title: The Debt You Can't Feel
dek: Two weeks of six-hour nights wrecks performance about as badly as a full night with no sleep. The people living it barely notice.

blocks.text: Ask anyone on a busy boat how much they sleep and you'll hear some version of the same answer: “Five, six hours. I'm used to it.” It sounds like a statement about toughness. It is actually a testable claim about the brain, and in 2003 a team of sleep researchers tested it more carefully than anyone had before.

The result is one of the most important findings in sleep science, and it has two halves. The first half is that modest, everyday sleep restriction does serious, steadily growing damage to performance. The second half is worse: the people it is happening to mostly can't tell.
The experiment

Hans Van Dongen, David Dinges and colleagues recruited 48 healthy adults between 21 and 38 years old. Before the study, they were all normal sleepers, averaging between about 7.6 and 7.9 hours a night. Then they moved into a lab where every hour of their lives was controlled.

They were split into groups. One group got **8 hours** in bed per night for 14 days. One got **6 hours**. One got **4 hours**. A fourth group got no sleep at all for three straight days, about 88 hours awake, to serve as a benchmark for what total deprivation looks like.

The design is what makes the study so convincing. Out in the real world, people who sleep less also tend to drink more coffee, stress more and live differently, so it is hard to tell what is causing what. In the lab, the only thing that differed between groups was the number of hours they were allowed to sleep. Their days were scheduled and supervised around the clock. Sleep was measured with brain-wave recordings, not self-report. Whatever happened to performance could be laid squarely at the feet of sleep.

Several times a day, everyone took a battery of tests. The key one was the **psychomotor vigilance task**, or PVT. It is aggressively boring: you stare at a screen and hit a button the instant a counter appears, again and again, for ten minutes. The measure that matters is *lapses*, responses slower than half a second. A lapse is a moment when your brain simply wasn't there. If you have ever watched a gauge without seeing it, you know exactly what a lapse feels like from the inside.
Why such a dull test? Because lapses in attention are what cause most fatigue mistakes. Nobody forgets how to do their job when tired. They just stop being present for a second at the wrong moment.
What two weeks of short nights did

The 8-hour group stayed flat. Across two weeks, their lapses didn't meaningfully increase. That is the control condition, and it is reassuring: given enough sleep, people can hold steady indefinitely.

The 4-hour and 6-hour groups did not hold steady. Their performance got worse day after day in a steady, cumulative slide. There was no point at which it leveled off within the two weeks. By the end, the numbers looked like this:

items.label: Total sleep loss matched by 14 days of 6 hours in bed
Total sleep loss matched by 14 days of 4 hours in bed
Wake time per day beyond which lapses built up

blocks.source: Van Dongen et al., Sleep, 2003

blocks.text: Let that land. Six hours a night, which most people would describe as “a bit short,” produced attention and working memory deficits equivalent to staying up for an entire night. Four hours a night matched two consecutive all-nighters. And unlike the total deprivation group, whose ordeal ended after three days, the restricted groups were still sliding when the experiment stopped.

The researchers also modeled the data to find the tipping point. Across all conditions, lapses started piling up once people were routinely awake more than about **15.84 hours** a day. Flip that around and it implies an average daily sleep need of a little over **8 hours** to avoid building deficits. That is a lab estimate for an average person, not a personal prescription, but it lines up with the official guidance discussed below.
Why you don't notice

Here is the part that should change how you think about your own sleep. Alongside the performance tests, participants rated how sleepy they felt. In the restricted groups, sleepiness jumped at first and then mostly flattened, creeping up by only about one point on a seven-point scale over two weeks. The 4-hour and 6-hour groups didn't even differ significantly from each other in how sleepy they felt.

So by day 14, when their performance was at its worst, the restricted groups reported feeling only slightly sleepy. Their subjective sense of being okay had stopped tracking reality. The total deprivation group, by contrast, *felt* terrible and knew it. Acute sleep loss announces itself. Chronic sleep loss whispers.

blocks.title: Chronic restriction: how it feels vs what it does

left.head: What you feel
items: A bit tired the first few days
Then roughly normal, just “used to it”
Sleepiness ratings barely rising
Confident you are adapting

right.head: What is happening
items: Lapses climbing day after day
Working memory steadily degrading
No plateau within two weeks
Deficits matching one or two all-nighters

blocks.text: This is the trap behind “I'm used to it.” What people get used to is the *feeling* of short sleep. Their brains keep paying the cost. And because the instrument you'd use to judge your own impairment is the same brain that is impaired, you are a poor judge of it. It is a bit like asking a gauge with a drifting zero whether it is calibrated.
The drunk comparison, and the slow recovery

If “equivalent to a night of total sleep deprivation” sounds abstract, a study in Australia gave it a more familiar yardstick. Ann Williamson and Anne-Marie Feyer tested 39 people, 30 transport workers and nine army personnel, both across 28 hours without sleep and after measured doses of alcohol.

After **17 to 19 hours** awake, which for most people is just 2230 to 0100 after a normal morning start, performance on some tests was as bad as or worse than at a blood alcohol level of **0.05%**. On some tasks, responses were up to 50% slower. Stay awake longer and performance sank to the level of the highest alcohol dose they tested, a blood alcohol level of **0.1%**.

items.label: Hours awake to match 0.05% blood alcohol on some tests
Slower responses on some tasks at that point

blocks.source: Williamson & Feyer, Occupational and Environmental Medicine, 2000

blocks.text: Then there is the question of paying the debt back. A companion study by Gregory Belenky and colleagues, published the same year, put 66 commercial drivers on 3, 5, 7 or 9 hours in bed for a week, then gave everyone three recovery nights of 8 hours in bed.

blocks.title: Average sleep actually obtained per night
blocks.note: Even with 7 hours in bed, people averaged about 6.3 hours of real sleep.
blocks.source: Belenky et al., Journal of Sleep Research, 2003

blocks.text: Look at the third bar. Seven hours in bed bought only about six and a quarter hours of actual sleep, because nobody falls asleep instantly or sleeps without waking. Time in the rack is not time asleep. If you are budgeting six hours of rack time, you are probably getting closer to five. Build that gap into how you plan, not just how you feel.

The recovery results were the real surprise. The 3-hour group bounced back quickly after the first recovery night but never returned to baseline. The 5-hour and 7-hour groups showed no clear recovery at all over three nights, and the 5-hour group's lapses were still elevated on the last day. Even the 7-hour group, a schedule plenty of people would call healthy, had taken a hit that three normal nights did not erase. The authors' interpretation was that the brain adapts to chronic restriction by settling at a lower level of performance, and that this adaptation slows the climb back out.
What a lapse looks like on watch

It helps to picture what is actually going wrong inside a sleep-restricted brain, because it is not what most people imagine. You don't get uniformly slower and dumber, like a computer with a throttled CPU. Most of the time, a tired person performs close to normal. The damage shows up as *instability*: normal response, normal response, then a sudden half-second or two-second gap where nobody was home, then normal again.

Belenky's data showed this directly. In the 3-hour group, the variability in reaction speed roughly doubled by the fourth day. The average got worse, but the spread got much worse. That pattern is what makes sleep debt dangerous in jobs built on vigilance. A logbook entry, a valve lineup, a reading that drifts out of spec: the risk isn't that you can't do the task, it's that you are absent for the one second the task needs you.

This also explains why tired people are so bad at judging themselves. Most of the time you *are* performing fine, so your memory of the last hour is mostly of things going fine. The lapses are brief and, by definition, you weren't paying attention during them. You can't remember the gaps you weren't present for.
Sleep debt doesn't make you consistently bad. It makes you unreliable: fine, fine, fine, gone. In watchstanding, the gone part is what matters.
What to do with this

Some honesty about limits first. These were small lab studies, dozens of people rather than thousands, and the PVT is a narrow test of attention rather than of judgment in a real job. People also differ in how much sleep they need and how hard restriction hits them. But the core pattern, cumulative decline with flat self-assessment, has been replicated in other labs and is a cornerstone of modern fatigue science.

The official guidance from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society is that adults should sleep **7 or more hours** per night on a regular basis. The same consensus notes that more than 9 hours may be appropriate for young adults and for people recovering from sleep debt. If you are in your early twenties and running a deficit, needing more than you think is not laziness. It is the guideline.

items: **Don't trust the feeling.** After a week of short sleep, “I feel fine” is the least reliable data you have. Judge by sleep hours, not by mood.
**Count rack time honestly.** Subtract time to fall asleep and wake-ups. Six hours in the rack is not six hours of sleep.
**Protect a consistent block.** A steady 7 hours beats a cycle of 5-hour nights and 10-hour crashes.
**Plan recovery longer than one night.** After a hard stretch, expect several nights of extra sleep, not one, before you are back to full speed.
**Use an objective check.** A simple reaction-time test, or your aim in a game you play often, can reveal slowing that you won't feel.

blocks.text: That last idea is worth trying. If you game, you already have a sensitive performance meter. Plenty of players notice their aim and reaction time fall apart on short sleep long before they would admit to being tired. Treat that as data. It is your PVT.

Be honest, too, about where the missing hour usually goes. On most days it isn't lost to the watchbill. It is lost to the last stretch of the evening: one more episode, one more match, twenty more minutes of scrolling in the rack. Those minutes feel free because you are tired and not doing anything demanding. By the logic of the Van Dongen data, they are among the most expensive minutes of your day, because they come straight out of tomorrow's attention.

The goal isn't perfect sleep every night, which isn't realistic on a submarine or anywhere else. It is to stop believing the comfortable story that your body has adapted to running short. It hasn't. It has just stopped telling you. If you are consistently sleeping badly despite having the time to sleep, or you feel drowsy in situations where you shouldn't, bring it to your corpsman or doctor.

takeaways: Six hours in bed for two weeks impaired attention about as much as a full night without sleep; four hours matched two all-nighters.
Sleepiness ratings barely rose while performance kept falling, so “I'm used to it” is not evidence.
17 to 19 hours awake can impair you like a 0.05% blood alcohol level.
Three normal nights did not fully undo a week of 5 to 7 hours; plan recovery over several nights.
Aim for 7 or more hours of actual sleep; young adults and people in debt may need more.

title: The Short Fuse Is a Sleep Symptom
dek: Losing sleep doesn't just make you slow. It turns up your brain's alarm, weakens the brake, and quietly convinces you the problem is everyone else.

blocks.text: It is 0340 and somebody is chewing too loudly in the crew's mess. Normally you would not even register it. Tonight it feels like a personal attack. The guy who forgot to log a reading becomes an idiot, the chief's question becomes an accusation, and a short message from home reads like the start of a fight. Twelve hours later, after real sleep, none of it seems like a big deal, and you're not sure why it got to you.

Most people file this under "I'm cranky when I'm tired" and move on. But the research behind it is stranger and more useful than that. Sleep loss doesn't just make you grumpier in general. It changes *what counts* as a threat, it makes you misread faces, it pushes you away from people, and it weakens the exact mental tools you would normally use to talk yourself down. The scariest part is that, from the inside, it feels like clear perception rather than a symptom.
The threshold drops

In 2012, a team at the University of Pennsylvania kept 53 healthy volunteers either rested or awake for a full night, then gave them cognitive tests under two conditions. In the easy version, the tasks were simple and relaxed. In the hard version, the researchers added time pressure, harder problems and discouraging feedback about performance.

The result was not what most people would guess. Under heavy stress, sleep-deprived and rested people reported about the same rise in stress and bad mood. Hard is hard for everyone. The difference showed up in the *easy* condition. After a sleepless night, people reported more stress, more anxiety and more anger in response to tasks that rested people barely noticed.

The authors' reading was that sleep loss lowers the threshold at which ordinary demands start to feel stressful. That matches the mess-deck scene exactly. A real emergency gets everyone's full attention whether they slept or not. It's the small stuff, the loud chewing and the routine question, that a tired brain promotes into a problem.

Notice what this means for self-awareness. When something big goes wrong, you know you're stressed, and you can account for it. When something small sets you off, the reaction feels like an accurate response to how annoying the thing really is. There's no internal warning light that says "a chunk of this irritation was manufactured by missing sleep." The distortion is in the measuring instrument itself, which is why it's so easy to blame the world.
A louder alarm, a weaker brake

The best-known brain study on this comes from Matthew Walker's lab, published in *Current Biology* in 2007. Twenty-six young adults were split into two groups. One slept normally; the other stayed awake for about 35 hours straight. Then everyone lay in an MRI scanner and looked at 100 pictures ranging from neutral to deeply disturbing.

The amygdala, a pair of almond-shaped structures that act as the brain's threat detector, responded far more strongly in the sleep-deprived group. In UC Berkeley's announcement of the study, Walker described the emotional centers as over 60 percent more reactive. Just as important was what had changed around the amygdala. In rested people it was tightly linked to the medial prefrontal cortex, the region that puts feelings in context and says "that's a movie, relax." In the sleep-deprived group, that link weakened, and the amygdala coupled instead with the brainstem's locus coeruleus, a source of noradrenaline, the body's fight-or-flight chemical.

blocks.title: The same brain, two nights

left.head: After normal sleep
items: Threat detector responds in proportion
Prefrontal cortex adds context and calms it
Small annoyances stay small
Faces read accurately

right.head: After a night awake
items: Threat detector over-responds to negative images
Link to the prefrontal 'brake' weakens
Ordinary demands register as stress
Angry and happy faces are misjudged

blocks.text: Put those pieces together and you get a simple model. Emotional control is a balance between an alarm that fires quickly and a slower, smarter system that checks whether the alarm is justified. Sleep loss pushes on both sides at once. The alarm gets more sensitive, and the checking system gets slower and less connected. It's like an overly sensitive smoke detector wired to a sprinkler system with the manual override disabled.

One honest caveat: this was a small study, and brain-imaging findings from small samples don't always hold up at the same size. Walker has also been criticised for overstating some claims in his popular writing. So treat "60 percent" as one experiment's result rather than a universal constant. The good news is that the overall direction doesn't rest on one scanner study. It rests on decades of experiments.
Fifty years of experiments, added up

In 2024 the journal *Psychological Bulletin* published the largest synthesis yet, led by Cara Palmer and Candice Alfano. The team pre-registered their plan and pooled every experiment they could find in which healthy people had their sleep deliberately cut, through all-nighters, shortened nights or repeated awakenings, and then had their emotions measured.

items.label: Experiments pooled, spanning more than 50 years
Participants, aged 7 to 79
Separate effect sizes analyzed

blocks.source: Palmer et al., Psychological Bulletin, 2024

blocks.text: Every form of sleep loss reduced positive emotion: less happiness, enthusiasm and contentment. Every form raised anxiety symptoms. And people's physical arousal in response to emotional pictures was blunted, which sounds like the opposite of the amygdala story until you remember that being flattened and being jumpy can happen at the same time. Some outcomes were less clear. Effects on negative mood and depressive symptoms were mixed and depended on the kind of sleep loss. The analysis also found that the relationship wasn't a straight line: the amount of sleep lost mattered in nonlinear ways, and losing REM sleep versus deep slow-wave sleep didn't produce identical effects. In other words, it's not only how many hours you miss, but which parts of the night get cut.

That pattern contains a reframe worth keeping. The most reliable effect of sleep loss isn't rage. It's *the joy draining out*. A tired person is less likely to enjoy the good parts of the day, while being a little more anxious about everything else. If a week of short nights makes your whole life feel gray and pointless, the meta-analysis suggests a boring explanation should be your first suspect, before you conclude your job, your friends or your future are the problem.
Misreading people, then pulling away

Emotions are social, so the damage doesn't stay inside your head. In a 2010 Berkeley study, 37 young adults rated faces that shifted gradually from neutral to sad, happy or angry. After a night without sleep, people were worse at judging the intensity of moderately angry and moderately happy faces, the kind of subtle expressions that make up most real conversations. One night of recovery sleep fixed it.

In 2018 Eti Ben Simon and Walker went further. Eighteen people were tested once rested and once after a night awake. Each time, a stranger walked toward them and they said stop when the person felt too close. After sleep loss, they wanted noticeably more space.

blocks.title: Extra personal space wanted after one night awake
blocks.note: Increase in preferred distance versus the same people when rested
blocks.source: Ben Simon & Walker, Nature Communications, 2018

blocks.text: The study's most interesting twist came next. The researchers filmed each participant answering ordinary interview questions, then showed the clips to 1,033 online viewers who had no idea about the experiment. Viewers rated the sleep-deprived versions as lonelier and were less interested in interacting with them. And after watching, the viewers themselves reported feeling a bit lonelier. The authors argued that sleep loss can start a self-reinforcing loop: tired people withdraw, others sense it and back off, and everyone ends up more isolated.

Now picture that loop inside a hull with a crew of tired people sharing tight living spaces for months. Shipmates misread each other's faces, want more room than exists, and come off as cold. A lot of the friction that gets blamed on personalities is at least partly a watchbill problem.
Why your usual tricks stop working

Most advice about handling emotions involves thinking differently: reframe the situation, take another perspective, distract yourself. Those are real skills, and they work. The catch is that they run on the same prefrontal machinery that sleep loss weakens.

A 2019 study tested this directly. Fifty-one young adults either slept normally or stayed up for 24 hours, then viewed upsetting pictures while their brain activity was recorded with EEG. Sometimes they just looked; sometimes they were told to distract themselves, reappraise the picture, or suppress their reaction. In rested people, distraction and reappraisal dampened the brain's response to the images. After a night awake, both strategies worked significantly less well.

Other experiments point the same way. A Loughborough University study found that one night of sleep loss made people worse at holding back a response to negative stimuli and quicker to make mistakes. At the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research, volunteers kept awake for more than two days scored lower on self-rated emotional intelligence, including empathy and impulse control. These are mostly small studies, but the theme is consistent: the more tired you are, the less you can rely on willpower and clever thinking to manage how you feel.
When you're badly underslept, don't plan on out-thinking your mood. Plan on routing around it: delay, defer and avoid decisions you can't undo.
Sleep as overnight therapy

The flip side is encouraging. Sleep isn't only something whose absence hurts; it seems to actively process emotional experiences. In a 2011 study, people viewed emotional images, then viewed them again 12 hours later, with either a night of sleep or a day awake in between. Those who slept showed a drop in amygdala response to the same images and rated them as less intense, and the size of that drop was tied to features of their REM sleep.

Deep sleep appears to matter for anxiety. In 2019, Ben Simon and colleagues reported that a night of sleep loss raised next-day anxiety, while the amount of deep, slow-wave sleep people got predicted how much their anxiety came down overnight. Looking more broadly across the population, even modest night-to-night drops in sleep predicted measurable rises in next-day anxiety. The phrase "sleep on it" turns out to be close to literal advice.
What to actually do with this

You can't always get more sleep. Duty sections, drills and rotating watches decide that for you. What you *can* change is how you interpret your own reactions and when you act on them. The point isn't to excuse bad behavior because you're tired. It's to recognize a known, temporary distortion and stop trusting it with big decisions.

blocks.title: A tired-brain protocol
items: Check the gauge first: before deciding someone is the problem, ask how many hours you slept in the last two nights.
Name it out loud to yourself: 'This is a tired reaction.' Labeling a feeling as a state, not a fact, makes it easier to wait out.
Delay anything permanent: angry messages home, big money moves and arguments with your chain of command can wait for a rested head.
Pick structural fixes over willpower: walk away, put the phone down, eat something, drink water.
Protect the night before what matters: an evaluation, a hard conversation or a board deserves sleep more than a few extra hours of gaming.
Extend the same grace to others: a shipmate snapping at 0400 is probably running the same broken software you are.

blocks.text: There's also a quieter lesson about mood over the long haul. Because positive emotion is the first thing to go, a stretch of short nights can masquerade as a motivation problem or even a personality problem: you feel flat, nothing seems fun, and you start doubting your goals. Before rewriting your life plan, try fixing your sleep for a week and see what's left.

If you ever end up leading people, as a watch supervisor, a leading petty officer, or someday the owner of a small business, this becomes a management tool too. When a normally solid person suddenly turns snappy or withdrawn, the first question isn't "what's wrong with them?" It's "when did they last sleep?" Sometimes the most effective fix for a conflict isn't a counseling session. It's making sure two exhausted people get a rack before they have the conversation.

Feeling low or anxious for weeks, not just after bad nights, is worth talking to the corpsman about; sleep and mood problems feed each other and both are treatable. If things ever feel hopeless, the Military Crisis Line is available any time: dial 988, then press 1.

takeaways: Sleep loss lowers the threshold for stress: small annoyances feel big, while real emergencies hit rested and tired people about equally.
Without sleep, the brain's threat detector gets louder and its connection to the calming prefrontal cortex gets weaker.
The most reliable effect across 154 experiments is less positive emotion, plus more anxiety; if life feels gray, check your sleep first.
Tired people misread faces and pull away, and others sense it and pull back too, which matters a lot in a small crew.
Reframing and willpower work worse when you're tired, so delay big decisions and use simple structural fixes instead.

title: The 18-Hour Day and Other Experiments Nobody Meant to Run
dek: Submarines, Antarctic stations and spacecraft are accidental sleep labs, and they keep teaching the same lesson about what happens when you take away the sun.

blocks.text: For decades, the US submarine force lived on a day that doesn't exist anywhere on Earth. Watchstanders stood six hours on and had twelve off for everything else: sleep, training, maintenance, meals. Then the cycle started over. Every 18 hours, a new day began.

On paper it was tidy. Three watch sections, clean rotations, plenty of total time off. In the body, it was something else. Nita Shattuck, a Naval Postgraduate School researcher who spent years arguing for change, compared it to forcing someone through six hours of jet lag every single day, like flying from the East Coast to Europe daily. Her view was that the schedule left sailors chronically short on sleep, with consequences that could show up as mistakes.

In 2014 the submarine force began moving to eight-hour watches with sixteen hours off, a schedule that finally matched a 24-hour clock. The story of how that happened, and of what researchers have found in Antarctic stations, the space station and a fake Mars mission, adds up to one of the clearest lessons in sleep science: when you remove the sun, the body doesn't stop needing a day. It just loses its best tool for keeping track of one.
The day that didn't exist

The human clock can be nudged, but only so far, typically by small amounts each day. An 18-hour day asks for a huge stretch: six hours shorter than the cycle the body is built around. There's no reason to expect most bodies to follow it, and plenty of reason to expect them to keep running on roughly 24 hours underneath, with sleep periods landing at random points in that internal day.

That's the core problem. Sleep isn't just about hours in the rack. It's about whether those hours line up with your biological night. Sleep that falls during your internal afternoon tends to be shorter and more easily broken than sleep during your internal night, as the Antarctic data later in this story shows.

Interestingly, the evidence wasn't a slam dunk at first. In a 2003 lab study by the Naval Submarine Medical Research Laboratory, nine enlisted submariners lived in the lab for three 8-day sessions, one on the 18-hour submarine schedule, one on a traditional maritime rotation and one on a compressed alternative. The researchers had predicted that the 24-hour schedules would beat the 18-hour one on performance tests. That prediction wasn't supported. The alternative schedule did produce more good-quality sleep, and the maritime rotation left people more fatigued, but there was no knockout result.

That's an important wrinkle, and an honest one. Eight days in a lab is a short window, and some costs of a bad schedule build slowly over months. When the fleet actually switched, the reports from the boats were striking. One officer on a fast-attack boat said nobody fell asleep on watch at the contact manager station under eight-hour watches, and that morale improved and complaints dropped. His summary was blunt:
Everything gets better with eight-hour watches.
blocks.by: Lt. Travis Nicks, quoted in Navy Times

blocks.text: An officer from a ballistic missile boat said her engineers no longer had dark circles under their eyes. Anecdotes aren't data, but when a whole community reports the same shift, it's worth taking seriously.

blocks.title: Two ways to run a submarine day

left.head: 18-hour day
items: 6 hours on, 12 off
A new “day” starts every 18 hours
Sleep lands at shifting points in your internal day
Like six hours of jet lag, daily

right.head: 24-hour day
items: 8 hours on, 16 off
Each day matches the body's cycle
Sleep can settle into a consistent window
Clock can align with the routine

blocks.text: Fixing the math, not the environment

So the 24-hour schedule solved everything? Not quite. In a 2024 study, Evan Chinoy, Rachel Markwald and Sarah Chabal tracked 58 crewmembers for 30 days of normal underway operations on the circadian-aligned schedule. Wrist trackers showed an average of about **6.6 hours** of sleep a day. When sailors reported their own sleep, they estimated even less, about **5.9 hours**.

The gap between those two numbers is worth a moment. Wrist trackers infer sleep from stillness, so lying quietly awake in a rack can get counted as sleep, which tends to push their estimates up. People, on the other hand, often remember the wakeful stretches of a broken night more vividly than the sleep in between. The truth probably sits somewhere in the range. Either way, neither number is generous for people doing demanding, safety-critical work.

There was good news. Over the underway, people's estimated circadian rhythms shifted steadily toward alignment with their watch schedules, meaning the 24-hour structure was doing its job: clocks were settling in. But sleep quality was rated low, meals were irregular, exercise was scarce, and mood dropped by the end of the underway.

The lesson is that the schedule fixed the math, but not the environment. A steel hull with no windows still has no sunrise. That's why Navy researchers have started experimenting with light itself. On an underway aboard USS Vermont in late 2020, researchers gave about half of 42 volunteers orange glasses to block blue light in the evening and light-emitting frames to deliver blue light in the morning. The early, not-yet-final reports were that the glasses group slept more and felt less sleepy during the day.
A good schedule gives your clock a chance to align. Light, meals, exercise and consistency are what actually pull it into line. On a boat, you supply those cues yourself.
Six months of night

Antarctica runs the opposite experiment. Instead of no windows, you get windows with nothing behind them. Through the winter at high latitudes, the sun barely rises or disappears entirely for weeks or months. The people who winter over at research stations are, in effect, living through a long natural blackout.

A 2022 study led by Tracey Sletten followed 51 expeditioners through six months of Antarctic winter. Their average sleep looked fine on the surface, about 7.2 hours. But averages hide things. About 41 percent of their sleep episodes were under seven hours, and about 19 percent were under six. The bigger story was alignment.

items.label: Expeditioners whose sleep was out of sync with their clock at some point
Average sleep when misaligned with the body clock
Average sleep when aligned

blocks.source: Sletten et al., Journal of Pineal Research, 2022

blocks.text: When sleep fell out of step with the internal clock, people lost more than an hour of it. And their performance and mood were worse when they were awake close to the peak of their melatonin rhythm, the clock's deepest night, and the longer they had been awake. That should sound familiar to anyone who has stood a mid-watch. Being awake during your biological night isn't just unpleasant. It measurably degrades how you think and feel.

For a watchstander, the practical point is that *when* you sleep relative to your clock matters almost as much as how long you're in the rack. Two people given the same eight-hour window can walk away with very different amounts of real sleep, depending on whether that window lands in their biological night or their biological afternoon.
Scheduled for 8.5, got 6

Then there's space. The International Space Station circles the planet so fast that sunrises and sunsets come around many times a day. The light outside the window is useless as a clock, so the crew depends on artificial lighting inside. Add a packed work schedule, a machine-filled environment and the strangeness of sleeping while floating, and you have a hard place to rest.

In 2014, Laura Barger and colleagues published a major study of astronaut sleep: 64 astronauts across 80 Space Shuttle missions, plus 21 astronauts on the ISS. NASA scheduled 8.5 hours of sleep per night. Here's what crews actually got.

blocks.title: Astronaut sleep: scheduled vs actual
blocks.note: Average nightly sleep in flight. Only 12% of Shuttle and 24% of ISS sleep episodes reached seven hours.
blocks.source: Barger et al., Lancet Neurology, 2014

blocks.text: The problem didn't start in orbit. In training about three months before launch, the same crews were already averaging under 6.5 hours a night. And sleep medication was common: Shuttle crews used it on about half of all nights in space, and roughly three-quarters of ISS crew members reported using it at some point.

These are some of the most carefully selected, highly trained, health-conscious people on Earth, with an official sleep schedule and the full attention of NASA's medical teams. They still came in more than two hours short. Discipline and toughness don't override the physics of light and the biology of the clock.
520 days in a box

The longest experiment of all never left the ground. From June 2010 to November 2011, six men lived sealed inside a mock spacecraft in Russia for 520 days, simulating a round trip to Mars. A team led by Mathias Basner tracked their sleep and movement the whole way.

Something unexpected happened: the crew slowed down. Over the mission, they spent more time resting and less time actively awake, and their sleep crept up rather than down. The waking light they lived under was dim, around 100 lux at the start and lower still by the end, a small fraction of typical outdoor daylight. Without strong light and a natural day, the crew drifted into something like a low-energy holding pattern.

And they drifted differently. One crewmember's sleep-wake cycle averaged nearly 25 hours, sliding later and later. Another developed a split sleep pattern. A third slept the least of anyone, rated his sleep poorly, and made far more errors on attention tests than the rest. In total, four of the six ran into at least one significant problem with circadian timing, sleep or alertness. Same capsule, same schedule, six different responses.

There was a reassuring finding, too. Across the whole crew, attention-test performance didn't steadily decline over the 520 days, and it actually improved in the second half. Humans can adapt to long isolation. But the slide into inactivity and dim, monotonous days is real, and it's a familiar risk on any long deployment where every day looks the same.

blocks.title: Learning to sleep without the sun

blocks.text: What every extreme place teaches

Line these places up and the same four lessons keep appearing. First, the body runs on a roughly 24-hour clock whether or not the schedule respects it. Second, people in extreme places sleep less than they're scheduled to, often by a lot, and their own estimates don't always match what trackers record. Third, without strong sunlight, individual differences explode: some people hold steady, some drift, some fragment. Fourth, being awake during your biological night hurts performance and mood in measurable ways.

The reframe is this. On land, the sun quietly does a huge amount of work keeping your clock on time, and you never notice because it's free. In a sealed hull, a polar station or a spacecraft, that work becomes your job. The people who sleep well in extreme places aren't tougher. They're the ones who deliberately rebuild the signals the sun used to provide.

items: **Anchor your day.** Keep your wake-up time and first meal as consistent as the watchbill allows. Consistency is a signal.
**Bright start, dim finish.** Seek the brightest light available right after waking and the dimmest in the last hour before sleep.
**Make the rack a cave.** Dark, quiet and cool. Every bit of light and noise you block helps.
**Move.** The Mars-500 crew drifted into inactivity. Exercise is both a clock signal and a guard against that slide.
**Don't trust your gut on sleep.** Submariners' own estimates differed from what their trackers recorded. Feeling fine on short sleep isn't proof that you are.
**Ask for help early.** If sleep problems drag on, talk to the corpsman. Sleep medication decisions belong with a professional.

blocks.text: None of these places is normal. That's exactly why they're valuable. They strip away the sun and show what's left: a clock that still wants its day, and a person who either gives it one on purpose or pays for it in sleep.

takeaways: The submarine force's old 18-hour day fought the body's 24-hour clock; the switch began in 2014.
Even on 24-hour schedules, submariners averaged about 6.6 hours of sleep a day, and estimated less.
Astronauts were scheduled 8.5 hours of sleep but averaged about 6 in flight.
In Antarctica, sleep out of sync with the body clock was over an hour shorter than aligned sleep.
Without sunlight, you have to rebuild the clock's signals yourself: consistent timing, bright mornings, dark nights, exercise.

title: Half Your Brain Is on Watch Tonight
dek: Dolphins, ducks and seabirds can sleep one side of the brain at a time. On your first night in a strange bed, so can you, a little.

blocks.text: Sleep labs have an awkward habit. When a volunteer shows up to have their sleep recorded, researchers often throw the first night of data in the trash. Volunteers take longer to fall asleep, wake up more, and get less deep sleep than they will on later nights. The pattern was written up back in 1966 under a name that stuck: the **first-night effect**. For half a century it was treated as noise, a nuisance to design around.

Anyone who has slept badly in a hotel, a barracks, or a fresh rack after a transfer knows the feeling from the inside. You're tired, the bed is fine, and still you drift in and out all night. The usual explanation was vague: new place, new sounds, a bit of nerves. In 2016 a team at Brown University found something more specific and much stranger. On that first night, one half of the sleeper's brain was standing watch.
To see why that's less weird than it sounds, you have to start with animals that do it all the time.
One eye open, literally

Most of us picture sleep as an all-or-nothing switch: the whole brain goes offline together. Birds broke that picture first. Some birds can put one hemisphere into slow-wave sleep while the other stays awake, and they keep the eye wired to the awake side open. This is called **unihemispheric slow-wave sleep**, and in birds it looks a lot like a lookout posted on one side of the body.

Niels Rattenborg and his colleagues tested that idea in 1999 with a simple setup. They lined up four mallard ducks in a row and recorded their brain waves and eye states while they slept. The two ducks in the middle were flanked by other ducks. The two on the ends had open space on one side, which is where a predator would come from.

The ducks on the ends spent **150 percent more** of their sleep in the one-hemisphere mode than the ducks in the middle. They also preferred to point their open eye outward, away from the group. When the researchers showed a threatening image to that open eye, the half-asleep ducks reacted fast. In other words, the birds weren't just sleeping lightly. They were deciding how much brain to put on watch, and which direction it should face.

items.label: One-hemisphere sleep in mallards at the exposed ends of a row
Longest continuous echolocation watch kept by a tested dolphin
Average daily sleep of elephant seals during 7 months at sea

blocks.source: Rattenborg et al., Behav Brain Res, 1999; Branstetter et al., PLoS One, 2012; Kendall-Bar et al., Science, 2023

blocks.text: Sleeping at sea without drowning

Dolphins and whales face a harsher problem. They breathe air, they live in water that steals body heat, and they can't haul out on a beach for a nap. A 2008 review by Oleg Lyamin and colleagues found that every cetacean species examined so far sleeps unihemispherically. One hemisphere shows the slow waves of deep sleep while the other looks awake, and they trade off. The sleeping animal keeps moving, surfaces to breathe, and often keeps one eye open. REM sleep, the dream-heavy stage people get several times a night, is tiny or absent.

Why evolve this? The obvious answer is breathing: a fully unconscious dolphin would drown. Lyamin's group argued that the deeper pressure may have been heat. Water pulls warmth out of a body fast, and a mammal that stopped moving for hours could chill dangerously, especially as a newborn. Keeping half the brain awake keeps the animal swimming and generating heat. Predator watch and breathing ride along as useful side effects.

How good is that half-awake brain at its job? In a 2012 study, researchers at the National Marine Mammal Foundation in San Diego trained two dolphins to find targets by echolocation and report them, nonstop. In five-day sessions one dolphin scored 75 to 86 percent correct and the other 97 to 99 percent. One dolphin then went **15 days** without a break and showed no meaningful decline. No human watchstander could do that. A dolphin can, because it never has to take the whole brain offline.

Fur seals show that this is a switch the animal can flip. On land, a northern fur seal sleeps like a dog or a person, with both hemispheres together. In the water, it switches to one-hemisphere sleep, paddling with one flipper to stay oriented. And something else disappears in the water. In a 2018 study, Lyamin's team found that fur seals in seawater go without REM sleep, or nearly so, for days or weeks. When they return to normal conditions, they show little or no REM "catch-up." That result bothered a lot of sleep scientists, because in land mammals, REM taken away usually comes back with interest. The authors suggested REM may exist partly to reheat and reactivate a brain cooled by deep bilateral sleep, which would explain why an animal that never sleeps fully on both sides barely needs it.
Asleep at 3,000 kilometers

For decades people assumed that birds which fly for weeks without landing must be sleeping on the wing, probably one hemisphere at a time. Nobody had ever measured it. In 2016 Rattenborg's group glued tiny EEG recorders to great frigatebirds nesting in the Galapagos. Frigatebirds can't rest on the ocean; their feathers aren't waterproof enough and taking off from the water is hard. The tagged birds flew trips lasting up to 10 days and covering up to about 3,000 kilometers.

They did sleep in the air. Mostly they slept while circling upward in rising air currents, and when they used one-hemisphere sleep, the open eye tended to face the direction they were flying. Sometimes both hemispheres slept at once, for a few seconds, which meant a fully sleeping brain could still keep the bird gliding. But the real surprise was how little they slept at all.

blocks.title: Frigatebird sleep per day
blocks.note: Flying birds slept in bursts averaging about 11 seconds, versus about 28 seconds on land.
blocks.source: Rattenborg, Interface Focus, 2017; Rattenborg et al., Nature Communications, 2016

blocks.text: In flight they averaged about 0.7 hours of sleep a day, in bursts averaging around 11 seconds. Back on land, the same birds slept 12.8 hours a day. So one-hemisphere sleep didn't let them get normal sleep while flying. It let them get a sliver of sleep without crashing, and then they paid it back on the ground. Rattenborg's reading: the ocean demanded more attention than even half a brain could spare.

Elephant seals push the same theme underwater. A 2023 study recorded brain waves from wild northern elephant seals diving off California and found they took naps of under 20 minutes during deep dives, down to 377 meters, away from the surface. Linking those recordings to dive data from 334 seals, the team estimated they average about **2 hours of sleep a day** for seven months at sea. That rivals the African elephant for the least sleep recorded in any mammal. The lesson from the ocean is consistent: when the environment is dangerous, animals don't stop needing sleep. They ration it, fragment it, and put part of the brain on lookout.
Your own night watch

Humans can't do what dolphins do. We don't split our sleep cleanly down the middle. But Masako Tamaki, Yuka Sasaki and their colleagues at Brown wondered whether the first-night effect might be a faint echo of the same strategy. Using brain imaging combined with standard sleep recordings in 35 young, healthy volunteers, they compared two lab nights about a week apart.

blocks.title: How the Brown team caught the night watch
items: Record deep-sleep brain waves in each hemisphere on a first and second lab night, about a week apart.
Compare the depth of sleep between the left and right sides, network by network.
Play regular beeps with occasional odd ones into one ear at a time during deep sleep.
Measure which hemisphere reacts more strongly to the odd sounds.
Ask sleepers to tap a finger when a sound wakes them, and time how fast they respond.

blocks.text: On the first night, deep sleep was shallower in the left hemisphere than the right, specifically in the **default-mode network**, a set of regions active when your mind wanders. The bigger that left-right gap, the longer the person took to fall asleep. The lighter-sleeping left side also reacted more strongly to unusual sounds, and odd sounds played to that side woke people up more often and faster. On the second session, all of that was gone. Both sides slept equally deep.

So the first-night effect isn't just your brain being bad at sleeping. It looks like a built-in security protocol. In a place your brain hasn't yet judged to be safe, one side sleeps a little lighter and keeps listening for anything that doesn't fit, ready to wake you. Once the place is familiar, the guard stands down. The study was small and done in a lab, so the details may shift with more research. But it lines up neatly with what ducks at the end of the row have been doing all along.

blocks.title: Same idea, different strength

left.head: Dolphins, seals, frigatebirds
items: One hemisphere fully asleep, the other awake
Open eye tied to the awake side
Used every day, for breathing, warmth or flight
Lets them keep moving while resting

right.head: Humans on night one
items: Both sides asleep, one a bit lighter
Lighter side listens for unusual sounds
Shows up mainly in a new place
Fades once the place feels familiar

blocks.text: Sleep is a dial, not a switch

Put all of this together and the old picture of sleep falls apart. Sleep isn't one state the whole brain enters at once. It can be local, partial and adjustable. Animals turn the dial depending on how dangerous their surroundings feel: deeper and longer when safe, shallower and split when exposed. Your brain does a quieter version of the same calculation every night, without asking you.

There's also a price on that dial. Vigilance and restoration trade off. The frigatebird gets through ten days on a fraction of an hour of sleep a day, but it sleeps for more than twelve hours once it's back on the nest. A sleeper whose left hemisphere spends the night on guard is getting less of the deep, restoring sleep it would get in a familiar bed. Watchfulness during sleep is paid for with the quality of that sleep.

That's worth knowing if your life involves a lot of first nights. A new boat, a new berthing space, a hotel on leave, a barracks room during training: each can trigger the guard. The tired, broken feeling after the first night somewhere new is not a sign that your sleep is falling apart or that you have insomnia. It's an old survival program doing its job, and the evidence suggests it fades as the place stops being new.
Don't judge your sleep, or your new rack, by night one. In the Brown study, the one-sided night watch was gone by the next session. The first night in a new place is supposed to be lighter.
Making a strange bed feel familiar

Nobody has run a trial on exactly which tricks shorten the first-night effect, so treat the following as reasonable bets rather than proven fixes. The logic is simple: the guard stays up when the brain detects something unfamiliar or unexpected, so the goal is to make the place as familiar and predictable as possible, as fast as possible.

items: Bring the same small cues everywhere: the same pillowcase, eye mask, earplugs, or a familiar sound like a fan app. They're portable pieces of home.
Steady noise is easier to tune out than sudden noise. The Brown sleepers reacted most to odd sounds that broke a pattern, not the regular ones.
Spend some awake time in the new space before you need to sleep there, so it's less of a stranger by lights-out.
Expect night one to be rough and plan around it: protect the second night instead of panicking about the first.
If sleep stays broken for weeks rather than nights, that's no longer the first-night effect. Talk to the corpsman.

blocks.text: The bigger idea is the one the animals teach. A sleeping brain is never completely gone. Some part of it is always weighing how safe you are, and it adjusts how deeply you're allowed to rest based on that judgment. The dolphin solved this with a brain that splits in two. You get a gentler version: a few uneasy hours in a new bed while half of you keeps an ear open, and then, once your brain decides the place is home, the watch is relieved.

takeaways: Some animals sleep one brain hemisphere at a time, keeping the eye tied to the awake side open as a lookout.
Frigatebirds sleep only about 0.7 hours a day in flight, then make it up with about 12.8 hours on land. Partial sleep buys survival, not full rest.
Humans show a faint version on the first night in a new place: one hemisphere sleeps lighter and reacts faster to odd sounds.
Bad sleep on night one somewhere new is normal and tends to fade. Judge your sleep by the nights after.
Familiar cues and steady background sound are reasonable, if untested, ways to help a strange bed feel like home.

title: Sleep Was Supposed to Be Nothing
dek: For most of history, scientists assumed the sleeping brain simply switched off. The story of how they found out otherwise is a lesson in how confident experts can be completely wrong.

blocks.text: In the early 1950s, a broke graduate student at the University of Chicago named Eugene Aserinsky was wiring his eight-year-old son, Armond, to an old brain-wave machine in the lab. His adviser, Nathaniel Kleitman, had given him a dull assignment: watch sleeping people's eyes. Partway through the night, the pens on the machine started swinging wildly, tracing the jerky movements of eyes darting back and forth under closed lids, along with brain waves that looked like those of someone awake. Aserinsky's first thought was that the equipment was broken.

It wasn't. He had stumbled onto rapid eye movement sleep, REM, a brain state as busy as waking life that every human enters several times a night. People had been sleeping, and watching other people sleep, for the entire history of the species. Nobody had noticed. That fact says something important about sleep, and something even more important about science: sometimes the biggest discoveries are hiding behind an assumption so obvious nobody thinks to test it.
The off switch

For most of recorded history, sleep was understood as an absence. The body got tired, the senses dimmed, and the mind went dark until morning, like a lamp being turned off. Dreams were a puzzle, but they were treated as flickers in an otherwise empty night rather than evidence of a working brain.

The first real window into the sleeping brain came in 1929, when the German psychiatrist Hans Berger published the first recordings of electrical brain waves from people, using electrodes on the scalp. The electroencephalogram, or EEG, let scientists see that brain activity changed character when someone fell asleep. But a tool doesn't automatically change minds. Through the 1930s, a leading view was still that sleep happened passively, when the brain stopped receiving enough stimulation from the senses to stay awake.

Clues against that view were already piling up. During and after World War I, a mysterious epidemic called encephalitis lethargica swept through Europe and beyond. The Austrian neurologist Constantin von Economo studied the brains of victims and noticed something strange: damage in one region of the hypothalamus tended to go with extreme sleepiness, while damage in a nearby area went with severe insomnia. If sleep were just the brain idling, why would it have specific control centers that could break?

In 1949, Giuseppe Moruzzi and Horace Magoun showed that stimulating a network deep in the brainstem could snap a sleeping animal's brain waves into an alert pattern. Wakefulness, it turned out, wasn't the brain's default setting. It was actively produced by a system that could be turned up or down. That reframed the question. If waking takes work, maybe sleep does too.
1953: the night gets crowded

Kleitman was the right person to be in charge when it happened. He had spent his career treating sleep as a serious scientific subject when few others did. In 1938 he famously moved into Mammoth Cave in Kentucky for about a month with a student, living on an artificial 28-hour day to see whether the body's daily rhythm could be pushed. The results were mixed: his younger student's rhythms shifted toward the new schedule, while Kleitman's own largely refused. He was used to the idea that the body runs its own programs at night, which may be why he took the swinging pens seriously when a less curious adviser might have told his student to fix the machine.

Aserinsky and Kleitman published their discovery in *Science* in September 1953. They described regularly recurring periods of rapid eye movement during sleep and linked them to dreaming: people woken during these periods usually reported vivid dreams. A few years later, Kleitman and a medical student named William Dement mapped out how the whole night is organized. Sleep wasn't one flat state. It moved in repeating cycles, from lighter to deeper stages and back up into REM, several times a night.

Around the same time, the French researcher Michel Jouvet found that during this stage in cats, the muscles of the body go almost completely limp even while the brain blazes with activity. He called it "paradoxical sleep": the most active brain state of the night paired with a nearly paralyzed body. That paralysis is what keeps you from acting out your dreams, and when it glitches at the edges of sleep, it produces sleep paralysis.

By 1968, researchers had agreed on a standard manual for scoring sleep into stages from EEG recordings, which let labs around the world compare results. Sleep had gone from "nothing happens" to one of the most structured, measurable things the brain does. The remaining question was the obvious one: what is all that activity *for*?

blocks.text: What happens if you just don't

One way to learn what something does is to take it away. In the winter of 1963 to 1964, a San Diego high school student named Randy Gardner tried to break the record for staying awake, for a science fair. William Dement, by then a researcher at Stanford, came to monitor him. Gardner made it 264 hours, a full 11 days, with mood swings, memory lapses and trouble concentrating along the way.

The most surprising part came afterward. At a normal eight hours a night, 11 days awake works out to nearly 90 hours of missed sleep. But he didn't need anything like that much to recover. His first night he slept just under 15 hours, and within a few nights he was sleeping normally.

blocks.title: Randy Gardner's recovery sleep after 264 hours awake
blocks.note: Sleep was back to roughly normal within days, far less than the hours lost
blocks.source: Gulevich, Dement & Johnson, Archives of General Psychiatry, 1966

blocks.text: That suggests sleep debt isn't a simple hour-for-hour loan. The brain seems to prioritize, packing recovery nights with deeper sleep. But it's a mistake to read Gardner's story as proof that sleep loss is harmless. He was one healthy teenager in one stunt. Later lab research found that people on chronically short sleep keep getting worse at attention tasks while feeling only a little sleepy, and that a few recovery nights don't fully restore performance. It's also worth remembering that Gardner was monitored by researchers and had people keeping him safe. A tired person driving or standing a safety-critical watch doesn't.

Animal experiments were blunter. In the 1980s, Allan Rechtschaffen's lab at the University of Chicago built a device that kept rats from sleeping: a rotating disk over shallow water that started turning whenever the rat dozed off, forcing it to walk. A paired control rat got the same movement but could sleep when the disk was still. Every totally sleep-deprived rat died or had to be euthanized within 11 to 32 days. Their energy use more than doubled, they lost weight while eating more, and no single organ failure explained it.

items.label: Randy Gardner's documented stretch of wakefulness, 1964

blocks.text: Two dials and a gene

By the 1980s, scientists had lots of data about sleep but no simple way to explain its timing. In 1982 the Swiss researcher Alexander Borbély offered one: the **two-process model**. One process is sleep pressure, a need that builds the longer you're awake and drains while you sleep. The other is the circadian clock, a roughly 24-hour rhythm that makes you more alert at some times of day than others, regardless of how long you've been up. When pressure is high and the clock stops pushing for wakefulness, you fall asleep.

The model was simple enough to fit on a napkin and powerful enough to explain jet lag, the afternoon slump, why pulling an all-nighter gets easier at dawn and why night shifts are brutal. More than 40 years later, it's still the backbone of how sleep timing is taught, and it's the framework behind why a rotating watchbill feels so wrong.

Then the clock got a mechanism. Working with fruit flies, Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young identified a gene that encodes a protein which builds up inside cells during the night and breaks down during the day, a self-running molecular loop. They and others went on to find more parts of the machine, and similar clockwork turned up in mammals, including humans. In 2017 the three shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.
The switch has a chemical

One of the strangest stories in sleep science came in 1998, when two separate teams, one in California and one in Texas and Japan, discovered the same brain chemical within about two months of each other and gave it two different names. One group called it **hypocretin** because it came from the hypothalamus. The other called it **orexin**, from the Greek word for appetite, because they thought it mainly drove hunger. Both names are still in use.

Within about a year, the real job became clear. In 1999, Stanford researchers found that a breed of dogs with narcolepsy, a disorder of sudden, uncontrollable sleep attacks, carried a mutation in the receptor for this chemical. The same month, a team working on mice that lacked orexin showed that those mice had narcolepsy-like attacks. In 2000, studies of human brains found that people with narcolepsy had lost most of their orexin-producing neurons. Orexin, it turned out, helps hold the brain steadily in the awake state. Without it, the wall between waking and sleep gets flimsy.

That discovery traveled fast from lab to pharmacy. Drugs that block orexin receptors are now prescribed for insomnia, working by turning down the wake signal rather than sedating the whole brain the way older sleeping pills do. A curiosity found in rat brains in the late 1990s became a treatment within two decades.
The question that still isn't settled

So what is sleep *for*? You might expect a final answer by now. There isn't one, and the most famous recent attempt shows why caution matters. In 2013, Maiken Nedergaard's lab at the University of Rochester reported in *Science* that in sleeping or anesthetized mice, the space between brain cells expanded by about 60 percent, letting fluid wash through and clear out waste, including the beta-amyloid protein linked to Alzheimer's disease. They named the plumbing the "glymphatic system."

The idea spread everywhere. Sleep as the brain's nightly cleaning cycle was intuitive, a little gross and great for headlines. Then in 2024 a team at Imperial College London published a study in *Nature Neuroscience* using a different method and found the opposite in mice: brain clearance was markedly *reduced* during sleep and anesthesia, not increased. The two camps disagree about methods, and the argument is ongoing. Brain waste clearance during sleep may turn out to be real, partial or mostly wrong.

blocks.text: That's the real lesson of this history. Nearly every generation of sleep researchers was confident about something that the next generation overturned. Sleep was passive, until it wasn't. It was one state, until it was several. It was obviously for cleaning the brain, until a careful replication pushed back. None of this means science is useless. It means science is a process of catching its own mistakes, and the people who made the big leaps were the ones who took an anomaly seriously instead of assuming their equipment was broken.

Which brings us back to Aserinsky and the swinging pens. The habit worth stealing from him isn't brilliance. It's noticing when the data doesn't match the story everyone believes, and checking instead of shrugging. That's useful at 0300 watching a panel, debugging a game script or reading the next viral sleep headline.

takeaways: For most of history, sleep was seen as the brain switching off; in fact the sleeping brain is busy, and REM went unnoticed until 1953.
Wakefulness is actively generated by brain systems, and the chemical orexin helps hold you awake; losing it causes narcolepsy.
Sleep timing comes from two dials: sleep pressure that builds while awake and a 24-hour circadian clock.
Recovery from sleep loss isn't hour-for-hour, but that doesn't make chronic short sleep harmless.
Even famous findings, like sleep washing waste from the brain, are still being debated; treat confident sleep headlines with care.

title: The Cold You Caught Last Week
dek: Getting sick after a brutal stretch isn't bad luck. Sleep is when your immune system trains, takes notes and stands its watch.

blocks.text: Picture a strange volunteer job. For a week, you wear a sensor on your wrist that records exactly how long you sleep each night. Then you check into quarantine, and a researcher drips a measured dose of live cold virus into your nose. For the next five days, they collect your snot, weigh your used tissues and check your blood to see whether you get sick.

That is what 164 healthy adults signed up for in a study led by Aric Prather and Sheldon Cohen, published in 2015. Everyone got the same virus, the same dose, the same quarantine. The difference was the week before. People who had slept **less than six hours** a night were about four times as likely to develop a real cold as people who had slept more than seven. Those in the six-to-seven-hour range weren't measurably worse off than the long sleepers.

Most people already suspect that running themselves into the ground makes them sick. The interesting part is *why*. The answer reveals something that sounds odd at first: your immune system, like your brain, does some of its most important learning while you sleep.
Same virus, different odds

Experiments where researchers deliberately expose people to a virus are rare and powerful, because they remove the biggest unknown in real life: who actually got exposed. In ordinary life, the person who sleeps four hours might also be the person who commutes on a packed train, skips meals and never washes their hands. In a quarantine study, everyone gets the same exposure on purpose.

The result also had a clear threshold. The six-to-seven-hour group looked much more like the long sleepers than the short ones. That matches a pattern seen across sleep research: the damage from short sleep isn't spread evenly, it piles up fast once you drop below about six hours. The researchers used wrist sensors precisely because self-reported sleep is unreliable. People often misjudge how long they slept, and older studies that relied on memory alone left room for doubt. Measuring sleep objectively closed that gap, and the link held.

blocks.title: Odds of catching the cold vs. sleep the week before
blocks.note: Odds ratios compared with people sleeping more than 7 hours. The 6-to-7-hour result was not statistically different from baseline.
blocks.source: Prather et al., Sleep, 2015

blocks.text: Two cautions. This was not a trial where people were assigned to sleep less; the researchers measured how people naturally slept, so some other hidden factor could still be involved, even though the team adjusted for many, including age, weight, season, stress and existing antibodies. And the margins of error were wide. The four-times figure could plausibly be anywhere from barely higher to far higher. What makes the result convincing isn't any single number but the fact that it lines up with experiments where sleep was directly controlled.
Your immune system has a memory, and it consolidates at night

Vaccines are the cleanest way to watch the immune system learn. A vaccine shows your body a harmless version of an invader, and your body responds by producing antibodies and building memory cells. Measure the antibodies weeks later and you have a scorecard for how well the lesson stuck.

In 2002, Karine Spiegel, John Sheridan and Eve Van Cauter at the University of Chicago restricted healthy young volunteers to four hours in bed for six nights and gave them a flu shot. Ten days after the shot, their antibody levels were **about half** those of people who slept normally. In 2003, a German team led by Tanja Lange and Jan Born gave people a hepatitis A vaccine at 9 a.m. Half slept normally that night; the other half stayed awake until the following evening. Four weeks later, the sleepers had nearly **twice** the antibody levels.

items.label: Flu vaccine antibodies after 6 nights of 4 h in bed
Hepatitis A antibodies when people slept the night after the shot
Pooled in a 2023 meta-analysis linking under 6 h of sleep to weaker vaccine response

blocks.source: Spiegel et al., JAMA, 2002; Lange et al., Psychosomatic Medicine, 2003; Spiegel et al., Current Biology, 2023

blocks.text: In 2023, Spiegel, Van Cauter and colleagues pooled seven studies covering about 300 people. Sleeping under six hours a night around the time of vaccination was linked to a clearly weaker antibody response. The researchers estimated the effect was comparable to about two months of antibody decline after a COVID-19 vaccine. Two details stood out. The effect was strong in men but not statistically significant in women, possibly because none of the studies accounted for hormone cycles. And it only showed up in studies that measured sleep objectively. When people simply reported how they slept, the link disappeared, a reminder that people are bad at estimating their own sleep.

Why would sleep help? A leading explanation is the hormonal environment of sleep. In Lange's study, the people who slept after their shot had lower levels of the stress hormones noradrenaline and adrenaline that night, and higher levels of growth hormone and prolactin, both of which stimulate immune activity. That mix appears to help the immune cells that present a new threat to the rest of the immune system, and the cells that build long-term memory of it, do their jobs.

If that sounds familiar, it should. Your brain uses sleep to turn the day's experiences into lasting memories. Your immune system appears to do something similar with the day's threats. In both cases, the learning happens during the day, but the filing happens at night. Skip the night and the lesson is weaker.

This also explains why timing matters. The window right after exposure, whether to a vaccine or a real virus, is when the immune system is deciding how seriously to take the threat and how much to remember about it. A bad night then may cost more than a bad night at a random point in the month. Researchers still don't know exactly how wide that window is, which is one of the open questions the 2023 meta-analysis flagged, but the nights immediately around a shot are the best bet.
Less sleep, more inflammation, worse defense
Here's a puzzle. If short sleep weakens immunity, you might expect the immune system to go quiet when you're tired. In some ways it does the opposite.

In 2006, Michael Irwin and colleagues at UCLA kept 30 healthy adults awake from 11 p.m. to 3 a.m. for just one night. The next morning, their immune cells were pumping out more inflammatory signaling molecules, called cytokines. Gene activity for one of them, interleukin-6, more than tripled. Another, tumor necrosis factor, roughly doubled.

So a sleep-deprived immune system is not off. It's agitated and unfocused, more like a crew on general quarters for no clear reason than one that's ready for a specific casualty. Inflammation is supposed to be a short, targeted response. Chronic low-grade inflammation is associated with problems that build up over decades, including heart disease, diabetes and arthritis, which is why researchers worry about what years of short sleep do to it. The worst version of an immune system is one that's both overreacting in general and underperforming against the actual threat, and that's roughly where chronic short sleep pushes it.

Weaker targeted defense, more background inflammation
Infection gets a foothold
Illness and congestion fragment sleep
Recovery takes longer

blocks.text: Why sickness makes you sleepy

The connection runs in both directions. When you catch something, some of the same cytokines that fight infection act on the brain to make you sleepy, slow and uninterested in doing anything. This package of symptoms, sometimes called **sickness behavior**, isn't just the bug knocking you down. It's partly your body deliberately taking you off the field.

There's some striking evidence that this extra sleep matters. In 1993, Linda Toth, Elizabeth Tolley and James Krueger infected rabbits with bacteria or fungus and tracked their sleep. Rabbits that showed a long stretch of increased sleep tended to have milder illness and better outcomes. Rabbits that died had slept less than those that survived. That's an animal study, and it shows a link rather than proof, but it fits the idea that the urge to sleep when sick is part of the treatment plan.

It's worth pausing on how strange this is. Evolution built a system where getting infected makes you vulnerable, immobile and unproductive, the opposite of what you'd want if a predator were nearby. The only reason that trade-off would survive is if sleep bought something valuable in return. The fact that it persisted across so many species is itself a clue to how much sleep matters for fighting infection.
The barracks problem

Military life is close to a worst-case experiment for this: early reveilles, shared berthing, physical stress, and lots of people breathing the same air. Researchers in Britain have studied it directly.

A 2018 study of 651 British Army recruits found that sleep dropped once basic training started. More than a third were sleeping under seven hours. Those sleeping under six hours a night were **four times** as likely to be diagnosed with an upper respiratory infection as those getting seven to nine, and each infection cost an average of almost three training days.

A larger 2023 study of 1,318 recruits added a twist. About half started training getting two or more hours less sleep a night than they had as civilians. Those sleep-restricted recruits were nearly three times as likely to get a respiratory infection, but only if they also rated their sleep quality as poor. Recruits who lost just as much sleep but felt they slept well didn't show the same increased risk. The researchers don't yet know why. It may be that good-quality sleep makes better use of fewer hours, or that the perception itself reflects something real about how restorative the sleep was.

items.label: Odds of respiratory infection for recruits sleeping under 6 h
Average training days lost per infection
Recruits starting training with 2+ h less sleep than civilian life

blocks.source: Wentz et al., Military Medicine, 2018; Walsh et al., Sleep, 2023

blocks.text: If you've ever watched a cold rip through a crew in close quarters, this will make sense. When a bug comes aboard, everyone is exposed, and whether you go down with it depends partly on what state your defenses are in. The stretch of short sleep before exposure may matter as much as the exposure itself.

Long underway periods add their own twist. A crew that has been sealed off for weeks has mostly been passing around the same germs. A port call can bring in new ones all at once, right when everyone is also staying up late, changing routines and running on adrenaline. It's close to a perfect setup for the familiar wave of illness after liberty. The virus is the trigger, but the sleep debt people carry into that exposure helps decide who goes down with it.
Using this on purpose
You often can't control your sleep schedule. You can control some of what happens around it, and the research points to a few high-leverage moments.

blocks.title: When sleep matters most for immunity
items: Before and after a vaccine: protect the nights around the shot. That's when the immune system is building its memory.
When a bug is going around: treat sleep as part of your defense, not something to trade for one more episode or match.
When you feel it starting: drop the hard workout and get the extra sleep. Your body is already asking for it.
During a stretch you can't control: guard the quality of the sleep you do get with darkness, earplugs and a consistent routine.
After the crunch: pay back sleep debt deliberately instead of jumping straight into the next push.

blocks.text: If you stand night watches, the same logic applies to day sleep. It counts, but it tends to be shorter and more broken, so it needs more protection, not less: blackout, earplugs, and telling people not to wake you for things that can wait. The recruit study suggests the quality of the sleep you get may matter almost as much as the hours.

None of this means sleep is a force field. Plenty of well-rested people catch colds, and the effects in these studies are about odds, not guarantees. Hand-washing, vaccines and not sharing water bottles still matter. And if you're getting sick constantly, or an illness isn't clearing up, that's a reason to see the corpsman or a doctor, not just to sleep harder.
The cold you catch this week may have been decided last week. Sleep doesn't just help you recover from being sick; it sets your odds of getting sick in the first place.

The bigger reframe is about how you think of rest. It's tempting to see sleep as downtime, the gap between the things that matter. The immune research says otherwise. While you're out, a large part of your defense system is doing its most important work: learning from what it saw today, filing memories of past invaders, and resetting from the background noise of stress. Treat sleep as a watch your body is standing for you, and cutting it short looks a lot less like toughness.

takeaways: In virus-exposure studies, people sleeping under 6 hours were about 4 times as likely to catch a cold as those sleeping over 7.
Sleep around vaccination helps decide how strong the response is; short sleep has cut antibody levels by about half in one study.
Short sleep makes the immune system both more inflamed and less effective against real threats.
The urge to sleep when sick is part of the body's defense, not weakness.
Protect sleep around shots and during outbreaks, and see medical if illnesses keep coming back.
