title: Rewrite the Dream
dek: A recurring nightmare feels like something that happens to you. One of the best-supported treatments says you can edit it while you're awake, with a pen and a few minutes a day.

blocks.text: The dream is always the same. Maybe it's a fire you can't reach in time, a fall, a fight you're losing, a door that won't hold. You wake with your heart going like you've run a mile, and the worst part isn't tonight. It's knowing that the same scene will be waiting in a week, or tomorrow. People with recurring nightmares often start dreading sleep itself, staying up later to avoid it, which leaves them more tired and more on edge, which doesn't help the dreams either.

In the 1990s a sleep physician in New Mexico named Barry Krakow and his colleagues tested an idea that sounds almost too simple. If the nightmare is a script your brain keeps replaying, what if you wrote a new script while you're awake and practiced it? Not analyzing the dream, not reliving it, just changing it and rehearsing the change. They called it **imagery rehearsal therapy**, IRT, and it has since become the one nightmare treatment that America's main sleep medicine organization calls "recommended."
What counts as a nightmare

Bad dreams are normal. Almost everyone has them, especially under stress, after a rough day, or when sleep is short and irregular. Sleep researchers usually reserve the word *nightmare* for a vivid, upsetting dream that wakes you up and that you remember clearly. When nightmares come often enough to cause real distress, wreck sleep, or make you afraid to go to bed, that's **nightmare disorder**, which affects about 4 percent of adults according to the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

Nightmares are also different from night terrors, which people often mix up. Nightmares mostly come out of REM sleep, which gets longer toward morning, so they tend to cluster in the second half of the night, and you wake up remembering the story. Night terrors come out of deep slow-wave sleep, usually early in the night. The person may scream or thrash but is hard to wake and usually remembers little or nothing. IRT is a treatment for the first kind, the dreams you remember.

A huge Finnish survey shows how common frequent nightmares are and who gets them. Across eight surveys from 1972 to 2007 covering nearly 70,000 adults, 3.5 percent of men and 4.8 percent of women reported frequent nightmares. Prevalence rose with age, especially in men. And people who had been through war, mostly World War II veterans in that sample, reported more frequent nightmares along with more insomnia, depression and anxiety, even decades after the fighting ended.

items.label: Adults with nightmare disorder
Finnish men reporting frequent nightmares
Finnish women reporting frequent nightmares

blocks.source: Morgenthaler et al., AASM position paper, 2018; Sandman et al., Sleep, 2013 (69,813 adults)

blocks.text: After trauma, nightmares take on a particular shape. Many people with post-traumatic stress disorder have dreams that replay the event, or a close variation of it, again and again. They're one of the most stubborn PTSD symptoms, and for a long time treatment focused on the daytime symptoms with the assumption that the nightmares would fade along with them. Often they didn't.
Why the same dream keeps playing

Krakow's key move was a reframing. Instead of seeing a chronic nightmare only as a symptom of something deeper, he treated it partly as a learned habit, a pattern the sleeping brain has practiced so many times that it runs on its own. Whatever started it, the nightmare had become a groove, and the brain kept sliding into it.

That framing points to a vicious circle. The nightmare wakes you in fear. You start dreading bedtime, sleep less, and lie in bed alert. Short, broken, anxious sleep tends to make emotional processing worse, which makes distressing dreams more likely. And each repetition of the nightmare is one more rehearsal of the old script. Researchers still argue about exactly what dreams do for emotional memory, so treat the details as a working model. But the loop explains why a nightmare can outlast whatever caused it by years.

blocks.title: The nightmare loop
items: Nightmare wakes you in fear
Dread of going to sleep
Short, broken, tense sleep
Worse emotional processing overnight
The old script runs again

blocks.text: The rewrite

IRT attacks the loop at the script. The method is short and doesn't require you to dig into the trauma behind the dream. In Krakow's version, people pick one nightmare, often not the worst one to start with. They change it in any way they want. The new version doesn't have to be happy or heroic, and it doesn't have to make logical sense. A monster can turn into a cardboard cutout, the burning building can have a door that wasn't there, the scene can switch to somewhere else entirely. Then they rehearse the new version in their imagination for a few minutes every day while awake, and they stop going over the old one.

blocks.title: Imagery rehearsal in practice
items: Pick one recurring nightmare, ideally a less intense one first.
Write it down briefly, then change it in any way you like.
Write out the new version so it's concrete and vivid.
Rehearse the new version in your imagination for a few minutes daily, awake.
Don't rehearse or retell the original version.
Once one dream shifts, work on the next.

blocks.text: Krakow's team tested it in a randomized trial published in JAMA in 2001. The participants were 168 women in New Mexico, nearly all survivors of sexual assault, 95 percent with moderate to severe PTSD. Half got IRT in three sessions; the rest went on a waitlist and continued whatever treatment they were already getting. Nothing else changed.

The treated group had large drops in how many nights a week they had nightmares and how many nightmares they had per week. Their sleep improved, and so did their PTSD symptoms, even though the therapy never targeted daytime symptoms directly. The control group barely moved. In the treatment group, 65 percent improved in PTSD severity, while 69 percent of the controls stayed the same or got worse. The gains held from three to six months without further contact.

blocks.title: IRT vs waitlist at 3 months (effect sizes)
blocks.note: Nightmares = nights per week with nightmares. An effect size of 0.8 or more is conventionally called large; under 0.2 is negligible.
blocks.source: Krakow et al., JAMA, 2001

blocks.text: Later work broadly backed this up. A 2012 meta-analysis of 13 studies found that imagery rehearsal had large effects on nightmare frequency, sleep quality and PTSD symptoms, sustained for 6 to 12 months. Adding insomnia treatment (CBT-I) improved sleep quality further but didn't make the nightmares or PTSD improve more.
Where it struggles

The honest version of this story has two big asterisks. The first is about comparison groups. Most IRT trials compared it to a waitlist or to no new treatment, which makes almost anything look good. The 2012 meta-analysis noted that in the single study that compared IRT to an active treatment, the effect sizes were small. That's a warning that some of IRT's benefit may come from the general ingredients of any structured help: attention, a sense of control, an expectation of improvement.

The second is about who it was tested on. In a 2010 trial, 124 male Vietnam veterans with chronic, severe, combat-related PTSD were randomly assigned to six group sessions of imagery rehearsal or to a comparison treatment. Both groups improved somewhat in sleep quality and PTSD symptoms, but IRT was no better than the comparison, and nightmare frequency didn't drop. Decades-old, severe combat nightmares in a group format turned out to be much harder to shift than the nightmares in Krakow's trial.

The authors of that trial discussed several possible reasons, and none has been settled. Combat nightmares that had run for decades may be more entrenched than newer ones. A group format gives each person less individual attention than one-on-one work. And chronic, severe PTSD comes tangled up with other problems that a few sessions focused on dreams can't reach. The fair conclusion is not that IRT fails for veterans, but that its effects depend on the person, the history, and how it's delivered.

The story of the main drug option is even more humbling. Prazosin, an old blood pressure medication that blunts the body's adrenaline response, looked promising for PTSD nightmares in several smaller trials and was widely prescribed to veterans. Then in 2018 the Department of Veterans Affairs ran a large trial: 304 veterans with chronic PTSD and frequent nightmares across 13 VA medical centers, prazosin versus placebo for 26 weeks. At 10 weeks there was no difference in distressing dreams, sleep quality or overall improvement, and still none at 26 weeks.

This pattern shows up all over medicine. Small early trials are noisy, and the ones with exciting results get noticed and repeated. When a big, careful trial finally runs, the effect often shrinks or vanishes. That doesn't mean everyone who felt prazosin helped them was imagining it, and some clinicians still use it for some patients. It means that on average, in a large and rigorous test, the drug didn't beat a sugar pill.

blocks.title: How the evidence moved
items: Krakow's JAMA trial: three IRT sessions cut nightmares and PTSD symptoms in 168 women
Group IRT fails to beat a comparison treatment in 124 Vietnam veterans
Meta-analysis of 13 studies finds large, lasting IRT effects, smaller against active controls
VA trial of 304 veterans: prazosin no better than placebo for nightmares
AASM lists IRT as the only recommended nightmare therapy; prazosin moves to "may be used"

blocks.text: After that trial, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine updated its position. Its 2018 paper listed image rehearsal therapy as the only treatment *recommended* for both PTSD-related nightmares and nightmare disorder. Prazosin and a long list of other options, including CBT, exposure-based therapies, and even lucid dreaming therapy for nightmare disorder, were placed in the weaker "may be used" category. So IRT isn't a guaranteed cure. It's the best-supported starting point we have, and it's cheap, short and low-risk.
Why editing a dream works at all

The strange and interesting part is that it works at all. You can't control what you dream. Yet a few minutes of deliberate, waking imagination seems to change what the sleeping brain produces at 0300. That says something about what dreams are made of. The dreaming brain isn't pulling from nowhere. It's drawing on material you've rehearsed, and you have more say over that material than it feels like.

It's the same principle athletes use when they rehearse a routine in their heads, or that you used in nuke school when you walked through a procedure step by step before doing it. Repetition builds a path, and the brain tends to follow well-worn paths, awake or asleep. IRT just points that ordinary learning process at the night shift. There's a second ingredient too: control. People who have rewritten a nightmare often say the biggest change was that sleep stopped feeling like a place where things happen *to* them. Less dread at bedtime means calmer sleep, which means one less push around the loop.
If it's you

For occasional bad dreams, the first fixes are boring ones: more regular sleep, enough of it, and less stress piling up right before lights-out. If one dream keeps coming back and it isn't tied to a trauma, a do-it-yourself rewrite is low-risk and worth trying. Write the change down, keep it simple, and practice the new version for a few minutes each day for a couple of weeks.

Living in shared berthing adds its own pressure. Waking up with a start, or wondering whether you said something in your sleep, can make the dread of bedtime worse. That's worth knowing because the dread is part of the loop. Treating the nightmares as a fixable sleep problem, rather than a private embarrassment, takes away some of their power before you've changed a single scene.

If the nightmares replay something that really happened, if they come more than once a week, or if you're starting to avoid sleep, don't white-knuckle it alone. Trauma nightmares are treatable, and a clinician can guide a rewrite safely and check for related problems like PTSD, insomnia or sleep apnea that make nightmares worse. The corpsman is the place to start, and asking is a normal medical request, not a sign of weakness.
If nightmares or what's behind them ever leave you feeling hopeless or thinking about ending your life, talk to the corpsman, or contact the Military Crisis Line: dial 988, then press 1.

The deepest idea here is that the sleeping mind is not sealed off from the waking one. What you rehearse by day shows up at night. Most of the time that happens by accident, with worries and replays. Imagery rehearsal does it on purpose. You don't get to choose your dreams directly, but you get more influence over them than you thought, and for a lot of people that's enough to change the ending.

takeaways: Nightmare disorder affects about 4% of adults, and nightmares are especially common and persistent after trauma.
Imagery rehearsal therapy means changing a nightmare's script while awake and rehearsing the new version daily.
It cut nightmares and PTSD symptoms sharply in a 2001 trial and is the only therapy the AASM rates as recommended.
It's not magic: effects shrink against active treatments, and a group version failed in chronic combat PTSD. A large VA trial also found prazosin no better than placebo.
For frequent or trauma-related nightmares, start with the corpsman. For a crisis, dial 988 and press 1.

title: The Demon on Your Chest Is a Glitch
dek: Sleep paralysis gave the world its witches, hags and night spirits. The real explanation is stranger, and knowing it can take the terror out.

blocks.text: In 1781, the Swiss-born painter Henry Fuseli finished a canvas that would make him famous. A young woman lies sprawled across a bed, head and arms hanging over the edge, deeply asleep. Squatting on her chest is a small, ugly demon staring straight out at the viewer. Behind the curtain, a horse with blank white eyes pushes its head into the room. He called it *The Nightmare*.

To modern eyes the horse looks like a pun, and it partly is. But the older meaning of the word explains the demon. In Old English, a *mare* was a spirit that crept onto sleepers at night and sat on them, pressing the breath out of their bodies. A night-mare wasn't a bad dream. It was an attack.

Here's the strange part. If you describe that attack to people around the world today, an enormous number of them recognize it, not from paintings or folklore, but from their own beds. They woke up and couldn't move. They felt something in the room. Something heavy sat on their chest. Many of them never told anyone, because it sounded insane.

It isn't insanity, and it isn't a demon. It's **sleep paralysis**, a temporary mismatch between the parts of your brain that wake up and the parts that don't. Understanding it explains centuries of folklore. It also offers one of the clearest examples of how the brain builds reality, and how much what you believe about an experience shapes what it does to you.
Waking up inside a dream

Every night, during REM sleep, your brain switches off most of your voluntary muscles. This **REM atonia** is a safety feature. REM is when the most vivid dreams happen, and the paralysis stops you from physically acting them out. Your eyes and diaphragm keep working; almost everything else goes limp.

You can see how important that switch is by looking at what happens when it fails in the other direction. In a condition called REM sleep behavior disorder, seen mostly in older adults, the paralysis doesn't fully engage, and people punch, kick and leap out of bed as they act out their dreams, sometimes injuring themselves or their partners. Sleep paralysis is the mirror image: the off switch stays on a little too long.

Normally, the paralysis switches off before you're aware of it. Sleep paralysis happens when the order gets scrambled: part of your brain wakes up and becomes aware of the room, while the REM machinery is still running. You're conscious, your eyes are open, and you can't move. Dream imagery and the emotional alarm of REM can spill into waking perception, so you may see, hear or feel things that aren't there. Episodes usually last from seconds to a few minutes, and they end on their own.

Episodes can strike as you're falling asleep or as you're waking up. Cheyne's research suggests that many of the episodes later in the night may begin with brief, unnoticed awakenings out of REM, possibly nudged by small breathing disruptions. That's part of why the timing feels random. You didn't do anything to cause it in that moment; your brain surfaced at a bad point in the cycle.

It's more common than most people would guess. In 2011, Brian Sharpless and Jacques Barber pooled 35 studies covering more than 36,000 people. About 1 in 13 people in the general population had experienced at least one episode. Among students, the figure was more than 1 in 4.

blocks.title: Who has had sleep paralysis at least once
blocks.note: Lifetime rates pooled from 35 studies, total of 36,533 people.
blocks.source: Sharpless and Barber, Sleep Medicine Reviews, 2011

blocks.text: The student figure is a clue. Students tend to sleep irregularly, pull all-nighters and run on stress, which are exactly the kinds of conditions that scramble the normal handoff between sleep stages. Reviews of the research have found that sleep paralysis is linked to poor and disrupted sleep, stress and trauma, certain psychiatric symptoms, substance use and genetics. It appears to be especially common in people with post-traumatic stress disorder. If your life involves rotating watches, broken sleep and stress, you're in the higher-risk group.
Why the demon looks the same everywhere

What makes sleep paralysis remarkable isn't the paralysis. It's how consistent the hallucinations are. In 1999, the Canadian psychologist J. Allan Cheyne and colleagues analyzed thousands of reports and found the experiences clustered into three groups. Each one maps neatly onto something the brain is doing in REM.

blocks.title: The three parts of the night visitor

left.head: What people experience
items: The Intruder: a sensed presence, dread, footsteps, whispers, a shadowy figure
The Incubus: crushing pressure on the chest, trouble breathing, sometimes pain
Unusual body sensations: floating, flying, leaving the body

right.head: What the brain is likely doing
items: Threat-detection circuits are on high alert with no real target, so the brain supplies one
Breathing muscles other than the diaphragm stay paralyzed, so deep breaths feel blocked
Balance and movement signals conflict with a body that can't move

blocks.text: The Intruder makes sense once you remember how jumpy the brain's alarm system is. Waking up paralyzed is objectively alarming, and the brain's threat circuits, built to err on the side of seeing danger, go into overdrive. A brain that senses danger but can't find its source tends to invent one. That's why the presence is so often felt before it's seen, lurking just out of view, usually malevolent.

REM itself also tilts the brain toward fear. The brain's emotional centers, including the amygdala, are highly active during REM, which is part of why dreams are so often anxious. Wake up partway through that state, unable to move, and you start the episode with your emotional alarm already turned up. The dread often arrives before any image does.

The Incubus, the thing sitting on your chest, comes from breathing in REM. The diaphragm keeps working, but the other muscles that help expand the chest are switched off. When you're awake and panicking, you try to take a big breath, and you can't. Your brain interprets that resistance as weight. Combine it with the Intruder and you get, quite literally, something sitting on you.

In a 2005 study of 5,799 people who had experienced sleep paralysis, Cheyne found the same three-part structure whether people had had one episode or hundreds, and regardless of the age at which their episodes started. That's evidence that the shape of the experience is built into the brain's wiring rather than learned from stories.

Body position matters too. In a 2002 study involving 6,730 people, Cheyne found that more people reported sleep paralysis while lying on their back than in all other positions combined. Being on your back was **three to four times** more common during episodes than when people were simply falling asleep normally.

items.label: How much more often people were on their backs during episodes than when normally falling asleep
Sufferers in a study that found the same three-part pattern in first-timers and veterans

blocks.source: Cheyne, Journal of Sleep Research, 2002 and 2005

blocks.title: The night visitor through history
items: Old English
The 'mare' is a spirit that sits on sleepers
Fuseli paints The Nightmare
First reported sudden night death among Hmong refugees in the U.S.
Folklorist David Hufford publishes his study of Newfoundland's Old Hag
Cheyne's team maps the three-part structure of the hallucinations
The same night-death syndrome is genetically linked to a heart rhythm disorder

blocks.text: Culture writes the script

If the core experience is universal, the story people tell about it is not. In Newfoundland it's the Old Hag. In Japan it's *kanashibari*, being bound as if by metal. Across much of the Muslim world, it's the jinn. The folklorist David Hufford spent years collecting accounts in Newfoundland and published them in 1982. One of his key findings was that people who had never heard of the Old Hag tradition still described the same experience in detail. The experience came first. The culture gave it a name and a face.

But the name and face aren't harmless decorations. They shape how the episode feels and, apparently, how it plays out. In 2013, Baland Jalal and Devon Hinton compared sleep paralysis in Egypt and Denmark. In Egypt, 44% of people surveyed had experienced it, against 25% in Denmark. Egyptians who had it reported far more episodes over their lifetime, and many feared they might die during an attack. Many of the Egyptians attributed their episodes to jinn, spirit beings from Islamic tradition, while few Danes reached for a supernatural explanation.

blocks.title: Same brain glitch, two cultures
blocks.note: Egyptian sufferers also reported about three times as many lifetime episodes as Danish sufferers (19.4 vs 6.0 on average).
blocks.source: Jalal and Hinton, Culture, Medicine and Psychiatry, 2013

blocks.text: Most striking, among Egyptians, believing the episode had a supernatural cause was linked to more fear and to longer periods of immobility. The studies can't prove the belief caused the longer episodes; other factors could explain the gap between countries. But the pattern fits a plausible loop. Terror is itself a stress response, and stress and fear may keep the brain stuck in that half-awake state for longer. A story that says *you are under attack* may lengthen the very attack it describes.
When the fear turns deadly

The darkest chapter in this story comes from the United States. Starting in 1977, dozens of apparently healthy Hmong refugees, mostly young men who had fled Laos after the Vietnam War, died suddenly in their sleep. Autopsies found nothing. The deaths became known as **sudden unexpected nocturnal death syndrome**.

The anthropologist Shelley Adler interviewed 118 Hmong men and women in Stockton, California, about a traditional night spirit called *dab tsog*, which was said to visit sleepers and press on them. She argued that the terror of these attacks, landing on people already under the extreme stress of war and displacement, and far from the traditional rituals that had once offered protection, could act as a trigger for death.

Later genetics added a crucial piece. The same pattern of sudden night deaths in young men had long been known in parts of Southeast Asia. In 2002, researchers studying affected families found mutations in a heart gene in some of them, the same gene involved in **Brugada syndrome**, a disorder that can trigger a fatal heart rhythm during sleep. They concluded the two were the same disorder. The most likely picture is a hidden, often inherited heart vulnerability, with stress and possibly terror acting as the spark. For people without that kind of heart condition, there's no evidence that sleep paralysis itself is dangerous. It feels like dying. It isn't.
What to do if it happens to you

The single most powerful tool is the one you now have: knowing what it is. The Egyptian data suggest the explanation you hold during an episode affects how frightening and how long it is. 'My brain woke up before my muscles did' is a very different thought than 'something is in the room.'

Baland Jalal has proposed a simple technique he calls meditation-relaxation therapy, built around that idea. In a 2020 pilot study of patients with narcolepsy, a sleep disorder in which sleep paralysis is common, six patients who practiced it for eight weeks cut the number of days with episodes by about half, while a comparison group of four who practiced deep breathing did not improve the same way. That's ten people in total, so it's a promising start, not proof.

blocks.title: Riding out an episode
items: Remind yourself what it is: a harmless glitch between sleep and waking that ends on its own.
Don't fight the paralysis or try to force a huge breath. Struggling tends to feed the fear.
Treat whatever you see or feel as a dream image, not a threat. Keep some emotional distance from it.
Focus attention inward on something calm, like a word or memory.
Relax your muscles deliberately. Some people find that wiggling a finger or toe helps break the episode, though that advice is anecdotal.

blocks.text: Prevention is mostly about the basics that keep sleep stages orderly: enough sleep, a schedule that's as regular as your watchbill allows, and less sleep deprivation in general. Since lying on your back is linked to episodes, sleeping on your side is worth trying if they bother you, though that's harder in a narrow rack.

It also helps to talk about it. Because sleep paralysis sounds so bizarre, many people quietly assume something is wrong with them, and that worry is its own source of stress. In a berthing compartment full of people on broken schedules, it's a safe bet you aren't the only one who has woken up unable to move. Saying it out loud tends to shrink it.

Occasional sleep paralysis is common and harmless. But frequent episodes, especially with heavy daytime sleepiness or sudden muscle weakness triggered by laughter or strong emotion, are worth raising with medical, because those can be signs of narcolepsy.

There's a broader lesson here about how perception works. Everything you experience is your brain's best guess, built from incoming signals and its expectations. Usually the guess is good enough that you never notice it's a guess. Sleep paralysis is one of the rare moments when you catch the guessing in action, and the brain, faced with paralysis, alarm and a heavy chest, constructs the most sensible explanation it can: a monster. For most of history, people took that construction at face value. You don't have to. The demon on the chest is real in the sense that your brain genuinely made it. It's just not out there.

takeaways: Sleep paralysis happens when you wake up mentally while the paralysis of REM sleep is still switched on.
About 1 in 13 people have had it, and more than 1 in 4 students; poor and irregular sleep and stress raise the risk.
The sensed presence, chest pressure and floating feelings have clear brain explanations, which is why the 'night visitor' looks similar worldwide.
Belief shapes the experience: supernatural explanations are linked to more fear and longer episodes.
Knowing what it is, staying calm and relaxing are the best tools; frequent episodes with daytime sleepiness are worth a medical check.

title: The Two-Hour Night Nobody Can Keep
dek: Polyphasic sleep promises an extra workday every day. When scientists finally tested it, the volunteers quit, the brain fought back, and the history behind it turned out to be more interesting than the hack.

blocks.text: The pitch shows up every few years on forums and YouTube. Instead of sleeping eight hours in one block, you take six 20-minute naps spread evenly around the clock, one every four hours. Total sleep: two hours a day. After a brutal adjustment period, the story goes, your brain learns to drop straight into the most valuable sleep stages, and you gain roughly six hours every single day. That's 42 hours a week. A full-time job's worth of extra life.

If you're trying to build a game, grow a channel and stay in shape around a Navy schedule, that pitch is hard to ignore. Time is the scarcest thing you have. So it's worth asking seriously: does it work? For years there was almost no real data, just blog posts and self-reports. Now there is. And the answer says something useful about where extra time actually comes from.
The schedules and the theory

Polyphasic sleep just means sleeping in more than one episode per 24 hours. Plenty of normal arrangements count: a night of sleep plus an afternoon siesta is biphasic. The controversial versions are the ones that try to cut total sleep drastically. The most extreme, nicknamed the "Uberman," is the six-naps-a-day plan. Milder ones pair a shortened core night with several naps.

The theory behind them goes something like this. Most of the value of sleep comes from deep slow-wave sleep and REM. Light sleep is filler. If you're starved of sleep for a while, your brain will learn to skip the filler and go straight to the good stages in every short nap, so two hours of compressed sleep can do the work of eight. It's a clever-sounding argument. It's also a set of testable claims, and they've now been tested.

The story usually comes with famous names attached. Leonardo da Vinci, Thomas Edison, Nikola Tesla and other high achievers are regularly held up as secret polyphasic sleepers. For most of these claims, the evidence is thin to nonexistent: retold anecdotes rather than records. Even if a genius really did sleep strangely, that wouldn't tell you whether the sleep pattern caused the genius or whether he succeeded in spite of it.

blocks.title: What the schedules promise vs. what studies found

left.head: The claim
items: Your brain adapts within a few weeks
Naps become pure deep sleep and REM
Two hours of sleep is enough
You'll feel sharp and productive
Anyone disciplined can do it

right.head: The evidence
items: Nine of ten motivated volunteers quit in the first month
Naps lose deep sleep and fill with light sleep
Sleep pressure keeps building and alertness falls
Vigilance and mood drop, worst in the early morning
No study has found a benefit

blocks.text: What happened when scientists tried it

In a study published in *Sleep* in 2024, researchers in Germany and the Netherlands recruited ten young, healthy volunteers who were genuinely enthusiastic about polyphasic sleep. The plan was eight weeks on the Uberman schedule: a 20-minute sleep opportunity at the end of every four hours, with no long core sleep at all. The team measured brain waves, hormones, mood and thinking.

Nine of the ten dropped out within the first month. The one who lasted longest, a 25-year-old man, managed five of the eight planned weeks. His cognitive test scores changed only modestly, which is the sort of detail polyphasic fans love to quote. But the researchers also found something dramatic in his blood: release of growth hormone, which normally pours out during deep sleep and is involved in tissue repair and muscle maintenance, had dropped by more than 95 percent. The authors concluded it was doubtful such schedules could cover the different jobs sleep does.

A 2026 study from the National University of Singapore went at the question more systematically. Forty healthy young adults were split into groups. One group got a normal eight-hour night. One got a single two-hour sleep opportunity. And one got the same two hours carved into six 20-minute Uberman naps. Every nap was recorded with full lab sleep monitoring, and attention and mood were tested every four hours.

items.label: Average sleep actually obtained in the first 20-minute nap
Less total sleep on six naps than on one 2-hour block
Drop in growth hormone release in the one volunteer who lasted 5 weeks

blocks.source: Koa & Lo, Sleep, 2026; Rosenblum et al., Sleep, 2024

blocks.text: Both short-sleep groups were sleepier, less vigilant and less cheerful than the rested group, which is no surprise. The interesting comparison was between the two short-sleep groups. Splitting the same two hours into six naps made things *worse*. Falling asleep over and over takes time, so people actually slept about 22 minutes less in total. Their naps contained more of the lightest sleep stage and less deep slow-wave sleep, the opposite of what the theory predicts. And their vigilance was worse than the one-block group's, especially in the morning.

In fairness, that study covered the first 24 hours, and advocates say adaptation takes weeks. That's exactly why the 2024 study matters: it gave motivated people weeks, and almost none of them could keep going. Put together, the two studies show a short-term picture that's worse than ordinary sleep restriction and a long-term picture where people mostly can't stick with it.

There's also a measurement problem built into self-experiments. Research on chronic sleep restriction has shown that people's own sense of how sleepy they are levels off after a few days, even while their performance on attention tests keeps sliding. So when someone on a forum reports feeling "fully adapted" in week three, that's exactly what you'd expect them to say whether or not they're actually functioning well. The only way to know is to measure, which is what the lab studies did.
The expert verdict

In 2021 the National Sleep Foundation convened a panel of prominent sleep and circadian scientists, including a Nobel laureate in circadian biology, to review the evidence on polyphasic schedules, not counting ordinary naps or siestas. They screened more than 40,000 publications and found just 22 that were relevant. Their conclusion was blunt: they found no evidence supporting benefits from polyphasic sleep schedules, and the sleep deficiency built into them was associated with worse physical health, mental health and performance.

It's worth being precise about what that means. The panel didn't say splitting sleep is always harmful. It said that using splits to *cut* total sleep far below normal, which is the whole selling point of the extreme schedules, doesn't hold up. The fantasy isn't that sleep can be broken into pieces. The fantasy is that the pieces can add up to two hours.
The twist: our ancestors did split their nights

Here's where the story gets more interesting. Polyphasic fans often claim humans are "naturally" polyphasic, and they're not entirely wrong. In 2001 the historian A. Roger Ekirch published a paper in the *American Historical Review* drawing on diaries, court records, medical books and literature from the British Isles. He found repeated references to a "first sleep" and a "second sleep," with a period of wakefulness in the middle of the night, when people prayed, talked, tended the fire or lay thinking. To writers of the time, this seemed so ordinary it rarely needed explaining.

A lab experiment around the same time pointed the same way. In a study published in 1992, psychiatrist Thomas Wehr at the National Institute of Mental Health moved volunteers from a normal 16-hour day of light to just 10 hours of light, leaving 14 hours of darkness each night. Over time, their sleep spread out and often split into two blocks of several hours each, separated by one to three hours of quiet wakefulness. Give people long, dark winter-style nights, and segmented sleep can appear on its own.

But the picture isn't universal. In 2015, researchers led by Jerome Siegel at UCLA tracked sleep in three pre-industrial societies in Tanzania, Namibia and Bolivia, using wrist activity monitors. These groups had no electric lighting. Their sleep was not interrupted by long periods of waking, and naps were uncommon. They slept between 5.7 and 7.1 hours a night on average, comparable to or a bit less than people in industrial countries.

blocks.title: Average nightly sleep in three pre-industrial societies (range)
blocks.note: Hadza, San and Tsimane groups; none showed long middle-of-the-night waking
blocks.source: Yetish et al., Current Biology, 2015

blocks.text: The fair reading of all three is that human sleep is flexible in its *shape*. Under long nights, one block can become two. In hot climates, an afternoon siesta is common. What none of this history shows is people thriving on two hours. Segmented sleepers in pre-industrial England were often spending a very long time in bed. They split their sleep. They didn't shrink it.
When splitting sleep actually works

There's one group that genuinely lives polyphasically: solo ocean sailors, who can't leave a boat unattended for eight hours. A 2020 study of 42 sailors in a solo transatlantic race found that about a quarter had trained in a polyphasic strategy beforehand, while others tried extending their sleep before the start. Neither approach made a clear difference in finishing times. Sailors nap in short bursts because the situation forces them to, not because it's an efficient way to live, and research on them generally suggests they're getting several hours of sleep a day in total, not two.

Splitting can even help when total sleep is fixed by circumstances. In a 2019 Singapore study, teenagers restricted to 6.5 hours of time in bed did better on attention, memory and mood when they got 5 hours at night plus a 90-minute afternoon nap than when they got 6.5 hours in one block. But there was a catch: their blood sugar responses got worse on the split schedule. And both groups were still worse off than teens who got a full night. Splitting changed the trade-offs; it didn't erase the cost of short sleep.

That's directly relevant underway, where the watchbill often decides for you that sleep will come in pieces. The lesson from this research is to protect the *total* first, keep one anchor block as long as you can, and use naps to top up rather than to replace. A split schedule is a tool for a broken day, not a way to beat biology.

blocks.title: If the watchbill splits your sleep anyway
items: Count total sleep across 24 hours, not just the longest block.
Guard one anchor block, ideally at the same clock time each day, as long as the schedule allows.
Use a nap to top up before a demanding watch, not to replace the anchor.
Expect grogginess right after waking from a longer nap and give yourself a few minutes before critical tasks.
When the schedule eases, pay back debt with longer sleep instead of keeping the split.

blocks.text: None of this means short naps are useless. A brief nap can restore alertness when you're already behind, and on a rotating watch it's often the smartest move available. The difference is in the goal. A nap that supplements sleep you're short on is a repair. A schedule that tries to make two hours of naps your entire supply is an experiment on yourself that, so far, nobody has been shown to win.
Where the extra hours really are

There are people who truly need less sleep. In 2009 researchers reported a mutation in a gene called DEC2 in two members of one family who had slept short their whole lives, averaging about 6.25 hours a day versus about 8 for their relatives; mice engineered with the same mutation slept less too. Since then, a handful of other short-sleep mutations have been found. These people are rare, and the trait is inherited, not trained. If you need an alarm and caffeine to function on six hours, you're not one of them.

So where does the extra time come from, if not sleep? Usually from the hours you're already awake but not really using. Most people who feel they have no time have a few hours a day that disappear into scrolling, background videos and low-effort browsing. Those hours cost nothing to cut, they don't wreck your growth hormone or your mood, and you don't have to fight your brain at 0400 to keep them. Do the math the polyphasic pitch does, but on your phone's screen-time report instead of your sleep. Recovering even two of those hours a day adds up to 14 hours a week, with no adaptation period, no dropouts and no hit to your mood or recovery. The cheapest productivity hack isn't sleeping less. It's being awake on purpose.

takeaways: Extreme polyphasic schedules like six 20-minute naps a day have been tested: most motivated volunteers quit within a month.
Splitting two hours into naps gave people less sleep, less deep sleep and worse alertness than one two-hour block.
An expert panel found no evidence of benefit from polyphasic schedules that cut total sleep.
Historical 'first and second sleep' was real in some places, but it split long nights rather than shrinking them.
Protect total sleep first; real extra hours come from wasted waking time, not from beating biology.

title: The Lag Is in Your Head
dek: Sleep loss doesn't just make you slower. It makes you inconsistent, it quietly changes how you play, and the place it hurts most isn't the game. It's the boring stuff.

blocks.text: In 2011, Stanford sleep researcher Cheri Mah asked the men's varsity basketball team to do something unusual: sleep more. For two to four weeks, the players kept their normal habits while she measured their performance after every practice. Then, for five to seven weeks, they aimed for at least ten hours in bed every night. They didn't change their training. They just slept.

items.label: Average extra sleep per night during the extension period
Timed sprint, before vs. after extra sleep
Free-throw percentage; three-point shooting rose by a similar amount

blocks.source: Mah et al., Sleep, 2011

blocks.text: The players also got faster on a standard reaction-time test, felt less sleepy and reported better mood. For a group of elite college athletes who were already training hard, those are big jumps from a change that cost nothing. There are real limits to the study: it involved only 11 players, had no separate control group, and the players knew they were in a sleep study, so some motivation effect is likely. But it raised an uncomfortable question that sports science has been chasing ever since. If more sleep makes good athletes better, how much are ordinary tired people leaving on the table?

For anyone who games competitively, the question is sharper. Reaction time, aim and split-second decisions are the whole job. So it's worth knowing what sleep loss actually does to those skills, and what it doesn't. The answer is less obvious than "tired people are slower."
What breaks first

In 2010, Julian Lim and David Dinges at the University of Pennsylvania pooled 70 studies containing 147 cognitive tests to answer a simple question: when people go 24 to 48 hours without sleep, which mental abilities take the biggest hit? They compared effects across categories, from basic attention to complex reasoning, using a standard measure of effect size where bigger numbers mean bigger damage.

blocks.title: How hard one to two nights without sleep hits each skill
blocks.note: Absolute size of the decline; around 0.2 is small, 0.5 moderate, 0.8 large
blocks.source: Lim & Dinges, Psychological Bulletin, 2010

blocks.text: The ranking is the opposite of what most people expect. Reasoning, the kind of thinking you'd assume needs a fresh brain, barely moved. The worst damage was to *simple* attention: sitting in front of a screen and responding the moment something appears. That's measured with tests like the psychomotor vigilance task, where you watch a box and hit a button as soon as a counter starts. It's about as dull as a test can be, and that's the point.

The most telling measure in those tests isn't average speed. It's **lapses**: responses that take half a second or longer, or don't happen at all. A sleep-deprived brain doesn't run uniformly slower, like a game at a lower frame rate. It runs normally most of the time and then briefly drops out, for a fraction of a second or longer, like a connection with random packet loss. Your average reaction time might look only a little worse. Your worst moments get much worse.

Researchers at Penn have a name for this: **state instability**. In a 2001 study, 13 volunteers stayed awake for 88 hours and took a 10-minute vigilance test every two hours, while a comparison group got a two-hour nap every 12 hours. As sleep loss continued, the deprived group's performance became wildly variable from one response to the next. They didn't just miss signals. They also jumped the gun, pressing the button when nothing had appeared. And the two kinds of errors rose together, which suggested people were trying hard to compensate rather than simply giving up. The authors described a brain flickering within seconds between waking and sleep, in a state that was neither fully one nor the other.

If you've ever whiffed an easy shot and then fired early on the next fight, that pattern might feel familiar. The tired brain alternates between too slow and too eager, and the effort you put into staying sharp can itself produce mistakes. It was Nathaniel Kleitman, one of the founders of sleep research, who first noted that sleep-deprived people could still perform a task; what they couldn't do was hold steady performance for more than a few minutes.

That distinction matters for any kind of performance. A gunfight you lose is rarely lost to your average reaction time. It's lost to the moment you didn't see the peek. Inconsistency is what sleep loss produces, and inconsistency is exactly what's hardest to notice in yourself.
The Rocket League experiment

Until recently, nobody had actually tested whether sleep loss hurts performance in an esport. In 2024, researchers at the University of Limerick in Ireland ran the first experiment. They recruited 40 Rocket League players and matched them into 20 pairs of similar skill, including some ranked in the top few percent of the game's 1v1 playerbase. Everyone played a baseline session rested. Then one player in each pair stayed awake for about 29 hours, while the partner slept normally, and they faced off again.

On the lab tests, sleep deprivation did exactly what decades of research predicted. The tired players felt sleepier and less motivated, their reaction times slowed, and they had roughly five times as many lapses on the vigilance test. But in the game itself, across 279 matches, their overall results didn't get worse. Measured against their rested partners, their overall in-game performance held steady.

The details hinted at why. After a night without sleep, players seemed to shift toward a safer, simpler style: less time high in the air going for difficult aerial plays, and somewhat more time sitting back on the defensive side of the ball. In other words, they adapted. They stopped attempting the hardest mechanics and leaned on lower-risk plays, and in short 1v1 matches that was enough to hold their results steady.

blocks.title: Same night without sleep, two different tests

left.head: Short, engaging game
items: Constant action keeps you alert
Motivation and adrenaline cover gaps
You can switch to safer plays
Results held steady in the study

right.head: Long, boring vigilance task
items: Nothing happens for long stretches
No excitement to mask fatigue
No strategy to fall back on
Lapses rose about fivefold

blocks.text: This is a genuinely surprising result, and it's tempting to read it as "sleep doesn't matter for gaming." That's not what it shows. It's one study of one game with fast, intense matches. The authors themselves pointed out that games requiring long stretches of sustained attention, like MOBAs, might behave very differently, and that chronic poor sleep is a separate concern from one bad night. What the study shows is subtler and more useful: engagement can temporarily hide sleep loss, and skilled players compensate by changing *how* they play, often without realizing it.
What the pros' data shows

Real competition is messier than a lab, but the data points in the same direction. A 2019 study by researchers at Stony Brook University used a clever proxy for sleep loss: NBA players' time-stamped tweets. When 112 players were active on Twitter between 11 p.m. and 7 a.m. before a game, they scored fewer points and grabbed fewer rebounds the next day, partly because they played fewer minutes. The clearest signal was shooting accuracy, which dropped by 1.7 percentage points. It's an observational study, and late-night tweeting isn't a perfect measure of sleep, but it's a hint from real games with real stakes.

Baseball offers a test of the body clock. A 10-year study of Major League Baseball looked at 24,121 games and assigned each team a "circadian disadvantage" based on how many time zones it had recently crossed without time to adjust. When one team was better adjusted than the other, it won 52 percent of the time. When the gap was three hours, the better-adjusted team won about 61 percent of games.

blocks.title: Winning percentage with a body-clock advantage, MLB
blocks.note: 10 seasons; the 3-hour group is small (160 games), so treat it as suggestive
blocks.source: Winter et al., International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 2009

blocks.text: The baseball numbers carry a lesson that goes beyond total sleep. A team that just flew three time zones may have slept a normal number of hours. What's off is *when* their bodies think it is. The same thing happens on a rotating watchbill: you can be technically rested and still be working at the bottom of your body clock's cycle, which is its own kind of handicap. Hours of sleep and timing of sleep are two different dials, and performance depends on both.

Raw physical output takes a measurable hit too. A 2022 meta-analysis pooled 69 studies on sleep loss and exercise, covering everything from sprints and strength to endurance and sport skills. On average, performance dropped by about 7.6 percent after a short night or none, and the longer people had been awake before the task, the worse they did, roughly 0.4 percent more for every extra hour. Interestingly, tasks done in the morning were largely unaffected; the damage piled up later in the day.
What actually helps

If sleep loss costs performance, the natural question is which fixes actually work. A 2023 systematic review looked at 25 intervention studies in athletes published between 2011 and 2021, covering everything from sleep hygiene advice and blue-light changes to naps, mindfulness, cold-water immersion and simply spending longer asleep. The two strategies that stood out as most effective were the least glamorous: extending sleep at night and adding naps.

Several popular tricks didn't show clear effects, including general sleep hygiene education, removing electronic devices at night and cold-water immersion, though the reviewers stressed that each of those rested on only a few studies, and the overall quality of evidence was limited. The broad lesson still holds up: when it comes to performance, the recovery gadgets and routines matter much less than the plain number of hours your brain spends asleep. There's no supplement or cold plunge that stands in for the thing itself.
Why your watch is harder than your game

Put these studies together and a pattern appears. Sleep loss hits hardest when a task is long, monotonous and requires you to respond to rare events. It hits least when the task is short, exciting and gives you room to adjust your strategy. A competitive match sits toward the easy end of that spectrum. A watch spent monitoring gauges in a quiet space at 0300 sits squarely at the hard end.

That flips a common bit of self-assessment on its head. "I played until 0200 and still dropped 30 kills, so I'm fine" is not good evidence that you're fine. The game was propping you up. The tasks that matter most for safety are the ones that look like the psychomotor vigilance test: nothing, nothing, nothing, then something you have to catch. That's precisely where lapses live, and there's no adrenaline to cover for them.

It also means the price of being tired in a game shows up in places a scoreboard won't. If you shift toward safer, simpler plays without noticing, you're not practicing the hard mechanics you're trying to build. For someone grinding aim or recording gameplay for a channel, a late-night session may feel productive while quietly training a cautious, sloppier version of your play.

There's a deeper point here about how you judge yourself. Every one of these studies separates two things that feel identical from the inside: how well you think you're doing and how well you're actually doing. The Rocket League players felt sleepier and less motivated but held their results; the vigilance tests showed damage they couldn't feel moment to moment. The only reliable way to know how sleep is affecting you is to look at outcomes over time, not at how sharp you feel right now.

blocks.title: Playing and working with the sleep you have
items: Schedule ranked matches, recordings and skill practice for when you're rested; save casual play for tired hours.
If you must perform tired, expect lapses rather than slowness: double-check critical actions and use checklists.
Notice if you're playing safer than usual; that's a fatigue signal, not a strategy upgrade.
Before a big event, a board or a qualification, protect several nights of sleep, not just the night before.
If you have flexibility, do your most demanding physical training earlier in your wake period.
Stop the late session when it starts to feel automatic; the boring parts are where the brain drops out.

blocks.text: Mah's basketball players didn't learn a new move or follow a new program. They just gave their brains the hours they needed, and the improvements showed up in sprints, shooting and reaction time. That's the most underrated upgrade in any competitive pursuit: it requires no talent, no gear and no money, only the discipline to stop playing and go to bed.

takeaways: Sleep loss hits simple, sustained attention hardest and reasoning least; boring tasks are where tired brains fail.
Tired brains aren't uniformly slower; they lapse, with occasional blank moments that wreck your worst reactions.
In a Rocket League study, players kept winning after 29 hours awake by switching to safer, simpler play, even though lapses rose about fivefold on a vigilance test.
Doing fine in a game after no sleep doesn't mean you're fit for a long, quiet watch.
Extra sleep improved sprint times, shooting and reaction time in Stanford basketball players; sleep is the cheapest performance upgrade.

title: Your Sleep Score Is Partly Fiction
dek: Wearables are good at some things and bad at others, and the number on your wrist can change how you feel whether or not it's right.

blocks.text: In a pair of experiments published in 2014, psychologists Christina Draganich and Kristi Erdal asked 164 volunteers how well they had slept the night before. Then they gave each person what was presented as a scientific readout of their sleep. Some were told they had spent **28.7%** of the night in REM sleep, which the researchers described as above average. Others heard they had managed only **16.2%**, which was below average.

None of it was real. The results were assigned at random, and had nothing to do with how anyone had actually slept. Yet on two of four mental tests, one of fast mental math and attention and one of verbal fluency, people's scores followed the fake result. The ones told they had slept well did better. The ones told they had slept badly did worse. How well they *said* they had slept didn't predict their scores. What they had been told did.

It was one small study, it hasn't been widely repeated, and two of the four tests showed no effect. Treat it as a warning sign rather than a law. But hold onto the question it raises, because it's the most important one about sleep tracking: if a fake number can shift how you perform, what does a real but inaccurate number do when you see it every single morning?
What's actually on your wrist

Sleep scientists define sleep stages with **polysomnography**, or PSG: an overnight lab recording of brain waves, eye movements, muscle tone, breathing and heart rhythm. Each 30-second chunk of the night gets labeled as wake, light sleep (N1 and N2), deep sleep (N3) or REM, mostly based on what the brain waves look like.

A ring or watch can't see brain waves. It sees how your arm or finger moves, your heart rate and how much it varies from beat to beat, and sometimes skin temperature and blood oxygen. From those indirect signals, an algorithm trained on people who wore both the device and a full lab setup makes a guess about what your brain was doing. That's the key word: everything a consumer tracker tells you about stages is an *estimate* built from proxies.

blocks.title: How a wearable builds your sleep score
items: Sensors log movement, heart rate, heart rate variability and sometimes temperature.
An algorithm decides when you were probably asleep, mostly from stillness and a slowing heart.
A second model guesses the stage of each chunk of the night from heart and movement patterns.
Those guesses are totaled into minutes of light, deep and REM sleep.
The company's own formula, which it usually doesn't publish, combines everything into a single score.

blocks.text: Here's a twist most people never hear: the gold standard is also partly a judgment call. Lab recordings are scored by trained humans reading squiggly lines. In 2013, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine compared more than 2,500 scorers, most with years of experience, on the same 1,800 chunks of sleep. On average, they agreed with the majority call **82.6%** of the time. For deep sleep, agreement dropped to 67.4%. For the lightest stage, N1, it was 63%.

blocks.title: Even experts disagree on sleep stages
blocks.note: Agreement of 2,500+ trained scorers with the majority call on the same lab recordings.
blocks.source: Rosenberg and Van Hout, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 2013

blocks.text: So when a device is graded against PSG, it's being graded against a reference that is itself fuzzy, especially at the boundary between light and deep sleep. That should make you more skeptical of any app that reports your deep sleep to the minute.

It also helps to know why stages are so hard to read from the wrist. During REM, your brain is busy but your body is nearly paralyzed, and your heart rate becomes irregular, a lot like it is when you're awake and lying still. Deep sleep and quiet light sleep can look similar from the outside too: a still body and a slow, steady pulse. The device is trying to tell apart states that differ mostly inside your skull, using signals that mostly come from everywhere else.
What trackers get right

The good news first. Modern trackers are genuinely good at one thing: telling whether you were asleep. A 2021 study from the Naval Health Research Center in San Diego, led by Evan Chinoy, tested seven consumer devices against lab recordings in 34 healthy young adults. Every device caught at least **93%** of the moments when people were actually asleep. A 2024 study at Brigham and Women's Hospital found the same for an Oura Ring, a Fitbit and an Apple Watch: all three caught at least 95% of sleep, and all three were close to the lab on total sleep time in healthy adults.

That's useful. Total sleep and consistent timing are among the most important things you could track, and a tracker gives you a far more honest record than memory does. Most people are poor judges of how long they slept, and a device that shows you've averaged five and a half hours across a hard week is telling you something true and actionable.

blocks.title: Where to trust the numbers

left.head: Fairly reliable
items: Whether you slept
Total sleep time on a normal night
Bedtime and wake time consistency
Trends across weeks
Resting heart rate

right.head: Treat with caution
items: Exact minutes of deep and REM sleep
How long you lay awake
Any single bad night
Scores on disrupted, restless nights
Comparisons between brands

blocks.text: What they get wrong

The weakness is the flip side of the strength. A tracker that's eager to call everything sleep is bad at noticing when you're *awake*. If you lie perfectly still in your rack with your heart rate down, scrolling nothing and thinking about tomorrow, a device can easily log that as sleep. In Chinoy's study, the share of awake moments correctly caught as wake ranged from just **18% to 54%** across devices. Every study of these devices finds the same pattern: catching wake is the weakest part of the job.

Stage estimates vary even more. A large 2023 study in Korea tested 11 consumer trackers, including watches, rings, bedside devices and phone apps, against lab recordings in 75 people. Using a standard score of how well the stage calls matched, where 1 is perfect, the best device scored 0.69 and the worst 0.26. Brand mattered a lot. In the 2024 Brigham study, the Apple Watch underestimated deep sleep by 43 minutes and overestimated light sleep by 45 minutes on average, while the Fitbit underestimated deep sleep by 15 minutes.

blocks.title: How far off stage estimates ran
blocks.note: Average error versus the lab in one night, healthy adults. The Oura Ring was not significantly different from the lab on any stage.
blocks.source: Robbins et al., Sensors, 2024

blocks.text: Two more problems are worth knowing. First, devices tend to get worse exactly when sleep gets worse. Chinoy's team found performance dropped on nights when sleep was deliberately disrupted, which is when people most want an accurate read. Second, follow the money. Several validation studies are funded by device makers or involve researchers who consult for them, and the 2024 Brigham study, for example, disclosed that its lead author advises Oura. That doesn't make the results wrong, but independent replications matter more than press releases.

And companies update their algorithms constantly. A validation study from two years ago may describe a device that no longer exists in that form, which makes it hard to know how accurate the one on your wrist is right now.

Then there's the score itself. A single number out of 100 feels scientific, but it's a design choice. Each company decides what goes into it and how much each piece counts, and the formula is usually secret. Two devices on the same person on the same night can hand out quite different scores. It's worth asking what the score is optimized for. A number that changes every morning and makes you curious to check it is great for keeping you engaged with an app. Whether it's also the best way to help you sleep is a separate question, and the companies have little reason to ask it.
When the tracker becomes the problem

In 2017, Kelly Glazer Baron and colleagues in Chicago described a pattern they had started seeing in their sleep clinic. Patients were coming in convinced they had a sleep disorder, not because they felt terrible, but because their tracker said they had too little deep sleep or too much restless time. Some trusted the device more than the clinic's own lab results. Their efforts to fix the numbers, like spending longer in bed, made their sleep worse. Baron's team named it **orthosomnia**: an unhealthy preoccupation with achieving perfect sleep data.

Notice the trap in that loop. You see a low deep-sleep number, so you go to bed earlier to get more. You lie awake longer, frustrated, which the device may not even catch as wake. You check the app first thing, see another mediocre score, and start the day already convinced you're running on empty. The tracker never caused the bad night, but it turned an ordinary night into a problem to solve, and the solving made things worse.

The name is a play on orthorexia, an obsession with eating perfectly. The mechanism is the same. Sleep is one of the few things in life that gets *worse* the harder you try. You can't force it; you can only set up the conditions and let go. A device that grades you every morning turns sleep into a performance, and performance anxiety is a classic driver of insomnia. The article in this library on treating insomnia explains why spending more time in bed chasing sleep usually backfires.

A 2018 experiment at the University of Oxford showed how direct the effect can be. Researchers gave 63 people with insomnia a watch that delivered next-morning feedback about their sleep, but the feedback was fake: half were randomly told they had slept well, half that they had slept badly. By evening, those given bad news reported feeling less mentally sharp and more sleepy and fatigued, while the good-news group's mood climbed more through the day. But on an objective reaction-time test that evening, the two groups performed about the same. The number changed how people *felt* about their day far more than it changed what they could actually do.

items.label: U.S. adults who have used a sleep tracker, up from 35% in 2023
Range of stage-matching scores across 11 trackers (1 = perfect)
Share of awake time correctly caught by seven devices tested in 2021

blocks.source: AASM survey (fielded 2025, published 2026); Lee et al., JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 2023; Chinoy et al., Sleep, 2021

blocks.text: This is why the shift toward **sleepmaxxing**, the trend of optimizing sleep with gadgets, routines and products, deserves some skepticism. A 2025 survey by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found that 48% of U.S. adults had used a sleep tracker. Many of them are healthy sleepers who are being nudged to worry about a deep-sleep number that even trained human scorers disagree about a third of the time.
Using a tracker without letting it use you

None of this means you should throw your watch overboard. Used well, a tracker is a decent mirror. On a rotating watch schedule, it can show you patterns your memory blurs: that your sleep collapses after a particular rotation, or that late gaming nights cost you more than you thought. The goal is to treat it like a gauge with known error, not like a verdict.

The most useful single thing a tracker can show on a submarine is regularity. With no sunrise to anchor you, the timing of your sleep drifts easily, and timing matters alongside total hours. A week-long view of when you actually fell asleep and woke up, across a watch rotation, can reveal whether your body is getting any consistent signal at all. That's information worth having, and it's exactly the kind of measure trackers handle well.

blocks.title: Rules for a healthy relationship with your tracker
items: Watch weekly averages of total sleep and timing, not single nights.
Treat deep and REM minutes as rough estimates. Never chase them.
If you feel fine, a bad score doesn't mean you slept badly. Believe your body first.
If you feel bad despite good scores, don't let the device talk you out of seeing medical.
If checking the score makes you anxious, hide it or take the device off for a week and see how you feel.

blocks.text: That fourth rule matters more than it looks. Trackers can miss real problems. Feeling exhausted despite plenty of hours in bed, loud snoring, gasping awake or falling asleep at the wrong moments are all reasons to talk to the corpsman or a doctor, whatever the app says. A consumer gadget isn't a diagnostic tool, and a good score can give false reassurance just as a bad one can create false alarm.
A tracker answers 'how long did I sleep?' fairly well and 'how well did I sleep?' poorly. Your own energy, mood and focus during the day are still the best sleep score you have.

The deeper lesson reaches past sleep. Any time you measure something, you change your relationship to it. Measurement is powerful when the number is accurate and tied to something you can act on. It turns harmful when the number is fuzzy, the thing being measured can't be forced, and you check it every morning first thing. Sleep tracking can land on either side of that line. Which side depends less on the device than on how you read it.

takeaways: Wearables are good at detecting sleep and estimating total sleep time in healthy people.
They are weak at detecting time spent awake and inconsistent at estimating deep and REM sleep.
Even expert human scorers agree on deep sleep only about two-thirds of the time.
Orthosomnia is real: chasing perfect sleep data can make sleep and mood worse.
Track weekly trends, trust how you feel, and see medical for real symptoms whatever the score says.

title: The Sleepless Night That Lifts Depression
dek: For about half of depressed patients, staying awake all night brings relief by morning. The catch is what happens when they sleep again, and what that says about how mood is wired to the body clock.

blocks.text: Picture a psychiatric ward at 0400. A handful of patients with severe depression are awake on purpose. Staff keep them talking, walking, playing cards, anything to stop them from dozing off. They've been told to stay up through the whole night and the following day. It sounds like the opposite of medicine. Poor sleep is one of the classic symptoms of depression, and everyone knows a sleepless night makes a normal person miserable.

And yet by morning, a lot of them feel noticeably better. Not just less tired of being sad, but lighter, more like themselves, sometimes for the first time in weeks. Standard antidepressants usually take around four to six weeks to work. This took one night.

This is **wake therapy**, also called therapeutic sleep deprivation, and it's one of the strangest reliable findings in psychiatry. It's also one of the most misunderstood, because the same thing that lifts a depressed patient in a hospital is, as a lifestyle, one of the strongest risk factors for becoming depressed. Untangling that paradox says something important about how mood actually works.

This article is about a supervised hospital treatment, not something to try on yourself. If you're feeling hopeless or thinking about ending your life, talk to the corpsman or contact the Military Crisis Line: dial 988, then press 1.
An accident that kept repeating

The observation that a sleepless night could lift depression circulated among German psychiatrists in the 1960s, and in 1971 Burkhard Pflug and Rainer Tölle published a systematic report on treating depression with sleep deprivation. Over the next two decades the finding was replicated over and over. By 1990, when Joseph Wu and William Bunney reviewed the field, there were 61 papers involving more than 1,700 patients, and over half of depressed patients had shown an antidepressant response.

The same review documented the problem that has haunted wake therapy ever since. Among unmedicated patients who responded, **83 percent relapsed after a single night of recovery sleep**. Even short naps could bring the depression back. The relief was real, but it seemed to be undone by sleep itself. Wu and Bunney suggested that something happening during sleep in these patients might be actively generating the depressed state, a strange idea that still hasn't been fully resolved.

items.label: Response rate to sleep deprivation in controlled studies
Unmedicated responders who relapsed after one night of sleep
Typical time for standard antidepressants to take effect

blocks.source: Boland et al., J Clin Psychiatry, 2017; Wu & Bunney, Am J Psychiatry, 1990; Martiny et al., J Clin Psychiatry, 2012

blocks.text: How big is the effect?

Because many early studies were small and uncontrolled, it was fair to wonder whether the effect was inflated. In 2017, a team at the University of Pennsylvania pooled 66 studies stretching back to 1974. Across studies that included a randomized control group, 45 percent of patients responded to sleep deprivation; in studies without one, the figure was 50 percent.

Just as interesting is what *didn't* matter. The response rate wasn't significantly affected by whether patients were kept awake the whole night or only part of it, by whether they had unipolar or bipolar depression, by whether they were on medication, or by their age or sex. A treatment that works for roughly half of a hard-to-treat population within a day, across all those variables, is not something psychiatry gets very often.

It's worth being clear about what "response" means here. Studies defined it in advance, with thresholds such as a 30 percent drop in a standard depression rating, and the meta-analysis found that the exact definition didn't change the picture much. A response isn't a cure. It means a meaningful, measurable lift, the kind a patient and their doctor would both notice, arriving in a day instead of a month.
The paradox

Now the uncomfortable part. Outside the hospital, poor sleep is one of the best-established predictors of future depression. A 2011 meta-analysis of 21 long-term studies found that people without depression who had insomnia were about twice as likely to develop depression later as people who slept well. The pooled odds ratio was 2.6 in one model and 2.1 in another.

So how can losing sleep both cause depression and cure it? The key is that these are completely different exposures. Wake therapy is one controlled night, done once or a few times, usually combined with other treatments, in people who are already severely depressed, with clinicians watching. Chronic insomnia or chronic short sleep is months of fragmented, anxious, irregular nights in people who may be fine to begin with. A single dose of something and a constant drip of it can have opposite effects. Think of a stress hormone spike that helps you in an emergency versus stress that never switches off.

blocks.title: Same ingredient, opposite effects

In people already severely depressed

Often lifts mood within a day

right.head: Chronic poor sleep
items: Months of short, broken or irregular nights
In people who may start out fine

About doubles the risk of later depression

blocks.text: What one night changes in the brain

Nobody has a complete explanation, but there are strong clues. In a 1992 study, Wu and colleagues used PET scans to measure brain metabolism in 15 unmedicated depressed patients before and after a night of sleep deprivation. The four who responded strongly had something in common: before treatment, their **cingulate cortex**, part of the brain's emotional circuitry, was running unusually hot, and after the sleepless night it calmed down toward normal levels. Non-responders and healthy controls showed no such change. That hints that wake therapy works best in a subset of depression marked by an overactive emotional system.

A more recent line of research focuses on synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen and rewire connections. One leading theory of sleep holds that waking hours build up connection strength and sleep scales it back down. In depression, some researchers argue, the brain's capacity to form new connections is stuck in an unhelpful range. Staying awake longer might push the system into a more flexible state, at least temporarily. That's a hypothesis under active study, not a settled account, and it's interesting partly because rapid-acting depression treatments seem to share this theme of quickly changing plasticity.

There's also the body clock. Many people with depression have disturbed circadian rhythms, with mood that varies by time of day and sleep that drifts out of alignment. Wake therapy is a large, abrupt jolt to that timing system. That's where the more modern versions of the treatment come in.
Making the relief last

If one night works but the next night undoes it, the obvious engineering question is how to lock in the gain. The answer researchers developed is called **chronotherapy**: combining wake therapy with bright morning light and a carefully controlled sleep schedule, sometimes moving bedtime earlier over several days, to stabilize the body clock in its new position.

The logic follows from the relapse problem. If sleeping at the wrong point in the body's daily cycle seems to drag mood back down, then controlling *when* recovery sleep happens might protect the gain. Bright light in the morning is the strongest signal the body clock has for setting its time, so it helps hold the clock where the treatment pushed it. A fixed, carefully timed sleep window keeps patients from drifting back into long, late or daytime sleep. Each piece is meant to stop the clock from snapping back.

A Danish trial published in 2012 tested a version of this. Klaus Martiny and colleagues randomly assigned 75 patients with major depression, all starting the same antidepressant, to either a chronotherapy package (three wake-therapy nights in one week, then daily morning light and a stable sleep schedule) or a daily exercise program. Both groups improved, but the wake-therapy group improved faster and further.

blocks.title: Patients responding to treatment
blocks.note: 75 patients with major depression; both groups also took the same antidepressant.
blocks.source: Martiny et al., J Clin Psychiatry, 2012

blocks.text: Not every trial has been that encouraging. A follow-up Danish trial in 2017 gave 64 hospitalized patients either standard treatment or standard treatment plus wake therapy, light and sleep stabilization. The wake-therapy group was clearly better after one week, but the difference faded and was no longer significant from week two through week nine. They did sleep better, wake less at night and nap less, and they reported a bigger gain in their confidence in handling life. But the fast antidepressant boost didn't hold.

Smaller studies have tested the approach in the sickest patients. In a 2014 pilot study in South Carolina, ten depressed inpatients with active suicidal thoughts received a "triple chronotherapy" package of one night of wake therapy, an earlier sleep schedule and bright morning light, on top of usual care. By day five their depression scores had dropped sharply, as had their suicidal-thinking scores, and six of the ten met criteria for remission. With only ten people, no comparison group and everyone knowing what treatment they got, it's a reason for bigger trials rather than a proof.
