title: The Slowest Emergency: Why We Age, and Whether We Have To
dek: Your risk of dying roughly doubles every decade of adult life. Biologists now argue about whether that curve is fate, or a treatable condition.

blocks.text: Here is aging, expressed as a single number. According to the Social Security Administration's life tables, a 20-year-old American man has about a **1 in 770** chance of dying in the next twelve months. At 50, it's about 1 in 176. At 80, about 1 in 16. At 90, about 1 in 6.

Nothing dramatic happens on any particular birthday. There's no switch. But the odds keep climbing, year after year, at a pace that accelerates. In 1825 a British actuary named Benjamin Gompertz noticed this pattern in mortality records and described it with a simple exponential curve. Two centuries later, his law still describes human populations remarkably well.

blocks.title: Chance of dying within a year, US men
blocks.source: US Social Security Administration, Period Life Table 2022 (2025 Trustees Report)

blocks.text: From 50 onward in that table, the annual risk roughly doubles or more every ten years. That curve is what aging *is*, from a statistician's point of view: not wrinkles or gray hair, but a steadily rising chance that something will go fatally wrong. The interesting questions are why the curve exists at all, and whether it has to bend upward the way it does.
Not a law of physics

You might assume that wearing out is simply what happens to complex machines, like a car accumulating rust. But aging isn't universal in the way physics is. The clearest counterexample is a small, wrinkled, nearly hairless animal from East Africa: the naked mole-rat.

Naked mole-rats are about the size of a mouse, yet they've been recorded living more than 30 years, where a lab mouse is old at two or three. In 2018, researchers analyzed more than 3,000 lifespan records and found something no one had documented in a mammal before. Their risk of death *didn't increase with age*, even at ages far beyond when they become able to breed. By Gompertz's standard, they barely age at all.

Some other species, including certain turtles, fish and the tiny freshwater animal hydra, also appear to show little or no rise in mortality with age. That doesn't make them immortal; they still die from predators, disease and accidents. But it proves that rising mortality isn't an unavoidable property of being alive. It's a trait, and traits have evolutionary explanations.
Why evolution lets us fall apart

The explanation that most biologists accept was developed in the mid-twentieth century by Peter Medawar, George Williams and later Tom Kirkwood. It starts with a simple observation: in the wild, most animals die young from external causes like predators, starvation, cold and disease, long before they could die of old age.

That means natural selection gets weaker with age. A gene that causes trouble at age 80 barely matters to evolution if almost nobody in the ancestral environment survived to 80, because by then they'd already have had their children. Harmful late-acting effects slip through the filter, generation after generation.

It gets worse. Some genes may be actively favored because they help early in life, even if they cause damage later. Williams called this *antagonistic pleiotropy*: one gene, two effects, pointing in opposite directions over a lifetime. Something that boosts growth and fertility at 20 can be selected for even if it raises cancer risk at 70.

Kirkwood added an economic version, the *disposable soma* theory. Every organism has a limited energy budget. Energy spent maintaining and repairing the body is energy not spent on growing and reproducing. Evolution tunes the budget for a body that's expected to last about as long as it's likely to survive in the wild, not a day longer. Repair is good enough, never perfect, and the small errors pile up.

From evolution's point of view, your body was never designed to last forever. It was designed to stay in good enough condition long enough to pass on your genes. Everything after that is running on leftover engineering.
What actually goes wrong

If aging is the slow accumulation of unrepaired damage, what kinds of damage are we talking about? In 2013, a team led by Carlos López-Otín in Spain proposed a list of hallmarks of aging in the journal *Cell*. It became one of the most cited papers in the field. In 2023 they updated it to twelve hallmarks.
To count as a hallmark, a process had to meet three tests: it shows up with age, making it worse in experiments speeds up aging, and fixing it slows aging down. The current list:

items: **Genomic instability:** DNA damage accumulates faster than it's fully repaired.
**Telomere attrition:** the protective caps on chromosomes shorten with cell divisions.
**Epigenetic alterations:** the chemical tags that control which genes are on or off drift out of order.
**Loss of proteostasis:** cells get worse at folding proteins correctly and clearing out the bad ones.
**Disabled autophagy:** the cell's internal recycling system slows down.
**Deregulated nutrient sensing:** growth and fuel-sensing pathways like mTOR and insulin signaling get miscalibrated.
**Mitochondrial dysfunction:** the cell's power plants become less efficient.
**Cellular senescence:** damaged cells stop dividing but don't die, and send out inflammatory signals.
**Stem cell exhaustion:** the reserves that replenish tissues run low.
**Altered intercellular communication:** signals between cells and tissues get noisy.
**Chronic inflammation:** a low-grade, constant immune activation sometimes called inflammaging.
**Dysbiosis:** the gut's microbial community shifts in unhealthy ways.

blocks.text: Notice that several of these are things the body normally handles well. Cells repair DNA constantly, recycle damaged parts, and clear out broken proteins. Aging isn't the sudden appearance of new problems so much as the slow erosion of maintenance systems that once kept up with routine wear.

Anyone who has worked on a ship will recognize the pattern. A well-run boat can stay in service for decades, not because nothing breaks, but because a maintenance system catches small failures before they spread. Let that system slip, even a little, and deferred repairs start compounding: one degraded component strains the next. Aging looks a lot like a body whose maintenance schedule is slowly falling behind.

These aren't independent problems. Damaged DNA can push a cell into senescence. Senescent cells drive inflammation. Inflammation impairs stem cells. The hallmarks feed each other, which helps explain why aging accelerates instead of creeping along at a constant pace. It's less like a single part rusting and more like an organization where small failures in one department start overloading the others.

Some of these were spotted early. In 1961, Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead showed that normal human cells grown in a dish can only divide a limited number of times before they stop. That limit, now called the Hayflick limit, was later linked to telomeres, and it overturned the belief that cells could divide forever if kept in the right conditions.
Slowing the clock, in animals
If the hallmarks are real causes, then targeting them should slow aging. In animals, that has now been shown several times, and the results are among the most striking in modern biology.

blocks.title: Milestones in the science of aging
items: Gompertz describes the exponential rise of death risk with age
Hayflick and Moorhead show normal human cells have a division limit
Rapamycin extends lifespan in mice even when started late in life
The original hallmarks of aging are published in Cell
Clearing senescent cells extends healthy lifespan in mice
Naked mole-rats shown to defy Gompertz's law
The hallmarks list is updated to twelve

blocks.text: In 2009, a US program that tests possible anti-aging compounds in genetically diverse mice reported that **rapamycin**, a drug that dampens the mTOR nutrient-sensing pathway, extended lifespan in both sexes. Remarkably, the mice didn't start the drug until they were 600 days old, well into middle age. The effect was replicated at three separate test sites.

In 2016, a team at the Mayo Clinic used genetically engineered mice whose senescent cells could be destroyed on command with a drug. Starting at one year of age, clearing those cells extended median lifespan and delayed age-related decline in the kidneys, heart and fat tissue, with no obvious side effects.

items.label: Lifespan gain in female / male mice given rapamycin from 600 days (age at 90% mortality)
Median lifespan gain in mice after clearing senescent cells

blocks.source: Harrison et al., Nature, 2009; Baker et al., Nature, 2016

blocks.text: Calorie restriction, eating well below normal intake without malnutrition, extends lifespan in many species. In monkeys, two long-running US studies started in the 1980s seemed to disagree: one found a survival benefit, the other didn't. A joint analysis in 2017 concluded that differences in study design explained much of the gap, and that the health benefits held up in both.

Now the caveats, which matter a lot. Mice aren't people. Rapamycin suppresses parts of the immune system and has real side effects. Strict calorie restriction is hard to sustain and risky for many people, particularly anyone young, training hard or with a history of disordered eating. None of this is a reason to self-experiment with drugs or extreme diets. Ask a doctor before trying anything marketed as anti-aging, and be especially skeptical of supplements with mouse data and a sales page.
Is aging a disease?

Here's where biology turns into philosophy. Aging is the biggest risk factor for almost every major killer in wealthy countries: heart disease, most cancers, stroke, dementia. Medicine attacks these one at a time. But if you cure one disease in an 85-year-old, the rising tide of aging tends to deliver another one soon after. Some researchers argue that this one-at-a-time approach has diminishing returns, and that we should target the underlying process instead.

That idea, often called *geroscience*, comes with a provocative claim: aging should be treated as a medical condition, something we could prevent or slow. Supporters point out that our current system only approves drugs for specific diseases, so a drug that delayed many diseases at once would have no obvious regulatory path. Trials like the proposed TAME study of metformin have been designed partly to test whether regulators would accept a combined set of age-related diseases as an outcome.

Critics push back from several directions. If something happens to every human who lives long enough, calling it a disease stretches the word until it means nothing. Labeling old age itself as pathology risks fueling ageism, or encouraging doctors to shrug off treatable problems as just aging. And some demographers argue there are hard limits. A 2016 analysis in *Nature* found that survival gains slow sharply after age 100, and that the maximum age at death had stopped rising since the 1990s. The oldest documented person, Jeanne Calment, died in 1997 at 122. Other researchers disputed that analysis, and the debate continues.

blocks.title: Should aging be treated as a condition?

left.head: The case for
items: Aging drives most major chronic diseases
Treating diseases one at a time has diminishing returns
Animal studies show aging can be slowed
A medical label could unlock research and approval

right.head: The case against
items: Something universal isn't a disease in the normal sense
Risk of ageism and dismissing treatable illness
Human evidence for anti-aging drugs is still thin
There may be hard limits to human lifespan

blocks.text: What this means at twenty

Aging feels irrelevant at twenty, but the biology says otherwise. The hallmarks don't switch on at 60. They accumulate from early adulthood, quietly, at a rate that's partly set by genes and partly by how you live. The tools with the strongest evidence for a longer healthy life in humans are unglamorous: regular exercise, keeping muscle, not smoking, sleeping enough, staying socially connected, and avoiding the slow damage of excess. None of them come in a bottle.

It also helps to separate two ideas that get blurred together: *lifespan*, how long you live, and *healthspan*, how long you live in good health. Many geroscientists say the second is the real goal. Stretching out the frail final years isn't the prize. Compressing them, so that people stay strong and sharp until close to the end, is. The mouse studies are exciting partly because the treated animals didn't just live longer; several of their organs aged more slowly too.

Researchers are also building ways to measure aging directly, rather than waiting decades to count deaths. One approach, the so-called *epigenetic clock*, estimates biological age from the pattern of chemical tags on DNA, one of the twelve hallmarks. These clocks are still being refined, and commercial tests that promise to reveal your true age deserve skepticism. But the idea behind them is powerful: two people born the same year can be aging at visibly different speeds.

The deeper reframe is this. We usually think of age as a date on an ID card. Biologists increasingly think of it as a *rate*: how fast damage builds up relative to how well it's repaired. You can't change your birth year. But the steepness of the curve, at least some of it, is still being decided, and much of the deciding happens decades before anyone thinks to worry about it.

takeaways: Aging, statistically, is a death risk that roughly doubles each decade of adult life.
Evolution lets us age because natural selection weakens after reproductive years.
Biologists list twelve interconnected hallmarks of aging, from DNA damage to chronic inflammation.
Rapamycin and clearing senescent cells extend lifespan in mice, but human evidence is thin. Don't self-experiment.
The best-supported tools for healthy aging are boring ones: exercise, muscle, sleep, not smoking.

title: The Construction Crew Under Every Scab
dek: A small cut kicks off a four-stage building project. What you do, how you sleep and even how stressed you are all change how fast that crew finishes.

blocks.text: In the 1990s, researchers at Ohio State University gave eleven dental students two small wounds each, on purpose. Each wound was a 3.5-millimeter punch biopsy on the hard palate, the roof of the mouth. The first was made during summer vacation. The second was made on the other side of the mouth three days before the first big exam of the term. Each student was their own comparison.

The wounds were identical, and the mouths belonged to the same people. The only difference was the calendar. Yet the exam-time wounds took an average of three days longer to close, which the authors described as about **40 percent longer**. No student healed as fast during exams as during vacation.

That result, published by Phillip Marucha, Janice Kiecolt-Glaser and Mahvash Favagehi in 1998, points to something most people never think about. Healing isn't a passive process where skin just grows back. It's a project run by your immune system, and like any project, it can be understaffed, underfunded or delayed. To see how your mind could reach into a hole the size of a pencil eraser, you first need to see who's working in there.
Four crews, one job site

The moment skin is cut, blood vessels leak and the body's first goal is to stop the loss. Platelets stick to the exposed tissue and to each other, and a protein called fibrin weaves through them into a mesh. That clot is more than a plug. It's scaffolding, and it's loaded with chemical signals that call in the next crew.

The second crew is inflammation, which is why a fresh cut turns red, warm and a little swollen. White blood cells called neutrophils arrive first and attack bacteria. Then larger cells called macrophages take over. They eat debris and dead cells, and they act like site foremen, releasing signals that tell the rebuilding crew to start. Inflammation gets a bad reputation, but here it's essential. A wound without it doesn't heal well.

The third crew builds. Cells called fibroblasts move in and lay down collagen, the protein rope that gives skin its strength. New capillaries sprout to feed the work, forming the bumpy pink tissue you see in a healing scrape. Meanwhile skin cells at the edges crawl across the gap to seal the surface. The final crew, remodeling, is the slowest. Over months the hasty first collagen is broken down and rebuilt in a more organized pattern, and the scar slowly fades and flattens.

blocks.title: How a cut closes
items: Stop the bleeding: platelets and fibrin form a clot that doubles as scaffolding (minutes)
Clean up: neutrophils fight bacteria, macrophages clear debris and signal the next stage (the first few days)
Rebuild: fibroblasts lay collagen, new vessels grow, skin cells crawl across the gap (days to weeks)
Remodel: collagen is reorganized and the scar matures (months, sometimes more than a year)

blocks.text: Why a scar is a patch, not a repair

Here's the part that surprises people: the skin you had before a deep cut never comes back. What you get is a patch. Scar tissue lacks hair follicles, sweat and oil glands, and many of the nerve endings of normal skin. And it's weaker. A 2012 review in *Stem Cell Research & Therapy* notes that scar tissue reaches only about 80 percent of the tensile strength of the skin around it, leaving a weak point that's easier to re-injure.

items.label: Strength of scar tissue compared with the surrounding skin, at best
Longer healing for identical mouth wounds during exam stress vs vacation

blocks.source: Jackson, Nesti & Tuan, Stem Cell Res Ther, 2012; Marucha et al., Psychosom Med, 1998

blocks.text: It doesn't have to be this way, which is the strange part. Through most of fetal development, skin wounds heal without scarring at all. Your mouth is another exception. Cuts inside the cheek heal faster and with less scarring than cuts on the outside of the body. A 2018 study led by Ramiro Iglesias-Bartolome at the National Institutes of Health compared paired wounds in human mouths and skin and found that the oral lining keeps many wound-response genes switched on even before any injury, as if it's always half-ready to repair.

So why does adult skin settle for a weaker patch? A common explanation is a trade-off between speed and quality. An open wound is a door for infection, and for most of human history, an infected wound could kill you. A system that seals the door fast with rough material would beat one that rebuilds slowly and perfectly. Your scars are the record of a body choosing *good enough, right now*.
Healing is a speed-versus-quality trade-off. Adult skin is built to close the door fast, not to rebuild the room perfectly.
The pig that killed the scab

For a long time, the standard advice was to let a wound air out and form a good scab. In 1962 a British researcher named George Winter tested that idea on young domestic pigs, publishing the results in *Nature*. He made shallow wounds and left some open to dry while covering others with a film that kept them moist. The covered wounds resurfaced with new skin about twice as fast as the ones left to dry.

The reason is mechanical. A dry scab is a hard crust that skin cells have to tunnel underneath to cross the gap. In a moist wound they can slide across the surface. Winter's study launched the modern era of wound dressings, and the principle still holds: clean it, cover it and keep it from drying into a crust.

Another common belief is that every cut needs antibiotic ointment. In 1996 dermatologists at Walter Reed Army Medical Center tested that in a randomized, double-blind trial of 922 patients after skin surgery. Half used plain white petrolatum, the stuff in a tub of petroleum jelly, and half used bacitracin ointment. Infection rates were low in both groups, 2.0 percent versus 0.9 percent, a difference that wasn't statistically significant, and healing looked the same at one, seven and 28 days. But four bacitracin users developed allergic skin reactions and nobody on petrolatum did. One honest caveat: all eight staph infections in the study occurred in the petrolatum group, so the authors' conclusion was *equally safe for clean surgical wounds*, not *antibiotics never help*.

blocks.title: Wound care beliefs vs evidence

left.head: Common belief
items: Let it air out and scab over
Every cut needs antibiotic ointment
Healing just takes the time it takes
A healed scar is as strong as skin

right.head: What studies show
items: Moist, covered wounds resurfaced about twice as fast (Winter, 1962)
Plain petrolatum matched bacitracin for clean surgical wounds, with fewer allergies
Stress, sleep loss and fitness all change the healing rate
Scar tissue tops out around 80% of normal strength

blocks.text: Your mind is on the job site

The dental student study was a follow-up to an earlier one. In 1995 Kiecolt-Glaser's team published a study in *The Lancet* comparing 13 women caring for a relative with dementia, an exhausting and chronic stress, with 13 women matched for age and income. Everyone got the same small punch wound on the arm. The caregivers took an average of 48.7 days to heal, compared with 39.3 days for the comparison group.

In both studies, the researchers also looked at a signaling molecule called interleukin-1 beta, one of the alarms that summons the cleanup and rebuilding crews. The caregivers' white blood cells made less of the genetic message for it. In the dental students, its production dropped by 68 percent during exams. The leading explanation is that stress hormones like cortisol damp down exactly the inflammatory signals a wound needs early on. The crew doesn't get called in on time.

It goes further. In a 2005 study, the same group gave married couples small blister wounds and then had them discuss a conflict. Couples who were consistently hostile toward each other healed at about 60 percent of the rate of low-hostility couples. On the flip side, a small randomized trial led by Charles Emery assigned healthy older adults to three months of exercise or no exercise, then gave everyone a standard wound. The exercisers healed in an average of 29.2 days, versus 38.9 days for the non-exercisers.

blocks.title: Days for a small standard wound to heal
blocks.note: Two separate studies; compare within each pair, not across them.
blocks.source: Kiecolt-Glaser et al., Lancet, 1995; Emery et al., J Gerontol, 2005

blocks.text: None of this is entirely new to doctors. Slow healing has long been recognized in conditions that change how the immune system behaves, such as diabetes and old age, which is why a foot sore in someone with poorly controlled diabetes gets so much attention. What the stress studies added was the uncomfortable idea that you don't need a disease to slow the crew down. A hard exam week was enough to do it in a group of healthy dental students.

There's an intuitive reason this might happen. When the body perceives a threat, stress hormones shift resources toward getting through the next few hours: alertness, energy and blood flow to muscles. Long-term projects like repair get pushed down the list. That's useful if you're running from a predator for ten minutes. It's a poor trade when the stress lasts for weeks and the wound needs attention the whole time.

These are small studies, and controlled experimental wounds aren't the same as a deep gash. But the pattern has held across different stressors, different wound types and different labs: the state of your body and mind sets the budget your repair crews work with.
Sleep debt slows the patch

The military has a practical stake in this, because service members get hurt more often than most people and often while short on sleep. So the U.S. Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine tested it. In a 2018 study, healthy volunteers had small blisters raised on their forearms by suction, and the tops were removed to create shallow wounds. When people had normal sleep, their skin barrier recovered in about 4.2 days. After two nights of a 72-hour stretch where they slept only two hours a night, it took about 5.0 days.

A 2022 follow-up from the same group, in volunteers averaging under 20 years old, asked whether nutrition could offset that. During the same kind of sleep restriction, one group ate a diet with 1.5 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight plus a drink containing arginine, glutamine, omega-3s, zinc, vitamin D and vitamin C. The other group ate 0.9 grams per kilogram with a placebo. The supplemented group's wounds recovered in a median of about 4 days versus about 5.25.

Read that one carefully. The earlier 2018 study found its supplement didn't change the healing rate, and because the 2022 drink mixed several ingredients with extra protein, there's no way to know which part mattered. The useful takeaway isn't to buy a wound-healing powder. It's that healing is real construction work, it costs raw materials, and someone who is both sleep-deprived and underfed is asking the crew to build without bricks.

Smoking belongs here too. A 2012 meta-analysis by Lars Tønnesen Sørensen pooled 140 cohort studies and found that smokers had more healing complications and infections after surgery than nonsmokers, and that quitting before surgery lowered infection rates. Nicotine narrows small blood vessels, and the carbon monoxide in smoke reduces how much oxygen the blood can deliver to a wound that needs it.
What this means in a steel hull

Small cuts and scrapes are part of working around machinery, and a submarine is a tough place for a wound: grime, shared surfaces, close quarters and sleep that comes in pieces. The evidence points to a simple routine that costs almost nothing.

items: Rinse a small cut with clean running water and get the dirt out.
Cover it and keep it moist; a thin layer of plain petrolatum under a bandage works for most minor wounds.
Change the dressing when it gets wet or dirty, which matters more in a dirty workspace.
Eat enough protein and actual meals while healing, especially during a stretch of bad sleep.
See the corpsman for deep or gaping cuts, anything from a dirty or rusty object, or signs of infection: spreading redness, increasing pain or warmth, pus, red streaks or fever.

blocks.text: The bigger idea is about the body as a whole. A healing wound is one of the few places where you can actually measure the cost of stress and sleep loss in days. The same immune crews that close a cut are the ones fighting off whatever is going around the boat. When the cut takes longer to heal, it's a visible sign of something you usually can't see: a body running its repair work on a short budget.

takeaways: Healing runs in four overlapping stages: clot, clean-up, rebuild and remodel.
Scars are fast patches, not perfect repairs, and top out around 80% of normal skin strength.
Covered, moist wounds heal faster than air-dried ones; plain petrolatum works for most minor cuts.
Stress, hostility and sleep loss measurably slow healing; exercise and adequate food help.
Get deep, dirty or infected-looking wounds checked by the corpsman.

title: Your Muscles Can't See the Gym
dek: Push-ups built as much muscle as bench press in a head-to-head trial. The catch is that body weight only works if you learn to turn its difficulty up.

blocks.text: In 2017, two researchers at Nippon Sport Science University in Japan, Kikuchi and Nakazato, ran a simple experiment that should be better known. They took 18 young men and split them into two groups. One group trained the bench press with a barbell loaded to 40 percent of their max. The other did push-ups, with the position adjusted, for example to kneeling, so that the load matched that 40 percent. Both groups trained twice a week for eight weeks.

Here is the strange part. At the end, both groups were tested on the bench press, including the push-up group, which had never touched a bench during the study. Both groups got stronger on it. The bench group's average max rose from 60.0 to 65.0 kilograms; the push-up group's rose from 61.1 to 64.2. Both groups also grew their triceps and chest muscles. The authors concluded that push-ups at a matched load were comparably effective for building muscle and strength.

items.label: Bench press max gain, barbell group
Bench press max gain, push-up group (no bench training)
Two sessions a week

blocks.source: Kikuchi & Nakazato, Journal of Exercise Science & Fitness, 2017

blocks.text: It's a small study, and the gains came from a light load. But it makes a point that matters to anyone who trains in a cramped berthing area, a hotel room or a garage with nothing in it: your muscles have no idea whether the resistance comes from an Olympic barbell or the floor. They only register how hard they are working.
Tension doesn't care where it comes from

The research on loads explains why body weight can work. When sets are taken close to failure, a wide range of loads, from fairly light to very heavy, build similar amounts of muscle. A 2017 meta-analysis by Brad Schoenfeld and colleagues, pooling 21 studies in which every set went to failure, found muscle growth was similar between low-load and high-load training. Heavy loads were still better for one-rep max strength.

There is a floor, though. In a 2018 study by Thiago Lasevicius and colleagues, a load of 20 percent of max built clearly less muscle than 40, 60 or 80 percent, even with volume matched. If an exercise is so easy that you could do it 60 or 80 times, the set ends from boredom, burning and fatigue long before your largest muscle fibers are forced to work.

That gives bodyweight training one rule that matters more than any other: **the exercise has to be hard enough that you approach failure in roughly 30 reps or fewer.** A beginner doing push-ups is well inside that window. Someone who can rattle off 50 clean push-ups is now doing an endurance test, and needs a harder version to keep building muscle. The whole craft of bodyweight training is managing that problem.
Your body weight is adjustable

With a barbell, you make an exercise harder by adding plates. With your body, you change the geometry. A 2011 study led by Ebben put people on a force plate and measured how much of their body weight they were actually pushing in different push-up positions. The answer ranged widely, and it gives you a ready-made ladder of difficulty.

blocks.title: Load in different push-up variations
blocks.note: Peak vertical force at the hands as a share of body mass.
blocks.source: Ebben et al., Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2011

blocks.text: A standard push-up loads your hands with about 64 percent of your body mass. Elevate your hands on a bench and that drops; put your feet on a bunk ledge or a step and it rises. For an 80-kilogram person, the gap between the easiest and hardest version on that chart is the difference between pressing roughly 33 kilograms and nearly 60. That's a wide spread of training loads, built out of furniture and floor space.

And that's only one lever. Other progressions change difficulty further: narrowing the hands to shift work onto the triceps, raising the hands on blocks or books to increase the range of motion, putting more weight over one arm in an archer push-up, or eventually working toward one-arm variations. Each step is a heavier plate, even though the scale never changes.
It works beyond beginners

A reasonable objection is that push-ups only work for people who are new to training. A 2018 study by Kotarsky and colleagues tested that with 23 moderately trained men. Half did a bench press program; half followed a **progressive calisthenic** program, moving to harder push-up variations to keep the difficulty in their target rep range. After four weeks, three sessions a week, both groups significantly increased their bench press max. Neither group showed significant changes in muscle thickness over that short window, which is typical for a four-week study.

A 2015 study by Calatayud and colleagues went further. They recruited 30 university students with advanced lifting experience and first measured muscle activity during a six-rep-max bench press and during push-ups made harder with elastic bands. Once the bands were set so muscle activity matched, they trained one group with the bench and one with banded push-ups for five weeks. Strength gains were similar in both, and both clearly beat a control group.

That design is the key to reading this whole body of research. When the push-up was made as demanding as the bench press, it produced the same result. The tool was irrelevant; the level of effort it created was everything. The flip side is equally true. A push-up that is far easier than your strength level will not keep you progressing, no matter how many you do.

Elastic bands deserve special mention for small spaces. They weigh almost nothing, fit in a pocket and can be anchored in a doorway or around a fixed object. A 2019 meta-analysis by Lopes and colleagues pooled eight studies comparing elastic resistance with weight machines and dumbbells. They found no meaningful difference in strength gains for either the upper or lower body. A couple of bands of different strengths solve most of the problems body weight alone can't.

items.label: Elastic bands vs machines and free weights
In upper- or lower-body strength gains

blocks.source: Lopes et al., SAGE Open Medicine, 2019

blocks.text: The weak spots: legs and pulling

Bodyweight training has two classic gaps, and both are fixable. The first is legs. Your legs carry your body all day, so a regular bodyweight squat quickly becomes too easy to build much muscle. The fix is to put more of your weight on one leg at a time. Split squats, step-ups, rear-foot-elevated split squats with the back foot on a bunk or bench, and eventually single-leg squats to a box all shift far more of the load onto one leg than a regular squat does.

Tempo helps too. Taking three or four seconds to lower into each rep and pausing at the bottom removes momentum and keeps the muscle under tension longer. A loaded backpack, a sea bag or a couple of water jugs held at your sides turns any leg movement into a weighted one. For the back of the legs, single-leg hip bridges and slow, controlled hamstring work fill in what squats miss.

The second gap is pulling. Push-ups, dips and squats only need a floor. Rows and pull-ups need something to pull on, and without them your training drifts out of balance, heavy on the chest and front of the shoulders and light on the upper back. A pull-up bar is ideal if you can rig one somewhere safe. Otherwise, a band anchored at chest height gives you rows and face pulls, and a sturdy, fixed bar or table edge at waist height lets you do inverted rows. Always test anything you hang from before trusting your full weight to it.

blocks.title: A push-up ladder from easiest to hardest
items: Hands elevated on a high surface, like a counter or top bunk
Hands on a lower step or bench
Standard push-up on the floor
Feet elevated on a step or low bench
Feet elevated with a slow 3-second lowering and a pause at the bottom
Archer push-ups, shifting most of the work to one arm
Banded or backpack-loaded push-ups for more resistance

blocks.text: The progression toolkit

The rule from the load research tells you when to move up the ladder: once a variation lets you do more than about 20 to 30 reps with good form, it is time for a harder one. Most people get stuck because they never move up. They keep doing the same push-ups and squats for months, getting better at doing many of them while the stimulus for muscle and strength slowly fades.

items: **Leverage:** change body angle or lever length, like feet elevated or arms farther from the body.
**One side:** shift weight to one limb, from split squats to single-leg squats, or from push-ups to archer push-ups.
**Range of motion:** go deeper, with hands on books for push-ups or a step under the front foot for split squats.
**Tempo and pauses:** lower slowly and hold the hardest position for a second or two.
**External load:** a band, a backpack, water jugs or a training partner's resistance.
**Density:** do the same work with less rest, useful when nothing else is available.

blocks.text: Use one change at a time and drop your reps back into the 8 to 15 range when you switch to a harder variation. Then build reps up again. It's the same logic as adding weight to a bar, just with a few more options.

Write down the variation and the reps, not just the reps. “Feet on bunk ledge, 3 sets of 11, 10, 9” tells you exactly what to beat next time. Without that, it's easy to drift back to the comfortable version on a tired day and not notice for weeks.

blocks.title: Gym equipment and small-space substitutes

left.head: In a gym
items: Bench press
Barbell squat
Lat pulldown or cable row
Romanian deadlift
Leg extension

right.head: In a small space
items: Feet-elevated or banded push-ups
Rear-foot-elevated split squat with a pack
Band rows or inverted rows under a fixed bar
Single-leg hip bridge or single-leg reach
Slow split squats with a long pause at the bottom

blocks.text: Put together, a complete session can fit in the floor space of a bunk and about 25 minutes: one push, one pull, one single-leg movement, one hip or hamstring movement and something for the core. Two to four hard sets of each, two or three times a week, covers every major muscle group. Pair a push with a pull and alternate between them to save time, since one group rests while the other works.
Think of body weight as a game with no difficulty slider in the menu. The slider still exists; you build it out of angles, single limbs, tempo and a couple of bands.
What body weight can't do, and why that's fine

Honesty matters here. If your goal is a heavy barbell squat or deadlift, you'll eventually need to train those lifts, because strength is specific to the movement and load you practice. Very strong legs and a powerful posterior chain are also hard to build without external weight once you're advanced. And measuring progress is fuzzier when difficulty comes from an angle instead of a number on a plate.

But most people are nowhere near those limits. For building a solid base of muscle and strength, staying capable through a long period with no gym, or maintaining what you built ashore, body weight plus a couple of bands covers most of the ground. A few square meters of floor, a fixed bar if you can find one and a willingness to make each set genuinely hard: that is a complete training setup.

Maintenance is even easier than building. A 2021 review by Spiering and colleagues found that in younger people, strength and muscle size could be held for months with as little as one strength session a week and one set per exercise, as long as each set stayed hard. If you go months without a real gym, a short weekly bodyweight and band session with genuine effort can keep most of what you built until you're back near a barbell.

If you have an injury or joint pain, check with a doctor or your corpsman before loading it, and favor variations you can control without pain. Otherwise, the main barrier isn't equipment. It's the habit of choosing the variation that's hard enough to count.

The deeper lesson is that the gym was never the stimulus. It's a convenience: a room full of preset difficulty levels. Your muscles respond to tension and effort, wherever those come from. Learn to create them with nothing but a floor, and you carry a full gym with you everywhere you go.

takeaways: Push-ups at a matched load built strength and muscle comparably to bench press in a head-to-head trial.
Bodyweight exercises work when they're hard enough that you near failure in about 30 reps or fewer.
Change leverage, go single-limb, slow the tempo or add bands and backpacks to keep progressing.
Bands match conventional weights for strength gains in pooled studies and fit anywhere.
Don't neglect pulling and single-leg work; they are the usual gaps in bodyweight programs.

title: The Long Road to One Arm
dek: The one-arm push-up looks like a feat of raw strength. It's really a puzzle about levers, and solving it teaches the rule behind every bodyweight skill.

blocks.text: Watch someone do a clean one-arm push-up and it looks like a party trick for the unusually strong. Feet spread wide, one hand behind the back, the body lowers in a slow, slightly twisted line and comes back up. It seems to require some special strength most people simply don't have.

Now do the physics. In a 2011 lab study, William Ebben and colleagues had people perform push-ups on a force plate. In a standard push-up, the hands supported a peak of about 64 percent of body weight. Split across two arms, that's roughly a third of your body weight per arm. Take one hand away and the remaining arm has to handle close to all of that load by itself, roughly double, while also stopping your body from rolling toward the empty side.

So the one-arm push-up isn't magic. It's a push-up with about twice the load per arm and a twisting problem added on top. Seen that way, it becomes something you can engineer your way toward, one adjustable variable at a time. And the method for getting there works for nearly every bodyweight skill.
Your body weight is a dial, not a number

With a barbell, progress is simple: add a plate. With body weight, your mass doesn't change, but how much of it your muscles have to handle does. That depends on leverage, meaning where your support points are relative to your center of mass, and on how many limbs share the work.

Ebben's measurements show how much range there is in the push-up alone. With hands on a box about two feet high, the hands carried about 41 percent of body weight. On the knees, about 49 percent. With feet on that same two-foot box, the load climbed to about 74 percent. Between the easiest and the hardest version tested, the load nearly doubled, without adding a single pound of equipment.

blocks.title: Load on the hands in push-up variations
blocks.note: Peak vertical force at the hands, measured on a force plate.
blocks.source: Ebben et al., Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2011

blocks.text: Notice the shape of that ladder. Each rung changes the angle of your body relative to the floor, which changes how much of your weight rests on your hands versus your feet. The higher your hands, the lighter the push. The higher your feet, the heavier. This is the master key for the whole progression: any time a variation is too hard, raise your hands. Any time it's too easy, raise your feet or take away a support point.

Load also changes *within* a single rep. A 2011 study by Suprak and colleagues held strength-trained men in the top and bottom positions of standard and knee push-ups on a force plate. In both versions, the hands supported more weight at the bottom than at the top. That matches what everyone feels: the bottom is where push-ups get hard. It also hands you a free tool. Pausing at the bottom, or lowering slowly through it, makes any rung tougher without changing the variation, and partial reps that stop short of the bottom quietly make it easier.
Does it build real strength?

A fair question is whether push-ups, however clever, can do what a bench press does. The evidence says they can, if they're hard enough. In a 2015 study by Calatayud and colleagues, 30 experienced lifters were split into three groups for five weeks. One did a bench press at a load they could lift for six reps. Another did push-ups with elastic bands across their back, tuned so they too could only do six reps. A third group didn't train. The bench press and band push-up groups improved their strength by similar amounts, and the control group didn't change.

items.label: Training period, bench press vs band-loaded push-ups
In 1-rep and 6-rep max strength when difficulty was matched

blocks.source: Calatayud et al., Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2015

blocks.text: The key phrase is *when difficulty was matched*. A broad 2017 meta-analysis by Brad Schoenfeld and colleagues found that muscle growth was similar across light and heavy loads when sets were taken close to failure, but maximal strength improved more with heavy loads. Translated to calisthenics: fifty easy push-ups can build muscle if you push the sets hard, but they won't teach you to produce high force. To get stronger in the sense the one-arm push-up demands, you need variations hard enough that you can only do a handful of good reps.

A 2018 study by Kotarsky and colleagues tested exactly this kind of ladder. Moderately trained men either trained the bench press or followed a push-up program that kept swapping in harder variations as they improved, three days a week for four weeks. Both groups significantly increased their bench press max, even though the push-up group never touched a bench, and the push-up group improved far more in push-up performance. It was a short study with small groups, but it is direct evidence that a progression ladder, not just push-ups in general, builds pressing strength.

The rule of calisthenics progression is to make the movement harder, not to do more of the easy version. Once you can do 15 to 20 clean reps of something, its strength value is mostly used up. Move to the next rung.
The four dials

Every bodyweight progression, from push-ups to squats to pull-ups, uses some combination of four dials. Knowing them means you can build your own ladder for any movement, which matters when you train in a tight space with whatever is available.

items: **Leverage:** change your body angle or lengthen the lever. Feet elevated, hands closer to your hips, arms reaching farther overhead.
**Base of support:** narrow it. Feet together instead of apart makes every push-up harder to stabilize and closer to the one-arm position.
**Distribution:** shift weight toward one limb. Archer push-ups, where one arm bends while the other slides out straight, move most of the load to one side while the straight arm helps.
**Range and tempo:** go deeper, slow the lowering to three to five seconds, or pause at the bottom where the muscles are weakest.

blocks.text: The one-arm push-up uses all four. Your one working arm carries most of the load, your base is reduced to two feet and one hand, your body must resist rotation, and the bottom position demands strength at a long muscle length. The progression is simply a matter of turning those dials one at a time.
The ladder

A sensible rule for moving up is *double progression*. Pick a rep range for each rung, say 5 to 10 for hard variations. Work in that range until you can do every set at the top of it with clean form. Then move to the next rung, where you'll probably drop back to the bottom of the range. Clean form here means a straight line from head to heels, elbows at roughly 45 degrees from your body rather than flared straight out, chest close to the floor at the bottom, and no hips sagging.

blocks.title: From push-up to one-arm push-up
items: Standard push-ups: build to 3 sets of 15 to 20 with full range before moving on.
Feet-together, slow push-ups: 3-second lowering and a 1-second pause at the bottom, 3 sets of 8 to 12.
Archer push-ups: one arm does most of the work while the other slides out straight; 3 sets of 5 to 8 per side.
Incline one-arm push-ups: one hand on a high, stable surface like a counter or bunk rail, feet wide; lower the surface over weeks.
One-arm negatives on the floor: lower yourself on one arm as slowly as you can, then reset with both hands; 3 to 5 reps per side.
Full one-arm push-up with a wide stance, then gradually narrow your feet as you get stronger.

blocks.text: The incline one-arm push-up is the most underrated rung. It lets you practice the exact movement, including the rotation control, at a load you can actually handle. Start with your hand on something about waist height, and each week or two drop to a slightly lower surface: a desk, a chair, a step, a stack of books. It's the same principle Ebben measured, applied to one arm.

Expect this to take months, not weeks. Early progress comes fast, partly because much of the strength gained in the first weeks of any new movement is neural. A classic 1988 review by Digby Sale described how early strength gains come largely from the nervous system learning to recruit and coordinate muscles more effectively, before the muscles themselves grow much. That's encouraging, because it means skill practice counts. It also means the later rungs, which require actual muscle and tendon adaptation, will feel slower. That's normal.

Sale's review also pointed to the *specificity* of training: strength gains tend to be largest in the exact movement you practice. That's why the progression keeps bringing you back to versions of the real thing. Generic chest and triceps work helps, but the nervous system learns the one-arm push-up by doing things that look like a one-arm push-up.
Practice like a skill, protect your joints

Because so much of the one-arm push-up is coordination, it rewards frequent, high-quality practice more than occasional exhausting sessions. A few crisp sets of your current rung, several times a week, with plenty of rest between sets, tends to beat one brutal session that ends in sloppy reps. Stop each set while form is still good, a rep or two before failure, and let the next session build on clean practice.

A workable week looks like this. Three days a week, do three to four sets of your current hardest rung, resting two or three minutes between sets. Follow that with two sets of the rung below it for more volume at a slightly lower difficulty. On one or two other days, do a few easy, crisp sets of the incline one-arm version purely as practice, nowhere near failure. The whole thing fits in a few square feet and fifteen to twenty minutes, and it can be squeezed between watches.

Joints and tendons tend to adapt more slowly than muscle, which is why people get hurt when they progress on enthusiasm instead of evidence. If your wrists complain, do push-ups on your fists or on a pair of handles to keep the wrist straight. If your elbow or shoulder starts to ache, back off a rung for a week or two rather than pushing through. Pain that sharpens during reps or lingers is worth having a corpsman look at.

The twisting component is also worth training directly. Shoulder taps from a push-up position, side planks and one-arm planks build the anti-rotation strength that keeps your hips square as you lower. Many people who can almost do a one-arm push-up are limited not by their pressing muscles but by their body rolling toward the free side.
The same logic, everywhere

Once you see the four dials, every bodyweight skill becomes a ladder you can build yourself. The squat path runs from a regular bodyweight squat to a split squat, then a rear-foot-elevated split squat, then a squat to a box on one leg, then a full pistol squat. The pulling path, if you have a fixed bar or a sturdy table edge, runs from inverted rows with bent knees to rows with straight legs and feet raised, to negative pull-ups, to full pull-ups, and eventually to archer pull-ups.

blocks.title: Building ladders for other movements

left.head: Squat ladder
items: Bodyweight squat
Split squat
Rear-foot-elevated split squat
Single-leg box squat
Pistol squat

right.head: Pull ladder
items: Bent-knee inverted row
Straight-leg inverted row
Feet-elevated row
Slow negative pull-up
Full pull-up, then archer pull-up

blocks.text: There's a reason this approach feels so much like a well-designed game. Good games keep you at the edge of your ability by raising difficulty just as you master the current level, and they show you the next challenge before you get there. A calisthenics ladder works the same way. Each rung is hard enough to demand effort and close enough to feel reachable. You always know your next unlock.

The deeper lesson is about what strength actually is. It isn't a fixed quantity you either have or don't. It's the ability to produce force in a particular position, and positions can be scaled. The person doing a one-arm push-up didn't start with special muscles. They started with a push-up and kept turning the dials. The road is long, but every step of it is visible from where you're standing.

takeaways: A standard push-up loads the hands with about 64% of body weight; a one-arm push-up roughly doubles the load per arm and adds rotation.
Push-ups made hard enough produced strength gains similar to bench press in a 5-week trial.
Progress by making the movement harder, not by doing more easy reps: leverage, base, distribution, range.
Use double progression: hit the top of the rep range on every set, then move up a rung.
Raise your hands to make a push-up easier; raise your feet or remove a support point to make it harder.

title: Does Cardio Really Kill Your Gains?
dek: A 1980 study taught a generation of lifters to fear running. Forty years of follow-up research says the interference is real, but it is smaller, narrower and easier to dodge than gym lore claims.

blocks.text: In 1980, the exercise physiologist Robert Hickson published a study that would echo through weight rooms for decades. He split volunteers into three groups for ten weeks. One group lifted, five days a week. One group did hard endurance work for 40 minutes, six days a week. The third group did **both** programs in full, every week, on top of each other.

For seven weeks the combined group gained leg strength at the same rate as the lifters. Then something odd happened. While the pure strength group kept climbing, the combined group's strength leveled off, and in weeks nine and ten it actually started to fall. Their aerobic fitness, meanwhile, was untouched by the extra lifting: VO2max rose by roughly 20 to 25 percent in both the endurance group and the combined group. Endurance training seemed to get in the way of strength, but not the other way around.

Hickson called it interference, and the idea spread into a slogan you have probably heard: cardio kills gains. It is one of those gym beliefs with a real study at its root. The question is what the study actually showed, and what happened when other researchers spent the next forty years trying to pin it down.
Read the fine print on the famous study

Look again at Hickson's combined group. They did around 30 to 40 minutes of lifting five days a week and 40 minutes of hard endurance work six days a week, which works out to about eleven sessions a week with almost no rest. That is not a normal person's program. It is closer to a stress test designed to see whether the two kinds of training could coexist at all when pushed to the limit.

And even under that load, the interference didn't show up for nearly two months. It appeared late, in the lower body, and in a group doing an enormous amount of total work. That should make you ask a different question than the gym slogan does. Not "does cardio hurt strength?" but "how much cardio, of what kind, and when?"
What forty years of trials found

In 2012, Jacob Wilson and colleagues pooled 21 studies that compared strength training alone to strength plus endurance training. Concurrent training still built a lot of strength and muscle, much more than endurance training alone, but it lagged a bit behind pure strength training on every measure. The biggest gap was in **power**, the ability to produce force quickly, as in jumping or sprinting. The details mattered, too. Running, but not cycling, was linked to meaningful losses in muscle growth and strength, and longer and more frequent endurance sessions were linked to bigger losses.

blocks.title: Gains in power by type of training (effect size)
blocks.note: Bigger number means a larger average improvement. Pooled from 21 studies.
blocks.source: Wilson et al., Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2012

blocks.text: A quick word on those numbers. An **effect size** expresses a change in units of how much people normally vary, so studies that measured different things in different ways can be pooled. As a rough guide, 0.2 is considered small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large. By that yardstick, strength training alone produced a large improvement in power, combined training a medium one, and endurance training alone almost none. Combined training still worked. It just worked less well for that one quality.

Ten years later, a larger and more careful review arrived. Moritz Schumann, Tommy Lundberg and colleagues gathered 43 studies in which people did an identical strength program either with or without added aerobic training for at least four weeks. Their 2022 analysis found essentially no difference in muscle growth and no meaningful difference in maximal strength. The one place interference clearly showed up was **explosive strength**, and that effect was stronger when both kinds of training happened in the same session than when they were separated by at least three hours.

items.label: Studies pooled in the 2022 meta-analysis
Difference in muscle growth with added cardio (standardized; zero = no effect)
Difference in explosive strength (a small but real penalty)

blocks.source: Schumann et al., Sports Medicine, 2022

blocks.text: Interestingly, that newer review found no clear difference between running and cycling, and no clear effect of training frequency, which conflicts with the 2012 analysis. Meta-analyses are only as good as the studies they pool, and most of these studies were short and small. The fair summary is that the evidence keeps shrinking the interference effect, but it hasn't erased it, especially for anyone whose sport depends on speed and power.

Why would explosive strength be the weak spot? Power depends on how fast your nervous system can recruit muscle and how quickly the muscle and tendon can transmit force, not only on how big or strong the muscle is. Long, steady endurance work trains the opposite quality: the ability to produce modest force over and over without tiring. Doing a lot of one seems to blunt the body's push toward the other. For a sprinter, a jumper or a fighter, that matters. For someone whose goals are a better run time, more push-ups and a healthier heart, it barely registers.

blocks.title: Gym lore versus the current evidence

left.head: What people say
items: Any cardio will eat your muscle
Running makes you weak
Lifters should avoid aerobic work
Interference shows up right away

right.head: What studies show
items: Muscle growth is mostly unaffected in pooled trials
Maximal strength is largely preserved
Explosive power takes the clearest hit
Effects grow with very high volume and same-session pairing

blocks.text: Why the two might clash

For years the favorite explanation came from cell biology. Endurance exercise activates an energy-sensing enzyme called AMPK, which pushes muscle cells toward building more mitochondria and burning fuel efficiently. Lifting activates a growth pathway called mTOR, which pushes cells toward building more protein. In lab dishes, AMPK can switch off mTOR. The story wrote itself: cardio flips a molecular switch that blocks growth.

It turned out to be too tidy. In a 2017 review, Vernon Coffey and John Hawley pointed out that in untrained or casually active people, both kinds of exercise trigger broadly similar signals at first, and that the mechanism behind interference is still unknown. They argued it likely comes from many processes working together rather than one switch.

The more boring explanations are probably doing a lot of the work. **Fatigue** is one: tired legs lift less weight, so the strength session that follows a hard run is a weaker stimulus. **Recovery budget** is another. Your body can only repair so much at once, and eleven sessions a week will overrun it. **Impact** is a third. Running involves thousands of landings that stress muscle in a way cycling doesn't, which may explain why some studies flagged running as worse. And there is **energy**: hours of cardio burn calories, and if you don't eat enough to cover them, there is less material left for building muscle.

That points to a useful self-check. If you are combining both and your lifts keep climbing, there is nothing to fix, whatever the slogans say. If your lifts stall or slide while your cardio is going up, look first at the boring causes before blaming biology. Are you doing your hardest runs the day before heavy legs? Are you sleeping less because of the watch bill? Are you eating less than usual because the extra work killed your appetite or the mess schedule doesn't line up? Those are fixable problems, and they usually explain more than any molecular switch.
The surprise: strength helps endurance

Hickson's original finding was that endurance training seemed to hurt strength but not the reverse. Eight years later he tested the reverse directly. His team took eight runners and cyclists who were already well trained and added heavy leg strength training three days a week for ten weeks, while keeping their endurance training the same.

Their leg strength rose about 30 percent, with no measurable change in thigh size. Their VO2max didn't change either. But their performance in short, hard efforts of four to eight minutes improved by 11 percent on the bike and 13 percent on the treadmill, and their time to exhaustion on the bike at a hard steady pace went from 71 minutes to 85. A 2014 review by Bent Ronnestad and Inigo Mujika reached a similar conclusion across many studies: adding heavy or explosive strength work tends to improve running economy and endurance performance in trained runners and cyclists.

There is even a study where cardio seemed to *help* growth. In 2013, Lundberg's team had ten men train both legs on the knee-extension machine for five weeks, but one leg also did about 45 minutes of one-legged cycling six hours before lifting. The leg that did both grew 14 percent in thigh muscle volume; the lifting-only leg grew 8 percent. Strength and power gains were similar in both legs. One small study proves nothing on its own, but it is hard to square with the idea that any cardio automatically kills gains.
How to combine them without the penalty

If you want to be strong and fit at the same time, which is exactly what the Navy PRT asks of you, the research points to a few practical rules. None of them require you to give up either kind of training.

blocks.title: Combining lifting and cardio
items: Decide which matters more right now, strength or endurance, and give it the fresh slot.
If strength is the priority and both happen in one session, lift first, then do cardio.
Better still, separate them by at least three hours, or put them on different days.
Keep most cardio easy to moderate; save the hardest intervals for days without heavy legs.
If running beats up your legs, use the bike or rower for some of your aerobic volume.
Eat enough to cover the extra work, especially protein and total calories.

blocks.text: The order rule has some support of its own. A 2018 meta-analysis by Lee Eddens and colleagues looked at ten studies that compared doing strength work first versus endurance first within the same session. Lifting first produced about 7 percent more gain in lower-body dynamic strength. It made no difference to muscle growth, aerobic fitness or body fat. So order is worth getting right if leg strength is your goal, and otherwise you can do whatever fits your schedule.

Put together, a sensible week for someone who wants both might look like this in shape, if not in exact numbers. Three short lifting sessions that hit the whole body. Two or three aerobic sessions, most of them at a pace where you could still talk, one of them harder. Heavy leg work and hard intervals kept apart, either on different days or at different ends of the day around your watch. If a session has to combine both, the quality you care about most goes first, while you are fresh.

Militaries have quietly been running this experiment for a long time. Soldiers and sailors have always needed to carry, lift, climb and run, often on the same day, and fitness tests like the PRT mix a strength-endurance event, a core event and a cardio event for that reason. Nobody expects a sailor to deadlift like a powerlifter or run like a marathoner. The goal is to be good at both and great at neither, which happens to be the zone where the interference effect is weakest.

On a boat with one treadmill, a few bikes and a tight schedule, the perfect split is rarely possible. That is fine. The penalty for imperfect timing is small. The penalty for skipping either kind of training altogether is much larger. Consistency over months beats a flawless schedule you can only follow for two weeks.

Here is the reframe. The interference effect is real, but it is mostly a problem for people at the edges: elite athletes chasing the last few percent of power, or anyone stacking extreme volumes of both kinds of training. For everyone else, the danger runs the other way. A lifter who avoids cardio out of fear gives up heart health, work capacity and recovery between sets. A runner who avoids lifting gives up injury resilience and, as Hickson found, some speed. The question isn't which one to choose. It's how to fit both into your week so they help each other more than they get in each other's way.

takeaways: The study that started the fear used about eleven hard sessions a week, and interference showed up only after seven weeks.
Large reviews find added cardio barely affects muscle growth or maximal strength; explosive power takes the clearest hit.
If strength matters most, lift first or separate cardio and lifting by at least three hours.
Heavy strength training tends to improve endurance performance, so runners and cyclists should lift too.
For most people the real risk is skipping one kind of training, not doing both.

title: Your Core Is Not Your Six-Pack
dek: In 2020 the Navy dropped the curl-up from its fitness test. The reasons reveal what the core actually does, and why most ab workouts train the wrong job.

blocks.text: For decades, sailors proved their core strength the same way: lie on your back, knees bent, and curl up as many times as you can in two minutes. Then, in November 2020, the Navy announced it was retiring the curl-up from the Physical Readiness Test and replacing it with a forearm plank. The official explanation was blunt. Navy researchers had concluded that the curl-up was not a true test of abdominal strength, did not prepare sailors for shipboard work, and had been linked to an increased risk of creating or aggravating lower back injuries.

The Navy said the plank, by contrast, reflects a movement pattern used in 85 percent of regular shipboard tasks, such as pushing, pulling, lifting and carrying. That's the Navy's own figure, not an independent study, but the logic behind it is the interesting part. It reflects a shift in how scientists think about the core, from a set of muscles that *bend* you to a system that *stops* you from bending when force passes through your body.
Understanding that shift changes what you should train, what you can expect from it, and what you can stop worrying about.
What the core actually is

Picture your torso as a pressurized can. The top of the can is the diaphragm, the dome-shaped muscle under your lungs. The bottom is the pelvic floor. The walls are a wrap of muscles: the six-pack muscle, the rectus abdominis, down the front; the obliques and the deep transverse abdominis wrapping around the sides like a belt; and the spinal erectors and smaller muscles like the multifidus along the back. Around the base sit the hip muscles, especially the glutes, which connect the can to your legs.

When you brace before lifting something heavy, all of those muscles tighten together. Pressure rises inside the can and the walls stiffen. That stiffness is the point. Your spine is a stack of small bones that would buckle under modest loads if nothing held it in place. A braced core turns it into something closer to a solid column, so that force from your legs can travel up through your torso into your arms without leaking out as wobble.

That is why reviews like Hibbs and colleagues' 2008 overview distinguish between core *stability*, the ability to control the position of the trunk, and core *strength*, the ability to produce force with it. In most real tasks, from carrying a heavy box up a ladder to throwing a punch, the core's main job is stability. It transfers force rather than generating movement. The legs and arms do the moving. The core makes sure their effort arrives where it is supposed to.

This also explains a common mistake: sucking the stomach in hard before a lift. McGill and other spine researchers have argued that pulling the belly button toward the spine narrows the can and makes it less stiff, not more. A better brace feels like getting ready to take a punch. Take a breath, then tighten everything around your midsection at once, front, sides and back, as if you were pushing outward against a belt. You should still be able to breathe and talk in short phrases while holding it. That 360-degree tension is the skill every core exercise below is really practicing.
Think of the core less like an engine and more like a drive shaft. Its job is to transmit power from the hips to the hands without twisting, sagging or bending under the load.
The case against the curl-up

The scientific skepticism about crunches and sit-ups traces largely to Stuart McGill, a spine biomechanist at the University of Waterloo. One of the most cited experiments from his lab, published in 2001 with Jack Callaghan, took spinal segments from pigs, a common stand-in for human spines in the lab, and mounted them in a machine that bent them forward and back once per second under a modest compressive load. Some specimens went through as many as 86,400 bending cycles, a full day of continuous flexing.

The discs herniated. The surprising part was what caused it: not heavy compression, but repeated bending with relatively light loads. Heavier compression made the injuries more frequent and severe, but the repetition was the key ingredient. McGill's broader argument was that the spine has a limited budget of bending cycles under load, and that spending it on hundreds of crunches is a poor trade.

items.label: Maximum flex-extend cycles applied to each spinal segment, one per second

blocks.source: Callaghan & McGill, Clinical Biomechanics, 2001

blocks.text: It's worth being fair about the limits of that evidence. These were isolated pig spines in a machine, without blood flow, without the ability to repair, and without the muscles that protect a living spine. Living tissue adapts to load over time, and plenty of researchers argue that controlled spinal flexion, done in sensible amounts, is not inherently dangerous. The debate is real. But there is no debate that the curl-up was a weak predictor of anything useful, and that is enough to justify a better test.
What ab training won't do

The biggest misconception about core training is that it burns belly fat. A 2011 study by Vispute and colleagues tested this directly. Twenty-four sedentary adults were randomly split into two groups. One did seven different abdominal exercises, two sets of ten reps each, five days a week for six weeks. The other did nothing. Both groups kept their diets stable.

At the end, the ab group could do significantly more curl-ups than the control group. But there was no meaningful difference in body weight, body fat percentage, belly fat measured by scan, waist circumference or skinfold thickness. Six weeks of targeted ab work made the muscles more capable and did nothing measurable to the fat sitting on top of them.

blocks.title: Curl-ups completed after six weeks
blocks.note: Endurance improved; abdominal fat measures did not change.
blocks.source: Vispute et al., Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2011

blocks.text: Visible abs are mostly a matter of overall body fat, which comes down to energy balance over time, not of how many crunches you do. That's freeing rather than discouraging. It means you can train your core for what it actually does and let your overall eating and activity handle what it looks like.
The core and your back

If the core isn't a fat burner, is it at least a back-pain shield? The answer is more nuanced than the fitness industry suggests. One of the classic studies here is from 1984, when Fin Biering-Sørensen examined about 900 adults in a suburb of Copenhagen and followed them for a year. Among men, good endurance in the back muscles, measured by how long they could hold their upper body horizontal off the edge of a table, predicted a lower chance of a first episode of low back trouble.

So trunk endurance seems to matter. But when researchers tested whether *specific* core stability programs beat general exercise for people who already have chronic back pain, the result was humbling. A 2012 meta-analysis by Wang and colleagues found that core stability training reduced pain and disability slightly more than general exercise in the short term. At six and twelve months, there was no significant difference.

The broader picture comes from a 2021 Cochrane review of 249 trials of exercise for chronic low back pain. Exercise, as a category, helped with pain compared with no treatment or usual care, with moderate certainty. The lesson from this body of research is that the core is not a magic spot. It is one part of a body that generally does better when it is regularly and progressively loaded.
If you do have back pain that is severe, spreads down a leg, comes with numbness or weakness, or doesn't improve, get it checked by a corpsman or doctor rather than trying to train through it.
What about performance?

Athletes are often told that a stronger core will make them faster, more powerful and more agile. A 2012 systematic review by Reed and colleagues examined 24 studies that targeted the core and measured athletic performance. Their conclusion was that targeted core stability training provides marginal benefits. Many studies that saw improvements had combined core work with broader strength programs, making it hard to credit the core work specifically. Some programs did not even measurably improve core strength.

This doesn't mean the core is unimportant. It means the core is already heavily trained by big, demanding movements. A heavy squat, a loaded carry, a push-up or a pull-up all require your trunk to stay rigid under load. If you do those regularly, a lot of your core training is already happening. Dedicated core work is best seen as a supplement: a way to cover the specific jobs those lifts might miss.
Training the jobs, in a small space

If the core's job is mostly to resist motion, then the smartest way to train it is around those jobs. There are three main ones. **Anti-extension** means resisting your lower back arching, as in a plank or a push-up. **Anti-rotation** means resisting twisting, as when you push or pull with one arm. **Anti-lateral flexion** means resisting side bending, as when you carry something heavy in one hand. Add **hip extension**, driving the hips forward with the glutes, and you have the core covered.

blocks.title: Core myths and what the evidence says

left.head: Myth
items: The core means the six-pack
Ab exercises burn belly fat
More crunches means a stronger core
Core work is the key to athletic power

right.head: Evidence
items: The core is a full ring of trunk and hip muscles
Six weeks of ab work didn't change abdominal fat
The core's main job is resisting movement
Targeted core work gives marginal performance gains

blocks.text: Every one of those jobs can be trained in a space the size of a bunk with no equipment, or with something as simple as a water jug, a backpack or a resistance band. What matters is progression: once a level is easy, make it harder by lengthening the lever, reducing your points of contact, or adding load.

One practical rule: once you can hold a plank cleanly for about a minute, stop chasing longer holds and make the exercise harder instead. A five-minute plank mostly trains patience. A 30-second plank in a tougher position, with more tension, trains the stiffness you actually want. The same goes for every exercise on this list. Quality of position first, then difficulty, and only then duration.

blocks.title: A plank progression that keeps getting harder
items: Forearm plank: build to 3 sets of 45 to 60 seconds with your ribs down and glutes squeezed, not your back sagging.
Long-lever plank: walk your elbows a few inches farther forward of your shoulders, which makes the same hold much harder.
Plank shoulder taps or reaches: lift one hand at a time without letting your hips twist, adding anti-rotation.
Side plank: build to 30 to 45 seconds per side, then raise the top leg to make it harder.
Body saw: in a forearm plank, slowly rock your body forward and back a few inches, ideally on a slick surface.
Ab rollout: with a wheel, a towel on a smooth floor or your hands walking out, extend as far as you can control and return.

blocks.text: Round out the week with a few simple additions. A **suitcase carry** with a heavy jug or loaded bag in one hand trains anti-lateral flexion. A **band press-out**, holding a band anchored to one side straight out in front of your chest, trains anti-rotation. A **bird dog**, reaching opposite arm and leg from all fours while keeping the back still, and **single-leg glute bridges** cover the back side of the can. McGill's own short routine for back health is built around a modified curl-up with one knee bent and the lower back supported, the side plank and the bird dog, done as short holds and repeated in descending sets.
What the plank really tests

There's a quiet irony in the Navy's switch. A plank isn't a perfect test either. Holding one for several minutes says more about tolerance for discomfort than about the ability to stay rigid while heavy force moves through the trunk. But it points in the right direction, toward the core as a stabilizer rather than a mover, and that is the direction that matters for real tasks: hauling stores, climbing ladders, moving in tight spaces with something heavy in your hands.

The deeper reframe is that the most important core work you do may not look like core work at all. Every time you carry something heavy with a braced, steady trunk, or press yourself off the deck with a body that stays straight as a plank, you are training the system exactly as it is meant to be used. The six-pack is just the part of the core that happens to be visible. The real thing is the whole can, and its job is to hold.

takeaways: The core is a full ring of trunk and hip muscles whose main job is resisting motion, not creating it.
Six weeks of daily ab exercises improved endurance but didn't change belly fat in a controlled trial.
Specific core programs beat general exercise for back pain only in the short term; exercise in general helps.
Train anti-extension, anti-rotation, anti-side-bending and hip extension, progressing by lengthening levers or adding load.
Heavy compound movements and loaded carries already train the core hard.
