title: Automate the Start, Not the Workout
dek: Most of a workout can't run on autopilot, and it doesn't need to. Research on "instigation habits" says the part worth automating is the moment you begin, and that changes what "start small" should really mean.

blocks.text: Think about the last workout you skipped. It probably wasn't the sets that beat you. Once you're under the bar, you usually finish. What beat you was the moment before: deciding to change, finding your shoes, walking to wherever you train. The hardest rep of most workouts is the first step toward the door.

Habit researchers have turned that intuition into a distinction that changes how you should build any complex habit. A workout isn't one behavior. It's a chain, and different links in the chain can be more or less automatic. In 2016, L. Alison Phillips and Benjamin Gardner asked 123 healthy adults to rate two things separately: how automatically they *started* exercising, and how automatically they *carried out* the exercise once they'd begun. Then they had participants keep a daily exercise diary for a month.

Only one of the two predicted how often people actually exercised. It was the automatic start. Once that was accounted for, how habitual the workout itself felt added nothing. And when people's exercise frequency rose or fell over the month, it moved with changes in the starting habit, not with the habit of doing the workout. The part of exercise that needs to be a habit, it seems, is the first sixty seconds.

The study checked one more thing that's easy to miss. It asked whether doing the same exercises in the same order every session, a fixed pattern, made any difference. It didn't. Changes in how often people trained tracked the starting habit, not how patterned their workouts were. That's good news if you get bored easily. You can vary your training as much as you want. What needs to stay stable is how the session begins.
Two habits hiding in one behavior

Gardner and colleagues call these **instigation habits** and **execution habits**. An instigation habit is a cue automatically triggering the decision to do something: you get off watch and find yourself heading to the gym without debating it. An execution habit is the smooth, automatic performance of the steps once you've started: your warm-up runs itself, your hands know the order of the sets.

For simple behaviors the two blur together. Brushing your teeth starts automatically and runs automatically. For complex behaviors they come apart. A 2026 study by Amanda Rebar and colleagues pinged 105 adults six times a day for a week and asked what they were doing and how habitual it felt. Most everyday behaviors were habitually started (65 percent) and habitually carried out (88 percent). But exercise stood out: it was more often habitually instigated, and *less* often habitually executed, than other kinds of actions.

items.label: Everyday behaviors that were habitually started
Everyday behaviors that were habitually carried out
Behaviors that matched what people intended to do

blocks.source: Rebar, Vincent, Kovac Le Cornu & Gardner, Psychology & Health, 2026

blocks.text: That makes sense once you think about it. A good training session can't be fully automatic. You're choosing weights, judging fatigue, pushing through sets that feel different every time. Studying is the same, and so is building a game or editing a video. A 2025 study by Saunders and More found that people kept using deliberate self-control strategies for complex behaviors even when those behaviors were habitually started. Simple habits run on autopilot. Complex ones still need a pilot.

So the goal isn't to make the whole workout effortless. It can't be. The goal is to make *starting* effortless, so the deliberate effort goes into the training itself instead of being burned on the daily argument about whether to train at all.

It also explains why the start is where so many habits die. At the moment of starting, every competing option is fully available: the rack, the phone, the movie someone's watching, the nap you've earned. Once you're ten minutes into a session, those options have mostly faded. The decision point is the most crowded moment of the whole behavior, so it's the one most worth taking off the table.

blocks.title: Two different habits inside one workout

left.head: Instigation habit
items: Cue triggers the decision to start
"Off watch, so I head to the gym"
Predicted how often people exercised
Can become close to fully automatic

right.head: Execution habit
items: Steps run smoothly once started
Warm-up order, set sequence, form
Didn't add to the prediction
Complex tasks still need active effort

blocks.text: The habit before the habit

If starting is the key link, then the routine that leads into starting deserves attention too. Navin Kaushal, Ryan Rhodes and colleagues split exercise into a preparation phase (packing your bag, changing clothes, getting to the gym) and a performance phase (the workout). In a study of 181 adults recruited from gyms, intention and preparation habit predicted exercise over six weeks. Performance habit didn't. The strongest single ingredient in building those habits was doing them at a consistent time.

They then tested whether you could build that habit on purpose. In a randomized trial, 94 new gym members who weren't yet meeting activity guidelines were split into two groups. One got a workshop on habit formation focused on preparation cues and consistent practice, plus a booster phone call at four weeks. After eight weeks, that group was doing significantly more moderate-to-vigorous exercise, measured both by accelerometer (an effect size of d = 0.39) and by self-report (d = 0.53).

Consistent timing is a problem when your schedule rotates, but timing doesn't have to mean a clock. An event that happens every day, like getting off watch or finishing a meal, gives the same consistency even when the hour moves. What matters is that the cue arrives reliably and the preparation follows it the same way each time.

A larger 2025 trial pushed the idea further. Phillips and colleagues followed 751 new users of an online exercise class platform for a year and tested three intervention pieces in every combination: one aimed at motivation and identity, one at building a preparation habit, and one at building an instigation habit. Only the preparation piece showed a clear effect on how often people took classes. Interestingly, it also strengthened the instigation habit, which suggests the prep routine may be how the automatic start gets built.

Don't try to make the workout a habit. Make getting ready a habit. Laying out your gear, changing clothes at the same point every day, and walking to the same spot are the links that carry everything after them.
The two-minute rule, examined

Popular habit advice has been circling this idea for years. James Clear's two-minute rule says to shrink any new habit to a version that takes two minutes or less: "read before bed" becomes "read one page." BJ Fogg's Tiny Habits method makes new habits absurdly small, like one push-up or flossing one tooth, and attaches them to an existing routine. The logic in both cases is that the tiny version is so easy that you'll do it every time, and repeating it in a consistent context builds the automatic start.

The instigation research gives that logic a scientific backbone. If what drives frequency is the automatic start, then making the start nearly effortless is a sensible way to build it. But direct evidence for the tiny methods themselves is still thin. One randomized trial of Tiny Habits, with 154 adults trying to increase gratitude, found both Tiny Habits groups improved more than an inactive control group. That's encouraging, but it relied on self-reports, included personal coaching, and lost a substantial share of participants by the end. It shows the method can help. It doesn't show it beats other approaches.

A tiny version has one more advantage that's easy to overlook. It's almost impossible to fail at. On a brutal day, after a long watch or a drill-heavy shift, the full workout may be out of reach, but putting your shoes on and doing one set is not. That keeps the cue and the start linked on exactly the days when the link would otherwise break, which are also the days that decide whether a habit survives.
Where tiny stops being enough

There's a trap in starting small, and one of the best-designed trials in this area shows it. The SNAP study randomized 599 young adults, aged 18 to 35, into three groups and followed them for an average of three years. One group got a "small changes" program: cut intake and increase activity by about 100 calories a day each. Another got a "large changes" program: lose about 2.3 to 4.5 kilograms up front to build a buffer against future gain. The third group was a control.

Both programs worked better than nothing. But the large changes group did better on weight. Over three years, average weight change was +0.26 kg in the control group, −0.56 kg with small changes and −2.37 kg with large changes. On the share of people who developed obesity, though, the two programs were about equal, and both roughly halved the rate seen in the control group.

blocks.title: Developed obesity over about 3 years (SNAP trial)
blocks.note: 599 adults aged 18 to 35. Average weight change: +0.26 kg, -0.56 kg and -2.37 kg respectively.
blocks.source: Wing et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 2016

blocks.text: The lesson isn't that small is bad. It's that small is a *starting mechanism*, not a target. A one-page reading habit or a single push-up is a way to install the automatic start. If you stay at one push-up forever, you have a very reliable habit of doing almost nothing. The research on instigation says the start is what keeps you showing up. The research on outcomes says what you do after you show up still decides the results.

So build in a ramp. Keep the start tiny and automatic, and raise the *floor* of what happens after it every couple of weeks once the start feels effortless. One push-up becomes one set, then a short circuit, then a real session. One page becomes ten. The start stays the same. What follows it grows. That way you get the reliability of a tiny habit and the results of a big one, instead of having to pick between them.
Designing your first sixty seconds

Put the findings together and you get a cleaner way to build any complex habit, whether that's training, studying for quals or working on a game project. Separate the start from the work. Make the start tiny, consistent and automatic. Then let the work be as demanding and deliberate as it needs to be, and scale it up on purpose once the start runs on its own.

blocks.title: Build the start, then build the work
items: **Pick a cue that happens every day.** Coming off watch, after the first meal, after evening hygiene. Consistency of timing was the strongest ingredient in the gym studies.
**Define a start action you can do in under a minute.** Shoes on and band out. Laptop open to the project file. Notebook open to the next qual item.
**Make preparation part of the routine.** Lay out your gear or set up your workspace ahead of time, so the start has nothing in its way.
**Make the start non-negotiable and the rest flexible.** On bad days, the start plus five minutes counts. On good days, keep going.
**Scale deliberately after a few weeks.** Once starting feels automatic, raise the floor: more sets, more pages, a longer work block.
**Plan the hard middle.** Complex work still needs active effort. Decide the session's main task before you start so you don't burn it deciding.

blocks.text: The same split applies to habits you want to break. Scrolling has a start, picking up the phone and opening the app, and an execution, the scroll itself. Most people fight the execution by setting time limits on sessions that have already begun, which is fighting the habit at its strongest point. The instigation research suggests aiming at the start instead: change what happens in the first second, by keeping the phone out of reach or the app logged out, so the automatic pickup has nothing to grab.

And it applies to anything you're building. For studying, the start action might be opening the qual card to the next unchecked item and reading the first question. For a game project, it might be opening the project file and playing the current build for one minute. For a video, it might be opening the editor on the last clip you touched. None of those is the real work. All of them make the real work much more likely to happen.

Back to that skipped workout. The fix probably isn't more motivation, a better program or a stricter streak. It's making the walk to the door so routine that the argument never starts. You'll still have to work hard once you're there. That's the part that builds strength, skill or a finished project. But you'll be there far more often, and the research suggests that is most of the battle.

takeaways: Complex habits have two parts: starting and doing. How automatic the start is predicted how often people exercised. How automatic the workout felt added nothing.
Preparation routines like laying out gear and changing at a set time are the link that carries the rest.
Tiny habits and the two-minute rule fit this research, but direct evidence for them is still limited.
Small is a way to start, not a goal. In a 3-year trial, bigger changes produced more weight loss.
Make the start automatic and non-negotiable, then put your deliberate effort into the work itself.

title: People Would Rather Shock Themselves Than Be Bored
dek: Boredom feels like a waste of time. It's actually a signal, and every time you kill it with a phone you lose the message it was trying to deliver.

blocks.text: The room was almost empty. No phone, no book, no pen. Volunteers at the University of Virginia were asked to put their belongings away and simply sit alone with their thoughts for up to 15 minutes. That was the whole task: think about whatever you like, stay in the chair, don't fall asleep.

It sounds easy. It turned out to be hard enough that psychologist Timothy Wilson and his colleagues built a series of experiments around it, published in *Science* in 2014. In the early studies, nearly half of the 409 participants said they didn't enjoy the experience. When the researchers sent people home to do the same thing on their own, nearly a third admitted they had cheated, sneaking a look at a phone or getting up to do something.

Then came the version that made headlines. Before sitting alone, participants got a small, unpleasant electric shock, and many said they'd pay money to avoid feeling it again. Then they were left alone in the room for 15 minutes, with a button that would deliver the same shock if they pressed it. Nobody told them to. Two-thirds of the men and a quarter of the women pressed it anyway.

blocks.title: Gave themselves a shock rather than just sit and think
blocks.note: Participants had already felt the shock, and many had said they would pay to avoid it.
blocks.source: Wilson et al., Science, 2014 (via Nature News)

blocks.text: Think about what that means. Faced with nothing but their own minds, a large share of people chose pain over boredom. Not because pain is fun, but because *anything* felt better than sitting with the empty feeling. That empty feeling is boredom, and in a world built to make sure you never feel it, it's worth understanding what it's actually for.
Why sitting alone with your thoughts is so hard

Wilson's results are often summarized as 'people hate thinking', but that's not quite right. Thinking is something you do constantly. What people struggled with was *undirected* thinking with no task attached: no problem to solve, no conversation, no input. Without a target, the mind tends to drift toward whatever is unresolved, worries, regrets, the argument from last week, and that is not a pleasant place to sit.

The participants who did enjoy the time alone tended to have something to steer toward. According to reports on the study, they often thought about future events, frequently involving people they cared about. That's a clue worth keeping. Being alone with your thoughts goes better when you bring a topic, the same way a long drive goes better with a destination in mind. Thinking for pleasure, it turns out, is partly a skill: you pick the subject instead of letting the loudest worry pick it for you.

It also helps explain why the shock button got pressed. When there's nothing to engage with, even a mildly painful stimulus is at least *something*. It breaks the loop, gives the mind an event to react to. That's the same pull that makes people pick at a scab, crack their knuckles or refresh an app they checked thirty seconds ago. The urge isn't for pleasure. It's for any change at all.
What boredom actually is

Boredom isn't the same as having nothing to do. You can be bored in a packed schedule, bored during a mandatory training, bored while scrolling an endless feed. Psychologists usually define it as an uncomfortable state of *wanting* to be engaged in something satisfying and not being able to get there. It's not emptiness. It's a gap between the engagement you want and the engagement you have.

In 2018, the psychologists Erin Westgate and Timothy Wilson proposed a model that breaks that gap into two parts. They call it the **MAC model**, for meaning and attentional components. According to the model, you get bored when an activity fails on one or both of two counts: your attention doesn't fit the task, or the task doesn't feel meaningful to you.

blocks.title: Two roads to boredom (the MAC model)

left.head: Attention mismatch
items: Task is too easy: under-stimulated, mind drifts
Task is too hard: can't get a grip, attention slides off
Fix: change the difficulty
Example: a lecture way below or way above your level

right.head: Meaning deficit
items: Task doesn't connect to anything you care about
Even if the difficulty is fine
Fix: find or build a reason it matters
Example: paperwork that feels pointless

blocks.text: This explains why boredom shows up in such different situations. Copying numbers into a log is boring because it's too easy. A dense technical manual can be boring because it's too hard to follow, so your attention keeps sliding off it. And a task at the perfect difficulty can still be boring if you can't see why it matters. Notice that the opposite of boredom on both counts, a challenge that fits your skill and feels worth doing, is basically a description of flow.
Boredom is a signal, not a bug

Many researchers now see boredom the way doctors see pain: unpleasant on purpose. Pain tells you to take your hand off the stove. Hunger tells you to find food. Boredom tells you that what you're doing right now isn't a good use of your attention, and that you should change something, either the task, how you're doing it, or what you're doing it for.

From an evolutionary angle, that's valuable. An animal that could happily stare at the same patch of ground forever would never explore, never find new food, never learn. A creature that gets restless when nothing is happening gets pushed toward new information. Boredom is the push. In that sense it's less like a void and more like an engine warning light: annoying, but there to make you look.
Boredom is a question your brain is asking: *is this worth my attention?* The answer can be 'no, change it' or 'yes, and here's why'. What matters is that you actually answer it.

The trouble is that the push can go in good or bad directions. The same restlessness that drives someone to start a project can drive someone else to pick a fight, drink too much or make a reckless choice. Researchers have found that people who get bored easily, what they call high boredom proneness, are more likely to report problems like depression, overeating, gambling and substance use. Those studies are correlational, so they don't prove boredom causes the problems, but they do suggest that handling boredom badly is not a harmless habit.
The case for a wandering mind

Boredom may also have a creative upside. In a 2014 study, the British psychologists Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman had some participants spend 15 minutes copying numbers out of a phone book, a task chosen to be mind-numbing. Then everyone did a classic creativity test: list as many uses as you can for a pair of polystyrene cups. The bored group came up with more ideas. In a follow-up, people who had to *read* the phone numbers, an even more passive task, did better still, possibly because reading leaves more room for the mind to wander.

The idea behind this is that boredom loosens the grip of focused attention and lets the mind drift. That drifting, daydreaming state is when the brain links distant ideas, replays problems from new angles and sometimes hands you the answer you couldn't force. Lots of people have had the experience of solving a bug in the shower or on a walk, after giving up at the keyboard.

An honest caveat: these creativity studies are small, use simple lab tasks, and haven't always replicated cleanly. Boredom doesn't automatically make you creative, and you won't write a great game just by staring at a wall. The more defensible claim is narrower. Mind-wandering is where a lot of loose thinking happens, and boredom is often the doorway into it. Close the doorway every time and you get less of that thinking.
What the phone actually takes

For almost all of human history, boredom was unavoidable. You waited in lines, sat through long evenings, stood watches with nothing to look at. Now there's a device in your pocket that can end boredom in under a second, every time. That sounds like pure progress. But think about what happens to a signal that's always silenced before it's heard.

If boredom is a message that says *change something*, the phone answers it with the cheapest possible change: a new stimulus that asks nothing of you. The restlessness goes away, but nothing about your situation improved. You didn't fix the boring task, find a better one or figure out why it bored you. Do that hundreds of times a day and you never learn what your boredom was pointing at.

blocks.title: The numbing loop
items: Feel a flicker of boredom
Reach for the phone
Instant relief, no real change
Tolerance for empty moments drops
Boredom shows up sooner and feels worse

blocks.text: There's also a tolerance effect, which anyone who has struggled with doomscrolling will recognize. Wilson's participants were ordinary college students and community members, and many of them already found 15 minutes alone hard to bear. The more reliably you escape boredom, the less practice you get at sitting with it, and the more unbearable short gaps start to feel. Scrolling doesn't cure boredom. It often just moves it, leaving you oddly flat afterward, bored and overstimulated at once.

Long deployments put this in sharp relief. Underway, much of the endless feed disappears, and the empty stretches come back: between watches, waiting for a drill to end, lying in the rack before sleep. For people used to filling every gap, that can feel brutal at first. It's also a rare chance to find out what your mind does when nothing is feeding it, and what it starts asking for.

It's worth separating boredom from rest, because they get confused. Rest is when you're not engaged and you're fine with it; your body and mind are recovering. Boredom is when you're not engaged and you want to be. After a brutal watch, an hour of staring at the overhead may be genuine rest. Feeling restless, irritated and itchy for something to happen is the signal. The response to rest is to let it happen. The response to boredom is to ask what it's pointing at.
How to use boredom instead of killing it

None of this means you should seek out misery or throw your phone overboard. The goal is to stop treating every flicker of boredom as an emergency and start treating it as information. A few simple habits help.

blocks.title: When boredom hits
items: Notice it and name it: 'I'm bored.' That alone breaks the autopilot reach for the phone.
Ask which kind: is this too easy, too hard, or pointless to me?
If it's too easy, make it harder: race the clock, add a constraint, turn it into a game.
If it's too hard, shrink it: break off a smaller piece you can actually grip.
If it feels pointless, connect it to something you care about, or decide it really isn't worth doing.
If it's just empty time, let your mind wander for a few minutes before filling it.

blocks.text: The middle steps are where the MAC model earns its keep. Field day is boring because it's too easy, so make it a race or a challenge with someone else. A qualification card full of dense system diagrams is boring because it's too hard to grip, so cut it into one small piece you can actually trace. A chore that feels pointless might connect to something real if you look for it, and if it truly doesn't, at least you know why it drains you.

The last step is the strangest one, and maybe the most valuable. Try a short walk, a workout or a stretch of rack time with no input at all, not even music. Keep a small notebook handy. The first few minutes will feel itchy. After that, a lot of people find their mind starts producing things: ideas for a project, a solution to a problem, a decision they'd been avoiding. That's not wasted time. It's the thinking that never gets a turn when every gap is filled.

And when a task is boring because it's genuinely pointless, boredom has done its job. Sometimes the right response to a boring thing is not to push through it but to ask whether you should be doing it at all, or whether there's a version of your life with less of it. A lot of people who built something of their own started with exactly that kind of restless question.

The reframe: boredom isn't the absence of something to do. It's your mind telling you it wants something better than what it's getting. Silence that message every time and you never find out what 'better' would be.

takeaways: In Wilson's 2014 study, 67% of men and 25% of women shocked themselves rather than sit alone with their thoughts for 15 minutes.
Boredom comes from attention mismatch (too easy or too hard) or a lack of meaning, and each has a different fix.
Boredom is a signal to change something; the phone silences it without changing anything.
Small studies suggest boredom can open the door to mind-wandering and creative thinking, though the evidence is limited.
Next time you're bored, name it, ask which kind it is, and give your mind a few minutes before you fill the gap.

title: You Can't Delete a Habit. You Can Outvote It.
dek: Building a habit and breaking one are different problems. The research on quitting says the old groove never fully disappears, so the real job is giving the cue somewhere better to go.

blocks.text: In 1987, the psychologist Daniel Wegner gave people one of the easiest instructions in the history of psychology. For five minutes, talk out loud about whatever comes to mind, but do not think about a white bear. If a white bear shows up, ring a bell. The bells kept ringing. People could not keep the bear out, and the effort of pushing it away left a mark: when they were later allowed to think about the bear, they thought about it more than people who had been told to think about it from the start.

That small experiment sits underneath one of the most common mistakes in self-improvement. Almost all habit advice is written for *building* things: start running, read before bed, practice aim every day. But a lot of what people actually want is subtraction. Stop reaching for the phone at every pause. Stop the late-night snacking. Stop biting nails, cracking knuckles, opening the same three apps in a loop. And subtraction turns out to follow different rules.

When you build a habit, you are carving a new path. When you break one, you are trying to stop walking a path that is already worn smooth, and the research says the path does not go away just because you stop using it. That sounds like bad news. It is actually the most useful thing to understand about quitting, because it tells you exactly where relapse comes from and what to do instead.
The groove stays

For about a century, learning researchers have studied what happens when a learned behavior stops paying off. A rat learns that pressing a lever brings food; then the food stops, and eventually the rat stops pressing. That process is called extinction, and it looks like forgetting. Mark Bouton at the University of Vermont spent decades showing that it isn't. In a 2002 review, he summarized the evidence that extinction does not destroy the original learning. Instead, the animal learns a *second* thing, something like "in this situation, pressing doesn't work," and stores it alongside the first.

Bouton's analogy is that the cue becomes an ambiguous word with two meanings. Which meaning wins depends on context: the room, the time, the body's internal state, even how much time has passed. And the newer meaning, the "don't do it" one, is the more fragile of the two. It is tied tightly to the context where it was learned. Change the context and the old meaning tends to come roaring back.

That one idea explains a whole catalog of relapse. You quit something in one setting and it returns the moment you're somewhere else. You're clean for weeks and then a stressful day, which changes your internal state, brings the urge back at full strength. You go a long time without the behavior and assume it's dead, then one exposure revives it. None of that means you failed. It means the old learning was sitting there the whole time, waiting for the right context to retrieve it.
A broken habit is not an erased habit. It is an old answer that a newer answer is currently outvoting. Your job is to keep the newer answer winning in as many contexts as possible.

The most famous real-world example comes from the military. In the early 1970s, Lee Robins and her colleagues studied US Army enlisted men who had served in Vietnam, where heroin was cheap, pure and everywhere. A 2017 review of her work by Wayne Hall and Megan Weier summarizes the striking numbers: about a third of the men used heroin in Vietnam and about one in five reported symptoms of dependence. Yet in the first year after returning home, only around 1 percent became re-addicted, even though about 10 percent tried the drug again.

items.label: Soldiers who used heroin while serving in Vietnam
Reported symptoms of heroin dependence there
Became re-addicted in the first year back home

blocks.source: Hall & Weier, Addiction, 2017 (on Robins' Vietnam veteran studies)

blocks.text: Hall and Weier warn against turning this into a simple slogan. Price, availability, social norms and life circumstances all changed when the soldiers came home, not just the scenery. But that is exactly the point. The cues that had driven the behavior (the place, the people, the boredom, the supply) were gone. A huge change in context did what willpower alone rarely does.
Don't plan a "don't"

If habits are cue-driven, the obvious tool is a plan for the cue. Implementation intentions, the "if X, then I will Y" plans, are among the best-supported techniques in behavior change. So a natural move is to write one for a bad habit: *if I feel bored at night, then I won't eat chips.*

A 2011 study by Marieke Adriaanse and colleagues tested exactly that structure, and found it can backfire. Plans that negated a habit ("if this, then *not* that") produced ironic rebound effects, both in what people thought about and in what they actually did, compared with simply intending to change or with a plan that named a *replacement* behavior. The effect was worst when the habit being negated was strong. The likely reason is the white bear problem: a "don't" plan still has to mention the forbidden response, and mentioning it keeps the link between cue and response alive.

Wegner's own second experiment pointed at the fix. People who were given a specific alternative thought to use as a distraction were less likely to become preoccupied with the white bear afterward. The brain is bad at holding a blank. It is good at running a different program.

This matters because the urge itself rarely goes away on command. Cravings and restlessness are signals, and a plan that only blocks the exit leaves the signal with nowhere to go. A replacement plan treats the urge as real and redirects it. It also gives you something to succeed at, which a plan made entirely of not-doing never can.

blocks.title: Two ways to write the same plan

left.head: Negation plan
items: If I'm bored at night, then I won't snack
If I sit down in the rack, then I won't open the app
Keeps the old response in the sentence
Tested: can strengthen the habit it targets

right.head: Replacement plan
items: If I'm bored at night, then I'll drink water and do 20 push-ups
If I sit down in the rack, then I'll open the book first
Gives the cue a new destination
Tested: no ironic rebound

blocks.text: There is one more wrinkle, from a 2010 diary study by Jeffrey Quinn, Wendy Wood and colleagues. They tracked how people tried to control unwanted behaviors in daily life. For temptations, controlling the environment worked well. But for *strong habits*, the strategy that worked best was vigilant monitoring: watching carefully for slip-ups and catching yourself in the act. A follow-up experiment suggested that monitoring didn't weaken the habit itself; it boosted the brain's ability to stop the response once it fired. In other words, the effective "don't" is not a plan you write in advance. It is an alert, real-time noticing at the moment the cue hits, paired with somewhere else to go.
The method clinicians actually use

There is a treatment built almost entirely on those two ingredients, noticing plus replacing. It was published in 1973 by Nathan Azrin and R. Gregory Nunn under the name habit reversal, originally for nervous habits and tics. Clinicians still use versions of it today for nail biting, hair pulling, skin picking, teeth clenching and similar repetitive behaviors.

The core moves are simple. First, awareness training: people learn to notice the behavior, and especially the earliest warning signs before it, such as the hand drifting toward the mouth. Second, a competing response: an action that is physically incompatible with the habit, like clenching a fist or holding an object for a minute or so when the urge arrives. Some versions add social support, with someone close giving a heads-up when they spot the habit and praise when it is replaced.

blocks.title: Habit reversal, adapted for everyday habits
items: Describe the habit in precise physical detail: what your hands, eyes or mouth actually do.
Find the earliest warning sign, the moment just before the behavior starts.
Choose a competing response you can't do at the same time as the habit.
Practice running the competing response for about a minute every time the warning sign appears.
Ask one person you trust to point it out when they see the habit, and to notice when you replace it.

blocks.text: Run that on a modern habit and it looks like this. The behavior: thumb unlocks the phone and opens a feed. The warning sign: the half-second of restlessness when a task ends, or the hand already moving toward the pocket. The competing response: put both hands on something else, pick up the book, stand up and stretch, write the next task on a card. The point is not that a stretch is more fun than a feed. It's that the cue now has a rehearsed second option, and every time you run it, that option gets a little stronger.

Does it work? A 2011 meta-analysis by Kylee Bate and colleagues pooled 18 studies with 575 participants covering stuttering, tics, nail biting, thumb sucking, jaw disorders and other repetitive behaviors. Compared with control conditions, habit reversal showed a large effect, an effect size of d = 0.80. Those are clinical populations with specific conditions, so don't expect a guaranteed fix for doomscrolling. But the logic transfers neatly. You stop fighting the urge in the abstract and start practicing a specific move at a specific moment.

Effect size versus control conditions (large)

blocks.text: Cold turkey or taper?

Most people instinctively want to ease out of a bad habit: cut back gradually, then stop. Sometimes that's sensible. But one of the best trials on the question points the other way, at least for one of the hardest habits there is.

In 2016, Nicola Lindson-Hawley and colleagues randomized 697 smokers in England to either quit abruptly on a set day or cut down by 75 percent over the two weeks before that day. Both groups got the same nurse support and nicotine replacement. Abrupt quitting won at four weeks and was still ahead at six months. The authors concluded that stopping abruptly was more likely to produce lasting abstinence even for smokers who initially preferred to cut down.

blocks.title: Still not smoking, by quit method
blocks.note: Validated abstinence; both groups had nurse support and nicotine replacement.
blocks.source: Lindson-Hawley et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2016

blocks.text: Smoking is a chemical addiction, and you shouldn't stretch one trial too far. But the result fits the bigger picture. A taper keeps the cue-response link in active use: every cigarette, every "just five minutes" of scrolling, is another rehearsal of the old answer. A clean break gives the new answer a chance to win repeatedly without competition. Notice also the drop between four weeks and six months in both groups. Quitting is not a single event. The old groove is still there, and relapse is the default, which is why planning for it matters more than promising it won't happen.
Using the moments when the map changes

Put all of this together and a strategy emerges that looks nothing like "try harder." Old habits are stored, not erased. They are triggered by context. Plans that only say "no" can strengthen them. What helps is noticing the cue early, giving it a new destination, and making the switch at a moment when the old context is already disrupted.

Those disruptions come more often than you might think. A move, a new job, a new rack, a new watch rotation, the start of an underway period, the return home. Each is a window where many of the old cues are temporarily gone, and the behavior you set up first in the new context gets a head start. The flip side is a warning: when you go back to an old environment, expect old habits to wake up with it. The guy who quit energy drinks at sea should not be surprised when the gas station near the base brings the craving straight back.

items: Name the cue, not just the behavior. "Phone at every pause" is a behavior; "the first ten seconds of downtime" is the cue.
Write a replacement plan, never a negation plan. Say what you will do, not what you won't.
Make the replacement physically incompatible with the habit when you can.
Expect relapse in new or stressful contexts and decide in advance what you'll do in the first minute after a slip.
Use big life transitions on purpose: set up the replacement before the new context starts.

blocks.text: And if the habit is a substance, a compulsion that's hurting your work, or something that keeps coming back no matter what you try, that's a medical conversation, not a willpower one. The corpsman is the place to start, and asking early is a lot easier than asking late.
The white bear never really leaves. What changes is how often it gets the floor. That is a quieter, more realistic goal than total elimination, and it is one you can actually win, one cue at a time.

takeaways: Quitting isn't erasing: the old habit is stored and can return when the context or your stress level changes.
Plans that say "if X, then I won't do Y" can backfire; always name a replacement behavior instead.
For strong habits, real-time noticing of the cue plus a competing response beats abstract resolve.
A clean break often beats a slow taper, because every "just a little" rehearses the old habit.
Big transitions are the best time to break habits, and returning to old places is the riskiest time for relapse.

title: Tie Yourself to the Mast
dek: Commitment devices let today's you lock in a decision that tomorrow's you would back out of. They work, sometimes dramatically, but the data shows almost nobody wants them, and a badly built one can leave you worse off than none at all.

blocks.text: In the *Odyssey*, Odysseus wants to hear the Sirens, whose song lures sailors onto the rocks. He knows exactly what will happen when he hears it: he will want to steer toward them, and no amount of good sense in that moment will stop him. So he makes the decision early. The crew plug their ears with wax, tie him to the mast, and get orders to ignore anything he says until they're clear. When the song comes, he begs to be untied. They tie him tighter.

Economists call this a commitment device: a choice you make now that restricts or penalizes the choices available to your future self. The story is about three thousand years old, but the idea behind it is very modern. It assumes you are not one consistent decision-maker. You are a series of selves who keep disagreeing, and the one making plans on a calm Sunday is not the one who will be standing in front of the vending machine at 0200 after a long watch.

Most self-improvement advice tries to change the 0200 version of you. Commitment devices skip that argument entirely. They let the calm version make a binding move, the way Odysseus did. The research on them is surprisingly rich, and it holds three lessons: they can work remarkably well, very few people will sign up for them, and building one wrong can cost you real money.
Putting money where your mouth is

One of the cleanest tests came from Xavier Giné, Dean Karlan and Jonathan Zinman, who designed a savings product for smokers in the Philippines. It was called CARES. Smokers who signed up deposited money into an account for six months. At the end, they took a urine test for nicotine and cotinine. Pass, and you got your money back. Fail, and it went to charity.

Only 11 percent of the smokers offered CARES took it. But because the offer was randomized, the researchers could measure its effect across everyone offered it, takers and non-takers alike. Smokers offered CARES were 3 percentage points more likely to pass the six-month test than the control group. More important, the effect held up in surprise tests at twelve months, after the money was no longer on the line. The device didn't just rent good behavior for six months. For some people, it seems to have changed the habit.

items.label: Smokers offered the CARES commitment account who signed up
Higher chance of passing the 6-month nicotine test for those offered it
Effect still present in surprise follow-up tests

blocks.source: Giné, Karlan & Zinman, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 2010

blocks.text: Karlan also co-founded stickK with the Yale law professor Ian Ayres, a website that turns the same idea into a consumer product. You set a goal, stake money if you want, choose a referee to confirm whether you did it, and pick where the money goes if you fail. One of its sharper options is the "anti-charity": an organization you dislike, so losing doesn't feel like a donation you can feel good about.
The medicine almost nobody takes

The most revealing study on commitment devices is a 2015 trial in the *New England Journal of Medicine* led by Scott Halpern. It enrolled 2,538 people, mostly CVS Caremark employees and their friends and family, and compared different ways of paying smokers to quit. Some programs simply offered a reward of about $800 for staying smoke-free. Others required a refundable deposit of $150 up front, which the smoker got back on success along with $650 in reward payments.

The deposit programs were, in effect, commitment devices. And people avoided them. Of those assigned to reward-only programs, 90 percent accepted. Of those assigned to deposit programs, 13.7 percent did. Because so few people took the deposit deal, the reward programs produced more quitters overall.

blocks.title: Six-month quit rates by program type
blocks.note: Intention-to-treat: everyone assigned to a program counts, whether or not they accepted it.
blocks.source: Halpern et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2015

blocks.text: But here's the twist buried in the paper. Using a statistical method to estimate effects among the kind of people who would accept *either* deal, the researchers found that the deposit programs produced six-month quit rates 13.2 percentage points higher than reward programs. Among people willing to put their own money at risk, having something to lose worked better than having something to gain. That fits a well-known pattern in behavioral economics: losses tend to sting more than equal gains feel good.

items.label: Accepted a reward-only quit program
Accepted a program requiring a $150 deposit
Estimated advantage of deposits among people who'd accept either

blocks.source: Halpern et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2015

blocks.text: Put those together and you get the central paradox. Commitment devices are strong medicine for the minority of people willing to swallow them, and most people won't. The fact that you're reading about them and thinking "maybe" already puts you in an unusual group.

Why do people refuse? Part of it is simple: nobody likes the idea of losing money. But economists point to a deeper reason. To want a commitment device, you have to admit, in advance and in writing, that you expect to fail without one. Most people believe their future self will behave. They are what economists call naive about their own impatience. Ask someone on a Sunday whether they'll skip the gym on Thursday and they'll say no. Ask them to bet on it and they get suspicious of the question.

The Halpern trial had one more finding worth knowing. Programs built around groups of six, where people's rewards were linked to how their teammates did, produced about the same quit rates as programs for individuals: 13.7 percent versus 12.1 percent at six months, a difference the researchers judged not significant. Social pressure alone, at least in that form, didn't add much on top of money. That's a useful reminder that "get an accountability buddy" is not automatically a powerful intervention. The details of what gets checked, and what's at stake, matter more than the fact that someone else is involved.
When betting on yourself backfires

Before you go stake your paycheck, read Anett John's 2020 study in *Management Science*. She randomly offered low-income people a commitment savings account. Clients chose their own savings plan and their own penalty for missing it. On average, the account boosted bank savings a lot. But 55 percent of clients defaulted on their plans and paid the penalty, ending up with monetary losses.

John's explanation is uncomfortable and useful. Many people chose penalties that were too small to actually change their behavior. They knew they had a self-control problem, but they underestimated how big it was. So they built a device strong enough to cost them money but too weak to hold them. In her data, the people who best understood their own impatience were more cautious about signing up, and better at picking contracts they could keep.
A commitment device has to be stronger than the temptation it's fighting. One that's just strong enough to punish you, but not strong enough to stop you, is a fee, not a fix.

There's a second caution about evidence. A famous 2002 study by Dan Ariely and Klaus Wertenbroch, often cited as proof that students who set their own deadlines perform better, carries a 2026 retraction notice in the journal *Psychological Science*. Treat the self-imposed-deadlines story you may have heard in books and talks with caution. The smoking and savings trials above stand on separate data.
Accountability: who's watching, and what they see

Not every commitment device involves money. The softer version is accountability: telling someone, reporting your progress, letting a referee check. Economists Gharad Bryan, Dean Karlan and Scott Nelson distinguish "hard" commitments with real financial or physical penalties from "soft" ones that mostly carry psychological costs, like the embarrassment of admitting you skipped. Soft commitments are easier to adopt, and the research suggests they can still carry real weight.

A 2016 meta-analysis by Benjamin Harkin and colleagues pooled 138 randomized studies with nearly 20,000 participants and found that interventions that got people to monitor their progress toward a goal improved goal attainment, with an average effect size of d = 0.40. Monitoring helped more in two conditions: when the progress was reported to others or made public, and when it was physically recorded rather than just kept in your head.

But there's a catch, and it's subtle. In 2009, Peter Gollwitzer and colleagues ran four experiments on identity goals, things like intending to become a lawyer or a psychologist. When other people took notice of a person's stated intention, that person then acted on it *less*. The announcement seemed to give a premature sense of already being the kind of person they wanted to be. Telling people "I'm going to be a YouTuber" can feel like progress, and that feeling can quietly replace the work.

blocks.title: Accountability that helps vs. accountability that hurts

left.head: Tends to help
items: Reporting what you actually did this week
Written, checkable records
A referee who confirms results
Specific behavior: three workouts, two uploads

right.head: Can backfire
items: Announcing who you're going to become
Progress kept vague or only in your head
Praise for the plan instead of the results
Identity claims: "I'm a content creator now"

blocks.text: This connects to how a lot of creators and builders talk online. Announcing a project, a channel or a game feels great and gets encouragement. But praise for an announcement rewards the plan, not the work. If you want an audience to hold you accountable, give them something checkable: a devlog, a weekly upload, a public changelog. That way the attention arrives only when the work does.

The resolution is simple: make the public part about *actions and results*, not identity. "I posted two videos this week" is accountability. "I'm starting a channel" is a dopamine hit that costs you nothing.

A 2015 workplace experiment by Heather Royer, Mark Stehr and Justin Sydnor adds one more piece. A four-week program paying employees to use the company gym produced only small lasting effects once the payments stopped. But when people were also offered a self-funded commitment contract at the end of the program, the effects persisted, detectable even several years later. Incentives can start a habit. Commitment, chosen by the person themselves, can help keep it going.
Building one that actually holds

Put the research together and a good commitment device has a recognizable shape. It targets a behavior that someone else can verify. It has a stake big enough to matter at the moment of temptation, not just on the calm day you set it. It runs for a defined period, long enough to build a routine but short enough that you can see the finish line. And it has a referee who isn't you.

blocks.title: Designing a commitment device
items: Pick one behavior that's checkable by someone else: a workout log, an uploaded video, a finished chapter.
Set a stake that would genuinely hurt to lose, sized to the temptation, not to your optimism.
Name a referee you won't argue with, ideally someone who will actually check.
Set a short, fixed window, such as four to eight weeks, then decide whether to renew.
Report results weekly in writing: what you did, not who you're becoming.

blocks.text: Not every device needs cash. Some of the most effective ones just remove options. Leaving a debit card with someone you trust before a weekend you know you'll overspend. Deleting an app and handing the password to a friend so reinstalling takes a conversation. Pre-paying for a coached session you'd be embarrassed to skip. Each one is a soft or hard commitment, depending on how painful it is to reverse, and the general rule from the research holds: the harder it is to undo in the moment, the more work it does.

It also helps to plan the exit before you need it. A device with no off-ramp tempts you to cheat it, and once you've cheated it once, it stops meaning anything. Decide in advance what counts as a legitimate exception, like illness or an unexpected duty day, and write it down. Then everything else counts.

Deployment life is an unusual setup for this, because some of the best commitment devices are built into it already. When you're underway, the environment itself restricts choices: no takeout, no store run, limited internet. That's Odysseus's rope, supplied for free. The harder test is the return. The weeks after coming home are when every option opens back up at once, and that's exactly when a pre-arranged stake, made while you're still at sea and thinking clearly, earns its keep.

A brother, a friend or a shipmate as referee; a deposit that goes to a cause you'd hate to fund; a weekly message that says what you did. None of it requires you to become a different person. It just requires the version of you who's thinking clearly right now to tie a knot that the tired version can't untie.

takeaways: Commitment devices work by letting your calm self restrict your future self's choices, like Odysseus at the mast.
Deposit-style stakes can outperform rewards for people willing to use them, but most people refuse them.
A stake that's too small just costs you money: size it to the temptation, not to your optimism.
Report actions and results to others; announcing an identity goal can make you do less.
Set up the device while conditions are calm, especially before big transitions like coming home.

title: Your Habits Don't Travel
dek: Change where you live or when you work, and your routines fall apart, good ones included. The same disruption is also the best opening you'll ever get to build new ones, and it doesn't stay open long.

blocks.text: In February 2014, a strike closed stations across the London Underground. Tens of thousands of commuters had to find another way to work. Some walked, some took buses, many rode lines they had never used. It was the kind of disruption everyone grumbles about and then forgets.

Three economists, Shaun Larcom, Ferdinand Rauch and Tim Willems, didn't forget. They pulled anonymized Oyster card data, more than 200 million records covering 20 days, and looked at what commuters did after the strike ended. About 1 in 20 of the regular commuters who were forced off their route never went back. They had found something better, a route they could have taken for years but never tried. The effect was strongest where the famous Tube map distorts real distances the most. The researchers concluded the time those switchers saved over the long run outweighed the time everyone lost during the strike.

Think about what that means. Thousands of people were making the same suboptimal trip every working day, not because they had weighed the options, but because the trip was a habit. It took a strike to knock them loose. Disruption is usually described as the enemy of good habits, and it often is. It's also the only thing that reliably gets the bad ones to loosen their grip.

The map detail is the clever part. The Tube map is a diagram, not a scale drawing, so some stations that look far apart are a short walk from each other and some that look close are not. Commuters had picked a route from the map once and then stopped checking. The researchers concluded that the hassle of searching alone was unlikely to explain it. The bigger problem was information: many commuters simply didn't know a better route existed, and their routine gave them no reason to find out. That's what a habit does. It stops you from sampling alternatives, so you never learn that one of them is better.

items.label: Disrupted commuters who kept their new route after the strike
Oyster card records analyzed
Span of travel data around the strike

blocks.text: Habits are glued to places

A habit isn't stored as "I work out." It's stored as something closer to "when I'm here, at this time, after this, I work out." Psychologists define habits as responses that cues in the environment trigger automatically, and the cue is doing more of the work than it feels like. You notice the behavior. You rarely notice the context holding it up.

Wendy Wood and her colleagues Tam and Witt tested this with students transferring to a new university, which is about as clean a context change as real life offers. They tracked habits like exercising, reading the newspaper and watching TV before and after the move. The habits survived the transfer only when some part of the old performance context came along. Students who had read the paper with other people and kept reading it with others kept the habit. When the context changed completely, the habit fell apart.

The study found something else. When the old habit broke, behavior started following people's *current intentions* again. Someone who had exercised out of habit but no longer cared much about it stopped. Someone who wanted to exercise more finally could, because the old automatic routine was no longer running the show. Disruption doesn't just delete habits. It hands control back to whatever you actually want right now, for better or worse.

That second finding is the hinge of this whole article. A habit is useful precisely because it doesn't consult your intentions. It runs whether you feel like it or not. When the habit breaks, the decision comes back to you, and what you do next depends on what you want in that moment and how easy each option is. If you've thought about what you want before the change, the window helps you. If you haven't, it just helps whatever is easiest.

This is why a move, a new job, a new ship or even a two-week trip can erase routines you thought were solid. You weren't less disciplined in the new place. The cues that ran the routine stayed behind.
Why travel kills good habits and spares bad ones

If disruption hit all habits equally, it would at least be fair. It doesn't. The habits that survive a big change are the ones whose cues come with you, and the most portable cue most people own is a phone. The gym was tied to a building and a time slot. Studying was tied to a desk and a quiet hour. Scrolling is tied to a device in your pocket and the feeling of having a spare minute, and both of those follow you everywhere. So you arrive somewhere new with your workout gone and your scrolling fully intact.

Stress makes this worse. In a 2013 set of five studies, David Neal, Wendy Wood and Aimee Drolet looked at what happens to habits when people are tired, stressed or low on self-control. One study followed students across a semester, including exam periods. Under exam stress, students didn't simply fall apart. They fell back on whatever habits they already had. Those who usually ate a junk breakfast ate more junk. Those who usually ate oatmeal kept eating oatmeal. Regular gym-goers were more likely to keep going. Students in the habit of reading a newspaper's editorial pages kept reading them even when they had little time.
Stress doesn't make you abandon habits. It makes you lean on them harder. The question during a hard stretch isn't whether you'll run on autopilot. It's which autopilot is installed.

Put those findings together and you get the double hit of a transition. A move or a schedule change strips the cues from the good habits you built in the old setting. The stress and fatigue that come with the change push you to rely on autopilot. And the habits still available on autopilot are mostly the portable ones, which for most people means the least useful ones.

There's a bitter irony here for anyone trying to cut back on screens. Every trip, every schedule shift and every stressful week quietly strengthens the phone habit relative to everything else, because it's the one routine that never loses its cue. If you only work on the habit during calm, stable stretches, you're fighting it on the days it's weakest and leaving it alone on the days it gets stronger.
The window that opens

Here's the other side. If a context change knocks habits loose, it also leaves a gap where new ones can take root more easily than usual. Bas Verplanken and colleagues call this the **habit discontinuity hypothesis**: interventions to change behavior work better when they land right after a life change.

Earlier studies hinted at it. One gave people who had recently moved a free one-day public transit ticket and information about local services, and transit use went up compared with other recent movers who got nothing. Another reanalyzed a program that handed out free one-month transit passes and found the passes only changed behavior among people who had recently moved house or changed workplace. For everyone else, a free month of transit didn't break the car habit.

In 2016, Verplanken and Deborah Roy ran a cleaner test in Peterborough, England. They recruited 800 households, half of which had moved in the previous six months. Half of each group got an intervention: a face-to-face interview plus information about sustainable choices like saving energy and water. Eight weeks later, they measured 25 everyday behaviors. Controlling for past behavior, habit strength, intentions and values, the intervention worked better for people who had recently moved. When the researchers broke it down further, the effect showed up for people who had moved within the previous three months and not for anyone else.

Caveats apply. The behaviors were self-reported, the effect was modest, and the three-month window comes from one study's subgroup analysis, which the authors themselves called tentative. But the pattern across these studies is consistent: a change of circumstances opens a window, and the window doesn't stay open. If you don't fill it on purpose, the old patterns, or whatever is most convenient, will fill it for you.

blocks.text: Build habits that pack light

If habits break because their cues stay behind, the obvious fix is to tie the habits you care about to cues that come with you. Clock times and locations are the worst anchors for anyone whose schedule or location changes. Things you do no matter where you are make far better ones: waking up, the first meal, changing into a uniform, coming off watch, the last time you brush your teeth.

A clock time like 1700
A workout partner who isn't coming
A desk, a chair, a view

right.head: Travel with you
items: Waking up, whenever that is
Your first meal of the day
Getting off watch or off shift
Putting on your boots or uniform
Brushing your teeth before sleep

blocks.text: Wood's transfer students point to a second trick. The habits that survived were the ones where *some* piece of the old context came along. You can do that on purpose. Bring a cue with you: the same playlist that always starts your workout, the same notebook you always study from, the same resistance band you always do your first set with. These sound trivial, and they matter, because they're part of what your brain has learned to treat as "time to do the thing."

Third, shrink the habit for the transition instead of pausing it. Phillippa Lally's well-known habit formation study found that missing a single day didn't materially affect how a habit built up. Missing one day is fine. Disappearing for three weeks is a different story. A ten-minute bodyweight circuit in a hotel room or a berthing passageway keeps the cue-response link alive until you can rebuild the full version.
A playbook for the next big change

Transitions are predictable even when life isn't. Leave, travel, a new duty station, the first weeks underway, the first weeks home after a long stretch away: you know they're coming. That means you can plan for the disruption before it hits instead of discovering on day ten that your routines evaporated.

blocks.title: Before, during and after a transition
items: **Before:** List your three most important habits and write down what actually cues each one. Circle any cue that won't exist where you're going.
**Before:** Re-anchor each one to a portable cue, and define a minimum version you can do anywhere in ten minutes or less.
**During:** Run the minimum version. Expect stress to push you toward autopilot, so make your worst portable habit a bit harder (app logged out, phone charging out of reach).
**After arriving:** Treat the first weeks as the window. Set up the routine you want on day one or two, not "once things settle down."
**After arriving:** Use the disruption to drop something. If an old habit didn't make the trip, ask whether you actually want it back before rebuilding it.

blocks.text: The last step is the one most people skip. When you come back from a trip and notice you haven't done some old routine in two weeks, the default reaction is guilt and a scramble to restart it. Sometimes that's right. But the strike commuters had been riding a slower route every working day because nothing had ever forced them to check. A disruption is a free experiment. Some of what broke deserves to stay broken.

Coming home deserves its own mention, because it's the transition people plan for least. Underway, the schedule is rigid and the environment is fixed, which can make some habits easy: the rack, the watch rotation and the mess decks give you cues every day. Ashore, all of those cues disappear at once and are replaced by unlimited choice. It's common to come off a long stretch with great routines and lose them within a week of getting home. That isn't weakness either. It's the same context change in reverse, and it calls for the same playbook.

Life in the Navy runs on transitions. Every one of them will break some habits whether you plan for it or not. The difference is whether it breaks them at random, leaving you with whatever was most portable and least useful, or whether you walk into the change knowing which habits to protect, which ones to let go and which new ones to start in the short window when starting is easiest.

takeaways: Habits are triggered by context. When the context changes, the habit often doesn't come with it.
Transitions hit good habits hardest, because portable habits like scrolling come along and gym routines don't.
Stress makes you fall back on whatever habits you have, good or bad, so install the good ones before a hard stretch.
Anchor important habits to cues that travel: waking up, meals, coming off watch.
After a big change there's a short window (about three months in one study) when new habits are easier to start. Use it on purpose.
