title: Your Pounding Heart Is Trying to Help
dek: The stress response evolved to make you perform. A decade of experiments suggests the story you tell yourself about it decides whether it does.

blocks.text: A group of college students sit in a Harvard psychology lab, about to take a practice version of the GRE, the entrance exam that decides a lot of graduate-school futures. Each one spits into a small tube so the researchers can measure a stress marker in their saliva. Then half of them read a short note. It says, in effect: feeling anxious before a test is normal, and recent research suggests that arousal doesn't hurt performance and may even help it. If you feel nervous, remind yourself that your body might be helping you do well.

That is the whole intervention. No breathing exercises, no meditation, no pep talk. One paragraph that changes the meaning of a racing heart. The students who read it went on to beat the control group on the math section, and the gap showed up again months later on the real exam. The study launched a line of research that now spans karaoke rooms, community colleges and nationwide online trials, and it points to an idea most of us were never taught: the problem is often not the stress itself, but what we think the stress means.
One paragraph, sixty-four points

The experiment was run by Jeremy Jamieson, Wendy Berry Mendes, Erin Blackstock and Toni Schmader and published in 2010 in the *Journal of Experimental Social Psychology*. Sixty students preparing for the GRE were recruited. All of them took a practice test in the lab. Those in the **reappraisal** group got the paragraph about arousal being useful; the control group got only the cover story about the saliva samples.

On the practice math section, the reappraisal group averaged about 739 against the control group's 684. The researchers then asked participants to send in their official scores from the real GRE, taken one to three months later. Twenty-eight did. The reappraisal group averaged 770 on quantitative reasoning; the control group averaged about 706. Verbal scores did not differ, which fits the authors' view that the effect works mostly on tasks where anxiety bites hardest, and for many students that is math.

blocks.title: GRE math scores after one paragraph
blocks.note: Means for the 28 students who reported their official scores. A small sample, so treat the size of the gap with caution.
blocks.source: Jamieson, Mendes, Blackstock & Schmader, JESP, 2010

blocks.text: The saliva told an interesting story. The researchers measured salivary alpha-amylase, a marker of sympathetic nervous system activity, the fight-or-flight branch. You might expect the reappraisal group to have calmed down. They did the opposite. Their arousal went *up* from baseline, while the controls' stayed flat, and within the reappraisal group, bigger increases went with better math scores. The note didn't remove the stress. It seems to have let the students use it.

A fair warning before going further: 28 people is a small study, and early effects in psychology often shrink when others try to repeat them. What makes this one worth taking seriously is not that single result. It is that the same basic idea kept producing similar patterns in different labs, with different tasks, and eventually in much larger samples.
Two ways a heart can race

To understand why reframing could matter, you need a distinction that stress researchers like Jim Blascovich, Joe Tomaka and Mendes spent years mapping. Your body has more than one way of being stressed. When you face a demanding situation and judge that you have the resources to handle it, you tend to enter a **challenge** state. When you judge that the demands outweigh what you've got, you slide into a **threat** state. From the outside, both look like stress: your heart speeds up, you sweat, your attention narrows. Under the hood they are different machines.

blocks.title: Same racing heart, different physiology

left.head: Challenge state
items: You judge your resources can meet the demand
Heart pumps more blood per beat
Blood vessels relax and open up
More oxygen and fuel reach brain and muscles
Attention stays on the task

right.head: Threat state
items: You judge the demand outweighs your resources
Heart rate rises, but output gains are weaker
Blood vessels tighten
The body braces for damage, not action
Attention drifts toward danger and failure

blocks.text: In a challenge state, the cardiovascular system looks a lot like it does during aerobic exercise: the heart pushes out more blood and the vessels widen to carry it. In a threat state, the heart still races but the vessels clamp down, a pattern that makes sense if you expect to be injured and want to limit bleeding. It is a terrible configuration for solving equations or giving a briefing.

In a 2012 follow-up in the *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General*, Jamieson, Matthew Nock and Mendes put people through a notoriously unpleasant lab stressor: giving a speech to stern, unsmiling evaluators. Participants told that arousal is a functional response showed a more challenge-like cardiovascular profile than controls, and they were less drawn to threatening cues on an attention task. Their bodies were still activated. They were activated in the more useful direction.

Notice what decides which state you land in: a quick, mostly automatic judgment of demands against resources. That judgment has two dials, and reappraisal only turns one of them. It changes how you read the demand, so a pounding heart stops counting as evidence that you're in over your head. The other dial is your actual resources: skill, knowledge, reps. This is why preparation and mindset aren't rivals. Training raises what you bring to the fight, and reappraisal stops your own nerves from being scored as a point against you.

Anyone who plays competitive games has felt both states. In a clutch round where you've drilled the angle a hundred times, the adrenaline sharpens you; time seems to slow and your aim tightens. In a round where you feel out of your depth, the same adrenaline turns into shaky hands, tunnel vision and a panicked spray. The hormone is the same. What differs is the verdict your brain has already reached about whether you can handle this.
Why 'calm down' is the wrong instruction

Most advice about nerves is about getting rid of them. Breathe. Relax. Calm down. Harvard Business School researcher Alison Wood Brooks noticed a problem with that advice: when your heart is pounding, dropping straight to calm is very hard. Going from a high-arousal state to a low-arousal state means fighting your own physiology. But anxiety and excitement are both high-arousal states. They differ mainly in whether you read the situation as a threat or an opportunity. So instead of trying to power down, what if you just relabeled the energy?

In studies published in 2014 in the *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General*, Brooks had people say a short phrase out loud before stressful tasks: either 'I am excited' or 'I am calm', among other conditions. Before a public speech, the 'excited' speakers talked longer and were rated by independent judges as more persuasive, competent and relaxed. Before a hard math test, they scored about 8% higher than the calm group and the controls. Then came the most memorable version: singing a rock song into a karaoke machine in front of an experimenter, with the game's software scoring pitch, rhythm and volume.

blocks.title: Karaoke accuracy by what singers told themselves
blocks.note: The APA summary groups the calm, angry and sad conditions together. 113 participants.
blocks.source: Brooks, JEP: General, 2014 (via APA press release, 2013)

blocks.text: The point is not that excitement is magic. It's that the move from anxious to excited is a short hop, because your body is already where it needs to be. The move from anxious to calm is a long climb. Brooks called this kind of relabeling arousal-congruent: you keep the energy and change the story.

Before a board, a qual checkout or anything else that makes your stomach drop, skip 'calm down.' Say 'I'm excited' or 'This is my body getting ready.' You're not lying to yourself. You're picking the more useful of two true descriptions of the same feeling.
The scary statistic, read carefully

If you've seen a popular talk about stress, you may have heard a striking number. In 2012, Abiola Keller and colleagues at the University of Wisconsin published an analysis in *Health Psychology* using a large national survey of about 28,750 American adults, linked to death records through 2006. People had been asked how much stress they had and how much they thought stress affected their health.

items.label: Higher risk of premature death for adults with high stress who also believed stress hurt their health a lot

blocks.source: Keller et al., Health Psychology, 2012

blocks.text: High stress on its own was not what stood out. The elevated risk showed up in people who had both high stress *and* the belief that it was harming them. It is tempting to conclude that the belief itself kills. Be careful. This was observational data, not an experiment. People who were already sick might reasonably have felt that stress was wrecking their health, which would produce the same pattern without the belief causing anything. The study is a clue, not a verdict.

Experiments help fill the gap. In 2013, Alia Crum, Peter Salovey and Shawn Achor showed that people can be nudged toward a stress-is-enhancing mindset with short videos, and that this shifted how they responded to stressful situations. That, along with the Jamieson and Brooks work, makes the belief story more plausible. But no one has shown that changing your view of stress will add years to your life, and anyone who tells you otherwise is overselling it.
Scaling it up

The real test of an idea like this is whether it survives being taken out of the lab and handed to thousands of ordinary people. In 2022, David Yeager, Jamieson and colleagues published a paper in *Nature* that tried exactly that. They built a roughly 30-minute self-guided online module that combined two messages: your abilities can grow, and the stress you feel when facing a challenge can be a resource rather than a sign you're failing. They called it a synergistic mindsets intervention.

items.label: Double-blind randomized experiments
Secondary and college students in the US
Length of the online module

blocks.source: Yeager et al., Nature, 2022

blocks.text: Across the studies, students who got the module showed healthier stress-related thinking, better cardiovascular responses in lab stress tests, lower daily cortisol, better well-being and, in one study, better academic outcomes. A final study found fewer anxiety symptoms during the 2020 COVID lockdowns. The effects were not enormous, and the module is not a substitute for actually being prepared. But it is notable that a half-hour lesson about what stress is for moved markers inside the body, not just answers on a survey.
What reappraisal is not

It is easy to turn this research into a slogan like 'stress is good,' which is wrong. The work applies most clearly to **acute performance stress**: an exam, a speech, a game, a drill, a job interview, where something hard is in front of you and the arousal is there to help you meet it. It says much less about chronic stress, the grinding kind that comes from months of bad sleep, money trouble, a toxic chain of command or grief. That kind wears the body down, and reinterpreting it is not a fix. Neither is it a tool for trauma, which needs real support from a professional, a chaplain or a corpsman.

Reappraisal also isn't denial. You are not pretending the situation is easy. You are acknowledging that it is hard and that your body is responding appropriately to something hard. The difference is between 'this feeling means I'm about to fail' and 'this feeling means I'm gearing up.' Both descriptions start from the same pounding heart.

blocks.title: Reappraising stress in the moment
items: Notice the signals: fast heart, tight stomach, shaky hands, quick breathing.
Name them as preparation: your body is sending oxygen and fuel where you need them.
Say it out loud or in your head: 'I'm excited' or 'I'm getting ready.'
Point the energy at the first concrete action of the task.
Afterward, recover on purpose: eat, move, sleep, and let the system power down.

blocks.text: That last step matters. The stress response is built for bursts, followed by recovery. On a boat with rotating watches and drills that come at any hour, the bursts are guaranteed. What you can influence is how you read them while they happen and whether you let your body come back down afterward.

There's a deeper reframe hiding in all this. For most of us, nervousness feels like evidence: proof that we are not ready, that we don't belong, that something has gone wrong. The research suggests that, for the kinds of challenges you choose or train for, nervousness is closer to the opposite. It is your body taking the task seriously. The heart pounding before a big moment is not a warning light. It is the engine spinning up.

takeaways: Stress arousal is fuel; how you interpret it helps decide whether it powers you or drags you down.
Switching from 'anxious' to 'excited' is easier than switching to 'calm', because both are high-energy states.
Challenge and threat look the same from outside but run your heart and blood vessels differently.
The famous 43% stat is correlational; the experiments are more convincing, but effects are modest.
Reappraisal is for acute performance stress, not chronic grind or trauma; recover after every burst.

title: The Translator Between You and the Chip
dek: A processor understands nothing but numbered instructions. Everything you type in a script editor has to be translated first, and how that translation happens explains why some languages are 70 times slower than others and why your Roblox code runs the way it does.

blocks.text: Type a line like *print("hello")* into a Roblox script and press Play. The words appear in the output window a moment later, and it feels like the computer read your line and did what it said. It did not. The processor inside your PC has never seen the word *print* and never will. It understands one thing: long runs of numbers, each one an instruction from a small fixed menu. Add these two registers. Copy this value to that memory address. If the last result was zero, jump to instruction 4,096.

Between your line of text and those numbers sits a translator, usually several of them stacked on top of each other. Most programmers use them every day without thinking about them, the way you flip a breaker without picturing the generator. But how the translation happens decides how fast your code runs, what errors you see and when, and even which devices your game can run on. It is also one of the best ideas in the history of computing, and a Navy officer was one of the first people to make it work.
What the chip actually understands

Every processor family has an **instruction set**: the complete list of operations its circuits can perform, each assigned a binary code. An instruction is a pattern of bits that, when it reaches the processor, opens and closes the right internal paths so that, say, two numbers get added and the result lands in a particular storage slot. A program, at the bottom, is just a long list of these patterns. That list is called **machine code**.

Machine code is miserable to write by hand. Instructions do almost nothing on their own, so a simple formula can take dozens of them, and every memory address has to be tracked manually. Change one thing near the top and addresses further down shift. The next step up, **assembly language**, replaces the bit patterns with short names like ADD and JMP, but it is still a one-for-one listing of machine instructions for one specific kind of chip. Code written for one processor family is useless on another.

That was programming in the early 1950s. IBM's own history of the era says programmers laboriously wrote out rows of ones and zeros, often spent up to half their time debugging, and cost at least as much as the computers they worked on. John Backus, who would lead IBM's fix for this, described the job as hand-to-hand combat with the machine, and noted that the machine often won.
The Navy officer who taught computers to translate

Grace Hopper joined the Navy Reserve in 1943 and was sent to Harvard's Computation Laboratory to work on early computers solving problems of military significance. After the war she moved to the company building UNIVAC, the first commercial electronic computer. There, in 1952, she built a program called **A-0** that took mathematical code written by a person and turned it into machine instructions. Yale's biography of her calls it the first compiler.

The idea sounds obvious now. At the time it was close to heresy. Computers were expensive and scarce, and the received wisdom was that their time should be spent computing, not translating. When Hopper proposed in 1953 that programs could be written in English words rather than symbols, she was told it would not work. She kept going anyway, and her work fed directly into **COBOL** in 1959, which became one of the most widely used business languages in history. She stayed in uniform long enough to retire as a rear admiral at 79, then the oldest serving officer in the armed forces.

Meanwhile Backus's team at IBM was attacking the same problem for scientists. They expected six months of work; it took three years. In 1957 they released **FORTRAN**, short for formula translation, for the IBM 704. IBM's history gives a striking example of the payoff: a job that once required keying in as many as a thousand machine instructions could be expressed in 47 FORTRAN statements. Just as important, a FORTRAN program was no longer welded to one machine. Any computer with a FORTRAN compiler could run it.

blocks.title: From hand-written numbers to translators
items: Grace Hopper joins the Navy Reserve and is assigned to Harvard's Computation Laboratory.
Hopper builds A-0, an early program that translates math notation into machine code.
She proposes writing programs in English words and is told it will not work.
IBM releases FORTRAN for the IBM 704 after a three-year effort.
COBOL is defined, with Hopper as a leading figure.
Roblox begins building Luau, its own language derived from Lua 5.1.
Roblox open-sources Luau.

blocks.text: Two strategies: translate first, or translate as you go

Every language since has had to choose how to get from text to machine instructions, and there are two basic answers. Think about turning a foreign book into English. You can translate the whole book once, carefully, and hand people the finished English version. Or you can hire an interpreter who sits next to the reader and translates each sentence aloud as it comes up.

A **compiler** is the first approach. It reads your entire program before anything runs, checks it, optimizes it and writes out a complete machine code file. C, C++, Rust and Go work this way. Because the compiler sees everything at once and has plenty of time, it can make deep improvements: removing work whose result is never used, keeping hot values in the fastest storage, rearranging loops. The price is a build step before every run, and a separate build for every kind of processor.

blocks.title: What a compiler does to your code
items: Lexing: chop the raw text into tokens such as names, numbers, operators and keywords.
Parsing: arrange the tokens into a tree that captures the program's structure, called an abstract syntax tree.
Analysis: check that the program makes sense, for example that types match and variables exist.
Optimization: rewrite the program into an equivalent version that does less work.
Code generation: emit machine instructions, or bytecode, for the target.

blocks.text: An **interpreter** is the second approach. It reads the program and carries it out directly, statement by statement, without producing a standalone machine code file. Classic Python and Lua work roughly like this. You get instant feedback, the same program runs anywhere the interpreter exists, and a crash points you straight to the line that caused it. The price is speed. Every time a loop runs, the interpreter has to figure out again what each step means, a bit like an interpreter retranslating the same sentence every time it is repeated.

blocks.title: Compiled vs interpreted, the classic trade

left.head: Compile ahead of time
items: Whole program translated before it runs
Slower edit-and-test loop
Fast execution, deep optimizations
Separate build per processor type
Many errors caught before the program runs

right.head: Interpret as you go
items: Program carried out step by step
Change a line and run it immediately
Slower execution, repeated decoding work
Runs anywhere the interpreter runs
More errors appear only when that line runs

blocks.text: The middle path, and how big the gap really is

In practice almost nothing is purely one or the other. Most modern interpreters first compile source code into **bytecode**, a compact set of instructions for an imaginary processor that is much easier and faster to step through than raw text. A program called a **virtual machine** then runs the bytecode. Java pioneered this at large scale; Python, Lua and Luau all do it too.

The other trick is **just-in-time compilation**, or JIT. The program starts out interpreted, but the runtime watches which functions get called over and over and compiles those hot spots into real machine code while the program is running. JavaScript engines in web browsers lean heavily on this, which is how a language once considered slow came to run large applications.

How much does all this matter? A 2017 study by Rui Pereira and colleagues at universities in Portugal ran the same ten benchmark problems in 27 languages and measured time, energy and memory. Normalized so that C equals 1, the spread in run time was enormous. Rust nearly matched C. Java, compiled to bytecode and then JIT-compiled, took under twice as long. JavaScript, with an aggressive JIT, took about six and a half times as long. Plain interpreted Python and Lua took roughly 72 and 83 times as long.

blocks.title: Relative run time across 10 benchmarks (C = 1)
blocks.note: Benchmark programs from 2017 language versions; real applications vary widely. Luau was not tested and is much faster than the standard Lua measured here.
blocks.source: Pereira et al., Energy Efficiency across Programming Languages, SLE 2017

blocks.text: Read that chart with care. These are small, number-heavy benchmark programs written in 2017 versions of each language, and real software spends much of its time waiting on disks, networks and graphics cards, where language speed barely matters. The authors also found that the fastest language was not always the most energy-efficient. But the broad pattern is real and has a simple cause: the less translation work left for run time, the faster the program goes.
How your Roblox scripts actually run

Roblox originally chose Lua because, as the Luau team explains, it was simple, easy to embed in a larger program, and the fastest of the popular scripting languages at the time. In 2019 Roblox started building **Luau**, its own language derived from Lua 5.1, partly to get more speed. The Luau team says a key constraint shaped the whole design: on many platforms Roblox runs on, generating native machine code at run time is either prohibited by the platform vendor or impractical because of tight memory. A JIT is not always allowed. So the core of Luau had to be a very fast interpreter.

Here is what happens to your code. When you publish, your source is compiled into Luau bytecode, and according to the Luau team that compilation happens on Roblox's servers, so players' devices never see your source code at all. The compiler is a multi-pass design that parses your script into a tree and optimizes it before producing bytecode, and it is quick: the team reports it compiles about 950,000 lines of Luau per second on one core of a desktop processor. On each device, a heavily tuned interpreter written in C steps through that bytecode.

Roblox also offers a way around the interpreter for code that needs it. Putting the comment *--!native* at the top of a script, or the *@native* attribute on a single function, asks Luau to compile that code straight to machine instructions. Roblox's documentation says this currently works for server scripts and for client scripts on Android devices, and helps most with heavy math on tables and buffers rather than code that mostly calls Roblox APIs. It also warns against putting it everywhere: native code takes longer to start up, uses extra memory, and each game has a cap on how much native code it can have.

Type annotations do double duty in Luau. They catch mistakes in Studio, and the native compiler uses them to generate faster code. Roblox's docs specifically recommend annotating Vector3 arguments in native functions.

For a pole-vault obby, almost none of this is the bottleneck. Physics, rendering and networking are handled by the engine in compiled C++, and your scripts mostly tell the engine what to do. The practical lesson is to measure before optimizing. Roblox's Script Profiler shows where time actually goes, and the usual culprit is doing something every frame that only needed to happen once, not the speed of the language.
The trade Hopper saw coming

Step back and the whole history is one trade, made over and over: spend machine effort to save human effort. In the early 1950s, critics thought it wasteful to make a scarce computer translate. Hopper and Backus bet that programmer time was the real bottleneck, and they were right. Every layer since, from bytecode to JIT compilers to Luau's server-side compiler, extends the same bet. The computer does more translation so you can think in terms closer to your problem.

That bet has a quiet consequence for anyone learning to code. When you write a script, you are not commanding the machine directly. You are writing for a translator that someone else built, and its rules shape what is fast, what is safe and what errors you get. Understanding the translator, even roughly, turns some of the mysteries of programming into cause and effect. It explains why a typo in an unused branch might not crash until a player finally walks into that room, and why the same algorithm can feel instant in one language and sluggish in another.

It also says something about the work itself. The biggest leap in programming productivity did not come from faster chips. It came from a translator, an idea that a Navy reservist was told would not work. The people who build the layers in between, compilers, engines, tools, often change more than the people who build on top of them.

takeaways: A processor understands only numbered machine instructions; every language needs a translator to get there.
Compilers translate the whole program ahead of time for speed; interpreters translate as they go for flexibility. Most modern languages mix both with bytecode and JIT compilation.
In one 2017 benchmark study, plain interpreted Python and Lua ran roughly 70 to 80 times slower than C, while JIT-compiled JavaScript was about 6.5 times slower.
Luau compiles your scripts to bytecode on Roblox's servers and runs them on a fast interpreter; --!native can compile hot math-heavy code to machine instructions where supported.
Profile before optimizing. In games, the usual slowdown is unnecessary work every frame, not the language.

title: The Cloud Is a Building With a Power Bill
dek: Every stream, search and chatbot answer runs inside a windowless warehouse full of hot silicon. For most of a decade those buildings got far busier without using much more power. AI is ending that streak.

blocks.text: Upload a clip, and a progress bar fills and the file goes "to the cloud." The word is a brilliant piece of marketing, because it makes the whole thing sound weightless, like vapor drifting overhead. The real cloud is a concrete building the size of several football fields, usually somewhere with cheap land and strong power lines. It has no windows, a fence, guards, a row of diesel generators out back and a constant roar of fans. Your clip is now a pattern of charges on a drive in a metal rack in one of those buildings, and another copy is probably sitting in a second building far away in case the first one burns down.

That building has an electric bill, and the bill is becoming one of the big stories in energy. In 2023, according to a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report released by the Department of Energy, data centers used about **4.4%** of all the electricity in the United States. By 2028 the same report expects somewhere between 6.7% and 12%. To understand why, you have to look inside the building, and then look at a strange decade when computing exploded and its energy use barely moved.
Inside the engine room

Strip a data center down and it has three jobs: deliver power, do computing, and get rid of heat. The computing happens in **servers**, which are flat computers without screens, stacked in tall cabinets called racks. Row after row of racks fills the floor. Each server has processors, memory and network connections; some racks are mostly hard drives and flash storage; others hold switches that tie thousands of machines into one network.

The power side would look familiar to anyone who has stood a watch in an engine room. Utility power arrives at high voltage and is stepped down by transformers. Switchgear routes it. Before it reaches the servers it passes through an **uninterruptible power supply**, a bank of batteries that can carry the load for the seconds or minutes it takes the backup generators to start. Then power distribution units split it out rack by rack. Almost everything is duplicated, two feeds and two supplies per server, because a single dropped breaker can knock a popular service offline for millions of people.

Then there is the heat. A processor is, from an energy point of view, an extremely sophisticated space heater. Nearly every watt that goes in comes out as warmth that has to be carried away, or the chips throttle and fail. Classic designs blow chilled air up through the floor into a cold aisle in front of the racks, let the servers exhale into a hot aisle behind them, and send that hot air back to cooling units that dump the heat outside through chillers or cooling towers. The newest AI racks pack so much power into so little space that air struggles to keep up, which is why liquid cooling plumbed straight to the chips is spreading.

Where these buildings go is not random. Operators hunt for three things: cheap and plentiful electricity, fat fiber-optic routes, and land near a substation that can be upgraded. Cool climates help, because outside air can do some of the cooling for free for much of the year. Google's own list of campuses runs from The Dalles, Oregon, on the Columbia River, to Hamina, Finland, and Fredericia, Denmark. The location decision is, at bottom, an electrical engineering decision.

Reliability drives the cost. A hospital or a bank cannot tell customers the cloud is down for a few hours. So designers stack layers of redundancy: spare cooling units, spare generators, fuel stored on site, and the ability to shift work to another building in another region if a whole site goes dark. All of that equipment sits idle most of the time, waiting, and some of it draws power just to stay ready. Redundancy is one reason a building's overhead never quite reaches zero.

blocks.title: Where a watt goes in a data center
items: High-voltage utility power is stepped down by transformers and routed by switchgear.
An uninterruptible power supply (batteries) bridges any gap until backup generators start.
Power distribution units feed each rack, usually by two independent paths.
Servers turn the electricity into computation, and nearly all of it into heat.
Fans, chillers, cooling towers or liquid loops carry that heat outside, which costs more electricity.

blocks.text: One number that grades the whole building

The industry's favorite scorecard is **PUE**, power usage effectiveness. It is the total power the building draws divided by the power that actually reaches the computers. A PUE of 2.0 means that for every watt doing computing, another watt is spent on cooling fans, power conversion losses and lighting. A perfect building would score 1.0, with every watt landing in a chip.

Google publishes its numbers, and in 2025 its fleet averaged a PUE of **1.09**, meaning overhead added only about 9% on top of the computing load. Google's own page cites the Uptime Institute's 2025 global survey, in which the average across respondents' data centers was **1.54**. That gap matters. In a typical facility, roughly a third of the electricity never touches a processor. In the best ones, almost all of it does.

items.label: Google's 2025 fleet-wide average PUE
Global average PUE, Uptime Institute 2025 survey
A theoretically perfect building

blocks.source: Google Data Centers efficiency page, 2026 (citing Uptime Institute, 2025)

blocks.text: PUE has a blind spot, though. It grades the building, not the work. A data center full of old, idle servers can post a beautiful PUE while wasting most of its power on machines doing nothing. To see the bigger picture you have to look at how much computing the whole system delivers per unit of energy, and that is where the story gets surprising.
The decade that broke the forecasts

Around 2010, a lot of people expected data center electricity to explode. Internet traffic was soaring, smartphones were taking off, and streaming video was about to swallow the evenings of half the planet. Simple projections that multiplied energy by traffic growth produced frightening numbers.

They were wrong. In 2020 a team led by Eric Masanet published a careful bottom-up recount in the journal *Science*, built from data on actual servers, drives, network gear and buildings. They estimated global data center energy use at about 194 terawatt-hours in 2010 and about 205 TWh in 2018, around 1% of the world's electricity. That is a rise of just **6%**. Over the same years, the number of computing workloads running in data centers rose by **550%**, about six and a half times. Storage capacity grew about 26-fold and data center internet traffic about 11-fold.

blocks.title: How much each measure grew, 2010 to 2018 (global)
blocks.note: Demand for computing grew several times over while total energy rose only about 6%.
blocks.source: Masanet et al., Science, 2020

blocks.text: How do you do six times the work on almost the same power? Three things happened at once. Servers got more efficient: the paper estimates energy per computation fell sharply, and the energy intensity per workload dropped about 20% a year. **Virtualization** let one physical server run many virtual ones instead of each company keeping its own half-idle box humming in a closet. And the work moved. In 2010, 79% of computing instances lived in smaller traditional data centers; by 2018, 89% lived in large cloud and hyperscale facilities, which run far lower PUEs because they can afford engineering that a small server room never could.
The cloud's quiet trick was consolidation. Thousands of underused server closets were replaced by a few giant, carefully engineered buildings. Same work, far less wasted power.

The authors did not declare victory. They warned that these efficiency gains were a resource that could be used up, and that the next doubling of computing demand might arrive within three to four years. That warning turned out to be prescient.
Why the curve is bending up

The Berkeley Lab report traces what happened next in the United States. Data centers used about 58 TWh in 2014 and about 176 TWh in 2023, roughly a tripling. The report projects 325 to 580 TWh by 2028, a range wide enough to show how uncertain everyone is, but even the low end is close to double. The International Energy Agency, looking at the whole world in its 2025 *Energy and AI* report, estimated data centers used about 415 TWh in 2024, around 1.5% of global electricity, and projected about 945 TWh by 2030. That is roughly what all of Japan uses in a year today.

blocks.title: US data center electricity use
blocks.note: 2028 values are the bounds of LBNL's projected range.
blocks.source: LBNL 2024 report via US Department of Energy, 2024

blocks.text: The driver is AI. Training a large model means running thousands of graphics processors flat out for weeks. Answering questions with it, called **inference**, is cheaper per request but happens billions of times. According to the IEA figures, servers built for AI accounted for about 24% of server electricity demand and 15% of total data center demand in 2024, and they are the fastest-growing slice. Some researchers think even those numbers are low.

Notice what is not happening: the hardware is not getting worse. Google says its data centers delivered more than three times as much computing per unit of energy in 2025 as five years earlier, largely thanks to its custom AI chips. Efficiency is still improving fast. Demand is simply growing faster.
The efficiency trap

Economists have a name for this, borrowed from a nineteenth-century argument about coal. William Stanley Jevons noticed that more efficient steam engines did not reduce Britain's coal use. They made steam power cheaper, so people found many more things to do with it, and total coal burned went up. The **Jevons paradox** says that when you make a resource cheaper to use, you can end up using more of it, not less.

Computing may be the cleanest example in history. Every time the cost of a calculation fell, someone found a new use for calculation that would have been absurd at the old price: streaming 4K video to a phone, keeping every photo you ever took, letting a language model draft an email. The 2010s were a race in which efficiency happened to keep pace with demand. In the 2020s, AI turned demand into a sprint. Efficiency did not lose; it was outrun.

This changes what the real bottleneck is. For years the limit on computing was chips. Increasingly the limit is electricity: getting enough generation built, and enough transmission lines and substations to deliver it. The IEA estimates that around a fifth of planned data center projects could face delays connecting to the grid. That is why tech companies now sign long contracts directly with power plants, including nuclear plants, and why utilities in data center hubs are rewriting their growth forecasts.

blocks.title: Two ways to read the same trend

left.head: Worry
items: Data center demand could double US share of electricity within a few years.
New load can strain local grids and raise prices for everyone else.
Efficiency gains are being swallowed by ever-larger AI models.

right.head: Context
items: Globally data centers are still around 1.5% of electricity use.
Per unit of computing, energy use keeps falling quickly.
Projections have been badly wrong before, in both directions.

blocks.text: What the meter is really measuring

It is tempting to ask whether all this power is wasted, and there is no clean answer, because it depends on what the computing is for. A data center that runs weather models, power grid controls and medical imaging is buying something real. One that spends its watts serving endless autoplay is buying something too, just something more debatable. The electricity meter cannot tell the difference. Only people can.

What the meter does do is puncture the idea that the digital world is weightless. Every "free" app has a physical cost that someone pays: in steel, copper, water for cooling, and megawatt-hours from a real generator turning somewhere. Next time a feed refreshes or a chatbot answers in two seconds, it is worth picturing the building behind it, the transformers humming, the chillers pumping, and the battery banks waiting for the moment the grid blinks.

And for anyone who spends their days keeping power flowing to critical loads, there is a quieter lesson. The most advanced software on Earth still depends on the oldest problem in electrical engineering: make enough power, deliver it reliably, and get the heat out. The AI age turns out to run on the same fundamentals as a ship's engine room.

takeaways: The cloud is physical: racks of servers plus transformers, batteries, generators and cooling, and nearly every watt ends up as heat.
PUE compares total building power to computing power; Google reports 1.09 versus a 1.54 global survey average.
From 2010 to 2018, data center computing grew about 6.5-fold while global energy use rose only about 6%, thanks to efficiency, virtualization and consolidation.
AI has broken that plateau: US data centers went from 58 TWh in 2014 to 176 TWh in 2023 and may reach 325 to 580 TWh by 2028.
Cheaper computing tends to create more demand for computing; the bottleneck is shifting from chips to power plants and grid connections.

title: Every Save Button Is a Promise
dek: Databases are the part of software that remembers. Their real job is not storing data but keeping promises when servers crash halfway through, and the ideas behind them decide whether a game's players ever lose their progress.

blocks.text: A player in a Roblox game spends 400 Robux on a new pole. At the exact moment the purchase goes through, the game server crashes. Three outcomes are possible. The player paid and got the pole, which is fine. The player did not pay and did not get the pole, which is also fine; they can try again. Or the player paid and got nothing, or got the pole and paid nothing. Those last two are the disasters, the ones that turn into angry posts, refund requests and players who never come back.

The difference between those outcomes is not luck. It is the job of a **database**, and it is one of the most quietly important ideas in computing. Banks, airlines, hospitals and every online game rely on the same handful of tricks to make sure that when something is saved, it stays saved, and that a crash halfway through never leaves the world in a half-finished state. Once you see how it works, you start noticing these promises everywhere.
The man who said: ask for what, not how

In the 1960s, storing business data was painful. According to IBM's history, early databases used rigid hierarchical structures with navigational paths spelling out where every record physically sat, often on magnetic tape. To get one fact out, a programmer frequently had to write an entire program that walked through the structure step by step. Change how the data was stored and every program that touched it broke.

In 1970 Edgar "Ted" Codd, a mathematician at IBM's San Jose research lab, published a paper called "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks." His idea was to put everything in plain **tables**, rows and columns, like a spreadsheet, and to link tables by matching values instead of physical pointers. A Players table and a Purchases table connect simply because both contain a player ID. More importantly, you would ask the database *what* you wanted, such as every purchase over 100 Robux this week, and let the database figure out *how* to fetch it.

Plenty of people were skeptical that this could be fast enough. IBM's System R project, started in 1973, proved it could. Along the way Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce designed the query language that became **SQL**, and Patricia Selinger built a cost-based optimizer that automatically chooses an efficient plan for each query. IBM shipped its DB2 database in 1983, and a small company that later renamed itself Oracle beat IBM to market with a commercial relational database in the late 1970s. Half a century later, the relational model is still the default way the world stores important data.

items: Codd proposes the relational model at IBM.
Bayer and McCreight publish the B-tree, the index structure most databases still use.
IBM's System R project begins; SQL is born inside it.
Haerder and Reuter coin the term ACID; IBM ships DB2.

blocks.text: Finding one row in a billion

Suppose a game has ten million players and a server needs one player's save file. The naive method is to read every row until you find the right ID. That works fine for a hundred rows and terribly for ten million. Databases avoid it with an **index**, the same idea as the index at the back of a technical manual: a sorted structure that tells you where to look, so you do not have to read every page.

The index structure almost every database uses was published in 1972 by Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight: the **B-tree**. Picture a tree in which each node holds hundreds of sorted keys and pointers. At the top node you see which range your ID falls into and follow that pointer down one level, then do it again. Because each node fans out so widely, the tree stays very shallow. If every node holds 500 keys, three levels can point to 500 × 500 × 500 = 125 million entries, so finding any one of them takes only a few hops instead of millions of reads. B-trees were also designed to match how disks work: each node fits in one block that the disk can read in a single trip.

blocks.title: Looking up player 48,213,907 with a B-tree
items: Read the root node: IDs from 40 million to 50 million are down pointer 7.
Read that node: IDs 48.0 to 48.5 million are down pointer 212.
Read that leaf node: it lists the exact disk location of player 48,213,907.
Read that one row. Three or four reads instead of scanning millions.

blocks.text: Indexes are not free. Every time a row is added or changed, every index on that table has to be updated too, so each extra index makes writes a little slower and takes extra space. Database design is full of trade-offs like that: making the common question fast, without making everything else slow.
The bank transfer problem

Here is the problem that keeps database engineers up at night. Moving $100 from account A to account B takes two steps: subtract 100 from A, add 100 to B. If the power fails between those steps, $100 has vanished. If two transfers from A run at the same moment, both might read the same starting balance and the account could go negative. Multiply that by millions of operations a second, any of which can be interrupted at any instant, and you see why this is hard.

The answer is the **transaction**: a group of operations the database treats as a single unit. In 1983 Theo Haerder and Andreas Reuter gave the guarantees a name that stuck, **ACID**, and it is worth knowing because nearly every serious database is described in those terms.

items: **Atomicity**: all of the transaction happens, or none of it does. No half-transfers.
**Consistency**: every transaction moves the data from one valid state to another; rules like "balances can't go negative" are never broken.
**Isolation**: transactions running at the same time do not see each other's half-finished work; the result is as if they ran one after another.
**Durability**: once the database says "committed," the change survives crashes and power loss.

blocks.text: Durability is usually achieved with a simple and very old-fashioned idea: write it down before you do it. The database first appends a description of the change to a **log** on disk and forces that log to stable storage. Only then does it report success. If the machine crashes, on restart the database reads the log, finishes any committed changes that had not been fully applied, and undoes anything that was not committed. Anyone who has kept a narrative log on watch knows the principle: if it is not written down, it did not happen, and the log is what lets the next person reconstruct the truth.

Isolation is handled differently. The classic tool is a **lock**: before a transaction changes account A, it claims A, and any other transaction that wants A has to wait its turn, much like a tagout keeps two people from working the same breaker at once. Locks are safe but can slow things down, and two transactions can end up each waiting on a lock the other holds, a standoff called a deadlock. Databases detect those and cancel one side so the other can finish. Many modern systems also keep several versions of a row, so readers can see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers at all.
Atomicity is what makes a crash survivable. If every change is all-or-nothing, the worst case is that you have to try again, never that you are left with a broken half-state.
How your Roblox game saves (and loses) progress

Roblox's data stores are not a full SQL database, but Roblox's own documentation says they behave similarly to tables in databases, and every one of the problems above shows up. A popular game runs many servers at once. A player might leave one server and join another a second later, while the first server is still saving. Two servers can try to write the same player's record at nearly the same moment. Network calls fail.

The documentation is blunt about the most common mistake. **SetAsync** simply overwrites a key without reading it first, and Roblox warns it can cause data inconsistency if two servers set the same key at the same time. **UpdateAsync** reads the latest saved value into your function before writing, which is slower and counts against both read and write limits, but it reduces lost updates. Roblox's best-practices page recommends UpdateAsync whenever a write depends on the current value or several servers might touch the same key. That is the bank transfer problem wearing a game skin.

blocks.title: Two ways to save a player's coins

left.head: SetAsync
items: Writes your value, ignoring what's there
Fast, uses only write budget
Two servers saving at once: the last one wins, the other's changes vanish
Fine for brand-new keys or values that don't depend on the old one

right.head: UpdateAsync
items: Reads the current saved value, then applies your change
Slower, uses read and write budget
Built for several servers touching the same key
Return nil from the function to cancel the write

blocks.text: The same docs give several other database lessons in miniature. Keep each player's data under one key when it fits within the **4 MB** per-key size limit, so related values can change together atomically. Keep a copy of the player's data in server memory during play and save periodically, when the player leaves and when the server shuts down; Roblox's own sample uses a 180-second save interval. Wrap every call in pcall and retry failures with growing delays, but be careful: an old save that retries after a newer one succeeds can overwrite fresh progress. And remember that a failed call only means the server never heard back. The write might have gone through anyway.

That last point is the deepest one. In distributed systems you cannot always know whether something happened. Good design assumes every step can fail at the worst moment and makes sure the result is still sane, which in practice means making saves all-or-nothing and making it safe to repeat an operation that might have succeeded already.
The most common database on Earth

Ask developers which databases they use and the answer is dominated by relational systems that descend directly from Codd's idea. In Stack Overflow's 2025 developer survey, PostgreSQL led, followed by MySQL and SQLite.

blocks.title: Databases developers used extensively in the past year
blocks.note: Based on about 26,000 respondents who answered the database question.
blocks.source: Stack Overflow Developer Survey, 2025

blocks.text: SQLite deserves a special mention, because you have almost certainly used it thousands of times today without knowing. It is a complete SQL database packed into a small library that runs inside an app, with no separate server. Its developers list it inside every Android device, every iPhone, every Mac, every Windows 10 and 11 installation and every major web browser. Since each smartphone holds hundreds of SQLite database files, they estimate there are likely over **one trillion** SQLite databases in active use. Your messages, browser history and many games' local settings very likely live in one.

Not everything on that chart is relational. Redis keeps data in memory for speed and is often used as a cache in front of a slower database. MongoDB stores flexible documents instead of fixed rows and columns, which is closer to how a Roblox data store holds a player's table of values. These so-called NoSQL systems usually give up some of the strict guarantees of a classic SQL database in exchange for speed or easier scaling across many machines. Picking one is mostly a question of which promises your data really needs.

Maximum size of one Roblox data store entry

blocks.text: Designing for the crash

Most people think of a database as a big box where data sits. Engineers think of it differently: as a machine for keeping promises under failure. Storing bytes is easy. The hard part is guaranteeing that a purchase, a transfer or a saved game is either fully recorded or not recorded at all, even when servers crash, networks drop and two people act at once.

That mindset is useful well beyond code. It asks one question of any process: what happens if it stops halfway? A good procedure, like a good transaction, has a clear point at which the change is committed, a record of what was done, and a way back to a safe state if something interrupts it. That is why plant procedures have steps you sign off and why logs are kept even when nothing seems to happen. The people who invented databases arrived at the same answer as the people who run reactors: assume the interruption will come, and decide in advance what a safe half-finished state looks like.

takeaways: Codd's 1970 relational model put data in tables linked by values and let you ask what you want instead of how to fetch it.
Indexes, usually B-trees, let a database find one row among millions in a handful of reads, at the cost of slightly slower writes.
ACID transactions (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) are how databases keep promises through crashes; a write-ahead log makes durability possible.
In Roblox, prefer UpdateAsync when several servers might write the same key, keep atomic data under one key, save periodically and handle failed or uncertain writes.
For any process, ask what happens if it stops halfway, and design so the answer is safe.

title: Pictures Pulled Out of Static
dek: Every AI-generated image begins as pure random noise. The model's only real skill is guessing which part of a picture is noise, and that one skill, repeated a few dozen times, is enough to paint almost anything.

blocks.text: Ask an image generator for a submarine surfacing through Arctic ice at dawn, and here is what happens first: the program fills a grid with random numbers. No sketch, no outline, no stored photo of a submarine. Just static, the visual equivalent of an untuned TV. Then it looks at that static and asks a strange question: *if this were a noisy photo of a submarine in ice, which part of it is the noise?* It subtracts a little of its guess. Then it asks again.

After a few dozen rounds, a picture is standing where the static was. Nothing was retrieved or collaged. The image was, in a real sense, pulled out of randomness by a system that had learned, from hundreds of millions of examples, what images tend to look like. This family of systems is called **diffusion models**, and they are behind most of the AI image tools people have used since 2022. The core idea is simple enough to explain on one page, and it says something odd about what creating actually is.
Destroy it, then learn to undo it

The idea came from physics. Drop ink into a glass of water and it spreads out, or diffuses, until the water is evenly gray. Going forward is easy and predictable. Going backward, gathering the ink back into a drop, seems impossible. In 2015 Jascha Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues at Stanford and Berkeley borrowed this picture from the physics of non-equilibrium systems. Their plan: slowly destroy the structure in data by adding noise step by step, then train a neural network to reverse each small step.

The trick is that while undoing *all* the noise at once is hopeless, undoing a *tiny* bit of it is a learnable problem. If you know an image was a clean picture plus a little noise, a network can learn to estimate what that noise was. Chain thousands of these small reversals together and you can walk from pure static all the way back to a clean image.

For years this was a curiosity. Then in 2020 Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel at Berkeley showed that a carefully designed version, which they called denoising diffusion probabilistic models, produced images rivaling the best methods of the time. Their setup used 1,000 noise steps between a clean image and pure static. Within two years, diffusion had become the main way AI makes pictures.
How the model is trained

Training a diffusion model is surprisingly repetitive. There is no artist feedback and no grading of beauty. The network plays one game, billions of times: here is a damaged picture, tell me how it was damaged.

blocks.title: One training step, repeated billions of times
items: Take a real image from the training set, along with its caption.
Pick a random noise level, from barely grainy to almost pure static.
Add exactly that much random noise to the image, and remember the noise.
Show the noisy image, the noise level and the caption to the network, and ask it to predict the noise.
Measure how far its guess was from the real noise and nudge millions of internal weights to do slightly better next time.

blocks.text: Notice what the network is never asked to do: draw anything from scratch. It only ever learns to separate signal from noise. But to do that well across every noise level, it has to absorb a huge amount about the world. To tell which specks on a nearly-static image are noise and which are the faint edge of a face, it needs to know what faces look like. At low noise levels it learns fine texture, like skin pores and brushed metal. At high noise levels it learns big layout, like where a horizon tends to sit and how a body is proportioned.

Generating an image runs the same skill in reverse. Start with fresh random static. Ask the network for its best guess of the noise, remove part of it, and repeat. Early steps decide composition; late steps sharpen detail. Ho's original method ran the network 1,000 times per image, once for every noise step, which was painfully slow. Later work, such as denoising diffusion implicit models from Stanford in 2020, made sampling 10 to 50 times faster by taking bigger, smarter steps. Stable Diffusion's published example code uses 50 steps by default.

One detail of this process will feel familiar to anyone who has played Minecraft. The starting static comes from a random number generator, and that generator is set by a number called a **seed**. Use the same seed, the same prompt and the same settings, and the model produces the same image every time, because all the randomness in the process flows from that one seeded generator. Change the seed and you get a different starting static, and so a different picture that still fits the prompt. It is the same principle a game uses when one seed number reproduces an entire world: a tiny amount of randomness, fed through fixed rules, unfolds into something huge and specific.

blocks.title: Generating an image
items: Start from pure random static
Network predicts the noise in the current image
Remove part of the predicted noise
The image is slightly cleaner; repeat
After the last step, decode to full-size pixels

blocks.text: Working in a compressed world

Diffusion on raw pixels is expensive. A 512 by 512 color image is 786,432 numbers, and the network has to process all of them at every step. In 2021 Robin Rombach and colleagues in Munich and Heidelberg published a fix that became the basis of Stable Diffusion: do the diffusion in a compressed space instead. First, train a separate network called an **autoencoder** to squash images into a compact code and expand them back with little visible loss. Then run the whole noise-and-denoise process on the compact code.

Stable Diffusion's model card spells out the numbers. The autoencoder shrinks each side of the image by a factor of 8 and keeps 4 channels, so a 512 by 512 image becomes a 64 by 64 by 4 grid: 16,384 numbers instead of 786,432, about 48 times fewer. The diffusion model works entirely in that small space, and only at the very end does the decoder turn the result back into full-size pixels.

blocks.title: Numbers the model must handle per image
blocks.note: Working in the compressed latent space cuts the work at every step by about 48 times.
blocks.source: Stable Diffusion v1-4 model card (CompVis); arithmetic from stated shapes

blocks.text: That compression has a cost, and you have probably seen it. The model card lists its own limitations plainly: the autoencoder is lossy, the model cannot render legible text, and faces and people may come out wrong. Small, precise details are exactly what gets squeezed out of a compressed code. That is one reason early AI images had garbled lettering and strange hands.

This is also why AI images often have a recognizable look: smooth, evenly lit, a little too perfect. Every denoising step nudges the picture toward what is most likely given everything the model has seen. Strange, rare or deliberately ugly choices are, by definition, unlikely, so the process tends to sand them off unless the prompt pushes hard in their direction. The model is not choosing a style. It is drifting toward the center of everything it learned.
How words steer the static

A picture of *something* is not useful; you want a picture of *your* thing. The link between words and images came largely from a 2021 OpenAI system called **CLIP**, trained on 400 million image and caption pairs from the internet to tell which caption goes with which image. In doing that, it learned to place words and pictures in a shared space of meaning. Stable Diffusion v1 uses a frozen CLIP text encoder to turn your prompt into a set of numbers, and the denoising network consults those numbers at every step through a mechanism called cross-attention.

There is one more trick, and it explains a setting you may have seen in image tools. In 2022 Ho and Tim Salimans described **classifier-free guidance**. During training, the caption is sometimes thrown away, so the network learns to denoise both with a prompt and without one; Stable Diffusion v1-4 dropped the text 10 percent of the time. When generating, the model makes both guesses and then pushes the image further in the direction the prompt pulls it, away from the generic guess. Turn the guidance scale up and you get images that follow the prompt more literally but look more alike; turn it down and you get variety at the cost of accuracy.
The model never looks up a matching image. Your prompt changes the model's guess about which parts of the static are noise, and the picture is whatever is left when the noise is gone.
Where the knowledge comes from, and what it owes

All of that learning had to come from somewhere. The open dataset behind Stable Diffusion, **LAION-5B**, contains 5.85 billion image and text pairs gathered from the public web and filtered with CLIP. Stable Diffusion v1 was trained on English-language subsets of it. The compute was substantial: the model card lists 256 Nvidia A100 GPUs and an estimated 150,000 GPU-hours.

items.label: Image and text pairs in the LAION-5B web dataset
A100 GPU-hours to train Stable Diffusion v1-4 (estimate)
Near-copies of training images found among 175 million generations

blocks.source: Schuhmann et al. 2022; Stable Diffusion v1-4 model card; Carlini et al. 2023

blocks.text: This raises the question artists, photographers and courts have been fighting over since 2023: does the model copy? A team led by Nicholas Carlini at Google, working with academic researchers, tested it directly. They took the 350,000 most-duplicated images in the training data, generated 500 images for each of their captions, 175 million images in total, and searched for outputs that matched training images. They found 109 near-copies. The paper's conclusion was that diffusion models can memorize and reproduce training images, and that they are less private than older kinds of image generators.

Both halves of that result matter. Memorization was rare, and it was concentrated in images that appeared in the training data many times, often a hundred copies or more; the Stable Diffusion model card admits the data was not deduplicated. A rough calculation shows why most images cannot be stored: Rombach's text-to-image model had 1.45 billion parameters and was trained on 400 million images, which leaves fewer than four parameters per training image. Mostly, the model learns patterns rather than pictures. But *mostly* is not *never*, and whether learning patterns from someone's work without permission is fair use is a legal question, not a technical one. Artists and Getty Images filed lawsuits over AI training in 2023 in the US and UK, and how copyright applies to training is still being argued in courts and legislatures. Check current rulings rather than trusting any summary, this one included.

There is also the question of whose world the model learned. The Stable Diffusion model card warns that because its training captions were mostly English, white and Western cultures are often set as the default, and prompts in other languages work worse. A model trained on the internet reproduces the internet's habits, including its blind spots.
What this means if you make things

For a small game team, these tools are genuinely useful for the parts of the job that are about exploring: rough concept art, mood boards, texture ideas, a dozen thumbnail directions to react to. Check the rules of whatever platform you publish on, and be careful with anything that looks like a real brand, a real person or a specific artist's signature style, because that is where both legal and memorization risks concentrate.

They are also a decent teacher, if you use them that way. Generating twenty variations of a scene and asking why some read clearly at thumbnail size and others turn to mush is a fast lesson in composition, contrast and silhouette. The tool is good at showing you the space of obvious options quickly. Deciding which option serves the game, and when to throw all of them out, is a design skill the tool does not have.

The deeper lesson is about what these models are. A diffusion model is, in a sense, a machine for producing the most plausible image given a prompt: what pictures with that caption *tend* to look like. That is powerful, and it is also the limit. Plausible is the average of what already exists. The weird mechanic, the color palette nobody uses, the specific feeling you want a player to have when they clear the last vault, none of that is in the noise. That part, for now, is still yours to bring.

takeaways: Diffusion models are trained only to predict the noise in damaged images; generating is the same skill run backward from pure static.
Stable Diffusion works in a compressed latent space about 48 times smaller than the pixel image, which makes it fast but costs fine detail like text.
Your prompt steers the denoising at every step; the guidance scale trades prompt accuracy against variety.
Copying is rare but real: researchers pulled 109 near-copies out of 175 million generations, mostly of heavily duplicated images.
AI images are the most plausible picture for a prompt. Originality, and the legal homework, are still on you.

title: The Year Chips Stopped Getting Faster
dek: For decades, software got quicker just by waiting for new hardware. Around 2005 that free ride ended, and nearly everything about computing has been bent around the loss ever since.

blocks.text: In November 1971, Intel advertised its first microprocessor, the 4004. It had 2,300 transistors, with circuit features about 10 microns, or 10,000 nanometers, across. Today, a single Nvidia Blackwell GPU carries 208 billion transistors. That's about 90 million times as many.

Now look at a different number. In 2004, Intel's Pentium 4 reached 3.8 gigahertz, meaning its clock ticked 3.8 billion times a second. Twenty years later, in 2024, Intel billed its Core i9-14900KS as the world's fastest desktop processor. Its top boost speed: 6.2 gigahertz. In two decades, while transistor counts kept exploding, clock speed went up by less than a factor of two.

So here's the puzzle. If we kept cramming in more and more transistors, why did processors stop getting dramatically faster at the thing everyone used to brag about? And where did all those extra transistors go? The answer explains why phones and laptops have so many cores, why AI runs on graphics cards, and why the next big gains in computing may come from programmers rather than physicists.

blocks.text: A prediction that became a schedule

In 1965, Gordon Moore, then research director at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote an article for *Electronics* magazine. He had five data points, from 1959 to 1964, showing how many components could be put on an integrated circuit at the lowest cost per component. The count was doubling every year. He extrapolated boldly: by 1975, a chip could hold 65,000 components.

He was roughly right. In 1975, now at Intel, Moore revised the pace to a doubling every two years, crediting better lithography, bigger wafers and what he called circuit and device cleverness. Somebody, often said to be the engineer Carver Mead, started calling it Moore's law, and the name stuck.

It's worth feeling how strong that compounding is. Doubling every two years for fifty years is 25 doublings, and 2 multiplied by itself 25 times is about 33 million. Few things people build have ever improved like that. Cars, planes and power plants got better by percentages per decade. Chips got better by factors of millions. That's why it was so easy to believe the trend was permanent.

Two things about the law are easy to miss. First, it was never a law of nature. It was an observation about economics: how many components you could put on a chip *at the lowest cost*. Second, it became self-fulfilling. Historian Cyrus Mody has argued that the whole semiconductor industry, from equipment makers to chip designers, used Moore's law as a shared target, planning years ahead to hit the next doubling on schedule. It worked less like a prediction and more like a drumbeat.

blocks.title: Fifty years of shrinking
items: Moore predicts components per chip will double every year
Intel 4004: 2,300 transistors, about 10-micron features
Moore revises the pace to doubling every two years
Clock speeds rise more than 200-fold
Pentium 4 reaches 3.8 GHz; the power wall arrives
