title: AI Has Died Twice
dek: Artificial intelligence has been declared the future, then a dead end, then the future again, for seventy years. The pattern explains a lot about today's hype, and about what actually made machines smart.

blocks.text: In July 1958 the US Office of Naval Research invited reporters to watch a computer learn. The machine was an IBM 704, a five-ton system that filled a room. Researchers fed it punch cards marked on either the left or the right. After 50 trials, according to Cornell's account of the event, it had taught itself to tell the two apart. Its creator, a young Cornell psychologist named Frank Rosenblatt, called his program the **perceptron** and described it as a machine capable of an original idea.

The press went wild. The *New York Times* headline read "NEW NAVY DEVICE LEARNS BY DOING." The *New Yorker* called it the first serious rival to the human brain ever devised. Within about a decade the idea was widely treated as a dead end, funding dried up, and Rosenblatt died in 1971 without seeing it vindicated. It took roughly half a century for the descendants of his perceptron to recognize faces, translate languages and hold conversations.

That arc, from wild promise to collapse to unexpected triumph, is not a one-off. It is the shape of the whole history of artificial intelligence. Knowing it is the best defense against both kinds of nonsense you hear about AI today: that it is about to do everything, and that it is just a fad.
The question that started it

In 1950 the British mathematician Alan Turing, who had helped break German naval codes during the war, published a paper in the philosophy journal *Mind* titled "Computing Machinery and Intelligence." It opened by proposing to consider whether machines can think, then immediately set that question aside as too vague to argue about. Instead he offered a test he called the imitation game: a judge exchanges typed messages with a hidden person and a hidden machine, and tries to tell which is which.

Turing's move was quietly radical. He stopped asking what thinking *is* and asked what thinking *does*. If a machine's conversation could not be told apart from a person's, on what grounds would you deny it was thinking? He also made a prediction: that in about fifty years, computers with far more memory than existed in 1950 would play the game well enough that an average judge would have no better than a 70% chance of picking correctly after five minutes. He was early on the date, but not on the direction.
One summer to crack intelligence

On August 31, 1955, four researchers, John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester of IBM and Claude Shannon of Bell Labs, wrote a funding proposal that gave the field its name. They asked for a two-month, ten-man study of "artificial intelligence" at Dartmouth College in the summer of 1956. Their founding assumption was that every aspect of learning or intelligence could in principle be described so precisely that a machine could simulate it. They were confident that a carefully chosen group could make a significant advance on language, abstraction and self-improvement in one summer.

One line in that proposal is worth rereading today. The authors wrote that the main obstacle was not the speed or memory of computers, but our inability to write programs that took full advantage of what we had. In other words: the hardware is fine, we just need to be cleverer. Hold on to that sentence. The next sixty years would turn it almost exactly upside down.

blocks.title: Booms and winters
items: Turing publishes the imitation game in Mind.
The Dartmouth summer project names the field.
The Navy-funded perceptron learns to sort punch cards.
Minsky and Papert's book Perceptrons highlights the limits of simple networks.
The Lighthill report helps cut British AI funding: the first winter.
Expert systems boom, then bust: the second winter.
Backpropagation makes multi-layer networks trainable.
Deep Blue beats world chess champion Garry Kasparov.
A deep network wins the ImageNet challenge by a wide margin.
Google researchers introduce the transformer.

blocks.text: Two camps and two winters

Early AI split into two tribes. The **symbolic** camp believed intelligence was manipulating symbols with rules, like a logician proving theorems, so the job was to write down the right rules. The **connectionist** camp, Rosenblatt's tribe, believed intelligence emerged from many simple neuron-like units adjusting their connections as they learned, so the job was to build learners and feed them examples.

For decades the symbolic camp held the money and the prestige. In 1969 Minsky and Seymour Papert published a book, *Perceptrons*, that rigorously showed what a single layer of artificial neurons could not do, including some embarrassingly simple pattern problems. Networks with more layers could in principle get around those limits, but nobody had a good way to train them. Interest and funding drifted away from neural networks.

Then the symbolic side hit its own wall. In 1972 the British Science Research Council asked the applied mathematician Sir James Lighthill to survey the field. His report, published in 1973, concluded that progress had been disappointing and that the most ambitious work, such as general-purpose robots, had been very disappointing indeed. His central technical complaint was the **combinatorial explosion**: methods that worked on toy problems collapsed on real ones, because the number of possibilities to search grows explosively with each added step. Funding in Britain was cut sharply, and AI entered its first winter.

In the 1980s the field revived with **expert systems**, programs that encoded the rules of human specialists, such as how to configure a computer order or diagnose an infection, as long chains of if-then statements. Companies spent heavily. But the systems were brittle. They failed in strange ways the moment a case fell outside their rules, and every new situation required an expert and a programmer to sit down and write more rules. By the end of the decade the market had collapsed. That was the second winter.
Both winters had the same cause: people promised general intelligence and delivered systems that only worked inside narrow, hand-built boundaries.
The comeback nobody scheduled

While the spotlight was elsewhere, the connectionists kept working. In 1986 David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams published a short paper in *Nature* describing **backpropagation**, a way to train networks with hidden layers by sending the error at the output backward through the network and nudging every connection in the direction that would shrink it. The idea had earlier roots, but this paper made it practical and popular. The technique is still the engine of nearly all modern AI.

For years, though, it did not win. Neural networks were slow to train, data was scarce, and on most benchmarks other methods were as good or better. When IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in New York in May 1997, it did so with very little learning at all. IBM's own history says it evaluated about 200 million chess positions per second. It won by brute-force search, a lot of hand-tuned chess knowledge, and special hardware.

blocks.text: The turn came from an unglamorous place: a giant labeled photo collection called ImageNet and an annual contest to classify its pictures into 1,000 categories. In 2010 the winning entry got 28.2% of its top-five guesses wrong. In 2011 the winner managed 25.8%. Then in 2012 a University of Toronto team, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Hinton, entered a deep neural network trained on graphics cards. It scored **16.4%**, and 15.3% in a version trained with extra data. That was not an incremental gain. It was a different league.

blocks.title: Winning error rate in the ImageNet classification challenge
blocks.note: One trained human annotator, tested on 1,500 images, erred on about 5.1%.
blocks.source: Russakovsky et al., IJCV, 2015; He et al., 2015

blocks.text: Within three years everyone had switched. By 2014 the winning network was down to 6.7%, and in 2015 a Microsoft team's 152-layer network hit 3.57%. The challenge organizers had measured a carefully trained human expert on a sample of the test images at about 5.1%, so the machines had, on this one narrow task, passed a person who had practiced hard. In 2017 Google researchers introduced the **transformer**, an architecture built for language, and at the end of 2022 a chatbot built on it reached the public and made AI a dinner-table subject.

Notice what the winning network actually used. Layers of artificial neurons: Rosenblatt's idea, 1958. Backpropagation: popularized 1986. What was new was the scale: millions of labeled images and graphics processors able to do the math fast. The old ideas had not been wrong. They had been starved.

There is a detail in that 2012 result any gamer will appreciate. The Toronto network was trained on two consumer graphics cards, the same kind of hardware sold to people who wanted smoother frame rates. Graphics chips are built to do enormous numbers of simple multiplications in parallel, because that is what drawing millions of pixels requires, and it happens to be exactly what training a neural network requires too. The gaming market had spent years funding the hardware that AI researchers were missing. Nobody planned that. It is one more example of how progress in this field kept arriving from directions no roadmap predicted.
The bitter lesson

In 2019 the reinforcement-learning pioneer Rich Sutton wrote a short essay called "The Bitter Lesson" that many researchers now treat as the moral of the whole story. Looking back over seventy years, he argued that general methods that use computation, mainly search and learning, end up beating methods built on human cleverness about the specific problem, and by a large margin. The reason is that computing keeps getting cheaper, so a method that can soak up more computation keeps improving, while hand-crafted knowledge stays stuck where its authors left it.
General methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective.
blocks.by: Rich Sutton, The Bitter Lesson, 2019

blocks.text: He called it bitter because researchers keep relearning it against their own wishes. Chess experts wanted programs that played like grandmasters think. Speech researchers wanted systems built on knowledge of phonemes and the vocal tract. In each case, a statistical method that simply crunched more data won. Set that next to the Dartmouth line about hardware being sufficient and the irony is sharp. The founders bet on clever programs over raw capacity. The field's biggest wins came from the opposite bet.

It is worth being honest about what the lesson does not prove. It does not prove that scaling up today's methods will produce human-level intelligence, and serious researchers disagree loudly about that. It also does not mean human insight is useless: backpropagation, the transformer and the design of ImageNet were all human insights. They were insights about how to build systems that learn, rather than insights handed directly to the machine.
Reading the hype cycle

Seventy years of AI history leave a few patterns that are useful whenever someone tells you what AI will do next. Short-term predictions have usually been too optimistic: one summer, ten years, just around the corner. Long-term dismissals have usually been too pessimistic: the perceptron was mocked, neural nets were unfashionable for decades, and they now run the most-used software on Earth. And there is a well-known habit researchers call the **AI effect**: once a machine can do something, people stop calling it intelligence. Chess was the summit of human intellect until a computer won; then it was just search.

There is also a personal version of the bitter lesson that applies to anyone learning a hard skill. Rules you are handed get you started, but they top out. What keeps improving is the general process that turns practice and feedback into skill: many repetitions, honest error signals, small corrections. That is what backpropagation does to a network, and it is roughly what qualification boards and drills do to a crew. The machines did not get smart because someone wrote down the answers. They got smart because someone built a way for them to learn from being wrong, then gave them enough examples and enough time.

Will there be a third winter? Nobody knows. The money flowing into AI now is far larger than in either earlier boom, and so are the promises. The safest bet, history suggests, is that some of today's predictions will be embarrassingly early and others embarrassingly timid, and that the people who keep building, through the hype and through the frost, are the ones who end up being right.

takeaways: Turing in 1950 replaced 'can machines think?' with a behavioral test, and predicted progress that arrived later than he guessed but in the direction he guessed.
AI went through two winters, in the 1970s and late 1980s, after promises of general intelligence ran into narrow, brittle systems.
The neural-network ideas that now dominate date to 1958 and 1986; what changed around 2012 was data and computing power.
ImageNet's winning error fell from 28.2% in 2010 to 3.57% in 2015, passing one trained human's 5.1% on that task.
Sutton's bitter lesson: general methods that learn and search with more computation tend to beat hand-built cleverness over time.

title: The Autocomplete That Learned Too Much
dek: Every chatbot answer is built one word-fragment at a time by a machine trained only to guess what comes next. The real question is what it had to learn to guess well.

blocks.text: Type a question into a chatbot and watch the answer come back. It doesn't arrive all at once. It streams in a few characters at a time, like someone typing on the other end. That stutter isn't a design flourish. It's a window into the machine: the model is literally producing its answer one small piece at a time, and every piece is a guess.

When OpenAI introduced GPT-2 in 2019, it boiled the whole training goal down to one line. The model was trained to “predict the next word, given all of the previous words.” That's it. No grammar rules, no built-in encyclopedia, no logic module. Everything a modern **large language model** (LLM) does, from writing code to explaining reactor physics, grows out of that one almost insultingly simple objective, repeated at enormous scale.
Which raises the real puzzle: how does next-word guessing turn into something that can debug your script or walk you through a circuit? To see it, you have to follow a sentence through the machine.
Step one: turning words into numbers

A neural network can only do arithmetic, so text has to become numbers first. The model's first move is to chop your input into **tokens**, chunks of text from a fixed vocabulary. A common word like “the” is usually a single token. A rarer word gets split into fragments, so “unbelievably” might become “un,” “believ” and “ably.” This is why models sometimes fumble at counting the letters in a word: they never see letters, only chunks.

Each token is then swapped for a long list of numbers called an **embedding**. Think of it as coordinates in a space with thousands of dimensions. In GPT-3, every token became a list of 12,288 numbers. Nobody hand-assigns those coordinates. They are learned during training, and they end up arranged so that tokens used in similar ways sit near each other. “Reactor” lands closer to “turbine” than to “sandwich,” not because anyone said so, but because of the company those words keep in billions of sentences.
Step two: attention, the trick that changed everything

For years, language models read text like a ticker tape: one word at a time, left to right, carrying a fading memory of what came before. Long sentences broke them. In 2017 a team at Google published a paper with a cocky title, “Attention Is All You Need,” introducing the **transformer**. Its central idea was to let every token look directly at every other token in the passage and decide which ones matter to it.

Mechanically, it works like this. For each token, the model computes three vectors: a **query** (what am I looking for?), a **key** (what do I offer?) and a **value** (what information do I pass along if chosen?). Each token compares its query against every other token's key. Strong matches get high scores, the scores are squashed into weights that add up to one, and the token absorbs a weighted blend of everyone's values. After one round of attention, each token's numbers carry a bit of context from the whole passage.

Take the sentence “The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big.” What does “it” mean? You know instantly: the trophy. In a transformer, the token “it” sends out its query, and a trained model weights “trophy” heavily, because big things not fitting into containers is how trophies and suitcases work. Change “big” to “small” and the right answer flips to the suitcase. Attention is the machinery that lets the model make that call.

blocks.title: What happens to your prompt
items: Your text is split into tokens, chunks from a fixed vocabulary
Each token becomes an embedding: a long list of learned numbers
Attention lets every token pull in context from every other token
Feed-forward layers transform each token's updated numbers
This repeats through dozens of stacked layers (96 in GPT-3)
The last layer gives a probability for every possible next token
One token is picked and appended, and the whole stack runs again

blocks.text: A transformer stacks this many times over. GPT-3 had 96 layers, each with 96 attention “heads” running side by side, so different heads can specialize: one tracking which noun a pronoun points to, another tracking open quote marks or unclosed brackets in code. The design also suited the hardware. Because all the tokens are processed at once instead of in sequence, transformers run well on GPUs, chips built to do thousands of multiplications in parallel. The original paper's base model trained in about 12 hours on eight GPUs. That efficiency is what made the next decade of scaling possible.

At the top of the stack, the model produces a score for every token in its vocabulary, converted into probabilities. After “The capital of France is,” almost all the probability piles onto “Paris.” The system then **samples** one token, appends it to the text, and runs the entire stack again to get the next one. A setting called **temperature** controls how adventurous that pick is: low temperature nearly always takes the top choice, high temperature gives long shots a chance. Every chatbot answer you have ever read was assembled this way, one draw at a time.

There's also a hard limit on how much the model can see at once, called the **context window**. GPT-3's was 2,048 tokens, roughly a few pages of text. Anything outside the window simply doesn't exist for the model; it has no memory between conversations unless the text is fed back in. When a long chat starts “forgetting” what you said at the beginning, that's usually the window, not a lapse in attention. Newer models have far larger windows, but the principle is the same: the model only knows what's in front of it plus what's baked into its parameters.
Step three: how 175 billion knobs get set

All of that machinery is defined by **parameters**, the numbers inside the model that decide how embeddings are formed, how queries and keys are computed, and how each layer transforms its input. Before training they are random, and the model outputs gibberish. Training is the process of nudging them, and the loop is brutally simple.

blocks.title: The training loop
items: Show a passage with the next token hidden
The model predicts probabilities for every token
Measure how wrong it was about the real next token
Backpropagation traces the error back to every parameter
Nudge every parameter slightly to shrink the error

blocks.text: The tracing step, **backpropagation**, is just the chain rule from calculus applied very carefully: it works out, for each of billions of parameters, which direction to move it so the right answer would have been a little more likely. Move them all a tiny bit, then repeat with the next chunk of text, trillions of times. This is **gradient descent**: walking downhill on a landscape of error, one small step at a time, without ever seeing the whole map.

Then comes scale. GPT-2 had 1.5 billion parameters. GPT-3, a year later, had 175 billion and was trained on 300 billion tokens, mostly filtered web pages plus books and Wikipedia. The industry assumption was that bigger was the main lever. In 2022, DeepMind ran a large set of training experiments and concluded the field had been following the wrong recipe.

blocks.title: Model size, billions of parameters
blocks.note: Chinchilla was a quarter of Gopher's size and beat it across a wide range of tests.
blocks.source: OpenAI, 2019; Brown et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022

blocks.text: Their finding: for a fixed computing budget, model size and training data should grow together. Double the parameters, double the tokens. By that rule, giant models like DeepMind's own 280-billion-parameter Gopher were badly undertrained, all brain and not enough reading. To prove it, they trained Chinchilla, a quarter of Gopher's size, on 1.4 trillion tokens, about 20 tokens per parameter, using the same compute. It outperformed Gopher and GPT-3 across a large range of tasks.

blocks.title: Training data, billions of tokens
blocks.note: Llama 3's figure is reported as “over 15 trillion” tokens.
blocks.source: Brown et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Hugging Face, 2024

blocks.text: The industry took the lesson and then sprinted past it. Meta's Llama 3 models, released in 2024 at 8 and 70 billion parameters, were trained on more than 15 trillion tokens. For the 8-billion model, that's nearly 2,000 tokens per parameter, nearly a hundred times Chinchilla's ratio. The logic is economic: a model is trained once but run for millions of users, so a smaller model that has read far more is cheaper every time anyone asks it something.
From autocomplete to assistant

A model trained only on next-token prediction, called a **base model**, isn't an assistant. It's a document continuer. Ask it “How do I troubleshoot a ground fault?” and it might reply with three more questions, because on the internet, questions often show up in lists of questions. It has learned the shape of text, not the job of answering.

Turning it into an assistant takes a second phase. First, people write example conversations showing good answers, and the model is fine-tuned on them. Then comes **reinforcement learning from human feedback** (RLHF): the model writes several answers, humans rank them, a separate model learns to predict those rankings, and the language model is tuned to produce answers that score well. In OpenAI's 2022 InstructGPT study, raters preferred answers from a 1.3-billion-parameter model trained this way over answers from the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3. A model more than 100 times smaller won, because it had been taught what the job was.

blocks.title: Base model vs. tuned assistant

left.head: Base model
items: Trained only to continue text
Treats your question as the start of a document
Imitates whatever it's shown, good or bad
Knows a lot, but not what you want

right.head: Tuned assistant
items: Further trained on example conversations
Treats your message as a request to answer
Shaped by human rankings of better and worse answers
Same knowledge, aimed at being useful

blocks.text: Why it makes things up

The flaw everyone has met is **hallucination**: a fluent, confident, completely wrong answer. A citation to a paper that doesn't exist. A function that isn't in the library. Once you understand the training objective, this stops being mysterious. The model was never trained to say true things. It was trained to say likely things, and most of the time likely and true overlap. When they don't, nothing inside the model raises a flag.

A 2025 paper by Adam Kalai and colleagues at OpenAI and Georgia Tech sharpened this into two arguments. First, some facts are essentially arbitrary, like a particular person's birthday. If a fact shows up only once in the training data, there's no pattern to learn from, and the authors argue the error rate on that kind of fact should be at least as high as the share of such facts that appear just once. Second, the grading makes it worse. Most benchmarks award a point for a right answer and nothing for “I don't know,” so a model that always guesses scores at least as well as one that honestly admits uncertainty.

If you've ever bluffed a multiple-choice question, you've done what the model does. When a blank scores zero, guessing is the rational move. Treat a chatbot's confidence as a writing style, not as evidence.

The practical upshot: LLMs are strongest where you can check the output. Code runs or it doesn't. A math step can be verified. A summary can be compared against the document in front of you. They are weakest on obscure specifics, such as exact figures, names, citations and niche regulations, which are precisely the things that appear rarely in training data. Use one like a sharp shipmate who has read everything once and never admits when he's fuzzy: great for ideas, explanations and first drafts, never the final word on a value that matters.
Is it “just” autocomplete?

Critics like to say an LLM is “just predicting the next word,” as if that settled things. It doesn't, because it hides how hard the prediction can get. To predict the next line of a physics derivation, it helps to model the physics. To predict how a character in a novel responds, it helps to model what she wants. Nobody programmed those abilities in. Training simply rewards whatever internal machinery lowers prediction error, and over trillions of tokens, some fairly sophisticated machinery pays for itself.

Researchers have started looking at that machinery directly. In 2024, Anthropic reported extracting millions of internal **features** from one of its Claude models: recurring patterns of neuron activity that line up with human concepts. One responded to the Golden Gate Bridge whether it was named in English, mentioned in other languages or shown in a picture. When researchers artificially turned that feature up, the model began insisting it was the bridge. That isn't proof of understanding in the human sense, and whether these systems “know” anything is a genuinely open argument. But it shows the inside isn't a lookup table of stored phrases. It's a learned map of concepts, and parts of that map can be read.

Here's the reframe worth keeping. Nuke school drills into you the difference between someone who can recite a procedure and someone who understands the plant well enough to predict what happens next. A language model sits in a strange spot on that spectrum. It was only ever graded on prediction, and prediction at this scale pushed it to build something like understanding along the way: patchy, alien and sometimes confidently wrong. So the interesting question isn't whether it's “just” predicting. It's how much of what we call understanding is, underneath, very good prediction.

takeaways: An LLM writes one token at a time; every token is a weighted guess about what comes next.
Attention lets every word look at every other word, which is how a model resolves context like what “it” refers to.
Since Chinchilla, data matters as much as size: today's models read trillions of tokens.
Hallucinations follow from the objective. The model learned what's likely, not what's true, so verify specifics.
“Just predicting the next word” undersells it: predicting well forces a model to learn a lot about the world.

title: The Internet Is a Garden Hose on the Seafloor
dek: Your messages get shredded into pieces, fired across a network that promises nothing, and rebuilt on the other side of an ocean in a blink. Here's how that actually works.

blocks.text: At 10:30 on the night of October 29, 1969, a UCLA student programmer named Charley Kline sat at a terminal and tried to log in to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute, hundreds of miles up the coast. He typed an L. It arrived. He typed an O. It arrived. He typed a G, and the system on the other end crashed.

So the first message ever sent over the network that became the internet was “lo.” About an hour later they got the full login working, and the rest is history: a network that started with a crash now carries video calls, bank transfers, game matches and nearly everything else. Yet most people who use it every waking hour couldn't tell you what happens between pressing send and the message showing up. The answer involves a radical design idea, a pair of protocols, and a lot of glass lying on the bottom of the ocean.
Chop it up: the packet idea

The old telephone network worked by **circuit switching**. When you made a call, the system reserved a continuous path of wire for you, end to end, for as long as you talked. That's simple and reliable, but wasteful: the line sits reserved even during silences, and if any link on the path fails, the call dies.

The internet does something stranger. It chops every message into small chunks called **packets**, each with a header stating where it's going and where it came from, like a label on a parcel. Packets are launched into the network independently. Each one may take a different route, and they can arrive out of order. Nobody reserves anything. The wire carries your packets, then someone else's, then yours again, interleaved with millions of other conversations.

It's the difference between booking a private train for one passenger and putting everyone in shared traffic. Shared traffic is messier, but it uses the roads far more efficiently, and when one road is closed, cars just go around. That resilience was the point: a network with no central switchboard has no single place where cutting a wire kills everything.
Two protocols, one division of labor

In May 1974, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn published a paper describing a way to link separate packet networks into one, an *inter-net*. Their design eventually split into two layers that still run your phone today, and the split is the most important idea in this article.

The bottom layer is **IP**, the Internet Protocol. Its job is addressing and forwarding, and nothing else. Every device gets an IP address, and every **router** (the specialized computers at network junctions) looks at a packet's destination address, consults a table, and passes it one hop closer. That's it. IP makes no promises. Packets can be dropped when a router is overloaded, duplicated, delayed or delivered out of order. Engineers call this **best effort**, which is a polite way of saying no guarantees.

How does a router know which way to send things? Each network on the internet, whether a phone carrier, a university or a cloud company, announces to its neighbors which blocks of addresses it can reach, using a protocol called **BGP** (Border Gateway Protocol). Those announcements ripple outward until every major router holds a rough map: for addresses in this range, hand the packet to that neighbor. No router knows the full path. Each knows only the next hop, like a messenger relaying a note down a passageway who only needs to know who's next in line.

BGP runs largely on trust, and that's its weak spot. If a network mistakenly announces that it can reach addresses it can't, traffic can be pulled toward it and vanish, and serious outages have started exactly that way. Internet routing is less a single designed machine than a constantly renegotiated agreement among a huge number of independent operators, none of whom is in charge.

The layer on top is **TCP**, the Transmission Control Protocol, and it turns that chaos into a reliable stream. Before sending data, two machines perform a **three-way handshake**: one says “let's talk” (SYN), the other says “got it, let's talk” (SYN-ACK), and the first confirms (ACK). Then every byte gets a sequence number. The receiver sends back acknowledgments of what arrived. Anything not acknowledged in time gets sent again. Out-of-order packets are put back in order before your app ever sees them. TCP also watches for signs of congestion, such as lost packets, and slows down when the network is clogged, so millions of users don't jointly stampede it into collapse.

blocks.title: Who does what

left.head: IP (the network)
items: Gives every device an address
Routers forward packets one hop at a time
No guarantee of delivery or order
Simple, fast, and dumb on purpose

right.head: TCP (the endpoints)
items: Handshake sets up a connection
Numbers every byte and confirms receipt
Resends whatever goes missing
Slows down when the network is congested

blocks.text: Notice where the intelligence lives. The network in the middle is kept dumb, and the reliability is built by the two computers at the ends. That's deliberate. A dumb core is cheap to build and easy to extend, and it doesn't need to understand what you're doing. It didn't need upgrading when video streaming or online gaming arrived. New ideas could be invented at the edges without asking permission from anyone in the middle.

Fast-paced online games often show the trade-off from the other side. Many skip TCP's guarantees for some traffic and use a lighter protocol called **UDP**, which just fires packets without handshakes or resends. If a position update from half a second ago went missing, resending it is pointless; the game wants the newest data, not a perfect history. When you see an enemy teleport, you're watching that design choice play out.

blocks.title: What happens when you hit send
items: Your app hands the message to TCP, which splits it into numbered segments
IP wraps each one in a packet stamped with source and destination addresses
Your router passes packets to your provider's network, then onto the backbone
Routers forward each packet hop by hop, possibly along different paths
Packets cross oceans as pulses of light in undersea fiber
The receiving TCP acknowledges, reorders, and requests anything missing
The rebuilt message is handed to the app on the other end

blocks.text: One step quietly happens before all of that: names. Computers route by number, but you type names. So your device first asks the **Domain Name System** (DNS), a distributed and hierarchical phone book, to translate a name like a website address into an IP address. Answers get cached at several levels, close to you, so popular lookups rarely have to travel far. When DNS breaks, the network can be perfectly healthy and yet nothing seems to load, which is why it gets blamed for so many mysterious outages.

The design spread slowly, then all at once. On January 1, 1983, DARPA required the ARPANET to switch from its older protocol to TCP/IP, a cutover remembered as a kind of flag day for the modern internet. The addressing scheme, though, was sized for a research network. The original version, IPv4, has 2 to the 32nd power addresses, a little over four billion. On February 3, 2011, the central pool of unassigned IPv4 blocks ran dry when the last ones were handed out to the regional registries.

blocks.title: From “lo” to now
items: First ARPANET message: “lo,” then a crash
Cerf and Kahn publish the design for TCP
ARPANET switches over to TCP/IP on January 1
The central pool of IPv4 addresses runs out
IPv6 passes 50% of users reaching Google

blocks.text: The fix is **IPv6**, with 2 to the 128th power addresses, roughly 340 trillion trillion trillion. Adoption crawled for years because IPv4 kept limping along with workarounds. Then, on March 28, 2026, Google's measurements showed IPv6 access to its services topping 50% of users for the first time. A transition decades in the making finally crossed the halfway mark.
The cloud is underwater

People talk about “the cloud” as if data floats through the sky. When your packets leave the continent, they almost certainly travel through glass on the seafloor. TeleGeography, the research firm that maps these systems, tracks more than 600 active and planned submarine cables and estimates over 1.5 million kilometers of them in service, enough to wrap around the planet dozens of times. Satellites carry only a sliver of international traffic. Using older FCC data, the firm notes satellites accounted for just 0.37% of U.S. international capacity.

items.label: Submarine cable in service worldwide (early 2026)
Cable faults per year
Share of faults caused by fishing gear and ship anchors

blocks.source: TeleGeography Submarine Cable FAQ, 2026 (citing the International Cable Protection Committee)

blocks.text: For most of their length, these cables are about as thick as a garden hose. Inside, the actual data rides in glass fibers about the width of a human hair, surrounded by layers of protection, with heavier armor near shore where the dangers are. Light pulses go in one end, are boosted by amplifiers spaced along the route, and come out the other. A single modern cable can carry staggering volumes; the MAREA cable across the Atlantic is rated at a potential 224 terabits per second.

They also break, a lot. The International Cable Protection Committee counts roughly 200 faults a year, and about two-thirds come from fishing gear and dragged anchors, not sabotage or sharks. Fish bites, a favorite internet myth, caused zero recorded faults between 2007 and 2014. When a cable goes down, traffic reroutes across other cables while a repair ship grapples the broken ends up from the bottom. That's the packet idea scaled to a planet: no single path is sacred.

Ownership has shifted too. Cables used to be built by consortiums of phone companies. Now the big buyers are content companies such as Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon, which lay their own routes to link their data centers. The physical internet is increasingly private infrastructure.
The speed limit you can't patch

Here's the part software can't fix. Light in glass travels slower than in a vacuum, roughly two-thirds as fast, around 204,000 kilometers per second. That works out to about 5 milliseconds of one-way delay for every 1,000 kilometers of fiber. Cross an ocean and back and you've spent tens of milliseconds before any computer does any work at all.

That limit is worth real money. In 2015, the Hibernia Express cable opened between New York and London advertising round trips under 58.95 milliseconds, explicitly aimed at financial traders. When a price difference between two exchanges lasts only milliseconds, the firm on the shorter cable wins.

Most traffic gets nowhere near the physical limit. A 2018 study of internet fiber infrastructure found that measured latencies typically run about three times longer than a signal traveling in a straight line at light speed would need. Part of that is physics, since light in fiber is slower. The rest is routing: cables follow roads, railways and coastlines rather than straight lines, packets detour through distant exchange points, and routers add small delays at each hop.

blocks.title: How much slower the real internet is than its limits
blocks.note: Median values. “Fiber path vs straight” is how much longer cable routes are than line-of-sight distance.
blocks.source: Bozkurt et al., “Dissecting Latency in the Internet's Fiber Infrastructure,” 2018

blocks.text: Your ping to a server is mostly geography. Fiber routes, the number of hops and the distance to the data center set a floor that no gaming chair, router upgrade or faster plan can beat. Picking the closest server region usually matters more than anything else you control.
Reliable from unreliable

Step back and the whole system rests on a counterintuitive bet. Instead of building a network that never fails, the designers built one that fails constantly, in small ways, and made recovery automatic. Packets get dropped every second of every day. Cables get snagged by anchors a couple hundred times a year. Routers crash. And yet the message gets through, because no single part was ever trusted to be perfect.

That's an idea that reaches well beyond networking. Anyone who has stood watch in an engineering plant knows systems are designed around the assumption that components will fail: redundancy, independent checks, multiple paths to a safe state. TCP is the same philosophy in software. Expect loss, number everything, confirm receipt, retry, slow down when things get crowded.

It also says something about how to build anything that lasts, including habits and projects. The fragile approach demands every day go to plan, and collapses at the first dropped packet. The robust approach assumes some days will be lost, keeps track of what actually got done, and resends without drama. The internet doesn't work because nothing goes wrong. It works because something goes wrong all the time, and the system was built to shrug.

So the next time a message lands on the far side of the planet in a fraction of a second, picture what actually happened: your words were shredded into numbered fragments, flung into a network that promised nothing, pushed as flickers of light through a hose-thick cable lying in the dark on the ocean floor, and stitched back together by a protocol designed in the 1970s that still assumes the worst. It's a little miracle of pessimism.

takeaways: The internet splits every message into packets that travel independently and get reassembled at the destination.
IP just addresses and forwards; TCP adds reliability at the endpoints by numbering, confirming and resending.
Over 1.5 million km of undersea cable carry nearly all intercontinental traffic, and they break about 200 times a year.
Light in fiber sets a hard floor on latency: about 5 ms per 1,000 km one way, which is why server distance matters.
The core design lesson: build reliable systems from unreliable parts by expecting failure and recovering automatically.

title: The Controlled Fire in Your Pocket
dek: A lithium-ion battery packs fuel and its own oxygen supply into one sealed can, kept apart by a thin sheet of plastic. Here's how it works, why it got so cheap, and what happens when that sheet fails.

blocks.text: In 2016, Samsung launched the Galaxy Note 7, one of the most hyped phones of the year. Within weeks, some of them were catching fire. By the time it was over, roughly three million had been sold and about 96 percent had been recalled. One of the most advanced consumer devices on the planet had been undone by tiny flaws inside a part most owners never think about.

Samsung's investigation found two different defects in two different batteries the phone had used. In the first, the negative electrode was bent in the upper-right corner of the cell until it touched the positive electrode. In the second, a burr left over from welding on the positive electrode poked through the insulating tape and the plastic separator, reaching the negative side. Two different mistakes, one result: the two halves of the battery touched.

That's the whole story of lithium-ion safety in miniature. The battery in your phone, vape, laptop, power tool and e-bike is a box of stored chemical energy with a thin barrier down the middle. As long as the barrier holds, it's one of the most useful inventions of the past century. When it fails, it can become a fire that feeds itself.
The rocking chair

A lithium-ion cell has four main parts. The *anode*, the negative side, is usually graphite, the same layered carbon as pencil lead. The *cathode*, the positive side, is a metal oxide such as lithium cobalt oxide or a nickel-rich blend. Between them sits the *electrolyte*, a lithium salt dissolved in an organic solvent, which lets lithium ions drift through. And keeping the two electrodes physically apart is the *separator*, a porous plastic film. Ions can squeeze through its pores. Electrons can't.

That last detail is the key to the whole design. When you use the battery, lithium ions leave the graphite and travel through the electrolyte to the cathode. Each ion leaves behind an electron, but the electron can't follow through the separator. It has to take the long way, out through the wires and through your phone's circuits, before it meets the ion again at the cathode. That forced detour *is* the current you're using.

Charging runs the process backward. The charger pushes electrons into the anode and drags the ions back into the graphite layers, uphill against the chemistry. Engineers call the design a *rocking chair* battery, because the lithium just rocks back and forth between two hosts without being consumed. The technical name for slotting ions between layers of a host material is *intercalation*, and it's why a good cell can survive hundreds or thousands of cycles.

blocks.title: What happens when you unplug and use your phone
items: Lithium ions sit packed between the graphite layers of the anode.
Your phone closes the circuit, giving electrons a path to the cathode.
Ions leave the graphite and drift through the electrolyte and separator pores.
Electrons, blocked by the separator, travel through the external circuit and power the device.
Ions and electrons recombine inside the metal oxide cathode.
Charging later forces both back to the anode, ready to go again.

blocks.text: If you think of it electrically, the separator is insulation. The whole cell is a stored potential difference, and the separator is the only thing keeping it from shorting internally. In a wiring run, a nick in the insulation is a hazard. In a battery, it's the beginning of a fire.
Three people and a thirty-year race

The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to the three scientists who made this possible. In the 1970s, Stanley Whittingham built a lithium battery with a titanium disulfide cathode, a material that could hold lithium ions inside its structure. Paired with a pure lithium metal anode, it produced just over two volts. But metallic lithium is violently reactive, and the battery was too explosive to be practical.

John Goodenough predicted that a metal oxide would make a better cathode than a sulfide, and in 1980 he showed that cobalt oxide could deliver as much as four volts. Then in 1985, Akira Yoshino replaced the dangerous lithium metal anode with petroleum coke, a carbon material that could also hold lithium ions. That made the first commercially viable lithium-ion battery. It hit the market in 1991.

blocks.title: How the lithium-ion battery was built
items: Whittingham: titanium disulfide cathode, lithium metal anode, just over 2 volts, too explosive
Goodenough: cobalt oxide cathode reaches about 4 volts
Yoshino: carbon anode replaces lithium metal, first commercially viable cell
Lithium-ion batteries go on sale
Nobel Prize in Chemistry for all three
Average pack price falls to $108 per kilowatt-hour

blocks.text: What happened next is one of the great cost collapses in industrial history. Researchers Micah Ziegler and Jessika Trancik at MIT found that the real price of lithium-ion cells per unit of energy fell about 97 percent from their 1991 introduction. Between 1992 and 2016, prices dropped around 13 percent a year, and every doubling of the cumulative market cut prices by roughly 20 percent. Over the same stretch, the best cells went from about 80 watt-hours per kilogram to over 250, and from about 200 watt-hours per liter to over 700.

items.label: Drop in real cell price per unit of energy since 1991
Watt-hours per kilogram, early cells vs. the best by the late 2010s
Average pack price per kilowatt-hour in 2025, down 8% in a year

blocks.source: Ziegler & Trancik, Energy & Environmental Science, 2021; BloombergNEF, December 2025

blocks.text: That curve is why phones last all day, why electric cars went from science projects to traffic, and why cheap e-bikes and disposable vapes exist at all. BloombergNEF reported that the average battery pack cost $108 per kilowatt-hour in 2025, and packs for stationary grid storage were down to $70. But the property that makes these batteries so valuable, cramming a lot of energy into a small space, is the same property that makes them dangerous.
Fuel and oxygen in the same can

Fire needs three things: fuel, oxygen and heat. A lithium-ion cell carries two of them inside a sealed can. The organic solvent in the electrolyte is flammable. And many cathode materials, when they get hot enough, break down and release oxygen. So once a cell starts burning, it doesn't fully depend on the air around it. That's why a cell fire can be so hard to smother.

The process that turns a hot battery into a burning one is called *thermal runaway*, and it happens in stages. A 2019 review by Xiangkun Wu and colleagues lays out the sequence. First to go is the *SEI*, or solid electrolyte interphase, a thin protective film that forms on the graphite during the cell's first charges, a bit like the oxide layer that protects aluminum. It starts breaking down somewhere between about 60 and 130 degrees Celsius, depending on charge level. With the SEI gone, the electrolyte attacks the anode directly, releasing more heat.

Around 135 degrees, a polyethylene separator melts. Some separators are built with a layer designed to melt and close its pores, shutting down ion flow, while a sturdier polypropylene layer keeps the electrodes apart. If the barrier fails, the electrodes touch and the cell shorts internally, dumping its stored energy as heat. Then, somewhere from about 150 to 250 degrees, the cathode starts to decompose and release oxygen. Nickel-rich cathodes, which hold more energy, tend to start breaking down at the lower end of that range.

blocks.title: Thermal runaway: heat that makes more heat
items: Cell heats up from a short, damage or charging fault
Protective SEI film breaks down, releasing heat
Separator melts and electrodes short internally
Cathode decomposes and releases oxygen
Flammable electrolyte burns, pushing temperature higher

blocks.text: If you've been through nuke school, this loop should make the hair on your neck stand up. A pressurized water reactor is designed so that if the core gets hotter, the reaction slows down. That's a negative temperature coefficient, and it's one of the most important safety features in the plant. A lithium cell in thermal runaway is the opposite: a positive feedback loop. Every increase in temperature speeds up reactions that produce more heat. Once it crosses a certain point, nothing inside the cell can stop it.

A failing lithium cell has a positive temperature coefficient: heat speeds up the reactions that make more heat. Safety isn't about stopping runaway once it starts. It's about never letting it start, and keeping one cell's fire from spreading to the next.

A phone usually runs on a single cell. Laptops, power tools and e-bikes string many cells together, and an electric car carries far more. In a pack, the most dangerous moment comes when one cell's runaway heats its neighbors past their own trigger points and the failure cascades down the row. Pack designers fight this with spacing, heat-resistant barriers, vent paths, and a *battery management system*, electronics that watch each cell's voltage and temperature and cut off charging when something looks wrong. Cheap packs tend to skimp on exactly these parts.
How good batteries go bad

The Wu review groups the triggers into three kinds of abuse. *Mechanical* abuse is crushing, bending or puncturing, like a phone run over in a parking lot or a pack damaged in a crash. *Electrical* abuse is overcharging, over-discharging or an external short. *Thermal* abuse is simply getting too hot, like a laptop left on a radiator. Nearly all of them end the same way: a short circuit inside the cell.

There's also a slower, sneakier failure. If a cell is charged too fast or in the cold, lithium can fail to slip into the graphite properly and instead plate onto its surface as metal. Over time, that plating can grow into needle-like structures called *dendrites*, which can work their way through the separator. Add manufacturing defects like the ones in the Note 7, a stray metal particle or a wrinkled electrode, and you have a battery that was born with a weak spot.

This is why cheap, uncertified batteries are such a problem. In New York City, fires from lithium-ion batteries, many of them from e-bikes and scooters, killed 18 people in 2023. The FDNY reported that deaths fell to 6 in 2024 after heavy public education and inspections, even though the number of battery fires barely moved, from 268 to 277. In the air, the Federal Aviation Administration said at least 84 lithium battery incidents on commercial flights were reported to it in 2024, a record, averaging more than one a week.

items.label: Lithium battery incidents reported on US commercial flights in 2024
NYC lithium-ion battery fire deaths, 2023 to 2024
NYC lithium-ion battery fires, 2023 to 2024

blocks.source: Federal Aviation Administration, March 2025; FDNY figures reported by Gothamist, 2025

blocks.text: Think about why aircraft care so much. A plane is a sealed tube with nowhere to go, full of people, and a burning cell gives off heat, smoke and toxic gas while it supplies part of its own oxygen. A submarine is that problem with the volume turned up. That's why ships and aircraft treat lithium batteries so seriously, and why your command's rules on personal devices exist. They aren't arbitrary.

If a device ever starts swelling, hissing, popping or smoking, treat it like the energy release it is. Don't pick it up to inspect it, and don't throw it in a trash can. Get distance, warn the people around you, and report it the way your space requires, whether that's calling the fire department ashore or following damage control procedures aboard. Once a cell commits to runaway, the job is containment, not rescue.
Living with the fire

The good news is that the same chemistry that fails dramatically also ages predictably, and you can control most of what ages it. Apple says a battery's chemical age depends on its temperature history and charging pattern, not just the calendar. Heat is the big one. Apple recommends using iPhones in surroundings of about 16 to 22 degrees Celsius, and warns that charging or using them above 35 degrees can permanently shorten battery life.

Time spent sitting at 100 percent also wears a cell. That's why newer iPhones let you set a charge limit between 80 and 100 percent, and why the optimized charging feature waits past 80 percent when it predicts you'll be plugged in overnight. Many laptops and Android phones offer similar settings. They trade a little range today for a battery that holds up longer.

blocks.title: Battery habits

left.head: Wears it out or raises risk
items: Charging under a pillow or in a hot space
Leaving it at 100% for days
Cheap, uncertified chargers and packs
Using a swollen, dented or punctured battery
Fast-charging in the cold

right.head: Keeps it healthy and safe
items: Charging on a hard surface with airflow
Using a charge limit or optimized charging
Chargers and packs from reputable makers
Retiring damaged batteries properly
Letting a cold device warm up before charging

blocks.text: The deeper idea is worth keeping. Every technology that stores a lot of energy in a small space is, in some sense, a controlled release waiting to happen. Gasoline, explosives, reactor fuel and lithium cells all share that bargain. The engineering that makes them safe isn't about making the energy go away. It's about barriers, margins and feedback: keeping the halves apart, keeping the heat down, and designing systems so that when something goes wrong, it goes wrong in one cell instead of a thousand.

Next time your phone gets warm in your hand, remember what's inside it: two electrodes, a flammable liquid, and a plastic film doing the job of a reactor's containment. It works billions of times a day, all over the world. That it works so reliably is the miracle. That it occasionally doesn't is just physics collecting on the bargain.

takeaways: A lithium-ion cell moves ions through a separator and forces electrons through your device; the separator is the insulation that keeps it from shorting.
Cell prices fell about 97 percent since 1991, which is why batteries are now in everything.
Thermal runaway is a positive feedback loop: heat breaks down layers and materials that release more heat and even oxygen.
Most failures come from damage, overcharging, heat, or manufacturing defects that let the electrodes touch.
Keep batteries cool, avoid parking them at 100 percent, use reputable chargers, and retire anything swollen or damaged.

title: Everything Is a Switch
dek: In the 1930s a graduate student noticed that relay circuits obey the same algebra as logic. That one insight, plus a lot of switches, is the whole secret of computers. If you can read a motor control circuit, you already understand more of it than you think.

blocks.text: Wire a light with two switches in series and it only turns on when switch A *and* switch B are closed. Wire the switches in parallel and the light comes on if switch A *or* switch B is closed. Any electrician learns this in the first week. It seems too simple to matter.

In the late 1930s, Claude Shannon, a young graduate student at MIT, saw something in that simplicity nobody had fully worked out. He had worked on a room-sized mechanical computer at MIT whose controls relied on relay circuits, and he realized that the behavior of switching circuits exactly matched an algebra of true and false that the English mathematician George Boole had published in 1854. Series was AND. Parallel was OR. A normally closed contact was NOT. Any logical statement could be built as a circuit, and any circuit could be analyzed as a logical statement.

Shannon published the idea in 1938 in a paper called *A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits*. It is one of the founding documents of the digital age, and it means something remarkable: every computer, from a calculator to the chip training AI models, is at bottom nothing but switches arranged so that their on and off states follow the rules of logic. Here is how you get from a light switch to a processor.
Series is AND, parallel is OR

Boole's algebra deals with values that are only ever true or false, which we can write as 1 and 0. Three basic operations do almost everything. **AND** gives 1 only if both inputs are 1. **OR** gives 1 if either input is 1. **NOT** flips its input. Shannon's insight was that a closed contact is a 1, an open one is a 0, and the wiring pattern performs the operation.

blocks.title: Shannon's translation table

left.head: Circuit
items: Two contacts in series
Two contacts in parallel
Normally closed contact
Lamp lit / current flows
Lamp dark / no current

right.head: Logic
items: A AND B
A OR B
NOT A
True, or 1
False, or 0

blocks.text: This mattered first for practical reasons. Telephone exchanges and industrial controls in the 1930s were huge tangles of relays designed by intuition and trial and error. With Shannon's method, an engineer could write the desired behavior as an equation, simplify the equation with algebra, and build the smaller circuit that resulted. Fewer relays meant cheaper, more reliable systems.

But the bigger consequence was philosophical. If switches can do logic, and arithmetic can be written as logic, then switches can do arithmetic. And if they can do arithmetic, they can do anything that can be expressed as a precise procedure. The question of building a thinking machine had quietly turned into a question of wiring.
The switch gets faster

A relay is a switch flipped by electricity: current through a coil pulls a contact closed. The key property is that the output of one relay can drive the coil of the next, so switches can control other switches. That is what lets you chain logic together. But relays are mechanical, so they are slow, noisy and wear out.

The first fully electronic computers replaced relays with vacuum tubes, which could switch with no moving parts. ENIAC, built for the US Army between 1943 and 1945 to compute ballistics tables, glowed with about 18,000 tubes. The Computer History Museum notes it lost a tube roughly every day or two, and its crew got good enough to find and replace the failed one in about 15 minutes. Its existence was revealed to the public on the front page of The New York Times in February 1946.

The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, did the same job in solid material: a small voltage on one terminal controls whether current flows between the other two. No vacuum, no glowing filament, and eventually it could be made microscopically small. Modern chips use a type called the MOSFET, and the standard way of building logic from them, called CMOS, pairs transistors so that almost no current flows except at the moment of switching. A CMOS NAND gate, the workhorse described below, takes just four transistors.

items.label: Vacuum tubes in ENIAC, which lost one every day or two
Transistors in Intel's 4004 processor on a single chip (1971)
Transistors in an NVIDIA Blackwell-architecture GPU

blocks.source: Computer History Museum; NVIDIA

blocks.text: One gate to build them all

Here is a surprising fact about logic: you only need one kind of gate. A **NAND** gate, meaning NOT-AND, outputs 0 only when both inputs are 1, and 1 otherwise. With nothing but NAND gates you can build every other gate. Tie a NAND's two inputs together and it becomes NOT. Put a NOT after a NAND and you have AND. Put NOTs on both inputs of a NAND and you get OR.

This property, called universality, is why a famous course and textbook by Noam Nisan and Shimon Schocken, *The Elements of Computing Systems*, better known as Nand to Tetris, starts students with a single NAND gate and has them build, layer by layer, a working computer that can run Tetris. Nothing is hidden. Every layer is built only from the layer below it.

It also explains why chip factories can be so uniform. A modern chip is not billions of unique inventions. It is a small vocabulary of gate designs, repeated and connected in staggering numbers, with software tools doing most of the arranging.
Teaching switches to add

Computers count in binary because switches have two states. Binary works like the decimal system you know, just with two digits instead of ten. In decimal, when a column passes 9 you write 0 and carry 1. In binary, when a column passes 1 you write 0 and carry 1. So 1 + 1 in binary is 10, which is two.

Why two states and not ten? Partly because a switch naturally has two, but mostly because of noise. Any electrician knows real voltages drift, sag under load and pick up interference. If a wire had to represent ten different levels, a small wobble could turn a 6 into a 7. With only two states, the circuit just has to tell high from low, and everything in a wide band near the top counts as 1 while everything near the bottom counts as 0. Each gate also restores a clean, full-strength output, so errors do not build up as a signal passes through thousands of stages. Binary trades efficiency per wire for near-perfect reliability, and with billions of switches, reliability is the trade you want.

Look at what adding two single bits requires. The sum digit is 1 when exactly one input is 1, which is an operation called XOR, or exclusive OR. The carry digit is 1 only when both inputs are 1, which is just AND. So a circuit that adds two bits, called a **half adder**, is one XOR gate and one AND gate side by side. That is the moment arithmetic becomes wiring.

To add longer numbers, each column also has to accept the carry coming in from the column to its right. A **full adder** handles three inputs, two bits plus a carry, and outputs a sum bit and a carry bit; it can be built from two half adders and an OR gate. Line up 64 full adders, each passing its carry to the next, and you can add two 64-bit numbers. Real chips use cleverer designs that work out the carries in parallel so they do not wait for each one to ripple down the line, but the principle is the same.

blocks.title: Adding 5 + 3 in binary, the way the circuit does
items: Write the numbers in binary: 5 is 0101 and 3 is 0011.
Rightmost column: 1 + 1 gives sum 0, carry 1.
Next column: 0 + 1 + carry 1 gives sum 0, carry 1.
Next column: 1 + 0 + carry 1 gives sum 0, carry 1.
Last column: 0 + 0 + carry 1 gives sum 1. The answer is 1000, which is 8.

blocks.text: Subtraction can be done with the same adder by a neat trick for representing negative numbers, called two's complement. Multiplication can be built from repeated shifting and adding. The block of a processor that does all of this is the **arithmetic logic unit**, or ALU, and it is nothing but gates.
Teaching switches to remember

Adding is not enough. A computer also has to hold on to results. Here, an electrician has a head start, because the trick is something you have almost certainly wired: the **seal-in circuit** on a motor starter.

Press the start button and the contactor coil energizes. One of the contactor's own auxiliary contacts, wired in parallel with the start button, closes and keeps the coil energized after you let go. The circuit is now holding itself on. Press the normally closed stop button and the loop breaks, the coil drops out, and it stays off. That circuit *remembers* which button was pressed last. In digital logic the same idea, two gates whose outputs feed back into each other's inputs, is called a **latch**, and it stores one bit.
A motor starter's seal-in contact and a computer's memory bit are the same idea: feedback that holds a state after the input that set it is gone. Memory is just a circuit that keeps itself on.

Add a timing signal and you get a **flip-flop**, a latch that only accepts a new value at the tick of a clock. The clock is a steady square wave, billions of ticks a second in a modern processor, and it keeps the whole chip in step: on each tick, results from the logic settle into flip-flops, ready to be the inputs for the next step. Group flip-flops in rows of 32 or 64 and you have **registers**, the processor's fastest scratch space.
The machine that follows instructions

Now put it together. A processor keeps a register called the program counter that holds the memory address of the next instruction. Each instruction is just a pattern of bits. The processor runs a cycle, over and over, for as long as it has power.

blocks.title: The instruction cycle
items: Fetch the instruction at the address in the program counter
Decode its bit pattern into control signals
Execute: route data through the ALU or to memory
Store the result in a register or memory
Advance the program counter and repeat

blocks.text: Decoding is the part that feels like magic, and it is not. The bits of an instruction feed into gates whose outputs open some paths and close others, exactly like a selector switch routing power to one circuit or another. One pattern sends two registers into the adder. Another sends a value out to memory. Another loads a new address into the program counter, which is how a program jumps and loops. The instruction is not understood. It is a physical setting of switches that determines which switches flip next.

Intel's 4004 did all of this in 1971 with about 2,300 transistors. Fifty-some years later a single high-end GPU holds more than 200 billion of them. The logic has gotten more elaborate, with caches, pipelines and many cores running at once, but nothing about the core idea has changed. It is still Shannon's series and parallel, Boole's true and false, and a clock ticking.

blocks.title: From logic to processors
items: George Boole publishes his algebra of true and false.
Shannon's paper shows relay circuits can be designed with Boole's algebra.
ENIAC is built with about 18,000 vacuum tubes.
The transistor is invented at Bell Labs.
Intel's 4004 puts a whole processor on one chip with 2,300 transistors.
GPUs pass 200 billion transistors.

blocks.text: What a stack of switches teaches

No single person understands a modern processor at the level of every transistor. Nobody needs to. Each layer, switches, gates, adders, registers, instructions, programming languages, game engines, trusts the layer below it to do its job and hides its details from the layer above. That is how a teenager can make a Roblox game without knowing what a flip-flop is, and how chip designers can build things far too large to hold in one mind. A submarine works the same way, with people qualified on systems they did not design, trusting components whose internals they never see.

But the layers are not magic, and knowing that is useful. When you write a line of Luau, it becomes bytecode, which becomes machine instructions, which become bit patterns that set switches that route electrons through adders and latches. People have even built working processors out of Minecraft redstone, because a game that gives you a switch, a wire and a way for one to control the other has, in principle, given you everything a computer needs. Shannon's insight was that thinking, at least the precise and mechanical kind, can be built out of the humblest component in the electrician's toolbox. The rest is just how many of them you can fit.

takeaways: Shannon showed in 1938 that switching circuits follow Boolean logic: series is AND, parallel is OR, a normally closed contact is NOT.
NAND alone can build every other gate, which is why a working computer can be built up from one gate type.
A half adder is just an XOR gate and an AND gate; chain full adders and switches can add numbers of any size.
Memory is feedback, the same principle as a motor starter's seal-in contact.
A CPU is a fetch, decode, execute loop where instructions are bit patterns that set which switches flip next.
