title: The Internet Runs on Strangers' Spare Time
dek: Open source software is worth trillions of dollars to the companies that use it, yet much of it rests on a handful of volunteers. One near-miss in 2024 showed how thin that thread is.

blocks.text: In early 2024 a Microsoft engineer named Andres Freund was running performance tests on a Linux machine when he noticed something tiny: logging in over SSH, the standard tool for remotely controlling servers, was taking a little longer than it should and burning more processor time than it had before. Most people would have shrugged. He dug in, and traced the slowdown to a compression library called xz Utils, a small, unglamorous piece of code that sits inside almost every Linux system.

What he found was a backdoor. A contributor using the name Jia Tan had spent about two years making helpful, legitimate contributions to the project, earning the trust of its overworked maintainer, until they had the access to slip in carefully hidden malicious code. It was designed to let an attacker run commands on affected servers without logging in. It had already started shipping in test versions of major Linux distributions when Freund caught it. Had it gone unnoticed for a few more months, it could have reached a huge share of the servers on the internet.

The scary part is not that someone attacked open source. It is what the attack revealed. A piece of software that much of the world quietly depended on had been maintained, for years, largely by one unpaid volunteer. That is not an exception. It is closer to the rule.
What open source actually means

Every program starts as **source code**, the human-readable instructions a programmer writes. Before it runs, that code is usually compiled into a binary, a blob of machine instructions that is almost impossible for a person to read or modify. Commercial software traditionally ships only the binary. **Open source** software ships the source too, under a **license** that gives anyone the right to read it, change it, and share their changes.

The movement started as a protest. In 1983 a programmer at MIT named Richard Stallman, frustrated that he could no longer fix software he used because companies had stopped sharing code, announced the GNU project to build a complete free operating system. He insisted the issue was freedom, not price: *free as in free speech, not free beer*. His GNU General Public License, the GPL, introduced a clever legal hack called **copyleft**. You can use, change and share GPL code however you want, but if you distribute a modified version, you must release your changes under the same terms. The license uses copyright law to keep code permanently open.

Other licenses, such as MIT, BSD and Apache, are **permissive**: do almost anything you want, including folding the code into a closed commercial product, as long as you keep the original credit. That split matters for anyone who builds things. Permissive code is easy for businesses to adopt. Copyleft code guarantees the improvements flow back to everyone.

blocks.title: Two philosophies of open licensing

left.head: Copyleft (GPL)
items: Use and modify freely
Distribute a changed version and you must share its source
Keeps the whole chain open forever
Used by Linux and many GNU tools

right.head: Permissive (MIT, BSD, Apache)
items: Use and modify freely
Can be built into closed, paid products
Only requirement is keeping the credit and license text
Common in libraries, web tools and game frameworks

blocks.text: Just a hobby

GNU had built compilers, editors and tools, but by 1991 it still lacked the core of an operating system, the **kernel** that manages memory, processes and hardware. That August, a 21-year-old Finnish student named Linus Torvalds posted a message to an online newsgroup about a free operating system he was writing for his own PC. He described it as just a hobby, one that would not be big and professional like GNU. Combined with the GNU tools and released under the GPL, his kernel became Linux.
Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow.
blocks.by: Eric S. Raymond, The Cathedral and the Bazaar

blocks.text: Linux grew in a way that made no sense by the rules of the software industry. Thousands of strangers on the internet, coordinating by email, sending patches that Torvalds and his lieutenants reviewed and merged. The writer Eric Raymond called this the bazaar model, in contrast to the cathedral model of a small, closed team carefully building toward a release. His essay argued that with enough people looking at the code, someone will spot almost any bug. In 2005 Torvalds wrote **Git** to manage Linux's flood of changes. Git now underpins nearly all software development, including GitHub, which hosts much of the world's open source code.

Today Linux is everywhere you do not look. It runs most of the servers behind websites and cloud services, the world's fastest supercomputers, and every Android phone, since Android is built on the Linux kernel. Much of the modern internet stack, from web servers to databases to the programming languages themselves, is open source.

blocks.title: How a protest became infrastructure
items: Richard Stallman announces the GNU project
First version of the GNU General Public License
Linus Torvalds announces the kernel that becomes Linux
The term open source is coined as a business-friendly label
Torvalds creates Git to manage Linux development
Heartbleed bug in OpenSSL exposes encrypted traffic across the web
Log4Shell flaw in a volunteer-maintained Java logging library hits millions of systems
xz Utils backdoor is discovered just before reaching stable Linux releases

blocks.text: Why anyone works for free

The obvious question is why. Some of it is the original motive behind Linux: a programmer needs a tool, builds it, and shares it because sharing costs nothing. Some of it is learning and reputation. Public code is a portfolio anyone can inspect, and plenty of engineers have been hired because of a project or a string of good fixes in someone else's project.

But a large share of open source work today is not volunteer work at all. Companies pay engineers to contribute, because they depend on the software and it is cheaper to improve a shared foundation than to build a private one. A great deal of Linux kernel development is done by developers employed by chipmakers, cloud providers and phone makers who need Linux to run well on their hardware.

There is also strategy. The software writer Joel Spolsky described a move he called *commoditizing your complement*: if your business sells one thing, make the things people buy alongside it cheap or free, so more money flows to you. Google gave away Android partly so that no other company could control the gateway to mobile search. Companies give away a database or a framework and earn money selling hosting, support or premium features on top. Red Hat built a large business selling support for free software, and IBM eventually bought it.

That bargain can sour. In recent years several companies that had built popular open source projects switched them to more restrictive licenses after cloud providers started selling the software as a service without contributing much back. The community's answer was the **fork**: because the old code was already open, developers copied the last open version and kept developing it under a new name. Forking is the ultimate check in open source. Nobody can take the code away once it has been released.
The trillion-dollar gift

How much is all this worth? Because nobody pays for it, open source barely shows up in economic statistics. In 2024 researchers Manuel Hoffmann, Frank Nagle and Yanuo Zhou of Harvard Business School tried to put numbers on it using data on how millions of firms actually use open source. They asked two questions. What would it cost to write the most widely used open source software once from scratch? And what would it cost every company that uses it to build its own version if open source vanished?

blocks.title: The value of widely used open source software
blocks.note: The gap exists because one piece of code is reused by millions of companies.
blocks.source: Hoffmann, Nagle & Zhou, Harvard Business School, 2024

blocks.text: The answers were $4.15 billion and $8.8 trillion. That gap of more than two thousand to one is the whole economic logic of open source. Code is written once and copied for free, endlessly. The researchers estimated that without it, firms would have to spend 3.5 times more on software than they do now.

The same study found something more unsettling. About 96 percent of that demand-side value was created by just 5 percent of open source developers. The software the world runs on is not built by a vast crowd evenly sharing the load. It rests on a small number of people, many of whom do the work in their spare time.

items.label: Estimated value of widely used open source to the firms that use it
Share of that value created by 5% of open source developers
Popular GitHub projects that would stall if 2 or fewer developers left

blocks.source: Hoffmann, Nagle & Zhou, 2024; Avelino et al., 2016

blocks.text: The bus factor

Software engineers have a grim metric called the **truck factor** or bus factor: how many developers would have to be hit by a bus, or simply quit, before a project stalls because nobody left understands it. In 2016 a team led by researchers at a Brazilian university estimated it for 133 popular projects on GitHub. They found that 65 percent had a truck factor of two or less. Two people leave, and the project is in serious trouble.

The failures follow a pattern. In 2014 a bug nicknamed **Heartbleed** turned up in OpenSSL, the library that encrypted a huge portion of web traffic. It let attackers read chunks of a server's memory, potentially including passwords and private keys. OpenSSL turned out to be run by a tiny team on very little money. In late 2021 **Log4Shell** hit Log4j, a free Java logging library maintained by volunteers. It let attackers take over systems simply by getting a specially crafted line of text logged, and it was buried inside software at millions of organizations, many of which did not know they used it.

The xz attack exploited the same weakness from the human side. Analyses of the incident describe how the attacker manipulated the project's community and development process, not just its code. Pressure from accounts urging the lone maintainer to hand over more control helped the newcomer gain the access needed. A burned-out volunteer, grateful for help, is the softest target in all of software security.

blocks.title: How a critical project ends up fragile
items: A volunteer writes something useful and shares it
Companies quietly build it into their products
Bug reports and demands grow faster than help or money
The maintainer burns out or leans on whoever offers help
A failure or an attack exposes how much depended on one person

blocks.text: After each crisis, money flows in for a while. Big tech companies and foundations have funded security audits and paid maintainers of critical projects. The deeper problem is structural: it is rational for each company to use free code and irrational for any one of them to pay for it, because everyone else benefits too. Economists call this a public goods problem, and it does not fix itself.
Standing on free shoulders

Open source is also the reason a solo developer today can build things that once took a company. A Roblox developer writes in Luau, a language Roblox derived from the open source language Lua and then open-sourced itself in 2021. Popular community tools let developers edit their game code in a normal code editor and track it with Git. Someone starting a small business can launch on open source web frameworks, databases and operating systems without paying a license fee for any of them. The starting line is decades of other people's work, handed over for free.

That also makes open source one of the best learning resources ever created. You can read the actual code of a production database, a game engine or a compiler, see how experienced engineers solved real problems, and watch their arguments play out in public issue threads. Fixing a small bug or improving documentation in a project you use is one of the most credible things a self-taught programmer can put on a résumé, because anyone can see the work. Before you depend on a library for your own project, it is worth a two-minute health check: when was the last commit, how many people actually merge changes, and do issues get answered? A popular package with one exhausted maintainer is a risk you are choosing to carry.

The reframe is this: a great deal of the software world is not a market at all. It is a gift economy that turned into critical infrastructure without anyone deciding it should. It works astonishingly well, until the day it depends on one tired person reading their email. The next time you install a package or a plugin with one command, it is worth asking a question nobody asked about xz Utils until it was almost too late: who actually maintains this, and are they okay?

takeaways: Open source means the human-readable code is shared under a license that lets anyone read, change and redistribute it.
Copyleft licenses like the GPL keep changes open; permissive licenses like MIT let code go into closed products.
Widely used open source would cost about $4 billion to write once but is worth an estimated $8.8 trillion to the firms that use it.
A small share of developers creates most of the value, and many critical projects would stall if one or two people left.
Reading and contributing to open source is one of the best ways to learn real-world coding and build a public track record.

title: Your Computer Is Lying to Every Program on It
dek: Every app on your PC believes it has the processor and all the memory to itself. The operating system keeps that lie going thousands of times a second, and it is the reason one crashed game doesn't take the whole machine down with it.

blocks.text: In 1969 a Bell Labs programmer named Ken Thompson had a game problem. He had written a game called Space Travel, a simulation of the solar system in which the player flew a ship around and tried to land on planets and moons. It ran on a big shared company computer, where, as his colleague Dennis Ritchie later recalled, the display was jerky, and each game cost about **$75** in computer time. So Thompson found a little-used PDP-7 minicomputer in the building and, with Ritchie, rewrote the game to run on it.

There was no useful software on the PDP-7, so they wrote their own: math routines, display code, a debugger. Then Thompson built a file system to store things, and tools to exercise the file system, and a way to run programs. Over the course of 1969 the pile of tools grew into a working operating system, soon named **Unix**. Its descendants and imitators now run most of the world's servers, every Android phone, every Mac and iPhone, and, as of every list since November 2017, all 500 of the world's fastest supercomputers. It started because someone wanted a better frame rate for a space game.

Most people never think about what an operating system actually does. It is easy to assume it is the desktop, the start menu and the settings app. Those are just the visible parts. The real operating system is a piece of software that sits between every program and the hardware and runs a set of carefully maintained illusions. Understanding those illusions explains a lot: why your PC can run a game, Discord, a browser and OBS at once, why a crashed app usually just disappears, and why some crashes take everything down.
Illusion one: you have the processor to yourself

Open the task manager on a gaming PC and you will see hundreds of processes running, each convinced it is executing continuously. Yet the processor has only a handful of cores, and each core can run exactly one stream of instructions at a time. The trick is **time-slicing**. The operating system lets a program run for a tiny slice of time, then a hardware timer fires an interrupt, the CPU jumps into the operating system's code, and the **scheduler** decides who runs next.

Switching from one program to another is called a **context switch**. The operating system saves everything the current program was doing, its place in the code and the contents of the processor's registers, then loads another program's saved state and lets it continue as if it had never stopped. This happens so often that, to the user and to the programs themselves, everything appears to run at the same time.

blocks.title: How one CPU core juggles many programs
items: A program runs for a short time slice
A hardware timer interrupts it
The kernel saves the program's state
The scheduler picks the next program by priority
The kernel restores that program's state and resumes it

blocks.text: The scheduler is where operating systems show their personality. It has to balance fairness against priority. Your game's rendering thread should beat a background updater, and the audio driver must never be starved, or your voice chat crackles. Priority scheduling is old and battle-tested; it is what let the Apollo 11 guidance computer shed low-priority work and keep flying through its famous 1202 alarms. When a modern PC stutters, the cause is often some low-priority task grabbing a resource the game needed at the wrong moment.
Illusion two: you have the memory to yourself

The second illusion is even stranger. Every program on your PC sees what looks like its own private memory, starting from the same addresses, as if no other program existed. Two programs can both store something at what they think is the same address and never collide. This is **virtual memory**, and it was pioneered in the early 1960s on the Atlas computer at the University of Manchester, as Peter Denning described in a classic 1970 survey.

Here is how it works. Memory is chopped into fixed-size blocks called **pages**. Each program has its own **page table**, a map from the addresses it thinks it is using to the real physical locations in RAM. A piece of hardware inside the processor called the memory management unit translates every single memory access through that map, billions of times a second. If a program asks for an address that is not in its map, the hardware stops it and hands control to the operating system.

That one mechanism buys three huge things. First, **isolation**: a program physically cannot see or scribble on another program's memory, because those addresses do not exist in its map. Second, **flexibility**: the operating system can place a program's pages anywhere in RAM. Third, the ability to pretend there is more memory than there is, by moving rarely used pages out to the SSD and bringing them back when needed. That last trick is why a PC with too little RAM does not usually crash outright; it just gets painfully slow as it shuffles pages back and forth.

When a game crashes with an access violation or segmentation fault, that is virtual memory doing its job: the program touched an address it did not own, and the operating system stopped it before it could damage anything else.
Illusion three: you are in charge

The most important line in a computer is one you never see. Modern processors have at least two privilege levels. Ordinary programs run in **user mode**, where certain instructions are simply forbidden: talking to hardware directly, changing page tables, disabling interrupts. The core of the operating system, the **kernel**, runs in **kernel mode**, where everything is allowed. The hardware enforces the boundary. A program cannot just decide to cross it.

So how does a program do anything useful, like open a file or send a network packet? It asks. It makes a **system call**, a special instruction that switches the processor into kernel mode at a fixed, guarded entry point. The kernel checks whether the request is allowed, does the work, and hands back the result. Ritchie's account of early Unix describes calls such as fork, exec, wait and exit for creating and managing programs; versions of them are still in use in Linux and macOS today.

That guarded doorway has a cost. Crossing into kernel mode and back takes far longer than an ordinary function call inside a program, which is why performance-minded programmers try to batch work into fewer, bigger system calls, and why game engines often load assets in large chunks rather than one tiny file at a time. Safety is not free, but it is cheap compared with what happens without it.

Unix added one more simplifying idea that still shapes computers today: treat as many things as possible as files. A document on disk, a terminal, a connection to another program and even some hardware devices can all be opened, read from and written to with the same few calls. A program does not need to know whether it is writing to an SSD, a USB stick or a network share. The kernel and its drivers deal with the differences, and the program sees one simple interface.

blocks.title: What happens when a game saves a file
items: The game, in user mode, asks to write data to a file through a system call.
The CPU switches to kernel mode at a guarded entry point.
The kernel checks permissions and finds where the file lives on disk.
A storage driver, also running in the kernel, tells the SSD what to write.
The kernel returns a result and the CPU drops back to user mode.

blocks.text: If you have worked under tagout rules, the logic is familiar. Not everyone gets to operate every piece of equipment. You go through the person who controls it, they verify it is safe, and the system enforces the rule even when someone is in a hurry. The kernel is that controlling authority for every resource in the computer.
When the trusted layer fails

The flip side is that code running in kernel mode has no safety net. **Device drivers**, the code that knows how to talk to a specific graphics card, network adapter or headset, usually run inside the kernel because they need direct hardware access. If a game makes a bad memory access, the operating system kills the game. If a driver makes the same mistake, there is nothing above it to step in, so the whole system halts. That is what a blue screen on Windows is: the kernel deciding it is safer to stop everything than to keep running in an unknown state.

The world got a vivid lesson in this on July 19, 2024. The security company CrowdStrike pushed a routine configuration update to its Windows sensor, software that, like many security tools, runs with deep kernel-level access. According to the company's own incident report, faulty content in that update triggered an out-of-bounds memory read that could not be handled, crashing Windows. Microsoft estimated about **8.5 million** devices were affected, less than 1% of Windows machines, yet airlines, hospitals and banks went down across the world. The same code in user mode would have crashed one program.

items.label: Windows devices Microsoft estimated were hit by the July 2024 CrowdStrike crash
Cost of one game of Space Travel on Bell Labs' big computer, the push behind Unix

blocks.source: Microsoft via TechCrunch, 2024; Dennis Ritchie, The Evolution of the Unix Time-sharing System

blocks.text: This is also the trade-off behind kernel-level anti-cheat in competitive shooters such as Valorant. Cheats that run with kernel privileges can hide from anything running in user mode, so anti-cheat software moves into the kernel too, where it can see everything. That makes cheating much harder. It also means trusting one more piece of third-party code with total control of your machine. Neither side of that argument is crazy; it is the same question the CrowdStrike crash raised, about how much code you allow inside the most trusted layer.
From a hobby to every supercomputer

Ritchie and Thompson published a description of Unix in 1974, and its ideas spread through universities: small tools that each do one thing, everything treated as a file, a simple set of system calls. On August 25, 1991, a Finnish university student named Linus Torvalds posted a message to an online newsgroup announcing a free operating system kernel he had been writing for his PC. He described it as just a hobby that would not be big and professional. That kernel became **Linux**.

Linux grew into the kernel under most web servers, under every Android phone, and under the machines that run the cloud. Its takeover of the world's fastest computers is especially stark. The TOP500 project, which ranks supercomputers twice a year, recorded one Linux machine on its November 1998 list. By November 2017 every one of the 500 ran Linux, and it has stayed that way on every list since.

blocks.title: Supercomputers on the TOP500 list running Linux (November lists)
blocks.source: TOP500.org operating system family statistics

blocks.text: The best lies are the useful ones

Step back and the operating system looks like a strange kind of magician. Its whole job is to tell every program a comfortable lie: you have the processor to yourself, you have your own memory, the hardware is simple and safe to use. Programs are written to believe those lies, and because they believe them, programmers can build a game without thinking about the antivirus, the browser and the voice chat running alongside it.

This is the core move in all of engineering: **abstraction**. Hide the messy details behind a simple, dependable interface, so the next person can build on top without understanding everything underneath. A breaker panel does it for electricity. A rank structure does it for a crew. Roblox does it for game developers, who write scripts without ever touching the operating system below the engine below them.

Abstractions are wonderful right up until the layer underneath fails, and then the people who understand what is really going on become the most valuable people in the room. That is the deeper reason to learn how the operating system works, even if you never write one. Most days the illusion holds. The day it breaks, you want to be the one who knows where the illusion ends and the machine begins.

takeaways: The operating system's kernel shares a few CPU cores among hundreds of programs by time-slicing and context switching.
Virtual memory gives each program a private address space, which is why one crashing app usually cannot corrupt another.
User mode and kernel mode split ordinary programs from the trusted core; programs must ask the kernel through system calls.
Bugs in kernel-level code, such as drivers or security tools, can crash the whole machine, as the 2024 CrowdStrike incident showed on about 8.5 million PCs.
Unix began in 1969 partly to run a space game; its Linux descendant has run all 500 TOP500 supercomputers since November 2017.

title: Nobody Guesses Your Password. They Ask for It.
dek: Hollywood hackers type furiously until the screen says ACCESS GRANTED. Real account theft is quieter: reused passwords from old breaches, and fake login pages that people fill in themselves. The data on what actually stops it is surprisingly clear.

blocks.text: Over one year, from March 2016 to March 2017, a team of researchers from Google and UC Berkeley watched the underground markets where stolen logins are traded. They found 1.9 billion usernames and passwords exposed in data breaches, 12.4 million potential victims of phishing kits, and 788,000 potential victims of keylogging software. And they stressed that this was only a sample of what was out there.

Notice what is missing from that list: clever hackers guessing passwords one by one. The movie version of account theft, someone in a hoodie typing until the screen flashes ACCESS GRANTED, is mostly fiction. In the real world, attackers rarely need to guess your password. Either it has already leaked from some other site, or they trick you into typing it into a page they control. Understanding those two routes, and the data on what stops them, will protect your accounts better than any rule about special characters.
The three pipelines

Kurt Thomas and colleagues, publishing in 2017, traced how stolen credentials reach attackers through three main routes. **Data breaches** dump millions of logins at once when some website gets hacked. **Phishing kits** are ready-made fake login pages that criminals buy and deploy, often copies of real sites. **Keyloggers** are malware that records what you type on an infected computer.

They then asked which pipeline actually leads to a hijacked account, using Google accounts as the case study. The answer was not close. Victims of phishing were about 400 times more likely to have their account successfully hijacked than a random Google user. Keylogger victims were roughly 40 times more likely, and data breach victims about 10 times.

blocks.title: How much each theft route raises hijacking risk
blocks.note: Compared with a random Google user, based on credentials seen on underground markets in 2016–2017.
blocks.source: Thomas et al., Data Breaches, Phishing, or Malware?, ACM CCS 2017

blocks.text: Why is phishing so much worse? Partly because it captures your *current* password for the exact account the attacker wants. Only 7 percent of breach victims had their current Google password exposed, compared with 25 percent of phishing victims. And partly because modern phishing kits steal more than a password. The researchers found 83 percent of kits collected the victim's location and many grabbed phone numbers and browser details, so the attacker could look like you when logging in and slip past security systems that flag strange sign-ins.
Your old passwords are still out there

The breach route works because of one human habit: reusing passwords. If you used the same password for a forum account in 2019 and your email today, then the day that forum gets breached, your email is exposed too. Attackers run huge automated lists of leaked username and password pairs against popular sites, a technique called **credential stuffing**. It costs them almost nothing, so they try everything.

The account that matters most is your email. Almost every other account lets you reset its password through email, so whoever controls your inbox can take over your bank, your Discord, your Roblox account and your YouTube channel one reset at a time. Thomas and colleagues described email as the root of trust for a person's whole online identity. Protect it first and best.
Unique passwords do not make breaches stop. They make each breach a dead end instead of a master key.
What actually makes a password strong

For years, websites demanded passwords like *P@ssw0rd!* and forced you to change them every 90 days. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology, whose guidelines shape security policy across government and industry, now says almost all of that was counterproductive. People responded to complexity rules with predictable patterns, a capital at the start and a number and symbol at the end, and to forced changes by bumping *Summer2024!* to *Fall2024!*.

NIST's 2025 revision of its digital identity guidelines, SP 800-63B-4, flips the old advice. Sites must not impose composition rules such as requiring a mix of character types. They must not force periodic password changes, only a change when there is evidence of compromise. They must check new passwords against lists of common and previously breached passwords. Passwords used as the only login factor must be at least 15 characters, and sites should allow at least 64. They must allow password managers and autofill, and should allow pasting.

blocks.title: Old password rules vs NIST's 2025 guidance

left.head: Old habits
items: Must include upper, lower, number and symbol
Change your password every 90 days
Eight characters is enough
Password hints and security questions
Pasting into the password box blocked

right.head: NIST SP 800-63B-4
items: No composition rules allowed
No forced changes unless compromised
At least 15 characters if it is the only factor
No password hints or security questions
Password managers and pasting allowed

blocks.text: To see why these rules work, it helps to know what happens when a site is breached. A well-run site never stores your actual password. It stores a **hash**, a scrambled fingerprint that is easy to compute from the password but practically impossible to reverse. When you log in, the site hashes what you typed and compares fingerprints. After a breach, attackers get the list of fingerprints and start guessing offline, on their own hardware, as fast as it will run: hash a candidate, compare, repeat, with no login page to slow them down or lock them out. Common passwords fall in seconds because they are the first guesses on every list. A long random password survives because there are simply too many possibilities to try.

Guessing against a live login page is a different game. NIST requires sites to limit failed attempts, so an attacker trying passwords against your account directly gets a limited number of tries before being slowed or blocked. That is why the real danger is not someone guessing your password on the login screen. It is your password, or its hash, leaking from somewhere else.

The math explains why length wins. Security people measure the strength of a randomly generated password in **bits**: each extra bit doubles the number of guesses needed. Eight random lowercase letters give about 38 bits. Eight random characters from the whole keyboard give about 53. But four random words from a 7,776-word list, the size used by the classic Diceware method and the Electronic Frontier Foundation's list, give about 52 bits, and they are far easier to remember and type. Six random words reach about 78.

blocks.title: Strength of randomly chosen passwords
blocks.note: Each extra bit doubles the guesses needed. Only true for randomly chosen passwords; human-picked ones are far weaker.
blocks.source: Arithmetic: length x log2(choices); 7,776-word list per EFF, 2016

blocks.text: The catch is the word *random*. These numbers assume the password was picked by dice or software. Passwords that humans invent cluster around the same patterns, names and keyboard walks, and attackers' cracking tools start with exactly those. A password you made up yourself is almost always weaker than its length suggests. That is why the best answer for most accounts is a **password manager** that generates and remembers a long random password for every site, so you only need to memorize one strong passphrase.
Why smart people click

Phishing works because it attacks judgment, not technology. One of the largest field studies of it ran inside a real company for 15 months. Daniele Lain, Kari Kostiainen and Srdjan Čapkun at ETH Zurich worked with an organization to send 117,864 simulated phishing emails to 14,733 employees during their normal workdays. About 32 percent of employees clicked at least one, and about 25 percent went further and did the dangerous thing, such as submitting their login credentials. Of the employees who clicked, nearly a third clicked on two or more, and one person fell for six of the eight campaigns.

Most phishing follows a recognizable recipe. A message borrows the look of something you trust, such as a platform you use, your bank, your chain of command or a friend's account that was already taken over. It creates a reason to act now: your account will be locked, a payment failed, someone reported your channel, you won a prize. And it offers a convenient link to fix it, leading to a login page that looks perfect but lives at a slightly different address. The page is the trap. Everything else in the message exists to get you there before you slow down. That is why checking the address bar, or better, never using the link at all, defeats so much of it.

Two findings cut against common practice. First, simple warnings worked. Employees were split into groups of nearly equal size; the group with no warnings clicked 3,964 times, while groups with a short or detailed warning banner on suspicious emails clicked about 1,300 to 1,400 times. Second, the industry-standard response to a click, sending the person to a training page, backfired. Employees who got that training were *more* likely to fall for later phishing, not less. In a follow-up questionnaire, 43 percent of those who remembered the training page said seeing it made them feel safe, and 40 percent said the company was protecting them from bad emails. A lesson meant to make people careful may have made them complacent.

blocks.title: Clicks on simulated phishing, by warning type
blocks.note: Groups of roughly equal size over 15 months.
blocks.source: Lain, Kostiainen and Čapkun, IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2022

blocks.text: The study also found something useful for anyone young: employees aged 18 to 19 stood out as the group most likely to click more than once. And it found that people collectively are a strong alarm system. Given a report button, employees reported phishing quickly, around 10 percent of reports arriving within five minutes of an email landing. The lesson is not that you are too smart to be fooled. Everyone is foolable on a tired, busy day. The defense is a habit: when a message creates urgency about your account, your pay or your orders, stop and check it through a channel you already trust, not the link in the message.
The second lock, and the one that cannot be phished

If passwords leak and people can be tricked, the fix is to require something besides the password. Google, working with researchers from New York University and UC San Diego, measured this in 2019. A text-message code to a phone blocked 100 percent of automated bot attacks, 96 percent of bulk phishing attacks and 76 percent of targeted attacks. An on-device prompt, where your phone asks if you are trying to sign in, did better: 100, 99 and 90 percent.

items.label: Drop in account compromise risk with multifactor authentication, Microsoft study
Drop even when the password had already leaked

blocks.source: Meyer et al., Microsoft, 2023

blocks.text: A 2023 Microsoft study of business accounts found that multifactor authentication cut the risk of compromise by 99.22 percent overall, and by 98.56 percent even for accounts whose passwords had already leaked. Authenticator apps beat text messages, but both were far better than a password alone.

There is one weakness left. A clever phishing page can ask for your code too and relay it to the real site within seconds. The defense against that is **phishing-resistant** login: hardware security keys and passkeys. These use public-key cryptography, and the browser only lets the key answer the website it was registered with. A fake site at a look-alike address simply gets nothing it can use. NIST requires this kind of phishing resistance at its highest assurance level. If an account offers passkeys, turn them on.

items: Lock down your email first: long unique password plus an authenticator app, security key or passkey.
Use a password manager and let it generate a different password for every site.
Turn on two-step verification for every account with money, rare items or your channel attached.
Never sign in from a link in an urgent message; go to the site or app yourself.
For government systems and devices, follow your command's cybersecurity rules; they override personal habits.

blocks.text: The pattern across all of this is that the weakest link in security is rarely the math. Encryption is strong. Humans reuse passwords, click when rushed and trust what looks official. Good security is less about being clever than about building a few defaults that protect you on the day your judgment slips.

takeaways: Most accounts fall to leaked or phished passwords, not guessing; phishing victims were about 400 times more likely to be hijacked.
Your email is the master key to everything else. Protect it first.
Length and randomness beat complexity: NIST now bans composition rules and forced changes and wants 15+ characters for password-only logins.
Warnings help and everyone can be fooled; when a message creates urgency, verify through a channel you already trust.
Any second factor helps enormously; passkeys and security keys are the ones phishing cannot steal.

title: How Two Strangers Agree on a Secret While Everyone Listens
dek: For thousands of years, sharing a secret meant meeting first. Then a few mathematicians found a way around it, and the entire internet now rests on their trick.

blocks.text: Open any website with a padlock in the address bar and something quietly impossible happens. Your phone and a server it has never met, possibly on another continent, agree on a secret key in a fraction of a second. Every message they exchange to set it up travels over cables, routers and Wi-Fi that anyone could, in principle, be recording. The eavesdropper sees every single bit of the conversation. And at the end of it, your phone and the server share a secret that the eavesdropper cannot work out.

If that doesn't strike you as strange, think about it for a second. How do you agree on a password with someone, out loud, in a crowded room, without anyone else learning it? For almost all of human history the answer was: you can't. The fact that we now can, billions of times a day, is one of the great intellectual tricks of the twentieth century. It is called **public-key cryptography**, and it rests on a surprisingly simple idea: some math problems are easy to do and brutally hard to undo.
The problem that stumped everyone

Classic encryption is symmetric: the same key locks and unlocks the message. That works beautifully as long as both sides already share the key. The trouble is getting it to them. Armies, navies and diplomats spent centuries solving this with couriers, sealed codebooks and lists of daily keys, physically carried from one place to another and guarded with real force. If the courier was intercepted or the codebook captured, every message was exposed.

This is called the **key distribution problem**, and it scales horribly. If a hundred people each want to talk privately with each other, they need a separate key for every pair, nearly five thousand keys, each delivered securely in advance. Now imagine billions of people and websites who want to talk to strangers they have never met. Symmetric cryptography alone simply can't do it. Something had to let two parties create a shared secret over a channel everyone can hear.
The paint trick

In 1976, two Stanford researchers, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, published a paper called 'New Directions in Cryptography' that showed it could be done. Their method is usually explained with paint, and the analogy is good enough to be worth learning.

blocks.title: Diffie–Hellman, with paint
items: Alice and Bob publicly agree on a starting color, say yellow. Everyone can see it.
Each secretly picks a private color: Alice picks red, Bob picks blue. They never share these.
Each mixes their private color into the yellow and sends the mixture to the other in public.
Alice adds her red to Bob's mixture; Bob adds his blue to Alice's mixture.
Both now hold yellow + red + blue, the same final color. The eavesdropper only saw the two mixtures.

blocks.text: The trick works because mixing paint is easy but unmixing it is practically impossible. The eavesdropper sees yellow, the yellow-red mixture and the yellow-blue mixture, but can't separate any of them back into their ingredients. Without Alice's red or Bob's blue, there's no way to produce the final shared color.

Real cryptography replaces paint with arithmetic on huge numbers. The everyday version uses what's called modular arithmetic, which is the math of clocks: on a 12-hour clock, 9 plus 5 isn't 14, it's 2, because you wrap around. Here's a toy example with tiny numbers. Alice and Bob publicly agree on a prime number, 23, and a base, 5. Alice secretly picks 6; Bob secretly picks 15. Alice computes 5 to the 6th power, wrapped around 23, which gives 8, and sends 8 in public. Bob does the same with his secret and sends 19.

Now Alice takes Bob's 19 and raises it to her secret 6, wrapped around 23, and gets 2. Bob takes Alice's 8, raises it to his secret 15, wrapped around 23, and also gets 2. They share the secret number 2, and nobody ever sent it. The eavesdropper saw 23, 5, 8 and 19. To find the secret, they would need to work backward from 8 to Alice's 6, a problem known as the **discrete logarithm**. With numbers this small you could guess it in seconds. With numbers hundreds of digits long, nobody knows how to do it in any reasonable time.
Locks anyone can close

Diffie and Hellman also sketched a bigger idea they couldn't yet build: a cipher with two different keys. One, the public key, could be handed out to the whole world and used to lock messages. The other, the private key, would be the only thing that could unlock them. Think of a padlock you can mass-produce and leave open on tables everywhere. Anyone can grab one and snap it shut on a box addressed to you. Only you have the key that opens it.

A year later, in 1977, three MIT researchers, Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman, found a way to build exactly that. Their system, RSA, rests on a different one-way problem: multiplying two large prime numbers is easy, but taking the result and finding the two primes again, called factoring, is enormously hard. Your private key is built from the two primes. Your public key contains only their product. Anyone can use the product to lock a message; only someone who knows the original primes can undo it.

Run the same idea backward and you get something just as important: **digital signatures**. If you lock something with your private key, anyone can unlock it with your public key, which proves it could only have come from you. That's how your phone knows a software update really came from the manufacturer, and how a website proves it really is your bank and not an impostor.

Signatures also solve a problem that public keys create. If anyone can publish a public key, what stops an impostor from publishing one and claiming to be your bank? The answer is a chain of signatures. A website's public key comes wrapped in a certificate, a small file that says 'this key belongs to this domain,' signed by a certificate authority. That authority's own key is in turn vouched for by a short list of root keys built into your phone or browser. When the padlock appears, your device has checked every link of that chain in the background.

If you've ever used a military Common Access Card, you've carried this system in your wallet. The chip on the card holds certificates and private keys, which is how it can digitally sign an email or log you into a government network. The PIN unlocks the private key on the card, and the private key never has to leave it.

blocks.title: Two kinds of cryptography

left.head: Symmetric (shared key)
items: One key locks and unlocks
Very fast, good for bulk data
Both sides must already share the key
Examples: AES, the cipher protecting most traffic

right.head: Public-key (key pair)
items: Public key locks or verifies, private key unlocks or signs
Much slower, used for small jobs
Strangers can start talking securely
Examples: RSA, Diffie–Hellman, elliptic curves

blocks.text: In practice, the internet uses both. Public-key math is slow, so it's used only at the start of a connection, to agree on a fresh symmetric key and to check who you're talking to. After that handshake, fast symmetric encryption carries the actual data. Every time you load a secure page, both kinds of cryptography have worked together before the first image appears.
The secret history

There's a twist to the story that wasn't revealed for more than twenty years. At GCHQ, Britain's signals intelligence agency, an engineer named James Ellis had already worked out that what he called 'non-secret encryption' should be possible. In 1973, a young mathematician there, Clifford Cocks, came up with a scheme essentially the same as RSA. His colleague Malcolm Williamson soon devised a method equivalent to Diffie–Hellman. All of it was classified. GCHQ made the work public only in late 1997, and Ellis died a month before the announcement.

blocks.title: How strangers learned to share secrets
items: James Ellis at GCHQ argues 'non-secret encryption' is possible
Clifford Cocks devises an RSA-like scheme in secret
Diffie and Hellman publish 'New Directions in Cryptography'
Rivest, Shamir and Adleman create RSA at MIT
Koblitz and Miller propose elliptic-curve cryptography
Peter Shor shows a quantum computer could break RSA
GCHQ reveals its earlier work
NIST publishes its first post-quantum encryption standards

blocks.text: It's a strange lesson about invention. The same idea arrived twice, independently, a few years apart. One version changed the world; the other sat in a safe. Secrecy can protect an idea, but only openness lets it be tested, improved and built into everything.
How hard is hard?

Everything depends on those one-way problems staying hard. The best measure we have is how big a number people have actually managed to factor. RSA Laboratories once published a list of challenge numbers with cash prizes, and they became a public scoreboard for the state of the art. In 2020, a team of researchers in France and the United States factored RSA-250, a number 829 bits long, using about 2,700 core-years of computing time spread across thousands of machines.

blocks.title: Largest RSA challenge number factored
blocks.note: Larger numbers reported factored in 2026 are still under 900 bits. Everyday RSA keys are 2,048 bits or more.
blocks.source: RSA Factoring Challenge records; UC San Diego, 2020

blocks.text: That curve climbs slowly, and it's still nowhere near the 2,048-bit keys in common use today. Each extra bit roughly doubles the size of the number, so going from 829 bits to 2,048 isn't a matter of a bit more effort; with known methods on ordinary computers, it's out of reach by an absurd margin. The progress that does happen comes from better algorithms and more computing power, which is why security standards plan for keys to grow over time.

It helps to know what the attackers are actually doing. Nobody factors these numbers by trying every possible divisor; that would take longer than the age of the universe even for modest keys. The record-setters use a sophisticated method called the number field sieve, which searches for mathematical relationships among many smaller numbers and then combines them. It is vastly better than brute force, but it still slows down steeply as numbers grow, and that steep slope is what keeps your keys safe.

In 1985, Neal Koblitz and Victor Miller independently proposed a newer family of systems based on the math of elliptic curves. The one-way problem there is harder to attack for a given key size, so you get the same security with far shorter keys. That's why most modern phones, messaging apps and websites lean on elliptic curves: smaller keys mean faster handshakes and less battery drain.

blocks.title: Key size needed for the same security
blocks.note: Security level roughly means an attacker needs about 2 to that power operations to break it.
blocks.source: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5, Table 2, 2020

blocks.text: The quantum clock

There's one known way all of this could fall. In 1994, mathematician Peter Shor showed that a large enough quantum computer could factor numbers and solve discrete logarithms efficiently, breaking RSA, Diffie–Hellman and elliptic curves at once. No quantum computer today is anywhere close to big or reliable enough to do it. But spies don't need to break messages today. They can record encrypted traffic now and wait. This threat even has a name: harvest now, decrypt later.

So cryptographers have spent the past decade building replacements based on different math problems that quantum computers aren't known to crack, many of them built on lattices, which are like enormous high-dimensional grids of points. In August 2024, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology published its first three finished post-quantum standards: one for agreeing on keys (ML-KEM) and two for digital signatures (ML-DSA and SLH-DSA). NIST says it plans to phase quantum-vulnerable algorithms out of its standards by 2035, and big messaging apps and browsers have already started mixing the new methods into their handshakes.

Here's the unsettling part: nobody has ever proven that factoring or discrete logarithms are truly hard. The world's security rests on the fact that very smart people have tried for decades and failed. That's strong evidence, but it's not a proof.

That's the deeper idea worth carrying away. Public-key cryptography didn't make secrets safe by hiding them better. It changed the question. Instead of asking how to keep a channel private, it asked how to make a secret that is safe even when the channel is completely public. The answer was to lean on asymmetry, on things that are easy in one direction and hard in the other. Once you start looking, you'll see the same pattern elsewhere: a reputation takes years to build and seconds to destroy; a habit is easy to break and hard to rebuild. The mathematicians just found a way to turn that kind of lopsidedness into a lock.

takeaways: Public-key cryptography lets strangers create a shared secret over a channel anyone can hear.
It works because some math is easy one way and hard to reverse: mixing, multiplying, exponentiating.
The internet uses public-key math for the handshake, then fast symmetric encryption for the data.
Elliptic curves give the same security as RSA with far smaller keys.
Quantum computers threaten today's schemes, so NIST has begun standardizing replacements.

title: Quantum Computers Aren't Faster Computers
dek: They don't try every answer at once. They do something stranger, it only pays off on a short list of problems, and one of those problems happens to be the lock on the internet.

blocks.text: In December 2024, Google announced a chip called Willow. It finished a benchmark calculation in under five minutes. Google estimated that one of the fastest classical supercomputers on Earth would need about 10 septillion years to do the same job. That's a 1 followed by 25 zeros, far longer than the universe has existed.

Read that and it's natural to imagine your next gaming PC running on qubits, loading instantly, rendering at a million frames per second. It won't. Willow can't run a web browser, and the problem it crushed was chosen because it is brutally hard for normal computers and almost useless for anything else.

So here's the puzzle: how can a machine be septillions of times faster than a supercomputer at one task and worse than your phone at almost everything else? The answer is the single most misunderstood idea in modern technology. A quantum computer isn't a faster computer. It's a different kind of instrument, and once you understand how it really works, you can tell the hype from the genuinely big deal.
The myth of trying every answer at once

Start with what a normal computer does. A *bit* is a switch that's either 0 or 1. Your CPU flips billions of them per second in a precise sequence. At every moment, the machine is in exactly one definite state, and you could, in principle, read out every bit without disturbing anything.

A *qubit* is different. Its state is described by two numbers called *amplitudes*, one attached to 0 and one attached to 1. Amplitudes behave a lot like waves: they have a size and a direction, so they can be positive, negative, or something in between. When you measure the qubit, you get a plain 0 or a plain 1, with odds set by the squared size of each amplitude. The measurement also destroys the delicate in-between state.

Now add more qubits. Two qubits need four amplitudes, one for each combination: 00, 01, 10, 11. Three need eight. Every added qubit doubles the count, so 300 qubits involve 2 to the 300th power amplitudes, a number vastly larger than the count of atoms in the observable universe. This is where the popular story comes from: a quantum computer explores all those possibilities in parallel, so it must be checking every answer at once.

Those combined amplitudes are also where *entanglement* comes from. When qubits are entangled, the amplitudes can't be split into separate descriptions for each qubit. The system only makes sense as a whole: measure one qubit and you instantly constrain what the others can show. Entanglement isn't a way to send messages faster than light, but it is the resource that lets a computation weave the possibilities of many qubits together instead of treating each one alone.

Here's the catch that the popular story leaves out. When you measure at the end, you get one answer, chosen at random according to the amplitudes. If all the possible answers have equal amplitudes, you just get a random guess. You could do that with a coin. All that enormous hidden state is worthless unless you can arrange for the wrong answers to fade and the right one to stand out before you look.

A quantum computer doesn't check every answer and report back. It sets up a pattern of waves so that wrong answers cancel each other out, then takes one measurement and hopes the right answer is the loudest thing left.
Interference is the real trick

If you've worked with AC power, you already have the intuition. Two signals in phase add up. Two signals 180 degrees out of phase cancel. Noise-cancelling headphones use the same idea, generating a wave that is the mirror image of the noise so that the two sum to nearly nothing.

Quantum algorithms are choreography for that kind of cancellation. Each step of the computation is a *gate*, an operation that rotates and mixes the amplitudes. A well-designed sequence of gates makes the paths leading to wrong answers arrive out of phase, so they cancel, while the paths leading to the right answer arrive in phase and reinforce. Then you measure, and with high probability you get the answer you wanted.

The hard part is that you can only build this choreography when the problem has some hidden structure the waves can lock onto, like a repeating pattern. Most everyday computing tasks have no such structure to exploit. That's why there is no quantum spreadsheet and probably never will be. The speedup is not a general property of the hardware. It belongs to specific algorithms for specific problems.

blocks.title: How a quantum algorithm actually runs
items: Prepare the qubits in a simple starting state, usually all zeros.
Apply gates that spread the amplitudes across many possible answers.
Apply more gates that encode the problem, shifting the phase of some paths.
Use interference so wrong answers cancel and the right one grows.
Measure once and read out a single classical answer.
Repeat several times and check the result on a normal computer.

blocks.text: The short list of things it's good at

The most famous example came in 1994, when Peter Shor, then at AT&T, showed that a quantum computer could factor large numbers efficiently. Factoring means taking a number like 15 and finding the primes that multiply to make it, 3 and 5. For numbers hundreds of digits long, the best known classical methods take an impractically long time. Shor's algorithm turns factoring into a problem of finding the period of a repeating pattern, exactly the kind of structure that interference can latch onto.

In 1996, Lov Grover at Bell Labs found a broader but much smaller speedup. Imagine a phone directory of N names in random order, and you want the one with a given number. A classical search has to check about half the entries on average. Grover's algorithm needs only about the square root of N steps. For a million entries, that's on the order of a thousand steps instead of half a million. Useful, but it's a square-root gain, not the exponential leap Shor offers.

The third big category may matter most in the long run: simulating nature itself. Molecules and materials are quantum systems, and tracking their electrons on a classical computer gets exponentially harder as they grow. A quantum computer speaks the same language as the thing it's simulating. That's the hope behind designing better catalysts, batteries and drugs, and it's the area Google pointed to in October 2025 with an algorithm called Quantum Echoes, aimed at revealing hidden dynamics inside quantum systems like molecules.

blocks.title: Where quantum helps, and where it doesn't

left.head: Strong candidates
items: Factoring big numbers (Shor)
Simulating molecules and materials
Some search and optimization problems, with smaller gains
Sampling tasks designed to be hard classically

right.head: Poor fits
items: Gaming, video and graphics
Web browsing and everyday apps
Most business software and databases
Anything that needs to read out huge amounts of data

blocks.text: The noise problem

If quantum computing is so powerful for these problems, why haven't we broken anything yet? Because qubits are absurdly fragile. Any stray interaction with the outside world, whether heat, vibration or a passing electromagnetic field, leaks information out of the qubit and scrambles the amplitudes. Physicists call this *decoherence*. Superconducting chips like Google's are cooled to a tiny fraction of a degree above absolute zero to slow it down, and even so, Willow's qubits hold their state for times approaching 100 microseconds.

Every gate also has a small chance of error. Google reported fidelities for Willow of 99.97 percent for single-qubit gates and 99.88 percent for the two-qubit gates that create entanglement. That sounds excellent until you remember that a useful algorithm needs millions or billions of operations, and errors stack up.

items.label: Physical qubits on Google's Willow chip
How long Willow's qubits hold their state
Fidelity of Willow's two-qubit gates

blocks.source: Google Quantum AI, Willow announcement (Dec 2024) and hardware update (Oct 2025)

blocks.text: The answer is *quantum error correction*. You spread one reliable *logical* qubit across many unreliable *physical* qubits and keep checking them for signs of damage, without directly measuring the information you're protecting. It's a bit like a RAID array or redundant instrument channels in a reactor plant: no single sensor is trusted, but the group can catch and correct a failure. The catch is that more qubits also means more places for errors to creep in. Error correction only wins if the hardware is already good enough. That cutoff is called the *threshold*.

There's a clever twist in how the checking works. You can't just look at the protected qubits, because measuring them would destroy the information. Instead, extra helper qubits are entangled with groups of data qubits and measured in their place. Their results reveal whether a neighbor has flipped, without revealing what the data actually is. A classical computer reads those results continuously and decides which corrections to apply, over and over in a continuous cycle for as long as the computation runs.

Willow's real headline wasn't the septillion years. It was that when Google grew its encoded qubit from a 3-by-3 grid of physical qubits to 5-by-5 and then 7-by-7, the error rate fell by half at each step. Bigger finally meant better. That's the first convincing sign that scaling up can work, though a useful machine needs vastly more qubits than 105.
A countdown on the internet's lock

Much of the internet's security has relied on public-key cryptography such as RSA, which depends on factoring being hopelessly slow. A big enough quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break it. So the question that matters is not whether a quantum computer is impressive. It's how big one would need to be.

In 2019, Craig Gidney and Martin Ekerå estimated that factoring a 2048-bit RSA key would take about 20 million noisy physical qubits running for eight hours. In May 2025, Gidney published a new estimate: fewer than a million noisy qubits, running for less than a week, assuming the same error rate of 0.1 percent per gate. The hardware didn't get 20 times better in six years. The *algorithms* did. That's a pattern worth remembering: in this field, the target moves from both ends.

blocks.title: Qubits needed to break RSA-2048 vs. qubits built
blocks.note: The 2025 figure is an upper bound ('less than a million'). Willow's bar is there; at 105 qubits it's too small to see.
blocks.source: Gidney & Ekerå, 2019; Gidney, arXiv 2505.15917, 2025; Google Quantum AI, 2024

blocks.text: Even so, the gap is enormous. Today's best chips have around a hundred physical qubits, and the requirement is still on the order of a million. Nobody can tell you with confidence when that gap closes. But there's a reason security agencies are moving now. Adversaries can record encrypted traffic today and simply store it, waiting for the day they can decrypt it. Security people call this *harvest now, decrypt later*. Secrets that need to stay secret for decades are already exposed to a future machine.

That's why, in August 2024, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalized its first three post-quantum encryption standards, built on math problems that are believed to be hard for quantum computers too. One is meant for general encryption and two for digital signatures. NIST noted that some experts expect a code-breaking quantum computer within a decade. The software migration is starting long before the hardware exists, which is exactly how it should work.

blocks.title: From theory to countdown
items: Peter Shor shows a quantum computer could factor large numbers efficiently
Lov Grover publishes a square-root speedup for unstructured search
Google's 53-qubit Sycamore claims a task in 200 seconds; IBM counters that a supercomputer could do it in about 2.5 days
Aug 2024
NIST finalizes its first three post-quantum encryption standards
Dec 2024
Willow: 105 qubits, errors halve as the encoded qubit grows
May 2025
New estimate: RSA-2048 needs under a million noisy qubits
Oct 2025
Google reports verifiable quantum advantage with Quantum Echoes

blocks.text: How to read the next headline

The 2019 Sycamore claim is a useful lesson. Google said its 53-qubit chip did in 200 seconds what a supercomputer would need 10,000 years to do. IBM quickly argued that a smarter classical approach on the Summit supercomputer could do it in about 2.5 days. Classical algorithms keep improving too, so every claim of quantum advantage is a race against a moving target. Some claims hold up, and some shrink.

It also helps to know what the famous benchmark actually is. *Random circuit sampling* means running a random jumble of gates and collecting the outputs. The results have no practical meaning. The point is that the pattern of outputs is extraordinarily hard to reproduce on a classical machine, which makes it a good stress test and a poor product. Google's October 2025 Quantum Echoes work was pitched as a step past this, because its result can be checked and is connected to real physics questions about molecules.

When you see the next big announcement, ask three questions. Is the task useful, or was it chosen because it's hard for classical machines? Can the answer be checked? And how many of the qubits are error-corrected logical qubits rather than raw physical ones? Those three questions cut through most of the noise.

The reframe to carry around is this. A quantum computer is to a normal computer what a telescope is to a truck. Nobody asks whether a telescope is faster than a truck. It does something a truck can't do at all, and it's useless for hauling groceries. The machines being built now are early, noisy telescopes. What they eventually reveal, whether it's new materials, new medicines or the contents of today's encrypted messages, depends on how fast the engineering closes a gap that is still measured in factors of ten thousand.

takeaways: Qubits hold many amplitudes, but a measurement gives one answer. The power comes from interference, not from checking every answer.
Big speedups exist only for problems with hidden structure: factoring, simulating molecules, and a few others.
Noise is the main obstacle; error correction spreads one logical qubit across many physical ones and only works below a quality threshold.
Breaking RSA-2048 was estimated at 20 million qubits in 2019 and under a million in 2025. Today's best chips have about a hundred.
Post-quantum encryption standards were finalized in 2024 because encrypted data can be stored now and decrypted later.
