title: The Feed Knows What You'll Do, Not What You Want
dek: Recommendation algorithms are prediction machines aimed at your behavior. Once you see how they score you, the endless scroll stops looking like a window and starts looking like a mirror.

blocks.text: It's 0130 and you just got off watch. You tell yourself you'll check one thing before you rack out. Forty minutes later you're watching a stranger restore a rusted pocketknife, and you couldn't explain how you got there if someone paid you. You didn't really choose most of those videos. You just never said no to them.

That isn't a character flaw so much as an engineering result. In January 2018, YouTube's chief product officer, Neal Mohan, said that about 70 percent of the time people spend watching YouTube is driven by its recommendations. Netflix engineers wrote in 2015 that their recommender influenced roughly 80 percent of the hours streamed on the service. Most of what the world watches is no longer picked by the viewer. It's picked by a prediction.

To use these systems instead of being used by them, it helps to know what they actually are. They aren't mind readers, and they aren't villains. They are machines built to answer one narrow question, billions of times a day: *what will this person do next?*

items.label: Share of YouTube watch time driven by recommendations (2018)
Share of Netflix hours streamed influenced by its recommender (2015)
How long a typical Netflix member browses before losing interest

blocks.source: Neal Mohan at CES, reported by Quartz, 2018; Gomez-Uribe & Hunt, ACM Transactions on Management Information Systems, 2015

blocks.text: A funnel, not a mind

Look at the problem from the platform's side. YouTube has an enormous library and a fraction of a second to fill your home screen. No model can carefully evaluate every video for every user in that time. So almost every large recommender is built as a funnel, with cheap, fast filtering at the top and slow, careful judgment at the bottom.

Google engineers described YouTube's version in a 2016 paper. The first stage, *candidate generation*, takes a corpus of millions of videos and pulls out a few hundred that are roughly relevant to you. It leans heavily on *collaborative filtering*: the idea that people who watched what you watched tend to want what those people watched next. The second stage, *ranking*, scores each of those few hundred carefully, using many more signals. A few dozen make it to your screen.

The trick that makes the first stage fast is called an *embedding*. Every video and every user gets turned into a list of numbers, a few hundred long, which you can picture as a point in a space with hundreds of dimensions. During training, the system nudges those points around so that the things you'd watch end up close to you. Finding candidates then becomes a geometry problem: grab the videos nearest your point.

Nobody writes down that one axis means tactical gear and another means sad piano covers. The model invents its own axes from billions of clicks, and many of them don't map onto any human category at all. That's part of why a feed can feel uncannily accurate and impossible to explain at the same time.

blocks.title: How a feed gets built in a fraction of a second
items: Start with the whole library: millions of items.
Candidate generation: cheaply pull a few hundred items that sit near your embedding.
Ranking: score each candidate with a bigger model and many more signals.
Filter and mix: drop repeats, spam and things you've seen; add some variety.
Show the top results and log everything you do with them.
Feed that log back into training, so tomorrow's model knows you a little differently.

blocks.text: What the machine is really predicting

Here is the part most people miss. The ranking model doesn't output a single verdict on how good a video is. It predicts a set of separate probabilities: the chance you'll click, watch to the end, like, reply, share, or tell it to go away. Then a plain formula combines those predictions into one score, and the highest scores win. The predictions are learned from data. The formula is chosen by people, and it encodes what the company has decided to value.

YouTube's 2016 paper is unusually frank about this. Its ranking objective was described as mostly a function of expected watch time per impression, rather than the chance of a click. The reason was practical: ranking by clicks tends to promote deceptive videos that people open and then abandon. Watch time was harder to fake. Notice what happened there. A human looked at a number, saw it being gamed, and swapped it for a different number.

We rarely get to see that formula. In 2023, Twitter (now X) published code for its home timeline ranker, including the weights it used as of April 2023. Each weight multiplies the predicted probability of one action. They're worth a close look, because they turn an abstract idea into a price list.

blocks.title: Twitter's ranking weights, April 2023 (like = 0.5)
blocks.note: Negative signals were weighted too: 'show less' or block at −74, a report at −369.
blocks.source: Twitter, the-algorithm-ml, home timeline ranker README, 2023

blocks.text: Read it like a menu. On that ranking, a predicted reply was worth 27 likes. A reply that the original poster then answered was worth 150 likes. A predicted report cost as much as 738 likes. Whoever set those numbers decided that conversation matters far more than quiet approval, and they were right that conversation keeps people on the app. What the formula didn't ask was whether the conversation was a friendly one or a shouting match.

Every platform makes a version of that choice. YouTube made a famous one in March 2012, when it told creators it would weight time watched more heavily than clicks when picking related and recommended videos. Clicks had been rewarding misleading thumbnails and titles. Watch time was supposed to reward videos people actually wanted to see.
Better serve videos that keep viewers entertained.
blocks.by: YouTube Creator Blog, March 2012

blocks.text: TikTok said in 2020 that one of its strongest signals is whether you finish a longer video from beginning to end, and that follower count is not a direct factor. Each of these is a sensible proxy for 'this person liked it.' None of them is the same thing as 'this person is glad they spent the time.'
The explore-exploit trap

A recommender faces a dilemma borrowed from casinos. Computer scientists call it the *multi-armed bandit* problem. A gambler facing a row of slot machines has to choose between pulling the one that has paid well so far (exploiting) and trying others that might pay better (exploring). Exploit too much and the feed goes stale. Explore too much and it fills with junk.

So feeds do both. Most of what you see is a confident bet, and a slice of it is a probe: something slightly outside your usual range, placed there to measure your reaction. That's why a strange video sometimes appears out of nowhere, and why one long look at it can tilt your feed for days. The system isn't messing with you. It's running an experiment, and you just answered it.

There's also a bias toward the past built into any model trained on yesterday's data. The YouTube engineers found that their system, left alone, underrated brand-new uploads, because popularity in the training data was averaged over the whole training window. Their fix was to tell the model how old each training example was, which raised watch time on fresh videos. Small design choices like that decide which creators get a shot and which never surface.

Put those pieces together and you get a loop, and loops are where the interesting behavior lives. Your actions train the model. The model decides what you see. What you see shapes your next actions. Anyone who has studied control systems knows that feedback can stabilize or it can drift. Watch three videos on a topic out of pure boredom, and the system may conclude that topic is who you are.

blocks.title: The feed loop
items: You act: watch, skip, like, linger
The model updates its picture of you
The feed shifts toward that picture
Your options narrow to what it shows
You act on those options

blocks.text: The same loop runs on the people making content. Anyone building a YouTube channel or a Roblox game is optimizing against a ranking formula whether they mean to or not. Strong hooks in the first seconds, faces in thumbnails, titles that open a question: creators drift toward these because the ranker rewards whatever predicts watching. The algorithm doesn't just learn its audience. It quietly trains everyone who makes things for it.
Wanting versus liking

If these models are so good at predicting behavior, why does an hour of scrolling so often feel like an hour you'd like back? Because behavior and satisfaction are different signals, and engagement only measures one of them.

A team led by Smitha Milli tested this directly. In February 2023 they recruited 806 Twitter users and compared the tweets the engagement-based algorithm showed each person with what a plain newest-first timeline would have shown. Participants then rated the tweets. The algorithmic feed carried noticeably more anger. Anger expressed by tweet authors was about half a standard deviation higher, and readers reported feeling angrier too. (A standard deviation is a measure of how spread out a set of scores is; half of one is a moderate effect, easily big enough to change the mood of a feed.) For political tweets the gap was even larger.

Here's the part that should stick. Users said they did not prefer the political tweets the algorithm picked for them. The system was serving content people engaged with but wouldn't have chosen. That isn't a conspiracy. Anger is engaging. It makes people reply, and on that 2023 price list a reply was worth 27 likes. The algorithm did exactly what it was told.

Economists have names for the gap. *Revealed preferences* are what your behavior shows you want. *Stated preferences* are what you say you want when someone asks you calmly. Feeds are built almost entirely on the first kind, because it's abundant, automatic and cheap to collect. The second kind takes asking, and asking is slow.

There's an old warning in economics, usually credited to Charles Goodhart: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Watch time and replies started out as decent clues that people were enjoying themselves. Turn them into the thing a billion-dollar system maximizes, and the system will find every way to raise the number, including ways that have nothing to do with enjoyment.

blocks.title: Two versions of you

left.head: What the model can see
items: You watched 90 percent of it
You replied within seconds
You stopped scrolling for eight seconds
You came back an hour later

right.head: What it can't see
items: You were annoyed the whole time
You were arguing, not enjoying
You were half asleep
You wish you'd gone to bed

blocks.text: It's worth being fair, too. Recommenders solve a real problem. Netflix's own research found that a typical member loses interest after 60 to 90 seconds of browsing, having looked at maybe 10 to 20 titles. Without a recommender, most of a giant library would be invisible, and plenty of great small creators would never be found. The issue isn't recommendation itself. It's what the system is told to maximize.
A feed is a mirror that reflects what you do, never what you meant. If you want it to show you something different, the only language it understands is behavior.
Taking back the controls

Once you see the machine as a behavior predictor wrapped in a weighting formula, the defensive moves become obvious. The model can't hear your intentions. It can only count your actions. So make your actions say what you mean.

items: Don't hate-watch. Lingering on rage bait is a vote for more of it, even if you never tap anything.
Use the negative buttons. 'Not interested' and 'don't recommend this channel' exist, and the published Twitter weights show how heavily negative feedback can count.
Search on purpose. A deliberate search hands the model a clear signal about what you want.
Finish what you value and bail fast on what you don't. Completion is one of the strongest signals platforms use.
Lean on subscription or following feeds when you can; they sit closer to your stated preferences.
Prune or pause your watch history if a binge has skewed things.

blocks.text: There's one more lever, and most people never get it: real time away. Months underway with no connection means you come back to apps running on an old picture of you. The first sessions back in port are fresh evidence. Spend them deliberately, and you're giving the model a new first draft instead of letting your most bored hours write it.

The deeper reframe is this. A feed isn't showing you what you like. It's showing you what a model predicted you would do, weighted by what a company decided to count. Once you see that, the scroll stops looking like a window onto the world. It's a very good guess about you, assembled as easily from your worst five minutes as from your best.

takeaways: Recommenders predict your actions, then rank by a formula that people chose. The formula defines what 'good' means.
On Twitter's published 2023 weights, a reply was worth 27 likes, which is one reason arguments travel so well.
Engagement measures what you do, not whether you're glad you did it.
Every linger, rewatch and reply is training data; deliberate searches and 'not interested' clicks are strong signals too.
Coming back online after time away is a chance to retrain your feed on purpose.

title: The Hard Problems Are Easy
dek: Computers beat the world chess champion in 1997. Getting a robot to fold a T-shirt was still a headline result in 2024. The reason says something deep about intelligence, and about which jobs machines will take first.

blocks.text: In May 1997, IBM's Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov at chess, largely by brute-force search through enormous numbers of possible moves. It was hailed as a machine conquering the peak of human intellect. Now picture a two-year-old in a messy room. She picks up a sock that is half inside a shoe, notices it is wet, drops it, steps over a toy truck without looking down, and hands you a crayon. None of that would impress anyone at a dinner party. For a robot, almost every piece of it is harder than chess.

Late in 2024, a team at a robotics startup called Physical Intelligence posted a research paper on a new general-purpose robot control model. Among the headline demonstrations listed in its abstract: **laundry folding**, table cleaning and assembling boxes. Twenty-seven years after a computer beat the best chess player alive, getting a machine to fold a shirt was still frontier research. That gap is not an accident or a temporary embarrassment. It has a name.
Moravec's paradox

In 1988 the roboticist Hans Moravec, then at Carnegie Mellon, wrote that it is comparatively easy to get computers to perform like adults on intelligence tests or checkers, and difficult or impossible to give them the perception and mobility of a one-year-old. Other researchers, including Rodney Brooks and Marvin Minsky, had noticed the same thing. The psychologist Steven Pinker later boiled it down to one line.
The hard problems are easy and the easy problems are hard.
blocks.by: Steven Pinker, The Language Instinct, 1994

blocks.text: Moravec's explanation was evolutionary. Seeing, balancing, grasping and moving through a cluttered world are skills animals have been refining for hundreds of millions of years. Enormous parts of your brain are dedicated to them, and they run below conscious awareness, so they feel effortless. Abstract reasoning such as arithmetic and chess is a very recent add-on. It feels hard to us precisely because our brains are not specialized for it, which also means it turns out not to be that hard to mechanize. Minsky put a related point sharply: we tend to be least aware of what our minds do best.

The paradox flips a common assumption. People tend to rank tasks by how hard they feel, so a chess grandmaster seems smarter than a dishwasher. Moravec's point is that feeling is a terrible guide to how much computation a task really takes. The things you never think about are often the most sophisticated things you do.

blocks.title: What feels hard versus what is hard

left.head: Easy for computers, hard for people
items: Multiplying ten-digit numbers
Searching millions of chess positions
Remembering every word of a manual
Following a fixed procedure perfectly a million times

right.head: Easy for people, hard for robots
items: Picking a single sock out of a tangled pile
Walking across a slippery, uneven deck
Folding a shirt that starts in a random crumple
Noticing something is wrong and improvising

blocks.text: What a robot actually has to do

Every robot, from a factory arm to a Mars rover, runs some version of the same loop. It **senses** the world with cameras, depth sensors, joint encoders that report each motor's angle, and sometimes force sensors in the wrist. It builds an estimate of where things are. It **plans** a motion. It **acts** by commanding electric motors. Then it senses again to see what actually happened, because what actually happened is never quite what it planned.

blocks.title: The robot control loop
items: Sense: cameras, encoders, force sensors
Estimate: where am I, where are things
Plan: choose the next motion
Act: drive the motors
Check: compare result with the plan

blocks.text: Anyone who has worked on a control system will recognize the hard part: everything is uncertain and errors stack up. A camera sees an object's position with some error. The arm's joints have slack. The object slides when touched. A rigid metal part on a fixture has a handful of possible positions; a T-shirt dumped on a table has essentially unlimited ones, and it changes shape every time you touch it. A plan computed from the first glance is wrong a moment later.

The fix engineers rely on is **feedback**. Instead of computing one perfect motion and executing it blind, the controller measures the error between where a joint is and where it should be, and corrects, over and over, many times a second. It is the same principle as a governor holding a turbine at speed or a thermostat holding a space at temperature. Feedback works beautifully when you know what to measure. The trouble with the messy world is that the robot often does not know which error matters: is the shirt sleeve folded under, or is that a shadow? Is the cup slipping, or just flexing?

Contact makes everything worse. The moment a gripper touches an object, the physics becomes hard to predict. Tiny differences in friction, in where exactly the finger lands, or in the object's weight can decide whether it is lifted cleanly, spun out of the grip or knocked to the floor. Simulators let researchers practice millions of grasps on a computer, but simulated friction and soft materials never quite match reality, a problem roboticists call the **reality gap**. A policy that looks flawless in simulation can fumble on the first real towel.

Human hands solve this with staggering sensing. In a classic 1979 study, Roland Johansson and Åke Vallbo recorded single nerve fibers from the hands of conscious volunteers and estimated how densely touch receptors pack the skin. At the fingertip they estimated about **241** sensory units per square centimeter, versus about 58 in the palm. That flood of information, combined with reflexes that adjust grip within a fraction of a second, is why you can hold an egg without crushing it, without thinking. Robot hands are improving, but nothing on the market matches that.

items.label: Estimated touch-sensing units at a human fingertip
Estimated touch-sensing units in the palm

blocks.source: Johansson and Vallbo, Journal of Physiology, 1979

blocks.text: Where robots already win

If robots are so bad at the physical world, how do factories run on them? The answer is that factories cheat, brilliantly. They change the world so the robot never has to deal with uncertainty. Parts arrive in exact positions on fixtures. Lighting is controlled. Humans are kept behind fences. The robot does not need to understand anything; it repeats a precise motion millions of times, which is the part of physical work that computers find easy.

When factories did need robots to see, they started tiny. The IFR's history notes that in 1981 General Motors put a machine vision system called Consight into production at a foundry in St. Catharines, Ontario, where it used three robots to sort up to six different castings coming down a conveyor, at up to 1,400 an hour. Even that took a carefully controlled belt and a short list of known parts. The robot was not seeing the world; it was recognizing six shapes.

That approach goes back to the beginning. According to the International Federation of Robotics, the first industrial robot on a production line, a Unimate, went to work at a General Motors plant in Trenton, New Jersey, in 1961. Following step-by-step commands stored on a magnetic drum, its 4,000-pound arm stacked hot pieces of die-cast metal, a dangerous job for people. It cost $65,000 to make and sold for $18,000.

Today the scale is enormous. The IFR's World Robotics 2026 report counts a record **5 million** industrial robots operating in factories worldwide in 2025, more than double the number seven years earlier, with over 600,000 installed in that one year. China alone installed 354,000, about 59% of the world total. Measured by robot density, the number of robots per 10,000 factory workers, South Korea led the 2023 rankings by a wide margin.

blocks.title: Industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers, 2023
blocks.source: International Federation of Robotics, World Robotics 2024

blocks.text: Almost all of those robots work inside carefully engineered cells. The hard frontier is everywhere else: homes, hospitals, farms, construction sites, ships. Those are the places Moravec's paradox lives.

The distinction matters for how to think about automation news. A headline that says robots are taking over factories usually means more precise, caged arms doing repetitive motions in a world rebuilt around them. A headline that says robots are about to clean your house is a claim about cracking Moravec's paradox, which is a different and much harder problem. The first has been steadily true for sixty years. The second has been announced as imminent for most of that time too.
Leaving the cage

In June 2015 the Pentagon's research agency, DARPA, held the finals of its Robotics Challenge in Pomona, California. The goal was human-supervised robots that could work in dangerous disaster zones built for people: drive a vehicle, open doors, turn valves, use tools. The top prize went to Team KAIST from South Korea, whose robot DRC-Hubo used a tool to cut a hole in a wall. The event also produced a famous collection of robots slowly toppling over while doing things a person would barely notice. Those were some of the best-funded machines in the world, operated by expert teams, often with a human supervising remotely.

The newest approach borrows a page from the rest of AI. Instead of hand-coding how to grasp each object, researchers train large neural networks on recordings of many robots doing many tasks, sometimes starting from models pretrained on internet images and text. The 2024 Physical Intelligence paper is one example: a single model trained on data from single-arm robots, two-armed robots and mobile platforms, then fine-tuned for chores like folding laundry. The main obstacle is data. Language models learned from a vast internet of text. There is no internet of robot hands touching things, so that data has to be collected, slowly and expensively, one demonstration at a time.

You will see a lot of humanoid robot videos in the next few years. The IFR's 2026 trends list says companies are moving humanoids beyond prototypes into real deployments, with carmakers leading and warehouses and factories next, and that reliability and efficiency are what they now need to prove. That is the right test. A clip of a robot doing something once is a demo. A robot doing it ten thousand times without breaking anything is a product. Watch for the second kind.

Why build robots shaped like people at all, when wheels and fixed arms are simpler? Because the world is already built for human bodies. Stairs, door handles, ladders, hand tools, vehicle seats and narrow passageways all assume two legs, two arms and a head about five to six feet off the ground. A machine with that shape could, in principle, work anywhere a person does without anyone rebuilding the space. In practice, every one of those joints is another source of error, cost and things to break.
When you see a robot demo, ask three questions: Was it remote-controlled? How many takes did it need? Would it still work if the objects moved a few inches?
What the paradox predicts

Moravec's paradox is more than a curiosity about robots. It is a forecast about work. If abstract, rule-following, screen-based tasks are the easy part for machines, then they will be automated first, and that is roughly what is happening as AI systems write code, summarize documents and draft reports. If skilled physical work in messy, unpredictable environments is the hard part, then it will be automated last. A technician tracing a fault through a cramped space, reading the smell of hot insulation and the sound of a bad bearing, is doing something no robot can yet come close to.

That is not a guarantee. Robot learning is improving, and some of today's limits will fall faster than expected, just as other AI limits did. But it is a useful correction to the usual picture, in which the smartest-seeming jobs are the safest. The paradox suggests the opposite ordering may be closer to the truth.

There is also a more personal takeaway. The skills you take for granted, keeping your balance on a moving deck, catching a tool before it falls, finding a valve by feel in the dark, represent a level of engineering nobody has managed to copy. The next time you feel slow at something abstract, remember the trade evolution made. Your brain spent most of its budget on the hard problems. It just made them feel easy.

takeaways: Moravec's paradox: abstract reasoning is relatively easy to mechanize, while perception and movement in a messy world are extremely hard.
Robots succeed in factories because factories remove uncertainty with fixtures, fences and fixed positions.
The IFR counts 5 million industrial robots working worldwide in 2025; South Korea had 1,012 per 10,000 factory workers in 2023.
Human fingertips pack an estimated 241 touch-sensing units per square centimeter, one reason grasping is so hard to copy.
Judge robot demos by reliability, not by a single impressive clip.

title: Search Engines Don't Find the Best Page
dek: They predict which page you will click and stay on, using proxies that everyone is trying to game. Here's how the machine actually decides what you see.

blocks.text: Type four words into a search box and hit enter. Before your finger has left the key, a system has looked at your words, pulled a few thousand candidate pages out of an index covering a huge slice of the public web, scored them, rescored the best ones with heavier machinery, and handed you ten links in an order it believes you will like. The whole thing takes a fraction of a second.

Here is the puzzle. No computer can actually tell which page is *best*. Best for whom? Best by what standard? A page about protein timing written by a researcher and one written by a supplement company can use exactly the same words. So search engines quietly answer a different question, one they can measure: *which page is this person most likely to be satisfied by?* Every ranking signal ever invented is a proxy for that guess. Understanding the proxies explains both why search works so well and why it keeps getting gamed.
The engine never searches the web

The first surprise is that when you search, nothing goes out onto the internet. That work happened earlier. Programs called **crawlers** (or spiders) fetch pages around the clock, follow the links on each one, and fetch those pages too. Every page they collect gets parsed: text extracted, language detected, duplicates spotted, links recorded.

Then comes the key data structure, the **inverted index**. Think of the index at the back of a textbook. Instead of reading every page to find the word *reactor*, you look up *reactor* and get a list of page numbers. A search engine builds the same thing at planetary scale: for every word, a list of every document containing it, often with the positions where it appears. A query becomes a lookup and an intersection. Pages containing *creatine* AND *loading* AND *phase* are the overlap of three lists, and that can be computed in milliseconds.

blocks.title: From your keystroke to ten blue links
items: Crawl: bots fetch pages and follow links, long before you search.
Index: each page is parsed and every word is filed in an inverted index pointing back to it.
Retrieve: your query is looked up and a few thousand candidate pages are pulled fast and cheap.
Rank: candidates are scored on hundreds of signals such as word match, links, freshness and location.
Rerank: the top slice gets a slower, smarter model that reads query and page together.
Serve and learn: results are shown, and what people click and skip feeds back into future rankings.

blocks.text: Matching words: why rare ones count more

The oldest signal is plain word matching, and even it has a clever twist. If you search *the reactor scram procedure*, the word *the* appears on nearly every English page, so a page containing it tells you nothing. *Scram* appears on very few, so a page containing it is a strong clue. In 1972 the British computer scientist Karen Spärck Jones formalized this as **inverse document frequency**, or IDF: weight a word by how rare it is across the whole collection. Multiply that by **term frequency**, how often the word shows up on the page, and you get the classic TF-IDF score.

The refined version that still underpins many search systems is called **BM25**, developed by Stephen Robertson and colleagues and tested at a U.S. government search competition called TREC in 1994. It adds two pieces of common sense. First, diminishing returns: the tenth mention of *scram* on a page adds much less than the first, so stuffing a keyword fifty times does not help much. Second, length normalization: a word appearing once in a short page is a stronger signal than once in a novel. BM25 is cheap, fast and surprisingly hard to beat, which is why many modern pipelines still use it to fetch the first batch of candidates.

But word matching has a fatal flaw that became obvious in the mid-1990s. Anyone can write any words on their own page. Early engines ranked whoever repeated the words most, so spammers hid hundreds of keywords in white text on white backgrounds. The engines needed a signal that page authors could not simply type.
Links as votes

In 1998 two Stanford graduate students, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, published a paper describing a prototype search engine called Google. Its core idea was **PageRank**: treat every link from one page to another as a vote, but weight each vote by the importance of the page casting it. A link from a page that many important pages link to is worth far more than a link from an unknown page.

That sounds circular, and it is, but the math resolves it. Picture a bored surfer who starts on a random page and keeps clicking random links. Most of the time, 85 percent in the original paper, they follow a link. The other 15 percent of the time they get bored and jump to a random page anywhere on the web. Run this for long enough and the share of time the surfer spends on each page settles to a stable number. That number is the page's PageRank. The random jump is not decoration. Without it, a surfer could get stuck forever in a little cluster of pages that only link to each other, and those pages would hoard all the rank. The jump guarantees every page gets a small baseline share and that the math always settles on one answer.

blocks.title: PageRank in a toy web of seven pages
blocks.note: F and B each have exactly one inbound link. F's comes from an important page, so F ranks nearly 9 times higher.
blocks.source: Worked example computed with the PageRank formula, damping 0.85 (Brin & Page, 1998)

blocks.text: The toy example above shows the key move. Pages F and B each have exactly one link pointing at them. But F's link comes from page A, which collects votes from four other pages, while B's comes from an obscure page. The result is a ranking gap of nearly nine to one. Quality of votes beats quantity, which made the signal much harder to fake than repeated keywords.

Harder, not impossible. Within a few years an industry sprang up selling links, building networks of fake sites that all linked to each other, and spamming blog comments with URLs. Search engines answered in 2005 with the *nofollow* tag, which lets sites mark links that should not count as votes, and in 2012 Google released an update known as Penguin that demoted sites with manipulative link patterns. Every signal that becomes valuable gets attacked. That arms race never ends.

blocks.title: How ranking evolved
items: Spärck Jones introduces inverse document frequency
Robertson's Okapi team brings BM25 to the TREC search competition
Brin and Page publish the PageRank-based Google prototype
The nofollow tag lets sites stop links from counting as votes
Google's Penguin update targets link schemes
Google starts using BERT language models in search
AI-written answer summaries appear above results; a U.S. court rules Google holds an illegal search monopoly

blocks.text: Your clicks are training data

A search engine sees something no page author can fake at scale: what millions of people do after they search. If people click result three, stay there and never come back, that is a good sign. If they click result one and bounce back within seconds to try something else, that is a bad sign. During the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, testimony and documents confirmed that the company uses a system called **Navboost** that learns from this kind of click behavior.

Clicks are a trap, though, and researchers have known it for two decades. In a 2005 study using eye-tracking, Thorsten Joachims and colleagues at Cornell concluded that clicks are informative but biased. People click the top result partly *because* it is the top result. They trust the engine's ordering and often never scroll. So a naive system that promotes whatever gets clicked will mostly promote whatever it already ranked first. The fix is to read clicks as relative preferences: if someone skips result one and clicks result three, that says something real about three versus one.

blocks.title: The click feedback loop
items: Engine ranks a page near the top
More people see it, so more people click it
Click data says the page is popular
Engine ranks it even higher
Pages that never got a fair shot stay buried

blocks.text: Clicks are not the only human input. Google publishes a long set of guidelines for thousands of contract **quality raters**, people who are shown queries and results and asked to judge them, paying special attention to experience, expertise and trustworthiness on topics like health and money. Raters do not directly move any one page. Their judgments are used to test whether a proposed ranking change makes results better or worse before it ships, a bit like a QA inspection on every software update.

This loop is the same one that drives YouTube recommendations and the Roblox discover page. A rich-get-richer dynamic is built into any system that learns from what it shows. The engineering answer is careful experimentation, including deliberately testing other orderings on small slices of users to see what people pick when the incumbent is not sitting on top.
From matching words to reading meaning

Word matching misses things a human finds obvious. Search *can you get medicine for someone pharmacy* and the word *for* is the whole point: you are picking up a prescription for another person. Classic systems mostly ignored small words like that. The breakthrough came from language models. In 2018 Google researchers published **BERT**, a model that reads a sentence in both directions at once and learns what words mean from context. Google said in 2019 that it was using BERT to understand search queries.

Researchers quickly showed how much this mattered for ranking itself. Microsoft had released a benchmark called MS MARCO, built from real Bing searches. A team at NYU fed each query and each candidate passage into BERT together and let it judge relevance directly. Their system beat the previous best result on the benchmark by 27 percent on its main ranking metric.

items.label: Real, anonymized Bing questions in the MS MARCO benchmark
Web passages in MS MARCO for systems to rank
Gain from BERT reranking over the prior best on MS MARCO

blocks.source: Nguyen et al., MS MARCO, 2016; Nogueira & Cho, 2019

blocks.text: A second trick from the same family changed retrieval itself. A model can turn any query or page into an **embedding**, a list of a few hundred numbers that acts like coordinates in a space of meaning. Pages about *submarine ventilation* and *how air is recycled underwater* land near each other even if they share no words. Finding relevant pages becomes a geometry problem: find the points closest to the query's point. Specialized indexes can do that nearest-neighbor search across billions of vectors quickly, which is why modern engines often run word-based and meaning-based retrieval side by side.

These models are expensive, so they run late in the pipeline. Cheap methods like BM25 or compact vector lookups pull thousands of candidates, and the heavy model rereads only the top few dozen. That two-stage design, fast and dumb first, slow and smart second, is how nearly every large search and recommendation system works. It is the same trade-off an engineer makes on watch: scan everything quickly, then look hard at what stands out.

blocks.title: What ranking looks like vs. what it is

left.head: How it feels
items: The engine finds the best page
Rankings are a neutral fact
Top result = most correct
One algorithm decides

right.head: How it works
items: The engine predicts which page will satisfy you
Rankings are a model's bet, learned from behavior
Top result = most likely to be clicked and kept
A pipeline of many models and hundreds of signals

blocks.text: The web bends toward the ranker

Every ranking signal starts as an honest measure and ends up as a target. Keywords were honest until people stuffed them. Links were honest until people bought them. Clicks are honest until people learn to write headlines that earn the click without earning the stay. This is Goodhart's law in action: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. The engine adapts, the optimizers adapt back, and the web you see is shaped as much by that contest as by the information itself.

Now a new layer sits on top. Search engines increasingly write an answer at the top of the page, drawing on the pages below. In 2024 a U.S. federal judge also ruled that Google had illegally maintained its monopoly in general search, partly through deals that made it the default on phones and browsers. Both changes raise the same question: if the engine reads the pages and answers for you, and one company controls the main gate, what reason do people have to keep writing the pages?

The useful reframe is this. A search result is not a verdict about truth. It is a prediction about what someone like you clicked and stayed on before. That makes search extraordinarily good at popular, well-trodden questions and weaker on narrow, technical or contested ones, where the crowd's behavior is a poor guide. Knowing that, the best searchers add specific terms the right page would contain, skip past the top result when it smells optimized, and go to primary sources whenever the stakes are real.

If you are trying to get something found, whether a game, a video or a page, the same logic applies: the system rewards what people choose and stay with. Optimize for the stay, not just the click, because that is the signal every ranker is ultimately trying to measure.

takeaways: Search engines never search the live web when you type; they look up a prebuilt inverted index.
Rare words count more than common ones (IDF), and repeating a keyword has sharply diminishing returns (BM25).
PageRank weighs links by the importance of the linking page, so one good link can beat many weak ones.
Clicks train rankers but are biased toward whatever was already on top, creating a rich-get-richer loop.
A ranking is a prediction of satisfaction, not a verdict on truth; for high-stakes questions, go to primary sources.

title: Why a 1-Terabyte Movie Fits in 4 Gigabytes
dek: Video compression throws away more than 99 percent of the data and you barely notice. The trick is a stack of ideas about how the world moves and what your eyes ignore.

blocks.text: Do the math on a movie and something seems wrong. A 1080p frame is 1,920 pixels wide and 1,080 tall, a little over two million pixels. Each pixel needs a red, a green and a blue value, typically 8 bits apiece, so 24 bits per pixel. That is about 6.2 megabytes for one frame. Films run at 24 frames per second, so one second of raw video is roughly 150 megabytes, and a two-hour movie comes to about 1.07 *terabytes*.

Yet that same movie downloads as a file of around 4 gigabytes, or streams to your phone over a cell connection. Somewhere between the camera and your screen, more than 99.6 percent of the data has vanished, and you mostly cannot tell. That is not a trick of one clever algorithm. It is a stack of five or six ideas, each exploiting a different weakness in your eyes or a different kind of repetition in the world, and together they squeeze video by a factor of a few hundred.

items.label: Raw 1080p video at 24 frames per second, 24 bits per pixel
Raw size of a two-hour 1080p movie
Compression needed to fit it in a 4 GB file

blocks.source: Arithmetic: 1,920 × 1,080 pixels × 24 bits × 24 frames/s × 7,200 s

blocks.text: Throw away what the eye ignores

The first cut is almost free. Your retina has far more cells that sense brightness than cells that sense color, and the color-sensing system is blurrier. So codecs stop storing red, green and blue directly. They convert each pixel to one **luma** value (brightness) and two **chroma** values (how blue and how red it is, relative to the brightness). Then they keep full detail for brightness but store color at half the resolution in each direction, one color sample for every block of four pixels. This is called **4:2:0 chroma subsampling**.

The effect on the data is immediate. Instead of 24 bits per pixel you are down to an average of 12, so that 1.07-terabyte movie is already about 540 gigabytes, and almost nobody can see the difference at normal viewing distance. It is the purest example of the principle that drives the whole field: compression is not about preserving the image. It is about preserving the *experience* of the image, and throwing away everything the brain would not miss.
Most of the next frame is the last frame

The biggest win comes from time. Watch any scene and ask how much actually changes from one frame to the next, a twenty-fourth of a second later. Usually almost nothing. The background holds still or slides a little. A character's face moves a few pixels. Storing every frame from scratch would mean saving the same wall a hundred times.

So codecs **predict**. The encoder chops each frame into blocks and, for each block, searches the previous frames for the patch that looks most like it. Instead of storing the block, it stores a **motion vector**, an instruction that says, in effect, take the patch from 6 pixels left and 2 pixels up in the last frame. Then it stores only the **residual**, the small difference between the prediction and reality. If the prediction is good, the residual is close to zero everywhere, and close-to-zero data compresses extremely well.

This creates three kinds of frames. **I-frames** (intra) are complete pictures, compressed on their own like a photo. **P-frames** (predicted) are built from earlier frames. **B-frames** (bi-directional) borrow from frames both before *and after*, which means the encoder sends some frames out of order so the decoder already has the future frame in hand. A typical stream has an I-frame every second or few, with long runs of P- and B-frames between them. That is why seeking in a video sometimes jumps to a nearby point: the player has to start from an I-frame.

blocks.title: What an encoder does to each block of a frame
items: Convert color to brightness plus two color channels and shrink the color channels.
Find the best prediction: from nearby pixels in the same frame, or a motion-shifted patch from another frame.
Subtract the prediction to get the residual, the part that could not be predicted.
Transform the residual into frequency patterns with a DCT-like transform.
Quantize: round the frequency values coarsely, dropping fine detail the eye barely notices.
Entropy-code the result so common values take fewer bits, then write it into the stream.

blocks.text: Turning pixels into waves, then rounding

The residual still needs to be stored, and here comes the mathematical heart of the system. In 1974 Nasir Ahmed, T. Natarajan and K. R. Rao published the **discrete cosine transform**, or DCT. It rewrites a block of pixels as a sum of simple wave patterns: one flat average, then gentle gradients, then finer and finer stripes and checkerboards. Any 8 by 8 block can be described exactly as a recipe of 64 of these patterns.

The magic is that in real images, nearly all the energy lands in the first few smooth patterns. Fine stripes have tiny amounts. That sets up the step where data is truly thrown away, **quantization**. Each pattern's strength gets divided by a step size and rounded to a whole number. Big steps for the fine patterns mean most of them round to zero. A block that started as 64 pixel values can end up as three or four meaningful numbers and a long run of zeros.

Quantization is the one dial that trades quality for size. Turn it up and you get the familiar ugly artifacts: **blocking**, where the grid of squares becomes visible, and **banding**, where a smooth dark sky breaks into visible stripes because there were not enough steps left to describe a subtle gradient. Everything else in the pipeline is lossless bookkeeping. Quantization is where the movie actually loses information.

The last stage, **entropy coding**, is pure efficiency. It assigns short codes to common values and long codes to rare ones, the same idea as Morse code giving the letter E a single dot. H.264 and later codecs use adaptive versions that keep updating their probability estimates as the stream goes on, squeezing out the remaining redundancy.

Confetti, rain, snow, film grain and fast-moving foliage are a codec's nightmare. None of them can be predicted from the last frame, so the residual stays large and the bitrate has to spike or the picture falls apart. That is why fireworks on a stream often turn to mush.
Each generation halves the bill

These ideas have been around since the 1990s. What changed with each new standard was how cleverly and flexibly they are applied. Older codecs used fixed block sizes. Newer ones split the frame into blocks that adapt to the content: big blocks for a smooth sky, tiny ones for a face. They offer dozens of directions for predicting a block from its neighbors, search more candidate motion vectors, and use loop filters that clean up blocking before a frame is used as a reference.

The results are measurable. When engineers compared HEVC (also called H.265) with its predecessor H.264 using human viewers, HEVC matched the picture quality using about 50 percent less bit rate on average. Its successor, VVC (H.266), finalized in July 2020, cuts bit rates by around another 50 percent versus HEVC, and about 75 percent versus H.264, according to the team that led its development. On the royalty-free side, the AV1 format from the Alliance for Open Media was reported to cut bit rate by more than 30 percent compared with Google's earlier VP9.

blocks.title: Bit rate needed for the same visual quality
blocks.note: Approximate averages from standardization tests; real savings vary by content and encoder.
blocks.source: Ohm et al., IEEE TCSVT, 2012; Bross et al., IEEE TCSVT, 2021

blocks.text: There is no free lunch. Every extra option the encoder can choose from is another option it has to *try*. One analysis puts VVC's compression gain at the cost of roughly ten times more encoder computation than HEVC. Decoding gets heavier too, which is why new codecs take years to reach phones: they need dedicated decoding hardware, or playback drains the battery. A 2024 study of decoder energy found that software decoding uses far more energy than dedicated hardware decoders, which brought consumption below 9 percent of the software figure.

blocks.title: Milestones in squeezing pictures
items: Ahmed, Natarajan and Rao publish the discrete cosine transform
JPEG standard brings DCT compression to photos
H.264 / AVC published; it goes on to power Blu-ray, YouTube and most streaming
HEVC / H.265 approved, about half the bit rate of H.264
AV1, a royalty-free codec from the Alliance for Open Media, is released
VVC / H.266 finalized in July

blocks.text: Live is harder than on-demand

A movie on a streaming service has a luxury that a live stream does not: time. The studio can spend hours encoding each title, running the encoder twice so the first pass can study the whole film and the second pass can spend bits where the first pass found trouble. It can look far ahead, use long chains of B-frames, and reuse a reference frame from many seconds earlier.

A live stream gets none of that. The encoder in your streaming software has a few milliseconds per frame and cannot see the future. Every B-frame it uses adds delay, because the frame after it has to arrive before it can be sent. Every second of lookahead is another second between your play and your viewers seeing it. So live encoders run faster, simpler settings, which is why a live stream at a given bit rate looks worse than a polished upload at the same bit rate.

Video calls push the trade-off further still. A conversation feels broken once the delay climbs past a fraction of a second, so call software uses almost no lookahead at all, adapts its bit rate constantly to the network, and would rather show you a blurry face on time than a sharp face late. The same codec family can be tuned toward quality, toward speed or toward low delay, and the settings that win for a Netflix film are exactly wrong for a squad call.

There is also the question of when to send a fresh I-frame. A complete picture is expensive, often many times larger than a predicted frame, so encoders want to send them rarely. But a viewer joining a live stream cannot start watching until one arrives, and any data lost in transit corrupts every frame predicted from it until the next I-frame resets things. Streaming platforms typically ask for one every couple of seconds as a compromise between efficiency and quick recovery.
Spending bits where you look

A standard defines only how to *decode* a stream. It says nothing about how to make a good one, and that freedom is where much of the progress lives. Two encoders producing legal H.264 at the same file size can look very different. The best ones run **rate-distortion optimization**: for each block they try many options and pick the one with the best trade between bits spent and visible error. They also spend bits unevenly, on purpose, giving more to faces and smooth gradients where errors are obvious and fewer to busy textures where errors hide.

Streaming services push this further. Instead of one fixed recipe for every title, they analyze each film or even each shot and pick encoding settings to match. A simple cartoon with flat colors can look perfect at a fraction of the bit rate needed for a grainy war film. Your player then picks from a ladder of versions at different resolutions and bit rates, switching every few seconds based on how fast data is arriving. That is why a stream sometimes goes soft for a moment before snapping back to sharp.

This matters if you ever upload gameplay. Platforms like YouTube re-encode everything you send. If you upload a file that is already heavily compressed, the platform compresses the compression, and the artifacts pile up. Fast games with particle effects, grass and constant camera motion are some of the hardest content to compress well. Uploading at a high bit rate, and at higher resolution where the platform gives higher-resolution uploads a larger bit budget, gives the second encoder more to work with.

The bigger idea is that a compressed video is not a recording of what the camera saw. It is a set of instructions for rebuilding something your brain will accept as the same thing. Each generation of codec is a better model of two things at once: how the world tends to move, and what the human eye cannot be bothered to notice. The 270-to-1 shrink is not a feat of storage. It is a feat of understanding the viewer.

takeaways: Raw 1080p video is about 1.2 gigabits per second; a two-hour film would be over a terabyte uncompressed.
Codecs store color at lower resolution than brightness because the eye is far less sharp for color.
Most of the data savings come from predicting each frame from others and storing only the difference.
Quantization after the DCT is the one truly lossy step; it causes blocking and banding when pushed too hard.
Each new codec roughly halves the bit rate for the same quality, at the cost of much more computing.

title: How Your Phone Pulls Gigabits Out of Thin Air
dek: Wi-Fi, 5G and the Navy's submarine radios all obey the same equation. Once you understand it, dropped calls, slow hotel Wi-Fi and billion-dollar spectrum auctions all make sense.

blocks.text: At periscope depth a submarine can hear the world. A few hundred feet down, it goes almost deaf. The ocean around the hull is soaked in the same kind of energy that carries every text, stream and voice call on land, but salt water is a decent electrical conductor, and conductors smother radio waves. To reach boats at depth, the U.S. Navy once ran a transmitter at 76 hertz, using antennas strung across tens of kilometers of Wisconsin and Michigan forest. Its reward for all that effort was a data rate of a few characters per minute.

Meanwhile a phone in a coffee shop pulls hundreds of megabits per second out of thin air. Same physics, same speed of light, same basic kind of wave. The gap between those two links is hundreds of millions to one, and the reason for it is the whole story of wireless: a short list of trade-offs that every radio engineer negotiates, from the Navy's ELF array to the router on your shelf.
A wave is just a carrier

Every radio signal is an oscillating electromagnetic field, the same stuff as visible light, only with a much longer wavelength. Two numbers describe it. **Frequency** is how many times per second the field flips direction, measured in hertz (Hz). **Wavelength** is the distance between peaks. Multiply them and you always get the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometers per second, so when one goes up the other goes down.

Run the numbers and the scale gets strange. Wi-Fi at 2.4 gigahertz (2.4 billion cycles per second) has a wavelength of 12.5 centimeters, about the length of your hand. The newer 6 GHz band is 5 centimeters. The Navy's 76 Hz signal had a wavelength of nearly 4,000 kilometers, longer than the distance from Seattle to Miami. That is why ELF antennas were measured in kilometers: an antenna works best when it is a sizable fraction of the wavelength it is trying to launch.

A pure, steady wave carries no information. It is like a dial tone. To send data you have to *disturb* the wave in a pattern the receiver can recognize, and the art of doing that is called **modulation**.
Writing bits onto a wave

A wave has three things you can tweak: its **amplitude** (how strong it is), its **frequency** (how fast it oscillates) and its **phase** (where in its cycle it is at a given instant, like the position of a clock hand). The simplest schemes change one of them. Flip the phase by half a cycle and you have sent a 1 instead of a 0. That is called binary phase-shift keying, and it moves one bit per **symbol**, a symbol being one short slice of time in which the transmitter holds a particular state.

Modern systems change amplitude and phase at the same time. Picture a dartboard where every possible combination of strength and timing is a dot. That pattern of dots is called a **constellation**, and the scheme is **quadrature amplitude modulation**, or QAM. With 16 dots, each symbol can land on one of 16 spots, which encodes 4 bits, because 2 to the 4th power is 16. With 1,024 dots you get 10 bits per symbol. Wi-Fi 7 goes to 4,096 dots, which is 12 bits per symbol.

blocks.title: Bits carried by each symbol
blocks.note: Bits per symbol = log2 of the number of constellation points. Each step up needs a cleaner signal.
blocks.source: HPE Aruba Networking, Wi-Fi 7 technical docs; constellation math

blocks.text: There is no free lunch. Pack 4,096 dots onto the same dartboard and they sit very close together. Any noise, from a microwave oven, a neighbor's router or just the random jiggle of electrons in the receiver, nudges the dart off its dot, and the receiver reads the wrong bits. HPE's Aruba engineering documentation puts the gain from 1,024-QAM to 4,096-QAM at up to 25 percent more raw speed, but only under good conditions. In practice that means a few meters from the router with nothing in between. Walk into the next room and your device quietly drops to a coarser constellation with fewer, wider-spaced dots. That automatic downshift is why your Wi-Fi speed falls off in steps, not smoothly.

blocks.title: What happens when your phone sends one packet over Wi-Fi
items: The data is scrambled and wrapped in error-correcting code, so some flipped bits can be repaired later.
The bit stream is split across many narrow subcarriers inside the channel, each one a slow, separate wave.
Groups of bits on each subcarrier are mapped to constellation points, setting its amplitude and phase.
All the subcarriers are combined into one signal and pushed out of the antennas, sometimes as several separate spatial streams.
The receiver measures each subcarrier, picks the nearest constellation point, runs error correction and sends back an acknowledgment.

blocks.text: Shannon's speed limit

In 1948 a Bell Labs mathematician named Claude Shannon worked out the maximum rate at which any channel can carry information without errors. His result says capacity equals the **bandwidth** (the width of the slice of spectrum you are using, in hertz) multiplied by the logarithm of one plus the **signal-to-noise ratio**, which is how much louder your signal is than the background hiss. No modulation scheme ever invented beats that ceiling. The best modern ones come close.

The shape of that formula explains almost everything about wireless. Capacity rises in a straight line with bandwidth: double the width of your channel and you double the ceiling. But it rises only with the *logarithm* of signal quality. If your signal is already a thousand times louder than the noise, doubling your transmit power buys you roughly one extra bit per second for every hertz. Shouting louder barely helps. Getting a wider road helps a lot.

That is why every Wi-Fi generation fights for wider channels. Wi-Fi 6 tops out at 160 MHz. Wi-Fi 7 allows 320 MHz, which only fits in the 6 GHz band, where regulators in some countries have opened up to 1,200 MHz of spectrum. In Aruba's tables a single Wi-Fi 7 stream, at 4,096-QAM on a 320 MHz channel, hits a raw rate of 2,882 megabits per second. Real throughput after overhead and sharing is always well below the raw figure.

items.label: Raw rate of one Wi-Fi 7 stream at 4096-QAM on a 320 MHz channel
Bid in the FCC's 2021 C-band auction for 280 MHz of spectrum
Typical data rate of VLF radio to submarines

blocks.source: HPE Aruba Networking; MITRE, 2021; Communication with submarines (Wikipedia)

blocks.text: It also explains why spectrum is so absurdly valuable. In the FCC's C-band auction, which wrapped up in early 2021, carriers bid $80.9 billion for 280 MHz of spectrum between 3.7 and 3.98 GHz, according to an analysis by MITRE. That works out to well over a quarter of a billion dollars per megahertz. They were not paying for anything you can touch. They were buying the right to use one strip of the Shannon formula across the United States.

Now go back to the submarine. Low frequencies punch deeper into seawater, which is why the Navy used them. VLF (very low frequency, 3 to 30 kilohertz) reaches only a few tens of meters down and carries around 300 bits per second. ELF reached hundreds of meters but crawled at a few characters per minute. The bandwidth simply is not there: you cannot carve a wide channel out of a signal that only oscillates 76 times a second. Penetration and data rate pull in opposite directions, and the ocean forces you to pick penetration. The U.S. ELF system was dismantled in 2004.
Sharing the air

The air is one medium, and everyone nearby is using it. Wireless systems survive this with a few clever tricks. The first is **OFDM**, orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing. Instead of blasting one fast signal across the whole channel, the transmitter splits it into hundreds or thousands of narrow subcarriers, each carrying a slow stream. Slow symbols are tougher, because a signal that bounces off walls arrives at your phone several times over, slightly delayed, and a long symbol shrugs off a short echo. Wi-Fi 6 and 5G add OFDMA, which hands different groups of subcarriers to different devices at the same moment, like assigning lanes on a highway.

The second trick is **MIMO**, multiple-input multiple-output. With several antennas on each end, a router can send different data streams from different antennas over the same frequencies at the same time. The receiver untangles them using the fact that each stream took a slightly different path through the room. Echoes, which used to be the enemy, become a resource: each distinct path is another lane.

The third trick is deciding who talks when, and this is where Wi-Fi and cellular split philosophies. Wi-Fi uses unlicensed spectrum that anyone can use, so devices behave like polite people at a party: listen first, talk only if nobody else is, and back off for a random time if two start at once. Cellular networks pay for exclusive licenses, so the tower acts as a conductor, scheduling exactly which phone transmits on which slice of frequency in each fraction of a millisecond.

blocks.title: Two ways to share the air

left.head: Wi-Fi
items: Unlicensed spectrum, free for anyone
Devices listen, then talk if the air is clear
Range of tens of meters
Cheap, fast, chaotic when crowded
Carries more than half of internet traffic

right.head: Cellular
items: Licensed spectrum bought at auction
Tower schedules every transmission
Range from hundreds of meters to many kilometers
Handoff keeps you connected at highway speed
Built to meet hard targets for latency and density

blocks.text: Cells, towers and the 5G promise

The word *cellular* is literal. A carrier divides territory into cells, each served by a base station, and reuses the same frequencies in cells far enough apart that they do not interfere. Small cells mean more reuse and more total capacity, which is why dense cities are packed with antennas on rooftops and light poles. When you drive, the network measures your signal against neighboring towers and hands your connection from one to the next in a fraction of a second.

Each generation has mostly been a better answer to Shannon. First-generation phones in 1979 were analog. Second generation, beginning with GSM in 1991, went digital. Third and fourth generations moved toward data, with 4G LTE built around OFDM. For 5G, the International Telecommunication Union set minimum requirements before anyone built a network: peak downloads of 20 gigabits per second, latency of 1 millisecond for ultra-reliable uses, and support for a million connected devices per square kilometer.

items: Hedy Lamarr and George Antheil patent frequency hopping for torpedo guidance

blocks.text: Those 5G headline numbers are ceilings, not what your phone sees. The giant speeds depend on millimeter-wave bands, around 24 GHz and higher, where wavelengths are about a centimeter. Those frequencies have enormous bandwidth available, but they barely get through a wall, a window or even a hand. The ITU's own target for typical user experience in a dense city is 100 megabits per second down, a fifth of a percent of the peak figure. That is why carriers paid so much for mid-band spectrum like the C-band: it is a compromise between reach and room, wide enough for real speed and low enough to get inside buildings.

Every wireless link trades the same three things: how far the signal reaches, how much bandwidth it has, and how clean it is. Low frequencies go far and through things but carry little. High frequencies carry a lot but give up easily. There is no setting that wins all three.
The air is a shared, noisy pipe

Once you see wireless this way, the frustrations make sense. Wi-Fi slows at a crowded event not because the router is weak, but because hundreds of devices are taking turns on the same channels. Your connection drops to a crawl in the far bedroom because walls eat signal-to-noise ratio, and your device steps down to a coarser constellation to stay reliable. Moving the router to a central, open spot often does more than buying a faster one, because it attacks the term in Shannon's formula that actually limits you. The same logic explains why the 6 GHz band feels blazing in the same room as the router and useless two walls away, and why a mesh system with several nodes often beats one powerful box: shorter hops mean cleaner signals, and cleaner signals unlock the dense constellations.

And the boat makes the point most cleanly of all. The fleet's link to shore at depth is not slow because the Navy lacks good engineers. It is slow because the problem is pinned to the bottom of the physics: a conducting ocean, wavelengths thousands of kilometers long, and a bandwidth measured in tens of hertz. Every engineer on land is playing the same game with friendlier numbers. The phone in your pocket is not a magic portal. It is a small radio, negotiating every millisecond with a formula written down in 1948.

takeaways: Data rides radio waves by changing their amplitude and phase; denser patterns carry more bits but need a cleaner signal.
Shannon's limit: capacity grows in a straight line with bandwidth but only logarithmically with signal strength, so wider channels beat louder ones.
Low frequencies reach far and through water or walls but carry little data; high frequencies carry a lot but are easily blocked.
Wi-Fi shares free spectrum by politely taking turns; cellular buys exclusive spectrum and schedules every transmission.
For better home Wi-Fi, improve signal quality (central placement, fewer walls) before buying a faster router.

title: The Clock Inside the Rock
dek: How we learned the Earth is 4.54 billion years old, why the most famous physicist of his era got it badly wrong, and how the answer ended up taking the lead out of gasoline.

blocks.text: About 50,000 years ago, an iron meteorite tens of meters across slammed into the desert in what is now northern Arizona. It left a crater more than a kilometer wide and scattered fragments of itself across the plain. Those fragments are called the Canyon Diablo meteorite, and a sliver of one of them holds the best single answer to one of the oldest questions people have asked: how old is the world?

The answer, 4.54 billion years, did not come from a single clever insight. It came from a century of wrong guesses, a scientific fight between physicists and geologists, the discovery of radioactivity, and a chemist named Clair Patterson who had to build what was then one of the cleanest laboratories on Earth because lead contamination kept ruining his measurements. Then he noticed where all that lead was coming from, and spent the rest of his career fighting to get it out of the air.
It is a story about deep time. It is also a story about two different ways of being wrong, and one very effective way of being right.
The physicist who was precisely wrong

By the 1800s, geologists reading layers of rock and fossils were convinced the Earth was very old. Charles Darwin needed it to be: evolution by natural selection is slow, and his theory assumed hundreds of millions of years at least. Then the physicists weighed in, led by William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, one of the most respected scientists alive.

Kelvin's argument was elegant. Assume the Earth started as a molten ball and has been cooling ever since. Measure how fast temperature rises as you go down into mines, which tells you how fast heat is leaking out of the surface. Then use the mathematics of heat conduction to work backward to how long it would take a molten planet to cool to today's state. In 1862 he published a range of 20 million to 400 million years. Over the following decades he narrowed it toward the young end of that range, and he used it to argue that Darwin's timeline was physically impossible.

The math was fine. The assumptions were not. In 1895, Kelvin's former assistant John Perry pointed out that if the Earth's interior could move and carry heat by convection, rather than only conducting it through solid rock, the surface could keep its observed temperature gradient for far longer. The planet could be billions of years old. Kelvin was unconvinced, and most scientists sided with him. A 2007 paper in GSA Today by geophysicists Philip England, Peter Molnar and Frank Richter called Perry's critique a missed opportunity: he had the right physics, roughly the mantle convection that also drives plate tectonics, decades early.

The other missing piece was a heat source no one knew existed. In 1896 Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity. Within a few years it was clear that radioactive elements in rock release heat as they decay, a steady internal furnace that Kelvin's cooling model left out. The Earth was not a cooling cannonball. It was more like a reactor that had been running at low power for a very long time.
Kelvin's error is the dangerous kind: a rigorous calculation built on an unexamined assumption. The more precise the math looks, the easier it is to forget to check what went into it.
How a radioactive clock works

Radioactivity did more than kill Kelvin's estimate. It handed scientists a clock. A radioactive isotope decays into a stable daughter at a fixed rate described by its half-life, the time it takes for half of any sample to decay. Temperature, pressure and chemistry do not change that rate in any meaningful way. Uranium-238 decays through a long chain into lead-206 with a half-life of about 4.5 billion years. Uranium-235 decays into lead-207 with a half-life of about 700 million years.

If a mineral formed with uranium in it but no lead, then every atom of lead you find inside it today was made by decay. Count the parent atoms and the daughter atoms, and the half-life tells you how long the clock has been running. Ernest Rutherford suggested this idea in 1904. The American chemist Bertram Boltwood applied it in 1907 and got ages for rock samples that, after later refinements, range from about 410 million to 2.2 billion years. In one stroke the scale of the argument had changed: Kelvin's tens of millions of years were not enough by a factor of a hundred.

blocks.title: Reading a radioactive clock
items: A mineral crystallizes and locks in uranium atoms, but rejects lead.
Over time, uranium atoms decay at a fixed rate into lead, which stays trapped in the crystal.
A mass spectrometer counts the ratio of daughter lead to remaining parent uranium.
The known half-life converts that ratio into years since the crystal formed.
A second, independent clock in the same sample (uranium-235 to lead-207) checks the first.

blocks.text: If you work around reactors, none of this is exotic. The same physics that governs how fission products build up and decay in a core, and why some isotopes matter for minutes and others for centuries, is what lets geologists read time in stone. Half-life is not a statistical hope. It is one of the most reliably measured quantities in physics.

There was still a catch. You cannot date the Earth just by finding the oldest rock, because the Earth keeps destroying its own records. Plate tectonics melts and recycles crust, and erosion grinds the rest down. According to the US Geological Survey, the oldest rocks found so far are the Acasta Gneisses in northwestern Canada at about 4.03 billion years. Tiny zircon crystals from the Jack Hills of Western Australia are older still: one was dated in 2001 at about 4.4 billion years. But those are survivors, not the starting line. To find the starting line, scientists had to leave the planet.
A clock that fell from the sky

Meteorites are leftover building material from the early solar system, the same stuff that clumped together to make the planets. If the Earth and the meteorites formed at about the same time from the same cloud, they should share an age. Some iron meteorites contain a mineral called troilite, an iron sulfide that holds lead but almost no uranium. That lead is essentially frozen at its original, primordial composition, the starting point before billions of years of uranium decay added to it.

Here is the clever part. Because uranium-235 and uranium-238 decay at different rates into two different lead isotopes, the ratio of lead-207 to lead-206 changes over time in a predictable way. Compare the primordial lead in Canyon Diablo troilite with the lead in other meteorites and in the average modern Earth, and you can calculate how long the uranium has been ticking. You do not need to know how much uranium was there at the start. Two clocks running at different speeds in the same box tell you the time on their own.

Clair Patterson, a young chemist working on this at the University of Chicago and then Caltech, spent years failing to get clean numbers. The problem was lead. It was in the air, the dust, the glassware, the reagents and his own skin. Every sample was contaminated by modern lead before he could measure the ancient kind. So he built an ultraclean lab, with filtered air, scrubbed surfaces and acid-washed equipment, and treated contamination as the enemy it was. According to the geochronologist Brent Dalrymple's history of the problem, Patterson calculated a valid age of 4.55 billion years in 1953. His full 1956 paper, Age of meteorites and the earth, gave 4.55 plus or minus 0.07 billion years. The modern accepted value of 4.54 billion years is within that range.
Different clocks, same answer

One measurement, however careful, is not why scientists are confident. The confidence comes from agreement among methods that share almost nothing except basic physics. Uranium-lead, samarium-neodymium, rubidium-strontium, rhenium-osmium and argon-argon dating use different elements with different chemistry, different half-lives and different lab techniques. If one of them had a hidden flaw, it would be a strange coincidence for all the others to have a flaw of exactly the same size in the same direction.

blocks.title: Ages of three meteorites by different dating methods
blocks.note: Five different radioactive clocks, three meteorites, all landing near 4.5 billion years. Each value has its own error bar of roughly 0.01 to 0.33 billion years.
blocks.source: Dalrymple, The Age of the Earth (Stanford University Press, 1991), as tabulated in Wikipedia, Age of Earth

blocks.text: The numbers have also been refined since Patterson. The oldest known solids in the solar system, tiny calcium- and aluminum-rich grains found in some meteorites, were dated by James Connelly and colleagues in 2012 to about 4.567 billion years. That is the closest thing we have to the solar system's birthday. The Earth took time to assemble after that, probably tens of millions of years of collisions, so the age of the Earth is slightly younger and slightly fuzzier. That is why the usual figure, 4.54 billion years, comes with an uncertainty of about 50 million years. Fifty million years sounds like a lot, but it is about 1 percent.

blocks.text: The lead in everyone's blood

Patterson's obsession with contamination led him somewhere unexpected. If the lab was full of lead, and the dust was full of lead, where was it coming from? Natural lead levels at the Earth's surface should be low. He began measuring lead in ocean water, in sediments, in ancient bones and in ice. In a 1965 paper, Contaminated and natural lead environments of man, he argued that people in industrial countries were carrying far more lead in their bodies than humans ever had in nature. In 1969, he and his colleagues Murozumi and Chow published measurements from Greenland ice and snow showing lead deposits rising steeply in modern times.

The main source was tetraethyl lead, added to gasoline since the 1920s to stop engine knock. Every car on the road was spraying fine lead particles into the air. Lead is a neurotoxin, especially for developing children's brains. The lead and petroleum industries pushed back hard, and Patterson lost some research funding along the way. But his data, and the work of others who followed, helped drive the phase-out of leaded gasoline in the United States through the 1970s and 1980s.

items.label: Mean US blood lead, micrograms per deciliter, 1976–80 vs 1988–91
Drop in average blood lead across ages 1 to 74
