blocks.text: The results showed up in national health surveys. A 1994 study in JAMA by James Pirkle and colleagues at the CDC found that the average blood lead level of Americans aged 1 to 74 fell by 78 percent between the late 1970s and the early 1990s. The authors judged the most likely cause to be the removal of 99.8 percent of lead from gasoline, plus the end of lead-soldered food cans. A question about meteorites ended up changing what was in the bloodstream of an entire country.
What deep time does to your head

A number like 4.54 billion is hard to feel. One way to make it concrete: squeeze the Earth's history into a single 24-hour day. The first simple life shows up within the first few hours. Animals with hard shells do not appear until after 9 p.m. Dinosaurs show up around 10:45 p.m. and are gone by about 11:40. All of recorded human history fits into the last fraction of a second. Every war, empire and invention you have ever heard of is a rounding error.

That should not make human things feel meaningless. If anything, it shows how much a few people with good instruments can figure out. A species that has been writing for about five thousand years worked out the age of a planet that is nearly a million times older, using the decay of atoms it cannot see, and checked the answer five different ways.

The story also offers a clean lesson in how knowledge actually advances. Kelvin was brilliant, rigorous and influential, and he was wrong because he trusted a model whose assumptions he never seriously questioned. Patterson was not famous when he started. He was right because he refused to trust a single measurement until he had eliminated every source of contamination he could find, and because he followed an anomaly, the lead in his lab, all the way to its source.

Two habits worth stealing: when your answer depends on a model, list the assumptions and ask which one would hurt most if it were wrong. And when something keeps messing up your results, do not just work around it. Find out where it comes from.

The meteorite fragment in Arizona did not care what anyone believed. It had been keeping time since before the Earth finished forming. All it took to read it was the right physics, a clean room and a person stubborn enough to keep scrubbing.

takeaways: The Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, give or take roughly 1 percent, based on meteorite lead and confirmed by several independent radioactive clocks.
Kelvin's estimate failed because of hidden assumptions (no internal heat, no convection), not bad math.
Radiometric dating works because half-lives are fixed; using two uranium clocks in one sample cancels out unknown starting amounts.
Patterson's fight against lab contamination revealed industrial lead pollution and helped drive leaded gasoline out of use; US blood lead fell 78% in about 12 years.
Confidence in science comes from agreement among independent methods, not from any single measurement.

title: Evolution on Fast Forward
dek: Antibiotics are one of the greatest inventions in history, and bacteria have been dismantling them since the first patient was treated. Watching how they do it is the clearest look at evolution you will ever get.

blocks.text: At Harvard Medical School in 2016, a team built the biggest petri dish most biologists had ever seen: a rectangle of agar two feet by four feet, about 14 liters of bacterial food. They divided it into bands. The outer edges had no drug at all. The next band held just enough of the antibiotic trimethoprim to kill ordinary *E. coli*. Each band toward the center held ten times more than the one before, until the middle strip held a thousand times the lethal dose.

Then they put bacteria on the edges, pointed a camera at the dish, and let it run. The bacteria filled the drug-free zone and stopped at the first wall of antibiotic, a wall that should have been fatal. For a while nothing happened. Then a small tuft appeared on the other side of the line: a mutant that could survive. It spread across the band and stopped at the next wall. Then another mutant broke through, and another.

Within about ten days, bacteria were growing in the center of the plate, in a thousand times the dose that had killed their ancestors. When the team tried another antibiotic, ciprofloxacin, the bacteria evolved resistance to a hundred thousand times the starting dose. The time-lapse video is one of the most striking things in modern biology, because it shows evolution happening the way it actually works: not as a slow slide but as a series of breakthroughs, each built on the last.

items.label: Trimethoprim dose E. coli survived after evolving on the MEGA-plate
Time to evolve that level of resistance
Resistance evolved against the starting dose of ciprofloxacin

blocks.source: Baym et al., Science, 2016 (Harvard Gazette)

blocks.text: Why bacteria win the arms race

Resistance is not something bacteria decide to develop, and they do not get stronger by being exposed to antibiotics the way a muscle gets stronger from training. It is natural selection, the same process Darwin described, running on a population so large and so fast that you can see it happen in a week.

Here is the math that makes it work. Under good conditions, some bacteria can divide every 20 to 30 minutes. A single infection can contain billions of cells. Every time a cell copies its DNA there is a small chance of a mistake, a mutation. Almost all mutations are useless or harmful. But when you have billions of cells dividing many times a day, even a one-in-a-billion mutation is likely to show up somewhere. If one of those happens to block the antibiotic, that cell survives while its neighbors die, and its offspring inherit the trick.

Put that in human terms. A bacterium that divides every 20 minutes can pass through about 70 generations in a single day. Seventy human generations, at roughly 25 years each, stretches back well over a thousand years. Bacteria get that many rolls of the evolutionary dice between breakfast one day and breakfast the next.

blocks.title: How resistance evolves
items: A huge bacterial population has random variation from mutations.
An antibiotic kills the susceptible cells.
A rare cell with a protective mutation survives.
With competitors gone, it multiplies and takes over.
Repeat with higher doses or new drugs, and resistance stacks up step by step.

blocks.text: The antibiotic did not cause the useful mutation. It removed everything that did not have one. That is the key idea, and it is why the MEGA-plate looks the way it does. Each wall of drug is a filter. Only the rare mutant passes, and then it has an entire empty band to itself.

What do the winning mutations actually do? There are only a few basic strategies, and bacteria use all of them. Some make enzymes that chop the antibiotic apart before it can act, the way staph learned to destroy penicillin. Some change the shape of the molecule the drug is supposed to latch onto, so it no longer fits, like changing the lock so the old key fails. Some build pumps in their outer wall that throw the drug back out as fast as it comes in. And some simply make their walls harder to get through.

items: Destroy it: enzymes that break the antibiotic apart.
Dodge it: change the target so the drug cannot bind.
Eject it: pumps that push the drug out of the cell.
Block it: tighter walls that keep the drug from getting in.

blocks.text: Bacteria have a second weapon that makes this far worse: they share. Many resistance genes sit on small loops of DNA called plasmids that bacteria can pass to each other, sometimes across different species. Imagine if a soldier in one unit could hand their body armor to a soldier in a completely different army just by standing next to them. A resistance gene that evolves in a harmless gut bacterium can end up in a dangerous one.

Resistance usually comes with a price. On the MEGA-plate, the early resistant mutants grew more slowly than their ancestors, because the changes that protected them also got in the way of normal life. Later mutations often fixed that, and the fully resistant strains grew at normal speed again. That second step is bad news. It means that simply stopping use of a drug does not always make resistance disappear, because the bacteria have already paid off the cost.
Antibiotics do not create resistance. They select for it. Every dose is a filter that clears out the vulnerable bacteria and leaves the field to whatever survives.
The warning was there from day one

Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mold contaminating one of his culture plates had killed the bacteria around it. That mold made penicillin. It took until the 1940s, and a massive wartime production effort, to turn it into a drug. When Fleming accepted the Nobel Prize in December 1945, he used part of his lecture to issue a warning that reads today like a prophecy.

He told a story about a hypothetical Mr. X with a sore throat who buys penicillin and takes too little, not enough to kill the bacteria but enough to train them. The surviving resistant germs pass to his wife, who later develops pneumonia. Penicillin fails her, and she dies. Fleming's point was that underdosing was more dangerous than overdosing, because it bred resistance. He was right, and the pattern he predicted has repeated with nearly every antibiotic since.

blocks.title: The race between drugs and bugs
items: Fleming notices mold killing bacteria on a culture plate
Penicillin is mass-produced and saves wartime lives
Fleming's Nobel lecture warns about breeding resistance
Methicillin is introduced to beat penicillin-resistant staph

blocks.text: The story of MRSA shows the speed. By the 1950s, much of the staph bacteria in hospitals had become resistant to penicillin. Chemists responded with methicillin, designed to resist the enzyme staph used to break penicillin down. It came into use in Britain around 1959. Within about two years, doctors were reporting methicillin-resistant staph. Today MRSA is one of the best-known hospital superbugs in the world.
How big the problem really is

The most complete estimate comes from a global research effort called GRAM, which published its latest analysis in The Lancet in 2024. It estimated that in 2021, about 1.14 million deaths worldwide were directly caused by drug-resistant bacterial infections, and resistant bacteria were involved in about 4.7 million deaths in total. Those are infections that once would have been cured with a standard pill.

blocks.title: Deaths directly caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria, worldwide
blocks.note: The forecast assumes current trends continue; it adds up to more than 39 million deaths from 2025 to 2050.
blocks.source: GRAM study, The Lancet, 2024 (via IHME)

blocks.text: The averages hide a striking split. Between 1990 and 2021, resistance deaths among children under five fell by about 60 percent, thanks to vaccines, cleaner water and better care for infants. But among adults 70 and older they rose by about 90 percent. Older people are more likely to be in hospitals, get surgery and have weaker immune systems, which is exactly where resistant bacteria thrive. As the world's population ages, the forecast rises with it.

blocks.text: In the United States, the CDC's most recent full threat report estimated more than 2.8 million antibiotic-resistant infections and 35,000 deaths each year. That was nearly twice the death toll the agency had estimated in its previous report. There was good news inside it, too: deaths had fallen since 2013, and by nearly 30 percent in hospitals, largely because of better infection control.
Why we are not just inventing new drugs

The obvious answer to resistance is to stay ahead with new antibiotics. The problem is economic as much as scientific. A new antibiotic that works against superbugs should be used as little as possible, saved for patients with no other options, so that resistance to it develops slowly. That is great public health and terrible business. A cancer drug or a cholesterol pill that people take every day for years earns back its development costs. A last-resort antibiotic sitting in a hospital cabinet does not, and several companies that brought new antibiotics to market went bankrupt.

The World Health Organization's 2024 review of the pipeline found that the number of antibacterial drugs in clinical testing had risen from 80 to 97. But of 32 antibiotics being developed against the most worrying bacteria, only 12 counted as truly innovative, and only 4 of those worked against at least one of the most critical threats. Since mid-2017, 13 new antibiotics had been approved, and only 2 were from a genuinely new chemical class. Most new drugs are variations on old ones, which bacteria have already practiced beating.

blocks.title: New antibiotics approved since July 2017
blocks.source: World Health Organization, antibacterial pipeline report, 2024

blocks.text: Hospitals are not the only place where the selection happens. A large share of the world's antibiotics goes into farm animals, in some places routinely, to prevent disease in crowded conditions or to speed up growth. Resistant bacteria and their genes can then move from farms into soil, water and food. Many countries have tightened rules on using antibiotics just to fatten livestock, but enforcement varies widely.

Researchers are exploring other routes: viruses called phages that infect bacteria, antibodies, drugs that disarm bacteria instead of killing them, and AI-assisted searches through millions of molecules. Some of these are promising. None is ready to replace antibiotics at scale.
What actually helps

If resistance is natural selection, then fighting it means changing the selection pressure. Use antibiotics less often, and only when they are needed, so fewer resistant strains get a head start. Stop infections from happening and spreading in the first place, so fewer bacteria get the chance to evolve and share genes. The biggest gains so far have come from exactly that: hand hygiene, vaccines, clean water and hospital infection control.

items: Antibiotics do nothing against viruses, which cause most colds, flu and many sore throats. Pushing for them only feeds resistance.
When you are prescribed an antibiotic, take it exactly as directed and ask the corpsman or doctor before stopping early or saving pills.
Never take someone else's leftover antibiotics or share yours.
In a confined space like a ship or submarine, hand washing and not working sick protect the whole crew, not just you.

blocks.text: One note on stopping early: the old rule of always finishing the course is being re-examined, because for some infections shorter courses work just as well and expose bacteria to less drug overall. That is a decision for whoever prescribed it, not something to guess at. The constant is to follow medical advice rather than improvising.
The bigger lesson

The MEGA-plate is worth remembering because it shows something true far beyond bacteria. Whenever you apply strong pressure to a large, fast-changing system, you select for whatever survives the pressure, not for what you intended. Pest control breeds resistant insects. Anti-cheat systems in games breed smarter cheats. Strict metrics at work breed people who game the metric.

The bacteria are not clever. They are numerous, fast and endlessly varied, and that is enough to beat some of the best chemistry humans have ever produced. The only durable strategy against a system like that is to stop handing it easy wins: use the pressure sparingly, and keep the population small.
Evolution needs three things: variation, selection and time. Bacteria have the first in enormous supply and the third in minutes. Every unnecessary antibiotic adds the second.

takeaways: Resistance is natural selection: antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria and leave rare resistant mutants to take over.
On the MEGA-plate, E. coli evolved to survive 1,000 times a lethal dose of trimethoprim in about ten days.
Resistant bacteria directly caused about 1.14 million deaths in 2021, and deaths among people over 70 rose by about 90% since 1990.
New antibiotics are scarce partly because good stewardship means using them as little as possible, which makes them unprofitable.
Antibiotics do nothing for viruses; take them exactly as prescribed and never share or save them.

title: How Do You Prove Something Nobody Can See?
dek: Around 1900, serious scientists doubted atoms existed. The case that settled it was not a photograph but a jittering yellow speck and thirteen numbers that refused to disagree.

blocks.text: In a Paris laboratory around 1908, Jean Perrin spent his days staring down a microscope at a drop of water with yellow grains floating in it. The grains came from gamboge, a tree resin artists used as paint. Each one was about three quarters of a micrometer across, and Perrin had spent months spinning batches in a centrifuge to sort them by size until they were nearly identical. Under the lens they never stopped moving. They twitched, drifted, reversed and twitched again, as if something invisible were kicking them from every side.

Something was. Perrin was using those grains to settle one of the longest arguments in science: whether atoms and molecules are real objects or just a convenient way of doing chemistry on paper. That sounds like a question with an obvious answer. It was not obvious in 1900, and the way it got answered is one of the best lessons available on how anyone can know anything about a thing they will never see directly.
The skeptics had a point

By the late 1800s, chemists had used atoms for most of a century. John Dalton's atomic theory explained why elements combine in fixed ratios. Amedeo Avogadro proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gas at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules. Ludwig Boltzmann built a whole theory of heat on the idea that gases are swarms of tiny colliding particles. The model worked beautifully.

But a model that works is not the same as a model that is true, and some very good scientists said so. The physicist and philosopher Ernst Mach, the chemist Wilhelm Ostwald and the physicist Pierre Duhem argued that science should describe what can be measured, such as pressure, temperature and energy, and should not invent invisible machinery underneath. To them, atoms were a bookkeeping device, like the lines of latitude on a map. Useful, but not things you could trip over.

This was not stubbornness for its own sake. Physics had already been burned by invisible stuff. Heat was once explained as a weightless fluid called caloric, and light was thought to travel through an invisible medium called the ether. Both were useful for a while, and both turned out not to exist. The skeptics were asking a fair question: what observation would prove atoms are real, rather than just handy? And for a long time, nobody had a good answer, because nobody could count them.

The real problem was not that atoms were invisible. It was that every theory using them could be rewritten without them. To prove they were real, someone needed an effect that only made sense if matter came in discrete lumps of a definite size.
A dance nobody could explain

The clue had been sitting in plain sight since 1827. That summer the Scottish botanist Robert Brown looked through a microscope at tiny granules released from the pollen of a wildflower, Clarkia pulchella, suspended in water. They moved constantly and erratically. Brown first wondered if this was some sign of life, so he tried other materials, including powdered rock and soot. Those jittered too. Whatever this motion was, it was not biology.

For decades, people proposed explanations: tiny currents, uneven heating, evaporation, light. Careful experiments knocked them down one by one. The motion did not fade over time, did not depend on the container being disturbed and got stronger in warmer, thinner liquids. Some physicists suspected molecular collisions, but suspecting is not proving. A grain of pollen debris is enormous compared with a water molecule, so why would individual hits move it at all? And how would you turn a vague jiggle into a hard number?

Notice what kind of problem this was. It was not a lack of cleverness. It was a lack of any measurement that could connect the invisible to the visible with a number attached. Atomists could say the jitter was molecules. Skeptics could say it was something else not yet understood. Without a prediction that could fail, both sides could keep talking forever.
Einstein's trick: make the invisible leave fingerprints

In 1905, a 26-year-old patent clerk named Albert Einstein published a paper with a long German title about the motion of small particles suspended in liquids at rest, as required by the molecular theory of heat. He did not try to track molecules. He asked what the molecules would do to something big enough to see.

His insight was statistical. A visible grain gets hit by water molecules from all sides, an enormous number of times every second. Most of those hits cancel out. But at any instant, slightly more might land on the left than the right, and the grain gets a tiny net shove. The next instant the imbalance points a different way. The result is a random walk, the same pattern as someone taking steps in random directions. A random walker does not drift away steadily. The average squared distance from the start grows in direct proportion to time, so going twice as far takes four times as long.

Size is the whole game here. A basketball in a pool also gets hit unevenly by water molecules, but it is so huge that the imbalances average out to essentially nothing. A grain a micrometer across is small enough that the leftover imbalance is noticeable, yet big enough to see in an ordinary microscope. Brownian motion lives in that narrow window, which is why it was a clue at all. It is the point where the graininess of matter leaks up into the visible world.

blocks.title: Einstein's argument in five moves
items: If water is made of molecules, they are moving faster at higher temperature and constantly hitting anything in the liquid.
A visible grain gets uneven hits from different sides, so it wanders in a random walk.
For a random walk, the average squared distance traveled grows in step with elapsed time.
The rate of that spreading depends on temperature, the liquid's viscosity, the grain's size and the number of molecules in a given amount of substance.
Measure the spreading of grains you can see, and you can solve for the count of molecules you cannot see.

blocks.text: That last step is the knife. Einstein's formula linked something you could measure with a microscope and a stopwatch to Avogadro's number, the number of molecules in a standard amount of a substance. If molecules were only a bookkeeping fiction, there was no reason for that number to come out of a pollen-sized speck dancing in water. If they were real, the dance would reveal how many of them there were. The theory made a prediction that could fail.
Perrin counts the uncountable

Einstein was a theorist. Turning his formula into a measurement took an experimenter with endless patience, and that was Perrin. He needed huge numbers of grains that were all the same size and density, which is why he spent months refining gamboge and later mastic. Then he attacked the problem from several directions at once.

First he treated his grains like a tiny atmosphere. In air, molecules thin out with height because gravity pulls them down while their motion spreads them up. If his grains really behaved like giant molecules, they should form the same kind of layered atmosphere in a drop of water, just squeezed into microscopic heights. They did. In his best measurements, the number of grains halved with every 6 micrometers of height. By counting grains at different levels he could calculate Avogadro's number.

Then he tracked individual grains, tracing their positions at regular intervals and checking Einstein's predictions directly. The mean squared displacement grew in proportion to time, just as the random-walk math said it should. He varied grain size over a range of about 70,000 to 1 and the liquid's viscosity over a range of about 125 to 1, and the predictions kept holding. Later he even watched larger spheres rotate, using tiny flaws inside them as markers, which gave yet another route to the same number.

items.label: Diameter of Perrin's sorted gamboge grains
Height over which his grain 'atmosphere' halved in density
Range of grain sizes over which the predictions held

blocks.text: Thirteen ways to get one number

Here is the part that actually won the argument. Perrin did not just produce one value of Avogadro's number. In his Nobel lecture he listed results from a dozen-plus methods, many having nothing to do with each other: the vertical layering of emulsions, the wandering and rotation of grains, the way light scatters off gas (the same physics that makes the sky blue), the radiation from hot objects, the electric charge on tiny droplets measured by Robert Millikan, and counting helium atoms produced by radioactive decay.

blocks.title: Avogadro's number, by method (×10²²)
blocks.note: Perrin's figures per gram-molecule; the modern SI value is 6.022 × 10²³ per mole.
blocks.source: Perrin, Nobel Lecture, 1926; NIST CODATA

blocks.text: Think about what that agreement means. Each method rests on different physics, different equipment and different assumptions. If molecules were fictional, there is no reason the jitter of resin grains, the color of the sky and the decay of radium should all point to roughly the same number. Each one could have come out a hundred times too big or too small. Instead they cluster within about 20 percent of each other, and close to the value we know today. Perrin said this convergence gave a certainty at least equal to that of the laws of thermodynamics.

Philosophers call this consilience: independent lines of evidence converging on one answer. It is the strongest kind of evidence science has, stronger than any single dramatic experiment, because a coincidence across unrelated methods is so unlikely.

It worked on the skeptics. In 1908, Ostwald, one of the leading anti-atomists, publicly conceded that the Brownian motion results allowed even a cautious scientist to speak of experimental proof that matter is made of atoms. Mach never fully came around. Perrin received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1926 for his work on the discontinuous structure of matter, and the presentation speech described his goal as ending the long struggle over whether molecules really exist.

blocks.title: From bookkeeping to reality

Avogadro: equal gas volumes hold equal numbers of molecules

blocks.text: What counts as seeing?

Today you can find images of individual atoms. In 1981 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at IBM Zurich built the scanning tunneling microscope, which moves a needle with an extremely sharp tip across a surface and measures the tiny current that leaks across the gap. They won the 1986 Nobel Prize for it. Later researchers used the same kind of instrument to push individual atoms around and spell out letters. So, finally, someone has seen one, right?

Not exactly. An STM image is not light bouncing into an eye. It is a computer map of electrical current, interpreted through quantum mechanics. It is the same kind of inference Perrin made, just with a sharper tool. And in 2019 the international system of units went a step further and defined the Avogadro constant as exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ per mole. The number of molecules in a mole is no longer something we measure. It is something we declare, because we trust it that much.

This should feel familiar to anyone who works around a reactor. Nobody has looked at a neutron. You know the neutron population in a core through detectors that turn particle hits into current, through power that shows up as heat, through predictions that match what instruments read. You trust the picture not because any single gauge proves it but because many independent indications agree. That is exactly the standard Perrin set for atoms.

The lesson reaches beyond physics. Most important things you believe, you have never seen directly: the age of the Earth, what is happening in another country, what is going on in someone else's head. The honest way to hold those beliefs is Perrin's way. Ask whether separate, unrelated lines of evidence point to the same answer. One source that agrees with you is a data point. Five independent sources that agree with each other are something close to knowledge.

And the skeptics deserve some credit too. Mach and Ostwald forced atomists to stop hand-waving and produce a number that could have come out wrong. Good skepticism is not saying no forever. It is naming the test that would change your mind, and then actually changing it when the test comes back.

takeaways: Around 1900, respected scientists doubted atoms were real, and their demand for proof was reasonable.
Einstein showed in 1905 that the random jitter of visible grains could reveal how many molecules exist.
Perrin's experiments and a dozen unrelated methods all gave roughly the same Avogadro's number, which is what settled the debate.
Independent lines of evidence agreeing (consilience) is stronger than any single experiment.
Good skepticism names the test that would change your mind, then accepts the result.

title: The Curve on the Mountain
dek: Skip the shouting. Here is what the measurements actually show about carbon dioxide and warming, how scientists know the extra CO2 is ours, and which parts of climate science are settled versus genuinely uncertain.

blocks.text: In March 1958, a young chemist named Charles David Keeling started measuring carbon dioxide in the air on the slopes of Mauna Loa, a volcano on the Big Island of Hawaii. He picked the site because it sits high above the local influence of cities, forests and traffic, sampling air that has mixed across the Pacific. Most people assumed CO2 levels varied too much from place to place to say anything meaningful about the whole planet. Keeling thought careful enough measurements could see through the noise.

Within a few years, his data showed two things nobody had seen clearly before. First, the Earth breathes. Every spring and summer, as forests and fields across the Northern Hemisphere grow leaves, CO2 drops. Every fall and winter, as leaves decay, it rises again. Second, underneath that seasonal breathing, the level was going up every single year.

That record, now kept by NOAA and the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, is called the Keeling Curve. It is one of the most important datasets in science, and it is a good place to start if you want to understand climate change from the evidence up rather than from the arguments down.

blocks.title: The planet breathing: Mauna Loa CO2 by month, 2024
blocks.source: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Mauna Loa monthly mean CO2

blocks.text: The curve

CO2 is measured in parts per million, or ppm: how many molecules out of every million molecules of dry air are carbon dioxide. In 1959, the first full year of the record, the annual average at Mauna Loa was about 316 ppm. In 2025 it was about 427 ppm. The rise has not been steady; it has been accelerating. In the early years the level rose by under 1 ppm a year. In recent years it has been rising by roughly 2 to 3 ppm a year.

blocks.title: Annual average CO2 at Mauna Loa
blocks.note: Every five years from 1959, plus 2025. The seasonal wiggle is averaged out here.
blocks.source: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory and Scripps, Mauna Loa annual mean CO2

blocks.text: To see further back, scientists use ice. Snow falling on Antarctica and Greenland gets compressed into ice over thousands of years, trapping tiny bubbles of ancient air. Drill a core, crack the bubbles open in a vacuum and you can measure the atmosphere as it was when the snow fell. Combined with other natural records, this lets researchers reconstruct greenhouse gases across hundreds of thousands of years.

The conclusions in the most recent major assessment, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) from 2021, are blunt. In 2019, CO2 concentrations were higher than at any time in at least 2 million years. Methane and nitrous oxide were higher than at any time in at least 800,000 years. CO2 had risen 47 percent since 1750. The IPCC notes that this increase far exceeds the natural swings between ice ages and warm periods over at least the past 800,000 years.

Living on a submarine, you already understand this in miniature. In a sealed space, CO2 builds up unless something removes it. The planet's only scrubbers are oceans, soils and plants, and they are not keeping up.
How we know the extra CO2 is ours

Volcanoes emit CO2. Oceans exhale it. Forests release it when they burn. So how can scientists be confident that the rise comes from human activity, mainly burning fossil fuels? There are at least three independent lines of evidence, and they all point the same way.

The first is simple accounting. We know roughly how much coal, oil and gas the world burns, because it is bought and sold and governments track it. That gives a reliable estimate of how much CO2 humans emit each year. The atmosphere is gaining less than that. According to the IPCC, land and ocean have absorbed a nearly constant share, about 56 percent per year, of human CO2 emissions over the past six decades. The rest stays in the air. If nature were the source of the rise, the oceans and land would be losing carbon, not gaining it. Measurements show the oceans are gaining it.

The second is isotopes. Carbon comes in different weights. Plants prefer the lighter carbon-12 over carbon-13, so fossil fuels, which formed from ancient plants, are depleted in carbon-13. They are also millions of years old, so they contain essentially no radioactive carbon-14, which decays with a half-life of about 5,700 years. As fossil CO2 floods the atmosphere, the share of carbon-13 drops and carbon-14 gets diluted. Both trends are measured, in air samples, tree rings and corals, as reviewed by Heather Graven, Ralph Keeling and Joeri Rogelj in 2020. Volcanic CO2 does not produce this signature.

The third is oxygen. Burning fossil fuel consumes oxygen. Volcanic CO2 does not. Starting in the late 1980s, Ralph Keeling, Charles Keeling's son, developed methods precise enough to measure tiny changes in atmospheric oxygen, publishing early results in Nature in 1992. Oxygen is declining, in step with fossil fuel burning. There is no risk of running out of oxygen to breathe; the decline is a tiny fraction of one percent of the oxygen in an atmosphere that is about 21 percent oxygen. But it is a clear chemical fingerprint of combustion.

items: Bookkeeping: humans emit more CO2 than the atmosphere gains; oceans and land are absorbing the difference, not releasing it.
Isotopes: the falling share of carbon-13 and diluted carbon-14 match old plant-based carbon, not volcanoes.
Oxygen: atmospheric O2 is dropping as expected from burning, which volcanic CO2 would not cause.

blocks.text: The physics is older than the airplane

None of this is new science. In 1856, the American scientist Eunice Foote reported that air containing more carbon dioxide heated up more in sunlight. A few years later, the Irish physicist John Tyndall showed in the lab that gases like water vapor and CO2 absorb infrared radiation, the heat that the Earth's surface gives off. In 1896, the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius worked through calculations by hand to estimate how much doubling CO2 would warm the planet.

Modern climate modeling started in the 1960s. In 1967, Syukuro Manabe and Richard Wetherald published a model that, for the first time, handled both the way heat moves up through the atmosphere by convection and the way it is radiated away. It gave a warming of a little over 2 degrees Celsius for doubled CO2, and correctly predicted that the lower atmosphere would warm while the upper atmosphere cooled. Manabe shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics for this line of work.

blocks.text: What the thermometers say

Global temperature is reconstructed from many thousands of land stations, ships, buoys and, more recently, satellites, by several independent groups in the US, Europe and Japan. They differ slightly in methods but agree closely on the trend. The IPCC concluded that each of the last four decades has been successively warmer than any decade before it since 1850.

blocks.title: Global surface temperature by decade
blocks.note: Decade averages computed from NOAA's annual global land and ocean values. Note the flat middle of the century, partly because sulfate pollution was reflecting sunlight, before the steep rise from the 1970s.
blocks.source: NOAA NCEI, Climate at a Glance, global land and ocean annual anomalies

blocks.text: Single years bounce around, which is where a lot of confusion comes from. In NOAA's record, 2020 came in about 1.01 degrees above the 20th-century average, and 2021 fell back to about 0.86. Then 2023 jumped to 1.17 and 2024 to 1.25, before 2025 eased to about 1.12. Much of that wobble comes from natural cycles such as El Niño and La Niña, which shift heat between the ocean and the air. If you looked only at 2020 to 2021, you might think warming had reversed. If you looked only at 2022 to 2024, you might think it was exploding. The way to read noisy data is the way you would read any gauge with a jumpy needle: look at the trend over many readings, not the last one. Decade averages strip out most of the bounce, and they have gone up every decade since the 1970s.

By the IPCC's numbers, the global surface in 2011 to 2020 was about 1.09 degrees Celsius warmer than in 1850 to 1900, with land warming faster, around 1.59 degrees, than the oceans, around 0.88. Its best estimate of the human-caused part over a similar period was 1.07 degrees, essentially all of it. Greenhouse gases likely contributed 1.0 to 2.0 degrees of warming, while other pollution, mainly sulfate aerosols that reflect sunlight, offset some of it. Natural factors such as the sun and volcanoes changed things by only about a tenth of a degree either way.

items.label: Observed warming, 2011–2020 vs 1850–1900
Best estimate of the human-caused part (2010–2019)
Estimated effect of natural drivers like the sun and volcanoes

blocks.source: IPCC AR6 Working Group I, Summary for Policymakers, 2021

blocks.text: One of the strongest pieces of evidence is a pattern, not a number. If the sun were driving the warming, the whole atmosphere would heat up, top to bottom. Greenhouse gases do something different: they trap heat in the lower atmosphere and cause the upper atmosphere to cool. A 2023 study in PNAS led by Benjamin Santer showed that satellite records include strong cooling in the middle and upper stratosphere, 25 to 50 kilometers up, of 1 to 2 degrees Celsius from 1986 to 2022, alongside warming lower down. That vertical fingerprint is what Manabe's 1967 model predicted, and it is hard to explain any other way.

For scale, the European Copernicus Climate Change Service reported that 2024 was the first calendar year more than 1.5 degrees above pre-industrial levels, at about 1.60 degrees in its main dataset; other datasets put it between 1.51 and 1.55. That does not mean the Paris Agreement's 1.5 degree goal has formally been breached, because that goal refers to a long-term average over about 20 years, not a single hot year. But it shows how close the world is to that threshold.
What is settled and what is not

Honest science distinguishes what is nailed down from what is still uncertain, and climate science has plenty of real uncertainty. The key unknown is climate sensitivity: how much the planet eventually warms if CO2 doubles. The answer depends heavily on clouds and other feedbacks. The IPCC's best estimate is 3 degrees Celsius, with a likely range of 2.5 to 4 degrees, narrower than the previous report's 1.5 to 4.5. That is real progress, but a spread between 2.5 and 4 degrees still matters a lot for planning.

Models are not gospel either. In 2022, the climate scientists Zeke Hausfather, Kate Marvel, Gavin Schmidt and colleagues published a commentary in Nature warning about a hot model problem: some of the newest climate models were warming faster than the observations and other evidence supported, and they argued those models should not be used naively. That is what healthy science looks like. The people building the models were the ones calling out the flaw.

blocks.title: Climate science: confidence levels

left.head: Very well established
items: CO2 is rising fast, mostly from fossil fuels
CO2 traps infrared heat; the physics is 150 years old
The planet has warmed about 1.1 °C
Human activity caused essentially all of it
Oceans and land absorb roughly half our emissions

right.head: Still genuinely uncertain
items: Exact climate sensitivity (likely 2.5 to 4 °C)
How clouds will respond
How much aerosol pollution is masking
Regional details: which places get wetter or drier
Whether carbon sinks keep absorbing at today's rate

blocks.text: The last item on that list matters. The IPCC projects that as cumulative emissions grow, land and ocean sinks will absorb a smaller proportion of them, leaving a larger share in the air. The planet's free cleanup service is not guaranteed to keep working at the same rate.
The power of a boring dataset

It is worth remembering what made the Keeling Curve possible. It was not a single brilliant insight. It was one person insisting on precise, calibrated measurements at a remote site, then others continuing them, year after year, for more than six decades. Funding was threatened more than once. The measurements were not exciting on any given day. But without that long, careful, boring record, we would still be arguing about whether CO2 was rising at all.

Whatever you think should be done about climate change, and that is a question about values, costs and trade-offs as much as science, the measurements themselves are not a matter of opinion. CO2 is going up. We know why. The physics says that warms the planet, and the thermometers say it has. The remaining debates are real and important, but they are about how much and how fast, not about whether.

takeaways: Mauna Loa CO2 rose from about 316 ppm in 1959 to about 427 ppm in 2025, and the yearly rise has accelerated.
Three independent fingerprints (emissions bookkeeping, carbon isotopes and falling oxygen) show the extra CO2 comes mainly from fossil fuels.
The IPCC puts observed warming at about 1.09 °C (2011–2020) and the human-caused part at about 1.07 °C, essentially all of it.
A cooling upper atmosphere alongside a warming lower one points to greenhouse gases, not the sun.
Real uncertainty remains about climate sensitivity, clouds, aerosols and regional effects; that is about how much, not whether.

title: The Yogurt Bacteria That Taught Us to Edit Life
dek: CRISPR started as a germ's immune system against viruses. Now it is curing sickle cell disease, and a baby in Philadelphia got a gene fix built just for him.

blocks.text: In the summer of 2019, a woman from Mississippi named Victoria Gray checked into a hospital in Nashville. She had sickle cell disease, and for most of her life it had meant sudden pain crises severe enough to put her in the emergency room again and again. Doctors took stem cells out of her bone marrow, shipped them to a lab, edited one spot in their DNA, and put them back. Within months her body was making healthy-looking blood. The pain crises stopped.

The tool that did that edit did not come from a medical lab. It came from bacteria, and specifically from scientists who were trying to make better cultures for yogurt and cheese. That is one of the strangest and best stories in modern science: the most powerful genetic tool humans have ever built was stolen, nearly whole, from a microbe's defense against viruses.
This article covers how it works, what it has already done, where the limits are, and why the most important part of the story might be the speed at which it is now moving.
A germ that remembers its enemies

Bacteria have a problem: viruses called phages hunt them constantly. A phage lands on a bacterium, injects its own DNA, and turns the cell into a factory for more phages until it bursts. Bacteria that cannot fight back die. Over billions of years, many of them evolved a defense that works a lot like a wanted poster.

When a bacterium survives a phage attack, it snips out a short chunk of the virus's DNA and pastes it into a special region of its own genome. That region is a stack of these stolen chunks, each separated by the same short repeated sequence. Japanese researchers first noticed the odd repeats in *E. coli* in 1987 without knowing what they were for. Years later they got a clunky name: clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats. CRISPR.

The bacterium copies those stored chunks into short strands of RNA. Each RNA strand pairs up with a protein, and the pair patrols the cell. If the RNA finds viral DNA that matches its sequence, the protein cuts it. The virus is chopped up before it can take over. The cell has a memory of every enemy its ancestors survived, written right into its genes and passed down to its offspring.

The proof that this really was an immune system came in 2007 from a team at Danisco, a food company. They were studying *Streptococcus thermophilus*, a workhorse of the dairy industry, because phage outbreaks can ruin a whole batch of yogurt. They showed that adding a phage's sequence to the CRISPR region made the bacteria resistant to that phage, and removing it took the resistance away. Industrial food science had just found a programmable weapon.

blocks.text: Turning a weapon into a tool

The leap came in 2012. Emmanuelle Charpentier, who studied the bacterium that causes strep throat, and Jennifer Doudna, a structural biologist at Berkeley, worked out exactly how one of these cutting proteins, called Cas9, finds its target. Then they did something clever. They showed that you could design the guide RNA yourself, swap in any sequence you wanted, and Cas9 would cut DNA at that spot. Not viral DNA. Any DNA.

That is the whole trick, and it is why CRISPR spread through biology labs like a wildfire. Before it, editing a gene meant engineering a custom protein for every new target, which could take months and a lot of money. With CRISPR, the protein stays the same. You just type a new 20-letter address into the guide RNA. Changing the target became closer to editing a line of code than building a new machine. In 2020 Charpentier and Doudna shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it, an unusually fast award for work only eight years old.

blocks.title: How Cas9 makes a cut
items: Scientists write a guide RNA whose 20 letters match the target spot in the genome.
The guide loads into the Cas9 protein, and the pair drifts through the cell's DNA.
Cas9 grabs onto a short tag sequence next to possible targets and pries the DNA open.
If the guide's letters match the DNA, Cas9 cuts both strands of the double helix.
The cell rushes to repair the break, and that repair is where the edit actually happens.

blocks.text: That last step matters more than most explanations admit. Cas9 does not really edit anything. It breaks the DNA, and the cell fixes the break. The cell's fast repair crew often glues the ends back together sloppily, adding or deleting a few letters. That usually wrecks the gene, which is exactly what you want if your goal is to switch a gene off. If you want a precise change instead, you can supply a template with the correct sequence, and the cell may copy it in. That second route is far less reliable.
The mental model: Cas9 is a search engine attached to a pair of scissors. The guide RNA is the search query. The cut is easy. Controlling what the cell does after the cut is the hard part.
The first cure: switching a baby gene back on

Sickle cell disease comes from a single wrong letter in the gene for adult hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells. That one error makes hemoglobin clump together, bending the cells into rigid crescents that jam in small blood vessels. The result is pain, organ damage and a shorter life. It is one of the most common inherited diseases in the world and falls hardest on people of African descent.

Here is the clever part of the treatment that eventually helped Victoria Gray. It does not fix the broken gene at all. Before birth, everyone makes a different version of hemoglobin, called fetal hemoglobin, which works fine. Around the time of birth, a gene called BCL11A acts like a switch that shuts fetal hemoglobin production down and turns the adult version on. Doctors had long noticed that people who naturally keep making some fetal hemoglobin into adulthood have milder sickle cell disease.

So the therapy, called exa-cel and sold as Casgevy, uses Cas9 to break the BCL11A switch in a patient's blood stem cells. With the switch broken, the cells go back to making fetal hemoglobin, which dilutes the faulty adult kind and keeps red cells round. It is a cut that disables, the easiest thing CRISPR does, aimed at exactly the right target.

items.label: Sickle cell trial participants who went a full year without pain crises
Date the FDA approved Casgevy, the first CRISPR medicine in the US
Estimated cost per patient at approval

blocks.text: The results were striking. In the trial data reported at approval, 29 of 30 sickle cell participants went a full year without a pain crisis. Britain's regulator approved the treatment in November 2023, and the US Food and Drug Administration followed on December 8, 2023. It was the first time a CRISPR-based medicine was approved anywhere.

But the honest picture includes the costs. The patient's own stem cells have to be harvested and edited in a specialized lab. Then the patient gets high-dose chemotherapy to wipe out the old bone marrow and make room for the edited cells, which carries real risks including infertility. Recovery means weeks in the hospital. And the price was estimated at up to two million dollars per patient. For a disease that affects millions of people, many in countries with limited health care, that is a cure most patients cannot reach yet.
Beyond scissors: pencils and erasers

Because cutting both strands of DNA is crude, scientists kept building better attachments. The most important upgrade is called base editing, developed in David Liu's lab starting in 2016. A base editor uses a disabled Cas9 that can still find its target but can no longer cut through both strands. Bolted onto it is an enzyme that chemically converts one DNA letter into another. No double-strand break, no messy repair. Just a single letter rewritten in place.

blocks.title: Two ways to change a gene

left.head: Classic Cas9
items: Cuts both strands of DNA
Cell repairs the break, often messily
Great for switching genes off
Precise fixes are unreliable

right.head: Base editing
items: Nicks or does not cut the DNA
Chemically swaps one letter for another
Built for fixing single-letter typos
Fewer large, unwanted changes

blocks.text: That is exactly what a baby in Philadelphia known as KJ needed. He was born in 2024 with severe CPS1 deficiency, a rare disorder in which the liver cannot clear ammonia, a toxic byproduct of breaking down protein. Ammonia builds up in the blood and damages the brain. Many babies with the severe form die young, and the usual long-term answer is a liver transplant.

KJ's mutation was unique to him. So a team at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and Penn Medicine did something nobody had done before: they designed a base editor for his specific typo, packaged it in tiny fat bubbles called lipid nanoparticles that travel to the liver, and had it manufactured in about six months. He got his first dose in late February 2025, with two more in the following months. By the time the results were published in the New England Journal of Medicine that May, he was tolerating more protein in his diet, needed less medication, and had shrugged off a cold without a dangerous ammonia spike. The team was careful to say he needs long-term follow-up.

Look at what changed between those two stories. Casgevy took years to develop and is a single product for a common disease. KJ's treatment was a one-off, built for one child, in months. If that process can be made routine, it flips the economics of rare disease, where thousands of conditions each affect too few people for any company to build a drug the normal way.
The lines we have not crossed (and one person who did)

Every treatment described so far edits *somatic* cells, the ordinary cells of one person's body. Those edits die with the patient. Editing embryos, eggs or sperm is different: those changes would be inherited by every descendant. In 2018 the Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced he had edited embryos that became twin girls, aiming to make them resistant to HIV. The scientific world reacted with near-total condemnation. The edits were medically unnecessary, poorly controlled and done with flawed consent. He was sentenced to prison in China.

There are also technical limits worth knowing. CRISPR can hit the wrong spot when an off-target sequence looks similar enough to the guide. Getting the editor into the right cells is often harder than the edit itself; blood and liver are popular targets precisely because they are the easiest to reach. And many diseases are not caused by one bad gene but by hundreds of small variants interacting with environment. There is no single typo to fix for most heart disease, depression or obesity.

items: Easiest targets: diseases caused by one gene, in tissues you can reach (blood, liver, eye).
Hard targets: brain, muscle throughout the body, and diseases driven by many genes.
Off the table for now: heritable edits to embryos, which scientific bodies broadly oppose.

blocks.text: Why this story is really about debugging

If you have ever written code, CRISPR's history looks familiar. First you need to be able to read the source; that was the Human Genome Project, finished in 2003. Then you need a way to make targeted changes; that was Cas9 in 2012. Then you build better tools for smaller, safer edits, the way programmers moved from rewriting whole files to changing a single line. Medicine is moving from treating symptoms toward patching the source.

The other lesson is about where breakthroughs come from. Nobody set out to find a gene editor in yogurt bacteria. The people who found it were curious about weird repeated DNA and about why dairy cultures kept dying. That kind of basic research looks useless right up until it changes everything. It is a good argument for paying attention to the odd thing you do not understand yet, whether that is a strange pattern in a reactor log or a bug that only happens on Tuesdays.
The pattern to remember: nature already solved a lot of hard engineering problems. Some of the biggest breakthroughs come from noticing a working system and asking what else it could be pointed at.

takeaways: CRISPR is a bacterial immune system: a guide RNA finds a matching DNA sequence and a Cas protein cuts it.
Cas9 only breaks DNA; the cell's own repair process makes the actual change, which is why switching genes off is easier than precise fixes.
The first approved CRISPR cure, Casgevy, works by breaking a switch so sickle cell patients make fetal hemoglobin again.
Base editing rewrites single letters without a full cut, and in 2025 it was custom-built for one baby in about six months.
The biggest limits now are delivery, cost and diseases with no single gene to fix, not the cutting itself.

title: The Dark Majority
dek: Most of the space on Earth where life can live is cold, crushing and pitch black, and we have looked at almost none of it. What we have seen rewrites what 'normal' life looks like.

blocks.text: In 2025 a team of ocean scientists tried to answer a simple question: how much of the deep seafloor has anyone actually seen? Not mapped with sonar from the surface, but looked at, with a camera or a pair of eyes through a viewport. They pulled together records from about 44,000 deep dives by submersibles, robots and towed cameras going back to 1958. Then they added up the area those cameras had captured.

The answer was less than 0.001% of the deep seafloor. All of humanity's direct visual record of the bottom of the deep ocean covers an area roughly a tenth the size of Belgium. And even that sliver is badly skewed: about 65% of the observations sit within 200 nautical miles of just three countries, the United States, Japan and New Zealand. Deep ocean, defined as water deeper than 200 meters, covers about two-thirds of the planet's entire surface. We have photographed a few parking lots and called it a map of a continent.

items.label: Share of Earth's surface covered by ocean deeper than 200 m
Share of the deep seafloor ever visually observed
Deep dives with visual records since 1958

blocks.source: Bell et al., Science Advances, 2025

blocks.text: If you serve on a submarine, you spend weeks inside the ocean without seeing any of it. That is close to the human relationship with the deep sea in general. It is the largest habitat on the planet, and it is mostly known through instruments, inference and the occasional startling photograph.
Going down

Sunlight fades fast in seawater. Red light is gone within the first few tens of meters, which is why blood looks greenish-black to divers at depth. By 200 meters there is too little light for photosynthesis, and that is where oceanographers draw the line for the deep sea. From there to about 1,000 meters is the twilight zone, where a dim blue glow still filters down during the day. Below 1,000 meters, sunlight is effectively zero. Everything below that line lives in permanent night.

Animals in the twilight zone are built around that last trickle of light. Many have enormous eyes for their size, and some fish, like the barreleye, have tube-shaped eyes that point straight up, scanning for the faint shadow of something swimming overhead. Deeper down, where there is nothing left to see from above, eyes often shrink. The only light worth watching for is the light other animals make.

Pressure climbs in the other direction. Every 10 meters of seawater adds roughly one more atmosphere of pressure. At the average depth of the ocean, about 3,682 meters, that is several hundred atmospheres pressing on every surface. At the bottom of the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, about 10,935 meters down, it is over a thousand. The temperature over most of the deep seafloor hovers just above freezing, day and night, summer and winter.

blocks.title: How deep is deep?
blocks.note: Below about 6,000 m lies the hadal zone, the trench country.
blocks.source: NOAA; Bell et al. 2025; Schorr et al. 2014; Smithsonian (Jamieson team, 2023)

blocks.text: Some air-breathing animals visit surprisingly far into this world. In 2014, researchers tagging Cuvier's beaked whales off Southern California recorded one diving to 2,992 meters, nearly two miles down, and one dive lasting over two hours. A later study of the same species logged a single dive of 222 minutes. These are mammals holding one breath for longer than a movie, in water near freezing, at pressures that would flatten an unprotected steel drum.

Here is the counterintuitive part about pressure. A submarine has to fight it, because it carries a bubble of air at surface pressure inside a hull, and the whole ocean is trying to squeeze that bubble flat. Most deep-sea animals have no bubble to defend. Their bodies are mostly water, which barely compresses, and many have no gas-filled swim bladder at all. A jellyfish at 3,000 meters is not straining against the weight above it. The pressure is the same inside and out. The real challenge is subtler: at high pressure, proteins and cell membranes misbehave, so deep animals have evolved chemistry that keeps their molecular machinery working.
A world that makes its own light

With no sunlight, you might expect the deep sea to be utterly dark. It is not. It flickers. Many deep-sea animals make their own light through chemical reactions, a trick called bioluminescence. A 2017 study by Séverine Martini and Steven Haddock went through 17 years of underwater video from off the California coast, from the surface down to 3,900 meters, and classified more than 350,000 animals. About 76% of the individuals they saw could produce light. Among jellyfish and their relatives, it was over 97%.

Light in the dark is used for every purpose you can imagine. Some animals have glowing patches on their bellies that match the faint light from above, erasing their silhouette from predators looking up. This is called counter-illumination, and it is basically a stealth coating. Anglerfish dangle a glowing lure in front of a mouth full of needle teeth. Some shrimp spew a cloud of glowing fluid at attackers, the way a jet drops flares. A few dragonfish produce red light, a color most deep-sea animals cannot see, giving them a private searchlight to hunt with.

There is even a strategy researchers nickname the burglar alarm. When some small animals are grabbed by a predator, they flash brightly. The point is not to scare the attacker. It is to attract something bigger that might eat the attacker. In a place where visibility is near zero, light is the loudest signal there is, and every flash is a gamble about who will see it.
The phantom seafloor

During the Second World War, Navy sonar operators noticed something strange. Their echo sounders showed a seafloor a few hundred meters down in places where the charts said the water was thousands of meters deep. Stranger still, this false bottom rose toward the surface at dusk and sank again at dawn. It was not geology. It was life: a dense layer of small fish, shrimp, squid and other animals thick enough to bounce sound back, now known as the deep scattering layer.

What the sonar operators were seeing is now understood as the largest migration on Earth, and it happens every single day. Huge numbers of animals hide in the dark twilight zone by day, where predators cannot see them, then swim up hundreds of meters at night to feed near the surface, and sink back down before sunrise. For a creature a few centimeters long, that is roughly like a person walking a marathon twice a day.

The scale is hard to grasp. For years, the total mass of fish in the twilight zone was estimated at about a billion tonnes. In 2014, a team analyzing acoustic data from a round-the-world research expedition argued that the true figure is at least ten times higher. If so, the small, mostly unnamed fish of the twilight zone outweigh all the fish humans catch by a huge margin, and they play a major role in carrying carbon from the surface into the deep when they feed above and respire, excrete and die below.

blocks.title: The daily migration
items: Daytime: hide in the twilight zone, 200 to 1,000 m down
Dusk: swim upward hundreds of meters
Night: feed on plankton near the surface
Dawn: sink back into the dark, carrying carbon down

blocks.text: Life without the sun

Until 1977, biologists assumed that essentially all life on Earth ran on sunlight. Plants and algae catch it; everything else eats them or eats something that did. The deep sea was supposed to survive on scraps, a slow snowfall of dead material drifting down from above. Then geologists diving in the submersible *Alvin* on the Galápagos Rift, looking for hot springs on the seafloor, found them, and found them crowded with life: clams the size of dinner plates, crabs, and dense thickets of tube worms.

These communities were not living on sunlight. The vents gush mineral-rich water heated by magma below, loaded with chemicals like hydrogen sulfide that would poison most animals. Bacteria at the vents pull energy out of those chemicals, a process called chemosynthesis, and use it to build food from carbon dioxide. The giant tube worms have no mouth and no gut as adults; they house these bacteria inside their bodies and live off what the bacteria make. It is a whole ecosystem whose power plant is chemistry, not light.

Hydrothermal vents changed the question of where life can exist. If an ecosystem can run on chemical energy in total darkness, the icy oceans hidden under the crusts of moons like Europa and Enceladus stop looking so impossible.

Vents are not the only oases. When a whale dies and sinks to the abyssal floor, its body becomes an island of food in a desert. Scavengers like hagfish and sleeper sharks strip the soft tissue first. Then come crowds of smaller animals working through what is left, including bone-eating worms that bore into the skeleton. Finally, bacteria break down the fats locked inside the bones, releasing sulfide that feeds chemosynthetic communities much like those at vents. A single carcass can sustain this sequence for years.

Some researchers think life itself may have started at vents like these, where energy, minerals and chemical gradients come together. That idea is still debated. But the discovery forced a basic rewrite: sunlight is not the only way to run a living world, just the one we happen to live in.
The bottom of the bottom

The deepest places on Earth are trenches, where one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The zone below 6,000 meters is called hadal, after Hades. Life persists here too: amphipods, sea cucumbers, worms and, surprisingly, fish. In 2023 a team led by Alan Jamieson of the University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of a young snailfish swimming at 8,336 meters in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench south of Japan, the deepest fish ever filmed.

Jamieson's team had predicted that fish would top out somewhere between about 8,200 and 8,400 meters. The limit is chemical. Deep-sea fish pack their cells with a small molecule that helps proteins keep their shape under pressure, and the deeper they live, the more they need. Past a certain depth, the concentration required would draw too much water into their cells. Below that line, crustaceans and other invertebrates carry on, but fish seem to run out of room.

blocks.text: Who is normal here?

Step back and the picture flips. We tend to think of the deep sea as the strange edge of the living world, full of oddities. By volume, it is the opposite. Most of the habitable space on Earth is dark, cold and under enormous pressure. The sunlit surface where humans, forests and coral reefs live is the thin unusual layer on top. If an alien biologist sampled Earth at random, the typical animal it found would probably glow, live in darkness and never see the sun.

That matters now, because the deep sea is no longer out of reach. Companies want to mine metal-rich nodules from the abyssal plains, and fishing fleets have started eyeing the twilight zone's enormous fish stocks. We are making decisions about a place we have barely looked at. The 2025 study found that 97% of all deep dives it compiled were run by just five countries, so even our sense of what the deep sea is like comes from a few well-studied corners.

The ocean you patrol is not empty water with a floor somewhere below. It is layered, crowded and lit by animals, with a rush hour every dusk and dawn, and most of it has never been seen by a human eye. The most alien ecosystems humans will meet this century may not be on another planet. They may be a few miles straight down.

takeaways: Deep ocean covers about two-thirds of Earth's surface, and less than 0.001% of its floor has ever been seen directly.
Around three-quarters of the animals filmed in the water column off California can make their own light.
Every night, animals from the twilight zone swim up hundreds of meters to feed, the largest daily migration on Earth.
Hydrothermal vents proved whole ecosystems can run on chemical energy instead of sunlight.
By volume, dark, cold, high-pressure life is the norm on Earth; the sunlit surface is the exception.
