title: You Are Not 90 Percent Bacteria
dek: For forty years, biology repeated that microbes outnumber your cells ten to one. Nobody had measured it, and the real numbers tell a stranger story.

blocks.text: For about forty years, one of the most repeated facts in biology was that you are mostly not you. Textbooks, documentaries, TED talks and science magazines all said it the same way: bacteria in your body outnumber your own cells ten to one. Some versions went further and claimed a hundred to one. The line was perfect for a headline. It made you feel like a walking colony, a spaceship crewed by strangers.

Then, in 2016, three researchers at the Weizmann Institute in Israel, Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo, decided to check where the number came from. They traced the citations backward, paper by paper, and found that every source for the bacterial count led to a single back-of-the-envelope calculation from the 1970s. Nobody had ever measured it. The number had simply been copied until it felt true.

When they redid the math with modern data, the ratio collapsed from 10 to 1 down to roughly 1.3 to 1. You and your bacteria are close to an even split by count. And the story of how that happened is more useful than the factoid ever was, because it is a clean lesson in how a confident number can outlive the evidence behind it.
Anatomy of a napkin estimate

The original estimate was not stupid. It was a Fermi problem, the kind of quick order-of-magnitude reasoning physicists and engineers use every day. In 1972 the microbiologist Thomas Luckey took a typical concentration of bacteria in gut contents, about 100 billion per gram, and multiplied it by an assumed gut capacity of about one liter, or roughly a kilogram. That gives around 100 trillion bacteria, written as 10^14. Human cells were commonly put at around 10 trillion. Divide one by the other and you get ten to one.

blocks.title: How the 10-to-1 ratio was built
items: Assume about 100 billion bacteria per gram of gut contents
Assume the whole digestive tract holds about 1 liter (roughly 1 kg) of contents
Multiply: about 100 trillion bacteria
Compare with a rough guess of 10 trillion human cells
Get a 10:1 ratio, then cite it for decades without rechecking the inputs

blocks.text: Every step there is reasonable for a rough guess. The problem is what happened next. As Sender and colleagues showed, later papers that gave a reference for the bacterial count could all be traced back to that one calculation. The guess got cited, then the citations got cited, and the error bars fell off along the way. By the 2000s, a rough sketch had hardened into a fact that people repeated with total confidence.

If that sounds familiar, it should. Anyone who has learned a technical system the hard way knows the danger of a number that everyone uses and nobody can source. In a plant or a ship, a value you cannot trace back to a procedure or a measurement is a value you should not trust. Biology had the same problem, just with less immediate consequences.
Redoing the math

The Weizmann team's key move was to notice that almost all of your bacteria live in one place: the colon. Bacterial density in the stomach and the upper small intestine is tiny by comparison, around a thousand to ten thousand per milliliter, because of stomach acid and the fast flow of food. The mouth, the skin and the lower small intestine each hold a lot of microbes, but their totals are dwarfed by the large intestine. So the count comes down to two questions: how much material is in the colon, and how densely packed is it with bacteria?

Their table of upper bounds makes the point vividly. The colon holds on the order of 10^14 bacteria at most. The skin, for all the talk about it, tops out around 10^11, a thousand times fewer, and the stomach holds perhaps 10^7. Even dental plaque and saliva, which are dense with microbes, add up to less than 1 percent of what lives in the colon. So the rest of the body barely moves the total. When people picture bacteria coating every surface of them, the picture is not wrong, but the numbers are overwhelmingly in one organ.

For the first question, they used newer measurements, including MRI studies of colon volume. The answer for a standard 70-kilogram adult man was about 0.4 liters of contents, not a full liter. For the second, they compiled bacterial densities from 14 earlier studies of stool and converted them to a common basis, landing on about 90 billion bacteria per gram of wet stool. Multiply and you get roughly 38 trillion bacteria. That is still an enormous number. It is just not 100 trillion.

Then they turned to the other side of the ratio, which turned out to be just as interesting. Earlier estimates of human cells had swung wildly, and many were based on dividing body mass by an average cell size, which is a bit like estimating the number of vehicles in a city by dividing the total weight of traffic by the weight of an average car. Instead, they counted by cell type. Their total came to about 30 trillion human cells.

blocks.title: Bacteria vs human cells in a 70 kg man
blocks.note: The old claim was an order-of-magnitude guess (10^14); the revised figures carry roughly 25% uncertainty.
blocks.source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology, 2016

blocks.text: The result: about 38 trillion bacterial cells to 30 trillion human ones, a ratio of about 1.3. The authors were careful to say this comes with an uncertainty of around 25 percent and varies by about 50 percent between individuals. They also pointed out a funny consequence of the colon being the main reservoir. A single bowel movement reduces the colon's contents by a quarter to a third. On a ratio this close to even, a trip to the head can shift the balance noticeably.
You are mostly blood

The most surprising part of the paper was not about bacteria at all. It was about what your own 30 trillion cells actually are. Red blood cells, tiny discs about 100 cubic micrometers in volume, make up about 84 percent of all your human cells by count. Add in platelets and other blood-forming lineages and the blood system accounts for roughly 90 percent of the total.

items.label: Share of your human cells that are red blood cells
Total mass of bacteria in the body, mostly in the colon
Revised ratio of bacterial to human cells

blocks.source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology, 2016

blocks.text: By mass, the picture flips completely. About three quarters of your cellular mass is fat cells and muscle cells, which are huge but relatively few. Meanwhile, all the bacteria in your body weigh about 0.2 kilograms, less than half a pound. So the bacteria outnumber you slightly, but you outweigh them by a factor of hundreds.

Here is the twist that makes the whole debate slippery. Mature red blood cells and platelets have no nucleus, which means they carry no DNA. By the paper's numbers, you have only about 3 trillion nucleated human cells. If you decide that a cell only really counts as you when it carries your genome, then the bacteria outnumber you more than ten to one after all. The old ratio comes back, for a completely different reason than the one people gave.

The question "are you mostly bacteria?" has no single answer. By count it is roughly even, by mass you win by hundreds to one, and by DNA-carrying cells the bacteria win by more than ten to one. The answer depends on what you decide to count.

A later study pushed the human count up a bit. In 2023, Ian Hatton and colleagues compiled data from more than 1,500 sources and estimated about 36 trillion cells in a reference 70-kilogram man, about 28 trillion in a 60-kilogram woman and about 17 trillion in a 10-year-old child. Different methods, similar ballpark. That is what healthy science looks like: estimates converging with stated uncertainties, instead of one unexamined number repeated forever.
Counting genes instead of cells

If you want a measure where the microbes truly dominate, stop counting cells and count genes. In 2010, the MetaHIT consortium sequenced fecal samples from 124 Europeans and cataloged about 3.3 million distinct microbial genes, roughly 150 times the number of genes in the human genome. Over 99 percent of them were bacterial. Each person carried at least 160 prevalent bacterial species, and the group as a whole carried roughly a thousand.

That is the more meaningful way to think about the microbiome. Your bacteria are not a crowd of extra bodies so much as an extra toolkit. Their genes code for enzymes you lack, letting them break down fibers you cannot digest, produce certain vitamins and short-chain fatty acids, transform bile acids and drugs, and occupy space that would otherwise be open to pathogens. Your genome is fixed at birth. Their combined genome is large, diverse and changes with what you eat, what medicines you take and where you live.

It is also worth being honest about what is not known. The microbiome is one of the most hyped areas in modern biology. Many headline findings come from mice raised in sterile conditions, or from studies that show correlation in humans without showing which way cause and effect run. A difference in gut bacteria between sick and healthy people can be a result of the illness, the diet that goes with it or the medications used to treat it, rather than the cause.
Where the evidence is strong

There is at least one case where manipulating the microbiome has worked dramatically in a randomized trial. Clostridioides difficile, usually called C. diff, is a gut infection that tends to take hold after antibiotics have wiped out a person's normal bacteria, and it often comes back after treatment. In a 2013 Dutch trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine, patients with recurrent C. diff were given either standard antibiotics or an infusion of stool from a healthy donor, a procedure called fecal microbiota transplantation.

blocks.title: Cure of recurrent C. diff without relapse at 10 weeks
blocks.note: Donor-stool figure is after the first infusion; groups had only 13 to 16 patients each.
blocks.source: van Nood et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2013

blocks.text: Thirteen of 16 patients in the infusion group were cured after a single infusion, compared with 4 of 13 on the antibiotic vancomycin alone. The difference was so large that the trial was stopped early. Afterward, the patients' gut bacteria became more diverse and looked more like the donors'. It was a small trial, and stopping early can exaggerate effects, but the result has broadly held up and transplantation is now an established option for recurrent C. diff.

The lesson there is narrower than the hype suggests. A badly disrupted gut ecosystem, knocked over by antibiotics and taken over by one pathogen, can be restored by reseeding it. That is very different from claiming a probiotic capsule will fix your mood, your weight or your focus. For most of those claims, the human evidence is thin, mixed or absent.

blocks.title: What the microbiome evidence supports

left.head: Well supported
items: Bacteria and human cells are roughly equal in number
Microbes carry far more genes than you do
Antibiotics can disrupt the gut community
Donor stool can cure recurrent C. diff

right.head: Still uncertain
items: Specific bacteria causing obesity in humans
Probiotic pills improving mood or focus
A single ideal healthy microbiome
Most claims tested only in mice

blocks.text: What the revised number really teaches

The microbiome did not get less important when the ratio fell from ten to one to roughly one to one. Thirty-eight trillion organisms with millions of genes, living in your gut and shaping what you absorb, is plenty remarkable without exaggeration. What changed is how much you should trust a fact just because everyone repeats it.

That is the real reframe. Ask where a number comes from. Ask what was actually measured and what was assumed. A good estimate is a tool for thinking, not a fact to memorize, and it should be revisited when better data shows up. Sender, Fuchs and Milo did not run a single new experiment on a human body. They did something more basic: they went back to the sources, checked the inputs and recalculated. That kind of skepticism is free, and it is available to anyone willing to pull the thread.

So, are you mostly bacteria? By count, it is close to a tie, and the lead changes hands depending on when you last used the head. By weight, you are overwhelmingly human. By genes, the microbes win by a landslide. The best answer is that you are a partnership, and the old line was never really about biology at all. It was about how easily a good story beats a good measurement.

takeaways: Bacteria and human cells are roughly even by count, about 38 trillion to 30 trillion, not 10 to 1.
About 84 percent of your human cells are red blood cells; by DNA-carrying cells, bacteria still win by more than 10 to 1.
Your microbes carry about 150 times more genes than you do, which is why they matter.
Fecal transplants for recurrent C. diff have strong evidence; most probiotic promises do not.
Before you repeat a number, ask what was actually measured and what was assumed.

title: Sending Your Cells the Recipe
dek: mRNA vaccines looked like an overnight miracle in 2020. They were actually thirty years of failure, one stubborn scientist and a fix to a single chemical letter. Now the same trick is being aimed at cancer.

blocks.text: On March 16, 2020, a volunteer in Seattle rolled up a sleeve for an experimental vaccine against a virus the world had first heard of less than three months earlier. Most vaccines take a decade or more to reach that point. This one had gone from a genetic sequence posted online to a needle in an arm faster than it takes to get through some Navy schools.

Nine months later, two vaccines built on the same technology were being given to the public, and their trials showed about 95 percent protection against symptomatic disease. To many people it looked rushed, even suspicious. How do you build a working vaccine in months when it normally takes years?

The real answer is that you don't. The speed in 2020 was the payoff of three decades of slow, unglamorous work, much of it by researchers who could barely get funding. Understanding that story explains both why mRNA vaccines work and why the same platform is now being pointed at cancer.
The messenger in every cell

Your DNA is the master blueprint, and it stays locked in the nucleus of each cell like the original drawings kept in a vault. When a cell needs to build a protein, it makes a temporary working copy of one gene. That copy is messenger RNA, or mRNA. It travels out of the nucleus to a ribosome, the cell's assembly machine, which reads the mRNA three letters at a time and strings together the matching amino acids into a protein.

Then the mRNA is destroyed. Cells chew it up within hours to days, on purpose. That short lifespan is how a cell controls production: stop making the message and the protein stops being built. Think of it as a work order that self-destructs after use rather than a permanent change to the plans.

The idea behind an mRNA vaccine follows directly. Instead of injecting a weakened virus or a purified piece of one, you inject the work order for one viral protein. Your own cells read it, build that protein, and display it. Your immune system sees a protein that does not belong, learns to recognize it, and stays ready for the real virus.

blocks.title: What happens after the shot
items: mRNA for the virus's spike protein is wrapped in tiny fat bubbles called lipid nanoparticles.
The bubbles fuse with cells near the injection site and release the mRNA inside.
Ribosomes read the message and build copies of the spike protein.
Immune cells spot the foreign protein and make antibodies and trained T cells against it.
The mRNA breaks down within days; the immune memory stays.

blocks.text: One common fear is that this changes your DNA. It doesn't. The mRNA never enters the nucleus where DNA is kept, and human cells have no normal way to write RNA back into their own genome. The message is read in the outer part of the cell, used and destroyed, which is exactly what your cells do with their own mRNA all day long.

The elegance of the approach is that the body does the manufacturing. A traditional protein vaccine needs a factory to grow and purify the protein. An mRNA vaccine ships the instructions and lets millions of your own cells act as temporary factories, which is part of why it can be designed and produced so quickly.
Thirty years of the immune system saying no

Scientists knew the basic idea could work by 1990, when a team injected mRNA into mouse muscle and the muscle made the protein it coded for. So why did it take so long? Because the body hated it. Lab-made mRNA set off alarms in the immune system, triggering inflammation and getting destroyed before it could do much. Animals got sick, and protein production was weak.

Katalin Karikó, a Hungarian-born biochemist at the University of Pennsylvania, spent years trying to make mRNA useful as medicine while grant after grant was rejected. She was demoted and pushed toward the edges of academia. Her break came from a chance meeting at a photocopier with Drew Weissman, an immunologist who wanted to build vaccines. Together they asked a precise question: why does our own mRNA not set off the alarm while lab-made mRNA does?

The answer was chemistry. RNA is written in four letters, A, U, G and C, but mammalian cells routinely attach small chemical tweaks to some of those letters. Lab-made mRNA had none. The immune system treated unmodified RNA as a sign of invasion, since that is what viral RNA often looks like. In 2005 Karikó and Weissman showed that swapping in modified versions of one letter, uridine, nearly abolished the inflammatory reaction. Later work showed the modified mRNA also made far more protein.
The key fix was tiny: change one of the four letters slightly so the cell's alarm system reads the message as friendly. That single tweak turned a promising idea into a workable platform.

The other missing piece was packaging. Naked mRNA is fragile and cannot easily get into cells. Researchers working on gene-silencing drugs spent years developing lipid nanoparticles, microscopic fat spheres that protect the cargo and slip it inside cells. By the late 2010s, companies like Moderna and BioNTech had both pieces and were testing mRNA vaccines against flu, Zika and cancer. None had reached the market. Then 2020 happened.

blocks.text: Why it was so fast, and what the trials showed

There was a price for using such a fragile molecule. mRNA falls apart easily, and the first Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine had to be shipped and stored at ultra-cold temperatures, far below an ordinary freezer, which meant special freezers, dry ice and careful logistics. That is one reason the technology was harder to roll out in places without reliable cold chains, and why later work has focused on more stable formulas.

With a traditional vaccine, every new virus means a new manufacturing process: growing the virus in eggs or cells, inactivating it, purifying proteins. With mRNA, the factory stays the same. Only the sequence changes. Once Chinese scientists published the virus's genetic code in January 2020, researchers could design the vaccine on a computer, mostly by picking the right protein to encode. It is closer to swapping one file in a working program than building a new machine.

The fast part was design and the first trials. The slower part, large trials to prove the vaccine works and is safe, still had to happen, and it did, with tens of thousands of volunteers. The trick was running steps in parallel that normally run in sequence, with governments paying to manufacture doses before anyone knew if they would work.

blocks.title: Symptomatic COVID-19 cases in the two big mRNA trials
blocks.note: Pfizer trial had about 43,400 volunteers; Moderna about 30,400. Efficacy was 95% and 94.1%.
blocks.source: Polack et al., NEJM, 2020; Baden et al., NEJM, 2021

blocks.text: The Pfizer-BioNTech trial enrolled about 43,000 people split evenly between vaccine and placebo. Of the 170 people who caught symptomatic COVID-19 during the study window, 162 had gotten the placebo and 8 the vaccine, an efficacy of 95 percent. Moderna's trial of about 30,000 people found 185 cases on placebo against 11 on vaccine, or 94.1 percent. In Moderna's trial, all 30 severe cases were in the placebo group.

Those numbers deserve honest context. They measured protection against symptomatic illness from the original strain, a few months after vaccination. Protection against infection faded over the following months and dropped further as the virus evolved, which is why boosters and updated versions followed. Protection against severe illness held up better. Side effects were real but mostly short: sore arms, fatigue, fever for a day or two. A rare one matters for readers in their twenties: heart inflammation called myocarditis, seen most often in young men after the second dose and usually mild. If you have questions about your own shots, the corpsman or medical officer is the right person to ask.
The next target: your own tumor

Before COVID, cancer was the main thing mRNA companies were working on, and it is where they have returned. The logic is elegant. Cancer cells carry mutations, and some of those mutations produce slightly abnormal proteins called neoantigens that exist nowhere else in your body. If the immune system could be trained to recognize them, it could hunt down cancer cells while ignoring healthy ones.

The problem is that every patient's tumor has a different set of mutations. So the vaccine has to be custom. Doctors sequence a patient's tumor and their normal cells, software picks out the mutations most likely to provoke an immune response, and an mRNA vaccine encoding them is manufactured for that one person. This only makes sense with a platform where changing the sequence is easy. mRNA is that platform.

blocks.title: Melanoma patients free of recurrence at 18 months
blocks.note: 157 patients with high-risk melanoma removed by surgery; a phase 2 trial.
blocks.source: Weber et al., KEYNOTE-942, AACR 2023

blocks.text: The most advanced example is a personalized vaccine from Moderna and Merck. In a phase 2 trial of 157 people whose high-risk melanoma had been surgically removed, patients got either the immunotherapy drug Keytruda alone or Keytruda plus a custom mRNA vaccine encoding up to 34 of their own tumor's neoantigens. After 18 months, 78.6 percent of the combination group were free of recurrence, against 62.2 percent with Keytruda alone, a 44 percent lower risk of the cancer returning or death.

That is promising, not proven. A phase 2 trial is small, and many cancer treatments that shine at this stage disappoint in larger trials. A bigger phase 3 study was launched to test the result properly. Researchers are also testing personalized mRNA vaccines against pancreatic cancer and other tumors, and mRNA versions of flu vaccines, where the ability to update the sequence quickly every season could be a real advantage.

The platform also has limits worth stating plainly. A shot in the arm trains immunity in the blood well but does a weaker job guarding the nose and throat, where respiratory viruses first get in, which is part of why vaccinated people could still catch and spread COVID-19. Side effects like fever are more common than with some older vaccines. And mRNA is not magic for every disease: if scientists do not know which protein to target, a faster factory does not help. Newer variants of the idea, such as self-amplifying RNA that copies itself inside the cell so a smaller dose goes further, are already in use in Japan, which approved one in late 2023.

There is also a political dimension now. The speed of 2020 left some people distrustful, and public funding for mRNA research has swung with that mood. Whatever your view, the science question and the policy question are different. The trial data above are public, large and published, and they are the place to start rather than anyone's headline.
What this story is really about

When Karikó and Weissman won the Nobel Prize in 2023, the committee pointed specifically to their 2005 finding about modified letters, published fifteen years before the pandemic. For most of those fifteen years, almost nobody cared. The paper did not make headlines. The work only looked obvious in hindsight, after it saved enormous numbers of lives.

There is a lesson there about how progress actually happens. The visible breakthrough in 2020 sat on top of decades of work that looked like failure from the outside: rejected grants, a demotion, mice that got sick, a packaging problem nobody had solved. Platforms take a long time to build and then suddenly pay off all at once, because every new use reuses the same foundation.

That pattern shows up far outside biology. A game engine, a content channel, a skill like reading reactor plant drawings: the first year looks slow and unrewarding. Then one day the foundation is in place and new things come together fast. From outside, it looks like overnight success. From inside, it was years of fixing one letter at a time.
Platforms are slow to build and fast to use. The question to ask about any long project is not how much it has produced yet, but whether it is turning into something you can reuse.

takeaways: mRNA is a temporary work order: cells read it, build a protein and destroy it within days. It never enters the nucleus or changes DNA.
The breakthrough that made it work was a small chemical change to one RNA letter, published in 2005 and largely ignored for years.
The 2020 vaccines were fast because the platform already existed; only the sequence had to change.
Trials showed about 95% protection against symptomatic COVID-19 at first, which faded against infection over time but held better against severe illness.
Personalized mRNA cancer vaccines showed a promising result in melanoma, but larger trials still have to confirm it.

title: The Brain That Grew a Map of London
dek: Learning is not just storing information. It physically rebuilds the organ doing the learning, and the same process that makes you skilled can also lock in the habits you wish you did not have.

blocks.text: To drive a black cab in London, you have to pass a test called the Knowledge. It requires memorizing roughly 25,000 streets within six miles of Charing Cross station, plus thousands of landmarks, and being able to recite the best route between any two points on demand, out loud, to an examiner. Trainees ride around the city on scooters for years. It typically takes three to four years, and many never make it.

Neuroscientists Katherine Woollett and Eleanor Maguire saw an experiment hiding in that ordeal. They recruited 79 trainee cabbies at the start of their training, plus 31 people who were not training, and scanned all of their brains. Years later they scanned them again. Only 39 of the trainees had qualified and came back for the second scan, and 20 more who had failed also returned.

In the trainees who passed, a specific part of the brain, the back of the hippocampus, had gained gray matter. In those who failed, and in the controls, it had not changed. Before training, all three groups had looked the same. The difference appeared only after years of hard spatial learning, and only in the people who did the learning successfully. Memorizing a city had physically reshaped their brains.

The design matters. Years earlier, Maguire's group had found that experienced London cabbies had larger posterior hippocampi than other people, and that the effect grew with years on the job. But that kind of snapshot cannot rule out the reverse explanation: maybe people born with a bigger hippocampus are drawn to the job and better at passing the test. Scanning the same people before and after, and comparing those who passed with those who failed, is what made the case that the learning caused the change.

items.label: London streets trainee cabbies must learn
Trainees scanned at the start vs those who qualified and were rescanned
Typical time to pass the Knowledge

blocks.source: Woollett and Maguire, Current Biology, 2011

blocks.text: What actually changes when you learn

Your brain has tens of billions of neurons, each connected to thousands of others through junctions called synapses. A thought, a memory or a skill is not stored in one cell. It lives in a pattern of connections, a particular set of neurons that tend to fire together. Learning means changing that pattern, and the brain can change it in several physical ways.

The most basic is strengthening synapses. In 1949 the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed that when one neuron repeatedly helps make another fire, the link between them gets stronger. It is often summarized as cells that fire together wire together. In 1973 researchers found the cellular version of this in the hippocampus of rabbits: a burst of activity made a synapse respond more strongly for hours afterward. It is called long-term potentiation, and it is still one of the main models of how memories form.

blocks.title: How practice rewires a circuit
items: You attempt a skill, and a specific chain of neurons fires together.
Repeated firing strengthens the synapses along that chain, so the signal passes more easily.
Neurons grow new connection points and prune ones that go unused.
Heavily used pathways get extra insulation called myelin, which speeds up signals.
Over time the skill runs with less effort and less conscious attention.

blocks.text: Beyond stronger synapses, neurons can sprout new connection points and lose old ones. Support cells wrap well-used nerve fibers in more myelin, a fatty insulation that makes signals travel faster and more reliably, a bit like upgrading from bare wire to shielded cable. Blood supply to busy regions can increase. Add all of that up across millions of cells, and the change can become large enough to show up on an MRI scan as more gray matter.

Losing connections is as important as gaining them. A young child's brain makes far more synapses than it will keep, and through childhood and the teenage years it prunes the ones that go unused, the way a sculptor removes stone. Expertise often looks less like adding more wiring everywhere and more like a cleaner, more efficient circuit with the useless branches cut away.
Practice does not just make a skill feel easier. It builds faster, better-insulated wiring for that skill. That is why something that once took all your concentration eventually runs on autopilot.
Use it, or the brain takes it back

The London cabbies are an extreme case, but smaller versions show up wherever scientists look. In 1995, a team scanned the brains of violin, cello and guitar players. The area of the touch-sensing cortex devoted to the fingers of the left hand, the hand that presses the strings, was larger than in non-musicians. The right hand, which bows or strums, showed no such difference. And the earlier a musician had started playing, the bigger the change.

In 2004, German researchers taught a small group of young adults to juggle three balls. Brain scans after they had mastered it showed growth in gray matter in regions that track moving objects. Then the jugglers stopped practicing for three months. On the next scan, the gain had shrunk, and many of them could no longer do the routine. The brain had built the hardware when it was needed and started dismantling it when it was not.

This is the part of neuroplasticity that is easy to miss. The brain is not a hard drive filling up with files. It is more like a city that keeps reallocating land. Brain tissue is expensive to run, burning a large share of your body's energy, and it does not keep unused circuits at full strength forever. Skills you practice get more space. Skills you abandon slowly lose it.

The taxi study found a trade-off too. Qualified cabbies were better than controls at judging distances between London landmarks, but worse at recalling a complex drawing after a 30-minute delay. The researchers were careful about what this means, and it is one result, not a law. But it hints that brain resources are not unlimited, and getting much better at one kind of thing may come with costs somewhere else.
Windows that close, and ones that do not

In the 1960s, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel ran experiments that won them a Nobel Prize and showed the darker side of plasticity. They found that if a kitten had one eye kept closed during a critical window early in life, the visual part of its brain rewired to favor the open eye. Open the closed eye later, and it never fully recovered, even though the eye itself was healthy. The same closure in an adult cat had little lasting effect.

Human brains also have critical periods, windows when certain circuits are especially easy to shape. It is why children who learn a language young usually speak it without an accent, while adults rarely manage that. For a long time, scientists took this to mean the adult brain was basically fixed, a finished building with no more construction allowed.

That view was wrong. The taxi drivers were adults. So were the jugglers. Adult brains are less plastic than children's in some ways, but they keep changing for life. The difference is that adult change seems to depend more on attention, effort and repetition. A child soaks up a language passively; an adult has to work at it. That is less a closed door than a door that now needs a push.

Medicine has put this to work. After a stroke damages the part of the brain controlling one arm, patients naturally lean on the good arm, and the weak one gets weaker. Constraint-induced movement therapy, developed by psychologist Edward Taub, who was also part of the string-player study, flips that. The good arm is restrained for much of the day, forcing hours of practice with the weak one. In many patients, other parts of the brain take over some of the lost control. The brain reorganizes, but only because it is pushed to.

blocks.text: Do adults grow new brain cells? The honest answer

One of the most exciting claims in pop neuroscience is that adults keep making new neurons in the hippocampus, and that exercise, learning or antidepressants can boost this. Strong evidence exists in mice and rats. In humans, it has become one of the field's genuine fights.

In March 2018, a team at the University of California San Francisco led by Shawn Sorrells and Arturo Alvarez-Buylla examined 59 human hippocampus samples from before birth to old age. Newborn brains had plenty of young neurons. The numbers fell steeply through childhood, and by early adolescence they were rare. In adults, the team found none. Their conclusion was that if adult neurogenesis happens in humans, it is extremely rare.

blocks.title: Young neurons in the human hippocampus by age
blocks.note: Adult value means none were detected in these samples; another lab reported the opposite.
blocks.source: Sorrells et al., Nature, 2018 (UCSF)

blocks.text: One month later, a team at Columbia University led by Maura Boldrini published the opposite result. They studied 28 people aged 14 to 79 who had died suddenly and had been healthy, and found thousands of new neurons even in the oldest brains. Older people did have fewer blood vessels forming and a smaller pool of the cells that give rise to neurons, but their production of new neurons was similar to younger people's.

blocks.title: Two labs, same question, opposite answers

left.head: Sorrells et al., 2018
items: 59 samples, prenatal to adult
Young neurons drop sharply in childhood
None found in adults
Adult neurogenesis, if any, is very rare

right.head: Boldrini et al., 2018
items: 28 healthy people, ages 14 to 79
Thousands of new neurons at every age
Fewer blood vessels and progenitors in old age
Neurogenesis persists through aging

blocks.text: Why the disagreement? Studying this in humans means working with brain tissue after death, and how quickly tissue is preserved, how it is treated and which markers are used to identify a young neuron can all change the result. The debate is not settled. The safe takeaway is that whether or not adults grow new neurons, the bulk of learning-related change happens through connections, not new cells. Your brain does not need new neurons to learn. It needs to rewire the ones it has.
Plasticity cuts both ways

The word neuroplasticity has become a marketing term, attached to apps, supplements and courses promising to rewire your brain. Be skeptical. A large 2016 review of brain-training research led by psychologist Daniel Simons found that people do get better at the specific games they practice, but there was little good evidence that the improvement spreads to everyday thinking, memory or intelligence. The brain gets better at what you actually do, and not much else.

That same principle has a darker edge. Plasticity does not care whether a habit is good for you. Whatever you repeat often, with strong reward attached, gets reinforced. Hours of short, fast, unpredictable videos train a brain to expect novelty every few seconds. Chronic pain can sensitize the nervous system so it produces pain more easily. Anxiety rehearsed every night gets better at showing up. The machinery that builds skill is the same machinery that builds ruts.

items: Plasticity is specific: you get better at the exact thing you practice, not at everything.
It is driven by repetition with attention: going through the motions builds less than focused effort.
It needs consolidation: much of the rewiring is cemented during sleep.
It is two-way: unused skills fade and repeated habits, good or bad, get stronger.

blocks.text: What this means for anything you want to get good at

If you made it through nuclear power school, you have already lived through a version of the taxi study. Months of dense material, memorized and re-memorized until diagrams and equations you could not parse at first became something you could reason with. Somewhere in your brain, the wiring for that is physically different than it was before you started.

The same rules apply to aim in a shooter, writing code for a game or speaking clearly in front of people. Your brain will build what you repeatedly ask it to do, at the level of difficulty you actually practice at. Easy reps build little. Reps right at the edge of your ability, with attention on what is going wrong, build the most. Stop practicing, and the brain will start reallocating the space.

The most useful reframe from this science is simple. Every day, whether you mean to or not, you are training your brain for something. The question is never whether it will change. It is what you are teaching it to become.
Your brain is shaped by demand. Whatever you do most, with the most attention and repetition, is what it builds the best hardware for. Choose those hours on purpose.

takeaways: Learning physically changes the brain: stronger synapses, new connections, more myelin and sometimes measurable gray matter growth.
London cabbies who passed the Knowledge grew gray matter in the back of the hippocampus; those who failed did not.
Use it or lose it: jugglers' brain gains shrank within months of stopping practice.
Whether adults grow new neurons is genuinely disputed; most learning works by rewiring existing cells.
Brain-training games mostly improve the games themselves. Plasticity is specific, and it builds bad habits as readily as good ones.

title: The Alien in the Tide Pool
dek: An octopus keeps most of its neurons in its arms, sees color while being colorblind and may even dream. It is the closest thing to an alien mind we can study, and it shows how many ways there are to be smart.

blocks.text: In 2001, a team of neuroscientists in Jerusalem did something that sounds like a horror movie. They took octopus arms whose connection to the brain had been cut, stimulated them, and watched what happened. The arms reached out in smooth, purposeful extensions, with movement patterns almost identical to those of a normal octopus reaching for food. The study, published in Science by German Sumbre, Binyamin Hochner and colleagues, concluded that the basic motor program for reaching is stored in the arm itself.

Think about what that means. If your arm were cut off, it would not reach for anything. Your arm is a tool run by your brain. An octopus arm is closer to a crew member that knows its job and needs only a general order. The more scientists study octopuses, the more they find that this is not a quirk. It is a whole different design for a mind, one that evolved separately from ours and arrived at intelligence by another road.

Nothing on Earth is truly alien, but octopuses are as close as we are likely to get before we meet something from another planet. Understanding how they work is a good way to stop assuming that our kind of mind is the only kind possible.
A mind that evolved twice

Your last common ancestor with an octopus lived somewhere around 600 million years ago, according to the philosopher of science Peter Godfrey-Smith in his book Other Minds. It was probably a small, simple, wormlike creature with a few neurons at most. From there, one branch eventually produced fish, mammals and us. Another produced snails, clams and, eventually, the cephalopods: octopuses, squid and cuttlefish.

That means that whatever intelligence octopuses have, they did not inherit it from any smart ancestor we share. Large brains, flexible problem solving, play-like behavior and sophisticated learning evolved at least twice on this planet, completely independently. Evolutionary biologists call this convergence, like eyes or wings evolving separately in different groups. It suggests that minds are not a one-off accident of the vertebrate line. Given the right pressures, nature can build them more than once.

Octopuses are also notably good at using whatever is around them. In 2009, Julian Finn and colleagues described veined octopuses in Indonesia that collect discarded coconut shell halves, carry them awkwardly across the seafloor stacked under their bodies, and later assemble them into a shelter. Carrying an object now for use later, at a cost to moving efficiently, is one of the stricter definitions of tool use. It was widely reported as one of the clearest examples of tool use ever seen in an animal without a backbone.
Where the neurons are

A common octopus has roughly 500 million neurons. That is far fewer than a human's 86 billion, but in the same general range as many mammals, and far beyond almost any other invertebrate. The surprise is where those neurons sit. Based on classic work by the anatomist J.Z. Young in 1963, about 330 million of them, roughly two-thirds, are outside the central brain, mostly in the arms.

items.label: Neurons in an octopus nervous system
Of those, outside the central brain, mostly in the arms
Neurons in an adult human brain, for comparison

blocks.source: Gendreau et al., Biology Open, 2025 (citing Young, 1963); Azevedo et al., J Comp Neurol, 2009

blocks.text: Each arm has its own thick nerve cord running down its length, with clusters of neurons at every sucker. Those suckers do more than grip. A 2020 study in Cell by Lena van Giesen, Nicholas Bellono and colleagues identified a family of chemotactile receptors in octopus suckers that detect chemicals on contact, essentially letting the arms taste what they touch. The authors concluded that the spread-out nervous system in the arms is a key site of information processing, not just a set of wires carrying signals up to headquarters.

Why build a body like this? Because an octopus arm has no joints and no bones. It can bend anywhere, twist, lengthen and shorten. A human arm has a handful of joints to control. An octopus arm has, in the words of Hochner's 2012 review, a virtually infinite number of degrees of freedom. Planning every movement from the center would be an enormous computing problem. So evolution pushed much of the work down to the arms, where local circuits handle the details.

blocks.title: Two designs for a smart animal

left.head: Vertebrate (you)
items: Most processing in a central brain
Rigid skeleton with a few joints to control
Brain keeps a detailed map of body position
Limbs mostly follow central orders
Long life, long childhood, learns from parents

right.head: Octopus
items: About two-thirds of neurons in the arms
Boneless arms that can bend anywhere
No clear body map in the higher motor centers
Arms run local reflexes and taste what they touch
Short life, no parenting, learns alone

blocks.text: You may have heard that octopuses have nine brains. That is a catchy simplification. There is one central brain, wrapped around the esophagus, plus large optic lobes behind the eyes, plus a nerve cord and chains of ganglia in each arm. The arm systems are not independent brains with their own goals. They are better described as powerful local controllers that can run complex routines, such as reaching, grasping, tasting and passing food toward the mouth, with only general direction from the center. The real point is not the count. It is that the line between brain and body, so sharp in us, is blurry in an octopus.

The trade-off is coordination. For years researchers found octopuses surprisingly bad at tasks requiring them to guide a single arm to a specific spot using vision. In 2011, Tamar Gutnick and colleagues finally showed they can do it: in a maze task, octopuses learned to steer one arm to a visually marked goal. But the process seems to involve the central brain checking in on the arm by sight rather than simply knowing where it is. The brain sets goals; the arms improvise. It is less like a puppet master and more like a commander who issues intent and trusts the people on the deck plates to execute.
Colorblind masters of camouflage

Octopuses are famous for changing color and texture in a fraction of a second, matching rocks, sand and coral so well that divers swim right past them. Here is the puzzle: most octopuses appear to have only one type of light-detecting cell in their eyes. By the usual rules of vision, they should be colorblind. How can an animal that cannot see color match colors so well?

Nobody fully knows. One hypothesis, proposed in 2016 by the father-and-son team Alexander and Christopher Stubbs in PNAS, is that octopuses exploit chromatic aberration. Different wavelengths of light come into focus at slightly different distances behind a lens, and the odd U-shaped and dumbbell-shaped pupils of cephalopods could exaggerate this effect. By shifting focus, an octopus might infer color from blur. It is a clever idea backed by computer modeling, but it has not been confirmed in living animals, and some researchers are skeptical.

Another clue comes from the skin itself. In 2015, Desmond Ramirez and Todd Oakley showed that patches of skin cut from a California two-spot octopus still responded to light by expanding their pigment cells, with no eye involved. The skin contains the same light-sensitive opsin proteins found in octopus eyes, most sensitive to blue light. Whether that helps with camouflage is still open. But it raises a strange possibility: part of what the octopus knows about its surroundings may be sensed directly by its skin.
A genome that edits itself

When the first octopus genome was published in Nature in 2015 by Caroline Albertin, Clifton Ragsdale, Daniel Rokhsar and colleagues, it turned up surprises. Two gene families were massively expanded: protocadherins, which help wire up neurons, and a large group of zinc-finger transcription factors that switch other genes on and off. Both were previously thought to be unusually large only in vertebrates. Again, convergence: two separate lineages building complex nervous systems reached for similar molecular tools.

Octopuses and their relatives also do something unusual with RNA, the working copies of genes that cells use to build proteins. A 2017 study in Cell by Noa Liscovitch-Brauer, Eli Eisenberg, Joshua Rosenthal and colleagues found that coleoid cephalopods edit their RNA at tens of thousands of conserved sites, especially in genes for the nervous system. That lets them tweak proteins on the fly without changing the DNA. The cost: to keep all those editing sites working, the surrounding DNA has to stay nearly frozen, so their genomes evolve unusually slowly in those regions. They traded genetic flexibility over generations for chemical flexibility within a lifetime.
Do octopuses dream?

Octopuses sleep, and their sleep has structure. In 2021, Sylvia Medeiros, Sidarta Ribeiro and colleagues in Brazil video-recorded Octopus insularis and found two distinct states. In quiet sleep, the animal went pale and still. Then, periodically, it entered a short active sleep state with rippling color and texture changes, eye movements and twitches, while staying unresponsive to stimulation. Active sleep recurred on a fairly regular cycle and mostly followed quiet sleep.

blocks.title: Two kinds of octopus sleep (median episode length)
blocks.note: Active sleep, with color flashes and eye movements, came mostly after quiet sleep and often recurred every 26 to 39 minutes. Based on only four animals.
blocks.source: Medeiros et al., iScience, 2021

blocks.text: The authors suggested this resembles the cycle between deep sleep and REM sleep in mammals and birds, the stage most associated with vivid dreams in humans. It is tempting to imagine an octopus replaying the day's hunt in flickering skin patterns. But the study was small, just four animals, and no one can ask an octopus what it experiences. What the data show is an ultradian cycle with intriguing parallels. Whether there is anything it is like to be in that state remains unknown.
Brilliant, solitary and brief

Here is the deepest puzzle. In mammals and birds, big brains usually go with long lives, social groups and long childhoods in which the young learn from older animals. Octopuses break all three rules. Most species are solitary. Many live only a year or two. Females typically guard their eggs without eating until they die; a 2018 study by Z. Yan Wang and Clifton Ragsdale traced this decline to dramatic hormonal changes in the optic gland, roughly the octopus equivalent of the pituitary. No parent teaches an octopus anything. Each one figures out the world from scratch, then dies.

Godfrey-Smith's suggestion is that octopus intelligence was driven less by social life and more by the body. Losing the protective shell their ancestors carried made them vulnerable but gave them an endlessly flexible form. Controlling that body, and surviving as soft prey in a world of fish with teeth, rewarded fast learning and improvisation. A mind built for handling a body and a complicated environment, rather than for handling other minds, may look very different from ours.

That has practical consequences. In 2022, the United Kingdom passed the Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act, which explicitly includes cephalopod mollusks, along with decapod crustaceans such as crabs and lobsters, in its definition of animals whose welfare government policy must consider. The decision followed a government-commissioned review of evidence on whether these animals can feel pain and other experiences.

This raises a question philosophers love. When an octopus arm tastes a crab hidden in a crevice and starts pulling it out before the central brain has weighed in, does the octopus experience that taste? Or does the arm know something the animal as a whole never feels? For humans, almost everything we sense ends up in one stream of awareness. For an octopus, there may be some experiences that stay local. We do not have the tools to answer this yet, but simply being able to ask it shows how much our ideas about minds are shaped by our own body plan.

The octopus is a reminder that intelligence is not a single ladder with humans at the top. It is a set of solutions to particular problems, and a very different body and life can produce a very different solution.

There is a lesson here for anyone who runs a team, a ship or a project. The octopus does not micromanage eight arms. It sets the goal, lets local systems with their own sensors handle the details, and checks in when something needs correcting. Whether that kind of distributed mind has a single point of view, or something more like a committee, is one of the open questions in the science of consciousness. Either way, the creature hiding in the tide pool is running an experiment in being smart that started 600 million years before we showed up.

takeaways: Octopus intelligence evolved independently of ours; our last common ancestor was a simple wormlike animal hundreds of millions of years ago.
Roughly two-thirds of an octopus's ~500 million neurons sit outside the central brain, and severed arms can still perform reaching movements.
Octopuses appear to be colorblind yet match colors expertly; how they do it is still unresolved, with chromatic aberration and light-sensing skin as leading ideas.
Small studies suggest octopuses cycle between quiet and active sleep states, but nobody knows whether they dream.
Distributed control, with clear intent from the center and autonomy at the edges, is a design that works for octopuses and for teams.

title: The Hardest Recipe: How Chemistry Turned Into Life
dek: Seventy years after a grad student made amino acids with fake lightning, scientists can build many of life's parts from scratch. The hard part was never the ingredients.

blocks.text: In 2008 a small team of chemists published results from samples that had sat in storage for more than half a century. They were small vials of dried brown residue, labeled in the handwriting of Stanley Miller, the chemist who in 1953 became famous for making the building blocks of life in a glass flask. Miller had died the year before. Some of his old samples came from a version of his experiment he never fully analyzed or published, and modern instruments found far more in them than he ever knew was there.

That rediscovery is a good summary of the origin-of-life field as a whole. It started with a stunning early success that made the problem look nearly solved. It then spent decades learning how much harder the real problem was. And it keeps uncovering more than anyone expected, even in old results. Where life came from is still one of the biggest open questions in science, but it is no longer a mystery in the sense of having nothing to say. It is a construction project with many parts built and some critical joints still missing.
Lightning in a flask

In 1953 Miller was a 23-year-old graduate student at the University of Chicago working with the Nobel laureate Harold Urey. At the time, many scientists thought the young Earth had an atmosphere rich in hydrogen-bearing gases like methane and ammonia. Miller built a closed loop of glass: a flask of boiling water for the ocean, a chamber filled with methane, ammonia and hydrogen for the sky, and a pair of electrodes throwing sparks through it as lightning. A condenser cooled the vapor so it rained back into the water.

blocks.title: Miller's 1953 setup
items: Boil water to simulate a warm early ocean and send vapor into the system.
Mix the vapor with methane, ammonia and hydrogen, the assumed early atmosphere.
Fire continuous electric sparks through the gas to stand in for lightning.
Cool the gas so droplets rain back down, carrying new products into the water.
After about a week, analyze the dark residue that collected in the water.

blocks.text: Within days the clear water had darkened noticeably. When Miller analyzed it, he found amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, including glycine and alanine. His short paper in *Science* in May 1953 reported five. Simple gases plus energy had produced molecules that every living cell depends on, with no biology involved. The result made headlines and helped launch an entire research field.

Miller also ran variations, including one where a jet of steam blasted into the spark chamber, mimicking a gas-rich volcanic eruption laced with lightning. Those samples were the ones that sat on a shelf. When Adam Johnson, Jeffrey Bada and colleagues reanalyzed them with modern equipment, the volcanic version had produced 22 amino acids and 5 amines. Even the classic experiment's vials held 14 amino acids, nearly three times what Miller could detect in 1953.

blocks.title: Amino acids found in Miller's experiments
blocks.note: Same 1950s samples; the difference is modern detection and the steam-jet design.
blocks.source: Miller, Science 1953; Johnson et al., Science 2008

blocks.text: The ingredients are everywhere

Since then, a complication emerged. Most geologists now think the early atmosphere was not as rich in hydrogen as Miller assumed, and was probably dominated by carbon dioxide and nitrogen. In that kind of air, spark experiments make far fewer amino acids. That is one reason the volcanic result matters: the authors argue that volcanic plumes could have released hydrogen-rich gases locally, along with frequent lightning, creating small chemical factories even if the global atmosphere was less helpful.

Meanwhile, space turned out to be full of the same kinds of molecules. Meteorites that fall to Earth contain amino acids. In 2023, a Japanese team reported finding uracil, one of the four letters of RNA's genetic code, in pristine samples the Hayabusa2 spacecraft brought back from the asteroid Ryugu. Because those samples were sealed away from Earth's air and microbes, contamination is far less of a worry. The authors concluded such molecules likely formed commonly on carbon-rich asteroids and were delivered to the early Earth.

So the raw parts of life are not rare or exotic. They form readily wherever simple carbon compounds meet energy. If origin-of-life research were only about the ingredients, it would be mostly done. The real problem is what happens next. A pile of amino acids is no more alive than a pile of bricks is a house, and the gap between them is where nearly all the hard questions live.

There is also a subtler gap: handedness. Many biological molecules come in mirror-image forms, like left and right gloves. Chemistry in a flask or on an asteroid makes both forms in equal amounts, and the amino acids in the Ryugu samples were exactly that kind of even mix. Life, though, uses almost only left-handed amino acids and right-handed sugars. How one hand won out early on is still an open question, with several proposed mechanisms and no consensus.
The chicken-and-egg problem

Every cell on Earth runs the same basic system. DNA stores instructions. Proteins do the work, including the work of copying DNA and reading it out. The trap is obvious: you need proteins to make DNA, and you need DNA to make proteins. Neither could have come first on its own, and both are huge, intricate molecules that would never assemble by chance.

Critics of origin-of-life research often point out that the odds of a working protein or gene assembling all at once by pure chance are absurdly small. They are right about that, and almost no researcher thinks it happened that way. The working assumption is that selection started before life did: molecules that were more stable, or that helped make more of themselves, would accumulate while others broke down. Chance supplies variation, and persistence does the sorting, the same logic that drives evolution once life exists.

The way out came from a surprise in the early 1980s. Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman independently found RNA molecules that act as enzymes, speeding up chemical reactions the way proteins do. They shared the 1989 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. RNA can store genetic information like DNA and catalyze reactions like a protein. If one molecule can play both roles, the trap disappears. This idea is called the RNA world: an early stage of life where RNA did everything, before DNA and proteins took over the specialized jobs.

The strongest clue sits inside your own cells. The ribosome is the machine that builds every protein in your body. In 2000, a team led by Thomas Steitz and Peter Moore published the atomic structure of the ribosome's working core and found that the part that actually joins amino acids together is made of RNA, not protein. The protein-building factory of modern life is, at its heart, an RNA enzyme. Many researchers read that as a molecular fossil left over from an RNA world.
The ribosome is like an old piece of legacy code still running at the center of a modern system. Nobody would design it this way from scratch, which is exactly why it hints at how things started.
Building the pieces in the lab

The RNA world created its own puzzle. RNA's building blocks, nucleotides, are hard to make. Each one is a sugar called ribose joined to a base and a phosphate. For decades, chemists could not find a plausible way to join the pieces under early-Earth conditions. Ribose is hard to make cleanly, and two of the bases simply would not attach to it.

In 2009, Matthew Powner, Béatrice Gerland and John Sutherland in Manchester sidestepped the problem. Instead of making the sugar and base separately and gluing them together, they found a route where the two grow together from simpler molecules, including cyanamide, cyanoacetylene and simple sugars, with phosphate guiding several steps along the way. It produced two of RNA's four nucleotides. It was a reminder that nature may not have followed the route that looks obvious on a chemist's whiteboard.

The same year, Tracey Lincoln and Gerald Joyce at the Scripps Research Institute built a pair of RNA enzymes that each assemble copies of the other from smaller pieces. Together they grew exponentially, doubling about every hour, with no proteins involved. When different versions competed for the same raw materials, new combined versions arose and took over. That is evolution happening in a test tube, in a system made only of RNA. There is a catch: the pieces they fed it were made in a lab, not by early-Earth chemistry. Joining every step together, from simple gases to a self-copying system, has still not been done.
A warm pond or a deep vent?

In 1871 Charles Darwin speculated in a letter to his friend Joseph Hooker that life might have begun in a warm little pond rich in ammonia and phosphate salts, with light, heat and electricity driving the chemistry. More than 150 years later, his pond is still one of the two leading candidates. Ponds and hot springs on land can dry out and refill again and again, and those wet-dry cycles help small molecules link into longer chains.

The other candidate is the deep sea. In 2000, researchers discovered a vent field in the Atlantic they named Lost City. Unlike the familiar black smokers, its towers are made of carbonate, and its fluids are relatively cool, around 40 to 75°C, and strongly alkaline. Some researchers argue that vents like this provide natural chemical and electrical gradients across thin mineral walls, similar to the gradients every living cell still uses to make energy. Each camp has real arguments, and some researchers think different steps may have happened in different places.

blocks.title: Two leading cradles for life

left.head: Warm ponds on land
items: Wet-dry cycles concentrate molecules and link them into chains
Sunlight and lightning supply energy
Fits much of the RNA chemistry done in labs
Requires dry land early in Earth's history

right.head: Deep-sea alkaline vents
items: Steady supply of energy and hydrogen from rock reactions
Natural gradients resemble those cells use for energy
Protected from UV and impacts
Molecules can dilute away in the open ocean

blocks.text: It happened fast

Whatever the place, the timing is striking. Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago. The oldest widely accepted microfossils date to about 3.5 billion years ago. A carbon inclusion found inside a 4.1-billion-year-old zircon crystal from Western Australia has a chemical signature consistent with life, though it could have other explanations. And a 2024 study that reconstructed the last universal common ancestor of all living things from modern genomes estimated it lived around 4.2 billion years ago, with a genome encoding roughly 2,600 proteins.

items.label: Estimated age of the last universal common ancestor
Proteins LUCA's genome likely encoded
Age of zircon with possibly biological carbon

blocks.source: Moody et al., Nat. Ecol. Evol. 2024; Bell et al., PNAS 2015

blocks.text: Those dates are uncertain and debated, but if they hold, they say something important. Our common ancestor was already a complex organism, comparable to modern bacteria, within a few hundred million years of a planet still being pounded by debris. Either life arises fairly easily when conditions are right, or Earth got extremely lucky early. Nobody knows which, and the answer matters a great deal for whether the universe is full of life or nearly empty.
Where the line actually is

The deepest lesson of this field may be that there is no sharp line between chemistry and life. Molecules that form on their own become molecules that speed each other up, then sets that copy each other, then copying with variation and competition. At some point along that path, something is clearly evolving. Asking for the exact moment it became alive may be like asking which line of code turned a project into a game.

That is also why progress is hard to see from the outside. No single experiment will announce that life has been made. Instead, researchers keep closing gaps one at a time: a nucleotide here, a self-copying enzyme there, a better guess about the early atmosphere. Be skeptical of headlines that say the mystery is solved, and equally skeptical of claims that it is impossible. The honest position is that we have plausible routes for many steps, gaps in several, and no complete demonstration yet.

takeaways: Miller's 1953 spark experiment made amino acids from simple gases; reanalysis of his samples in 2008 found far more than he reported.
Life's building blocks form easily, even on asteroids; organizing them into a self-copying system is the hard part.
RNA can both store information and act as an enzyme, which is why many scientists think an RNA world came first.
Warm ponds and deep alkaline vents are the leading candidate cradles; the evidence does not yet decide between them.
Life appeared early in Earth's history, but no one has yet built the full path from chemistry to life in a lab.
