title: The Sugar Pill That Knows Its Price
dek: Placebos can cut pain, ease nausea and even work when patients know they are fake. They cannot shrink a tumor. The line between those two facts tells you a lot about how your brain builds what you feel.

blocks.text: In a study published in 2008, a team including behavioral economist Dan Ariely gave 82 people a series of mild electric shocks to the wrist and asked them to rate the pain. Then each person took a pill, described as a new painkiller, and got shocked again. Half were told the pill cost $2.50 a dose. The other half were told it had been discounted to 10 cents. Every pill was the same: inert, a placebo.

Among people who thought they had the full-price drug, 85 percent reported less pain. Among the bargain group, 61 percent did. Nothing in the pills differed. Only the story did. The brain, it seems, reads the price tag.

blocks.title: People reporting less pain after an identical fake pill
blocks.note: Both groups got the same inert pill; only the stated price differed.
blocks.source: Waber, Shiv, Carmon and Ariely, JAMA, 2008

blocks.text: The placebo effect is one of the most misunderstood ideas in science. Some people treat it as proof the mind can cure anything. Others treat it as a polite word for nothing happening. The truth is more interesting than either: placebos are real, measurable brain events with a narrow and specific reach. Knowing where that reach ends is useful for understanding medicine, and for understanding your own body.
Most of the placebo response is not a placebo effect

Start with a trap that fools even researchers. In a drug trial, people who get the sugar pill often improve a lot. That improvement is called the placebo response, and it is tempting to credit it all to the power of belief. But most of it has more boring explanations.

The first is that many conditions get better on their own. Colds end. Back pain flares and fades. The second is a statistical effect called regression to the mean. People tend to join a trial or see a doctor when their symptoms are at their worst, and from a peak, the most likely direction is down, whatever you do. The third is that people in trials are watched, encouraged and cared for, and they often want to please the researchers by reporting improvement.

The way to separate these out is to compare placebo against *no treatment at all*. A Cochrane review led by Asbjørn Hróbjartsson and Peter Gøtzsche did exactly that across many trials. Their conclusion was sobering: overall, placebo pills did not have large, important effects on objective outcomes like blood tests or survival. But they could affect what patients report, especially pain and nausea. That is the true territory of the placebo.

blocks.title: What placebos can and cannot touch

left.head: Responds to placebo
items: Pain
Nausea
Fatigue and how bad symptoms feel
Some IBS and other gut symptoms

right.head: Does not respond
items: Tumor size
Infections and bacterial counts
Broken bones healing faster
Blood sugar in diabetes

blocks.text: A useful rule: placebos change how the brain processes signals from the body, not the underlying damage. They can turn the volume down on pain; they cannot rebuild the speaker.
The chemistry of expectation

If placebo pain relief were just people being polite, it would have no chemistry. It does. In a classic 1978 experiment, researchers studied patients after dental surgery who reported relief from a placebo. Then they gave some of them naloxone, a drug that blocks the body's opioid receptors, the same drug used to reverse overdoses. The placebo relief largely vanished. The conclusion: expecting relief had caused the brain to release its own opioids, natural painkillers called endorphins.

Later brain-imaging work found that when people expect a placebo to work, activity drops in brain regions that process pain, and rises in regions involved in controlling it. The pain signal from the body still arrives. The brain simply turns down how much of it reaches awareness. This fits what pain researchers now believe more generally: pain is not a direct readout of damage, but the brain's best guess about how much danger the body is in, built from nerve signals, context and expectation.

blocks.title: How a placebo eases pain
items: A cue arrives: a pill, an injection, a white coat, a price tag.
The brain predicts relief based on past experience and what it has been told.
It releases natural opioids and other signaling chemicals.
Pain-processing regions quiet down and the same nerve input feels less intense.
Relief confirms the expectation, strengthening the next response.

blocks.text: That last step explains why placebo effects are bigger with things that *seem* more powerful. Injections tend to beat pills. Brand names beat generic labels. Two pills often beat one. And, as the price-tag study showed, expensive beats cheap. Every one of those is a cue the brain uses to predict how much relief is coming.

Learning matters too. If you have taken a real painkiller many times, your body starts associating the act of swallowing a pill with relief. That is conditioning, the same process Pavlov's dogs went through with a bell. A placebo can then trigger part of the response on its own. Your past experience is quietly shaping what any new treatment does for you.

The effect is not limited to pain. In patients with Parkinson's disease, a condition caused by the loss of dopamine-producing brain cells, brain scans have shown that a placebo they believed was medication triggered a measurable release of dopamine. The patients' expectation of improvement drove the very chemical their disease was starving them of. It was not a cure, and it did not stop the disease, but it showed how directly a belief can reach into brain chemistry.
The evil twin: nocebo

If expecting relief can reduce pain, expecting harm can create symptoms. This is the nocebo effect, and it may matter even more in daily life. Read a long list of side effects, and you are more likely to feel some of them, whether or not the drug causes them.

The COVID-19 vaccine trials gave researchers a huge natural experiment. A team led by Julia Haas and Ted Kaptchuk pooled 12 trials with more than 22,000 people who received placebo injections of salt water. After the first shot, more than 35 percent of placebo recipients reported a systemic side effect like headache or fatigue. Headache alone hit nearly 1 in 5. Comparing that to the vaccine groups, the team estimated that about 76 percent of the side effects reported after the first dose could be put down to nocebo rather than the vaccine itself.

items.label: Placebo recipients reporting a systemic side effect after the first shot
Share of first-dose side effects in vaccine groups attributed to nocebo
Pooled, with more than 22,000 placebo recipients

blocks.source: Haas et al., JAMA Network Open, 2022

blocks.text: That does not mean vaccine side effects are imaginary; the vaccine groups reported more than the placebo groups did. It means a big part of what anyone feels after a shot or a pill is driven by expectation, anxiety and paying close attention to normal body sensations. A headache you would have ignored on a normal day becomes a side effect the moment you are watching for one.

Doctors are starting to use this. Some researchers argue for telling patients about common side effects in a way that is honest but does not prime them to expect misery, for example by noting that most people feel fine, or that mild aches are a sign the immune system is working. The information is the same. The prediction it sets up in the brain is not.
Honest placebos and sham surgery

For a long time, doctors assumed a placebo only works if you are fooled. In 2010, Ted Kaptchuk's team at Harvard tested that by giving 80 patients with irritable bowel syndrome either no treatment or a bottle of pills plainly labeled as placebo. Patients were told the pills were inert, like sugar pills, but that placebos had helped IBS symptoms in earlier studies. After three weeks, the open placebo group reported significantly more improvement than the no-treatment group.

That was a small study, and patients knew which group they were in, so their reports could be colored by hope. Later trials of open-label placebos have had mixed and generally modest results. But the core finding is striking: the ritual of treatment seems to do some work even without deception.

Placebo research has also humbled surgery. In a famous 2002 study, patients with knee arthritis got either real arthroscopic surgery or a sham: small incisions in the skin and nothing else. For two years, the sham group reported as much improvement in pain and function as the real surgery groups. A procedure performed on hundreds of thousands of people a year had not beaten a fake. Sham-controlled trials have since questioned several other common operations.

There is an uncomfortable flip side for everyday medicine. Doctors cannot ethically hand out sugar pills while claiming they are drugs, but some still prescribe real drugs that cannot help the problem in front of them, such as antibiotics for a cold caused by a virus. Researchers call these impure placebos. The patient feels better, mostly because colds end on their own, and both sides credit the pill. The cost is real: unnecessary antibiotics feed the evolution of resistant bacteria.
The placebo is getting stronger

Here is a strange twist. Researchers at McGill University led by Alexander Tuttle and Jeffrey Mogil looked at 84 trials of drugs for chronic nerve pain published between 1990 and 2013. In trials run in the United States, the placebo groups were reporting more and more relief over time. The drugs did not get worse, but their edge over placebo shrank sharply.

blocks.title: How much better nerve-pain drugs did than placebo
blocks.note: The rise in placebo response appeared only in trials conducted in the US.
blocks.source: Tuttle et al., Pain, 2015 (reported in Nature)

blocks.text: The effect showed up only in US trials, not those in Europe or Asia. The researchers pointed to how American trials had changed: they became much longer and larger, with more sites and more of the hope and attention that come with being in a big study. One possibility is that direct-to-consumer drug advertising, legal in the US, has raised expectations of what pills can do. Whatever the cause, it means a new painkiller today has to beat a tougher fake than one tested in the 1990s.

This matters beyond pharmacology. When a drug fails to beat placebo, the trial counts as a failure even if the drug genuinely helps, because the fake is helping too. Promising treatments can be abandoned for that reason alone. It is also a reminder that every number from a placebo-controlled trial is a comparison, not an absolute. A drug that is 9 points better than a placebo might still help a patient a great deal, because the patient gets both the drug and the expectation.
What to do with this

The placebo effect is not a reason to skip real medicine. A sugar pill will not fix an infection, a torn ligament or a heart problem, and anyone selling a remedy because it beats nothing in a small study is selling hope, not treatment. If something feels wrong, talk to the corpsman or a doctor.

But the research does say something practical about the part of your experience that runs through your brain's predictions. How you frame pain, fatigue or discomfort is not just commentary. It changes how much of it you feel. Bracing for a miserable watch makes the same watch feel worse. Reading every side effect on a label makes you feel more of them. Expecting your body to handle a hard workout changes how the effort registers.

items: Before a painful task or a long watch, describe it to yourself accurately rather than catastrophically. 'This will be uncomfortable for a while' beats 'this will be awful.'
Skim side-effect lists for the serious warning signs you need to act on, then stop scanning your body for every minor sensation.
Treat recovery routines you trust, like a cool-down or a set bedtime, as legitimate cues. Part of their benefit is that your brain expects them to work.
Be suspicious of any product whose evidence is a small study where people rated how they felt. That is exactly where placebo effects are strongest.

blocks.text: This is not positive thinking as magic. It is a mechanical fact about a prediction machine that sits between your nerves and your awareness. You cannot think a tumor away. You can, within limits, change the volume.

The takeaway is not that belief cures. It is that what you feel is always the brain's interpretation, and the inputs to that interpretation include context, expectation and attention, which you have some control over.

takeaways: Most improvement in a trial's placebo group comes from natural recovery and regression to the mean, not belief.
True placebo effects are real but narrow: mostly pain, nausea and other symptoms the brain interprets, not underlying disease.
Placebo pain relief runs on the brain's own opioids; blocking them with naloxone weakens it.
Nocebo works in reverse: in COVID vaccine trials, more than a third of placebo recipients reported side effects after the first shot.
Framing and expectation shape how intense symptoms feel, so watch how you brace for discomfort.

title: The Idea That Geology Laughed At
dek: Continental drift was dismissed for decades. Then Navy echo sounders and submarine-hunting magnetometers found the evidence under the sea floor.

blocks.text: In November 1930, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener set out across the Greenland ice cap on a resupply trip for a remote research station. He never made it home. His body was found the following spring, buried in the snow. He was 50 years old, and the idea he was most famous for, that the continents move, was widely considered by geologists to be wrong, even a little embarrassing.

Within about forty years, that idea had become the foundation of modern earth science. Today it explains earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain ranges, ocean trenches and the shapes of the continents themselves. What changed in between was not a single brilliant argument. It was a flood of new data from the deep ocean, much of it gathered with tools built for war, including echo sounders on Navy ships and magnetometers derived from submarine hunting.

The story is worth knowing for its own sake. It is also one of the best case studies in how science actually works: how a right idea can be rejected for reasonable reasons, and how the decisive evidence often comes from somewhere nobody was looking.
A jigsaw puzzle nobody wanted to solve

People had noticed for centuries that the coastlines of South America and Africa look like they could fit together. Wegener went much further. In a 1912 paper and a 1915 book, The Origin of Continents and Oceans, he gathered evidence from multiple fields. Rock formations and mountain belts seemed to continue across the Atlantic. Identical fossils of land plants and reptiles turned up on continents now separated by thousands of kilometers of ocean. Traces of ancient glaciers appeared in places that are now tropical.

His conclusion was that all the continents had once been joined in a single supercontinent he called Pangaea, which later broke apart and drifted into its current arrangement. It was a bold and sweeping theory, and in broad outline it was correct.

The geological establishment, especially in Britain and the United States, mostly rejected it. Some of that was turf protection against an outsider. Wegener was trained in astronomy and meteorology, not geology. But a lot of the resistance was legitimate. Wegener proposed that continents plowed through the ocean floor like ships through ice, pushed by forces tied to Earth's rotation and tides. Physicists calculated that those forces were far too weak to move a continent. Some of his evidence, including longitude measurements he believed showed Greenland moving many meters a year, turned out to be simply wrong.

Wegener's critics were not just stubborn. He had a lot of correct observations and no workable mechanism. In science, "this fits the data" is not enough if the proposed cause breaks the laws of physics.

So for decades, continental drift sat in a strange limbo. A few scientists kept it alive, and some geologists in the Southern Hemisphere, who could see the matching rocks for themselves, found it convincing. But in most textbooks it was a curiosity at best. The problem was that the evidence that would settle it was hidden under kilometers of seawater, and nobody had seriously looked.
The war maps the ocean floor

World War II changed that. Navies needed to understand the ocean to fight in it, and especially to hunt and hide submarines. That meant echo sounders that bounced sound off the seafloor to measure depth, and later magnetometers sensitive enough to detect the steel hull of a submerged submarine. Both technologies turned out to be perfect tools for geology.

Harry Hess, a Princeton geologist and Naval Reserve officer, was called to active duty after Pearl Harbor and ended up commanding the attack transport USS Cape Johnson in the Pacific, through landings at the Marianas, Leyte, Lingayen Gulf and Iwo Jima. Between operations, he kept the ship's echo sounder running day and night, collecting thousands of miles of seafloor profiles. In them he found flat-topped undersea mountains, which he named guyots. They looked like volcanoes that had been eroded flat at sea level and then sunk.

After the war, the mapping exploded. At Columbia University's Lamont Geological Observatory, Marie Tharp worked through sounding profiles from across the Atlantic and plotted them into maps of the ocean floor. In the early 1950s she noticed a deep V-shaped valley running down the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a great undersea mountain range. Her colleague Bruce Heezen was initially skeptical, because a rift valley there implied the crust was being pulled apart, which sounded uncomfortably like continental drift. Earthquake locations soon lined up with her rift, and their 1957 map of the North Atlantic floor made it impossible to ignore.
Stripes on the seafloor

Then came the evidence that cracked the case. In the 1950s, scientists from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, Ronald Mason and Arthur Raff, towed magnetometers behind ships off the west coast of North America. Their 1961 maps showed something nobody expected: the magnetism of the seafloor rocks formed long parallel stripes, alternating strong and weak, like a zebra pattern. Nothing on land looked like it.

Meanwhile, Hess had put the pieces together into a bold hypothesis. In his 1962 paper, History of Ocean Basins, he proposed that hot material rises from the mantle at mid-ocean ridges, creates new seafloor, and spreads sideways in both directions until it sinks back into the mantle at deep ocean trenches. The seafloor would be a conveyor belt, and the continents would ride along on top rather than plowing through anything. Hess himself was careful to frame it as speculative, but it solved Wegener's mechanism problem in one stroke.

In 1963, Frederick Vine and Drummond Matthews at Cambridge, and independently Lawrence Morley in Canada, connected the stripes to Hess's conveyor. Earth's magnetic field has flipped its polarity many times in the past. When new rock forms at a ridge and cools, it locks in the direction of the field at that moment. If the seafloor is spreading, you should find a symmetrical pattern of normal and reversed stripes on both sides of the ridge, like a tape recording of Earth's magnetic history being played outward in two directions. Morley's version, famously, was rejected by journals before Vine and Matthews's paper appeared in Nature.

blocks.title: How the seafloor records its own age
items: Molten rock rises at a mid-ocean ridge and forms new crust
As it cools, magnetic minerals lock in the direction of Earth's field
The new crust moves away from the ridge on both sides
Earth's magnetic field periodically reverses
The result is mirror-image magnetic stripes on each side of the ridge, getting older with distance

blocks.text: By 1966, the stripes measured across ridges matched the timeline of magnetic reversals that other scientists had dated from volcanic rocks on land. The best match, across the East Pacific Rise, was so close to the calculated pattern that it convinced many skeptics almost overnight.
From drift to plates

The rest came fast. In 1965, the Canadian geophysicist J. Tuzo Wilson described a new class of faults, transform faults, that connect offset segments of ridges and trenches and explained the strange geometry of the ocean floor. In 1967 and 1968, Dan McKenzie and Robert Parker, Jason Morgan, and Xavier Le Pichon showed that Earth's surface could be described as a set of rigid plates rotating across a sphere. Seismologists showed earthquakes clustered along plate boundaries, with deep quakes tracing slabs of seafloor diving back into the mantle.

The clincher was drilling. In 1968, the drill ship Glomar Challenger began pulling up cores from the deep seafloor. Sediment and rock ages increased steadily with distance from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, exactly as seafloor spreading predicted. The US Geological Survey calls that voyage the clinching evidence.

blocks.title: From mocked to proven
items: Wegener presents continental drift; book follows in 1915
Wegener dies on the Greenland ice cap, theory largely rejected
Hess runs a Navy echo sounder across the Pacific and finds guyots
Tharp maps the Mid-Atlantic rift valley
Mason and Raff publish magnetic stripes off western North America
Hess publishes seafloor spreading
Vine and Matthews (and Morley) explain the stripes
Wilson describes transform faults
Plate tectonics formulated on a sphere; Glomar Challenger drills proof

blocks.text: One consequence is striking. Because the seafloor is constantly created at ridges and destroyed at trenches, it is young. According to the USGS, the oldest ocean floor is only about 180 million years old, a small fraction of Earth's age of about 4.5 billion years. Continents, which are too light to sink, preserve rocks billions of years old. The ocean floor is recycled; the continents are the attic where Earth keeps its old stuff.

items.label: Age of the oldest ocean floor
Mid-Atlantic spreading per million years

blocks.source: USGS, This Dynamic Earth

blocks.title: How fast plates move
blocks.note: Mid-Atlantic is an average spreading rate; the East Pacific Rise near Easter Island exceeds 15 cm/yr.
blocks.source: USGS, This Dynamic Earth

blocks.text: Those speeds sound tiny, and they are, on human time scales. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge averages about 2.5 centimeters a year, roughly 25 kilometers per million years. But give it the 100 to 200 million years the Atlantic has been opening and you get an ocean. The San Andreas Fault slips at about 5 centimeters a year on average, which is why California keeps having earthquakes. Today, GPS stations can measure these motions directly, year by year, so plate motion is no longer inferred. It is observed.

What actually drives the plates is still an active research question, but the broad answer is heat. Earth's interior is hot from its formation and from radioactive decay, and the mantle, though solid rock, creeps slowly over millions of years like an extremely stiff fluid. The biggest single push seems to come from the plates themselves. Old seafloor grows cold and dense as it moves away from a ridge, and where it sinks into the mantle at a trench, its weight drags the rest of the plate along behind it. Geologists call this slab pull. Elevated ridges add a smaller push from the other side.

Once you see the planet this way, its surface starts to make sense. The Ring of Fire around the Pacific is a ring of trenches where seafloor sinks and melts, feeding chains of volcanoes in Japan, Alaska, the Cascades and the Andes. The Himalayas exist because India, riding on its plate, crashed into Asia and is still pushing north, crumpling the crust upward. Iceland sits right on top of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, one of the few places you can walk across a spreading boundary on dry land. Wegener died on the ice of Greenland, the big island just to the west, without ever seeing the ridge that would prove his central idea right. He had the continents moving; he just could not see the machinery underneath them.
What the story teaches

It is tempting to tell this as a simple morality tale: a lone genius was right, closed-minded experts were wrong. That version misses the useful part. Wegener was right about the big picture and wrong about the mechanism and some of the data. His critics were wrong to dismiss the observations but right that his proposed forces were impossible. The theory that won, plate tectonics, is not Wegener's continental drift. It is something better, built from evidence he never had.

blocks.title: Continental drift vs plate tectonics

left.head: Wegener's drift (1915)
items: Continents plow through ocean floor
Driven by rotation and tidal forces
Evidence mostly from land: fossils, rocks, coastlines
No way to test the mechanism

right.head: Plate tectonics (late 1960s)
items: Whole plates move, with continents riding on them
Driven by mantle heat, seafloor creation and sinking slabs
Evidence from seafloor maps, magnetism, quakes and drilling
Testable predictions that were confirmed

blocks.text: The other lesson is about where breakthroughs come from. The tools that proved plate tectonics were not built for geology. Echo sounders and magnetometers were built to fight and hunt submarines, and later, a worldwide seismometer network built in part to monitor nuclear weapons tests sharpened the map of earthquakes along plate boundaries. Military budgets paid for the surveys that turned a fringe idea into the core of earth science.

And a final thought for anyone who spends time underwater. The ocean floor below a submarine is not a fixed landscape. It is a moving conveyor, born at ridges and swallowed at trenches, carrying a magnetic record of Earth's history written in stripes. Much of what we know about it came from people doing their jobs at sea and paying attention to data nobody had asked them to collect. Hess was running an echo sounder between amphibious landings. The best ideas often start with someone noticing a pattern in work that looked routine.

takeaways: Wegener had strong evidence that continents move but no workable mechanism, so most geologists rejected him.
Wartime echo sounders and magnetometers revealed ridges, rift valleys and magnetic stripes on the seafloor.
Seafloor spreading, magnetic reversals and drilling cores proved the plates move.
The oldest ocean floor is only about 180 million years old because it is constantly recycled.
Being right about the pattern is not enough; you also need a mechanism that holds up.

title: The Year Science Proved ESP
dek: When researchers went back and re-ran famous experiments, a huge share did not hold up. What went wrong, how much of science it touches, and how to tell a solid finding from a shaky one.

blocks.text: In 2011, one of the most prestigious journals in social psychology published nine experiments by Daryl Bem, a respected Cornell professor, claiming that people can sense the future. In one setup, students were more likely to remember words they would be asked to practice *after* the memory test was over. The studies used standard methods, standard statistics and passed standard peer review. By the rules of the field, they were good science.

Almost nobody believed the result. That was exactly the problem. If the normal toolkit of a respected field could produce convincing evidence for precognition, what else had that toolkit 'proven'? Later the same year, three researchers published a paper showing how easy it was to manufacture a statistically significant result for something impossible. They ran a real experiment and, by making a series of small, common analysis choices, 'showed' that listening to a Beatles song made people literally younger. Their point was not about the Beatles. It was that the ordinary habits of working scientists could turn noise into findings.

That year kicked off what is now called the replication crisis: a decade-plus effort to go back, re-run famous experiments, and see how many held up. The answer was humbling, and it reaches well beyond psychology.
Running it again

The landmark test came in 2015. A large team of researchers organized as the Open Science Collaboration took 100 studies published in three top psychology journals and repeated them as faithfully as they could, often with the original materials and larger samples. Of the original studies, 97% had reported statistically significant results. Of the replications, 36% did. On average, the effects in the replications were about half the size of the originals.

Other fields followed. Economists re-ran 18 lab experiments from two top journals and got the same significant result in 11. A team re-ran 21 social science experiments that had been published in *Nature* and *Science*, the most famous journals in the world, with samples about five times larger than the originals. Thirteen replicated, and even those showed effects averaging about half their original size. A massive project called Many Labs 2 ran 28 findings across 125 samples in 36 countries; 15 held up.

blocks.title: Share of findings that replicated
blocks.note: Each project used its own standard for success, so compare loosely. Cancer biology figure is for positive effects judged successful by at least three of five methods.
blocks.source: Open Science Collaboration 2015; Klein et al. 2018; Camerer et al. 2016 and 2018; Errington et al. 2021; Begley and Ellis 2012

blocks.text: Some caution is fair here. A failed replication does not prove the original was false; the second team might have done something differently, or been unlucky. Critics of the 2015 project argued exactly that, and the debate over how to score it went on for years. But the overall pattern across many independent projects is hard to argue with. A published, peer-reviewed, statistically significant finding in these fields has something like a coin-flip chance of holding up when someone checks carefully, and the effect is usually smaller than first claimed.

If you have read about power posing, ego depletion, or some of the bolder claims around growth mindset and the marshmallow test, you have already met this crisis. Each of those ideas was a famous, widely taught result that shrank or stumbled when larger teams tried to repeat it.

Bem's precognition claim, by the way, never went away quietly. In 2016 he and colleagues pooled 90 experiments from 33 labs and reported overall evidence for seeing the future at a level beyond six sigma, the kind of number physicists use to announce new particles. Almost no one outside that circle was persuaded. The episode is a useful warning: stacking up many studies only helps if the individual studies are clean. Pile up biased results and you get a very confident wrong answer.
How honest people produce false results

The striking thing is that the crisis is mostly not about fraud. Fraud exists, and 2011 also brought the exposure of a Dutch psychologist who had fabricated data for years. But most unreliable findings come from ordinary scientists following the incentives and habits of their field. Nobody has to lie. The system just has too many ways for luck to sneak in and get treated as discovery.

The core issue is flexibility. A researcher collecting data faces dozens of small choices: which participants to exclude, when to stop collecting, which of several measures to report, whether to control for age or gender, which test to run. Each choice is defensible on its own. But if you try several paths and report the one that crossed the line of statistical significance, you have quietly turned a 1-in-20 false alarm rate into something much worse. Statisticians call this the garden of forking paths, or p-hacking when it is done more deliberately.

blocks.title: How noise becomes a published finding
items: Run a small study, where random variation is large.
Measure several outcomes and try several reasonable ways of analyzing them.
Report the version that reaches p below 0.05; the others feel like false starts.
Write the paper as if that result was the plan all along.
Journals prefer exciting positive results, so this one gets published while null results sit in file drawers.
The published record now overstates both how often effects exist and how big they are.

blocks.text: The last step is the quietest and maybe the most damaging. Journals, reviewers and readers want news. A study that finds nothing is hard to publish, so it often never gets written up. That means the literature you can read is a filtered sample of everything that was tried, tilted toward lucky hits. Think of it like a highlight reel: if you only ever see the clips where a player hits every shot, you will badly overestimate their aim.

Small samples make all of this worse in a sneaky way. In a tiny study, random noise swings results around a lot. The only versions that clear the significance bar are the ones where noise happened to push the effect up. So even when an effect is real, the first small study to find it usually overstates it, sometimes by a lot. Researchers call this the winner's curse. It is a big reason replications with larger samples so often find effects about half the original size, rather than zero.

There is a base-rate problem underneath all of this too. A 2015 study used prediction markets, where researchers bet on which psychology findings would replicate, and used the results to estimate how likely the tested ideas were to be true before anyone ran the experiment. The median came out around 9%. When most of the ideas you test are long shots, even a well-run study with a significant result is far from proof. In 2005 the epidemiologist John Ioannidis laid out the math in a paper with a title that became a rallying cry: 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False.'
It is not just psychology

Psychology took the most public beating, partly because it was the first field brave enough to check itself at scale. The problem is broader. In 2012, scientists at the biotech company Amgen reported that they had tried to confirm 53 'landmark' cancer studies before building drug programs on them. They could confirm 6. A team at Bayer had reported the year before that only about a quarter of the published findings it checked held up in its own labs.

A careful academic follow-up, the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, repeated 50 experiments from 23 high-profile papers. For positive results, the median effect in the replications was 85% smaller than in the originals, and 92% of replication effects came out smaller. When *Nature* surveyed 1,576 researchers in 2016, more than 70% said they had tried and failed to reproduce another scientist's experiment, and more than half had failed to reproduce one of their own.

items.label: Researchers who have failed to reproduce someone else's experiment
How much smaller the median replicated cancer-biology effect was
Landmark cancer studies Amgen could confirm

blocks.source: Baker, Nature, 2016; Errington et al., eLife, 2021; Begley and Ellis, Nature, 2012

blocks.text: Medicine learned a version of this lesson earlier, because the stakes were patients. Drug companies were caught publishing their successful trials while trials that found nothing stayed in a drawer. Since the mid-2000s, major medical journals have required clinical trials to be publicly registered before the first patient enrolls, so a missing result can at least be noticed. It did not solve everything, but it made the most dangerous kind of selective reporting much harder to hide.

The fields with the fewest problems tend to share some traits: very large datasets, strong theory that makes precise predictions, and a culture of independent checking. Particle physics, for example, demands evidence far stronger than the usual 1-in-20 standard before anyone announces a discovery. The physics that runs a reactor plant has been tested billions of times over by engineers who would notice if it were wrong. That is not because physicists are more honest. It is because their system makes luck much harder to mistake for signal.
The repair job

Here is the hopeful part. The replication crisis is the scientific method working, slowly and painfully, on itself. The same researchers who exposed the problem built fixes, and many of those fixes are now standard. The most important is **preregistration**: writing down your hypothesis, sample size and analysis plan before you collect data, and posting it publicly with a timestamp. You can still explore, but you can no longer quietly pass off exploration as a planned test.

A stronger version is the **registered report**, where a journal reviews and accepts the study design before results exist, and promises to publish whatever comes out. A 2021 comparison found the difference this makes is enormous. In ordinary psychology papers, 96% of first hypotheses were supported. In registered reports, only 44% were.

blocks.title: Share of studies reporting a positive result
blocks.note: Psychology papers, first hypothesis tested in each. Registered reports are accepted before results are known.
blocks.source: Scheel, Schijen and Lakens, Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 2021

blocks.text: Real science should look more like the second number. Most good ideas are wrong when you test them, and an honest literature reflects that. Alongside preregistration, journals increasingly expect open data and code, bigger samples, and teams of labs running the same protocol in parallel. There is even evidence that scientists have decent instincts about which findings are shaky: in the 2018 project, peer predictions of which studies would replicate tracked the actual results closely.

The incentives are the harder part to fix. Careers are still built on publishing papers, especially splashy ones, and a replication rarely makes anyone famous. Some funders and journals now reward replication work directly, and young researchers increasingly treat open methods as a point of pride rather than a chore. The culture is shifting, but it is shifting the way an aircraft carrier turns.
How to read a claim

You will hear scientific claims constantly: in fitness content, nutrition videos, productivity books, and the YouTube growth advice that fills your feed. You do not need a statistics degree to filter them. A handful of questions catch most of the problems.

items: How many people were studied, and were they anything like you?
Has anyone other than the original team found the same thing?
How big is the effect in plain terms, not just whether it was significant?
Was the plan written down before the data came in?
Who benefits if you believe it: a supplement seller, a course, a book deal?

blocks.title: Shaky versus solid

left.head: Red flags
items: One small study, especially with a few dozen people
A surprising, life-changing effect from a tiny intervention
Only one lab has ever found it
Results announced in a press release or book before a paper
Effect sizes not mentioned, only 'significant'

right.head: Green flags
items: Many studies, ideally summarized in a careful meta-analysis
A modest effect that fits with what else is known
Independent teams have replicated it
Preregistered or a registered report
Data and methods are public

blocks.text: One more filter is worth keeping: ask how the result would look if it were just luck. If a single study of 40 college students says a two-minute pose changes your hormones, the boring explanation is noise plus a good story. If dozens of studies across decades and countries show that sleep loss slows reaction time, noise is no longer a plausible explanation.
A finding is not true because it was published, and it is not false because it failed once. Treat every single study as a rumor and a body of replicated evidence as news.

The deepest lesson of the crisis is not that science is broken. It is that science was never a pile of facts handed down from authorities. It is a process for catching mistakes, including its own. The part that failed was the shortcut, trusting a single exciting result. The part that worked was people going back, running it again, and publishing what they found even when it was embarrassing. That habit is worth stealing for your own life: when something you believe matters, check whether it holds up the second time.

takeaways: When famous findings were re-run carefully, roughly a third to two-thirds held up depending on the field, and effects usually shrank.
Most unreliable results come from small samples, flexible analysis and publication bias, not fraud.
Preregistration and registered reports cut the share of positive results in psychology from 96% to 44%, closer to how often ideas are actually right.
Trust replicated bodies of evidence over single studies, and be most skeptical of big effects from tiny interventions.
The crisis is science correcting itself; the failure was trusting one exciting result.

title: Your Nose Is Better Than Your Reputation
dek: Humans were written off as poor smellers because of a 19th-century hunch. The evidence says otherwise, and smell turns out to be wired straight into memory, flavor and health.

blocks.text: In 2006, a team of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, did something that sounds like a prank. They laid a trail of chocolate scent through a grassy field, then blindfolded volunteers, plugged their ears, put them in thick gloves and asked them to find it with their noses alone. The volunteers got down on all fours and sniffed along the ground like dogs.

Most people assume that would fail. Humans are supposed to have a weak sense of smell, a leftover from ancestors who needed it more. But the volunteers could follow the trail. With practice, they got faster and more accurate. And when the researchers blocked one nostril, people did worse, which revealed something nobody had shown before: humans, like many animals, compare the slightly different samples from each nostril to steer toward a scent.

That experiment is part of a quiet reversal in how scientists think about human smell. The old story is that we are visual creatures with a vestigial nose. The newer evidence says our nose is far better than our reputation, and that smell is wired into memory, emotion and health in ways the other senses are not.
Where the bad reputation came from

In 2017, the Rutgers neuroscientist John McGann published a review in Science with a blunt title: poor human olfaction is a 19th-century myth. He traced the belief back not to experiments but to the French anatomist Paul Broca. Broca noted that the olfactory bulb, the brain structure that first processes smell, is small in humans relative to the rest of the brain. He tied that to a philosophical idea: that humans had traded animal instincts like smell for free will and reason.

The problem is that relative size is a misleading measure. Our bulb looks small mainly because the rest of our brain is enormous. In absolute terms, the human olfactory bulb is fairly large, and McGann's review notes it contains a similar number of neurons to the bulbs of other mammals. In tests, humans are more sensitive than rodents and dogs to some specific odors. We just rarely use the ability deliberately, because modern life does not demand it.
A belief can be backed by a famous name and repeated for a century without ever having been tested. The idea that humans smell poorly came from philosophy dressed up as anatomy.
A lock for every key, sort of

Smell starts when molecules drift into your nose and dissolve in the mucus over a small patch of tissue high in the nasal cavity, the olfactory epithelium. There, millions of sensory neurons wait, each one tipped with receptor proteins that can bind certain molecules. When the right molecule latches on, the neuron fires.

How so few cells could tell apart so many smells was a mystery until 1991. That year, Linda Buck and Richard Axel at Columbia University discovered a huge family of genes that code for odor receptors. Their work, which earned the 2004 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, revealed that the receptors form the largest gene family in mammals. A later analysis found that humans have about 400 functional odor receptor genes, along with more than 400 broken ones, called pseudogenes, that have accumulated mutations and no longer work.

The trick is combinatorial. Each sensory neuron uses just one type of receptor. Each receptor responds to a range of molecules, and each odor molecule activates a particular set of receptors, some strongly and some weakly. Your brain reads the pattern, the way you read a word from a combination of letters. With around 400 letters, the number of possible words is astronomically large.

blocks.title: How a smell becomes a perception
items: Odor molecules enter the nose by sniffing or rise from food in your mouth
They bind receptors on sensory neurons, each neuron carrying one receptor type
Neurons with the same receptor send signals to the same spot in the olfactory bulb
The bulb turns this into a spatial pattern, like a fingerprint for the odor
The signal goes straight to areas tied to emotion and memory, and on to the cortex

blocks.text: Then the signal does something unusual. Vision, hearing, taste and touch all pass through the thalamus, a relay station, before reaching the cortex. Smell does not, at least not first. From the olfactory bulb, signals go directly into regions including the piriform cortex, the amygdala, which handles emotion, and areas next to the hippocampus, which is central to memory. That short, direct wiring is one reason a smell can drag a vivid memory or a wave of emotion into your head before you can even name the odor.
Receptors lost and kept

Comparing species shows how flexible this system is. In a 2014 study, Yoshihito Niimura and colleagues at the University of Tokyo cataloged odor receptor genes in 13 placental mammals. They estimated that the common ancestor of placental mammals had roughly 781 functional receptor genes. Along the human line, many were lost and some new ones were gained, leaving 396. African elephants, by contrast, had expanded their repertoire to 1,948, the largest ever found in a single species.

blocks.title: Functional odor receptor genes
blocks.note: Intact receptor genes; the ancestral figure is estimated from 13 living species.
blocks.source: Niimura, Matsui & Touhara, Genome Research, 2014

blocks.text: It is tempting to read that chart as proof that humans smell poorly. But the number of receptor types is not the same as performance. Having fewer receptor types might limit the range of distinctions you can make, but sensitivity, training and how the brain processes the signal matter just as much. A pianist and a beginner have the same 88 keys. Mice have well over twice as many receptor genes as humans, yet as McGann points out, there are odors humans detect at lower concentrations than mice can.

Those broken genes have a strange side effect: no two people live in quite the same smell world. Many receptor genes come in variants that work differently, and some people carry versions that barely work at all. A famous example is androstenone, a compound derived from testosterone that turns up in sweat and in pork. Some people find it sweaty and urine-like, some find it sweet or floral, and some cannot smell it at all. In 2007, Andreas Keller, Hiroaki Matsunami and colleagues showed that much of this difference traces to a single receptor, OR7D4. People carrying a common impaired variant were less sensitive to the smell and found it less unpleasant.

Multiply that across hundreds of receptors, each with its own variants, and the result is that your nose is to some degree personal. Two people standing in the same galley can genuinely be having different sensory experiences, and neither is wrong. Arguments about whether something smells good or bad are sometimes arguments about genetics.
How many smells can you tell apart?

For decades, textbooks claimed humans can distinguish about 10,000 odors. Nobody had actually tested it. In 2014, a team at Rockefeller University led by Caroline Bushdid and Andreas Keller tried. They mixed together dozens of odor molecules in different combinations and asked people whether pairs of mixtures smelled the same or different. From the results, they calculated that humans can discriminate at least one trillion olfactory stimuli. The headline went everywhere.

Then two critiques landed. In 2015, Richard Gerkin and Jason Castro, and separately the Caltech neuroscientist Markus Meister, showed that the math behind the estimate was fragile. Gerkin and Castro found the same framework could produce numbers many orders of magnitude bigger or smaller from the same data, and that the formula actually gave an upper bound, not a lower one. Meister called the claim wrong outright. In 2024, Science published an erratum to the original paper.

blocks.title: The trillion-smells debate

left.head: Bushdid et al., 2014
items: Tested real people on odor mixtures
Estimated at least 1 trillion discriminable smells
Challenged the untested 10,000 figure
Widely reported as fact

right.head: Critics, 2015
items: Estimate depends heavily on modeling assumptions
Same data can give wildly different totals
Formula gives a ceiling, not a floor
The true number is still unknown

blocks.text: The honest summary is that nobody knows how many smells humans can tell apart. It is probably far more than the old textbook number, which was never measured either. The bigger lesson is about extraordinary claims built on a chain of calculations. When the final number is enormous, check how much of it comes from the data and how much from the math in between.
Smell, flavor and health

Most of what you call taste is actually smell. Your tongue detects only a handful of basic qualities: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savory. Everything else, the difference between a strawberry and a cherry or between coffee and burnt toast, comes from odor molecules rising from your mouth to the back of your nose as you chew and swallow. Hold your nose while eating a jelly bean and you get sweetness with almost no flavor. Let go and the flavor rushes in.

Your nose also tunes itself out. Smell adapts quickly to any steady odor, which is why you stop noticing the smell of your own home, your own clothes or a space you live in. Sailors often find that their gear carries a distinctive smell that people ashore notice right away while the crew stopped registering it long ago. That is not a defect. A system built to detect change is more useful than one that keeps reporting the same background.

Smell loss became a household topic during the COVID-19 pandemic, when a sudden inability to smell turned out to be one of the most distinctive early signs of infection. Most people recovered their sense of smell over weeks or months, but some were left with a reduced or distorted sense, where familiar things like coffee or toothpaste smelled wrong or even disgusting. Many of them discovered for the first time how much of daily life, from appetite to mood to noticing smoke or spoiled food, quietly depends on a working nose.

Smell may also be a window into overall health. In a 2014 study of more than 3,000 older Americans aged 57 to 85, Jayant Pinto and colleagues at the University of Chicago tested smell and then tracked who died over the next five years. Even after accounting for age, disease, nutrition, cognition, smoking and other factors, people who could not smell at all had more than three times the odds of dying within five years compared with those whose smell was normal.

items.label: Odds of death within 5 years for older adults who had lost their sense of smell
Adults aged 57 to 85 in the study

blocks.source: Pinto et al., PLoS One, 2014

blocks.text: That does not mean losing your sense of smell kills you. The researchers suggested it may be a marker of something broader, such as slowing cell renewal or accumulated environmental damage. Olfactory sensory neurons are among the few neurons in the body that are routinely replaced throughout life, so a nose that stops working may be a sign that repair systems elsewhere are struggling too. It is a correlation in older adults, not a diagnosis. Still, a sudden or lasting change in your sense of smell, whether after an illness, a head injury or for no clear reason, is worth mentioning to medical.
Training the sense you ignore

If human smell is better than its reputation, the gap between what we can do and what we actually do is mostly a matter of attention. Wine tasters, perfumers and chefs are not born with special noses. They practice naming and comparing smells until distinctions that once blurred together become obvious. The Berkeley scent-tracking volunteers improved just by doing the task a few times.

That reframes smell as a skill, not a fixed trait. You can try it any time: when you eat, pause and try to name what you are smelling rather than just tasting. When you walk into a space, notice the first impression before adaptation erases it. A sense you have ignored your whole life is still sitting there, wired straight into your memory and emotions, waiting for you to use it on purpose. In a world that trains your eyes and ears constantly, through screens and headsets, the nose may be the one sense with the most unused headroom. It is also the only one that can still surprise you with a memory you forgot you had.

takeaways: The idea that humans smell poorly came from a 19th-century anatomist's theory, not from tests.
About 400 receptor types combine like letters to encode a huge range of odors.
Smell signals skip the thalamus at first and reach emotion and memory areas directly.
The famous claim of 1 trillion distinguishable smells was mathematically fragile; the true number is unknown.
Most flavor is smell, and lasting smell changes are worth mentioning to medical.

title: The Wire With No Resistance
dek: Superconductors carry current with zero loss and push magnetic fields out of themselves. They already run MRI machines and particle colliders. The hunt for one that works at room temperature has produced Nobel Prizes, a 40-year-old mystery and some spectacular failures.

blocks.text: In 1963, two physicists named John File and Robert Mills ran a current through a loop of superconducting wire, disconnected the power supply, and watched the current keep going. They measured the magnetic field it produced, waited, and measured again. The decline was so small it was hard to detect at all. Their results, published in Physical Review Letters, and later experiments like theirs set a lower limit on how long such a current could circulate: more than 100,000 years.

Anyone who has worked with electrical systems knows how strange that is. Every conductor you have ever touched has resistance. Current through it turns some of its energy into heat, which is why cables are sized for load, why breakers trip and why switchboards need cooling. A superconductor has exactly zero DC resistance. Not low. Zero. Once a current is flowing in a closed superconducting loop, there is nothing to slow it down.

That property, and an even weirder one involving magnetic fields, has made superconductors one of the most important and most frustrating materials in physics. They power the strongest magnets on Earth. They have also spent more than a century refusing to work at anything close to room temperature.
The day the resistance vanished

The story starts with cold. In 1908, the Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes became the first person to liquefy helium, reaching temperatures a few degrees above absolute zero. He then started measuring how the electrical resistance of metals changed at those temperatures. Scientists expected resistance to drop smoothly as things got colder, or perhaps to rise again near absolute zero.

On April 8, 1911, his team cooled a sample of solid mercury to about 4.2 kelvin, roughly minus 269 degrees Celsius, and the resistance did not drop smoothly. It vanished abruptly. Onnes called the new state superconductivity, and it earned him the 1913 Nobel Prize in Physics. Over the following decades, many other metals and alloys turned out to superconduct, each below its own critical temperature, usually called Tc.

In 1933, Walther Meissner and Robert Ochsenfeld found the second signature. When a material becomes superconducting, it actively pushes magnetic fields out of its interior. This Meissner effect is why a superconductor can float above a magnet, or a magnet above it. It also proves that a superconductor is not just a very good conductor. A perfect conductor would merely trap whatever field was already inside it. A superconductor expels it. It is a distinct state of matter, as different from a normal metal as ice is from water.

Two tests separate a real superconductor from a lookalike: resistance must drop to zero, and the material must expel magnetic fields. Plenty of materials show one hint of either. Real ones show both, clearly, and reproducibly.
Why electrons stop bumping into things

For almost 50 years nobody could explain superconductivity. Then, in 1957, John Bardeen, Leon Cooper and Robert Schrieffer published what became known as BCS theory, and it earned them the 1972 Nobel Prize. It was Bardeen's second physics Nobel; his first was for co-inventing the transistor.

Normally, resistance happens because electrons moving through a metal scatter off vibrations of the atomic lattice and off defects, losing energy each time. BCS theory showed that at low temperatures, those same lattice vibrations can do something surprising. An electron moving through the lattice slightly pulls the positive ions toward it, leaving a faint wake of extra positive charge. A second electron is attracted to that wake. The result is a loose partnership called a Cooper pair.

Cooper pairs behave very differently from lone electrons. Huge numbers of them can pile into a single shared quantum state and move together, like one coordinated fluid. To scatter one pair, you would have to break it apart, which costs a minimum amount of energy known as the energy gap. At low enough temperatures, the ordinary bumps and vibrations in the metal simply do not have that much energy to give. So nothing slows the flow down. Heat the metal up, and thermal vibrations break the pairs apart, and resistance comes back.

blocks.title: How a conventional superconductor works (BCS theory)
items: An electron passing through the metal tugs the nearby positive ions slightly toward it.
That shift leaves a brief region of extra positive charge in its wake.
A second electron is attracted to the wake, forming a weakly bound Cooper pair.
Vast numbers of pairs condense into one shared quantum state and move together.
Breaking a pair costs a minimum energy; when the metal is cold enough, nothing supplies it, so current flows with zero resistance.

blocks.text: The 1986 surprise and the record board

By the 1970s, progress had stalled. According to the Nobel committee's later summary, the best superconductor known by 1973 worked at about minus 250 degrees Celsius, or about 23 kelvin. Many physicists suspected BCS-type superconductivity could not go much higher. Everything practical needed liquid helium, which is expensive, scarce and hard to handle.

Then, in 1986, Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller at IBM's research lab in Zurich tried something unfashionable: ceramic copper oxides, materials that are normally poor conductors. A barium-lanthanum-copper oxide superconducted at a temperature about 12 degrees higher than the old record. The field exploded. Within months, labs around the world were mixing ceramics. In early 1987, a group led by Maw-Kuen Wu and Paul Chu reported a yttrium-barium-copper oxide that superconducted at 93 kelvin. Bednorz and Müller received the Nobel Prize in 1987, one of the fastest awards in its history.

The 93 kelvin number mattered because it is above 77 kelvin, the boiling point of liquid nitrogen. Liquid nitrogen is cheap and plentiful; it is made from air. For the first time, superconductors could be cooled with something you can buy by the tankful instead of rare helium. In 1993, Andreas Schilling and colleagues pushed the record for a mercury-based copper oxide to about 133 kelvin. More than three decades later, that is still the highest confirmed critical temperature for a superconductor at ordinary pressure.

blocks.title: Record superconducting temperatures (Tc)
blocks.note: Mercury, the first superconductor, managed about 4.2 K in 1911. Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K; room temperature is about 293 K. The two hydrides only work squeezed in diamond anvils at roughly a million or more atmospheres.
blocks.source: Nobel Prize in Physics 1987 press release; Wu et al., PRL, 1987; Schilling et al., Nature, 1993; Drozdov et al., Nature, 2019 (which also reports the 2015 H3S result)

blocks.text: Here is the part that should bother you: nobody fully understands why the copper oxides work. They do form pairs, but the pairing does not seem to come mainly from lattice vibrations the way BCS theory describes. Magnetic interactions among the copper atoms are thought to be involved, but after nearly 40 years and many thousands of papers, there is still no agreed theory. It is one of the biggest unsolved problems in physics, and the lack of a theory is a big reason no one can simply design a room-temperature version.
Squeezed hydrogen, retracted papers and LK-99

The newest records came from a different direction. Theory predicted that hydrogen-rich compounds, crushed to enormous pressures, should be excellent conventional superconductors because hydrogen's light atoms vibrate at high frequencies. In 2015, Alexander Drozdov, Mikhail Eremets and colleagues reported superconductivity at 203 kelvin in sulfur hydride. In 2019, the same group reported about 250 kelvin in lanthanum hydride at roughly 170 gigapascals, around 1.7 million times atmospheric pressure. That is nearly as warm as a cold winter day, but only in a speck of material smaller than a grain of sand, crushed between the tips of two diamonds.

The race to reach room temperature also produced some of the most embarrassing episodes in recent physics. A 2020 Nature paper from a group including Ranga Dias at the University of Rochester claimed room-temperature superconductivity in a carbon-sulfur-hydrogen compound under pressure. It was retracted in 2022. A 2023 Nature paper from the same group claimed near-ambient superconductivity in a nitrogen-doped lutetium hydride. It was retracted that November after other scientists raised concerns about the data.

Then came LK-99. In July 2023, a team in South Korea posted preprints claiming that a copper-doped lead apatite superconducted above the boiling point of water at ordinary pressure. Videos of a small fleck of the material partly levitating over a magnet went viral, and amateur and professional labs rushed to replicate it. Within weeks the answer was in. Replication teams found that a copper sulfide impurity in the samples undergoes a structural change that produces a sharp drop in resistivity, mimicking one signature of superconductivity. A team in India that synthesized phase-pure LK-99 found it behaved like an insulator, not a superconductor. No group has confirmed zero resistance or a true Meissner effect in the material.

It would be easy to read these stories as science failing. They are closer to the opposite. The claims were tested quickly and publicly, the two-test rule did its job, and the record board did not change. A result that cannot be reproduced does not survive, no matter how famous the journal or how exciting the video.
Where superconductors already run the show

You do not need room temperature for superconductors to be indispensable. Most hospital MRI scanners use coils of niobium-titanium wire cooled by liquid helium. Because the coil has no resistance, it can carry a large current continuously and hold a steady, powerful magnetic field without a huge electrical bill.

The Large Hadron Collider at CERN is the extreme case. Its 27-kilometer ring uses 1,232 main dipole magnets, each 15 meters long and weighing 35 tonnes, generating fields of about 8.3 tesla with currents of roughly 11,000 amps. CERN says the main magnets run at 1.9 kelvin, colder than outer space, and the cryogenic system needs about 120 tonnes of helium. With ordinary copper magnets, CERN estimates the ring would have to be about 120 kilometers long to reach the same energy.

items.label: Superconducting main dipole magnets in the LHC
Operating temperature, colder than deep space
Field of each dipole, over 100,000 times Earth's field

blocks.source: CERN, Superconducting electromagnets and Cryogenics pages

blocks.text: Superconductors also demand respect. If part of a superconducting magnet warms above its critical temperature, that section suddenly has resistance, and the enormous current flowing through it starts dumping energy as heat. This is called a quench, and protection systems exist to detect it and safely discharge the stored energy. On September 19, 2008, just days after the LHC first circulated beams, a faulty electrical connection between two magnets triggered a quench and an arc. About six tonnes of liquid helium escaped, more than 50 magnets were damaged, and repairs took about 14 months. One bad joint, in a machine worth billions, took the whole thing down.

The LHC incident is an electrician's lesson at the largest scale: the conductor can be perfect and the system can still fail at a connection. Splices, joints and terminations are where high-current systems usually break.

The newest application may be fusion. Copper oxide superconductors can now be made into flat tapes. In 2021, Commonwealth Fusion Systems and MIT tested a large magnet built from such tape that reached 20 tesla, a record for a fusion magnet of its kind. MIT says the technology allows the same performance in a device about 40 times smaller in volume than one using conventional low-temperature superconductors. Whether compact fusion plants pan out is another question, but the magnets are real.
What room temperature would and would not change

A practical room-temperature, ambient-pressure superconductor would be a big deal. It could make powerful magnets cheap to run, shrink MRI machines, and allow power cables that carry large currents without resistive loss. But it would not be magic. Every superconductor also has a maximum current density and a maximum magnetic field above which it stops superconducting. Many good superconductors are brittle ceramics that are hard to turn into wire. And grid losses are not only about resistance in lines; transformers, switching and conversion all matter too.

The deeper lesson is about how progress actually happens. The biggest jump in the history of the field came from two researchers trying materials everyone else considered unpromising. The best-understood superconductors are the least useful at warm temperatures, and the most useful ones are still not understood. And the most hyped results of the past five years were the ones that fell apart. Being able to tell those apart, by asking whether both tests were passed and whether anyone else can reproduce the result, is a skill worth more than any single headline.

takeaways: Superconductors have exactly zero DC resistance and expel magnetic fields; both signs must be present and reproducible.
BCS theory explains conventional superconductors through Cooper pairs, but the copper oxide high-temperature superconductors are still not understood after nearly 40 years.
The ambient-pressure record (about 133 K, set in 1993) still stands; warmer results need extreme pressure.
Room-temperature claims in 2020 and 2023 were retracted, and LK-99's signals came from a copper sulfide impurity.
In real systems, failures often happen at connections: the LHC's 2008 shutdown started with one faulty joint.
