title: Worlds Nobody Has Seen
dek: There are more than 6,400 confirmed planets around other stars, and almost none of them has ever been seen directly. Here is how you find a world from a wobble, a shadow, and a signal of 84 parts per million.

blocks.text: In 1994 no one had confirmed a single planet orbiting a normal, Sun-like star other than our own. As of November 5, 2026, the NASA Exoplanet Archive lists **6,451 confirmed planets** in 4,847 star systems. Almost none of them has ever been photographed. They are known the way a sonar operator knows a contact he will never lay eyes on: by what they do to something we *can* measure.

That is the core trick of the field, and it is worth understanding properly, because it shows how science gets real answers out of signals that look hopeless. A planet is a dim speck next to a star that outshines it by a factor of millions to billions, sitting so close to it in the sky that the two blur together. So astronomers mostly stopped trying to look at planets. They learned to watch the star instead and read the planet off the star's behavior.

items.label: Confirmed exoplanets (NASA Exoplanet Archive, checked Nov 5, 2026)
Host stars with at least one known planet
Planets that share their star with other known planets

blocks.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive, Planetary Systems Composite table, queried Nov 5, 2026

blocks.text: The wobble: weighing a planet you can't see

A planet doesn't simply orbit its star. Both orbit their shared center of mass, so the star traces a small loop of its own. Seen from Earth, the star moves slightly toward us and then away, again and again, once per orbit. That motion stretches and squeezes the star's light by the Doppler effect, shifting thousands of dark absorption lines in its spectrum a tiny bit red, then a tiny bit blue.

The numbers are brutal. Run the orbital mechanics for our own solar system and Jupiter drags the Sun around at about **12.5 meters per second**, about the top speed of an elite sprinter. Earth moves the Sun by only about **9 centimeters per second**. To detect an Earth twin this way you need to measure a star's speed, from across light-years, to better than a slow crawl, while the star's own boiling surface jitters by more than that.

The method still delivered the moment that launched the field. In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz reported a planet around the Sun-like star 51 Pegasi. It had at least half of Jupiter's mass and whipped around its star every 4.2 days, far inside where Mercury sits. Theory said giant planets should form far out, where ice is plentiful, so the first planet found broke the textbook. That discovery earned them a share of the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.

The lesson theorists took from 51 Pegasi b reshaped planetary science: planets don't necessarily stay where they are born. A young giant can form far out and then spiral inward, dragged by the disk of gas it grew in, or get flung around by gravitational fights with its siblings. Our own solar system now looks less like the template and more like one outcome among many. A model that worked perfectly for the only example you had turned out to be a sample size of one.

Precision has kept climbing. In 2022 a team using the ESPRESSO spectrograph in Chile reported another planet around Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, from a wobble with an amplitude of just **39 centimeters per second**, slower than a casual stroll. The planet has at least a quarter of Earth's mass, about twice the mass of Mars. One catch is built into the physics: the wobble only reveals the part of the motion along our line of sight, so it gives a *minimum* mass, not the true mass.

This is also why so many headline planets orbit small red dwarfs. A lighter star gets yanked around harder by the same planet, and a smaller star is blocked more by the same disk. TRAPPIST-1, the host of seven Earth-sized worlds, is only about 12 percent of the Sun's width. Its planet TRAPPIST-1 e, a bit smaller than Earth, dims it by about half a percent per transit, roughly sixty times deeper than Earth's dip across the Sun. Small stars turn an impossible measurement into a merely hard one.

Credit where it's due: the first confirmed planets outside the solar system weren't found by either famous method. In 1992 Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail found planets orbiting a pulsar, a dead star whose radio ticks arrived early and late as planets tugged it around.
The shadow: a dip of 84 parts per million

The second method waits for a planet to pass in front of its star. During that transit the planet blocks a slice of starlight, and the star dims by a fraction equal to the planet's disk area over the star's disk area. That is the ratio of their radii, squared. For Jupiter crossing the Sun the dip is about 1 percent. For Earth it is about **84 parts per million**, like one pixel going dark on a screen of twelve thousand.

Geometry adds a second problem. A transit only happens if the orbit is lined up almost edge-on to us. For an Earth-Sun setup, the odds of a random alignment are about the Sun's radius divided by Earth's orbital radius, roughly **half a percent**. So you can't watch one star and hope. You watch a crowd of stars, continuously, for years, because you need to see the same dip repeat on schedule at least a few times before you believe it.

That is exactly what NASA's Kepler telescope was built to do. Launched in March 2009, it stared at one patch of sky in the constellation Cygnus and tracked the brightness of about 150,000 stars without blinking. Kepler is why the discovery chart below has those enormous spikes in 2014 and 2016: those were years when hundreds of Kepler candidates at a time were confirmed using statistical validation instead of one-by-one follow-up. TESS, launched in April 2018, now scans nearly the whole sky for planets around brighter, closer stars that are easier to study afterward.

blocks.title: Exoplanets confirmed per discovery year
blocks.note: 2026 is partial (through Nov 5). Spikes in 2014 and 2016 are bulk confirmations of Kepler candidates.
blocks.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive, queried Nov 5, 2026

blocks.text: Transits come with a trap. Lots of things can make a star dip: a pair of stars eclipsing each other in the background, starspots, instrument glitches. A large share of the effort in this field goes into ruling out impostors. The workflow below is roughly how a flicker becomes a planet.

blocks.title: From flicker to confirmed planet
items: A survey telescope logs a star's brightness every few minutes for months or years.
Software flags repeating dips with the same depth, duration and spacing.
Analysts rule out impostors such as eclipsing binary stars blended into the same pixels.
Follow-up spectra measure the wobble to get the planet's mass, or statistics show a planet is far more likely than any false alarm.
The planet is published and added to the archive with its radius, period and, if known, mass.

blocks.text: Two methods are better than one
Each method on its own leaves you half-blind. A transit gives you the planet's **size** but not its mass. A wobble gives you a **minimum mass** but not its size.

Get both for the same planet and you have its density, and density is where planets stop being dots and become places. A dense planet is rock and iron. A puffy one is wrapped in thick gas. Something in between might be a water world.

blocks.title: What each main method actually measures

left.head: Transit (shadow)
items: Planet's radius, from the depth of the dip
Orbital period, from the spacing of dips
Works only for edge-on orbits
Favors big planets close to small stars

right.head: Radial velocity (wobble)
items: Planet's minimum mass, from the size of the wobble
Orbital period and shape
Works for most orientations
Favors heavy planets close to quiet stars

blocks.text: The other tricks: lenses, pictures and timing

The two big methods account for nearly 93 percent of known planets, but the rest come from cleverer physics. **Microlensing** uses Einstein's general relativity: when one star drifts almost exactly in front of a more distant one, its gravity bends and focuses the background light, and the background star brightens for a few weeks. If the foreground star has a planet, the planet adds its own brief spike. Each event happens once and never repeats, but it can reveal planets far from their stars and even planets drifting alone between stars, which no other method can catch.

**Direct imaging** is the one method that produces an actual picture. It works best for young, giant planets far from their stars, which still glow in infrared from the heat of their formation. Instruments called coronagraphs block the star's light inside the telescope, a bit like holding your thumb over the Sun to see a bird near it. Only 98 planets have been found this way so far, but each one is a world you can point to. A few dozen more were found by **timing**: a planet tugging on a pulsar's ticks, or on the schedule of a neighbor planet's transits.
Reading another world's air

The transit has one more gift. When a planet crosses its star, a thin ring of starlight passes through the planet's atmosphere on the way to us. Different molecules absorb different colors, so comparing the star's light during and outside the transit gives a spectrum of the planet's air. This is where the James Webb Space Telescope has changed the game. In 2023 Webb measured heat from TRAPPIST-1 b, an Earth-sized planet 40 light-years away, and found it consistent with bare rock and no thick atmosphere.

Webb has also produced the field's loudest argument. In 2025 a Cambridge-led team reported evidence at about **3 sigma** for dimethyl sulfide, a gas that on Earth comes mainly from marine life, in the atmosphere of the sub-Neptune K2-18 b.

Other groups re-analyzed the same public data and pushed back hard. One found that a flat line, meaning no spectral features at all, fit as well or better in five of six tests. Another found that most of their retrievals did not favor the gas. For comparison, particle physicists won't claim a discovery below 5 sigma. The honest status: interesting, unconfirmed, and a live lesson in how extraordinary claims get stress-tested.

blocks.title: How the 6,451 confirmed planets were found
blocks.note: Methods with fewer planets include eclipse timing, pulsar timing and astrometry.
blocks.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive, queried Nov 5, 2026

blocks.text: What the catalog tells us, and what it hides

The headline result is simple: planets are normal. Kepler's statistics showed that most stars have planets, which means the Milky Way holds more planets than stars. And our solar system turns out to be a bit odd. The most common kind of planet Kepler found is something between Earth and Neptune in size, a super-Earth or sub-Neptune, and we don't have one. Many systems pack several planets into orbits tighter than Mercury's.

The question everyone actually cares about is how common Earth-like planets are. A 2020 analysis of Kepler data by Steve Bryson and colleagues estimated that, for stars similar to the Sun, there are between about **0.37 and 0.60** rocky planets in the conservative habitable zone per star. Read the error bars, though: the uncertainty is large because Kepler caught very few small planets on Earth-like orbits. Even the low end means rocky planets in the habitable zone are common, not rare exceptions.

Here is the part worth carrying around. Every chart in this article is a portrait of our *instruments* as much as of the universe. Transits favor big planets close to small stars, because those give deep, frequent dips. Wobbles favor heavy planets on tight orbits. So the catalog is crowded with hot, close-in worlds and nearly empty of true Earth twins, not necessarily because twins are rare, but because they are the hardest things to hear. Astronomers call this selection bias, and correcting for it is half the job.

Flip it around for a moment. Suppose astronomers on a planet a few hundred light-years away pointed instruments like ours at the Sun. Unless their orbit happened to line up edge-on, they would never see Earth transit at all. Their wobble data would show Jupiter clearly, Saturn eventually, and Earth as a whisper buried in the Sun's surface noise. By our current standards, their catalog might list our solar system as a star with a couple of giant planets and nothing that looks like home.

That idea travels well beyond astronomy. Sonar detects loud contacts first. A game's analytics show you the players who stayed, not the ones who quit in the first minute. Whenever you look at data, ask what your detector was built to notice, and what it would have missed even if it was there.

The next leap is already designed: future telescopes aim to block a star's glare and image Earth-sized planets directly, then read their atmospheres for oxygen, water and methane together. For the first time, the question of life elsewhere is an engineering problem with a budget line.

takeaways: As of Nov 5, 2026, NASA's archive lists 6,451 confirmed exoplanets, most found by watching their stars rather than seeing the planets.
Transits give a planet's size; wobbles give its minimum mass; together they give density, which tells rock from gas.
An Earth twin dims its star by about 84 parts per million and moves it about 9 cm/s, which is why true Earth analogs are still so hard to confirm.
Big claims like the K2-18 b biosignature get re-analyzed by independent teams; 3 sigma is a hint, not a discovery.
Every catalog reflects what its detector can notice. Ask what your data would miss.

title: Where Is Everybody?
dek: Enrico Fermi's lunchtime question has collected 75 years of answers. One of the best says the paradox came partly from a math mistake, and that silence is itself a piece of data.

blocks.text: Los Alamos, summer 1950. Four physicists are walking to lunch at Fuller Lodge: Enrico Fermi, Edward Teller, Herbert York and Emil Konopinski. They're joking about a cartoon in that spring's *New Yorker*, which blamed a rash of trash cans vanishing from New York streets on flying saucers. Fermi needles Teller about the odds of anyone proving, within ten years, that a material object can move faster than light. Then, at the table, Fermi suddenly asks a question that made everyone laugh and that nobody has answered since.
But where is everybody?
blocks.by: Enrico Fermi, as recalled by Emil Konopinski (Los Alamos report, 1985)

blocks.text: Fermi was the man who built the first nuclear reactor, Chicago Pile-1, and a famous master of quick estimates. According to York's later account, he went on to run rough numbers on how many Earth-like planets there should be, how likely life and technology were, and how long civilizations last. His conclusion was that we should have been visited long ago and many times over. So why hadn't we been?
The argument in four lines

The paradox isn't really about UFOs. It is a collision between a strong expectation and a blank observation. The expectation goes like this, and every step is now on firmer ground than it was in 1950.

blocks.title: Why the silence is strange
items: Planets are everywhere: NASA's archive lists 6,451 confirmed exoplanets, and Kepler showed most stars have planets.
Earth-sized planets in the habitable zone are common: Kepler data suggest roughly one for every two or three Sun-like stars, with large uncertainty.
Many of those planets had a head start: about 75 percent of stars in the galaxy's habitable zone are older than the Sun.
Spreading through the galaxy should be fast: even at modest speeds, a civilization could settle it in a few million years, a blink compared with those billion-year head starts.
Yet we see no visitors, no probes, no engineering on the sky, and no signals.

blocks.text: The fourth line is the one that bites. In 1975 the astronomer Michael Hart argued that a civilization able to travel between stars could fill the galaxy in a few million years, simply by settling nearby systems and letting each new colony do the same. That is exponential growth, the same math as a viral video. If even one civilization had done this in the billions of years available, it should be everywhere, including here. Hart concluded that there probably aren't any.

Notice that this argument doesn't need starships full of colonists. A civilization could send self-copying robot probes that land, build copies of themselves from local material and send those onward. Even our own Voyager 1, crawling along at about 17 kilometers per second, would need around 75,000 years to cover the distance to the nearest star. That sounds hopeless on a human scale, yet a wave of probes moving that slowly would still sweep the galaxy in a small fraction of the time the oldest planets have existed.
Drake's equation: a way to organize ignorance

In November 1961 the radio astronomer Frank Drake hosted the first scientific meeting on searching for extraterrestrial intelligence at Green Bank, West Virginia. To give the meeting an agenda, he wrote down a product of factors that has been on posters ever since: the number of civilizations we could detect, N, equals the rate of star formation times the fraction of stars with planets, times habitable planets per system, times the fractions that develop life, then intelligence, then detectable technology, times how long such civilizations keep broadcasting.

It is a beautiful framework and a terrible calculator. In 1961, only the first term was reasonably known. Thanks to exoplanet surveys, the planet terms are now known to within a factor of two or three, according to the SETI Institute. Everything after that, life, intelligence, technology and lifespan, is still essentially a guess. Drake himself suggested an answer around 10,000 civilizations in our galaxy. Other researchers have published answers from less than one to millions.
The Drake Equation is a wonderful way to organize our ignorance.
blocks.by: Jill Tarter, SETI astronomer

blocks.text: The math mistake hiding in the paradox

In 2018, three Oxford researchers, Anders Sandberg, Eric Drexler and Toby Ord, pointed out something that seems obvious once you hear it. People plug a single best guess into each term of Drake's equation and multiply. But when you are uncertain about a quantity across many orders of magnitude, a single guess throws away the most important information you have: how uncertain you are.

Their toy example makes it vivid. Imagine nine factors, each with a best guess of 0.1, multiplied across 100 billion stars. The point-estimate answer is 100 civilizations, and the chance of an empty galaxy is about 10 to the minus 44th power. Effectively zero, so an empty sky is a paradox.

Now admit you only know each factor lies somewhere between 0 and 0.2. Run that uncertainty through a simulation and the galaxy comes out **empty about 21 percent of the time**. Same averages; completely different conclusion.

They then did it properly, building probability distributions for each factor from the scientific literature, with special attention to the chance of life arising at all, which could plausibly be anywhere from near-certain to astronomically rare. Their model's *mean* number of civilizations in the galaxy was about 27 million. Its *median* was 0.32. Both numbers describe the same distribution. The mean is dragged up by a long optimistic tail, while the typical outcome is less than one civilization per galaxy.

blocks.title: Chance we are alone in the Milky Way (Sandberg, Drexler & Ord)
blocks.note: Last two bars update the model on the fact that we see no one; the range depends on how strong that evidence is judged to be.
blocks.source: Sandberg, Drexler & Ord, 'Dissolving the Fermi Paradox', arXiv 2018

blocks.text: Their model gave about a **52 percent** chance that we're alone in the Milky Way, and about 38 percent that we're alone in the entire observable universe. Then they took the silence into account as evidence. Depending on how much weight you give it, the odds of being alone in the galaxy rise to somewhere between 53 and 99.6 percent. Their verdict: once you are honest about uncertainty, an empty sky isn't surprising. The paradox, they argue, mostly dissolves.

The transferable lesson: when uncertainty spans orders of magnitude, the average is a liar. A few wildly optimistic scenarios can inflate the mean while the typical outcome is tiny. The same is true of startup returns, YouTube views and Roblox game revenue.
If they exist, where are they? The answer menu

Not everyone accepts that the paradox is dissolved, and the question of *why* life might be rare is interesting on its own. The explanations fall into two camps: life or intelligence is genuinely rare, or it is out there and we're not seeing it.

blocks.title: Two families of answers

left.head: They're rare or gone
items: Life's origin is a fluke that almost never happens
Complex cells, brains or technology are huge hurdles
Civilizations tend to destroy themselves
Habitable planets are rarer than they look

right.head: They exist, but we don't see them
items: Distances and timing: we're early, or they're too far
They don't expand or don't broadcast
Their signals don't look like what we search for
We've barely searched

blocks.text: The economist Robin Hanson framed the first camp in 1998 as the **Great Filter**. Somewhere between dead rock and a civilization spreading across the stars, there must be at least one step that is extremely unlikely, because we see no one who made it all the way. The unsettling question is *where* that filter sits. If it is behind us, say the origin of life or of complex cells, then we are rare and lucky. If it is ahead of us, then most civilizations that get as far as we have don't survive what comes next.

That logic produces one of the strangest ideas in science: finding fossil microbes on Mars would be bad news. Two independent origins of life in one solar system would suggest life starts easily, which pushes the filter forward, toward our own future. A dead Mars, by the same reasoning, is mildly reassuring.

There is a hint about where the hard steps might be, and it comes from Earth's own timeline. Life shows up early in the geological record, but complex animals and then intelligence arrive late, near the end of the window in which Earth will stay habitable as the Sun slowly brightens. Physicist Brandon Carter argued decades ago that this pattern is what you'd expect if evolution had to pass through a few extremely unlikely "critical steps." Later work has complicated the picture: a 2022 study by Andrew Snyder-Beattie and Michael Bonsall showed that repeated catastrophes, which can undo evolutionary progress, can mimic or hide such steps. The timeline is suggestive, not decisive.

Hanson and colleagues later added a twist called **grabby aliens**. If some civilizations expand fast and visibly reshape their region of space, they would quickly fill the volume around them and prevent new civilizations like ours from appearing there. That would explain why we find ourselves so *early* in cosmic history: later on, the grabby ones will have taken everything. Their model estimates that such civilizations may already control 40 to 50 percent of the universe's volume, and that we might meet one in somewhere between 200 million and 2 billion years. It's speculative, but it's testable in principle, which is more than most answers can claim.

And then there is the darkest option, popularized by Liu Cixin's novel *The Dark Forest*: everyone is out there and everyone is hiding, because in a universe where you can't verify anyone's intentions, revealing yourself is dangerous. It is game theory applied to galaxies. It is more thought experiment than scientific hypothesis, since it's hard to see how you would ever test it. But anyone who has served on a submarine already understands the core point: being quiet is a choice, and the quietest platform in the ocean is the one you never hear.
Have we actually looked?

Before deciding the sky is empty, it's fair to ask how hard we've listened. Not very, it turns out. In 2018 Jason Wright and colleagues estimated how much of the possible search space for radio signals had been covered, counting directions, frequencies, sensitivities and more. Their answer: the fraction searched is comparable to the volume of a large hot tub compared with all of Earth's oceans. If you dipped a hot tub into the sea and found no fish, you wouldn't conclude the ocean was empty.

There is also the matter of what a signal would even look like. The most famous candidate, the Wow! signal recorded by Ohio State's Big Ear radio telescope in August 1977, was a strong narrowband burst that never repeated, which leaves it permanently unexplained and permanently unconvincing. Modern searches have widened the net beyond radio: astronomers look for laser flashes, for the waste heat that giant energy-harvesting structures would emit in infrared, and, with telescopes like Webb, for industrial gases in exoplanet atmospheres.

The largest modern search, Breakthrough Listen, published results in 2020 covering 1,327 nearby stars observed with big radio telescopes in West Virginia and Australia. After removing interference from human sources, there were **zero** candidates. That rules out powerful transmitters beamed our way from those particular stars at those frequencies. It says nothing about weaker signals, other frequencies, or the hundreds of billions of other stars in the galaxy.
Why the answer matters down here

The Fermi paradox looks like a question about aliens. It is really a question about us, and about how to reason when evidence is thin. The honest scorecard is this: we know planets are common; we have no idea how often life starts; and our search has barely begun. Strong opinions in either direction outrun the data.

But the Great Filter gives the question real stakes. If the hard step is behind us, then intelligent life may be vanishingly rare, and what happens on this one planet carries enormous weight. If the hard step is ahead of us, then surviving it is the most important project there is. Either way the practical conclusion is the same: don't count on a universe full of others to make our choices matter. They already do.

There is something almost freeing in that. Fermi's question started as a lunchtime joke among men who had just built the most dangerous technology in history, and it has turned into one of the most serious questions science can ask about the future. The answer may arrive in your lifetime: a biosignature in an exoplanet's air, a microbe on Mars or Europa, or a signal that repeats. Or it may never come. Either outcome would tell us something about our place in the universe.

Fermi's question still works because it treats silence as data. In any field, the absence of an expected signal tells you something; the hard part is figuring out whether it's telling you about the world or about the limits of your detector.

takeaways: Fermi asked 'where is everybody?' at lunch at Los Alamos in 1950; the paradox is a clash between a strong expectation and an empty sky.
Planets are common and many are older than Earth, but the odds of life, intelligence and technology are still unknown.
Sandberg, Drexler and Ord showed that honest uncertainty gives a substantial chance, roughly 53 to 99.6 percent after accounting for the silence, that we're alone in the galaxy.
When uncertainty spans orders of magnitude, the median matters more than the mean.
We've searched only a hot tub's worth of the cosmic ocean. Silence so far is weak evidence, not proof.

title: The Day We Heard Two Black Holes Collide
dek: In 2015 a pair of machines in Louisiana and Washington felt space itself stretch by less than a thousandth of a proton's width. Since then, gravitational waves have become a new sense for astronomy, with hundreds of cosmic collisions recorded.

blocks.text: At 09:50:45 UTC on September 14, 2015, a signal lasting about a fifth of a second passed through two machines 3,000 km apart, one in Livingston, Louisiana, and one in Hanford, Washington. It arrived at Livingston first and at Hanford 7 thousandths of a second later. On a plot it looked like a wiggle that got faster and stronger, sweeping upward in frequency from 35 to 250 cycles per second, then abruptly stopped. Turned into sound, it is a short rising *whoop*, which physicists call a chirp.

That chirp was the sound of two black holes, each roughly 30 times the mass of the Sun, spiraling into each other and merging about 1.3 billion light years away. In the last fraction of a second, the collision converted about three Suns' worth of mass into pure energy, released not as light but as ripples in the shape of space itself. For a brief instant it outshone every star in the observable universe combined, and none of that power was visible to any telescope.

Albert Einstein had predicted these ripples in 1916 and doubted anyone would ever detect them. He had good reason. By the time they reached Earth, the waves from this cosmic catastrophe stretched and squeezed the planet by an amount smaller than a thousandth of the width of a proton.
What a gravitational wave actually is

In general relativity, gravity is not a force pulling through space; it is the shape of space and time. Mass curves spacetime, and objects follow the curves. When massive objects accelerate, especially when two of them whirl around each other, they send out ripples in that curvature, traveling at the speed of light. A gravitational wave passing through you stretches you slightly in one direction while squeezing you in the perpendicular direction, then reverses, over and over.

The size of that effect is called the strain: the fractional change in length. For the 2015 event, it peaked at about 1 part in 10^21. To put that in perspective, stretch the distance from Earth to the Sun by 1 part in 10^21 and it changes by roughly the width of an atom. Nothing in ordinary experience comes close to being that small. Building a machine to measure it was one of the hardest engineering problems physicists have ever taken on.

Why so small? Because spacetime is incredibly stiff. Shaking it takes enormous masses moving at a good fraction of the speed of light, and even then the ripples weaken the farther they travel, falling off with distance. Two Suns orbiting each other slowly would make waves too faint to ever notice. Only the most extreme objects in nature, black holes and neutron stars locked in tight orbits in their final seconds, produce waves strong enough to detect from across the universe. That is also why the signal is a chirp: as the pair loses energy to the waves, it spirals closer, orbits faster, and the pitch and loudness rise until the two objects merge.

blocks.title: How LIGO measures a stretch smaller than a proton
items: A laser beam is split in two and sent down two 4 km arms at right angles to each other.
Each beam bounces between mirrors hundreds of times, which effectively makes the arms far longer.
The beams are recombined so that, normally, their light waves cancel and almost nothing reaches the detector.
A passing gravitational wave lengthens one arm and shortens the other by a tiny amount.
The cancellation becomes imperfect, a flicker of light leaks out, and its pattern traces the wave.
A second detector thousands of kilometers away must see the same pattern within milliseconds.

blocks.text: The instrument is an interferometer, a design over a century old, scaled up to an absurd degree. Each LIGO site has two arms, each 4 km long, inside some of the largest ultra-high vacuum systems ever built. The mirrors are 40 kg slabs of ultra-pure glass hung from glass fibers in multi-stage pendulums, so that ground vibration from trucks, ocean waves and earthquakes is filtered out before it reaches them. After a major upgrade finished in 2015, called Advanced LIGO, the detectors could sense a change in arm length smaller than one ten-thousandth the diameter of a proton.
Why one detector is never enough

When your instrument is that sensitive, almost everything is noise. A logging truck, a thunderstorm, a hiccup in the power supply or a stray magnetic pulse can all wiggle the mirrors. That is why LIGO has two sites, separated by about 3,000 km. Local disturbances will not show up at both at the same moment. A real gravitational wave, traveling at light speed, has to appear at both within about 10 milliseconds and with matching shapes.

This idea, requiring agreement between independent channels before you believe a signal, will be familiar to anyone who has worked with protection systems built on coincidence logic. One channel tripping might be a bad sensor. Two independent channels agreeing is a different story. LIGO pushed the idea to the extreme: for the 2015 event, the team estimated that noise would produce something that strong and that well matched by chance less than once in 203,000 years.

items.label: Masses of the two black holes, in Suns
Mass converted to gravitational-wave energy
Peak strain: the fractional stretch of space at Earth

blocks.source: LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo, Physical Review Letters, 2016

blocks.text: The masses reveal the most striking part of the bookkeeping. The two black holes had about 36 and 29 times the mass of the Sun. The black hole they made had about 62. The missing 3 solar masses did not vanish; they left as energy in the waves, via Einstein's E = mc^2. The discovery was announced in February 2016, and three of the project's founders, Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish, shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Trust, but test the people too

A detector this sensitive raises a darker question: how do you know you are not fooling yourself? Scientists who have spent decades hunting a signal badly want to find one, and wanting a result is how good people talk themselves into bad conclusions. LIGO's answer was to attack its own analysts. A small group had the ability to secretly inject fake signals into the detectors by physically nudging the mirrors, and nobody else knew whether a given event was real or planted.

In 2010, during an earlier version of the detectors, the collaboration found an apparently strong event, analyzed it for months, and wrote up a paper. Only then was the envelope opened: it had been a blind injection. The exercise proved the analysis pipeline could find a real signal, and it proved the team would follow the process rather than their hopes. So when the 2015 event arrived, one of the first checks was whether it was another planted test. It was not; the injection system had not been in use. Months of further checks followed before anyone announced anything.

This is one of the most useful habits in any technical field. Test your own detection system with known fakes, under conditions where you cannot tell the difference. Drills work the same way. If a process only works when everyone knows it is a test, it does not really work.
When gravity and light arrived together

Black hole mergers give off no light, so for the first two years LIGO was hearing events no one could see. That changed on August 17, 2017. LIGO and the European Virgo detector in Italy caught a much longer, gentler signal, about 100 seconds as it swept through their frequency band, from two neutron stars, collapsed stellar cores each a little more massive than the Sun. Just 1.7 seconds after the merger, NASA's Fermi satellite detected a burst of gamma rays from the same patch of sky.

Because three detectors had recorded the gravitational wave, astronomers could narrow its location to a region of about 28 square degrees. Within hours, telescopes found a new glowing source in a galaxy about 130 million light years away. Around 70 observatories, using every kind of light from radio waves to gamma rays, then watched it fade over weeks. It was the birth of *multi-messenger astronomy*, observing one event with completely different kinds of signals.

That single event settled several questions at once. The near-simultaneous arrival of gravity and light after a 130-million-year trip showed that gravitational waves travel at the speed of light to extraordinary precision, ruling out a whole family of alternative gravity theories. It confirmed that neutron star mergers produce short gamma-ray bursts. And the glow of the debris showed signs of freshly made heavy elements, strong evidence that collisions like this are a major source of the universe's gold and platinum. Some of the metal in a wedding ring was likely forged in an event like this.
From one event to hundreds

The first detection was a single event. Now they are routine. LIGO, Virgo and Japan's KAGRA detector run in long observing campaigns, and each round of upgrades lets them hear farther, which means a much larger volume of space and many more events. The official catalog grew from 11 confident detections after the first two runs, to 90 after the third, to 218 when the catalog covering the first part of the fourth run was released in 2025.

blocks.title: Gravitational-wave catalog size
blocks.note: Each catalog includes all earlier ones. Most events are black hole pairs.
blocks.source: LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration, GWTC-1 (2019), GWTC-3 (2023), GWTC-4.0 (2025)

blocks.text: With hundreds of events, the questions change from "does this exist?" to population science: how many black holes of each size exist, how they spin, and how they pair up. The latest catalog includes a pair, GW231123, that is probably the most massive binary observed so far, with a heavier black hole of roughly 137 solar masses. That is a puzzle. Standard stellar physics predicts that stars in a certain mass range blow themselves apart completely instead of collapsing, so black holes this heavy are hard to make from a single dying star. One popular explanation is that some of these heavyweights are second-generation black holes, the products of earlier mergers that went on to merge again in crowded star clusters.

There is a rhythm to this that is worth noticing. The first detection proved a new kind of sense works. The next hundred turned a curiosity into statistics. Discovery often works like that: the spectacular first result gets the headline, but the steady accumulation of ordinary data is where most of the knowledge comes from.
The next ears

Ground-based detectors hear only a narrow band of frequencies, roughly tens to thousands of cycles per second, which suits merging black holes a few dozen times the Sun's mass. Bigger, slower systems sing at lower notes that are buried under Earth's seismic rumble. To hear them, you need to leave Earth.

In January 2024 the European Space Agency formally adopted LISA, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna. It will be three spacecraft flying in a triangle 2.5 million km on a side, trailing Earth around the Sun and bouncing lasers between them, with launch planned for 2035. LISA should hear supermassive black holes merging at the centers of colliding galaxies and thousands of white dwarf pairs in our own galaxy. At even lower frequencies, radio astronomers use pulsars, spinning dead stars that tick like clocks, as a galaxy-sized detector. In 2023 the NANOGrav collaboration reported evidence, from 15 years of timing 67 pulsars, for a faint background hum of gravitational waves, likely from many supermassive black hole pairs.

Neutron star merger GW170817 seen in gravitational waves and light
Pulsar timing finds evidence for a low-frequency background hum
GWTC-4.0 catalog reaches 218 confident detections
Planned launch of ESA's LISA space detector

blocks.text: For all of human history, astronomy meant collecting light: visible at first, then radio, X-rays, infrared. Light is great, but it is easily blocked by dust and gas, and many of the most violent events in the universe, like black holes colliding, emit almost none. Gravitational waves pass through everything, carry information straight from the heart of the event, and can be heard from objects that are perfectly dark. Astronomers like to say that before 2015 they could only see the universe, and now they can also hear it. The deeper point is that the universe was shaking the whole time. It took a century of work, and a machine sensitive to a ten-thousandth of a proton, before anyone could notice.

takeaways: Gravitational waves are ripples in the shape of space, made when massive objects like black holes whirl around each other and merge.
LIGO measures arm-length changes smaller than a ten-thousandth of a proton's width, and needs two distant detectors to agree before trusting a signal.
The first detection turned 3 solar masses into wave energy; a 2017 neutron star merger showed these collisions forge heavy elements like gold.
The catalog has grown from 11 confident events to 218, turning a single discovery into population science.
Requiring independent channels to agree is how you separate a real signal from noise, in a physics lab or on a watch station.

title: The Reactor That Runs Itself
dek: A star is a fusion reactor with a built-in negative feedback loop. Its whole life story, from steady burn to white dwarf or supernova, is about what happens when that thermostat finally fails.

blocks.text: Every second, the Sun turns about **4.26 million tonnes** of its own mass into energy. That sounds ferocious until you divide by the Sun's mass. NASA's fact sheet puts its average output at about **0.19 milliwatts per kilogram**. A person eating the standard 2,000-calorie day runs at roughly 97 watts, which for a 70-kilogram body is about 1.4 watts per kilogram. Kilogram for kilogram, you put out several thousand times more heat than the Sun does.

So the Sun isn't intense. It is enormous and extraordinarily patient. Understanding why it burns so slowly, and why it doesn't run away or fizzle out, is the key to understanding the whole life of a star. And if you have ever stood watch on a pressurized water reactor, you already know the core idea.

items.label: Mass the Sun converts to energy every second
Modeled temperature at the Sun's center
Sun's average power output per kilogram of its mass

blocks.source: NASA Sun Fact Sheet (NSSDC)

blocks.text: Gravity squeezes, fusion pushes back

A star is a balance between two forces. Gravity tries to crush the whole thing toward the center. Pressure from hot gas, heated by fusion in the core, pushes outward. Where the two match, the star sits in what physicists call hydrostatic equilibrium. That balance is the star's entire job description, and it holds for billions of years.

The fusion itself is harder than it sounds. Hydrogen nuclei are protons, and protons repel each other electrically. Even at the Sun's core temperature of about 15 million degrees, almost none of them have enough energy to touch. Fusion happens only because quantum mechanics lets a few protons *tunnel* through the barrier they classically can't climb. Even then, the first step requires one proton to turn into a neutron through the weak nuclear force, which is so improbable that a typical proton in the Sun's core waits billions of years before it fuses. That bottleneck is why the Sun lasts so long.

The payoff per reaction is still huge. Four hydrogen-1 atoms weigh 4.0313 atomic mass units; one helium-4 atom weighs 4.0026. The missing **0.71 percent** of the mass leaves as energy, about 26.7 MeV per helium nucleus, by E = mc². For comparison, a uranium-235 fission releases around 200 MeV but from a nucleus of 236 nucleons, so it converts less than a tenth of a percent of the mass. Gram for gram, hydrogen fusion is several times richer than fission.
A negative temperature coefficient the size of a star

Here is the part a nuke will recognize. Suppose fusion in the core speeds up a little. The extra heat raises the pressure, the core expands, and expanding gas cools and thins out. Cooler, thinner gas fuses more slowly, so the rate drops back. Suppose fusion slows instead: pressure falls, gravity squeezes the core, it heats up, and the rate climbs. The star has a built-in negative feedback loop, the same principle that makes a reactor with a negative temperature coefficient stable.

blocks.title: The stellar thermostat
items: Fusion rate rises
Core heats and pressure climbs
Core expands and cools
Fusion rate falls
Gravity compresses the core and it heats again

blocks.text: This loop is so effective that the Sun's output barely changes over millions of years, even though the energy takes a long time to get out. NASA estimates that energy bouncing through the Sun's radiative zone takes about **170,000 years** to reach the top of the convection zone. The sunlight on your face left the core before humans had invented agriculture. And in 4.6 billion years of shining, the Sun has converted roughly a hundred Earth masses into energy, which sounds dramatic until you notice it's about 0.03 percent of the Sun's mass.
Keep this thermostat in mind, because the rest of a star's life is about two things: running out of fuel, and the specific moments when the thermostat stops working.
Mass is destiny

The single most important number about a star is its mass at birth. A heavier star has stronger gravity, so its core is squeezed hotter and denser, and fusion rates rise steeply with temperature. Heavy stars have more fuel, but they burn it far faster than the extra fuel can make up for. The result is a cruel inversion: the bigger the star, the shorter its life.

The spread is enormous. NASA notes that the most massive stars live only a few million years. The Sun is a little less than halfway through a life of about 10 billion years. And small red dwarfs, which churn their whole interior so that fresh hydrogen keeps reaching the core, can shine for trillions of years. NASA estimates some could last up to about 14 trillion years, roughly a thousand times the current age of the universe.
Red dwarfs also make up about **75 percent** of the stars in the Milky Way. The typical star is small, dim, and will outlive everything else.

How do we know any of this, when no one can watch a star for a billion years? Star clusters are natural experiments. All the stars in a cluster formed from the same cloud at the same time, so they differ mainly in mass. Plot their brightness against their color and you see the heavy ones have already left the main sequence while the light ones haven't. The mass at which stars are just now peeling away works like a clock hand, giving the cluster's age. Astronomers check their stellar models against thousands of these snapshots.

blocks.title: Two ways to die

left.head: Low-mass star (like the Sun)
items: Burns hydrogen for billions of years
Swells into a red giant, then fuses helium
Gently sheds its outer layers as a glowing nebula
Leaves an Earth-sized white dwarf that slowly cools

right.head: High-mass star (above ~8 Suns)
items: Burns hydrogen in a few million years
Fuses heavier and heavier elements in layers
Builds an iron core that cannot release energy
Core collapses in about a second; supernova; neutron star or black hole

blocks.text: Small stars: the thermostat breaks quietly

When the Sun's core runs out of hydrogen in about 5 billion years, fusion there stops. Gravity wins for a while: the core contracts and heats, while hydrogen keeps fusing in a shell around it. The extra energy puffs the outer layers up enormously. The Sun becomes a red giant, swelling far beyond its current size and cooling at the surface to a dull orange-red.

Mercury and Venus will very likely be swallowed. Whether Earth is engulfed or merely scorched depends on how much mass the Sun sheds as it swells, which loosens its grip and lets the planets drift outward; models still disagree. Either way, Earth's oceans will have boiled away long before then, because the Sun slowly brightens even during its stable middle age.

Inside, something strange is happening to the core. It gets so dense that electrons are packed as tightly as quantum mechanics allows. Matter in that state is called *degenerate*, and its pressure comes from the Pauli exclusion principle rather than heat. That breaks the thermostat. When helium finally ignites, the extra heat no longer makes the core expand, so nothing slows the reaction. In stars like the Sun the helium ignites in a runaway burst called the helium flash, until the core heats enough to stop being degenerate and the feedback loop returns.

After the helium is spent, the Sun will lose its outer layers into space as a glowing shell, a planetary nebula, and leave behind its exposed core: a **white dwarf** about the size of Earth but hundreds of thousands of times more massive. It no longer fuses anything. It just cools, for longer than the universe has existed.

In 1931, a 20-year-old Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar showed that degenerate electron pressure has a limit. With modern values, it works out to about **1.4 solar masses**; above that, no white dwarf can hold itself up. A white dwarf in a close binary that steals gas from its partner and creeps toward that limit can ignite carbon fusion with no working thermostat at all. The entire star detonates in a thermonuclear explosion, a Type Ia supernova, and leaves nothing behind.
Big stars: an onion with a one-second fuse

A star above roughly eight solar masses never stalls. After hydrogen and helium, its core gets hot enough to fuse carbon, then neon, then oxygen, then silicon, each stage building the ash the next one burns. The star ends up layered like an onion, with a different fusion shell at each depth. And each stage is shorter than the last, because at these temperatures the core loses energy as **neutrinos** that stream straight out of the star. The faster it loses energy, the faster it has to burn.

blocks.title: Core burning stages of a 15-solar-mass star
items: Hydrogen
About 11 million years
Helium
About 2 million years
Carbon
About 2,000 years
Neon
About 0.7 years
Oxygen
About 2.6 years
Silicon
About 18 days
Iron core collapse
About 1 second

blocks.text: Those durations come from a stellar model published by Stan Woosley and Hans-Thomas Janka in Nature Physics in 2005. Silicon burning makes iron and nickel, and that is the dead end. Iron sits at the top of the nuclear binding-energy curve, the same curve that explains why fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light ones both release energy. Fusing iron *absorbs* energy instead of releasing it. The core has no fuel left that pays.

When the iron core grows too heavy to support itself, it collapses in a fraction of a second. Electrons are crushed into protons to make neutrons, and the inner core bounces off its own nuclear-density stiffness. In seconds, the newborn neutron star radiates about 10 percent of its rest mass as neutrinos. According to Woosley and Janka, that is a hundred times or more the kinetic energy of the explosion we see. A core-collapse supernova is, overwhelmingly, a neutrino event with a light show attached.

A neutron star is the closest thing in nature to one giant atomic nucleus. NASA describes it as packing more mass than the Sun into a ball about as wide as Manhattan is long. Many spin many times per second and sweep beams of radio waves across space; we see those as pulsars, the same objects whose ticking revealed the first known exoplanets.

We have checked this directly. In February 1987 a star exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, and underground detectors in Japan, the United States and the Soviet Union recorded a burst of about two dozen neutrinos, a few hours before anyone noticed the light. Those few particles, out of an unimaginable flood, confirmed the core-collapse picture. What remains after a collapse is a neutron star, a city-sized ball denser than an atomic nucleus, or, for heavier cores, a black hole.
You are made of reactor products

Every star is also a factory. The Big Bang made almost nothing but hydrogen, helium and a trace of lithium. The carbon in your cells, the oxygen you breathe and the calcium in your bones were fused inside stars and blown back into space by their deaths. A large share of the iron in your blood came from exploding white dwarfs. And in 2017, when gravitational-wave detectors caught two neutron stars merging, astronomers watched the glow of freshly made heavy elements, strong evidence that collisions like that are a major source of the universe's gold and platinum.

The hydrogen in your body's water is a different story. Its nuclei formed within minutes of the Big Bang, and stars only ever destroy hydrogen; they never make it. So you are a mix of the oldest material that exists and the recycled waste of stellar reactors that lived and died before the Sun was born.

There is a quiet lesson in all this for anyone who works on engineered systems. The Sun's steadiness isn't a sign that nothing is happening inside it; it is the visible result of a control loop correcting constantly. The dramatic moments in a star's life come exactly when a parameter drifts outside the range where the loop works: degenerate matter, iron ash, too much mass. Reactors, budgets and habits fail the same way.

The big idea: a star is stable for exactly as long as its negative feedback loop works. Small stars lose the loop briefly and recover; big stars lose it for good when their core turns to iron. Stability isn't the absence of change; it's a control system doing its job.

takeaways: Per kilogram, the Sun produces less heat than your body. It lasts billions of years because the first step of fusion is extremely slow.
Hydrogen fusion converts about 0.71 percent of mass to energy, several times more per gram than uranium fission.
Stars are stable because they have negative feedback: hotter core, expansion, cooling, slower fusion.
Mass decides fate: red dwarfs can last trillions of years, while stars above about 8 Suns live a few million and end in core collapse.
Most of a supernova's energy leaves as neutrinos, and nearly every atom in you heavier than helium was made in a star.

title: The Telescope That Launched Nearsighted
dek: Hubble's mirror was polished almost perfectly to the wrong shape, thanks to 1.3 millimeters and a chipped patch of paint. How it got fixed is the better story.

blocks.text: On June 27, 1990, two months after the space shuttle Discovery released it into orbit, NASA had to announce that its brand-new, multibillion-dollar space telescope could not focus. Both of Hubble's cameras showed the same smeared halo around every star. The flaw had to be in the main mirror, the one part nobody could reach, sitting hundreds of kilometers above the Earth.

The jokes came fast. A comedy film that year put Hubble in a montage of famous disasters alongside the Titanic and the Hindenburg. Politicians asked whether NASA could build anything. But three and a half years later, astronauts gave the telescope a pair of glasses in orbit, and Hubble went on to become arguably the most productive scientific instrument ever built. The gap between those two facts is a lesson in how errors happen, and in why designing something to be fixable can matter more than designing it to be perfect.

The telescope's road to orbit had already been long. Congress cut funding in the 1970s, the planned mirror shrank from 3 meters to 2.4 to save money, and a launch set for October 1986 evaporated when Challenger was lost that January. For years Hubble waited in a clean room, powered up and purged with nitrogen, at a reported cost of around $6 million a month. By launch day the total bill was roughly $4.7 billion in 2010 dollars. Every one of those dollars was riding on a mirror nobody had tested end to end.
Perfectly wrong

Hubble's primary mirror is a disk of ultra-low-expansion glass 2.4 meters across and weighing 828 kilograms. To take sharp pictures from above the atmosphere, it had to be shaped with absurd precision: its surface was polished smooth to roughly 10 nanometers, a small fraction of a wavelength of visible light. By that measure, it was one of the finest mirrors ever made.

The trouble was not roughness. It was shape. The mirror had been ground into a slightly wrong curve, too flat toward the edge. Light bouncing off the outer rim came to a focus at a different point than light bouncing off the center, an error called spherical aberration. The investigation board found the resulting wavefront error was about ten times the specified tolerance. Commonly cited figures put the edge too flat by about 2.2 micrometers, a few hundredths of the width of a human hair.

items.label: Spacing error in the test instrument that guided the polishing
How far the mirror's error exceeded its specified tolerance
Time the faulty test rig sat untouched before investigators measured it

blocks.source: NASA, Hubble Space Telescope Optical Systems Failure Report (Allen Board), 1990; NASA Science, Hubble's Mirror Flaw

blocks.text: That is the strange part. A mirror can only be polished as accurately as it can be measured, and Hubble's was measured beautifully. It was measured against the wrong standard. The error was not sloppy craftsmanship. It was a precise answer to a wrongly posed question.
The ruler that lied

Big telescope mirrors are made in cycles: polish a little, test the shape, polish again. The test uses a device called a null corrector, a small arrangement of mirrors and lenses that makes a perfectly shaped mirror look perfectly flat to an interferometer. If the pattern of light fringes comes out straight, you are done. The contractor, Perkin-Elmer, built a new reflective null corrector for Hubble and relied on it as the only test for both making and verifying the mirror.

In 1990 the investigation board, led by Lew Allen, found that null corrector preserved in the test chamber exactly as it had been during manufacture. When they measured it, one lens sat about 1.3 millimeters too far from its neighboring mirror. Feed that error into the math and it explains, in detail, the blur coming down from orbit.

blocks.title: How 1.3 millimeters got into the mirror
items: Technicians position the null corrector's lens using a precision metal rod, sighting a laser on the rod's polished end.
A cap over the rod end is supposed to be covered in non-reflective coating, but a small patch of the coating has flaked off.
The instrument picks up a reflection from the bare cap instead of the rod tip, so the lens is set 1.3 mm out of place.
The adjustment screws run out of travel, so spacers are added to push the lens into the 'correct' position.
Every later test of the mirror uses this flawed reference, so the mirror is polished until it matches the error.

blocks.text: The board could not find records proving exactly how it happened, so it reconstructed the most likely scenario in the lab and found the mistake was easy, even probable, with the setup used. Notice the step where the adjustment ran out and someone added spacers. That was the moment the hardware itself was saying something was off. It got shimmed instead of questioned.
Two warnings, both dismissed

The most painful finding in the report is that the error was caught, twice, and explained away both times. A second device, an inverse null corrector built to mimic a perfect mirror, clearly showed the main test rig was off. A cruder backup tester made only of lenses also showed the finished mirror was wrong. Both results were dismissed on the grounds that the cheaper instruments must be the flawed ones.

blocks.title: What the team assumed vs. what the data said

left.head: Assumption at the time
items: The main null corrector is the most precise tool, so it must be right
Disagreeing results come from cruder, less trustworthy instruments
An end-to-end test of the whole telescope costs too much to justify
Quality inspectors would only slow down a project already over budget

right.head: What the board found
items: The most precise tool was precisely wrong
Both cruder tools were pointing at the real error
No independent test existed to catch a single mistake
Quality staff had been kept out of key areas at critical times

blocks.text: The board was blunt about why. Relying on a single test was a process clearly vulnerable to simple error, and such errors had happened on other telescopes. Simple checks to guard against a gross mistake were considered and rejected. Competitive, cost and schedule pressures kept the test data away from people qualified to read it. Meanwhile, the backup mirror for Hubble, polished by Kodak using different null correctors, came out matching its specifications.

There was another quiet failure in the paperwork. Perkin-Elmer's quality assurance staff reported to the same project manager who was answerable for cost and schedule, and they were kept out of the optical test area during the critical work. If the written quality plan had been followed, the board concluded, the error probably would never have happened. And because full records were not kept, even the investigators had to reconstruct the likely mistake by experiment rather than read it from a logbook.

The lesson is not 'trust the cheap tool.' It is that when two independent measurements disagree, you have found the most valuable fact in the project, and the expensive instrument does not get to win the argument by default.

Hubble was not useless in the meantime. The core of each blurred star image was still sharp, so bright targets and spectra of single points of light could still be studied, and astronomers used image-processing tricks to partly undo the known blur. What died were the faint, deep observations that had justified the telescope in the first place, the distant galaxies at the edge of the visible universe. Those needed every photon to land where it belonged.
Glasses for a telescope

Here is the twist. Because the faulty null corrector had been preserved untouched, engineers knew the mirror's error almost exactly. A known, stable error can be canceled. An unknown one cannot. Hubble's flaw was a terrible accident, but it was a well-characterized terrible accident, and that made it fixable.

The fix came in two parts. Engineers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory redesigned the next main camera, Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2, with corrective optics built inside it. For the other instruments, they built COSTAR, a package about the size of a large refrigerator that slid into an instrument bay and put small corrective mirrors in front of three of them, like eyeglasses. To make room, the High Speed Photometer had to come out.

None of this would have mattered if Hubble had been built like most satellites, sealed and untouchable. But Hubble was the first space observatory designed from the start to be serviced by astronauts, with handholds, standard bolts and swappable instrument drawers, because it was planned around the space shuttle. In December 1993, the crew of Endeavour caught it, installed both fixes and much more over a series of spacewalks, and released it. The before-and-after images of the galaxy M100 went from a fuzzy smudge to crisp spiral arms.

blocks.text: By the numbers, astronauts spent 23 days doing spacewalks on Hubble across five servicing missions, 171 hours in total. By 2002, every original instrument that needed COSTAR had been replaced by one with built-in correction, so in 2009 astronauts pulled COSTAR out and brought it home. It now sits in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum, a refrigerator-sized monument to a 1.3 millimeter mistake.
What a fixed telescope found

Once it could see, Hubble went to work on the biggest question its namesake left behind: how fast is the universe expanding? Edwin Hubble showed in the 1920s that galaxies are flying apart, but for decades astronomers could not pin the expansion rate, the Hubble constant, down tightly. A Hubble Key Project team led by Wendy Freedman measured the distances to pulsating stars in nearby galaxies and in 2001 reported a value of 72 kilometers per second per megaparsec, give or take 8.

The method is a chain of rulers. Certain pulsating stars, Cepheids, blink at a rate tied to their true brightness, so comparing how bright they look with how bright they are gives a distance. Hubble could pick out individual Cepheids in galaxies far enough away to also host exploding stars of known brightness, and those supernovae carry the ruler out to galaxies being swept along by cosmic expansion. A blurry Hubble could not have resolved those single stars in crowded galaxies. The fix was the whole ballgame.

blocks.title: How fast is the universe expanding?
blocks.note: Uncertainties: about 8, 1.04 and 0.5. The gap between the last two is the 'Hubble tension.'
blocks.source: Freedman et al., ApJ, 2001; Riess et al., ApJL, 2022; Planck Collaboration, A&A, 2020

blocks.text: Then the plot thickened. A later team using Hubble, SH0ES, shrank the uncertainty to about 1 and got 73. But the Planck satellite, reading the afterglow of the Big Bang and running it forward through the standard model of cosmology, predicts about 67.4. The SH0ES team reports the gap at five sigma, with no sign it comes from measurement error. Either one side has a subtle problem nobody has found, or the standard model of the universe is missing something. Hubble helped start that fight and is still in it.

That is only one thread. Hubble observations fed the discovery that the universe's expansion is speeding up, work that led to a Nobel Prize. Its Ultra Deep Field, staring at a patch of seemingly empty sky, revealed about 10,000 galaxies. NASA counts more than 1.7 million observations and over 23,000 peer-reviewed papers built on its data. Not bad for a joke.
The last service call

Hubble has no engine of its own. Like everything in low Earth orbit, it is slowly sinking as thin traces of atmosphere drag on it, and the shuttles that used to boost it higher retired in 2011. NASA's current analysis says it will likely reenter the atmosphere around 2033 to 2034. On October 29, 2026, NASA asked companies to describe what they could offer: a mission to boost Hubble to a higher orbit, servicing to improve it, or a safe controlled reentry at the end. Any mission would need to fly by about 2032.

That request is the old design decision paying out one more time. Hubble's successor, the James Webb Space Telescope, sits about 1.5 million kilometers away, far beyond any repair crew, so it had to be right the first time. Hubble got to be wrong the first time because someone decided, years before launch, that it should have handholds.

Two habits from this story travel well: never let a single measurement be the only check on something that matters, and build the things you care about so they can be opened, inspected and fixed later.

Anyone who has worked in a technical trade will recognize both halves. The failure mode was not stupidity. Skilled people trusted their best tool, were under schedule pressure, and treated the instruments that disagreed with them as noise. The recovery was not genius alone either. It depended on a preserved record of the mistake and on hardware that let people reach in and fix it. When something you build goes wrong, and something will, those are the two things you will wish you had.

takeaways: Hubble's mirror was polished to the wrong shape because its test rig had a lens 1.3 mm out of place, probably from a reflection off a chipped coating.
Two independent checks caught the error before launch and were dismissed as the faulty ones; disagreement between measurements is a signal, not noise.
The flaw was fixable because the faulty test rig was preserved and the telescope was designed for astronauts to service.
A fixed Hubble helped measure the universe's expansion rate, which now disagrees with early-universe predictions: the unresolved 'Hubble tension.'
Hubble is expected to reenter around 2033 to 2034 unless a reboost mission flies by about 2032; NASA asked industry for options in October 2026.

title: A Submarine That Can Never Surface
dek: The International Space Station has kept people breathing inside a sealed can for over 25 years. Its hardest problems are ones every submariner already knows: air, water, leaks, and a hull that slowly wears out.

blocks.text: In 2019, the people who watch the International Space Station's air pressure noticed something they did not like. The station was losing air a little faster than it should. Not fast enough to be an emergency, but steady, and steady is what worries engineers. The source was eventually traced to a short tunnel at the back of Zvezda, the Russian service module. By April 2024 the leak had reached its highest rate yet, and NASA rated it a 5 by 5 on its risk matrix: the worst possible score for both likelihood and consequence.

The fix, at least for now, will sound familiar to anyone who has stood a damage control watch. Keep the hatch to that section shut whenever nobody needs to be in there. Isolate the compartment. Monitor the rate. Argue about the point at which you stop opening it at all. NASA and Roscosmos, according to NASA's Inspector General, still have not agreed on what leak rate would count as untenable.

The ISS is, in a real sense, a submarine. It is a sealed pressure vessel that has to manufacture its own atmosphere, recycle its own water, and keep a crew healthy in a cramped space for months at a time, with help a long way off. But the two vessels differ in ways that are just as instructive as the similarities. Looking at one through the lens of the other makes both easier to understand.

items.label: Mass of the station
Habitable volume, shared by a crew of seven
Sunrises and sunsets the crew passes through every 24 hours

blocks.source: NASA, International Space Station Facts and Figures

blocks.text: An inside-out pressure hull

A submarine hull is built to keep the ocean out. At depth, the sea pushes inward with enormous force, and the hull is designed so it doesn't collapse. The ISS has the opposite problem. Its modules hold roughly one atmosphere of air pressure on the inside, with vacuum on the outside, so the force on the walls pushes outward. The pressure difference is only about one atmosphere, far less than a deep-diving submarine feels, but it never lets up and there is nothing outside to push back.

That changes what failure looks like. A submarine's nightmare is sudden flooding or collapse. The station's chronic enemy is slow leakage: air escaping molecule by molecule through tiny cracks, seals and welds, plus the small but real chance of a puncture from orbital debris. Every bit of air that leaks out is gone for good and has to be replaced from supplies launched from Earth.

By NASA's numbers, the station's pressurized volume is about 1,005 cubic meters, of which 388 are habitable living and working space. That's often compared to a six-bedroom house, with six sleeping quarters, two bathrooms and a gym. Split among a crew of seven, it works out to around 55 cubic meters each, a bit more than a single-car garage. It's spacious by submarine standards, but every cubic meter of it has to be kept airtight.
Open to energy, closed to mass

Here is the difference that matters most. A nuclear submarine is sealed off from the atmosphere, but it is not a closed system. It sits in an effectively unlimited supply of seawater, and its reactor provides enough power to turn that seawater into fresh water and oxygen without much worry about running out. The previous article on making air and water underway, *The Atmosphere Is Something You Manufacture*, covers how that works. The key point here is that a submarine is rich in both energy and raw material.

The station has energy, too. Its eight solar arrays generate about 75 to 90 kilowatts. What it lacks is an ocean. Nothing flows in from outside except what arrives on cargo ships, and launching mass into orbit is expensive. So on the ISS, every kilogram of water is either delivered or recycled. That single constraint shapes the whole life support system, because water is also where the oxygen comes from. Like a submarine, the station makes oxygen by splitting water with electricity. Lose water and you lose air.

This is why NASA treats water recycling on the station as something close to a moonshot. In June 2023 the agency announced that the station's life support system had reached 98% water recovery, the target NASA considers necessary for long missions beyond low Earth orbit. NASA's fact sheet adds that the Water Recovery System cuts the crew's dependence on delivered water by 65%, from roughly a gallon per person per day to about a third of a gallon.

blocks.title: How the station turns waste back into drinking water
items: Dehumidifiers pull moisture out of the cabin air, catching the water astronauts breathe and sweat out.
The Urine Processor Assembly boils urine under vacuum and condenses the vapor, leaving behind a concentrated brine.
The Brine Processor Assembly squeezes the remaining water out of that brine, the last step that pushed recovery to 98%.
The Water Processor Assembly filters and treats all the recovered water until it is safe to drink.
Some of that water goes to the oxygen generator, which splits it into oxygen for breathing and hydrogen.

blocks.text: The reframe is worth holding onto. A submarine can afford to be wasteful with water because the ocean is right outside. The station can't afford to waste anything because nothing is outside. How closed a system is depends on what's cheap to bring in, not on whether the hatch is shut. A submarine is closed to air but open to the sea. A spacecraft is closed to almost everything.
Air with no up

On a submarine, or in your bedroom, warm exhaled breath rises and drifts away from your face because warm gas is less dense than the cooler air around it. That process, convection, depends on gravity. In orbit, there is no up. Exhaled carbon dioxide can hang around your head in a stale bubble unless a fan moves it. That's why ventilation on the station isn't a comfort feature. It's life support, and astronauts pay attention to where they sleep relative to the airflow.

Getting the CO2 out works on a different principle than on most submarines. The station's main US scrubber uses beds of zeolite, a mineral sponge with pores sized to trap CO2 molecules. When one bed is full, it's heated and exposed to the vacuum of space, which pulls the gas back out so the bed can be reused. Some of the captured CO2 goes to a Sabatier reactor, which combines it with leftover hydrogen from the oxygen generator to make water and methane. So the station recovers water from the very gas its crew breathes out.

Carbon dioxide on the station has been studied more carefully than on most submarines, because astronauts reported headaches and fogginess. A 2014 NASA analysis by Jennifer Law and colleagues compared crew headache reports with measured CO2 levels. They found that for every 1 mmHg increase in CO2 partial pressure, the odds of a crew member reporting a headache roughly doubled. To keep headache risk below 1%, they estimated the seven-day average would need to stay under 2.5 mmHg, at a time when station levels ranged from about 1 to 9 mmHg.

blocks.title: Carbon dioxide on the ISS (partial pressure)
blocks.note: At sea-level pressure, 1 mmHg of CO2 is about 1,300 ppm, so 2.5 mmHg is roughly 3,300 ppm.
blocks.source: Law et al., Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine, 2014

blocks.text: For context, 2.5 mmHg works out to roughly 3,300 parts per million, which is in the same general range as the CO2 levels discussed for submarines in *The Atmosphere Is Something You Manufacture*. The evidence is not settled, though. A 2024 study in *Neurology* followed 24 astronauts on long missions and found that 22 of them had at least one headache, but it did not find a link between headache episodes and the station's measured CO2, oxygen, temperature or pressure. One possible explanation is that cabin sensors miss the local pockets that form around a person's face. Another is that space headaches have several causes at once. It's an open question.
The body as a maintenance item

A submarine crew doesn't lose bone just by being aboard. An astronaut does. Without gravity loading the skeleton, the body starts to break down bone it no longer seems to need. A study of cosmonauts on the Mir station, published in *The Lancet* in 2000, found that bone loss in the shin was already measurable after one month in orbit and got worse with longer missions. Even more striking, the loss continued during recovery back on Earth, which suggested that rebuilding takes longer than the mission itself.

That's why NASA has astronauts exercise at least two hours a day, using a treadmill, a stationary bike and a resistance machine that imitates lifting weights. On the station, exercise isn't a lifestyle choice. It's scheduled maintenance on the most important equipment aboard. The mental side of long confinement, including crew friction, monotony and the mid-mission slump, follows patterns very similar to those seen on submarines and at polar stations. The article *What a Sealed Hull Actually Does to People* goes into that research.

Crew of more than a hundred spreads the social load

right.head: Space station

No convection; fans are life support
