Crew of about seven, each one critical

blocks.text: No emergency blow

Every submariner knows that the ultimate fallback is reaching the surface. If the ship is flooding or burning, the procedures are built around getting up to air and daylight. The ISS has nothing equivalent. There's no surface to reach. Its lifeboats are the crew spacecraft docked to it, the Soyuz and Dragon capsules, and each crew member's seat has to be accounted for at all times.

NASA's Inspector General lists the main threats as fire, structural leaks, toxic gas leaks such as ammonia from the cooling system, and impacts from micrometeoroids and orbital debris. The standard response looks a lot like damage control: isolate the affected section, protect the crew, and only if that fails, get into the spacecraft and prepare to leave. The report also points out an uncomfortable gap. If the return vehicle itself is damaged, the options for evacuating get very limited.

That isn't a hypothetical. In December 2022, a Soyuz docked to the station was unexpectedly damaged and began leaking coolant, which made it potentially unsafe for the three people who were supposed to ride it home. According to the Inspector General, there were no specific rules at the time about where the crew should shelter if their own return vehicle was compromised. The partners ended up launching a replacement Soyuz. The damaged one came home empty in March 2023, and the crew finally returned that September, turning a roughly six-month mission into one lasting more than a year.

Submariners will recognize the logic. The ship is only as safe as its last line of escape, and nobody notices that line until it's damaged. Afterward, NASA wrote a contingency plan for exactly that situation. The station's procedures, like a ship's, are partly a record of things that went wrong once.
Every hull ages

The station has been continuously occupied since November 2000. That's an unbroken human presence in orbit lasting longer than the lives of many of the people who now work on it. But a sealed vessel is never finished. It is a long-running argument with fatigue, corrosion, worn seals and parts that are no longer manufactured. The Zvezda tunnel leak has been tracked since 2019, the root cause is still unknown, and investigators have narrowed their search to internal and external welds.

blocks.text: The end is already scheduled. In June 2024 NASA selected SpaceX to build the US Deorbit Vehicle, a single contract worth up to $843 million. Its job is to push the station down into a controlled reentry over a remote stretch of ocean, where the station is expected to break apart, with the deorbit vehicle breaking up along with it. The US, Japan, Canada and the European partners have committed to operating it through 2030. Russia has committed through at least 2028.

There's a lesson in how the station got here. The leak wasn't caught by an alarm. It was caught by people paying attention to a trend: a rate that crept up from very low to the highest yet. Most problems on a sealed vessel arrive like that, slowly, in the logs, before they ever show up as an emergency. The skill that keeps a crew alive is less about heroics than about noticing when the reading you took today doesn't quite match the one you took last month.

A closed system makes the invisible visible. On land, clean air and water seem free. On a submarine or a space station, every breath and every liter shows up as a line in somebody's log, and somebody has to keep that log honest.

takeaways: The ISS is a pressure hull turned inside out: it holds one atmosphere in against vacuum, so its chronic threat is slow leakage, not crushing.
A submarine is closed to air but open to the sea; the station is closed to almost everything, which is why it recycles 98% of its water.
Without gravity there's no convection, so exhaled CO2 can pool around your face. Evidence linking station CO2 levels to headaches is suggestive but mixed.
In orbit, exercise is scheduled maintenance: astronauts train at least two hours a day and still lose bone.
Most failures on a sealed vessel show up first as a slow trend in the logs. Noticing trends is the real survival skill.

title: Mars Is Not a Rocket Problem
dek: Getting a ship to Mars is the easy part. Landing 20 tonnes through almost-vacuum, absorbing a career's worth of radiation, making fuel for the ride home and keeping a crew sane for two and a half years are the hard parts.

blocks.text: Right now, in late 2026, Earth and Mars are lined up for one of the launch windows that open roughly every 26 months. For a while, this was supposed to be the window when SpaceX sent its first uncrewed Starships to Mars; the company had talked about five of them. In February 2026, the *Wall Street Journal* reported that SpaceX had pushed Mars back to concentrate on landing on the Moon for NASA, targeting an uncrewed lunar landing in March 2027. The window will close with no ships headed to Mars.

Meanwhile, in a 1,700-square-foot 3D-printed habitat at NASA's Johnson Space Center, four volunteers were scheduled to finish a 378-day simulated Mars mission on October 31. That contrast says a lot. Mars keeps being a decade away, not mainly because rockets are too weak, but because everything *around* the rocket is hard. This is a tour of those problems, the physics behind them and the trade-offs engineers are wrestling with.

items.label: Average time between Earth–Mars alignments (synodic period)
Mars surface pressure compared with Earth's (about 6.4 mb vs 1,014 mb)
One-way light delay between Earth and Mars

blocks.source: NASA Mars and Earth Fact Sheets (NSSDC); NASA 'What Is a Light-Day?'

blocks.text: The clock: orbital mechanics sets the schedule

You can't fly to Mars whenever you like, at least not cheaply. The cheapest route is a **Hohmann transfer**: an ellipse that touches Earth's orbit at one end and Mars's at the other. Kepler's third law gives the trip time directly. The ellipse's average radius is about 1.26 AU, so a full orbit on it would take 1.26 to the power 1.5, or about 1.42 years. You only fly half of it, so the trip takes about **259 days**. Curiosity's actual cruise in 2011–2012 took 253 days and covered about 560 million kilometers.

For that ellipse to end where Mars actually is, Mars has to be about 44 degrees ahead of Earth when you leave. That geometry repeats only once every synodic period, about 780 days. Miss the window and you wait two years. Leaving low Earth orbit on that path takes a burn of roughly 3.6 kilometers per second, and the rocket equation makes every extra bit of speed expensive.

The return is the part people forget. When you arrive, Earth has raced ahead of Mars by about 75 degrees, the wrong position for heading home. You have to wait for Earth to lap Mars and come back around to the right spot. With simple circular-orbit math, the wait comes out to roughly **454 days** on Mars. Add the two transfers and a minimum-energy round trip runs about 970 days, more than two and a half years. Faster trajectories exist, but they cost much more propellant, and there's no option to come home early if something goes wrong.

blocks.title: A minimum-energy Mars mission, roughly
items: Wait for the launch window that opens every ~26 months
Burn about 3.6 km/s out of low Earth orbit onto the transfer ellipse
Coast about 8.5 months through deep space
Slow down and land roughly 20 tonnes through a very thin atmosphere
Live on Mars about 15 months while the planets realign
Launch off Mars on fuel made there and coast about 8.5 months home

blocks.text: The dose: a career's worth of radiation in transit

On the way to Mars, Curiosity carried a radiation detector inside the spacecraft, about where a crew would sit. Its measurements, published in *Science* in 2013, showed that the dose equivalent for just the round-trip cruise, using the shortest trip possible with current propulsion and similar shielding, would be about **0.66 sieverts**, give or take 0.12. That doesn't include any time on the surface.

Put that next to the limits. NASA's current standard caps an astronaut's total career spaceflight dose at **600 millisieverts**, the same for every age and sex. The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission's annual limit for a radiation worker is **50 millisieverts**. In other words, the cruise alone could exceed an astronaut's lifetime limit, and it equals more than thirteen years of maximum allowed exposure for someone working at a nuclear plant.

blocks.title: Radiation doses compared
blocks.note: Cruise value is the dose equivalent measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument, scaled to the shortest round trip; uncertainty is about ±120 mSv.
blocks.source: Zeitlin et al., Science, 2013; NASA-STD-3001 technical brief, 2022; 10 CFR 20.1201

blocks.text: The problem is the kind of radiation. Most of the dose comes from galactic cosmic rays: atomic nuclei, some as heavy as iron, moving at a large fraction of light speed. They're so energetic that thin shielding barely slows them, and thick metal can make things worse by shattering them into showers of secondary particles. Hydrogen-rich materials like water and polyethylene work better per kilogram, which is why designers like the idea of wrapping crew quarters in the water and food supplies they're carrying anyway. Solar storms are a separate, short, intense threat; NASA limits exposure to any single event to 250 millisieverts, which means ships need a heavily shielded storm shelter.

Landing doesn't end the exposure. Mars has no global magnetic field and only a thin blanket of air, so cosmic rays reach the surface far more easily than on Earth. The planet itself blocks half the sky, which helps, but long stays would likely mean living under thick layers of Martian soil or in caves, the same logic as a reactor compartment: put mass between people and the source.

Here's a trade-off a nuke will appreciate. Nuclear propulsion could shorten the trip, but the reactor adds its own dose. NASA's radiation technical brief works an example: if a nuclear engine saves 90 days of transit at about 1.5 millisieverts per day, that avoids 135 millisieverts; if the engine's own radiation gives the crew 150, the crew comes out 15 millisieverts *worse*. The standard tells engineers to make that trade explicitly, applying the same principle every nuclear worker learns: keep exposure as low as reasonably achievable.
The landing: 20 tonnes through air that's almost not there

Mars's atmosphere is the worst of both worlds. At about 0.6 percent of Earth's surface pressure, it's too thin for parachutes to slow a heavy vehicle enough, but thick enough to heat an incoming spacecraft's shield to well over a thousand degrees Celsius. Every fully successful Mars landing so far has put down a payload of roughly one metric ton or less; Curiosity and Perseverance, the heaviest, needed a heat shield, a supersonic parachute and a rocket-powered sky crane.

Human missions need far more. NASA's landing studies assume a usable payload of about **20 tonnes** per lander, enough for a Mars ascent vehicle, the small rocket that will lift the crew back to orbit. NASA engineers have called that a twentyfold increase over the state of the art. Parachutes don't scale that far in such thin air, so every architecture in NASA's 2016 human-landing study relies on **supersonic retropropulsion**: firing rocket engines into the oncoming supersonic airflow to brake. It's the same basic move SpaceX uses to land boosters on Earth, but performed in a different atmosphere, millions of kilometers from help, with no chance for a second attempt.

blocks.title: Robot landings vs. human landings

Heat shield, then supersonic parachute
Sky crane lowers rover on cables
A failure loses a robot

right.head: Human-class lander

Heat shield or lifting body, then engines
Supersonic retropropulsion all the way down
A failure loses a crew

blocks.text: The ride home: make your fuel on Mars

The rocket equation punishes you twice on Mars. Whatever propellant you need for the trip home has to be carried there first, which means even more propellant leaving Earth. The obvious escape is to make the return propellant on Mars, from Mars. The raw material is everywhere: the atmosphere is about 95 percent carbon dioxide.

NASA has tested the first step. MOXIE, a device about the size of a microwave oven, rode on the Perseverance rover and split oxygen out of Martian carbon dioxide electrochemically. Over 16 runs it made a total of **122 grams** of oxygen, about what a small dog breathes in 10 hours. At its best it produced 12 grams an hour at 98 percent purity or better, twice its original goal. It proved the chemistry works on Mars, in real dust and real cold.

Now the gap. A rocket that lifts a crew off Mars needs propellant measured in tonnes, mostly liquid oxygen, which is the heavier half of a methane-oxygen mix. Scaling from grams per hour to tonnes over a year or so means bigger machines and, above all, steady power, day and night, through months-long dust storms. That's why NASA has been developing small fission reactors for surface power. The likely recipe for a Mars base looks familiar to anyone who works in a reactor plant: a compact nuclear power source running a chemical plant that makes air and fuel.
The crew: confinement, bones and a 22-minute delay

The body pays too. NASA reports that in weightlessness, astronauts' bones lose an average of **1 to 1.5 percent** of their density per month on four-to-six-month missions, even with daily exercise. A crew would spend months in zero gravity in transit, then land on a planet with 38 percent of Earth's gravity, an environment no one has ever lived in long-term. Nobody knows yet whether that partial gravity is enough to keep bones and muscles healthy.

Then there's the mind. In the Mars-500 experiment, six men spent 520 days sealed in a mock spacecraft in Moscow. Wrist monitors showed that as the months went on, the crew moved less and slept and rested more, their light exposure dropped, and most of them had disrupted sleep, vigilance lapses or drifting body clocks. The researchers concluded that a real crew would need deliberately engineered light, meal and exercise schedules to stay on a normal rhythm. Anyone who has done a long underway with no sunlight and rotating watches knows exactly what they found.

And there's no Houston in real time. With a one-way light delay of 3 to 22 minutes, a conversation with mission control becomes an exchange of messages, and a fast-moving emergency has to be handled by the people on scene. That changes who you send and how you train them. A Mars crew will look less like ISS astronauts, who have experts on the radio around the clock, and more like a submarine crew on patrol: small, self-reliant, cross-trained on every system, and expected to fix what breaks with the parts on board.

And sometimes there's no Houston at all. Roughly every 26 months, Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from Earth, and the Sun's hot, turbulent outer atmosphere scrambles radio signals passing near it. NASA routinely stops sending commands to its Mars robots for a couple of weeks around these solar conjunctions. A crew would go through at least one such blackout, alone, during a long surface stay.
So what would it really take?

This is why the current plan runs through the Moon first. NASA's Artemis II crew took about three days to reach the Moon, and a radio signal crosses that gap in 1.3 seconds. That makes the Moon a place to practice landers, surface power, propellant production and long stays where a crew can still get home within days if something breaks. SpaceX's architecture adds another piece that has to be proven there: refilling a ship's tanks in orbit from multiple tanker launches, a step SpaceX's own plans depend on to send a ship that large beyond Earth orbit.

Put the pieces together and the shape of the problem becomes clear. Mars isn't one giant leap; it's a systems problem with no resupply and no abort. Every subsystem, from life support to the propellant plant to the crew's sleep schedule, has to work for roughly a thousand days, far from help, and failures have to be fixable with what's on board.

The good news is that each piece has a path. Big reusable rockets are flying; propellant production works in miniature; radiation shielding is mostly a question of mass and trip time; and long-duration isolation studies keep teaching us how crews break and how to prevent it. The bad news is that nobody has put all of the pieces together yet, and the integrated version is where programs usually slip by years.

The reframe: the hardest part of Mars isn't getting there. It's being *self-sufficient* there. The closest existing model for that isn't a space station; it's a nuclear submarine on a long deployment.

takeaways: Planetary geometry sets the schedule: windows every ~26 months, ~259-day minimum-energy transfers and a ~15-month wait on Mars before the trip home.
Curiosity measured about 0.66 Sv for a round-trip cruise, above NASA's 600 mSv career limit and 13 times the NRC's annual worker limit.
Human landers need about 20 tonnes of payload, roughly 20 times anything landed so far, which means braking with engines, not parachutes.
MOXIE made 122 g of oxygen on Mars; a crew's ride home needs tonnes, so power, likely nuclear, is the real bottleneck.
A Mars crew will need to operate like a submarine crew: self-reliant, cross-trained and on a carefully engineered daily rhythm.

title: The Moon Is Leaving, and It's Taking Our Time
dek: Born from a collision that nearly destroyed the young Earth, the Moon has been drifting away ever since, stretching our days as it goes. Here is how we know, what still doesn't fit, and why astronauts are heading back.

blocks.text: Several times a month, an observatory in New Mexico fires a powerful laser at the Moon. The beam spreads out to a few kilometers wide by the time it gets there, and a handful of its photons hit a suitcase-sized panel of glass corner reflectors left by Apollo astronauts. A corner reflector sends light straight back where it came from, so a tiny fraction of those photons make the return trip. Out of the enormous number of photons fired in each pulse, only a few typically come home. Timing their round trip, about 2.5 seconds, tells scientists the distance to the Moon to within millimeters.

Fifty years of these measurements have revealed something that sounds like a fact from a children's book but is completely true: the Moon is drifting away from us. Lunar laser ranging puts the rate at 3.82 cm per year, about the pace your fingernails grow. At the same time, Earth's spin is slowing, so every day is very slightly longer than the one before.

Those two facts are connected, and following that connection backward leads to one of the most violent events in the history of our planet, the birth of the Moon itself. It also explains why, after more than 50 years away, people are going back.
Born in a collision

Before Apollo, there were three main ideas about where the Moon came from. Maybe it was a passing body captured by Earth's gravity. Maybe it formed alongside Earth from the same cloud of debris. Or maybe a fast-spinning young Earth flung off a chunk of itself. The six Apollo landings brought back 382 kg of rock and soil, and the samples did not fit any of those stories cleanly.

The rocks showed the Moon had once been covered by a deep ocean of molten magma, which takes a lot of energy. They were very low in water and easily evaporated elements, as if the material had been baked. And the Moon has very little iron: Earth's iron core makes up about 30 percent of its mass, while the Moon's core is only around 1.6 to 1.8 percent. The idea that emerged in the 1970s and became the leading explanation is the giant impact hypothesis. About 4.5 billion years ago, within roughly 60 million years of the solar system's formation, a body about the size of Mars, nicknamed Theia, slammed into the young Earth. The collision threw a ring of molten and vaporized rock into orbit, mostly from the outer, iron-poor layers of both bodies, and that debris pulled itself together into the Moon.

blocks.title: The giant impact story
items: About 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body, Theia, strikes the young Earth at an angle.
The impact melts and partly vaporizes the outer layers of both bodies.
Iron from Theia's core mostly sinks into Earth's core, so the debris is iron-poor.
A disk of molten and vaporized rock forms around Earth.
The debris clumps together into the Moon, much closer to Earth than it is today.
The new Moon is covered by a deep ocean of magma, which slowly cools into its crust.

blocks.text: The twin problem

The giant impact explains a lot, but it created a stubborn puzzle. Elements come in slightly different versions, called isotopes, and the mix of oxygen isotopes works like a fingerprint for where in the solar system a rock formed. Mars and the asteroids each have their own distinct fingerprint. In the simplest computer models, most of the Moon should be made from Theia, so its fingerprint should differ from Earth's.

It does not. In 2016, Edward Young and colleagues at UCLA measured oxygen isotopes in Apollo samples and Earth rocks with extreme precision and found them indistinguishable, with a difference of -1 plus or minus 5 parts per million, statistically zero. Either Theia happened to have formed in the same neighborhood as Earth, or the impact was so violent that the two bodies mixed thoroughly before the Moon formed. Young's team favored the second: a high-energy impact that churned everything together.

Newer simulations have explored ever more dramatic versions, including impacts so energetic that Earth and the debris became a single spinning, partly vaporized blob, and one NASA and Durham University simulation suggesting the Moon may have assembled in a matter of hours. None of this is settled. It is a good example of science working properly: the leading theory is strong enough to be widely accepted, while a specific detail stubbornly refuses to fit and keeps researchers honest.

It is not the only loose end. The Moon's two faces are strangely different. The crust on the near side, the side we always see, is about 70 km thick, while the far side's crust is about 150 km. The near side is covered in dark plains of ancient lava, the "seas" visible to the naked eye, and is rich in radioactive elements, while the far side is mostly rugged, bright highlands with little sign of volcanism. Nobody has a fully agreed explanation for why one world ended up so lopsided.
How the Moon is stealing our day

The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans and raises two bulges of water, one facing the Moon and one on the far side. Earth spins underneath them once a day, which is why most coastlines get two high tides and two low tides daily. But Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, so friction drags the bulges slightly ahead of the line between Earth and Moon.

That offset is the key. The leading bulge pulls the Moon forward along its orbit, giving it a little extra energy, which lifts it into a slightly higher, wider orbit. In exchange, the Moon's pull on the bulge acts like a brake on Earth's spin. Angular momentum, the spin quantity that physics insists must be conserved, is being transferred from Earth's rotation to the Moon's orbit. Earth slows; the Moon recedes. It is the same principle as a figure skater who slows down by extending her arms, only here the arm is 384,000 km long.

blocks.title: The tidal exchange
items: Moon's gravity raises tidal bulges
Earth's faster spin drags the bulges ahead
Bulge pulls Moon forward, lifting its orbit
Moon pulls back on bulge, braking Earth's spin
Longer day, more distant Moon

blocks.text: The same braking already finished its work on the Moon. Earth raises tides in the Moon's rock, too, and over time that friction slowed the Moon's spin until it matched its orbit exactly. That is why the Moon always shows us the same face: it is tidally locked, turning once on its axis for every trip around Earth. No human saw the far side until a Soviet spacecraft photographed it in 1959. In principle, Earth's spin would keep slowing toward the same locked state, but the process is so slow that the Sun will change dramatically long before it could finish.

The slowdown is measurable even in human history. Astronomers Richard Stephenson, Leslie Morrison and Catherine Hohenkerk analyzed records of eclipses going back to 720 BC, from Babylonian clay tablets to Chinese, Arab and European chronicles. Because an eclipse is only visible along a narrow path, its recorded location reveals how far Earth had rotated at that moment. They found the length of a day has been growing by about 1.8 milliseconds per century on average. Tidal friction alone would add 2.3 milliseconds per century; other effects, such as Earth's crust slowly rebounding since the ice ages, partly offset it.

Run that process backward over hundreds of millions of years and the numbers become dramatic. Rocks record it too. Tidal sediments laid down in layers, called tidal rhythmites, preserve the count of tides per month and days per year, the way tree rings preserve years.

blocks.title: Length of a day on Earth
blocks.note: Ancient values come from layered sedimentary rocks that recorded tides and climate cycles.
blocks.source: Meyers & Malinverno, PNAS, 2018; Williams, Reviews of Geophysics, 2000

blocks.text: A 2000 review by geologist George Williams found that 620 million years ago a year held about 400 days of about 21.9 hours each. Going back further, a 2018 study by Stephen Meyers and Alberto Malinverno used climate cycles recorded in 1.4-billion-year-old rocks to estimate a day of about 18.7 hours, with the Moon around 341,000 km away instead of today's 384,000.

There is a twist. Williams found that since 620 million years ago, the Moon has receded at an average of about 2.2 cm per year, little more than half today's rate. The modern rate is unusually fast. The amount of tidal braking depends on the shape and size of the ocean basins, which keep changing as continents drift, and today's oceans happen to be very efficient at dissipating tidal energy. A rate measured over 50 years is not necessarily the rate over a billion. That warning applies far beyond geology.

Some scientists have also argued that the Moon keeps Earth's tilt stable, and with it our seasons. An influential 1993 study by Jacques Laskar and colleagues found that without the Moon, Earth's axis could swing chaotically over very long times. Later simulations, such as a 2012 study led by Jack Lissauer, suggested the wobble of a moonless Earth might be much smaller than first feared. It remains an open debate, so treat the popular claim that we owe complex life to the Moon with some caution.
Why we are going back

On April 1, 2026, NASA's Space Launch System rocket sent the Orion capsule on Artemis II, carrying NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch and Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen around the Moon. They splashed down on April 10 after a mission of a little over nine days, the first people to travel to the Moon since Apollo 17 in 1972.

The next step looks different from Apollo. Under NASA's current plan, detailed in October 2026, Artemis III is a 14-day mission in low Earth orbit, planned for 2027, with astronauts docking Orion with test versions of two commercial lunar landers, Blue Origin's Blue Moon and SpaceX's Starship, to practice rendezvous, docking and living aboard before risking a landing. It means launching three spacecraft on three different heavy rockets and making them work together, something NASA says it has never attempted. Doing the hard, unfamiliar part close to home, where a problem is survivable, is classic risk reduction. NASA is aiming to land astronauts near the Moon's south pole in 2028. Schedules like this have slipped many times, so the dates are goals, not guarantees.

The south pole is the target for a reason. Because the Moon's axis is barely tilted, some craters near the poles never see sunlight, and their floors may be among the coldest places in the solar system. In 2009, NASA's LCROSS mission deliberately crashed a spent rocket stage into one of them, a crater called Cabeus, and watched the plume. It found water: about 5.6 percent of the excavated soil by mass, plus or minus 2.9 percent. Water on the Moon means drinking water, breathable oxygen and, split into hydrogen and oxygen, rocket propellant. A base that can make its own fuel changes everything about how far people can go.

blocks.text: Samples from the south pole, from rock that is far from the Apollo sites, may also help close the twin problem. Apollo explored a small patch of the Moon's near side. Rocks from new regions, especially from deep in the Moon's past, are exactly what researchers need to test how the collision really unfolded.
The power of a small number

Here is the idea worth taking away. Four centimeters a year is nothing. You could not see it, feel it or measure it with any normal instrument. Yet sustained over billions of years, that tiny drift, paired with a fraction of a millisecond per century, turned an 18-hour day into a 24-hour day and pushed the Moon tens of thousands of kilometers farther out. Long timescales make small, steady forces dominant.

The same principle runs through physics, through erosion, through compound interest and through habits. What changes the world is rarely the dramatic moment. More often it is a small, unglamorous effect that never stops. The Moon's birth was the most violent thing that ever happened to Earth. Its slow retreat, one fingernail's growth per year, may end up mattering just as much.

takeaways: The Moon most likely formed when a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.
Earth and Moon rocks have identical oxygen fingerprints, a puzzle that still pushes scientists to refine the impact story.
Tides transfer spin from Earth to the Moon: the Moon recedes 3.82 cm a year and days grow about 1.8 ms per century.
A day was about 21.9 hours long 620 million years ago and about 18.7 hours 1.4 billion years ago.
Artemis II flew around the Moon in April 2026; the target for a landing is the south pole, where craters hold water ice.

title: The Best Clocks in the Universe Are Dead Stars
dek: A neutron star crams more mass than the Sun into a ball the width of a city and can spin hundreds of times a second. Astronomers have turned these stellar corpses into clocks, scales, gravitational-wave detectors and a GPS for deep space.

blocks.text: In the summer of 1967, a Cambridge graduate student named Jocelyn Bell was running a new radio telescope she had helped build: a field of wire antennas strung across posts, feeding pens that scratched signals onto long rolls of paper chart. Her job was to scan that paper by eye for flickering radio sources. In among the expected squiggles, she noticed a small patch of something that didn't belong. When she and her supervisor, Antony Hewish, recorded it at higher speed later that year, it turned out to be a string of sharp pulses arriving about every 1.3 seconds, with a regularity that looked man-made.

The team ruled out interference, ruled out the building next door, and, half-jokingly, labeled the source LGM-1, for little green men. Then Bell found a second one in a different part of the sky. Two alien civilizations broadcasting on the same odd schedule seemed unlikely, so the answer had to be natural. The paper describing a rapidly pulsating radio source came out in *Nature* in February 1968. Within a year, astronomers had worked out what they were looking at: a neutron star, the collapsed core left behind by a supernova, sweeping a beam across Earth like a lighthouse.

Hewish shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery. Bell did not, which is still one of the most debated omissions in the prize's history. But the bigger story is what pulsars turned into. That chart-paper anomaly became one of the most precise tools in physics.
A signal that measured its own size

Before anyone knew what pulsars were, the pulses themselves gave away a key fact. An object can't brighten and dim as a whole faster than light can cross it, because one side of it has no way of knowing what the other side is doing any sooner than that. A source that switches on and off in a fraction of a second has to be small. When pulsars were later found that pulse in milliseconds, the size limit dropped to roughly the scale of a city.

That kind of reasoning is worth stealing. Sometimes the most informative thing about a signal isn't what it says but how fast it changes. A fault that comes and goes in milliseconds is not a slow thermal drift. A pressure swing that cycles every few seconds isn't a leak. Timing alone can rule out whole categories of explanation.

Only a few kinds of objects are small enough, dense enough and strong enough to spin that fast without tearing apart. White dwarfs are too large. That left neutron stars, which had been predicted in the 1930s and never seen. The previous article on stellar life cycles, *The Reactor That Runs Itself*, explains how they form when a massive star's iron core collapses. This article is about what happens after: what a neutron star is like, and what we've learned by timing them.
A city-sized atomic nucleus

Picture a ball about 25 kilometers across, small enough to fit inside a large city, holding more mass than the Sun. In 2019, a team using NASA's NICER X-ray telescope on the space station measured one such object, the pulsar PSR J0030+0451, by modeling how hot spots on its surface rotate in and out of view. They found a mass of about 1.34 Suns and an equatorial radius of about 12.7 kilometers, each with an uncertainty of roughly 10%.

Do the arithmetic on those numbers and the average density comes out to around 300 million billion kilograms per cubic meter, comparable to the inside of an atomic nucleus. A teaspoon of that material would weigh about 1.5 billion metric tons, more than every human on Earth put together. Gravity at the surface is so strong that light leaving it gets bent noticeably, which is why the NICER team had to trace light paths through curved spacetime to read the star's size from its pulses.

Its measured equatorial radius
Weight of a teaspoon at its average density (calculated)

blocks.source: Riley et al., Astrophysical Journal Letters, 2019 (density calculated from their mass and radius)

blocks.text: Two things get dramatically amplified when a star's core collapses to that size. The first is spin. A figure skater spins faster by pulling her arms in, and a stellar core shrinking from thousands of kilometers to about 25 does the same thing on a huge scale. The second is magnetism, because the star's magnetic field gets squeezed into a much smaller area. The most extreme neutron stars, called magnetars, have the strongest magnetic fields known. About 30 had been identified by 2017, according to a review by Victoria Kaspi and Andrei Beloborodov.
Lighthouses that keep perfect time

A pulsar isn't actually pulsing. Its magnetic poles shoot out beams of radiation, and those poles are tilted relative to the axis the star spins around. Each rotation sweeps the beams across space. If Earth happens to sit in the path, we see a blink once or twice per turn. Most neutron stars probably beam somewhere else, so we never detect them as pulsars at all.

The young Crab pulsar, left by a supernova recorded by Chinese astronomers in 1054, spins about 30 times a second. Jodrell Bank Observatory has tracked it for decades. Since 1968, its spin rate has dropped by about half a rotation per second as it slowly loses energy, interrupted by 24 sudden small speed-ups called glitches. Those glitches are thought to happen when the star's interior and crust briefly fall out of sync and then re-lock.

The fastest pulsars are old, not young. These are millisecond pulsars, spun up over millions of years by pulling in material from a companion star, much as a merry-go-round speeds up when you keep shoving it. The record holder, found in 2006 in the star cluster Terzan 5, spins 716 times per second. Its surface is moving at a meaningful fraction of the speed of light.

blocks.title: How fast pulsars spin
blocks.note: B1937+21 held the speed record for 23 years until J1748-2446ad was found in 2006.
blocks.source: Lyne et al., MNRAS, 2015; Hessels et al., Science, 2006; Romani et al., ApJ Letters, 2022

blocks.text: How heavy can a dead star get?

PSR J0952-0607 isn't just one of the fastest spinners. In 2022 Roger Romani and colleagues used the Keck telescopes to measure how its faint companion moves, and they calculated the pulsar's mass at about 2.35 Suns, give or take 0.17. That's the heaviest well-measured neutron star known. They estimated it has pulled in nearly a full Sun's worth of mass from its partner, which the pulsar's own wind is now slowly evaporating. For that reason, astronomers call systems like this black widows.

What's actually inside? The outer crust is thought to be a rigid lattice of atomic nuclei, held so tightly by gravity that the surface is almost perfectly smooth. Deeper down, the pressure squeezes electrons into protons until neutrons dominate, and much of that neutron matter is expected to behave as a superfluid that flows without friction. Nobody knows for sure what's at the very center. Proposals range from ordinary neutrons packed even tighter to exotic states where neutrons dissolve into free quarks. That uncertainty is exactly why mass measurements matter.

Why does a heavy neutron star matter? Somewhere above a certain mass, a neutron star can't hold itself up and collapses into a black hole. That limit depends on how matter behaves at densities no laboratory on Earth can reach. Each precise mass and radius measurement rules out some theories of nuclear matter. The honest status: the exact limit is still unknown, and the error bars on radius measurements are still about a kilometer, which is a big deal for an object only about 25 kilometers across.

Neutron stars don't always end quietly, either. When two of them spiral together and merge, the collision throws out neutron-rich debris where heavy elements like gold and platinum are forged. In 2017, gravitational-wave detectors and telescopes watched one of these mergers happen. The stellar life cycle article covers that event. What makes it possible to study these systems for decades before they merge, though, is the pulsar's remarkable clock.
A clock that tested Einstein

In 1974, Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found a pulsar orbiting another neutron star. General relativity predicts that a pair like that should radiate gravitational waves, lose orbital energy, and slowly spiral inward. Because the pulsar is such a good clock, you can measure that spiral just by watching its pulses arrive a little earlier, year after year. Hulse and Taylor won the 1993 Nobel Prize for this work.

By 2016, Joel Weisberg and Yuping Huang had analyzed 9,257 pulse arrival times collected over 35 years. The observed rate at which the orbit is shrinking came out to 0.9983 times Einstein's prediction, with an uncertainty of 0.0016. That's agreement to a fraction of a percent, using a clock thousands of light-years away. It was the first strong evidence that gravitational waves exist, decades before LIGO detected them directly in 2015.

Astronomers have now scaled up the trick. If many pulsars across the sky all drift in a particular correlated pattern, it suggests gravitational waves are gently stretching the space between us and them. In 2023 the NANOGrav collaboration reported evidence for exactly that pattern in 15 years of timing data from 67 pulsars. The most likely source is a background hum from pairs of supermassive black holes in galaxies across the universe, though other explanations haven't been ruled out. The result is described as evidence, not yet a confirmed detection.

blocks.text: A GPS made of dead stars

Here's the application a navigator will appreciate. GPS satellites only work near Earth. Deep-space probes are tracked from the ground by radio, which gets less precise the farther away they are. But millisecond pulsars are scattered across the sky, and their ticks are known in advance. If you know exactly when a pulse should arrive at a reference point, and you measure when it actually arrives at your spacecraft, the difference tells you how far you are along the line toward that pulsar. Combine several pulsars and you have a position fix.

In November 2017, NASA's SEXTANT experiment did that for real, using the NICER X-ray telescope on the space station. Working autonomously and in real time, it tracked the station's position to within 10 kilometers using only pulsar timing, while the station was moving at nearly 8 kilometers per second. Ten kilometers isn't GPS-grade precision, but it was a first demonstration, and it works anywhere in the solar system.

Why X-rays rather than radio? Radio pulsars are easier to find, but catching their faint signals takes a big dish antenna, which is not something you can bolt onto a probe. Many millisecond pulsars also give off X-rays, and an X-ray detector can be made compact. The tradeoff is that X-ray photons arrive sparsely, a few at a time, so a navigator has to collect them over minutes to hours and fold them together to rebuild each pulse. It's slow but steady, more like a fix taken at regular intervals than a live readout.

Submariners will see the parallel. A submerged boat relies on inertial navigation, which slowly drifts, and every so often it needs an outside reference to correct the error. Sailors once used a sextant and the stars. A spacecraft heading to the outer planets might use an X-ray detector and a handful of dead stars.

The first pulsar was a tiny smudge of odd squiggles on a very long roll of chart paper. The discovery came from someone who knew what normal looked like well enough to notice the one thing that wasn't. That's as true on a watch log as it is on a radio telescope.

takeaways: A neutron star packs over a solar mass into a sphere about 25 km across, so densely that a teaspoon would weigh more than a billion tons.
Pulsars are lighthouses, not flashing stars: tilted magnetic beams sweep past Earth as they spin, up to 716 times a second.
Timing a pulsar orbit for 35 years matched Einstein's gravitational-wave prediction to within a fraction of a percent.
How fast a signal changes can reveal how big its source is, a useful way to diagnose any system.
Pulsar timing has already navigated a spacecraft to within 10 km, with no GPS required.

title: The Hidden Oceans Under the Ice
dek: Some of the solar system's most promising places for life aren't planets at all. They're frozen moons of Jupiter and Saturn, heated from the inside, with salty seas under their ice, and one of them is spraying its ocean into space.

blocks.text: In 2005, NASA's Cassini spacecraft was a year into its tour of Saturn when it took a close look at Enceladus, a small icy moon about as wide as Arizona. Enceladus was already odd. Its surface is the most reflective in the solar system, as white as fresh snow, and its south pole had almost no craters, which meant the surface there was young. Then the cameras caught something nobody expected: jets of water vapor and ice grains spraying out of long cracks near the south pole at around 400 meters per second, building a towering plume above a moon that should have been frozen solid.

Enceladus was spraying its ocean into space. Over the next decade, Cassini flew through the plume again and again, sampling it with instruments that were never designed for the job, and essentially tasted a sea on another world without landing. What it found turned a tiny moon nobody cared about into one of the best places in the solar system to look for life.

Enceladus is not alone. Jupiter's moon Europa almost certainly hides a salty ocean holding more than twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans combined. A whole class of worlds that used to be dismissed as balls of ice turns out to have liquid water inside. And a spacecraft is on its way right now to find out whether one of them could support life.
How can there be liquid water out there?

Saturn is about ten times farther from the Sun than Earth. Sunlight there is roughly a hundredth as strong, and surface temperatures on its moons sit far below minus 150 Celsius. By the old logic, which said liquid water needs a planet at the right distance from its star, these moons should be frozen to the core. The old logic missed a second heat source: gravity.

Enceladus is locked in a rhythm with a bigger neighbor, the moon Dione. It orbits Saturn exactly twice for every one orbit Dione makes, so the two line up at the same points again and again, and Dione's regular tugs keep Enceladus's orbit slightly oval. That means Enceladus is sometimes closer to Saturn and sometimes farther away. Saturn's enormous gravity squeezes and relaxes the little moon on every orbit, flexing its interior. Flexing makes friction, and friction makes heat. Europa gets the same treatment from Jupiter, thanks to a similar rhythm with its neighbors Io and Ganymede. Io gets so much of it that it is the most volcanic body in the solar system.

blocks.title: Tidal heating: how a frozen moon keeps an ocean
items: A neighboring moon's regular tugs keep the orbit oval
The moon swings closer to and farther from the giant planet
The planet's gravity squeezes and relaxes the moon's interior
Flexing rock and ice turn motion into heat
Heat keeps an ocean liquid under the ice shell

blocks.text: This is a reframe worth sitting with. The usual picture of a habitable world is a planet warmed by its star. Ocean worlds are warmed from the inside by orbital mechanics. If that works here, it probably works around many other stars too, which means the number of places in the galaxy with liquid water could be far larger than counts of Earth-like planets suggest.
Finding an ocean you cannot see

Nobody has seen these oceans directly. They lie under kilometers of ice. Their existence was worked out the way a detective works out a crime, from several independent clues that all point the same way.

blocks.title: Four ways to detect a hidden ocean
items: Magnetism: Jupiter's field sweeps past Europa, and a salty, conductive ocean responds with its own induced magnetic field, which the Galileo spacecraft detected.
Wobble: Cassini measured a slight back-and-forth rocking of Enceladus that is too large unless the ice shell floats on a global liquid layer.
Gravity: tracking a spacecraft's radio signal during flybys reveals how mass is distributed inside the moon.
Plumes and geology: young, cracked surfaces and spraying jets show material moving up from below.

blocks.text: The magnetic clue is the most elegant, and it uses physics any electrician knows. Jupiter's huge magnetic field is tilted, so as Jupiter rotates, the field at Europa's position keeps changing. A changing magnetic field passing through a conductor induces currents, and those currents create a magnetic field of their own. Ice is a poor conductor. Salt water is a good one. When the Galileo spacecraft flew past Europa in the late 1990s, it measured exactly the kind of induced field you would expect from a global layer of salty water beneath the surface. Europa is, in effect, the secondary winding of a transformer the size of a planet.
Tasting the sea of Enceladus

Enceladus made things easier by throwing its ocean at the spacecraft. The plume is made of tiny ice grains and gas from the ocean below, so every pass through it was a sample. Over the years, Cassini's instruments built up a chemistry report that reads like a checklist for life's needs.

First came salts, sodium chloride and carbonates, showing the grains came from liquid water in contact with rock. Then, in 2015, a team led by Hsiang-Wen Hsu reported tiny grains of silica, only 2 to 8 nanometers in radius, that had been flung out of the Saturn system. Making silica grains like that requires water hotter than about 90 Celsius reacting with rock. The likeliest explanation is hydrothermal activity on the seafloor, the same kind of hot springs that support rich ecosystems in total darkness at the bottom of Earth's oceans.

In 2017, a team led by Hunter Waite reported molecular hydrogen in the plume, most plausibly from ongoing reactions between hot water and rock. Hydrogen matters because it is food. On Earth, some microbes make their living by combining hydrogen with carbon dioxide to make methane, no sunlight required. The amount Cassini found suggests that chemical energy for exactly this kind of metabolism is available.

The last major missing piece was phosphorus, the least abundant of the key elements life uses, essential for DNA and for the molecules cells use to store energy. In 2023, Frank Postberg and colleagues reanalyzed Cassini's dust data and found sodium phosphates in the ice grains. Their estimate put phosphorus concentrations in the plume's source water at least 100 times higher than in Earth's oceans. NASA also notes that organic material in the plume was about 20 times denser than scientists had expected.

The way Cassini read these grains is clever in itself. Its Cosmic Dust Analyzer was a target plate that ice grains hit at several kilometers per second. At that speed a grain is instantly vaporized into a puff of charged fragments, and timing how long each fragment takes to fly to a detector reveals its mass. Different molecules leave different patterns. The instrument was built to study dust in Saturn's rings, not to analyze an alien ocean, which is why some of these results came out years after the mission ended, when researchers went back through the archive with new questions and new lab experiments.

blocks.text: Put it together: liquid water, salts, rock, heat, a chemical energy source, carbon compounds and phosphorus. That is not evidence of life. It is evidence of a place where life, as we understand it, would not obviously be impossible. For astrobiologists, that is a big deal, because it narrows the search from "anywhere" to a short list of addresses.
Europa: the bigger ocean

Europa is slightly smaller than our Moon, yet NASA estimates its ocean may hold about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans, because it wraps around the entire moon and is thought to be very deep. The surface is crisscrossed with cracks, ridges and jumbled regions called chaos terrain, where the ice seems to have broken apart and refrozen. In 2022, NASA's Juno spacecraft flew past Europa and used its microwave radiometer to peer into the ice. A study published in 2026 estimated the shell's thickness at about 29 km, give or take 10, with cracks and pores reaching hundreds of meters down. That matters, because a thinner and more fractured shell could let oxygen and other chemicals made at the surface by Jupiter's radiation reach the ocean below.

On October 14, 2024, NASA launched Europa Clipper on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy. With its solar arrays unfolded it spans more than 30 meters, about the length of a basketball court, because sunlight at Jupiter is so weak that it needs huge panels to run on solar power. It is traveling 2.9 billion km to arrive at Jupiter in April 2030, and it will make 49 close flybys of Europa, swooping in and back out again to limit its exposure to Jupiter's brutal radiation belts. Europe's Juice spacecraft, launched in April 2023, will arrive in July 2031 to study Ganymede, Callisto and Europa.

Europa may be spraying too. Over the past decade, observations with the Hubble Space Telescope have reported possible signs of water vapor plumes above Europa's surface, but the detections are faint and have not been firmly confirmed. If Europa Clipper catches a plume during a flyby, its instruments could sample ocean material directly, the same trick that made Enceladus so productive.

blocks.text: A key detail: Europa Clipper is not a life-detection mission. It carries nine instruments to map the ice, measure the ocean's depth and saltiness, analyze surface chemistry and sample any gas or dust near the moon. Its job is to answer whether Europa *could* support life, and to scout where a future lander might dig. Science usually advances this way, one carefully scoped question at a time, rather than in one dramatic leap.
Protecting what we might find

In September 2017, nearly out of fuel after 13 years at Saturn, Cassini was deliberately steered into Saturn's atmosphere, where it burned up. NASA did this on purpose. A spacecraft left to drift could eventually crash into Enceladus or Titan, and despite careful cleaning, it could carry hardy Earth microbes. If we ever found life in that ocean, we would need to be certain we had not brought it ourselves. Mission planners destroyed a working spacecraft to protect a possible ecosystem nobody has proven exists.

That decision says something about how seriously scientists take the question. It is easy to say "maybe there's life out there." It is harder to build every mission so that, if the answer is yes, the result will be believable.
Why it matters

On Earth, life in deep-sea hydrothermal vents lives in total darkness, feeding on chemical energy from the rocks rather than sunlight. Anyone who has lived for weeks in a sealed hull under the sea knows that a world without sunlight is not necessarily a world without life. Ocean moons are that idea scaled up to an entire world.

The deeper stakes are about numbers. So far, we know of exactly one origin of life: ours. One example tells you nothing about whether life is common. If even simple microbes turned up in an ocean under the ice of Europa or Enceladus, and they arose independently from life on Earth, life would have started twice in a single solar system. That would strongly suggest it starts easily, wherever conditions allow, and the galaxy would suddenly look like a crowded place.

Proving independence would take care. Impacts have blasted rocks from Mars to Earth (scientists have collected Martian meteorites), so microbes could in principle hitch rides between planets. But the outer moons are far harder to reach, and a truly separate origin might leave a signature. Life on Earth builds its proteins from one mirror-image form of amino acids and stores information in DNA using a specific chemical alphabet. Life that used a different set of building blocks, or the opposite handedness, would be very hard to explain as a cousin of ours.

If the oceans turn out to be sterile despite having every ingredient, that would be a profound answer too. Either way, the most important water in the solar system outside Earth may be hidden under kilometers of ice, and we finally have the tools to start asking.

takeaways: Moons like Europa and Enceladus stay warm inside through tidal heating, the squeezing of their interiors by a giant planet's gravity.
Hidden oceans are detected indirectly, through induced magnetic fields, rocking motions, gravity and erupting plumes.
Cassini found salts, signs of hot seafloor springs, hydrogen, organics and plenty of phosphorus in Enceladus's plume: ingredients, not proof of life.
Europa Clipper arrives at Jupiter in April 2030 to judge whether Europa could support life, with 49 close flybys.
Finding a second, independent origin of life in our own solar system would suggest life is common in the universe.

title: The Crowded Sky
dek: Earth orbit is a commons with no garbage truck. A 1978 paper predicted what happens when the junk starts hitting itself, and the catalog has nearly quadrupled in twenty years.

blocks.text: At 16:56 GMT on February 10, 2009, high over northern Siberia, two satellites arrived at the same point at the same moment. One was Iridium 33, a working American communications satellite of about 560 kilograms. The other was Cosmos 2251, a dead Russian satellite of about 900 kilograms that nobody had controlled in years. Their orbits crossed at nearly a right angle, and they met at more than 11 kilometers per second, many times faster than a rifle bullet.

The first sign anything had happened was that Iridium 33 stopped talking. Then the U.S. Space Surveillance Network began spotting new objects strung along both satellites' paths. By the end of March, 823 pieces had been cataloged, with more tracked and countless smaller fragments too small to see. It was the first accidental collision between two intact satellites. It will not be the last, and understanding why requires understanding why satellites are where they are.
Why orbits are where they are

An orbit is just falling sideways fast enough to keep missing the ground. The lower you are, the faster you must go and the shorter your lap. Close to Earth, in what is called low Earth orbit, below about 2,000 kilometers, objects travel at 7 to 8 kilometers per second and circle the planet in roughly an hour and a half. Hubble, at about 483 kilometers, laps the Earth every 95 minutes. The International Space Station, imaging satellites and the new internet megaconstellations all live down here, because close means sharp pictures, fast signals and cheap launches.

Go higher and the lap slows. GPS satellites, in the middle region, take about twelve hours. At roughly 36,000 kilometers, the lap takes exactly as long as Earth takes to spin once, so a satellite over the equator appears to hang motionless above one spot. That geostationary belt is prime real estate for weather and TV satellites, since a dish on the ground never has to move. It is also a single thin ring around the planet, which means everyone wants the same slots.

Geostationary operators have their own cleanup ritual. Nothing up there falls back to Earth on any human timescale, so near the end of a mission, operators typically spend their last fuel nudging the satellite a few hundred kilometers higher into a graveyard orbit, out of the working ring. NASA describes the debris problem at geostationary altitude as generally less severe than in low orbit, largely because the belt is so far up and so carefully managed.

Altitude also decides how long junk sticks around. The thin upper atmosphere drags on everything in low orbit, slowly pulling it down to burn up. That drag is the only garbage collector space has, and it fades quickly with height.

items.label: Typical time for debris below 600 km to fall back to Earth
Typical decay time at 800 km
Debris above 1,000 km normally keeps orbiting

blocks.text: Notice where the 2009 crash happened: 790 kilometers. The fragments from that collision will be drifting through some of the busiest altitudes in orbit for generations. NASA says the greatest concentration of debris sits between about 750 and 1,000 kilometers, right in the zone where nature cleans up slowest.
Counting the junk

The U.S. Space Surveillance Network, a web of radars and telescopes, tracks objects larger than about 10 centimeters, roughly the size of a softball. As of August 2026 it had cataloged 34,054 objects in Earth orbit: 19,154 spacecraft, working or dead, and 14,900 spent rocket stages and pieces of debris. NASA estimates about 50,000 large objects are up there in total, plus around 100 million fragments about a millimeter across.

blocks.title: Objects cataloged in Earth orbit
blocks.note: Only objects big enough to track (roughly 10 cm and up). The 2007-2010 jump is mostly debris; the post-2020 climb is mostly new satellites.
blocks.source: NASA Orbital Debris Quarterly News, Satellite Box Score, 2006-2026

blocks.text: That curve has two very different stories in it. The early jump is wreckage. On January 11, 2007, China destroyed its own retired Fengyun-1C weather satellite with a missile in an anti-satellite test. Within a year, nearly 2,600 large tracked pieces had been tied to it, and NASA radar data suggested at least 150,000 pieces a centimeter or larger. Two years later came the Iridium-Cosmos crash. On November 15, 2021, Russia did its own test, blowing up the derelict Cosmos 1408 and creating more than 1,500 trackable fragments. NASA's catalog history shows these three events as the three big upward steps in fragmentation debris.

blocks.title: Tracked fragments from three events
blocks.note: Counts a few weeks to a year after each event; smaller untracked fragments are far more numerous.
blocks.source: NASA Orbital Debris Quarterly News, Jan 2008, Apr 2009, Feb 2022

blocks.text: Explosions do not just add pieces; they scatter them. Cosmos 1408 had been circling at roughly 465 to 490 kilometers, but the blast flung fragments into new orbits, some reaching as high as about 1,440 kilometers, and around 60 percent ended up on more steeply tilted paths than their parent. One dead satellite at one altitude became a spray of hazards crossing many altitudes, including the one the International Space Station uses. NASA scrambled to work out measures to protect the station's crew, and even after the cloud spread out, it estimated the debris risk to the station had settled at about twice its pre-test level.

The later climb is a different thing: launches. The catalog held 2,970 payloads in January 2006. In August 2026 it held 19,154 spacecraft. Most of that is the arrival of megaconstellations, thousands of small satellites working together to beam internet around the planet.
Kessler's warning

In 1978, a NASA scientist named Donald Kessler and his colleague Burton Cour-Palais published a paper with a dry title and an alarming idea. They calculated how often satellites would collide as their numbers grew, and pointed out a feedback loop. Every collision makes fragments. Fragments make further collisions more likely. Past a certain density, the debris population would keep growing on its own, even if nobody launched anything else, eventually forming a belt of junk around the Earth.

blocks.title: The collision cascade
items: Objects crowd a popular altitude
Two of them collide at kilometers per second
Hundreds or thousands of fragments spread along the orbit
More fragments mean higher odds of the next collision
Drag is too weak at that height to clear them out

blocks.text: The idea became known as the Kessler syndrome, and movies have made it look like a chain reaction that shreds every satellite in an afternoon. The real version is slower and, in a way, more unsettling. NASA's long-term debris models once ran a thought experiment: what if launches stopped completely after 2006? The answer was that the low-orbit population would hold roughly steady for about 50 years, as new collision fragments balanced old junk falling out, and then start growing anyway over the following centuries. The cascade is a process measured in decades, which is exactly the kind of problem humans are bad at taking seriously.

A Kessler cascade does not need a dramatic trigger. It only needs the rate at which collisions create debris to exceed the rate at which the atmosphere removes it. At some altitudes, models suggest that line may already have been crossed.

Kessler himself is still being recognized for the warning. In May 2026 his alma mater, the University of Houston, gave him an honorary doctorate, nearly half a century after the paper that named a problem the rest of the world is only now budgeting for.
Living in a shooting gallery

At orbital speeds, size is a poor guide to danger. NASA says debris strikes other objects at an average relative speed of about 10 kilometers per second. Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed, so at 10 kilometers per second every gram of debris carries about 50,000 joules, more than ten times the chemical energy in a gram of TNT. A paint fleck can pit a window; a bolt can kill a satellite. The International Space Station is the most heavily shielded spacecraft ever flown, and its critical modules can normally take hits from debris up to about a centimeter across.

Bigger things it has to dodge. When a tracked object is predicted to pass within a few miles and the chance of collision tops 1 in 10,000, the station normally fires its thrusters to move. It has done that 41 times since 1999. The hardest band is the middle: pieces between 1 and 10 centimeters are too big for the shielding and too small to track reliably. For most robotic spacecraft in low orbit, NASA says millimeter-sized debris is actually the highest mission-ending risk, simply because there is so much of it.

items: Under 1 mm: strikes constantly, usually harmless, wears surfaces over time.
1 mm to 1 cm: the main killer of unshielded robotic satellites; untracked.
1 to 10 cm: can puncture shielded modules; mostly untracked; the blind spot.
Over 10 cm: tracked and cataloged; spacecraft can maneuver around it.

blocks.text: Historically, the biggest single source of large debris was not collisions at all but explosions: rocket upper stages and spacecraft left in orbit with leftover fuel or charged batteries that eventually ruptured. That is why debris guidelines now stress passivation, venting propellant and draining batteries at the end of a mission so the hardware is inert. It still goes wrong. On June 9, 2026, the upper stage of a Chinese ZhuQue-2E rocket broke apart shortly after releasing its payload. Because it was only a few hundred kilometers up, the drag cleanup was quick: of the 7 fragments added to the catalog by mid-July, 4 had already reentered.

Why should anyone below care? Because modern life quietly runs through this shell of space. GPS timing synchronizes cell networks, power grids and bank transactions. Weather satellites feed every forecast, and ships far from shore rely on satellite links for navigation and communication. A debris belt would not fall on anyone's head. It would just make the most useful real estate above Earth more expensive, more dangerous and, at worst, unusable for generations.
Megaconstellations: the problem or the fix?

SpaceX's Starlink is the elephant in the sky. According to astronomer Jonathan McDowell's running tally, SpaceX had launched 13,096 Starlink satellites by early November 2026, with 11,214 still in orbit. Compare that to the 19,154 spacecraft of every kind in the August catalog and one company now operates more than half of all the spacecraft circling the planet. Amazon's Kuiper and Chinese constellations such as Qianfan are following.

That sounds like a recipe for Kessler, and critics worry it is. But the same tally shows something reassuring: 1,528 Starlinks have already completed controlled disposal, deliberately steered down to burn up. Constellations that fly low, below a few hundred kilometers where drag works fast, are partly self-cleaning even when a satellite dies. The real danger is not the number of satellites so much as their discipline: whether dead ones are removed quickly, whether operators share their orbits and dodge each other, and whether anyone ever blows one up on purpose again.

In the end, orbit is a classic commons, like a fishery or a shared pasture. Each operator gains the full benefit of launching, while the risk of debris is spread across everyone, including countries that have never launched anything. There is no international treaty on orbital debris, NASA notes, only mitigation guidelines from bodies such as the Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee and a United Nations subcommittee. The economist Elinor Ostrom won a Nobel Prize for showing that commons can be governed well when users can monitor each other and face consequences. Orbit has the monitoring. It is still working on the consequences.

Anyone who has worked around sensitive machinery knows the rule: the cheapest piece of foreign material to deal with is the one you never let in. Orbit works the same way. Removing debris after the fact is expensive and barely possible; not creating it is almost free.

takeaways: Altitude decides lifetime: junk below about 600 km falls within years, but above 1,000 km it can circle for a thousand years or more.
The U.S. catalog held 34,054 tracked objects in August 2026, up from about 9,400 in 2006; NASA estimates 100 million millimeter-sized fragments.
Two deliberate anti-satellite tests and one accidental collision created the biggest single jumps in orbital debris.
The Kessler syndrome is a slow feedback loop, not an instant catastrophe: collisions make fragments that make more collisions.
Megaconstellations add enormous numbers of satellites; whether they worsen debris depends mostly on how fast dead ones are removed.

title: The Planet That Kept Shrinking
dek: Pluto was found by a prediction built on bad data, demoted by a vote, and then turned out to be one of the most interesting worlds we have visited. Now astronomers are chasing another invisible planet the same way.

blocks.text: In 1980, two space physicists published a tongue-in-cheek note in the newsletter of the American Geophysical Union titled, roughly, the pending disappearance of Pluto. Their joke was simple. Every new measurement of Pluto's mass had come out smaller than the last. Draw a line through the estimates and extend it, they noted, and Pluto would soon weigh nothing at all.

Pluto did not vanish. But the joke pointed at something real and a little embarrassing: the ninth planet had been discovered on the strength of a calculation that was wrong, and its status as a planet had been resting on an assumption nobody had checked. The story of how Pluto went from planet to dwarf planet, and why astronomers are now hunting a hidden Planet Nine using a similar method, is really a story about how science decides what things are, and how it fools itself with patterns.
Found by a mistake

The method had a famous success behind it. In 1846, astronomers noticed Uranus drifting slightly off its predicted path, worked backward to where an unseen planet would have to be, and found Neptune almost exactly there. Percival Lowell, the wealthy founder of an observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, believed Uranus still was not behaving and spent his last years computing the position of a massive Planet X beyond Neptune.

In February 1930, years after Lowell's death, a young assistant at his observatory named Clyde Tombaugh found a faint moving dot by comparing photographic plates of the same patch of sky taken days apart. The search was brutal, patient work: a blink comparator flipped rapidly between two glass plates, each crowded with faint stars, so that anything that had moved would seem to jump back and forth. Tombaugh spent months staring at plates like that. The dot was close enough to the predicted region to look like vindication. A schoolgirl in Oxford, England, Venetia Burney, suggested the name Pluto over breakfast, her grandfather passed it along, and the observatory chose it.

Then the estimates of its mass began to fall. In 1931 it was calculated to be about as heavy as Earth, based on its supposed tug on the giant planets. By the late 1940s, measurements of its size cut that to around a tenth. In 1976, astronomers found methane ice on its surface, meaning Pluto was bright and reflective and therefore much smaller than it looked. In 1978, James Christy and Robert Harrington at the U.S. Naval Observatory spotted a moon, Charon, and used its orbit to weigh the pair directly. Pluto came in at about one five-hundredth of Earth's mass.

blocks.title: Pluto's estimated mass, as a share of Earth's
blocks.note: The last two bars are too small to see. That is the point.
blocks.source: Nicholson & Mayall 1931; Wylie 1942; Kuiper 1948; Cruikshank et al. 1976; Christy & Harrington 1978; Buie et al. 2006 (compiled in Wikipedia, Planets beyond Neptune)

blocks.text: A body that small could not possibly have nudged Uranus. Lowell's prediction had been a coincidence: Tombaugh found Pluto because he searched carefully, not because the math pointed to it. And the wobbles themselves turned out to be fake. After Voyager 2 flew past Neptune in 1989 and measured its mass precisely, astronomer E. Myles Standish showed in 1993 that Neptune's mass had been slightly overestimated. Plug in the corrected number and the unexplained motion of Uranus disappears. There had never been a Planet X to find.
Pluto is a reminder that a correct result can come from a wrong reason. A lucky hit does not validate the method that produced it, and anything you build on that method inherits its weakness.
A crowd beyond Neptune

For sixty years Pluto seemed alone out there. That changed in 1992, when astronomers spotted another small icy body beyond Neptune. Then another, and another. Today thousands are known, forming the Kuiper Belt, a wide ring of frozen leftovers from the formation of the solar system. Pluto turned out not to be a lonely planet but one of the biggest members of a large family, sharing its region with countless smaller bodies, some on orbits that cross its own.

The breaking point came in 2005, when Mike Brown's team at Caltech announced a distant body later named Eris. Using the orbit of its small moon Dysnomia, Brown and Emily Schaller weighed it in 2007: Eris turned out to be about 27 percent more massive than Pluto. Astronomers now faced a choice. Either Eris was the tenth planet, and probably dozens more would follow, or the word planet needed a definition, which, remarkably, it had never had.

Length of one Pluto orbit around the Sun
