blocks.text: The vote

On August 24, 2006, at the International Astronomical Union's general assembly in Prague, astronomers voted on a definition. A planet, they decided, is a body that orbits the Sun, is massive enough that its own gravity pulls it into a nearly round shape, and has cleared the neighborhood around its orbit. A body that meets the first two tests but not the third, and is not a moon, is a dwarf planet. Pluto, sharing its zone with the Kuiper Belt, failed the third test.

blocks.title: Two ways to define a planet

left.head: Dynamical (the IAU rule)
items: Asks what a body does to its surroundings
A planet dominates its orbit and sweeps or herds everything nearby
Gives exactly eight planets, with a huge gap below them
Pluto is a dwarf planet, like Eris and Ceres

right.head: Geophysical (favored by many planetary scientists)
items: Asks what a body is like itself
Anything round from its own gravity counts
Gives dozens of planets, including some large moons by some versions
Pluto, with mountains and glaciers, is clearly a planet

blocks.text: This had happened before. In 1801 astronomers found Ceres orbiting between Mars and Jupiter and called it a planet. Within a few years they found Pallas, Juno and Vesta in the same zone, and for a while the official count of planets swelled well past the familiar list. As the count kept climbing, astronomers quietly moved them into a new category, asteroids. Ceres was demoted for exactly the reason Pluto would be: it turned out to be the biggest member of a crowd rather than a lone world. In 2006 Ceres was promoted back, as a dwarf planet.

The dynamical rule has real numbers behind it. Astronomer Steven Soter showed in 2006 that if you measure how thoroughly each body dominates the mass sharing its orbital zone, the eight planets stand apart from asteroids and Kuiper Belt objects by a gap of four to five orders of magnitude. That is not a fuzzy boundary; it is a cliff. Earth is not simply bigger than Pluto. It is a different kind of thing in how it shapes its surroundings.

But the vote itself drew fire, partly because only a small share of the union's members took part. Alan Stern, who leads NASA's New Horizons mission to Pluto, has been one of the most vocal critics, arguing that a definition based on a body's own properties makes more sense to planetary geologists. The fight is not really about facts. Everyone agrees on Pluto's mass, size and orbit. It is about which feature of reality a category should track.
Pluto up close

Nine years after the demotion, on July 14, 2015, New Horizons flew past Pluto, and the dwarf planet turned out to be anything but dull. It is about 2,377 kilometers across, roughly a fifth the width of Earth, with mountains, valleys, craters, plains and glaciers. A pale heart-shaped region stretches across one side. It has a thin atmosphere of nitrogen, methane and carbon monoxide at an average temperature of minus 232 degrees Celsius. Its largest moon, Charon, is about half its size, so the two are often described as a double planet.

That was the geophysicists' best argument. A world with active-looking geology and a layered atmosphere does not feel like a piece of rubble. The honest answer is that both camps are describing something true. Pluto is small in the sense that matters for orbits and big in the sense that matters for geology. The word planet was invented long before anyone knew about either distinction, and it simply cannot carry both meanings at once.
Hunting Planet Nine

Here is the irony. Ten years after Mike Brown's discovery of Eris helped demote Pluto, he and Caltech colleague Konstantin Batygin proposed that a real ninth planet is out there after all, far beyond Pluto. In 2016 they pointed out that the most distant known Kuiper Belt objects, on long stretched orbits, seemed to have their orbits lined up, pointing in roughly the same direction. They calculated only a 0.007 percent chance that the alignment was random, and showed it could be explained by an unseen planet of more than about ten Earth masses on a distant, tilted orbit, herding the small bodies with its gravity.

The mechanism is counterintuitive. In their models, the planet's orbit points the opposite way from the clustered objects, and over immense stretches of time its gravity herds them into a stable, anti-aligned pattern, much like a sheepdog circling a flock from the far side. The same planet would naturally explain other oddities: objects like Sedna that never come close enough to Neptune to have been flung out by it, and a handful of bodies on orbits tilted steeply, even past vertical. One hypothesis, several puzzles solved. That economy is what made Planet Nine so attractive.

In 2021, after updating their accounting for observational biases, Brown and Batygin refined the estimate: a planet of about 6 Earth masses, averaging roughly 380 times Earth's distance from the Sun, with the clustering still significant at 99.6 percent confidence. A planet like that would be faint, slow and very hard to spot. It would also be a super-Earth or mini-Neptune, a common type of planet around other stars that our own solar system seems to lack.

blocks.title: Invisible planets, inferred from wobbles
items: Neptune found where Uranus's drift said it would be: a hit
Pluto found near Lowell's Planet X position: luck, not math
Corrected Neptune mass erases the Planet X evidence
IAU vote makes Pluto a dwarf planet
Batygin and Brown propose Planet Nine from clustered orbits
Survey-bias study finds no clear evidence of clustering
Larger sample: clustering signal falls from 2.7 to 1.9 sigma

blocks.text: The skeptics' case is exactly the lesson of Planet X. Telescopes do not survey the whole sky evenly; they look where weather, seasons and the Milky Way allow, and faint distant objects are easiest to catch near the closest point of their orbits. That can make random orbits look lined up. In 2021, Kevin Napier and colleagues modeled the pointing history of three surveys in detail and concluded that the objects they found were consistent with no clustering at all. In 2025, astronomers reported a large new distant body, 2017 OF201, whose orbit points outside the supposed cluster. And in April 2026, a team led by Amir Siraj applied a new bias-proof method to 25 objects and found the clustering signal had weakened from 2.7 sigma to 1.9, below what physicists normally accept as evidence.

Meanwhile, that same group reported a different hint in 2025: the outer Kuiper Belt appears slightly warped relative to the plane it should sit in, which they suggest could come from a smaller unseen world, somewhere between the mass of Mercury and Earth, at 100 to 200 times Earth's distance. It is a separate idea from Planet Nine, and it might also turn out to be noise.

The test is coming. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory's ten-year survey is expected to find many more distant objects across the whole southern sky, enough to show whether the clustering and the warp are real. Planet Nine is a falsifiable prediction, which is exactly what good science should produce.

So the scorecard for planets inferred from wobbles is one clean hit, Neptune, and one famous false alarm, Planet X, with Planet Nine still pending. That is not a reason to dismiss the search. It is a reason to respect the two questions this whole story keeps asking. First, is the pattern real, or is it an artifact of where we happened to look? Second, when we put things in categories, are we describing nature, or choosing which of nature's features we care about? Pluto does not care what we call it. It is still out there, 248 years per lap, with a nitrogen sky and a heart on its face.

takeaways: Pluto was found near a predicted spot, but the prediction rested on wrong data; the 'Planet X' wobbles vanished once Neptune's mass was corrected in 1993.
Estimates of Pluto's mass fell from about Earth's mass in 1931 to about 1/500 of it once Charon was discovered in 1978.
The 2006 IAU rule demoted Pluto because it has not cleared its orbit; the eight planets dominate their zones by a gap of four to five orders of magnitude.
Planet Nine was proposed from clustered distant orbits; newer, bias-aware studies have weakened that signal, and the Rubin Observatory should settle it.
A pattern in data can be an artifact of where you looked. Check how the sample was collected before trusting the pattern.

title: The Tyranny of the Rocket Equation
dek: One short formula from 1903 explains why a moon rocket is almost entirely fuel, why rockets come in stages, and why reusability changed everything.

blocks.text: Stand next to a fully fueled Saturn V and you are looking at about 2.8 million kilograms of machine, taller than a 30-story building. Now ask what it actually delivered to the Moon. According to NASA, the answer is about 43,500 kilograms: the Apollo spacecraft, the lunar lander and the crew inside them. Everything else, roughly 98 percent of what sat on the pad, existed only to push that small fraction out of Earth's gravity well.

That ratio is not a sign of bad engineering. The Saturn V was one of the best-engineered machines ever built. The ratio comes from a single equation written down by a self-taught Russian schoolteacher named Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, published in 1903, the same year the Wright brothers first flew. Engineers sometimes call it the tyranny of the rocket equation, because once you understand it, you see that the universe charges compound interest on every kilogram you try to move.

items.label: Saturn V fully fueled at liftoff
What it could send toward the Moon
Share of liftoff mass that went to the Moon

blocks.source: NASA, What Was the Saturn V? (percentage calculated from NASA figures)

blocks.text: A rocket pushes itself by throwing itself away

A rocket in space has nothing to push against. No road, no water, no air for a propeller. The only way it can change its speed is by throwing mass out the back. Every kilogram of hot gas shoved backward gives the rocket a kick forward, the same momentum trade you feel if you throw a heavy ball while standing on a skateboard. Conservation of momentum is the whole engine.

Here is the catch that makes rockets different from cars. The fuel a rocket burns at liftoff has to lift not just the rocket, but all the fuel it will burn later. Early in the flight, the engines are mostly accelerating fuel that hasn't been used yet. As the tanks drain, the same engines are pushing less and less mass, so each kilogram of propellant buys more speed than the one before it. Tsiolkovsky worked out exactly how those two effects balance, and the result is this:
**Δv = v_e × ln(m0 / mf)**. The change in speed a rocket can achieve equals its exhaust velocity times the natural logarithm of its starting mass divided by its ending mass.

Every term matters, so take them one at a time. **Δv** (delta-v) is the total change in velocity the rocket can produce, in meters per second. Think of it as the rocket's fuel gauge, measured not in gallons but in speed. Every mission, from reaching orbit to landing on Mars, has a delta-v price, and if your rocket's budget is smaller than the price, you don't get there.

**v_e** is the exhaust velocity: how fast the gas leaves the nozzle relative to the rocket. Faster exhaust means more momentum per kilogram thrown away. Rocket engineers usually quote this as **specific impulse (Isp)**, measured in seconds, where v_e = Isp × g0 and g0 is standard gravity, 9.80665 m/s². The SpaceX Merlin Vacuum engine on Falcon 9's upper stage is rated at about 348 seconds, which works out to an exhaust velocity of about 3,413 m/s, roughly ten times the speed of sound at sea level.

**m0** is the rocket's mass at the start of the burn, fuel included. **mf** is its mass at the end, after the propellant is gone: structure, engines, and payload. Their ratio is called the **mass ratio**. And **ln** is the natural logarithm, the function that asks what power you have to raise e (about 2.718) to in order to get a given number. That logarithm is where the tyranny lives.
Why the logarithm is so cruel

A logarithm grows painfully slowly. Doubling the mass ratio doesn't double your delta-v; it just adds a fixed amount. Flip the equation around and the cruelty becomes obvious: the mass ratio you need is e raised to the power of Δv divided by v_e. Required fuel grows **exponentially** with the speed you want. Every extra kilometer per second multiplies, rather than adds to, the size of the rocket.

Run the numbers with that 348-second engine. To gain 1 km/s, you need a mass ratio of about 1.34, meaning about a quarter of the starting mass is propellant. Easy. To gain 5 km/s, the ratio climbs to about 4.3, so roughly 77 percent of the vehicle is fuel. To gain 10 km/s, you need a ratio near 18.7, which means almost 95 percent of the rocket must be propellant and everything else, tanks, engines, wiring, payload, has to fit in the last 5 percent.

blocks.title: Mass ratio needed vs. delta-v (Isp 348 s)
blocks.note: The curve bends upward because required fuel grows exponentially with speed.
blocks.source: Calculated with the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation using the Merlin Vacuum Isp of 348 s

blocks.text: For perspective, a soda can is about 95 percent contents and 5 percent aluminum. A rocket that needs a mass ratio of 18.7 is built to the standards of a soda can, except it also has to survive enormous vibration, hold cryogenic liquids, and carry engines producing millions of newtons of thrust. This is why rocket tanks are so thin that some early designs, like the Atlas, were pressurized just to keep from collapsing under their own weight.

Notice also what the equation does *not* contain: the size of the rocket. A rocket ten times bigger with the same mass ratio and the same engine gets exactly the same delta-v. Scaling up lets you carry a bigger payload, but it doesn't let you go faster or farther. That is counterintuitive, because in everyday life a bigger truck with a bigger tank goes farther. In rocketry, the only things that buy more speed are a better ratio of fuel to everything else, or faster exhaust. Size is just a multiplier on the payload, never on the destination.
The price of orbit

So what does it cost to reach orbit? Orbit isn't about altitude; it's about sideways speed. An object in low Earth orbit is falling toward the planet constantly, but moving sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it as quickly as it falls. You can calculate that speed from Newton's gravity: v = √(GM/r), where GM for Earth is about 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and r is the distance from Earth's center. At 200 kilometers up, r is about 6,578 km, which gives roughly 7.8 km/s, around 28,000 kilometers per hour.

But the rocket has to pay more than 7.8 km/s, because it loses speed on the way. **Gravity losses** come from the minutes spent thrusting partly upward while gravity pulls back down. **Drag losses** come from punching through the thick lower atmosphere. Add in the work of climbing to altitude, and the realistic price of reaching low orbit comes to about 9.3 to 10 km/s of delta-v. Launching east gives a small discount: Earth's surface at the equator spins at about 465 m/s, and at Cape Canaveral's latitude you get roughly 400 m/s for free.

blocks.title: Where a rocket's delta-v goes on the way to orbit
items: Reach orbital speed: about 7.8 km/s sideways at low altitude.
Pay gravity losses: speed lost while thrusting upward against gravity.
Pay drag losses: speed lost to air resistance in the lower atmosphere.
Climb to altitude: energy spent rising above the atmosphere.
Subtract Earth's spin: launching east returns a few hundred m/s.
Total bill: roughly 9.3 to 10 km/s.

blocks.text: Now plug 9.4 km/s into the equation with a 348-second engine and you need a mass ratio of about 15.7. That means a single-stage rocket would have to be roughly 94 percent propellant at liftoff. Using a sea-level engine with lower efficiency, around 283 seconds, the ratio jumps to about 30. No one has ever flown a practical single-stage-to-orbit vehicle, and this calculation is the reason.
The cheat code: staging

The way around the tyranny is to stop carrying dead weight. When a stage runs out of fuel, its empty tanks and engines are useless mass that the rest of the flight would have to keep accelerating. So you throw them away. Every stage gets its own fresh mass ratio, and the delta-v from each stage simply adds up.

Falcon 9 makes a clean worked example. Its liftoff mass is about 549 tonnes. The first stage carries about 396 tonnes of propellant. Burn all of it and the vehicle drops to roughly 153 tonnes, a mass ratio of about 3.6. With Merlin engines averaging somewhere between their sea-level and vacuum ratings, that buys around 3.5 to 3.9 km/s. Then the first stage falls away, taking about 26 tonnes of empty structure with it.

The second stage starts life at roughly 119 tonnes: about 4 tonnes of structure, 93 tonnes of propellant, and a 22.8-tonne payload, ignoring the nose fairing for simplicity. When its fuel is gone, about 27 tonnes remain, a ratio of about 4.5. At 348 seconds, that is worth about 5.1 km/s. Add the two stages and you get roughly 8.6 to 9 km/s, plus Earth's spin, which lands right in the range needed for orbit. The equation predicts the real rocket almost exactly.

blocks.title: One stage vs. two stages to orbit

items: Must carry all tanks and engines the entire way
Needs about 94% propellant at liftoff

blocks.note: Reusable Falcon 9 keeps fuel in reserve to land, so it carries less.
blocks.source: Calculated from NASA (Saturn V) and SpaceX figures via Wikipedia (Falcon 9)

blocks.text: Three ways to fight back

If the equation is fixed, engineers only have a few levers. The first is **raising exhaust velocity**. Because v_e sits outside the logarithm, it pays off linearly, which makes it the most valuable lever there is. This is why the Saturn V's upper stages burned liquid hydrogen, the lightest propellant, despite the miserable engineering of storing it at about 20 kelvin. It is also why engineers keep returning to nuclear thermal rockets, where a reactor heats hydrogen directly instead of burning it. Light, extremely hot exhaust leaves the nozzle faster than any chemical reaction can manage, though it comes with heavy reactors and shielding.

The second lever is **refueling**. The equation only cares about the mass ratio for each burn. If a spacecraft can reach orbit nearly empty and fill its tanks there, it starts the trip to the Moon or Mars with a fresh ratio, as if the climb out of Earth's atmosphere never happened. That is the logic behind plans for orbital propellant depots and tanker flights.

The third lever isn't physics at all. It's **economics**. The rocket equation says most of the rocket must be fuel, but fuel is cheap; the expensive part is the hardware. For decades, rockets were thrown into the ocean after one use, like scrapping an airliner after every flight. Landing and reusing boosters doesn't make the equation any kinder. Look at the chart: the reusable Falcon 9 actually carries less, because it has to save propellant to fly itself home. What reuse does is stop the hardware from being lost, which changes the cost of every kilogram even though it slightly worsens the mass ratio.
What the equation teaches beyond rockets

The deepest lesson of Tsiolkovsky's formula is about where effort pays off. In a system governed by an exponential, brute force loses. Want a little more speed? You need a lot more fuel, which needs bigger tanks, which need more fuel to lift them. Piling on more of the same input produces smaller and smaller gains. The winning moves are the ones that change the shape of the problem: a better exhaust velocity, dropping dead weight, refueling partway, or reusing what used to be thrown away.

That applies far outside aerospace. Anyone who has stood a watch rotation knows the difference between grinding harder and changing the system. A sailor carrying old habits, half-finished projects and gear he never uses is a rocket hauling empty tanks. Staging is a mindset: finish a phase, drop what it needed, and start the next one lighter.

Next time you watch a launch, look at the rocket and remember the soda can. That white column of fire is mostly a machine for throwing away mass as fast as possible, so that a tiny capsule at the tip can reach a speed where it never comes back down. Every kilogram on that capsule was fought for, and the fight was decided by a logarithm a schoolteacher worked out with pen and paper more than a century ago.

takeaways: Δv = v_e × ln(m0/mf): a rocket's speed budget depends on exhaust velocity and the ratio of full to empty mass.
Required fuel grows exponentially with the speed you want, which is why rockets are about 90 to 95 percent propellant.
Reaching low Earth orbit costs about 9.3 to 10 km/s once gravity and drag losses are included.
Staging works by dropping dead weight so each stage gets a fresh mass ratio; reuse cuts cost, not physics.
In exponential systems, changing the shape of the problem beats adding more brute force.

title: One in a Hundred Thousand
dek: NASA managers believed the space shuttle would fail once in 100,000 flights. Engineers said closer to 1 in 100. NASA's own later math says the early shuttle was nearer 1 in 10.

blocks.text: After the space shuttle Challenger broke apart in 1986, the physicist Richard Feynman, serving on the presidential commission that investigated it, asked people around NASA a simple question: what are the odds of losing a shuttle and its crew? The answers were wildly different. Working engineers tended to say something like 1 in 100. Management gave numbers as optimistic as 1 in 100,000.

Feynman did the arithmetic on the optimistic figure. One loss in 100,000 flights meant you could launch a shuttle every single day for 300 years and expect to lose only one. Yet NASA had just lost one on its 25th flight. His appendix to the commission's report asked where that faith in the machinery came from. The answer is a story about two accidents, a missing set of data points, and a trap that catches smart people everywhere: treating a string of successes as proof that something is safe.

items.label: Loss odds claimed by NASA management, per Feynman
Rough figure from working engineers
NASA's 2011 estimate of the real risk on Challenger's flight

blocks.source: Feynman, Rogers Commission Report Appendix F, 1986; Hamlin et al., NASA/AIAA, 2011

blocks.text: The cold morning

Each shuttle rode to orbit strapped to two solid rocket boosters, built in segments and joined by field joints. Rubber O-rings sealed those joints against the searing gases inside. Rubber stiffens in the cold, and a stiff O-ring springs back slowly when the joint flexes at ignition. On the morning of January 28, 1986, the air temperature at the pad was 36 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 degrees colder than any previous launch. One spot on the right booster's aft joint was estimated at about 28 degrees.

The night before, engineers at Morton Thiokol, the company that built the boosters, held a teleconference with NASA. Roger Boisjoly and his colleagues had seen O-ring damage on earlier flights and were worried about the cold. Thiokol's first written recommendation was not to launch below 53 degrees, the coldest temperature they had flight experience with. NASA officials pushed back. During an off-line caucus, a Thiokol senior manager told the engineering vice president to take off his engineering hat and put on his management hat. Thiokol reversed itself. According to testimony, no engineer in the room spoke in favor of launching.

At 11:38 a.m., Challenger lifted off. A plume of flame was visible leaking from the right booster's joint at 58 seconds. At about 73 seconds, the vehicle broke apart, and seven astronauts died, including Christa McAuliffe, a schoolteacher. The commission later found that the people who made the final call did not know about Thiokol's initial recommendation against launching or the engineers' continued opposition.

Feynman later made the physics impossible to ignore. At a televised hearing, he squeezed a piece of O-ring rubber in a small clamp, dropped it into a glass of ice water, then released it. The rubber did not spring back. No equations were needed: in the cold, the seal could not keep up with the joint it was supposed to seal.
The missing dots

The most instructive mistake was not in the hardware. It was in a chart. When managers looked at whether temperature mattered, they compared only the flights where O-rings had shown damage, plotting them against joint temperature. Those few points were scattered between 53 and 75 degrees with no obvious pattern. Conclusion: temperature did not seem to matter.
The commission redrew the chart with all the flights, including the ones where nothing went wrong. Suddenly the pattern jumped out. Warm flights were mostly clean. Cold flights were all damaged.

blocks.title: Flights with O-ring damage, by joint temperature
blocks.note: Challenger's joints were far colder than any flight in this data.
blocks.source: Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, Vol. 1, Ch. 6, 1986

blocks.text: That is a textbook case of what statisticians call selection bias. By looking only at failures, the managers threw away the information that made the failures meaningful: how often things went fine under the same conditions. The commission concluded that, judged against the whole flight history, the chance of O-ring distress approached certainty when the joint was colder than 65 degrees. Challenger's was far below that.
Whenever you ask 'did X matter?', check that you are looking at the cases where nothing happened, not just the ones where something did. The successes are where the pattern hides.

Feynman found another bent idea in the reports. Engineers had noted that on one earlier flight, an O-ring burned through a third of its thickness, while a lab test showed it took a cut the full depth to fail. Officials called that a safety factor of three. Feynman pointed out that a safety factor means a part designed not to be damaged at all can take three times the load. A seal that is not supposed to erode, eroding a third of the way, is not a margin. It is a warning that you do not understand what is happening. He compared it to Russian roulette: the first safe pull says nothing about the next.
Foam

Seventeen years later it happened again, in a different way. Columbia launched on January 16, 2003, on mission STS-107, the shuttle program's 113th flight. At 81.7 seconds, as the stack climbed past Mach 2, a briefcase-sized chunk of insulating foam broke off the external fuel tank near a strut called the left bipod ramp. It struck the leading edge of Columbia's left wing, made of reinforced carbon-carbon panels, at roughly 545 miles per hour relative to the orbiter.

Foam shedding was not new. The investigation board found foam loss on more than 80 percent of the 79 missions with usable imagery, and loss from that same left bipod ramp on about 10 percent. Each time the shuttle came home safely, foam strikes slid further from 'threat to the vehicle' toward 'maintenance problem.'

Engineers on a debris assessment team wanted on-orbit images of the wing to see the damage. Shuttle program managers declined. Without pictures, the team used a model called Crater, which had been calibrated on debris around 3 cubic inches. The board estimated the actual foam piece was about 400 times larger. Using a model hundreds of times outside its validated range, the analysis could not prove the wing was badly damaged, and managers treated the strike as a turnaround issue to handle after landing.

Mission Management Team calls it a turnaround issue

blocks.text: On February 1, superheated air entered the breach in the left wing during reentry and melted it from the inside. Columbia broke apart over Texas. Months later, investigators fired a 1.67-pound block of foam from a gas gun at a real wing panel at the speed and angle of the strike. It punched a hole roughly 16 by 17 inches. Light, soft foam, moving fast enough, was a cannonball. Nobody had been allowed to see that before it mattered.
What the real odds were

In 2011, as the shuttle program wound down, NASA analysts led by Teri Hamlin did something unusual: they took the shuttle's mature risk model, built with 30 years of hindsight, and ran it backward to estimate how dangerous each earlier flight had really been. The results are sobering.

blocks.title: Estimated shuttle risk, flight by flight
blocks.unit: 1 in N chance of losing crew and vehicle (higher is safer)
blocks.note: Risk only improved in steps, mostly after accidents or near misses exposed the true risk drivers.
blocks.source: Hamlin et al., Shuttle Risk Progression, NASA/AIAA, 2011

blocks.text: Feynman, notably, got close to the truth without any risk model at all. He went looking for a base rate. A range safety officer had studied nearly 2,900 solid rocket flights and found 121 failures, about 1 in 25. Discount the early design bugs and a mature rocket might reach 1 in 50; with great care, perhaps better than 1 in 100. The shuttle carried two boosters, which doubles the exposure. Instead of asking 'how safe do we believe our design is?', he asked 'how often do things like this fail?' That outside view beat the inside view by orders of magnitude.

By this estimate, the very first shuttle flight had about a 1 in 12 chance of ending in disaster, and the odds stayed near 1 in 10 through Challenger's flight. Management's 1 in 100,000 was off by a factor of about ten thousand. Even the engineers' 1 in 100 was optimistic for those years. The analysts found risk did not fall smoothly as experience piled up. It dropped in steps, and mostly after an accident or close call revealed what the real dangers were.

Some of those steps came from close calls rather than disasters. On STS-27 in 1988, insulation tore off the right booster's nose cap and battered Atlantis's underside, leaving more than 298 damage marks larger than an inch. Atlantis survived. The material was replaced with a tougher one, and the estimated risk improved from about 1 in 17 to 1 in 36. That was the system working as it should: a near miss treated as a failure, before it became one.

One step went the wrong way. Around flight STS-86 in 1997, after an environmental ban on a Freon-based blowing agent, the tank's foam was applied with a new process. Damage to the orbiter's underside jumped from about 13 hits larger than an inch per flight to about 45, and the estimated risk worsened from about 1 in 38 to 1 in 21. Venting holes added to the foam later brought hits down again. The hazard that killed Columbia had been measurable years earlier.

After Columbia, NASA finally treated debris as a threat it had to see. Every later shuttle inspected its heat shield in orbit, crews trained to make repairs, and a rescue option was planned in case a wing was badly damaged. By the analysts' estimate, that cut the risk from ascent debris from about 1 in 130 to about 1 in 600, and the overall flight risk improved to about 1 in 73.

The final record stands at 135 missions and two lost crews, fourteen astronauts in all. That works out to about one loss every 67 flights, far closer to the engineers' instinct than management's confidence.
Why you can't prove a rare risk by surviving it

Feynman put his finger on the deepest problem. If the true risk really were 1 in 100,000, you could never confirm it from experience: you would see nothing but a long string of successes. But a long string of successes is also exactly what you would see if the risk were 1 in 100, for a while. Success is weak evidence about rare failures. Two dozen good flights cannot tell 1 in 100 apart from 1 in 100,000. Only understanding the mechanism can.

blocks.title: Two ways to read a clean record

left.head: Success as proof
items: It worked last time, so the margin must be fine
Damage that did not cause a failure is acceptable damage
Data outside our experience can be extrapolated
Pictures and extra tests just slow us down

right.head: Success as a question
items: It worked last time; do we know why?
Any unexpected damage means our model is wrong somewhere
Outside the tested range, we know nothing
If we can look, we look

blocks.text: The same trap shows up in small, everyday forms. A lifter who has never been hurt doing sloppy reps, a driver who has always made it home after skipping sleep, a player who keeps winning fights with bad positioning: each has a clean record that says less than it seems to. Outcomes are noisy. Mechanisms are not. If you understand why something works, a lucky streak cannot fool you.

The organizational side of this story, how anomalies get quietly reclassified as normal, is covered in the Navy safety-culture piece in this library. The statistical side is just as useful on its own. In both disasters, people had real data. In the first, they plotted half of it. In the second, they fed it into a model far outside its tested range and declined to collect the one measurement, a photograph, that could have settled the question.

Feynman closed his appendix with a line that has outlived the shuttle: for a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations. Then he added the part worth taping inside a locker.
Nature cannot be fooled.
blocks.by: Richard Feynman, Rogers Commission Report, Appendix F, 1986

blocks.text: In anything you run, from a plant to a project to your own training, the most dangerous sentence is 'we have done it this way many times and nothing happened.' Ask instead: what would I expect to see if I were wrong, and have I actually looked?

takeaways: Managers put shuttle loss odds at 1 in 100,000; a 2011 NASA reanalysis estimated the early flights, including Challenger's, at about 1 in 10.
Challenger's managers plotted only flights with O-ring damage; adding the clean flights showed cold launches were damaged every time.
Columbia's foam strike was analyzed with a model built for debris about 400 times smaller, and requests for wing imagery were declined.
A string of successes cannot prove a risk is tiny; only understanding the mechanism can.
When you ask whether something matters, include the cases where nothing went wrong.

title: The Rocket That Comes Back
dek: For half a century, every orbital rocket was thrown away after one flight. Landing boosters changed that, but the real breakthrough wasn't saving hardware. It was speed.

blocks.text: On the night of December 21, 2015, a Falcon 9 lifted off from Cape Canaveral carrying 11 communications satellites. That part was routine. What happened next wasn't. About ten minutes later, the first stage, a tube of aluminum and engines that had just been traveling several times the speed of sound, came falling back out of the dark on a column of fire. It slowed, stood upright and set itself down on a concrete pad a few miles from where it had launched. For the first time, the main stage of an orbital rocket had come home in one piece.

By August 2026, one Falcon 9 booster, serial number B1067, had flown 37 times. In 2025, SpaceX launched 165 Falcon missions using just 25 different boosters. Ninety-five percent of those flights used a booster that had already been to space.

It's tempting to tell this as a simple story: rockets used to be disposable, now they're reusable, so space got cheap. The real story is more interesting, and more useful for anyone who wants to build something. Reuse had been tried before, at enormous expense, and it made things worse. What made the difference the second time was not just recovering hardware, but what recovery made possible.
Fifty years of flat prices

In a 2018 NASA paper, Harry Jones of Ames Research Center collected launch costs for dozens of rockets and converted them into 2018 dollars per kilogram delivered to low Earth orbit. His summary is striking. After a steep drop in the first years of the space age, costs basically stopped improving. From 1970 to 2000, the average was about $18,500 per kilogram, with most rockets between $10,000 and $32,000.

The space shuttle was supposed to break that pattern. It was the original reusable spacecraft. Instead, it became the most expensive system of its era, at about $61,700 per kilogram by Jones's figures, based on a total program cost of roughly $1.5 billion per flight from a lifetime analysis by Roger Pielke Jr. and Radford Byerly. The orbiter came back, but rebuilding it between flights took a huge workforce and months of inspection. An older NASA analysis that Jones quotes put it bluntly: launch operations alone needed about 10,000 contractors and 1,000 civil servants, and the shuttle's low flight rate meant those high fixed costs were spread over only a handful of missions a year.

blocks.title: Cost to launch one kilogram to low Earth orbit
blocks.note: Based on advertised price divided by maximum payload. Reused boosters carry less, and internal costs aren't public.
blocks.source: Jones, NASA Ames, ICES-2018-81

blocks.text: The chart hides another clue. The Saturn V, the giant moon rocket, was one of the cheapest launchers per kilogram in Jones's data, at about $5,200, even though it was thrown away after every flight. It was enormous, and big rockets spread their fixed costs over more payload. Size, simplicity and flight rate all matter, not just whether you get the hardware back.

The lesson of the shuttle is worth remembering: reusable doesn't automatically mean cheap. If refurbishing something costs nearly as much as building a new one, and you can only fly it a few times a year, reuse just turns a manufacturing cost into a maintenance cost. The economics depend on two numbers: how much it costs to turn the vehicle around, and how often you fly it.
How a booster comes home

Landing a rocket is harder than launching one. A booster coming back is mostly empty, which makes it light and top-heavy, like a tall, empty soda can. Its engines were built to lift a full rocket, so even one engine at its lowest throttle setting pushes harder than the empty stage weighs. That means it can't hover. It has to time its final burn so it reaches zero speed at the exact moment it reaches zero altitude. Start the burn too early and the stage stops in midair and starts climbing. Start too late and it hits the ground hard.

blocks.title: A Falcon 9 booster's trip home
items: Stage separation: the booster shuts down and releases the upper stage a couple of minutes after liftoff.
Flip and boostback: cold-gas thrusters turn it around, and some missions fire engines to head back toward land.
Entry burn: engines relight to slow the booster before it hits the thickest air.
Steering: grid fins at the top guide it through the atmosphere toward the pad or a drone ship.
Landing burn: a single engine fires so speed hits zero right at touchdown, and the legs deploy.

blocks.text: All of that takes fuel the rocket could otherwise have used to lift payload. Jones points out that reusable rockets cost more to develop and carry less, because they have to save propellant for the trip home. The previous article, *The Tyranny of the Rocket Equation*, shows how much payload Falcon 9 gives up when it lands its booster. Reuse doesn't beat physics. It just stops throwing away the most expensive part.

The first reflight came on March 30, 2017, when a booster that had already flown a space station supply mission launched the SES-10 satellite. SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said at the time that refurbishing that booster cost substantially less than half the price of a new one. That was with an early design, on the first attempt.

Reuse also wasn't the only thing SpaceX did differently. Jones points out that the company is vertically integrated: it designs, builds, tests and launches most of its own hardware, largely in one big facility, instead of acting as a systems integrator managing hundreds of subcontractors. That cuts out layers of overhead and makes it faster to change a design. Cheap reuse depended on that kind of control, because you can only refly hardware quickly if you understand every part of it.
The real product is tempo

Here's the part the simple story misses. Once boosters started coming back reliably, the most important change wasn't the cost of each one. It was how often SpaceX could fly. A company that has to build a new first stage for every launch is limited by its factory. A company that can refly a stage within weeks is limited mostly by how fast it can process vehicles at the pad.

blocks.text: Using Jonathan McDowell's catalog of every launch since Sputnik, Falcon rockets made up about 51% of all orbital launch attempts worldwide in 2024, and about half again in 2025. One company's single rocket family now accounts for roughly as many launches as the rest of the planet combined.

High flight rates feed on themselves. Every launch is a test that produces data. Problems that show up once in a hundred flights get found and fixed within months instead of years. Fixed costs like the launch team, the pads and the engineers get spread over far more missions. Jones listed raising production and launch rates among the most important ways to cut launch costs, and noted that the shuttle's low flight rate was part of what made it so expensive. Reuse is what made high rates possible without needing a factory to build 165 boosters a year.

Anyone who has built a game or edited videos knows this pattern. The project that ships an update every week learns faster than the one that ships a polished release every year, even if each weekly update is rougher. Iteration speed is a kind of capital. SpaceX turned a rocket into something closer to a product you can patch.

blocks.text: Where did the savings go?

If reuse made launches so much cheaper, you might expect prices to drop by the same amount. That's not obviously what happened. In 2018, SpaceX advertised a Falcon 9 launch for $62 million, which Jones divided by the rocket's maximum payload of 22,800 kilograms to get his $2,720 per kilogram. That calculation already flatters the rocket, because a reused booster can't lift its full expendable payload. SpaceX is a private company and doesn't publish what a launch actually costs it, so outsiders can only estimate the margin.

What the launch records do show is who the main customer became. In 2025, 122 of the 165 Falcon launches carried SpaceX's own Starlink internet satellites, about three out of four. The company used cheap, frequent launches to build a global satellite network, a business that only works if launches are cheap and frequent. In effect, reuse paid off less through lower prices for customers and more by letting SpaceX become its own biggest customer.

The savings also depend heavily on what you're launching. Jones ran the same comparison for cargo going to the space station, where Falcon 9 has to carry a Dragon capsule that adds cost and takes up lifting capacity. By his figures, a Falcon 9 and Dragon cargo run cost about $140 million for roughly 6,000 kilograms, around $23,300 per kilogram. The shuttle's comparable figure was about $93,400. That's still a fourfold improvement, but nowhere near the twentyfold drop the per-kilogram-to-orbit chart suggests. Headline numbers about launch costs usually describe the best case.

There's a strategy lesson here for anyone building a business. A cost advantage is good. A cost advantage that unlocks a product competitors can't afford to build is much better. SpaceX didn't just sell cheaper rides. It used those rides to build something only a company with cheap rides could build, and that business then paid for more launches.

That concentration has downsides, and they're worth stating plainly. When a single rocket family flies about half the world's launches, its failures become everyone's problem. NASA now depends on SpaceX to carry astronauts and cargo to the space station, and in 2024 it picked SpaceX to build the vehicle that will eventually bring the station down. A monopoly-like position also reduces the pressure to lower prices. Competition, from Blue Origin, Rocket Lab and Chinese launch providers among others, is the main thing that could shift that.
The next bet

Falcon 9 reuses only its first stage. The upper stage, which reaches orbit, still burns up or is left in space after each flight. SpaceX's Starship is meant to fix that by making both stages fully reusable, with the giant booster caught by arms on the launch tower instead of landing on legs. McDowell's catalog records 14 Starship flights from April 2023 through September 2026. Several ended in failure, including the first two in 2023 and two more in early 2025, and a third version of the vehicle began flying in 2026.

Upper stages are much harder to bring back. A first stage separates at a few kilometers per second and falls back through the atmosphere relatively gently. An upper stage reaches full orbital speed, close to 8 kilometers per second, so coming home means surviving reentry heat the way a crew capsule does, with a heat shield, flaps and landing fuel. Every kilogram of that equipment rides all the way to orbit, so it comes almost directly out of the payload. That's why fully reusable rockets are so hard to build, and why it would matter so much if Starship works.

It's worth keeping old promises in view. In 2016, Elon Musk suggested that full reusability could cut the cost of spaceflight by a factor of about a hundred, to around $10 per pound, by 2025, as Jones noted. That didn't happen on schedule. Big claims in this industry tend to come true later and less completely than promised, but they sometimes do come true, as landing boosters did.

blocks.text: The cost of something depends less on what it's made of than on how many times you can use it and how quickly you can turn it around. That's true of rockets, and it's just as true of code, skills and content you only have to build once.

That may be the most transferable idea in the whole story. The shuttle proved that reuse with slow turnaround is a trap. Falcon 9 showed that reuse with fast turnaround compounds. Whether you're building a game, a channel or a business, the useful question isn't just whether you can reuse what you've made. It's how quickly you can ship it again.

takeaways: Launch costs barely moved from 1970 to 2000; the reusable shuttle was the most expensive system of its era.
Reuse only saves money when turnaround is cheap and fast. Otherwise it just moves the cost.
Landing boosters let SpaceX reach 165 Falcon launches in 2025 with only 25 boosters, about half of all launches worldwide.
Much of the benefit went into SpaceX's own Starlink network rather than lower prices for customers.
Speed of iteration, not just the cost of each unit, is what compounds.

title: When the Sun Reaches Out and Touches the Grid
dek: In 1859 a solar storm set telegraph wires sparking. In 1989 one blacked out Quebec, and in 2022 a moderate one knocked dozens of satellites out of the sky. Our star has weather, and we are wired straight into it.

blocks.text: On the morning of September 1, 1859, an English amateur astronomer named Richard Carrington was doing what he did most clear days: projecting an image of the Sun onto a screen and sketching its sunspots. Suddenly two beads of intensely bright white light flared up inside one sunspot group, brightened, drifted, and faded within about five minutes. He ran to find a witness and came back to find it almost gone. Nobody had ever recorded anything like it.

The following night, the sky over much of the planet caught fire. Auroras, normally a polar sight, were reported far toward the tropics. Telegraph systems, the internet of the day, went haywire as currents surged through the wires on their own. A cloud of magnetized gas from that flare had crossed the 150 million kilometers to Earth in roughly 17 hours, a pace that later reconstructions of the magnetic records still put among the fastest ever recorded.

In 1859 the damage was mostly a curiosity. Today the same event would hit power grids, GPS, satellites, high-frequency radio and aviation. The Sun is not just the thing that lights the day. It is a variable star with weather, and we have quietly built a civilization that is exposed to it.
Three kinds of bad day

Space weather is a catch-all for what the Sun throws at Earth beyond ordinary sunlight, and it comes in three main flavors that arrive on very different clocks. A **solar flare** is a burst of light, including X-rays, released when twisted magnetic fields near a sunspot snap and reconnect. Because it is light, it arrives in about eight minutes, with no warning at all. It mostly disrupts high-frequency radio on the sunlit side of the planet.

A **solar radiation storm** is a flood of fast protons accelerated by a flare or shock. These arrive in tens of minutes to hours and are the hazard for astronauts, polar flights and satellite electronics. The third and most dangerous to the ground is a **coronal mass ejection**, or CME: billions of tons of magnetized plasma blasted off the Sun. CMEs usually take one to three days to arrive. When one hits Earth with its magnetic field pointed the wrong way, southward, opposite to Earth's own field, the two fields link up, energy pours into Earth's magnetosphere, and you get a geomagnetic storm.

blocks.title: How a solar storm reaches the ground
items: Tangled magnetic fields above a sunspot group snap and reconnect, releasing a flare and often a CME.
The CME, a cloud of magnetized plasma, crosses space in roughly 1 to 3 days (the Carrington cloud took about 17 hours).
A spacecraft at the L1 point, 1.5 million km sunward, sees the shock arrive and gives 15 to 60 minutes of warning.
If the cloud's magnetic field points south, it couples to Earth's field and drives a geomagnetic storm.
Rapidly changing magnetic fields induce currents in long conductors: power lines, pipelines and old telegraph wires.
The upper atmosphere heats and swells, dragging on satellites and scrambling GPS and HF radio signals.

blocks.text: NOAA rates all three on five-step scales, much like hurricane categories: R for radio blackouts, S for radiation storms and G for geomagnetic storms. The G scale is the one that matters most for the grid. Its top level, G5, comes with an official description that reads like a casualty list: possible grid collapse, transformer damage, HF radio propagation impossible in many areas for one to two days, and satellite navigation degraded for days.

It is worth being clear about what space weather does *not* do. The radiation from even a severe storm does not reach people on the ground in any meaningful dose, because Earth's magnetic field and the thick atmosphere absorb it. Water is an excellent shield too, so anyone at sea or underwater is even better off. The danger is to technology, and to people whose safety depends on that technology working. Ships and aircraft that lean on satellite navigation and HF radio feel it first: during the strongest storms, GPS position errors grow, HF links over the poles can black out completely, and some airlines reroute polar flights to keep crews and passengers lower in latitude.

The grid problem comes from a basic piece of physics any electrician knows: a changing magnetic field through a loop induces a current. A geomagnetic storm makes Earth's field swing slowly, over seconds to minutes, and a power line hundreds of kilometers long, grounded at both ends, becomes a giant loop. The result is a nearly direct current pushed through transformer windings designed for alternating current. That drives the transformer cores into saturation, which heats them, distorts the waveform and makes protective relays trip. Long lines on old, resistive rock, such as the Canadian Shield, are the worst case.

blocks.title: How often each geomagnetic storm level happens
blocks.note: Average number of storm days per solar cycle. Extreme storms are rare, not hypothetical.
blocks.source: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Space Weather Scales

blocks.text: The night Quebec went dark

The modern proof came in March 1989. A large, complex sunspot region produced an X-class flare on March 10 and another eruption on March 12. According to a 2019 reconstruction by Canadian geophysicist David Boteler, two CMEs followed, the second traveling at about 1,320 km per second and catching Earth just over 31 hours after it left the Sun. The storm that followed produced the largest value of the main storm index, Dst, in the record that began in 1957.

At 2:44 a.m. on March 13, the magnetic field over Quebec started swinging violently. Long transmission lines act like giant antennas for these slow magnetic swings, and the induced currents flowed into transformers that were never designed for them. Hydro-Québec's protective systems tripped, and the entire grid collapsed in under a minute. The province sat in the dark for more than nine hours, in March, in Canada.

Two details from Boteler's analysis are worth noticing. First, the blackout did not happen at the storm's peak. It happened early, when a sharp local surge hit, before the global index had reached its worst. Second, the fix was not exotic. Hydro-Québec recalibrated protective relays, added a real-time alert system, changed operating procedures to reduce power flow during storms, and installed series compensation on its lines. The utility says intense storms since 1989 have not caused problems. Engineering for a known hazard works, but only after someone admits the hazard is real.
Starlink and the storm nobody worried about

You might think only the monster storms matter. In February 2022, SpaceX launched 49 Starlink satellites into a deliberately low parking orbit around 210 km up, planning to raise them later with onboard thrusters. A couple of *moderate* geomagnetic storms arrived at the same time. Nothing about them would have made the evening news.

But a storm does not just shake the magnetic field. It dumps energy into the upper atmosphere, which heats and puffs outward, so the thin air at satellite altitudes gets thicker. A 2022 study by Ryuho Kataoka and colleagues found that air drag at around 200 km rose by up to 50 percent, more than the standard atmospheric model predicted. The satellites could not climb out in time. About 38 of the 49 fell back and burned up; some analyses count up to 40.

The lesson is subtle and important. Risk depends on the storm *and* on what you happen to be doing when it hits. A moderate storm against satellites sitting at their most vulnerable point did more economic damage than many larger storms that hit when nothing was exposed. That is true of a lot of systems: the dangerous moment is often a transition, like a launch, a startup, or a shift change, when margins are thinnest.
Exposure matters as much as severity. A moderate storm that hits satellites during their most vulnerable phase can do more damage than a bigger storm that hits when everything is secured.
The Sun's 11-year heartbeat

The Sun's activity rises and falls on a cycle of about 11 years, tracked since the 1700s by counting sunspots. At solar minimum, the face of the Sun can go spotless for weeks. At solar maximum, it is crowded with active regions, and flares and CMEs become far more common. The Royal Observatory of Belgium keeps the official international sunspot record, and its yearly averages show the current cycle, number 25, climbing steeply out of a deep minimum in 2019 and 2020.

blocks.title: Yearly mean sunspot number, 2008 to 2025
blocks.source: SILSO, Royal Observatory of Belgium, yearly mean total sunspot number (version 2)

blocks.text: Cycle 25 turned out stronger than its weak predecessor, and 2024 was its busiest year in the record so far. In May 2024, a cluster of CMEs from one huge sunspot region piled into Earth starting May 10. NASA reported that the resulting storm reached G5, the first since the Halloween storms of 2003. Auroras were photographed from the southern United States and northern India, and NASA noted that sightings as low as about 26 degrees magnetic latitude may rank among the lowest-latitude auroras in five centuries. Operators had warning: NOAA sent notices to grid and satellite operators ahead of time, and several NASA missions powered down sensitive instruments. Even so, NASA's ICESat-2 satellite dropped into safe mode, likely because of the extra drag.
Peaks do not mean the danger is over once the count drops. Big storms can and do happen on the declining side of a cycle, and history's worst storms have not always come in the strongest cycles.
The bullet that missed

On July 23, 2012, the Sun launched one of the fastest CMEs ever measured, with an initial speed estimated at 2,500 km per second, plus or minus 500. It was aimed away from Earth and hit NASA's STEREO-A spacecraft instead, which happened to be in the line of fire and recorded it in detail. Daniel Baker and colleagues then ran the numbers for a hypothetical in which Earth had been in the way. Their worst-case scenario produced a storm larger than estimates for Carrington's. It arrived during a cycle widely seen as weak, which is the uncomfortable point: extreme events do not need an extreme cycle.

How likely is the real thing? In 2012, physicist Pete Riley looked at how often storms of different sizes occur and found that their frequency falls off as a power law, the same kind of pattern seen in earthquakes. Extending that line, he estimated about a 12 percent chance of a Carrington-class storm in a given decade. Riley was explicit about the weakness: the estimate assumes the pattern holds at sizes we have barely observed, and that the Sun's behavior does not drift over centuries. Other researchers using different methods have gotten different numbers. Treat 12 percent as a reasoned estimate, not a fact.

Even so, the logic is the logic of any serious engineering plant. You do not design a reactor plant for the average day. You design it for credible worst cases and drill the response until it is boring. A one-in-ten chance per decade is not a doomsday prophecy, but over a career or a lifetime it is not a rounding error either.
Watching the weather at its source

Most of our warning comes from a handful of spacecraft. Coronagraphs, which block the Sun's disk to see the faint corona around it, catch CMEs leaving the Sun and let forecasters estimate arrival times a day or more out. The precise warning comes later, from NOAA's DSCOVR satellite at the L1 point between Earth and Sun. When the shock wave of a CME sweeps over it, forecasters typically get 15 to 60 minutes of notice before it hits Earth, enough time for grid operators to reconfigure and satellite operators to safe their spacecraft.

Meanwhile, NASA's Parker Solar Probe has been diving into the Sun's outer atmosphere itself, coming within about 6.2 million km of the Sun at speeds near 700,000 km per hour, the fastest any human-made object has gone. Its job is to answer questions that still limit forecasting: why the corona is millions of degrees hotter than the surface, and how the solar wind gets accelerated. The hardest problem remains predicting the magnetic orientation of a CME before it arrives, because that single factor decides whether a big cloud does little or a lot.

There is a deeper reframe here. People tend to picture the Sun as a fixed background condition, as constant as gravity. It is actually a dynamic system with moods and seasons, and modern life is wired into it through every long conductor and every satellite link. For anyone who works in a world of HF radio, satellite navigation and electrical distribution, space weather is not astronomy trivia. It is part of the operating environment, and the professionals who manage it treat it the same way a good watch team treats any other hazard: know the indications, know the warning time, and have the procedure ready before you need it.

takeaways: Solar flares arrive in minutes as light, radiation storms in hours, and CMEs in one to three days; the CME is the one that threatens power grids.
In 1989 a geomagnetic storm collapsed Quebec's grid in under a minute and left it dark for more than nine hours; better relays and procedures fixed the weakness.
A moderate storm in 2022 raised air drag by up to 50 percent and brought down about 38 new Starlink satellites, because they were caught at their most exposed moment.
One estimate puts the odds of a Carrington-class storm at about 12 percent per decade, a reasoned guess with real uncertainty, not a prophecy.
Treat space weather like any other plant hazard: know the indications, know the warning time, and have the procedure ready.

title: One Light-Day From Home
dek: This month Voyager 1 becomes the first human-made object a full light-day from Earth, running on 1970s computers, a fading plutonium power supply and a team that keeps refusing to let it die.

blocks.text: On Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 10:16 UTC, a machine the size of a small car will cross a line nothing built by humans has crossed before. NASA calculates that at that moment Voyager 1 will be **25.902 billion kilometers** from Earth, the distance light covers in exactly 24 hours. After that, a command sent from California will need more than a full day to arrive, and the reply another full day to come back.

Voyager 1 launched in September 1977. It was built to work for five years and visit two planets. It is now in its 50th year, still sending data from outside the Sun's bubble, powered by a source that weakens every year, with computers that have less memory than a single photo on a phone. The story of how it got there, and how it is still talking, is one of the best engineering stories ever told.

blocks.text: A shortcut that opens once every 175 years

In the late 1960s, mission planners noticed that Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune would line up in the late 1970s in a way that happens only about once every 175 years. A spacecraft launched at the right moment could swing past each planet in turn, using each one to bend its path toward the next. NASA estimates this cut the flight time to Neptune from 30 years to 12.

The trick is the **gravity assist**, and it seems to break the rules until you change frames. Seen from the planet, the spacecraft falls in and climbs back out at the same speed, only in a new direction; no energy is gained. But the planet is moving around the Sun at tens of kilometers per second. Seen from the Sun, the spacecraft has borrowed a little of the planet's orbital momentum, like a ball bouncing off the front of a moving train. The planet slows by an amount far too small to measure, and the spacecraft leaves much faster than it arrived.

Engineers studied more than 10,000 possible trajectories before choosing two. Voyager 2 launched first, on August 20, 1977, on a path that kept the outer planets open. Voyager 1 launched on September 5 on a faster route that traded Uranus and Neptune for a close pass of Saturn's moon Titan. That Titan flyby bent Voyager 1 up and out of the plane of the planets, which is why it is now heading north at about 35 degrees, while Voyager 2 dives south.

blocks.text: Engineering for a mission nobody planned

Between them, the Voyagers explored all four giant planets, 48 of their moons, and their rings and magnetic fields. The project cost $865 million through the Neptune encounter, launch and power supplies included. But the more remarkable number is the one nobody budgeted: the decades of extra life.

Each Voyager runs on three computers, each with a backup. The command computer has 4,096 words of memory; the flight data system, which packages science for transmission, has about 8,000 words. All of it together is smaller than a single photo on your phone. Engineers have been rewriting that code from billions of kilometers away since the 1970s, patching around failures and giving the spacecraft abilities they didn't have at launch.

Designers also assumed the spacecraft would sometimes be on its own. About 10 percent of the command computer's memory holds fault-protection routines: if something goes wrong and Earth is hours away, Voyager is supposed to detect it, switch to backups and point its antenna home without waiting for orders. That philosophy of building in self-rescue, rather than relying on help arriving in time, is a big part of why it survived.

Power comes from three radioisotope thermoelectric generators, or RTGs. Each holds plutonium-238 oxide, which stays hot from its own radioactive decay; thermocouples turn the heat flowing through them into electricity. There are no moving parts. Together the three RTGs produced about **470 watts** at launch. Plutonium-238 has a half-life of 87.7 years, so the fuel itself fades slowly, and the thermocouples degrade with age too. NASA says each spacecraft now loses about **4 watts every year**.

Why not solar panels? Because of the inverse-square law. At 173 AU, sunlight is 173 squared, or about 30,000 times, weaker than it is at Earth. A solar array big enough to run Voyager out there would be absurd. Outer-planet missions need a power source that carries its own heat, and nuclear decay is the only practical one.

Then there is the radio. Voyager talks through a 3.7-meter dish at a normal science rate of **160 bits per second**, about 20 characters a second. By the time that signal reaches Earth, it has spread over such a vast area that only NASA's Deep Space Network, with huge dishes in California, Spain and Australia, can still hear it. Radio waves obey the same inverse-square law as light, so after crossing 25 billion kilometers, what reaches a 70-meter dish from Voyager's modest transmitter is an almost unimaginably small trickle of energy. Every bit of telemetry is a feat of antenna engineering and patience.

blocks.title: How far is far? Distances in astronomical units
blocks.note: 1 AU is the Earth–Sun distance. Termination shock: where the solar wind abruptly slows.
blocks.source: NASA Voyager Fast Facts and What Is a Light-Day?; JPL Horizons, Nov 5, 2026

blocks.text: Troubleshooting with a two-day round trip

Imagine diagnosing a fault on a system you can't see or touch, where every test takes two days to report back, and where one bad command could end the mission. That is daily life for the small Voyager team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

In November 2023, Voyager 1 stopped sending usable data and began transmitting gibberish. Engineers sent a command to dump the flight data system's memory, then spent weeks decoding the readout. About **3 percent** of that memory had been corrupted, most likely because a single chip had failed, either from a cosmic-ray hit or plain old age after 46 years. The chip couldn't be fixed, so the team rewrote the affected code and moved it into other parts of the memory, piece by piece, checking that nothing else broke. By spring 2024 Voyager 1 was sending engineering data again, and science data followed.

Even routine operations work on that clock. When the team shut off an instrument in April 2026, the commands took about 23 hours to reach Voyager 1, and the shutdown itself ran for over three hours more. Every sequence is written, simulated and checked days ahead, because by the time anyone on Earth sees a mistake, the spacecraft has been living with it for a full day.

This is the unglamorous side of exploration: maintenance. Keeping a legacy system alive takes as much skill as building a new one, sometimes more, because you're working within constraints that someone else set fifty years ago. Anyone who has kept old shipboard equipment running with the parts and procedures on hand knows that feeling.
Finding the edge of the Sun's bubble

The Sun blows a constant wind of charged particles outward at hundreds of kilometers per second. That solar wind inflates a vast bubble, the heliosphere, inside the thin gas between the stars. Nobody knew exactly where the edge was until the Voyagers flew into it. Voyager 1 hit the termination shock, where the solar wind abruptly slows, in December 2004 at about 94 AU from the Sun; Voyager 2 crossed it in August 2007 at about 84 AU.

Proving Voyager 1 had actually left the bubble took clever physics, because its instrument built to measure plasma directly had long since stopped working properly. The team used the plasma wave instrument instead. When outbursts from the Sun sent shock waves rolling past the spacecraft, the surrounding gas rang like a bell, and the pitch of that ringing depends only on how many electrons are packed into each cubic centimeter. In April 2013 Voyager 1 heard oscillations at about **2.6 kilohertz**, which works out to roughly 0.08 electrons per cubic centimeter.

That was about forty times denser than the outer solar wind and almost exactly what theory predicted for interstellar gas. Working backward, the team concluded that Voyager 1 had crossed the heliopause on August 25, 2012. Voyager 2, whose plasma instrument still worked, confirmed the boundary directly when it crossed in November 2018. Two spacecraft, two different methods, one answer: that is how you make a measurement believable.
Turning off the lights, one by one

Every year the power budget shrinks, so every year something has to be turned off. Years ago the science and engineering teams agreed on the order in which instruments would be shut down, so that no decision would have to be made in a panic. Heaters have been switched off too, which is risky, because the spacecraft must stay warm enough that its thruster fuel lines don't freeze.

Of the 10 instruments each Voyager carries, seven have now been shut off. In April 2026, after Voyager 1's power fell unexpectedly earlier in the year, the team turned off its low-energy charged particle instrument, which had been running almost without a break since launch. Voyager 1 is now down to two working science instruments: a magnetometer and a plasma wave detector. Engineers expect that to buy about a year. They are also preparing a larger power-saving reshuffle nicknamed "the Big Bang," which swaps several powered devices for lower-power alternatives at once. They will try it on Voyager 2 first, because it has slightly more power to spare and is closer to home.

NASA has said the Voyagers could stay within range of the Deep Space Network until about 2036, depending on power. Voyager 2 is expected to reach one light-day in November 2035. Whether either will still be transmitting then is an open question that the team is actively fighting to answer with a yes.
Why this matters: the Voyagers are the only spacecraft ever to measure interstellar space directly. Every watt saved buys data from a region no other machine can reach for decades.
The photo it took on the way out

On February 14, 1990, about 6 billion kilometers from the Sun, Voyager 1 turned its cameras around and photographed the planets for the last time. Earth came out as a point of light about a pixel in size, sitting in a band of sunlight scattered inside the camera. Carl Sagan, who had pushed for the picture, named it the Pale Blue Dot. Soon after, the cameras were switched off for good to save power and memory.

Both spacecraft also carry a golden phonograph record, assembled by Carl Sagan and colleagues, with sounds and images of Earth, greetings in dozens of languages, and music. It is not likely to be found. In about 40,000 years, Voyager 1 will pass within 1.7 light-years of a faint star in the constellation Ursa Minor, and Voyager 2 will pass a similar distance from a star called Ross 248. They will drift through the galaxy for far longer than any human structure is likely to survive on Earth.

That's the strange inversion at the heart of the mission. The machines were sent out to look at other worlds, and their most famous image is of us. And the most lasting lesson isn't about Jupiter's storms or Neptune's moons. It is about what good margin, careful design and stubborn people can do: a five-year mission, still running after almost fifty, because nobody involved treated "good enough for now" as good enough.

Perspective check: Voyager 1 has been flying at around 17 km/s for 49 years and has covered one light-day. The nearest star is about 4.24 light-years away. At this speed, it would take roughly 75,000 years to get that far.

takeaways: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day (25.9 billion km) from Earth on Nov 18, 2026; Voyager 2 should follow in Nov 2035.
Gravity assists borrow orbital momentum from planets; a once-in-175-years alignment made the Grand Tour possible.
Each Voyager started with about 470 W of RTG power and loses about 4 W a year, forcing a planned, ordered shutdown of systems.
In 2024 engineers fixed a failed memory chip by relocating code from 24 billion km away. Maintenance is engineering too.
Built for 5 years, still running at nearly 50. Margin and stubbornness compound.
