title: This Sentence Cannot Be Proved: Gödel and the Limits of Math
dek: In 1931 a 25-year-old logician proved that no set of rules can capture all mathematical truth, and the same idea later showed that some questions about computer programs can never be answered.

blocks.text: On September 7, 1930, in the German city of Königsberg, a quiet 24-year-old from Vienna made a brief remark during a round-table discussion at a mathematics conference. Most of the room missed its significance. One person did not: John von Neumann, one of the sharpest mathematical minds of the century, understood immediately that something enormous had just happened.

The next day, in the same city, the great mathematician David Hilbert gave a major address, soon repeated for a radio broadcast. He was the most influential mathematician alive, and his speech ended with a defiant line aimed at anyone who claimed some questions were beyond human reach: *Wir müssen wissen. Wir werden wissen.* We must know. We will know. The words are carved on his gravestone.

The young man was Kurt Gödel, and what he had announced the day before showed that Hilbert's dream, in the form Hilbert wanted it, could never come true. Gödel published the full proof in 1931. It is one of the strangest and most important results in the history of thought, and the core idea can be followed by anyone willing to go slowly.
The dream of a perfect rulebook

Around 1900, mathematics had a crisis of confidence. Paradoxes had turned up in the foundations, especially in the new theory of infinite sets. Mathematicians wanted to rebuild everything on solid ground. Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead tried to derive all of mathematics from pure logic in *Principia Mathematica*, a three-volume monster published from 1910 to 1913.

Hilbert pushed a sharper plan. Write down a small set of starting assumptions, called **axioms**, and precise rules for deriving new statements from old ones. Then prove that this system is **consistent**, meaning it can never prove both a statement and its opposite, and **complete**, meaning every true statement about numbers can be proved within it. Picture a game engine where the axioms are the starting state and the rules are the allowed moves. Hilbert wanted a guarantee that every true fact is a reachable state and no contradiction ever is.

If that worked, mathematics would become, in principle, mechanical. Any question could be settled by grinding through the rules. Gödel showed that for any system strong enough to handle ordinary arithmetic, that guarantee is impossible.
Turning math into numbers

Gödel's first move was a brilliant piece of encoding, the kind of thing a programmer would appreciate. He gave every symbol in the formal language a number, then turned whole formulas into single numbers, and whole proofs, which are just lists of formulas, into numbers too. Statements *about* the system became statements about numbers, which the system itself can talk about.

Here is a toy version. Say the symbol 0 gets code 1, the symbol = gets code 2, and the symbol S, meaning "the next number after", gets code 3. To encode the formula 0 = 0, take the first three primes, 2, 3 and 5, and raise each to the code of the symbol in that position: 2¹ × 3² × 5¹ = 2 × 9 × 5 = 90. The formula 0 = 0 becomes the number 90. Because every number factors into primes in exactly one way, you can always decode it again: 90 = 2¹ × 3² × 5¹ gives back codes 1, 2, 1, which spell 0 = 0.

This is the same trick every computer uses. A song, a photo and the source code of a game are all, at bottom, very large numbers. Gödel did it in 1931, before any computers existed, and he used it for a purpose no one had imagined: to let arithmetic describe itself. With his encoding, "the formula numbered *x* is provable" becomes an ordinary statement about numbers, like "*x* is prime", only far longer.
The sentence that talks about itself

You probably know the liar's paradox: "This sentence is false." If it is true, it is false, and if it is false, it is true. It breaks logic, which is why formal systems are built to keep it out. Gödel did not use falsity. He used *provability*, which can be expressed in arithmetic, and built a sentence that says, in effect: **"This sentence cannot be proved in this system."** Call it G.

blocks.title: The first incompleteness theorem, in five moves
items: Encode every formula and every proof as a number, so "P is a proof of formula F" becomes a checkable fact about two numbers.
Using a self-reference technique called diagonalization, build a formula G that says "the formula with my own number has no proof".
Suppose the system proves G. Then G is provable, so what G says is false, and the system has proved a falsehood. A consistent system cannot do that.
So if the system is consistent, G has no proof. But that is exactly what G claims, so G is true.
Result: a true statement the system cannot prove. Adding G as a new axiom does not help, because the bigger system has its own new unprovable sentence.

blocks.text: That is the **first incompleteness theorem**: any consistent formal system that can do basic arithmetic contains true statements about numbers that it cannot prove. The phrase "basic arithmetic" matters. Very weak systems, such as arithmetic with addition but no multiplication, can be complete. The trouble starts once a system is strong enough to encode itself.

It is worth being careful about the word "true" here. G is true about the ordinary counting numbers, 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. But because the system cannot prove G or its opposite, logicians can build strange alternative number systems, with extra "numbers" beyond all the normal ones, where every axiom still holds and G comes out false. The axioms simply do not pin down the numbers we have in mind. Something about what we mean by "number" always slips through the rules.

The **second incompleteness theorem** landed even closer to Hilbert's heart. Such a system cannot prove its own consistency, unless it is actually inconsistent, in which case it can prove anything, including its own consistency. Von Neumann worked this out on his own shortly after Königsberg and wrote to Gödel about it, only to learn Gödel had already found it. To establish that a system is safe, you have to step outside it and use a stronger system, whose safety is then in question too.
An instrument cannot be calibrated against itself. You need an outside standard, and that standard needs its own check. Gödel proved that mathematics has the same structure all the way down.
What it does not mean

Few results in math have been abused as much as this one. It gets dragged into arguments about God, the law, the mind and literary theory. Most of these uses are stretches at best. The theorem is precise, and its limits are worth knowing.

blocks.title: Gödel's theorem: claims versus reality

left.head: Common claim
items: Math is broken or unreliable
Nothing can ever really be known
Every system of rules is incomplete
Humans can see truths no machine can
Unprovable statements are exotic word games

right.head: What it actually says
items: Math works; it just cannot be captured by one fixed rulebook
Specific formal systems have specific limits
It applies to formal systems strong enough to do arithmetic
This is a contested philosophical argument, not part of the theorem
Natural statements about numbers can be unprovable too

blocks.text: That last point took decades to establish. Gödel's sentence G is artificial, built only to talk about itself. Mathematicians wondered whether any *natural* question would ever be undecidable.

The answer turned out to be yes. Goodstein's theorem, from 1944, is about simple sequences of whole numbers that grow to astronomical size and then, surprisingly, always shrink back to zero. It is true, but it was later shown that it cannot be proved using the standard axioms for arithmetic. In set theory, the continuum hypothesis, Cantor's question about the sizes of infinity, was shown by Gödel in 1940 and Paul Cohen in 1963 to be undecidable from the standard axioms.
From proofs to programs

In 1936, a young British mathematician named Alan Turing took Gödel's idea into a new world. He imagined a simple abstract computer, now called a Turing machine, and asked: can there be a program that looks at any other program and its input, and tells you whether it will eventually stop or run forever? This is the **halting problem**, and Turing proved no such program can exist.

The proof has Gödel's fingerprints all over it. Suppose someone hands you a perfect checker called halts(P), which returns true if program P stops. Now write a contrarian program: it asks halts about itself, and if the answer is "stops", it loops forever, and if the answer is "runs forever", it stops.

Whatever the checker says about the contrarian, the contrarian does the opposite. So the perfect checker cannot exist. This is why no antivirus, compiler or code reviewer can ever be guaranteed to catch every infinite loop or every malicious behavior in general. They catch a lot, but they can never catch everything.

The most vivid modern example is the **busy beaver** problem. Among all Turing machines with *n* internal states that eventually halt, which one runs the longest? For two states the answer is 6 steps, for three it is 21, and for four it is 107. For five states the answer took decades: in 2024, an online collaboration called bbchallenge proved it is 47,176,870 steps, with the proof checked by the Coq proof assistant after it sorted through more than 181 million machines.

items.label: Steps run by the champion 5-state Turing machine, confirmed in 2024
5-state machines the proof had to classify as halting or not
States in a machine that standard set theory cannot prove runs forever (2016)

blocks.source: bbchallenge collaboration, arXiv 2509.12337; Yedidia and Aaronson, Complex Systems, 2016

blocks.text: And there is a hard ceiling. In 2016, Adam Yedidia and Scott Aaronson built a Turing machine with 7,910 states that searches for a contradiction in a set of axioms stronger than the standard foundation of mathematics, known as ZFC. Through Gödel's second theorem, they showed that if ZFC is consistent, it can never prove that this machine runs forever, even though it almost certainly does. A specific, finite machine, the kind you could in principle write down and run, poses a question that mathematics as we normally practice it cannot answer.

blocks.text: Puzzles to try

items: **Decode a Gödel number.** Using the toy code above (0 is 1, = is 2, S is 3), decode 4,200. Answer: 4,200 = 2³ × 3¹ × 5² × 7¹, so the codes are 3, 1, 2, 1, which spell S0 = 0, meaning "1 = 0". The encoding handles false statements just as easily as true ones. Provability is a separate question.

**Russell's barber.** A town's barber shaves exactly those men who do not shave themselves. Who shaves the barber? Either answer contradicts the rule. Bertrand Russell found the same self-reference trap in set theory around 1901, and it is one reason Hilbert wanted a rock-solid foundation.

**A program that settles a famous problem.** Goldbach's conjecture says every even number above 2 is the sum of two primes. Imagine a program that checks 4, 6, 8 and so on forever, and halts only if it finds an even number that breaks the rule. If you had a perfect halting checker, you could settle Goldbach without any clever math. Yedidia and Aaronson actually built Turing machines like this for Goldbach and for the Riemann hypothesis.

**The smallest boring number.** Suppose some whole numbers are uninteresting. Then there is a smallest uninteresting number, which is a pretty interesting thing to be. Spot the self-reference, the same move that powers Gödel's sentence.

blocks.text: Living with limits

Gödel's own story has a sad ending. He moved to the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in 1940, where his closest friend was Albert Einstein. Late in life he became convinced that people were trying to poison him. When his wife, who had looked after him, fell seriously ill herself, he refused to eat, and he died in Princeton in January 1978 of what was essentially starvation. The man who proved the limits of formal certainty could not escape his own need for it.
For the rest of us, incompleteness is not a counsel of despair. Mathematicians did not stop proving theorems in 1931. They kept going, more productive than ever.

What changed was the picture. Mathematics is not a finished machine that will one day print every truth. It is an open system that can always be extended with new axioms, new ideas and new ways of seeing, and it will never run out of questions.

That reframe applies well beyond math. No rulebook, procedure manual or checklist can cover every situation, no matter how carefully it is written, because some cases will always fall outside what the rules can decide. That is not an argument against rules. They are how complicated, dangerous systems get run safely. It is an argument for people who understand *why* the rules exist, because when the book runs out, judgment is all that is left.

takeaways: Gödel proved in 1931 that any consistent formal system able to do basic arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove.
His second theorem shows such a system cannot prove its own consistency; you always need an outside standard.
The key trick was encoding formulas and proofs as numbers, the same idea that lets computers store everything as data.
Turing's halting problem carries the idea into software: no program can decide in general whether every other program halts.
Incompleteness is precise, not mystical; it limits fixed rulebooks, not human inquiry.

title: Every Frame Is a Math Problem
dek: Behind every 3D game is a small toolkit of linear algebra: arrows, a dot product, a few matrices and one strange four-dimensional number system. Learn it and you start seeing how the engine thinks.

blocks.text: About two hours after Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, Mission Control radioed Michael Collins, orbiting alone in the command module, to warn him that he was maneuvering very close to *gimbal lock*. Collins steered around it, then quipped back, more or less, that what he really wanted was a fourth gimbal for Christmas.

The joke was about a math problem. Apollo's guidance platform measured the spacecraft's orientation with three nested rings, one per axis. If the middle ring swung to 90 degrees, two of the axes lined up, the platform lost track of one direction of rotation, and the guidance computer's formula for extracting the angles ended up dividing by the cosine of 90 degrees, which is zero. The lunar module's computer flashed a warning at 70 degrees and froze the platform at 85. The astronauts then had to realign it against the stars.

Every 3D game has the same problem lurking inside it, along with the same fixes. The camera in your favorite shooter, the character in a Roblox obby, the way light falls across a wall: all of it is a small set of mathematical tools from a subject called **linear algebra**, applied millions of times per second. It's worth knowing, because once you see it, the engine stops being a black box.

items.label: Pixels in one 1080p frame
Pixels to compute per second at 60 frames per second

blocks.text: Arrows that know where they point

The basic object is the **vector**: an arrow with a length and a direction, written as three numbers (x, y, z). Roblox calls it a Vector3. The same three numbers can mean two different things. As a *position*, (10, 5, 0) is a point 10 studs along x and 5 up. As a *direction*, it's an arrow pointing that way, no matter where it starts. Keeping those two meanings straight is half the battle in game code.

Vectors add tip to tail. A character at position P moving with velocity V for one second ends up at P + V. Subtract two positions and you get the arrow from one to the other: target minus shooter is the direction a bullet needs to travel. The length of a vector comes from Pythagoras, extended to three dimensions: the square root of x squared plus y squared plus z squared. That's the distance check behind every "is the player close enough to open this door?" prompt.
Divide a vector by its own length and you get a *unit vector*, length exactly 1, pure direction. Unit vectors are everywhere in engines because they make the next tool work cleanly.

A lot of beginner scripting bugs live right here. Want a part to fly forward at 50 studs per second? Take the direction it's facing, a unit vector, multiply by 50, and add that times the frame time to its position each frame. Forget to normalize the direction first and the speed silently depends on how far away the target was. Mix up a position and a direction and the part flies toward the center of the map instead of straight ahead.
The dot product: how light knows which way you face

Multiply two vectors component by component and add the results: a.x times b.x, plus a.y times b.y, plus a.z times b.z. That's the **dot product**, and it hides a small miracle. It always equals the lengths of the two vectors multiplied together, times the cosine of the angle between them. For two unit vectors, the dot product *is* the cosine of the angle. One multiply-and-add tells you how aligned two directions are: 1 means the same way, 0 means perpendicular, minus 1 means opposite.

Games use this constantly. Is the enemy in front of the player or behind? Take the dot product of the player's look direction with the direction to the enemy. Positive means in front, negative means behind. Is the enemy inside a 90-degree vision cone? Check whether the dot product is above the cosine of 45 degrees, about 0.707. No angles computed, no trigonometry, just a few multiplications.

The dot product also splits motion into pieces. Dot a velocity with a wall's normal and you get exactly how much of that velocity is pushing into the wall. Subtract that part and what remains slides along the surface. That one line of math is why a character running diagonally into a wall glides along it instead of sticking, and why a ball bounces off at the right angle when you flip that component instead of deleting it.

Lighting runs on the same idea. In 1760 Johann Heinrich Lambert described how a matte surface looks brightest when light hits it straight on and dimmer as the light grazes it at a slant, falling off with the cosine of the angle. In code, that's the dot product of the surface's outward-facing direction, called its *normal*, with the direction toward the light. Clamp negatives to zero, since a surface facing away gets no direct light, and you've got the core of diffuse shading.

blocks.title: Diffuse brightness of a matte surface by angle of incoming light
blocks.note: This is why the top of a box under a high sun is bright and its sides are dim.
blocks.source: Calculated: brightness = max(0, n · l) = cos(angle), Lambert's cosine law

blocks.text: The dot product has a partner, the **cross product**, which takes two vectors and returns a third one perpendicular to both. Give it two edges of a triangle and out comes the triangle's normal, which is how engines figure out which way each little piece of a mesh faces. In 1975 Bui Tuong Phong published a lighting model that added shiny highlights on top of Lambert's matte shading, again built from dot products of normals, light directions and the direction to the viewer. Versions of that recipe lit games for decades.
Matrices: machines that move everything at once

A model in a game is thousands of points. To rotate it, you need to rotate every point the same way. A **matrix** is a grid of numbers that does exactly that: multiply any vector by the matrix and out comes the transformed vector. A 3 by 3 rotation matrix has a beautifully simple meaning. Its three columns are just where the x, y and z axes end up after the rotation. Roblox's own CFrame documentation lays this out: the columns of a CFrame's rotation matrix are its RightVector, its UpVector and the reverse of its LookVector.

The real power is composition. Rotating by one matrix and then another is the same as multiplying the two matrices together once and applying the result. Engines chain whole stacks of these: the part's position relative to its model, the model's position in the world, the world's position relative to the camera. Order matters. Rotating and then moving is not the same as moving and then rotating, just as turning left then walking forward lands you somewhere different than walking forward then turning left. Matrix multiplication is famously not commutative, and this is why.

There's one snag. Rotation and scaling can be written as matrix multiplication, but sliding something sideways, a *translation*, can't: it's an addition. The fix is a trick borrowed from 19th-century geometry called *homogeneous coordinates*. Add a fourth number, w, set to 1 for positions. Now a 4 by 4 matrix can rotate, scale and translate in a single multiplication, and the whole pipeline becomes one long chain of matrix products. Roblox stores a CFrame as 12 numbers, three for position and nine for the rotation matrix, which is exactly a 4 by 4 matrix whose bottom row is always the same and can be left out. Its documentation also notes that a CFrame's inverse just transposes the rotation part, flipping it along its diagonal, because rotation matrices are special: undoing one is as cheap as reading it sideways.

blocks.title: The journey of one vertex to your screen
items: Model space: the point as the artist built it, relative to the model's own center.
World space: multiplied by the model's matrix to place it in the level.
Camera space: multiplied by the inverse of the camera's matrix, so the camera sits at the origin looking down one axis.
Clip space: multiplied by a projection matrix that sets up perspective and the field of view.
Screen space: divided by w, the perspective divide, then scaled to pixel coordinates and handed to the rasterizer.

blocks.text: This is also why graphics cards exist. Transforming one vertex by a 4 by 4 matrix takes 16 multiplications and 12 additions. Doing it for a million vertices is the same tiny job repeated a million times with different inputs, which is perfect for a chip with thousands of small cores working side by side. GPUs were built for exactly this. Then researchers noticed that neural networks are, at their core, also giant stacks of matrix multiplications, and the hardware designed to spin game worlds became the hardware that trains AI. The math you use to rotate a part in Studio is the same math behind large language models.
Perspective is a division

Why do far things look small? Draw a line from your eye to the top of a distant tower and see where it crosses a window in front of you. By similar triangles, the height on the window equals the tower's height times the window's distance, divided by the tower's distance. Renaissance painters worked this out with string and grids. A GPU does it with one division per vertex: the projection matrix tucks the distance into w, and dividing by w shrinks everything in proportion to how far away it is.

blocks.title: On-screen height of a 10-stud-tall object as it moves away
blocks.note: Double the distance, half the size. Assumes a 70-degree vertical field of view.
blocks.source: Calculated: screen height = f × h / z, with f = 540 / tan(35°) ≈ 771 px and h = 10 studs

blocks.text: That 1-over-distance curve explains a lot of game design. Objects shrink fast up close and then slowly, so a level's foreground dominates the screen while distant mountains barely change as you walk. It's why widening the field of view makes everything look farther away, and why engines swap distant objects for simpler versions: past a certain distance, a detailed model covers only a handful of pixels anyway.
Gimbal lock and the four-dimensional fix

Now back to Collins. The natural way to describe an orientation is three angles: yaw (turn left-right), pitch (tilt up-down) and roll (twist). These are called Euler angles, and they're what Roblox's CFrame.fromEulerAnglesXYZ takes. They're intuitive, and they have the exact flaw Apollo's gimbals had. Pitch straight up 90 degrees and yaw and roll become the same motion. You've lost a degree of freedom. In a game, that shows up as a camera that suddenly spins or jitters when you look straight up, or an animation that takes a bizarre detour between two poses.

The fix is older than airplanes. On 16 October 1843, the Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton was walking along the Royal Canal in Dublin when he finally cracked a problem he'd been stuck on for years. He was so excited he carved the key formula into the stone of Broome Bridge: i squared equals j squared equals k squared equals ijk equals minus 1. These were **quaternions**, numbers with one real part and three imaginary parts. A plaque marks the spot today.
i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1
blocks.by: William Rowan Hamilton, carved into Broome Bridge, Dublin, 1843

blocks.text: A unit quaternion, four numbers, can represent any 3D rotation with no gimbal lock at all, because it describes the rotation as a single turn around a single axis rather than three turns stacked in sequence. Quaternions also blend smoothly. In 1985 Ken Shoemake showed computer graphics researchers how to interpolate between two orientations along the shortest arc at constant speed, a technique called *slerp*, for spherical linear interpolation. Roblox's CFrame:Lerp uses exactly that for the rotation part, and CFrame.new will even accept a quaternion's four components directly.

blocks.title: Three ways to store a rotation

left.head: Euler angles (yaw, pitch, roll)
items: Three numbers, easy for humans to read
Suffer gimbal lock at certain angles
Blend badly between poses
Great for an editor's input boxes

right.head: Matrices and quaternions
items: Nine numbers (matrix) or four (quaternion)
No gimbal lock
Quaternions blend smoothly with slerp
What the engine actually uses inside

blocks.text: Here's the reframe. A 3D game is not really a world. It's a gigantic linear algebra problem: lists of vectors pushed through chains of matrices, dotted against light directions and divided by distance, re-solved from scratch about 60 times a second. Hamilton's bridge graffiti, Lambert's cosine and a Renaissance painter's similar triangles are all running inside the device in your hand. When your camera script jitters or a part spins the wrong way, the bug is almost always in this math: the wrong order of multiplication, a position treated like a direction, or a rotation built from angles that hit a pole.

Practical rule for Roblox scripting: think in CFrames, not angles. Build rotations with CFrame.lookAt or by multiplying CFrames, blend them with Lerp, and remember that a * b is not b * a. Save Euler angles for the moments a human has to type a number in.

takeaways: Vectors are arrows; subtracting positions gives directions, and their length comes from 3D Pythagoras.
The dot product measures alignment. It decides front versus behind, vision cones and how bright a lit surface is.
Matrices transform every point at once; their columns show where the axes go, and the order you multiply them matters.
Perspective is a division by distance, so on-screen size falls as 1 over distance.
Euler angles suffer gimbal lock; engines store rotations as matrices or quaternions and blend them with slerp.

title: The Ruler That Counts Zeros: Logarithms in Sound, Earthquakes and Acid
dek: Decibels, magnitudes and pH are the same trick wearing different uniforms. Once you see it, you can add noise sources in your head, size an earthquake from a fault, and see why the ocean's tiny pH change is not tiny.

blocks.text: On February 28, 2001, the magnitude 6.8 Nisqually earthquake shook Seattle and the whole Puget Sound region, from Olympia up past Everett. Now compare it with the 1964 Alaska earthquake, magnitude 9.2. On paper the gap is 2.4, small enough to sound like the difference between a bad day and a slightly worse one. In reality the Alaska quake's seismic waves were about 250 times larger in amplitude, and it released roughly 4,000 times as much energy.

That gap between how the numbers look and what they mean is the whole story of logarithmic scales. Decibels, earthquake magnitudes and pH all compress enormous ranges into small, friendly numbers by counting powers of ten instead of counting units. If you came through nuke school, you have used decibels and logs plenty. The goal here is to go past the definitions to the things the definitions let you do, plus the traps they set for anyone who reads them like a normal ruler.
A logarithm is a zero counter

The base-10 logarithm of a number is, roughly, how many zeros it has. The log of 1,000 is 3, the log of a million is 6, and the log of 2 is about 0.301, because 2 is about three tenths of the way to 10 in multiplicative terms. The key property is the one John Napier built his 1614 tables around: logs turn multiplication into addition. Log of a times b equals log a plus log b. For three centuries, slide rules and log tables let engineers multiply by sliding sticks and adding numbers.

There is evidence the human brain starts out on this kind of scale. In a 2008 *Science* study, Stanislas Dehaene and colleagues asked members of the Mundurucu, an Amazonian group with few number words and little formal schooling, to place quantities on a line. They spaced them logarithmically, giving lots of room to small numbers and squeezing big ones together. Western adults did the same with dot clouds when counting was discouraged. The even-spaced number line, the authors argued, is something school installs. That matters, because log scales feel natural right up until you have to read them, and then they lie to your linear-trained eye.
Decibels: the parts the formula sheet skips

A decibel is ten times the log of a power ratio. Ten decibels is a factor of 10 in power, 20 dB is 100, and 3 dB is almost exactly a factor of 2, since 10 times log 2 is 3.01. When you measure amplitudes, like voltage or sound pressure, the formula becomes 20 log instead of 10 log, because power goes as amplitude squared. So 6 dB doubles a voltage but quadruples the power. Mixing up those two conventions is one of the most common errors in any field that uses dB.

The useful skill is adding sources. Decibels from independent, incoherent sources don't add; their powers do. Two pumps each at 90 dB together make 93 dB, not 180. Ten of them make 100 dB. To combine any set of levels, convert each back to power, add, and take the log again: L total equals 10 log of the sum of 10 to the L over 10. A source 3 dB quieter than another adds about 1.8 dB. A source 10 dB quieter adds only 0.4 dB, which is why turning off the quieter of two machines barely changes the noise, and why the loudest source is the only one worth fixing first.

Worked example: a space has an 85 dB fan and an 82 dB pump. Convert to relative powers of 10^8.5 and 10^8.2, which are about 3.16 and 1.58 hundred million. The sum is 4.75 hundred million, and 10 log of that is 86.8 dB. Kill the fan and you drop to 82; kill the pump and you only drop to 85.

Hearing protection rules are logs in disguise. NIOSH recommends a limit of 85 dBA averaged over 8 hours with a 3 dB exchange rate: every 3 dB louder halves the allowed time. That is pure physics, because 3 dB is double the acoustic energy, and equal energy means equal dose. OSHA's legal limit uses 90 dBA with a 5 dB exchange rate, which is a regulatory compromise rather than an energy rule, and it lets you spend far longer at high levels. At 100 dBA, the NIOSH rule allows 15 minutes; OSHA's allows 2 hours.

Distance is a log problem too. In open air, sound from a small source spreads over a sphere, so its intensity falls with the square of distance. Double your distance and the intensity drops by a factor of 4, which is 10 log 4, about 6 dB. Ten times farther is 20 dB quieter. That is why stepping back from a loud machine helps more than people expect at first and less than they hope later: going from 1 meter to 2 buys you 6 dB, but going from 10 meters to 11 buys you less than 1. Inside a steel hull, with reflections everywhere, the drop is smaller, because the reflected sound fills the space.

blocks.title: Allowed daily exposure under the NIOSH 3 dB rule
blocks.note: Each 3 dB step doubles the energy, so it halves the time.
blocks.source: Calculated: T = 480 / 2^((L − 85)/3), from the NIOSH 85 dBA, 3 dB exchange-rate criterion (NIOSH, 1998)

blocks.text: Earthquakes: from a seismograph squiggle to fault physics

Charles Richter's 1935 scale was the log of the amplitude of a squiggle on a particular seismograph, corrected for distance. It worked for California but saturated for great earthquakes: past a certain size, bigger ruptures didn't produce proportionally bigger squiggles at the frequencies it measured. In 1979 Thomas Hanks and Hiroo Kanamori defined the moment magnitude, which seismologists now prefer for large quakes because it is tied to physics rather than to an instrument.

The seismic moment, M0, is rigidity of the rock times the area that slipped times the average slip. It is measured in newton-meters, and moment magnitude is two thirds of the quantity log M0 minus 9.1. Two consequences fall right out. First, each whole magnitude step is 10 times the wave amplitude but about 32 times the energy, because energy scales with the 1.5 power: 10 to the 1.5 is 31.6. Second, you can reason about faults. Double both the slip and the rupture area and M0 goes up by 4, but magnitude only rises by two thirds of log 4, about 0.4.

blocks.title: Energy released relative to Nisqually 2001 (M6.8)
blocks.note: Nisqually's bar is there; it is just 1/11,220 the height of Chile's.
blocks.source: Calculated: 10^(1.5 × (M − 6.8)); magnitudes from USGS

blocks.text: USGS uses this to put a ceiling on the planet. Summing the energy of every earthquake over the past century or so gives the equivalent of a single quake around magnitude 9.95. A full end-to-end rupture of the San Andreas would be about 8.5. Even the entire South American subduction zone, about 6,400 kilometers long, rupturing at once would come out near 9.86. A magnitude 10 would need roughly 14,000 kilometers of fault slipping together. The log scale makes 10 sound like the next number up from 9.5. The physics says it is close to impossible.

Logs also reveal a law hiding in the earthquake catalog. USGS figures put the yearly average at about 1 earthquake of magnitude 8 or above, 15 in the 7s, 134 in the 6s and 1,319 in the 5s, with about ten times more for each step down. Plot the log of those counts against magnitude and you get a nearly straight line, known as the Gutenberg–Richter law. Small quakes are common, big ones are rare, and the ratio is steady enough to forecast long-run odds.

blocks.title: Earthquakes per year: one step down, ten times more
blocks.note: From 1 a year to about 1.3 million a year. Counts below magnitude 5 are USGS estimates.
blocks.source: USGS Earthquake Facts and Statistics (log10 of counts calculated)

blocks.text: pH: a negative log that hides big changes

The chemist Søren Sørensen introduced pH in 1909 as the negative log of hydrogen ion concentration. The minus sign is why lower pH means more acid, and the log is why each unit is a factor of ten. Pure water at 25°C sits at pH 7 because its hydrogen ion concentration is 10 to the minus 7 moles per liter. Dilute a pH 2 acid tenfold and you get pH 3. To get it to 7 you would need to dilute it 100,000 times.

Here is where the eye gets fooled. NOAA reports that the pH of surface ocean water has fallen by about 0.1 units since the start of the industrial era. A tenth of a unit sounds like rounding error. But 10 to the 0.1 is 1.26, so even an exact 0.1 drop means 26 percent more hydrogen ions; NOAA's rounder figure is about 30 percent. On a log scale, a decimal in the first place is a big deal.

The flip side is why buffers work. The Henderson–Hasselbalch relation says a buffer's pH equals its pKa plus the log of the ratio of base to acid. Near a 1 to 1 ratio, you can push that ratio around a lot and the log barely moves: doubling the ratio shifts pH by only 0.3. The same compression that hides changes on the way in also makes systems stable against them. Swimming pools, lab solutions and the bicarbonate system in your bloodstream all lean on that flatness.
Thinking in logs

The deep habit worth stealing is this: whenever a quantity grows by multiplying rather than adding, think in its log. Money compounding, subscriber counts, reactor power on a startup, the number of possible game states, the strength of a password. Log base 2 counts bits, the number of yes-or-no questions needed to pick something out. Twenty questions can single out one item among 2 to the 20, which is 1,048,576, which is why that game is so hard to lose if you ask good questions.

Log scales on charts are worth learning to read, too. On a chart with a log vertical axis, a straight line means a constant percentage growth rate, and the slope tells you the rate. On a log-log chart, with both axes logarithmic, a straight line means a power law, and the slope is the exponent. The Gutenberg–Richter chart above is the first kind. Inverse-square spreading, plotted on log-log axes, is a straight line with slope minus 2. Spotting which kind of straight line you are looking at tells you what kind of process made the data.

blocks.title: Combining decibel levels in your head
items: Find the difference between the two levels.
0 dB apart: add 3 to the louder.
3 dB apart: add about 1.8.
6 dB apart: add about 1.
10 dB or more apart: add about 0.4 or less, so ignore the quieter source.

blocks.text: Puzzles

items: **The crowd.** One person shouting measures 70 dB at some distance. How many people shouting equally loud, at the same distance, to reach 90 dB? (Answer: 20 dB is a factor of 100 in power, so 100 people.)
**The dial.** An amplifier gain goes from 20 dB to 26 dB. What happened to output voltage and to output power? (Answer: voltage doubled, power quadrupled.)
**The fault.** A fault ruptures with ten times the area and the same slip as another. How much bigger is the magnitude? (Answer: two thirds of log 10, about 0.67.)
**The step back.** You measure 94 dBA 1 meter from a compressor outdoors. Roughly what will you measure at 4 meters? (Answer: two doublings of distance, so about 12 dB less, around 82 dBA.)

**The acid.** A solution's hydrogen ion concentration is 4 × 10 to the minus 8 moles per liter. What is its pH, and is it acidic or basic? (Answer: log of 4 × 10^−8 is about −7.40, so pH 7.4, slightly basic.)

blocks.text: A log scale is an honest tool with a dishonest look. It lets one number line hold a whisper and a jet engine, a tremor and the Chile earthquake, lemon juice and lye. The price is that equal-looking steps hide wildly unequal changes. Read every log number by asking how many factors of ten it represents, and the scales stop lying to you.

takeaways: Logs turn multiplication into addition; every log scale is counting factors, not units.
Incoherent decibel sources add by power: two equal sources give +3 dB, and a source 10 dB quieter adds about 0.4 dB.
Each earthquake magnitude step is 10 times the wave amplitude and about 32 times the energy.
A 0.1 drop in pH means at least 26 percent more hydrogen ions; NOAA puts the ocean's change at about 30 percent.
When something grows by multiplying, reason in its log.

title: A 1% Drop Is Not 100 Tries
dek: The math hiding inside every loot table: why bad luck lasts longer than you think, why collecting a full set costs triple, and why game designers quietly rig randomness to feel fair.

blocks.text: You have killed the same boss 140 times. The wiki says the mount drops 1% of the time. Your buddy got it on kill 12 and will not stop talking about it. Somewhere in your head a voice is doing math that feels obvious: one percent means one in a hundred, so after a hundred kills you should have it, and after 140 the game must be broken.

The game is not broken. Your intuition is. A 1% drop does not mean you get it in about 100 tries. It means that after 100 tries roughly a third of players still have nothing, and a few unlucky ones will still be farming at kill 400. Once you see the shape of that math, you look at every loot table, gacha banner and egg hatch differently, and if you build games, you start to understand why so many designers secretly cheat their own random number generators.
The curve behind every drop

Each kill is an independent roll. If the chance of a drop is *p*, the chance of missing on one kill is 1 − *p*, and the chance of missing *n* times in a row is (1 − *p*) multiplied by itself *n* times. So the chance you have the item after *n* tries is 1 − (1 − *p*)^*n*. Mathematicians call the number of tries until the first success a *geometric distribution*, and it has a shape that surprises almost everyone.

Plug in a 1% drop. After 50 kills, only about 39.5% of players have it. After 100, it is 63.4%, not 100%. To reach 95% of players you need about 300 kills, and to reach 99% you need about 459. The curve rises fast at first and then crawls, because every new kill only converts 1% of the people who are still empty-handed.

blocks.title: Chance you have a 1% drop after n tries
blocks.note: Halfway at 69 tries; 95% only at about 300.
blocks.source: Calculated: P(at least one) = 1 − (1 − 0.01)^n

blocks.text: Here is the strangest part. The *average* number of tries is exactly 100, which is where the folk rule comes from. But the *median*, the point where half of players have the item, is only 69. Those two numbers disagree because the distribution has a long right tail. Most people get lucky earlier than 100, and a smaller group gets crushed far beyond it, dragging the average up. If you ask 'what usually happens', the answer is 69. If you ask 'what happens on average', it is 100. Neither tells you what will happen to *you*.

items.label: Tries until half of players have a 1% drop (the median)
Average tries, pulled up by the unlucky tail
Players still empty-handed after 200 tries

blocks.source: Calculated: median = ln 0.5 / ln 0.99; mean = 1/p; 0.99^200

blocks.text: That last number is the one that matters for player experience. If 10,000 people farm a 1% drop, about 1,340 of them will go 200 kills with nothing. That is not a rare glitch. It is a guaranteed crowd of furious players, built into the math, posting on forums that the drop rate is bugged.
The dice have no memory, but you do

The geometric distribution has a property called *memorylessness*. If you have already missed 140 times, your chance of getting the item in the next 100 kills is exactly the same 63.4% as it was for a fresh player. The 140 failures are sunk. They do not make the next roll more likely, and they do not 'count toward' anything, unless the designer built a counter.

Humans are terrible at accepting this. In 1971 psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described what they called the belief in the law of small numbers: people expect short runs of random events to look like the long-run average. We expect a 1% item to show up roughly once per hundred tries, the way we expect a coin to alternate heads and tails more than it really does. When luck clumps, which it always does, we assume something is wrong.

Before you farm, decide how many tries the item is worth to you. Use the 95% number, not the average: for a drop rate p, it is about 3 divided by p. For a 1% drop, budget 300 tries, not 100. If that is too many, skip it now rather than after you have sunk 200.
Is the drop rate lying?

Sometimes the drop rate really is bugged, so it helps to know how to tell. The honest test is not 'I have gone way past 100.' It is 'how likely is my drought if the stated rate were true?' At a true 1%, going 300 kills without the item happens to about 1 player in 20. Going 459 happens to about 1 in 100. Unusual, yes, but with thousands of players farming, somebody is always living in that tail. One person's bad run is weak evidence. Many players pooling their kill counts is strong evidence.

Statisticians have a handy shortcut for the case where you have seen zero successes, called the *rule of three*. If something has not happened in *n* independent tries, you can be about 95% confident its true rate is below 3/*n*. Zero drops in 300 kills means the rate is probably under 1%. Zero in 1,000 means it is probably under 0.3%. This is how player communities crowdsource drop tables: they log thousands of kills, count the drops, and put error bars on the result instead of trusting one loud forum post.
Collecting the whole set costs far more

Now suppose a game has 10 pets in an egg, all equally likely, and you want all ten. The first hatch is always new. The second is new 9 times out of 10. But by the time you have nine, each hatch has only a 1-in-10 chance of being the one you are missing, so you wait about 10 hatches for that last pet alone. Add up the waits and the expected total is 10 × (1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... + 1/10), which is about 29.3 hatches. This is the classic *coupon collector's problem*, named after people collecting cards from cereal boxes.

blocks.title: Average draws to collect a full set (equal odds)
blocks.note: The last few items eat most of the cost; uneven rarities make it far worse.
blocks.source: Calculated: expected draws = N × (1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/N)

blocks.text: Notice that collecting 100 items costs more than five times the number of items. And that is the friendly version, where every item is equally common. Real games make one item in the set rare, which turns the last slot into a long geometric grind stacked on top of the collection grind.

This math once got a whole game mechanic banned. Japanese mobile games in the early 2010s sold 'complete gacha' (kompu gacha), where you had to pull every card in a set from paid random draws to unlock a special prize. In May 2012 Japan's Consumer Affairs Agency said the method was illegal under its law against unjustifiable premiums and misleading representations, citing charges that were in some cases excessive, and the big platforms DeNA and Gree said they would drop it. The regulators were, in effect, reacting to the coupon collector's problem with money attached.
Why designers rig the dice

At the 2010 Game Developers Conference, Civilization creator Sid Meier described playtesters who saw 3-to-1 odds in their favor before a battle and expected to win every time, even though they should lose a quarter of the time. They also treated 20-to-10 as much stronger than 2-to-1, though it is the same ratio. Meier's team tweaked the math so players won more than the displayed odds implied, and made outcomes take previous battles into account so long losing streaks were less common.

Blizzard's Rob Pardo told a similar story at the same conference about World of Warcraft quest items. Players on long dry streaks blamed the random number generator instead of accepting variance, so the team changed the code: the drop chance rose after each kill without the item, until it reached 100%, then reset. Pure randomness was mathematically fair and emotionally unacceptable, so they replaced it with something that feels fair.

A general version of this trick, which Warcraft III and Dota players know as *pseudo-random distribution*, is used for effects like critical hits. Instead of a flat 25% chance every swing, the chance starts low and grows by a fixed step each time you miss, resetting when you hit. If you choose the step correctly, the long-run rate is still exactly 25%. For a 25% effect, the step works out to about 8.5%: the first swing has an 8.5% chance, the second 17%, and so on, guaranteed by the twelfth.

blocks.title: Same 25% long-run rate, very different streaks

left.head: True random (flat 25%)
items: Every swing has a 25% chance
Miss 10 in a row about 5.6% of the time
Hits can come back to back often
No upper limit on a drought

right.head: Pseudo-random (starts 8.5%, +8.5% per miss)
items: Chance climbs after every miss
Miss 10 in a row about 0.05% of the time
Back-to-back hits are rarer
Guaranteed by swing 12

blocks.text: The trade is subtle. Pseudo-random distribution removes both tails: fewer frustrating droughts, but also fewer glorious streaks of luck. For something like crits in a competitive game, that is usually what you want, because it makes skill matter more than coin flips. For a rare celebratory drop, you might want to keep some of the wild luck, because the story of 'I got it on my third try' is part of what players share.
Pity timers: the guarantee does the real work

Gacha games formalize this as a *pity* system: after a set number of pulls without a top-rarity result, the next one is guaranteed. Let us design a hypothetical banner to see what that does. Say the rare character has a 0.6% chance per pull, and pull 90 is guaranteed if you have not gotten one yet.

Run the numbers and something surprising appears. The chance of missing 89 pulls in a row at 0.6% is about 58.5%. So more than half of all players never win the 0.6% roll at all. They reach the pity counter and get the character because of the guarantee. The average cost works out to about 69.7 pulls, which means the effective rate is about 1.43%, more than double the advertised base rate. The headline percentage is almost decoration. The pity number is the real price.

blocks.title: Hypothetical 0.6% banner: chance you have it by pull n
blocks.note: Without the guarantee the curve would still be at 41.8% on pull 90.
blocks.source: Calculated: 1 − (1 − 0.006)^n, with a guaranteed result on pull 90

blocks.text: This is why the earlier library article on loot boxes noted that pity can turn 'just a few pulls' into 'only twenty away from guaranteed.' A visible counter is a progress bar, and progress bars pull people forward. The math itself is neutral. It caps the worst case, which is genuinely kinder to unlucky players. But it also hands players a concrete target, and targets close to completion are powerful motivators.
Building it into your own game

If you are building a Roblox game, none of this is abstract. Roblox's policy on paid random items requires creators to show every possible outcome with its odds as percentages before purchase, and it explicitly treats luck boosts and pity systems as part of the odds. So you will be publishing these numbers whether you like it or not. You might as well understand what they do to players.

blocks.title: A designer's checklist for any random reward
items: Write down the drop rate and compute the median and 95th-percentile tries, not just the average
Ask how many players will be stuck at the 95th percentile and whether that experience is acceptable
If droughts are the problem, add a rising chance or a hard pity cap rather than raising the base rate
For collections, compute the coupon-collector cost and consider letting duplicates convert into the missing items
If the item is paid, publish odds including pity, and price a direct-buy version near its real expected cost

blocks.text: One trick that game designers use for collections is a duplicate converter: extra copies turn into shards or currency that can buy the missing piece. Mathematically, it chops off the brutal tail of the coupon collector's problem, because the last item no longer depends on one tiny probability. Players experience it as fairness. The underlying randomness is the same; the worst case is just no longer unbounded.

The deeper lesson reaches beyond games. Whenever something has a small chance per attempt, like a job application, a video blowing up, or a cold message getting a reply, you are living on a geometric curve. The average hides a long tail, the past attempts do not make the next one more likely, and the useful question is never 'when will it happen?' It is 'how many attempts can I afford, and what is the chance it happens within that budget?' Real life rarely gives you a pity timer. Knowing that is exactly why it helps to do the math before you start farming.

takeaways: For a drop chance p, the chance of having it after n tries is 1 − (1 − p)^n. A 1% drop is only 63% likely after 100 tries.
The average hides the tail: a 1% drop has a median of 69 tries but needs about 300 to reach 95% of players.
Past failures do not raise your odds unless the game has a counter. Random rolls have no memory.
Collecting a full set costs about N × (1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/N) draws, roughly 29 for just 10 equal items.
In pity systems the guarantee, not the base rate, sets the real price. Design and spend accordingly.

title: Three Doors and 23 Birthdays: The Puzzles That Break Your Intuition
dek: Two famous probability puzzles where the right answer feels flat-out wrong, why thousands of experts got them wrong, and how to retrain your gut.

blocks.text: In September 1990, a reader wrote to Marilyn vos Savant's "Ask Marilyn" column in *Parade* magazine with a game-show puzzle. You face three doors. Behind one is a car; behind the other two are goats. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens door 3 to show a goat, then asks if you want to switch to door 2. Should you?

Vos Savant said yes: switching wins two times out of three. The response was a flood. By her estimate, about 10,000 readers wrote in, close to 1,000 of them holding PhDs, and most insisted she was wrong and that the odds were 50/50. Paul Erdős, one of the most prolific mathematicians of the twentieth century, reportedly refused to believe it until he was shown a computer simulation. She was right. They were wrong. And the reason is worth understanding, because the same mental glitch shows up far from game shows.

items.label: Letters vos Savant estimated she received
Of those letters, from people with PhDs
Chance that switching wins

blocks.source: Monty Hall problem, summary of vos Savant's own estimates (Wikipedia)

blocks.text: The rules that matter

The puzzle had actually been posed years earlier, by statistician Steve Selvin in two 1975 letters to *The American Statistician*, the second of which gave it the name "the Monty Hall problem" after the host of *Let's Make a Deal*. Before solving it, pin down the rules, because the answer depends on them completely. The host **knows** where the car is. He **always** opens a door you did not pick. He **always** reveals a goat. And he **always** offers the switch.

Those rules mean the host's action is not random. He is forced. If you picked a goat, he has exactly one door he is allowed to open, and the car is behind the other one. That single fact is the key to the whole puzzle.
Three ways to see why switching wins

**Way one: list every case.** You pick door 1. The car is equally likely to be behind door 1, 2 or 3, each with probability 1/3. If it is behind door 1, the host opens either other door, and switching loses. If it is behind door 2, the host must open door 3, and switching wins. If it is behind door 3, the host must open door 2, and switching wins. Switching wins in two of the three equally likely cases. Sticking wins in one.

blocks.title: Stick or switch, starting from door 1

left.head: Always stick
items: Car behind 1: you win
Car behind 2: you lose
Car behind 3: you lose
Wins 1 of 3 cases

right.head: Always switch
items: Car behind 1: you lose
Car behind 2: you win
Car behind 3: you win
Wins 2 of 3 cases

blocks.text: **Way two: blow it up.** Imagine 100 doors. You pick one. The host, who knows where the car is, opens 98 of the other doors, all goats, and leaves exactly one closed. Do you still think your random first pick and that one surviving door are equally likely? Your door had a 1 in 100 chance when you picked it, and nothing the host did changed that. The surviving door collects the other 99 in 100. With three doors the same logic gives 1/3 versus 2/3; it is just less obvious.

**Way three: think about what you are really choosing.** Sticking means betting that your first pick was right, which happens 1/3 of the time. Switching means betting that your first pick was wrong, which happens 2/3 of the time. The host's reveal turns "my first pick was wrong" into a specific door you can walk to.

If none of that convinces you, do what convinced Erdős and simulate it. A short Python script that plays the game 100,000 times, choosing doors at random and letting a host follow the rules, gives this:

blocks.title: 100,000 simulated Monty Hall games
blocks.note: Random car placement and first pick each game; the host always opens a goat door you did not choose.
blocks.source: Calculated: Python simulation, 100,000 games, seed 1

blocks.text: The twist: it depends on what the host knows

Here is the part that teaches the real lesson. Change one rule: the host does *not* know where the car is and opens one of the other two doors at random. Sometimes he accidentally reveals the car and the game is spoiled. But in the games where he happens to reveal a goat, switching now wins only half the time. My simulation of that version gives 50.1 percent. Same doors, same goat, same moment on stage, and the odds are different.

Why? Because when the host is forced, his choice carries information about where the car is. When he is guessing, it carries none, and a revealed goat just eliminates one possibility evenly. Probability is not a property of the doors. It is a property of **what you know and how you came to know it**. That idea, that the process that produced your evidence matters as much as the evidence itself, is the foundation of real statistical thinking, from intelligence analysis to medical tests.

Outside game shows, the host is usually invisible. A store page decides which reviews you see first. A streamer's clip channel shows the shots that hit, never the hundred that missed. A recruiter tells you about the sailors who loved the job. Each of those is a door someone chose to open for a reason. Before you update on any piece of evidence, ask the Monty Hall question: was this shown to me at random, or was someone forced, or motivated, to show me exactly this?

Psychologists have offered a few reasons the wrong answer feels so right. One is a habit of treating any set of unknown options as equally likely: two closed doors, so 50/50. Another is regret. Losing a car you already had by switching away from it feels far worse than losing by sticking with a goat, even though the two losses are equally real. People will pay a real price in expected winnings to avoid the sharper sting of a mistake they actively chose. If you have ever stuck with a bad build in a game because changing felt like admitting you were wrong, you have felt this pull.

And here is a humbling footnote. In a 2010 study in the *Journal of Comparative Psychology*, Walter Herbranson and Julia Schroeder ran pigeons through a version of the game for grain. The birds learned to switch and moved toward the optimal strategy. Humans tested on the same procedure did not adopt the optimal strategy, even with extensive training. The pigeons were not smarter. They simply learned from outcomes, while people kept trusting a story in their heads that said two doors must mean even odds.
Twenty-three people, one birthday

Now a second puzzle. How many people need to be in a room for there to be a better than even chance that two of them share a birthday? Ignore leap years and assume all 365 days are equally likely. Many people guess around 183, half of 365. The answer is **23**.

The gut goes wrong because it quietly answers a different question: how many people do I need before someone shares *my* birthday? That really does take a crowd, 253 people for a 50 percent chance. But the puzzle asks about *any* pair. With 23 people there are 23 × 22 / 2 = 253 different pairs, and each pair is a fresh chance for a match. You are not running 22 trials. You are running 253.

Here is the exact calculation, using a standard trick: compute the chance of *no* match, then subtract from 1. The first person can have any birthday: 365/365. The second must avoid the first: 364/365. The third must avoid both: 363/365. Keep going to the 23rd person, who must avoid 22 taken days: 343/365. Multiply all 23 fractions and you get about 0.493. So the chance of at least one shared birthday is 1 − 0.493 = 0.507, or 50.7 percent.

There is a beautiful shortcut hiding in that number. Each pair has a 1 in 365 chance of matching, and for small chances the odds that none of 253 pairs match is close to e^(−253/365). Now look at the exponent: 253/365 is about 0.693, which is the natural log of 2. So the chance of no match is about e^(−ln 2) = 1/2. The number 23 is simply where the count of pairs reaches 365 × ln 2. The general rule is that the chance of no match is roughly e^(−n²/730), which is why the curve climbs so fast: pairs grow with the *square* of the group size.

blocks.title: Chance at least two people share a birthday
blocks.note: Assumes 365 equally likely birthdays.

blocks.text: Real-world check: at the 2014 World Cup, every squad had 23 players, almost exactly the 50 percent line. The BBC went through the official squad lists and found that 16 of the 32 teams had at least one pair of players sharing a birthday. Half. The math predicted 50.7 percent. Real birthdays are not perfectly uniform, since births cluster a little in certain seasons, and uneven distributions actually make matches slightly *more* likely, not less.

There is a bigger lesson here about coincidence. Statisticians sometimes call it the law of truly large numbers: with enough people and enough chances, astonishing coincidences are not just possible but close to guaranteed. Two shipmates with the same birthday, running into someone from your hometown on liberty in a foreign port, a dream that seems to come true. Each one feels like it means something because you only notice the hits. You never count the millions of pairs and moments where nothing lined up.
Where the birthday problem bites

This is not just a party trick. In computing it is called the **birthday bound**, and it shapes how systems are designed. Suppose you are building a game and give each new player a random six-digit code, a million possibilities. It feels like collisions would be rare until you have hundreds of thousands of players. Run the same calculation and with just 1,000 players there is already about a 39 percent chance that two of them got the same code. The rough rule: collisions become likely after about the *square root* of the number of possibilities.

That is why cryptographic hash functions use enormous outputs. A hash with n bits of output has 2^n possible values, but an attacker hunting for any two inputs that collide only needs to try around 2^(n/2) of them. Engineers have to design for the square root, not the full number. The birthday problem is the reason a 128-bit hash only gives about 64 bits of collision resistance.

blocks.title: How to beat a probability puzzle
items: Write down the exact rules, especially who knows what and who is forced to act.
List every equally likely case, or the outcomes that matter, before trusting a feeling.
Push it to an extreme (100 doors, 1,000 people) to see the structure.
Use the complement: computing the chance of nothing happening is often easier.
Count pairs or combinations, not people or objects.
If you still doubt it, simulate it a few thousand times.

blocks.text: Puzzles to try

items: **Four doors.** Same game, but four doors, and the host opens one goat door and offers you either of the two remaining. What is your chance if you switch? (Answer: your first pick holds 1/4. The other 3/4 is spread across the two remaining doors, so each is 3/8. Switching still beats sticking, 37.5 percent to 25 percent.)

**The three cards.** One card is red on both sides, one is white on both sides, one is red on one side and white on the other. You draw a card at random and see a red face. What is the chance the other side is red? (Answer: 2/3, not 1/2. There are three red faces you could be looking at, and two of them belong to the red-red card.)
**Your crew.** In a group of 60, what is the chance two people share a birthday? (Answer: just over 99 percent. In any large crew, a shared birthday is close to guaranteed.)

blocks.text: Both puzzles fool people for the same reason. The mind grabs the most visible feature of a situation, two doors left, 365 days in a year, and builds its answer around that, ignoring the structure underneath: a host who is forced to act, or 253 hidden pairs. The fix is not to become a genius. It is to slow down long enough to ask what process produced what you are seeing. The thousands of people who wrote angry letters to *Parade* were not stupid. They just trusted the first story that made sense.

takeaways: In Monty Hall, switching wins 2 of 3 games because the host is forced to avoid the car.
If the host opens a door at random and shows a goat, switching drops to 50/50: information depends on the process.
23 people give a 50.7% chance of a shared birthday because they form 253 pairs.
Collisions become likely around the square root of the number of possibilities, the birthday bound.
When a probability answer feels obvious, list the cases or simulate before trusting it.

title: When to Stop Looking: The 37 Percent Rule and Its Fine Print
dek: There is a provably best way to choose when options arrive one at a time and you can't go back. It is elegant, it is famous, and it is answering a stranger question than most people think.

blocks.text: In 1611, after his first wife died, the astronomer Johannes Kepler went looking for a second one. He was methodical about it, the way you'd expect from a man who spent years fitting planetary orbits to data. He ended up considering 11 candidates. He liked the fifth one, but hesitated, kept looking, and she withdrew. After working through the rest of the list, he went back to her, she agreed, and in 1613 they married.

Kepler was stuck in what mathematicians now call an *optimal stopping* problem. Options arrive one at a time. You can evaluate each one only against the ones you've already seen. If you pass, it may be gone for good. If you commit, you never see what came after. Apartments in a tight market, job offers, hires, a used car on Marketplace, even when to stop rerolling a loadout: the structure keeps showing up. And for one clean version of it, there is an exact answer.
The secretary problem

The puzzle reached a wide audience in Martin Gardner's Mathematical Games column in *Scientific American* in February 1960, and it picked up the name "secretary problem" from its usual framing. You are hiring for one job. There are n applicants, they arrive in random order, and you interview them one at a time. After each interview you can rank the applicant against everyone you've already seen, but you have no absolute scale. You must hire or reject on the spot, and rejections are final. You win only if you hire the single best applicant of all n. Anything else counts as a loss.

The solution has a simple shape: look, then leap. Interview and reject a fixed number of applicants no matter how good they are, just to calibrate. Then hire the first applicant who is better than everyone you've seen so far. The only question is how long to look. The statistician Thomas Ferguson, in a 1989 survey of the problem's tangled history, traced versions of it through several mathematicians in the 1950s and 1960s, including Dennis Lindley's 1961 solution using dynamic programming.
Where 37 percent comes from

Here's the derivation in a few lines. Say you reject the first r applicants and then take the first one who beats them all. For you to win, the best applicant must be at some position i after r, which happens with probability 1/n for each i. Given that, you'll pick them only if you didn't stop earlier, which happens exactly when the best of the first i − 1 applicants was inside your looking phase. That chance is r/(i − 1). Add up over every i and the success probability is r/n times the sum of 1/(i − 1) from i = r + 1 to n.

For large n, that sum is close to the natural log of n/r. Write x for the fraction r/n and the success probability becomes x times ln(1/x). Take the derivative, set it to zero, and you get ln(1/x) = 1, so x = 1/e, about 0.368. Plug it back in and the success probability is also 1/e. That is the double coincidence behind the famous rule: **look at the first 37 percent, then leap, and you'll land the very best about 37 percent of the time,** no matter how big n is.

blocks.title: Chance of hiring the best of 100, by length of the look phase
blocks.note: A Monte Carlo run of 200,000 shuffles at r = 37 gave 37.0 percent.
blocks.source: Calculated: P(r) = (r/n) × Σ 1/(i−1) for i = r+1 to n, n = 100

blocks.text: Notice how flat the top of that curve is. Rejecting anywhere from 30 to 45 applicants gives nearly the same odds. The exact cutoff matters much less than having one. The real failures are at the edges: leap immediately and you're at 1 percent; look forever and you run out of applicants.

It's worth pausing on how surprising the result is. With a million applicants, blind luck gives you a one-in-a-million shot at the best. A rule that only ever compares candidates against each other, with no idea what a good score looks like, gets you better than one in three. The look phase is doing real work: it converts ignorance about the absolute scale into a usable bar. That is the general move behind every calibration period, from the first weeks at a new command to the placement matches in a ranked game.

blocks.title: The look-then-leap rule
items: Decide how many options you'll see, or how long you'll search.
Explore the first 37 percent without committing to anything.
Remember the best one you saw during that phase as your bar.
After that, take the first option that beats the bar.
If nothing beats it, you're left with whatever comes last.

blocks.text: Small numbers you can check by hand

The formula is for large n, but the logic works at any size, and small cases make good puzzles. With 3 applicants, the best plan is to reject the first, then take the next one who beats them. There are six equally likely orderings, and this plan wins in three, so 50 percent. With 10 applicants, reject 3 and you win about 39.9 percent of the time. As n grows, the best cutoff settles toward 36.8 percent of n and the odds slide down toward 36.8 percent, never below it.

Kepler's 11 candidates make a tidy test. For n = 11 the exact optimum is to reject 4, which gives a 39.8 percent chance of the best. Kepler passed on the first four, and if the fifth really did beat all of them, as his eventual choice suggests he thought, the rule says to commit right there instead of auditioning the remaining six. The catch is that Kepler did something the classic problem forbids: he went back. Real life sometimes allows recall, and that changes the math.
Change the rules, change the answer

The 37 percent rule is optimal for a specific and slightly strange goal: the best or nothing, with only relative rankings. Loosen any of those assumptions and the answer moves, often a lot. If you can score candidates on an absolute scale, for example by percentile, you no longer need a pure look phase. Gilbert and Mosteller worked out this full-information version in 1966: you use a sliding threshold that starts high and drops as options run out, and your odds of getting the best rise to about 58 percent. My own simulation with 100 candidates gave 58.2 percent.

Now change the goal. Most people don't need the single best apartment; they want a really good one and would hate a bad one. In 2006, Neil Bearden analyzed the case where you still only see rankings but your payoff is the candidate's actual quality. The best look phase shrinks to roughly the square root of n. For 100 candidates, my simulation puts the sweet spot at about 9. Here is how the two strategies compare when you score them every way that matters.

blocks.title: 100 candidates: 37% rule vs. skip 9
blocks.note: Average rank of the pick: about 20 with the 37% rule, about 9.6 when skipping 9.
blocks.source: Calculated: Monte Carlo, 100,000 random orderings per strategy

blocks.text: That last pair of bars is the fine print. Under the 37 percent rule, you fail to find anyone better than your bar 37 percent of the time, because the best candidate was already in your look phase and you let them go. In the classic puzzle that's just a loss, so who cares. In real life it means settling for whatever is left when the lease runs out. If your goal is a good outcome rather than a perfect one, look for less time. If you want to minimize your expected rank instead, the best possible strategy for 100 candidates gets you an average rank of about 3.6, by my dynamic programming calculation, using a sliding standard that relaxes as time runs out.

The rule also works with time instead of counts. If you'll search for 30 days and offers arrive at a roughly steady rate, explore for about 11 days, then take the first option better than anything you saw in those 11 days. If you only need good, not best, explore for much less.

Two more rule changes matter in practice. First, options can say no. If each offer you make has only some chance of being accepted, the math pushes you to start making offers earlier, because each attempt is less likely to end the search. Second, you often don't know n. You don't know how many apartments will list this month or how many people you'll meet this year. The fix is the time version of the rule: spend the first 37 percent of your *time window* calibrating, which works as long as options arrive at a fairly steady pace.
What real people do

In lab experiments that give people the classic setup, they usually leap too soon. In a 2006 *Management Science* study, Bearden, Amnon Rapoport and Ryan Murphy found participants stopped searching earlier than the optimal policy, and a follow-up task suggested they overrated the quality of early applicants and underweighted those still to come. Earlier experiments by Darryl Seale and Rapoport pointed the same way. Stopping early isn't always irrational: real searches cost time, energy and money, and the classic model counts all of that as zero. But it is a known tilt, and it's worth checking against.

There's a more general tool hiding here too. In 2000, F. Thomas Bruss proved what he called the odds theorem. Suppose you're watching a sequence of independent events and want to stop on the last success, for example the last good offer, and you know the odds of success at each step. Add up the odds from the end backward until the sum reaches 1, and start acting from there. Applied to the secretary problem it gives back the 1/e answer, and Bruss showed that 1/e is a typical lower bound across a wide class of such problems. Sometimes the right policy is not "wait for perfect" but "start acting when the remaining chances, added up, are about one."

Optimal stopping is one corner of a bigger family of problems about exploring versus exploiting: keep trying new things to learn, or cash in on what you already know works. Gamers know it from the meta. Early in a season you experiment with loadouts; late in a season you play your best one. Builders know it too. Spend some fixed fraction of a project prototyping several game ideas, set a bar from what you learn, and then commit hard to the first idea that clears it. The worst version is the one with no cutoff at all, where every new idea resets the clock and nothing ships.

blocks.title: Is your decision really a secretary problem?

left.head: Classic assumptions
items: You know how many options are coming
Only rankings, no absolute scores
Rejected options never come back
Only the very best counts
Searching is free

right.head: Real life, usually
items: The count is a rough guess
You can score many things on an absolute scale
Some options can be revisited
Good enough is a real win
Searching costs time and stress

blocks.text: Puzzles

items: **Three applicants.** List all six orderings of ranks 1, 2 and 3 and confirm that "reject the first, take the next better one" wins exactly three times. Then check that "take the first" and "reject two, take the last" each win only twice.

**The apartment hunt.** You'll look at up to 20 listings. Under the classic rule, how many do you tour just to calibrate? (Answer: the exact optimum for 20 is 7, giving a 38.4 percent chance of the best.)

**The deployment window.** You have a 45-day window to pick a used car and only care about getting a good one. Why should your look phase be shorter than 37 percent, and roughly how short? (Hint: square root of the number of cars you expect to see.)
**Why 1/e twice?** Show that x ln(1/x) is maximized at x = 1/e and that its maximum value is also 1/e.

blocks.text: The 37 percent rule is a beautiful piece of math, and the most useful lesson in it isn't the number. It's that the right amount of exploring depends on what you're actually trying to win. Decide that first, set a bar on purpose instead of drifting, and then, when something clears it, commit. Kepler's hesitation cost him a year. Yours probably costs you something too.

takeaways: For best-or-nothing choices with only rankings, explore the first 37 percent, then take the first option that beats them all; you get the best about 37 percent of the time.
The curve is flat near the top, so having a cutoff matters more than its exact value.
The rule leaves you stuck with the last option 37 percent of the time; if good enough counts, explore for much less, about the square root of n.
With absolute scores instead of rankings, a sliding threshold raises the odds of getting the best to about 58 percent.
In experiments people tend to stop too early, partly by overrating early options.
