title: Confucius Thought You Could Practice Your Way to Being Good
dek: Twenty-five centuries ago, a failed government official turned teacher argued that character is not something you have. It is something you build, rep by rep, through small habits most people think are pointless.

blocks.text: Near the start of the *Analects*, the collection of sayings that has shaped East Asian life for two thousand years, Confucius sums up his own life in six short lines. At fifteen he set his heart on learning. At thirty he stood firm. At forty he had no doubts. At fifty he understood what Heaven asked of him. At sixty his ear was attuned. And at seventy, he says, he could follow whatever his heart desired without crossing the line of what was right.

Read that last line again, because it is the whole project. Confucius did not end up with iron self-control, forcing himself to do good things he didn't want to do. He ended up not needing force at all. After fifty-five years of practice, what he wanted and what was right had become the same thing. That is a bold claim about human beings: that your desires are not fixed, and that you can train them the way you train a body.

blocks.title: Confucius's own progress report (Analects 2.4)

Set his heart on learning
Age 30
Stood firm on his own feet
Age 40
Was free of confusion
Age 50

blocks.text: A minor official who changed everything

Tradition dates Confucius's life to 551–479 BCE. He was born in the small state of Zou, near the larger state of Lu, in what is now Shandong Province in eastern China. His father died when he was small, leaving the family poor but with some social standing. As a young man he became known as an expert in the rituals and ceremonies of the old Zhou dynasty, whose power was crumbling into a patchwork of rival states.

His career was not glamorous. One early source says he kept the accounts at a granary and the books on pasture animals. Later biographers credit him with much grander offices, but those stories grew with his reputation. What seems clear is that he spent years moving from state to state, looking for a ruler who would put his ideas into practice, and never really found one. Late in life he turned to teaching. The great historian Sima Qian, writing about three centuries later, counted 77 direct disciples and some 3,000 students in all.

items.label: Traditional dates for Confucius's life
Chapters in the received Analects, compiled after his death
Direct disciples counted by the historian Sima Qian, out of about 3,000 students

blocks.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Confucius"

blocks.text: A caution about sources. Confucius did not write the *Analects*. His students and their students did, and scholars still argue about when. Some argue that writers only started paying close attention to the text in the second and first centuries BCE. Ancient copies dug up in China and North Korea date to the middle of the first century BCE. So the Confucius we meet is partly a portrait painted by people who admired him. The ideas still matter, whoever polished them.
Gentlemen are made, not born

The ideal in the *Analects* is the *junzi*. The word originally meant something like "son of a lord," a person of noble birth. Confucius quietly changed its meaning. In his hands it became a moral rank, not a social one: the exemplary person, usually translated as "gentleman" or "superior person." And it was open to anyone willing to do the work. One of his disciples put it this way: the gentleman works on the roots, and once the roots are set, the Way grows from them.

Underneath this is a claim about human nature that sounds modern. In one passage Confucius says people are close to one another by nature, and grow far apart through practice. Birth does not decide who you become. Repetition does. That is why the *Analects* is not a rulebook. It is closer to a coaching log: short scenes of a teacher correcting particular students in particular moments, nudging each toward the right habit.

items: **Ren (humaneness):** caring about others from their point of view; the broadest of the virtues.
**Yi (rightness):** doing what is right when profit points the other way.
**Li (ritual propriety):** knowing and fulfilling the roles and forms that hold a community together.
**Zhi (wisdom):** reading people and situations accurately, and knowing what you don't know.
**Xin (trustworthiness):** being someone whose word others can build on.

blocks.text: Notice what is missing from that list: wealth, rank, comfort. Confucius was openly poor for much of his life and said it did not bother him. With coarse rice to eat, water to drink and a bent arm for a pillow, he said, there was still joy to be had, while riches gained the wrong way were to him like floating clouds. He was not against prosperity. He just refused to let it be the measure of a person.

The last one carries more weight than it looks. When a disciple asked what a government needs, Confucius listed food, weapons and the people's trust. Pressed to drop one, he dropped weapons. Pressed again, he dropped food. Without trust, he said, a state cannot stand.
Why ritual is a training tool

The part of Confucius modern readers find hardest to take seriously is his obsession with ritual, or *li*. He cared about how to receive guests, how to bow, how long to mourn, even what color trim belonged on a garment. When a student suggested skipping the sheep offered at a monthly ceremony, Confucius answered that the student cared about the sheep, but he cared about the ceremony. The poet Ezra Pound mocked the detail of these passages. It is easy to join him.

But Confucius had a theory about why form matters, and it is psychological. Performing a ritual is practice in feeling the right way at the right moment. Bowing to an elder rehearses respect. Following mourning customs gives grief a shape. Over time, the outer form trains the inner response, the way drilling a procedure eventually makes the correct response feel natural. One text compares the gentleman's way to an embankment dam that holds back a flood of raw desire, buying you room to think before you act.

Crucially, he insisted that empty form is worthless. In one passage he says he cannot stand ritual performed without reverence or mourning done without grief. Asked about the root of ritual, he said that at a funeral, real sorrow matters more than perfect arrangements. The form is a tool for building the feeling. If you go through the motions forever without the feeling ever arriving, you have missed the point.

Military life is full of Confucian ritual: uniforms, salutes, formal watch turnovers, saying back an order word for word. Confucius would say the real question is not whether you do these things but what they are training in you. Done with attention, they build respect and precision. Done on autopilot, they are just motions.

Psychologists have started studying ritual directly. A 2018 review by Nicholas Hobson and colleagues argued that rituals seem to help people regulate emotions, prepare for performance and bond with others. The field is young, though, and it has had stumbles: a widely cited 2016 study claiming that pre-performance rituals reduce anxiety was retracted in 2024. The fair summary is that the idea is plausible and being tested, not settled.
Call things by their right names

One of Confucius's strangest-sounding ideas is also one of his most useful. A disciple asked what he would do first if put in charge of a government. His answer: rectify the names. The disciple thought this was absurdly beside the point. Confucius explained the chain. If names are not correct, language does not match reality. If language does not match reality, nothing gets done. If nothing gets done, ritual and music decay, punishments go wrong, and people no longer know how to move hand or foot.

He meant, in part, that people should live up to their titles: let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son. A ruler who does not act like one is not really a ruler, whatever he is called. But the idea scales down to private life. Calling a dead project "on pause" lets you avoid deciding about it. Calling an hour of scrolling "winding down" keeps you from noticing what it costs. Calling yourself a content creator while making nothing is a name that does not match the thing.

Rectifying names is not about harsh labels. It is about refusing to let comfortable words hide uncomfortable facts, so that you can actually act. Anyone who has worked with technical procedures already knows the principle: if the label on a valve is wrong, everything downstream goes wrong too.
Lead the way wind moves grass

Confucius had a clear view of how influence works, and it was not mainly through orders. In a famous image, he compared the gentleman's character to the wind and ordinary people's to grass: when the wind blows over the grass, the grass bends. Another classic text spells out the corollary. A good leader only asks of others what he already does himself, and only condemns in others what he has already rooted out of himself.

For anyone who leads even a small team, this is blunt advice. Lectures about standards from someone who does not meet them have almost no effect. Quiet consistency has a lot. It also connects back to self-cultivation. You cannot shortcut your way to influence by learning the right speeches. The influence is a side effect of the person you have built.
The arguments against him

Confucius has serious critics, and they deserve a hearing. His ethics is built around roles and hierarchy: ruler and subject, father and son, elder and younger. In one passage he says that true uprightness means a father and son covering for each other, even when one has stolen a sheep. Modern reformers in China, including the May Fourth movement of the early twentieth century, attacked his teachings as a prop for inequality and blind obedience. That critique has real force.

He also drew fire from the other direction. Early Daoist writers argued that all this deliberate cultivation was itself the problem. In their view, the very need to teach humaneness and rightness showed that natural goodness had already been lost, and that forcing virtue through effort only made people more self-conscious and fake. Even within his own tradition, his followers split. Mencius argued that human nature contains sprouts of goodness that need tending. Xunzi argued that nature is crooked and ritual is the tool that straightens it, like steam bending wood.

blocks.title: Two heirs of Confucius on human nature

left.head: Mencius (4th c. BCE)
items: Humans are born with sprouts of goodness, like compassion
Cultivation means nurturing what is already there
Don't force growth; tend it patiently
Moral failure is neglect of good instincts

right.head: Xunzi (3rd c. BCE)
items: Raw human nature leans toward selfish desire
Cultivation means reshaping it from outside
Ritual and teachers work like tools on warped wood
Moral failure is skipping the training

blocks.text: A practice, not a belief

You do not have to accept the hierarchy to use the method. Strip it down and Confucius offers a handful of practical ideas. Character is built through repeated action, not decided in a single moment of resolve. Small forms, done with attention, shape big feelings. Words should match reality, especially the words you use about yourself. And the most reliable way to change others is to become the example first.

blocks.title: A Confucian practice for one month
items: Pick one small daily form, like a proper greeting at watch turnover, and do it with full attention every time
Rename one thing honestly: a stalled project, a habit, a label you use for yourself
Before correcting someone, check whether you meet the standard yourself
After each study session, spend five minutes asking what you actually understood
At the end of the month, notice which forms started to feel natural

blocks.text: He also gave a warning about how to learn, which fits anyone studying hard material. Learning without thinking, he said, is labor lost; thinking without learning is dangerous. Memorizing without reflection gives you facts you can't use. Reflecting without study gives you confident opinions built on nothing. Real growth needs both, over and over, for years.

That last part is the uncomfortable truth in the *Analects*. Confucius said he only reached ease at seventy. Self-cultivation is not a thirty-day challenge. It is a direction you walk in for the rest of your life. The encouraging flip side is that every rep counts, and nobody is locked out by birth. In his scheme, the gentleman is just a person who kept practicing.

takeaways: Confucius held that people start out similar and grow apart through practice, so character is trained, not inherited.
Rituals and small forms are tools for shaping feelings, but only if you do them with real attention.
"Rectify the names": call things what they are so you can act on them, especially when describing yourself.
Influence flows from example: ask of others only what you already do yourself.
Learning without reflection is wasted; reflection without learning is dangerous.

title: Tip Out the Whole Basket
dek: Descartes decided to doubt everything he had ever believed, all at once, to see what survived. What he found, and where his method breaks, still shapes how we test what we know.

blocks.text: On the night of 10 November 1619, a 23-year-old French gentleman soldier was stuck in winter quarters in a small town in southern Germany. He had been to the coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor and was heading back to the army when the weather closed in. He knew nobody worth talking to and had nothing to do, so he spent the whole day shut up alone in a heated room, thinking.

That night he had three vivid dreams. He took them as a sign that he had a mission: to rebuild human knowledge from the ground up, on foundations so solid that nothing could shake them. The soldier was René Descartes, and the method he eventually built from that winter's thinking is one of the most famous moves in the history of philosophy. Take everything you believe. Doubt all of it. Then see what is left standing.
It sounds like a recipe for paranoia. It was actually a construction project, and its logic is surprisingly close to how good engineers, troubleshooters and investigators work.
A soldier who wanted certainty

Descartes was born in 1596 in La Haye, a town in western France that has since been renamed Descartes in his honor. His mother died when he was about a year old. He was educated by Jesuits at the college of La Flèche, one of the best schools in Europe, then took a law degree to please his family and never practiced. Instead he became a gentleman volunteer in the Dutch army, where he met a mathematician named Isaac Beeckman who set him puzzles about falling bodies and geometry.

Looking back on his schooling, Descartes wrote that it had left him buried in so many doubts and errors that his main gain was discovering his own ignorance. Everything he had been taught in philosophy was disputed by someone. Only mathematics seemed solid, because it started from a few clear principles and built step by step. He wanted the rest of knowledge to work like geometry. He would later invent part of the bridge between the two himself: the technique behind what we still call Cartesian coordinates, the x-y graph every student learns.

blocks.title: Descartes's four rules for thinking (Discourse on Method, 1637)
items: Accept nothing as true unless you know it so clearly that there is no room for doubt.
Divide each problem into as many parts as needed to solve it.
Start with the simplest things and work up step by step to the complex.
Make your lists so complete and your reviews so thorough that nothing is left out.

blocks.text: If those rules sound like a troubleshooting procedure, that is not an accident. Isolate the fault, break the system into parts, check the simple things first, and do not trust a single reading you have not verified. Descartes wanted to apply that discipline to everything, including his own mind.
The basket of apples

When critics asked why he did not just question his beliefs one at a time, Descartes answered with an image. Suppose you have a basket of apples and you are worried some are rotten. If you leave them all in and poke around, the rot keeps spreading. The sensible thing is to tip the whole basket out, inspect each apple, and put back only the ones you can see are sound.

Beliefs, he argued, work the same way. You have been collecting them since childhood, many of them without checking. Some are surely false, and a false belief that sits underneath other beliefs quietly contaminates everything built on it. If you test beliefs one by one while trusting the rest, you can be fooled, because the belief you are testing may look solid only because it leans on another one you never questioned. So you empty the basket all at once.

Anyone who has chased an electrical fault knows the trap. You assume the meter is good, or that the breaker you checked yesterday is still closed, or that the drawing matches what is actually installed. Every test you run after that leans on the unchecked assumption, and you can spend hours proving the wrong thing very carefully. The fix is the same as with the apples: list what you are taking for granted, set it all aside, and confirm each piece before you let it back into the reasoning.

He also wanted the doubt to be as extreme as possible. A modern commentator compares it to choosing a bulldozer for clearing ground: a small one cannot tell a big boulder from bedrock, because both feel immovable to it. Only the heaviest possible doubt can show you what is truly unshakable. So in his *Meditations on First Philosophy*, published in 1641, Descartes brought out three escalating waves of doubt.

blocks.title: Three waves of doubt in the Meditations
items: Wave 1
The senses sometimes deceive, especially about small or distant things, so they can't be the foundation.
Wave 2
You might be dreaming right now, and dreams can feel completely real while they last.
Wave 3
An evil demon, powerful and cunning, might be feeding you false experiences of everything, even 2 + 3 = 5.
Bedrock
Even if all that is true, something is doing the doubting. I think, therefore I am.

blocks.text: You might be dreaming

The dream argument is the one that tends to stick. Descartes noticed that while you are dreaming you usually have no idea it is a dream. The dream world feels real, you accept its absurd rules, and only on waking do you realize none of it happened. So what, exactly, entitles you to be sure you are awake now?

Modern sleep research backs up his premise in an interesting way. A lucid dream is one in which you realize, inside the dream, that you are dreaming. A 2016 meta-analysis pooling 50 years of studies estimated how common that is.

blocks.title: How often do people realize they're dreaming?
blocks.note: Pooled estimates; 95% confidence intervals roughly 49-62% and 20-25%.
blocks.source: Saunders et al., Consciousness and Cognition, 2016

blocks.text: Read the other way, those numbers make Descartes's point. Nearly half of people say they have never once noticed they were dreaming, and only about one in four catches it as often as once a month. Most of the time, a dreaming brain swallows its own illusions whole. If your mind can do that every night, its sense that "this is obviously real" cannot be the final word.

The evil demon goes further still. It imagines a deceiver who could fake not only the outside world but your reasoning, making you feel certain of arithmetic that is false. It is the 17th-century ancestor of the brain in a vat and of simulation scenarios in science fiction. Descartes did not believe there was such a demon. He used it as the heaviest bulldozer he could find.
The one thing left standing

Here is the turn. Suppose the demon is real and fooling you about everything. To be fooled, you have to exist. To doubt, you have to be thinking. However far the doubt goes, the very act of doubting proves that there is a doubter. In the *Discourse on Method* Descartes put it in what may be the most famous line in philosophy: I think, therefore I am.

It is worth being precise about how little this proves. It does not show that you have a body, that your memories are accurate, or that anyone else exists. It shows only that, at the moment you are thinking, a thinking thing exists. Descartes then tried to rebuild everything else on that one point, arguing that a perfect God exists and would not deceive us, so that whatever we perceive with complete clarity and distinctness must be true. From there he hoped to recover mathematics, the physical world and science.

Even if that rebuilding fails, the starting point has a lasting lesson. The one thing you cannot be wrong about is that you are having the experience you are having right now. You can be wrong that the noise was a pump, but not that you heard something. You can be wrong that a shipmate meant an insult, but not that you felt stung. Separating the raw experience from the story you attach to it is exactly the move Descartes made, and it is a surprisingly useful one when emotions run hot in a small space.

Sets of objections from critics, printed with his replies
Died in Stockholm, months after joining Queen Christina's court

blocks.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "René Descartes"

blocks.text: That middle number is worth pausing on. Before publication, Descartes and his friend Marin Mersenne sent the manuscript around to theologians and philosophers, including Thomas Hobbes, Pierre Gassendi and Antoine Arnauld, collected their attacks, and printed seven sets of objections in the book alongside his answers. He was building a system on certainty, yet he invited the strongest critics he could find to try to knock it down in print. That is a habit worth stealing.
Doubt in the head, decision in the field

Descartes knew perfectly well that you cannot live while doubting everything. While the rebuilding was underway, he adopted what he called a provisional moral code to get through daily life. Its second rule is the most practical thing he ever wrote.

Imagine travelers lost in a forest, he said. The worst thing they can do is wander back and forth or stand still. Better to pick a direction, even one chosen by chance, and walk in a straight line. They may not reach exactly where they wanted, but they will end up somewhere better than the middle of the forest. In the same way, when action cannot wait and you do not know the truth, act on the most probable option, and once committed, carry it out as firmly as if it were certain.

Descartes split the job in two: ruthless doubt when you are thinking, firm commitment when you have to act. Watchstanders and troubleshooters live this split. Question every assumption during the investigation, then execute the procedure decisively when it is time to act.

This is the part people forget. Radical doubt was never meant to make anyone timid. It was meant to make the foundation solid so that action built on it could be confident. Doubt that never ends in a decision is not Descartes's method; it is just a more sophisticated way of being lost in the forest.
Where the method cracks

Descartes's critics found real problems, and some of them sat right in that book of objections. Arnauld spotted what is now called the Cartesian circle. Descartes says we can trust our clear and distinct perceptions because God exists and is no deceiver. But how do we know God exists? Because we clearly and distinctly perceive the proof. The reasoning seems to use the very tool it is trying to certify. Philosophers still argue over whether Descartes had a good answer.

Gassendi complained that pretending everything is false is not neutral doubt at all, just a new prejudice in place of the old ones. Much later, the American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce made a sharper point: you cannot actually doubt everything at will. You start with the beliefs you have, and real doubt arises when you hit a specific reason to question one of them. The philosopher Otto Neurath later gave this view a famous image: inquiry is less like tipping out the whole basket and more like sailors rebuilding their ship at sea, plank by plank, without ever being able to put into dry dock.

The deepest challenge came from Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia, who corresponded with Descartes in the 1640s. He had concluded that the mind is a thinking thing with no size or location, and the body is an extended physical thing. Then how, she asked, can a mind with no physical extension move an arm? Descartes admitted to her that he did not have a good answer. The puzzle she raised, how mind and matter connect, is still open today under the name of the mind-body problem.

So the foundation he hoped would be unshakable turned out to have cracks, and most philosophers no longer think knowledge rests on a single point of certainty. But the habits he modeled have outlived the system: break problems into parts, distrust what you have never checked, recognize how convincingly your own mind can fool you, invite the toughest critics in, and when it is time to move, pick a direction and walk.

takeaways: Descartes doubted everything at once, like tipping out a basket to find the rotten apples, so hidden bad assumptions could not contaminate the rest.
The dream argument still bites: most people rarely or never realize they are dreaming while it happens.
"I think, therefore I am" proves only that a thinker exists while thinking, which is why rebuilding from it was so hard.
Doubt while thinking, commit while acting: walk straight out of the forest instead of circling.
Invite your strongest critics before you ship; Descartes printed seven sets of objections in his own book.

title: The Pleasure Philosopher Lived on Bread and Water
dek: Epicurus built an entire school around pleasure, then asked a friend for a little pot of cheese so he could feast. His real target was not fun. It was the kind of wanting that never ends.

blocks.text: Somewhere around 300 BCE, a man in Athens wrote a letter asking a friend to send him a small pot of cheese, so that, as he put it, he could have a feast whenever he liked. That line survives because a later biographer, Diogenes Laertius, thought it said something important about the writer. The writer was Epicurus, the philosopher who taught that pleasure is the goal of life. His idea of a luxury was cheese. Most days, by his own account, he was happy with plain bread and water.

Today the word *epicurean* means a person who loves fine food and wine. That would have baffled him. The real Epicurus was not running a party. He was running something closer to a training program for the mind, built on one hard question: if pleasure is what we all want, why are so many people who chase it miserable?
A school in a garden

Epicurus was born in 341 BCE and grew up on the island of Samos, where Athenian settlers had been given land. He came to Athens at eighteen, studied under a follower of the atomist Democritus, and taught for years in cities around the Aegean. Around 306 BCE he came back to Athens for good and bought a property with a garden for eighty minae. The school that met there became known simply as the Garden.

It was an odd place by the standards of the time. Ancient sources say his brothers joined, and so did a slave named Mys. Women took part too. The members lived simply, drinking mostly water with a little thin wine. Epicurus refused to make them pool their property, which some philosophers recommended, because he thought a group that has to force sharing does not really trust itself. He died in 270 BCE, in his early seventies, after about two weeks of agony from kidney stones. His will freed several of his slaves, Mys among them, and set aside support for the children of a friend who had died before him.

blocks.title: How a garden school reached us

blocks.text: Pleasure means no pain

The center of the system is a definition. When Epicurus says pleasure is the goal, he does not mean nonstop excitement. In his *Letter to Menoeceus* he says flatly that he is not talking about drinking bouts, sex or fancy fish. Pleasure, for him, is the absence of pain in the body and of turmoil in the mind. He had words for both: *aponia*, freedom from bodily pain, and *ataraxia*, a calm, untroubled mind.

Later writers split his pleasures into two kinds. *Kinetic* pleasures are the ones in motion: the first gulp of water when you're thirsty, the rush of a clutch round, the scroll that lands on something funny. *Katastematic*, or static, pleasures are the steady state of being fine: not hungry, not afraid, not in pain, not anxious about tomorrow. Scholars still argue over the exact line between them, but the direction of his argument is clear. The steady state is the real prize. The rushes are fine as seasoning.

His rivals, the Cyrenaics, took the opposite view. They said to stack up as many intense pleasures as you can. Epicurus thought that was a losing strategy. Intense pleasures usually depend on a painful lack that comes first, and feeding desires tends to grow them. If your happiness requires a constant supply of new highs, you have signed up for a constant supply of craving. Anyone who has finished a long session of short videos and felt worse than when they started has run his experiment.

blocks.title: Two ways to chase pleasure

left.head: The Cyrenaic plan
items: Maximize intense, moment-to-moment highs
Grow your appetites so there is more to enjoy
Happiness is a running total of good moments
Needs a steady supply of new stimulation

right.head: The Epicurean plan
items: Aim for a body without pain and a mind without dread
Trim desires that can never be filled
Happiness is a stable state you can return to
Simple things become enough, so luck matters less

blocks.text: Three kinds of wanting

The most practical tool Epicurus left is a way of sorting desires. Some desires are **natural and necessary**: food, water, shelter, sleep, safety, friends. They have built-in limits. When you have eaten, you are done being hungry. Some are **natural but not necessary**: a great meal instead of a decent one, a better bed, a nicer view. Fine to enjoy, no tragedy to lose. And some are **empty**, born from what he called empty opinion rather than nature.

His examples of empty desires are telling: limitless wealth, power, fame, the wish for statues of yourself, the wish never to die. What they share is that they have no finish line. There is no amount of fame at which you feel you have enough fame, because the desire was never really about the fame. It was about feeling safe and valued, and fame cannot deliver that. So the desire keeps going, and so does the anxiety that comes with it.

Translate that into the present and the statues are easy to spot. Follower counts. Ranked badges. View counts on a video. A nicer truck than the one you paid off. None of these is evil, and Epicurus would not say so. His question is about the shape of the desire. Does it have a natural stopping point? If not, chasing it will feel like running on a treadmill that speeds up whenever you catch up.

blocks.title: The Epicurean desire check
items: Name the desire plainly: what exactly do I want right now?
Ask what it is really for: comfort, safety, connection, status?
Ask whether it has a limit: would there be a point where I'd feel done?
Ask what happens if I get it, and what happens if I don't
Keep the natural ones, enjoy the optional ones lightly, starve the empty ones

blocks.text: The fourth step comes from one of the sayings later collected from his school: put every desire to the question of what will happen to you if you get it, and what will happen if you don't. It sounds almost too simple. In practice it is a fast way to notice that a lot of wants are just itches, and that the cost of not scratching is close to zero.
Does modern research back him up?

Partly. Psychologists have studied people who put a high priority on money, possessions and image, which is close to what Epicurus meant by chasing empty goods. In 2014 Helga Dittmar and colleagues pulled together 259 independent samples into a single meta-analysis. People who held more materialistic values reported lower well-being on average. The link was strongest for things like risky health and spending behavior and for negative views of oneself.

items.label: Independent samples combined in the materialism meta-analysis
Average link between materialist values and well-being (higher materialism, lower well-being)
Stronger links for risky health and spending behavior and negative self-views

blocks.source: Dittmar, Bond, Hurst & Kasser, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2014

blocks.text: Two caveats keep this honest. First, these are correlations, mostly from surveys. They do not prove that wanting stuff makes you unhappy; unhappy people may also reach for stuff. The authors themselves called for more experimental and long-term studies. Second, money itself is not the enemy. In 2023 Matthew Killingsworth, Daniel Kahneman and Barbara Mellers settled a long argument by showing that for most people, day-to-day happiness keeps rising with income, even at high levels. Only among the least happy people did it flatten out.

Epicurus would not be surprised. He was not against money; he was against the belief that more of it would finally make you feel secure. Money that pays for food, a safe place to live and time with friends serves natural and necessary desires. Money chased as a scoreboard serves an empty one. The difference is not in the dollars. It is in what you are asking them to do.
Death is nothing to us

The fear Epicurus most wanted to cure was the fear of death. His argument is short. Where death is, you are not; where you are, death is not. Being dead is not a terrible experience, because it is not an experience at all. Bad things have to happen to someone, and after death there is no one for them to happen to. So fearing being dead is fearing nothing. His Roman follower Lucretius added a mirror image: you were not distressed by the endless time before you were born, so why dread the endless time after?

Not everyone is convinced. The modern philosopher Thomas Nagel argued that death can still be bad for you, not because you feel it but because it takes away the good things you would otherwise have had. A death at twenty-five robs someone of decades. That is a serious objection, and it is worth noticing what it leaves standing. Epicurus may be wrong that death costs you nothing. He is right that the dread of it, carried through every ordinary day, is a separate burden that you pay while alive.

The Romans took his view to heart in a way you can still see. A common inscription on Roman tombstones, often shortened to initials, translates roughly as: I was not, I was, I am not, I don't care. It is a strange thing to carve over a grave, and a cheerful one.
Death is nothing to us.
blocks.by: Epicurus, Principal Doctrines 2 (trans. R. D. Hicks)

blocks.text: Friends are the real wealth

For a philosopher accused of selfishness, Epicurus was intensely focused on other people. One of his principal doctrines says that of everything wisdom provides for a happy life, by far the greatest is friendship. The Roman writer Seneca passed along another Epicurean idea: before you look at what you will eat, look at who you will eat with, because dining alone is living like a lion or a wolf.

His reasoning starts out practical. Friends make you safe. They help when things go wrong, and knowing they will is a big part of a calm mind. But he did not stop there. One saying holds that friendship begins in usefulness but is worth choosing for its own sake. Scholars have argued for two thousand years about how a pleasure-based philosophy gets there. The lived answer is easier than the theory: people who have real friends are less afraid.

He tested this on himself at the very end. On his last day he wrote to a friend that his pain was so severe nothing could make it worse. Then he said he set against it the gladness of remembering their conversations, and asked the friend to look after a dead colleague's children. It is the whole philosophy in one letter. He did not deny the pain. He just refused to let it be the only thing in the room.

He also gave advice that sounds strange now: *lathe biosas*, live unnoticed. Stay out of the scramble for public status. That might seem at odds with building an audience online. But the core warning still holds for anyone making things in public. If your sense of being okay depends on strangers noticing you, you have handed your calm to people who are not paying attention.

Underway, the Epicurean list of essentials is short and mostly covered: food, a rack, safety, a crew. That makes a deployment an unusually clean test of his idea. Which of the things you miss are natural and necessary, and which were just habits wearing the costume of needs?
Living it, not just reading it

Epicurus thought philosophy that does not heal the mind is as useless as medicine that does not cure the body. He packaged his teachings into short, memorable sayings so his students could carry them around and repeat them under stress. Later followers boiled the core down to a four-part cure: there is nothing to fear in the gods, nothing to dread in death, what is good is easy to get, and what is terrible is easy to endure.

You do not have to accept all four to use the method. Its practical core is a habit of checking your wants before they run you. When a craving shows up, whether for a purchase, a status marker or another hour on the feed, ask what it is actually for and whether it has an end. Then make the simple pleasures count. A hot meal after a long watch, a real conversation, a decent night of sleep: Epicurus would say these are not consolation prizes. They are the main event, and most people only notice once they've lost them.

That is the quiet surprise in his philosophy. The man who put pleasure at the center of life ended up recommending less, not more. Not because pleasure is bad, but because a mind that needs very little is a mind that is very hard to knock over.

takeaways: For Epicurus, pleasure meant no pain in the body and no turmoil in the mind, not a string of highs.
Sort desires into natural and necessary, natural but optional, and empty. Empty desires have no finish line.
Ask of any desire: what happens if I get it, and what happens if I don't?
Materialist values are linked to lower well-being, but money that meets real needs still helps. The trap is wanting without limit.
He ranked friendship as the greatest thing wisdom provides for a happy life.

title: The Psychiatrist Who Took Notes in Hell
dek: Viktor Frankl lost his wife, his parents, his brother and his life's work to the Nazi camps. What he noticed about who held on, and why, became one of the most influential books of the century.

blocks.text: In early 1945, in a camp at Türkheim in Bavaria, a prisoner with typhus was fighting to stay awake. The fever brought delirium, and he was determined to get through the nights without slipping under. So he kept his mind busy. On tiny scraps of paper he had scrounged, in shorthand, he was rebuilding a book.

The original manuscript had been sewn into the lining of his coat when he arrived at Auschwitz. He had begged to keep it. The coat was taken, and with it years of work. Now, starving and sick, Viktor Frankl was writing it again from memory, one keyword at a time. He later said that the urge to finish that book was one of the things that kept him alive.

That detail is the whole of Frankl's philosophy in miniature. He did not claim that having a purpose protects you from harm. It plainly does not. His claim was narrower and harder: when almost everything has been stripped away, a person can still be pulled forward by something that needs them, and that pull changes how they endure what they cannot escape.
A doctor who studied despair before he lived it

Frankl was born in Vienna on March 26, 1905, the city of Freud and Adler, and he trained in their shadow before breaking with both. Freud said people are driven by pleasure; Adler said by power. Frankl came to believe the deepest drive was something else: the need for meaning. He called his approach **logotherapy**, from the Greek *logos*, which here means meaning.

He did not arrive at this in an armchair. In 1928 and 1929 he set up free counseling centers for teenagers in Vienna, and a special program he ran around end-of-year school reports in 1930 was credited with a sharp drop in student suicides. From 1933 to 1937 he ran the pavilion for suicidal women at Vienna's Steinhof psychiatric hospital, seeing roughly 3,000 patients a year. Despair was his specialty before it became his circumstance.

In 1938 Germany annexed Austria. As a Jew, Frankl was soon only allowed to treat Jewish patients, and he became head of neurology at Vienna's Rothschild Hospital. In 1940 he obtained a visa to emigrate to the United States. He let it lapse rather than leave his elderly parents behind. He married Tilly Grosser, a nurse at the hospital. In September 1942 the couple and his parents were deported to the Theresienstadt ghetto.

blocks.title: Frankl's war
items: Born in Vienna, March 26
Runs Steinhof's pavilion for suicidal women, about 3,000 patients a year
Gets a US visa, lets it lapse to stay with his parents
Sept 1942
Deported to Theresienstadt with wife Tilly and his parents
Sent to Auschwitz, then to Kaufering and Türkheim, subcamps of Dachau
Liberated at Türkheim by US troops
Dictates the book that becomes Man's Search for Meaning in nine days

blocks.text: His father died in Theresienstadt after about six months, of exhaustion. In 1944 Frankl, Tilly and his mother were shipped to Auschwitz. His mother was murdered in the gas chamber on arrival. His brother was also killed at Auschwitz. Tilly was later moved to Bergen-Belsen. Frankl spent only days at Auschwitz before being sent to the Kaufering camps, slave-labor sites attached to Dachau, and finally to Türkheim, where he worked as a doctor through a typhus epidemic. US soldiers liberated the camp on April 27, 1945. Within days he learned Tilly was dead.
What he saw in the camps

Frankl went into the camps as a psychiatrist, and some part of him never stopped observing. He described prisoners passing through stages. First came shock, including a strange, grim curiosity about what would happen next. Then came apathy, an emotional numbness that he saw as a kind of armor: when you see death every day, you stop feeling it, because feeling it would break you.

Inside that numbness he noticed differences. Some men gave up. A prisoner would refuse to get up one morning, lie in his own filth, and smoke the cigarettes he had been hoarding to trade for food. The others knew what that meant. Within a short time he would be dead. Frankl came to see the moment a man stopped looking forward as the moment his body started to fail.

He reported a grim piece of evidence from the camp's chief doctor. In the week between Christmas 1944 and New Year's 1945, deaths rose sharply, beyond anything explained by work, food or weather. The doctor's explanation, which Frankl shared, was that many prisoners had pinned their hopes on being home by Christmas. When the date came and went, the hope collapsed, and so did their resistance.

Frankl also described a kind of freedom that survived inside the fences. He wrote about men who walked through the huts comforting others and giving away their last piece of bread. They were few, he admitted. But they proved to him that the guards could control nearly everything except the stance a person took toward what was happening to him. That inner choice, he argued, was the one freedom that could not be confiscated.
Whoever has a why to live for can bear almost any how.
blocks.by: Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols, 1889, quoted by Frankl (author's translation)

blocks.text: Frankl leaned on that line from Nietzsche constantly. His job as a doctor in the camp, he said, was to help men find their *why*. One story stuck. Two prisoners told him separately that they had nothing left to expect from life. Frankl did not argue with them about hope. He turned the question around. One man had a child waiting for him abroad. The other was a scientist with a series of books only he could finish. Neither man's suffering got lighter. But each now had a reason the suffering was worth getting through.
Flipping the question

That reversal is the core of the book, and it is the idea most worth carrying around. Most of us ask what life owes us: happiness, fairness, a good draw. Frankl said that question is upside down. Life is the one asking. Each situation poses a question, and you answer it not with a theory but with what you do. Meaning, in this view, is not something you invent to feel better. It is something you discover in the particular demands of your actual situation.

He named three main places meaning shows up. You can find it by **creating or doing** something: a piece of work, a task, a contribution. You can find it by **experiencing** something or someone: beauty, truth, and above all love. And when neither of those is open to you, you can find it in **the attitude you take toward suffering you cannot avoid**. That third road is his most distinctive claim, and the most easily misread.

blocks.title: Frankl's three roads to meaning
items: Work: make something, do a task well, contribute something that would not exist without you
Love: experience something or someone fully; for Frankl, love was the highest form
Attitude: when suffering cannot be avoided, choose how you carry it
Rule for road three: if suffering can be fixed or escaped, fix or escape it; bearing avoidable pain is not noble, it is a mistake

blocks.text: Frankl was blunt that suffering is not required for meaning. If the cause of your pain can be removed, remove it. Enduring pain you could have fixed is not heroism. The third road applies only to what genuinely cannot be changed: a death, an illness, a sentence you cannot appeal. In later years he called this stance **tragic optimism**: staying oriented toward meaning in the face of pain, guilt and death, the three facts no life escapes.

One morning on a forced march in the dark, stumbling over ice and stones while guards shouted, Frankl found himself talking in his mind to Tilly. He did not know whether she was alive. He realized it did not matter to the conversation. Love, he concluded, reaches past the physical presence of the person you love. In the most degraded setting he could imagine, he had found something that made him feel, for a moment, rich.
Does purpose actually help?

Frankl's evidence was his own observation, which is powerful and also limited. Modern researchers have tried to test the broader idea that a sense of purpose is good for you. In 2016, cardiologists at Mount Sinai pooled ten prospective studies covering 136,265 people. After adjusting for other factors, people with a higher sense of purpose had about 17 percent lower risk of dying during the studies, and a similarly lower risk of heart attacks and strokes.

items.label: People in 10 prospective studies pooled in the meta-analysis
Relative risk of death for people with higher purpose in life (1.0 = no difference)

blocks.source: Cohen, Bavishi & Rozanski, Psychosomatic Medicine, 2016

blocks.text: Treat that number with care. These are observational studies, so they show a link, not proof that purpose causes longer life. Purpose may travel with things like good health, money, friends and exercise, and adjusting for those is never perfect. Still, the association held across countries, ages and different questionnaires. It is at least consistent with what Frankl claimed.

There is a harder objection, and Frankl stated it himself. Survival in the camps was overwhelmingly a matter of luck and of the decisions of guards. Millions of people with every reason to live were murdered anyway, including his own family. He wrote that the best among the prisoners often did not come back. Some Holocaust scholars and survivors have criticized readers who take his book as a story of willpower conquering death. Read carefully, it makes no such promise. Meaning did not decide who lived. It shaped how people lived while they could.
Meaning in a steel tube

Nothing on a submarine resembles a death camp, and the comparison should never be stretched. But Frankl identified a trap that shows up in any long, enclosed stretch of life you cannot leave on your own schedule. He called it **provisional existence**. Prisoners who did not know when their sentence would end began to live as if their real life were on pause, somewhere in the future. The present became a waiting room. Nothing in it counted.

A deployment invites the same move. No sunlight, three-section duty, the same faces, the same food, the days blurring together. It is easy to start treating the patrol as dead time: just get through it, real life resumes when we pull in. The Christmas story is a warning about where that leads. If everything hangs on a date, then the date becomes a cliff.

Frankl's roads are all open underway, in small versions. **Work:** a qualification that actually makes you better at the plant, teaching a newer guy something you struggled with, building a game design doc on the off-watch. **Love:** a letter written properly instead of quickly, attention to the people in the berthing next to you, who are also counting days. **Attitude:** the long watch, the field day, the drill at 0300 that you cannot change, met with a stance you chose instead of one that happened to you.

The question to ask on a bad day is not what this patrol owes you. It is what this patrol is asking of you. Sometimes the honest answer is small: stand a sharp watch, be decent to someone who is struggling, get one thing done. Frankl rebuilt a book on scraps of paper while delirious. The point was never the size of the task. The point was that something out ahead of him needed him to keep going.

If the question of whether life is worth it ever stops feeling abstract, treat that as a signal, not a philosophy problem. Talk to the corpsman, your chain of command or a shipmate you trust, and when you have a phone, the Military Crisis Line is there around the clock: dial 988, then press 1.

Frankl died in Vienna on September 2, 1997, at 92. He remarried, had a daughter, wrote dozens more books and taught at the University of Vienna for decades. In 1991 the Library of Congress listed *Man's Search for Meaning* among the ten most influential books in America. He once suggested that the Statue of Liberty on the East Coast should be matched by a Statue of Responsibility on the West. Freedom, he thought, was only half the story. The other half was what you answer when life asks.

takeaways: Stop asking what life owes you; ask what this situation is asking of you.
Meaning comes from three places: work you do, people and things you love, and the stance you take toward suffering you cannot change.
Fix avoidable suffering. Only unavoidable suffering is a place to find meaning, never a goal in itself.
Beware provisional existence: treating a deployment as dead time until real life resumes makes the end date a cliff.
Purpose is linked to better health and lower mortality in large studies, but it is a correlation and it guarantees nothing.

title: Did You Choose to Read This?
dek: Brain scans that seem to catch decisions before you make them, a 2,000-year-old argument, and a surprising result about what happens when people stop believing in free will.

blocks.text: In a lab in San Francisco in the early 1980s, a volunteer sat in front of a special clock. Instead of hands, a single dot swept around the face, completing a lap in about two and a half seconds. The instructions were simple: whenever you feel like it, flex your wrist. No plan, no countdown. Just do it when the urge strikes, and remember where the dot was at the moment you first felt that urge.

Meanwhile, electrodes on the volunteer's scalp were recording a slow electrical ramp called the **readiness potential**, a buildup of brain activity known to come before voluntary movement. The neuroscientist Benjamin Libet wanted to know which came first: the brain's ramp or the person's conscious decision.

The brain won. In the trials where subjects said the urge came spontaneously, the ramp began on average about 350 milliseconds before the moment they reported deciding. The conscious urge itself came only about 200 milliseconds before the wrist moved. Read one way, the brain had already started the action, and the feeling of choosing showed up late to take credit. The study, published in the journal *Brain* in 1983, has been argued about ever since.

items.label: Average lead of the brain's readiness ramp over the reported urge to move
Gap between the reported urge and the actual movement
Subjects in Libet's original study

blocks.source: Libet, Gleason, Wright & Pearl, Brain, 1983

blocks.text: The problem is older than neuroscience

Libet did not invent the worry. He just gave it a stopwatch. The old version goes like this. Everything that happens is caused by what came before it. Your decision to flex your wrist was caused by brain states, which were caused by earlier brain states, your genes, your upbringing, last night's sleep, and so on back to before you were born. If that chain is complete, then given the past, you could not have done anything other than what you did. So in what sense was it up to you?

In 1814 the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace imagined an intellect that knew the position and force of every particle in the universe. For such a mind, he wrote, the future would be as visible as the past. Physics has since complicated that picture, because quantum events appear to be genuinely random. But randomness is no rescue. If your choices are caused by coin flips inside your neurons, they are not more yours. They are just less predictable.

That leaves three broad camps. **Hard determinists**, or free will skeptics, accept the chain and conclude that free will, at least the kind that would make people truly deserve blame and praise, does not exist. **Libertarians** (no relation to the political party) argue that agents can genuinely start new causal chains, so the past does not fix what you do. **Compatibilists** argue that the whole debate rests on a mistaken idea of freedom, and that free will is perfectly compatible with a caused universe.

blocks.title: What philosophers believe about free will
blocks.note: Share of 1,758 philosophers accepting or leaning toward each view; some accepted more than one, and 13.5% chose other answers.
blocks.source: PhilPapers Survey 2020 (Bourget & Chalmers)

blocks.text: Among professional philosophers, compatibilism wins by a wide margin. That does not make it true. Philosophy is not settled by vote, and the experts may share blind spots. But it should make you suspicious of any headline that says science has proven free will is an illusion. The people who think about this for a living mostly think the question is being framed wrong.

The libertarian minority deserves a fair hearing, because it is defending the view most people start with. Philosophers like Robert Kane argue that indeterminism in the brain does not have to mean randomness running the show. Picture a moment of real inner conflict, duty pulling one way and temptation the other. If either outcome is genuinely open, and whichever wins does so because you were trying to make it win, then the choice was yours in the deepest sense. Kane calls these *self-forming actions*: the hard choices through which you make yourself into the person whose later choices flow more easily. Critics reply that if the outcome was not settled by anything about you, it is hard to see why you deserve credit for it.
What the brain experiments actually show

The most famous follow-up came in 2008. John-Dylan Haynes and colleagues in Germany put people in an fMRI scanner and let them press a button with their left or right hand whenever they chose. By reading patterns in prefrontal and parietal cortex, the team could predict which hand a person would use up to about 10 seconds before the person reported deciding. That sounds devastating. The fine print is less so. The predictions were clearly better than chance but far from perfect, and Haynes himself said the study did not show where the final decision is made or whether it could still be reversed.

Then in 2012 Aaron Schurger and colleagues in France proposed a different explanation for Libet's ramp. Brain activity constantly drifts up and down at random. When you are told to move at some unspecified moment, the movement tends to happen when that background noise happens to drift past a threshold. If you then line up all the trials by the moment of movement and average them, the random drifts add up to what looks like a smooth ramp. On this account the readiness potential is not a hidden decision. It is noise that has been made to look like one by the way it was averaged.

blocks.title: The fight over the readiness potential
items: German researchers Kornhuber and Deecke first record the readiness potential
Libet finds the ramp starts before the reported urge to move
Soon, Haynes et al. predict a left or right choice seconds early, imperfectly
Schurger et al. model the ramp as random drift crossing a threshold
Sapolsky's book Determined argues for no free will from biology

blocks.text: There is a deeper problem with all these studies. They test the most meaningless choice imaginable: flick now or a moment later, left or right, with nothing at stake. That is precisely the kind of decision where you would expect the brain to hand off to random fluctuation. It tells us little about choices that involve reasons, like whether to reenlist, how to answer a hard question from the chief, or whether to start the project tonight. Even Libet believed people retained a window to veto an action after the urge appeared.
Freedom without magic

Compatibilists start by asking what we actually want when we want free will. Not, they argue, the power to act uncaused, which would make actions random. We want our actions to come from us: from our own reasons, values and deliberation, rather than from a gun to the head, a brain tumor or a manipulation we would reject if we saw it. The philosopher Daniel Dennett called these the varieties of free will worth wanting, and argued that a determined world is full of them.

blocks.title: Two pictures of free will

left.head: Freedom as magic
items: You are an uncaused cause
Could have done otherwise with the past exactly the same
Threatened by any discovery of causes
Neuroscience seems to refute it

right.head: Freedom as capacity
items: You act from your own reasons and values
Your choices respond when the reasons change
Threatened by coercion, compulsion, manipulation
Neuroscience studies how it works

blocks.text: Two years earlier Frankfurt had already knocked out one pillar of the old debate with a thought experiment. Imagine a neuroscientist, Black, who wants Jones to vote for a certain candidate. Black has secretly wired Jones's brain so that if Jones shows any sign of choosing the other candidate, the device will flip him. As it happens, Jones decides on his own to vote the way Black wanted, and the device never fires. Jones could not have done otherwise. Yet he seems fully responsible, because the choice came entirely from him. Frankfurt's conclusion: what matters for responsibility is not whether alternatives existed, but where the action actually came from.

Harry Frankfurt sharpened this in 1971 with an idea that feels very modern. Humans do not just have desires; we have desires about our desires. An addict may want a drug and also want not to want it. Frankfurt argued that you act freely when the desire that moves you is one you endorse on reflection. The unwilling addict is unfree not because his choice was caused, but because it was caused by a craving he disowns.

Run that on yourself. At 0200 after watch, you want to keep scrolling. You also want to be the kind of person who sleeps and gets up for the gym. When the scroll wins, it does not feel like freedom. It feels like being dragged. On Frankfurt's view, that feeling is accurate. Freedom is not the absence of causes. It is a match between what moves you and what you would choose to be moved by.

Free will skeptics are not convinced. The philosopher Galen Strawson argues that to be truly responsible for what you do, you would have to be responsible for who you are, and nobody built themselves from scratch. The neuroscientist Robert Sapolsky makes a similar case from biology: every trait you used to make a choice came from genes, hormones and history you did not pick. Their conclusion is not that nothing matters, but that deep blame and deep desert make no sense.
What happens if people stop believing

Here the debate seemed to get practical. In 2008 psychologists Kathleen Vohs and Jonathan Schooler had people read a passage arguing that behavior is fully determined, then gave them a chance to cheat on a math test. Those who read the anti-free-will passage cheated more. The study was widely cited as a warning: tell people free will is fake, and they behave worse.

It did not hold up well. In 2020 a team led by Thomas Nadelhoffer ran five studies, four preregistered, with samples up to nearly 1,000 people, closely copying the original methods. Their attempts were largely unsuccessful. Then a 2023 meta-analysis pulled together 145 experiments, 95 of them never published, and found that anti-free-will messages do nudge people's beliefs, but found no evidence that the shift changes how they behave.

items.label: Experiments in the meta-analysis, 95 of them unpublished
Evidence found that the belief shift changes behavior

blocks.source: Genschow et al., Personality and Social Psychology Review, 2023

blocks.text: That is reassuring in one direction and humbling in another. Reading an argument about determinism does not turn people into cheaters. But it also suggests that our everyday behavior does not run on our metaphysics. People act on habits, situations, relationships and goals, not on their position in a philosophy debate.
How to live with an unsolved question

Whichever camp is right, one popular conclusion is plainly wrong: that if everything is caused, effort is pointless. That is **fatalism**, and determinism does not imply it. Fatalism says the outcome will happen no matter what you do. Determinism says the outcome happens because of what you do. Your deliberation, your plans, the alarm you set and the phone you leave in your locker are all links in the chain. Remove them and the chain goes somewhere else.

Practical compatibilism: you cannot will yourself into a different person in the moment, but you can change the inputs that the next moment's choice will run on. Phone in the locker before watch, gym bag packed the night before, a friend who expects you. Those are not tricks around free will. They are what free will looks like from the inside.

The nuclear Navy already runs on something like this view. When something goes wrong in the plant, a critique asks two questions at once. What caused this: procedures, training, fatigue, design, culture? And who owns it? Nobody thinks finding the causes cancels the ownership. Fixing the causes is how ownership gets exercised. That is compatibilism in coveralls.

The skeptics still have a point worth keeping. If you could trace every bad choice a shipmate made back through his sleep, his history and his brain chemistry, you might be slower to sneer at him. Sapolsky argues that should make us less vengeful and more interested in fixing conditions. You can accept that and still hold yourself to a standard. The best reason to hold yourself accountable is not that you are an uncaused cause. It is that holding yourself accountable is one of the causes that makes you better.

takeaways: Libet-style experiments test trivial, reasonless flicks; they say little about decisions that involve reasons.
Most philosophers (about 59%) are compatibilists: free will means acting from your own reasons, not escaping causation.
Determinism is not fatalism. Your choices, plans and environment are part of what causes the outcome.
Frankfurt's test: are you moved by a desire you endorse, or one you disown? Scrolling at 0200 usually fails it.
The famous finding that disbelief in free will makes people cheat largely failed to replicate.

title: Why You Can't Prove the Sun Will Rise Tomorrow
dek: In the 1730s a young Scotsman noticed that nearly everything you believe rests on an assumption no one can justify. Nearly 300 years later, nobody has fully answered him, and that should change how much you trust a good track record.

blocks.text: Consider a chicken. Every morning of its life, a farmer walks into the yard and scatters feed. The chicken learns. Footsteps mean breakfast. After hundreds of mornings without a single exception, its expectation is about as well supported as any expectation can be. Then one morning the farmer walks in, reaches down, and wrings its neck.

Bertrand Russell used that chicken in 1912 to illustrate a problem that had been bothering philosophers for almost two centuries. The chicken was not stupid. It did exactly what you do every day: it assumed that the future would look like the past. The question is whether you have any better reason for that assumption than the chicken did.

The man who first asked that question sharply was David Hume, and his answer was unsettling. You do not. Not for the sun rising, not for gravity, not for the floor holding your weight. You believe these things, rightly and unavoidably. But you cannot prove them, and every attempt to prove them quietly assumes what it is trying to prove.
The book that fell dead-born

Hume was born in Edinburgh in 1711. In his early twenties, after a breakdown from overwork, he moved to La Flèche in France and, at 23, began writing *A Treatise of Human Nature*. It came out anonymously in 1739 and 1740. Hume later said it fell dead-born from the press. That was an exaggeration, but it sold poorly, and what attention it got painted him as a dangerous skeptic. The reputation cost him at least one university chair.

He tried again. In 1748 he published a shorter, sharper version of his ideas on knowledge, later titled *An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding*. He became famous instead as a historian and essayist, much loved in Paris salons, and a friend of Adam Smith. The argument about induction, buried in a book that flopped and then a book written to rescue it, went on to become one of the most discussed ideas in the history of philosophy.
Hume's fork

Hume starts by splitting everything you can know into two kinds. **Relations of ideas** are truths you can work out by thinking alone: two plus two is four, a triangle has three sides. Denying them leads to contradiction. **Matters of fact** are claims about how the world actually is: water is wet, fire burns, the sun rises. Denying them is false, maybe, but not contradictory. You can picture fire freezing things. You can picture the sun failing to come up.

Hume's own example is memorable. The proposition that the sun will not rise tomorrow is, he wrote, no less intelligible than the proposition that it will. Nothing in logic forbids it. So logic alone cannot guarantee it.

He also points out that all our knowledge of cause and effect comes from experience, not reasoning. Imagine the first human, his mind as sharp as possible but with no experience at all. Hume says Adam could not have figured out from looking at water that it would drown him, or from looking at fire that it would burn him. A billiard ball rolls toward another. Before you have ever seen it happen, the first ball stopping dead, bouncing back or flying straight up are all equally conceivable. Only experience tells you what actually happens.
So far, so reasonable. Here is the trap.

blocks.title: Hume's argument in five moves
items: Every belief about the unobserved, including tomorrow, rests on cause and effect.
Our knowledge of cause and effect comes only from past experience.
Using past experience to predict the future assumes that nature is uniform: the future will resemble the past.
That assumption is not a logical truth, since its denial is perfectly conceivable.
Nor can experience prove it, since arguing that the future will resemble the past because it always has assumes the very thing in question.

blocks.text: That last step is the knife. The obvious defense of induction is that it has always worked. But "it has always worked, so it will keep working" is itself an inductive argument. You are using induction to prove induction. The chicken could have made the same argument on its last morning.
Custom, the great guide

What did Hume conclude? Not that we should stop expecting the sun to rise. He thought that would be impossible and insane. His point was that our expectations are not produced by reasoning at all. They come from **custom**, or habit. See one thing follow another enough times, and the mind is simply carried from the first to the expectation of the second. Nature built us that way, and nature is stronger than any argument.

Hume has a wonderful passage about this at the end of the first book of the *Treatise*. After pages of skeptical gloom, he says, he goes to dinner, plays a game of backgammon and talks with friends. When he comes back hours later, the doubts look so cold and strained and ridiculous that he cannot bring himself to take them up again. Life overrides the skeptic. That does not mean the skeptic was wrong.

Hume did not think this made all beliefs equal. A wise man, he wrote, proportions his belief to the evidence. Some patterns have held without exception across enormous experience. Others have shaky records. You should expect the first with near-total confidence and the second with caution. Induction cannot be proven, but it can be done carefully or carelessly.

Scholars still argue about which Hume is the real one: the skeptic who showed that our beliefs have no rational foundation, or the naturalist who showed that they do not need one. When the 2020 PhilPapers Survey asked philosophers familiar with Hume's work, the naturalist reading won, but far from unanimously.

blocks.title: Was Hume a skeptic or a naturalist?
blocks.note: 872 philosophers answered. Many accepted both readings, so totals exceed 100%.
blocks.source: PhilPapers Survey 2020 (Bourget & Chalmers)

blocks.text: Three centuries of trying to answer him

The first big attempt came from probability. In 1814 the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace worked out a rule for estimating the chance of an event repeating, given how many times it has happened before. He took recorded history to be about 5,000 years, or 1,826,213 days of sunrises, and calculated the odds that the sun would rise tomorrow.

items.label: Laplace's 1814 odds that the sun rises tomorrow, based on 5,000 years of sunrises
The same estimate as a probability

blocks.source: Laplace, Essai philosophique sur les probabilités, 1814; via Zayana & Rioul, 2024

blocks.text: It is a clever result, but it does not beat Hume. Laplace's math only works if you start by assuming that whatever governs sunrises is stable over time. That is the uniformity of nature again, wearing a lab coat. Laplace also knew perfectly well that astronomy gives far better reasons to expect sunrise than a tally. But those reasons rest on laws of physics, and our confidence in those laws rests on induction too.

Karl Popper, in the 1930s, took a different exit. He agreed induction could never be justified, so he argued that science does not actually use it. Scientists propose bold guesses and then try to kill them. A theory that survives many attempts at refutation is not proven, just not yet disproven. Critics reply that we still rely on surviving theories to build bridges and reactors, and trusting them to keep working is an inductive bet.

In 1955 Nelson Goodman made things worse. Define a color word, **grue**, meaning green if first observed before some future date and blue after. Every emerald ever seen is green. Every emerald ever seen is also grue. The same evidence supports both "all emeralds are green" and "all emeralds are grue," which predict opposite colors for emeralds dug up after the date. Something other than the data tells us which pattern to project. Nobody has fully explained what.

Hume's challenge spilled well beyond induction. He argued that we never actually observe causation itself, only one event regularly followed by another, plus the feeling of expectation in our own minds. Immanuel Kant later wrote that reading Hume interrupted his dogmatic slumber and set him on the path to his own philosophy. The argument is still live. In the 2020 PhilPapers Survey, about 31 percent of philosophers accepted or leaned toward a Humean view of the laws of nature, on which laws are just summaries of regular patterns, while about 54 percent thought laws are something more, something that actually makes the patterns happen.

blocks.title: The long fight over induction
items: Hume's Treatise appears anonymously and sells poorly
The Enquiry restates the problem more sharply
Laplace calculates the odds of sunrise
Russell's chicken, in The Problems of Philosophy
Popper's Logic of Scientific Discovery argues science runs on falsification
Goodman's grue shows that the problem goes deeper

blocks.text: Good induction, bad induction

If induction can never be proven, is every prediction equally a guess? No, and the difference is practical. Go back to the chicken. Its problem was not too little data. It had hundreds of perfect mornings. Its problem was that it had a pattern without a mechanism. It never understood *why* the farmer fed it. A chicken that understood farms would have seen that the very thing producing the pattern, a farmer raising birds for meat, also predicted its end.

Compare the sun. Your confidence that it will rise is not a tally of past sunrises. It rests on a web of connected knowledge: the Earth's rotation, the conservation of angular momentum, the physics of the Sun's fusion, all cross-checked by millions of independent observations. None of that escapes Hume in principle. But a prediction backed by a mechanism you understand, and that many separate lines of evidence support, is far sturdier than a streak.

blocks.title: Two ways to trust the future

left.head: Pattern only
items: It has always happened
One source of evidence
Breaks without warning
The chicken's method

right.head: Pattern plus mechanism
items: It happens because of a known cause
Many independent checks agree
You can see what would break it
The engineer's method

blocks.text: The most important inductions you make may be about yourself. "I have always been bad at this." "I never stick with anything." "People always get tired of me." Each one is a prediction drawn from past cases, and each one usually skips the mechanism. Why did it happen before? Was it a fixed trait, or a situation, a skill you had not learned yet, a habit nobody taught you to break? A pattern in your past is real evidence. It is not a law of nature, and Hume is the best argument you will ever find that the future is not obliged to copy it.
The danger of a perfect record

This is not just a puzzle. It describes one of the most dangerous ways real systems fail. Before the space shuttle *Challenger* broke apart in 1986, engineers had seen damage to the rubber O-ring seals on earlier flights. Each time the shuttle came home safely, the damage looked a little more acceptable. Success became evidence that the problem was under control. The sociologist Diane Vaughan later called this the **normalization of deviance**: a warning sign gets reclassified as normal because nothing bad has happened yet.

That is the chicken's logic, applied to hardware. It is also why serious engineering cultures refuse to treat a clean history as proof. A component is not trusted because it has never failed. It is trusted because it was built to a known standard, tested, inspected and documented. Periodic tests exist precisely because yesterday's good reading tells you less about tomorrow than it feels like it does. The deep-diving submarine safety programs that grew out of past losses are, in a sense, institutional answers to Hume.

The same logic hits anything that learns from the past. A strategy that won hundreds of matches dies with one balance patch. A video format that grew a channel stops working when the algorithm shifts. Machine learning systems, which are induction engines on a massive scale, can be confidently wrong the moment the world they are deployed in stops matching the world they were trained on.

None of this is a reason for paralysis. You have to act on patterns; there is nothing else to act on. Hume's lesson is about the size and shape of your confidence. Hold strong expectations where a mechanism is understood and the evidence is broad. Hold loose ones where all you have is a streak. And treat any small anomaly in a long run of success as information, not noise, because that is usually what the first crack looks like.

The Hume question for any track record: what is actually keeping this pattern in place, and what would have to change for it to break? If you cannot answer the first part, your confidence is coming from habit, not understanding.

Hume never claimed we should stop trusting experience. He claimed we should know what we are doing when we trust it. The sun will almost certainly rise tomorrow. But almost certainly is not proof, and the gap between them is where chickens, shuttles and overconfident strategies go to die.

takeaways: Every prediction about the future assumes nature will keep behaving the same way, and that assumption can't be proven without circular reasoning.
Hume's answer: we believe from habit, not logic, and the wise move is to scale confidence to the evidence.
Probability, falsification and other fixes help in practice but don't fully escape the problem.
A clean track record is not a reason. Ask what mechanism keeps the pattern going.
Normalization of deviance is induction gone wrong: treating 'nothing bad happened yet' as proof of safety.
