title: Six Minutes at Midway
dek: In June 1942 a team of sleep-deprived codebreakers in a windowless basement told the Navy where Japan would strike. Then the battle came down to luck, nerve and about six minutes over the open ocean.

blocks.text: In May 1942, the most important room in the Pacific had no windows. It was a basement at Pearl Harbor called Station HYPO, and its commander, Joseph Rochefort, sometimes went days without leaving it. He worked shifts of twelve hours or more, often wearing a bathrobe and slippers over his khakis. Around him, analysts sorted through stacks of punched cards and printouts full of five-digit numbers.

Those numbers were Japanese naval radio traffic, and somewhere inside them was a plan. Messages kept mentioning an upcoming operation against a target called **AF**. Rochefort was convinced AF meant Midway, a tiny atoll about halfway between Hawaii and Japan. Washington was not convinced. If he was right, the Navy could set an ambush. If he was wrong, the last American carriers in the Pacific would be waiting in the wrong place.

What happened next is often told as a story about codebreaking. It is, but only partly. The code got the Americans to the right patch of ocean. What won the battle was a messier mix of courage, bad luck, good luck and one officer who decided to keep searching when his fuel gauge told him to turn back.
Six months after Pearl Harbor

By spring 1942, Japan had run the table. Its carrier striking force, the Kido Butai, had hit Pearl Harbor and swept across the western Pacific. Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto wanted to finish the job. His plan, Operation MI, was to seize Midway and draw out what was left of the US Pacific Fleet, then destroy it in a decisive battle. Four of his fleet carriers, *Akagi*, *Kaga*, *Soryu* and *Hiryu*, would lead the attack.

The plan was elaborate, like most Japanese naval plans of the war. It split the fleet into several groups spread over hundreds of miles of ocean, including a diversion toward the Aleutian Islands. It also rested on a bad assumption: Japanese intelligence believed only two American carriers, *Enterprise* and *Hornet*, could respond. The third, *Yorktown*, had been badly damaged a month earlier at the Battle of the Coral Sea.

Admiral Chester Nimitz had other ideas about *Yorktown*. Estimates said she needed months in a West Coast shipyard. Instead, the Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard worked around the clock and had her ready for battle in about 72 hours, good enough for a few weeks of combat. Her air group was rebuilt with whatever squadrons and pilots could be found. Three carriers, not two, would be waiting.
How to read an enemy's mind

The Japanese Navy's main operational code, which the Americans called JN-25, worked in two layers. First, words and phrases were replaced with five-digit code groups from a codebook. Then a second set of numbers, taken from a separate table of additives, was mixed in to scramble the groups again. To read a message you needed both the codebook and the right additives, and the codebreakers had neither in full. They rebuilt them piece by piece, from repetition, guesswork and patterns in the traffic.

The work was grinding. In May 1942, Rochefort's team decrypted, translated and analyzed as many as 140 messages a day. In the final week before Nimitz issued his orders, the volume rose to somewhere between five hundred and a thousand a day. Most messages could only be partly read. Analysts filled the gaps with context, the way you can follow a conversation in a noisy room even when you miss every third word.

The fight over AF was as much bureaucratic as technical. The Navy's codebreaking headquarters in Washington, known as OP-20-G, argued the target might be the Aleutians, Port Moresby in New Guinea, or even the US West Coast, and that the attack would come in mid-June. Rochefort said Midway, in early June. Admiral Ernest King, the top officer in Washington, sided with his own people.

So HYPO set a trap. One of Rochefort's analysts, Jasper Holmes, suggested making Midway lie about its water supply. Nimitz approved the idea. Using the secure undersea cable, the garrison was told to send an uncoded radio message saying its fresh-water plant had broken down. Soon afterward, the codebreakers intercepted a Japanese message reporting that AF was short of water. The enemy had answered the question for them.

blocks.title: The water trick, step by step
items: Japanese messages refer to an upcoming target called AF; Washington and Pearl Harbor disagree on what it means.
Pearl Harbor sends orders to Midway by undersea cable, which Japan cannot intercept.
Midway radios an uncoded message claiming its water plant has broken down.
Japanese listeners pick it up and pass along, in code, that AF is short of water.
HYPO decrypts that report: AF is Midway, and the argument is over.

blocks.text: Knowing the target was not enough; Nimitz also needed the date. Japanese messages encrypted their dates and times with an extra cipher layered on top of the code. HYPO's team cracked it by hunting through old traffic for matching number sequences, and one analyst, Lieutenant Joseph Finnegan, worked out the method. The verdict was June 4 or 5. Timing helped too. Japan delayed switching to a new codebook until May 24, and by then the key breaks had been made.

The water ruse is the kind of move worth stealing. When two smart groups argue about what the data means, stop arguing and design a test whose result will settle it. Rochefort didn't win the debate with better reasoning; he won it with an experiment.
A morning of failures

At 4:30 a.m. on June 4, Admiral Chuichi Nagumo launched 108 aircraft against Midway. The island's radar spotted them at 5:53, and the outnumbered Marine fighters that rose to meet them were cut to pieces. Bombers and torpedo planes based on Midway then attacked the Japanese carriers. Almost none of their bombs or torpedoes hit. By mid-morning, the Americans had lost a lot of planes and had very little to show for it.

Nagumo now faced the dilemma that would undo him. His reserve aircraft were armed with torpedoes for ships, but his pilots said Midway needed a second strike. At 7:15 he ordered the reserve planes rearmed with bombs for land targets. Shortly afterward, one of his scout planes reported American ships to the east, and he reversed the order. His crews spent the morning swapping weapons back and forth, while also recovering the Midway strike force.

Admiral Raymond Spruance, commanding *Enterprise* and *Hornet*, made a hard call. Launching a fully coordinated strike would take too long, so he sent his squadrons as soon as they were ready, accepting that they would arrive piecemeal and suffer for it. His reasoning was to hit Nagumo while his decks were busy, before the Japanese could hit back. The Japanese could launch 108 planes in seven minutes. It took *Enterprise* and *Hornet* more than an hour to launch 117.

Then things went wrong. *Hornet*'s air group flew a heading of 265 degrees instead of 240 and never found the enemy; ten of its fighters ran out of fuel and ditched. Torpedo Squadron 8, led by Lieutenant Commander John Waldron, broke away from the group and found the carriers on its own. It attacked at about 9:20 with no fighter cover. All fifteen of its slow TBD Devastators were shot down. Of thirty men, only Ensign George Gay survived, floating in the water as the battle went on around him.

Two more torpedo squadrons followed. *Enterprise*'s lost most of its planes. *Yorktown*'s lost ten of twelve. Not one torpedo hit, partly because early-war American torpedoes were notoriously unreliable. On paper, it was a massacre. In practice, it pulled the Japanese fighters down to sea level and to one side of the fleet, chasing torpedo planes, and kept the carriers maneuvering hard instead of launching their own strike.
Six minutes

High above, Lieutenant Commander Wade McClusky was leading a 32-plane formation of *Enterprise* dive bombers at about 20,000 feet. He had reached the expected intercept point and found empty ocean. His planes were low on fuel. The safe choice was to turn back. He kept searching, and spotted a lone Japanese destroyer, the *Arashi*, racing at full speed. He guessed it was rejoining the carriers and followed its heading. About ten minutes later, the Kido Butai appeared on the horizon.

By sheer chance, *Yorktown*'s dive bombers arrived at nearly the same moment from a different direction. Beginning at 10:22, the Dauntlesses rolled into their dives. Both *Enterprise* squadrons went for *Kaga* by mistake, hitting her several times and killing her captain on the bridge. Lieutenant Richard Best and his two wingmen pulled out, swung toward *Akagi*, and planted a single bomb that exploded among fueled and armed aircraft in her hangar. *Yorktown*'s bombers struck *Soryu*.

The Japanese hangars were packed with planes full of gasoline, and bombs and torpedoes from the morning's rearming were stacked around them instead of stowed in the magazines. Within about six minutes, *Kaga* and *Soryu* were burning from end to end, and *Akagi* soon followed. Three of the four carriers that had attacked Pearl Harbor were finished.

blocks.text: A popular version of this story says the Japanese were just five minutes from launching a devastating counterstrike, decks lined with ready planes. That account came largely from Mitsuo Fuchida, a Japanese officer aboard *Akagi*. Later research, especially by historians Jonathan Parshall and Anthony Tully, showed it was wrong: the few planes on deck were mostly fighters, and spotting and launching a full strike would have taken at least half an hour. The carriers were not seconds from victory. They were floating bombs, made that way by a morning of indecision.
The cost

*Hiryu*, the last carrier, hit back. Her planes found *Yorktown* and struck her twice, first with bombs, then with torpedoes. Damage control was so effective after the first attack that the second wave thought they were hitting a different, undamaged carrier. Late that afternoon, American dive bombers found *Hiryu* and left her burning; she sank the next morning. *Yorktown* survived under tow until June 6, when the Japanese submarine *I-168* slipped through her escorts and torpedoed both her and the destroyer *Hammann*. *Yorktown* sank on June 7.

blocks.text: The losses were lopsided in hulls, but historians now argue about what they meant. Parshall and Tully point out that Japan lost about 110 carrier aircrew, under a quarter of those embarked, and still had a large pool of trained pilots. The deeper damage was to the carriers themselves, and to the skilled mechanics, deck crews and armorers who went down with them. Meanwhile American shipyards, already years into a buildup, would commission more than two dozen fleet and light carriers in the time Japan built three.
Prepared for luck

So was Midway won by codebreaking or by luck? The honest answer is both, in a particular order. Intelligence did not sink a single ship. What it did was put three American carriers northeast of Midway, unseen, on the morning Japan least expected them. That position turned a long run of mistakes and failures into a survivable morning, and gave lucky breaks, like a destroyer's wake, the chance to matter.

There is a harder lesson in the torpedo squadrons. Their attacks failed by every measure anyone could see at the time. Yet without them, the Japanese fighters would have been at altitude when the dive bombers arrived. Effort that looks wasted in the moment can be what makes the decisive move possible. Spruance accepted that trade on purpose: speed and pressure over a perfectly coordinated plan.

Rochefort's own ending was bitter. Nimitz recommended him for the Distinguished Service Medal, and King rejected it. After complaints from rivals in Washington, he was moved out of codebreaking and given command of a floating dry dock in San Francisco. He never served at sea again. The medal was finally awarded in 1986, ten years after his death.

On a watch team, the person who spots the anomaly in the data is rarely the one who gets the credit for the outcome. Midway is a reminder that the quiet work done before the fight often decides where the fight can even happen.

takeaways: Codebreaking didn't win Midway on its own; it put the fleet in the one place where courage and luck could pay off.
When an argument over data stalls, design a test that settles it, the way HYPO did with the water message.
Failed efforts can still shape the outcome: the doomed torpedo attacks pulled Japanese fighters out of position.
Indecision has a cost. Nagumo's back-and-forth rearming left fuel and bombs exposed at the worst possible moment.
Be skeptical of tidy versions of history; the famous five-minutes story came from one participant and didn't hold up.

title: Nautilus 90 North
dek: The first nuclear submarine reached the top of the world on her third try. The bravest call of the whole voyage was the one where her captain turned around.

blocks.text: In June 1958, USS *Nautilus* crept north through the Chukchi Sea, the shallow stretch of water above the Bering Strait, on a mission so secret that her hull numbers had been painted over. Above her was pack ice. Below her, never far away, was the sea floor. Then the sonar picked up something that ended the mission: a block of ice about a mile wide, hanging 63 feet down into the water, deep enough to threaten the sail.

Commander William R. Anderson had a choice. He could try to thread the gap between the ice and the bottom and press on toward the North Pole, with the President of the United States waiting for good news. Or he could admit that he did not have a clear enough picture of what lay ahead, and go home. He went home. *Nautilus* turned around and steamed back to Pearl Harbor to wait.

Six weeks later, the same submarine and the same captain passed under the North Pole, the first ship ever to reach it. It is one of the great exploration stories of the twentieth century. But the part worth studying is not the triumph. It is the retreat that made the triumph possible, and the engineering and judgment that turned a stunt into something the Navy could repeat.

items.label: Men aboard Nautilus at the North Pole
Distance under the ice, covered in 96 hours
Depth of the sea beneath the Pole

blocks.source: Submarine Force Museum (NHHC); Naval History magazine, August 2008

blocks.text: Underway on nuclear power

To understand why the Pole mattered, you have to remember what a submarine was before *Nautilus*. A diesel boat was really a surface ship that could hide for a while. Its diesels needed air, so underwater it ran on batteries that drained in hours at speed. It had to come up to the surface or to snorkel depth to recharge, and that was when it was easiest to find and kill. Speed underwater was a sprint you paid for later.

*Nautilus* broke that rule. Truman laid her keel at Groton in June 1952, First Lady Mamie Eisenhower christened her in January 1954, and she was commissioned that September as the first nuclear-powered ship in the Navy. On January 17, 1955, she left the pier and her captain, Eugene Wilkinson, had the message sent that announced a new era: underway on nuclear power.

The records came fast. She ran submerged from the Connecticut coast to San Juan, Puerto Rico, about 1,300 miles, farther underwater than any submarine had gone before. On a later run she covered 1,396 miles at an average of more than 20 knots. For a diesel boat, either would have been impossible. For *Nautilus* it was just a transit. The question became where else a submarine that never had to come up could go.

blocks.title: What changed in 1955

left.head: Diesel-electric submarine
items: Needs air for its engines
Battery limits underwater speed and time
Must surface or snorkel to recharge
Most exposed when recharging

right.head: Nautilus

blocks.text: Why the Pole

In 1956, after a trip to the Arctic, Senator Henry Jackson of Washington suggested that nuclear submarines might be able to operate under the polar ice cap. The idea had strategic logic. The Arctic Ocean sits between North America, Europe and the Soviet Union. A route under the ice would be a shortcut between the Atlantic and the Pacific, hidden from anyone watching on the surface.

Then politics added urgency. In October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite, and the American reply, the Vanguard rocket, blew up on the launch pad in front of the press. The United States looked like it was losing the technology race. President Dwight Eisenhower wanted a dramatic answer. A submarine crossing the top of the world, something no ship had ever done, would be exactly that.

There was a practical payoff, too. According to the museum association that cares for *Nautilus* today, a typical voyage from London to Tokyo ran about 11,200 miles, and a route over the top of the world would cut roughly 4,900 miles off it. For merchant shipping that was a dream for the distant future. For submarines that could travel under the ice, it was a highway that already existed, if anyone could prove it was safe to drive.
The first two failures

*Nautilus* had already tried once, from the Atlantic side, in 1957. She pushed into the Arctic basin between Greenland and Spitsbergen. Then things started to go wrong. A collision with ice damaged her periscope. Her gyrocompass, which finds north by sensing the rotation of the Earth, became erratic as she approached the top of the planet, where that rotation stops being a useful guide. She turned back about 180 miles from the Pole.

That failure exposed the real problem. Getting under the ice was the easy part. Knowing where you were once you got there was the hard part. Magnetic compasses are useless near the magnetic pole. Stars and the sun are invisible from under the ice. A submarine that lost track of its position under a solid roof of ice, with no way to surface and get a fix, could wander until it ran out of luck.

The fix came from an unexpected place. For the 1958 attempt, *Nautilus* carried an N6A inertial navigator, adapted from the Navajo missile project and looked after by two technicians from the contractor, North American Aviation. Instead of looking outward at stars or magnetic fields, an inertial navigator measures every acceleration the ship makes and calculates its position from them. It does not care where the Pole is. She also carried an upward-looking sonar designed by Navy scientist Waldo Lyon that drew the profile of the ice overhead, so the crew could see the shape of the roof they were sailing under.

The principle is simple even if the hardware was not. Accelerometers measure every push and turn the boat makes. Gyroscopes hold a stable reference so the system knows which way those pushes point. A computer adds up acceleration to get speed, and adds up speed to get distance traveled. The catch is drift: tiny errors pile up over time, which is why inertial systems need to be checked against a known position whenever possible. Under the ice, there would be no such check for days, so the crew had to trust the math.

blocks.title: How Nautilus navigated where compasses fail
items: Magnetic compasses are useless near the magnetic pole, so they are set aside
Gyrocompasses lose accuracy at very high latitudes, so they become a backup
An inertial navigator senses every acceleration and computes position continuously
Upward-looking sonar maps ice thickness and shows where the roof is thin
Depth sounders track the sea floor below, so the boat knows its gap from top to bottom

blocks.text: The second attempt, code-named Operation Sunshine, came from the Pacific side in June 1958, and it is the one that ended with the ice block in the Chukchi Sea. The Navy had kept the whole mission secret precisely so that a failure would not become another public embarrassment like Vanguard. Anderson's decision to turn around meant the mission quietly vanished. No headlines, no disaster. Just a submarine back in Pearl Harbor, waiting for the ice to retreat.

Turning back felt like failure, but it preserved the only thing that mattered: the chance to try again. A captain who forced the gap and wedged his boat between the ice and the bottom would have ended the program, not just the voyage.
Ninety north

*Nautilus* left Pearl Harbor again on July 23, 1958. This time the ice had pulled back, and she headed for a deep undersea valley off Point Barrow, Alaska, which gave her a road into the Arctic basin with room to spare. On August 1 she dove into that trough, 1,094 miles from the Pole. Once in the deep basin, she ran at about 400 feet and more than 20 knots, with the ice sliding by overhead on the sonar traces.

At 11:15 p.m. Eastern time on August 3, 1958, she passed under the geographic North Pole, in water more than 13,000 feet deep. Anderson spoke to the crew over the announcing system and dedicated the moment to the world, the country and the Navy. Then the boat kept going. She had no way to tell anyone yet. There was solid ice above and the nearest open water was days away.

In all, she covered 1,830 miles under the ice in 96 hours. She came up northeast of Greenland and sent a message that has become one of the most famous signals in naval history, just three words long: Nautilus 90 North. A helicopter lifted Anderson off near Iceland and he was flown to Washington, where Eisenhower gave him the Legion of Merit. The crew received the first Presidential Unit Citation ever awarded in peacetime, and New York threw them a ticker-tape parade.

The secrecy held to the end. Anderson did not contact Washington until the boat came up in the Greenland Sea, about a day and a half after crossing the Pole, so the first the world heard of the voyage was the announcement of its success. Then *Nautilus* finished the job in style, crossing the Atlantic to England and later returning home with a submerged run of more than 3,100 miles in six days, averaging over 20 knots. She was back in Connecticut by the end of August.

blocks.text: From stunt to routine

The voyage changed the map of naval strategy almost overnight. Within days, USS *Skate* reached the Pole too, and within a few years nuclear submarines were meeting each other under the ice, a story told in the article on record voyages in this library. The Arctic stopped being a blank wall and became an operating area, a place submarines could hide, transit and patrol. It has stayed one ever since.

*Nautilus* kept working. Between 1959 and 1960 she went through the first complete overhaul of any nuclear ship and got a fresh reactor core, then deployed to the Mediterranean, took part in fleet exercises, and spent her last years on testing programs. She was decommissioned on March 3, 1980, after a 25-year career and more than half a million miles. In 1986 she opened to the public in Groton, Connecticut, where she sits today next to the Submarine Force Museum, a short drive from the yard that built her.

Anderson was 37 when he took her under the Pole. He later retired from the Navy and served four terms in Congress from Tennessee. He died in 2007. His career is a reminder that the people on these early boats were not superhuman. They were young officers and sailors working with brand-new equipment, a lot of uncertainty and a deadline set by politicians.
The hard call

There is a version of this story where Anderson is a hero for pressing on. That is not what happened, and it is worth thinking about why. The success in August was built on two failures: the 1957 attempt, which revealed the navigation problem and led to the inertial navigator, and the June 1958 attempt, which taught the crew that the shallow route was too dangerous and pushed them toward the deep valley off Barrow. Each retreat bought information.

Anderson's own explanation for turning back was simple: he did not have a solid picture of what lay ahead. That is a standard any watchstander would recognize. When you do not understand what your plant or your boat is doing, you do not push harder and hope. You stop, get more information and come back. The pressure to keep going, from schedules, from bosses, from your own pride, is almost always strongest at exactly the moment when stopping is the right call.

It is a useful lens for anything long and uncertain. A failed first attempt at a project is not wasted if it tells you what you did not know. The question to ask after a setback is not whether you failed, but what the failure showed you, and whether your next attempt is actually different. *Nautilus* did not get to the Pole by trying harder. She got there by coming back with a better navigator and a better route.

takeaways: Nautilus reached the North Pole on her third Arctic attempt; the first two failures each taught something essential.
The real problem under the ice was not depth but navigation, solved by an inertial navigator borrowed from a missile program.
Anderson's decision to turn back in June 1958, with the President waiting, is what made August possible.
When you lack a clear picture of what is ahead, stopping to get one is a strength, not a retreat.
After a setback, ask what it revealed and make the next attempt genuinely different.

title: The Torpedoes That Didn't Work
dek: American submarines sank more than half of Japan's merchant fleet in World War II, after spending a year and a half fighting with broken weapons. Fifty-two boats never came home.

blocks.text: In July 1943, the submarine USS *Tinosa* found the kind of target skippers dreamed about: a Japanese tanker of about 19,000 tons, one of the biggest in the enemy's fleet, steaming alone toward Truk. Lieutenant Commander Lawrence Daspit attacked. Two torpedoes exploded, and the tanker went dead in the water. She could not run. She could barely fight back. For a submarine captain, it does not get easier than that.

Daspit lined up carefully and fired again, from an ideal angle, square to the target's side. The torpedo hit and nothing happened. He fired again. Another hit, another dud. As historian Clay Blair tells it, *Tinosa* fired 15 torpedoes at that tanker over two days, and the great majority that hit failed to explode. Daspit finally stopped, kept his last torpedo, and took it all the way back to Pearl Harbor so someone could find out what was wrong with it.

That single torpedo helped break open one of the worst weapons failures in American military history. It also captures the strange shape of the submarine war in the Pacific: a small force of diesel boats that ended up strangling an empire, after fighting the first year and a half of the war with weapons that betrayed them. The men who did it paid a higher price than any other American force in the war.

items.label: Share of Japanese merchant tonnage sunk by US submarines
US submarines lost in World War II
Submariners lost, by the Navy's loss report count

blocks.source: JANAC, Japanese Naval and Merchant Shipping Losses, 1947; Naval History and Heritage Command, United States Submarine Losses

blocks.text: A war on shipping

Japan was an island empire that could not feed its factories on its own. Oil, iron ore, rubber, rice and the troops who held its conquests all moved by sea. That made its merchant fleet the jugular, and within hours of the attack on Pearl Harbor, the United States ordered unrestricted submarine warfare against Japan. Any Japanese ship, warship or freighter, was a legitimate target.

It is worth remembering that Germany tried the same strategy against Britain, on a much larger scale. Germany built 1,162 U-boats in World War II, sank about 3,000 Allied ships, and lost the large majority of its boats in the attempt. The Atlantic was the campaign that nearly worked. The Pacific was the one that did, partly because Japan, despite being even more dependent on imports than Britain, was slow to build the convoys and escorts that eventually beat the U-boats.

The submarine force was not ready for that war. Before 1941, American submarines had trained mostly to scout for the battle fleet and make cautious attacks on warships. Peacetime exercises rewarded skippers who stayed safe, not ones who pressed in close. In the first year of the war, a number of commanding officers proved too cautious for the job and were relieved, and younger, more aggressive officers took their places.

The patrols themselves were brutal. A typical war patrol lasted 45 to 60 days in a cramped diesel boat with limited fresh water and a crew of roughly 60 to 80 men. Crews got about two weeks of rest between patrols and a few days of refresher training before going out again. Boats ran on the surface at night to charge batteries and dove at dawn, spending the day submerged and waiting.

Danger was not spread evenly. According to the Navy's loss records, no American submarine was lost in the Central Pacific until *Pickerel* in April 1943, sixteen months into the war. Shallow, mined waters near the Japanese home islands and narrow straits were far deadlier. The sea itself was an enemy too: four boats were lost to groundings, though in every one of those cases the whole crew was rescued.
Three failures stacked on top of each other

The Mark 14 torpedo was supposed to be one of the most advanced weapons in the world. Its Mark 6 exploder had a magnetic feature that was meant to detonate the warhead under a ship's keel, breaking its back. The problem was that it had never been properly tested. To save money, the Navy's Bureau of Ordnance had not fired live production torpedoes against real targets before the war. Test shots used exercise heads with instruments in place of the warhead.

The first failure was depth. When Rear Admiral Charles Lockwood ran tests into fishing nets in mid-1942, he found that the torpedoes ran about ten feet deeper than set. They were passing harmlessly under their targets. By then, Pacific Fleet submarines had fired more than 800 of them. The Bureau's first response was to blame the skippers.

Fixing the depth uncovered the second failure. With torpedoes now running at the right depth, the magnetic exploder started setting them off early, before they reached the target. In April 1943 the submarine *Tunny* fired all ten tubes at a group of three aircraft carriers; most would have hit, but they exploded prematurely, causing only light damage. Skippers begged to disable the magnetic feature. Some did it on their own. In June 1943, with Admiral Chester Nimitz's approval, the order went out to deactivate it.

That exposed the third failure, which is what *Tinosa* ran into. The contact exploder, the backup that was supposed to fire on impact, had a design flaw. Tests ordered by Lockwood, including torpedoes dropped from heights and fired into the cliffs of Kahoolawe island off Maui, showed that a square, 90-degree hit, the perfect shot, slowed the firing pin so much that it often failed to fire. Glancing hits were more likely to work. Skippers were told to aim for worse angles while fixes were made. By early 1944, more than two years into the war, the Mark 14 was finally reliable.

blocks.title: How fixing one fault revealed the next
items: Torpedoes run about 10 feet deep and pass under targets
Depth is corrected, so torpedoes now reach the magnetic zone
Magnetic exploder fires early; it is deactivated in June 1943
Contact exploder now does all the work, and fails on perfect hits
Firing pin is redesigned; torpedoes are reliable by early 1944

blocks.text: Each fault hid the next one. As long as torpedoes ran too deep, nobody could see that the exploders were bad. Anyone who has troubleshot a plant or a piece of code knows the feeling: the first fix does not solve the problem, it just shows you the next one.

There was one more cruelty. Torpedoes sometimes ran in a circle and came back at the boat that fired them. The Navy's loss records attribute two submarines to their own circular runs. One was *Tang*, commanded by Richard O'Kane, one of the most successful skippers of the war. On October 25, 1944, her last torpedo of a patrol turned around and hit her. O'Kane and a handful of his crew survived and were taken prisoner. He received the Medal of Honor after the war.

The contrast with the enemy stings. Japan's Type 93 torpedo, a 24-inch weapon with a warhead of more than a thousand pounds, could run far longer distances than American torpedoes and left almost no wake. Japan had tested its torpedoes with live firings. According to the Naval History and Heritage Command, Type 93s sank seven American cruisers, nine destroyers and the carrier *Hornet*, and killed more than 3,100 American sailors. The side that tested its weapons the way it planned to use them had torpedoes that worked.
Learning to win

Once the weapons worked, the campaign changed fast. A new generation of skippers attacked aggressively, often on the surface at night using radar. Boats hunted in coordinated groups. Japan was slow to organize convoys and escorts, and when it did, its anti-submarine forces were often outmatched. Submarines also sank warships, including the battleship *Kongo* and the giant carrier *Shinano*, sunk by USS *Archerfish* in November 1944 on one of her first voyages.

The cost of command was personal. In February 1943, Commander Howard Gilmore of USS *Growler* was on the bridge when his boat collided with a Japanese ship that then raked it with gunfire. Wounded and unable to get below in time, he ordered his crew to take the boat down without him. *Growler* survived. Gilmore received the Medal of Honor, and his last order has been told to every class of submariners since.
Take her down.
blocks.by: Cmdr. Howard Gilmore, USS Growler, February 1943

blocks.text: By the end of the war, the postwar Joint Army-Navy Assessment Committee counted 1,113 Japanese merchant ships and 201 naval vessels sunk by American submarines. That was about 4.8 million tons of merchant shipping, roughly 55 percent of all the Japanese merchant tonnage lost to every cause. Aircraft, mines and surface ships together accounted for most of the rest.

blocks.title: Japanese merchant tonnage sunk, by cause
blocks.note: Selected categories; total merchant losses from all causes were about 8.6 million tons.
blocks.source: Joint Army-Navy Assessment Committee (JANAC), Japanese Naval and Merchant Shipping Losses During World War II, 1947

blocks.text: The effect on Japan was strangulation. Oil from the conquered East Indies, the reason Japan had gone to war in the first place, stopped arriving in useful quantities. Factories ran short of raw materials, and garrisons on distant islands were cut off from food and reinforcements. The submarine war did not win the Pacific alone, but it starved the Japanese war machine of what it needed to fight.
On eternal patrol

The price was enormous. The Navy lost 52 submarines in World War II. The official loss report counts 374 officers and 3,131 enlisted men lost, 3,505 in all, although other Navy counts run somewhat higher. That was about 16 percent of the officers and 13 percent of the enlisted men who served in the boats operationally, and roughly 18 percent of all submarines that saw combat. The National Park Service calls it the highest casualty rate of any American force in the war.

blocks.title: Why the 52 boats were lost
blocks.note: Half-values reflect losses split between two probable causes.
blocks.source: Naval History and Heritage Command, United States Submarine Losses, World War II

blocks.text: Most of those boats simply disappeared. They sailed on patrol and were never heard from again, and their fates were pieced together after the war from Japanese records, which were often incomplete. Submariners say that those boats are still on eternal patrol. Some survivors came home only at war's end, from prison camps: men from *Grenadier*, *Perch*, *Sculpin*, *Tang* and a few others.

Those Japanese records carried their own lesson about the fog of war. The Navy's loss report notes that Japanese forces claimed 468 positive sinkings of American submarines, against 52 boats actually lost from all causes. Anti-submarine crews saw oil slicks, debris and explosions and reported kills that had not happened. Japan's own submarine force fared far worse in reality: it lost 128 boats, and many of the 58 left at the end of the war were not fit for operations.
What the war left behind

The men who survived built the submarine force that came next. Many of the officers who took the first nuclear boats to sea had learned their trade on war patrols. Edward Beach, who later commanded *Triton* on her voyage around the world underwater, had served on *Trigger* during the war. They brought with them a hard-earned respect for equipment that works and a distrust of anyone who says it works without proving it.

The torpedo scandal is the lesson worth carrying. A weapon was never tested the way it would be used, because testing was expensive. When the people using it reported that it failed, the people who designed it blamed the users. It took skippers who kept careful records, a commander willing to run his own tests and one captain who brought home his last torpedo as evidence to fix it, and it took the better part of two years.

That pattern still shows up everywhere, from shipyards to software. Test things the way they will actually be used. When the people closest to the work say something is broken, treat it as data, not complaining. And when the first fix does not solve the problem, do not assume you were wrong. There may be another fault hiding behind the first one, waiting for you to clear the way.

takeaways: US submarines sank about 55 percent of Japan's lost merchant tonnage, strangling its oil and supply lines.
The Mark 14 torpedo had three stacked defects: it ran deep, its magnetic exploder fired early and its contact exploder failed on perfect hits.
Each fix revealed the next fault, and full reliability took until early 1944.
52 boats and about 3,500 men were lost, the highest casualty rate of any US force in the war.
Test the way you fight, and treat reports from the people using the gear as data.

title: The Canal the Mosquitoes Almost Won
dek: France spent eight years and an estimated 22,000 lives trying to dig a sea-level ditch across Panama. The Americans finished the job by changing two ideas: what was killing the workers, and what a canal should be.

blocks.text: In 1883, a talented French engineer named Jules Dingler arrived in Panama to run the biggest construction project in the world. He brought his family with him. Within about two years, every one of them had died of yellow fever. Dingler resigned in August 1885 and went home alone.

His story was not unusual. On the French canal, chief engineers came and went, many of them because of illness. By 1884, the death rate among workers was over 200 a month. Hospitals filled and emptied. Nobody understood why the jungle killed people so efficiently, so nobody could stop it.

The cause was a small striped mosquito, *Aedes aegypti*, which carries yellow fever, along with other mosquitoes carrying malaria. The French never figured that out in time. That single gap in knowledge, more than money or machines, is the difference between the canal that failed and the canal that ships still pass through today.
The hero of Suez

People had dreamed of cutting through the isthmus since the Spanish conquest. The California gold rush made it urgent. After 1848, one of the fastest routes from New York to San Francisco was by steamship to Panama, a trek across the jungle, and another steamship north. Americans built a railroad across the isthmus to speed that up. It was supposed to take two years. It opened in 1855, cost six times its estimate, and killed large numbers of workers through cholera, dysentery and malaria. It was a warning about what Panama did to builders. Almost nobody heeded it.

The man behind the French attempt was Ferdinand de Lesseps, the most famous builder alive. In 1869 he had opened the Suez Canal, connecting the Mediterranean to the Red Sea through 100 miles of flat Egyptian desert, a project experts had said was impossible. He was a diplomat and a promoter, not an engineer. Suez taught him a lesson that would ruin him in Panama: trust your vision and ignore the doubters.

In 1879 he called an international congress in Paris to approve a canal across Panama, then part of Colombia. He had already decided what kind: a sea-level canal, a straight trench from ocean to ocean with no locks, like Suez. A French engineer at the congress, Adolphe Godin de Lépinay, proposed something different. Dam the rivers, create a lake in the middle, and use locks to lift ships up to the lake and back down. The plan was ignored. It was, almost exactly, the design that would be built 35 years later.

Digging began on 1 January 1881. Panama was not Suez. Instead of sand there was rock, clay that slid when wet, a mountain ridge in the way, and the Chagres River, which could rise many feet in a single storm. The workforce reached about 40,000 by 1888, nine out of ten of them laborers from the Caribbean islands. Steel equipment rusted in the rain. Slopes collapsed into the cut faster than crews could dig them out.

De Lesseps visited only a few times, in the dry season. He kept raising money from small French investors and kept insisting on a sea-level canal long after the engineers on site knew it was hopeless. Only in October 1887 did he accept locks, as a last-ditch rescue. It was too late. On 15 May 1889, the company went bankrupt. About 800,000 investors lost their savings. The death toll for the French era is estimated at over 22,000. De Lesseps and his son were convicted in the scandal that followed.

De Lesseps' greatest strength, refusing to listen to people who said it couldn't be done, became his fatal flaw when the people saying it were right. Confidence is only useful if it can still be updated.
The mosquito problem

When the United States took over the project in 1904, buying the French equipment and excavations for $40 million, it also inherited the disease problem. But science had moved. In Cuba, the physician Carlos Finlay had long argued that mosquitoes spread yellow fever, and in 1900 an Army team under Walter Reed proved it with experiments on volunteers. In Havana, an Army doctor named William Gorgas then went after the mosquitoes. Yellow fever cases in the city dropped from 784 to zero within a year.

Gorgas was sent to Panama as chief sanitary officer. His approach sounded crazy to many officials, who still believed tropical disease came from filth and "bad air." He wanted to fight insects. His teams drained ponds and swamps, oiled standing water, fumigated buildings, put screens on windows and nets over beds, and built piped water systems so people did not keep open water barrels where mosquitoes could breed.

It was expensive and labor-intensive, and his bosses fought him. The canal commission's chairman wanted him replaced. President Theodore Roosevelt asked doctors for advice and was told, in effect, that he could have Gorgas or he could have no canal. Roosevelt backed Gorgas. Within about two years, yellow fever and malaria were close to eliminated in the canal zone.

blocks.title: How Gorgas fought a disease he couldn't see
items: Accept the new evidence: mosquitoes, not dirt or swamp air, spread yellow fever and malaria.
Map where the mosquitoes breed: standing water, barrels, gutters, swamps.
Remove the breeding sites: drain, fill, or spray oil and larvicide on water.
Block contact: screens on buildings, nets over beds, isolation of sick patients behind screens.
Supply clean piped water so people stop storing open water.
Keep doing it every day, even when the bosses complain about the cost.

blocks.text: Changing the plan

The Americans also inherited the sea-level question. In January 1906, a panel of engineers voted eight to five to recommend a sea-level canal, the same idea that had broken the French. The chief engineer on the ground, John Stevens, had a different view. He had built railroads through the mountains of the American West and had watched the Chagres in full flood. He called a sea-level canal "an entirely untenable proposition."

Stevens argued for the lock-and-lake design. Build a huge earthen dam across the Chagres at Gatun. That would create a lake 85 feet above sea level, which ships could sail across for much of the route. Locks at each end would lift ships up to the lake and lower them back to the sea. The water to work the locks would come from the lake itself, by gravity. Stevens convinced Roosevelt and Congress. Gatun Dam became the largest dam in the world, and Gatun Lake the largest artificial lake.
Stevens resigned abruptly in 1907. Roosevelt replaced him with an Army engineer, George Washington Goethals, who ran the project with military discipline until it was finished.
Moving a mountain

The hardest part was the Culebra Cut, an eight-mile slice through the continental divide. About 6,000 men worked in the cut at a time. They drilled holes and packed them with dynamite, using about 27,000 tonnes of it over the project, then loaded the broken rock onto as many as 160 trains a day. Over a hundred steam shovels did the digging.

The mountain fought back. The rock underneath was weak and kept sliding. Landslides added about 30 million cubic yards of extra material that had to be dug out a second time. Workers would clear a section only to watch the walls collapse back into it after a rainstorm. The engineer in charge, David Gaillard, led the work calmly through the chaos, but fell ill and died in 1913, before the canal opened; the cut was later renamed in his honor. On 26 May 1913, steam shovels finally broke through the length of the cut at the canal's bottom level.
The machine at the heart of it

For anyone who works on electrical systems, the locks are the most impressive part. Each chamber has a usable length of 1,000 feet and is 110 feet wide. Filling one takes about 26.7 million gallons of water, which flows in from the lake through huge culverts in the walls, with no pumps, just gravity and valves. The giant steel gates are hollow and buoyant, like ship hulls, and so well balanced that two 25-horsepower electric motors can swing each leaf. If one motor fails, the other can still move the gate, slowly.

Ships move forward under their own engines, but they do not steer themselves through. Electric locomotives called mules run on tracks along the lock walls, holding the ship with cables to keep it centered and to brake it, up to eight mules for a large ship. And because everything was electric from the start, the whole lockage could be run from a central control room on the lock wall.

That control board was a beautiful piece of safety engineering. It included a working scale model of the locks, with moving indicators that showed the real position of every gate and valve. Mechanical interlocks were built into the controls so an operator physically could not open a valve that would drain a chamber while another valve was filling it, or move a gate in the wrong sequence. The designers assumed operators would someday make mistakes and made those mistakes impossible. If you have ever worked with interlocks on a switchboard or a reactor plant, you know the philosophy. It was there in 1914.

blocks.text: Opening day, and who paid

The canal opened to commercial traffic on 15 August 1914, when the cargo ship *Ancon* went through from the Atlantic to the Pacific. World War I had started weeks earlier, so the grand celebration was cancelled. The US share of the project cost about $375 million, including the payments to the French company and to Panama, and came in about $23 million under the 1907 estimate.

The human cost was smaller than the French era but still large. Between about 5,600 and 5,850 workers died during American construction, from disease and accidents. Only around 350 were Americans. The great majority were Black laborers from the West Indies, especially Barbados. The canal zone ran a segregated pay system: mostly white American workers were paid on the "gold roll," with better housing and better mosquito protection, while mostly Black Caribbean workers were on the "silver roll" with worse pay and conditions. The disease campaign that made the canal possible did not protect everyone equally.

The canal also carried a political cost. The US had backed Panama's 1903 break from Colombia to get control of a canal zone, and the arrangement remained a source of anger in Panama for decades. Treaties signed in 1977 began the handover, and Panama took full control on 31 December 1999. In 2016 a new set of larger locks opened alongside the old ones, which still operate.

blocks.text: Being right about the wrong thing

It is tempting to tell this story as the Americans being smarter than the French. That misses the point. The French had good engineers, huge resources and a proven leader. What they lacked was a correct model of two things: what was killing their workers, and what the land would allow. The right design was proposed in 1879 and ignored. The cause of yellow fever was argued by Finlay for years before anyone acted on it.

The Americans succeeded partly because they arrived after the science changed, and partly because their leaders were willing to throw out a plan, even one an expert panel had voted for, when the evidence on the ground said it would fail. Gorgas fought for his idea against bosses who thought it was nonsense. Stevens overruled a committee because he had seen the river flood.

That is a pattern worth recognizing in your own projects. When something keeps failing no matter how much effort you pour in, the problem may not be effort. It may be that your model of the problem is wrong. The hardest and most valuable move is to stop, find the mosquito, and change the plan.

takeaways: The French effort (1881-1889) failed because of disease and an insistence on a sea-level canal; an estimated 22,000 people died.
William Gorgas nearly eliminated yellow fever and malaria by attacking mosquitoes, an idea many officials resisted.
John Stevens overruled an expert panel to choose a lock-and-lake design, the same plan the French had ignored in 1879.
The locks used electrical interlocks and a model control board so operators could not open the wrong valve: safety by design in 1914.
The benefits were shared unequally: most of the roughly 5,600 deaths in the American era were West Indian laborers on segregated pay.

title: The Submarine in the Desert
dek: Before a nuclear submarine ever touched water, a stubborn electrical officer built one in the Idaho desert, bet everything that it would work, and nearly got fired for it.

blocks.text: In the spring of 1953, the most important submarine in the world sat in the high desert of Idaho, hundreds of miles from the nearest ocean. It was not really a submarine. It was a section of hull built to the exact shape of one, with a reactor inside, sitting in a big tank of water that served as shielding. Its spray ponds, not the sea, carried away the heat. On March 30, 1953, the reactor inside that land-locked hull went critical for the first time.

A few weeks later, the crew ran it for roughly 100 hours straight at power, a run designed to simulate a submerged crossing from the American East Coast to Ireland. Nothing like it had been done before. No one had ever driven a ship's propeller shaft with fission, let alone for four days without a break. If the plant failed, the real submarine, already under construction at Groton, Connecticut, would be a very expensive steel tube.

The man who insisted on building a submarine in the desert, and who had already started building the real one before the desert version ever ran, was a captain named Hyman G. Rickover. He had been passed over for promotion twice, was disliked by much of the Navy's leadership, and was months away from forced retirement. The story of how he got from there to 63 years of service, and why every nuke still trains on a prototype before going to sea, is a story about what it takes to build something genuinely new inside an organization that does not want it.

blocks.text: An outsider from Makow

Rickover was born on January 27, 1900, in Makow, a town in what was then the Russian-ruled Kingdom of Poland. When he was about four, he, his mother and his sister fled anti-Jewish pogroms and joined his father in New York. The family later moved to Chicago, where a congressman nominated him to the Naval Academy. He got in as a third alternate, which is the Navy's way of saying he was nobody's first choice.

He graduated 107th out of 540 in the class of 1922: solid, not brilliant. What stood out early was where he chose to spend his career. He served as an engineering officer on a destroyer, then as **electrical officer** on the battleship *Nevada*, then earned a master's degree in electrical engineering from Columbia. The man later called the father of the nuclear Navy began as, essentially, the ship's senior electrician.

He volunteered for submarines in 1929 and served three years on S-48, an old boat with a troubled reputation, rising to executive officer. He later commanded a minesweeper in China for about three months. Then, in August 1939, he reported to the Navy's engineering bureau in Washington, and spent most of World War II running electrical work for the fleet. It was the job that formed him. He learned how the Navy bought equipment, how contractors cut corners, and how much damage a bad part could do to a ship in combat.

He also learned that he was not built for the Navy's social side. He was blunt, impatient with ceremony and ruthless about standards. Plenty of officers who worked with him admired him. Plenty of others could not stand him. Both groups would matter.
Oak Ridge, 1946

In May 1946, the Navy sent Rickover and a handful of other officers to Oak Ridge, Tennessee, the Manhattan Project's sprawling industrial site, to learn about atomic energy. It was an assignment that could easily have been a dead end, a year of classes before a return to routine duty. Rickover treated it as a mission. By November 1946 he was standing in front of the Submarine Officers' Conference arguing that the Navy should build nuclear-powered submarines.

The idea was not his alone. Physicists had talked about nuclear propulsion for years. What made Rickover different was that he understood the problem was not physics. Everyone knew fission released heat. The hard part was engineering: materials that would survive years of radiation, pumps and valves that would never leak, a plant compact enough to fit in a hull and reliable enough that 100 men could bet their lives on it every day.

Over the next three years he maneuvered himself into a uniquely powerful spot. In August 1948, the Bureau of Ships set up a Nuclear Power Branch under him. In February 1949 he was also appointed to the Atomic Energy Commission's reactor development division. He now sat in both the Navy, which wanted the submarine, and the civilian agency that controlled everything nuclear. Requests and approvals that would normally bounce between two bureaucracies for months could move through one office, his.

Rickover's real innovation was organizational. He built one small group that owned the whole problem, from reactor physics to the last valve, and answered to no one who could water it down. That structure, now called Naval Reactors, still runs the program today.
Mark I equals Mark II

The normal way to build a radically new machine is in sequence. Build a test version, learn from it, then design the real thing. Rickover set himself a deadline of January 1955 to have a submarine at sea and decided the normal way was too slow. Westinghouse's Bettis laboratory would design the land prototype, called the Submarine Thermal Reactor Mark I, and the shipboard plant, Mark II, at the same time. The slogan around the program was blunt: Mark I equals Mark II.

That slogan contained a huge bet. If the prototype revealed a basic flaw, the submarine would have to be redesigned while half-built. Construction of the Idaho prototype began in August 1950. The contract for the submarine went to Electric Boat in August 1951. On June 14, 1952, President Harry Truman laid the keel of USS *Nautilus* at Groton. That was less than a year before the prototype in Idaho went critical. The ship was being built on faith in a machine that had never run.

The decision to build the prototype as a full-size hull section was the hedge. A simple test reactor would have proven the physics. A reactor jammed into the actual shape and space of a submarine proved the engineering: where the pipes ran, whether men could reach the valves, how heat and noise behaved in a cramped space. Anything that went wrong in Idaho would go wrong in a place where you could walk outside, not 400 feet down.

blocks.text: Then came the test that mattered. The plant reached power in the spring of 1953, and instead of a short demonstration, it ran for about 100 hours, simulating a submerged voyage across the Atlantic. Rickover wanted proof that the plant could do the job it was built for, continuously, not just that it could start. The run succeeded. On January 17, 1955, *Nautilus* went to sea, and her commanding officer, Eugene Wilkinson, had the message sent that every submariner knows: underway on nuclear power. Rickover had hit his own deadline almost to the day.

blocks.text: The admiral who almost wasn't

Here is the part of the story that should bother anyone who has ever watched a large organization work. While Rickover was building the most important new weapon system of the decade, the Navy was trying to get rid of him. Promotion boards passed him over for rear admiral twice. Under the rules of the time, an officer passed over again would have to retire. The man running the nuclear submarine program was on track to be shown the door before his submarine went to sea.

The reasons were partly personal. Rickover had stepped on a lot of senior toes, he had little patience for the Navy's traditions, and he was an engineering specialist in a service that promoted line officers who commanded ships. Some historians have also pointed to antisemitism as a factor, though that is hard to prove from the record. What is clear is that his supporters, in Congress and in the press, made his treatment a public issue. In July 1953 he was selected for rear admiral. He made vice admiral in 1958 and later four-star admiral, and he did not leave active duty until January 31, 1982.

There is an uncomfortable lesson in that episode. Institutions are built to reward people who fit in, and a person building something genuinely new usually does not fit in. The Navy's promotion system worked exactly as designed. It just happened to be designed for a different job than the one that most needed doing.
Did you do your best?

Rickover understood that a reactor is only as safe as the people running it, so he chose them himself. For decades he personally interviewed officers who wanted into the nuclear program. The interviews became legendary for their strangeness: hostile questions, long silences, candidates sent to sit in a closet to think about an answer. Behind the theater was a single question, which was whether this person would tell the truth when it was uncomfortable.

The most famous of those interviews involved a young lieutenant named Jimmy Carter, who served under Rickover from 1952 to 1953. Carter, proud of his class standing, was asked whether he had done his best at the Naval Academy. He started to say yes, then stopped and admitted that he had not always done his best. Rickover asked one more question: why not? Then he ended the interview. Carter was accepted anyway, and more than twenty years later he used those two words as the title of the autobiography he published while running for president.
Why not?
blocks.by: Rickover to Jimmy Carter, as Carter told it in Why Not the Best? (1975)

blocks.text: Rickover also built the training pipeline that every modern nuke has gone through. He required that people in the program qualify on a land-based plant before being assigned to a nuclear-powered ship. The Idaho hull section was not just a test article. It became the first classroom. The logic was the same as the logic of the prototype itself: make your mistakes where the consequences are small, so you do not make them where the consequences are fatal.

items: **Responsibility is personal.** A problem belongs to a named person, not a committee.
**Technical facts beat rank.** An engineer who is right outranks an admiral who is wrong.
**Bad news travels up fast.** Hiding a problem is worse than having one.
**Train on the real thing.** Prototypes and qualification come before the ship, not after.

blocks.text: What he left behind

Rickover served 63 years, longer than almost anyone in the Navy's history. He died on July 8, 1986, in Arlington, Virginia, and is buried at Arlington National Cemetery. A Los Angeles-class attack submarine was named for him while he was still alive. The culture he built, with its procedures, its watch standards and its obsession with honest reporting, has been studied by NASA and the commercial nuclear industry, a story told in its own article in this library.

He was not a simple hero. He could be cruel to subordinates, he feuded endlessly, and by the end even many admirers thought he had stayed too long. In the early 1980s, the Navy's civilian leadership finally eased him out. But the thing he built outlasted all of it, and that is the point worth carrying away. Rickover's genius was not that he was likable or even that he was a great physicist. It was that he refused to accept that a hard thing had to be done slowly, and he refused to trust any result he had not tested himself.

For anyone building something on their own, whether it is a game, a channel or a business, the Idaho desert holds a useful idea. You can build the real thing and the test version at the same time, as long as the test version is honest. Make it the real shape and the real size. Run it longer than feels necessary. And when it breaks, be glad it broke in the desert.

takeaways: The nuclear Navy began with an electrical officer who treated an Oak Ridge study assignment as a mission.
Rickover built the prototype as a real hull section and started Nautilus before the prototype ever ran: speed with an honest test.
The Navy nearly forced out the man building its future; institutions reward fit, and new things rarely fit.
His interview question, 'Did you do your best?', was really a test of whether you would tell the truth about yourself.
Make mistakes where they are cheap: prototypes and qualification exist so the real thing does not fail.

title: Endurance: The Expedition That Failed Its Way Into Legend
dek: In 1915 the Antarctic ice crushed Shackleton's ship and left 28 men on a frozen sea, 1,000 miles from anyone. Every one of them came home. In 2022 the ship was found 3,008 meters down, her name still readable on the stern.

blocks.text: In March 2022, an underwater robot was sweeping the floor of the Weddell Sea off Antarctica, nearly two miles down, in water just below freezing. On a screen aboard the South African icebreaker *S.A. Agulhas II*, a shape appeared out of the dark: a wooden ship sitting upright on the seabed, masts toppled, rigging draped over the rails. Then the camera slid across the stern and found a single word arched over a star: ENDURANCE.

She had been lost since 21 November 1915, when the pack ice finally let her go and she slid under. The searchers found her about five nautical miles from where her captain, Frank Worsley, had calculated she sank, using a sextant, a chronometer and dead reckoning while camped on a moving ice floe. More than a century later, his numbers were good enough to find a shipwreck at 3,008 meters.
The ship is famous not because of what her expedition achieved. It achieved nothing it set out to do. She is famous because of what happened to the 28 men who were aboard her when the ice won.
The last great journey

By 1914 the South Pole had been reached, by Roald Amundsen in 1911. Ernest Shackleton, an Anglo-Irish explorer who had come within about a hundred miles of the Pole himself a few years earlier, wanted the one big prize left: walk across the entire continent, from the Weddell Sea to the Ross Sea, via the Pole. About 1,800 miles on foot, with dogs and sledges.

He called it the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition. A famous newspaper ad supposedly read "Men wanted for hazardous journey... safe return doubtful." Nobody has ever found the original, and historians think it is a myth. What is real is that more than 5,000 people applied. One ship, *Endurance*, would carry the crossing party south. A second, *Aurora*, would land a team on the far side to lay food depots for the end of the march.

*Endurance* sailed from South Georgia, a whaling island in the South Atlantic, on 5 December 1914. World War I had just begun. Shackleton had offered the ship and crew to the Navy, and was told to carry on.
Frozen in like an almond in chocolate

The Weddell Sea that year was choked with pack ice. *Endurance* pushed through for six weeks, sometimes making less than 30 nautical miles a day, and got within sight of the coast. Then, around 19 January 1915, the ice closed around her and never opened again.

They were stuck tantalizingly close to their planned landing site. The ship began drifting with the ice, slowly at first, then faster, northwest and away from the continent. Shackleton ordered normal ship routine dropped and turned the vessel into winter quarters. The sun set in May and would not rise again for months.

This is the part of the story that sounds most familiar to anyone who has spent long stretches sealed in a small space with the same people. Shackleton's main enemy for the next ten months was not cold. It was morale. He kept everyone on a schedule. Men exercised the dogs and raced them. They put on shows, celebrated every holiday they could find and took moonlit walks on the ice. He paid close attention to who was struggling and stepped in early.

In late October 1915, the ice began to squeeze. The hull bent and splintered, and timbers broke with noises the crew compared to gunfire. Water poured in. On 27 October, at about 5 p.m., with temperatures below minus 26 degrees Celsius, Shackleton gave the order to abandon ship. Three lifeboats, supplies and dogs went onto the ice. The wrecked hull stayed on the surface, held by the ice, for another three and a half weeks before sinking.
Living on a raft of ice

Now 28 men were camped on floating sea ice, roughly 350 miles from the nearest known food depot, with no radio contact and no one on Earth aware of where they were. The rules changed overnight. Shackleton ordered each man to keep only two pounds of personal gear. The photographer Frank Hurley had shot around 550 glass-plate negatives; he picked the best 120 and smashed the rest. The carpenter's cat, Mrs Chippy, was put down because there was no way to feed her.

They tried to march toward land, dragging lifeboats on sledges over ridges of broken ice. In three days they covered about two miles. A second attempt managed seven and a half miles in seven days. Shackleton calculated it would take more than 300 days to reach land at that rate and gave up. They would wait for the ice to carry them north and break up.

Not everyone took it calmly. On 27 December the carpenter, Harry McNish, refused to work, arguing that his duty ended when the ship sank. Shackleton faced him down and McNish went back to hauling. Shackleton never forgave him, even though McNish's craftsmanship would later help save all their lives.

They spent more than three months on a floe they named Patience Camp. Food ran short. They lived mostly on seal and penguin. The dogs were shot, and eventually eaten. On 9 April 1916, their floe split under the camp, and they launched the three lifeboats into a sea full of grinding ice.

blocks.text: Eight hundred miles in a lifeboat

Six days of rowing and sailing through freezing spray, with almost no sleep, brought them to Elephant Island, a lump of rock and glacier off the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula. It was the first time they had stood on land in 497 days. It was also a place no ship ever visited. Staying meant dying slowly.

The nearest place with people who could help was the whaling stations on South Georgia, about 800 miles away across the Southern Ocean, the stormiest water on the planet. Shackleton chose the strongest lifeboat, the *James Caird*, just 22.5 feet long. McNish raised her sides and built a makeshift deck from canvas, sledge runners and boxes. Shackleton picked five men to go with him: Worsley, the navigator; Tom Crean, a tough Irish sailor and Antarctic veteran; McNish; and seamen John Vincent and Timothy McCarthy. He took food for four weeks. If they had not reached land by then, they never would.

They launched on 24 April 1916. Everything was soaked, all the time. Ice built up on the boat and had to be chipped off to keep her from capsizing. Worsley managed only a few sextant sights in the whole voyage, snatching the sun through brief gaps in the cloud while the boat pitched under him. The margin was brutal: miss South Georgia, a target about 100 miles long, and there was nothing beyond it but thousands of miles of open ocean.

Around midnight one night, Shackleton, at the tiller, saw what he thought was a line of clear sky. It was the crest of an enormous wave. In his own account he wrote that in 26 years at sea he had never seen one so big. The boat was flung forward and half filled, and the men bailed for their lives. On 8 May, after 14 days, they sighted the cliffs of South Georgia. A hurricane kept them off the coast for two more days. They landed on 10 May.

blocks.text: The walk across the mountains

They had landed on the wrong side of the island. The whaling stations were on the north coast. The boat was too battered and two of the men too weak for another voyage around the coast. So Shackleton, Worsley and Crean set out to cross South Georgia's mountainous interior, which had never been crossed, with no map, a length of rope, a carpenter's adze for an ice axe, and screws driven through their boot soles for grip.

They walked for 36 hours without stopping to sleep. At one point, trapped on a ridge with night falling, they coiled the rope into a makeshift sledge, held on to each other and slid down a mountainside into the dark. At 7 a.m. on 20 May, they heard the steam whistle at Stromness whaling station calling the men to work. It was the first sound from the outside world they had heard in 17 months. They walked in, filthy and bearded, and frightened the children who saw them.

All three later said they had felt the presence of a fourth person walking with them across the mountains. Shackleton wrote that it seemed to him "often that we were four, not three." Mountaineers, divers and polar explorers have reported the same experience under extreme stress. It even ended up in a T. S. Eliot poem.
All safe, all well

Rescuing the 22 men on Elephant Island took four tries. A whaler, a Uruguayan trawler and a schooner were all turned back by pack ice. Meanwhile, on the island, Frank Wild, Shackleton's second in command, held the group together under two upturned boats. He kept a permanent lookout and cooking rotas, ran Saturday concerts, and refused to let anyone talk as if rescue might not come. The surgeons amputated the frostbitten toes of the youngest man, Perce Blackborow, by candlelight, using the last of their chloroform.

On 30 August 1916, the small Chilean Navy tug *Yelcho*, commanded by Luis Pardo, came through a gap in the ice. Shackleton stood in the bow of a boat shouting to ask if everyone was well. Wild answered that they were. All 22 were alive. Within an hour they were aboard.

The full record is less tidy than the legend. On the other side of the continent, the *Aurora* party, which had faithfully laid depots for a crossing that never came, was stranded when their ship blew out to sea. Three of them died. Shackleton had cut that team's budget in half and never sent word that the crossing was delayed. And the Weddell Sea men came home to a world war. Two of them, McCarthy and Alfred Cheetham, were killed within two years. Shackleton himself died of a heart attack on South Georgia in 1922, on yet another expedition.

blocks.text: Why a failure became the story

Endurance was found in a remarkable state because of where she lies. The cold, dark water of the Weddell Sea lacks the wood-eating shipworms that destroy wrecks elsewhere. The 2022 team, organized by the Falklands Maritime Heritage Trust, filmed and 3D-scanned her but touched nothing. She is a protected monument under the Antarctic Treaty.

Finding her took more than a good robot. Earlier searches had failed, and one in 2019 lost its underwater vehicle under the ice. Before the 2022 attempt, researchers went back to Worsley's original logbooks and re-ran the timings he and the expedition physicist had made of the Moon passing in front of stars, using modern star catalogues to correct the old position. In other words, the wreck was found partly by re-checking a 107-year-old sailor's math, and discovering that it was very nearly right.

It is worth asking why we remember this expedition and not the one that actually succeeded at something. The answer says a lot about what leadership is. Shackleton's original goal died in the ice in 1915. Most leaders would have spent the next year trying to save the plan, or mourning it. He dropped it almost immediately and replaced it with a single goal anyone could understand: everybody gets home. Then he made every decision, from the two-pound gear limit to which camp to stay on, serve that goal.

The other lesson is quieter. Survival on the ice and on Elephant Island did not come from heroics. It came from routine: a watch kept even when no ship had ever come, meals at fixed times, concerts on Saturdays, a leader who checked on the men who were sinking into despair. Endurance, in practice, was mostly the discipline of doing small ordinary things well for a very long time.
When the plan dies, the best leaders do not hold its funeral. They pick a new goal fast, make it simple enough for everyone to repeat, and build every routine around it.

takeaways: Shackleton's expedition failed every goal it set, yet all 28 men of the Weddell Sea party survived nearly two years stranded.
The James Caird crossed about 800 miles of the Southern Ocean in a 22.5-foot boat, guided by a handful of sextant sights.
Morale was managed like a resource: schedules, lookouts, concerts and close attention to the people who were struggling.
The legend leaves things out: three men of the Ross Sea party died, partly because of Shackleton's planning and budget cuts.
In 2022 the wreck was found 3,008 meters down, close to where Worsley's century-old navigation said she sank.

title: The Silk Road Was Never a Road
dek: For about 1,500 years a web of caravan trails linked China to the Mediterranean. It carried silk, but also paper, religions, camels, parasites and plague. The most important things it moved were the ones nobody was selling.

blocks.text: In the desert of northwest China, near the oasis town of Dunhuang, archaeologists excavated the latrine of a Han dynasty relay station called Xuanquanzhi. The station was built in 111 BCE and used until about 109 CE. It gave travelers a bed and gave government couriers a fresh horse. In the latrine, the excavators found something unusual: wooden sticks with cloth wrapped around one end, the ancient version of toilet paper. Some still had dried feces on them.

In 2016, a team of researchers who study ancient parasites examined those sticks under a microscope. They found the eggs of whipworm, roundworm, tapeworm and the Chinese liver fluke. The last one is the surprise. The liver fluke needs a wet environment with snails and freshwater fish to complete its life cycle, and Dunhuang sits on the edge of one of the driest deserts on Earth. The nearest area where it was common in the 20th century is about 1,500 kilometers away.

Someone had caught it in the well-watered east or south of China, then traveled a very long way before stopping to use that latrine. It is the earliest archaeological proof that people moving along the Silk Road carried disease with them. It is also a reminder of what trade networks really are. They carry whatever is moving through them, wanted or not. The other parasites on those sticks, whipworm and roundworm, spread through food and water contaminated with human waste. Travelers on the road were eating from the same pots and drinking from the same wells, and they carried the consequences home.

blocks.text: A name invented in 1877

Nobody who traveled it called it the Silk Road. The name was popularized in 1877 by Ferdinand von Richthofen, a German geographer who made seven expeditions to China. He wrote of the *Seidenstrasse*, the silk road, and the romantic label stuck. Even Marco Polo, the traveler most linked with it, never used the term. Some historians today prefer Silk Routes, because the word road suggests something that never existed.

There was no single highway from China to Rome. There was a shifting web of trails, river crossings, mountain passes and oasis towns, stretching more than 6,400 kilometers overland, plus sea lanes running alongside it. Routes split around the Taklamakan Desert, one skirting the north edge, one the south. Wars, droughts and changing dynasties opened some paths and closed others for decades at a time.

Very few people ever traveled the whole thing. Instead, goods moved in what historians call relay trade. A bolt of silk might change hands many times, each merchant carrying it a few hundred miles to the next market and selling it at a markup. A Roman buying silk had no idea where it came from. Famously, Roman writers like Virgil and Seneca thought silk was combed from the leaves of trees. Pliny the Elder knew better, describing creatures that spun webs like spiders.

Travel was slow and dangerous. The network was decentralized, and for long stretches no one was in charge of security. Caravans faced bandits, raids by nomadic horsemen, mountain passes, and deserts where a missed well could kill a whole party. That is part of why relay trade made sense. A merchant who knew one stretch well, its wells, its tolls and its local rulers, could move goods across it far more safely than an outsider trying to cross the entire continent.
