title: The Wright Brothers Didn't Have a Better Engine. They Had Better Data.
dek: In December 1903 the best-funded flying machine in America fell into the Potomac. Nine days later two bicycle makers from Ohio flew. The difference was a homemade wind tunnel and a willingness to doubt the experts.

blocks.text: On December 8, 1903, a strange machine sat on top of a houseboat on the Potomac River in Washington, D.C. It had two pairs of wings set one behind the other, spanning nearly 50 feet, and an engine that produced a remarkable 52.4 horsepower. The War Department had put $50,000 into it. Its designer, Samuel Langley, was the head of the Smithsonian Institution and one of the most respected scientists in America.

The catapult fired. The Aerodrome, as Langley called it, reared up, folded in on itself and plunged into the freezing river, trapping its pilot under the wreckage until he was pulled out. It was the machine's second crash in two months. Newspapers mocked it, the government refused more money, and Langley never tried again.

Nine days later, on a cold beach in North Carolina, a machine built by two bicycle shop owners from Dayton, Ohio, lifted off under its own power with a man aboard. Its engine made about 12 horsepower. The Wrights had no government grant, no university position and no engineering degrees. What they had was a method, and that method is the real invention.

blocks.title: Engine power, 1903
blocks.note: The machine with more than four times the power never flew as built.
blocks.source: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, Langley Aerodrome A and 1903 Wright Flyer collection records

blocks.text: Two brothers and a box

Wilbur and Orville Wright had been tinkering since childhood. When they were boys, their father brought home a toy helicopter powered by twisted rubber bands, and they built bigger copies of it. As adults they ran a printing business and then a bicycle shop, where they built and sold their own bikes. What turned them toward flight was a death: in 1896, the German glider pioneer Otto Lilienthal crashed and was killed.

On May 30, 1899, Wilbur wrote to the Smithsonian asking for whatever it had on aeronautics. The reading convinced the brothers that most experimenters were focused on the wrong problem. Inventors were building bigger engines and bigger wings. But nobody had worked out how a pilot would actually control a machine in the air, balancing it in gusts and turning it on purpose. Lilienthal had steered his gliders by swinging his body around, and it had killed him.

Bicycles gave the brothers an important intuition. A bicycle is unstable when it stands still, yet a trained rider controls it easily by making constant small corrections. They suspected an airplane could work the same way: it didn't need to be perfectly stable, it needed to be controllable. Their solution was wing warping, twisting the tips of the wings in opposite directions with cables so that one side lifted more than the other, rolling the machine like a bike leaning into a turn.

They tested it cheaply first. In the summer of 1899 they built a biplane kite with a five-foot wingspan and flew it from a field in Dayton, twisting the wings with control lines. The only witnesses were some schoolboys who watched a grown man in business clothes playing with an odd kite. It responded quickly and precisely. The control idea worked, and it had cost them almost nothing to find out.
When the numbers lied

Dayton was too calm and too crowded for full-sized gliders, so the brothers asked the US Weather Bureau where to find steady wind and soft sand. The answer was Kitty Hawk, a tiny fishing village on the Outer Banks of North Carolina. In September 1900 they made their first trip there with a piloted glider. The controls worked well. The lift was a disappointment.

In 1901 they came back with a bigger glider, the largest anyone had built, and it was worse. It produced only about a third of the lift their calculations predicted, and it had new control problems: when they warped the wings to turn, the glider would start to turn and then swing the opposite way. Wilbur went home deeply discouraged. He later admitted that around this time he told Orville that people would not fly for fifty years.

Here is where most people would have quit, or blamed their own workmanship. The Wrights did something else. Their gliders had been designed with the accepted equations for lift, using Lilienthal's published tables and a number called the Smeaton coefficient, which described air pressure on a surface. The brothers began to suspect that the problem was not their glider. It was the data everyone had been relying on.

First they rigged a test on a bicycle. They mounted a free-spinning wheel flat across the front, attached a model wing and a flat plate to its rim, and pedaled hard so the moving air pushed on both until the wheel settled into balance. The result suggested a wing had to meet the wind at more than three times the angle Lilienthal's data predicted. Something in the accepted numbers was badly off.
A wind tunnel in a bike shop

In the fall of 1901, after a quick trial with a small one, they built a proper wind tunnel. Others had used wind tunnels before, but the Wrights' innovation was the instruments inside: two balances they designed to measure the lift and drag on small model wings in numbers they could plug straight into the design equations. Between October and December 1901, they ran preliminary tests on as many as 200 wing shapes and made formal, recorded tests on nearly 50, varying curvature, thickness and proportions.

The results were a revelation. The tunnel let them check Lilienthal's table against his own wing shape and gather data on dozens of others. The biggest error was the Smeaton coefficient, a number that had been in use since the 1700s. Everyone, including Lilienthal and Langley, used a value of about 0.005. Using their Kitty Hawk glider measurements and the lift equation, the Wrights calculated a value closer to 0.0033. Modern physics puts it at about 0.00327. Generations of experimenters had been designing wings with a number that was off by roughly half.

blocks.title: The Smeaton coefficient: accepted vs measured
blocks.note: An inflated coefficient makes every wing look like it will lift more than it does.
blocks.source: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics: Smeaton Coefficient; Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

items.label: Wing shapes given preliminary tests in the wind tunnel
Shapes formally tested and recorded
October to December 1901

blocks.source: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, Researching the Wright Way

blocks.text: The Wrights' breakthrough was not courage or genius in the movie sense. It was refusing to treat a published number as true just because everyone used it, and then building a cheap tool to check it themselves.

Their 1902 glider, designed from the tunnel data, finally worked. To fix the strange reverse turns, they added a vertical tail, then made it movable and linked it to the wing warping so the two worked together. That gave them control in all three axes: pitch, roll and yaw. Every airplane since, from Piper Cubs to F-35s, is controlled in those same three axes.

Their layout also had a safety feature built in. The Wrights put the elevator, the surface that controls pitch, in front of the wings rather than behind them. With that arrangement, called a canard, a machine that stalls tends to settle rather than drop violently. A violent stall is what killed Lilienthal. The Smithsonian notes that the forward elevator saved the brothers' lives on several occasions. Their designs were full of details like this, down to making the 1903 Flyer's right wing four inches longer than the left to balance the engine, which was heavier than the pilot beside it.

That fall they made somewhere between 700 and 1,000 glides at Kitty Hawk. The best covered 622.5 feet in 26 seconds. Just as important, the brothers became genuinely skilled pilots. While other experimenters tried to leap straight to powered flight, the Wrights had spent hundreds of flights learning to fly before they ever added an engine.
Twelve seconds

Powered flight still needed two things they could not buy. No carmaker could supply an engine light enough, so their shop mechanic, Charlie Taylor, did nearly all the machining for a small four-cylinder engine with an aluminum crankcase, the first use of aluminum in an aircraft engine. It made about 12 horsepower. The propellers were harder. There was no theory for them, so the Wrights invented one, treating each propeller as a wing turned on its side and spinning, producing forward lift.

They returned to Kitty Hawk in September 1903 and spent weeks assembling the Flyer and fighting problems with its propeller shafts. On December 14, Wilbur won a coin toss and made the first try, but the attempt failed and the machine was slightly damaged. After repairs, they were ready again. On December 17, in a cold, strong wind, it was Orville's turn.

At 10:35 a.m. the Flyer lifted off and flew for 12 seconds, covering 120 feet. The brothers made three more flights that morning, taking turns. On the fourth, Wilbur stayed up for 59 seconds and covered 852 feet. Then, as they stood around discussing it, a gust caught the parked Flyer and sent it tumbling across the sand. It was badly damaged and never flew again. It didn't need to.

items.label: First flight, 120 feet, Orville at the controls
Best flight that day, 852 feet, Wilbur
Wilbur's flight of October 5, 1905, covering 24.5 miles

blocks.source: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, 1903 Wright Flyer

blocks.text: Those first hops were just the start of the engineering. Over the next two years, flying from a cow pasture called Huffman Prairie outside Dayton, the brothers refined the design into a practical airplane that could bank, circle and stay up. On October 5, 1905, Wilbur flew for 39 minutes and covered 24.5 miles. The airplane was no longer a stunt. It was a machine.

Strangely, much of the world didn't believe it. The brothers were secretive while they tried to secure patents and sell their airplane, and few reporters bothered to come and watch. Skeptics, especially in France, called them bluffers. That changed in August 1908, when Wilbur flew in public near Le Mans, banking and circling with an ease no European aviator could match. Within days, many of the same critics were praising them.

The original 1903 Flyer, meanwhile, had a rough retirement. After the crash at Kitty Hawk, the brothers crated it and shipped it home, where it sat in a shed behind the bicycle shop for more than a decade. In March 1913, a great flood swept through Dayton and the crates sat submerged in water and mud for eleven days. The airplane was not uncrated until 1916, when Orville repaired it for an exhibition at MIT.
The fight over who was first

The story has a bitter epilogue. In 1914 the Smithsonian hired aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss, who was locked in a patent fight with the Wrights, to rebuild Langley's Aerodrome. With significant changes, he got it to make a few short hops. The Smithsonian then put the Aerodrome on display, restored to its original form, with a label that misleadingly suggested it was the first airplane capable of manned flight.

Wilbur had died of typhoid in 1912. Orville, furious, did the one thing guaranteed to embarrass the Smithsonian: in 1928 he sent the original 1903 Flyer to the Science Museum in London. It stayed in Britain for twenty years, and during World War II it was stored in an underground facility outside London alongside other national treasures. The Smithsonian finally corrected the record in 1942. The Flyer came home in 1948, the year Orville died, and was unveiled in Washington on December 17, the 45th anniversary of the first flight.
The method is the invention

blocks.title: The Wright method
items: Identify the real bottleneck (control, not power).
Test the core idea cheaply first, with a kite.
Fly real prototypes and measure what actually happens.
When results disagree with theory, question the theory's data.
Build your own tool to get better data, then redesign.
Practice until you're skilled before raising the stakes.

blocks.text: Langley's approach was to scale up a working model and pour in money and horsepower. It is a common strategy in any field, and it fails whenever the underlying assumptions are wrong, because spending more just builds a bigger version of the mistake. The Wrights spent their money on finding out what was true, then built exactly what the truth required.

The pattern shows up everywhere. A game developer can follow published advice about what players want, or watch real players and record where they get stuck. A trainee can memorize procedures, or understand the system well enough to notice when the gauges don't match the theory. The Wrights' advantage was not that they were smarter than everyone else. It was that they trusted measurements over reputations, including their own.

takeaways: Identify the real bottleneck. Everyone else chased engine power; the Wrights solved control first.
When results don't match the theory, check the theory's inputs. The accepted Smeaton coefficient was off by about half.
Test ideas cheaply before scaling them, the way a kite proved wing warping.
Skill compounds: hundreds of glider flights made them pilots before they ever added an engine.
Money and horsepower can't fix a design built on wrong assumptions.

title: Chernobyl: The Night the Stop Button Started It
dek: At 01:23:40 an operator pressed the button designed to shut the reactor down. Understanding why that made things worse explains the entire disaster.

blocks.text: At 01:23:40 on 26 April 1986, an operator in the control room of Chernobyl unit 4 pressed AZ-5, the emergency button that drives every control and safety rod into the core. It is the most basic safety action in reactor operation, the move every operator is trained to make when things look wrong. Three seconds later, reactor power had passed 530 megawatts thermal and was still climbing. Within seconds more, the core had torn itself apart.

The usual story of Chernobyl is reckless operators breaking rules during a late-night test. That story is not wrong, but it is incomplete in a way that matters. The reactor had a design flaw that turned the shutdown button, under the conditions that night, into an accelerator. The flaw had been seen three years earlier at another plant. The fix was promised and never made. The operators had never been told.
Here is the sequence, decision by decision, and what it teaches anyone who runs a plant that can hurt people.
A reactor with a hidden trapdoor

Chernobyl 4 was an RBMK-1000, a Soviet design found nowhere outside the Soviet Union. It produced 3,200 megawatts of heat and 1,000 megawatts of electricity. Unlike Western light water reactors, it used blocks of graphite as the moderator to slow neutrons, while ordinary water flowed up through hundreds of vertical pressure tubes as the coolant, boiling as it rose. Fuel was only about 2% enriched. There was no Western-style containment building. The core, about 7 metres high and 12 metres across, sat under a 1,000-tonne steel cover plate.

Separating the moderator from the coolant created the first trap. In a water-moderated reactor, steam bubbles mean less moderation and less power. In an RBMK, the graphite keeps moderating no matter what the water does, but the water also absorbs neutrons. Turn water to steam and you remove an absorber without removing the moderator, so power goes up. This is a positive void coefficient. In a fresh core it was small and manageable. But as fuel burned and absorbers were removed, and especially at low power with most control rods pulled out, it could grow large enough to dominate everything else.

The second trap was in the control rods. Most RBMK rods had a 4.5-metre graphite section, called a displacer, attached below the boron absorber. With a rod fully withdrawn, the displacer sat in the middle of the core with about 1.25 metres of water beneath it in the channel. When the rod started to fall, the first thing to happen at the bottom of the core was graphite replacing that water. Less absorber, same moderation: a brief burst of added reactivity at the core bottom before the boron arrived. Full insertion took about 18 seconds.

blocks.title: What the crew believed versus what was true

left.head: Belief that night
items: Pressing AZ-5 always reduces power
The 15-rod margin exists so there are enough rods to shape and steer power
The rundown test is an electrical test, not a nuclear one
Low power is a safe place to wait

right.head: Reality
items: With rods fully withdrawn, the first seconds of a scram added reactivity at the bottom of the core
The margin also kept the void coefficient tolerable and the scram effective, a reason the operators were never taught
The test cut coolant flow through an unstable core
At low power with rods out, the RBMK was at its most dangerous

blocks.text: A test nobody treated as nuclear

Unit 4 was due for a routine maintenance shutdown on 25 April. The plan was to use the shutdown to run a test: if the plant lost outside power, could the turbine, coasting down, generate enough electricity to keep the main coolant pumps running until the diesel generators took over? The test had been tried the year before and failed because the turbine's output dropped off too fast. New voltage regulators had been built, and this was the retry.

The test was viewed as an electrical exercise, and it was planned without real coordination between the people running it and the people responsible for reactor safety. The program even called for isolating the emergency core cooling system so it would not interrupt the test. That did not cause the accident, but it showed how the test was regarded.

Then the grid intervened. The power reduction began at 01:06 on 25 April and was halted at 1,600 megawatts thermal, half power, at 03:47. At 14:00 the emergency cooling system was isolated as planned. But the grid controller in Kiev asked the plant to keep supplying power to meet demand, and the reactor sat at half power for most of the day. Reductions resumed only at 23:10. The test that would have happened on the day shift slid onto the night shift, after the midnight turnover.
The night, step by step

At 00:05 on 26 April, power was down to 720 megawatts and still dropping. At 00:28, with power around 500 megawatts, control was transferred between regulating systems, and power unexpectedly plunged to about 30 megawatts, essentially near shutdown. Whether an operator missed a setting or the system failed to respond is still debated.

That plunge set a second trap. At low power, xenon-135, a strong neutron absorber produced by fission products, builds up in the fuel faster than it burns away. The core was poisoning itself. To claw power back, operators withdrew control rods, many of them. By 01:00 power had recovered only to about 200 megawatts, well below the 700 to 1,000 megawatts the test plan called for. The decision was made to run the test anyway, at 200.

blocks.title: Chernobyl 4 thermal power before the explosion
blocks.note: The last point is a floor: power passed 530 MWt and kept rising toward many times the 3,200 MWt rating.
blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Chernobyl Accident Appendix 1: Sequence of Events

blocks.text: Next, at 01:03 and 01:07, two additional main circulating pumps were started as part of the test program. More flow through the core carried heat away faster, cooled the water and reduced boiling, which in this reactor reduced reactivity, so still more rods came out. The flow exceeded allowed limits and the steam drum levels became hard to control. Around 01:19, with drum level near its emergency setpoint, the operator increased feedwater, which cooled the core further and forced even more rod withdrawal. With pressure and level control giving them trouble, the crew disabled the automatic trips on the steam drums.

Post-accident calculations found that at 01:22:30 the operating reactivity margin, the number of equivalent control rods still in the core, was eight. The operating rules required at least fifteen. The reactor was now at low power, most of its rods pulled out, its coolant near the boiling point, and its void coefficient strongly positive. The crew may not have known the margin had been violated. The IAEA later noted that the margin was not conveniently available to the operators and was not tied into the reactor protection system.

items.label: Operating reactivity margin at 01:22:30
Minimum the operating rules required
Time for a full scram insertion, before post-accident fixes

blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Chernobyl Appendix 1 and RBMK Reactors

blocks.text: At 01:23:04 the turbine stop valves closed and the test began. Four pumps began coasting down with the turbine. For about 30 seconds, according to the IAEA's later analysis, the unit's parameters stayed within expected limits. But reduced flow meant more boiling in the core, and more boiling meant more reactivity. At 01:23:40, AZ-5 was pressed. Analysts still debate whether the excursion started from boiling alone or was triggered by the scram itself. Either way, the rods began entering from the top, displacers first, adding reactivity at the bottom of a core that had almost none to spare.

At 01:23:43, power-excursion alarms sounded and power passed 530 megawatts. Fuel ruptured, steam generation surged, and the positive void coefficient fed it back into more power, toward around 100 times the reactor's rated output. Pressure from ruptured channels lifted the 1,000-tonne upper plate, jamming the rods about halfway down. At 01:24 the chief reactor control engineer logged severe shocks and rods that had stopped moving. Two explosions followed, seconds apart: first steam, then probably hydrogen from zirconium reacting with steam.
Ten days of fire

The explosions killed two workers. Roughly a quarter of the core's 1,200 tonnes of graphite was thrown out, and burning graphite and fuel started fires across the site, including on the bitumen roof of the turbine hall. The first 14 firefighters arrived at 01:28. Roof fires were out by about 05:00, but the exposed core kept burning. From the second to the tenth day, helicopters made about 1,800 flights to drop roughly 5,000 tonnes of boron carbide, lead, sand, clay and dolomite onto it. Radioactive material poured out for about 10 days, about 14 exabecquerels in total, over half of it noble gases.

Pripyat, the plant's town of about 45,000 people three kilometres away, was evacuated on 27 April, the day after the explosion. By 14 May about 116,000 people within 30 kilometres had been moved, and about 220,000 more were resettled in later years.

By the end of July 1986, 28 people, six of them firemen, had died of acute radiation syndrome. Acute radiation syndrome was confirmed in 134 people. Among people who were children at the time, about 20,000 thyroid cancers were diagnosed between 1991 and 2015; UNSCEAR judged that about a quarter were probably caused by radiation, mostly through iodine-131 in milk, with wide uncertainty. Fifteen of the cases diagnosed through 2005 proved fatal. UN bodies have found no clear rise in other cancers in the general population. The question is not fully closed: the NRC notes that a 2015 study found a statistically significant increase in solid cancer risk among emergency workers. Much larger death tolls that still circulate have been dismissed by UNSCEAR as unsupported by scientific assessment.
Who was to blame?

The first international review, INSAG-1 in 1986, put most of the weight on operator violations. Six years later, the IAEA's INSAG-7 revised that view. A Soviet state commission had found that the positive scram effect was identified at the Ignalina RBMK plant in Lithuania in 1983. The chief design organization told other RBMK plants it would restrict full rod withdrawal and fix the rods. Neither happened, and the matter was apparently forgotten. The operators were also never told the specific safety significance of the reactivity margin. A rule existed; the reason for it did not reach the people who had to obey it.

Even the question of which rules were broken is murkier than the popular version suggests. The operating procedures themselves were ambiguous in places. The deputy chief engineer who supervised the test, Anatoly Dyatlov, acknowledged choosing a lower test power than first planned but argued that the regulations allowed it. A 1991 Soviet state report concluded that while the crew had put the reactor in a condition that made an accident almost inevitable, several of the vital safety principles they supposedly broke had never actually been spelled out for them. You can be harsh about the judgment shown that night and still recognise that the system had set them up to fail.

After the accident, every RBMK was modified. The required margin was raised from 26 to 30 equivalent rods in steady operation to 43 to 48. Enrichment went from 2% to 2.4% to support extra fixed absorbers that tamed the void coefficient. Rods were redesigned so no water column could sit beneath a withdrawn displacer, scram time was cut from 18 to 12 seconds, and a fast-acting system was added that could insert strong negative reactivity in under 2.5 seconds.

blocks.title: How the flaw went from known to catastrophic
items: Positive scram effect identified at Ignalina; fixes promised to all RBMK plants
Promised rod restrictions and design changes never made
Test delayed by grid demand into the night shift
Power drops to about 30 MWt; xenon builds; rods withdrawn
AZ-5 pressed; displacers add reactivity at the core bottom
Explosions destroy unit 4
IAEA's INSAG-7 shifts emphasis from operators to design and safety culture

blocks.text: A procedure limit without its reason is fragile. The crew understood the 15-rod margin as a tool for steering power. Had they known it was also what kept the scram from making things worse, they would have been far less likely to trade it away to finish a test.

The lesson that lasts is not that Soviet operators were reckless, or even that the RBMK was badly designed, though both are partly true. It is that a dangerous condition was known, written down, and allowed to fade, while the people closest to it were left without the knowledge that would have made the rules make sense. That failure mode is not Soviet. It shows up anywhere schedule pressure, a culture that does not question, and a gap between designers and operators line up on the same night. The best protection is boring and personal: know the reason behind every limit you stand watch over, and treat any test that touches a reactor as a reactor test.

takeaways: The RBMK combined a positive void coefficient with control rods whose graphite tips briefly added reactivity when inserted.
Grid demand pushed the test to the night shift; a power drop to about 30 MWt led operators to pull nearly all rods.
At 01:22:30 the reactivity margin was 8 equivalent rods, against a required 15; the scram at 01:23:40 triggered or worsened the excursion.
The positive scram effect was identified in 1983, but the promised fixes were never made and operators were never told.
Know the reason behind each operating limit; a limit understood only as paperwork is the first to be traded away.

title: The Duck That Swallowed California's Afternoon
dek: Solar power got so cheap and so plentiful that on spring middays California's wind and sun now out-produce the state's entire grid demand. The hard problem is no longer making clean energy. It is making it at 7 p.m.

blocks.text: At noon on Sunday, April 13, 2025, California's grid operator recorded something that would have sounded like science fiction a decade earlier. Net demand, the electricity the state needed after subtracting everything its wind and solar farms were producing, was negative 3,821 megawatts. Wind and sun were making more power than the entire grid was using.

Seven hours later, the sun was setting and the picture had flipped. Net demand was over 20,700 megawatts and climbing toward a peak near 22,700. In the space of an afternoon, the grid had to find more than 26,000 megawatts of other power, roughly the output of two dozen large 1,000-megawatt nuclear reactors, and bring it online in a few hours. That daily whiplash has a name in the power industry. They call it the duck.

blocks.title: California net demand, Sunday April 13, 2025
blocks.note: Net demand is total demand minus wind and solar output. Readings on the hour.
blocks.source: California ISO, Today's Outlook historical data, 2025

blocks.text: Drawing the duck

Grid operators care less about total demand than about net demand, because wind and solar run whenever the weather lets them, and everything else has to fill the gap. In the early 2010s, the California Independent System Operator, CAISO, plotted what net demand on a spring day would look like as more solar came online. The curves sagged lower each year in the middle of the day, then shot up steeply in the evening. Someone noticed the shape: a duck's tail in the early morning, a fat belly at midday, a tall arching neck at sunset.

CAISO's own explainer laid out the problem. As solar fades after about 4 p.m., the operator must call on other resources to meet the steepest ramp of the day. For its 2020 scenario, it projected the system would need to add about 13,000 megawatts in roughly three hours. It flagged two other risks: oversupply, when there is more generation than demand, and weaker frequency response, because fewer spinning generators would be online to stabilize the grid automatically.

The duck shows up in winter too, just in a different pose. CAISO's study of a January day described four distinct ramps: an upward climb of about 8,000 megawatts starting around 4 a.m. as people wake up, a drop after sunrise as solar takes over, a steep rise of about 11,000 megawatts as the sun sets, and a final slide as people go to bed. Each ramp has to be met by machines that someone has scheduled, started and synchronized to the grid ahead of time.
The projection turned out to be conservative. The duck grew faster than its creators drew it.
The duck got deeper

Pull CAISO's published data for a similar day in successive years, a mid-April Sunday when demand is mild and sunshine strong, and you can watch the belly sink. On April 14, 2019, net demand bottomed out at about 6,900 megawatts. On April 11, 2021, it reached about 4,600. On April 16, 2023, it briefly went below zero. On April 13, 2025, it fell to about negative 3,800.

Here is the striking part. Total demand on those days barely changed. The highest demand of the day was about 25,200 megawatts in 2019 and about 25,500 in 2025. Californians did not suddenly use less power at noon. What changed was supply: peak solar output on the grid went from about 8,000 megawatts on the 2019 day to about 18,600 on the 2025 day. The duck is not a story about demand. It is a story about one source growing so large that it reshapes the job of every other source.

blocks.title: Steepest 3-hour climb in net demand, mid-April Sundays
blocks.note: Largest rise in net demand over any three-hour window, always starting between about 4 and 5 p.m. Single days vary with weather; compare the trend, not one year.
blocks.source: Calculated from California ISO Today's Outlook data (Apr 14 2019, Apr 11 2021, Apr 16 2023, Apr 13 2025, Apr 12 2026)

blocks.text: The evening ramp grew with it. On the 2019 day, the steepest three-hour climb in net demand was about 12,900 megawatts, almost exactly what CAISO had forecast. By the 2025 day, it was about 21,200 megawatts. These are single days, and a cloudy or windless afternoon changes everything, but the direction is unmistakable. The duck's neck has become a cliff.

If you have stood a watch on a propulsion plant, the operator's problem will feel familiar. Steady state is easy. The hard moments are transients: big, fast changes in demand where every system has to respond in sequence and nothing can lag. The duck turns every sunny evening into a scheduled transient across an entire state, and the grid operator has to have the right equipment warmed up and ready before the sun goes down.
Why a glut of free power is a problem

Too much electricity sounds like a nice problem. It is not, because the grid has no slack. Supply and demand must match every second, or frequency drifts and protective relays start tripping equipment offline. When the sun overproduces, someone has to absorb or shed the excess.

The options are all imperfect. Neighboring states can import the surplus, if transmission and their own conditions allow. Prices can go negative, paying anyone who can use more or produce less. And operators can curtail, ordering solar and wind farms to throw away power they could have made. Meanwhile, plants that cannot ramp quickly, including nuclear reactors designed to run flat out, have to keep running through a midday glut and then the evening surge has to be met by something fast.

There is a deeper economic trap too. Every solar panel in California produces at the same time as every other one. The more solar a grid has, the lower the price at exactly the hours solar sells, so each new panel earns less than the last. Analysts call this value deflation or cannibalization. The energy is clean and cheap to make, but its timing makes it worth less. Solar did not run out of sunlight. It ran out of afternoon.

Electricity is not one product. A megawatt-hour at noon in April and a megawatt-hour at 7 p.m. in August are different goods with different prices. The grid's problem has shifted from making enough energy to making it at the right time.
Enter the batteries

The answer arriving fastest is the obvious one: store the noon surplus and release it after sunset. Until recently, batteries were too expensive to do this at grid scale. Then lithium-ion costs collapsed, driven largely by electric cars, and utility-scale battery installations took off.

The numbers from the US Energy Information Administration's generator inventory are startling. Battery systems that came online before 2021 and are still operating add up to about 1.5 gigawatts. By September 2026, the total operating battery capacity in the country was about 56 gigawatts, with more than 16 gigawatts added in 2025 alone. Texas, with about 19 gigawatts, and California, with about 16.5, hold most of it. Measured in power, America's batteries now exceed its pumped-hydro storage by more than two to one.

blocks.title: US utility-scale battery capacity, cumulative by year online
blocks.note: Nameplate capacity of batteries operating in September 2026, summed by the year each came online.
blocks.source: Calculated from US EIA Form 860M, Preliminary Monthly Electric Generator Inventory, September 2026

blocks.text: You can see them working in California's data. On the 2019 Sunday, batteries never discharged more than 76 megawatts. On the 2025 day, they soaked up about 7,000 megawatts at noon, much of the solar surplus, and pushed out about 7,800 megawatts at 7:30 in the evening, right on the duck's neck. The same machines that charge on the belly now discharge on the cliff.

How a battery plant earns money explains why it behaves this way. It buys power when prices are low and sells when they are high, a trade called arbitrage, and it also gets paid for standing by to correct the grid's frequency in an instant. In 2021, according to the EIA, frequency regulation was the most common job for US grid batteries, reported for 63% of battery capacity, while storing excess solar and wind was reported for only 30%. Most systems do several jobs. As the duck deepened, the midday-to-evening spread became one of the most reliable trades on the grid, and batteries followed the money.

blocks.title: Peak battery output in California, mid-April Sundays
blocks.source: California ISO, Today's Outlook fuel source data

blocks.text: Texas shows the same pattern from the market side. The ERCOT market monitor reported that as solar surged at midday, real-time prices dropped, sometimes below zero, letting batteries charge cheaply or even get paid to charge. Storage also took over much of the job of keeping reserves ready, which helped cut the cost of those reserve services sharply in 2024.
What batteries can't do yet

Batteries are a superb answer to the daily duck. They are a weak answer, so far, to longer problems. The EIA data implies the typical American grid battery holds roughly two to three hours of energy at full power. That is ideal for shifting noon solar to evening. It does almost nothing for a week of cloudy, windless winter weather, or for a multi-day emergency like the Texas freeze of 2021.

There is also a seasonal mismatch. California's solar output is strongest in late spring and summer, while some grids face their hardest days in winter, when the sun is low and heating demand is high. A battery that cycles once a day cannot carry summer sunshine into January. Covering those gaps takes either a lot more storage of a different kind, more transmission to borrow power from distant regions where the weather differs, or plants that can run on demand for days.

The old storage technology fills part of that gap. Pumped-storage hydro uses cheap power to pump water uphill into a reservoir and lets it run back down through turbines when power is needed. The US had 40 such plants in 18 states in 2022, with about 22 gigawatts of capacity, most built in the 1970s. The largest, Bath County in Virginia, can deliver about 2,860 megawatts for six hours or more. But good sites are scarce and new projects take many years.

blocks.title: Two ways to store a grid's worth of energy

left.head: Lithium-ion batteries
items: About 56 GW in the US by Sept 2026, mostly built since 2021
Typically a few hours of storage
Can be built in months, almost anywhere

Degrade with use; fire risk must be managed

items: About 22 GW in the US, mostly from the 1970s
Often six hours or more

Spinning machines that also help stabilize the grid
Lasts for many decades

blocks.text: Where firm power fits

The duck curve changes what the grid values. In a fossil-fuel world, the most valuable plants were the cheapest per megawatt-hour. In a solar-heavy world, plain megawatt-hours at noon are almost worthless, and the valuable things are flexibility, which means ramping fast, and firmness, which means being there at 7 p.m. in a heat wave or at 6 a.m. in a freeze.

That reframes the debate over nuclear power. A reactor that runs flat out is a poor fit for the duck's belly, where its output just adds to the glut. But it is a strong fit for the long nights, the windless weeks and the winter peaks that batteries cannot yet cover. Engineers already know reactors can follow load; naval reactors change power constantly to match what the ship needs. Whether civilian plants are designed and paid to do that is mostly a question of market rules, not physics.

Supply is only half of the toolkit. The other half is moving demand. Utilities increasingly charge different prices at different times of day, which nudges people to run dishwashers, charge cars and pre-cool houses during the sunny hours instead of after sunset. Electric vehicles parked at work could soak up midday solar the way batteries do. Larger regional markets help too, letting California send its noon surplus to neighbors and import their power at night. None of these alone flattens the duck, but each one shaves a little off the neck.

The bigger lesson is that solving one problem reveals the next one. Clean power was once too expensive. Now it is cheap but arrives at the wrong time. Batteries are fixing the daily timing gap, and the remaining problem is the rare long gap. Each layer of the solution makes the next layer visible. That is how most hard engineering problems actually get solved: not with one breakthrough, but by stacking fixes until what is left is small enough to handle.

takeaways: Net demand is total demand minus wind and solar; its daily shape in California looks like a duck.
The midday belly has sunk below zero on some spring days, and evening ramps now exceed what CAISO projected.
More solar lowers prices exactly when solar produces, so timing, not cost, is now the main challenge.
US grid batteries grew from about 1.5 GW (pre-2021) to about 56 GW by September 2026, and they now shift noon solar into the evening.
Batteries handle hours; long, multi-day gaps still need firm power such as nuclear, hydro or gas.

title: Why the Last Power Plant Sets Everyone's Price
dek: In most of the US grid, electricity is sold in an auction that runs every few minutes, and every winner gets paid the price of the most expensive plant needed. That one rule explains cheap wind, struggling reactors, negative prices and a $59 billion week in Texas.

blocks.text: In 2020, the average wholesale price of electricity in Texas was $25.73 per megawatt-hour. In 2021 it was $167.88, more than six times higher. Almost all of that jump came from a single week in February, when Winter Storm Uri froze the state. For several days the price sat pinned at the legal maximum of $9,000 per megawatt-hour, roughly 350 times the previous year's average. The independent market monitor later calculated that the electricity traded during the event was valued at $59 billion.

To understand how that is possible, and why it is not a glitch but the system working as designed, you need to understand one rule. It also explains why wind farms sometimes pay people to take their power, why some excellent nuclear plants closed for economic reasons, and why a reactor that shut down in 2019 is being restarted for a tech company. The rule is this: in a competitive electricity market, the last plant needed sets the price for everyone.
An auction every few minutes

Across much of the United States, an independent grid operator runs a wholesale electricity market. Examples include ERCOT in Texas, CAISO in California and PJM in the mid-Atlantic. Electricity cannot be stored cheaply in bulk, so supply must match demand second by second. The operator handles this with a continuous auction, re-run every few minutes.

blocks.title: How a uniform-price electricity auction clears
items: Every generator offers a quantity of power and the lowest price it will accept, usually close to its fuel and operating cost.
The operator stacks the offers from cheapest to most expensive. This ranking is called the merit order.
It forecasts demand for the next interval and walks up the stack until supply equals demand.
The offer of the last plant needed becomes the clearing price.
Every plant that runs gets paid that same clearing price, no matter what it offered.
Repeat a few minutes later with new demand, new offers and new transmission limits.

blocks.text: That fifth step is the one that surprises people. If a wind farm offered power at $0 and a gas plant at $40, and the gas plant was the last one needed, the wind farm gets $40 too. It looks like a giveaway. Why not pay each plant what it asked?

Because the asking prices would change. Under pay-as-bid rules, nobody would offer their true cost. Every generator would try to guess the highest price that would still get accepted and bid that, so the cheap plants would bid near the expensive ones anyway. Prices would end up about the same, but with more guessing, more gaming and less efficient choices about which plants run. Uniform pricing lets a cheap plant simply bid its real cost and trust the market to pay the going rate. Economists call the gap between a plant's cost and the clearing price inframarginal rent, and it is not a bug. For capital-heavy plants with cheap fuel, it is how the construction loan gets paid.
Think in margins. The price of electricity at any moment is not an average of what it costs to make. It is the cost of the next megawatt, from the most expensive plant you had to turn on.
Gas sets the price

In most US markets, most of the time, the last plant needed burns natural gas. Coal, nuclear, wind, solar and hydro usually sit lower in the stack. So the wholesale price of electricity tends to follow the price of gas, almost one for one.

The Texas market monitor, Potomac Economics, shows this year after year. In its 2021 report it noted the historically close link between average real-time power prices and gas prices, consistent with a market where gas generators set the price in most hours. When gas averaged $1.99 per million BTU in 2020, power averaged $25.73. When gas averaged $4.32 in 2014, power averaged $40.64.

blocks.title: ERCOT average real-time wholesale price
blocks.note: 2021 includes Winter Storm Uri; without the storm week, the 2021 average was $40.73.
blocks.source: Potomac Economics, ERCOT State of the Market Reports 2021 and 2024

blocks.text: There is one more wrinkle: location. Power lines have limits, and when a line is full, cheap power on one side cannot reach customers on the other. So the auction actually computes a separate price at each point on the grid, called a locational marginal price. Where lines are congested, prices on the two sides split apart. That congestion is not small change. In Texas it added up to about $2.1 billion in the real-time market in 2021 and $1.9 billion in 2024, according to the market monitor. A wind farm in the wrong place can be surrounded by cheap power it cannot sell, while a city a few hundred miles away pays more.

This is also why most consumers barely notice wholesale swings. Retail customers usually pay rates set to cover average costs over a season, plus the cost of the wires. According to the US Energy Information Administration, Americans paid an average of about 13.6 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2025. Homes paid about 17.3 cents, while big industrial users, who take power at high voltage and pay close to the wholesale price, paid about 8.6 cents.
The plants that win by having no fuel bill

Now look at the market from the point of view of a nuclear plant. Its fuel is cheap and its costs are mostly fixed: the plant has to pay for staff, security, maintenance and the debt on its construction whether it runs or not. It offers power at a very low price so that it always runs, and it lives entirely on the gap between its low running cost and whatever the clearing price is.

That works well when gas is expensive, because gas sets the clearing price high. When gas gets cheap, as it did after the shale boom, the clearing price falls, and the nuclear plant's margin shrinks even though nothing about the plant itself changed. Several US reactors have closed largely for this reason. Three Mile Island Unit 1, which had run among the best-performing plants in the country for years after the 1979 accident at its sister unit, was shut down in September 2019 when it could no longer compete.

Five years later the economics flipped from an unexpected direction. In September 2024, its owner, Constellation, announced a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft and plans to restart the reactor, since renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center. A data center wants power that is steady, carbon-free and available around the clock, and it is willing to pay a fixed price for it under a long contract, outside the minute-by-minute auction. The physics of the plant never changed. What changed was who valued its particular product.
When the price goes negative

Under the auction rules, a price below zero is perfectly possible. It happens when there is so much power that the cheapest way to balance the grid is to pay someone to use more or produce less. Two kinds of plants make this happen.

The first is renewables with production-based subsidies. A wind farm that earns a federal tax credit for every kilowatt-hour it produces can bid below zero and still come out ahead, as long as the negative price is smaller than the credit. The second is inflexible plants. A nuclear reactor or a big coal unit cannot cheaply ramp down for a few hours and back up, so it may accept a negative price rather than go through a costly cycle.

In Texas, negative prices cluster where the wind and sun are strongest and transmission is weakest. The market monitor's 2024 report found the West zone had the most hours below $0, largely because wind and solar output could not be moved out of the region over congested lines, and it noted that the Panhandle often sees negative prices. Midday solar now pushes prices down so far that batteries can charge cheaply, or even get paid to charge. Texas added about 7.5 gigawatts of solar and 5 gigawatts of energy storage in 2024 alone.
When the price hits the ceiling

The opposite extreme is scarcity. Texas runs what is called an energy-only market: generators earn money only by selling electricity, with no separate payment for simply being available. The theory is that rare, very high prices during shortages provide the profits that justify building and weatherizing plants. In 2021 the cap was $9,000 per megawatt-hour, set equal to the estimated value of lost load, what customers would pay to avoid being cut off.

items.label: Generation unavailable in ERCOT at the height of Winter Storm Uri
Price per MWh held through mid-morning Feb 19, 2021
Total value of electricity during the event

blocks.source: Potomac Economics, 2021 State of the Market Report for ERCOT

blocks.text: Uri tested that theory brutally. From February 13 to 19, 2021, extreme cold knocked out more than 52 gigawatts of generation through frozen equipment and fuel shortages. Demand was so far above supply that the grid operator ordered rolling outages to prevent a collapse, and many could not rotate because the shortfall was so deep. Prices sat at or near the cap for days. The market monitor criticized the pricing in both directions: early in the storm, prices briefly dipped as low as about $1,200 because the rules did not account for the outages, and later, prices were held at $9,000 through mid-morning on February 19, even though the last outage orders had been recalled just before midnight on February 17.

The market even had a circuit breaker for exactly this situation. Once the profits a new peaking plant would have earned over the year passed three times the annual cost of building one, the cap was supposed to drop to a lower level for the rest of the year. On February 16, 2021, that threshold was crossed for the first time in ERCOT's history. But the lower cap was defined as the greater of $2,000 or 50 times the natural gas price, and gas had spiked above $400 per million BTU during the outages, compared with around $3 in normal years. The supposedly lower cap worked out higher than $9,000. A safety valve tied to fuel prices failed precisely because fuel prices were part of the crisis.

For companies that had promised to deliver power they could not produce, or that bought wholesale power without a hedge, the result was ruinous losses. The episode shows the hard edge of marginal pricing. A price spike is a powerful signal to build capacity and prepare for the next storm. It is also a very blunt instrument when people are freezing in the dark.
Paying plants to exist

Other regions add a second market. PJM, which runs the grid across much of the mid-Atlantic and Midwest, also holds a capacity auction. Instead of buying energy, it buys a promise: plants commit years in advance to be available when called. The price is set the same marginal way.

blocks.title: PJM capacity auction clearing price (RTO)
blocks.source: PJM, 2025/2026 Base Residual Auction Report, 2024

blocks.text: For years those prices drifted down. Then, in the auction held in July 2024 for the 2025/26 delivery year, the price jumped from $28.92 to $269.92 per megawatt-day, and the total cost rose from about $2.2 billion to $14.7 billion. Less capacity cleared, about 135,700 megawatts versus 147,500 the year before, and the reserve margin fell from 21.7% to 18.6%. The marginal rule worked exactly as intended, sending a loud signal to build. Those costs flow through to the utilities that serve homes and businesses, and from there toward customers' bills.
Price is information

The deepest idea here is that a price is a message. A $9,000 price says the system is out of power and anyone who can add some, or use less, should do it now. A negative price says the system has too much and anyone who can soak it up should. A capacity price jump says the region is short of firm supply years from now. Each of those messages is computed from one question asked over and over: what does the next unit cost?

That marginal way of thinking carries well beyond electricity. The value of an extra hour of sleep depends on how much you have had. The worth of another practice session depends on how close you are to your plateau. The price of your time on a project depends on the next-best thing you could do with it. Averages tell you where you have been. Margins tell you what to do next.

takeaways: In most competitive power markets, every running plant is paid the price of the last, most expensive plant needed.
Gas plants usually set that price, so wholesale power tracks gas prices closely.
Nuclear and renewables earn the gap between their low running costs and the clearing price; cheap gas squeezes them.
Negative prices come from production subsidies, inflexible plants and congested lines; batteries now profit from them.
Think at the margin: the next unit's cost, not the average, drives decisions.

title: From Rock to Reactor: The Long Road of a Fuel Pellet
dek: Before a fuel pellet ever sees a core it has been dug, dissolved, turned into a gas, spun thousands of times and baked like pottery, often crossing several continents. The rock is the easy part.

blocks.text: Uranium is not rare. It is about 500 times more abundant than gold and roughly as common as tin. Granite, which makes up much of the continental crust, holds about four parts per million. Some phosphate fertilizers contain up to 400 parts per million, and there is uranium dissolved in seawater and in rivers. If you have ever walked on a granite countertop, you have touched it.

So why is reactor fuel expensive, strategic and the subject of sanctions and international treaties? Because the hard part of nuclear fuel is not finding the element. It is the chain of chemistry and machinery that turns a rock that is 99.9% useless into a ceramic pellet that can run a power plant for years. That chain is called the front end of the nuclear fuel cycle, and very few countries can do all of it.

blocks.title: The front end of the fuel cycle
items: Mining: dig ore from a pit or underground, or dissolve it in place with in-situ leaching.
Milling: crush and leach the ore, precipitate uranium oxide concentrate (yellowcake), pack it in drums.
Conversion: refine it and turn it into uranium hexafluoride (UF6), which becomes a gas at modest temperatures.
Enrichment: spin the gas in centrifuges to raise U-235 from 0.7% to around 3.5 to 5%.
Deconversion and fabrication: turn it back into uranium dioxide powder, press and bake pellets, load them into rods and assemblies.
Reactor: about three to six years in the core, then the used fuel goes to storage.

blocks.text: Where the rock comes from

Ore is just rock with enough of something valuable to be worth digging. For uranium, a deposit might be as little as 0.1% uranium, though the richest Canadian mines are far higher grade. Where the ore sits close to the surface, miners use open pits. Deeper than about 120 meters, they go underground, which disturbs less land but needs heavy ventilation to keep radon and airborne radioactivity away from workers.

The method that now dominates is different from both. In-situ leaching, also called in-situ recovery, pumps oxygenated groundwater with a weak acid or alkaline solution through a porous ore body, dissolves the uranium where it lies and pumps the solution back up. There is no pit and no pile of waste rock. According to the World Nuclear Association, in-situ leaching accounted for about 55% of world production in 2024, with conventional mines at 40% and by-product recovery, like uranium pulled out alongside copper at Australia's Olympic Dam, at about 5%.

Geography is concentrated. Kazakhstan, mostly through in-situ leach fields in its southern steppe, produced 39% of the world's mined uranium in 2024. Canada, home to the two biggest mines on Earth, McArthur River and Cigar Lake in northern Saskatchewan, produced 24%. Namibia made 12%. Those three countries supplied about three-quarters of the world.

blocks.title: Uranium mined in 2024, by country
blocks.note: World total was 60,213 tonnes of uranium, which covered about 90% of reactor demand; the rest came from stockpiles and recycled material.
blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, World Uranium Mining Production, 2026

blocks.text: Resources tell a different story from production. Australia holds about 27% of the world's identified uranium recoverable at moderate cost, more than any other country, yet produced less than 8% of the 2024 total. Mining is shaped by politics, permits and price as much as by geology.

The United States is a striking case. American mines produced 1,256 tonnes of uranium in 2015, then the output collapsed as prices fell, to just 6 tonnes in 2020. By 2024 it had recovered only to 260 tonnes. The country runs the largest reactor fleet in the world on fuel that is overwhelmingly imported, and in 2025 only about 7% of the uranium delivered to its reactor owners was American in origin. Low prices made it cheaper to buy from Canada and Kazakhstan than to keep domestic mines open, which is efficient right up until a supplier becomes unreliable.
Yellowcake that isn't yellow

Mined ore goes to a mill, usually close by. The ore is ground into a fine slurry and leached with sulfuric acid or a strong alkaline solution, which pulls the uranium into solution and leaves the rock behind. The uranium is then recovered, precipitated as an oxide, dried and packed into 200-liter drums. The product is called yellowcake, although the modern version is usually khaki. It is more than 80% uranium, compared with perhaps 0.1% in the ore.

Here is a detail that surprises people. Most of the radioactivity in natural uranium ore is not from uranium. It is from the decay products uranium has built up over geologic time, such as radium. Those stay behind in the mill tailings, which is why tailings have to be isolated in engineered facilities, often a mined-out pit. The yellowcake itself is only mildly radioactive. A large 1,000-megawatt reactor burns through the output of roughly 200 tonnes of it a year.
Turning a solid into a gas

Natural uranium is 99.3% uranium-238 and only 0.7% uranium-235, the isotope that fissions easily with slow neutrons. Most power reactors need that U-235 share raised to somewhere between 3.5% and 5%. The problem is that the two isotopes are chemically identical. No chemical reaction can tell them apart. The only handle is their mass, which differs by about 1%.

To sort atoms by weight you need them moving freely, which means a gas. That is the job of conversion. Yellowcake is refined and reacted with fluorine to make uranium hexafluoride, UF6, a compound that turns to vapor at relatively low temperature and solidifies again when cooled. It is shipped as a solid in steel cylinders that hold 14 tonnes each, then heated back into a gas at the enrichment plant. Fluorine has a lucky property here: it has only one natural isotope, so every bit of mass difference between UF6 molecules comes from the uranium.
The spinning heart: enrichment

Modern enrichment plants are halls full of tall, thin centrifuges spinning at enormous speed. The heavier U-238 molecules drift slightly toward the wall, the lighter U-235 slightly toward the center. One machine only nudges the mix a little, so thousands are linked in series, called cascades, each stage feeding the next. Out one end comes enriched product. Out the other comes tails, uranium depleted below its natural 0.7%.

The industry measures this work in a strange unit: the separative work unit, or SWU. It captures how much sorting effort it takes to split a given amount of feed into product and tails at given concentrations. The numbers show the trade-off at the heart of the business. Making one kilogram of 5% fuel takes 7.9 SWU and 10.4 kilograms of natural uranium if the tails are left at 0.25% U-235. Squeeze the tails down to 0.20% and you need 8.9 SWU but only 9.4 kilograms of uranium. In other words, you can substitute machine time for mined ore. When uranium is cheap, enrichers leave more U-235 in the tails. When uranium is expensive, they spin harder.

items.label: Enrichment work for one year of fuel for a typical 1,000 MW reactor
kWh per SWU: old gaseous diffusion vs modern centrifuges

blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Uranium Enrichment, 2026

blocks.text: That second statistic is one of the quiet engineering triumphs of the century. The old American method, gaseous diffusion, pushed UF6 through porous barriers thousands of times and used about 2,500 kilowatt-hours of electricity per SWU. Centrifuges need about 50. America's diffusion plants have all since closed.

Enrichment is where the geopolitics bite. The technology that makes 5% reactor fuel can, in principle, keep going to the much higher enrichments used in weapons, which is why it is tightly controlled and why only a handful of companies sell it commercially. Russia's Rosatom has the largest capacity in the world. According to the US Energy Information Administration, about a quarter of the enrichment services bought by American reactor owners in 2025 still came from Russia, with large shares from France, the United Kingdom and the Netherlands, and only 23% from US-origin plants.
Pellets, rods and the strangest fuel source of all

After enrichment, the gas is converted back into uranium dioxide powder, pressed into small cylinders and sintered, which means baked at over 1,400 degrees Celsius until it becomes a hard ceramic. The pellets are stacked inside metal tubes to make fuel rods, and the rods are bundled into assemblies built to tight tolerances. A large reactor core holds about 75 tonnes of low-enriched uranium in several hundred assemblies and needs about 27 tonnes of fresh fuel a year.

Fabrication plants have their own quiet safety rule. Any container holding enough fissile material in the wrong shape could, in principle, start a small chain reaction on its own, called a criticality accident. So the size and shape of every tank, tray and pipe is designed so that it cannot happen, no matter what an operator does. With low-enriched fuel the risk is very small, but the geometry is still controlled. It is the same philosophy you see throughout nuclear work: make the dangerous configuration physically impossible rather than relying on people to avoid it.

Inside the core, something interesting happens to the supposedly useless U-238. Some of it absorbs neutrons and becomes plutonium-239, and about half of that plutonium fissions in place. Over a fuel load's life, that plutonium provides about one-third of a typical reactor's energy. Used fuel comes out still about 95% U-238, with roughly 1% U-235, about 1% plutonium and about 3% fission products and other heavy elements.

For twenty years, some American power plants ran on fuel from Soviet nuclear weapons. Under the Megatons to Megawatts program, Russia took 500 tonnes of highly enriched uranium from warheads and military stockpiles, the equivalent of around 20,000 bombs, and blended it down to reactor-grade fuel for sale to the United States. The last of it was down-blended in 2013, producing about 14,446 tonnes of low-enriched uranium in total. Material designed to destroy cities ended up lighting them.

blocks.text: The real meaning of energy density

Why go through all this trouble? Because the payoff is absurd. According to the World Nuclear Association, one tonne of natural uranium, after enrichment and use in a typical reactor, produces about 44 million kilowatt-hours of electricity. Getting the same from fossil fuels would take more than 20,000 tonnes of coal or 8.5 million cubic meters of natural gas. That ratio is why a nuclear plant gets fuel deliveries every year or two while a coal plant of the same size needs a steady stream of coal trains.

items.label: Electricity from one tonne of natural uranium
Coal needed to produce the same electricity

blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Nuclear Fuel Cycle Overview, 2026

blocks.text: It also explains a fact that seems backward. Uranium prices can double and the cost of nuclear electricity barely moves, because the raw material is a small slice of the total. In 2025, American reactor owners paid an average of about $58 per pound of uranium oxide, per the EIA. The reactor's construction loan, staff and maintenance dwarf that. For a gas plant, by contrast, fuel is usually the biggest cost, which is why gas price spikes show up directly on electricity bills.

Utilities also buy uranium very differently from how a gas plant buys fuel. Most of it is locked in years ahead. In 2025, 87% of the uranium delivered to US reactor owners came under long-term contracts at an average of about $56 a pound, while the 13% bought on the spot market cost about $76. Paying a steady price for a fuel you can store on site for years is part of why nuclear output is so predictable.

blocks.title: Where US reactors' uranium came from, 2025
blocks.note: Shares of uranium delivered to US civilian reactor owners by country of origin; remaining shares from other countries.
blocks.source: US EIA, 2025 Uranium Marketing Annual Report, 2026

blocks.text: The bottleneck is never where you think

The fuel cycle has a lesson that applies far outside nuclear power. When people worry about the supply of something, they usually picture the raw material running out. With uranium, the rock is plentiful, and the dangerous chokepoints are in the middle: a few conversion plants, a few enrichment companies, a few fuel fabricators licensed for each reactor design. A country can sit on huge reserves and still be unable to fuel its reactors without help from abroad.

The same pattern shows up in computer chips, where sand is cheap and a handful of machines from a single company are not, and in batteries, where the bottleneck is often refining rather than mining. If you want to understand any supply chain, follow the material step by step and ask where the hard, slow, specialized work happens. That is usually where the real power sits.

Next time you see a drawing of a fuel assembly, picture its history: a Kazakh well field or a Saskatchewan mine shaft, a drum of khaki powder, a steel cylinder of frozen gas, a hall of humming centrifuges, a furnace, a rod. Years of chemistry, physics and politics, compressed into a stack of ceramic pellets each about the size of a fingertip.

takeaways: Uranium is common; the hard, strategic parts of nuclear fuel are conversion, enrichment and fabrication.
Kazakhstan, Canada and Namibia mined about three-quarters of the world's uranium in 2024, and in-situ leaching now produces most of it.
Enrichment is measured in SWU, and plants can trade machine work for raw uranium by changing the tails assay.
One tonne of natural uranium yields about 44 million kWh, the same as over 20,000 tonnes of coal, so fuel is a small slice of nuclear's cost.
In any supply chain, look for the specialized middle steps; that is usually where the real chokepoint is.
