title: Fukushima: Every Reactor Shut Down. Three Melted Anyway.
dek: The earthquake did its worst and the reactors stopped exactly as designed. What destroyed them was a wave someone had already calculated, and the heat that never stops.

blocks.text: At 2:46 p.m. on Friday, 11 March 2011, a magnitude 9.0 earthquake ripped along a stretch of seafloor 650 kilometres long. Eleven reactors at four nuclear plants in the region were running. Every one of them shut down automatically, control rods in, chain reactions stopped, exactly as designed. Later inspections found no significant earthquake damage at any of them.

Less than an hour later, three of those reactors had lost every means of cooling. Over the next three days, all three cores largely melted, hydrogen explosions tore open three reactor buildings, and the Fukushima Daiichi plant became the second accident ever rated level 7, the top of the international scale. The paradox is the lesson. Stopping fission was never the problem. The problem was the heat that keeps coming after fission stops, and a wall of seawater that knocked out everything needed to carry it away.
The quake the plant survived

Fukushima Daiichi, on the coast about 180 kilometres from the epicentre, had six boiling water reactors of an early 1960s General Electric design. Units 1 to 3 were operating; units 4 to 6 were shut down for maintenance. Ground acceleration at Daiichi peaked at 0.56 g, and units 2, 3 and 5 exceeded their design response in one direction by about 20%. Even so, Japan's regulator later confirmed the earthquake itself had not damaged unit 1, and the reactors shut down cleanly.

The shaking did knock out all six external power lines feeding the site. That was an anticipated event. Emergency diesel generators in the basements of the turbine buildings started up and began running the pumps that would remove decay heat. For about 40 minutes, the plant was in a bad but fully manageable situation.
The wave the plant did not

At 3:42 p.m. the first tsunami wave arrived, followed by a second eight minutes later. The site sat about 10 metres above sea level, with its seawater pumps at 4 metres. The water came ashore at about 15 metres. It drowned the seawater pumps that dumped heat to the ocean, flooded 12 of the 13 backup generators, and swamped electrical switchgear and batteries, almost all of it located low in the turbine buildings. The turbine halls sat under about 5 metres of seawater.

The result was a station blackout plus loss of the ultimate heat sink: no AC power, and nowhere to send the heat even if there were. In units 1 and 2 the 125-volt DC batteries also flooded, leaving operators without instruments, controls or even lights. Unit 3's batteries lasted about 30 hours. Meanwhile, an hour after shutdown, decay heat was still about 22 megawatts in unit 1 and 33 megawatts in units 2 and 3, roughly 1.5% of full power and more than enough to boil off the water covering the fuel.

One detail shows how thin the margin was. The single generator that survived was an air-cooled unit at unit 6, which did not depend on the drowned seawater pumps. It kept power flowing to units 5 and 6, and both of those reactors were brought safely to cold shutdown. One diverse backup, placed where the water could not reach it, was the whole difference between those two units and their neighbours.

A reactor can be shut down in seconds and still melt days later. Every safety system that matters after a scram depends on two things: electricity to run it and somewhere to dump the heat. Fukushima lost both at once.
Three reactors, three clocks

Each unit failed on its own timeline, set by what backup cooling it had left. Unit 1 had an isolation condenser, a passive system that cools the reactor by condensing its steam in a big tank of water, needing no pumps. But its valves were designed to fail closed when DC power was lost, and when the batteries died the valves shut. With no alarm and no lights, the control room did not realize the condenser had stopped working. According to a University of Tokyo analysis, the emergency response headquarters only began to doubt that it was working at 11:50 p.m., more than eight hours after it stopped.

By then it was far too late. In unit 1 the water level had dropped to the top of the fuel about three hours after the scram, and core damage began about an hour later. Fuel temperatures reached around 2,800 °C, and by 16 hours after the scram most of the core had slumped to the bottom of the reactor vessel. Much of it eventually went through the vessel bottom and ate about 65 centimetres into the concrete below. Venting the containment was delayed by the lack of power and compressed air. On Saturday afternoon, hydrogen that had leaked into the top of the reactor building exploded, blowing off its roof and walls.

Two pieces of physics made everything harder. First, fire trucks and other low-pressure pumps cannot push water into a reactor vessel sitting at high pressure. Before they could help, crews had to depressurize the vessel by venting steam into the suppression pool, and that took power and nitrogen they did not have. Second, once fuel is uncovered, its zirconium cladding reacts with steam, releasing heat that adds to the decay heat and producing hydrogen. Japan's regulator later estimated 800 to 1,000 kilograms of hydrogen in each of the three units. Hydrogen that escaped containment collected under the roofs of the reactor buildings, waiting for a spark.

Units 2 and 3 bought more time with steam-driven injection systems that could run without AC power, but those failed too. Unit 3's high-pressure injection stopped early on Sunday, core damage began around 44 hours after the earthquake, and a very large hydrogen explosion destroyed the top of its building on Monday morning. Hydrogen vented from unit 3 also backflowed through shared ducts into unit 4, whose building exploded on Tuesday even though its reactor held no fuel. Unit 2 lasted longest, about 70 hours, before cooling failed; its containment then appears to have leaked, and it was probably the source of most of the radioactive release on Tuesday, 15 March.

blocks.title: Hours from the earthquake until core damage began
blocks.note: Each unit's clock was set by how long its remaining backup cooling lasted. Times are from TEPCO's 2012 accident modelling.
blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Fukushima Daiichi Accident (citing 2012 MAAP analysis)

blocks.text: In the middle of this, crews were working in darkness and rising radiation, many of them having just lost homes or family members to the tsunami. Fire trucks became reactor injection pumps. Seawater injection began in unit 1 on Saturday evening. When the prime minister's office instructed TEPCO to stop it, plant management ignored the order, and the instruction was withdrawn shortly afterward. The heavily loaded spent fuel pool at unit 4, holding 1,331 assemblies, including a full core offloaded for maintenance, became a fear of its own, though later checks found the fuel there had stayed covered.
The wave someone had already calculated

When Daiichi was designed in the 1960s, its design-basis tsunami was 3.1 metres, based on the 1960 Chilean tsunami. The estimate was raised to 5.7 metres in 2002 and 6.1 metres in 2009. But in 2008, TEPCO's own calculation produced a potential tsunami of 15.7 metres at the site. Senior managers asked an engineering society to review the model, and no major action followed from either TEPCO or the regulator. A government earthquake committee report, due out in April 2011, described an earthquake more than 1,140 years earlier that had flooded much of the same coast.

blocks.title: Daiichi tsunami estimates versus what arrived
blocks.note: The worst-case number existed three years early. It was studied, not designed for.
blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Fukushima Daiichi Accident

blocks.text: Japan's parliamentary investigation commission was blunt. It called the accident a manmade disaster and found that TEPCO had known since 2006 that flooding could cause a station blackout, while the regulator had told operators it was not necessary to plan for one. Plans for venting and for manually operating emergency cooling were incomplete, so crews were improvising procedures under the worst possible conditions.
The control group down the coast

The strongest evidence that Daiichi's fate was not inevitable sits a few kilometres away. Fukushima Daini, about 11 kilometres south and run by the same company, was built 13 metres above sea level and was hit by a tsunami of about 9 metres. Its heat exchangers were damaged, but its diesel generators were less affected and one external power line survived. Staff laid and energized 8.8 kilometres of heavy cable in 30 hours, and all four reactors reached cold shutdown.

Onagawa, owned by Tohoku Electric farther up the coast, sat on an embankment almost 14 metres above sea level. Four of its five power lines were lost, but the one that survived was enough to bring all three reactors to cold shutdown. Same earthquake, same ocean, similar machines. The difference was a few metres of elevation and a few surviving power sources.
Counting the harm honestly

items.label: Cases of acute radiation sickness from the accident
Disaster-related deaths among Fukushima evacuees
Killed by the earthquake and tsunami

blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Fukushima Daiichi Accident

blocks.text: The release was serious, an estimated 940 petabecquerels in iodine-131 equivalent, contaminating about 3,000 square kilometres above the threshold used at Chernobyl, versus 29,400 there. But no one developed radiation sickness, and UNSCEAR's 2020 report concluded that future radiation-linked health effects among residents are unlikely to be discernible. In 2018 the Japanese government did recognise a link between one former plant worker's lung cancer and his radiation exposure.

The evacuation was another matter. More than 100,000 people were moved, and by 2020 Japanese authorities counted 2,313 disaster-related deaths among Fukushima evacuees, about 90% of them people over 66, from the stress of shelters, disrupted care and forced moves. An IAEA mission in 2013 said decontamination targets were unrealistic and that many evacuees could return. The last evacuation order, for Futaba, was lifted only in August 2022. Cleanup continues: treated water releases began in August 2023, and TEPCO extracted its first sample of melted fuel, about 0.7 grams, in November 2024, out of an estimated 880 tonnes.

That does not mean evacuating was wrong. UNSCEAR found that prompt evacuation cut people's radiation doses by about a factor of ten. The hard lesson is that protective actions have their own casualty count, especially for the elderly and sick, and that plans should weigh how long people are kept away and how they are moved, not just how far they are moved.
What changed

In March 2012 the NRC ordered every US plant to be able to maintain key safety functions with installed power sources lost, to add reliable spent fuel pool level instruments, and, for reactors similar to Daiichi's, to install vents that can work in severe accident conditions. Plants now keep portable pumps and generators on site, and the industry stocked two regional response centres. Every site re-analysed its earthquake and flood hazards. Japan replaced its regulator with a new, more independent Nuclear Regulation Authority.

Part of this was already familiar. After the September 2001 attacks, the US industry had prepared every plant to cope with an extended station blackout using portable water sources independent of normal systems, including plants of the same design as Daiichi's, and that preparation became a licence condition in 2008. The equipment that might have saved Fukushima existed in principle. It had not been made a requirement where it was needed.

The deeper lesson is about design bases. A design basis is a line someone draws through uncertainty, and nature does not read it. Daiichi did not fail because the engineers of the 1960s were careless; it failed because a known, credible threat sat in a report for years while the plant kept running on the old number. The questions worth asking of any system, on a reactor plant or anywhere else, are what happens one step beyond what we planned for, and what single location, like a flooded basement full of generators and batteries, takes out all of our backups at once.

takeaways: All eleven reactors in the region scrammed safely; the meltdowns came from losing power and cooling, not from failing to stop fission.
The tsunami flooded diesels, switchgear and batteries placed low in turbine buildings, causing a station blackout and loss of heat sink.
Unit 1's isolation condenser valves failed closed on loss of DC power, and operators did not realize it for hours.
TEPCO had calculated a 15.7-metre tsunami in 2008; nearby Daini and Onagawa, higher and with surviving power, reached cold shutdown.
No radiation deaths were recorded early on, but 2,313 evacuee deaths show that emergency response itself carries real risk.

title: Fusion Ignition: 3.15 Megajoules Out, 300 Megajoules From the Wall
dek: In December 2022 a laser lab got more energy out of a fusion target than it put in. Here is what that milestone proved, what it did not, and how far it is from a power plant.

blocks.text: On 5 December 2022, at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, 192 laser beams delivered 2.05 megajoules of ultraviolet light to a fuel capsule about the size of a peppercorn. For a tiny fraction of a second the capsule produced 3.15 megajoules of fusion energy. For the first time in history, a controlled fusion experiment had released more energy than the laser energy used to drive it. The US Department of Energy announced it on 13 December, and headlines called it the dawn of limitless clean power.

Here is the number that did not make most headlines. To produce that 2.05-megajoule pulse, the laser system drew roughly 300 megajoules from the electrical grid, according to the lab's director. By that accounting, the shot returned about 1% of the energy the facility consumed. So was it a breakthrough or a stunt? The honest answer is that it was a genuine scientific milestone and nowhere near a power source, and understanding both halves is the best way to understand fusion.

blocks.title: The energy ledger of the first ignition shot
blocks.note: Ignition is measured against laser energy on target, not against the electricity the facility used.
blocks.source: LLNL, Dec 2022; grid figure from LLNL director Kim Budil via Optica OPN, 2022

blocks.text: Why fusing atoms is so hard

Fission and fusion both turn a little mass into a lot of energy, but they run in opposite directions. Fission splits heavy nuclei like uranium. Fusion joins light ones. The usual fuel is two heavy forms of hydrogen: deuterium, with one proton and one neutron, and tritium, with one proton and two neutrons. Fuse them and you get a helium nucleus, also called an alpha particle, plus a fast neutron. The products weigh slightly less than the ingredients, and that missing mass comes out as energy.

The obstacle is that every nucleus is positively charged, and like charges repel. Two hydrogen nuclei have to be slammed together hard enough to get close enough for the strong nuclear force, which only works at extremely short range, to grab them. That takes temperatures and pressures found in the cores of stars. Fission is easy by comparison: a slow neutron carries no charge, so it walks right into a uranium nucleus at room temperature. That is why the first fission chain reaction ran under a Chicago stadium in 1942, while controlled fusion that releases net energy took another eight decades.

Making fusion happen at all is not the hard part; small machines can fuse a few atoms. The hard part is making it pay. A fusion fuel has to be hot enough for nuclei to collide fast, dense enough that collisions are frequent, and held together long enough for enough of them to happen before the energy leaks away. Physicists bundle those three into a single figure of merit, often called the triple product after the physicist John Lawson's criterion. You can trade one factor against another, but you cannot skip any of them, and every approach to fusion is really a strategy for maximizing that product.

There are two broad ways to make a star on Earth. Magnetic confinement, used in doughnut-shaped tokamaks, holds a thin, hot plasma in place with powerful magnetic fields for seconds or longer. Inertial confinement, NIF's approach, does the opposite: it crushes a tiny amount of fuel so fast and so hard that it fuses before it has time to fly apart, held together for an instant only by its own inertia.
How NIF lights a star

blocks.title: Indirect-drive inertial fusion at NIF
items: 192 laser beams fire into a hollow cylinder about a centimetre long, called a hohlraum
The beams heat the hohlraum's inner walls, which glow with a bath of X-rays
The X-rays blow off the outer surface of a peppercorn-sized fuel capsule
Like a rocket in reverse, the blow-off drives the capsule inward at more than 400 km per second
The partly frozen deuterium-tritium fuel is crushed, forming a hot spot at the centre
Alpha particles from fusion reheat the fuel and a burn wave spreads outward

blocks.text: The key physics is in that last step. Fusion in the hot spot produces alpha particles, which are charged and get stopped inside the dense fuel around them, dumping their energy back in. If that self-heating outruns the ways the hot spot loses energy, through X-ray emission, heat conduction and simple expansion, the reaction starts feeding itself. When alpha heating supplies more than half of the fuel's heating, physicists call it a burning plasma. Beyond that, a burn wave can sweep outward through the colder fuel and multiply the yield.

Getting there took far longer than planned. NIF researchers had to tame instabilities, asymmetries in the X-ray drive, and the mixing of capsule material into the fuel. Even the thin membranes holding the capsule in place and the tube used to fill it with fuel turned out to disturb the implosion. Better 3D simulations, more diagnostics and machine learning helped close the gap between models and experiments, shot by shot.

Each shot is a one-off. Capsule, hohlraum and laser pulse are designed together, the target is cooled until the fuel freezes into a thin layer on the inside of the capsule, and the implosion itself is over in a tiny fraction of a second. Diagnostics then reconstruct what happened from the neutrons, X-rays and particles that fly out. Researchers learn from it, adjust the design, and wait for the next shot. The December 2022 success came after years of shots that fell short, each one feeding the models that made the next one better.
Repeating it, and climbing

A single result can be a fluke. Repeating it is science. Since December 2022, NIF has achieved ignition again and again, and its records keep moving. In April 2025 a shot delivering 2.08 megajoules produced 8.6 megajoules, a target gain of 4.13. By June 2026 the lab had reached ignition 11 times, the latest yielding 7.9 megajoules.

The milestones in between tell the story of a team learning to push the same machine harder. In February 2024 a shot produced an estimated 5.2 megajoules from 2.2 megajoules of laser energy, more than doubling the input for the first time. In February 2025 a 2.05-megajoule shot yielded 5.0 megajoules for a target gain of 2.44. In June 2025 a team led by Los Alamos National Laboratory, working with Livermore, reached ignition on NIF and created a burning plasma, a sign that more than one group can now hit the target.

blocks.title: Selected NIF ignition shots: fusion yield
blocks.note: Laser energy on target was about 2 to 2.2 MJ where LLNL reported it. Some shots served other goals, so yields go up and down.
blocks.source: LLNL, Achieving Fusion Ignition (accessed 2026)

blocks.text: It is worth knowing why NIF exists. Its primary mission is national security: the National Nuclear Security Administration uses it to study matter at extreme conditions for maintaining the nuclear stockpile without explosive testing. Some ignition-class shots are designed for that work rather than for maximum yield, which helps explain why the yields bounce around. Energy research is a major beneficiary, not the original purpose.
The gap to a power plant

Target gain, fusion energy out divided by laser energy on target, is the number NIF reports. A power plant cares about a harsher ratio: electricity sold divided by electricity used. On that scale NIF is roughly a hundredfold short of merely breaking even, because its laser, by its director's own description, is built on 1980s technology and converts well under 1% of wall power into light on target. And NIF can fire about once a day.

blocks.title: NIF today versus what a laser fusion plant needs

left.head: NIF ignition shots
items: About one shot per day
Target gain up to about 4
Laser converts under 1% of grid energy into light on target
Each capsule hand-built over weeks
No tritium breeding

right.head: Inertial fusion power plant
items: 10 to 20 shots every second
Target gain of roughly 50 to 100
Laser efficiency above 10%
Millions of cheap, identical targets per day
Tritium bred and recovered inside the plant

blocks.text: Each of those gaps is a whole engineering field. Lasers that fire many times per second without destroying their optics. Targets cheap enough to mass-produce by the million, injected and hit while flying. A chamber that survives a fusion blast ten times a second while capturing neutron energy as heat. A blanket that breeds new tritium, because there is very little of it in the world. The director put it plainly at the time: very significant hurdles, in the technology as well as the science, and a few decades of research ahead.

There is also a problem a nuclear electrician will recognise. In deuterium-tritium fusion, most of the energy leaves with the neutron, and neutrons carry no charge, so no magnetic field or chamber wall can steer them. They slam into the surrounding structure, which is how the heat gets captured, but they also damage materials and make them radioactive over time. Fusion produces no long-lived fission products and cannot run away like a chain reaction, but a fusion plant will still be a radiation workplace, with shielding, activated components and remote maintenance.

Watch the denominator. Target gain, plasma gain, and engineering or wall-plug gain are different numbers. Fusion headlines often quote the most flattering one. A power plant only cares about the last.
The magnetic road

The other big path is magnetic confinement, and it has its own landmarks. In its final tritium experiments in late 2023, Europe's JET tokamak in England sustained high fusion power for 5 seconds and produced 69 megajoules, a record for energy from a single fusion experiment, from only 0.2 milligrams of fuel. JET was built as a stepping stone toward ITER, not as a net-energy machine.

ITER, the international megaproject under construction in southern France, is designed to get 500 megawatts of fusion power from 50 megawatts of heating, a gain of 10, in pulses of 400 seconds. Its giant superconducting magnets store 41 gigajoules of energy at 12 tesla. It is also badly behind schedule. Its 2024 baseline pushed the start of research operations to 2034 and deuterium-tritium operation to 2039, about four years later than the previous plan.

A tokamak works by driving an enormous electrical current through the plasma itself, while external superconducting coils wrap it in a twisted magnetic cage. ITER is designed for a full plasma current of 15 million amperes. In the hands of an electrician, ITER is less a physics experiment than a giant power-distribution and magnet-protection problem: those coils have to be cooled to a few degrees above absolute zero, charged, and safely discharged if something goes wrong.

blocks.text: Private companies are trying to move faster. Commonwealth Fusion Systems is building SPARC, a compact tokamak using high-temperature superconducting magnets, in Massachusetts, and says it will produce more fusion energy than it takes to heat the plasma in 2027, ahead of a planned grid-connected plant called ARC. Treat company timelines as goals, not forecasts; fusion has a long history of dates that slipped.
What ignition actually proved

A useful comparison is fission itself. The first controlled chain reaction ran in Chicago in December 1942. The first US commercial nuclear power plant, at Shippingport, Pennsylvania, started generating in 1958, after an enormous wartime and postwar push. Proving that the physics works and building a machine that makes cheap, reliable electricity are separated by years of unglamorous engineering, materials science and money, even when the physics is easy. Fusion's physics is not easy.

There is a second, quieter result that matters for both roads to fusion. NIF showed in the lab that a fusion fuel can enter the burning-plasma regime, where the fusion reactions themselves supply most of the heating. Every future fusion power plant, laser-driven or magnetic, has to live in that regime, and ITER was designed largely to study it in a tokamak. Seeing it achieved, measured and repeated gives modellers on every side real data instead of extrapolation.

So December 2022 deserves its place in history, just not the one the headlines gave it. It settled a decades-old physics question: can a laboratory fusion reaction heat itself enough to release more energy than was delivered to it? Yes. The open questions now are engineering and economic ones, the same kind that decide whether any product, from a reactor plant to a game studio, actually ships. Physics breakthroughs make good headlines. Repetition rate, efficiency and cost per unit decide what reaches the grid.

For anyone weighing a civilian career after naval nuclear work, that is the part worth noticing. Whoever builds the first fusion power plants will need people who understand radiation protection, high-power electrical systems, instrumentation, vacuum and cryogenic plant, and the discipline of operating something unforgiving by procedure. Those skills transfer from today's fission plants. The physics headline belongs to the scientists; the decades after it will belong to the people who can run machines.

takeaways: NIF's December 2022 shot made 3.15 MJ of fusion energy from 2.05 MJ of laser light: ignition, or scientific breakeven.
The laser drew about 300 MJ from the grid, so the facility as a whole was nowhere near net energy.
NIF has since repeated ignition 11 times through June 2026, peaking at 8.6 MJ and a target gain of 4.13.
A laser fusion plant would need roughly 10 to 20 shots per second, gains of 50 to 100 and lasers over 10% efficient.
ITER's current plan starts deuterium-tritium operation in 2039; private timelines are earlier but unproven.

title: Geothermal Power Is Half Nuclear
dek: About half the heat leaking out of the Earth comes from radioactive decay. For a century we could only tap it in a few lucky places. Shale drilling tricks may change that.

blocks.text: Deep under Japan, inside a mine in the mountains near Kamioka, sits a tank holding about a thousand tonnes of liquid scintillator, a fluid that gives off a faint flash when a rare particle hits it. Most of the particles it was built to catch are antineutrinos from nuclear power reactors. But some come from somewhere stranger: the rock beneath our feet. In 2011, the KamLAND collaboration combined its measurements of these "geoneutrinos" with data from Italy's Borexino detector and published a striking result.

The Earth leaks about 44 terawatts of heat into space, a steady glow far too faint to feel but enormous when added up over the whole planet. The radioactive decay of uranium-238 and thorium-232 inside the planet supplies roughly 20 terawatts of it, and potassium-40 adds about 4 more. Put together, about half of the heat flowing out of the Earth is nuclear energy, released by slow radioactive decay rather than by fission. The rest is leftover heat from the planet's formation that has not yet escaped.

items.label: Total heat flowing out of Earth's surface
Heat from decay of uranium-238 and thorium-232
Share of Earth's heat flow from radioactive decay

blocks.source: KamLAND Collaboration, Nature Geoscience, 2011

blocks.text: So geothermal energy is, in a real sense, half nuclear power, running on a reactor no one has to refuel. It is clean, it runs day and night regardless of weather, and the resource is so large it is effectively endless. Which raises an obvious question: why does it supply almost none of our electricity?
Five light bulbs in Tuscany

The story starts in Italy. In the hills of Tuscany, natural steam vents out of the ground at a place called Larderello, and long before anyone thought of electricity, the area was an industrial site extracting boric acid from the hot springs. In 1904 Prince Piero Ginori Conti, who ran the boric acid business, hooked a small generator to the natural steam. It produced about 10 kilowatts, enough to light five light bulbs. It was the first time anyone had made electricity from the Earth's heat.

By 1913 a commercial geothermal power plant was running at Larderello, and the field never really stopped. Today the area hosts 34 plants operated by Enel Green Power, with a total capacity around 800 megawatts. In the United States, the big equivalent is The Geysers in Northern California, which the US Energy Information Administration calls the largest known dry steam field in the world. It has been producing electricity since 1960.

Getting electricity out of that heat uses the same basic machine as a nuclear plant: hot fluid spins a turbine, which spins a generator. Geothermal plants come in three main flavors, according to the EIA. Dry steam plants, like The Geysers, pipe steam straight from the ground into the turbine. Flash plants take very hot water under pressure and let it boil suddenly into steam at lower pressure. Binary plants handle cooler water by passing its heat through a heat exchanger to a second fluid with a lower boiling point, which then drives the turbine. That last design looks a lot like a PWR's two loops: the geothermal water never touches the turbine, just as primary coolant never leaves the reactor plant.

blocks.text: Why so little, so far

Larderello and The Geysers share a lucky geology. Conventional geothermal power needs three things at once: rock that is very hot near the surface, water to carry the heat, and enough natural cracks and porosity for that water to flow. That combination occurs mostly near the edges of tectonic plates and over volcanic hot spots. Iceland, which sits right on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, is the poster child. According to its government, geothermal supplied about 27% of its electricity in 2015, and about 85% of all Icelandic homes are heated with geothermal energy.

blocks.title: Geothermal share of electricity generation
blocks.note: Years differ by source. Kenya has the highest geothermal share of any country.
blocks.source: US EIA, Geothermal Explained, 2026; Government of Iceland, Energy

blocks.text: Most places are not Iceland or Kenya. In 2025, according to the EIA, the United States had geothermal power plants in only seven states, producing about 0.4% of the country's utility-scale electricity. California alone produced about 69% of the nation's geothermal power. Everywhere else, the heat is there, but it is too deep, or the rock is too tight for water to move through it, or both.

And deep is expensive. The temperature of the crust climbs as you go down, but in most regions you would need to drill several kilometers to reach rock hot enough for efficient power generation. Drilling through hard, hot crystalline rock is slow, wears out bits and costs a fortune. For a century, that meant geothermal was a geographic accident: a great deal for the few places born with the right plumbing, and irrelevant for everyone else.

It is worth clearing up one common confusion. The "geothermal heat pumps" sold for houses are a different thing. They do not tap deep volcanic heat at all. They use the fact that the ground a few feet down stays at a fairly constant temperature all year, warmer than winter air and cooler than summer air, and pump heat into or out of a building using that steady reservoir. They are a smart efficiency technology, but they do not generate electricity.
Borrowing the shale playbook

The idea of making your own plumbing is not new. If the rock is hot but has no natural pathways, you could drill into it, crack it open with pressurized water, and then circulate water through the cracks to pick up heat. This is called an enhanced geothermal system, or EGS. Early attempts struggled. The rock did not fracture the way engineers wanted, the water short-circuited through a few big cracks, and costs ran high.

Then the oil and gas industry spent two decades and enormous sums perfecting exactly the skills EGS was missing. The shale revolution was built on drilling down, turning sideways, running long horizontal wells through rock, and fracturing them in many separate stages to create a wide web of flow paths. A startup called Fervo Energy bet that the same toolkit would work in hot granite instead of oily shale.

blocks.title: How an enhanced geothermal system works
items: Drill an injection well several kilometers down into hot, dense rock, then turn it horizontal.
Pump in water at high pressure in stages to open a network of small fractures along the well.
Drill a parallel production well that crosses the same fractured zone.
Pump cool water down the first well; it flows through the fractures and heats up against the rock.
Bring the hot water up the second well and use it to drive a turbine, often via a secondary fluid.
Send the cooled water back down and repeat, in a closed loop.

blocks.text: In 2023 Fervo's pilot, called Project Red, began producing about 3.5 megawatts in Nevada, supplying power to the local grid that serves Google's data centers there. In 2024 a 30-day test at its much larger site in Beaver County, Utah, produced more than 10 megawatts from a single well pair, with peak flow of 107 kilograms of water per second. Oil and gas workers made up about 90% of the labor hours at that site, according to the Journal of Petroleum Technology. Fervo's technology chief described it as the company's "Mitchell Energy moment," a nod to the wildcatter who cracked shale gas.

In September 2026, Fervo reported first power from Cape Station. Its first phase is about 100 megawatts, built as three 33-megawatt blocks, with another 400 megawatts under construction and expected around 2028. Right next door sits Utah FORGE, a field laboratory funded by the Department of Energy where researchers test EGS techniques and publish the data openly. Circulation tests there in 2024 sent water through fractured rock at around 370°F and recovered most of what was pumped in.

The economics hinge on a learning curve. In shale, crews got dramatically faster at drilling each new well as they repeated the same design over and over in the same kind of rock. Geothermal developers are betting on the same effect: standardize the well, drill dozens of them, and let practice drive the cost down. That is the opposite of how big one-off energy projects usually behave, and it is the main reason investors suddenly care about a technology that has been around for more than a century.

The breakthrough in next-generation geothermal was not a new physics discovery. It was a transfer: a mature skill set from one industry applied to another. Some of the most valuable innovations are moves like that, taking a tool that already works somewhere and carrying it across a border nobody bothered to cross.
The earthquake problem

Cracking rock miles underground has a known side effect: it can make the ground shake. Most induced quakes are tiny and felt only by instruments. But in November 2017, a magnitude 5.5 earthquake struck the city of Pohang in South Korea, one of the most damaging quakes in the country's modern history. Two teams publishing in *Science* in 2018 concluded that the quake was very probably triggered by fluid injection at an EGS project being developed nearby. The possibility of pure coincidence was not ruled out, but the location and pattern of aftershocks pointed strongly to the project.

Pohang did not kill enhanced geothermal, but it changed how it is done. Modern projects map faults carefully before drilling, monitor seismic activity in real time, and use "traffic light" rules that slow or stop injection when small tremors exceed set thresholds. The trade-off is familiar to anyone who has worked in nuclear power: the technology can be run safely, but only if operators treat warning signs as hard stops rather than suggestions.
What's actually at stake

The Department of Energy's GeoVision analysis projected that with better technology, US geothermal capacity could grow more than 26-fold, to 60 gigawatts by 2050, providing about 8.5% of the country's electricity. A later update suggested that newer estimates of enhanced geothermal potential could push that to 90 gigawatts. Those are projections, not promises, and they depend heavily on drilling costs continuing to fall.

What makes geothermal valuable is less the size of the resource than its shape. Solar and wind deliver cheap energy when the weather cooperates. Geothermal delivers steady power around the clock, the same way a nuclear plant does, and it can be sited on a small patch of land. In a grid that is adding huge amounts of variable power and huge new loads like data centers, a source that simply runs all the time is worth more per megawatt-hour than its raw cost suggests.

There is a nice symmetry here for anyone in the nuclear business. A reactor concentrates a nuclear reaction into a small, intensely controlled core and harvests its heat. Geothermal harvests heat from a nuclear process spread thinly through an entire planet. One is a triumph of concentration, the other of access. For a century, the limiting factor for geothermal was never the heat itself. It was the cost of drilling down to where it is. If that cost keeps falling, the biggest energy resource under your feet stops being a geographic accident and becomes something nearly anyone can reach.

takeaways: About half of Earth's 44 TW heat flow comes from radioactive decay of uranium, thorium and potassium.
Conventional geothermal needs heat, water and permeable rock together, which is why it supplies only about 0.4% of US electricity.
Enhanced geothermal borrows horizontal drilling and multi-stage fracturing from the shale industry to build its own plumbing.
Induced earthquakes like Pohang 2017 are a real risk, managed by fault mapping, monitoring and hard stop rules.
Geothermal's value is that it runs around the clock; drilling cost is the main thing holding it back.

title: The Most Complicated Way Ever Invented to Boil Water
dek: A pressurized water reactor is a kettle built around one strange fact: less than 1% of its neutrons arrive late, and that delay is the only reason anyone can steer it.

blocks.text: Burn one carbon atom in a lump of coal and you get about 4 electron-volts of energy. Split one uranium-235 nucleus and you get about 200 million. That ratio, roughly fifty million to one, is the whole reason nuclear power exists. It is also why a single ceramic fuel pellet, about the size of a fingertip, holds roughly as much energy as 150 gallons of oil.

And yet the thing we do with all that energy is almost embarrassingly ordinary. We boil water, spin a turbine and push electrons down a wire, exactly like a coal plant from 1920. A pressurized water reactor, or PWR, is the most common power reactor on Earth, with about 300 operating for electricity worldwide. The interesting part is not the boiling. It is all the physics that has to go right so the water boils at a steady, boring, controllable rate for eighteen months straight.
This is a tour of that physics, from a single neutron to the switchyard, with the numbers that make it work.

items.label: Energy released by one U-235 fission
Energy from burning one carbon atom
Share of U-235 fission neutrons that arrive delayed

blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Physics of Uranium and Nuclear Energy

blocks.text: Slowing down the bullets

When a U-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, it wobbles and splits into two smaller nuclei, usually somewhere in the middle of the periodic table. About 85% of the released energy shows up as the kinetic energy of those two fragments. They can only travel a microscopic distance inside solid fuel before slamming to a stop, so their motion becomes heat right there in the pellet. The fission also throws off two or three fresh neutrons, about 2.45 on average for U-235.

Here is the catch. Those new neutrons are born moving at about 7% of the speed of light, and at that speed they mostly fly past U-235 nuclei without interacting. U-235 is far more likely to fission when hit by a slow, or thermal, neutron, one that has bounced around until it moves at roughly the speed of the surrounding atoms. So a reactor needs a moderator, a material full of light nuclei that neutrons can ricochet off, losing energy with each collision like a cue ball hitting other balls.

In a PWR the moderator is ordinary water. Hydrogen nuclei are about the same mass as a neutron, which makes them excellent at soaking up its speed. The drawback is that light water also absorbs some neutrons outright. Natural uranium is only 0.7% U-235, which is not enough to keep a chain reaction going in a sea of neutron-hungry water. That is why PWR fuel is enriched, commonly to 3.5 to 5% U-235.

The fuel itself is uranium dioxide, a ceramic that melts at about 2,800 °C, pressed into pellets roughly 1 cm wide and 1.5 cm long. Pellets are stacked inside zirconium-alloy tubes, chosen because zirconium is tough, resists corrosion and barely absorbs neutrons. A large PWR holds about 150 to 250 fuel assemblies of 200 to 300 rods each. A 1,000-megawatt-class plant might contain 51,000 fuel rods and more than 18 million pellets.
The 0.66% that makes control possible

Of the roughly two and a half neutrons each fission releases, exactly one, on average, has to go on to cause another fission for the reactor to hold steady. The rest leak out of the core or get absorbed by something that does not fission. When the balance is exactly one, the reactor is critical, and critical is the normal, desired state. It does not mean danger. It means steady power.

Now the puzzle. In a water-moderated core, a neutron goes from birth to its next absorption in a tiny fraction of a second. If every neutron were born instantly, even a small nudge above critical would multiply the population so many times per second that no mechanical system could possibly respond. You could not drive a car whose speed doubled before your foot reached the brake.

The rescue is a statistical quirk. About 0.66% of the neutrons from U-235 fission are not emitted at the moment of fission. They come out later, when certain fission products undergo radioactive decay, with the longest-lived group having a half-life of about 56 seconds. Those stragglers stretch the effective generation time from fractions of a millisecond to something closer to human scale. As long as the reactor is kept below the point where it could sustain itself on prompt neutrons alone, power changes at a pace that rods, pumps and people can follow.

Every reactor operator is, in a sense, managing a budget of less than 1%. Stay inside the delayed-neutron margin and the plant responds in seconds to minutes. Exceed it and the response time collapses toward nothing. Chernobyl is what happens when that margin is lost.

Operators and automatic systems steer the balance with neutron absorbers. Control rods made of materials like boron, cadmium or hafnium slide in from the top of a PWR core. Pull them out slightly and the reactor goes a hair supercritical, so power rises; once it reaches the desired level, the rods go back to the critical position. For slower, long-term adjustment, PWRs dissolve boron in the primary coolant and lower its concentration as the fuel burns up over the cycle. Many cores also include burnable poisons, absorbers built into the fuel that fade away as they soak up neutrons, smoothing out the excess reactivity of fresh fuel.
Brakes built into the physics

The most important safety features of a PWR are not systems at all. They are feedback effects baked into the materials. The first is the Doppler effect in the fuel: as uranium heats up, U-238 nuclei absorb more neutrons without fissioning, which pushes the chain reaction down. The fuel itself pushes back against overheating, and it does so almost instantly.

The second is the moderator. If the water in the core heats up and becomes less dense, or starts to form steam bubbles, it slows neutrons less effectively. Fewer thermal neutrons means fewer fissions, which means less heat. Engineers call this a negative temperature coefficient and a negative void coefficient. In plain terms, the reactor makes less power when it gets hotter, which is exactly the opposite of a runaway.

blocks.title: The negative feedback loop in a water-moderated core
items: Power rises and the core heats up
Fuel gets hotter and U-238 absorbs more neutrons
Water expands or forms voids and moderates less
Fewer thermal neutrons cause fewer fissions
Power falls back toward where it started

blocks.text: The same feedback has a quietly elegant side effect: in a PWR, the reactor tends to follow the turbine. Open the turbine valves to draw more steam and the steam generators pull more heat out of the primary loop. The water returning to the core arrives a little cooler and denser, moderates a little better, and power rises to match the new demand. Close the valves and the opposite happens. Within limits, the core adjusts itself to the load without anyone touching a rod, the way a well-designed system should: the physics does the routine work, and people handle the exceptions.

This is why commercial reactors are deliberately designed with negative coefficients. It is also why the Soviet RBMK design at Chernobyl was so dangerous. In that reactor, graphite did the moderating while water did the cooling, so steam bubbles removed a neutron absorber without removing the moderator. Under the conditions of April 1986 its void coefficient turned strongly positive, and more steam meant more power.
Two loops and a pressurizer

Water boils at 100 °C at sea level. The water flowing through a PWR core reaches about 325 °C and still does not boil, because it is held at roughly 150 times atmospheric pressure. That pressure is set by the pressurizer, a tall tank connected to the primary loop where a bubble of steam sits on top of the water. Heaters and sprays in the pressurizer nudge the steam bubble's temperature, and with it the pressure of the entire loop.

The primary loop never sends its water to the turbine. Instead, it runs through steam generators, enormous heat exchangers that can weigh up to 800 tonnes and contain anywhere from 300 to 16,000 tubes about 2 cm across. Hot primary water flows inside the tubes; cooler secondary water outside them boils into steam. The two waters never touch. That matters because primary water picks up radioactivity, including nitrogen-16, made when neutrons hit oxygen in the water. N-16 has a half-life of about 7 seconds, and plants watch for it in the steam as an early sign that a tube is leaking.

blocks.title: From fission to the grid in a PWR
items: Fission in the fuel heats the pellets and cladding
Primary water at about 325 °C and 150 atmospheres carries heat out of the core
Steam generators pass the heat to a separate secondary loop, where water boils
Steam spins the turbine, which turns the generator
A condenser cools the spent steam back to water using a river, lake, sea or cooling tower
Feed pumps return the water to the steam generators, and the cycle repeats

blocks.text: Because the steam is relatively cool by power-plant standards, a light water reactor converts only about 33 to 37% of its heat into electricity, up to about 38% in the newest PWRs. The other two-thirds leave through the condenser. That is not a nuclear quirk. It is the second law of thermodynamics, and it applies to every steam plant ever built.
The heat that will not shut off

Drop every control rod into the core and fission stops within seconds. The heat does not. The fuel is packed with radioactive fission products that keep decaying, and their decay keeps warming the core. At the moment of shutdown this decay heat is about 6.5% of the reactor's full power. After an hour it is about 1.5%, after a day about 0.4%, and after a week about 0.2%.

blocks.title: Decay heat after shutdown
blocks.note: Small percentages of a very large number: enough to melt a core if cooling is lost.
blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Nuclear Power Reactors

blocks.text: A few percent sounds trivial until you remember what it is a percentage of. At Fukushima Daiichi, an hour after the reactors shut down, decay heat was still about 22 megawatts in unit 1 and 33 megawatts in each of units 2 and 3. That is plenty to boil away the water around a core and melt it. Almost every serious reactor accident in history, including Three Mile Island and Fukushima, was not a failure to stop the chain reaction. It was a failure to keep cooling the fuel after the chain reaction had already stopped.

That is why so much of a PWR's design exists for the hours after a shutdown rather than the years of operation. There are emergency injection pumps, backup diesel generators, auxiliary feedwater to keep the steam generators supplied, and, around everything, a containment building typically about a metre of steel-reinforced concrete. The fuel pellet, the zirconium cladding, the reactor vessel and primary piping, and the containment form successive barriers between fission products and the outside world.
Why they run flat out

Once all of this is built, the fuel is cheap and the plant is expensive, so the economic logic is simple: run it as hard as possible, as often as possible. Most PWRs refuel every 12, 18 or 24 months, swapping out a quarter to a third of their fuel assemblies at a time. Between outages they hum along near full power around the clock.

blocks.title: US capacity factors by source, 2025
blocks.note: Capacity factor compares actual generation with what the plant could produce running full-time.
blocks.source: US EIA, Electric Power Monthly, Tables 6.07.A and 6.07.B (2025 final values)

blocks.text: In 2025 the US nuclear fleet ran at a capacity factor of about 91%, far above any other source. As of March 2026 there were 94 operating commercial reactors at 54 plants in 28 states, with an average age of about 44 years. They supplied about 17% of US electricity in 2025. The newest, Vogtle unit 4 in Georgia, entered service in April 2024.

It is worth sitting with the shape of the whole machine. The PWR descends directly from a submarine power plant, and its civilian form kept the same core idea: pick materials so that the physics argues for stability, then surround that physics with layers of engineered backup. The operator is not really driving a beast that wants to run away. The operator is guarding margins, the delayed-neutron margin, the subcooling margin, the decay-heat margin, so that the plant's natural tendency toward calm never gets overridden.

That reframe matters for anyone who has stood a watch. The dramatic picture of nuclear power is a chain reaction on the edge of control. The real picture is a heat source that is almost stubbornly steady, attached to a cooling problem that never takes a day off. The hard part was never splitting the atom. It was boiling water, reliably, forever, including on the day everything else goes wrong.

takeaways: A U-235 fission releases about 200 MeV, roughly fifty million times the energy of burning one carbon atom.
Delayed neutrons, only about 0.66% of the total, are what make a reactor controllable on a human timescale.
Water moderation gives a PWR negative feedback: hotter water or steam voids mean less power, not more.
Decay heat is about 6.5% of full power at shutdown and still about 1.5% after an hour, so cooling must never stop.
US reactors ran at about a 91% capacity factor in 2025, higher than any other power source.

title: Hydrogen Isn't a Fuel. It's a Leaky Battery.
dek: The world already uses almost 100 million tonnes of hydrogen a year, nearly all of it dirty. The physics shows where clean hydrogen makes sense and where it is mostly hype.

blocks.text: Every year the world makes and uses close to 100 million tonnes of hydrogen. That is not a forecast or a pilot program. It is a giant, boring, century-old industry, and according to the International Energy Agency, less than 1% of that hydrogen is made in a low-emissions way. Almost all of it comes from natural gas or coal, and almost all of it goes into fertilizer factories and oil refineries. New uses like cars, trucks and power plants together account for less than 1% of demand.

Keep that picture in mind the next time you see a glossy ad for a hydrogen car or a headline about the coming "hydrogen economy." Hydrogen is real, useful and important. But it has been sold for decades as a near-magical clean fuel, and the physics tells a more modest story. The best way to see through the hype is to treat hydrogen not as a fuel at all, but as what it really is: a way of storing energy that somebody else already produced.
Not a source, a carrier

There are no hydrogen wells in the usual sense. Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe, but on Earth it is almost always locked up with something else, in water or in hydrocarbons like methane. To get pure hydrogen you have to break those bonds, and that takes at least as much energy as you will ever get back by burning the hydrogen or running it through a fuel cell. That makes hydrogen an *energy carrier*, like electricity or a charged battery, not an energy *source* like uranium, sunlight or gas.

How it is made is the whole ballgame, and the industry uses colors as shorthand. In the United States, according to the Department of Energy, about 95% of hydrogen comes from natural gas reforming, where methane reacts with high-temperature steam. That releases carbon dioxide, and the result is often called gray hydrogen. Capture and bury that CO2 and you get blue hydrogen. Split water with electricity from renewables and you get green hydrogen; use nuclear electricity and some call it pink.

blocks.title: The color code, decoded

left.head: Made from fossil fuels
items: Gray: steam reforming of natural gas, CO2 released
Black or brown: gasified coal, even more CO2
Blue: gray plus carbon capture, only as clean as the capture rate and methane leaks allow

right.head: Made by splitting water
items: Green: electrolysis powered by wind or solar
Pink: electrolysis powered by nuclear plants
Clean only if the electricity is clean and would not have been used better elsewhere

blocks.text: Blue hydrogen has its own fine print. Carbon capture never grabs all the CO2, and natural gas leaks on its way from the wellhead to the plant. Methane is a far more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 over the short term, so a leaky supply chain can erase much of the benefit. Whether a given blue hydrogen project is genuinely low-carbon depends on numbers that have to be measured, not assumed.

That last line matters more than it looks. If you run an electrolyzer on grid power that is partly coal and gas, the hydrogen can end up dirtier than plain gray hydrogen, because you burned fossil fuel to make electricity and then lost a big chunk of it in conversion. A clean color label depends entirely on where the electrons came from.
The energy math nobody puts in the ad

Electrolysis is something any nuke-school graduate can picture: pass a current through water, and hydrogen bubbles off one electrode while oxygen comes off the other. Submarines have used the same basic chemistry for decades to make breathing oxygen. The question is how much electricity it takes.

The DOE's published figures for current proton exchange membrane electrolyzer systems are about 55 kilowatt-hours of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen, which works out to roughly 61% efficiency. Its long-term target is 46 kWh per kilogram. For scale, the DOE's Alternative Fuels Data Center says one kilogram of hydrogen holds about the same energy as one gallon of gasoline. So today it takes around 55 kWh of electricity to make the hydrogen-equivalent of one gallon of gas.

items.label: Electricity used per kg of hydrogen by current PEM electrolyzer systems
Gasoline with about the same energy as 1 kg of hydrogen
Efficiency hydrogen fuel cells are capable of

blocks.source: US DOE Hydrogen and Fuel Cell Technologies Office; Alternative Fuels Data Center

blocks.text: Getting the energy back out is electrolysis run in reverse. In a fuel cell, hydrogen flows over one electrode, where a catalyst strips each molecule into protons and electrons. A thin membrane lets only the protons through. The electrons have to take the long way around, through an outside circuit, and that flow is your electric current. On the far side, protons, electrons and oxygen from the air meet and form water. No combustion, no moving parts, and the only exhaust is water vapor. It is elegant. It is also never perfectly efficient, because every step sheds some energy as heat.

Now follow the energy all the way around. Turn electricity into hydrogen at about 61%. Turn the hydrogen back into electricity in a fuel cell at around 60% at best. Multiply, and you get back roughly 37 units of electricity for every 100 you started with, and that is before the energy needed to compress, chill, store or truck the gas. Compare that with storing electricity in a battery or a pumped-hydro reservoir.

blocks.title: Electricity returned for every 100 units stored
blocks.note: Battery and pumped hydro are measured US fleet averages for 2019. Hydrogen is calculated from DOE electrolyzer (61%) and fuel cell (about 60%) figures and excludes compression and storage losses.
blocks.source: US EIA, Today in Energy, 2021; US DOE Hydrogen and Fuel Cell Technologies Office

blocks.text: For short-term storage, that gap is brutal. If a battery can return more than twice as much of the electricity you put in, hydrogen has to win on something else to make sense, such as storing energy for months rather than hours, or doing a job that electricity simply cannot do directly.

Long-duration storage is where that something else might live. Batteries are superb at shifting energy by hours, but storing a summer's worth of solar power for a dark winter would take an absurd number of them, sitting mostly idle. Hydrogen can be pumped into underground salt caverns and left there for months at low cost per unit of energy stored. When the alternative is having no stored energy at all during a long cold, windless stretch, a 37% round trip can still be worth it. Efficiency is a cost, not a verdict.
Why cheap hydrogen is hard

Efficiency is only half the problem. The other half is money. The DOE lists the current uninstalled cost of a PEM electrolyzer system at around $1,000 per kilowatt, and the cost of producing hydrogen this way at more than $3 per kilogram, and that is assuming very cheap electricity available almost all the time. Its Hydrogen Shot goals are $2 per kilogram by 2026 and $1 per kilogram by 2031.

Here is the trap. Green hydrogen's big pitch is to soak up surplus solar and wind when power is nearly free. But an expensive machine that only runs when the sun is shining sits idle much of the time, and its capital cost gets spread over fewer kilograms. Run it around the clock and you need around-the-clock power, which is either fossil, nuclear or a lot of extra renewables. This is one reason nuclear plants keep coming up in hydrogen discussions: a reactor runs flat out day and night, which is exactly what an expensive electrolyzer wants.

A useful habit for any energy claim: ask what it replaces and what the round trip costs. Hydrogen that replaces gray hydrogen in a fertilizer plant cuts emissions directly. Hydrogen that replaces a battery usually wastes most of the electricity it was made from.
Where hydrogen is already irreplaceable

On October 13, 1908, the German chemist Fritz Haber filed his patent on making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen. Industrialized by Carl Bosch, the Haber-Bosch process turned air into fertilizer, and it changed the world. A 2008 analysis in *Nature Geoscience* by Jan Willem Erisman and colleagues estimated that nitrogen fertilizer made this way sustained about 48% of the world's population. Roughly half of humanity eats food grown with hydrogen-derived fertilizer.

Refineries are the other big user. They use hydrogen to strip sulfur out of fuels and to crack heavy oil into lighter products. Methanol and some steelmaking add more. None of these uses can simply plug into an outlet instead, because the hydrogen is a chemical ingredient, not just an energy source. Every one of them currently runs mostly on gray hydrogen.

Steel is the next frontier. Traditional blast furnaces use coke, made from coal, both as fuel and as the chemical agent that pulls oxygen out of iron ore, which makes steelmaking one of the largest industrial sources of CO2. Hydrogen can do the same chemical job in a process called direct reduction, leaving water instead of CO2. A few plants are being built to try it at scale. This is a use where electricity alone cannot easily substitute, which is exactly the kind of niche where hydrogen's high cost might be worth paying.

That points to the least glamorous but most sensible plan for clean hydrogen: before inventing new markets, clean up the giant market that already exists. Swapping gray for green or pink hydrogen in fertilizer plants needs no new pipelines to homes, no new cars and no consumer behavior change.
The hydrogen ladder

The energy analyst Michael Liebreich turned this logic into a ranking he calls the Clean Hydrogen Ladder. Version 5.0, published in October 2023, sorts possible uses into rows from A to G by how likely hydrogen is to win a meaningful share by about 2035, considering cost, convenience, safety and the alternatives, not just efficiency.

blocks.title: The Clean Hydrogen Ladder, simplified (Liebreich, v5.0, 2023)
items: Row A, no real alternative: existing uses such as fertilizer and oil refining.
Row B, likely: jet fuel production and chemical feedstocks.
Rows C to D, some to small share: off-road machinery, long-haul trucks, high-temperature industrial heat.
Rows E to F, niche: regional trucks, short-term grid balancing, remote trains, local ferries, backup power.
Row G, unlikely: hydrogen cars, burning hydrogen for power without storage, bulk e-fuels.

blocks.text: Notice where cars sit: on the bottom row. A hydrogen car is an electric car that carries a chemical plant on board, buys its energy at the end of a long and lossy supply chain, and competes with battery cars that charge from any outlet. Liebreich's broader point is that clean hydrogen will be scarce for decades, so every kilogram spent on a weak use case is a kilogram not spent where it is irreplaceable.

Practical problems add up too. Hydrogen is the smallest molecule, so it leaks through seals and fittings that hold other gases, and it can make some steels brittle over time. It ignites over a very wide range of mixtures with air. And by volume it holds little energy, so it has to be squeezed to very high pressure or chilled to near absolute zero. Industry handles all of this safely every day, but each fix adds cost and energy losses.
Separating the hype from the hope

None of this means hydrogen is a dead end. It means hydrogen is a specialist, not a universal fuel. It looks strongest where there is no good electric alternative: making fertilizer and chemicals, possibly steel, long-duration seasonal storage, and as a building block for synthetic fuels for planes and ships. It looks weakest where it competes head-on with batteries and wires.

There is a nuclear twist worth knowing. The energy needed to split water does not all have to arrive as electricity. At high temperatures, a solid oxide electrolyzer can take part of that energy as heat instead, so it needs noticeably less electricity per kilogram. A reactor produces enormous amounts of heat, and heat is cheaper than electricity, because turning heat into electricity loses about two-thirds of it. Pairing reactors with high-temperature electrolysis is one of the more serious ideas in the field, and it is the kind of job a future civilian nuclear workforce may find itself running.

The deeper lesson is about how to read any energy pitch. Start with the conversion chain and multiply the efficiencies, because losses compound. Then ask what the new thing replaces and whether there is a simpler way to do the same job. A technology that sounds clean at the tailpipe can still be wasteful at the system level. Hydrogen's real story is less exciting than the brochures and more useful: a clean version of a molecule the world already cannot live without.

takeaways: Hydrogen is an energy carrier, not a source: making it always costs more energy than you get back.
Electricity to hydrogen to electricity returns roughly a third of the input, versus about 80% for batteries and pumped hydro.
Today's hydrogen is mostly made from natural gas; under 1% is low-emissions.
The best first use of clean hydrogen is replacing dirty hydrogen in fertilizer and refining.
For any energy claim, multiply the conversion efficiencies and ask what it replaces.

title: The Atoms That Find Disease: How Radioactivity Became Medicine
dek: Every day, hospitals inject people with radioactive material on purpose. The story runs from a chemist's trick with lead to a lunchtime question at Harvard to a six-hour isotope whose supply depends on a few aging reactors.

blocks.text: Somewhere right now a patient is lying still under a large camera while a technician watches a screen. Half an hour earlier, the patient was injected with a radioactive substance. Nobody in the room is alarmed. In developed countries, according to the World Nuclear Association, the chance that any given person will have this kind of test at some point is about one in two, and rising.

The same physics that makes reactors need shielding and makes sailors wear dosimeters is used, deliberately, tens of millions of times a year to look inside living bodies and to kill tumors from the inside. Nuclear medicine is the clearest example of a theme that runs through all of nuclear science: radiation is not good or bad. It is a tool whose meaning depends entirely on dose, location and timing.

items.label: Nuclear medicine procedures performed worldwide each year
Share of procedures that use technetium-99m
Half-life of technetium-99m

blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Radioisotopes in Medicine, 2026

blocks.text: The spy atom

The idea at the root of nuclear medicine came from a Hungarian chemist named George de Hevesy. In 1913, working in Vienna with Friedrich Paneth, he ran the first radioactive tracer experiment. The insight was simple and powerful. A radioactive atom behaves chemically exactly like its stable twin, so if you slip a few radioactive atoms into a system, they go wherever the ordinary atoms go. But unlike ordinary atoms, they announce their position by emitting radiation. You can follow them.

Hevesy had already shown that a mysterious substance called radium D was really a radioactive form of lead. In 1923 he used radioactive lead to trace how plants absorb and move the metal, proving that labeled atoms could reveal what happens inside a living organism without cutting it open. Over the following decades he extended the method to animals and people, and in 1943 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for using isotopes as tracers. Nearly every scan in a nuclear medicine department today is a descendant of that idea: put a spy atom on a molecule the body uses, and watch where it goes.
A question at lunch

The jump from watching to treating started with a single question. On November 12, 1936, Karl Compton, president of MIT, gave a talk at a Harvard Medical School faculty luncheon about what physics could do for medicine. Saul Hertz, a young physician who ran the thyroid unit at Massachusetts General Hospital, asked whether iodine could be made radioactive artificially.

The question was not random. The thyroid gland soaks up iodine from the blood to make its hormones, more greedily than any other tissue. If iodine could be made radioactive, it would carry radiation straight to the thyroid and almost nowhere else. For patients with an overactive thyroid, that could mean treating the gland from the inside with no surgery.

The answer was yes. Hertz teamed up with an MIT physicist, Arthur Roberts. Using a short-lived iodine isotope made with a radium-beryllium neutron source, the method Enrico Fermi had pioneered, they injected rabbits and confirmed that radioactive iodine concentrated in the thyroid. But the isotope had a half-life of only 25 minutes, far too short for treatment. They needed more, and longer-lived. With a $30,000 grant, MIT built a cyclotron largely for medical work. It came online in November 1940.

On March 31, 1941, Hertz gave a woman with hyperthyroidism a dose of radioactive iodine made in that cyclotron, a mixture of iodine-130 and iodine-131. She became the first patient treated with radioiodine for thyroid disease. A Berkeley team began treating patients the same way later that year. Radioiodine is still a mainstay treatment for overactive thyroid and for thyroid cancer, given in much the same way Hertz gave it more than eighty years ago.

Credit turned out to be its own fight. While Hertz was away on wartime military service, a colleague familiar with his work wrote up radioiodine results, and in 1946 that paper reached the journal without crediting his earlier work. The editor of the Journal of the American Medical Association invited Hertz and Roberts to write up their own results, on 29 patients. Both papers ran in the same issue, with Hertz and Roberts placed first. It is a reminder that in science, as in any team, doing the work and getting recognized for it are separate problems, and the second one is often solved only by writing things down.

The war then changed everything about supply. The Manhattan Project built reactors that could make radioactive isotopes in quantities no cyclotron could match, including iodine-131 as a by-product of fission. In June 1946, partly inspired by Hertz's work, the project announced that radioisotopes would be made available for civilian research and medicine. Hertz himself had little time to benefit. He died of a heart attack in 1950 at age 45, and for decades his role was largely overlooked.

blocks.text: The six-hour isotope

The workhorse of modern nuclear medicine is technetium-99m. Emilio Segre and Glenn Seaborg identified it in 1938, but it stayed a laboratory curiosity for two decades. Then, in 1958, Walter Tucker and Margaret Greene at Brookhaven National Laboratory, working on a different parent-daughter isotope pair, built the first technetium-99m generator. Around 1960 their colleague Powell Richards began pushing technetium as a medical tracer, and through the 1960s, helped by better gamma cameras, its use spread worldwide.

Technetium-99m is close to ideal for imaging. Its six-hour half-life is long enough to prepare a dose, inject it and scan, but short enough that the patient's radiation dose stays small. It emits a gamma ray with an energy that cameras detect well. And it can be chemically attached to many different carrier molecules, each built to collect in a different organ: bone, heart muscle, kidneys, lungs. Change the carrier, and the same isotope becomes a different scan.

That six-hour half-life is also a trap. You cannot stockpile technetium. Within a day, almost all of it is gone. The solution is the generator: a shielded container holding molybdenum-99, which has a 66-hour half-life and decays into technetium-99m. A hospital receives the generator, washes the fresh technetium out with salt water each morning, and sends the generator back for recharging after two weeks or less. The slower parent keeps producing the fast daughter, like a well that refills overnight.

blocks.title: From reactor to scan
items: Uranium targets are irradiated in a research reactor; some fissions produce molybdenum-99.
The targets are dissolved and the molybdenum-99 is separated and purified.
Molybdenum-99 is loaded into shielded generators and shipped fast, since it loses about 1% of its strength per hour.
At the hospital, saline washes out the technetium-99m its parent has produced.
Technetium is attached to a carrier molecule chosen for the organ being studied, then injected.
A gamma camera maps where the radiation comes from, building a picture of function, not just shape.

blocks.text: Seeing what tissue is doing

An X-ray or CT scan shows anatomy, where things are. Nuclear medicine shows physiology, what things are doing. A heart scan can show which part of the muscle is not getting enough blood under stress. A bone scan can light up spots where bone is being rebuilt unusually fast, which can mean a hidden fracture or a cancer that has spread.

The scale is large. More than 10,000 hospitals worldwide use radioisotopes, and about 90% of procedures are diagnostic. The United States performs over 20 million nuclear medicine procedures a year and Europe about 10 million, of which around 2 million are treatments rather than scans. Most patients never think of it as anything nuclear. To them it is just the heart test, or the bone scan, or the pill for an overactive thyroid.

Positron emission tomography, or PET, takes the idea further. The most common PET tracer is a modified sugar called FDG, labeled with fluorine-18. Cells take it up like glucose but cannot fully break it down, so it accumulates in proportion to how hard the tissue is working. Many cancers are hungry for sugar, so they glow. Fluorine-18 has a half-life of just under two hours, which means it has to be made in a cyclotron within a couple of hours' reach of the scanner. Hospitals combine PET with CT so doctors can see both the activity and the anatomy in one image.

blocks.title: Two workhorse imaging isotopes
