Made from molybdenum-99 from research reactors
Delivered via generators that last up to two weeks
Used in about 80% of nuclear medicine procedures
Bone, heart, kidney, lung and many other scans

right.head: Fluorine-18 (PET)
items: Half-life just under 2 hours
Made in cyclotrons, no reactor needed
Must be used within a couple of hours of production
Main tracer FDG maps sugar use
Most important clinical role is cancer

blocks.text: A fragile pipeline

Here is the part most people never hear about. According to the World Nuclear Association, about 95% of the world's molybdenum-99 comes from just six reactors, and five of them are more than 50 years old. Because the product decays constantly, there is no warehouse to fall back on. If a key reactor goes down unexpectedly, scans get canceled within days.

That is exactly what happened in 2009 and 2010, when Canada's NRU reactor at Chalk River and the High Flux Reactor at Petten in the Netherlands both needed major repairs and were offline for long stretches. Hospitals around the world rationed technetium, postponed tests and switched to older, less convenient methods where they could. NRU stopped isotope production in 2016 and closed for good in 2018. A replacement for the Petten reactor, called PALLAS, began construction in 2025 with operation planned for 2032.

The industry has also made a quiet nonproliferation shift. Molybdenum-99 used to be made by irradiating targets of highly enriched uranium, the kind of material that worries security experts. As of March 2023, every reactor producing it uses low-enriched targets instead, which adds about 20% to production costs, small next to the cost of the hospital visit. Meanwhile, cyclotron routes that make technetium without a reactor are emerging; Health Canada approved the first cyclotron-produced technetium product in 2020.

A medical supply chain that depends on a handful of half-century-old reactors and a product that loses about 1% of its strength every hour is a lesson in hidden fragility. Systems can work smoothly for decades and still have a single point of failure.
From seeing to treating

The newest chapter loops back to Hertz. If a molecule can carry a camera-friendly isotope to a tumor, the same molecule can carry a destructive one. This pairing of diagnosis and therapy is now called theranostics. Doctors first image a patient with a diagnostic version to confirm the tumor takes up the carrier, then treat with a version carrying a beta emitter such as lutetium-177, whose short-range radiation damages cells close to where it lands.

The strongest evidence so far comes from advanced prostate cancer. Many prostate tumors carry a surface protein called PSMA. In the VISION trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021, 831 men with metastatic prostate cancer that had stopped responding to hormone therapy and chemotherapy were randomly assigned to standard care with or without lutetium-177 attached to a PSMA-seeking molecule. The radioactive drug extended median survival from 11.3 to 15.3 months and more than doubled the median time before scans showed the cancer progressing, from 3.4 to 8.7 months.

blocks.title: VISION trial: median months, advanced prostate cancer
blocks.note: Serious side effects (grade 3 or higher) were also more common with the drug: 52.7% vs 38.0%.
blocks.source: Sartor et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2021

blocks.text: Those numbers deserve honest reading. Four extra months is meaningful for men who had run out of options, and the trial found quality of life was not made worse. But it is not a cure, and serious side effects were more frequent. The excitement around theranostics is real, and so are its limits.
Dose, place, time

If you work around reactors, you are trained to treat radiation with respect: time, distance and shielding, and keeping dose as low as reasonably achievable. Nuclear medicine runs on the same principles turned inside out. Its designers choose isotopes for half-lives that match the job, pick carrier molecules that put the radiation exactly where it is wanted, and use the smallest dose that gets the image or kills the target.

The reframe is this: there are no dangerous substances in the abstract, only dangerous doses in the wrong place at the wrong time. Hevesy's spy atoms, Hertz's radioiodine and today's tumor-seeking drugs all work because someone figured out how to control those three variables. That is also, in the end, what every reactor operator is doing on every watch.

takeaways: Hevesy's tracer principle (1913): radioactive atoms behave chemically like normal ones, so you can follow them through a living body.
Saul Hertz's 1936 lunchtime question led to the first radioiodine treatment in 1941, still a standard thyroid therapy.
Technetium-99m powers about 80% of nuclear medicine; its six-hour half-life makes it ideal for scans and impossible to stockpile.
About 95% of molybdenum-99 comes from six reactors, mostly over 50 years old, a textbook single point of failure.
Theranostics uses the same targeting molecule to find and treat cancer; results are real but modest so far.

title: One Design, Two Missions: Naval vs. Commercial Reactors
dek: Both are pressurized-water reactors. One is built to sell electricity cheaply; the other is built to survive combat and never stop for fuel, and that changes everything.

blocks.text: Two machines share almost the same blueprint. Each splits uranium inside a steel pressure vessel, heats water that is kept under so much pressure it cannot boil, and hands that heat through a steam generator to a second loop of water that does boil and spins a turbine. One of them sits on a riverbank in Georgia and sells electricity by the megawatt-hour. The other is welded into a hull, dives, and is expected to run for the whole life of the ship without anyone opening it up to add fuel.

On paper they are the same invention: the pressurized-water reactor. In practice they are as different as a work truck and a race car that happen to share an engine layout. The useful question is not how each one works, but what each one is *for*. Change the mission and every downstream choice changes with it: fuel, materials, size, staffing, regulation, and even what counts as winning.

The numbers the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program publishes show how far the naval branch has pushed. USS Nautilus steamed about 62,000 miles on her first core before she was refueled in 1957. The program now says its submarine and aircraft carrier cores have an endurance of more than a million miles.

items.label: Naval reactors in operation (Dec 2024)
Reactor-years of naval operation
US commercial power reactors operating (Mar 2026)

blocks.source: Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, The U.S. Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, 2025; US EIA, U.S. Nuclear Industry, 2026

blocks.text: Same loop, different job description

Start with what is shared. The NRC's public description of a commercial PWR and the Navy's public description of a naval plant read almost line for line the same. Water in a closed primary loop carries heat from the core to steam generators. Across a watertight boundary, a secondary loop at lower pressure boils, drives turbines, condenses and returns. Keeping the loops separate keeps radioactivity in the primary system away from the turbines and the people who work on them.

The family resemblance is not a coincidence. President Eisenhower made the naval program responsible for building the Shippingport Atomic Power Station in Pennsylvania, the world's first full-scale atomic plant built only to make electricity. The program says Shippingport's PWR design and original cores became the prototypes for most commercial nuclear stations, and it also credits itself with the uranium-dioxide fuel system and the zirconium alloys that civilian plants still use.

Where the two branches split is in the requirements written above the engineering. A commercial reactor has one overriding job: make as much electricity as possible, as cheaply and safely as possible, for decades, from a fixed spot on the grid. A naval reactor has a stranger job: deliver power on demand to a warship that may be hunted, has to stay quiet, keeps its crew close to the core, and can never pull into a gas station.

blocks.title: What each reactor is optimized for

left.head: Commercial PWR
items: Lowest cost per megawatt-hour
Runs near full power almost all year
Refuels part of the core every 12 to 24 months
Low-enriched fuel, about 3 to 5% U-235
Licensed and inspected by the NRC

right.head: Naval PWR
items: Endurance, speed and stealth
Frequent, rapid power changes
Newer cores built to last the life of the ship
Highly enriched fuel in most navies
Run cradle to grave by Naval Reactors

blocks.text: The fuel decision that drives everything

Commercial fuel is uranium enriched to about 3 to 5% uranium-235, pressed into ceramic pellets and stacked into metal tubes. According to the EIA, operators typically replace about a third of the core every 12 to 24 months. Those refueling outages are planned like any other maintenance, because a power plant sits next to a road, a rail line and a crane, and the spare fuel is waiting in a storage bin on site.

A warship has none of those luxuries. Refueling one means a long stretch in a shipyard with the reactor opened up, so the naval program has pushed toward cores that last as long as the hull. Its 2025 overview says the Virginia-class reactor plant is designed to last the planned 33-year life of the ship without refueling, and that the coming Columbia class will have a life-of-the-ship core supporting more than 40 years of service. The program credits that shift with lower life-cycle costs and more time on mission.

How does a core last three decades? Part of the public answer is enrichment. The World Nuclear Association notes that most or all of the world's nuclear submarines are fuelled by highly enriched uranium, which by international definition means 20% uranium-235 or more, far above commercial fuel. More fissile atoms packed into a small volume means more energy stored before the core runs out of reactivity. Specific details of US naval fuel are not public, and an open article should not guess at them.

France shows the trade-off from the other side. The WNA reports that newer French naval reactors use low-enriched fuel close to civilian levels, and that its Barracuda-class submarines refuel roughly every ten years. Lower enrichment spares France a separate military enrichment line, but the price is periodic refueling and a somewhat larger core. Neither path is free. Each navy bought the thing it valued more.

blocks.title: Naval core endurance, then and now
blocks.note: Today's figure is the program's floor: submarine and carrier cores now exceed one million miles.
blocks.source: Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, The U.S. Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, 2025

blocks.text: Built to take a hit

The Department of Energy spells out why naval components are held to a stricter standard than civilian ones. Warship reactors must be designed for battle shock, limits on radiated noise, a crew living close to the plant, and frequent, rapid changes in power. The heavy components take four to eight years of precision machining, welding, heat treatment and inspection of large specialty forgings before they are ready to install.

Each of those requirements pushes the design somewhere a utility never has to go. A commercial plant is anchored to bedrock and designed for earthquakes, but no one expects it to absorb an underwater explosion. It can be as loud as it likes. Its operators sit in a control room behind thick concrete. And it spends most of its life at a steady 100% power, because that is when it earns the most money.

The Navy's description of its own philosophy stresses stability and simplicity. It calls its reactors small and relatively uncomplicated, inherently stable, and able to ride through operational transients without immediate operator action. It also says something revealing about the human side: the plants are designed to be operated and maintained by highly trained Navy crews, without scientists and engineers aboard. The machine is built around the sailors who will run it, far from help.
Every engineering choice is downstream of a mission. To understand any machine, from a reactor to a game engine, ask what its designers were told to optimize and what they were allowed to sacrifice.
Two different scoreboards

Commercial nuclear power keeps score in capacity factor, the share of the year a plant spends producing its maximum possible output. The EIA reports that the US nuclear fleet averaged 91% in 2025, higher than any other type of power plant. As of March 2026 there were 94 operating commercial reactors at 54 plants in 28 states, with combined capacity of about 98,000 megawatts. A reactor sitting idle is losing money, so the whole business is built around running flat out and refueling fast.

A warship keeps score differently: availability when needed, speed when needed, and silence the rest of the time. The program's overview points to the 1964 cruise in which three nuclear-powered warships went around the world, 30,000 miles in 65 days, with no refueling or logistics support, and to USS Nimitz's 321-day deployment in 2021 with no port calls. A naval reactor that loafs at low power for weeks and then sprints is doing exactly its job.

Even the money is counted differently. A utility weighs a design change against the price of electricity it will sell. The naval program weighs it against the ship's whole life: its overview says the Columbia class's new life-of-the-ship core and propulsion plant will let the planned 12 boats cover the nation's deterrent requirements, with expected savings of more than $40 billion. For comparison, the program says Nimitz-class carriers go more than 20 years without refueling and need one refueling in the life of the ship. Spending more up front to avoid a refueling decades later only makes sense when you count years at sea, not megawatt-hours.

The safety scoreboards are kept differently too. Commercial plants are measured through NRC inspections, performance indicators and enforcement. The naval program reports its own record in public documents: more than 7,600 reactor-years and over 177 million miles steamed on nuclear power, with, in its words, no reactor accident and no release of radioactivity that has harmed human health or the environment.

blocks.text: Who regulates the regulators

The biggest institutional difference is who is in charge. Commercial reactors are licensed and inspected by the NRC, an independent agency, and their operators hold individual NRC licenses. Naval reactors sit outside that system entirely. Under Executive Order 12344 and the laws that codify it, Naval Reactors, a joint Department of Energy and Navy organization, holds total responsibility for naval propulsion plants: research, design, construction, operation, maintenance, personnel selection and training, and final disposal.

That cradle-to-grave model shows up in places a civilian might not expect. Commercial plants plan around a plume exposure emergency planning zone about 10 miles in radius and an ingestion zone of about 50 miles. The naval program states that, because of how its ships are designed and operated, ordinary civil emergency plans for things like chemical spills or earthquakes are also sufficient for a radiological emergency aboard a nuclear-powered ship. Naval spent fuel, built ruggedly enough for combat, makes up about 0.05% of all spent nuclear fuel in the country.

Training follows the same split. The naval program selects, trains and assigns its own people through Nuclear Field A School and Nuclear Power School in Charleston, then hands-on qualification on land-based prototypes and moored training ships, so that every operator has qualified on a working plant before a first sea tour. Its statistics count more than 127,000 enlisted sailors trained or in training since the beginning. A commercial plant, by contrast, trains operators on its own unit and its own full-scale simulator, and the NRC tests and licenses each of them for that one plant.

Radiation exposure tells a similar story. The program says its plants are shielded so well that typical operators at sea receive less radiation than they would from natural background ashore over the same period. Its latest occupational report put the average 2025 exposure of nuclear-trained sailors living aboard at less than 3% of what the average American gets from natural background. Since 1980, no one in the program has exceeded 2 rem in a year, against a federal limit of 5.
What carries over to the civilian side

If the two branches are so different, why do commercial plants hire so many former Navy nukes? Because the deepest similarity is not hardware. It is a way of operating: procedure compliance, formal communications, conservative decisions, and a refusal to treat a strange indication as noise. Those habits were built into the naval program from the start and carried into civilian power by the people who left it. A former submarine operator walking into a commercial control room will find bigger panels, different systems and a different regulator, but the same expectation that every action is briefed, every reading is believed until proven wrong, and every surprise gets reported.

The hardware is also drifting back together. Many small modular reactor designs advertise features that would sound familiar in a submarine engine room: compact cores, longer intervals between refuelings, natural circulation for decay heat removal and factory-built components. What still separates them is the objective. A civilian SMR has to sell electricity at a price someone will pay, which is a big reason most designs stay with low-enriched fuel and accept refueling outages.

So the honest answer to how different they are: the physics is identical, the engineering overlaps, and the missions are almost opposite. A commercial reactor is an asset tuned for cost per megawatt-hour. A naval reactor is part of a weapon system tuned for endurance, stealth and survivability, and it pays whatever that costs. Once you see the mission, the other differences stop looking arbitrary and start looking inevitable.

takeaways: Naval and commercial plants are both pressurized-water reactors; the commercial PWR descends directly from the naval program's Shippingport project.
Commercial fuel is 3 to 5% enriched and partly replaced every 12 to 24 months; newer US naval cores are designed to last the life of the ship.
Naval components must handle battle shock, noise limits, crew proximity and rapid power swings, so they are built to stricter standards.
Commercial plants win on capacity factor (91% in 2025); warships win on availability, endurance and stealth.
The NRC regulates civilian reactors; Naval Reactors runs the naval program cradle to grave under Executive Order 12344.

title: The License Exam: What It Takes to Become a Civilian Reactor Operator
dek: A Navy nuke already knows the theory. The NRC license tests something harder: whether you know one specific plant well enough to be trusted with it alone.

blocks.text: For more than thirty years, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission gave every applicant for a reactor operator license the same opening test: a 50-question exam on reactor theory, thermodynamics and plant components. About 13,000 people took it between 1989 and 2021. The NRC kept careful statistics, and one pattern held for two decades.

On questions pulled straight from the published question bank, examinees scored around 94 to 95%. On bank questions that had been significantly modified, scores fell to the mid-to-high 80s. On brand-new questions, they dropped to the low-to-mid 70s. Same people, same subject, same day. The only difference was whether they had seen the question before.

That 20-point gap is the best one-line summary of what an operator license is really testing. It is not whether you have memorized answers. It is whether you understand a plant well enough to handle the question nobody wrote down in advance. For anyone leaving the Navy's nuclear program and eyeing a civilian control room, that is both the challenge and the opportunity.

items.label: Average score on unchanged question-bank items
Average on significantly modified bank items
Average on newly written items

blocks.source: US NRC, Generic Fundamentals Examinations for Reactor Operators, 2026

blocks.text: A license is a key to one door

Start with what the license is. Under federal regulations in 10 CFR Part 55, the NRC licenses every person who operates or supervises the controls of a commercial power reactor. According to the NRC, about 3,600 people hold active power reactor operator licenses in the United States. There are two levels: reactor operator, or RO, who manipulates the controls, and senior reactor operator, or SRO, who supervises and directs licensed activities.

The most important fact about the license is how narrow it is. An NRC license is valid only for the facility named on it. It expires after six years, or sooner if you leave that employer or the plant decides you no longer need it. You cannot earn a license on your own and then shop it around. A plant hires you, trains you on its unit, and then sponsors you.

That design is deliberate, and it is worth understanding rather than resenting. Two pressurized water reactors can share a vendor and still differ in hundreds of ways that matter at 3 a.m.: which pump trips on which signal, which valve fails open, which procedure step comes first. A license that certified general competence would certify the wrong thing. The NRC is not asking whether you are a good operator. It is asking whether you are a good operator of *this* plant.

That sponsorship is formal. The application, NRC Form 398, requires an authorized representative of the plant to certify that you have completed its training program and that it needs you as an operator. You also need a medical examination certified on NRC Form 396 showing you are physically and mentally fit for the job. If a medical condition does not meet the standards, the NRC can still approve the application with conditions written into the license to accommodate it. And the regulations require evidence that, as a trainee, you have performed at least five significant control manipulations affecting reactivity or power, either on the actual plant or on a simulator that models it.

blocks.title: The road to an NRC operator license
items: Get hired by a nuclear plant into its operator training pipeline
Complete the plant's licensed-operator training program
Perform at least five significant reactivity or power manipulations as a trainee
Plant certifies your training and need for you on NRC Form 398, with a medical on Form 396
Pass the written exam: 75 questions for RO, 100 for SRO
Pass the operating test: plant walkthrough plus simulator scenarios
Receive a license for that one plant, valid for six years

blocks.text: What the written exam covers

The written exam for an RO is 75 multiple-choice questions, and you need 80% to pass. SRO applicants take an additional 25 questions and must score 80% on all 100 and at least 70% on the SRO-only portion. Either the plant writes the exam and the NRC reviews and approves it, or the plant asks the NRC to write it. Either way, it follows the agency's examination standards in NUREG-1021.

The regulation lists 14 knowledge areas the RO exam samples from. Some will feel like a reunion with nuke school: fundamentals of reactor theory, including neutron multiplication, reactivity coefficients and poison effects; heat transfer, thermodynamics and fluid mechanics; radiological safety principles. Others are pure plant knowledge: the design of this core, its control and safety systems with their interlocks and failure modes, its emergency systems, and its normal, abnormal and emergency operating procedures.

To decide which specific facts are fair game, the NRC publishes knowledge and abilities catalogs: NUREG-1122 for pressurized water reactors, NUREG-1123 for boiling water reactors and a separate catalog for the Westinghouse AP1000. These catalogs rate thousands of knowledge statements by importance to safe operation. If you want a concrete preview of what a civilian license expects, skimming the catalog for your target plant type is one of the most useful free things you can do.

One detail in the regulation is easy to skim past. The NRC says the knowledge tested is identified partly from a systematic analysis of the operator's actual duties, and partly from the plant's own documents: its final safety analysis report, system manuals, operating procedures, license amendments and Licensee Event Reports. Those event reports are the plant's official record of things that went wrong. In other words, your future plant's past mistakes are legitimate exam material, which is exactly how it should be.
The written exam samples fundamentals, but most of its weight lands on one plant's systems and procedures. Theory gets you in the door; plant-specific knowledge gets you the license.
The operating test

Passing the written exam is only half. The NRC also gives an operating test, which has two parts: a walkthrough of the plant, where you demonstrate tasks and explain systems at the actual equipment, and a performance demonstration on the plant's simulator. The regulation lists 13 kinds of things the test can ask you to do, from pre-startup procedures and console manipulations between shutdown and power to identifying annunciators, running heat removal and emergency systems, and handling radiation hazards.

The simulator is not a generic training toy. NRC rules require a plant-referenced simulator to reproduce the expected response of that specific plant to operator input and to normal, transient and accident conditions. When it is used for a trainee's required control manipulations, its nuclear and thermal-hydraulic models must replicate the plant's most recent core load. In other words, the control room you train and test in behaves like your plant's control room, with this cycle's fuel, on its worst day.

SRO candidates face a more demanding operating test, because their job is to supervise the crew and direct licensed activities. If you pass both the written exam and the operating test, the NRC's regional office issues the license, with any conditions it considers necessary.
The fundamentals exam that disappeared

That 50-question fundamentals test from the opening, the Generic Fundamentals Examination, no longer exists. The NRC says the last one was given in September 2021, and the current examination standards took effect for all exams on or after March 17, 2022, with no more GFEs scheduled. Over its life, the exam split its questions into 22 on components, 14 on reactor theory and 14 on thermodynamics, and examinees averaged about 91% with a pass rate near 96%.

Reactor theory and thermodynamics did not leave the regulations, though; they remain among the knowledge areas the written exam samples. What the GFE data leaves behind is a lesson about how to study. The NRC published its GFE question bank and past exams, and the numbers show why drilling them feels so effective: recognition is easy. The scores on new questions show what it costs. If your preparation is mostly drilling known questions, you are training for the 95% case and hoping you never meet the 70% one.

There is a practical way to use this while you are still in uniform. The NRC still posts the entire PWR question bank from the old fundamentals exam, organized by topic, along with past exams. It is free, public and squarely in a Navy nuke's wheelhouse. The trick is to use it the way the statistics suggest: cover the answer choices, work the problem from first principles, then explain to yourself why each wrong option is wrong. If you can do that on questions you have never seen, you are training for the 70% case instead of the 95% one.

blocks.text: What transfers from the Navy, and what doesn't

A Navy nuke arrives with the theory, years of watchstanding, comfort with procedures and formal communications, and the habit of being examined constantly. Oral boards, qualification cards and drills are close cousins of the walkthrough and the simulator scenario. The NRC leaves education and experience requirements to each plant, pointing to criteria in the National Academy for Nuclear Training guidelines, so how much your naval time counts is a question to ask each employer directly.

blocks.title: Navy qualification vs. NRC license

left.head: What carries over
items: Reactor theory, heat transfer and fluid flow
Years of watchstanding and casualty drills
Procedure compliance and formal communications
Comfort with oral boards and frequent exams
Radiation worker habits

right.head: What starts over
items: The specific plant, its systems and layout
Technical specifications and emergency procedures
Possibly a different reactor type, such as a BWR
A new regulator, the NRC
A license issued to you personally

blocks.text: What does not transfer is the plant. A commercial unit is larger and laid out differently, with systems a submarine never needed and its own technical specifications and emergency procedures, all of which the exam will probe in detail. You might also land at a boiling water reactor, which works on a different principle from the pressurized water plants the Navy runs. The regulator is different too. Your license is personal, issued in your name by a federal agency, and the NRC can take enforcement action against you as an individual, including fines or suspending or revoking the license.

The job market is worth seeing clearly. O*NET, drawing on BLS data, lists about 5,200 nuclear reactor operators in 2025 with a median wage of $122,890, and projects a decline in that occupation through 2035, with roughly 400 openings a year, mostly from people retiring or moving on. That is a small, high-paying, competitive field. The neighboring roles in maintenance, radiation protection and grid operations employ more people and in some cases are growing.
Life after the license

Earning the license is not the finish line; keeping it is a permanent part of the job. Licensed operators must complete their plant's requalification program, which runs in continuous cycles of no more than 24 months. Within each cycle they must pass a comprehensive written exam and an operating test every year.

They need a medical exam every two years, must take part in the plant's drug and alcohol testing program, and must keep their proficiency current on shift. They may not perform licensed duties under the influence of alcohol or any drug, prescription or otherwise, that could impair them. Renewal every six years requires evidence of your licensed experience, the plant's certification that you are a safe and competent performer who has completed requalification, and a fresh medical certification.

The NRC also inspects the requalification programs themselves, generally every other year, checking that plants are genuinely testing whether operators and crews have mastered their training, including high-risk actions. When new reactors are built, the agency administers license exams before the plant is finished. The NRC acknowledges the oddities this creates: candidates may need to complete reactivity manipulations without a finished plant or a fully plant-referenced simulator, and the walkthrough portion of the test may come before the plant is even constructed. The industry has a template training program for this so-called cold licensing, and the NRC has said it intends to address some of these challenges in rulemaking. Every new reactor that comes online will need its own crews to go through this process.

For someone who survived nuke school and qualified on a submarine, the honest framing is this. You already know how to learn hard material under pressure and how to stand a watch. The license asks you to do it again, deeper and narrower, for one machine, with your own name on the paper. The people who do best treat it the way the GFE statistics suggest: not as a test to memorize, but as a plant to understand.

takeaways: An NRC operator license is tied to one plant, lasts six years and requires the plant to certify and sponsor you.
ROs need 80% on a 75-question written exam plus an operating test; SROs answer 100 questions and must also score 70% on the SRO-only 25.
The old fundamentals exam showed scores of about 95% on familiar questions but low-to-mid 70s on new ones: understand, don't memorize.
Navy theory, watchstanding and procedure habits transfer; the plant, its procedures and the regulator do not.
Licensed operators requalify every 24 months or less, with annual operating tests and medicals every two years.

title: The Reactor Nobody Built
dek: Two billion years ago, groundwater and uranium in Gabon ran a self-regulating nuclear reactor for hundreds of millennia, and it was found because someone took a third decimal place seriously.

blocks.text: In May 1972, a worker at a French nuclear fuel-processing plant ran a routine measurement on a batch of uranium and got a number that should not have been possible. Natural uranium contains 0.720% uranium-235, the isotope that sustains a chain reaction. This sample, from the Oklo mine in Gabon, came in at 0.717%.

Three thousandths of a percent sounds like nothing. In the nuclear world it was an alarm bell. Further checks showed that ore from part of the mine was short by roughly 200 kilograms of uranium-235, enough, as the physicist Alex Meshik later put it, for about half a dozen nuclear bombs. Either someone had diverted fissile material, or something stranger had happened.

That is not paranoia. The entire system of nuclear safeguards rests on bookkeeping: uranium is tracked by mass and by isotope ratio at every step, precisely so that material siphoned off for weapons shows up as a discrepancy. An unexplained shortfall of fissile uranium is the exact signature inspectors are trained to fear. The French had to find out where it went.

It was stranger. The missing uranium had been burned in a nuclear reactor. Nobody built it. It switched itself on deep underground about two billion years ago, ran on and off for hundreds of thousands of years, and shut itself down long before there were any animals on land to notice.

items.label: U-235 share in natural uranium almost everywhere: crust, Moon, meteorites
U-235 share measured in the Oklo samples in 1972
U-235 share in natural uranium about two billion years ago

blocks.source: Meshik, Scientific American, 2005

blocks.text: A discrepancy in the third decimal place

The reason a tiny deviation mattered is that the 0.720% figure is astonishingly uniform. Uranium from mines around the world, from lunar rocks and from meteorites shows essentially the same isotope ratio, because they all came from the same well-mixed cloud of material that formed the solar system. Chemistry cannot separate isotopes easily, and geology almost never does. So when a sample is off, the explanation is usually nuclear.

For weeks, specialists at the French Atomic Energy Commission were stumped. Then someone remembered a prediction. In 1953, George Wetherill and Mark Inghram had suggested that some uranium deposits might once have operated as natural fission reactors. In 1956, Paul Kuroda, a chemist at the University of Arkansas, worked out what it would actually take for an ore body to go critical on its own, and published the conditions in the Journal of Chemical Physics.

Proof came quickly once people looked. The ore was loaded with the lighter elements that fission produces, in the specific isotope patterns that only fission makes. Researchers eventually mapped 16 separate reaction zones in the Oklo and neighboring Okelobondo mines, plus another at a site called Bangombe, about 35 kilometers away. The scientific community gathered in Gabon's capital, Libreville, in 1975 to compare notes on what became known as the Oklo phenomenon.
Kuroda's recipe

Kuroda's conditions read like a checklist for any reactor designer. First, the uranium deposit had to be thicker than the average distance a fission neutron travels, about two thirds of a meter, so that neutrons hit more uranium before escaping. Second, there had to be enough uranium-235. Third, something had to slow the neutrons down, because slow neutrons are far more likely to split uranium-235. Fourth, there could not be much boron, lithium or other neutron-absorbing poisons around.

The second condition is the clever part. Today, no natural deposit can go critical, because 0.720% uranium-235 is too thin to sustain a chain reaction with ordinary water as the moderator. But uranium-235 decays about six times faster than uranium-238. Run the clock backwards and the fissile fraction climbs. Two billion years ago it was about 3%, roughly the enrichment that most commercial power reactors use today. When Earth formed, it was above 20%.

In other words, nature did the enrichment for free, simply by being younger. The Oklo ore happened to concentrate in thick seams at a moment when its natural enrichment matched a modern fuel assembly, and groundwater soaked through it to act as moderator. Every condition on the checklist was met at once.

It is worth being precise about what 'critical' means here, because the word sounds dramatic. A reactor is critical when each fission, on average, leads to exactly one more fission. Fewer than one and the reaction dies out; more than one and it grows. Oklo did not need to be a bomb or even a power plant. It only needed to hover around that balance point, and the geology let it do so for an extraordinarily long time.

blocks.title: Oklo versus a modern pressurized water reactor

left.head: Oklo, about 2 billion years ago
items: Fuel: natural uranium at about 3% U-235
Moderator: groundwater seeping through the rock
Control: water boiled off and power stopped
Average power: probably under 100 kilowatts
Ran in pulses for a few hundred thousand years

right.head: Modern PWR
items: Fuel: uranium enriched to roughly 3 to 5% U-235
Moderator: pressurized light water
Control: control rods, boron and temperature feedback
Output: around 1,000 megawatts of electricity
Refueled every 18 to 24 months over decades

blocks.text: By modern standards, Oklo was a weakling. From the amount of uranium-235 consumed, researchers estimate it released about 15,000 megawatt-years of energy in total. Spread over its long life, that works out to an average output probably under 100 kilowatts, enough, Meshik noted, to run a few dozen toasters. Along the way, uranium-238 soaking up neutrons produced more than two tons of plutonium-239, nearly all of which has since decayed away.
A reactor that breathed

For three decades one question lingered. Did these reactors run steadily, or in fits and starts? The answer came from xenon, a noble gas that fission produces and that rarely reacts with anything. Meshik, Charles Hohenberg and Olga Pravdivtseva at Washington University in St. Louis used a laser to release xenon from individual mineral grains in a single Oklo fragment, just 4 millimeters across.

The xenon was not where they expected. Most of it sat in aluminum phosphate grains that contain no uranium at all, at the highest xenon concentration ever measured in a natural material. And its isotope mix was wrong for ordinary fission. The heavier isotopes, xenon-134 and xenon-136, were depleted, while xenon-131 and xenon-132 were enriched.

The explanation was timing. Each xenon isotope comes from a different chain of radioactive parents with different half-lives, so each one appears on its own schedule after fission begins. If the reactor was hot at certain points in that schedule, gas escaped. If it was cool and wet, the parent iodine got trapped in freshly forming minerals. Modeling those schedules, the team concluded in Physical Review Letters in 2004 that the reactor ran for about 30 minutes, then shut down for at least 2.5 hours, again and again.

blocks.title: How Oklo regulated itself
items: Groundwater fills the pores in the uranium ore
Water slows neutrons and the chain reaction starts
Fission heat builds for about 30 minutes
Water boils away, the moderator is lost and fission stops
The rock cools for 2.5 hours or more and water seeps back

blocks.text: Meshik compared it to a geyser: heat up, boil off, refill, repeat. Anyone who has studied reactor theory will recognize the deeper principle. Oklo had a strong negative feedback. More power meant more heat, which meant less water, which meant fewer slowed neutrons and less power. That is the same logic that makes a water-moderated reactor stable, and it kept Oklo from melting down or blowing itself apart for hundreds of thousands of years with no operator and no control rods.

Low power density helped too. Oklo's heat was spread through large volumes of rock, so it never came close to the conditions inside a modern core, where fuel is packed tightly and cooled hard. A natural reactor that ran too hot simply boiled itself into a pause. Engineers have to design that kind of self-limiting behavior into a reactor deliberately. At Oklo it fell out of the geology.

Oklo is a reminder that a reactor is not an exotic machine. It is a set of physical conditions. Engineers did not invent the chain reaction in 1942. They rediscovered how to arrange it on purpose, with a far better control system than boiling groundwater.
Two billion years of waste storage

The most practical lesson from Oklo may be about what happens to nuclear waste left underground for geologic time. Oklo is a natural experiment in exactly that, so scientists have tracked where its fission products went. The picture is mixed in an instructive way. Water-soluble elements such as iodine clearly moved, washed out by the same groundwater that moderated the reactor. Other elements stayed remarkably close to where they were made.

A 2018 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, led by Evan Groopman at the US Naval Research Laboratory with Meshik and Pravdivtseva, found that radioactive cesium and the barium it decays into were captured by ruthenium-rich grains within about five years of a reactor zone shutting down, and then held there despite later volcanic activity in the region. The same sample contained the most uranium-235-depleted natural uranium ever measured, 0.3655%, from the most active part of the reactors.

It would be wrong to read Oklo as proof that any repository will be safe. A purpose-built site with copper canisters and clay is a different system, and Oklo's own iodine did not stay put. But it is real evidence, over a timescale no laboratory can match, that many dangerous fission products can stay locked in rock and minerals, and it gives modelers data to test their predictions against.

Oklo even hints at new tricks. Those aluminum phosphate grains held on to xenon gas for nearly half of Earth's history, which is remarkable for an element that normally escapes from almost anything. Meshik has suggested that minerals like these might one day be used to lock away radioactive noble gases such as krypton-85, which power plants and reprocessing facilities have historically released to the atmosphere because it is so hard to capture.
Is the speed of light's cousin constant?

Oklo also turned out to be a tool for fundamental physics. The fine-structure constant, written as alpha, sets the strength of the electromagnetic force. If it had been even slightly different two billion years ago, the energy at which samarium-149 nuclei absorb neutrons would have shifted. Oklo's reactors ate samarium-149 at a measurable rate, so the leftover samarium records how strongly that absorption worked back then.

In 1996, Thibault Damour and Freeman Dyson reanalyzed the Oklo data and concluded that alpha could not have changed by more than about one part in ten million since the reactors ran. A 2015 analysis by Edward Davis and Leila Hamdan tightened that to about one part in a hundred million. Not everyone agreed along the way: in 2004, two Los Alamos physicists argued that Oklo data pointed to a real change. The weight of later work favors constancy, but the result depends on assumptions about the reactors' temperature and neutron spectrum, which is exactly why details like Meshik's on-off cycle matter.

blocks.title: From natural reactor to physics laboratory

Groundwater-moderated reactors run in pulses in Gabon
Fermi's team builds the first human-made reactor

blocks.text: The reactor nobody built

Oklo is still the only known natural reactor, though Meshik has suggested that traces of xenon could help find others. Conditions two billion years ago were not wildly unusual. What made Oklo rare was that the evidence survived erosion, burial and tectonics, and then that someone happened to measure it closely enough to notice a third decimal place.

That last point deserves attention. The discovery did not come from a grand theory. It came from a routine check, a number slightly out of spec, and people who refused to wave it away. Anyone who has stood a watch and caught a gauge drifting a hair outside its normal band knows the feeling. Most of the time it is a sensor. Once in a while, it is two billion years of history trying to get your attention.

Deep time makes the scale hard to feel, so try compressing it. Squeeze Earth's 4.6-billion-year history into a single 24-hour day. Oklo switches on at roughly half past one in the afternoon, and its entire working life, a few hundred thousand years of pulsing on and off, lasts about five seconds. The whole of human civilization fits into the final fraction of a second before midnight, and in that sliver we rediscovered, by calculation, what a seam of wet rock in Africa had already done.

takeaways: Natural uranium is 0.720% U-235 almost everywhere; Oklo's 0.717% revealed that fission had consumed some of it.
About two billion years ago natural uranium was roughly 3% U-235, the same range as modern reactor fuel, so groundwater alone could moderate a chain reaction.
Xenon trapped in minerals shows the reactor pulsed about 30 minutes on and at least 2.5 hours off, regulated by water boiling away.
Oklo is a partial analogue for waste disposal: some fission products stayed put for eons, while soluble ones like iodine moved.
Small anomalies in routine data are worth chasing; most are noise, but some are discoveries.

title: The Machine the Size of a Continent
dek: The US power grid is really three giant synchronized machines, and in February 2021 one of them came within minutes of a collapse that could have lasted weeks.

blocks.text: Shortly after 1 a.m. on February 15, 2021, the operators at the Electric Reliability Council of Texas watched the most important number on their screens start to fall. It was not a price or a temperature. It was frequency, the speed at which every generator in the Texas grid spins together, normally held at 60 cycles per second.

Winter Storm Uri was knocking power plants offline faster than anyone had planned for. Frozen equipment and gas supply problems took out generator after generator, and as supply fell behind demand, the whole system began to slow down. Frequency bottomed out at 59.302 hertz. That sounds like a rounding error. It was not. ERCOT later reported that frequency stayed below 59.4 hertz for 4 minutes and 23 seconds, and that more generating units would have tripped if it had stayed there for 9 minutes. Operators ordered massive rolling blackouts to pull demand down, and the grid held, with roughly four and a half minutes to spare.

Had it collapsed, ERCOT's chief executive later told Congress, power could have been out for most Texans for weeks. To understand why a fraction of a hertz matters that much, you have to see the grid the way engineers do: not as wires, but as one enormous machine.

items.label: Lowest ERCOT frequency on Feb 15, 2021 (normal is 60)
Share of ERCOT generating capacity out at the worst point
Peak load shed through rolling blackouts

blocks.source: ERCOT, Review of February 2021 Extreme Cold Weather Event, presentation to US House Energy and Commerce, March 2021

blocks.text: One machine, spinning together

Every large generator on an alternating-current grid is a spinning magnet, and every one of them on the same interconnection turns in lockstep. In the lower 48 states there are three such machines. The Eastern Interconnection covers everything east of the Rockies, the Western Interconnection covers the West, and ERCOT covers most of Texas. According to the Energy Information Administration, they mostly operate independently and rarely transfer power among themselves.

Within each one, a basic law rules everything: supply must match demand at every instant. The grid stores almost nothing, so every kilowatt used somewhere must be produced somewhere else in the same moment. Organizations called balancing authorities keep that equation true, minute by minute, across their regions.

Frequency is how the machine reports whether the equation holds. When a large load switches on, the extra demand is first supplied by the kinetic energy stored in thousands of spinning rotors, which slow down slightly. Frequency dips. Governors on the generators sense it and open up more steam, water or gas flow to push back. When load drops, the reverse happens. If you have ever paralleled a generator onto a bus or watched a ship's frequency sag when a big pump starts, you have seen the grid's core physics at small scale.

blocks.title: How a grid holds 60 hertz
items: Demand rises above generation
Spinning rotors give up kinetic energy and slow down
Frequency drops below 60 hertz
Governors and operators add generation
Frequency recovers, and the loop runs again

blocks.text: If generation falls too far behind, protection systems take over. Generators trip off to protect themselves from damage at low frequency, which removes even more supply, which drops frequency further. That is the spiral ERCOT was racing in 2021. The last defense is deliberately cutting customers off, called load shedding, to bring demand back down to what the remaining generators can carry. It is painful, but it keeps the machine spinning so that power can be restored in hours or days rather than weeks.
From turbine to outlet

The path electricity takes to your wall is a story about voltage. Power is voltage times current, and the losses in a wire grow with the square of the current. Double the voltage for the same power and you halve the current, which cuts resistive losses to a quarter. That is why the grid moves power across long distances at hundreds of thousands of volts and only lowers it near the end.

blocks.title: The journey of a kilowatt-hour
items: A generator at a power plant produces alternating current
A step-up transformer raises it to transmission voltage, often hundreds of kilovolts
High-voltage transmission lines carry it long distances between regions
Substation transformers step it down for local distribution feeders
A pole-top or pad-mounted transformer drops it to 120/240 volts for a home
It reaches your breaker panel and outlet, still alternating 60 times a second

blocks.text: The last step is the one electricians know best. The transformer on the pole or in the green box down the street has a center-tapped secondary winding. The center tap becomes the neutral, and the two ends become two hot legs, 180 degrees apart. Measure from either hot leg to neutral and you get 120 volts for lights and outlets. Measure across both hot legs and you get 240 volts for the dryer, the range and the air conditioner. Most American houses run on this split-phase arrangement, a single-phase service even though the transmission system upstream is three-phase.

Transformers are the quiet heroes here, and they only work with alternating current. That single fact settled the late-1800s fight between AC and DC power systems in favor of AC for most of the grid. The EIA describes the US grid as thousands of miles of high-voltage lines and millions of miles of low-voltage lines, connecting thousands of power plants to hundreds of millions of customers.

Even with high voltage, some energy turns into heat along the way. The EIA estimates that transmission and distribution losses averaged about 5% of the electricity moved across the US from 2018 through 2022. On a system this large, 5% is an enormous amount of energy, but it is also a sign of how efficient the design is. Few machines move energy across a continent and lose only one part in twenty.

It was not always one connected system. At the start of the 20th century, the EIA notes, more than 4,000 isolated electric utilities operated in the United States, each with its own small grid. As demand grew, especially after World War II, they tied their systems together to share large power plants and to back each other up. Those ties are what make today's grid both remarkably reliable and capable of failing on a very large scale.

Ownership is just as patchwork as the history. The company that sends your bill might be a city-owned municipal utility, a member-owned electric cooperative or an investor-owned corporation. A few federal power authorities, such as the Tennessee Valley Authority and the Bonneville Power Administration, generate and sell power on a huge scale. In some states you can buy electricity from a separate power marketer. But whoever sells it, the local utility owns and runs the distribution wires that actually reach your house, and it is their crews who show up after a storm.
Where the power comes from

The machine is fed by a changing mix of sources. In 2025, natural gas generated about 41% of US utility-scale electricity, according to the EIA. Nuclear supplied about 18%, the second-largest share, and coal about 17%. Wind, solar and hydropower together provided most of the remaining renewable share, which reached about 24% in total.

blocks.title: US utility-scale electricity generation by source, 2025
blocks.note: Renewables together supplied about 24%, up from about 12% in 1990.
blocks.source: US EIA, Electricity explained: Electricity in the United States, 2026

blocks.text: These sources behave very differently from the grid's point of view. Nuclear plants run nearly flat out around the clock. Gas plants, especially fast-starting turbines, can ramp up and down to follow demand. Wind and solar produce when the weather allows, which means other resources or batteries must fill the gaps. A good grid operator thinks less about which source is 'best' and more about whether the whole portfolio can keep supply and demand matched through a heat wave, a cold snap or a windless night.
Three ways a grid can fail

Texas in 2021 was a failure of supply: not enough generation, so frequency fell. ERCOT's own numbers show how far outside its planning the storm went. At the worst point, 52,277 megawatts of its 107,514 megawatts of installed capacity were unavailable. During a 2011 cold snap, ERCOT had asked for a maximum of 4,000 megawatts of load shed for about 7.5 hours. In 2021 it asked for up to 20,000 megawatts, and the load shed request lasted 70.5 hours.

That is the brutal arithmetic of rolling blackouts. Millions of homes lost heat during a deep freeze, and people died during the storm. But the alternative, a full collapse of the Texas interconnection, would have meant restarting a dead grid from scratch, plant by plant, in a process ERCOT warned could take weeks. Load shedding is the grid's version of damage control: sacrifice part of the system to save the whole.

The great Northeast blackout of August 14, 2003 was a different kind of failure. According to the US-Canada task force that investigated it, the outage hit an area with about 50 million people and 61,800 megawatts of load across eight states and Ontario. It began a few minutes after 4 p.m., and some parts of the United States did not get power back for four days.

The 2003 blackout started small. Transmission lines in northern Ohio, heavily loaded on a hot afternoon, sagged into trees that had not been trimmed, and tripped. A failure in the utility's alarm software meant operators did not realize what was happening. As each line dropped, its power shifted onto neighboring lines, overloading them in turn. Within minutes, the cascade spread across the interconnection, and protective relays split the system into islands that could not stay balanced. Nobody had a full picture until it was over.

Then came a failure that grid engineers had never seen at that scale. At 12:33 in the afternoon on April 28, 2025, the entire mainland power systems of Spain and Portugal went dark. ENTSO-E, the association of European grid operators, convened a 49-member expert panel, and its final report in March 2026 called it a first-of-its-kind event. The cause was not a shortage of generation. It was a combination of oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive power control, differing voltage regulation practices and rapid generator disconnections, which together produced fast voltage increases and a cascade of generators tripping offline.

Grids fail in different ways: frequency collapses when supply falls short, cascades spread when lines overload, and voltage can run away when control is uneven. Each failure teaches the same lesson: the grid is a single control system, and weak points anywhere can become everyone's problem.
A changing machine

Part of what makes these failures newly relevant is that the machine itself is changing. Large spinning generators provide inertia automatically: their heavy rotors resist sudden changes in speed, buying operators seconds to react. Solar panels and batteries connect through power electronics called inverters, which have no spinning mass. They can be programmed to support frequency and voltage, often faster than any turbine, but only if they are designed and required to do so.

ENTSO-E's panel stressed that the Iberian blackout had many interacting causes, not a single villain, and called for stronger operating practices, better monitoring and regulations that keep pace with how power systems are evolving. In the United States, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation sets mandatory reliability standards, and debates about inverter behavior, winter preparation and transmission expansion now sit at the center of grid planning.

For an electrician, there is a satisfying reframe hiding in all this. The outlet on the wall is the end point of a real-time control system the size of a continent, run by people watching frequency to three decimal places. The skills that keep a ship's electrical plant stable, such as understanding generators, protection, switching and procedures, are the same skills that keep this machine running. Utilities need them in substations, relay shops, line crews and control rooms, and the BLS puts median pay for power dispatchers at $106,730 and for substation and relay technicians at $103,020 as of May 2025.

Next time a light flickers when a big load kicks on, picture what just happened: a tiny dip in speed shared by thousands of machines, sensed and corrected before you could blink. The grid works so well that most people never think about it. The people who run it think about almost nothing else.

takeaways: Each US interconnection is one synchronized machine; frequency at 60 Hz is the live signal that supply and demand match.
High-voltage transmission exists because losses scale with current squared; US T&D losses average about 5%.
In 2025, gas supplied about 41% of US utility-scale power, nuclear 18%, coal 17% and renewables about 24%.
Grids fail by frequency collapse (Texas 2021), cascading overloads (2003) or voltage runaway (Iberia 2025).
Ship electrical skills such as generators, protection and switching map directly onto utility, substation and dispatcher jobs.

title: Counting the Invisible: How Radiation Detectors Actually Work
dek: Every radiation instrument, from a frisker to the badge on your belt, works by catching the damage radiation leaves behind. Knowing how each one does it tells you when to trust it.

blocks.text: Between 2015 and 2024, investigators in South Korea worked a series of small radiation accidents in which workers and bystanders were exposed. To reconstruct how much radiation each person had absorbed, the team turned to what people had been carrying. They pulled the display glass and tiny surface-mounted resistors out of the victims' mobile phones, heated or illuminated them in the lab, and read the dose straight out of the materials.

That study, published in *Scientific Reports* in 2026, is a good reminder of something every radiation worker learns and then forgets: there is no such thing as a radiation sensor that senses radiation directly. Every detector, from a hundred-dollar Geiger counter to a germanium crystal cooled to cryogenic temperatures, works the same basic way. Radiation passes through some material and leaves damage behind. The instrument's whole job is to collect that damage and turn it into a number.

Understanding how each instrument does that is not just trivia. It tells you what a reading means, what it cannot tell you, and the specific ways each tool can lie to you. A detector is a machine for answering one question, and the most dangerous mistake is asking it a different one.
Radiation leaves a trail

Ionizing radiation earns its name by knocking electrons off atoms as it passes, leaving a trail of charged pairs: a freed electron and a positive ion. Alpha particles leave short, dense trails. Beta particles leave longer, sparser ones. Gamma rays and neutrons are indirect: they first hand their energy to an electron or a nucleus, which then does the ionizing. Detection is the art of catching those pairs, or the energy they leave, before they recombine and vanish.

Different instruments measure different quantities, which is why radiation units are famously confusing. The NRC offers a mnemonic, R-E-A-D: radioactivity (how many atoms decay per second, in curies or becquerels), exposure (radiation passing through air, in roentgens), absorbed dose (energy deposited in a material, in rads or grays), and dose equivalent (absorbed dose weighted for biological effect, in rem or sieverts). For gamma and beta radiation, the NRC notes that 1 roentgen, 1 rad and 1 rem are close enough to equal for practical purposes.

That is why the frisker at a control point and the dosimeter clipped to your belt answer different questions. One asks whether contamination is present right here, right now. The other asks how much energy your body has absorbed over weeks. Treating one as a substitute for the other is a category error.

blocks.title: Two questions, two kinds of instrument

left.head: Survey meters
items: Ask: what is here, right now?
Report count rate or dose rate
Used for surveys, frisking and finding sources
Readings change as you move
Can saturate or under-respond in some fields

right.head: Dosimeters
items: Ask: how much have I absorbed?
Report accumulated dose
Worn on the body for the whole issue period
Read later in a lab, or live on a display
Record of legal dose for the worker

blocks.text: One tube, three personalities

The oldest family of detectors is the gas-filled tube: a sealed cylinder of gas with a thin wire running down the middle and a voltage between the wire and the wall. When radiation ionizes the gas, the electrons drift toward the positive wire and the ions toward the wall, and the moving charge becomes a tiny electric signal. What happens next depends almost entirely on how much voltage you apply.

At low voltage, the tube simply collects the charge the radiation created. That is an *ionization chamber*. Its signal is small but faithfully proportional to the energy deposited, which makes it a good choice for measuring dose rate, including in strong fields. Turn the voltage up and electrons near the wire gain enough energy to knock loose more electrons, multiplying the signal while still keeping it proportional to the original ionization. That is a *proportional counter*, which can tell alpha from beta by pulse size.

Turn the voltage up further still and the multiplication runs away. A single ionizing event triggers an avalanche that spreads along the entire wire, and every pulse comes out the same size no matter what started it. That is the *Geiger-Müller* region. Ernest Rutherford and Hans Geiger described an electrical method for counting alpha particles in 1908, and Geiger and Walther Müller published their improved counting tube in 1928. Nearly a century later, the same principle clicks away in friskers and survey meters across the nuclear world.

blocks.title: What happens inside a Geiger-Müller tube
items: A gamma ray or beta particle ionizes a few gas atoms inside the tube
Freed electrons race toward the thin central wire under high voltage
Near the wire they gain enough energy to ionize more atoms, starting an avalanche
The avalanche spreads along the whole wire and produces one large, uniform pulse
A quench gas stops the discharge so the tube can reset for the next event
The meter counts pulses per unit time and converts them to a count rate or dose rate

blocks.text: The price of a loud click

The Geiger tube's huge, uniform pulse is its great strength. It needs very little electronics, it is cheap and rugged, and it can detect a single event. But that uniformity is also its blind spot. Because every pulse looks identical, a GM tube cannot tell you the energy of the radiation that triggered it, and so it cannot by itself identify which isotope is present. It counts; it does not identify.

Its second weakness is time. After each avalanche, the tube is effectively dead for a short interval while the discharge clears, and any event that arrives during that window is lost. At low count rates this hardly matters. At high rates, more and more events fall into those blind windows, and the meter reads lower than the true field. Meters correct for this mathematically, but the correction only works if the dead time, often called resolving time, is short and well characterized.

A 2026 study in the *Annals of the ICRP* shows why that matters in practice. Researchers at Fukushima Medical University measured the resolving times of GM survey meters used to screen evacuees for contamination after a nuclear disaster. Every one exceeded the Japanese industrial standard value of 250 microseconds.

The authors recommend keeping resolving time below about 2,000 microseconds and pulling meters above that from contamination inspections, because their corrected readings could overestimate contamination. The instrument looked fine. Its timing was the problem.

A meter that reads low is not necessarily telling you the area is safe. Before you trust any instrument, ask what it measures, what it cannot see, and whether it was response-checked against a known source before use.
Crystals that turn radiation into light

If you need to know *which* isotope is present, you need an instrument that measures energy. The workhorse for that is the scintillator: a crystal or plastic that emits a flash of light when radiation deposits energy in it. A photomultiplier tube or, increasingly, a small silicon photomultiplier converts that flash into an electrical pulse. Crucially, the brighter the flash, the more energy was deposited, so a scintillator can sort events by energy and build a spectrum.

A 2021 review in the journal *Sensors* compared common scintillator crystals. Sodium iodide doped with thallium, the classic NaI(Tl) detector, has been the reference standard for decades. Newer crystals like cerium-doped lanthanum bromide produce more light per unit of energy, which translates into sharper energy peaks. The review lists energy resolution at the 662 keV line of cesium-137 of about 2.6% for LaBr3(Ce), versus just under 7.5% for NaI(Tl).

blocks.title: Light output of common scintillators
blocks.note: More light per unit of deposited energy generally means sharper energy peaks and easier isotope identification.
blocks.source: Marques, Vale and Vaz, Sensors, 2021

blocks.text: Every gain comes with a trade-off. The same review notes that lanthanum bromide has its own internal radioactivity, which can swamp very weak sources, and that both NaI and LaBr3 absorb moisture and must be sealed. For the finest energy resolution, the gold standard is a high-purity germanium semiconductor detector. Its drawback is that it must be cooled to cryogenic temperatures to work, which makes it heavy and power-hungry. Room-temperature semiconductors like cadmium zinc telluride now reach better than 2% resolution at 662 keV, but only in small, expensive crystals.

The pattern is worth noticing because it shows up everywhere in engineering. No detector wins on every axis. Cheap, rugged and sensitive pulls against precise, which pulls against portable. The right instrument depends on the question, which is why a single radiological controls locker holds several kinds.
Your badge is a memory, not a meter

The dosimeter you wear works on a completely different principle: it remembers. The Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program's annual occupational exposure report describes how this technology evolved. Before 1974, workers wore film badges similar to dental x-ray film, and the darkening of the developed film was converted into dose. Tests by the shipyards found film readings averaged about 15% higher than the actual exposure, a deliberate conservatism so the recorded dose would never understate the real one.

In 1974 the program switched to thermoluminescent dosimeters, or TLDs. Certain crystals trap energy from radiation in their structure. When the crystal is later heated, it releases that stored energy as light, and the amount of light is proportional to the dose. The program's original calcium fluoride TLDs could be read in about 30 seconds, and the heating also zeroed them for reuse. Since 2010, every ship has used lithium fluoride TLDs with four chips behind different filters, which let the reader estimate deep and shallow gamma dose, beta dose and neutron dose separately.

items.label: How much film badges over-read, on average, by design
TLD cards one automated reader can process in a run
Average error of the Navy's TLD system in blind tests

blocks.source: Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, NT-26-2, 2026

blocks.text: Two details in that report reveal how carefully a dose number is built. First, every TLD also picks up natural background radiation, so control dosimeters are stored aboard ship far from the propulsion plant, and their reading is subtracted from each person's badge. What ends up in your record is occupational dose only. Second, the program runs blind tests: dosimeters exposed to known amounts of radiation are sent to each processing site without telling the site the answer. The report says the system measures dose with an average error of less than 10%.

The same report is candid about which kinds of radiation actually matter aboard ship. Neutrons are the hardest to detect, because they carry no charge and must first trigger a nuclear reaction or knock a nucleus loose inside the detector before anything can be counted. Yet more than 20 years of neutron film badge monitoring aboard ships found that monitored individuals did not receive neutron exposure above the film's minimum detection level.

Beta radiation is largely stopped by the metal of the reactor coolant system, clothing and even eyeglasses, and alpha contamination is not encountered in normal operations, apart from radon progeny that occur naturally in air. The program's recorded doses are therefore almost entirely gamma. Knowing that is part of reading the badge correctly: the instrument is tuned to the radiation that is actually there.

blocks.title: From counting tubes to dose badges
items: Rutherford and Geiger describe electrical counting of alpha particles
Geiger and Müller publish their counting tube
Film badges plus pocket dosimeters for high radiation areas
Calcium fluoride TLDs replace film badges
Shipyards and prototypes adopt lithium fluoride TLDs
All ships complete the switch to lithium fluoride TLDs

blocks.text: Badges that are read only once a quarter cannot warn you in the moment, which is why electronic personal dosimeters, with a live display and a dose alarm, are widely used alongside them for work in higher radiation areas. The older equivalent was the pocket dosimeter, which radiological controls personnel read as workers left the area and then compared against the monthly film badge. The principle has not changed: one device for the legal record, another for real-time control.
Detectors in disguise

Back to those phones. The South Korean team reconstructed doses ranging from below the detection limit to several grays using phone glass, resistors and electronic dosimeters. At lower doses, up to about 320 milligrays, their luminescence results agreed with the standard biological method, which counts chromosome damage in blood cells. At higher doses the methods sometimes disagreed: in one case the phone suggested a much larger dose than the chromosome test, and in another the phone caught an exposure the blood test missed.

The authors' conclusion is appropriately cautious. Luminescence from personal belongings cannot yet stand alone as a measure of individual dose, but it can add valuable evidence alongside other methods. It is an honest example of a promising technique that is useful, imperfect and still being validated.

The bigger idea is the one to keep. Anything that stores energy from radiation in a readable way is a detector, whether anyone designed it to be or not. The instruments in a radcon locker are just materials chosen and calibrated to make that memory precise. Once you see detection that way, every reading becomes a question about the material: what it responds to, what it misses and how it was checked. That habit is what turns a number on a meter into something you can act on.

takeaways: Every radiation detector measures what radiation leaves behind: ionization, light or stored energy.
Ion chambers, proportional counters and Geiger tubes are the same basic design run at different voltages.
GM tubes count but cannot identify isotopes, and dead time makes them under-read in high fields unless corrected.
Scintillators and germanium detectors measure energy, so they can identify isotopes; better resolution costs size, money or cooling.
Your TLD is a memory read in a lab; Navy blind testing puts its average error under 10%.
