title: The Banana Problem: Radiation Doses in Perspective
dek: A year standing watch on a nuclear sub can deliver less dose than one chest x-ray, while the biggest source in most American lives seeps up through the basement floor.

blocks.text: In 2025, the average person monitored for radiation aboard the Navy's nuclear-powered ships picked up about 6 millirem of occupational dose for the entire year. A single chest x-ray is about 10 millirem. A full-body CT scan is about 1,000. The average American, who has never stood a watch anywhere near a reactor, absorbs roughly 620 millirem every year just by breathing, eating, flying and going to the doctor.

Those numbers sound backwards to most people. The reactor is the scary thing, so it should carry the big dose. But radiation does not care about how frightening its source looks. It cares about energy deposited in tissue, and once you measure that honestly, the ranking of everyday risks gets rearranged in ways that are worth understanding, especially if you work around the stuff.
This is a tour of the dose ladder, from bananas to CT scanners, with real numbers and a frank look at what those numbers mean for your health.

items.label: Average yearly dose per person in the US (6.2 mSv)
Share of that average from medical procedures
Average 2025 occupational dose of Navy fleet personnel

blocks.source: NCRP Report 160 via US NRC and Bolus, J Nucl Med Technol, 2013; Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program report NT-26-2, 2026

blocks.text: Where the 620 comes from

The standard reference for American radiation exposure is NCRP Report No. 160, published in 2009 by the National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements using mostly 2006 data. It put the average yearly dose at 6.2 millisieverts, or 620 millirem. (One millisievert equals 100 millirem; the Navy and the NRC tend to talk in rem, most of the world in sieverts.) About half came from natural background and about half from human activity.

It helps to know what that unit is measuring. Effective dose is a bookkeeping tool. It starts with the energy radiation deposits in tissue, then weights it by the type of radiation and by how sensitive each organ is, so that a dose to the lungs and a dose to the whole body land on the same scale. It was built for protecting populations and setting limits, not for predicting what will happen to one particular person.

The natural half is dominated by one thing: radon. This colorless gas seeps out of soil and rock as uranium decays, collects in basements and poorly ventilated rooms, and is inhaled. NCRP puts the inhaled share at about 228 millirem a year, roughly three quarters of all natural exposure. Cosmic rays add about 33 millirem, the potassium-40 and other radionuclides in your own body add about 29, and the ground under your feet about 21.

Those are averages, and real lives vary a lot. Someone in Denver gets more cosmic radiation than someone at sea level, because a mile of thinner air overhead does less shielding. Radon swings far more, from house to house and county to county, depending on local geology and ventilation. It is not a harmless curiosity, either. The EPA ranks radon as the second leading cause of lung cancer in the United States after smoking, responsible for an estimated 21,000 lung cancer deaths a year.

The human-made half is almost entirely medicine. The NRC notes that medical procedures account for about 96% of exposure from human-made sources. Consumer products, fallout and the entire nuclear power industry are rounding errors by comparison. The NRC caps the dose any member of the public may receive from a licensed facility at 100 millirem per year.

Here is the twist. In the early 1980s, the average American dose was about 3.6 millisieverts. By 2006 it had jumped to 6.2. Background radiation had not changed at all. Medical exposure went from about 15% of the total to 48%, driven by an explosion in CT scanning, which by itself accounted for about half of all medical dose. The country's radiation problem, to the extent it had one, was in the hospital, not the power plant.

That trend has since reversed. A 2020 follow-up study for NCRP by Fred Mettler and colleagues found that per-person medical dose fell from about 2.9 millisieverts in 2006 to 2.3 in 2016, even though the number of CT scans rose from 67 million to 84 million. Better machines and more careful dose settings did that. It is a good example of a technical community noticing a number creeping up and actually bending it back down.
The everyday ladder

Radiation doses span an enormous range, so it helps to split them into two ladders. The first covers the small stuff you encounter without thinking about it. The NRC lists a dental x-ray at about 1.5 millirem and a chest x-ray at about 10. The CDC estimates that a one-way flight across the United States delivers about 3.5 millirem of cosmic radiation, so two transcontinental trips roughly equal one chest x-ray. Natural radioactivity in food and water adds about 30 millirem over a year.

blocks.title: Small doses: everyday exposures
blocks.note: Banana value is the 'banana equivalent dose' of about 0.1 microsievert. Fleet value is occupational dose only, with background subtracted.
blocks.source: US NRC, Doses in Our Daily Lives; CDC, Radiation from Air Travel; University of Groningen; NNPP report NT-26-2

blocks.text: The second ladder starts where the first one ends. A head CT is about 200 millirem, a chest CT about 700, and a full-body CT about 1,000, according to the NRC's table. A nuclear medicine study averages around 400. One full-body scan delivers about as much dose as three years of everything nature throws at you. That is not a reason to refuse a scan your doctor thinks you need. It is a reason to ask whether a scan is needed, and to keep a rough mental count of how many you have had.

blocks.title: Big doses: medical imaging and limits
blocks.note: The NRC's occupational limit for adult radiation workers is 5,000 mrem (50 mSv) per year.
blocks.source: US NRC, Doses in Our Daily Lives and Man-Made Sources

blocks.text: Why the banana is a trick question

Bananas are the internet's favorite radiation unit. They contain potassium, a small fraction of which is radioactive potassium-40, and someone once worked out that eating one delivers about 0.1 microsievert, or 0.01 millirem. The 'banana equivalent dose' is a joke unit, but a useful one: it reminds people that radioactivity is everywhere, including inside them.

Here is the catch, and it is the most interesting part. The University of Groningen's radiation protection academy points out that eating extra bananas barely changes your actual dose, because your metabolism keeps total body potassium nearly constant. Eat more, and you excrete more. The potassium-40 dose you carry is set mainly by your body chemistry, not your fruit intake.

That small detail holds a bigger lesson. A dose figure is not a property of an object. It depends on what the radioactive material is, where it ends up, how long it stays and which tissues it reaches. Iodine-131 concentrates in the thyroid. Radon's decay products lodge in lung tissue. Cesium spreads through muscle and leaves over months. The same activity, measured in becquerels or curies, can mean very different doses depending on biology. That is why health physicists talk about pathways, not just sources.
Radiation is a quantity, not a quality. The useful question is never 'Is it radioactive?' Almost everything is. It is 'How much dose, to which tissue, over what time, in exchange for what benefit?'
What a dose actually costs

So what does any of this do to your odds of getting sick? The most widely cited answer comes from the National Academies' BEIR VII report from 2006. Its risk model predicts that if 100 people each received a single dose of 0.1 sievert (10 rem, or 10,000 millirem) above background, about one of them would develop cancer from it. For context, about 42 of those same 100 people would be expected to develop cancer from all other causes over their lifetimes.

BEIR VII then assumes that lower doses carry proportionally lower risk, so 1 rem would mean about one extra case per thousand people. This is the linear no-threshold model, or LNT, and it is where honest scientific argument begins. At doses below roughly 10 rem, the predicted effects are so small that no epidemiological study can cleanly detect them against the 42-in-100 baseline. LNT is an assumption that fits the high-dose data and is extended downward because it is cautious.

Some researchers argue that cells repair low-level damage well enough that small doses carry less risk than LNT predicts, or even none. Others argue that certain effects could be worse than linear. Large studies of nuclear workers and veterans who were exposed slowly over decades are under way precisely because this question is still open. Regulators keep using LNT because, for setting limits, erring on the cautious side is cheap. The fair summary is that low-dose risk is small, uncertain, and not zero by assumption.
The quietest radiation environment you have lived in

Now back to the sailors. The Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program publishes an annual report on occupational radiation exposure, and the 2026 edition contains some striking numbers. In 2025, fleet personnel averaged about 0.006 rem of occupational dose. Since 1954, the average yearly dose per person monitored aboard ships has been 0.058 rem, compared with about 0.3 rem a year that an average American gets from natural background. No program worker has exceeded 2 rem in any year since 1980, well below the 5 rem federal limit.

The report also makes a claim that surprises many people. For crew stationed outside the propulsion plant, total exposure at sea, including the reactor, is lower than what the public receives from natural background ashore. Seawater blocks cosmic radiation, and ship construction materials have low natural radioactivity. Operators actually pick up more dose in port, during maintenance and overhaul, than from running the plant underway.

The shielding design is deliberately conservative. According to the report, a person would have to spend more than 48 hours a day in a ship's living quarters to exceed exposure limits, which is a polite way of saying it cannot happen. Every rack, mess deck and passageway was laid out with that margin in mind.

For comparison, the same report notes that workers at the 95 commercial power reactors covered in its 2024 data averaged about 0.06 rem each. Across the roughly 156,000 officers and enlisted people trained to operate naval plants, average lifetime dose from that work is around 0.54 rem. That is less than one year of average American exposure from all sources.

blocks.text: Thinking in doses

The practical value of all this is a habit of mind. When a headline says something is 'radioactive,' convert it to a dose and put it on the ladder. When a doctor suggests a CT, weigh it: the benefit of catching a problem is often far larger than a risk measured in fractions of a percent, but repeat scans add up. When you buy or rent a house, remember that radon is the largest single source of exposure for most Americans and is cheap to test. The EPA's suggested action level is 4 picocuries per liter of air.

For anyone working in the nuclear field, the deeper lesson is that the dosimeter on your belt is measuring a tiny slice of your lifetime exposure. The program behind it is designed so that slice stays small, through shielding, time limits, distance and monitoring. The tools are the same ones you learned early: time, distance and shielding. Halve the time and you halve the dose. Double your distance from a small source and the dose rate drops to roughly a quarter, the same inverse-square rule that governs light from a bulb. Put dense material in between and most gamma rays never reach you. Respect for radiation and fear of radiation are different things. Respect means knowing the numbers well enough to spot both carelessness and panic.

takeaways: The average American gets about 620 mrem (6.2 mSv) a year; about half is natural, mostly radon, and nearly half is medical.
Medical imaging drove US dose up from 3.6 mSv in the 1980s to 6.2 mSv in 2006; per-person medical dose then fell from 2.9 to 2.3 mSv by 2016.
A full-body CT (about 1,000 mrem) outweighs years of typical occupational dose for naval nuclear personnel.
BEIR VII estimates about 1 extra cancer per 100 people from 10 rem; below that, risk is extrapolated with the cautious linear no-threshold model and remains debated.
Ask 'how much dose, to which tissue, for what benefit?' and test your home for radon.

title: The Safest Power Plant Is the One People Fear Most
dek: Count the dead per unit of electricity and the ranking flips: the energy source with the scariest reputation sits at the bottom of the chart, next to wind and solar, while the quiet killer is the one nobody protests.

blocks.text: Picture a town of 150,000 people somewhere in the European Union. Call it Euroville. In a year its homes, shops and streetlights use about one terawatt-hour of electricity, which is a billion kilowatt-hours. Now power Euroville entirely from one source and count the funerals.

If the town runs on coal, at least 25 of its residents die early every year because of it, most of them from breathing the smoke. Run it on oil and the number is 18. Gas, 3. Now run it on nuclear power. In an average year, nobody dies. Statistically, one person dies about every 33 years. Solar comes out at one death every 50 years, wind about one every 25.

Those figures come from Hannah Ritchie at Our World in Data, who built the Euroville comparison to make an abstract number feel real. The number is deaths per terawatt-hour, and it is one of the most clarifying statistics in the whole energy debate. It is also one of the most ignored, because it describes a world that feels backwards: the power source that inspires protest marches and disaster movies is among the safest ways humans have ever made electricity.

items.label: Early deaths per year in a coal-powered town of 150,000 (Euroville)
Same town, powered entirely by nuclear

blocks.source: Hannah Ritchie, Our World in Data, 2017 (updated 2022)

blocks.text: Why you have to divide

You cannot compare energy sources by total deaths. Fossil fuels still make most of the world's electricity, so of course they kill more people in absolute terms. A fair comparison divides the harm by the work done. Deaths per terawatt-hour does exactly that: it asks how many people die, through accidents and pollution across the whole supply chain, for each fixed chunk of electricity delivered.

The supply chain part matters. The counts include miners killed digging coal or uranium, workers who fall during construction, people killed in transport accidents moving fuel, and the far larger number who die from air pollution after the fuel is burned. For wind it includes technicians falling from towers and helicopter crashes at offshore farms. For solar it includes installers falling from roofs and fires during construction. Nothing is zero.

blocks.title: Deaths per terawatt-hour of electricity (accidents + air pollution)
blocks.note: The bottom three bars are not missing. They are too small to see at this scale, which is the point.
blocks.source: Our World in Data (Markandya & Wilkinson 2007; Sovacool et al. 2016), data for 2021

blocks.text: Look at the chart and notice that you can barely see the last three bars. Coal kills roughly 800 times as many people per unit of electricity as nuclear. Our World in Data puts it this way: nuclear causes 99.9% fewer deaths than brown coal, 99.7% fewer than oil and 97.6% fewer than gas. Wind and solar sit in the same tiny range as nuclear.
The killer you can't see

Almost all of the fossil fuel number is air pollution, not explosions or mine collapses. Burning coal releases fine particles, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides that lodge deep in the lungs and bloodstream. They raise the risk of heart attacks, strokes, lung cancer and respiratory disease. None of these deaths make the news, because each one looks like an ordinary death from an ordinary illness. Nobody's death certificate says coal plant.

The fossil fuel rates in the chart come from a 2007 paper in The Lancet by Anil Markandya and Paul Wilkinson. Ritchie argues they are probably far too low. They were based on European power plants, which have strict pollution controls and tend to sit farther from big cities than plants in many other countries. And research since 2007 has found air pollution to be more harmful than earlier models assumed.

She runs a sanity check. Multiply the 2007 death rates by the world's actual fossil-fuel electricity in 2021 and you get about 280,000 deaths a year. But newer air-pollution research, combined with estimates of how much pollution comes from power generation, suggests that 1.1 to 2.55 million people die each year from fossil fuels burned for electricity. If that is right, the true global death rate from coal could be 93 to 224 deaths per terawatt-hour, four to nine times higher than the chart shows. The gap between nuclear and coal would be even wider than it looks.

The deadliest power source in the world kills mostly by a slow, statistical process: a few extra heart attacks in every city downwind. Risks that kill quietly and spread thin are the ones societies most easily ignore.
Counting the disasters honestly

The obvious objection is Chernobyl and Fukushima. Any honest safety number has to include them, and these do. Ritchie's calculation assumes 433 deaths from Chernobyl and 2,314 from Fukushima, and the nuclear rate of 0.03 per terawatt-hour already has both baked in.

The Chernobyl figure is worth unpacking because it is contested. Two workers died in the explosion, and 28 more died within weeks from acute radiation syndrome. Among children who drank milk contaminated with iodine-131 in the days after the accident, there was a real rise in thyroid cancer; the UN scientific committee on radiation, UNSCEAR, judged about a quarter of 19,233 cases in that group to be radiation-linked. Thyroid cancer in young people is usually survivable, which is why the confirmed death toll is under 100 and Ritchie's best estimate of the total is 300 to 500. Higher estimates exist. In 2005 the WHO projected a possible 4,000 eventual deaths, and some reports went much higher. Those projections assume that even tiny doses spread across millions of people add up to cancers, an assumption called the linear no-threshold model. UNSCEAR's later reviews did not find detectable health effects in the general population, but the long tail of Chernobyl is genuinely uncertain, and anyone who tells you the exact number is overselling.

Fukushima teaches a stranger lesson. The earthquake and tsunami that wrecked the plant were a national catastrophe, but in 2018 the Japanese government attributed exactly one death to radiation, a worker who later died of lung cancer. The 2,314 figure is mostly something else: elderly and sick people who died from the stress and disruption of a rushed evacuation. Fear of radiation, not radiation itself, did most of the killing. That is not an argument against evacuating. It is an argument that the response to a nuclear accident carries its own body count, and that the plan should weigh both.

Hydropower shows the same disaster-driven pattern. Its rate of 1.3 deaths per terawatt-hour is almost entirely one event, the 1975 Banqiao dam failure in China, which killed about 171,000 people. Strip it out and hydro drops to about 0.04, right alongside nuclear and wind. Most people have never heard of Banqiao. Almost everyone has heard of Chernobyl.
Why fear doesn't track the numbers

In 1987 the psychologist Paul Slovic published a now-classic paper in Science on how ordinary people judge risk. He found that people do not rank hazards by expected deaths. They rank them along a few gut dimensions, the most powerful being what he called dread: whether a risk feels uncontrollable, catastrophic, fatal, involuntary and unfair. A second dimension was how unknown the risk felt: invisible, new, poorly understood, delayed in its harm. Nuclear power scored at the extreme of both. It was the textbook case of a dreaded, unknown risk.

blocks.title: What makes a risk feel scary vs. what makes it deadly

left.head: Feels scary
items: Rare, sudden, big events
Invisible hazard you cannot sense
Victims you can name and picture
Harm that is new or poorly understood
Imposed on you by someone else

right.head: Actually kills more
items: Constant, small, everyday harm
Pollution you can see but have stopped noticing
Victims spread thinly through statistics
Harm so familiar it seems normal
Chosen by everyone at once, so nobody objects

blocks.text: Coal fails almost none of those gut tests. Its smoke is visible and familiar. Its victims are scattered across decades and millions of people, each death indistinguishable from the background rate of heart disease. A nuclear accident is the opposite: one place, one date, a name, a cloud on a map. Our brains evolved to notice the lion in the grass, not the slightly elevated mortality rate across a continent.

The same mismatch shows up everywhere. Many people are more afraid of flying than driving, even though a mile on a commercial airliner is far safer than a mile on the highway. A shark attack makes international news while drowning, which is vastly more common, barely registers. The pattern is consistent: we overweight vivid, catastrophic, uncontrollable risks and underweight common, chronic ones.
What the numbers don't settle

None of this means nuclear is risk-free or that the debate is over. Ritchie herself warns against reading too much into the differences at the bottom of the chart. Nuclear, wind and solar are close enough, and uncertain enough, that their ranges overlap. Arguing over whether 0.019 beats 0.03 misses the point. The real gap is between that whole group and fossil fuels.

There are also costs these numbers do not capture. Nuclear power leaves long-lived waste that has to be managed for a very long time, and it raises proliferation questions that wind turbines do not. It is expensive and slow to build, which is a different kind of risk: the risk that money spent on a delayed plant could have cut more pollution somewhere else. The accident database behind the renewable figures is patchy, built partly from English-language news reports, and nobody keeps a timely global register of energy accidents. Mining for the metals in panels, turbines and batteries carries health costs that are not well counted for any source.

Climate is the other column in the ledger, and it points the same way. Coal emits more than a hundred times as much greenhouse gas per unit of electricity as nuclear, once mining, construction and fuel are included. A 2013 study by Pushker Kharecha and James Hansen estimated that by displacing fossil fuels, the world's nuclear plants had already prevented an average of 1.84 million air-pollution deaths. That estimate depends on assumptions about what would have been burned instead, but even generous error bars leave a very large number.

items.label: Air-pollution deaths estimated to have been prevented by nuclear power displacing fossil fuels
Greenhouse gas from coal vs. nuclear per unit of electricity, lifecycle

blocks.source: Kharecha & Hansen, Environ. Sci. Technol., 2013; Our World in Data, 2024

blocks.text: Ritchie's conclusion is less pro-nuclear than you might expect. Because low-carbon sources are also the safest, she argues, it matters less whether a country picks nuclear or renewables and more that it stops burning fossil fuels. The safety data does not crown a winner among the clean options. It identifies a loser.
Thinking like the denominator

The deepest lesson here is not about energy at all. It is about the denominator. Almost every misleading risk claim comes from a number with no denominator, or the wrong one. Deaths from an energy source mean nothing until you ask: per what? Crimes in a city mean nothing until you divide by population. Injuries in a sport mean little until you divide by hours played. Learning to ask for the denominator is one of the cheapest upgrades you can make to your thinking.

The second lesson is to separate how a risk feels from how big it is. Dread is useful information about what people will tolerate, and engineers ignore it at their peril. Public fear shaped the regulations, training and safety culture that make modern reactors so safe. But dread is not data. A plant that operates for decades with no one hurt and a smokestack that quietly shortens thousands of lives are not equally dangerous just because one of them makes better headlines.

items: Ask for the denominator: per terawatt-hour, per mile, per hour of exposure.
Count the whole chain: mining, building, transport, pollution, not just the plant.
Separate the dramatic from the deadly; the quiet risks usually win.
Look for the response's own cost, like Fukushima's evacuation deaths.
Be suspicious of precise numbers for contested events; ranges are more honest.

blocks.text: When someone back home learns you work around a reactor and asks if it is dangerous, the honest answer has two parts. Yes, the physics is powerful and demands respect, which is exactly why the procedures, training and margins are what they are. And measured by the bodies it leaves behind per unit of power, splitting atoms sits at the very bottom of the chart, next to sunlight and wind, while the fuel most of the world still burns every day sits at the top.

takeaways: Per unit of electricity, coal causes roughly 800 times the deaths of nuclear; nuclear, wind and solar are all in the same very low range.
Most fossil fuel deaths come from air pollution, a slow, invisible killer that rarely makes news, and the standard estimates are probably too low.
Chernobyl and Fukushima are included in nuclear's safety rate; at Fukushima the rushed evacuation killed far more people than radiation did.
People rank risks by dread and unfamiliarity, not by expected deaths (Slovic, 1987), which makes rare disasters feel worse than chronic harm.
Before trusting any risk number, ask for the denominator.

title: Small Reactors, Big Bets: Where a Navy Nuke Fits in Civilian Power
dek: Small modular reactors are finally getting construction permits, while federal forecasts still show operator jobs shrinking; here is how to read both, and what the civilian paths actually look like.

blocks.text: In September 2026, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued the Tennessee Valley Authority a licence to build a 300-megawatt reactor at Clinch River, near Oak Ridge, Tennessee. Six months earlier it had authorized TerraPower to build a sodium-cooled reactor in Kemmerer, Wyoming, the agency's first construction permit for a commercial non-light-water power reactor in more than 40 years. Dow Chemical's subsidiary is lined up behind them with four small gas-cooled units for a chemical plant on the Texas coast.

Read only those headlines and civilian nuclear power looks like it is about to boom. Now read a different source. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects that employment of nuclear power reactor operators will shrink about 6% between 2025 and 2035, from roughly 5,200 jobs to 4,900. At the start of November 2026 the World Nuclear Association listed zero power reactors officially under construction in the United States.

Both pictures are true at once. For anyone weighing civilian nuclear work as a career, especially from the Navy's nuclear pipeline, the useful skill is learning to hold both in your head: real momentum, real risk, and a job market that rewards people who are licensed and qualified when the momentum turns into concrete.

items.label: Median annual wage, US nuclear power reactor operators, May 2025
Active NRC-licensed operators at US power reactors
Operable US power reactors in late 2026

blocks.source: BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, 2026; US NRC Operator Licensing; World Nuclear Association, Nuclear Power in the USA, 2026

blocks.text: What makes a reactor small

A small modular reactor, or SMR, is generally defined as one producing 300 megawatts of electricity or less. A typical large reactor produces around 1,000 megawatts or more. The smallest designs, under about 20 megawatts, are often called microreactors. The 'modular' part matters as much as the size. The idea is to build reactor modules in factories, ship them to sites and assemble them, the way aircraft are built in series rather than one at a time.

Under that label sits a zoo of technologies. Most near-term designs are simplified light-water reactors, close cousins of today's plants and of naval reactors, using familiar low-enriched fuel. Others are more radical: fast reactors cooled by liquid sodium or lead, high-temperature reactors cooled by helium gas, and reactors that use molten salt. The water-cooled designs carry the least technical risk. The exotic ones promise higher temperatures for industrial heat, longer fuel life or better use of uranium, in exchange for less operating history.

Developers also pitch safety benefits from smallness. A small core holds less decay heat and can often be cooled by natural circulation and passive systems, without pumps or operator action. That, in turn, may justify smaller emergency planning zones, which would let reactors sit closer to towns and factories. TVA's early site permit for Clinch River was written with the expectation that the emergency planning zone could extend only to the site boundary. Regulators decide these questions plant by plant, so the promise is real but not automatic.

This is a deliberate reversal of history. The World Nuclear Association notes that early power reactors in the 1950s and 1960s were small. From the 1970s, utilities pushed vendors to build bigger and bigger plants to spread fixed costs over more output, which is economies of scale. SMR developers are betting on economies of series instead: build many identical units, learn on each one, and drive the cost down the way manufacturing does.

blocks.title: Electrical output per reactor unit
blocks.note: Gross electrical output per unit as listed by the World Nuclear Association; several SMR plants combine multiple modules.
blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Nuclear Power in the USA, 2026

blocks.text: Small reactors are not a new idea to the military. The Army ran a program from 1954 to 1977 that built reactors for remote sites, including one at McMurdo Sound in Antarctica that generated 78 million kilowatt-hours between 1962 and 1972, and a floating plant on a converted Liberty ship in the Panama Canal Zone. And of course the Navy has operated compact, high-reliability reactors at sea for seven decades. Much of what SMR vendors advertise, such as small cores, long fuel cycles and passive safety, would sound familiar in a submarine engine room.

The military is coming back for more. In October 2025 the Army launched its Janus Program to put commercial microreactors on military installations, and in August 2026 it picked five developers. In October 2026 the Navy selected Radiant's 1-megawatt Kaleidos microreactor for Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana, which would be the state's first power-producing reactor.
The scoreboard in late 2026

It is easy to lose track of who is actually building what, so here is the state of the leading US projects as of this writing. The common thread is that licensing, which used to be the bottleneck, has been moving faster than many expected. Construction and cost are now the real tests.

TerraPower's Natrium plant is a good example of where things stand. It is a 345-megawatt sodium-cooled fast reactor that runs on metallic high-assay fuel, sited near a coal plant in Wyoming. Non-nuclear construction began in April 2026, with the first safety-related concrete planned for 2027. Kairos Power, meanwhile, is building Hermes, a 35-megawatt-thermal test reactor cooled by molten fluoride salt in Oak Ridge, and expects construction to finish in 2028. Test reactors like Hermes produce no electricity for sale. Their job is to prove the technology and train the first people who will run it.

blocks.text: Alongside new builds, the industry is doing something nobody expected a decade ago: restarting closed plants. Holtec's Palisades plant in Michigan, shut in 2022, was authorized to receive fresh fuel in July 2025. Constellation is working to restart the undamaged unit at Three Mile Island, renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center, and NextEra is pursuing a restart of Duane Arnold in Iowa. The Department of Energy has also put $400 million each behind TVA's Clinch River project and Holtec's planned SMR-300s at Palisades.
Why the skeptics are not wrong

The cautionary tale is NuScale. It was the first SMR design to win NRC approval, and a group of Western municipal utilities planned a six-module plant at Idaho National Laboratory. By late 2022 the estimated price of its power had risen from about $55 per megawatt-hour to between $90 and $100, partly because of inflation in steel and construction. In November 2023 the project was cancelled. A good design and a licence were not enough without customers willing to pay first-of-a-kind prices.

Fuel is another constraint. More than half of SMR designs in development need high-assay low-enriched uranium, enriched to between 5% and 20% uranium-235. The World Nuclear Association notes that only Russia and China can produce it at scale today; the US company Centrus began producing small amounts from a demonstration cascade in October 2023. And economies of series only arrive once there is a series. The first few units of any design are almost always the most expensive.

That is why the BLS projection is not crazy. It is a projection for the occupation as it exists today, and it cannot count jobs at plants that have not been built. If even a fraction of the announced projects reach operation in the 2030s, each one will need its own trained, licensed crew. If they stall, the job market looks more like the BLS line. The honest planning stance is to be ready for the upside without betting your rent on it.

New reactors do not come with operators. Every NRC operating licence is tied to one specific facility, so each new plant must train and license its own crews before it can run. Experienced people who can pass that process will be the scarce input.
The civilian paths for a Navy nuke

The BLS notes that some nuclear power reactor operators gain their experience in related roles in the Navy. In practice, people leaving the naval program usually land in a few kinds of civilian jobs. Pay figures below are national medians from the BLS for May 2025; actual offers vary by region, plant, shift work and overtime, so treat them as rough benchmarks rather than promises.

blocks.title: Median annual wage by occupation, May 2025

blocks.text: Licensed operations is the path most people picture. You typically start as a non-licensed operator, sometimes called an equipment operator, working rounds in the plant while you complete the site's training program. When the plant certifies that you have met its training and experience requirements, it sponsors you for an NRC licence as a reactor operator (RO) or senior reactor operator (SRO). The requirements are set by the facility using industry guidelines from the National Academy for Nuclear Training, and some plants run classes that take experienced candidates directly to SRO.

blocks.title: How an NRC operator licence works
items: Get hired by a plant and complete its training program, often starting as a non-licensed operator
The plant certifies your training and experience on NRC Form 398 and sponsors your application
Pass a medical exam certifying you are fit to operate
RO candidates must score at least 80% on a 75-question written exam; SROs take 25 more questions and need 70% on that portion
Pass an operating test with a plant walkthrough and simulator scenarios
Hold a licence valid for that plant only, renewed every 6 years, with requalification and a medical exam every 2 years

blocks.text: Maintenance is the other big door, and it is the natural fit for an electrician. Plants employ electrical maintenance technicians who work on breakers, motors, switchgear, batteries and protective relays, and the BLS lists powerhouse, substation and relay repairers at a $103,020 median with about 20,900 jobs nationally. Those skills also transfer outside nuclear, to utilities, substations and large industrial sites. Radiation protection and chemistry technicians, grouped by the BLS as nuclear technicians, earn a $110,240 median.

There is also the grid side. Power distributors and dispatchers, the people in control centers who balance generation and load and route power across transmission networks, earned a $106,730 median in May 2025. Their work is a direct extension of what a ship's electrical division does on a smaller scale: keep frequency and voltage steady while generators and loads come and go. It is a path that does not depend on any particular reactor getting built.

Whichever door you choose, expect to be a student again. The BLS notes that power plant operators typically need several years of onsite training and experience to become fully competent, and that nuclear operator licences must be maintained through ongoing requalification exams. For people who got through nuke school, that rhythm of classroom, qualification cards and oral boards will feel familiar. The difference is that the plant, the procedures and the regulator are new.
What transfers and what does not

A Navy nuke leaves with things civilian plants value: deep theory training, years of watchstanding, comfort with procedures and formal communications, and the habits of a radiation worker. Those are hard to teach and slow to build, which is why the naval program has long been a feeder for the industry.

Some things do not transfer directly. Commercial plants run different designs, much larger and with different systems, and every licence is site-specific. The regulator is the NRC, not Naval Reactors, with its own rules and inspection culture. Plants are businesses that care about refueling outage schedules and electricity prices in a way a submarine never does. And an NRC licence takes real time and effort to earn, even for experienced candidates, because you have to learn a specific plant in depth.

A few practical moves make the transition easier. Keep copies of qualification records, watch hours and evaluations, because plants assess experience against written criteria. Talk to the command career counselor about transition programs and education benefits, and confirm the current rules, since they change. If a degree is on your horizon, know that technical degrees open doors to SRO and engineering roles later. And remember that the licensed operator path is not the only one: maintenance, radiation protection, training and grid operations all draw on the same core skills.

The deeper point is that the safety net is not a particular plant or a particular reactor design. It is a rare and portable ability: running high-consequence machinery by procedure, under pressure, without cutting corners. SMRs may or may not boom on schedule. People who can do that work well will be needed either way.

takeaways: SMRs are reactors of about 300 MWe or less, built to win on factory production and repetition rather than sheer size.
Licensing momentum is real in 2026 (Clinch River, Kemmerer, Long Mott), but cost and fuel supply remain the big risks, as NuScale's cancelled Idaho plant showed.
The BLS put the May 2025 median wage for nuclear reactor operators at $122,890, and still projects a 6% decline in those jobs by 2035.
NRC operator licences are tied to one plant, so every new reactor will need its own licensed crews.
Electrical maintenance, relay and substation work, radiation protection and grid operations are strong paths beside licensed operations.

title: Thorium: The Fuel of the Future Since 1965
dek: Thorium has been called the clean, abundant, meltdown-proof answer to nuclear power for sixty years. The physics is real. So are the reasons it still isn't running the grid.

blocks.text: In October 2024, a small experimental reactor in Wuwei, in China's Gansu province, made history. The 2-megawatt TMSR-LF1 became the first molten salt reactor in the world to have thorium loaded into it. A year later, its operators announced they had converted thorium into uranium-233 inside the reactor. To thorium's fans, it looked like proof that the thorium age had finally arrived, and that the West had been asleep.

Look at the details the World Nuclear Association reports, though, and the picture gets more interesting. TMSR-LF1 holds about 50 kilograms of thorium and has a conversion ratio of about 0.1, meaning it makes roughly one new fissile atom for every ten it burns. It runs on uranium enriched to just under 20% as its main fuel. It is a genuine milestone, and it is also a 2-megawatt test rig taking the first step on a road that Oak Ridge National Laboratory first walked in the 1960s.

That combination, real progress wrapped in decades of hype, is the story of thorium. If you have watched a video promising that thorium will end the energy crisis, this is the version with the asterisks put back in.

items.label: Thorium's abundance relative to uranium in rocks and soils
Thorium inventory in China's TMSR-LF1 test reactor
TMSR-LF1 conversion ratio: new fissile atoms per atom burned

blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Thorium and Molten Salt Reactors, 2026

blocks.text: What thorium actually is

Thorium is a slightly radioactive silvery metal, named after Thor and found in small amounts in most rocks and soils. The WNA says it is about three times as abundant as uranium in rocks and soils. Almost all of it is a single isotope, thorium-232, which decays so slowly that its half-life is about three times the age of the Earth. In a sense, the planet is full of it.

The catch is in one word: thorium is *fertile*, not *fissile*. It cannot sustain a chain reaction by itself. When thorium-232 absorbs a neutron it becomes thorium-233, which beta-decays in about 22 minutes to protactinium-233, which decays again with a 27-day half-life into uranium-233.

That uranium-233 is an excellent fuel. But to start the process you need neutrons, and to get neutrons you need a fissile driver already in the reactor: uranium-235, plutonium-239 or uranium-233 made earlier. As the WNA puts it, none of these is easy to supply.

blocks.title: How thorium becomes fuel
items: Thorium-232 absorbs a neutron supplied by a fissile driver fuel
It becomes thorium-233, which decays in about 22 minutes
That produces protactinium-233, which decays with a 27-day half-life
The result is uranium-233, a fissile fuel that splits much like U-235
Each U-233 fission releases about 200 MeV and new neutrons to keep the cycle going

blocks.text: If this sounds familiar, it should. It is the same trick a uranium reactor plays with uranium-238, which absorbs neutrons and turns into plutonium-239. Every light-water reactor quietly breeds some plutonium and burns part of it. Thorium is not a magic new kind of fuel. It is the other fertile material, with a different set of strengths and weaknesses.
The real case for thorium

The strengths are genuine, and they explain why serious engineers have kept working on thorium for six decades. The first is abundance, and in particular where it is. The OECD and IAEA's 2016 uranium 'Red Book' put known and estimated world thorium resources at about 6.2 million tonnes, with India at the top of the country list. A nation with lots of thorium and little uranium has a strategic reason to care that has nothing to do with internet enthusiasm.

blocks.title: Identified thorium resources by country
blocks.note: In-situ resources regardless of cost category; some figures are estimates based on mineral sands.
blocks.source: OECD NEA and IAEA, Uranium 2016 (Red Book), via World Nuclear Association

blocks.text: The second strength is physics. Uranium-233 releases enough neutrons per absorption that a carefully designed thorium reactor can produce more fissile fuel than it consumes, even with slow neutrons. The WNA notes that thermal breeding of this kind is unique to thorium; it is not possible with uranium fuels. Thorium oxide is also an excellent fuel material, with a much higher melting point and better thermal conductivity than uranium oxide, and it releases less fission gas.

The third is waste and weapons. Thorium fuels produce fewer of the long-lived heavy elements beyond uranium, such as plutonium and americium, that make used fuel hazardous for so long. And uranium-233 bred from thorium is always contaminated with traces of uranium-232, whose decay products emit intense gamma radiation. That makes the material hard to handle and easy to detect, which is a real barrier to diversion, though the WNA notes it is not an absolute one: uranium-233 can be used in a weapon, and the United States produced about 2 tonnes of it during the Cold War.
It has already been done

Here is a fact the hype videos usually skip: thorium reactors are not a new idea waiting for permission. They have been built and run, including by the program that trains Navy nukes. Shippingport, the Pennsylvania plant the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program developed in the 1950s, later hosted a light water breeder reactor core using uranium-233 and thorium. It produced electricity for Duquesne Light from 1977 for five years, and end-of-life inspections found 1.39% more fissile material than it started with. The program says breeding occurred at a higher rate than predicted.

That result mattered because, as the program's own history puts it, conventional wisdom in the 1960s held that breeding was impossible in a pressurized water reactor; the Atomic Energy Commission was betting on liquid-metal fast breeders instead. The Shippingport team did it with movable seed regions of uranium-233 fuel surrounded by thorium, inside a reconfigured early PWR running at 60 megawatts electric. The fuel was never chemically reprocessed afterward, so the closed cycle, the part that would actually make thorium self-sustaining, was never demonstrated at scale.

Oak Ridge's Molten-Salt Reactor Experiment ran from 1965 to 1969 at up to 7.4 megawatts thermal, and in its second campaign it was fuelled mainly with uranium-233. Gas-cooled reactors in the US, Britain and Germany used thorium-bearing fuel for years. The 330-megawatt Fort St. Vrain plant in Colorado used almost 25 tonnes of thorium between 1976 and 1989. Germany's 300-megawatt THTR ran on thorium fuel pebbles from 1983 until it was shut down in 1989 because of technical problems.

Peach Bottom 1 gas-cooled reactor runs on thorium fuel
Fort St. Vrain in Colorado uses almost 25 tonnes of thorium
Shippingport light water breeder proves breeding with thorium
Germany's THTR runs, then shuts over technical problems

Apr 2026

blocks.text: Notice what those early projects had in common. Many of them used highly enriched uranium as the driver fuel, which the WNA notes would not be considered today. They proved the physics worked. None of them proved that thorium could beat uranium on cost, which is the test every energy technology eventually has to pass.
The catches

The first catch is economics. The WNA reports that thorium fuel studies keep reaching the same conclusion: it is not economical to use low-enriched uranium as the driver unless fuel can stay in the reactor to very high burnups, well beyond what today's light-water reactors with zirconium cladding achieve. Meanwhile uranium is not scarce enough to force the issue, and enormous stockpiles of depleted uranium already exist for any future fast reactors. In fast reactors, the WNA adds, thorium offers no particular advantage over that depleted uranium.

The second catch is the same uranium-232 that makes the fuel proliferation-resistant. Its gamma-emitting decay products make recycled thorium fuel expensive to fabricate, because the work has to be done remotely behind heavy shielding. Thorium itself carries a similar headache from thorium-228. And protactinium-233, the intermediate step, is a neutron absorber that can steal the very neutrons the cycle depends on.

The third catch belongs to the reactor type most often paired with thorium: the molten salt reactor, where fuel is dissolved in a liquid fluoride salt. The concept has real appeal, including operation at near atmospheric pressure and a freeze plug that drains fuel into a safe tank if power is lost. But Oak Ridge's experiment also exposed problems that are still being worked on: corrosion of structural metals, a primary loop that becomes intensely radioactive, toxic beryllium in common salt mixtures, and tritium production unless the lithium is enriched to nearly pure lithium-7.

The fourth catch is time. Any new fuel has to be qualified: irradiated, examined and proven safe before a regulator will let it into a power reactor. The ANEEL thorium fuel shows the pace. In 2024 it became the first thorium-based fuel for Candu reactors to complete the first phase of Canada's pre-licensing vendor design review, and twelve test rodlets went into Idaho's Advanced Test Reactor that May, to be irradiated toward burnup targets of 20, 40 and 60 gigawatt-days per tonne. Each step is measured in years, and that is for a solid fuel in a reactor type that already exists.

blocks.title: Thorium: the pitch vs. the fine print

left.head: The pitch
items: About three times as abundant as uranium
Can breed fuel even with slow neutrons
Fewer long-lived heavy elements in the waste
Bred U-233 is hard to handle and easy to detect

right.head: The fine print
items: Cannot start a chain reaction without a fissile driver
Breeding demands an extremely tight neutron economy
Recycling it is costly because of strong gamma emitters
Uranium remains plentiful, so few countries are forced to switch

blocks.text: Who is actually betting on it

The country with the clearest reason to pursue thorium is India, which has huge thorium resources and relatively little uranium. Its long-standing plan has three stages: heavy water reactors, then sodium-cooled fast breeders to make plutonium, then advanced reactors that run largely on thorium. It is slow going. The 500-megawatt prototype fast breeder at Kalpakkam, started in 2004 and originally due in 2010, reached first criticality only in April 2026, and India's Department of Atomic Energy says large-scale thorium use will come only after enough fast breeder capacity is built.

Heavy water reactors are the other practical route. Their excellent neutron economy and on-line refueling make them well suited to thorium, and Indian heavy water reactors have long used thorium-bearing fuel bundles in some channels to flatten the power distribution, especially in new cores. Canada's laboratories have irradiated thorium fuels for more than 50 years, and Norway's Thor Energy tested thorium-plutonium fuel rods at the Halden research reactor until it shut down in 2018. All of that is real engineering. None of it has yet become a commercial thorium fuel cycle.

China is moving faster on molten salt. After TMSR-LF1, the WNA reports a 10-megawatt-electric successor planned at the same site, targeting first criticality in 2030, with a 100-megawatt-thermal demonstration aimed at around 2035. In the West, the efforts are smaller and more incremental: a thorium and high-assay uranium fuel called ANEEL has been tested in Idaho National Laboratory's Advanced Test Reactor, and European startups are designing thorium molten salt reactors.

It also helps to separate thorium from the broader wave of alternative reactors. Many of the advanced designs closest to operation in the US, such as gas-cooled pebble beds and fluoride salt-cooled reactors with solid fuel, run on high-assay low-enriched uranium, not thorium. The salt-cooled Hermes test reactor under construction at Oak Ridge, for example, uses uranium TRISO fuel pebbles. Thorium is one branch of the advanced reactor tree, not the trunk.
How to read the hype

None of this means thorium is a scam. It means the bottleneck in nuclear power was never a shortage of fuel. The hard parts are materials that survive decades of heat, radiation and corrosion; supply chains for new fuels; licensing; and building plants on budget. Thorium changes the fuel and leaves most of those problems in place, and in some cases makes them harder.

A useful habit, for thorium or any hyped technology, is to ask a few blunt questions. What is the fissile driver, and where does it come from? What is the conversion ratio in a machine that actually exists, not in a slide deck?
Who is paying for the first plant, and at what cost per megawatt-hour? A project that answers those clearly is worth watching. A video that answers none of them is selling a feeling.

items: Ask what fissile fuel starts the reaction and how it is supplied
Ask for measured conversion or breeding ratios from a real reactor
Ask how used fuel will be handled and recycled, and at what cost
Ask who is paying for the first plant and the price of its power

blocks.text: Sixty years in, thorium remains what it has always been: a fuel with genuinely attractive physics, a strong strategic case for a few countries and an unproven economic case everywhere else. The interesting question is no longer whether thorium works. Shippingport answered that in the 1980s. It is whether anyone can make it cheaper than the uranium fuel cycle that already runs nearly every power reactor on Earth.

takeaways: Thorium-232 is fertile, not fissile: it needs a driver like U-235 or plutonium before it can breed U-233.
Its real strengths are abundance, thermal breeding, good fuel properties and fewer long-lived heavy elements in waste.
Thorium reactors have run before, including the naval program's Shippingport breeder core, which bred more fuel than it used.
The barriers are economics, costly recycling due to U-232's gamma emitters, and unsolved molten-salt engineering issues.
India and China are the serious bets; ask any thorium pitch for its driver fuel, real conversion ratio and cost.

title: Three Mile Island: The Light That Said Closed
dek: A stuck valve, an indicator that reported a command instead of a fact, and a crew doing exactly what it was trained to do melted half a reactor core in 1979.

blocks.text: At 4 a.m. on Wednesday, 28 March 1979, the control room of Three Mile Island unit 2, near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, was quiet. The reactor was almost brand new, a 959-megawatt pressurized water reactor running at 97% power on the night shift. Within the next few hours, about 45% of its core would melt, and nobody in that room would realize it for a very long time.

Nothing exploded. No one was hurt. The radioactive release was tiny. And yet TMI-2 became the most serious accident in US commercial nuclear history and reshaped the industry more than any event before or since. The reason is uncomfortable: the operators were not reckless. They were careful, well-intentioned and following their training. The plant was lying to them, and their training made the lie convincing.
A minor trip, then a valve that stayed open

It started on the non-nuclear side. A mechanical or electrical failure stopped the main feedwater pumps that send water to the steam generators. With no feedwater, the steam generators could no longer pull heat out of the primary loop. The turbine tripped, and the reactor scrammed automatically, a shutdown that took about one second. So far this was a routine transient that plants were designed to ride out.

With heat removal suddenly reduced, the primary coolant heated up, expanded and pushed pressure up. As designed, the pilot-operated relief valve, or PORV, on top of the pressurizer popped open to bleed off the excess. About 10 seconds later, once pressure fell, it should have closed. It did not. It stuck open, and reactor coolant began pouring out as steam into a drain tank.

Here is the detail that turned a stuck valve into a meltdown. The control room had a light for the PORV, and that light showed the valve closed. But it was not wired to the valve's actual position. It only showed that a close signal had been sent to the valve's solenoid. The plant was reporting what it had been told to do, not what it had done. The crew had a small-break loss-of-coolant accident in progress and an instrument telling them, in effect, that there wasn't one.
Design rule written in molten fuel: an indicator should show the state of the equipment, not the command sent to it. If a light can be lit while the valve is open, sooner or later it will be.
Trained to do exactly the wrong thing

As coolant drained out, pressure fell and the high-pressure injection pumps started automatically, pumping emergency water into the primary system. This was the safety system doing its job. Then the operators made the decision that every investigation would circle back to: they throttled it back.

They had a reason. The pressurizer level, the water level in the tall tank that controls primary pressure, was rising. Their training told them that pressurizer level was the one dependable measure of how much water was in the system, and that they must never let the pressurizer fill solid with water, because then they could lose control of pressure and risk rupturing the system. A rising level looked like a system getting too full.

What was actually happening was the opposite. Steam escaping through the open valve at the top of the pressurizer was drawing water up into it, and steam pockets forming elsewhere in the primary system were pushing water into the pressurizer too. Level went up while the total inventory went down. There was no instrument to show the water level in the reactor vessel itself, because in normal operation the vessel is always completely full. So the crew assumed that a full pressurizer meant a covered core.

blocks.title: How a stuck valve became a meltdown
items: Feedwater lost; turbine and reactor trip automatically
PORV opens to relieve pressure, then sticks open while its light shows closed
Emergency injection starts, but rising pressurizer level convinces operators the system is overfilling
Operators throttle injection to keep the pressurizer from going solid
Steam forms in the primary loop; the coolant pumps vibrate and are shut off
Without forced flow or enough makeup water, the core uncovers and overheats

blocks.text: Steam kept forming in the primary loop. Pumping a mix of steam and water made the big reactor coolant pumps vibrate violently, and to protect them the operators shut them down. That ended forced cooling of the core. The water level in the vessel kept dropping as coolant boiled away through the stuck valve, until the top of the core was uncovered and the fuel began to overheat. The zirconium cladding reacted with steam, producing hydrogen and releasing radioactive material into the coolant.
Nearly sixteen hours to restore cooling

At 6:22 a.m., about two hours and twenty minutes in, operators closed a block valve between the PORV and the pressurizer, and the coolant leak finally stopped. By then the damage was well under way, and steam and gases inside the system were blocking flow through the core. The rest of the day was a struggle to collapse those steam bubbles and get circulation back. In the afternoon, a sudden spike in containment pressure revealed that hydrogen had burned inside the reactor building. Not until 7:50 p.m. did the crew get one reactor coolant pump running again and restore forced cooling.

Think about what the crew was facing. Alarms were ringing and lights were flashing across the boards, and every individual reading had an innocent explanation. Pressurizer level high: too much water. Coolant pumps shaking: protect the pumps. Relief valve light: closed, so that leak was ruled out. Each clue was explained away by a mental model that was internally consistent and wrong. That is the signature of the hardest accidents to stop, the ones where nobody is panicking because everybody is confident.

The reactor reached cold shutdown, with natural circulation and water below 100 °C, only on 27 April, a month later. When engineers finally removed the vessel head in July 1984 and looked inside, they found that at least 45% of the core, about 62 tonnes, had melted, and 19 tonnes had flowed down into the bottom of the vessel. The steel vessel had held. So had the containment building.

items: Feedwater lost; turbine and reactor trip; PORV opens and sticks
Early morning
Injection throttled; coolant pumps shut off; core uncovers
Block valve closed, stopping the leak
Afternoon

Hydrogen bubble fears; venting; public alarm

blocks.text: The bubble, the panic and the dose

For the public, the worst days were Friday and Saturday, 30 and 31 March. A deliberate venting of radioactive gas produced a reading of 1,200 millirem directly above a plant stack. Through garbled phone calls between people who did not know the plant's status, officials came to believe it was an off-site reading. A hydrogen bubble had also collected at the top of the reactor vessel, and for a time NRC officials feared it could explode. It never could have; there was not enough oxygen in the system. But the fear drove a weekend exodus, and the communication failures became as famous as the meltdown.

The actual release was small. About 2 million people around the plant received an average dose of about 1 millirem above normal background, according to the NRC. A chest X-ray is about 6. The maximum possible dose to someone at the site boundary was under 100 millirem. The Pennsylvania Department of Health tracked more than 30,000 people living within five miles for 18 years and found no unusual health trends, and more than a dozen independent studies found no excess cancers.

The cleanup was its own engineering saga. Defueling did not even begin until October 1985, after years of preparation; crews on a platform over the open, flooded vessel fished out damaged fuel with long-handled tools, keeping it underwater the whole time. By 1990, 342 canisters of fuel and debris had gone to the Idaho National Laboratory. More than 2 million gallons of accident-generated water were processed and evaporated. About 1% of the fuel is still in the vessel, and final decommissioning of unit 2 is expected to run until about 2052.

blocks.title: TMI doses in context
blocks.note: The site-boundary figure is an upper bound; the true maximum was below it.
blocks.source: US NRC, Backgrounder on the Three Mile Island Accident

blocks.text: It had already happened once

The most haunting part of TMI is that it was a rerun. On 24 September 1977, at the Davis-Besse plant in Ohio, which also used a reactor from the same vendor, Babcock and Wilcox, a loss of feedwater led to a pressurizer relief valve sticking open. The operators throttled high-pressure injection when pressurizer level rose, for the same reason TMI's crew would. Shift supervisor Mike Derivan later wrote that for the first 20 minutes the two events were nearly identical. At Davis-Besse, he worked out what the plant was really doing and acted on it, and the event ended as a footnote instead of a disaster.

Derivan has argued that the TMI operators did what they were trained to do. In his account, the vendor's training stressed the rule for throttling injection so hard that failing to apply it could cost an operator a certification exam, while neither that vendor nor others in the industry correctly understood how a plant behaves when the leak is in the steam space at the top of the pressurizer. About a dozen operators at two plants, 18 months apart, made the same choice and believed it was correct. An engineer at the vendor raised concerns in a memo in November 1977, but the warning was soft and the lesson never reached TMI's control room.
What changed

TMI permanently changed how US reactors are run. Training shifted from picking an event-specific procedure out of a book to symptom-based procedures that walk operators through yes-or-no questions, starting with whether the core is covered, before they try to diagnose the specific fault. Full-scale control room simulators became central. Control rooms were redesigned around human factors, and requirements for relief valves, instrumentation and auxiliary feedwater were tightened. The NRC put at least two resident inspectors at every plant, required emergency plans tested with state and local agencies, and opened a 24-hour operations center.

The industry also policed itself. In 1979 utilities created the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations, which set performance standards, shared operating experience across plants and, from 1985 through its National Academy for Nuclear Training, accredited training programs. The point of sharing was exactly the Davis-Besse lesson: one plant's near miss should become every plant's training scenario.

There was a price, too. Public confidence in nuclear power in the US dropped sharply after the accident, and TMI became a major reason that new reactor construction stalled through the 1980s and 1990s. An accident that injured no one ended up shaping the American energy mix for a generation, which says as much about communication and trust as it does about engineering.

items.label: Significant events per US reactor, 1985 vs 1997
Median US plant capability factor, 1980 vs after 2000
Cost of the nearly 12-year TMI-2 cleanup

blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Three Mile Island Accident

blocks.text: The results showed up in the numbers. Significant events per reactor fell from 2.38 in 1985 to 0.10 by the end of 1997. Median capability factor rose from about 65% in 1980 to over 80% in 2000 and above 90% afterward. TMI-1, the undamaged twin, restarted in 1985 with revamped training, ran an uninterrupted 616 days in 1997 and stayed among the country's best performers until it closed in 2019 for economic reasons. In 2024 its owner announced plans to restart it under a power deal with Microsoft, renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center. Cleaning up TMI-2 took nearly 12 years and about $973 million.

The deeper lesson is about what an operator can know. The TMI crew was not ignorant or lazy. They read their instruments correctly and applied their training faithfully, and the core melted anyway, because the instruments answered a different question than the one that mattered and the training rested on an incomplete model of the plant. The fix was not just better people. It was instruments that report reality, procedures built around protecting the core first, and a system that moves every near miss to every control room. For anyone who stands watch, the useful habit is simple: when the indications do not add up, ask what each one is actually measuring.

takeaways: The PORV light showed that a close signal was sent, not that the valve was closed; indicators must show actual state.
Operators throttled emergency injection because rising pressurizer level looked like overfilling; there was no vessel level gauge.
About 45% of the core melted, yet the vessel and containment held and the average public dose was about 1 millirem.
A nearly identical event at Davis-Besse in 1977 was a warning that never reached TMI's operators.
Symptom-based procedures, simulators, INPO and shared operating experience came out of TMI and drove big safety gains.
