title: The Best Thing Money Can Buy Is an Hour
dek: Most people use spare cash to get more stuff. Research led by Ashley Whillans suggests buying back time makes people happier, and almost nobody does it.

blocks.text: Picture two Saturdays. On the first, you spend $40 on something you can hold: a game, a hoodie, a new set of earbuds. On the second, you spend the same $40 to make a chore disappear. Maybe you pay for a laundry service, order dinner instead of shopping and cooking, or pay a neighbor's kid to deal with the car. Which Saturday leaves you happier by the evening?

Most people bet on the stuff. It's tangible, it lasts, and spending money on a chore feels slightly lazy, even a little embarrassing. A team of psychologists led by Ashley Whillans, then at Harvard Business School, ran almost exactly this experiment. The time-saving Saturday won. And the more interesting finding came next: when they asked people how they'd spend extra money, almost nobody chose to buy time, even very rich people who could easily afford it.

That gap, between what makes people happier and what they actually do with spare cash, says something important about how badly we keep score with money. We count every dollar. We almost never count the hours.
Two weekends, one experiment

The study, published in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* in 2017, came in two parts. The first was a set of large surveys covering 6,271 adults in the United States, Canada, Denmark and the Netherlands. People reported whether they regularly spent money to offload tasks they disliked, such as cleaning, cooking or errands, and how satisfied they were with their lives. Those who bought time this way reported higher life satisfaction. The pattern wasn't limited to the rich; the senior author, Elizabeth Dunn, stressed that the benefits of buying time aren't just for wealthy people.

Surveys can't tell you which way the arrow points, though. Maybe happier people are simply more likely to hire a cleaner. So the team added a field experiment. Sixty working adults received $40 on two separate weekends. On one, they had to spend it on something that saved them time. On the other, they had to buy a material thing for themselves. The order was randomized. At the end of each day, people reported their mood and how pressed for time they felt.

On the time-saving weekend, participants reported more positive feelings and less time stress than on the material weekend. The money was identical. The difference was what it bought. The researchers' explanation is simple: feeling short on time is a steady background stressor, and paying to remove one draining task shrinks it, which leaves more room for the rest of the day to feel good.

items.label: Adults surveyed in four countries; those who paid to offload disliked tasks reported higher life satisfaction
Share of 98 working adults who said they'd use a $40 windfall to save time
Share of about 850 millionaires who spent nothing to outsource tasks they disliked

blocks.source: Whillans et al., PNAS, 2017; University of British Columbia, 2017

blocks.text: Why almost nobody does it

Here's the puzzle. When the researchers asked 98 working adults how they would spend an unexpected $40, only 2% said they would use it to save time. In a separate survey of roughly 850 millionaires, almost half said they spent no money at all outsourcing tasks they disliked. These are people for whom a cleaner or a meal service is a rounding error, and many of them still mop their own floors and resent it.

A few forces seem to push in the same direction. Stuff is visible and lasting. A new monitor sits on your desk and reminds you that you own it; the two hours you didn't spend at the laundromat leave no trace. Time also feels strangely elastic. Next week always looks emptier than this week, so trading money for time feels unnecessary, because surely you'll have more time later. You won't. Next week fills up exactly like this one did.

There's an identity piece, too. Many people, especially those who grew up without much money, feel that paying someone to do something you *could* do yourself is wasteful or self-indulgent. That instinct is useful when money is tight. It becomes a blind spot once it isn't, because it treats your hours as worth nothing. Money gets a price tag and a budget. Time gets neither, so it gets spent carelessly.

Think about how this plays out in a game you care about. Nobody who plays seriously grinds a low-value activity for hours when a better route exists; they optimize for progress per minute without thinking twice. Yet the same person will happily spend a free afternoon doing errands that could have been batched, delivered or skipped, because real-life hours don't come with an efficiency readout. The tools for valuing time are already in your head. They just aren't pointed at your actual life.
You track your money to the dollar and your time not at all. That's why time leaks. Before buying anything, it's worth asking: does this give me hours back, or does it cost me hours later?
Time poverty is a real cost

Researchers call the feeling of having too much to do and not enough time to do it *time poverty*, and it has been linked to stress and lower well-being. The Whillans paper opens with an odd observation: as countries around the world have grown richer, people's sense of time scarcity has grown too. More money hasn't bought more breathing room. If anything, the hours of people whose time is worth more get claimed by more things.

Other studies point the same way. In 2016, Hal Hershfield, Cassie Mogilner and Hanna Barnea found that people who said they would choose more time over more money tended to be happier than people who chose money. In a 2019 preregistered study, Whillans and colleagues followed about 1,000 graduating university students. Those who valued time over money went on to pick more intrinsically rewarding activities and jobs, and were happier a year later, even after accounting for how happy they were to begin with.

Commuting is the cleanest real-world example. In a classic study of German workers, economists Alois Stutzer and Bruno Frey found that people with longer commutes reported systematically lower well-being, and that they were not making up for it with better pay or cheaper housing. Standard economics predicts people would only accept a longer commute if something compensated them for it. In their data, nothing did. They called it the commuting paradox. For anyone choosing between a cheap apartment far from base and a pricier one ten minutes away, that's worth knowing: the cheaper place may cost you an hour a day, every day.

There's an important twist. A 2021 paper by Marissa Sharif, Cassie Mogilner and Hal Hershfield, using data from 35,375 Americans, found that well-being rises with free time only up to a point. Too little discretionary time was linked to lower well-being through stress. But having a lot of free time was also linked to lower well-being, apparently because people felt unproductive. When those people spent their free time on something purposeful, the drop shrank. So the goal isn't maximum leisure. It's enough time, used on things that matter.
What actually counts as buying time

Not every purchase that claims to save time does. A food delivery that replaces an hour of shopping and cooking you dread buys time. A gadget that needs setting up, updating and fixing often costs time. A subscription you forget to cancel costs time and money. The test is whether the purchase removes a task you actively dislike, and whether the hour it frees goes to something you value more.

blocks.title: Buying time vs. looking like it

left.head: Usually buys time
items: Paying to skip a chore you dread, like laundry or deep cleaning
Living closer to work, even for a bit more rent
A direct flight instead of a cheaper one with a long layover
Buying a used tool once instead of borrowing it every time

right.head: Often costs time
items: Gadgets that need constant setup, updates and troubleshooting
Cheap things that break and must be replaced
Saving $10 by driving 30 minutes to another store
Freed-up hours that go straight to the phone

blocks.text: That last item matters. Whillans has described how modern time gets shredded into what she calls *time confetti*: small scraps of a few minutes, broken up by notifications and quick checks. Buying back an hour does little if the hour gets confettied into scrolling. The research finding is about time spent on rest, people and meaningful work, not about time in general.

The idea also has limits. If paying for a service leaves you anxious about rent, you've swapped one stressor for a bigger one. The studies found benefits across income levels, but nobody is arguing that a person with no cushion should hire a housekeeper. The principle is about where the next dollar of *discretionary* money goes, after the bills and the savings are handled.
A system for your own hours

Military life complicates this in useful ways. Underway, you can't buy time at all. The schedule is set, the chores are assigned, and no app delivers to a boat at depth. That makes in-port time more valuable, not less. A long duty rotation leaves only so many free days, and every one spent doing errands you hate is a day you didn't spend training, building something or seeing people.

Think about what a typical in-port week actually contains: duty days, qualifications, PT, the drive in, the laundry that piled up during the last underway, meals, a car that needs attention, and the errands you put off. Most of those are fixed. A few aren't. The ones that drain you most are rarely the longest; they're the ones that feel pointless, like waiting in line, cleaning up after a week of not cleaning, or doing paperwork you could have done in five minutes if it hadn't been buried. Those are the best candidates for spending a little money, or a little planning, to make them go away.

blocks.title: Run a simple time audit
items: List the recurring tasks in a normal in-port week and roughly how long each takes.
Mark the ones you actively dread, not just the ones that take long.
For each dreaded task, find the cheapest way to make it disappear or shrink.
Try one for a month and notice how your free days feel, not just how many hours you saved.
Decide in advance what the freed time is for, so it doesn't leak into scrolling.

blocks.text: A rough way to frame the trade: figure out what an hour of your after-tax pay is worth, then ask whether paying someone that much or less to take a dreaded hour off your hands feels like a good deal. It's not a precise formula, and it ignores the fact that your free hours are scarce in a way your work hours aren't. But it breaks the habit of treating your own time as free.

The biggest version of this idea is saving itself. Money in the bank is stored time. Six months of expenses saved means six months you could spend between jobs, in school, or building a business without panic. Seen this way, buying time and saving money aren't opposites. They're two versions of the same move: using money to get control over your hours instead of letting money control them.
What the evidence can and can't say

It's worth being honest about how solid this is. The field experiment that gives the causal evidence had 60 people, which is small, and it relied on self-reported mood. The large surveys are correlational, so they can't fully rule out that happier, more organized people just tend to hire help. Most samples come from wealthy Western countries. The effects are real but modest; buying a meal kit will not transform your life.

Still, the core point is hard to dismiss, and it has the advantage of being cheap to test. You don't need a peer-reviewed study to find out whether paying $20 to skip a chore you hate improves your Saturday. You can run that experiment on yourself next time you're in port, and keep the result.

A good way to run that test is to compare two in-port weekends, one where you outsource or skip a single dreaded chore and one where you don't, and simply notice how the evenings feel. Keep the experiment honest by spending the same amount either way. That's essentially the design of the study, shrunk to a sample size of one. It won't prove anything to a scientist. It might tell you something about yourself.

The deeper reframe is this: money is a tool for buying the life you want, and a life is made of hours. People who get that tend to spend differently. They worry less about owning the newest thing and more about whether their days feel like theirs.

takeaways: In a randomized field study, spending $40 to save time made people happier than spending $40 on stuff.
Almost nobody does it: 2% chose to buy time with a windfall, and about half of millionaires surveyed outsourced nothing they disliked.
Long commutes are linked to lower well-being that pay and cheaper housing don't make up for.
Buy time only with discretionary money, and decide what the freed hours are for.
Savings are stored time: every month of expenses saved is a month of freedom.

title: Who Pays for Your Cashback?
dek: A credit card is a free tool for some people and one of the priciest legal loans for others. How the business works, and how to stay on the right side of it (rules as of 2026; not financial advice).

blocks.text: Here is a puzzle. A bank hands you a card that lets you borrow thousands of dollars with no collateral, no interview and no questions about what you buy. Every time you use it, it pays you: one or two percent back, points, miles, a sign-up bonus worth a few hundred dollars. If you pay the bill in full every month, you never pay a cent of interest. So who is paying for all of this?

The answer is that a credit card is not one product. It is two products sharing a piece of plastic. For some people it is a free payment tool that pays them to use it. For others it is one of the most expensive loans sold legally in the United States. The business works because the same card can be both, and because most people never stop to ask which one they are holding.
Three ways the machine gets fed

Card issuers make money in three main ways. The first is **interchange**: every time you tap a card at a store, the merchant pays a fee, a small percentage of the purchase, and most of it flows to the bank that issued your card. You never see it. It is baked into the price of everything in the store, which is why some small shops add a surcharge or ask for a minimum on card purchases. For debit cards from large banks, federal law caps that fee under the Fed's Regulation II. For credit cards, there is no such federal limit.

The second is **interest** on balances people do not pay off. The third is **fees**: late fees, annual fees, cash-advance and balance-transfer fees. Interest is by far the biggest of the three that cardholders pay directly. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, which reviews the card market every two years under the CARD Act of 2009, found that in 2024 cardholders were charged **$160 billion in interest**, up from $105 billion just two years earlier. On top of that came $31.3 billion in fees, more than half of it late fees.

blocks.title: What US cardholders paid and earned, 2024
blocks.note: Late and annual fees are part of the $31.3B fee total. Rewards are paid out to cardholders, not collected from them.
blocks.source: CFPB, The Consumer Credit Card Market, Dec 2025

blocks.text: Look at that chart again. Cardholders as a group earned $47.5 billion in rewards in 2024, nearly double the 2020 figure. That sounds generous until you set it next to the interest bill. The rewards are real, but they are funded, and a large part of the funding comes from the people who carry a balance.
Transactors and revolvers

The industry has names for its two kinds of customer. **Transactors** pay their full statement balance by the due date. **Revolvers** carry some of it into the next month and pay interest. The CFPB found that about half of active accounts revolve, back up to the pre-pandemic level after dipping to 45 percent in late 2021. About 15 percent of general-purpose cardholders made only the minimum payment in 2024, the highest share since at least 2015.

blocks.title: Same card, two different products

left.head: Transactor
items: Pays the full statement balance every month
Pays zero interest
Collects rewards funded partly by merchants and other cardholders
Builds credit history for free
The bank earns mainly interchange

right.head: Revolver
items: Carries a balance month to month
Pays an APR that averaged about 25% on general-purpose cards in 2024
Often pays late fees as well
Rewards are small next to the interest
The bank earns interest, fees and interchange

blocks.text: A transactor is not a great customer for a bank in the short run. The bank lends them money for free for up to a month or more and pays them rewards on top. It earns interchange, and it keeps them around hoping that some month, after a car repair or a bad deployment budget, they become a revolver. A revolver is where the margin is. As the CFPB's analysis notes, an issuer pays to fund balances for both groups but earns interest only from revolvers who do not default.

Researchers have tried to measure how much money moves between these groups. A 2010 Boston Fed paper by Scott Schuh, Oz Shy and Joanna Stavins estimated that, because stores charge everyone the same price whether they pay with cash or card, each cash-paying household was transferring about **$149 a year** to card users, and each card-using household was receiving about **$1,133**. Their numbers were disputed by industry-friendly economists at the time, so treat them as an estimate, not a law of nature. A 2023 Federal Reserve working paper by Sumit Agarwal and colleagues used account-level data and reached a similar conclusion from a different angle: people they classified as financially sophisticated profit from rewards cards at the expense of less sophisticated ones, an estimated **$15 billion a year** in redistribution. Reward cards, they found, also nudge people to spend more.
The price of a balance

Credit card rates are not set the way most people imagine. A typical card has a variable APR built from two pieces: the prime rate, which moves with the Federal Reserve's policy rate, plus a margin the bank chooses. When the Fed raised rates in 2022 and 2023, card rates rose with it. But the CFPB found something else going on underneath. Between 2013 and 2023, the average margin itself rose by 4.3 percentage points, to the highest level on record, even though defaults were lower and the share of subprime borrowers was roughly stable. In other words, cards got more expensive partly because banks decided to charge more, not only because money got more expensive.

blocks.title: Average credit card interest rate, all accounts
blocks.note: 2026 averages the first three quarterly readings. Accounts that actually pay interest are charged more than this all-accounts average.
blocks.source: Federal Reserve G.19 via FRED (series TERMCBCCALLNS), accessed Nov 2026

blocks.text: Here is what that means in practice. Take a $3,000 balance at 25.2 percent, the CFPB's 2024 average APR for general-purpose cards. Suppose the minimum payment is the month's interest plus 1 percent of the balance, with a $25 floor, a common formula. If you pay only the minimum and never charge another dollar, it takes about **15 and a half years** to clear the debt, and you pay roughly **$5,160 in interest**, more than the original balance. Pay a flat $150 a month instead and it is gone in a little over two years with about $930 in interest. Same debt, same rate. The only difference is the payment you choose.

Fees follow the same pattern as interest: they land hardest on the people with the least slack. The CFPB found that cardholders with deep subprime scores hold about 14 percent of card accounts but generate about 40 percent of late fees. Store-branded cards, the kind a cashier offers you with 10 percent off today's purchase, averaged an APR of 31.3 percent in 2024, and their subprime holders racked up nearly five late fees a year on average. The discount at the register is the bait. The APR is the hook.

Zero percent introductory offers are the friendliest-looking product in the lineup, and they can be genuinely useful if you have a plan to clear the balance before the promotion ends. But the CFPB noted that accounts opened with these promotions tend to carry higher balances over the longer term. A free first year is how a lot of revolvers are made.

The minimum payment is not a recommendation. It is the smallest amount that keeps the account current while keeping the balance, and the interest, alive for as long as possible. Since the CARD Act, your statement has to show how long minimum payments would take. Read that box once.
The score that follows you

Cards matter beyond their interest rates because they are how most young adults build a credit history, and that history shapes the price of everything else you borrow: car loans, apartment applications, eventually a mortgage. FICO, the most widely used scoring model, publishes the rough weights of its five categories.

blocks.title: What goes into a FICO Score
blocks.note: These are general weights for the population; the importance of each varies by person.
blocks.source: myFICO, What's in my FICO Scores

blocks.text: Two of those categories, worth 65 percent together, come down to habits a single card can teach. Pay on time, every time, and keep the amount you owe low relative to your limit. Nothing in the formula rewards carrying a balance. The persistent myth that you need to pay a little interest to build credit is false. A card used for one small recurring bill and paid in full by autopay builds the same history as one that bleeds interest.

Length of history is the slow one. It rewards the boring move of opening a no-annual-fee card early, using it lightly and simply never closing it. At 20, that is a cheap head start you cannot buy later.
Rules written for people in uniform

Service members get legal protections civilians do not, because lenders have a long history of setting up shop outside the gates of bases. Two are worth knowing as of 2026. Rules change, so confirm the current details with the command financial specialist or the base legal office.

items: **Military Lending Act (MLA):** for active-duty members and their dependents, most consumer credit, including credit cards, payday loans and many installment loans, cannot cost more than a 36 percent Military Annual Percentage Rate. That rate counts most fees and add-on products, not just interest. Lenders also cannot force arbitration or require a military allotment for repayment. Mortgages and auto loans secured by the vehicle are not covered.

**Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (SCRA):** debt you took on *before* entering active duty, such as a card or a car loan from your civilian life, can be capped at 6 percent interest while you serve (and for a year after, for mortgages). Interest above 6 percent is forgiven, not deferred. You generally have to notify the lender in writing and send a copy of your orders.

blocks.text: Notice what the MLA cap actually tells you. Congress decided that 36 percent, all-in, is the line beyond which lending to service members becomes predatory. The ordinary credit card in your wallet often sits in the mid-20s before fees. It is legal. It is also not that far from the line.
Using the machine without feeding it

None of this means cards are evil. For a transactor, a card is genuinely useful: fraud protection that is stronger than a debit card's, a month of float, a way to build credit, and rewards partly paid for by other people. The CFPB found that, in 2024, a third of card purchase volume was on cards with zero percent introductory rates, and some of those people used them well. The card is a tool. The question is whether you are using the tool or the tool's designers are using you.

The honest test is simple. If you have carried a balance more than once in the last year, you are a revolver, whatever you intended, and the rewards are almost certainly smaller than what you are paying. The fix is not a better rewards card. It is paying the balance down, switching the card to autopay in full, and treating the card as a debit card that happens to build credit.

blocks.title: A low-drama card setup
items: Pick one no-annual-fee card from a mainstream bank or a military credit union.
Put one or two predictable bills on it, like a phone plan or a streaming subscription.
Turn on autopay for the full statement balance, not the minimum.
Keep your total balance well below your limit and never take cash advances.
Check the statement once a month, especially before and after an underway period.
Keep the card open for years, even when you stop using it much.

blocks.text: That last step matters more on a submarine than almost anywhere else. When you cannot log in for weeks, autopay is the difference between a card that quietly builds your score and one that racks up a late fee, a penalty rate and a mark on your report while you are out of contact. The bank's model is built on people who are busy, distracted and occasionally late. The best defense is setting things up so busy and distracted does not cost you anything.

So, back to the puzzle. Who pays for the cashback, the points and the sign-up bonuses? Partly the stores, through prices everyone pays. Mostly the people who carry balances, through interest and late fees. Once you see that, the card in your wallet stops looking like a perk. It looks like a deal with two sides, and you get to choose which side you are on.

takeaways: In 2024 US cardholders paid $160 billion in interest and $31.3 billion in fees, while earning $47.5 billion in rewards.
Pay the full statement balance on autopay; carrying a balance does nothing for your credit score.
Paying only the minimum on $3,000 at about 25% APR can take over 15 years and cost more than the original debt.
Payment history and amounts owed make up about 65% of a FICO Score.

As of 2026 the MLA caps most consumer credit to active-duty members at 36% MAPR, and the SCRA can cap pre-service debt at 6%; confirm details with your command financial specialist or base legal office.

title: The Damage Control Locker for Your Money
dek: An emergency fund is the least exciting thing you will ever own, and the thing most likely to keep a bad week from becoming a bad year. What the Federal Reserve's data says about who has one, and how big yours should be.

blocks.text: Every year since 2013, the Federal Reserve has asked thousands of Americans the same simple question: if you faced an unexpected expense of $400, how would you pay for it? In the survey conducted in October 2025, **63 percent** of adults said they would cover it entirely with cash, savings or a credit card they would pay off at the next statement. That leaves more than a third of the country one dead alternator away from borrowing. Twelve percent said they could not pay a $400 bill right now by any means at all.

Four hundred dollars is not a disaster. It is a tow, a cracked phone, a last-minute flight home. The point of the question is not the dollar amount. It is what the answer reveals about how close people live to the edge, and how small the shock needs to be to push them over it.

blocks.title: Adults who would cover a $400 emergency with cash or its equivalent
blocks.note: Cash or its equivalent includes a credit card paid in full at the next statement.
blocks.source: Federal Reserve, Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (SHED), May 2026

blocks.text: On a submarine there are lockers full of gear that nobody hopes to use: patches, plugs, firefighting equipment, emergency breathing devices. The crew trains on them constantly anyway, because when something goes wrong underwater there is no time to go shopping. An emergency fund is the same idea applied to money. It is boring by design. Its entire job is to sit there, fully stocked, so that when something breaks you are responding with a plan instead of a panic.

General education, not financial advice. Data are from surveys published in 2025 and 2026. For a plan built around your own pay and obligations, talk to the Personal Financial Manager at your Fleet and Family Support Center or your command financial specialist.
Small shocks, expensive answers

Unexpected expenses are not rare events. In the same Federal Reserve survey, **59 percent** of adults said they had faced at least one major unexpected expense in the prior twelve months. The most common was a major vehicle repair or replacement, hit by 30 percent of adults. Among people who knew what the most common emergencies cost, the median bill landed between $1,000 and $1,999.

blocks.title: Major unexpected expenses in the prior 12 months
blocks.note: 59% of adults had at least one major unexpected expense.
blocks.source: Federal Reserve, Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (SHED), May 2026

blocks.text: The danger is not the bill itself. It is how you pay for it. Among adults who would not cover a $400 expense with cash, the most common fallback was putting it on a credit card and carrying the balance. That is where small shocks get expensive. In August 2026, the average interest rate on credit card accounts that were actually charged interest was about **22 percent** a year, according to the Federal Reserve's consumer credit report. Carry a $1,500 car repair on a card for a year at that rate and you pay well over $300 in interest on top of the repair itself.

Worse, debt from one emergency weakens you for the next one. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau puts it plainly in its guide to emergency savings: research suggests that people who struggle to recover from one financial shock end up with less savings to protect them from the next. A card balance eats the money that would have rebuilt the cushion. One emergency becomes a slow leak that lasts for years.

blocks.title: The debt spiral an emergency fund breaks
items: Unexpected bill arrives
No cash, so it goes on a card
Interest eats part of each paycheck
Less is left to save
Next surprise hits with no cushion

blocks.text: How much is enough?

You have probably heard the rule: keep three to six months of expenses in savings. It is a sensible starting point, but it was built for civilian workers whose biggest risk is losing a job. The CFPB's own advice is less tidy and more useful: the right amount depends on your situation, and a good way to set a goal is to look at the kinds of unexpected costs you have actually faced and what they cost.

For an active-duty sailor, the risk profile is unusual. Your paycheck is about as stable as income gets. Medical care is covered, and if you live in the barracks or on the boat, housing and much of your food are handled. Losing your job next month is unlikely. That means the classic six-month cushion is less urgent right now than it would be for a civilian in a shaky industry.

But stable income does not mean no emergencies. Cars still break, and a junior sailor is more likely than most to own one. Family emergencies at home mean last-minute travel. A deployment can leave a car, an apartment or a bill on autopay sitting unattended for months. And there is one financial cliff that almost every service member eventually walks toward, whether they think about it or not: the day they get out.

To turn any of this into a number, you need to know what a month of your life actually costs. Pull up the last three months of bank and card statements and add up everything that left: car insurance, phone, subscriptions, gas, food off the boat, gaming, gifts, the random stuff. Divide by three. Most people guess low, often by a lot, because irregular costs like a new tire or a trip home are easy to forget. The real figure is the foundation for every tier that follows, and it is worth fifteen minutes in port to get it right.

blocks.title: A tiered target for a single sailor
items: Tier 1: a starter fund of about $1,000 to $2,000, matching the typical cost of a major surprise expense.
Tier 2: one full month of your real expenses, including car insurance, phone, subscriptions and anything on autopay.
Tier 3: three to six months of estimated civilian living costs, fully built before your separation date.
Refill rule: whenever you use the fund, rebuilding it becomes the next savings priority.

blocks.text: Money worry takes up mental space

There is a second, less obvious reason to keep a cushion, and it has to do with your head rather than your wallet. In a 2013 paper in *Science*, Anandi Mani, Sendhil Mullainathan, Eldar Shafir and Jiaying Zhao asked shoppers at a New Jersey mall to think through a hypothetical car repair before taking reasoning tests. When the imagined repair was expensive, lower-income participants scored worse; when it was cheap, they did fine. Higher-income participants did about the same either way. The authors argued that financial worry acts like a background process that eats into the attention you have left for everything else.

That idea, often called the scarcity mindset, deserves some caution. When a team led by Michael O'Donnell tried to replicate 20 studies from the broader scarcity literature in 2021, the results varied widely: some held up strongly and others clearly failed. So treat the specific effect sizes with skepticism. The everyday version is harder to argue with, though. Anyone who has stood watch while worrying about an overdue bill knows that money stress does not stay in its compartment. A fund that makes a breakdown merely annoying instead of frightening gives you back some of that bandwidth.
The separation cliff

When you leave active duty, a lot of things that are invisible today become bills: rent, food, health insurance, sometimes a gap of weeks or months before a civilian paycheck starts. For people who have not planned for it, this is when the trouble shows up. A January 2025 CFPB report on auto lending to servicemembers found that **33 percent** of servicemembers with an auto loan who left the military after seven to 35 months of service became 90 days delinquent or defaulted on that loan within a year. For those with longer service, the share was under 15 percent.

items.label: Short-service members with auto loans who went 90 days delinquent or defaulted within a year of leaving
Same measure for servicemembers with longer service

blocks.source: CFPB, Auto Lending to Servicemembers, January 2025

blocks.text: That gap is not about intelligence. It is about a sudden change in cash flow with no buffer in place. If you already know you do not plan to make the Navy a career, the most valuable thing your emergency fund can become is a transition fund. Several months of civilian expenses, saved while your housing and food are still covered, turns the first year out from a scramble into a choice. It is the difference between taking the first job that answers and taking the right one.
Where to keep it

An emergency fund has three requirements, in this order: it must be safe, it must be reachable within a day or two, and it should earn something. That rules out the stock market. Stocks are a fine place for long-term money, but they can drop sharply at the exact moment the economy is wobbling and emergencies are most likely. Selling at a loss to pay a bill turns a temporary dip into a permanent one.

It also rules out your regular checking account, for a different reason: money that sits next to your spending money tends to get spent. The best home is a separate savings account at a federally insured bank or credit union, ideally a high-yield account, with no debit card attached. Inflation will nibble at it, which is a real cost. Think of that small loss as the premium you pay for having cash that is guaranteed to be there.

A practical detail: some sailors keep the fund at a credit union near their home port and the spending account at a bank with good ATM access overseas, or the reverse. The specific institution matters less than two things. Make sure deposits are federally insured, which banks and credit unions advertise clearly, and make sure you can move the money from your phone if you are on the other side of the world when you need it.

Your retirement account is not an emergency fund either. Pulling money out of the TSP early, or borrowing against it, can trigger taxes, penalties or lost growth that compounds for decades. Treat it as a last resort behind your own savings. For true crises, the Navy-Marine Corps Relief Society exists to help sailors with interest-free loans and grants. Knowing that backstop is there is useful. Planning to depend on it is not.
What counts as an emergency

The hardest part of an emergency fund is not building it. It is leaving it alone. Every fund eventually meets a moment that feels urgent: a game sale, a buddy's trip, a deal on a new phone that will be gone tomorrow. A simple test helps. An emergency is something that is unexpected, necessary and urgent. If any one of those three is missing, it belongs in a regular savings goal, not in the locker.

blocks.title: Use the fund or not?

left.head: Emergency
items: Car repair you need to get to the base
Last-minute flight home for a family crisis
Deductible after an accident or theft
Rent and bills during a gap between jobs

right.head: Not an emergency
items: A limited-time sale on gear or games
A trip planned weeks in advance
Annual bills like registration and insurance
A new phone when the old one still works

blocks.text: Notice that predictable expenses sit on the right side. Car registration, yearly insurance premiums and holiday travel are not emergencies; they are bills with long fuses. They deserve their own small savings buckets, so the emergency fund is not quietly drained by things you could see coming.
Building it without thinking about it

The Federal Reserve's data has a revealing pattern. Among adults who said they always had money left over at the end of the month, **86 percent** had savings to cover three months of expenses. Among those who never had money left over, only 13 percent did. That sounds obvious, but the lesson is about order. People with savings are not necessarily disciplined at the end of the month. They tend to take the money out first, before the month has a chance to spend it.

blocks.title: Have three months of expenses saved, by how often money is left over
blocks.source: Federal Reserve, Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (SHED), May 2026

blocks.text: For a sailor, the mechanics are easy. Set up an allotment so a fixed amount goes straight to the separate savings account each payday, and pick a number small enough that you will not cancel it. Deployments help too: with fewer chances to spend, money piles up, and the trick is deciding before you leave where that pile will go. When you hit a tier, raise the target or redirect the allotment toward investing.

The real payoff is not measured in dollars. Young adults are among the groups the Fed found least likely to have a three-month cushion: only 37 percent of adults aged 18 to 29 said they did. Being in that minority changes how you move through the world. You can say no to a bad deal, leave a bad situation and handle a breakdown without a knot in your stomach. Nobody brags about their emergency fund. But almost everyone who has one sleeps a little better because of it.

takeaways: In 2025, 63% of US adults would cover a $400 surprise with cash or its equivalent; 12% could not pay it at all.
The most common major surprise expense is a car repair, typically $1,000 to $1,999.
Build in tiers: a starter fund, then one month of expenses, then a full transition fund before you separate.
Keep it in a separate, insured savings account, not in stocks, checking or the TSP.
Automate it with an allotment, and refill it every time you use it.

title: The Twelve People Who Set the Price of Money
dek: The Federal Reserve controls a rate you will never pay, and it still decides what your car loan, credit card and future mortgage cost. How the thermostat works, as of November 2026 (not financial advice).

blocks.text: On September 16, 2026, twelve people in a room in Washington voted 12 to 0 to nudge one number up by a quarter of a percentage point. The number was the target range for the federal funds rate, now 3.75 to 4 percent. Almost nobody in the country pays that rate. You have never borrowed at it and never will. And yet it reaches your car loan, your credit card, the savings account your paycheck lands in, and the price of every house you might someday buy.

The Federal Reserve is one of the most powerful institutions in the world, and one of the least understood. People talk about it like a weather system, something that happens to them. It is better understood as a thermostat with a very long delay, run by humans who are trying to steer by instruments that report what the economy was doing months ago. Once you see how the thermostat works, interest rates stop being random noise and start being something you can plan around.
The rate nobody pays

Banks keep accounts at the Fed, the way you keep an account at a bank. Every night, some banks end up with more money in those accounts than they need and some with less, so they lend to each other overnight. The interest rate on those overnight loans is the **federal funds rate**. It is the shortest, safest borrowing in the system, and almost every other interest rate is priced as some distance above it.

The decision about where it should sit belongs to the **Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)**: the seven members of the Fed's Board of Governors, the president of the New York Fed, and four of the other eleven regional Fed presidents on a rotating basis. They meet eight times a year. In 2026 the chairman is Kevin Warsh. The committee does not order banks to charge a particular rate. Instead it sets a target range and then uses its own administered rates to herd the market into it.

The main lever today is the interest the Fed pays banks on the money they park with it, called interest on reserve balances. After the September 2026 decision, the Board set that rate at 3.90 percent. Think about why that works. No bank will lend to another bank overnight for much less than it can earn, risk free, by leaving the money at the Fed. Raise what the Fed pays and you raise the floor under the whole market. A standing repo facility at 4.0 percent acts as a rough ceiling. In October 2026 the effective federal funds rate averaged 3.88 percent, right where the committee wanted it.

This is a newer setup than most textbooks describe. Before the 2008 crisis, reserves were scarce, and the New York Fed's trading desk steered the rate by buying and selling Treasury securities every day to add or drain just enough cash. Since then the banking system has been flooded with reserves, and the FOMC's statements now say it maintains ample reserves. With that much money sloshing around, fine-tuning the supply no longer moves the price, so the Fed sets the price directly by deciding what it pays.
Why anyone would want to slow an economy down

Congress gave the Fed its marching orders in the Federal Reserve Reform Act of 1977: promote maximum employment and stable prices. This is the **dual mandate**, and the Fed interprets stable prices as inflation of 2 percent a year over the longer run. The two goals usually point the same way, but not always. When the economy runs hot, businesses hire, wages rise, spending rises, and prices can start climbing faster than anyone planned. Higher interest rates cool that by making borrowing more expensive and saving more rewarding. Lower rates do the opposite.

The clearest demonstration of the Fed's power, and its cost, came around 1980. Inflation in the 1970s had become entrenched. When Paul Volcker became chairman in August 1979, prices were rising more than 11 percent a year. Measured by the consumer price index, inflation peaked at about 14.6 percent in March 1980. The Volcker Fed squeezed money growth and let short-term rates soar: the effective federal funds rate averaged about 19 percent in early and mid 1981, the highest in its history.

blocks.title: Effective federal funds rate, selected months
blocks.note: Monthly averages at uneven intervals, chosen to show peaks and troughs.
blocks.source: Federal Reserve via FRED (series FEDFUNDS), accessed Nov 2026

blocks.text: It worked, and it hurt. The economy fell into recession in July 1981 and stayed there until November 1982. Unemployment hit 10.8 percent in November 1982. But inflation broke: by the end of that recession it was back under 5 percent, and by mid 1983 CPI inflation was about 2.5 percent. At the time, Volcker was one of the most unpopular officials in the country; today he is mostly remembered for proving that inflation could be beaten. Fighting inflation is a choice to accept some pain now to avoid more pain later, and the people who feel the pain are rarely the people who make the choice.
How a decision in Washington reaches your wallet
The federal funds rate is the first domino. What makes the Fed powerful is how many dominoes stand behind it.

blocks.title: From the FOMC to your account
items: The FOMC announces a new target range and the Fed resets the rate it pays on reserves.
Overnight lending rates between banks move into the new range within a day.
Banks' prime rate moves with it, and prime is the base for most credit card APRs and many variable loans.
Rates on savings accounts, CDs and money market funds follow, usually with some lag and less enthusiasm.
Markets reprice expectations of where short rates will be for years, which moves Treasury yields and, through them, mortgage rates.
Over months, more expensive borrowing changes what households buy and what businesses build, which eventually shows up in jobs and prices.

blocks.text: That last step is the slow one. Milton Friedman described monetary policy as acting with long and variable lags: a hike today may not show up fully in inflation for a year or more. That is why the Fed can look like it is always too late. It is reacting to data about the past while trying to influence a future it cannot see.

The lags cut both ways, and the most recent cycle shows it. As prices took off in 2021, Fed officials at first described the jump as likely to be transitory, a side effect of reopening supply chains that would fade on its own. It did not fade quickly. CPI inflation peaked at about 9 percent in June 2022, the highest in four decades, and the Fed then raised rates faster than at any time since the Volcker era. Critics said it started too late. Defenders pointed out that unemployment stayed low through the whole fight, which almost nobody had predicted. Both things can be true.

It also matters what the Fed cannot do. Interest rates are a blunt tool that works on demand: they make people and companies want to borrow and spend less. They do nothing to grow more wheat, pump more oil or unclog a port. When inflation comes from a supply shock, the Fed can only cool demand until it matches the reduced supply, which is why fighting that kind of inflation tends to cost jobs. The Fed also has a second lever, buying or letting run off huge amounts of Treasury and mortgage bonds, which pushes longer-term rates around. But the overnight rate remains the main dial.

Mortgage rates deserve special mention because they do not follow the Fed directly. A 30-year mortgage is priced off longer-term bond yields, which depend on what investors expect the Fed and inflation to do over many years. That is why mortgage rates can rise while the Fed holds still, or fall before the Fed cuts. In 2026, the 30-year average in Freddie Mac's weekly survey started the year near 6.2 percent and was above 7 percent by October.

blocks.title: Average 30-year fixed mortgage rate by year
blocks.note: *2026 is the average of weekly readings through October 29.
blocks.source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey via FRED (MORTGAGE30US), accessed Nov 2026

blocks.text: Same house, different decade

Here is why this matters to someone who is not buying anything today. Take a $300,000, 30-year fixed loan. At the 2021 average rate of 2.96 percent, the monthly principal and interest payment works out to about **$1,258**, and total interest over the life of the loan is about $153,000. At 7.24 percent, the rate in Freddie Mac's survey at the end of October 2026, the same loan costs about **$2,044** a month and roughly $436,000 in interest. Same house, same buyer, nearly $800 a month more, purely because of where rates sat the week the loan was signed.

items.label: Monthly payment on $300,000 at 2.96% (2021 average)
Same loan at 7.24% (late October 2026)

blocks.source: Rates: Freddie Mac PMMS via FRED; payments: standard 30-year amortization, author's calculation

blocks.text: The same arithmetic runs in reverse for savers. When the Fed held rates near zero from 2009 to 2015 and again in 2020 and 2021, cash in a savings account earned almost nothing. When it raised rates eleven times between March 2022 and July 2023, from a 0 to 0.25 percent range to 5.25 to 5.5 percent, high-yield savings accounts and money market funds started paying real money again. Higher rates are bad for borrowers and good for people holding cash, and which one you are can change over your life.

For a sailor, the rate environment shows up in a few specific places. The TSP's G Fund pays a rate tied to Treasury yields, so it pays more in high-rate years. A car loan from a credit union is priced off the same rate structure as everyone else's. And if you are ever offered a re-enlistment bonus or a lump of deployment savings, high rates make a plain insured savings account a reasonable place to park it while you decide what to do, instead of a reason to rush.

Variable-rate debt, like a credit card, moves with the Fed within a statement cycle or two. A fixed-rate loan locks in whatever the world looked like the day you signed. That single difference is worth understanding before you borrow anything large.
A hard job done in public

The 2026 decisions show how uncertain this all is, even for the experts. In September the committee voted unanimously to raise rates, saying inflation remained elevated and the move would support a more timely return to 2 percent. CPI inflation was running around 3.7 percent over the previous year. Six weeks later, in October, the committee held rates steady, but two members, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, dissented because they wanted another hike. Twelve well-informed people looking at the same data did not agree.

The Fed's independence is part of its design. Congress sets the goals but leaves the decisions to the committee, so that rates are set on economic evidence rather than on the election calendar. Politicians in both parties have complained about the Fed over the decades, usually when it raises rates. The bet behind independence is that a central bank willing to make unpopular moves keeps inflation lower over the long run, and history, Volcker included, is the main evidence for that bet.

blocks.title: Turning points for the federal funds rate
items: Federal Reserve Act signed, creating the central bank
Reform Act makes jobs and stable prices the Fed's explicit goals
Paul Volcker becomes chairman with inflation above 11%
Effective fed funds rate averages about 19%
Target cut to 0 to 0.25% in the financial crisis
Back to near zero as the pandemic hits
Eleven hikes take the range to 5.25 to 5.5%
Sept 2026
First hike since 2023, to 3.75 to 4%

blocks.text: Thinking like the thermostat

You cannot predict interest rates, and neither can most professionals. What you can do is borrow, save and plan in ways that do not depend on guessing right. Keep variable-rate debt, especially credit cards, at zero, because it reprices against you as soon as the Fed moves. When rates are high, cash savings earn something, so an emergency fund in a high-yield account is not dead money. When you eventually borrow for something big, a car or a house, know that the rate environment can swing your monthly payment by hundreds of dollars, and that waiting, a bigger down payment or a smaller purchase are all ways to take that risk off the table.

The deeper lesson is the Fed's own. Every decision it makes trades some pain now against more pain later, with incomplete information and a delayed response. That is not a bad description of personal finance either. The people who do well with money are rarely the ones who called the market. They are the ones who built a setup that holds up whichever way the thermostat turns.

takeaways: The FOMC sets a target for the overnight rate banks charge each other; nearly every other rate is priced off it.
The Fed's goals are maximum employment and 2% inflation; in September 2026 it raised the target range to 3.75 to 4%.
Mortgages follow long-term bond yields, not the Fed directly, and can move while the Fed holds still.
A $300,000 30-year loan cost about $1,258 a month at 2021 rates and about $2,044 at late-October 2026 rates.
Keep variable-rate debt at zero and build plans that work whether rates go up or down.

title: The Real Math of Retiring Early
dek: How soon you can stop working depends mostly on one number you control. The famous 4% rule behind it is shakier for long retirements than the internet admits.

blocks.text: Two people start working at 20. The first earns a big salary and saves 10% of it, like the standard advice says. The second earns half as much but lives on half of what comes in and invests the rest. Who can stop working first? It isn't close. Under one common set of assumptions, the high earner needs about 51 years. The saver needs about 17.

That result is the engine behind FIRE, short for Financial Independence, Retire Early, a movement that grew online through the 2010s with blogs, forums and a lot of spreadsheets. Its central claim sounds too simple to be true: how soon you can stop needing a paycheck depends far more on what fraction of your income you keep than on how much you earn.

The math is real. But the internet version usually leaves out the hard parts: where the famous 4% rule came from, why it gets shakier the earlier you retire, and why people who reach the finish line sometimes find it isn't what they wanted. This is the full picture, so you can decide what to take from it.
The one equation

Start with your *FI number*, the amount of invested money that could cover your yearly spending indefinitely. The FIRE rule of thumb is 25 times annual spending. If you spend $40,000 a year, the target is $1 million. The 25 comes from the 4% rule, which says you can withdraw 4% of a portfolio in the first year and raise that amount with inflation each year after. One divided by 0.04 is 25.

Now notice what your savings rate does. When you save more, two things happen at once. You put more money toward the goal each year, and you shrink the goal itself, because you've proven you can live on less. A person who lives on 90% of their income needs to replace 90% of it. A person who lives on 50% only needs to replace half. That double effect is why the curve below is so steep.

blocks.title: Years of work until financially independent, by savings rate
blocks.note: Assumes starting from $0, a 5% annual return after inflation, and retiring at 25x annual spending
blocks.source: Calculated using the assumptions in Mr. Money Mustache, The Shockingly Simple Math Behind Early Retirement, 2012

blocks.text: Income is missing from that chart on purpose. Under these assumptions, two people with the same savings rate reach independence in the same number of years whether they earn $40,000 or $400,000. Income still matters a great deal in practice, because it's far easier to save 50% of a large paycheck than of a small one. But the chart's point stands: lifestyle creep, the habit of spending every raise, quietly erases the advantage of earning more.

It also tells you where to look for savings. Daily coffee gets the attention, but the big levers are the few large, recurring costs: housing, vehicles and food. A cheaper car payment or a roommate changes your savings rate every single month without requiring willpower every single day. One good decision about a big fixed cost often beats a hundred small acts of self-denial.

Two assumptions in that math deserve suspicion. A 5% return after inflation is a reasonable long-run guess for a stock-heavy portfolio, not a promise; real returns have been much lower for a decade at a time. And the 4% withdrawal rule wasn't designed for early retirees at all.
Where 4% came from

In 1994, a financial planner named William Bengen tested withdrawal rates against historical US market returns. He asked a simple question: what's the highest starting withdrawal, adjusted for inflation each year, that would have survived every 30-year retirement in the record? His answer was roughly 4%. A few years later, a study by three professors at Trinity University reached similar conclusions, and the 4% rule became the most famous number in retirement planning.

The key words are *30-year*. Bengen was modeling a person retiring around 65. Also, 4% was the *worst case* in the historical record, not a typical outcome. In many historical periods, a retiree following it would have ended up with plenty left over. In the worst ones, such as retiring just before a long stretch of high inflation or a deep crash, it barely held.

Morningstar publishes an updated estimate every year using forward-looking assumptions about stock and bond returns. Its figure for a 30-year retirement with a 90% chance of not running out of money has bounced between 3.3% and 4.0% in recent years, moving mainly with its expectations for future stock and bond returns. Its 2025 estimate was 3.9%. The lesson isn't that one of these numbers is right. It's that the safe rate depends on conditions at the moment you retire, which you can't choose.

blocks.title: Morningstar's safe starting withdrawal rate, 30-year retirement
blocks.note: 90% probability of success, 30% to 50% stocks, excluding Social Security
blocks.source: Morningstar, The State of Retirement Income, 2025

blocks.text: The 4% rule is a historical worst case for a 30-year retirement. Retire at 40 and you might need your money to last 50 years or more, which is a different problem.
The 40-year problem

Karsten Jeske, an economist who writes the *Early Retirement Now* blog, ran one of the most detailed public studies of withdrawal rates for long retirements, using US market data going back to 1871. One example from his work captures the issue. With a portfolio split evenly between stocks and bonds, a 4% withdrawal survived about 95% of historical 30-year periods but only about 65% of 60-year periods. Stretching the timeline made failure roughly seven times more likely.

His conclusion for early retirees was that 3.5% is closer to the real safe number, possibly lower if stock prices are high when you retire. That sounds like a small tweak. It isn't. At 3.5%, the multiple rises from 25 times spending to about 28.6 times, so the $1 million target becomes about $1.14 million. At 3.25%, it becomes about $1.23 million.

The reason long retirements are fragile is *sequence-of-returns risk*. If the market drops hard in the first few years after you stop working, you're selling investments at low prices to pay your bills, and those shares are gone before the recovery. The same average return in a different order can leave you rich or broke. Over a 30-year retirement, a bad start can be survived. Over 50 years, it has more time to compound.

blocks.title: Two kinds of retirement

left.head: Traditional, at 65
items: About 30 years to fund
Social Security and Medicare arrive on schedule
4% has held up in the historical worst case
Little time for a bad start to compound

right.head: Early, at 40
items: 50 years or more to fund
Decades of health insurance to buy yourself
Safer to plan around 3.5% or less
A crash in year two can shape the next five decades

blocks.text: What the spreadsheet leaves out

Health insurance is the biggest blind spot. People who stop working before 65 lose employer coverage and aren't yet eligible for Medicare, so they pay for decades of coverage out of their portfolio. Kids, aging parents, a house that needs a roof, and the simple fact that spending is hard to predict thirty years out all push the real number higher.

The other blind spot is psychological. A 2021 study by Marissa Sharif, Cassie Mogilner and Hal Hershfield, drawing on data from 35,375 Americans, found that well-being rises with free time only to a point. Too little was linked to stress. But a lot of free time was also linked to lower well-being, because people felt unproductive. When people with abundant free time spent it on productive or purposeful activities, the downside shrank. The lesson for FIRE is clear: retiring *from* something is not the same as retiring *to* something.

There are practical snags too. Most retirement accounts, including the TSP, are built for people who stop working in their late 50s or 60s, and pulling money out early can trigger taxes and penalties unless you use one of the specific exceptions. Early retirees need a plan for how to reach their money in the gap years, which usually means some savings in regular taxable accounts as well. Inflation is another quiet threat: a budget that feels comfortable at 40 can feel tight at 70 if your personal costs rise faster than average.

Critics of the movement also point out that extreme frugality can become its own trap. Someone who spends a decade saying no to friends, travel and experiences to hit a number has traded away years that don't come back. The research on time and happiness suggests that money spent on relationships and on reducing daily stress pays real dividends. A plan that makes your twenties miserable to make your forties free is a trade worth questioning, not an automatic win.

That's why many people in the FIRE world don't actually stop working. They change the deal. *Barista FIRE* means covering part of your spending with a low-stress job. *Coast FIRE* means investing heavily early, then saving nothing more and letting compounding finish the job while you earn just enough to live. These versions are far more forgiving. Even a small income in the early years of retirement sharply reduces sequence-of-returns risk, because you sell fewer shares when prices are down.

Flexibility works the same way on the spending side. Retirees who are willing to trim their withdrawals for a year or two after a bad market can usually start with a higher rate than those who insist on a fixed, inflation-adjusted paycheck no matter what. The 4% rule assumes total rigidity. Real people rarely need to be that rigid, and the ability to adapt is worth a lot.

Here's the coast idea in numbers. Money growing at 5% a year after inflation roughly doubles every 14 years. If a 25-year-old had $100,000 invested and never added another dollar, at that rate it would be worth about $432,000 in today's money at 55. The earliest dollars do the heaviest lifting, which is the single most important point for someone in their early twenties.
The young-sailor version

A junior sailor has a few unusual advantages here. Housing and food are partly covered through allowances or provided outright. There's no commute while underway and few chances to spend. The Thrift Savings Plan comes with government matching, covered in detail in a separate article. And most importantly, a 20-year-old has the one ingredient no high earner can buy: decades of compounding ahead.

There's also a built-in version of early retirement in the military itself. Someone who serves 20 years can collect a lifetime, inflation-adjusted pension starting around age 40, along with military health coverage. Not everyone wants to stay that long, and that's a legitimate choice. But it's worth recognizing the pension for what it is in FIRE terms: a large, guaranteed income stream that would take a big portfolio to replicate.

For someone leaving after one enlistment, the most valuable FIRE lesson may not be early retirement at all. It's that a high savings rate during your twenties buys options in your thirties: the freedom to go to school full time, take a lower-paying job you love, or start a business without the pressure of needing it to pay rent in month three.

blocks.title: Find your own numbers
items: Track what you actually spend for three months, including irregular costs.
Multiply your yearly spending by 25 for a traditional target, or about 28 to 30 for an early one.
Calculate your savings rate: what you invest divided by your take-home pay.
Count your runway: how many months of expenses you could cover with no income.
Raise the savings rate by cutting big fixed costs before small daily ones.

blocks.text: Freedom is a spectrum

The most useful reframe from FIRE has nothing to do with retiring at 40. It's measuring wealth in time instead of dollars. Divide your savings by your monthly spending, and you get the number of months you could live without a paycheck. Three months means a job loss is a crisis. Two years means it's an opportunity. Ten years means work becomes optional.

Every month added to that number is a small piece of independence, and you don't have to reach the end to benefit. A person with a year of runway negotiates differently, takes smarter risks and tolerates a bad boss less. The finish line is optional. The direction is what changes your life.

The honest version of FIRE, then, is less a promise than a set of tools: know your spending, push your savings rate as high as you can sustain without hating your life, invest simply, and treat the 4% rule as a rough guide that gets less reliable the longer you need the money to last.

takeaways: Your savings rate, not your income, mostly decides how many years until you're financially independent.
The 4% rule came from 30-year retirements and was the historical worst case, not the typical outcome.
Early retirees face a longer horizon; 3.5% or less is a safer planning number.
Health insurance and purpose are the two biggest things FIRE spreadsheets leave out.
Measure wealth in months of runway; every month added is a piece of freedom.

title: The Business of Selling You a Business
dek: Dropshipping courses, done-for-you stores and crypto hype share one pattern: the steady money goes to whoever sells the dream. What FTC data and court cases show.

blocks.text: The pitch was polished. A company called Click Profit promised buyers a hands-off online store on Amazon, Walmart or TikTok, run by its own AI-powered system. Ads talked about six- to eight-figure incomes and the chance to sell the store later at a multiple. The price of entry was a management fee of at least $45,000, plus thousands more for inventory.

In March 2025, the Federal Trade Commission sued. According to the FTC's complaint, over a fifth of the Amazon stores earned nothing after fees, and another third made less than $2,500 in gross sales over their entire lifetime. Amazon blocked, suspended or terminated roughly 95% of them. Most buyers, the FTC alleged, lost everything they paid, and some were left with credit card debt and boxes of unsold products. These are allegations; a court decides the case. But the pattern is one the FTC has seen again and again.

This article is about that pattern, the business of selling people the dream of a business. It shows up in dropshipping courses, done-for-you Amazon stores, trading signal groups and crypto hype. Not everything in these worlds is a scam. But the reliable money is very often made by the person selling the dream, not the person buying it.
The scale of it

Each year the FTC publishes data from its Consumer Sentinel Network, a database of fraud reports from the public. For 2025, the FTC reported about 3 million fraud reports and $15.9 billion in reported losses. Investment scams were the largest category by far, at $7.9 billion. A year earlier, the totals were $12.5 billion lost, with investment scams at $5.7 billion and business and job opportunity scams at about $750 million.

Two things make these numbers worse than they look. First, they only count what people reported, and most fraud victims never report. Second, the share of reporters who actually lost money is rising: 38% in 2024, up from 27% the year before. Younger adults aren't immune. In the 2024 data, 44% of people in their twenties who reported fraud said they lost money.

Military consumers show up in the data too. In 2024, service members, veterans and their families filed 99,443 fraud reports with $584 million in losses. The median loss was $700. But in the investment category, the median loss was $10,000, and in business and job opportunities it was $2,800. These are the categories where people hand over real savings, not pocket change.

blocks.note: Top fraud categories reported by service members, veterans and families

Median loss in business and job opportunity scams
Median loss across all fraud reports

blocks.text: Selling the shovel

During the California Gold Rush, many of the people who reliably made money weren't miners. They were the merchants selling picks, pans and jeans to miners. The modern online version is the course. When someone with a rented sports car and a screenshot of a big sales day offers to teach you their system, it's worth asking a simple question: which business is actually making this person money, the store or the course?

The FTC's recent cases sketch a common shape. Ecommerce Empire Builders sold training programs costing nearly $2,000 and done-for-you online storefronts costing up to $35,000, promising profits of $10,000 a month. In May 2025, a court order permanently banned the company and its owner from selling business opportunities, with a $9.8 million judgment, partly suspended because they couldn't pay. In June 2025, the FTC announced a settlement banning the operators of Ascend Ecom, which it said had taken at least $25 million from consumers with promises that AI-powered tools would bring in thousands of dollars a month in passive income.

Several of these operations also tried to stop customers from complaining. The FTC said Click Profit cited a non-disparagement clause to threaten people who complained, and the Ascend and Empire orders specifically banned contract terms that keep consumers from posting reviews or reporting problems. When a business needs to legally prevent you from describing your experience, that tells you something about the experience.

blocks.title: The guru funnel
items: Free video showing a lifestyle and big sales screenshots
Cheap course or community that teaches the basics
Expensive coaching, mastermind or done-for-you store
Poor results blamed on your effort or mindset
Pitch for the next, more advanced tier

blocks.text: Notice how the loop protects the seller. If you fail, the problem was your execution, so the solution is more coaching. The model works for the seller regardless of whether anyone downstream makes money. That is the core tell of a get-rich-quick product: the seller's income doesn't depend on the buyer's success.

It's also worth knowing how to read the proof. A screenshot of a $50,000 month usually shows revenue, the total money customers paid, not profit. Take out the product cost, ad spend, fees and refunds and the real number can be small or negative. And the people posting screenshots are a filtered group: the few who did well, plus the ones paid to say so. You never see the thousands who tried quietly and stopped.

None of this is a judgment on the people who buy in. These pitches are designed for ambitious people who want more than a paycheck, who are willing to work and who are tired of being told to be patient. That's exactly why they work. The target isn't the lazy or the foolish. It's the hungry.
Dropshipping, honestly

Dropshipping itself is a real, legal business model. You run an online store, a customer orders, and a supplier ships the product directly to them. You never touch inventory. Some people do build profitable businesses this way. The question isn't whether it's possible. It's whether the version being sold to beginners makes sense.

Here's the problem in plain terms. If you can set up a store selling a product from a supplier in an afternoon, so can thousands of other people, often selling the identical item. There's no barrier to entry, which means there's no protection from competition. The only way to win is to find customers more cheaply than everyone else, which usually means paid ads, which means your profit is decided by an auction you don't control.

Run some made-up but realistic-looking arithmetic. Say you sell a gadget for $30 that costs you $10 including shipping. That looks like a $20 profit. Now subtract the payment processing fee, the store platform's monthly cost, and refunds from customers annoyed by slow shipping. Then subtract the ad spend needed to get each sale. If it takes $15 of ads to land one $30 order, most of your margin is gone before you've paid yourself anything. Courses tend to show revenue screenshots. The number that decides everything is ad cost per sale, and it rarely appears in the highlight reel.

You'll often see claims like "90% of dropshippers fail." Be skeptical of those too. There's no reliable public dataset on dropshipping success rates, and many of the statistics floating around trace back to companies selling apps or courses. The honest answer is that nobody outside the platforms knows the real number. What the FTC cases do show is what happens in the worst version: stores that never open, stores suspended by the platform, and buyers who end up in debt.

There's also platform risk. A store that lives on Amazon, Shopify or TikTok exists by permission. One policy change, one complaint pattern or one automated review can freeze the account and the money in it. The Click Profit allegation that about 95% of stores were blocked, suspended or terminated is an extreme case, but the underlying risk applies to anyone building on someone else's platform. If you do want to try dropshipping, do it with a small budget you're prepared to lose, treat it as paid lessons in marketing, and never pay someone tens of thousands of dollars to do it for you.
A business that anyone can start in an afternoon is a business anyone can copy in an afternoon. Ask what makes yours hard to copy. If the answer is nothing, you're competing on ad spend alone.
Crypto: hype as a business model

Crypto has its own version of the shovel problem. Researchers at the Bank for International Settlements studied crypto exchange app use in 95 countries from 2015 to 2022. They estimated that between 73% and 81% of retail investors had likely lost money on their initial bitcoin investment. The reason was timing: app downloads surged when prices were rising, so most people arrived after the run-up, just in time for the fall.

Then there are outright scams. Investment fraud was the FTC's largest loss category in both 2024 and 2025, and in 2024 the losses paid through bank transfers or cryptocurrency exceeded losses through all other payment methods combined. A common pattern starts with a friendly stranger on social media or a dating app, slowly builds trust, then introduces a "platform" that shows impressive fake gains until the victim tries to withdraw. Crypto payments are hard to reverse, which is exactly why scammers prefer them.

Influencer coins and pump-and-dump schemes follow the same shovel logic as the courses. Early insiders buy cheap, hype the coin to their audience, and sell into the wave of late buyers they created. The audience provides the exit.

A few habits filter out most of this. Real investments don't guarantee high returns, because nothing that can rise a lot is free of the risk of falling a lot. Real brokers and advisers can be looked up on FINRA's free BrokerCheck tool. Real platforms let you withdraw your money without a surprise fee or a sudden "tax" to unlock it. And no legitimate opportunity requires you to decide before you've had time to sleep on it. Urgency is a tactic, not a feature.
Red flags and the honest alternative

items: Promises of passive, guaranteed or effortless income.
"AI does everything" or "fully automated" claims.
Income screenshots without full costs, refunds and ad spend.
The seller makes most of their money teaching the method, not using it.
Pressure: limited spots, countdown timers, "price goes up tonight."
Encouragement to use credit cards, loans or retirement money to pay.
Contracts that bar you from complaining or posting reviews.
Payment requested in crypto, gift cards or wire transfers.

blocks.text: The FTC's Business Opportunity Rule requires sellers of many money-making opportunities to give buyers a short disclosure document before they pay, and to have written evidence for any earnings claims they make. If a seller dodges that question, or the earnings claims can't be backed up, walk away. And if you've been hit, report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov; those reports are exactly the data that builds the cases above.

None of this means building a business is a bad idea. It means the real version looks different. Real small businesses usually start slow and cheap: a few hundred dollars, not tens of thousands. They sell something with an edge, such as a skill, an audience, a product you made, or knowledge of a niche others don't have. They test demand before scaling. A Roblox game, a YouTube channel or a small online store built around something you know well all fit that mold. The skills involved, like marketing, writing, building and analyzing data, compound over years.

blocks.title: Two ways to start

left.head: Get-rich-quick pitch
items: Pay thousands up front for a system
Promised results in weeks
Sell what everyone else sells
Failure blamed on your mindset

right.head: Real small business
items: Spend little and test demand first
Expect months or years to profit
Sell something with an edge
Failure treated as data to adjust

blocks.text: The most useful question to carry around is simple: who is making money here, and from whom? If the honest answer is that the money comes from people like you buying the program, then you're not the business owner. You're the customer, and the product is hope.

takeaways: Americans reported $15.9 billion in fraud losses in 2025; investment scams were the biggest category.
In FTC cases, done-for-you store schemes charged up to tens of thousands and most buyers lost money.
Dropshipping is legal but easy to copy; ad cost per sale decides profit, and courses rarely show it.
An estimated 73% to 81% of retail bitcoin app investors likely lost money, mostly by arriving late.
Always ask: is the seller's income coming from the business or from selling it to you?
