title: Two GI Bills and One Decision Not to Rush
dek: The Montgomery and Post-9/11 GI Bills pay for school in completely different ways, and court rulings in 2024 and 2025 changed the rules for people who have both. The rules as of November 2026.

blocks.text: Thirty-six months at the current full-time Montgomery GI Bill rate comes to $93,636. That's real money, and it's only one of the two education programs many sailors can draw on. Yet plenty of people spend more time comparing phones than figuring out how their GI Bill actually works.

A common belief goes something like this: the Montgomery GI Bill covers about three years of college plus housing. That sentence mixes up two different programs. The Montgomery GI Bill sends you a flat monthly check and leaves the rest to you. The Post-9/11 GI Bill pays the school directly and adds a separate housing allowance. Which one is better depends on where and how you study, and a Supreme Court case in 2024, followed by a second court ruling in 2025, changed the rules for many people who have both.

These are the rules as published on VA.gov as of November 2026. Benefits law and VA policy change. Confirm everything with the VA and your base education office before making a decision. This is general information, not financial or legal advice.
Two different machines

The Montgomery GI Bill for active duty, known as Chapter 30 or MGIB-AD, is the one you pay into. If you entered active duty after June 30, 1985, and didn't opt out, $100 a month was taken from your pay for your first 12 months, $1,200 in total. To use it, you generally need an honorable discharge, a high school diploma or equivalent, and enough continuous service, typically three years, or two if that was your enlistment agreement. Most people get up to 36 months of benefits, and you usually have 10 years after leaving the service to use them.

MGIB-AD pays a fixed monthly rate directly to you. For October 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027, the full-time rate for someone with at least three years of continuous active duty is $2,601 a month. Three-quarter-time students get $1,950.75 and half-time students get $1,300.50. Out of that check, you pay your own tuition, books and rent. The rate goes up most years; the same full-time rate was $2,358 in 2023–24 and $2,438 in 2024–25.

items.label: MGIB-AD full-time monthly rate, 3+ years of service (Oct. 1, 2026 to Sept. 30, 2027)
Full-time rate with 2 to 3 years of service
What you paid in: $100 a month for 12 months

blocks.source: US Department of Veterans Affairs, VA.gov, 2026

blocks.text: The Post-9/11 GI Bill, Chapter 33, works differently. You don't pay into it. Anyone with at least 90 days of active duty after September 10, 2001, qualifies for some level of benefit, and the percentage rises with service time. At 100%, it covers full in-state tuition and fees at public schools, paid straight to the school. Private and foreign schools are capped; for August 1, 2026, through July 31, 2027, the cap is $30,908.34 a year.

On top of tuition, Post-9/11 pays a monthly housing allowance when you attend more than half time. For in-person classes, it's based on the military housing allowance for an E-5 with dependents at your school's location, so it's much larger in expensive cities. For fully online students, it's half the national average, up to $1,198 a month. There's also up to $1,000 a year for books and supplies. Benefits don't expire for anyone whose service ended on or after January 1, 2013, and with Defense Department approval, service members can transfer some or all of the benefit to a spouse or child.

Two smaller details matter at the edges. Benefits are counted in months of entitlement, so going full time burns them faster than part time but also pays the full rate. And for private schools that cost more than the yearly cap, the Yellow Ribbon Program lets participating schools cover part of the gap, with the VA matching their contribution, for students at the 100% benefit level. Not every school participates, and those that do often limit the number of spots.

blocks.title: Post-9/11 GI Bill benefit level by active-duty service
blocks.note: Service on or after Sept. 11, 2001. Some other paths, such as a Purple Heart, also qualify for 100%.
blocks.source: VA.gov, Post-9/11 GI Bill rates, effective Aug. 1, 2026

blocks.text: Where each one wins

blocks.title: The two GI Bills side by side

left.head: Montgomery (Chapter 30)
items: You paid $1,200 to join
Flat monthly check paid to you
You cover tuition, books and rent from it
Usually must be used within 10 years of leaving

right.head: Post-9/11 (Chapter 33)
items: No buy-in
Tuition paid to the school, plus housing and books
Housing tied to E-5 BAH where you study
No expiration for service ending in 2013 or later

blocks.text: For many people attending in person, especially at a public school in a high-cost area, Post-9/11 is the bigger package. It covers the tuition outright and then pays a housing allowance on top, which in an expensive city can be large. That's where the "college plus housing" idea comes from. It describes Post-9/11, not Montgomery.

Montgomery can come out ahead when tuition is low. Because it pays the same flat amount no matter what the school charges, a cheap community college or low-cost program leaves more of the check in your pocket. Online study is a good test case. Under Post-9/11, a fully online student gets tuition covered plus up to $1,198 a month for housing. Under Montgomery, the same student gets $2,601 a month and pays tuition out of it. On those numbers alone, Montgomery leaves more cash whenever monthly tuition is under about $1,400. That's rough arithmetic, not a verdict; the real comparison depends on your enrollment, your benefit percentage, breaks between terms and the specific school.

The VA's online GI Bill Comparison Tool runs these calculations for a specific school and situation. It's worth using before you choose, because the gap between the two programs can be thousands of dollars a year in either direction.

It also helps to know that the GI Bill isn't only for four-year degrees. According to the VA, the benefits can pay for non-college degree programs, apprenticeships and on-the-job training, flight training, and licensing and certification tests. For a sailor planning to move into civilian nuclear power, skilled trades or technical work, those uses can be more valuable than a degree program, and the right program choice can look different for each one. A flat Montgomery check during a paid apprenticeship works very differently from a Post-9/11 housing allowance tied to a campus.
What Rudisill changed

For years, people eligible for both programs faced a hard choice. To use Post-9/11, you generally had to give up Montgomery, and your Post-9/11 benefit was capped at whatever Montgomery time you had left. Older VA material says that choice can't be changed once made.

Then an Army veteran named James Rudisill, who had served multiple separate periods of active duty, challenged that limit. On April 16, 2024, the Supreme Court ruled in *Rudisill v. McDonough* that veterans with separate periods of service qualifying for each program may use both, up to a combined 48 months. In 2025, the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims went further in *Perkins v. Collins*, holding that a veteran with a single obligated period of service may also qualify for both, if that period is long enough and contains qualifying time for each program.

blocks.title: How the GI Bill rules got here
items: The original GI Bill helps World War II veterans attend college
Montgomery GI Bill begins for those entering active duty after June 30
Congress creates the Post-9/11 GI Bill
Forever GI Bill removes the time limit for service ending in 2013 or later
Apr 2024
Supreme Court decides Rudisill v. McDonough
Perkins v. Collins extends the idea to some single periods of service
Mar 2026
VA says veterans no longer need to request a Rudisill review
Oct 2026
Current MGIB-AD rates take effect

blocks.text: According to the VA's Rudisill page, last updated in October 2026, people eligible under these decisions no longer have to give up Montgomery to use Post-9/11, Post-9/11 is no longer capped at your remaining Montgomery time, and people who previously gave up Montgomery can revoke that choice. The overall limit across programs is still 48 months. The VA says it is automatically reviewing the files of about 1.04 million affected veterans rather than requiring them to apply.

The VA's Montgomery page adds a useful line: if you served 56 months or more on active duty, you may qualify for up to 48 months combined across both programs. With less than 56 months, you can generally use only one benefit, with Post-9/11 capped at 36 months. Nuclear-field sailors usually sign up for six years, which is longer than 56 months. That doesn't guarantee anything. How your months are counted toward each program is a VA decision, and the details are new enough that it's worth getting a written answer.

Why does an extra 12 months matter? A typical bachelor's degree takes about four academic years of roughly nine months each, which is about 36 months of benefits. A 48-month limit can stretch to cover a full degree with room for a graduate certificate, part of a master's, or a summer of extra courses. For someone starting from scratch, a year of paid school is a serious difference.

It's also a reminder that VA's own pages don't always agree. The older comparison chart on the VA site, last updated in 2025, still says the choice between programs cannot be changed, while the newer Rudisill page says earlier waivers can now be revoked. When official sources conflict, the newest specific guidance usually reflects current policy, but that's exactly the kind of thing to confirm with a person, not a webpage.

One more detail: if you relinquish Montgomery, use Post-9/11 and have less than 56 months of active duty, the VA refunds part or all of your $1,200 contribution. And if you paid into the optional $600 Montgomery buy-up program, which increases Montgomery payments, that money does nothing for you under Post-9/11.
Using it while you're still in

While you're on active duty, both programs pay less. Montgomery pays the monthly rate or your actual tuition and fees, whichever is lower. Post-9/11 pays no housing allowance to active-duty members. In other words, the most valuable parts of each benefit are designed for after you leave.

That's why most service members take classes on active duty through Tuition Assistance, a separate military program that pays for courses without touching your GI Bill entitlement. There's also a Tuition Assistance Top-Up option that uses your GI Bill to cover what Tuition Assistance doesn't, but it spends GI Bill months to do it. The months are the scarce resource, so it's worth thinking twice before using them on courses that Tuition Assistance could mostly cover.

If you ever want to transfer Post-9/11 benefits to a future spouse or child, timing matters. A transfer generally has to be requested while you're still serving, and it usually comes with an additional service obligation. Leave first, and that door typically closes. It's a decision to make deliberately before separating, not to discover afterward.

For someone who spends long stretches underway, the practical window for classes is usually shore duty or the time between deployments. A few online courses through Tuition Assistance, finished before leaving the service, can mean starting school as a civilian with credits already banked and the full GI Bill still intact.
What to check before you choose

blocks.title: Before you use either benefit
items: Confirm on your pay records that the $1,200 Montgomery contribution was actually taken.
Visit your base education office or Navy College office and ask about Tuition Assistance first.
Check your eligibility and remaining entitlement on VA.gov.
Run your target schools through the VA's GI Bill Comparison Tool under both programs.
Ask the VA in writing whether Rudisill or Perkins applies to your service history.
Don't give up Montgomery or make an election until you're about to enroll and understand the trade.

blocks.text: Be careful with schools, too. Because GI Bill money is reliable, some schools recruit veterans aggressively, with fast enrollment, glossy promises about careers and pressure to sign up before you've compared options. The VA's comparison tool shows whether a school follows its Principles of Excellence program, which commits schools to things like clear cost information and no high-pressure recruiting, and flags cautionary information about schools. A school that pushes you to decide this week is a school to slow down with.

The bigger point is about attitude. Many people treat the GI Bill as a vague promise that school will be paid for someday. It's better understood as a large, specific asset with rules, deadlines and trade-offs, worth tens of thousands of dollars, sometimes much more. Assets like that deserve a plan.

Rules may have changed by the time you read this, and your situation has details no article can see. Before you decide, confirm the current rules with the VA, at VA.gov or by phone at 1-800-698-2411, and with your base education office.

takeaways: Montgomery pays a flat monthly check to you; Post-9/11 pays the school plus housing and books.
As of Oct. 1, 2026, the full-time Montgomery rate is $2,601 a month for 3+ years of service.
Post-9/11 usually wins for in-person school in high-cost areas; Montgomery can win when tuition is low.
Rudisill (2024) and Perkins (2025) let some people use both, up to 48 months combined.
Use Tuition Assistance on active duty, and confirm everything with the VA and your education office.

title: Does Money Buy Happiness? The Rivals Who Settled It Together
dek: One famous study said happiness stops rising at $75,000. Another said it never stops. Then the authors teamed up, and the answer turned out to depend on who you are.

blocks.text: In 2010, two Nobel-winning economists published a short paper with a number that escaped into the wild. Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton reported that Americans' day-to-day happiness rose with income, but only up to about $75,000 a year. After that, the line went flat. The figure spread everywhere: in articles, in talks, and famously in 2015, when a Seattle CEO cited it while raising his company's minimum salary to $70,000.

Eleven years later, a younger researcher named Matthew Killingsworth looked at a much bigger pile of real-time data and found no plateau at all. Happiness kept climbing with income, well past $75,000. Two credible studies, two opposite answers. What happened next is rarer in science than it should be: the rivals sat down together, with a neutral referee, to figure out who was right. The answer is more interesting than either original claim, and it says a lot about what money actually does for people.
Two kinds of happiness

The first step is to notice that "happiness" means two different things. One is how you feel in the moments of your life: whether this afternoon was pleasant, stressful, boring or fun. Researchers call this emotional or experienced well-being. The other is how you judge your life when you step back and think about it, often measured by asking people to rate their life on a ladder from worst possible to best possible. That's life evaluation.

These two don't always move together. Someone grinding through a hard but meaningful stretch, like nuke school or a demanding deployment, might rate their life highly while feeling pretty rough most hours of the day. Someone drifting through easy, pleasant days might feel fine moment to moment and still rate their life as going nowhere. Any honest answer about money has to say which kind of happiness it means.
The $75,000 plateau

Kahneman and Deaton analyzed more than 450,000 responses to a daily Gallup survey of US residents. For life evaluation, the pattern was simple: the more money people had, the better they rated their lives, with no sign of stopping. For emotional well-being, measured by asking whether people had felt things like enjoyment, stress or sadness the previous day, the picture was different. It rose with income, then stopped improving at around $75,000 a year.

They also found that low income made life's other blows hurt more. Divorce, illness and loneliness were associated with more emotional pain among people with less money. And they noted that for everyday emotions, other factors, such as health, caregiving, loneliness and smoking, were relatively stronger predictors than income. Their summary was memorable: high income buys life satisfaction but not happiness.

One detail people often forget: that $75,000 figure was in 2008 and 2009 dollars. Adjusted with the Consumer Price Index, it's roughly $118,000 in late-2026 prices. Even if the plateau were real, it would sit far higher than the number still quoted online.

items.label: Gallup survey responses in Kahneman & Deaton (2010)
Real-time happiness reports in Killingsworth (2021), from 33,391 employed US adults

blocks.source: Kahneman & Deaton, PNAS, 2010; Killingsworth, PNAS, 2021

blocks.text: The challenger

Killingsworth used a different method. Through a smartphone app, people were pinged at random moments and asked how they felt right then, on a continuous scale from very bad to very good. Over time, he collected 1,725,994 of these reports from 33,391 employed US adults. Instead of yes-or-no questions about yesterday, he had fine-grained snapshots of the moment.

His result, published in 2021: both kinds of well-being rose steadily with income, and the slope was just as steep for higher earners as for lower earners. There was no sign of a plateau at $75,000. Higher incomes went with more positive feelings, such as confidence and interest, and fewer negative ones, such as sadness and boredom.

There's a key detail in how both studies measured income: they used its logarithm. In plain terms, that means what matters is the *percentage* change, not the dollar amount. Going from $40,000 to $80,000 is a doubling, and so is going from $80,000 to $160,000. In Killingsworth's data, each doubling bought roughly the same bump in happiness. So an extra $10,000 matters enormously to someone earning $30,000, and barely registers for someone earning $300,000. Money kept mattering, but each additional dollar mattered less.

Money and happiness follow a curve of doublings, not dollars. A raise that doubles your income changes a lot; the same dollar raise later in life changes much less. That's diminishing returns, not a hard ceiling.
The adversarial collaboration

Instead of trading rebuttals for a decade, Killingsworth and Kahneman did something unusual. They agreed to an adversarial collaboration, a joint project between researchers who disagree, with psychologist Barbara Mellers as arbiter. They reanalyzed Killingsworth's data, looking not just at the average person but at people across the range of happiness, from the least happy to the most.

The answer, published in 2023, reconciled both papers. For the least happy fifth or so of people, happiness rose with income up to about $100,000 and then flattened, just as Kahneman and Deaton had described. For everyone else, happiness kept rising with income, and for the happiest people it rose even faster at higher incomes. The overall average looked like a smooth climb because these different patterns blended together.

Think about what that split implies. If you're broadly doing okay, more income tends to keep adding something, whether that's more comfort, more experiences or simply less friction. If you're deeply unhappy because of grief, illness, loneliness or depression, money helps up to the point where basic stresses are handled, and then it stops reaching the real problem. Same paycheck, different curve, because the sources of unhappiness are different. That's why one-size-fits-all claims about money and happiness kept failing.

blocks.title: How fast happiness rose with income above $100k, by happiness level
blocks.note: Regression slope of happiness on log income above $100,000. The three lowest groups were not statistically different from zero.
blocks.source: Killingsworth, Kahneman & Mellers, PNAS, 2023 (Table 1)

blocks.text: Why did the 2010 study miss this? The authors concluded its yes-or-no questions about yesterday's emotions could tell unhappy people apart but couldn't distinguish degrees of happiness. Once someone was doing reasonably well, the measure had nowhere higher to go. In effect, Kahneman and Deaton had measured unhappiness, and what they found was real: money reduces misery up to a point, and beyond that point, for the most unhappy people, their remaining problems aren't the kind more income fixes.

The process itself is worth a moment. Kahneman, who died in 2024, spent years promoting adversarial collaboration as a better way to settle scientific fights than dueling papers. The usual pattern in research is that each side digs in, picks at the other's methods and talks past them. Here, a famous senior scientist agreed to test whether his own best-known finding had been misread, and published the answer. Being willing to be wrong in public is rarer than being smart, and it's how a field actually gets closer to the truth.

It's an honest, almost humble conclusion, and the authors said so. Both original studies relied on standard practices, such as assuming everyone follows the same curve, that turned out to hide what was going on.
What money actually buys

Killingsworth's 2021 data also offered clues about why income and well-being move together. People were asked how much they felt in control of their lives. Statistically, that sense of control accounted for about 74% of the link between income and moment-to-moment happiness. Financial insecurity, measured by trouble paying regular bills, accounted for about 38%. The overlap is the point: a big part of what money provides is the feeling that life isn't pushing you around.

items.label: Share of the income–happiness link accounted for by feeling in control of your life
Share accounted for by financial insecurity (trouble paying bills)

blocks.source: Killingsworth, PNAS, 2021

blocks.text: Two other findings are worth sitting with. First, higher earners reported feeling *more* pressed for time, not less, so a bigger paycheck didn't automatically buy breathing room. Second, people who strongly equated money with success were less happy on average, and there was no income level at which that belief went with feeling better. Simply thinking money was important wasn't linked to being happier or unhappier overall. Valuing money for what it does seemed harmless. Treating it as a scoreboard did not.

How you spend may matter too. In a well-known 2008 study, psychologist Elizabeth Dunn and colleagues found that spending money on other people was linked to greater happiness than spending on yourself, including in an experiment where people were randomly assigned to spend a small sum on themselves or on someone else. Research on spending to buy back time, such as paying to skip chores you hate, points in a similar direction. These lines of research come from smaller studies than the income work and deserve more caution, but they suggest that how money is used matters, not just how much there is.
What the debate doesn't settle

All of this is correlational. Richer people are happier on average, but that doesn't prove the money made them happier. Healthier, more energetic or more optimistic people might earn more in the first place. In a published commentary, psychologists Julia Rohrer and Sebastian Wenz argued that the 2023 paper leaned on causal assumptions the data couldn't support. Both data sets come from the United States, and Killingsworth's included only employed adults. And in Kahneman and Deaton's data, health and loneliness predicted daily emotions more strongly than income did.

blocks.title: Myth vs. what the research shows

left.head: Popular version
items: Happiness stops at $75k
Money doesn't buy happiness
More money fixes everything

right.head: Closer to the evidence
items: No universal plateau; it depends on the person
On average, more income goes with more well-being, by doublings
For the unhappiest people, gains fade past about $100k

blocks.text: None of this makes the question pointless. It makes it more precise. Instead of asking whether money buys happiness, the better questions are which problems money can solve for you, how much it takes to solve them, and what you're trading away to get it, whether that's time, health or relationships.

For someone at the start of a career, the most useful takeaway might be about the shape of the curve. The steepest happiness gains in the data come from escaping money stress and gaining a sense of control. You don't need a huge salary for that. You need a cushion that turns emergencies into inconveniences, no debt that dictates your choices, and enough saved that a bad job or a bad boss isn't a trap. Savings, seen this way, are not just future money. They are present-day freedom.

The doubling rule has a practical edge, too. Early in a working life, income can double in just a few years through promotions, new qualifications or a jump into a better-paid civilian field, and those doublings are exactly where the research finds the biggest changes in how people feel. Later on, doubling a large income is much harder and, by the same curve, buys no more than the early doublings did. That's an argument for investing heavily in skills and earning power while you're young, and for not assuming that the next raise will feel as big as the last one.

There's also the problem of adjustment. People get used to new levels of comfort surprisingly fast, so a lifestyle that felt like a reward one year becomes the baseline the next. That's part of why spending every raise on upgrades can leave people no happier than before, while the same money set aside to build security keeps paying off in the form of options. A habit of saving doesn't just buy a future. It quietly buys a feeling of control today, which is the very thing the data links most closely to income and happiness.

And the warning is just as clear: if more money isn't fixing what's making you unhappy, more money probably won't. The researchers' own conclusion was that for the least happy people, beyond a certain income, the remaining miseries come from places a paycheck doesn't reach.

takeaways: Money and happiness move together by doublings: each extra dollar matters less as income rises.
The famous $75,000 plateau holds only for the least happy fifth of people, and at about $100,000 in the 2023 reanalysis.
A big part of money's link to happiness is a sense of control and freedom from bill stress.
Treating money as a scoreboard is linked to lower well-being at every income.
The evidence is correlational; health and relationships still matter more than income.

title: Four Hundred Years of Bubbles
dek: From Dutch tulips to Newton's losses to the dot-com crash and crypto, manias follow a recognizable pattern. What the evidence says about spotting one, and why timing it is nearly impossible (not financial advice).

blocks.text: In the winter of 1636 to 1637, people in the Dutch Republic were paying extraordinary sums for tulip bulbs they could not see. The bulbs were in the ground. Nobody would know until spring whether a given bulb would produce the flamed, streaked flower that made it precious. Buyers and sellers traded promises written on paper, often in taverns. Then, in early February 1637, the prices stopped rising, and almost overnight the market was gone.

You have probably heard this story as the ultimate tale of human stupidity: people mortgaging houses for flowers. The real history is more interesting, and more useful, than the legend. Bubbles are not just episodes of crowds going mad. They are what happens when a good story, easy money and the fear of missing out line up, and they have been happening for four centuries to people who were not stupid at all. If you are 20 now, you will live through several more. The question is whether you will recognize the pattern while you are inside one.
The tulip story is mostly a myth

Most of what people think they know about tulip mania comes from Charles Mackay's 1841 book, *Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds*, which drew heavily on satirical pamphlets written right after the crash. In 2007 the historian Anne Goldgar published *Tulipmania*, based on years in Dutch archives, and argued that the familiar picture is badly overdrawn. She found no endless wave of bankruptcies and no national economic collapse. The bulb trade was a niche market run by a network of collectors and merchants who knew each other.

What did happen, in her account, was a crisis of trust. Because bulbs were traded in winter for delivery later, the market ran on honor: a written promise to pay. When prices broke, many buyers simply refused to pay, and a society built on keeping your word had to reckon with the fact that its merchants had not. The pamphlets that turned the episode into a morality tale were, in effect, the memes of their day.

Not every scholar buys the full revision. The economist Peter Garber argued in 1989 that the prices of the rarest bulbs were less crazy than they look, because brand-new, rare varieties have always commanded high prices that fall as growers propagate them. A Dutch reviewer of Goldgar's book praised her archival work but felt she went too far toward treating the prices as rational, noting that bulbs could multiply, sicken, rot and go out of fashion in a way gold never does. The prized streaked patterns, it turned out centuries later, were caused by a plant disease. The honest summary: something speculative happened, it was smaller and stranger than the legend, and we are still arguing about it.
The smartest man in England

Eighty-three years later, in 1720, Britain had its own mania, centered on the South Sea Company, a trading company that took on government debt in exchange for shares. Its stock soared and then collapsed within the same year. One investor in it was Isaac Newton, then Master of the Royal Mint and arguably the greatest scientist who ever lived.

The popular story says Newton made a tidy profit early, sold, watched his friends keep getting richer, bought back in near the top and lost a fortune. Some writers, including John Maynard Keynes, doubted it. In 2018 the mathematician Andrew Odlyzko went through the surviving records and concluded that the folk tale is almost certainly correct, and that it probably understates how badly Newton misjudged the bubble. A famous line about being able to calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies but not the madness of people is often attached to the episode, though the evidence that he said it is thin.

Newton's problem was not intelligence. It was that he could see other people getting rich on something he had already sold. Being right early and then watching the price keep rising is one of the hardest feelings in investing, and bubbles are built to exploit it.
Stability breeds instability

Why do bubbles keep happening to smart people? The economist Hyman Minsky offered one of the most influential answers. In his financial instability hypothesis, summarized in a 1992 working paper, he argued that long stretches of prosperity change how people borrow. In calm times, most borrowers can pay both interest and principal from their income; he called this hedge finance. As good times continue, more borrowers can only cover interest and must keep rolling the debt over, which he called speculative finance. Eventually some can pay neither and depend on prices continuing to rise; he called that Ponzi finance. The longer things stay calm, the more the system tilts toward the fragile end, until a small shock can topple it.

The economic historian Charles Kindleberger, building on Minsky, sketched a recurring sequence in his book *Manias, Panics, and Crashes*, first published in 1978. The details differ every time. The shape is remarkably consistent.

blocks.title: The anatomy of a bubble
items: Displacement: a real innovation or change creates real profits
Boom: credit expands and prices rise on genuine good news
Euphoria: people buy because prices are rising, and new buyers pour in
Distress: insiders sell, prices stall, borrowers get nervous
Panic: everyone heads for the exit at once and prices crash

blocks.text: Notice that the cycle starts with something real. Railways really did transform the world. The internet really did change everything. Houses really are worth owning. That is exactly why bubbles are hard to see from inside: the story is true, and the price has merely run ahead of it.

Late in the cycle, a different logic takes over. People stop asking what something is worth and start asking whether someone else will pay more for it next month. Economists call this the greater fool theory: it is fine to overpay as long as there is a bigger fool behind you. It works right up until the supply of new buyers runs out, and nobody gets a warning when that day arrives. You can hear this stage in how people talk. Valuation questions get waved off with phrases like *this time is different* or *you just don't get it*, and the main argument for buying becomes the fact that the price went up.
Modern bubbles, by the numbers

The dot-com boom is the cleanest recent example. The Nasdaq Composite, heavy with technology stocks, rose from about 744 at the start of 1995 to a closing peak of 5,048.62 on March 10, 2000. It then fell to 1,114.11 by October 9, 2002, a drop of about 78 percent. The internet did go on to change everything, and some companies from that era became giants. But it took until April 2015, fifteen years, for the index to close above its 2000 peak again.

blocks.title: Nasdaq Composite through the dot-com boom and bust
blocks.note: Closing values; Mar 2000 is the March 10 peak and Oct 2002 the October 9 low.
blocks.source: Nasdaq OMX Group via FRED (NASDAQCOM), accessed Nov 2026

blocks.text: Housing came next. Using the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller national home price index, US home prices peaked in July 2006 and fell about 27 percent to their low in February 2012, before inflation is even considered. The national index did not regain its 2006 level until January 2017. That bust was not just a stock market story: it took down banks, triggered the 2008 financial crisis and cost millions of people their homes, because the asset in question was bought with borrowed money by ordinary families.

The contrast between those two busts is the most important lesson in this article. When the dot-com bubble popped, most of the losses fell on stockholders who had bought with their own money; the recession that followed was comparatively mild. When housing popped, the losses fell on assets bought largely with borrowed money, held by households and by banks that had lent against them. Debt is what turns a bubble from a painful loss into a crisis. A falling price hurts. A falling price on something you still owe money on can ruin you.

Crypto has run the cycle several times in a single decade. Bitcoin's price on Coinbase fell about 84 percent from its December 2017 high to December 2018, and about 77 percent from its November 2021 high to November 2022. It then set a new record of about $124,700 in October 2025 before falling about 53 percent to a low near $58,600 by the end of June 2026. Believers point out that it has recovered every time. Skeptics point out that people who bought near any of those peaks waited years just to break even.

blocks.title: Peak-to-trough declines in recent manias
blocks.note: Home prices are nominal and national; local markets fell far more in some places. Bitcoin uses Coinbase prices.
blocks.source: FRED series NASDAQCOM, CSUSHPINSA and CBBTCUSD, author's calculation, Nov 2026

blocks.text: Can you spot one in time?

For decades, the Nobel-winning economist Eugene Fama argued that the word bubble is mostly hindsight: if bubbles were real and predictable, sharp price run-ups would be followed by poor returns, and on average they are not. In a paper titled *Bubbles for Fama*, first circulated in 2017 and later published in the Journal of Financial Economics, Robin Greenwood, Andrei Shleifer and Yang You tested that claim on US industry returns from 1926 to 2014 and international sectors from 1985 to 2014. Their answer was subtle. Fama was right that a big run-up does not, on average, predict low returns afterward. But it does strongly predict a **crash**, which they defined as a 40 percent drop at some point in the next two years.

blocks.title: Chance an industry crashes 40% within two years
blocks.note: US industries; run-ups are two-year returns above the overall market. Many crashes came after prices kept rising for months.
blocks.source: Greenwood, Shleifer and You, Bubbles for Fama, NBER Working Paper 23191, 2017

blocks.text: So a huge run-up is a real warning sign. But here is the catch that makes bubbles so cruel: the timing is almost impossible. In their data, even industries that eventually crashed tended to keep rising for about six more months after the run-up was obvious. And nearly half of the 100 percent run-ups did not crash within the next two years at all. Simply selling everything that doubled would have slightly underperformed just holding on. You can often tell that something is dangerous. You usually cannot tell when.
What to do with all this

The point of studying bubbles is not to become the person who calls the top. Almost nobody does that reliably, and Newton shows what happens when a brilliant person tries. The point is to build a financial life that a bubble cannot destroy, whether you are on the inside of it or the outside.

This matters more in a small, tight community. On a boat, one shipmate's winning trade becomes everyone's topic for a week, and nobody brags about the losing ones. That is the same selective view of other people's money that fuels every mania, compressed into a berthing compartment. A few simple rules, decided before the next hot tip arrives, do more than any amount of market forecasting.

items: Own the broad market through low-cost index funds, so no single mania can sink you and you never need to guess which story wins.
Never use borrowed money to buy something because its price is rising. Every bubble's worst damage lands on people with debt.
Size speculative bets so that losing all of it would sting, not wreck you. If a crypto or single-stock bet would hurt your rent or your emergency fund, it is too big.
Watch your own feelings. The urge to buy because everyone around you is getting rich is the euphoria stage of the cycle, happening inside your head.
Remember the timeline. Nasdaq took 15 years to recover. Ask whether you could wait that long.

blocks.text: There is something oddly comforting in the long history. The Dutch merchants of 1637, the London investors of 1720, the day traders of 1999 and the crypto buyers of 2021 were not fools. Most of them were reacting sensibly to what they could see: a real innovation, rising prices, and people they knew making money. That is exactly why the next bubble will feel reasonable from the inside too. You cannot make yourself immune to the story. You can make sure that when the story ends, it does not take your future with it.

takeaways: Tulip mania was real but far smaller than the legend; historians now see it mostly as a crisis of trust.
Bubbles start with something real; the price simply runs ahead of a true story.
After an industry's price doubles relative to the market, the chance of a 40% crash within two years rises to about half, but the timing is unpredictable.
The Nasdaq took 15 years to regain its 2000 peak; diversification and patience beat trying to call tops.
Never buy a rising asset with borrowed money, and size speculative bets so losing them won't hurt your basics.

title: Money Was Never About Gold
dek: A stone at the bottom of the sea, clay tablets full of debts, lion-stamped lumps of metal and a 1971 TV address. The history of money suggests it was never really a thing at all, but a shared memory of who owes what.

blocks.text: On the Pacific island of Yap, money came in the form of huge limestone discs, some taller than a man, with a hole in the middle for a carrying pole. The stone wasn't from Yap. It was quarried on islands hundreds of miles away and brought back by canoe at great risk. Large stones rarely moved after they arrived. When one changed owners, everyone simply agreed it now belonged to someone else, and it stayed leaning against the same house.

The best story comes from an American visitor, William Furness, who published a book about the island in 1910. A family on Yap was considered rich because of an enormous stone that their ancestors had been bringing home when a storm hit and it sank. Nobody alive had ever seen it. It lay on the sea floor. And yet everyone agreed it was still theirs, and it still counted as wealth that could pay for things. The economist John Maynard Keynes found the book delightful enough to review it in 1915, and he saw the joke at once: was this really so different from gold sitting in a bank vault that nobody ever touches?

The sunken stone is a good place to start, because it breaks the picture of money most of us carry around. We tend to think of money as a *thing*, something valuable in itself, like gold. The history says something stranger. Money is mostly a record that people agree to trust. The thing, when there is one, is just a way of keeping score.
The barter story that never happened

Open almost any economics textbook and you'll find the same origin story. Before money, people bartered: I trade you my fish for your shoes. That's clumsy, because you have to find someone who has what you want and wants what you have. So people gradually settled on one handy commodity, such as silver, that everyone would accept, and money was born. Adam Smith gave the classic version in *The Wealth of Nations* in 1776, built on what he called a human propensity to truck, barter, and exchange.

It is a tidy story. Anthropologists went looking for it and could not find it. In a much-cited 1985 paper, the Cambridge anthropologist Caroline Humphrey reviewed the evidence and concluded that no one had ever described a pure barter economy, much less watched money emerge from one. Barter does happen, but mostly between strangers, or when money breaks down, as in prisoner-of-war camps or collapsing economies. Inside communities, people mostly ran on credit: you give me fish now, I owe you, and we both remember.

The prison camp is a revealing exception. In 1945 a British economist named R. A. Radford, freshly released from German POW camps, described how prisoners with no money traded Red Cross parcels and quickly settled on cigarettes as currency. Prices were quoted in cigarettes, and they rose and fell with supply, including when a fresh shipment arrived. So commodity money can emerge from barter, but notice the setting: strangers thrown together, with no shared history and no authority they trusted. That is precisely the situation in which credit fails.

The anthropologist David Graeber built a bestselling book, *Debt: The First 5,000 Years* (2011), around that point. His argument, simplified, is that the order in the textbook is backward. Credit and debt came first. Coins came much later. Barter is mostly what people fall back on when trust and credit fail, not what they did before money existed. Economists still argue about parts of Graeber's account, but the absence of a real barter economy is now widely accepted.

blocks.title: Two origin stories of money

left.head: Textbook version
items: Barter comes first
A handy commodity like silver emerges as money
Credit is a later invention built on money
Money is fundamentally a thing

right.head: What the record suggests
items: Credit and IOUs come first
Rulers and temples set units to keep accounts
Coins arrive thousands of years later
Money is fundamentally a record of debts

blocks.text: Debts written in clay

The earliest written evidence of money looks a lot like accounting. In ancient Mesopotamia, the cities of what is now Iraq, temple and palace administrators tracked grain, labor and debts on clay tablets thousands of years before anyone stamped a coin. Silver was used as a unit of account, measured by weight in shekels, but most people rarely handled it. A farmer could run up a tab in silver terms at an alehouse and settle it in barley at harvest.

Because these were debts, they came with interest, and with trouble. Laws from Hammurabi's era set maximum interest rates on loans of silver and grain. Farmers who fell behind could lose land, or family members, to debt bondage. Mesopotamian kings periodically issued decrees that canceled certain debts and freed debt-bondsmen, wiping the slate clean so the economy, and the king's army of free farmers, didn't collapse. The idea of a clean slate is older than the coin.
Coins: money you can carry

Coins appear in the 7th century BC in Asia Minor, in what is now western Turkey. The kingdom of Lydia struck lumps of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver found in local rivers, at regular weights and stamped them with a lion's head, the badge of its royal dynasty. One later Lydian king, Croesus, who ruled from about 560 to 546 BC, was so wealthy that we still say rich as Croesus.

Why would a state bother? A stamped coin of known weight solves a trust problem between strangers: you don't need to weigh and test the metal if a king vouches for it. Graeber adds a darker explanation. Coins spread fastest where there were large armies. A soldier on the move can't run a tab at the village alehouse, but he can carry coins. Rulers paid soldiers in coin and then demanded taxes in the same coin, which forced everyone to start selling things to the army to get it. Money and the state, on this view, grew up together.

blocks.title: A short history of money
items: Mesopotamian temples track debts on clay tablets, with silver as the unit of account
7th c. BC
Lydia strikes the first stamped coins, in electrum
11th c. AD
Song China issues government paper money
Adam Smith popularizes the barter origin story
Bretton Woods ties the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce
Nixon closes the gold window on August 15
Major currencies float; Bretton Woods is effectively over
Bitcoin launches, money with no issuer at all

blocks.text: Paper, promises and the end of gold

China took the next big step. In the early 11th century, during the Song dynasty, merchants' deposit receipts in Sichuan were taken over by the government and turned into official paper money. Later visitors like Marco Polo were amazed that a ruler could make people accept printed paper as payment. Chinese dynasties also discovered the obvious problem: when a government in trouble prints too much, the paper loses value. Inflation is as old as paper money.

For much of modern history, Western governments tried to solve that problem by tying paper to metal. After World War II, the Bretton Woods system fixed the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce, and other major currencies were fixed to the dollar. Foreign governments could, in principle, turn in dollars for American gold.

By the late 1960s, there were far more dollars around the world than the US had gold to back at $35 an ounce. On August 15, 1971, President Nixon announced that the US would stop converting dollars to gold. A patched-up deal in December 1971 failed, and by March 1973 major European currencies were floating against the dollar. Since then, the dollar has been backed by nothing physical at all. Its value rests on trust in the US government, its economy and the Federal Reserve. Most people didn't notice the difference in their wallets.
Where money actually comes from now

Here is the part that surprises people the most. Most money today isn't printed by anyone. In 2014, economists at the Bank of England published an unusually blunt article explaining that most money in a modern economy is created by ordinary commercial banks when they make loans. When a bank approves your car loan, it doesn't hand over someone else's savings. It types a new deposit into your account. That deposit is new money. When you pay the loan off, the money disappears again.

items.label: Share of UK broad money that was bank deposits, not notes and coins (Dec 2013)

blocks.source: McLeay, Radia & Thomas, Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin, 2014 Q1

blocks.text: Banks can't do this without limit. They are constrained by whether loans are profitable, by regulation and, above all, by central banks that set interest rates. But the image of a bank vault full of cash waiting to be lent out is mostly wrong. The US looks similar. Physical currency is a small slice of the broad money supply, and a large share of US paper dollars is held overseas.

blocks.title: US money supply, September 2026
blocks.note: Seasonally adjusted. Currency is about 10% of M2; the rest is mostly bank deposits and money market balances.
blocks.source: Federal Reserve, via FRED series CURRSL and M2SL (accessed Nov 2026)

blocks.text: Because bank money is a promise, it can fail when trust fails. A bank run is just a crowd of people deciding at once that they would rather hold something else. In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in about two days after depositors, many of them connected through the same networks and group chats, tried to pull their money out together. That is why governments insure deposits; in the US the FDIC covers up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Insurance doesn't make the promise physical. It makes it more believable, which, for money, is the same thing.

You already live inside this system in miniature. Robux is money too: a currency issued by a single company, accepted only on its platform, with an official exchange rate set by the issuer. Roblox's standard Developer Exchange rate has been $0.0038 per earned Robux since September 2025. Robux has value because millions of players agree it does and because Roblox promises to honor that rate for qualifying developers. That is a very small version of the deal every national currency makes.

Bitcoin, launched in 2009, was an attempt to escape the issuer entirely: a fixed supply, no central bank, and a public ledger anyone can check. Whatever you think of it as an investment, notice what it is. It's a giant shared record of who owns what, kept by thousands of computers rather than temple scribes. Even the newest money ends up looking like the oldest.
So what is money?

In 1998 the economist Narayana Kocherlakota published a paper with a memorable title: *Money Is Memory*. His point was technical but intuitive. If everyone could perfectly remember everything everyone had ever given and received, you wouldn't need money at all; you'd just keep score. Money exists because our collective memory is imperfect. A coin, a bill or a bank balance is a portable record of credit that strangers can trust without knowing your history.

That is why the Yap stone at the bottom of the sea could still be money. What mattered was never the stone. It was that everyone remembered whose it was and agreed to honor it. When that agreement breaks, money fails no matter what it is made of. When it holds, almost anything works: clay, metal, paper, digits or limestone.

It also explains why money feels so emotional. A paycheck is not just purchasing power; it is society's running tally of what it thinks it owes you for your time. Saving is storing up claims on other people's future work. Debt is promising your own future work to someone else. Put that way, the question of how much money is enough becomes a question about how much of your future you want to be free, and how much you're willing to sign away.

Seeing money this way changes a few everyday instincts. Gold isn't real money while dollars are fake; both are things people have agreed to value. A bank balance isn't a pile of cash in a vault with your name on it; it's a promise from the bank, backed by deposit insurance up to a limit. Debt isn't a modern invention; it's the original form of money. And trust, which sounds soft, turns out to be the hardest asset in the whole system.

Next time you look at your bank app, remember what the number actually is: not a stack of bills somewhere, but a record of what the bank owes you, honored because of a web of rules, insurance and trust that took about 5,000 years to build.

takeaways: There's no good evidence that a pure barter economy ever existed; credit and debt came first.
Coins appeared in Lydia in the 7th century BC, thousands of years after Mesopotamian debt records.
Since 1971 the dollar has been backed by trust in the government and economy, not gold.
Most modern money is created by banks when they lend; physical currency is about a tenth of US M2.
Money is best understood as a shared memory of who owes what, which is why trust is the real asset.

title: Where Millionaires Actually Come From
dek: Social media says wealth comes from a hustle, a course or a lucky trade. The Federal Reserve's newest survey of American family finances tells a slower, stranger and more useful story.

blocks.text: Here is a statistic that sounds like good news: the average American family is a millionaire. According to the Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, released in October 2026, mean family net worth was **$1,241,500**. Here is the statistic that tells you what is really going on: the median family, the one exactly in the middle, had **$215,900**. The average is pulled up by a relatively small number of extremely wealthy households, the way one boss fight with a million hit points would wreck the average health of every enemy in a game.

That gap between the mean and the median is the first lesson of wealth: it is lopsided, and stories about it usually come from the far tail. Your feed is full of twenty-somethings in rented supercars explaining that the 9-to-5 is a trap. The data on how millionaires actually got there is quieter, and it comes from a survey that has been run every three years since 1989, with thousands of families interviewed in detail about everything they own and owe.

General education, not financial advice. Figures are from Federal Reserve data published in 2026 and from research cited by name. For decisions about your own money, talk to a Personal Financial Manager at Fleet and Family Support.
How rare is a million, really?

The Fed's 2025 survey shows where the cutoffs sit. A family at the 75th percentile of net worth had about $812,800; at the 90th percentile, about $2.54 million. So a net worth of $1 million puts a family somewhere between those two lines: richer than roughly three-quarters of households, but not in the top tenth. It is uncommon, but it is not a lottery outcome. Millions of ordinary families cross it.

And most of them cross it late. The single strongest pattern in the data is age. Families headed by someone under 35 had a median net worth of just $33,000 in 2025. The median roughly climbs with each decade of life after that, topping out at about $505,000 for families 75 and older. The typical millionaire is not a 24-year-old with a trading app. It is someone in their fifties or sixties who has been accumulating for thirty years.

blocks.title: Median family net worth by age, 2025
blocks.note: Age of the family's reference person; 2025 dollars.
blocks.source: Federal Reserve, Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 (SCF), Oct 2026

blocks.text: Young families also had the worst three years. Between 2022 and 2025, median net worth for families under 35 fell 23 percent, and the Fed attributes the decline mainly to the unwinding of business equity gains young families had made between 2019 and 2022. Gains that arrive quickly can leave quickly too.

That should change how you read your own position. At 20, a low net worth is not a verdict. It is a starting point on a curve that almost everyone follows. What matters at your age is not where you are on the chart. It is the slope you set up: how much you save, what you own and how long you leave it alone. Time is the one input to wealth that the young have in abundance and the rich cannot buy back.
What wealthy households own

The Survey of Consumer Finances tells you who has wealth. The Fed's Distributional Financial Accounts, which combine survey data with the national accounts every quarter, show what that wealth is made of. The contrast between groups is stark. In the second quarter of 2026, the top 1 percent held about 68 percent of their assets in corporate stock, mutual funds and private businesses. For the bottom half of households, that share was about 5 percent.

blocks.title: Share of assets in stocks, funds and private businesses
blocks.note: Calculated from Fed category totals: corporate equities and mutual funds plus unincorporated businesses, divided by total assets.
blocks.source: Federal Reserve, Distributional Financial Accounts, 2026 Q2

blocks.text: Where does the bottom half keep its wealth instead? Mostly in homes and in consumer durables, the official term for things like cars, furniture and electronics. By the same calculation, about 68 percent of the bottom half's assets were real estate and durable goods, against about 13 percent for the top 1 percent. And the bottom half's debts equaled roughly 58 percent of its assets. A lot of what lower-wealth households own is stuff that loses value, bought with money that costs interest.

That one comparison explains a great deal. Wealthy households mostly own things that produce income or grow: shares of businesses, public or private. Everyone else mostly owns things they use. There is nothing wrong with owning a car or a home. But a portfolio made of depreciating possessions cannot compound, while a portfolio of productive assets compounds automatically. The rich are not just people with more stuff. They own different kinds of stuff.

Stock ownership follows the same line. In 2025, 56 percent of all families held stock in some form, directly or through retirement accounts, according to the Fed. Among families in the top tenth of income, it was 97 percent. Among the bottom half, 31 percent. For families who held stock, the median holding rose from $56,900 in 2022 to $77,400 in 2025, as markets climbed. When markets rise, the gains go to people who already own the market, which is one quiet reason wealth gaps persist.

For a sailor, the barrier to joining the owners is unusually low. The TSP gives you access to broad, very low-cost index funds, and under the Blended Retirement System the government adds matching money when you contribute. You do not need to pick winners or watch charts. You need to be in, and to stay in through the years when the market falls, because those years are when long-term owners are separated from short-term tourists.
The business owners and the working rich

Private businesses are a big part of the picture at the top, and they are more common than you might think. In 2025, about 15 percent of all families owned a privately held business, according to the Fed. But ownership rises steeply with income: about 8 percent of families in the bottom half of the income distribution owned one, compared with 40 percent of families in the top tenth.

What do those businesses look like? A 2019 study in the *Quarterly Journal of Economics* by Matthew Smith, Danny Yagan, Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick linked tax records for 11 million firms to their owners. They found that top business income mostly goes to working-age owners of closely held, mid-sized firms in skill-intensive industries. When those owners retired or died, the firms' profits fell by about three-quarters. The authors concluded that the typical top earner's income comes mostly from human capital, meaning the owner's own skills and effort, rather than from financial capital sitting in an account.

In other words, a large share of the very top is not idle heirs or day traders. It is people who built expertise in something valuable and then owned the business that sold it, often a fairly unglamorous one. That is encouraging if you want to build your own business someday. It is also a warning: the profits were tied to the owner's continued work. A business is less a lottery ticket than a demanding job you own, and most of its value walks out the door with you.
The inheritance argument

The most heated question in this whole topic is how much wealth is simply handed down. Here the honest answer is that economists still disagree, and the reason is technical. To estimate how much of today's wealth came from past gifts and inheritances, you have to assume what that money earned in the years since it was received. Small differences in that assumption produce huge differences in the answer.

A 2018 Federal Reserve analysis by Laura Feiveson and John Sabelhaus shows the problem clearly. Using the Survey of Consumer Finances, they estimated that intergenerational transfers account for about 26 percent of total household wealth if transferred money earns a 3 percent real return, and about 51 percent if it earns 5 percent. They note that earlier studies landed anywhere from roughly 20 percent to 80 percent. Transfers are also concentrated: more than half of all transfer dollars went to households already in the top 10 percent of wealth, and only 8 percent went to the bottom half.

items.label: Share of US household wealth traced to gifts and inheritances, depending on assumed returns
Share of transfer dollars going to the top 10% of the wealth distribution
Share going to the bottom half

blocks.source: Feiveson and Sabelhaus, FEDS Notes, Federal Reserve, 2018

blocks.text: Now compare that with a number you may have seen on social media: that 79 percent of millionaires received no inheritance at all. It comes from the National Study of Millionaires by Ramsey Solutions, a company that sells personal finance programs. It surveyed more than 10,000 millionaires in 2017 and 2018, partly through a third-party panel and partly through Ramsey's own research panel. Both findings can be true at once. Most individual millionaires may never inherit a cent, while the minority who do inherit receive enough to account for a large share of total wealth.

The same Ramsey study, read closely, undercuts some of its own messaging. It reports that 88 percent of the millionaires it surveyed had graduated from college and 52 percent held a master's or doctoral degree. About a third never earned six figures in a single year, but 31 percent averaged $100,000 a year over their careers. The punchline that ordinary people can become millionaires through steady investing is broadly supported. The implication that education and income do not matter much is not.

blocks.title: Two stories about getting rich

left.head: The feed's story
items: One big move: a coin, a store, a viral hit
Fast, ideally before 25
Your job is the enemy
Spend to look successful

right.head: The data's story
items: Decades of saving into productive assets
Wealth climbs steeply with age
Skills and income drive the savings
Own things that grow, not things that shrink

blocks.text: Education, homes and the boring middle

The Fed's 2025 numbers show other strong patterns. Families headed by a college graduate had a median net worth of about $505,400, compared with $106,700 for families headed by a high school graduate. Homeowners had a median net worth of $458,900, renters $10,600. These are correlations, not recipes. A degree does not cause wealth by itself, and owning a home is partly a result of already having money. But both point in the same direction: the people who end up wealthy usually build earning power and then convert part of their income into assets, steadily, for a long time.

That pattern is close to the opposite of what an algorithm rewards. Videos about slow accumulation do not get clicks. A 30-second story of a single trade that changed someone's life does, even if a thousand people who made the same trade lost money and never posted about it. When you see wealth content, ask the survivorship question: how many people tried this and failed, and would I ever hear from them?
What this means at 20

Put the evidence together and a fairly clear playbook emerges, none of it secret. Build skills that raise your income, because income is the fuel. Save a meaningful slice of it automatically. Put long-term money into productive assets, such as broad stock index funds through the TSP or an IRA, and leave it there for decades. Avoid borrowing to buy things that lose value. If you want to start a business, treat it as a skill you are building and an asset you will own, not a shortcut around the work.

blocks.title: The unglamorous path the data points to
items: Grow your earning power: certifications, skills, a degree if it fits your goals.
Automate saving before spending, starting small if you need to.
Own productive assets for the long run, like broad index funds.
Avoid debt on depreciating things like cars and gadgets.
Build a business as a skill-based asset, alongside a stable income rather than instead of it.
Give it time: the curve bends upward with decades, not months.

blocks.text: The most hopeful thing in the data is also the least exciting. Wealth in America is unequal and partly inherited, and pretending otherwise helps no one. But for families without a big inheritance, the path to a million is mostly the same: earn well, save steadily, own growing assets and wait. That is not a story anyone will make a viral video about. It is just the one that keeps showing up in the numbers.

takeaways: In 2025, median US family net worth was $215,900; the $1.24 million mean is pulled up by the very top.
A $1 million net worth sits between the 75th and 90th percentiles, and most families who reach it are older.
The top 1% hold about two-thirds of their assets in stocks and businesses; the bottom half mostly holds homes, cars and debt.
Inheritances matter a lot at the top, but estimates of their share of total wealth range widely, from about a quarter to half or more.
The repeatable path is boring: build skills, save automatically, own productive assets and give it decades.
