title: The Boring Machine That Turned $100 Into a Million
dek: Compound growth and index funds are the least exciting idea in finance and the one with the best track record. The math is easy. Sitting still is the hard part.

blocks.text: Picture someone in January 1928 putting $100 into the biggest companies in America and then doing nothing for the rest of their life. No trading, no watching the news, no clever moves. Just reinvesting the dividends and leaving it alone. By the end of 2025, according to the long-running dataset kept by NYU finance professor Aswath Damodaran, that $100 would have grown to about **$1.16 million**.

The same $100 parked in three-month Treasury bills, about the safest thing you can own, would have grown to roughly $2,600. Nobody in this thought experiment picked a hot stock or dodged a crash. They simply owned the whole market and gave it time. That is the entire idea behind index investing, and it's worth understanding properly, because the same forces that make it work are the ones that make most people quit before it pays off.

items.label: $100 in the S&P 500 from 1928 to 2025, dividends reinvested (before inflation)
The same $100 in 3-month Treasury bills
Average yearly S&P 500 return, 1928–2025 (compounded)

blocks.source: Damodaran, NYU Stern, Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills (2026 update)

blocks.text: Growth on top of growth

Compounding just means your returns start earning returns of their own. In the early years it's almost invisible: a 10% gain on $1,000 is $100, which is nice but changes nothing. The action lives at the far end of the curve, where a single year's growth can be bigger than everything you originally put in. Human intuition is built for straight lines, which is why this curve keeps surprising people (the Math section digs into why).

Here's the version that should change how a 20-year-old thinks about money. Using Damodaran's actual year-by-year S&P 500 returns, imagine someone who invested $1,200 at the start of every year, about $100 a month, from 1986 through 2025. Over 40 years they put in $48,000. They ended with roughly **$766,000**. Someone who did exactly the same thing but started ten years later, in 1996, put in $36,000 and finished with about $240,000.

blocks.title: $1,200 a year into the S&P 500, value at end of 2025
blocks.note: Total put in: $48k, $36k and $24k. Nominal dollars, before fees and taxes.
blocks.source: Calculated from Damodaran, NYU Stern historical returns (data through 2025)

blocks.text: The late starter contributed only $12,000 less but ended with less than a third as much. Those first ten years of deposits weren't powerful because they were large. They were powerful because they had the longest runway. A dollar invested at 20 can end up doing more work than several dollars invested at 40.

Look closely at the late part of that 40-year run and the curve becomes obvious. In 2024 alone, the 1986 starter's account grew by about $129,000, more than two and a half times everything they had contributed in four decades. Two years earlier, in 2022, the same account dropped by about $90,000 in a single year. Both numbers come from the same source: once a balance is large, the market's ordinary swings move more money in a year than your paycheck ever could. That's the payoff of compounding, and it's also why the late years feel so volatile.

There's a useful way to think about the two phases. Early on, your deposits do the heavy lifting: in the first few years of that 1986 run, the yearly $1,200 was usually bigger than the market's gain. By the mid-1990s that flipped, and the account was growing by more in a typical year than the owner was putting in. Saving is what builds the base; time is what turns it into an engine. Neither works without the other.

One more honest adjustment: these are nominal dollars. Prices rose a lot between 1928 and 2025, so that $1.16 million buys far less than it sounds. Damodaran's figures put the inflation-adjusted value at about $61,000 in 1928 dollars, an average real gain of roughly 6.8% a year. That's less dramatic, but it's still more than a 600-fold increase in buying power over one long lifetime. Cash in a drawer over the same period lost most of its value.
You don't control the market's return. You do control your start date and your consistency, and over long periods those two inputs matter more than almost anything else you can choose.
What an index fund actually is

A stock is a slice of one company. An index is just a list, like the S&P 500, which tracks around 500 large US companies weighted by their size. An index fund buys everything on that list in the same proportions, so its return is the market's return minus a small fee. No star manager, no research team, no bets on which company wins next year.

The S&P 500 isn't the only index. Total-market funds add thousands of smaller US companies, international funds hold companies in other countries, and bond index funds do the same trick with loans to governments and corporations. The principle is identical every time: don't try to find the winners inside a category, just own the category cheaply. How much to hold in stocks versus bonds mostly depends on when you'll need the money, since money you need in two years shouldn't be riding on a market that can drop a third in one.

That sounds like settling for average. It isn't, for a reason the Nobel-winning economist William Sharpe laid out in a two-page 1991 paper called "The Arithmetic of Active Management." Before costs, the average actively managed dollar has to earn the market's return, because all investors together *are* the market. Active management costs more to run. So after costs, the average active dollar has to trail the average index dollar. It's not a theory about markets; it's arithmetic.

The scoreboard agrees. S&P Dow Jones Indices publishes a regular report called SPIVA that compares professionally managed funds with their benchmarks. Over the 15 years ending in 2024, about 90% of actively managed US large-company funds trailed the S&P 500. And 2025 was another rough year for stock pickers: according to the year-end 2025 SPIVA report, 79% of active large-cap funds lagged the index.

blocks.title: Active US large-cap funds that trailed the S&P 500
blocks.note: Periods ending December 2024.
blocks.source: S&P Dow Jones Indices, SPIVA U.S. Year-End 2024

blocks.text: Why owning everything beats owning a few things

There's a second, stranger reason to own the whole haystack instead of hunting for needles. Finance professor Hendrik Bessembinder studied every US common stock in the CRSP database back to 1926 and found that the majority of individual stocks, over their lifetimes, did worse than one-month Treasury bills. The entire net gain of the US stock market came from the best-performing 4% of companies. The rest, taken together, roughly matched T-bills.

Think about what that means for a stock picker. Market returns are driven by a small number of huge winners that are hard to spot in advance. If you own five or ten stocks, the most likely outcome is that you miss most of them. An index fund guarantees you own the few that end up mattering, because it owns all of them. It's like a loot table where almost all the value sits in a handful of rare drops: the only way to be sure you get them is to open every box.

The few managers who do beat the market in one stretch rarely keep doing it in the next, which is why the losing share tends to stay high or climb as the time window gets longer. Picking the fund that will win the next 15 years is just as hard as picking the stock.
The silent leak

Fees look harmless because they're quoted as tiny percentages. According to the Investment Company Institute, the average actively managed US stock mutual fund charged 0.64% a year in 2025, while the average index stock mutual fund charged 0.05%. The Thrift Savings Plan, the retirement plan for the military and federal workers, reported net expenses of about 0.034% for 2025, or 34 cents a year for every $1,000.

items.label: Average active stock mutual fund expense ratio, 2025
Average index stock mutual fund, 2025
TSP net expense ratio, 2025

blocks.source: ICI, Trends in the Expenses and Fees of Funds, 2025 (March 2026); FRTIB administrative expense review (January 2026)

blocks.text: Half a percent sounds like rounding error until you remember that fees compound too, just in the wrong direction. A fee is charged on your whole balance every year, including all the growth you've piled up. With an assumed 7% yearly return, shaving 0.6 percentage points off every year leaves a 40-year balance about a fifth smaller. You never get a bill for it. The money just quietly isn't there.
The part that's actually hard

If this were easy, everyone would be rich. The math is easy. Living through it is not. In Damodaran's data, the S&P 500 lost money in 26 of the 98 years from 1928 to 2025. It fell almost 44% in 1931 and about 37% in 2008. Anyone who invested at the start of 2000 was still behind ten years later, after two crashes, with nothing to show for a decade of patience.

But watch what happens as the holding period stretches. Using the same data, every 20-year stretch since 1928 ended with a gain, even after adjusting for inflation. The odds of losing money shrink quickly with time, because the good years get more chances to outweigh the bad ones.

blocks.title: How often the S&P 500 lost money, by holding period
blocks.note: Share of rolling periods from 1928 to 2025 with a negative total return (dividends reinvested, before inflation).
blocks.source: Calculated from Damodaran, NYU Stern historical returns (data through 2025)

blocks.text: That chart is the whole strategy in one picture. The risk in stocks is real, but it's mostly short-term risk. The bigger danger is selling during a crash, which turns a temporary drop into a permanent loss and often means missing the rebound. The year after the 2008 collapse, the S&P 500 returned about 26%, while the news still felt like the end of the world.

Could you just dodge the crashes? It's the obvious question, and the answer is that almost nobody does it reliably. To win by timing, you have to be right twice: when to get out and when to get back in. Rebounds often start while things still look terrible, so the person waiting for good news to buy back in usually pays a higher price than the person who never left. A plan that requires you to predict the future isn't a plan.

There's an honest caveat. The US market of the last century is one of history's great success stories, and it's where these numbers come from. Not every market was so kind: Japan's stock market took more than three decades to get back to its 1989 peak. Past returns are a record, not a promise. That's one reason many investors also hold international stocks and bonds, and why nobody can tell you what the next 40 years will return.
Boring on purpose

blocks.title: Two ways to invest

left.head: Picking and timing
items: Feels skilled and active
Higher fees, more trading costs and taxes
Needs you to be right again and again
Most professionals trail the index over 15 years

right.head: Owning the index
items: Feels like doing nothing
Fees close to zero
Needs only time and patience
Gets the market's return, by design

blocks.text: The reason this approach is so hard to follow is that it gives your brain nothing to do. Games, social feeds and trading apps are all built on tight feedback: you act, something happens, you get a hit. Index investing pays you for *not* acting. The winning behavior is to set up automatic contributions, choose something broad and cheap, and then mostly ignore it, especially on the days the headlines are screaming.

For service members, a simple version of this already exists. The TSP's C Fund tracks the S&P 500, and its Lifecycle (L) Funds mix stocks and bonds automatically based on when you expect to need the money. Contributions come out of your pay before you ever see them. The companion article on the TSP and the Blended Retirement System covers the matching money and the rules. None of this is a recommendation of a particular fund; it's a description of how the tools work.

blocks.title: The boring system
items: Pick a contribution rate and have it taken from every paycheck automatically
Use a broad, low-cost index fund instead of a handful of individual stocks
Raise the rate whenever your pay goes up, before you get used to the bigger check
Check in once or twice a year, not daily
When the market crashes, change nothing and keep buying on schedule

blocks.text: Life on a submarine is oddly well suited to this. You can't refresh a stock app from a watch station. You can't panic-sell in the middle of a long underway. Weeks go by, contributions keep landing, and the market does whatever it does without your help. A lot of investors on land would do better with that kind of enforced distance.

This is how the mechanics work, based on historical data, not personal financial advice. Your timeline and situation matter. Before changing anything, talk to your command financial specialist or the personal financial counselors at Fleet and Family Support.

takeaways: Starting early beats investing more later: the first dollars get the most years to compound.
An index fund owns the whole market; after fees, most professional stock pickers trail it over long periods.
Fees compound against you, so fractions of a percent matter over decades.
US stocks often lose money in a single year but never lost over any 20-year stretch from 1928 to 2025. That's history, not a guarantee.
The hard part is behavior: automate it, then leave it alone, especially during crashes.

title: The Leak in Every Savings Account
dek: Inflation is a tax nobody votes on and nobody sends you a bill for. Here's what it is, why it spiked after 2021, and why the money that feels safest is the money guaranteed to shrink.

blocks.text: In June 2022, the price of the typical basket of things Americans buy was 9.1% higher than a year earlier. That was the fastest yearly increase since November 1981, before most of today's sailors' parents had finished school. Gas, groceries, rent and used cars all jumped at once, and for a while it felt like every receipt was a small shock.

But the dramatic year isn't the most important part of the story. The quieter part is what happens in ordinary years. By the government's own price index, a $100 bill tucked in a drawer in January 2000 now buys roughly what $50 bought back then. Nobody took the money. Nothing went wrong. Prices just kept rising a little at a time, and the bill stayed $100.

items.label: Yearly rise in consumer prices, June 2022: the highest since 1981
What $100 from January 2000 is worth in buying power (September 2026)

blocks.source: BLS CPI-U (series CUUR0000SA0 / CPIAUCNS) via FRED; calculated

blocks.text: What inflation actually measures

Inflation is a rise in the general level of prices, which is the same thing as a fall in what each dollar can buy. It isn't about one item getting expensive; a bad orange harvest raises orange prices without being inflation. It's about the overall cost of living drifting upward across thousands of goods and services at once.

The number you hear in the news usually comes from the Consumer Price Index, published monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Government data collectors track the prices of a large, weighted basket of goods and services that urban households buy, from rent and car insurance to haircuts and coffee, and compare the cost of that basket over time. The Federal Reserve prefers a similar measure, the price index for personal consumption expenditures, and aims for inflation of 2% a year on that measure over the long run.

Two things are worth knowing about any index like this. First, it's an average, and your personal inflation rate depends on what you actually buy. Someone who lives aboard ship and doesn't pay rent barely feels rising housing costs, while someone with a long commute feels every gas spike. Second, a target of 2% means the plan is for prices to keep rising, slowly and predictably. Stable prices, in central-bank language, still means your cash loses a little every year.

Measuring this is harder than it sounds. Products change: a phone that costs the same as five years ago is a much better phone, and the index tries to adjust for that. People also switch to cheaper options when prices rise. Critics on one side argue the official numbers understate what families feel; a government-appointed commission in the 1990s concluded the opposite, that the CPI was overstating inflation at the time, and the method was revised. Neither camp thinks the index is perfect, but it's the best common yardstick there is.
Why prices rise

Economists group the causes into a few families. **Demand-pull** inflation happens when people and businesses want to buy more than the economy can produce, so sellers can raise prices. **Cost-push** inflation happens when it suddenly costs more to make things, such as when energy prices spike, and producers pass that on. And **expectations** matter: if everyone expects prices to rise, workers ask for bigger raises and businesses raise prices preemptively, which helps make the prediction come true.

The 2021–2022 surge had all three. Supply chains snarled during the pandemic, demand rebounded strongly as economies reopened, supported by relief spending and very low interest rates, and energy and food prices spiked after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Economists still argue about how much each factor mattered. The Federal Reserve responded by raising interest rates sharply in 2022 and 2023, making borrowing more expensive to cool demand, and yearly inflation fell back to around 3% by mid-2023.

blocks.title: How much prices rose over the previous 12 months, each June
blocks.note: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, not seasonally adjusted.
blocks.source: BLS CPI-U (series CUUR0000SA0 / CPIAUCNS) via FRED; calculated

blocks.text: Notice that the line never goes back down to where it started. Inflation falling from 9% to 3% doesn't mean prices fell. It means they rose more slowly. The higher prices from 2021 and 2022 are baked in, and yearly inflation picked up again in spring 2026, reaching 4.2% in May. That's the uncomfortable truth about price levels: they tend to ratchet in one direction.
The math of slow erosion

A handy shortcut called the rule of 72 tells you how long it takes for something growing at a steady rate to double: divide 72 by the rate. At 3% inflation, prices double in about 24 years. At 6%, about 12. For a 20-year-old, that means the cost of living could plausibly double before age 45 even if inflation stays fairly tame. A retirement plan that ignores that is planning to retire poorer than it thinks.

This is why any long-range money number should come with a question attached: in whose dollars? A retirement calculator promising a million dollars in 45 years sounds enormous, but at 3% inflation a future million buys roughly what a quarter of a million buys today. Good calculators let you show results in today's dollars. If one doesn't, mentally cut big long-term numbers down to size before getting excited, or worried, about them.

Over the long run, US inflation has averaged about 3% a year since 1928, according to the CPI figures in NYU professor Aswath Damodaran's historical dataset. That small-sounding number, compounded over 98 years, means the price level rose almost nineteenfold. A dollar kept in cash since 1928 kept its face value and lost about 95% of its buying power.

Falling prices aren't the cure, by the way. Prices fell sharply from 1930 to 1932, by more than 6% in 1930 and roughly 9 to 10% in each of the next two years, during the Great Depression. When people expect prices to fall, they put off spending and borrowing, businesses cut jobs, and debts become harder to repay. That's one reason central banks aim for low, steady inflation rather than zero.

Inflation also plays tricks on perception. Psychologists Eldar Shafir and Amos Tversky and economist Peter Diamond studied what they called **money illusion**: the tendency to think in face-value dollars instead of buying power. In scenarios they posed, people often judged a worker who got a bigger raise in a high-inflation year as happier than one who got a smaller raise with no inflation, even when the second worker was better off in real terms. Bigger numbers feel like progress. Your brain sees the raise and doesn't do the subtraction.

The subtraction is simple once you know to do it. What you really earn on savings is the interest rate minus inflation, called the real return. A savings account paying 4% in a year of 3% inflation leaves you about 1% richer in buying power. One paying 0.5% in the same year leaves you about 2.5% poorer, even though the balance went up. The statement shows growth either way; only one of them is real.
Winners and losers

Inflation doesn't hit everyone equally. People holding cash or money owed to them at a fixed rate lose, because they get repaid in cheaper dollars. People who owe money at a fixed rate quietly gain, because their payment stays the same while their pay and prices rise. That's part of why a fixed-rate mortgage can be a good deal in inflationary years, and why a variable-rate credit card balance is the opposite: card rates tend to rise along with interest rates.

People on fixed incomes, like retirees with pensions that aren't adjusted for prices, get squeezed the hardest. That's why it matters that military retired pay and Social Security include cost-of-living adjustments tied to inflation. Workers are somewhere in between: wages do tend to catch up, but usually after prices have already moved, which is exactly what the military pay data shows.
Safe isn't the same as safe

This is where inflation flips the usual idea of risk. Cash feels safe because its number never goes down. But measured in what it can buy, cash is the one asset that is guaranteed to lose over time. Investments that bounce around from year to year have, historically, been the ones that outran rising prices. The chart below uses Damodaran's data to show average yearly returns after inflation from 1928 through 2025.

blocks.title: Average yearly return after inflation, 1928–2025
blocks.note: Compounded annual real returns; stock returns include reinvested dividends.
blocks.source: Calculated from Damodaran, NYU Stern, Historical Returns (2026 update)

blocks.text: Short-term Treasury bills, the classic safe asset, barely stayed ahead of inflation over that span. Bonds did a little better. Stocks, with all their crashes, grew buying power by almost 7% a year on average. That doesn't make stocks right for every dollar. Money you'll need soon shouldn't be exposed to a market that can fall by a third in a bad year. But it does mean that keeping long-term money in cash isn't the cautious choice it looks like. It's a slow, guaranteed loss traded for the comfort of a number that never drops.

Every pile of money has a job and a timeline. Money for emergencies and near-term plans needs to be stable and easy to reach. Money for 10, 20 or 40 years from now has to beat inflation, or it's shrinking while you sleep.
Your paycheck versus prices

Military basic pay has its own built-in inflation defense. By law, the annual raise is tied to the Employment Cost Index, a measure of how fast private-sector wages are growing, unless the President or Congress sets a different number. In practice, that means raises follow wages, which tend to follow prices with a lag.

blocks.title: Annual military basic pay raise
blocks.note: Across-the-board raise each January. In 2025, junior enlisted also received an extra targeted raise from April 1.
blocks.source: Congressional Research Service, Defense Primer: Military Pay Raise (IF10260), Jan 2026

blocks.text: That lag showed up clearly in the inflation spike. The across-the-board raises from 2021 through 2025 add up, compounded, to about 21.6%. Over roughly the same stretch, from December 2020 to December 2025, consumer prices rose about 24.4%. The bigger raises of 2023 and 2024 were partly catch-up, and the targeted 2025 increase for junior enlisted helped those ranks further. But for a member whose pay rose only by the general raise, the paycheck lost a little ground to prices over those five years.

items.label: Military basic pay, general raises 2021–2025 combined
Consumer prices, December 2020 to December 2025

blocks.source: CRS IF10260 (Jan 2026); BLS CPI-U via FRED; calculated

blocks.text: The real lesson is that annual raises mostly just keep you in place. Actual gains in buying power come from promotions, years-of-service steps, new skills and, over time, from owning assets that grow faster than prices. That's true in uniform and it will be just as true in a civilian career.
Living with a leaky bucket

blocks.title: Protecting money from inflation
items: Keep an emergency fund in an insured savings account that pays interest, so it loses less to inflation than cash at zero
Don't hold large piles of idle cash for years without a specific purpose
Invest long-term money in diversified assets that have historically outpaced inflation
Commit part of every raise to savings, so savings grow at least as fast as your pay
Watch your own lifestyle inflation; it's the part of the cost of living you control

blocks.text: There's also a quieter form of inflation that has nothing to do with the CPI: the gradual rise in what you consider normal. Better phone, bigger subscription bundle, more takeout. Each upgrade feels small and permanent at once. Economists measure the national price level, but your personal cost of living is mostly set by your own choices, and it's the only part of the problem you fully control.

The deeper reframe is this: inflation means that doing nothing with money is itself a decision, and usually a losing one. Leaving savings in a zero-interest account isn't neutral. It's a bet that the next 20 years will have no inflation, a bet that history says almost never wins. Understanding that doesn't require predicting the economy. It just requires noticing that the bucket has a small hole in it and deciding what to do about it.

This explains how inflation works, not what to do with your specific money. For a personal plan, including where to keep an emergency fund and how to invest, talk to your command financial specialist or Fleet and Family Support's personal financial managers.

takeaways: Inflation is a falling value of money: $100 from January 2000 buys about what $50 did then.
When inflation cools, prices still rise, just more slowly. They rarely go back down.
Cash is the only asset guaranteed to lose buying power; over 1928–2025, US stocks gained about 6.8% a year after inflation.
Military raises track wages with a lag; real gains come from promotions, skills and investing.
Doing nothing with money is a decision, and usually a losing one.

title: Insurance Is a Bet You Hope to Lose
dek: SGLI, renters insurance, car coverage and the policies you can skip. How to think about insurance like an engineer: protect against the failures you cannot survive, and absorb the ones you can. Rules and rates as of 2026.

blocks.text: Every month, a line on your LES quietly buys you half a million dollars. If you have the default amount of Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance, you pay **$26 a month**: $25 for $500,000 of life coverage and $1 for traumatic injury protection. Most sailors never think about it again after in-processing. That is a shame, because SGLI is one of the best insurance deals available to anyone in the country, and understanding why it is good teaches you how to judge every other policy someone will try to sell you.

Insurance is a strange product. You pay money every month hoping you will never get anything back. If you do collect, it means something bad happened. And on average, buyers as a group must lose: insurers pay claims, salaries and overhead out of premiums and still need to make money. So insurance is a bet you expect to lose. The question is never whether it is a good bet on average. It is whether losing small and steady is worth it to avoid losing catastrophically.

General education, not financial or insurance advice. Rates and rules are from VA and other sources current as of 2025 and 2026 and can change. Confirm your coverage in milConnect and with your personnel office, the VA or a licensed agent before making changes.
The engineer's rule: insure the failures you cannot survive

Nuclear plants are designed around a simple idea: you cannot prevent every failure, so you rank them by how likely they are and how bad the consequences would be, and you put your heaviest protection where the consequences are unrecoverable. Personal insurance works the same way. A cracked phone screen is likely but survivable; you can pay for it from savings. A lawsuit after a car crash, a fire that destroys everything you own or your death leaving family with bills are unlikely but devastating. Those are what insurance is for.

blocks.title: Insure it or absorb it?

left.head: Insure it
items: Your death, if anyone depends on you or would face your bills
Injuring someone with your car
Losing everything you own to fire or theft
Major medical costs (TRICARE covers this on active duty)

right.head: Absorb it with savings
items: A cracked phone or controller
Minor dents and scratches
Small repairs and replacements
Anything you could pay for in a month or two

blocks.text: This rule explains why an emergency fund and insurance are partners. The bigger your savings, the more small risks you can handle yourself, which means higher deductibles, cheaper premiums and fewer add-on policies. Every protection plan offered at a checkout counter is a tiny insurance policy on something you could replace yourself, and the price is set so that the seller comes out ahead.
SGLI: the deal you already have

According to the VA, if you are on active duty you are automatically enrolled in SGLI through your service branch. Coverage goes up to $500,000 in $50,000 increments, and the basic premium is five cents per $1,000 of coverage each month, plus a flat $1 for Traumatic Injury Protection, known as TSGLI. You can lower your coverage or decline it entirely, and you choose your beneficiaries, all through the SGLI Online Enrollment System in milConnect.

items.label: Maximum SGLI coverage, in $50,000 steps
Total premium at the maximum, including $1 for TSGLI
TSGLI payment range for qualifying traumatic injuries

blocks.source: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, SGLI and TSGLI pages, 2026

blocks.text: TSGLI is the part people forget. It pays $25,000 to $100,000 to service members insured under SGLI who suffer certain traumatic injuries, such as qualifying losses that occur within two years of the injury, to help cover recovery. Separately from any insurance, the military pays a $100,000 death gratuity, a tax-free lump sum to designated survivors, according to Military OneSource. The two are not the same thing, and one does not replace the other.

So should a single 20-year-old with no kids keep $500,000? There is a real argument for less. Life insurance exists to replace income for people who depend on you, and if nobody does, the strict logic says you need only enough to cover debts and final expenses. But there are arguments the other way. Parents or siblings may rely on you more than you think, or would face costs if something happened. At $25 for the full amount, the premium is small. And coverage you keep now carries forward into options after you leave, as the next section shows. Whatever you decide, decide it on purpose.

The most important part of SGLI is not the amount. It is the beneficiary designation. Policies pay whoever is named on the form, regardless of what you might have said out loud or written somewhere else. Check yours in milConnect after any big life event: marriage, divorce, a new child, a death in the family. An out-of-date beneficiary is one of the most common and most painful insurance mistakes, and it takes five minutes to prevent.

If you marry someday, the system expands automatically. Family SGLI covers a spouse for up to $100,000, never more than your own SGLI amount, with premiums deducted from your pay, and covers each dependent child for $10,000 at no cost, according to the VA. It is one more reason to revisit your insurance whenever your life changes rather than once at boot camp.
When you get out: the rate cliff

SGLI does not follow you into civilian life on its own. The VA says coverage continues free for 120 days after you leave the military. After that, you can convert to Veterans' Group Life Insurance (VGLI) for up to the amount you had through SGLI. If you apply within 240 days of leaving, there is no health review, which means coverage even if you have developed medical conditions. You can also convert SGLI to an individual commercial policy within 120 days without proving good health.

VGLI is renewable term insurance, and its price is based only on your age and coverage amount. At 29 or younger, $500,000 of VGLI cost $30 a month as of the July 2025 rate table. That is still cheap. But look at what happens to the same coverage as the years go by.

blocks.title: Monthly VGLI premium for $500,000 of coverage, by age
blocks.note: Rates effective July 1, 2025; selected age bands shown.
blocks.source: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, VGLI premium rates, 2025

blocks.text: This chart is a lesson about every kind of term life insurance, not just VGLI. Term coverage is cheap when you are young because you are very unlikely to die soon, and it gets dramatically more expensive as that probability rises. That is why most people only need life insurance during the years when others depend on their income: while kids are young and a mortgage is large. Many veterans compare VGLI with private term policies when they separate, especially if they are young and healthy. The guaranteed, no-health-questions conversion is what makes VGLI valuable for anyone whose health has changed.
Renters insurance: the cheapest protection you are not buying

If you live off base or keep belongings somewhere other than the boat, renters insurance deserves a look. A standard renters policy, called an HO-4, covers your personal property against a list of named perils such as fire and theft. Most policies also include personal liability coverage, which protects you if someone is hurt in your place or you accidentally damage someone else's property, and coverage for extra living costs if your apartment becomes unlivable.

It is also cheap. Insurance regulators collect premium data from every state, and according to the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, as reported by the Insurance Information Institute, the average renters premium in 2022 was **$171 a year**, less than $15 a month. Average renters premiums actually fell for most of the decade before that, even as homeowners insurance climbed. Your price depends on where you live, how much coverage you choose and your deductible.

blocks.title: Average annual renters insurance premium (HO-4)
blocks.source: NAIC data via Insurance Information Institute, 2025

blocks.text: Now add up what you own. A gaming PC, monitors, a mic and camera, a laptop, a TV, clothes, tools, maybe a bike or gym equipment. For a lot of young sailors, that total is several thousand dollars, sometimes much more, and replacing it after a fire or a break-in would wipe out a year of savings. That is the textbook definition of a risk worth insuring: unlikely, but expensive enough to hurt badly.

Two details matter when you buy. First, choose **replacement cost** coverage if you can, which pays to buy a new equivalent item, rather than actual cash value, which pays what your three-year-old PC is worth after depreciation. Second, take photos or a short video of your gear and save receipts in the cloud. If you live in the barracks, ask an insurer directly whether a policy will cover your belongings there before you assume it will not; theft in shared spaces happens. The military claims system can pay for certain losses connected to service, such as damage during a government-arranged move, but it is not designed to replace everyday coverage.
The deductible is a dial, not a detail

Almost every policy you buy has a deductible: the amount you pay out of pocket before the insurer pays anything. Most people pick whatever the website defaults to. That is a missed opportunity, because the deductible is the dial that sets how much risk you keep and how much you rent out to the insurer. A low deductible means higher premiums every month in exchange for smaller bills when something goes wrong. A higher deductible means lower premiums and a bigger hit when you file a claim.

The right setting depends almost entirely on your savings. If a $1,000 surprise would push you onto a credit card, a low deductible is worth paying for. If your emergency fund could cover $1,000 without drama, you are paying the insurer to handle a risk you could handle yourself. Raising the deductible and banking the difference is how people with savings quietly pay less for the same protection. It is also why building the emergency fund first makes every other insurance decision cheaper.
Car insurance and the paid-off car

Car insurance is mostly about the liability portion: the coverage that pays when you hurt someone else or damage their property. Every state sets a legal minimum, and those minimums are often far below what a serious crash can cost. Liability is the part of car insurance where cheaping out is most dangerous, because the downside is a judgment against you that can follow you for years.

Collision and comprehensive, the coverages that fix or replace your own car, are a different calculation. If you owe money on a car, the lender usually requires them. If you own the car outright, as you do, they are optional, and the question becomes whether the car is worth enough to justify the premium. An old car worth a few thousand dollars may not be, especially if your emergency fund could replace it. A newer car you could not afford to replace probably is. For context, AAA's 2026 driving cost study put full coverage at about $2,098 a year for an experienced driver; younger drivers usually pay more.
What you can probably skip

Some insurance products are sold far more often than they are needed. Extended warranties and protection plans on electronics, add-on products in the car dealer's finance office, credit life insurance attached to loans and expensive cash-value life policies pitched to young servicemembers all deserve skepticism. Not every one is a bad deal for every person, but you should be able to explain exactly which catastrophe the policy protects you from and why your savings could not handle it instead.

blocks.title: A one-evening insurance checkup
items: Log in to milConnect and confirm your SGLI amount and beneficiaries.
List what you own and what it would cost to replace; get two or three renters quotes if it is more than you could absorb.
Check your car policy's liability limits, and reconsider collision on an older paid-off car.
Cancel small add-on policies that cover things your emergency fund can handle.
Put a reminder on your calendar for the months before you separate: SGLI, VGLI and health coverage.

blocks.text: Good insurance decisions are mostly about imagination. You have to picture the worst plausible day, the fire, the crash, the phone call nobody wants to get, and ask what it would do to you and the people you care about. Then you buy protection for that day and nothing more. Done right, insurance is invisible and boring, a few small lines on a statement. That is exactly what a bet you hope to lose should look like.

takeaways: Insure against losses you could not recover from; pay for small ones from savings.
SGLI costs $26 a month for $500,000 plus TSGLI; check your beneficiaries in milConnect after every life change.
After separation, SGLI runs free for 120 days, and VGLI is available without a health review if you apply within 240 days.
Renters insurance averaged $171 a year in 2022 and protects your gear and your liability.
Be skeptical of add-on warranties and pricey policies sold to young servicemembers.

title: Where Your Raise Went
dek: Spending rises to meet income so reliably that it has a name. The psychology of lifestyle creep, why willpower loses to it, and the pre-commitment trick that beats it (not financial advice).

blocks.text: Think back to the first paycheck that felt big. Maybe it was boot camp pay landing in an account that used to hold a couple hundred dollars. Maybe it was the bump that came with a promotion. For a few weeks it felt like a lot of money. Then, quietly, it stopped feeling like a lot. Nothing dramatic happened. A slightly better phone plan, a few more meals out, a car payment that made sense at the time. The paycheck was bigger, and yet the end of the month felt exactly as tight as before.

This is lifestyle creep: the tendency for spending to rise to meet income, so that every raise gets absorbed before it can change anything. It is one of the main reasons people with good incomes still live paycheck to paycheck. And it is not mainly a willpower problem. It is the predictable result of how human brains handle comparison and change, which means the fix is not trying harder. It is setting things up so the creep has nowhere to go.
The treadmill under your feet

In 1978, psychologists Philip Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman published one of the most cited studies in happiness research. They interviewed 22 people who had won major lottery prizes and compared them with 22 similar people who had not. The winners were not happier than the controls, and they took noticeably less pleasure from ordinary things like a compliment, a joke or breakfast. The authors argued two forces were at work: **contrast**, because everyday pleasures look dull next to the thrill of winning, and **habituation**, because the new pleasures money buys stop feeling new.

That idea became known as the hedonic treadmill: you can run faster, but you stay in the same place. It is a powerful image, and it explains a lot about lifestyle creep. The first month in a nicer apartment feels great; by month six it is just where you live. But the original study was tiny, and later research has complicated the story in ways that matter.

In 2006, Ed Diener, Richard Lucas and Christie Scollon reviewed the evidence and argued the treadmill needed serious revisions. People's baseline happiness is not neutral; it differs between people; different parts of well-being can move in different directions; and, most importantly, set points can actually change. Then in 2020, economists Erik Lindqvist, Robert Östling and David Cesarini surveyed a large sample of Swedish lottery players 5 to 22 years after their wins, using pre-registered methods. Large-prize winners reported **sustained increases in life satisfaction** that showed no sign of fading over more than a decade, with smaller effects on day-to-day happiness. The gains seemed to run largely through financial satisfaction.

Put those together and you get a more useful picture than the old slogan. Money does improve how people rate their lives, and financial security seems to be a big part of why. What adapts quickly is the pleasure of the *stuff*. The upgraded car, the bigger place, the subscription bundle all fade into the background. So the trap is not earning more. The trap is converting every raise into new baseline spending, which buys the part that fades and gives up the part, security, that lasts.

blocks.title: How a raise disappears
items: Income goes up
An upgrade feels earned and affordable
The upgrade becomes the new normal
Fixed costs are now higher than before
The budget feels tight again, so the next raise feels necessary

blocks.text: Keeping up with the people next door

Adaptation is half the engine. The other half is comparison. People judge what is enough by looking around, and what they see around them is mostly other people's spending, not their savings or their debts.

The Dutch Postcode Lottery offers a rare natural experiment. Each week it picks a postal code at random and hands cash, and a new BMW, to participating households in that code. Peter Kuhn and colleagues used it to study what happens next, and published the results in the American Economic Review in 2011. Winners mostly spent on cars and other durable goods. But the striking result was next door: neighbors who had not even entered the lottery had significantly higher car spending than other non-participants. A new car in the driveway next to yours is, apparently, contagious.

A study of neighborhoods published in 2019 in the Review of Financial Studies pushed the idea further. Sumit Agarwal, Slava Mikhed and Barry Scholnick looked at what happened around lottery winners and found that the bigger a neighbor's win, the more the people around them borrowed afterward, and the more of them later filed for bankruptcy. The winners got richer. Some of their neighbors went broke trying to look like they had too.

The economist Robert Frank has argued, in books like *Luxury Fever*, that this is not irrational at the individual level. Some goods are **positional**: their value depends on how they compare with what others have. A house, a car, a watch are judged partly against the ones around them. Other things, like free time, health, a short commute or money in the bank, are valued mostly for themselves. Frank's point is that when everyone competes on positional goods, everyone spends more and nobody ends up ahead, because the comparison just resets. Each person's upgrade quietly raises the bar for everyone else.

Comparison is aimed at what is visible. You see a shipmate's new truck in the parking lot; you do not see the 84-month loan, the insurance bill or the empty savings account behind it. Spending is public. Wealth is mostly invisible.

Military life is tuned almost perfectly for this. Pay is public and standardized, so everyone knows roughly what everyone else makes. Raises arrive on a schedule: the annual pay raise, time-in-service steps, promotions, special pays. Large lump sums show up at predictable moments, such as a reenlistment bonus or months of underway pay that piled up because there was nothing to spend it on. And there is a whole economy of car dealers and lenders near every base that understands all of this very well. The moment after a long underway, when the money is sitting there and you feel like you earned something, is the most dangerous moment in a sailor's financial year.

It is worth being fair to the lottery winners, though. The Dutch study found that their own spending looked fairly sensible: it went mostly into durable goods, consistent with people spreading a windfall over time, and most of the BMW winners sold the car. The people who got into trouble in the neighborhood studies were often not the ones with the money. They were the ones reacting to it.
Why willpower loses

The usual advice is to be disciplined: when you get a raise, just do not spend it. The research on human decision-making suggests that advice fails for predictable reasons. Spending happens in the present, with a clear and immediate reward. Saving pays off in an abstract future. And once a spending level is established, cutting it back feels like a loss, and losses feel bigger than equivalent gains. Trying to downgrade your life after it has crept up is fighting all of that at once.

Behavioral economists took this seriously and designed around it rather than lecturing people. One of the most influential findings came from Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea in 2001. When a large company switched its 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment, participation among new employees jumped dramatically. Nothing about the plan's value changed. Only the default did.

blocks.title: 401(k) participation, opt-in vs automatic enrollment
blocks.note: New employees at one large US firm.
blocks.source: Madrian and Shea (2001), as summarized by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, 2017

blocks.text: Saving more tomorrow

Richard Thaler, who later won the 2017 Nobel Prize in economics, and Shlomo Benartzi built a program aimed squarely at lifestyle creep. They called it **Save More Tomorrow**. The design is clever because it works with human biases instead of against them. Employees agree, well in advance, to increase their retirement contribution starting with their next raise. Because the decision is about the future, it is easier to make. Because the increase comes out of new money, take-home pay never drops, so nobody feels a loss. The contribution keeps stepping up with each raise until it reaches a preset cap, and inertia keeps people in. They can quit at any time, but few do.

In tests at three companies it raised savings substantially, especially when it was offered in one-on-one meetings. The idea spread. It helped shape the Pension Protection Act of 2006, which encouraged automatic enrollment and automatic escalation in 401(k) plans. Benartzi and Thaler later estimated that about 4.1 million Americans were in some kind of automatic escalation plan by 2011, adding an estimated $7.6 billion a year in savings by 2013.

items.label: Americans in automatic savings escalation plans by 2011
Estimated added annual savings by 2013

blocks.source: Benartzi and Thaler (2013), as summarized by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, 2017

blocks.text: The deep lesson is that the best time to decide what to do with a raise is before you get it. Once the money is in your account and has been spent once, it has become part of your normal. Before it arrives, it is still hypothetical, and hypothetical money is easy to give away to your future self.
Building a creep-proof setup

The Blended Retirement System already applies part of this logic: it defaults service members into contributing to the Thrift Savings Plan, because the people who designed it know defaults work. You can take the same approach further on your own. None of this requires a spreadsheet or tracking every coffee. It requires a few decisions made once, in advance, in the systems that already touch your pay.

blocks.title: Pre-commit your raises
items: Decide a rule now: for example, half of every raise or promotion goes to savings or the TSP, half is yours to enjoy.
When a raise is announced, change your TSP percentage or savings allotment before the first bigger paycheck lands.
Send lump sums, such as bonuses or underway savings, to a separate account the day they arrive, then decide calmly what to do with them.
Before any new monthly bill, like a car payment or a pricier plan, wait a set period, such as 30 days.
Judge fixed costs by how much freedom they cost you, not by whether the monthly payment fits.

blocks.text: That last step is the one most people skip. Lifestyle creep does its real damage through **fixed costs**, the recurring bills that lock in. A one-time splurge after a long underway is fine; it is gone and done. A $700 car payment is a decision you remake every month for six years, and it quietly raises the income you need just to feel okay. Each new fixed cost raises the floor you are standing on, and a higher floor makes it harder to take risks later, such as leaving a job you hate, starting a business or going back to school.

If you want a single number to watch, make it your savings rate: the share of each paycheck that goes to savings and the TSP rather than to spending. Your income will rise on its own as you promote. If your savings rate rises with it, you are beating the treadmill. If your income keeps going up and that percentage stays flat, lifestyle creep is winning, no matter how disciplined each individual purchase felt at the time.

blocks.title: Two ways to spend a raise

left.head: Lifestyle creep
items: Raise arrives, spending rises to match
New fixed costs feel permanent
Savings rate stays flat
Freedom shrinks as the floor rises

right.head: Lifestyle by design
items: Split decided before the raise arrives
Upgrades are mostly one-time, chosen on purpose
Savings rate climbs with every promotion
Freedom grows as savings outpace costs

blocks.text: None of this means never enjoying money. The point of a raise is that your life gets better. The question is which kind of better. The research suggests the pleasure of new things fades fast, while the security of having savings keeps paying out. Splitting raises lets you have some of both: you get a real upgrade now, and the other half builds something that does not fade.

There is one more reason to care about this at 20. Your spending level becomes a habit, and habits formed early are sticky. If you get used to living on less than you make while your pay is still climbing, every future raise widens the gap. If you get used to spending everything, every future raise just resets the treadmill. The difference between those two paths is not talent or income. It is a handful of default settings, chosen once, before the next raise shows up.

takeaways: The pleasure of new stuff fades fast; the life satisfaction that comes from financial security appears to last.
Spending is contagious: neighbors of Dutch lottery winners bought more cars, and bigger wins nearby were followed by more borrowing and bankruptcies.
Defaults beat willpower: automatic enrollment raised 401(k) participation from 49% to 86% at one firm.
Decide what happens to a raise before it arrives, and change your TSP or savings allotment before the first bigger paycheck.
Watch fixed costs most closely; they raise the floor you need just to feel okay.

title: The $89,000 Sailor: What Your Navy Paycheck Is Really Worth
dek: A civilian offer of $75,000 sounds like a raise to someone whose basic pay is $50,000. It might be a pay cut. How to count what the military actually pays you, how to price a civilian offer honestly, and how SkillBridge can bridge the gap. The 2026 numbers.

blocks.text: Imagine a recruiter from a utility calls a second-class petty officer a year before his contract ends. The offer: $75,000 a year to start, plus benefits. His basic pay is about $50,000. The math in his head is simple and exciting. Fifty percent raise. Where do I sign?

The math is wrong, and not in a small way. Basic pay is only the most visible part of what the Navy pays. Once you add the tax-free allowances, the tax break those allowances create, free health care and a handful of other benefits, a typical E-5 is being paid something closer to $89,000 a year in cash and near-cash, before counting medical care at all. The $75,000 offer might be a raise. It might also be a cut. You can't tell until you count both sides the same way.

This article walks through how to do that count. It uses 2026 figures, it is general education rather than financial or career advice, and the specifics of your pay, bonuses and benefits should be confirmed with your command's career counselor and the base finance office.
The paycheck you don't see

Defense officials and Congress use a standard measure called Regular Military Compensation, or RMC, to compare military and civilian pay. It is defined in federal law and has four parts: basic pay, the Basic Allowance for Housing, the Basic Allowance for Subsistence, and the federal tax advantage that exists because the two allowances are not taxed. If you live aboard or in barracks, you receive the housing benefit as a room instead of cash, but the value is still part of what you are paid.

blocks.title: Example E-5 Regular Military Compensation, 2026
blocks.note: Total about $89,148. BAH varies by location and dependents; the tax advantage varies by individual.
blocks.source: CRS, Defense Primer: Regular Military Compensation (IF10532, July 2026), using DoD data for Jan 1, 2026

blocks.text: Notice how much of the total is invisible on a quick glance at the Leave and Earnings Statement. Basic pay is just 56 percent of this E-5's RMC. The tax advantage line is the strangest one, because no money ever arrives labeled as tax advantage. It is the extra salary a civilian would need to earn, and then pay tax on, to end up with the same take-home money. A civilian salary is fully taxable. Comparing it to basic pay alone compares a taxed number to a mostly untaxed one.

RMC also places junior military pay surprisingly high against civilians. The 14th Quadrennial Review of Military Compensation, published in 2025, compared RMC to civilian earnings for people of similar age and education. It found enlisted members with up to 20 years of service at about the 83rd percentile, meaning they out-earned roughly 83 percent of comparable civilians. The Pentagon's long-standing benchmark had been the 70th percentile.

items.label: Percentile of civilian pay matched by enlisted RMC (up to 20 years of service)
DoD's historic target percentile

blocks.source: 14th QRMC (2025), as summarized by CRS IF10532, July 2026

blocks.text: What even RMC leaves out

RMC is conservative, because it skips several things worth real money. It excludes special pays and bonuses, which for a submarine nuke can be large: submarine duty pay, nuclear incentive pays and reenlistment bonuses. It excludes the government's contributions to the Thrift Savings Plan under the Blended Retirement System, up to 5 percent of basic pay once you contribute 5 percent yourself. It excludes education benefits like the GI Bill and tuition assistance, and it excludes health care.

Health care is the biggest blind spot for people leaving the service. Active-duty members pay no premium and essentially nothing out of pocket for TRICARE. Civilians usually pay a share of the premium and then face a deductible before insurance pays much. According to KFF's 2025 survey of employer health benefits, the average total premium for single coverage was $9,325 a year, of which workers paid $1,440 on average. The average deductible for single coverage, among workers with one, was $1,886. For a family plan, the worker's share of the premium averaged $6,850.

items.label: Average worker share of a single-coverage premium, per year
Average worker share of a family-coverage premium, per year
Average single-coverage deductible (workers with a deductible)

blocks.source: KFF, 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey

blocks.text: Then there is time off. Service members earn 30 days of leave a year from their first year, plus federal holidays when the schedule allows. Many entry-level civilian jobs start with far less paid vacation, and new hires at a plant running shifts may not get to choose when they take it. Leave you can't use underway is not worth much, so be honest about what you actually take. But if you are comparing offers, ask about paid time off in days, and price a missing week as a week of pay.

Those are averages, and individual plans swing widely. But the direction is clear: a sailor with a spouse and kids could easily spend several thousand dollars a year more on health care as a civilian, money that comes straight out of a paycheck that is already taxed.
Pricing a civilian offer honestly

The fix is to stop comparing headline numbers and compare what you keep. Strip both offers down to the same basis: after-tax money, after health costs, plus retirement money someone else puts in for you. It takes an hour with a pay stub and the offer letter, and it can change the decision.

blocks.title: Turning an offer letter into a real number
items: Start with the military side: total your basic pay, BAH, BAS and taxable special pays for the last 12 months from your LES. Add the government's TSP contributions.
Estimate federal tax on the taxable parts only. Remember that BAH and BAS are tax-free.
On the civilian side, start with salary and any guaranteed bonus. Ignore 'target' bonuses until you know how often they actually pay.
Subtract federal tax, state income tax for where the job is, and your share of health premiums. Add a realistic estimate of deductibles and copays.
Add the employer's retirement match only up to what you will actually contribute.
Compare the two after-tax, after-health totals. Then compare the hours it takes to earn each one.

blocks.text: Here is a rough version for the E-5 in the chart, using 2026 federal brackets and ignoring special pays and state tax. Basic pay plus BAH and BAS is about $82,809 in cash. Federal income tax on the basic pay is about $3,816, and Social Security and Medicare take about $3,822, leaving roughly $75,170. Now the $75,000 civilian offer: federal income tax of about $7,670, payroll taxes of about $5,738 and the average $1,440 single-coverage premium leave about $60,150. The 'fifty percent raise' turns into roughly $15,000 a year less in hand, before deductibles, state tax or any retirement match. Your own numbers will differ, which is exactly why you run them.

State taxes deserve their own line. Many service members keep their legal residence in a state with no income tax, which can carry into a civilian job only if they actually live and work there. A job in a state with an income tax takes a slice that never touched your military pay. Housing works the other way: BAH is set to roughly match local rents, while a civilian salary doesn't move just because rents near the plant are high.

Retirement matches also need a careful read. An offer might say the company matches 50 cents per dollar up to 6 percent of pay. That is worth 3 percent of salary, but only if you contribute the 6 percent. A match that vests over several years is worth less if you might leave before it vests, just as the BRS automatic contribution only became yours after two years of service.
The hourly truth

Annual pay hides the most important number: what you are paid per hour of your life. This is where many sailors' comparisons flip back toward the civilian job. On a rotating duty schedule, with long days in port and longer ones underway, the hours behind that $89,000 can be far more than 2,080, the standard 40 hours times 52 weeks.

Try the arithmetic with your own numbers. If your real average is 60 hours a week, the E-5's $89,148 works out to about $28.57 an hour. A civilian salary of $75,000 at 40 hours a week for 50 weeks, with two weeks off, works out to $37.50 an hour. On a per-hour basis the civilian job pays more, even if the yearly total is a bit lower. Shift work at a plant brings nights, weekends and overtime of its own, so ask what a normal month actually looks like rather than assuming 40 hours.

Combine the two lenses and the picture gets clearer. Using the take-home estimates from earlier, about $75,170 spread over 60-hour weeks all year is roughly $24 an hour kept. About $60,150 over 2,000 civilian hours is roughly $30 an hour kept. The Navy job pays more per year; the civilian job pays more per hour. Both statements are true at once.

This is not an argument for leaving or staying. It is an argument for measuring the thing you actually care about. If what you want is the most money per year, count total compensation. If what you want is time to build a business, a game or a channel, count dollars per hour and hours you control. Those can point in opposite directions, and only you know which one matters more.
What doesn't fit in the spreadsheet

Two more differences are real but hard to put a dollar sign on. The first is risk. Military pay arrives on the 1st and 15th no matter how the economy is doing; nobody gets laid off from a submarine because quarterly sales came in light. Civilian jobs, even good ones, can disappear in a downturn or a plant closure. Stable income is worth something, which is part of why economists treat a steady paycheck almost like a bond.

The second is freedom, and it cuts the other way. In uniform you cannot quit, cannot negotiate your hours, and cannot easily pick where you live. A civilian can walk across the street to a competitor for a raise, and that option has value even if it's never used. People who chafe at a rigid schedule often underrate how much that flexibility will be worth to them, especially if they plan to build something of their own on the side. Neither of these shows up in RMC, and neither should be ignored.
Where Navy nukes often land

For a nuclear-trained electrician, the most direct civilian path is the commercial nuclear power industry, which values Navy training and discipline. Operators of commercial reactors must earn a Nuclear Regulatory Commission license, which means more training and exams after hiring. The pay reflects that. In May 2023, the Bureau of Labor Statistics counted about 5,760 nuclear power reactor operators in the US, with a median annual wage of $120,350.

blocks.title: Annual pay, US nuclear power reactor operators, May 2023
blocks.note: Licensed reactor operators. Plant technician and other entry roles often start lower.
blocks.source: BLS, Occupational Employment and Wages, May 2023 (SOC 51-8011)

blocks.text: Not every Navy nuke walks straight into a licensed operator seat, and entry roles like technician or non-licensed operator often start lower. But the chart shows why the commercial nuclear path is a strong safety net: even the 10th percentile of licensed operators out-earns the E-5's RMC on a pre-tax basis, before overtime.
SkillBridge: the last 180 days

The Defense Department's SkillBridge program is built for exactly this transition. It lets service members spend up to their last 180 days of service working with an approved civilian employer in training, an apprenticeship or an internship. During that time you keep receiving your military pay and benefits, and the employer pays nothing for your time. Companies participate partly because it is a free, extended job interview.

The catch is approval. Participation requires your chain of command to sign off, with written authorization from a field-grade commander, and the command can say no if it can't spare you. On a submarine with tight manning and an operational schedule, that is a real constraint. Start the conversation early with your career counselor, look up approved partners in your field on the official SkillBridge site, and have a fallback if the timing doesn't work.

Used well, SkillBridge is also a way to test a career before betting on it. Six months inside a plant, a lab or a tech company will tell you more about whether you'd like the work than any recruiter's pitch. If the fit is wrong, you've learned that while still on military pay, and you can adjust before the paychecks stop.

Before deciding anything, pull your last 12 LES statements, total every line, and compare after-tax, after-health dollars and dollars per hour. Then ask your career counselor and the Fleet and Family Support Center's transition staff to check your numbers. Rules and rates here are as of 2026.

takeaways: A typical E-5's Regular Military Compensation was about $89,000 in 2026, not the $50,000 of basic pay.
BAH and BAS are tax-free, so compare civilian salaries to military pay on an after-tax basis.
Civilian health care costs real money: KFF found workers paid $1,440 a year on average for single coverage, $6,850 for family, plus deductibles.
Measure dollars per hour, not just dollars per year, especially if time for your own projects matters.
SkillBridge lets you work for a civilian employer during your last 180 days on full military pay, if your command approves.
