title: The $12,863-a-Year Machine in the Parking Lot
dek: The sticker price is the smallest part of what a car costs. AAA's 2026 numbers, the Federal Reserve's loan data and a CFPB study of servicemembers show where the money really goes, and why a paid-off car is a quiet superpower.

blocks.text: Walk past any base parking lot near payday and you can read a whole economy in the rows of vehicles: lifted trucks, new sedans with dealer plates, the occasional sports car with an E-3 sticker. Every one of them comes with a number most owners never calculate. In September 2026, AAA put it at **$12,863 a year**, or about $1,072 a month, for the average new vehicle. That is not the payment. That is the full cost of owning and running the car once you add everything up.

AAA has published its Your Driving Costs study every year since 1950, using top-selling models and assuming five years of ownership and 15,000 miles a year. The 2026 edition is worth reading closely, because it shows that the things people shop on, monthly payment and gas mileage, are not where most of the money goes.

blocks.title: What owning a new car costs per year, 2026
blocks.note: Fuel and maintenance converted from AAA's per-mile figures at 15,000 miles a year.
blocks.source: AAA, Your Driving Costs 2026

blocks.text: General education, not financial advice. Prices and rates are as of 2025 and 2026 and change often. Before a big purchase or loan, talk to your command financial specialist or the Personal Financial Manager at Fleet and Family Support.
The cost you never see

The biggest line on AAA's list is one that never shows up as a bill. **Depreciation**, the gap between what you pay for a car and what it is worth when you sell it, averaged $4,422 a year for new vehicles in the 2026 study. Nobody mails you an invoice for it. It simply disappears, quietly, every day the car exists, and you only feel it when you trade in and the dealer offers far less than you expected.

Depreciation is steepest early in a car's life, which is why the first owner of a new car absorbs the worst of it. It also explains why the cheapest car to own is usually not the one with the best gas mileage. AAA found that electric medium sedans had roughly twice the depreciation of gas models, which helped make them about 29 percent more expensive to own overall in that category even though charging costs ran about two-thirds below gas. The lesson is not about EVs. It is that the cost you cannot see tends to beat the one you can.

Fuel is the cost people feel most, because they pay it in person every week. In the 2026 study, regular gas averaged $4.152 a gallon, up 31.8 percent from the year before, and AAA's average new vehicle burned about 17 cents of fuel per mile. Vehicle type swings everything: AAA found half-ton pickups cost $1.10 a mile to own and operate, 48 cents more than small sedans, which adds up to about $7,191 more per year. Choosing a vehicle that fits what you actually do with it, rather than what you might someday do with it, is one of the biggest levers you have.

This is where owning a paid-off car becomes an advantage most people underrate. If you already own your vehicle outright, someone else, possibly you a few years ago, has already eaten the steepest part of the depreciation curve. Your remaining costs are insurance, fuel, maintenance and registration. The single most expensive decision available to you is not a repair. It is replacing a working car before you need to.
The payment trap

Dealers sell monthly payments, not cars, and it works because a monthly payment is a number your brain can compare to your paycheck. The total cost is a number it cannot feel. According to the Federal Reserve's consumer credit report, the average new-car loan from a finance company in the second quarter of 2026 was **$41,705**, stretched over 67 months. Commercial banks were charging about 7.5 percent on 60-month new-car loans in August 2026.

Run the math on a round example. Borrow $40,000 at 7.54 percent for 60 months and the payment is about $802 a month. Over five years you pay roughly **$8,100 in interest** alone, on top of the car, and you still face depreciation, insurance and fuel. Stretch the same loan to 72 or 84 months and the payment shrinks while the total interest grows, and you are more likely to spend years owing more than the car is worth.

items.label: Average new-car amount financed by finance companies, Q2 2026
Average loan length on those loans
Average 60-month new-car rate at commercial banks, Aug 2026

blocks.source: Federal Reserve, G.19 Consumer Credit, 2026

blocks.text: That last condition has a name: negative equity, or being underwater. It matters because life changes. A PCS move, a separation or a deployment can make you want to sell, and if you owe more than the car is worth, you either write a check for the difference or roll the leftover debt into your next loan. Rolling it over feels painless at the dealership. It is how people end up paying for two cars while driving one.
Why the lot outside the gate is a battlefield

Servicemembers are a favorite market for car lenders, and the data shows why. In January 2025, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau published a study comparing auto loans to servicemembers and civilians from 2018 to 2022. Servicemembers paid about the same prices for their vehicles but borrowed more to buy them. The average amount financed for a new vehicle was about $39,000, more than $2,200 above civilian borrowers.

The rest of the findings form a pattern. Servicemembers were less likely to make a cash down payment. They were more likely to roll negative equity from an old car into a new loan, and when they did, the average amount rolled in on new-car purchases was about $5,900. They paid more for add-ons such as extended warranties and service plans, averaging over $3,300 per new-vehicle loan. Their interest rates averaged 5.3 percent on new cars and 9.3 percent on used cars, slightly higher than civilians even after accounting for credit scores.

blocks.title: Servicemember auto loans: averages, 2018 to 2022
blocks.note: Approximate averages for new-vehicle loans; negative equity is the average among loans that included it.
blocks.source: CFPB, Auto Lending to Servicemembers, Jan 2025

blocks.text: The CFPB also cites research that young servicemembers are almost twice as likely as civilians their age to have taken out an auto loan. And the report contains the sharpest warning in this whole topic: a third of servicemembers with a vehicle loan who left the military after seven to 35 months of service went 90 days delinquent or defaulted within a year. The car that felt affordable on active duty pay became a crisis on a civilian budget.

None of this means car dealers near bases are villains or that buying a car is a mistake. It means the default path, walking onto a lot with no preapproval, focusing on the payment and saying yes to the add-ons in the finance office, is expensive, and young sailors walk it more often than anyone. The fix is not willpower. It is a process you follow before you ever set foot on the lot.
The paid-off car strategy

Here is the reframe. A car payment is a habit, not a law of nature. The CFPB found the average servicemember new-car payment was over $644 a month. If you own your car outright and simply set aside that same amount in your own account every month for four years, you end up with about $30,900 before any interest. That is enough to buy your next car in cash, or to fund a business, a transition out of the Navy or a big chunk of a house down payment.

The person paying $644 to a lender and the person paying $644 to themselves have the same monthly budget. The difference is where the money ends up four years later. One has a car that is worth much less than they paid. The other has the cash and still has a car. Keeping a reliable, paid-off vehicle running for an extra three or four years is one of the highest-return financial moves available to a young person, and it looks like doing nothing.

Doing nothing does require a little upkeep. Follow the maintenance schedule, because the cheapest repair is the one that never happens. Remember too that vehicle repairs were the single most common major unexpected expense in the Federal Reserve's 2025 survey of household finances: 30 percent of adults had one in the prior year. An older car paired with an emergency fund is a far better deal than a newer car paired with a payment.
Insurance: the line item that punishes youth

One line in AAA's breakdown deserves an asterisk for anyone in their early twenties. The $2,098 insurance figure assumes a full-coverage policy for a driver with more than six years behind the wheel and a clean record. A 20-year-old does not fit that profile, and insurers price young drivers higher because, statistically, they crash more. Your premium can easily be the biggest cash cost of keeping a paid-off car on the road.

That makes insurance the place where a little effort pays the most. Get quotes from several companies every year or two rather than renewing on autopilot, and ask specifically about military and good-driver discounts. Consider a higher deductible once your emergency fund can cover it, because a deductible you can pay from savings is a cost you no longer need to rent from the insurer. And as your car ages, check whether collision coverage still makes sense: when the car is worth only a few thousand dollars, you may be paying a meaningful share of its value every year to insure against losing it.

blocks.title: Feels cheap versus is cheap

left.head: Feels cheap
items: Low monthly payment on a long loan
Zero down, drive it home today
Rolling the old loan into the new one
Bundled warranty for a few dollars a month

right.head: Is cheap
items: Keeping a reliable paid-off car longer
A down payment and a short loan
Selling the old car before buying
Saving for repairs in your own account

blocks.text: Owning a car when you are underway

Submarine life adds its own twist: your car may sit for weeks or months while you are gone. A car that does not move still costs money. Insurance keeps running, registration keeps expiring and batteries quietly die. Before a long underway or deployment, decide who has a key, how it will be started or kept on a battery maintainer, and where it will be parked safely.

Insurance is worth a phone call. Many insurers let you reduce coverage on a vehicle in long-term storage, but the rules depend on your state and your lender, and dropping liability on a registered car can be illegal. Ask what your options are rather than canceling anything on your own. If you lease, the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act lets you end an auto lease without early termination penalties in certain cases, including deployments of 180 days or more, according to the CFPB. If you finance, check before a move overseas: many lenders will not let a financed car leave the country.
A process for the next car

Eventually, your current car will need replacing, and when it does the goal is to buy it on your terms instead of the dealer's. AAA's own buying advice lines up with the CFPB data: get preapproved by a bank or credit union before you talk financing, and keep the vehicle price, the loan rate and your trade-in as three separate negotiations. Dealers prefer to blend them into one monthly number because blended numbers are harder to compare.

blocks.title: Before you sign anything
items: Price the total cost: payment, insurance quote, fuel, maintenance and registration for a year.
Get preapproved at a bank or credit union so you know your real rate.
Negotiate the out-the-door price first, then financing, then the trade-in, separately.
Decline add-ons in the finance office; you can research and buy most of them later.
Never roll negative equity into a new loan if you can avoid it.
Sleep on it. A deal that vanishes overnight was built on pressure, not value.

blocks.text: Cars are not just transportation for a lot of young people. They are freedom, status and a reward for surviving a hard stretch of life, and those are real things. But a vehicle is a depreciating asset, and the money that flows through it every year is enough to build an emergency fund, max out a Roth or seed a business. You do not have to drive a beater forever. You just have to know what the shiny one actually costs, and decide whether it is worth more to you than what that money could become.

takeaways: AAA puts the full cost of owning a new car at $12,863 a year in 2026; depreciation is the biggest piece.
A paid-off car has already absorbed its steepest depreciation; replacing it early is the most expensive move you can make.
Servicemembers tend to borrow more, put less down and buy more add-ons than civilians, according to the CFPB.
Pay yourself the car payment: $644 a month for four years is about $30,900 for your next car or your future.
Get preapproved, negotiate price, rate and trade-in separately, and skip the add-ons.

title: Roth or Traditional? The Math Says It's a Tie, Until It Isn't
dek: Paying tax now or paying it later sounds like a huge choice. Run the numbers and the two come out identical, except for a few levers that happen to matter a lot to a young sailor. The 2026 rules, worked out with real arithmetic.

blocks.text: Take $1,000 of pay and run two experiments. In the first, you put it in a traditional account before tax. It grows tenfold over the decades to $10,000, and when you withdraw it you pay 12 percent tax, leaving $8,800. In the second, you pay the 12 percent first, leaving $880, which goes into a Roth account. It grows the same tenfold to $8,800, and you withdraw it tax-free. Same answer, to the dollar.

That result surprises most people, because the internet treats Roth versus traditional like a sports rivalry. One camp says never pay tax before you have to. The other says tax-free growth is the best deal in finance. The arithmetic says that, on its own, neither door is better. What decides it is a small set of details: what rate you pay now, what rate you will really pay later, and a few rules that make one account more flexible than the other. Those details tilt hard in one direction for a 20-year-old on a Navy paycheck, and then often tilt back the other way later in a career.

This is general education using the 2026 federal rules, not personal financial advice. Tax law changes, and your own situation has details this article can't see, so run your numbers with a command financial specialist or the base financial counselor before you change your elections.
Why the two doors lead to the same room

The tie in the opening is not a coincidence. It is the commutative property of multiplication, the same rule that says 2 × 3 equals 3 × 2. The traditional route is: money, times growth, times (1 minus the tax rate). The Roth route is: money, times (1 minus the tax rate), times growth. The order of the multiplication changes; the product does not. It doesn't matter whether growth is tenfold or fiftyfold, or whether the account sits for ten years or forty.

blocks.title: Same $1,000 of pay, two doors (12% tax both times, tenfold growth)

left.head: Traditional
items: $1,000 goes in before tax
Grows to $10,000
Pay 12% on the way out: $1,200
You keep $8,800

right.head: Roth
items: Pay 12% now: $120
$880 goes in
Grows to $8,800
Withdraw tax-free: you keep $8,800

blocks.text: So the whole debate collapses into one question: is the tax rate on the way in higher or lower than the tax rate on the way out? If you pay 12 percent now and would pay 22 percent later, Roth wins. If you pay 24 percent now and 10 percent later, traditional wins. Everything else is a footnote, but a few footnotes are big enough to change the answer, and we will get to them.

One trap hides in the equal-rate example: it assumes you invest the tax savings. A traditional contribution lowers your tax bill today. If that saved tax gets spent on a new headset rather than invested, the traditional route quietly falls behind. Roth forces the issue, because the tax is already paid. For people who don't trust themselves to invest the difference, that is a real behavioral point in Roth's favor.
The rate you pay now, and the rate you pay later

Federal income tax uses brackets. Each slice of taxable income is taxed at its own rate, and only the dollars above a threshold pay the higher rate. For 2026, after the standard deduction of $16,100 for a single filer, the brackets look like this.

blocks.title: 2026 federal brackets, single filer: where each rate starts
blocks.note: Taxable income is income after the $16,100 standard deduction. Only dollars above each threshold pay that rate.
blocks.source: IRS, IR-2025-103, 2026 inflation adjustments (Oct 2025)

blocks.text: The rate that matters for a contribution today is your *marginal* rate, the rate on your last dollars of income, because those are the dollars a traditional contribution removes from your taxable pay. The rate that matters later is subtler. Retirement withdrawals from a traditional account stack up from the bottom: the first $16,100 (in 2026 terms, adjusted for inflation each year) is covered by the standard deduction and taxed at zero, the next slice at 10 percent, then 12 percent. If traditional money is your main retirement income, its average tax rate can be well below the marginal rate you avoided when you put it in.

Here is a concrete case using 2026 brackets. Suppose in retirement you pull $40,000 a year from a traditional account and have no other income. Taxable income is $23,900. The tax is $1,240 on the first $12,400 plus $1,380 on the next $11,500, for $2,620 in all, about 6.6 percent of the withdrawal. Someone who saved those dollars at a 22 or 24 percent marginal rate made a clear profit by choosing traditional. Someone who saved them at 12 percent came out modestly ahead too, but by much less, and Social Security, a pension or Roth conversions can push later withdrawals into higher brackets. This is why the standard advice is: Roth when your bracket is low, traditional when it is high.
Why a sailor's tax bill is unusually small

Here is where military pay changes the math. A big part of a sailor's compensation is never taxed at all. The Congressional Research Service, using Defense Department figures for January 2026, put a typical E-5's Regular Military Compensation at about $89,148 a year. Only the basic pay part of that, $49,965, is taxable. Housing and food allowances, worth about $32,844 together, are tax-free, and CRS values that tax break alone at around $6,339 a year.

items.label: Example E-5 Regular Military Compensation, 2026
The part that is taxable basic pay
Marginal federal bracket on that basic pay alone, after the 2026 standard deduction

blocks.source: CRS, Defense Primer: Regular Military Compensation (IF10532, July 2026); IRS IR-2025-103

blocks.text: Run that E-5's basic pay through the 2026 brackets. After the $16,100 standard deduction, taxable income is $33,865. The tax comes to about $3,816. That is a 12 percent marginal rate, and roughly 4 percent of the full compensation package. Special pays, such as submarine duty pay and nuclear incentive pays, are generally taxable and can push the number up, and a large reenlistment bonus landing in one year can push some income into the 22 percent bracket. But for most junior sailors, the marginal rate is about as low as it will ever be while working full time.

What about the future tax code itself? Roth fans often argue that rates must rise someday to pay for federal debt, so locking in today's rate is a safe bet. Maybe. But the honest answer is that nobody knows. The top federal rate was 70 percent in 1980 and 28 percent in 1988, and brackets have been rewritten many times since. Betting your whole retirement on one forecast of Congress is not a plan. What you can know is your own likely path: a junior enlisted income now, and probably a higher one later. That forecast is far more reliable than any guess about Washington, and it is the one to lean on.

Now picture the same person later. A civilian nuclear plant operator, the career many Navy nukes move into, earned a median of about $120,000 in May 2023 according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Without tax-free allowances, that salary sits in the 22 or 24 percent bracket. So the classic pattern fits: Roth while in uniform, when the rate on the way in is 12 percent, and a serious look at traditional later, when the rate on the way in is 22 or 24.

Combat zone pay is the extreme version. Pay earned in a designated combat zone can be excluded from income, and contributions made from it go into the TSP as tax-exempt money. In the traditional TSP those contributions come out tax-free later, but their earnings are taxed. In the Roth TSP, both the money and its growth come out tax-free if you meet the Roth rules. Submariners rarely qualify, so treat this as a bonus to ask about if it ever shows up on your Leave and Earnings Statement, not a plan.
The footnotes that can flip the answer
If the only question were tax rates, this would be a short article. A few other rules break the tie, and most of them favor Roth for someone young.

items: **The bigger box.** The 2026 limit for your own TSP contributions is $24,500, traditional and Roth combined. A Roth dollar is an after-tax dollar, so $24,500 in Roth holds more real spending power than $24,500 in traditional, which still owes tax. This only matters if you are close to the limit.

**Flexibility.** With a Roth IRA (2026 limit: $7,500), the amounts you contributed, not the earnings, can generally be withdrawn at any time without tax or penalty. That makes it a backstop, though raiding it costs you decades of growth.
**No forced withdrawals.** Since 2024, Roth money inside workplace plans like the TSP is no longer subject to required minimum distributions during the owner's lifetime. Traditional balances are.
**Tax diversification.** Nobody knows tax rates in 2066. Having both kinds of money lets you choose each year which bucket to draw from, keeping taxable income in a low bracket.

**A point for traditional: the Saver's Credit.** Traditional contributions lower your adjusted gross income. For 2026 a single filer with AGI up to $40,250 may qualify for a credit worth 10 to 50 percent of up to $2,000 of retirement contributions, Roth or traditional. Lowering AGI can move you into a better tier. Full-time students and people claimed as dependents don't qualify, and the credit is scheduled to become a government match starting in 2027.

blocks.text: One thing that is not a choice: the government's automatic and matching contributions under the Blended Retirement System always go into the traditional side of the TSP. So even a sailor who elects 100 percent Roth ends up with some traditional money. That is tax diversification you get for free.

And since January 28, 2026, the TSP lets participants convert traditional money to Roth inside the plan. The converted amount is added to your taxable income for that year, and the TSP says you must pay that tax from other money, not from the amount being converted. For a sailor in the 12 percent bracket with a modest traditional balance built from matching, a small conversion in a low-income year is worth asking a counselor about. A huge conversion in one year can push you into a higher bracket and defeat the point.
A simple way to decide

blocks.title: Choosing your split, in order
items: Contribute at least 5% of basic pay so you get the full BRS match. The match is worth more than any Roth-versus-traditional optimization.
Find your marginal bracket: basic pay plus taxable special pays, minus the standard deduction, against the 2026 table.
If you are in the 10 or 12 percent bracket, lean Roth. If you are in 22 percent or higher, weigh traditional more heavily.
Check whether a traditional contribution would drop your AGI into a better Saver's Credit tier. If so, run both versions.
Split if unsure. A 50/50 split is never the worst answer, and it buys flexibility.
Revisit after any big change: promotion, bonus, separation or a civilian job offer.

blocks.text: Picture two sailors who each put $300 a month into the TSP for six years in uniform, then leave for civilian jobs paying in the 22 percent bracket. The first chooses all traditional the whole time, saving 12 cents of tax per dollar now and owing tax on every dollar later. The second chooses Roth in uniform and switches to traditional in the civilian job. The second sailor paid tax at 12 percent on the Navy years, when that rate was cheap, and avoided it at 22 percent on the civilian years, when it was expensive. Neither made a reckless choice, but the second matched each dollar to the cheaper year to pay tax. That matching, done consistently over a career, is the entire game.

Notice what is missing from that list: predicting the stock market, picking the perfect fund, or guessing what Congress will do in 2050. The Roth-versus-traditional decision is mostly a bet about your own future income, and you know more about that than any pundit does. If the plan is to leave the Navy for a six-figure civilian job, you are probably earning less taxable income now than you ever will again in your working life.

The deeper lesson is about how to read money advice in general. Whenever two options are argued about endlessly, check whether they are mathematically the same thing wearing different clothes. Often the loud debate is about the clothes, and the real decision is a single number you can look up: here, today's bracket versus tomorrow's.

These are 2026 federal rules. State taxes, special pays, bonuses and future law changes all affect the answer. Before changing your TSP elections or opening an IRA, check your LES and sit down with your command financial specialist or the Fleet and Family Support Center's financial counselor. It costs nothing.

takeaways: At equal tax rates, Roth and traditional produce exactly the same money; the order of multiplication doesn't matter.
The real question is your marginal rate today versus your effective rate on withdrawals later.
Tax-free BAH and BAS keep many sailors in the 12% bracket, which is a strong case for Roth while in uniform.
Get the full 5% BRS match first; the government's money always lands in traditional, giving you both kinds.
Revisit the split when your income jumps, especially in a 22% or 24% civilian job.

title: Your Tax Refund Is Not a Bonus
dek: Brackets, withholding and the combat-zone exclusion, explained for a sailor filing his own return. The rules as of tax year 2026, and why the biggest refund is usually a sign of a mistake.

blocks.text: Every spring, a familiar scene plays out in barracks and berthing: somebody gets a fat IRS deposit and treats it like a gift. New headphones, a weekend trip, maybe a down payment on a truck. In the 2026 filing season the average refund was **$3,273**, according to IRS figures through early May. It feels like free money. It isn't. It is your own pay, lent to the federal government for up to sixteen months at zero percent interest, and handed back to you as if it were a reward.

Taxes are one of those topics nobody actually teaches. You learn reactor theory in a classroom with a qualified instructor, but you learn taxes from a guy in your division who is fairly sure you can write off your energy drinks. The system is less mysterious than it looks. Once you understand three ideas, brackets, withholding and what counts as income, most of the anxiety disappears. Military pay adds a few twists, including one of the most generous breaks in the tax code.

This is general education, not tax advice. Figures are for tax year 2026 (returns filed in 2027) unless noted. Rules change every year, so confirm your situation with your base tax center, your command's finance office or a MilTax consultant before you act.
Brackets: the myth of the raise that costs you

The most common tax misconception is that moving into a higher bracket can make you take home less. People turn down overtime or worry about a bonus pushing them over a line. That is not how it works. The US uses **marginal** rates: each slice of income is taxed at its own rate, and only the dollars above a threshold get the higher rate. Crossing into the next bracket changes nothing about the dollars below it.

Think of it as a set of buckets stacked on top of each other. Your income fills the bottom bucket first, then spills into the next. For 2026, a single filer's first $16,100 is covered by the standard deduction and is not taxed at all. The next $12,400 of taxable income is taxed at 10 percent. Taxable income above that, up to $50,400, is taxed at 12 percent. Only taxable income beyond $50,400 sees 22 percent.

blocks.title: Where each 2026 federal rate stops (single filer)
blocks.note: Taxable income above $640,600 is taxed at 37%. Thresholds apply after the $16,100 standard deduction.
blocks.source: IRS, tax year 2026 inflation adjustments (Rev. Proc. 2025-32), 2025

blocks.text: Here is a worked example with round numbers. Suppose you had $40,000 of taxable wages in 2026 and took the standard deduction. Subtract $16,100 and you have $23,900 of taxable income. The first $12,400 is taxed at 10 percent, which is $1,240. The remaining $11,500 is taxed at 12 percent, which is $1,380. Total federal income tax: **$2,620**.

items.label: 2026 standard deduction, single filer
Marginal rate in the example: tax on the next dollar earned
Effective rate in the example: $2,620 of tax on $40,000

blocks.source: IRS 2026 inflation adjustments; example calculation

blocks.text: Two numbers matter here, and they are different. Your **marginal rate** is 12 percent: an extra $1,000 of taxable pay costs you $120 in federal income tax. Your **effective rate** is about 6.6 percent: the share of your total wages that actually went to federal income tax. The marginal rate is what to think about when you weigh extra income. The effective rate is what you actually pay. Social Security (6.2 percent) and Medicare (1.45 percent) come out separately, and those are flat, not bracketed.
What counts as income when you wear a uniform

Military pay is a mix of taxable and tax-free money, and the split is bigger than most junior sailors realize. According to the IRS Armed Forces' Tax Guide (Publication 3), basic pay is taxable. So are most special and incentive pays, including career sea pay, submarine duty pay and enlistment and reenlistment bonuses. That nuclear bonus that looked enormous on paper was taxed like any other wage.

Living allowances are a different story. Basic Allowance for Housing and Basic Allowance for Subsistence are excluded from gross income, along with moving allowances, many travel allowances and in-kind benefits like medical care. That is why the wages on your W-2 are lower than what your LES shows you were paid over the year. It also means that comparing military pay to a civilian salary by looking only at taxable wages undersells the job.

State taxes add another layer. Under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, you generally keep your legal state of residence when the Navy moves you somewhere else on orders. If your domicile is a state with no personal income tax, such as Texas or Washington, your military pay is not taxed by the state where you happen to be stationed. Changing your state of legal residence has consequences, so check before you do it, not after.

One practical habit follows from all this: read your W-2 against your LES. If box 1 looks too high, a tax-free allowance or a combat zone month may have been coded wrong. If your state withholding shows a state you never meant to claim, that is worth a visit to finance. Errors on military pay records are not rare, and the person with the strongest incentive to catch them is you. Finding a mistake in February is a short conversation. Finding it after the IRS sends a letter is a much longer one.
The combat zone exclusion, and the catch for submariners

Now for the generous part. If you are enlisted and serve in a designated combat zone, your active duty pay for that month is excluded from federal income tax. Not reduced. Excluded. Publication 3 is explicit that serving in a combat zone for any part of a single day counts as service for the entire month. Officers get a capped version; for enlisted members and warrant officers the exclusion covers all of that month's military pay.

Some of the details are surprisingly powerful. A reenlistment bonus is excluded if the reenlistment or voluntary extension happens in a month you served in a combat zone. Imminent danger or hostile fire pay is excluded. Leave you earn during combat zone months can be excluded when you later cash it in. You do not have to file anything special: the exclusion should already be reflected on your W-2, which should leave the excluded pay out of box 1.

blocks.title: How the exclusion works, month by month
items: DoD designates combat zones by executive order or law; the IRS lists them in Publication 3.
If you serve in a designated area for any part of a day, that whole month qualifies.
For enlisted members, all military pay earned that month is excluded from federal income tax.
Finance applies the exclusion; your W-2 should already leave that pay out of taxable wages.
You also get extra time to file and pay: at least 180 days after you leave the zone.

blocks.text: The catch for submariners is geography. The combat zones are specific places, such as the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, the Gulf of Oman, the Gulf of Aden and part of the Arabian Sea, plus certain land areas and areas certified for direct support. A boat on patrol somewhere else does not qualify just because the deployment is long, hard and secret. Whether any particular month counts is decided by where you actually were, and that determination comes from the chain of command and finance, not from you.

So do not build a budget on hoping for tax-free months. Treat any combat zone exclusion as a windfall when it shows up on your LES. If it does, two questions are worth asking your finance office: whether a reenlistment decision could be timed into a qualifying month, and whether Roth contributions to the TSP make sense while your pay is tax-free. Both can be worth a lot of money, and both depend on details you should confirm rather than assume.
Why a low bracket is an opportunity

Here is the reframe most people miss. At 20, with a modest taxable wage and tax-free housing and food allowances, you are likely in the lowest tax brackets you will ever see as a working adult. If your plans work out, a civilian nuclear job, a business, a channel that pays, your income later should be higher, and so might your rate. That makes right now an unusually cheap time to pay tax on money you are setting aside for the future.

This is the logic behind Roth accounts, including the Roth option in the TSP. With a Roth, you pay tax on the money today and qualified withdrawals in retirement come out tax-free, including the growth. With a traditional account you skip the tax today and pay it on withdrawal, at whatever rate applies to you then. Nobody knows future tax law. But if you are taxed at 12 percent on the margin now and expect to earn more later, locking in today's rate is a reasonable bet, and it is one of the few tax decisions where a young sailor has a real edge over an older one.

The same thinking applies to timing. A bonus, a reenlistment or a big side-business year changes which bracket your last dollars fall into. You cannot control everything, but you can notice when a year is unusually low or high and ask whether it changes the right move. That habit of asking, not any single trick, is what separates people who pay what they owe from people who pay extra out of confusion.
Withholding: the dial you actually control

Withholding is the tax taken out of each paycheck in advance. Your employer, in this case DFAS, estimates your annual tax from your W-4 and sends a slice of each check to the IRS. In April you settle up: if too much was withheld, you get a refund; if too little, you owe. A refund is not a sign that you did well on your taxes. It is a sign that the withholding estimate was too high.

There is a reasonable case for a small refund. Owing a large amount in April is stressful, and if you owe enough you can face an underpayment penalty. But a refund of several thousand dollars means several hundred dollars a month that could have been sitting in your emergency fund or your TSP. The IRS Tax Withholding Estimator is a free online tool that compares your year-to-date pay and withholding with your expected tax and tells you how to adjust your W-4. Run it after any big change, like a promotion, a bonus or a move.

There is a behavioral argument for refunds too, and it deserves an honest hearing: some people only save when the money is forced out of reach. But you can get the same effect without the interest-free loan. An allotment that moves a fixed amount to a separate savings account every payday does what an oversized refund does, except the money is yours all year and can earn interest while it waits.

blocks.title: Two ways to think about a refund

left.head: Common view
items: A refund is a bonus
Bigger refund means you did taxes right
Owing anything is a failure
Bracket jumps can shrink your take-home pay

right.head: What is actually happening
items: A refund is your own money returned without interest
A big refund means too much was withheld
Owing a small amount means withholding was close
Only the dollars above each threshold get the higher rate

blocks.text: Filing from a steel tube

Deployments and underway periods make deadlines awkward, and the tax code recognizes it. Publication 3 says that if you are on military duty outside the United States and Puerto Rico on the due date, you get an automatic two-month extension to file, though interest still runs on any tax you owe. Combat zone service brings a longer extension. Even so, the simplest move is to file early, before you go, or right after you get back.

You also do not need to pay for software. MilTax, run through Military OneSource, offers free tax software and free consultations with tax professionals for active duty members, and covers a federal return and up to five state returns. Many bases also run volunteer tax centers in the spring. A paid preparer is not wrong, but a refund-anticipation product that charges you to get your own money a few days early is a bad deal.

blocks.title: A once-a-year tax routine
items: In January, check your LES and confirm your state of legal residence is correct.
When your W-2 arrives on myPay, compare box 1 with your LES and look for combat zone months.
File with MilTax or a base tax center, and pick direct deposit.
Run the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator and adjust your W-4 if the refund was large.
Send the refund straight to savings or investments before it turns into stuff.

blocks.text: The bigger lesson is about attention. Taxes reward people who understand the system just enough to avoid expensive mistakes: they file on time, keep the tax-free parts of their pay tax-free, and do not let thousands of dollars ride along with the government for a year. None of that requires genius. It requires one evening a year and the willingness to read your own pay documents. For a sailor who can trace a reactor plant on a whiteboard, a 1040 is not the hard part. Caring about it is.

takeaways: Tax brackets are marginal: crossing a threshold only raises the rate on the dollars above it.
BAH and BAS are not taxable; base pay, sea pay, sub pay and bonuses are.
For enlisted members, all military pay for any month with combat zone service is excluded, but most submarine patrols are not in designated zones, so treat it as a windfall.
A big refund means too much was withheld; use the IRS Withholding Estimator to adjust your W-4.
File free through MilTax or a base tax center, and confirm anything unusual with your finance office.

title: The Retirement Deal Most Sailors Don't Understand
dek: Under the Blended Retirement System, the government matches part of what you save, but only if you know the rules. How the TSP and BRS work, as of 2026.

blocks.text: In 2022 the Defense Department asked thousands of active-duty members a basic question about how their own retirement system works. Among junior enlisted members, only 41% got it right. Across all ranks it was 48%. Those numbers come from the Pentagon's annual report to Congress on the financial literacy of the force, based on the 2022 Status of Forces Survey.

That's a strange gap, because the Blended Retirement System is one of the few places in life where someone will hand you free money for doing something that's good for you anyway. The catch is that the free money has conditions, deadlines and a couple of traps. This is a plain-language tour of how it works under the rules in effect in 2026. Rules change, so treat this as a map, then confirm the details for your own situation with your command financial specialist or the personal financial counselors at Fleet and Family Support.

items.label: Junior enlisted who answered the BRS knowledge question correctly (2022)
All active-duty members who answered it correctly

blocks.source: OUSD(P&R), Financial Literacy and Preparedness of Members of the Armed Forces: 2022 Status of Forces Survey (Dec 2023)

blocks.text: From all-or-nothing to portable

For decades, military retirement worked like a cliff. Under the legacy "High-36" system, serve 20 years and you earned a pension for life: 2.5% of your average highest 36 months of basic pay for every year served, so 50% at 20 years. Leave at year 12 and you walked away with no retirement benefit at all. Since the large majority of people who join leave long before 20 years, most of the force was serving under a retirement plan they would never collect.

The Blended Retirement System, which took effect on January 1, 2018, kept a pension but made it smaller and added a savings account that goes with you whenever you leave. Everyone who first entered service on or after that date is automatically in BRS. Members already serving with fewer than 12 years had the option to switch during 2018. If you enlisted any time after 2017, this is your system.

items: **A smaller pension at 20 years:** 2.0% of your highest-36-month average basic pay per year served, instead of 2.5%.
**TSP contributions from the government:** an automatic 1% of basic pay plus matching of up to 4% more.
**Continuation pay:** a one-time mid-career bonus for agreeing to serve four more years.
**A lump-sum option at retirement:** trade part of your early pension checks for cash up front.

blocks.text: The TSP piece is the one that matters for almost everyone, because it pays out whether or not you ever reach 20. The Thrift Savings Plan is the government's version of a civilian 401(k): an investment account inside your name, funded from your paycheck, with the government adding money on top.
The free money, exactly

Here are the rules, as published by the TSP and the Defense Department. About 60 days after you enter service, the government starts putting 1% of your basic pay into your TSP every pay period, even if you contribute nothing. That 1% vests, meaning it becomes permanently yours, once you have two years of service. After your second full year, the government also starts matching what you put in: dollar for dollar on the first 3% of basic pay, then 50 cents per dollar on the next 2%. Matching money is yours immediately.

Add it up and the math is simple. Put in 5% of basic pay and the government puts in 5% too: the automatic 1% plus a 4% match. Put in more than 5% and there's no extra match, though the extra savings still count. Put in less and you leave part of the match unclaimed. Both the automatic and matching contributions stop after 26 years of service.

blocks.title: What the government adds, by what you contribute
blocks.note: After two years of service. Before then, only the automatic 1% applies.
blocks.source: TSP booklet TSPBK34; Air Force benefits BRS fact sheet (reviewed Jan 2026)

blocks.text: Since October 1, 2020, new members are automatically enrolled to contribute 5% of basic pay, up from 3% before that date. That default was chosen on purpose: it's exactly the amount that captures the full match. If you never touched your TSP election, you're probably at 5% already. If you lowered it or stopped it to free up cash, you may be turning down part of your pay.

The choice of default isn't a small detail. In a well-known 2001 study, economists Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea tracked a large company that switched its 401(k) from opt-in to automatic enrollment. Participation rose sharply, and many new employees simply kept whatever contribution rate and fund the company had pre-selected, even though few people had picked that combination when they had to choose it themselves. People treat the default as advice. The military's 5% default is a good one, but it's still worth deciding on purpose rather than by inertia, especially as your pay grows.

To make that concrete, take an E-5 with more than three years of service. Under the 2026 pay table, monthly basic pay is about $3,776. Contributing 5% means roughly $189 a month comes out of the paycheck, and the government adds another $189. Over a year that's about $2,266 from the sailor and about $2,266 from the government, a little over $4,500 going to work. Contribute nothing, and the government's share drops to the automatic 1%, about $38 a month.

The match is effectively an instant 100% return on the first 3% of basic pay you contribute and 50% on the next 2%. No stock, fund or side hustle reliably offers that. Whatever else you decide, understand what you give up by contributing less than 5%.
Where the money actually goes

Contributions don't just sit there; they buy into one or more TSP funds. The G Fund holds special government securities and can't lose value, but it grows slowly. The F Fund holds bonds. The C Fund tracks the S&P 500, the S Fund holds smaller US companies, and the I Fund holds international stocks. The Lifecycle, or L, Funds are pre-built mixes of the other five, set to a target year. If you were auto-enrolled and never chose, your money goes into the L Fund matched to your age, which starts out heavy on stocks and shifts toward safer assets as that date approaches.

The TSP is also unusually cheap. Its board reported net expenses of about 0.034% for 2025, meaning roughly 34 cents a year on every $1,000. Most retail mutual funds charge many times that. Low costs matter because fees, like returns, compound over decades. The companion article on index funds and compounding explains why that matters more than it sounds.
Traditional or Roth

Every dollar you contribute goes in one of two tax doors. **Traditional** contributions come out before federal income tax, which lowers your taxable pay now, but you pay tax on the money and its growth when you withdraw it in retirement. **Roth** contributions come out after tax, so they don't lower today's bill, but qualified withdrawals, including all the growth, come out tax-free later. To qualify, at least five years must have passed since your first Roth contribution and you generally need to be 59½ or older.

The usual way people reason about it: if you expect to be in a higher tax bracket later than you are now, paying the tax now (Roth) tends to look better. Young enlisted members often have relatively low taxable income, partly because allowances such as BAH and BAS aren't taxed. That's not a rule, just the logic. You can split contributions between both, and it's worth running your numbers with a financial counselor rather than guessing.

There's one military-specific wrinkle. Pay earned in a designated combat zone is tax-exempt, and TSP contributions from that pay follow special rules. Traditional contributions from tax-exempt pay don't count against the normal yearly limit, though they do count against a larger overall cap. If you ever earn combat-zone pay, ask finance how it interacts with your TSP.
Limits, cliffs and traps

For 2026, the IRS caps your own traditional plus Roth contributions at $24,500, with a total limit of $72,000 including tax-exempt and government contributions. Few junior sailors will hit that, but anyone who does should know about the front-loading trap. The TSP warns that if you max out early in the year, your contributions stop, and the government's matching stops with them for the rest of the year. Spreading contributions across every pay period keeps the match flowing.

items: **The two-year cliff:** leave service before two years and the automatic 1% contributions are forfeited. Your own money and any matching stay yours.

**The 90-day exit:** members who were auto-enrolled can ask for a refund of their own automatic contributions within 90 days of the first one. The government's automatic 1% stays in the account; matching on the refunded money is forfeited.
**Cashing out early:** money pulled out before retirement age usually means income tax plus, in most cases, an extra 10% early-withdrawal tax. That can wipe out years of growth.
**Pay raises:** your contribution is a percentage, so it rises automatically with promotions and annual raises, like the 3.8% raise on January 1, 2026.

blocks.text: When you leave the military, the TSP comes with you. You can leave the money in the plan, keep investing it at the same low cost, or roll it into another retirement account. What you can't do is keep receiving government contributions once you're out.
The pension still matters

blocks.title: BRS milestones for someone who joined after 2017
items: ~Day 60
Auto-enrolled at 5%; government's automatic 1% begins
2 years
Automatic 1% vests; matching begins
7–12 years
Continuation pay window, for a four-year commitment
20 years
Pension: 2.0% × years served × high-36 average basic pay
26 years
Automatic and matching contributions end
Retirement
Option to take 25% or 50% of early pension value as a lump sum

blocks.text: For those who do stay 20, the pension is still the biggest single asset in the package: a monthly payment for life, adjusted for inflation. Under BRS, 20 years earns 40% of the high-36 average instead of the legacy 50%. Continuation pay is a mid-career offer between roughly the 7th and 12th year of service in exchange for four more years. For 2026, the published active-duty amount is 2.5 times monthly basic pay, though the timing and amount can vary by service and year. At retirement, you can choose to receive a lump sum of 25% or 50% of the pension's discounted value, in exchange for smaller monthly checks until full Social Security retirement age, usually 67, when the full pension resumes.

The lump sum is a classic test of how people value now versus later. Because the government calculates it with a discount rate, the cash up front is generally worth less than the monthly payments you give up. It can still make sense for some people. It's the kind of decision worth making slowly, with real numbers in front of you.
The real point of BRS

The deeper change in BRS is philosophical. The old system rewarded only the minority who stayed for a full career. The new one assumes, realistically, that most people serve for a while and then do something else, and it makes sure they leave with something. A sailor who serves six years, contributes 5% throughout and lets it sit invested could walk out with a meaningful head start on retirement, money that under the old system simply wouldn't exist.

That shifts responsibility, too. A pension needs nothing from you except time. The TSP needs you to contribute, pick sensible funds, and not raid it the first time you change jobs. The system gives you the tools; the 41% question is whether people know they're holding them.

Check your Leave and Earnings Statement for your TSP contribution percentage and the government contribution lines. If anything looks off, or you're not sure which BRS rules apply to you, ask your command financial specialist or base finance office. These are the 2026 rules; Congress and the TSP can and do change them.

takeaways: If you joined after 2017, you're in BRS: a smaller pension plus government TSP contributions you keep even if you leave before 20.
Contributing 5% of basic pay captures the full match; the government then adds 5% as well.
The automatic 1% vests at two years; matching starts after two years and is yours immediately.
Don't front-load to the yearly limit, or you lose matching for the rest of the year.
Rules change: confirm yours on your LES and with a command financial specialist.

title: No Money Down, Real Strings Attached
dek: The VA home loan lets a sailor buy a house with no down payment and no mortgage insurance. How it works under 2026 rules, what it really costs, and why the best time to use it is often not right now (not financial advice).

blocks.text: Most 20-year-olds are told that buying a house means saving for a down payment for years. Here is a strange fact: an active-duty sailor who has served 90 continuous days can already qualify for a mortgage benefit that, in most cases, requires no down payment at all and no monthly mortgage insurance. It is one of the most valuable benefits the military offers, and one of the least understood. It is also easy to misuse.

The VA home loan does not hand you money. It makes banks willing to lend you money on terms they would never offer a 20-year-old with no down payment. Understanding why it works that way is the key to using it well, and to knowing when not to use it yet. Everything below reflects VA rules as published in 2026. Rules and fees change, so confirm current details with the VA, a lender and your base housing or legal office before you act. This is general information, not financial advice.
A promise from 1944

President Franklin Roosevelt signed the Servicemen's Readjustment Act on June 22, 1944, days after D-Day. It became known as the GI Bill of Rights, and besides paying for college it offered help buying homes and businesses. The home loan piece helped millions of returning veterans buy houses and helped build the postwar suburbs.

It is worth knowing the uglier part of that history too. The National Archives notes that Black veterans were often unable to get bank loans for mortgages in Black neighborhoods and were largely shut out of buying in white suburbs. The federal guarantee was available on paper; the private lenders and neighborhoods were not. The program you can use today is the same idea, open to everyone who qualifies, and it is still delivered through private lenders.
How the guarantee actually works

The VA usually does not lend you anything. A bank, credit union or mortgage company makes the loan, and the VA promises the lender that if you default, it will pay back a portion of the loan. That promise is called the **guaranty**, and your share of it is called your **entitlement**. Because a quarter of the loan is effectively backed by the government, the lender does not need your down payment as a cushion.

Your Certificate of Eligibility (COE) shows a basic entitlement of $36,000. That is not how much you can borrow. It is how much the VA guarantees on a loan of $144,000 or less. Above that, the VA guarantees up to 25 percent of the loan amount. Since January 1, 2020, there is no VA loan limit at all for borrowers with **full entitlement**: if you have never used the benefit, or used it and had it restored, the VA does not cap the loan. The lender still decides how much you can afford based on your income, debts, credit and assets, and the loan can never exceed the appraised value or the purchase price, whichever is lower.

blocks.title: The path from benefit to keys
items: Confirm eligibility: for service members, at least 90 continuous days of active duty.
Request a Certificate of Eligibility online, or have your lender pull it.
Get preapproved by more than one lender; the VA sets no minimum credit score, but lenders often do.
Make an offer; the home must be your primary residence (for active duty, a spouse or dependent living there can count).
The VA appraisal sets the property's value; the loan cannot exceed it.
Close, paying the funding fee (or financing it) and the other closing costs.

blocks.text: A few details surprise people. The VA does not require a minimum credit score, though many lenders set their own, which is one reason to shop more than one. You can buy a property with up to four units, as long as you live in one of them. And VA loans are assumable: a qualified buyer can take over your existing loan, rate and all, which can be a real selling point if you locked in a low rate and rates later rose.
What it costs: the funding fee

The trade for no down payment and no mortgage insurance is a one-time **VA funding fee**, which the VA says exists to reduce the program's cost to taxpayers. It is a percentage of the loan amount, and it depends on whether this is your first use and how much you put down. The current rates took effect April 7, 2023.

blocks.title: VA funding fee on a purchase loan (rates effective April 7, 2023)
blocks.note: Applies to veterans, active-duty, Guard and Reserve borrowers. Listed on VA.gov, page updated October 2026.
blocks.source: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, VA funding fee and loan closing costs

blocks.text: On a $300,000 house with nothing down, a first-time user pays 2.15 percent, or $6,450. You can pay it at closing or roll it into the loan, which makes the loan $306,450 and means you pay interest on the fee for decades. Put 5 percent down and the fee drops to 1.5 percent of the smaller loan. Some borrowers pay no fee at all, including anyone receiving VA disability compensation and active-duty members who provide evidence of a Purple Heart before closing.

Other closing costs, such as the lender's origination fee, the appraisal, title insurance and recording fees, cannot be rolled into a VA purchase loan. Only the funding fee can. You can negotiate for the seller to pay closing costs, and the VA caps seller concessions (things of value beyond closing costs, like paying off your debts or covering the funding fee) at 4 percent of the home's reasonable value. In practice, buying with no down payment still takes some cash, and it pays to read the lender's Loan Estimate line by line.

items.label: Down payment required on most VA purchase loans
First-use funding fee with under 5% down
Cap on seller concessions, of the home's reasonable value

blocks.source: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, VA.gov home loan pages, 2026

blocks.text: The catch nobody puts on the brochure

No down payment means no equity on day one. That is fine as long as you stay put and the house holds its value. It becomes a problem when you have to sell soon. Selling a house usually costs real money in agent commissions and closing costs, and in the first few years most of your monthly payment goes to interest. Buy with zero down, sell after two or three years in a flat market, and you can owe money at the closing table just to get out.

Run the numbers. Finance the $6,450 funding fee into a $300,000 purchase and you owe $306,450 on a house worth $300,000 the day you move in. At 7.24 percent, your first payment of about $2,088 sends roughly $1,850 to interest. After three years of on-time payments, the balance has only fallen to about $296,850, a little over $9,600 paid down. If the house has not gained value, selling it at that point means covering the agent's commission and closing costs out of pocket, because the equity to pay them simply is not there yet. Rising home prices can rescue this math. Flat or falling prices make it worse.

Now add the military's favorite habit: moving you. A sailor on sea duty might PCS every few years, and a submariner may spend long stretches away from the house entirely. The VA's occupancy rule centers on living in the home as your primary residence, and for active-duty members a spouse or dependent living there can satisfy it. Plenty of service members later keep the house as a rental when orders come. That can work out well, but it turns you into a landlord, often from hundreds of miles away or from somewhere with no email at all, with a property manager's fee, vacancies, repairs and tenant problems you will hear about weeks late.

There is also an opportunity cost in the benefit itself. Your entitlement stays tied up in that loan until the house is sold or the loan is paid off. You may still be able to buy again with whatever entitlement remains, but the math changes: with partial entitlement, county loan limits come back into play, and you may need a down payment to buy at the next duty station.

The multi-unit option deserves a sober look, because it is popular online. Buying a duplex or fourplex with a VA loan and living in one unit while renting the others, often called house hacking, can make the numbers work in an expensive area. It also means being a landlord to your neighbors from day one, and lenders will scrutinize whether the rents are realistic. Treat it as a small business decision, not a hack.
Rent or buy: the sailor's version

For most civilians the rent-or-buy question is about lifestyle and money. For a service member it has an extra variable: Basic Allowance for Housing, a tax-free payment that depends on where you are stationed, your paygrade and whether you have dependents. Single junior sailors assigned to a ship or submarine may not draw it at all, depending on their situation. Whether BAH covers a mortgage near your base is the question that decides whether buying is even on the table.

blocks.title: Renting vs buying with a VA loan near your duty station

left.head: Rent
items: Easy to leave when orders come
No repair bills, no tenant problems
No equity built
Rent can rise every year
Keeps your VA entitlement unused for later

right.head: Buy with a VA loan
items: No down payment, no mortgage insurance
Fixed rate locks in your payment for 30 years
Little equity for several years; selling early can cost you
You own every repair and, after a PCS, every tenant problem
Uses entitlement that may be worth more at a later, longer stop

blocks.text: Interest rates matter more than almost anything else. At the 2021 average 30-year rate of 2.96 percent, a $300,000 loan costs about $1,258 a month in principal and interest. At 7.24 percent, the rate in Freddie Mac's weekly survey at the end of October 2026, the same loan costs about $2,044, before property taxes, homeowners insurance and maintenance. Mortgage rates in 2026 have run from about 6 percent in winter to over 7 percent by October. You cannot control that number, but you can control when you buy and how much house you take on.

One small consolation if you do buy in a high-rate year: the program includes an Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loan, often called an IRRRL or streamline refinance, for swapping an existing VA loan into a lower rate later. Its funding fee is 0.5 percent, far below a purchase loan's. People call this marrying the house and dating the rate. That only works if rates actually fall, though, and refinancing still has closing costs, so never buy a payment you can only afford if a future refinance comes through.

blocks.title: Average 30-year fixed mortgage rate
blocks.note: Annual average of weekly readings; 2026 runs through October 29. VA loan rates are set by lenders and differ from this survey.
blocks.source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey via FRED (MORTGAGE30US), accessed Nov 2026

blocks.text: When it makes sense

The VA loan is a powerful tool with a narrow sweet spot. It shines when you expect to stay in one area long enough to ride out selling costs, when the payment fits comfortably inside your income or BAH, and when you have cash for closing costs and an emergency fund left over afterward. That last part is non-negotiable: a house will hand you a broken water heater or a roof leak at the worst possible time, and on a submarine you may not even hear about it until you pull in.

For a 20-year-old on a first sea tour with no fixed location, the benefit is often more valuable unused. It does not expire. A shore tour, a final duty station, or a civilian job near a nuclear plant after you separate may be a far better place to spend it. Your entitlement is a one-time head start on full terms; a later, longer stop is usually where it pays off most.

items: Get your COE now so you know where you stand, even if you are not buying.
Keep building credit and savings; lenders will look at both even though the VA does not require a down payment.
Ask yourself honestly how long you will live within commuting distance of the house.
Run the numbers with taxes, insurance and repairs included, not just principal and interest.
Before signing anything, talk to the base housing office, your command financial specialist and more than one lender.

blocks.text: The 1944 promise was that serving the country should make it easier, not harder, to put down roots. The benefit is still there for you, and it does not go stale. The smart move is not to use it as soon as you can. It is to use it when the roots are actually going to stay put.

takeaways: The VA guarantees part of your loan so a private lender can skip the down payment; it is not free money.
Since 2020 there is no VA loan limit with full entitlement, but lenders still cap what you can afford.
The 2026 funding fee for first use with under 5% down is 2.15% of the loan; disability compensation recipients are exempt.
Zero down plus frequent PCS moves can mean owing money when you sell, or becoming a long-distance landlord.
The benefit does not expire; often it is worth more at a longer duty station or after you separate. Confirm details with the VA, lenders and your base housing office.

title: The Thousand People Who Pay the Rent
dek: Kevin Kelly's famous napkin math says a creator needs only 1,000 true fans to make a living. The math is right. What it quietly assumes is where the real lessons are.

blocks.text: A thousand people is not many. It is a mid-sized high school, a few crews' worth of a big ship, the attendance at a minor league ballgame on a slow night. In 2008 the writer Kevin Kelly, a founding editor of Wired, argued that this is roughly how many people a creator needs to make a living. Not a million followers. Not a viral hit. A thousand people who care enough to pay.

His math fit on a napkin. If each of those thousand true fans spends about $100 a year on your work, you earn about $100,000 a year. The essay, called 1,000 True Fans, has been passed around ever since by musicians, writers, podcasters, game makers and YouTubers, often as a kind of permission slip: you do not have to be famous, you just have to matter a lot to a few people.
The arithmetic is not the interesting part. The interesting part is what each number in that equation is hiding, and what happens when you look at a real platform's data instead of a napkin.
What Kelly actually claimed

Kelly defined a true fan narrowly. It is someone who will buy anything you make: drive a long way to see you, preorder the deluxe edition, buy the version they already own because it has a new cover. He imagined them at the center of a set of rings. Around the true fans sit many more casual fans who buy now and then, and around them, a much larger crowd who know your name. The true fans are the ones who reliably pay.

He set the price at about $100 a year because that is roughly a day's wages for many people, an amount a devoted fan can spend without much pain. And he attached two conditions that tend to get dropped when the idea is retold. First, the creator has to make enough new work each year to give fans something to spend $100 on. Second, the creator needs a direct relationship with those fans, so that the money flows to the creator instead of mostly to a label, publisher or store in between.

It helps to remember when this was written. Kickstarter did not launch until 2009 and Patreon until 2013. Kelly was describing a world that was only starting to exist, in which the internet would let small creators reach small audiences directly. Much of what he predicted arrived. Some of it arrived in a shape he did not expect.
The number that moves is the price

In 2020 the investor Li Jin, then at the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, wrote a response called 1,000 True Fans? Try 100. Her point was that the $100 assumption was the weakest part of the napkin. If a creator can offer something worth $1,000 a year to the right person, 100 fans produce the same $100,000. She pointed to course platforms where individual creators had earned six figures from a few dozen students.

blocks.title: Fans needed for $100,000 a year
blocks.note: Simple division of $100,000 by yearly spend per fan; before any platform fees, taxes or costs.
blocks.source: Kelly, The Technium, 2008; Jin, a16z, 2020

blocks.text: One example from her essay: an art advisor who sold a course on Teachable earned about $110,000 from 76 students, an average of more than $1,400 each. Those were not casual buyers. They were people paying for a specific result they badly wanted. That is the real shift in Jin's version. A fan at $10 a year is supporting you. A fan at $1,000 a year is buying a transformation, and expects one.

items.label: Earned by one Teachable creator from a single course
Students who paid for it, about $1,440 each on average

blocks.source: Li Jin, 1,000 True Fans? Try 100, a16z, 2020

blocks.text: Jin's other observation was that fans do not all have to pay the same amount. She pointed to a podcast on Patreon with tiers running from $5 a month up to $500, a top tier priced a hundred times the bottom one. The many people at the low end keep the lights on and feel included. The handful at the top, who want access and recognition, can account for a surprising share of the total. Free-to-play games discovered the same pattern long ago, which is why a game can be free for almost everyone and still make money.

The chart above makes one thing obvious. The difference between needing 10,000 fans and needing 100 is entirely about what you offer each one. Most new creators spend all their energy on the left side of the equation, getting more people, and almost none on the right side, giving each person something worth more.
A viewer is not a fan, and neither is a subscriber

Here is where platforms complicate the napkin. On YouTube, subscriber counts feel like a measure of fans. They are not even close. In September 2026, Todd Beaupré, who runs YouTube's growth and discovery team, said in an interview that the click rate from the subscriber row on the home page is often around 10 percent or less, even for a channel's best videos. Nine in ten subscribers who are shown a new upload pass on it, and YouTube considers that normal.

Roblox shows the same gap from the spending side. In its annual report for 2025, Roblox said it averaged 127 million daily active users, while about 1.8 million people paid for something on a typical day. On average, those paying users spent a little over $10 on the days they paid. Divide the two figures and roughly 1 or 2 percent of the people in the building on any given day are the ones paying the rent.

items.label: Average daily active users on Roblox in 2025
Average daily unique paying users
Average daily spend per paying user

blocks.source: Roblox Corporation, Form 10-K for fiscal 2025

blocks.text: That is not a Roblox quirk. It is the shape of almost every audience. A large crowd watches. A smaller group engages. A very small group pays, and an even smaller group would follow you anywhere. Kelly's rings are real; they are just much steeper than most people expect when they start.

blocks.title: The fan ladder, from widest to narrowest
items: Strangers who see a thumbnail or a game icon
Viewers or players who try one thing
Regulars who come back without being reminded
Buyers who have paid you at least once
True fans who would buy almost anything you make

blocks.text: What the napkin leaves out

The most pointed critique came from Dave Karpf, a political scientist who studies digital media. Writing in 2022, he argued that the essay leaned on a hopeful idea from the 2000s, that the internet would let niche work be found as easily as hits. In practice, recommendation systems tend to funnel attention toward what is already popular. Being one click away from a hit is not the same as being found.

He also pointed out that platforms take cuts, so the direct relationship is rarely direct. Roblox keeps 30 percent of a game pass sale before a developer can cash out. App stores take their share of purchases on phones. And $100,000 of revenue is not $100,000 of income. As Karpf notes, a self-employed American pays roughly 15 percent in Social Security and Medicare tax on earnings, covering both the worker's and the employer's share, and buys their own health insurance, equipment and software on top of that.

blocks.title: The napkin vs. the spreadsheet

left.head: Napkin version
items: You sell to fans directly
Fans find you because the internet is flat
Every dollar spent reaches you

right.head: What actually happens
items: A few percent of an audience ever pays
Platforms sit between you and the fan
Algorithms concentrate attention on hits
Fees, taxes and costs come off the top

blocks.text: Karpf's sharpest point is that the model favors creators whose fans have money to spare. A thousand true fans of a niche finance newsletter can pay far more than a thousand true fans of a game aimed at twelve-year-olds, whose spending depends on a parent's card. That is not a reason to give up. It is a reason to think hard about who your audience is and what they can actually afford.
What a true fan of a game or a gaming channel buys

For a small studio or channel, the useful question is not how to get 1,000 fans. It is what a true fan of this specific thing would want to buy that a casual viewer would not. For a Roblox game, the answer is mostly inside the game: passes and items that make the experience better for people who already love it, private servers to play with friends, early access to new levels. For a gaming channel, it might be memberships, a Discord where the creator actually shows up, or eventually something more valuable, like coaching or a course for people trying to fix the same problem the channel documents.

Notice that none of those work until people care. A game pass in a game nobody returns to sells nothing. A membership on a channel nobody watches twice has no members. This is the quiet message under Kelly's essay. The money is downstream of a relationship, and relationships are built with consistency and trust, one returning viewer or player at a time. (The articles on retention and on a channel's first 1,000 subscribers come at the same truth from other directions.)

It also helps to be honest about time. Kelly's thousand fans are usually the residue of years of steady work, not the output of one good month. If a channel posts once a week and each video converts a handful of strangers into regulars, and a small fraction of regulars eventually become buyers, the curve is slow at first and then compounds. Most people quit during the slow part, when the numbers feel like they mean nothing. They do mean something; they are just measuring the wrong ring.

A better scoreboard for the first year is a short list of depth numbers. How many players came back the next day and the next week? How many viewers watched a second video? How many people joined a Discord and actually talked? Those numbers are small and unglamorous, and they are the best early predictor of whether a true-fan base is forming.
A useful test for any new project: can you name ten real people who would be disappointed if it disappeared? If not, work on that before working on monetization.
Depth beats breadth, at first

The lasting value of 1,000 True Fans is not the number. It is the direction of attention. Most creators measure breadth, because breadth is what dashboards show: views, impressions, subscribers, visits. Kelly's essay asks you to measure depth instead: how many people come back, how many would pay, how many would tell a friend without being asked.

Depth is also the part a small builder can control. You cannot make an algorithm favor you, and you cannot make a game go viral. You can make something a small group of people genuinely loves, show up for them on a schedule, and give them ways to support you that feel worth the money. If that group reaches a few hundred or a thousand, Kelly's napkin starts to look less like a fantasy and more like a plan. If it never does, no amount of reach would have saved it.

There is one more reason depth matters for a two-person project in particular. A small, devoted group gives you something a big, shallow audience cannot: honest feedback from people who want you to succeed. They will tell you which update they loved and which level they hated, test things early, and forgive a rough patch. For builders who can only work in the gaps between other duties, that kind of group is not just a revenue source. It is the reason the project keeps going when motivation dips, because someone is waiting for the next thing.

Kelly was right that a thousand is not many. He was perhaps too hopeful about how easy they are to find. The reframe worth keeping is that you are not looking for an audience. You are looking for your people, and they are worth more than the crowd around them.

takeaways: Kelly's math: 1,000 fans spending $100 a year is $100,000 in revenue, before fees, taxes and costs.
The lever most creators ignore is value per fan; 100 people paying $1,000 equals 1,000 paying $100.
Subscribers and players are not fans. On big platforms only a few percent of an audience pays.
Platforms sit between you and fans and concentrate attention on hits; plan for that, do not wish it away.
Measure depth (returners, buyers, people who would miss you) before breadth.
