title: Your First Hire: How to Bring In Help Without Wrecking Your Project
dek: Adding people to a project can slow it down, cost you ownership of your own game, and trigger tax rules you never thought about. Here is how to do it right.

blocks.text: In 1975, a manager named Fred Brooks wrote a book about the worst project of his career. He had run software development for IBM's System/360, one of the biggest computing projects in history, and it ran badly late. His instinct, and everyone's, was to throw more programmers at it. It got later. Out of that experience came a line that every software team eventually learns the hard way: adding people to a late software project makes it later.

Brooks's law is usually quoted about giant companies. It matters even more when you are two people with a game and a few hours a week. Sooner or later you will hit a wall, maybe 3D models you cannot make, music you cannot write, a thumbnail that looks amateur, and the obvious answer will be to bring someone in. Sometimes that is exactly right. Done badly, it costs you money, months, friendships and even ownership of your own game. Here is how to do it well.
Why one more person is not one more unit of work

Brooks had two explanations. The first is ramp-up. A new person does not arrive knowing your codebase, your style or what you meant by "make it feel bouncier." Someone has to teach them, and that someone is you, which means the first weeks of a new helper often subtract from your output before they add to it.

The second is communication. Every pair of people on a project is a line that needs to be kept in sync. With two people, there is one line. With three, there are three. The formula is n(n−1)/2, and it grows much faster than the team does.

blocks.title: Communication links as a team grows
blocks.note: Each pair is a relationship where misunderstandings can happen
blocks.source: Brooks, The Mythical Man-Month, 1975 (n(n−1)/2)

blocks.text: Going from two to three people does not add 50 percent more coordination. It triples it. That is why the best first helpers are not "another developer" who touches everything. They are people who can do a well-defined, separate chunk of work without needing to be in every conversation.

blocks.title: What to hand off and what to keep

left.head: Good first hand-offs
items: Separable: can be done without touching the rest of the game
Specifiable: you can describe "done" in a few sentences
Checkable: you can tell if it is good quickly
Examples: 3D models, icons, music, sound effects, thumbnails, trailer edits

right.head: Keep in-house for now
items: The core game loop and what makes it fun
Systems everything else depends on (saving, economy, progression)
Anything you cannot evaluate yourself
Your relationship with your players

blocks.text: There is also a simpler question to ask before hiring anyone: should you learn this skill yourself instead? If the task comes up constantly and sits close to the heart of your game, learning it may pay off for years. If it is occasional, specialized and far from your strengths, like composing a soundtrack, paying someone who already does it well is usually cheaper than the dozens of hours it would take you to get mediocre at it. Your scarcest resource is not money. It is the few hours a week you actually get to build.
Write the brief before you write the check

Most freelance disasters start the same way: a vague request, a fast yes, and a delivery that technically matches the words but not what you meant. The fix is a written brief. It feels like extra work. It is the work. If you cannot describe the job in a page, you are not ready to hand it off.

A good brief describes the deliverable in concrete terms, such as "five low-poly pole models, under 2,000 triangles each, in our color palette." It includes references, because a picture of what you like communicates more than a paragraph of adjectives. It sets the format, the deadline and the number of revision rounds included. And it says what "accepted" means, so both sides know when the job is finished and the payment is due.

blocks.title: Hiring a freelancer without regret
items: Write a one-page brief: deliverable, references, format, deadline, revisions, acceptance
Look at portfolios of finished work similar to what you need
Pay for a small test task before the real job
Put the deal in writing, including who owns the result
Pay in milestones tied to deliverables, not all up front
Give the minimum access needed, and remove it when the job is done

blocks.text: The paid test task is the single best filter. Ask two or three candidates to do a small, real piece of the job, and pay them for it. You will learn more from how they handle a five-dollar task, whether they ask good questions, hit the deadline and take feedback well, than from any portfolio. Paying for tests also signals that you respect people's time, which attracts better people.

Once work comes back, how you give feedback decides whether the second round is better or worse. Be specific and point at the brief: "the silhouette reads well, but the poles are about twice the triangle budget" is fixable; "it just doesn't feel right" is not. Separate must-fix problems from preferences, and say which is which. Bundle your notes into one message per round instead of a stream of thoughts across a day, because every extra message is another chance to be misread. And if the work is good, say so plainly. Good freelancers remember the clients who are clear and pay on time, and those clients get first call next time.

Watch for red flags early. Someone who refuses any paid test, pushes for full payment before showing anything, asks for your account password or high-level group permissions, or wants to move the deal somewhere you cannot see it is telling you how the job will go. So is someone who agrees to everything instantly without asking a single question about your game. Good collaborators ask questions, because they are trying to understand what you actually want.
Paying: cash, Robux or a cut
On Roblox there are three common ways to pay someone, and each has a trap.

**A fixed price, in money or Robux.** This is the cleanest option for a defined job. Roblox lets group owners send *one-time payouts* of Robux to members from the group's funds, with safety checks like two-step verification. The tradeoff is that Robux and dollars are not the same thing to the person receiving them. At the standard DevEx rate of $0.0038 per earned Robux (since September 5, 2025), Robux are worth far less in cash than what players pay for them, and cashing out requires meeting DevEx requirements. Be clear up front about which currency you are paying in and what it is worth.

**A percentage of revenue.** Roblox also supports *recurring payouts* that split a game's or group's income by percentage among members. This feels generous and saves cash, which is why it is so popular with new teams. But think about it from the freelancer's side: 10 percent of a game that earns nothing is nothing. Skilled people know this, so revenue share mostly attracts beginners or people who believe in the project for other reasons. It also creates a long-term relationship with someone you hired for a short-term task. Roblox's own documentation warns that private-server subscription splits are locked in at the percentage in place when the player subscribed, so changing the split later does not change those payments.

**A mix.** A modest fixed price for the work plus a small, time-limited share can work for people who will keep contributing. Whatever you choose, write down what happens if the game is renamed, rebuilt or abandoned, and when the share ends. Ambiguity is fine while nothing is earning. It becomes a fight the day something does.
Never pay a stranger everything up front, and never give a new helper full ownership-level permissions in your group or game. Pay in milestones and grant only the roles the job requires.
Who owns the work?

This is the part most small teams never think about until it is too late. Under U.S. copyright law, the person who creates something generally owns it, even if you paid them, unless the work counts as a *work made for hire* or the rights are transferred in writing.

The U.S. Copyright Office explains that a work made for hire is either created by an employee within the scope of their job, or specially commissioned work that fits one of nine specific categories, such as a contribution to a collective work or part of an audiovisual work, and only if both sides sign a written agreement saying it is a work made for hire. If the work fails any of those requirements, it is not a work made for hire. A Discord message saying "yeah it's yours" is not that agreement.

For a small team, the practical habit is simple: before work starts, get a short written agreement in which the freelancer either agrees the work is made for hire or assigns you the copyright, in exchange for the payment. Include what they are allowed to do with it, like showing it in their portfolio. The same logic applies inside the team. If you and a partner build a game together, write down who owns what and what happens if one of you leaves. That conversation is awkward for ten minutes. Not having it can be awkward for years.
Taxes, rules and the uniform

If you are paying people as part of running a business, U.S. tax rules care whether they are an independent contractor or an employee. The IRS looks at three kinds of evidence: behavioral control (do you control how the work is done?), financial control (who provides tools, how they are paid, whether expenses are covered) and the type of relationship (contracts, benefits, how permanent it is). A freelancer who sets their own methods and hours and delivers a finished product looks like a contractor. Someone you direct hour by hour may look like an employee, even if they work remotely.

Reporting thresholds changed recently. For tax years beginning after 2025, the IRS's minimum threshold for reporting many payments on information returns such as Form 1099-NEC rose to $2,000, and it may be adjusted for inflation starting in 2027. On your side, if your projects make money, net self-employment earnings are subject to self-employment tax at 15.3 percent, made up of 12.4 percent for Social Security and 2.9 percent for Medicare. These rules are current as of 2026 and change often, so confirm them with the IRS or the free tax help on base before filing. This is general information, not tax or legal advice.

items.label: Form 1099-NEC reporting threshold for tax years after 2025
Self-employment tax rate (Social Security plus Medicare)

blocks.source: IRS, Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC and Self-Employment Tax page, 2026

blocks.text: Two more checks matter if you serve. First, off-duty business activity can be subject to command approval and ethics rules, so talk to your chain of command or the command's ethics counselor before you start paying or being paid. Second, be careful about hiring other service members, especially anyone senior or junior to you in the same chain of command. Business dealings between seniors and subordinates can run into fraternization rules even when everyone is friendly. Asking first costs nothing.

Platform rules matter too. Roblox requires an age check before you can add collaborators to a game through Team Create, and by default you can only collaborate with creators in compatible age groups. That is worth knowing before you promise someone access.
The real job is becoming someone worth working for

Underneath the contracts and tax forms is a shift in your own role. The moment you hire your first helper, part of your job becomes management: deciding what matters, explaining it clearly, giving feedback and paying on time. Many people who are great at building things find this uncomfortable. It is also one of the most valuable skills you can learn, and the military has probably already taught you more of it than you realize: clear orders, defined standards and a known way to check the work.

Start small. Hire one person for one well-defined job with a written brief, a test task, a simple agreement and milestone payments. Learn what went wrong, and there will be something. Then do it again a little better. Brooks's law is a warning about adding people carelessly, not a rule against adding people at all. The teams that grow well are the ones that keep the number of things everyone has to talk about small, and make every hand-off clear enough that nobody has to guess.

takeaways: Brooks's law: new people add ramp-up and communication costs; three people have three times the links of two.
Hand off work that is separable, specifiable and checkable; keep the core loop in-house.
Write a brief, pay for a small test task, pay in milestones and limit access.
Get ownership in writing; paying someone does not automatically make the work yours.
As of 2026, the 1099-NEC threshold is $2,000 and self-employment tax is 15.3%; check with your command before paying or earning off duty.

title: The 98 Percent Who Never Pay
dek: Dropbox had 500 million users and only 11 million customers, and that was the plan. How free products make money, why free is a different kind of price, and what that means for a Roblox game.

blocks.text: At the end of 2017, Dropbox had more than 500 million registered users. About 11 million of them paid. Put the other way around, roughly 98 out of every 100 people using the product gave the company nothing, and Dropbox still went public a few months later as a business generating over a billion dollars a year.

That looks like a charity with a sales team. It is actually one of the most effective business models ever designed, and it is the same model that runs Fortnite, Spotify, most mobile games and nearly every successful experience on Roblox. To understand it, you have to stop thinking of free users as people who did not pay and start thinking of them as something else entirely.
Free is a marketing budget

Dropbox's IPO filing said it plainly. The company acquired users cheaply through word of mouth, referrals inside the product and people sharing files with each other, and it made more than 90 percent of its revenue from people who signed up and paid on their own, without ever talking to a salesperson. One line in the filing captures the whole strategy: *Our 500 million registered users are our best salespeople.*

Every free user who shares a folder shows the product to someone new. That is acquisition. Most of them never pay, but they do the marketing a sales team would otherwise be paid to do. The free tier is not a loss the company tolerates; it is the advertising budget, spent as product instead of ads.

This approach has a name in the software world: **product-led growth**. In a traditional sales-led company, salespeople find customers and persuade them to buy. In a product-led company, the product itself does the finding, the persuading and much of the selling. People try it for free, get real value, bring in others, and eventually some of them hit a limit that is worth paying to remove.

The numbers in Dropbox's filing show the loop working. Paying users grew from 6.5 million at the end of 2015 to 8.8 million in 2016 and 11.0 million in 2017, while revenue rose from about $604 million to $845 million to $1.1 billion. The company did not need most people to pay. It needed a steady trickle of the people who got the most value to decide the product was worth it.

blocks.title: The product-led loop
items: Someone tries the product for free
They get real value quickly
They share it or invite others
Heavy users hit a limit or want more
Some of them upgrade and pay
Revenue funds a better free product

blocks.text: Slack ran the same loop inside companies. Its 2019 filing reported more than 600,000 organizations using it, of which more than 88,000 paid. A team would start on the free plan and build its work around the tool. The filing said many organizations upgraded to search and access more than 10,000 messages, the free plan's limit, which is exactly the moment a team's history becomes too valuable to lose. The paying customers had, in effect, been sold by their own daily habit.
Why free is a different kind of price

There is a psychological reason this works, and it is stranger than it sounds. In 2007, Kristina Shampanier, Nina Mazar and Dan Ariely ran experiments in which people chose between a fancy chocolate and a cheap one. When both had a small price, people mostly chose based on value. When the researchers lowered both prices by the same amount, so the cheap one became free, demand for the cheap one jumped dramatically, even though the gap between them had not changed.

Their conclusion was that people do not treat zero as just a very low price. A free option seems to carry extra benefit of its own, probably because it feels good and removes any risk of making a bad purchase. For a product, this means the step from $1 to free is much bigger than the step from $2 to $1. Free removes the first and hardest decision a customer has to make: whether to try at all.

Free users are not literally free to serve, of course. Every one of Dropbox's non-paying users needed storage space, and every free Roblox player needs a server slot. That cost is why the model only works when serving one more user is cheap compared with what a converted user brings in. Software and games fit that description well, which is a big reason free-to-play took over those industries and not, say, restaurants.

But free creates a second, harder decision later: whether to pay. Products that get the first decision right and the second one wrong end up with millions of users and no business. The whole craft of free-to-play is designing the line between what is free and what is paid.
How many people actually pay

Notice what both companies charged for. Dropbox sold more storage; Slack sold more history and team features. In each case the paid limit grew with how much someone relied on the product. Light users never hit it, so they stayed happy and kept spreading the product, while heavy users hit it precisely when the product had become hard to live without. A good free tier puts the price on the thing that grows with value, not on the thing that makes people try it.

blocks.title: Share of users who pay (approximate)
blocks.note: Calculated from each company's reported totals. Slack counts organizations, not people, so the bars are not strictly comparable.
blocks.source: Dropbox Form S-1, 2018; Slack Form S-1, 2019; Spotify company page, accessed Nov 2026

blocks.text: The share of users who pay varies enormously, and the differences reveal what each product is really selling. Spotify, which reports about 788 million users including 306 million subscribers, converts far more people than Dropbox did, and its free tier comes with ads and fewer controls. Dropbox's free tier was enough for many people's needs, which kept conversion low but made the free product a superb advertisement. Neither approach is wrong. They are different bets about how good the free version should be.

Roblox shows a third pattern, and also a lesson in reading numbers carefully. In the third quarter of 2026, the company reported 138 million daily active users and 30 million average monthly unique payers, with $1.7 billion in bookings. It is tempting to divide one by the other, but a daily count and a monthly count measure different things, so the result would not mean what it seems to. What the numbers do show is scale: a large paying population sitting inside a much larger free one.

items.label: Roblox daily active users, Q3 2026
Average monthly unique paying accounts, Q3 2026
Bookings in the quarter

blocks.source: Roblox Q3 2026 shareholder letter

blocks.text: The trap of selling impatience

Much of mobile gaming learned to make money by selling relief from friction it created itself: timers you can skip, energy bars you can refill, waits you can pay to end. A 2023 paper by Taylor Lundy, Narun Raman, Hu Fu and Kevin Leyton-Brown looked at a puzzle in this design. Skip prices are usually set so high that few players buy them, which seems to contradict designers' claims that they care about player happiness.

Their proposed explanation is interesting. If players value a task more when it feels harder, then cheap skips can actually make the game *less* satisfying, because they cheapen the achievement. In their model, high revenue, happy players and low purchase rates can all exist together, mostly because a small number of big spenders account for much of the money. It is a model, not proof, but it captures something every gamer recognizes: a win you bought feels hollow.

Roblox's own creator documentation goes further. It warns that timers and appointment mechanics that work on other platforms tend to be unpopular with Roblox players, who resent having their fun cut short, and that players may downvote games whose monetization they dislike. It also splits players into *tourists*, who hop between games and like items with an immediate, visible effect, and *locals*, who settle into a few games and value long-term purchases like a battle pass. Most of a game's dedicated players are locals.

This matters directly for an obby. Selling a stage skip is the most obvious way to monetize a hard course, and the Lundy model suggests why it can backfire: the whole pleasure of an obby is having earned the next checkpoint. A player who skips their way to the end has bought the ending and thrown away the reason to want it. Cosmetics, trails, a faster or flashier launcher that does not trivialize the course, and private servers for friends sell something people enjoy without hollowing out the game itself.

blocks.title: Two ways to design free-to-play

left.head: Selling relief
items: Creates frustration, then sells the fix
Timers and energy walls
Purchases feel like ransom
Players resent the game and leave

right.head: Selling more of what's fun
items: The free game is complete and good
Cosmetics, status, convenience, extra content
Purchases feel like support or self-expression
Players stay longer and bring friends

blocks.text: What a free player is really worth

Here is the reframe at the center of free-to-play: in a multiplayer game, the free players are part of the product. A paying player who buys a rare cosmetic wants other people to see it. Someone who buys a faster launcher in a pole vault obby wants a full server to show it off to. Without a crowd of free players, there is nothing to pay for.

Roblox's current creator payout program makes this logic explicit, and with a twist. Under its Creator Rewards program, a game earns 5 Robux a day for each *active spender*, defined as someone who has bought at least $9.99 of Robux or subscriptions in the past 60 days, who plays it for ten minutes or more as one of the first three games they open that day. Creators who bring brand-new or returning players to Roblox through their share links can also earn 35 percent of what those players spend anywhere on the platform, up to their first $100, during their first 60 days, as long as the game keeps averaging 100 or more daily users.

Read carefully, that is a platform paying creators for two things: holding the attention of people who spend, and doing product-led growth on Roblox's behalf. Both reward the same qualities, a game good enough to be someone's first choice of the day and good enough that players invite their friends. The rules can change, as Roblox's documentation notes, but the direction is telling.

Roblox lists the main ways a game can charge: passes, developer products, subscriptions, paid access, private servers and selling models to other creators. The choice among them matters less than the line you draw. A simple test for any paid item is to ask whether a player who never buys it still gets a complete, fair, fun game. If yes, the purchase is an extra. If no, it is a wall, and walls drive away the free players who make the paid ones care.

In a free-to-play game, the people who never pay are not freeloaders. They are your marketing, your audience and the crowd that gives every purchase its meaning. Design the free game for them and the paid extras for the people who love it most.
Free is a promise

Product-led growth and free-to-play are often described as tricks for extracting money. The successful versions work the opposite way. They give away something genuinely valuable, earn trust and habit, and then offer more to the minority who want more. Dropbox's free tier was good enough that hundreds of millions of people used it. Slack's free plan was good enough that whole teams depended on it before anyone paid.

For a small team, this changes where to put effort. The first job is not designing the store. It is making the free experience good enough that players come back and tell their friends. Monetization is the last layer, not the foundation: a game that is fun for free has something to sell, and a game that is only fun after paying has nothing.

takeaways: In free products, free users are the marketing budget: they bring in others and give paying users an audience.
People treat free as special, not just cheap, so free removes the first decision. The hard part is designing the second one: what is worth paying for.
How good the free tier is sets the trade-off between how many people use you and how many pay.
Selling relief from frustration you created makes players resent the game; selling more of what is fun keeps them.
Test every paid item: does a player who never buys it still get a complete, fair game?

title: The Video That Was the Product
dek: Dropbox tested its idea with a three-minute screencast before the software worked for the public. The lean startup turned that trick into a method, and the best evidence for it comes from an experiment that treated founders like scientists.

blocks.text: Building a file-syncing service that actually works across every kind of computer is brutally hard. Drew Houston, the founder of Dropbox, knew that years of engineering stood between him and a product anyone could use. So before finishing it, he made a short demo video showing how it would work, packed it with in-jokes for the tech crowd on the news site Digg, and posted it. According to Houston, the beta waiting list jumped from 5,000 people to 75,000 overnight.

Eric Ries, who told the story in a 2011 guest post on TechCrunch, drew the lesson in one line: in that case, the video was the minimum viable product. Nobody could use it. Nobody could buy it. But it answered the question that mattered most at that stage, which was whether enough people wanted this thing to justify the years of work. The answer came back in a day.

items.label: Dropbox beta waiting list before the demo video
Waiting list the next day, per Drew Houston

blocks.source: Eric Ries, TechCrunch, October 2011

blocks.text: That is the core of what became known as the lean startup, the method Ries laid out in his 2011 book of the same name. It is often summarized as ship fast. A better summary is: figure out what you most need to learn, and find the cheapest way to learn it. (The separate article on shipping early covers why version one should embarrass you. This one is about what version one is for.)
A startup is an experiment

Ries's central claim is that a startup is not a small version of a big company. A big company executes a known plan to serve known customers. A startup is searching for a plan, under so much uncertainty that most of its early guesses about customers, pricing and features will be wrong. He built on the work of Steve Blank, a serial founder and teacher whose customer development approach insisted that founders get out of the building and talk to real customers before scaling anything.

Blank put the distinction neatly: a startup is a temporary organization whose job is to search for a business model that can repeat and grow, while an established company's job is to execute one it already has. The tools that serve execution, such as detailed plans, fixed deadlines and feature roadmaps, can actively mislead during the search, because they reward doing the plan rather than finding out whether the plan is right.

Under that kind of uncertainty, Ries argued, the unit of progress is not code written or features shipped. It is what he called validated learning: something you now know about customers that you did not know before, backed by evidence from their behavior rather than your hopes. A team can work flat out for a year, ship a polished product and have learned almost nothing, because it never put a risky assumption in front of real people.

He knew this from experience. His earlier company, IMVU, spent months building a 3D chat product as an add-on to existing instant messaging networks, on the theory that people would not want to switch networks. When real users finally tried it, the theory fell apart; they were happy to use a new, standalone network and were reluctant to invite their existing friends into something odd. Months of careful engineering had gone into supporting an assumption that a cheap test would have broken in days.

blocks.title: Build, measure, learn
items: Ideas: state the riskiest assumption as a testable guess
Build: make the smallest thing that can test it
Measure: watch what real people actually do
Learn: decide to persevere, change course, or stop

blocks.text: The loop runs backward from how it is drawn. You start by deciding what you need to learn, then what you would have to measure to learn it, and only then what you need to build to get that measurement. Most builders run it the other way: build what seems cool, see what happens, and try to learn something from the result.
An MVP is an experiment, not a small product

The phrase minimum viable product has been stretched so far it now often just means a rough first version. Ries meant something sharper: the version of a product that lets a team learn the most about customers with the least effort. The emphasis is on learning, and the minimum refers to effort, not quality.

blocks.title: Two ways to read 'minimum viable product'

left.head: MVP as a small product
items: Build fewer features, but build them
Ship when it feels sort of ready
Success means people use it
Next step: add more features

right.head: MVP as an experiment
items: Build only what tests one assumption
Ship when it can answer the question
Success means you learned something true
Next step: test the next riskiest assumption

blocks.text: Seen that way, an MVP can be almost anything. A video, a landing page with a sign-up button, a version where humans quietly do by hand what software will eventually automate. For a game, it might be a single level that contains only the core loop, played by twenty strangers, with nothing else built around it. The question is not whether the thing is good. It is whether it can tell you what you need to know.

Ries also warned about the numbers people use to fool themselves, which he called vanity metrics. Total sign-ups, total visits and total views only ever go up, so they always feel like progress. What matters are actionable metrics: numbers tied to a specific change that tell you whether that change worked. For a Roblox game, total visits is a vanity metric. The share of new players who return the next day, measured before and after an update, is an actionable one.
What the evidence says

For years the lean startup was mostly supported by stories, and stories select for winners. Nobody writes up the startups that ran perfect experiments and still died. So it matters that someone tested a version of the idea properly.

In a randomized controlled trial published in Management Science in 2020, Arnaldo Camuffo and colleagues worked with 116 early-stage Italian startups and tracked them at 16 points over about a year. Both groups got ten sessions of training on getting feedback from the market. But one group was taught to work like scientists: to build a theory of why their idea would succeed, turn it into explicit hypotheses, and run rigorous tests. The control group was left to judge its ideas by intuition.

items.label: Startups randomly assigned in the trial
Training sessions given to both groups
Tracking period, with 16 data points per startup

blocks.source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella & Spina, Management Science, 2020

blocks.text: The founders who behaved like scientists performed better, were more likely to pivot to a different idea, and were no more likely to drop out early. The authors' explanation is about precision. Testing hypotheses made founders less likely to keep chasing ideas that only looked good, and more likely to spot ideas that looked weak but were actually promising. It is one study, in one country, with fairly small firms, so it is not the final word. But it is a real experiment, and it points the same way as the method.

Notice what the trial did not test. It did not compare launching fast against launching slow. It compared thinking clearly about assumptions against going with your gut. That distinction matters, because the most serious critique of the lean startup is about speed.
The critique: false starts

Tom Eisenmann, a Harvard Business School professor, studied failed ventures for his 2021 book Why Startups Fail. One pattern he named was the false start: founders who took launch fast and fail fast so literally that they rushed out a product without first doing basic research on what customers needed. When it flopped, they had learned only that this particular version did not work, not why. Then they repeated the process, burning time and money on a series of half-informed guesses.

Eisenmann's point is not that the lean startup is wrong, but that it is often read as permission to skip thinking. The cheapest test of an idea is frequently not a product at all. It is a conversation with ten potential users, a look at what similar products already do, or a careful list of what has to be true for the idea to work. Building an MVP is the second-cheapest test, not the first.

Before building anything, write down the one assumption that would kill the project if it were false. Then ask what the cheapest possible test of that assumption is. It is usually smaller than a prototype.

There is a second limit worth knowing, and it matters for games in particular. Some products only reveal their value when they are reasonably finished. A gray-box prototype can make a good mechanic look dull, because so much of what makes a game satisfying comes from feedback, sound, animation and the feeling of control. (The article on game feel covers why.) A team that tests a rough build, sees flat reactions and kills the idea may have thrown away something that only needed a little juice.

The answer is not to skip testing but to test the right layer. A core loop can be tested with placeholder art as long as the moment-to-moment feel is roughly there; a story or a world usually cannot be tested that way at all. Part of the skill is knowing which of your assumptions a cheap test can actually answer, and which ones need a more complete build before the data means anything. Lean thinking says to spend the least effort that gives a trustworthy answer. Sometimes the least effort is still a real chunk of work.

Finally, experiments only help if someone is willing to read them honestly. Every builder is tempted to explain away a bad result: the testers were the wrong people, the timing was off, the next update will fix it. Sometimes that is true. The discipline the lean method asks for is to write those excuses down before the test, so that you cannot invent them afterward.
Lean for a two-person game and a new channel

For a small team working in stolen hours, this method is less a business philosophy than a survival skill. Time is the scarcest resource, and the most expensive mistake is spending months polishing something built on an untested guess. The lean move is to name the guess out loud and test it before it costs much.

For a Roblox game, the riskiest assumption is almost always whether the core loop is fun on its own, before any progression, cosmetics or story. That can be tested with one rough level, a few friends of friends, and the game's own retention numbers. If people do not come back to the bare loop, more features will not save it. (The articles on retention and on deciding with data go deeper into what to measure.)

For a YouTube channel, the risky assumptions are about the audience and the promise. Does anyone want this particular angle? Does this packaging make the promise clear? Those can be tested with a handful of videos made quickly, each built around a single question, rather than with one perfect launch video that took two months. Each upload is a small experiment; the analytics are the lab results.

blocks.title: A lean cycle you can run in a month of spare evenings
items: Write the project's riskiest assumption as a single sentence.
Decide what result would prove it wrong, before you test it.
Build the smallest thing that could produce that result.
Put it in front of real players or viewers, not just friends.
Read the numbers that tie to the assumption, not the vanity totals.
Decide: keep going, change direction, or stop and start the next idea.

blocks.text: The hardest step is the last one. Ries called it the choice to pivot or persevere, and it requires something founders rarely have: a willingness to be wrong in public, even if the public is only your brother. Deciding in advance what result would change your mind makes that easier, because the decision was made by a calmer version of you before the result arrived.

Houston's video worked because it was aimed at a question, not at an audience. He did not need applause. He needed to know whether to spend the next several years building Dropbox. The real lesson of the lean startup is to keep asking which question you are trying to answer, and to refuse to build anything bigger than the answer requires.

takeaways: An MVP is the cheapest experiment that tests your riskiest assumption, not a small version of the final product.
Measure actionable metrics tied to a specific change, such as next-day return rate, not ever-rising totals.
A 2020 randomized trial of 116 startups found founders taught to test hypotheses like scientists did better and pivoted more.
Fail fast is not a license to skip thinking; talking to users is often a cheaper test than building anything.
Decide in advance what result would make you change course.

title: Who Owns the Game?
dek: When two people build something that starts making money, the law already has default answers about who owns it, and they are often not the ones partners assume. Business structures, contracts and IP for side businesses, in plain language. General information, not legal advice.

blocks.text: Imagine two brothers building a Roblox game together. One writes most of the scripts; the other builds the maps and designs the store. The game lives in a group that one of them created. It starts earning real money, and then one brother leaves for months with almost no connection. A question nobody asked at the start suddenly matters: who actually owns this game?

Most people assume the answer is "both of us, obviously." The law has its own default answers, and they are not always what partners assume. The money follows whoever controls the group. The code may legally belong to both of them in ways neither can untangle alone. And without a written agreement, any disagreement becomes one memory against another.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Business and tax rules vary by state and change over time. For decisions with real money at stake, talk to a lawyer or tax professional, and see the section below on rules for service members before earning anything.

None of this is a reason to be afraid of starting. It is a reason to spend one calm evening on paperwork now, while the stakes are small, instead of a miserable month later. The good news is that the basics are simpler and cheaper than most people expect.
You are already a business

You do not need to file anything to be in business. According to the U.S. Small Business Administration, if you do business activities without registering as anything else, you are automatically a **sole proprietorship**. That is simple, but it means your business and you are legally the same: you are personally responsible for the business's debts and obligations.

When two people go into business together without setting up any structure, the default in most states is a **general partnership**, even if neither of them ever uses that word. The SBA's comparison of business types lists unlimited personal liability for partnerships unless they are set up as a limited partnership. In plain terms, each partner can be on the hook for obligations the business takes on, including some the other partner created.

For a game earning a few hundred dollars, this risk is usually small. It grows when there are contracts, paid freelancers, real revenue, or anything that could lead to someone claiming they were harmed. That is the point at which most people start looking at a more formal structure.
What an LLC does, and what it does not

The most common choice for small businesses is the **limited liability company**, or LLC. You create one by filing a document with a state, usually called articles of organization, and paying a filing fee that varies by state. The SBA describes the main benefit as protecting personal assets, like your car and savings, if the business is sued or goes bankrupt, in most instances.

An LLC is also flexible on taxes. The IRS treats a single-member LLC as a *disregarded entity* by default, so the profit simply goes on the owner's personal tax return, typically on Schedule C. An LLC with two or more members is treated as a partnership for federal taxes unless it elects otherwise. Either way, the SBA notes, LLC members are generally considered self-employed and pay self-employment tax.

items.label: Self-employment tax rate (Social Security plus Medicare) on net self-employment earnings
Net self-employment earnings that trigger the tax filing requirement
Cost of an EIN from the IRS; the IRS warns against sites that charge

blocks.source: IRS self-employment tax and EIN pages, accessed Nov 2026

blocks.text: That self-employment tax applies whether or not you form an LLC, and it surprises many first-time sellers. It covers the Social Security and Medicare contributions an employer would normally split with you. Roblox earnings cashed out through the Developer Exchange count as income, as the article on the Robux economy explains, so keep records from the first dollar.

An LLC is not a force field. The SBA itself notes that the liability protection has limits and that business insurance can fill gaps. It also points out that in some states, when a member joins or leaves an LLC, the company may have to be dissolved and re-formed unless an agreement is already in place for transferring ownership. That is one reason the SBA recommends an **operating agreement**, the document that sets out how decisions are made and what each member owns, even in states that do not require one.

Whatever structure you choose, keep the business's money separate from your own from the start. A dedicated bank account, and a simple record of every payout, expense and transfer, makes taxes far easier and makes it obvious to everyone, including the partners, where the money went. Mixing business and personal money is one of the habits that can weaken the protection an LLC is supposed to provide, so it is worth getting right early.

items: Default partnership in most states
Each partner personally exposed
Ownership of code and name unclear

right.head: LLC with a written agreement
items: The company holds the game, name and accounts
Personal assets protected in most cases
Ownership percentages written down
Rules for decisions, payouts and leaving
Disputes come down to the document

blocks.text: The right moment to form an LLC is a judgment call, and there is no prize for doing it before you have anything worth protecting. A reasonable trigger is when real money starts arriving, when you sign contracts or pay contractors, or when you are about to spend significant money of your own. The SBA offers free business counseling, including through Small Business Development Centers, which is a good place to ask before you file.
Who owns the code, the art and the name

Copyright is automatic. Under the federal Copyright Act, copyright in a work belongs initially to the person who created it. The moment someone writes a script or builds a model, they hold the copyright in it, with no registration needed.

When two people create something together, the law has a specific category for it. A **joint work** is one made by two or more authors who intend their contributions to merge into a single whole, and the authors of a joint work are co-owners of the copyright. A game built by two partners can easily fall into this category. Co-ownership sounds fair, but it means neither of you cleanly owns the game alone, which gets complicated if you ever split up, sell the game, or want to take it in different directions.

Two other rules matter just as much. First, copyright does not protect ideas, systems or methods, only the specific expression of them. Your idea for a pole vault launcher is not owned by anyone; the actual code and art are. Second, transferring copyright ownership requires a signed written document. A verbal promise that "it all belongs to the company" does not transfer anything.

This is why the cleanest setup for partners is for each person to assign their work on the project, in writing, to the company. The LLC then owns the game, its code, its art and its name, and the partners own the LLC in whatever percentages they agreed. If someone leaves, the question becomes what happens to their share of the company, which is far easier to handle than trying to split a game's code in two.

Freelancers need the same care. If you pay an artist for a thumbnail or a composer for music, the default is that they own what they made unless you agree otherwise in writing. The Copyright Act allows some commissioned work to count as a *work made for hire*, owned by the person who commissioned it, but only in certain categories and only with an express written agreement signed by both sides. A short written assignment in the deal avoids the guesswork.

The game's name is a separate kind of property. Names are protected by trademark law, not copyright, as the article on branding explains, and you gain trademark rights by using a name for your product. Decide early that the name belongs to the company, not to whoever thought of it.
Write it down, on one page

A contract does not need to be long or written by a lawyer to be useful. Its first job is to be shared memory: what you both agreed, on a calm day, before money changed anyone's mood. The partner article on roles and decisions covers how to split work and revenue; the legal version adds a few lines about ownership and exits.

blocks.title: A one-page ownership memo for two partners
items: Who owns what: the game, its code, art, name and accounts belong to the business (or name exactly who holds them).
The split: each partner's percentage of ownership and of revenue, and whether those can differ.
Control: who owns the Roblox group, who can change payouts, and what changes need both signatures.
Contributions: each partner assigns their work on the project to the business in writing.
Leaving: what happens to a partner's share if they stop contributing, want out, or cannot work for months.
Changes: how and when you will revisit the deal, and that changes must be written and signed by both.

blocks.text: Roblox makes the control question concrete. Its documentation explains that group owners, and members given permission, can set recurring percentage splits and send one-time payouts. It also states plainly that if a conflict arises inside a group, Roblox cannot help arbitrate or resolve it. Whoever holds the keys holds the money, so put in writing who that is and what they may not do alone.

For partners where one person is regularly unreachable for weeks, add one more line: what the other partner may do alone while you are away, and what must wait. Shipping updates and paying agreed splits might be fine; selling the game, changing the split or bringing in a new partner should not be. Deciding this in advance means the business keeps moving without either brother feeling the other took advantage of an absence.

Once real money is involved, it is worth paying a lawyer to turn your memo into a proper operating agreement. The memo makes that meeting shorter and cheaper, because the hard conversations will already be done.
First rule for a sailor: check before you earn

Active-duty service members carry an extra layer of rules that civilians do not. The federal standards of conduct for government employees, in Title 5 of the Code of Federal Regulations, bar using a public position for private gain or to endorse a product or business, using government property for unauthorized purposes, and using official time for anything other than official duties. The rules list government computers, email and social media accounts as government property.

The same regulations say outside work must not conflict with official duties, and that agencies can require prior approval before employees take on outside activities. The Defense Department has added its own approval requirement for some personnel doing business with certain outside parties, and the Navy and individual commands may have further rules on off-duty work. Which ones apply depends on your situation, so do not guess.

Before the business earns money, ask your command about its outside-employment and business-activity policy, and talk to an ethics counselor through your command's legal office. Do it in writing, keep the answer, and ask again if the business changes.

In practice, that means never building the game on a government computer or during duty hours, never using your rank, title or Navy position to promote it, and getting a clear answer on whether your command requires approval. A partner who is a civilian, such as a brother who has already left the service, is not bound by these rules, which is one more reason to divide roles thoughtfully and write down who handles what.
Paperwork is a gift to your future selves

It is tempting to treat contracts between family members as a sign of mistrust. The opposite is closer to the truth. Memories drift, and money changes how people remember promises. A one-page agreement written while the game earns nothing protects the business, but more importantly it protects the relationship, because it takes the most explosive questions off the table before anyone is emotional about them.

The order is simple: check the military rules first, then write down who owns what. Keep business money separate and keep records. Form an LLC when there is something real to protect, and get a professional to look at the documents when the stakes justify it. None of it is glamorous, but it is the foundation that lets two people keep building together for years.

takeaways: Without paperwork you are a sole proprietor, and two people working together are usually a general partnership with personal liability.
An LLC can protect personal assets in most cases and is taxed simply by default, but it is not a force field. Self-employment tax applies either way.
Copyright starts with the creator. Partners can end up co-owning the code, and transfers only work in a signed writing, so assign your work to the business on paper.
Roblox will not settle group disputes. Write down who controls the group and payouts.
As a service member, check your command's outside-employment rules and talk to an ethics counselor before earning anything.

title: Whoever Speaks First
dek: In study after study, the first number on the table drags the final deal toward it. Six decades of negotiation research explain when to use that, how to defend against it, and why so many people never ask at all.

blocks.text: Two people sit across a table, one playing a buyer and one a seller in a simulated business deal. They have the same information sheet, the same deadline and the same instructions. The only difference between pairs is who speaks first. In a series of experiments published in 2001, the psychologists Adam Galinsky and Thomas Mussweiler found that this one detail decided a great deal. Whichever side made the first offer, buyer or seller, tended to walk away with the better deal, and the first offer was a strong predictor of the final price.

It sounds like a trick. It is closer to a law of how minds handle uncertainty. When nobody knows exactly what something is worth, the first concrete number becomes the reference point that everything else is measured against. Negotiation research has spent six decades mapping when that works, when it backfires and how to defend against it. Most people never use any of it, because most people never negotiate at all.

That is a costly habit. In a study of newly hired employees across many industries, Michelle Marks of George Mason University and Crystal Harold of Temple University found that those who negotiated their starting salary raised it by about $5,000 on average, and more than half of the negotiators also won something extra, like vacation time. The researchers projected that, with 5 percent yearly raises compounding on top, a $5,000 higher start could add up to more than $600,000 over a 40-year career.

items.label: Average starting-salary gain for new hires who negotiated
Of negotiators also won a non-salary benefit

blocks.source: Marks & Harold, Journal of Organizational Behavior, 2011 (via George Mason University)

blocks.text: How strong is the anchor?

A single study can mislead, so the useful question is what happens when you pool many. In 2006, Dan Orr and Chris Guthrie ran a meta-analysis of anchoring in negotiation studies, combining 19 effect sizes from 16 articles. They found a correlation of about 0.5 between the opening anchor and the final outcome. Put plainly, roughly a quarter of the variation in where deals landed was associated with where the first number was set. For social science, that is a big effect.

Two details from that analysis are more interesting than the headline. The anchor's pull was weaker for people with real professional experience, though only a few studies included them, so that finding is tentative. And it shrank as negotiators had more information. When people knew little about the other side, the correlation was about 0.54. With moderate information it was 0.47, and with lots of information it fell to 0.38.

blocks.title: How much the opening anchor tracks the final deal
blocks.note: Higher numbers mean final deals follow the first offer more closely. Information and experience weaken the pull.
blocks.source: Orr & Guthrie, Ohio State Journal on Dispute Resolution, 2006

blocks.text: That pattern is the whole game in miniature. An anchor is powerful exactly to the degree that the person hearing it is unsure what the thing is worth. Homework is the antidote. So if you know more about the market than the other side does, it usually pays to speak first. If you know less, your priority is to find out more before any number gets said.
Defending against someone else's number

Galinsky and Mussweiler's study had a second, more hopeful finding. The first-mover advantage disappeared when the person receiving the offer deliberately focused on information that contradicted it. In separate experiments, thinking about the other side's alternatives, thinking about the other side's bottom line, or simply focusing on one's own target price all cancelled out the anchor's effect. This worked both face to face and over email.

That is the scientific case for the oldest advice in negotiation: know your alternatives before you sit down. In their 1981 book *Getting to Yes*, Roger Fisher and William Ury of the Harvard Negotiation Project called it your BATNA, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement. If the deal on the table is worse than your BATNA, you walk. If you have not worked out your BATNA, you have no way to know when an offer is bad, and the other side's anchor fills the gap.

What if you do not have a strong alternative? A 2018 set of studies by Michael Schaerer, Martin Schweinsberg and Roderick Swaab found that simply imagining a strong alternative helped people with weak positions negotiate more ambitiously and reach more profitable deals, mainly because it raised their aspirations and their first offers. But the effect had limits. It stopped helping when the imaginer did not make the first offer or when the other side was doing the same thing, and it backfired when the two positions were very hard to reconcile. Imagination can lift your aim, not change reality.

Put those findings together and you get a simple script for the moment someone else names a number first. Do not treat their number as the starting point for haggling. Pause, bring your own target back to mind, and answer with your own number and the reason behind it, as though their figure had never been said. Then shift the conversation to the evidence: comparable prices, results, alternatives. The anchor loses its grip when the discussion is about reasons instead of about the distance between two figures.

The same logic answers the dreaded question in job interviews, "What salary are you looking for?" If you have done your research and know the market range, giving a specific, reasoned number near the top of it is often the stronger move. If you genuinely do not know, the smarter play is to ask what range they have budgeted for the role, and to treat the answer as information rather than as a ceiling.

blocks.title: A one-page prep sheet before any negotiation
items: Research the market: what do similar jobs, items or deals actually go for?
Write down your target, the ambitious but defensible result you are aiming for.
Write down your walk-away point and your best alternative if there is no deal.
Guess the other side's alternatives and bottom line. What happens to them if you say no?
List the issues beyond price: timing, extras, responsibilities, flexibility.
Decide whether you know enough to make the first offer, and prepare a reason for it.

blocks.text: The shape of a good first offer

A 2026 review by Loschelder and Petrowsky of Leuphana University sums up the trade-off. First offers can anchor outcomes in your favor, but an offer that is too aggressive can alienate the other side, raise the chance of no deal at all and leave a bad taste even if you win. The advantage is strongest when the offer is shaped well, and four features keep coming up: precision, framing, ranges and rationales.

Precision is the most surprising. In studies with 1,254 participants, Malia Mason, Daniel Ames and colleagues at Columbia Business School found that a precise opening number, like $5,015, made recipients assume the person knew the item's value well, so they answered with more conciliatory counteroffers than they did after a round number like $5,000. In a real-world check, only about 2 percent of home listings they looked at used precise prices. Most people round, and rounding signals a guess.

Ranges can work too, with care. Ames and Mason found that some range offers, such as asking for $7,200 to $7,600 for a car, got better terms without hurting the relationship, because the listener takes both ends as clues about your real bottom line and an extreme counter starts to feel rude. Ranges that are too wide or too extreme lose that benefit. And a rationale helps any number: an offer tied to a reason, such as comparable sales or measured results, invites a discussion about the reason instead of a flat no.
A good first offer is ambitious, specific and explained. An outrageous one is not an anchor. It is an insult, and the research says insults raise the odds that nobody gets anything.
The pie is usually not fixed

Everything so far treats negotiation as a tug-of-war over one number. Many real negotiations are not like that, and assuming they are is one of the most common mistakes people make. In a review of 32 experiments, the negotiation researchers Thompson and Hrebec described what they called the lose-lose effect: two sides often share an interest without realizing it, and they settle on a deal that is worse for both than one that was easily available.

Negotiation teachers love a simple story to illustrate this. Two siblings fight over one orange and eventually split it down the middle. One then squeezes her half for juice and throws away the peel. The other grates his half's peel for baking and throws away the fruit. Each could have had twice as much if either had asked the other one question: what do you want it for?

blocks.title: Two ways to negotiate the same deal

left.head: Fighting over positions
items: I want 60 percent
Each concession is a loss
Hide your priorities
Split the difference at the end

right.head: Trading on interests
items: Why does each side want what it wants?
Trade things you value less for things you value more
Share priorities selectively to find trades
Add issues so both sides can win something

blocks.text: This matters for anyone building something with a partner. Two brothers splitting the work on a Roblox game are not really negotiating over one number. One might care more about creative control of the map, the other about the code or the money. Treating every disagreement as a split-the-difference fight leaves value on the table. (The separate article on partner roles covers why those conversations are worth having before money arrives.) The negotiation research adds how: ask about interests first, then trade.
Who asks, and who pays for asking

If negotiation pays, why do so many people skip it? Part of the answer is that asking feels risky, and for some people it really is riskier. A 2015 meta-analysis in *Psychological Bulletin* by Jens Mazei and colleagues pooled 123 effect sizes from nearly 11,000 people and found that men, on average, got somewhat better economic outcomes than women. But the gap depended heavily on context. It shrank when negotiators had experience, when they knew the bargaining range and when they were negotiating on behalf of someone else, and it even reversed in the conditions least stacked against women. A 2026 review by the same research group concludes that gaps in outcomes persist in some situations, while the gap in willingness to start negotiating has largely narrowed.

Social class shows a similar pattern. In a 2026 paper in *PNAS*, researchers at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, MIT and Stanford studied more than 10,000 people across four studies and found that people from lower-class backgrounds were less likely to start negotiations, partly because they felt less powerful and feared backlash. In a fifth experiment with HR professionals, that fear turned out to be partly justified: the identical request drew more backlash when it came from a lower-class candidate. The authors call it a double bind. Staying quiet keeps you behind, and asking carries a higher social price.

The common thread in both lines of research is that information and practice shrink the gaps. Knowing the market range, having done it before and having a clear reason to ask all made a difference. Those are things you can build on purpose.

For anyone in the military, this is a skill that may need deliberate practice. Military pay is set by tables, not bargaining, so years can pass without ever negotiating a salary. That changes the moment you look at civilian jobs. A nuclear-trained technician with real plant experience walking into a utility hiring process has market information to gather, alternatives to line up and a precise, reasoned number to prepare. The first civilian offer is an anchor too.
How sure is the science?

One honest caveat. Much of negotiation research comes from simulated negotiations, often between students with play money. A 2026 analysis of 50 recent negotiation studies by Joachim Hüffmeier and colleagues found that independent replications and other transparency practices are still uncommon in the field, especially in specialty journals. The first-offer effect has been found many times by many labs, which is reassuring, but exact numbers like a correlation of 0.5 should be read as rough guides, not physical constants.

Still, the practical message is unusually consistent across studies. Do the homework, because information weakens anchors. Know your alternative, because it tells you when to walk. Make a specific, reasoned first offer when you know the market. Look for trades instead of only splitting differences. And above all, ask. The research is clearest on one point: the deal you never negotiate is the one that is guaranteed not to get better.

takeaways: First offers anchor outcomes, especially when the other side is unsure what things are worth.
Defend against an anchor by focusing on your target, your alternatives and the other side's alternatives.
Make first offers specific and explained. Precise numbers and reasoned ranges outperform round guesses.
Look for trades on what each side cares about most. Many deals that look like tug-of-war are not.
Information and practice shrink negotiation gaps. Prepare like it is an exam, then actually ask.

title: The Plan Is Not the Point: What Research Says About Business Plans
dek: Investors barely read them and plan writers aren't more profitable, yet founders who plan quit less. The trick is knowing which kind of plan helps.

blocks.text: Researchers once got access to the inbox of an American venture capital firm and pulled 722 funding requests from it. Some came with polished business plans. Some came with almost nothing. The team, led by David Kirsch, then checked which requests actually got money. Business plans should have mattered a lot here. Investing in startups is exactly the situation the business plan was invented for.

They barely mattered. Published in the *Strategic Management Journal* in 2009, the study found that whether a plan was included, and much of what it said, was only weakly linked to funding. And the useful information in those plans was information the investors were learning anyway, through other channels.

If the people a business plan is supposedly written for are not reading it closely, why does every entrepreneurship class still make you write one? And should you bother, if you are building a game or a channel on the side? The research gives a surprisingly clear answer, and it is not "yes" or "no." It is that the document is rarely the point. The thinking is.
Plans are worthless, but planning is everything.
blocks.by: Dwight D. Eisenhower, 1957

blocks.text: The case against the business plan

Start with the skeptics, because they have real data. Benson Honig and Tomas Karlsson followed 396 people in the process of starting businesses over two years. Writing a plan, they found, was predicted less by whether it was useful and more by outside pressure: banks or programs requiring one, and people copying what other founders did. Most importantly, they found no evidence that the people who wrote plans ended up more profitable over those two years.

Their explanation is that a written business plan often works like a ritual. It signals to outsiders that you are a serious, legitimate business, the way a suit signals you are serious at an interview. That signal can be useful. But a ritual is not the same thing as a tool, and you can perform the ritual perfectly while learning nothing about your business.

Put that next to the venture capital study and a pattern appears. The formal document, the 30-page thing with a market-size slide and five-year projections, is mostly theater. Nobody, including the founder, should believe a revenue forecast for year four of a product that does not exist yet.

items.label: VC funding requests studied; plans only weakly tied to funding
Nascent founders followed; no profit edge for plan writers
Swedish ventures; planners less likely to quit

blocks.source: Kirsch et al., SMJ, 2009; Honig & Karlsson, J. of Management, 2004; Delmar & Shane, SMJ, 2003

blocks.text: There is a second, quieter problem with planning: it feels like work. Writing a detailed plan gives you the satisfaction of progress without the risk of showing anything to a real player. For anyone who has ever spent a weekend designing a perfect system instead of using it, this will sound familiar. Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky gave a related trap a name, the *planning fallacy*: people consistently underestimate how long their own projects will take, even when they know similar projects ran late before. A thick plan does not cure that. It can make it worse, because the more effort goes into a forecast, the more attached you get to it.
The case for planning

Now the other side. Frédéric Delmar and Scott Shane studied 223 new ventures started in the first nine months of 1998 by a random sample of Swedish founders. They argued that planning is not a substitute for action but a precursor to it. Planning helps founders make decisions, match the resources they have to what they need, and turn vague goals into specific steps. Their data supported it: ventures that planned were less likely to be abandoned, and they moved faster on developing products and organizing the business.

That is a different claim from the one the skeptics attacked. Delmar and Shane are not saying a document impresses anyone. They are saying the act of working through decisions in advance helps you actually do the work and keeps you from quitting. For someone building on the side, with a few hours a week, that second effect might be the most valuable one. Most side projects do not fail because the market rejected them. They fail because the builder drifted away.

So which is it? In 2010, Jan Brinckmann, Dietmar Grichnik and Diana Kapsa pooled the existing research in a meta-analysis titled, wonderfully, *Should entrepreneurs plan or just storm the castle?* Their answer: planning is beneficial on balance, but context changes how much. In particular, the newness of the firm and the cultural environment significantly affected the relationship. Their recommendation was an approach that combines planning with learning, adjusting the plan as you go rather than treating it as a contract with yourself.

The research split is less about plans and more about what kind of plan. A static document written to impress outsiders does little. A working plan that turns goals into next steps, and gets revised as you learn, helps you act and keeps you from quitting.
Prediction versus control

A different line of research explains why traditional plans fit new ventures so badly. In 2001, Saras Sarasvathy published a paper in the *Academy of Management Review* contrasting two ways of reasoning. *Causation* starts with a goal and picks the best means to reach it: decide the destination, then plan the route. *Effectuation* starts with the means you already have and asks what effects you could create with them, letting the goal take shape along the way.

Sarasvathy studied how expert entrepreneurs, people who had founded multiple companies, actually thought through problems, and found they leaned heavily on effectual reasoning. Her later work boiled it down to a few principles. Start with who you are, what you know and whom you know. Decide what you can afford to lose rather than chasing an expected return. Bring in partners who commit early. Treat surprises as material rather than threats. And focus on the parts of the future you can control rather than trying to predict the rest.

blocks.title: Two ways to start something

left.head: Causation (classic plan)
items: Start with a fixed goal
Research the market and predict demand
Calculate expected returns
Avoid surprises; stick to the plan
Works best when the future is knowable

right.head: Effectuation (expert founders)
items: Start with the skills, time and people you have
Decide what you can afford to lose
Get partners and players involved early
Use surprises to change direction
Works best when the future is unknowable

blocks.text: This matters for a Roblox game or a YouTube channel because those markets are about as unpredictable as markets get. Nobody can tell you in advance how many players a pole-vault obby will hold on day 7, or which video will catch. A plan built on predictions is guesswork dressed up in a spreadsheet. A plan built on affordable loss is honest: here is what I will put in, here is how I will know if it is working, here is when I stop.
The one-page plan worth writing

Put the research together and you get a clear design brief. The useful plan is short, because nobody updates a 30-page document. It focuses on decisions and next steps, because that is where Delmar and Shane found the benefit. It is built around what you can control and afford, as Sarasvathy suggests. And it is revised as you learn, as Brinckmann and colleagues recommend. It is not a tracking system or a spreadsheet you maintain every day. It is a page you write once, look at weekly, and rewrite when reality disagrees with it.

blocks.title: A one-page plan for a side project
items: What are we building, for whom, in one sentence?
What do we already have: skills, time per week, tools, people, audience?
What is our affordable loss: the maximum hours and money we will put in before re-deciding?
What is the riskiest assumption, and the cheapest test that could prove it wrong?
What result by what date means keep going, change course or stop?
What are the next three concrete actions, and who does each one?

blocks.text: Here is what that might look like for a small Roblox project, as an illustration rather than a template. *What:* a launcher obby where every jump makes you stronger, for players who like quick progression. *What we have:* one scripter, one builder, about six hours a week each, and a small Discord. *Affordable loss:* ten weeks of those hours and no paid ads until the game proves itself. *Riskiest assumption:* that the core jump is still fun after the first ten minutes. *Cheapest test:* a rough build played by twenty strangers, watching where they quit. *Decision rule:* if most of them leave before the second area, change the core loop once; if that fails too, move on. *Next actions:* named, small and due this week.

Notice what is missing: market size, five-year projections, competitor tables. Those things matter for some decisions, but for a two-person project they mostly give you a feeling of progress without any progress. The questions on this list are the ones that change what you do on Saturday.

The kill criteria in step five deserve special attention. Deciding in advance what result would make you stop is one of the few defenses against the sunk cost effect, the tendency to keep investing because of what you have already spent. If you decide before you start that a game needs a certain day-1 return rate in its first real playtest, you can judge the result calmly. If you decide afterward, you will find a reason to keep going.

There are times when the formal version is the right tool. If you ever apply for a bank or Small Business Administration loan, bring on an investor or ask a partner to put real money in, they may expect a traditional plan, and they are entitled to see your thinking in a standard format. The SBA itself describes two common formats: a traditional plan that can run dozens of pages, and a lean startup plan that is typically a single page and can take as little as an hour to make. Its guidance is refreshingly practical: there is no right or wrong format, only the one that meets your needs. When the readers are lenders, write for lenders. When the reader is you, write the page that changes your next move.

The two formats can also live together. Start with the one-page version while you are testing whether the idea works at all. If it does, and you need outside money or a formal partnership, the one page becomes the skeleton of the longer document, filled in with real numbers from real players instead of guesses. That is the order Brinckmann and colleagues pointed toward: learn first, then plan in more detail as the uncertainty shrinks.
Plans that survive contact

One more tool is worth adding, because it attacks the biggest weakness of every plan: optimism. Psychologist Gary Klein described the *premortem* in the *Harvard Business Review* in 2007. Before starting a project, the team imagines it is months later and the project has failed completely. Then everyone writes down why it failed. Because the failure is treated as a fact rather than a possibility, people stop defending the plan and start finding its holes.

For a small team, a premortem takes fifteen minutes. Imagine it is six months from now and the game is dead. Why? Maybe one of you stopped having time. Maybe the core loop was fun for five minutes and boring after twenty. Maybe nobody ever found the game because there was no plan to get players in the door. Each answer points to something you can add to the one-page plan now, while it is cheap to change.

That is the deeper lesson in Eisenhower's line. A military commander knows the plan will not survive the first hours of contact; that is not a reason to skip planning. The value is that, having thought through the problem, the people involved understand the goal, the resources and the risks well enough to adapt when things change. A business plan should do the same job. If it is sitting in a folder, it is a ritual. If it changes what you do this week, it is a tool.

takeaways: In a study of 722 VC funding requests, business plans were only weakly linked to who got funded.
A two-year study of 396 nascent founders found no profit advantage for writing a plan; many plans are written for show.
Planning that turns goals into concrete steps made Swedish ventures less likely to be abandoned.
For unpredictable projects, plan around what you have and can afford to lose, not around forecasts.
Write one page with kill criteria and next actions, run a premortem, and revise it when reality disagrees.
