title: The Number That Arrives First
dek: Students bid triple for the same keyboard because of their Social Security numbers. Pricing psychology is real, but smaller and stranger than its reputation, and Roblox's own data says most creators charge too much.

blocks.text: In a marketing class at MIT, students were shown a handful of ordinary products: a cordless keyboard, a bottle of wine, a box of chocolates. Before bidding on each one, they were asked to write down the last two digits of their Social Security number and say whether they would pay that many dollars for it. The number was meaningless. Everyone knew it was meaningless. It still bent their bids.

Students whose numbers ended between 80 and 99 bid an average of $56 for the keyboard. Students whose numbers ended between 1 and 20 bid $16. Across the products, the high-number group's bids ran roughly 216 to 346 percent higher. The economist Dan Ariely, who ran the study with George Loewenstein and Drazen Prelec, used it to make a provocative claim: people often do not know what things are worth, so they grab whatever number is nearby and adjust from there.

items.label: Average keyboard bid, Social Security digits 80 to 99
Average keyboard bid, Social Security digits 1 to 20

blocks.source: Ariely, Loewenstein & Prelec, 'Coherent Arbitrariness', QJE 2003; Ariely, HuffPost, 2008

blocks.text: That idea, that value is partly invented on the spot, sits under almost every pricing trick you have seen: the crossed-out "was" price, the $9.99 tag, the three-tier menu with one option nobody buys. Some of these effects are among the most solid findings in behavioral science. Others are much smaller and shakier than their reputation. And for someone selling game passes on Roblox, the most useful pricing evidence available turns out to come from Roblox itself.
The anchor drops first

The classic demonstration came from Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman in 1974. They spun a wheel of fortune rigged to stop at either 10 or 65, then asked people what percentage of United Nations member countries were in Africa. People who saw 10 gave a median estimate of 25 percent. People who saw 65 said 45 percent. A random number, visibly produced by a wheel, moved a factual guess by twenty points.

This is anchoring: the first number you encounter becomes the starting point, and people adjust away from it, but not far enough. Unlike many famous psychology results, the basic effect has held up well. When the Many Labs project re-ran classic experiments across dozens of labs in 2014, anchoring was among the effects that replicated most strongly.

The size of the effect in real purchases is another matter. In 2014, the economists Zacharias Maniadis, Fabio Tufano and John List re-tested anchoring on valuations and found weaker effects than the original studies, and they used the episode to warn that a single striking result is a poor guide to how big an effect really is. There is a further reason for caution with this particular body of work. In 2021, a separate 2012 paper co-authored by Ariely was retracted after investigators found that some of its data had been fabricated. Ariely denied fabricating it, and the anchoring findings rest on many other labs too, but it is a reminder that the most quotable numbers deserve the most skepticism.

In practice, sellers use anchors constantly. A store shows the expensive model first. A software page lists the enterprise plan beside the basic one. A sale tag shows a crossed-out higher price. The last one has legal limits: the US Federal Trade Commission's long-standing guides on deceptive pricing say a "former price" has to be one the item was genuinely offered at, not a number invented to make the discount look bigger. An honest anchor is a real comparison. A fake one is a lie with a price tag.
Anchoring is real and robust. What is not settled is how much it moves money in a real market where people can compare prices, read reviews and walk away.
The decoy nobody is meant to buy

The second famous trick works on choice rather than price. In 1982, Joel Huber, John Payne and Christopher Puto showed that adding a clearly inferior third option can shift people toward the option it most resembles. They called it the attraction effect. Marketers call it the decoy.

The best-known illustration comes from Ariely's book *Predictably Irrational*. He described an old subscription offer from *The Economist*: web only for $59, print only for $125, or print and web together for $125. Nobody sane picks print only when print plus web costs the same. But in his classroom test, its presence seemed to matter. With all three options, 16 percent of students chose web only and 84 percent chose the bundle. With the useless print-only option removed, 68 percent chose web only and just 32 percent took the bundle.

blocks.title: Share choosing the $125 bundle
blocks.note: A classroom demonstration with students, not a market test. Treat it as an illustration of the idea.
blocks.source: Dan Ariely, Predictably Irrational, 2008

blocks.text: That demo is vivid, but it was a classroom poll, not a field experiment with real money. And the academic picture has grown more complicated. In 2014, Shane Frederick, Leonard Lee and Ernest Baskin argued in the *Journal of Marketing Research* that the attraction effect mostly appears when products are reduced to tidy numbers on a page. When people actually taste a drink, or see hotel rooms in photos, the effect tends to vanish. Huber and his colleagues replied that the effect is real but only under specific conditions: the two main options have to be close, the decoy has to be obviously worse, and the comparison has to be easy to see.

That is a useful correction. A decoy works best on a confusing menu of numbers, when the buyer cannot easily judge quality. It works worst on things people can experience directly. A game pass that players can see in action is closer to the hotel photo than to the spreadsheet.
Why $9.99 still works

Then there is the oldest trick of all, the price ending in 9. It sounds too silly to matter: $2.99 versus $3.00 is a one-cent difference. But in 2005, Manoj Thomas and Vicki Morwitz showed through five experiments that people really do perceive $2.99 as meaningfully cheaper than $3.00, and only when the leftmost digit changes. $2.99 versus $3.00 triggers it. $2.79 versus $2.80 does not. They call it the left-digit effect. We read numbers left to right, and the first digit gets most of our attention.

Field evidence backs this up. Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester ran three experiments with a mail-order clothing retailer, printing different versions of the same catalog with different prices for the same items. A price ending in $9 increased demand in all three tests. The boost was larger for new items, which customers had no prior price for, and weaker when items were already marked with a "Sale" sign.

That pattern reveals what is really going on. A 9-ending is partly a signal. It says "this is a deal" to someone who does not know what the item should cost. When customers already know the price, or already see a sale tag, the signal adds less. That is also why many premium brands avoid 9s entirely: they do not want to look like a discount.

Virtual currencies add one more layer. On Roblox, players see prices in Robux, not dollars, so the anchors that matter are other Robux prices: what the last game charged for a similar pass, what a skin costs in the avatar shop. Few players convert back to dollars in their heads. That makes the left-digit effect and familiar price points inside the game's own currency more relevant than any rule about $9.99.
More choices, fewer buyers? Not so fast

You may have heard of the jam study. In 2000, Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting booth in a grocery store and found that a display of 24 jams attracted more browsers but led to fewer purchases than a display of 6. It became the founding story of "choice overload" and has been quoted in countless pricing pages to justify cutting options.

The follow-up research is much less dramatic. In 2010, Benjamin Scheibehenne, Rainer Greifeneder and Peter Todd pooled 50 experiments with more than 5,000 participants and found an average effect of virtually zero. Some studies found that more options hurt, others found they helped, and nobody could pin down reliable conditions for when overload kicks in. The honest takeaway is not "always offer three options." It is that the menu matters, but no magic number works everywhere, and you have to test yours.

blocks.title: Pricing claims versus the evidence

left.head: What the blogs say
items: Anchors can triple what people pay
Always add a decoy tier
Three options is the magic number
Psychological prices are a growth hack

right.head: What the research shows
items: Anchors are robust, but real-market effects are smaller
Decoys work mainly on abstract, numeric menus
Choice overload averages out to about zero
Real tests typically find single-digit gains

blocks.text: What a real pricing lab found

Here is the part most pricing blogs cannot offer: results from a platform running experiments on millions of real purchases. In October 2024, Roblox launched Price Optimization, a tool that tests different prices for a game's items and passes on small groups of players for two weeks and recommends the best one. Its announcement contained a blunt line for creators: most of them unknowingly price their in-game items too high, and in many cases the fix would be to cut prices.

In April 2025 Roblox added regional pricing, which automatically lowers prices in countries where Robux are expensive relative to local incomes. In June 2026 it folded both into one system called Managed Pricing and published results. Among the top 2,500 games, those using regional pricing saw an average 4 to 10 percent increase in overall Robux spending, 1 to 6 percent more players and playtime, and 43 to 52 percent more pass purchases in the discounted regions. Creators using price optimization saw average earnings growth of 4 percent.

blocks.title: Roblox regional pricing results, top 2,500 games, 2025
blocks.note: Low and high ends of the ranges Roblox reported. Pass purchases were measured in the discounted regions. Averages, not guarantees.
blocks.source: Roblox Developer Forum, Managed Pricing announcement, June 2026

blocks.text: Four percent sounds small next to the $56-versus-$16 keyboard. That is the point. When real buyers can compare, wait and walk away, good pricing usually adds single-digit percentages, not miracles. The dramatic lab effects shrink in the wild. And the biggest gain on Roblox did not come from a psychological trick at all. It came from lowering prices for players who could not afford them, which brought in buyers who had been priced out entirely.

This connects to the economics covered in the separate article on Roblox developer earnings. Because a creator keeps only a slice of each Robux spent, and because a digital pass costs nothing to deliver to one more player, selling twice as many passes at a lower price is often better than selling a few at a high one. Volume is cheap to serve when the product is code.
A pricing playbook for a game pass
Put the research together and a sensible approach emerges. It uses the real effects lightly, ignores the hype and leans on testing.

blocks.title: Pricing your first passes
items: Look at what similar games charge for similar passes. That is the anchor players already carry.
Show the most valuable pass first, so cheaper ones look reasonable next to it, but make sure it is genuinely worth its price.
Keep the menu short and clearly different: each option should do a different job for a different player.
Price for volume at launch. A digital pass costs nothing to deliver, and Roblox's data says most creators start too high.
Turn on regional pricing and price testing once you have enough buyers, and let real behavior pick the number.
Change one thing at a time and watch revenue per player, not just sales count.

blocks.text: Anchoring also explains why your launch price matters more than later ones. The first price your early players see becomes their reference point. Lowering it later feels like a gift; raising it feels like a betrayal, even if the new price is fair. If you are unsure, it is usually easier to start a little low and add value, or create a new premium pass, than to push an existing price up on the players who know what it used to cost.

One warning sits on top of all of this. Tricks that make players feel cheated, like fake "was" prices or decoys that only exist to confuse, may win a sale and lose a player. Your audience on Roblox is young and talks to each other constantly, so trust is a pricing asset too. The anchoring research says first impressions of value stick. That cuts both ways: a pass that feels like a rip-off anchors how players see everything else in your game.

The deeper lesson from the Social Security experiment is not that people are easy to fool. It is that value is uncertain, and people reach for whatever reference point is nearby. Your job as a seller is to give them an honest one: a clear comparison, a fair price, a product that obviously earns it. Then test, because the market's answer is worth more than any psychology blog's.

takeaways: Anchoring is one of psychology's most robust effects: the first number people see shapes what they think is fair.
Decoys and choice-overload effects are real only under narrow conditions. Do not build a strategy on them.
A 9-ending signals a deal. It helps most when buyers do not already know the price.
In real markets, good pricing usually adds single-digit percentages. Roblox's price optimization averaged 4 percent.
For digital goods with near-zero delivery cost, test lower prices before higher ones.

title: The 17-Year Overnight Success: What Roblox's Own Filings Reveal
dek: Roblox's SEC filings tell a story of slow building, billion-dollar 'losses' that aren't what they look like, and an economy where 1 percent of players pay for everyone.

blocks.text: In 1989, two engineers wrote a piece of software that let students crash virtual cars into virtual walls. It was called Interactive Physics, and you could build a little house on screen and watch it fall apart under simulated gravity. David Baszucki and Erik Cassel did not know it yet, but they had just written the first draft of a company that, thirty-six years later, would have 127 million people showing up every single day.

That company is Roblox. Most people experience it as a game, or a thousand games, or a place where their little cousin spends their allowance. But Roblox is also a public company, which means it has to tell the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission the truth about itself, in writing, every year. Those filings are boring to look at and fascinating to read. They tell a story that is very different from the one most people assume: not a rocket ship, but a slow climb, a long stretch of losing money on paper, and an economy where a tiny fraction of players and creators carry almost everything.
If you build on Roblox, this is your landlord's diary. It is worth knowing what it says.
The overnight success that took seventeen years

Roblox's 2021 prospectus, the document it filed before its shares started trading, opens with that physics program. Baszucki worked at Knowledge Revolution, the company behind Interactive Physics, from 1989 until it was bought by MSC Software in December 1998. He then founded an online car-sales company. Roblox itself was incorporated in 2004, and Baszucki has been its CEO since March of that year.

Here is the part that gets skipped in the highlight reel. By 2018, fourteen years after incorporation, Roblox averaged about 12 million daily active users. That sounds big, and it was, but the company still reported a net loss of $88 million that year. The founders were not new to this. They already had one exit behind them. They still spent well over a decade building before the numbers turned into the kind that make headlines.

blocks.title: From physics lab to stock ticker
items: Baszucki and Cassel program Interactive Physics, a 2D physics simulator for students
Knowledge Revolution is acquired by MSC Software
Roblox is incorporated; Baszucki becomes CEO
About 12 million average daily users; $88M net loss
Pandemic year: daily users nearly double to 32.6 million

Shares begin trading on the NYSE via a direct listing
127 million average daily users, about 1.8 million of them paying each day

blocks.text: Then came 2020. The prospectus says plainly that the COVID-19 pandemic increased its users, bookings and cash flow. Daily users went from 17.6 million in 2019 to 32.6 million in 2020. Kids stuck at home needed somewhere to hang out with their friends, and Roblox had spent sixteen years building exactly that place. Luck mattered. But luck only pays out if you are already standing in the right spot when it arrives.

blocks.title: Roblox average daily active users
blocks.source: Roblox S-1/A (2021) and Form 10-K filings, 2021–2025

blocks.text: Notice the shape after 2020. The pandemic spike did not collapse. Growth kept going, and 2025 added more users than any year before it. A curve like this looks inevitable in hindsight. From inside 2009 or 2014, it looked like a niche kids' site that might never matter.
Losing a billion dollars while swimming in cash

Here is a fact that breaks most people's mental model of business. In 2025, Roblox reported a net loss of about $1.07 billion. In the same year, it generated about $1.35 billion in free cash flow. Its accumulated deficit, the running total of every loss it has ever booked, stood at about $5.06 billion. How can a company lose that much money and also be gushing cash?

Two things explain most of it. The first is how Roblox counts revenue. When a player buys Robux, Roblox gets the cash right away, but under accounting rules it spreads the revenue out over the estimated time that paying players stick around. So the company tracks a second number, *bookings*, which is closer to what players actually spent in the year. In 2025, revenue was $4.89 billion, but bookings were $6.79 billion. The gap is money already in the bank that has not shown up on the income statement yet.

The second is stock-based compensation. Roblox pays a lot of its employees in shares, and in 2025 that cost was about $1.13 billion. It is a real cost to shareholders, because it dilutes them, but it does not drain cash. Strip it out, along with depreciation and interest, and the company's own adjusted measure of profit was positive.

items.label: Roblox net loss, 2025
Free cash flow, 2025
Bookings (what players spent), 2025

blocks.source: Roblox Form 10-K for fiscal 2025

blocks.text: This is not a trick, and it is not a scandal. It is a reminder that *profit* is a definition, not a fact of nature. The question you should ask about any business, including a small one, is not just whether it shows a profit but where the cash actually goes and when it arrives. A Roblox game that sells a big one-time gamepass and a game that sells a cheap monthly subscription can have the same yearly income and feel completely different to run.
The economy inside the economy

Roblox does not make most of its content. Creators do, and the company pays them. The filings call these payments *developer exchange fees*, the dollars Roblox hands over when qualifying creators cash out their earned Robux through the DevEx program. That line has grown faster than almost anything else on the income statement.

blocks.title: What Roblox paid creators through DevEx
blocks.note: Developer exchange fees as reported on the income statement
blocks.source: Roblox S-1/A (2021) and Form 10-K filings

blocks.text: In 2025, those fees came to about 31 percent of Roblox's revenue. As of the end of that year, more than 35,500 creators were registered for DevEx, over 10,500 of them newly qualified during 2025. The standard rate is $0.0038 per earned Robux (since September 5, 2025), and a higher $0.0054 applies to qualifying purchases from age-verified U.S. players 18 and up (since June 8, 2026). When a creator sells an item inside their own experience, the 10-K says they keep 70 percent of the Robux spent.

Those payouts are not spread evenly. The 2020 prospectus gives a rare look at the distribution. That year, more than 1.25 million developers and creators earned some Robux. About 3,300 actually cashed out. Around 1,250 earned $10,000 or more, and about 300 earned $100,000 or more. The same document says roughly 90 percent of in-experience engagement went to the top 1,000 experiences.

The player side is just as lopsided. In 2025, of 127 million average daily users, only about 1.8 million were paying on a given day, roughly 1.4 percent. The average daily spend across all users was about 15 cents. Across paying users it was about $10. Free-to-play economics in one sentence: almost everyone plays for free, and a small group pays for everyone.

Put those numbers next to the DevEx rate and you get a sobering bit of arithmetic. Roblox's own documentation says 30,000 earned Robux convert to $114 at the standard rate. To cash out $1,000, you need roughly 263,000 earned Robux. And earned Robux are what is left after the platform's share of each sale, so players have to spend noticeably more than that inside your game. None of this means small games cannot make money. It means a game that earns a few thousand Robux a week is a hobby that pays for itself, not a business yet, and the jump between the two is mostly about how many people come back.

That is why the filings keep returning to engagement. Roblox reports hours engaged next to daily users, because time spent is the raw material for everything else: spending, ad impressions and the engagement-based payouts it makes to creators whose experiences hold Premium subscribers. For a creator, the lesson is to watch the same thing the company watches. Revenue is downstream of people choosing to return tomorrow.

Read the filings of the platform you build on. Roblox's 10-K tells you how many people pay, how payouts are split and what the company worries about in its risk factors. That is better market research than any YouTube video about "how much Roblox games make."
The good news hiding in the concentration

A hits-driven economy sounds hopeless for a two-person team. But one line in the 2021 prospectus cuts the other way. Looking at the top 100 grossing experiences each month from 2015 through 2020, Roblox reported that almost half of them had been made in the previous two years. The top of the charts was not a locked club of old games. New ones kept breaking in.

That fits the company's incentives. Roblox earns money when people spend time and Robux, and players get bored. The platform needs a steady supply of new games that feel fresh, which means the front page is never permanently owned. Compare that to a market where the same ten titles dominate for a decade. On Roblox, the barrier is not that the old guard holds every slot; it is that the bar for a new game keeps rising as the platform matures and big studios and brands move in.

It also says something about the audience. In 2020, Roblox reported that 54 percent of its daily users were under 13. By 2021 that had dropped to 49 percent. The platform is aging up, and the higher DevEx rate for spend from verified adults shows the company wants that older audience. A game designed with teenagers and adults in mind is swimming with the current, not against it.
What a small studio should take from a giant

It is easy to read a company story like this and pull out the wrong lesson, something like "keep going and you'll be a billionaire." Survivorship bias is real. For every Roblox there were dozens of virtual-world startups in the 2000s that kept going and still disappeared. Persistence is necessary, not sufficient.

The better lessons are narrower and more useful. First, the founders' earlier work mattered. A physics simulator for students taught them that people love building things and watching them behave realistically. Roblox was not a random idea; it was a bigger version of something they had already seen work. Your own earlier projects, even the abandoned ones, are research. Second, the company tracked the right numbers long before anyone was watching: daily users, hours engaged, bookings per user. A tiny studio can track the same things for one game.

Third, timing and position compound. Roblox did not create the pandemic, but it had built a social platform for kids long before the moment arrived that everyone needed one. Small builders cannot predict their moment either. What they can do is keep a project alive and improving long enough to be ready when luck shows up, instead of starting over every few months and always being at version zero.

It is also worth reading what the company says it is afraid of. The risk-factor section of a 10-K is a list, written by lawyers, of everything that could go wrong. Roblox's includes child-safety and privacy law, the app stores that take a cut of mobile purchases, its dependence on a small share of paying users and on creators continuing to build. Every one of those risks flows downhill to the people making games on the platform. When the company tightens age rules or changes payout rates, it is usually responding to something already sitting in that section.

blocks.title: Reading a 10-K in 20 minutes
items: Search the company on SEC EDGAR and open the latest Form 10-K
Read the business overview for how the company describes itself and its users
Find the key metrics (for Roblox: daily users, hours, bookings) and compare years
Read the risk factors for what management is actually worried about
Check the cash flow statement, not just net income, to see where money really moves

blocks.text: Finally, remember who you are in this picture. On Roblox you are not the company in the filings; you are one of the 35,500 or so creators in a single line of them. The platform's choices about rates, discovery and age rules shape your income more than almost anything you control. That is not a reason to stay away. It is a reason to read what the platform says about itself, keep your own audience close, and build a game good enough that the algorithm has a reason to show it.

takeaways: Roblox was incorporated in 2004 and had about 12 million daily users by 2018; the explosion came after more than a decade of building.
Net loss is not the same as no money: in 2025 Roblox lost about $1.07B on paper but produced about $1.35B in free cash flow.
Only about 1.4 percent of daily users paid on a typical day in 2025, and payouts to creators are highly concentrated.
Almost half of the top-grossing experiences from 2015 to 2020 were made in the previous two years, so new games can break in.
Read your platform's own filings and docs before trusting anyone's summary of them.

title: Follow the Robux: Where a Player's Dollar Actually Goes
dek: Roblox paid its creators about $1.5 billion in 2025, and the typical creator who cashed out got a few hundred dollars a year. Tracing a single dollar through the system explains both numbers.

blocks.text: Two numbers from Roblox's own reports sit next to each other uneasily. In 2025, according to the company's annual filing, creators earned about $1.5 billion through its Developer Exchange program, up from about $923 million the year before. And in the twelve months that ended in December 2024, the median creator in that program received $1,575.

Both numbers are true at once, and the gap between them is the whole story of Roblox as a business for small developers. There is a lot of money moving through the platform, it is growing fast, and almost all of it lands on a small number of games. To see why, it helps to follow one dollar from a player's parent's card to a developer's bank account and count what happens along the way.

items.label: Earned by Roblox creators through DevEx in 2025
The same figure for 2024
Median yearly payout to a DevEx creator (12 months to Dec 2024)

blocks.source: Roblox Form 10-K for fiscal 2025; Roblox Annual Economic Impact Report, 2025

blocks.text: Following one dollar

Start with the purchase. Players buy Robux in bundles, and the price per Robux depends on the bundle and how it is bought. Roblox's annual report puts the average selling price in 2025 at about one cent per Robux. So, roughly, a dollar of real money becomes 100 Robux in a player's account.

Next, the player spends those Robux in your game, say on a game pass. Roblox's filing says that when creators sell their own items inside their own experiences, they receive 70 percent of the Robux and the platform keeps 30 percent. Of the 100 Robux, 70 land in your account as what Roblox calls earned Robux.

Finally, you cash out through the Developer Exchange, usually shortened to DevEx. Since September 5, 2025, the standard rate has been $0.0038 per earned Robux, up from $0.0035 before that. Seventy Robux times $0.0038 is about 27 cents. That is the core fact of Roblox economics for a small developer: of each dollar a player spends in your game, roughly a quarter reaches you, before any taxes.

blocks.title: Cash to the developer per $1 a player spends
blocks.note: Assumes Robux bought at the 2025 average of about $0.01 each and the 70% creator share on in-game sales. Real bundle prices vary.
blocks.source: Roblox Form 10-K FY2025; Roblox DevEx documentation, 2026

blocks.text: Where does the rest go? The 30 percent fee pays for the platform itself: servers, moderation, payments, discovery. Purchases made on phones also pass through app stores, which take a cut of their own before Roblox sees the money. And the gap between what Robux cost players and what Roblox pays to buy them back is how the company funds everything else. None of that is hidden, but it rarely appears in the stories about teenage developers buying houses.
Rule of thumb: under the standard rate, a game keeps roughly a quarter of what its players spend. A game pass priced at 100 Robux is worth about 27 cents to its creator, not a dollar.
The 18+ rate, and who it is really for

On April 30, 2026, Roblox announced a higher exchange rate for a specific slice of spending, starting June 8. The DevEx documentation now lists a rate of $0.0054 per earned Robux, about 42 percent above the standard rate. It applies only to certain purchases, namely developer products, passes, subscriptions and private servers, made by players in the United States who have been verified as 18 or older through facial age estimation or a government ID, in eligible games. The announcement tied eligibility to games using the R15 avatar type.

The company was open about the motive. It said its U.S. users aged 18 to 34 were growing by more than half year over year and spent about 50 percent more than under-18 players, while flagging that those figures were early estimates. In plain terms, Roblox is paying developers more to build games that adults want, because adults have their own money.

For most small games, the honest reading is that this rate will cover a minority of revenue at best. A casual obby whose players skew young will see most of its earnings at the standard rate, and every Robux that was earned before September 5, 2025 still cashes out at the old $0.0035 rate first. The higher rate is a signal about where the platform wants to grow, not a raise for everyone. It is worth knowing about when choosing what to build next, and not worth counting on when estimating what the current game will earn.
A power law, not a ladder

Roblox's 2025 economic impact report gives a rare look at how earnings are spread among developers. In 2024, the top 10 developers averaged $33.9 million each. The top 100 averaged $6 million. The top 1,000 averaged $820,000. The median DevEx creator, the one in the exact middle of the more than 24,500 creators in the program, got $1,575. A footnote says some of these figures were measured in Robux spent, so treat them as approximate, but the shape is unmistakable.

blocks.title: Average yearly earnings by developer rank, 2024
blocks.note: The median bar is too small to see. That is the point. Roblox notes some figures are measured in Robux spent.
blocks.source: Roblox Annual Economic Impact Report, September 2025

blocks.text: This is what a power law looks like. It is not a ladder where each rung is a bit higher than the last; it is a cliff. And remember that the median here is the median of people who already qualified to cash out, which requires at least 30,000 earned Robux. The many developers who never reach that threshold are not in the sample at all.

The cliff should change how a small team thinks about success. If the distribution were a ladder, steady effort would produce steady income. On a cliff, most of the return goes to games that break out, and breaking out depends on things like retention and the ability to ship updates fast enough to ride a trend. (The articles on retention and on shipping early cover those levers in depth, and the one on platform risk covers what happens when Roblox changes the rules.)
Designing for the few who pay

The power law exists inside each game too. Using the filing's figures, only about 1.4 percent of Roblox's daily users paid for anything on an average day in 2025. Those who did spent a little over $10 on average. So a game's income does not come from everyone spending a little. It comes from a small group spending a meaningful amount, supported by a much larger group who play for free and make the game feel alive.

That has a design consequence that is easy to get wrong. The free players are not freeloaders; they are the crowd, the competition, the friends who get invited, and the reason a paying player bothers to show off a rare trail or a flashy effect. A game that squeezes them with constant purchase prompts or walls them out of the fun tends to shrink, and a shrinking game earns less from its payers too. The healthier pattern is to sell things that make a game the player already loves feel better, faster or more personal, and to leave the core loop open.

A useful exercise is to imagine the player most likely to spend real money in your game and ask what they would happily pay for that a casual player would not miss. Often the answers are cosmetic flair, convenience, a private server to play with friends, or a way to support the creators they like. Rarely is the answer a paywall in front of the fun. The 18+ rate pushes in the same direction from the other side: Roblox is signaling that it wants games adults enjoy enough to spend on, which means games with depth, not just games with more store buttons.

There is also a timing lesson. Monetization added to a game nobody returns to does almost nothing, because the people who would eventually pay never stick around long enough to want anything. The order that works is retention first, then a small number of well-made things to buy, then more of whatever the data says players actually value.
What it takes to cash out

The Developer Exchange has a short list of requirements. You must be at least 13, have a verified email on your Roblox account, hold at least 30,000 earned Robux, have a DevEx portal account, and have a tax form on file: a W-9 for U.S. taxpayers or a W-8 for everyone else. You can cash out once per calendar month. At the standard rate, the 30,000-Robux minimum is worth $114.

items: Counts as earned: in-game sales of passes, developer products and subscriptions, paid access and private servers, Creator Store and Marketplace sales, Creator Rewards, and legitimate group payouts.
Does not count: Robux you bought, monthly subscription grants, trading or reselling items, Robux transferred or gifted to you, or anything from content that was moderated.
Older balances: Robux earned before September 5, 2025 cash out at $0.0035 and must be cashed out before newer Robux.

blocks.text: Work the minimum backward and it gets concrete. To earn 30,000 Robux at a 70 percent share, players must spend about 43,000 Robux in your game, which at the 2025 average price is roughly $430 of real money. That is the first real milestone for a new game: not a million visits, but a few hundred dollars of player spending that adds up to your first cash-out of a bit over a hundred dollars.

Two practical cautions apply to anyone in the military. The tax form is there because this is taxable income, so keep records and talk to a tax preparer or the free tax help offered on base. And service members are generally expected to follow their command's rules on outside work and business activity, so ask your chain of command or legal office what applies before money starts flowing.
Running your own numbers

The useful formula is simple. Daily players, times the share who pay, times what they spend, times 0.7 for the platform fee, times the exchange rate. Every term except the last two is something your game controls through design, and every one of them shows up in Roblox's own analytics dashboard once the game has players.

For a sense of the ceiling, Roblox's filing says the platform averaged about 15 cents of player spending per daily user per day in 2025, and roughly 1.8 million of its 127 million daily users paid for something on a typical day. Those averages include avatar shopping and the biggest hit games, so a typical small game will earn well below them per player. Even at the platform average, 1,000 daily players would generate about $150 a day of spending and around $40 a day for the developer. Use that as an upper bound for daydreams, and your own dashboard as the real answer.

blocks.title: Estimating what your game earns
items: Pull average daily active users from your analytics.
Find the share of players who buy anything, and what they spend on average.
Multiply to get daily player spending in Robux.
Multiply by 0.7 for your share, then by $0.0038 for dollars.
Compare that to the 30,000-Robux minimum to see how long until a first cash-out.

blocks.text: The economics are not a reason to quit. They are a reason to aim carefully. Roblox gives two people with no studio, no publisher and no budget access to an audience of well over a hundred million daily players, and it pays real money when a game works. What it does not do is pay much for a game that is merely fine. The money follows players who come back, and players come back to games that are built around one strong idea and keep getting better.

So the question for a two-person team is not whether Roblox pays fairly in the abstract. It is whether this particular game can find a group of players who return every week and care enough to spend. Answer that with real data from a released version, and the DevEx math becomes a simple multiplication instead of a hope.

takeaways: Of each dollar a player spends in your game, about 27 cents reaches you at the standard DevEx rate of $0.0038.
The $0.0054 rate covers only qualifying purchases by age-verified U.S. adults in eligible games; most young-audience games will earn mostly at the standard rate.
Earnings follow a power law: top-10 developers averaged $33.9M in 2024, while the median DevEx creator got $1,575.
Your first milestone is 30,000 earned Robux ($114), which takes roughly $430 of player spending.
DevEx income is taxable, and military members should check outside-work rules with their command.

title: Champagne for the Dead: Why Supercell Kills Most of Its Games
dek: The studio behind Clash of Clans built a multibillion-dollar company by cancelling projects early, toasting every failure and publishing what went wrong.

blocks.text: In the fall of 2011, five people at a small Finnish startup had spent nearly six months working day and night on a game codenamed *Magic*. It looked amazing. The team loved it. The company was running on the founders' savings and government loans, and it had already watched its first game fade. Then the founders made a call that sounds insane: kill *Magic*, kill everything else in production for web and Facebook, and bet the whole company on the iPad.

The same five people went back to work on something new for tablets. Supercell's own history page tells what happened next with obvious delight. That team built *Clash of Clans*, a game whose working codename was, once again, *Magic*. Launched globally in August 2012, it reached number one on the U.S. top-grossing chart three months later.

Supercell is now one of the most successful mobile game companies in the world. In 2025 it reported $3.01 billion in revenue. But the thing it is most famous for inside the industry is not its hits. It is how often it kills its own games, and the fact that it throws a party with champagne every time it does.
A company built on the delete button

Supercell was founded in 2010 in Espoo, Finland. According to the company, the first office was a single 30-square-meter room with six desks from a recycling center and a coffee maker. At one point fifteen people were crammed into it, and the CEO, Ilkka Paananen, had to move out to make room. The original plan was cross-platform online games you could play from any device.

The first game, *Gunshine*, was a browser MMO that peaked at about half a million monthly players in the summer of 2011. That is not nothing. But the team saw that players got bored after a month or two, and that the game was too hard for newcomers to ever become a mass hit. So they killed it, and with it the whole cross-platform strategy.

blocks.title: Supercell's early kill list
items: Founded in Espoo with founders' savings and loans from Tekes
Gunshine peaks near 500,000 monthly players, then is killed; Magic is killed too
Feb 2012
Pets vs. Orcs, the first mobile game, is killed
Spring 2012
A game codenamed Tower is killed
Jun 2012
Hay Day launches globally after a strong beta in Canada
Aug 2012
Clash of Clans launches globally; No. 1 grossing in the U.S. within three months
Battle Buddies never escapes beta and is killed
Spooky Pop and Smash Land are killed after betas

blocks.text: By early 2012 the company had five small teams working on tablet and mobile games, knowing that at least one had to succeed for Supercell to survive. Two of the five became hits. Three were killed. Supercell's history page states the lesson bluntly: it is usually better to kill a game early, and if you start feeling that a game is not fun enough, that feeling usually means you should have killed it already.

Even the wins were chaotic. *Hay Day* went global on June 21, 2012, which happened to be Midsummer's Eve, one of Finland's biggest holidays. The company had almost no player support set up, because nobody expected that kind of response, so nearly everyone ended up answering support tickets from their summer cottages. Success arrived before the company was ready for it. That is a recurring pattern in these stories: the teams that win are usually the ones that kept shipping attempts until one landed, not the ones that predicted which one would.
Why kill a game that might work?

Most people treat cancelling a project as a confession of failure. Supercell treats it as part of the production pipeline. Its games usually get judged at a milestone the company calls a *company playable*, when the team hands a build to everyone in the company. Plenty of projects die there. When the company wrote its early history, it said that only five games had made it all the way through beta to global launch, against what it called countless kills.

The logic comes from the economics of hits. Mobile games are an extreme winner-take-most market. A Supercell market analyst looked at roughly 53,000 mobile games launched since 2020 and found that only 22 of them grossed $1 billion or more. That is about 0.04 percent. If your goal is to make one of those, an average game is not a small success; it is a cost. Every month a team spends polishing something that will never be great is a month it cannot spend finding the thing that might be.

items.label: Mobile games launched since 2020 in Supercell's analysis
Of those that grossed $1 billion or more
Share that reached that level

blocks.source: Ilkka Paananen, "The Best Games Haven't Been Made Yet," Supercell, 2026

blocks.text: There is a psychological trap here, and it has a name. In a classic 1985 experiment, Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer sold season tickets to a university theater series at different prices. People who paid full price went to more plays than people who got a discount, even though the money was already gone either way. That is the *sunk cost effect*: we keep investing in things because of what we have already put in, not because of what they will give us next. Game teams feel it constantly. Two years of work feels like a reason to keep going. Supercell's champagne ritual exists to break that spell.
Champagne for the dead

In a January 2026 post, Supercell described the ritual directly. When a project gets killed, people pop champagne, not to celebrate the failure but to honor the courage it took to try. The reasoning is that if failure feels dangerous, people play it safe, and if failure feels survivable, they take real risks. The company even put people on stage in front of 800 colleagues to talk through the projects they had watched die.

Three of those stories are worth stealing. *Clash Mini* spent years making small changes and putting off hard decisions about its art and identity. Only when the team was told it had time for one last update, and needed to multiply its numbers roughly tenfold, did it make the bold moves that actually shifted the metrics. By then it was too late. One of its leads said the constraint was what finally forced real choices: with a hundred options, you pick safe ones; with one shot, you pick the one that matters.

*Hay Day Pop* was a puzzle game made by a strong team that did not actually play or love puzzle games. They executed well and followed the data, but never innovated on the core. One programmer contrasted it with working on *Clash Royale*, where the team played every day and knew exactly what players wanted. Without that love, he said, you are just guessing from metrics. And in 2013, Supercell cancelled its first big outdoor ad campaign for *Clash of Clans* at a cost of roughly $2 million, because the finished creative was not good enough. The lesson the marketer took away was to ask not only whether something will work, but whether you will be proud of it.

Supercell's three tests for any project: Is there a hard constraint forcing bold choices? Does the team genuinely love this kind of game? Would we be proud to ship it? A "no" on any of them is a warning, not a detail.
When the system fails: Squad Busters

The best evidence that this culture is real is that Supercell publishes its expensive failures. *Squad Busters* started development in 2020. Its first closed beta, in February 2023 with 5,000 players, missed its goals, with day-7 retention of 29 percent. The team spent three months making real changes, and the second beta, with more than 140,000 players, looked much better.

blocks.title: Squad Busters beta retention
blocks.note: Day 7 jumped from 29% to 38% after a three-month redesign
blocks.source: Ilkka Paananen, Supercell, 2026

blocks.text: Top creators loved it. Apple and Google were excited. And Supercell had not launched a game in six years, so there was quiet pressure to finally take a swing. The game launched with 40 million pre-registrations and passed 75 million downloads in its first year, and players spent over $100 million on it. Then retention after global launch failed to match the betas, and after an aggressive redesign Supercell shut it down. It was the company's first game ever killed after a global launch.

The postmortem is refreshingly concrete. Even a 100,000-player beta did not predict how the whole world would behave. The betas tested the core gameplay and only checked seven-day retention, not long-term retention or the meta-game. The soft launch lasted just one month. And the company built a huge marketing push before the vision was proven. The team's own conclusion was that one more, longer beta might have exposed the problem in time.

Notice what that means. The kill-early philosophy is not a magic shield. Supercell knew the rules and broke one under pressure, because a long drought made everyone hungry to ship. That is the most human part of the story and the most useful. Discipline is easy when you have a hit. It gets tested when you have not had one in years.
Small teams, big bets, and what to do with this

Underneath the rituals is a structural choice. Supercell has always organized around small, independent teams, the *cells* in its name, and its early history describes the explicit goal of staying as small as possible, because less management means less process. Teams decide what to build. Leadership mostly decides how much to support them. As of 2026, new game teams also share in their game's profits if it launches, which turns team members into something closer to founders.

You do not need a billion-dollar company to use any of this. A two-person Roblox team is about as small a cell as it gets, and the same rules apply with even more force, because your scarcest resource is not money but hours. Every week on a game that is not working is a week not spent on one that might.

Why does Supercell share all of this publicly, including the embarrassing parts? Paananen's explanation is partly self-interested. He credits the Finnish game industry's habit of helping each other, and says Rovio's success with *Angry Birds* made it easier for Supercell to raise money in its early days. When one studio wins, investors and talent take the whole scene more seriously. Writing openly about failure is a way of paying that forward and, not by accident, of recruiting people who want to take big swings.

He is also candid that the industry is stuck. Citing Newzoo estimates, he says the mobile games market has grown only about 3 percent a year on average over the last five years, and that most of the industry has become very good at optimizing proven formulas through A/B tests and small tweaks. His argument is that optimization keeps a live game healthy but rarely creates the next one. New hits come from genuinely new gameplay, and new gameplay means a lot of attempts that do not work.

blocks.title: A kill-early system for a tiny team
items: Before building, write down what the game must prove and by when (for example, day-1 and day-7 return rates from a real playtest)
Build the smallest playable version and get strangers, not just friends, to try it
Check retention at the deadline you set, not when it feels convenient
If it misses, change one big thing under a hard deadline, not a dozen small things forever
If it still misses, kill it, write down three lessons, and celebrate the attempt

blocks.text: The hard part is the last step. Killing a project can feel like admitting you wasted months. Supercell's answer is that the months were the price of the lesson, and that a team which never kills anything is not succeeding more often; it is just not taking risks. As the company put it in its early history, if it realizes it has not failed in a while, that is a sign it has not been bold enough.

There is a balance, though. Killing too quickly is its own trap. *Clash Royale* is nearly ten years old, and in 2025 its returning players doubled and new players grew almost 500 percent, which Supercell's CEO credited to a focused team and, after public pushback, to creators who brought the game back into the spotlight. Some games deserve patience. The skill is knowing the difference between a game that is not working yet and a game that is never going to, and being honest enough to measure it.

takeaways: Clash of Clans came from a team whose previous game was killed; killing projects freed people for the hit.
In hit-driven markets an average game is a cost: about 0.04 percent of mobile games since 2020 grossed $1 billion.
Set kill criteria and deadlines before you build, so the sunk cost effect cannot make the decision for you.
Constraints force bold choices; love for the genre and pride in the work are real tests, not soft extras.
Even Supercell broke its own rules under pressure with Squad Busters; test long-term retention before going big.

title: The Business That Grew Itself to Death
dek: Blue Apron went from 213,000 customers to more than a million in two years and still ended up worth a fraction of what it raised. The reason fits on one line: what a customer costs versus what a customer is worth.

blocks.text: In June 2017, a meal-kit company called Blue Apron sold its shares to the public for the first time. Its prospectus, the long legal document every company files before an IPO, had a section with a confident heading: *Attractive unit economics*. The growth behind that claim looked spectacular. In early 2015 the company had about 213,000 customers in a quarter. Two years later it had more than a million.

The cost of that growth was in the same document. Blue Apron's marketing spending went from $14.0 million in 2014 to $51.4 million in 2015 and $144.1 million in 2016, roughly a tenfold rise in two years. Customers were arriving, but each one was being bought, and the open question was whether enough of them would stay long enough to pay that money back.

blocks.title: Blue Apron customers per quarter
blocks.note: Growth bought with marketing did not hold. Points are selected quarters, not a continuous series.
blocks.source: Blue Apron IPO prospectus, 2017; Blue Apron Form 10-K for 2022

blocks.text: By the last quarter of 2022, the company reported about 298,000 customers, fewer than it had in mid-2015, and an accumulated deficit of about $777 million. In 2023 a food-delivery company called Wonder made a tender offer to buy it outright. Plenty of things went wrong at Blue Apron, but the shape of the chart tells the core story: the company could buy customers far faster than it could keep them.

That gap, between what a customer costs and what a customer is worth, is what *unit economics* means. It is the most useful single idea in business, and it applies just as much to a Roblox game or a YouTube channel as to a company on the stock exchange.
Shrink the business down to one customer

Unit economics asks you to stop looking at the whole business and look at a single unit of it. For most businesses the unit is one customer. For a game it is one player. For a channel it might be one video or one subscriber. Then you ask two questions: what did it cost to get this unit, and what will it give back over its life?

The first number is the **customer acquisition cost**, or CAC. It is everything you spent on marketing and sales in a period, divided by the new customers you got. If you spent $1,000 on ads and gained 100 customers, your CAC is $10. The second number is **lifetime value**, or LTV: the total profit you expect from that customer before they leave.

The word *profit* in that definition matters more than anything else in this article. Lifetime value is not lifetime revenue. If a meal kit sells for $60 and the food, packing and shipping cost $45, the customer is worth $15 a box, not $60. The amount left after the costs that come with each sale is called the **contribution margin**, and it is the only money that can pay back the cost of acquiring the customer.

blocks.title: A back-of-the-envelope LTV (made-up numbers for illustration)
items: Start with what one customer pays you per month: say $20.
Subtract the costs that come with serving them: if those are $8, your contribution margin is $12 a month.
Estimate how many customers leave each month (churn): say 6 percent.
Average customer lifetime is roughly 1 divided by churn: 1 / 0.06, or about 17 months.
LTV is margin times lifetime: $12 x 17, or about $200.
Compare to CAC: if each customer cost $50 to acquire, each one pays back about four times over. If they cost $250, every sale loses money.

blocks.text: The arithmetic is simple, which is exactly why it is dangerous to skip. A business where LTV is below CAC loses money on every customer it adds. Growth makes that business worse, not better, because it multiplies the loss. This is how a company can look healthier every quarter while marching toward the point where it runs out of cash.
The lever that matters most

Once you see LTV as margin times lifetime, a question follows: which part should you work on? In 2004, the marketing researchers Sunil Gupta, Donald Lehmann and Jennifer Ames Stuart tried to answer it with real companies. They built a model that valued firms by adding up the expected future profits of their customers, then tested it with public data on five real companies.

Their answer was lopsided. Improving customer retention by 1 percent raised the estimated value of the firm by about 5 percent. The same 1 percent improvement in margin raised it by about 1 percent. Cutting acquisition cost by 1 percent raised it by only about 0.1 percent. In their numbers, keeping customers was worth roughly fifty times more than getting them cheaper.

blocks.title: Firm value gained from a 1% improvement in each lever
blocks.note: Averages from a model of five firms; real effects vary by business.
blocks.source: Gupta, Lehmann & Stuart, Journal of Marketing Research, 2004

blocks.text: The reason is compounding. A customer who stays one more month does not just add one month of margin; they also get another chance to stay the month after that. Go back to the made-up example above. Cutting monthly churn from 6 percent to 5 percent stretches the average lifetime from about 17 months to 20, which raises LTV by roughly a fifth without spending a single extra dollar on ads.

The same study found that a 1 percent gain in retention was worth almost five times as much as a 1 percent drop in the cost of capital, the interest-rate-like number that finance people obsess over. That is a striking result for a field that usually treats customers as a marketing problem and money as a finance problem. The customers *were* the money.

This is why the research on retention matters so much for games, which the separate article on D1, D7 and D30 retention covers in depth. A player who quits on day one has a lifetime value of almost nothing, no matter how cheaply you got them.
When customers grow on their own

The best businesses push this even further. In 2019, the workplace chat company Slack reported a measure called *net dollar retention* in its IPO filing. It takes a group of paying customers from a year ago and compares what that same group pays today, after subtracting everyone who cancelled or downgraded. Slack's figure was 143 percent.

items.label: Slack's net dollar retention: a year later, the same paying customers spent 43% more
Blue Apron's marketing spending in 2016, about 18% of its revenue

blocks.source: Slack Form S-1, 2019; Blue Apron IPO prospectus, 2017

blocks.text: Read that number slowly. Slack was not just keeping its customers; the customers who stayed were spending more, because more people inside each company started using the product. Even with some cancellations, the old customers grew on their own. A business like that can afford to spend heavily on acquisition, because every customer it wins becomes a slowly expanding source of revenue.

Put the two companies side by side and the contrast is sharp: both spent large sums to win customers. One sold a product whose users kept pulling more colleagues in. The other sold a weekly box of groceries that many people tried, enjoyed for a while and then stopped ordering. The marketing budgets looked similar on paper. The units underneath them were completely different.
Where the numbers lie

Unit economics is powerful, but the inputs are easy to fool yourself with. Lifetime value is a forecast, not a measurement. A young business does not yet know how long customers will stay, so it guesses, and the guess is usually optimistic. A company that has existed for eight months cannot honestly claim a three-year customer lifetime.

Averages hide things too. A CAC that blends free word-of-mouth customers with expensive paid ones can look healthy while every paid customer loses money. The article on finding your first hundred customers tells how Dropbox discovered exactly this: paid search was costing it far more per customer than the product earned. The blended number would never have shown it.

items: **Revenue dressed up as value.** If the LTV uses revenue instead of margin, it is wrong by the size of your costs.
**Early cohorts treated as typical.** The first customers are often the most enthusiastic. Later ones usually churn faster.
**Ignoring the payback period.** Even a good LTV-to-CAC ratio can sink a small business if the money takes two years to come back and you run out of cash in six.
**Forgetting your own time.** For a side project, the biggest acquisition cost is usually hours, not dollars.

blocks.text: The fix for most of these is to look at *cohorts* instead of totals. Group customers or players by the week or month they arrived, then follow each group over time. If the March group is still 30 percent active after two months and the June group is only 15 percent, something changed, and a total user count that keeps rising would have hidden it completely. Roblox and YouTube both show versions of this in their analytics, and reading them is a skill worth practicing before there is money on the line.

Investors often quote rules of thumb, such as wanting lifetime value to be several times acquisition cost. Treat these as rough sanity checks, not laws. The honest version of the question is simpler: if you stopped all marketing tomorrow, would the customers you already have keep paying back what you spent to get them?
The unit economics of a Roblox game

Everything above translates directly to a small game. The unit is a player. Roblox's own Ads Manager reports a number it calls cost per play, which is the acquisition cost of one session. That number is meaningless on its own. What matters is what happens after the play: how many of those players come back, how many ever buy something, and how much of each purchase actually reaches you after the platform's share, which the article on the Robux economy walks through.

Roblox's documentation hints at the same logic. It notes that campaigns usually need several days to show results, and that if a campaign is not working after three to five days, you should improve the game's onboarding and first-time experience before spending more. It also says the ad system can offer discounts to games that keep players engaged. In other words, the platform rewards good retention with cheaper acquisition, which is unit economics enforced by an algorithm.

Purchases are not the only way a player pays back, either. A player who stays and brings friends lowers the cost of every future player, which is why sharing and inviting count as part of lifetime value even though no money changes hands. On a social platform, a loyal player is both a customer and a small marketing department.

For a two-person team, this leads to a clear order of work. First, make a game that keeps the players it already gets. Then find out what a retained player is worth. Only then decide how much you can afford to pay for a new one. Buying players for a game that cannot hold them is the Blue Apron chart in miniature.

The same thinking works for a channel. The unit can be a video: what did it cost in hours to make, and what did it return in views, subscribers and future views from those subscribers? A video that takes forty hours and brings in viewers who never return has poor unit economics, however good it looks. A short format that takes three hours and keeps people coming back may be the better business, even if each video is smaller.

Growth is not evidence that a business works. Growth can be bought. The evidence is whether each customer, player or viewer pays back what it cost to get them, and whether they stay long enough to do it.
The question to carry around

The deepest lesson of unit economics is a habit of mind. Whenever something is growing, ask what it is costing to make it grow, and what each new unit is actually worth. Most failed businesses could have answered that question early. They just did not ask it, because the top-line numbers were going up and everyone was excited.

That habit is cheap to build now, while the stakes are small. Track what a new player costs, in money or hours, and what a retained player brings in. Keep the numbers honest: margin, not revenue; real churn, not hoped-for churn. If the unit works, growth will multiply something good. If it does not, no amount of growth will save it.

takeaways: Unit economics means judging one customer, player or video at a time: what it cost to get versus the profit it returns.
Lifetime value uses margin, not revenue, and it is a forecast that young businesses usually overestimate.
Retention is the strongest lever: in one study, 1% better retention raised firm value about fifty times more than 1% cheaper acquisition.
If each unit loses money, growth multiplies the loss. Fix retention before paying for players or customers.
For side projects, count your hours as acquisition cost.

title: The Company With No Bosses: How Valve Built Half-Life, Then Steam
dek: Valve restarted its first game, hired the modders who made its best hits, built a store for its own patches, and wrote a handbook arguing against the military model of management.

blocks.text: In 2012, a game company in Bellevue, Washington, printed a handbook for new employees with cartoon diagrams and a glossary of inside jokes. Early on, it explains why the company has no managers. Hierarchy, it says, is great for predictability and control from the top down, which is why military organizations rely on it so heavily. Then it argues that a company trying to hire the most creative people on Earth should do the opposite.

That company was Valve, the studio behind *Half-Life*, *Counter-Strike*, *Portal* and *Dota 2*, and the owner of Steam, the store where most PC gamers buy their games. If you live inside a chain of command, Valve's handbook reads like a dispatch from another planet. Desks on wheels. No bosses. Everyone picks their own projects. And yet the company built one of the most dominant platforms in gaming. How much of that is the org chart, and how much is something else?
A game that wasn't good enough

According to the timeline in Valve's own handbook, the company was formed in 1996 in Kirkland, Washington, by Gabe Newell and Mike Harrington, both former Microsoft employees. The formation papers were signed on the same day as Newell's wedding. They licensed the *Quake* engine from id Software and started building a shooter that would become *Half-Life*.

Then, in 1997, they did something most first-time studios cannot afford to do. After an internal review, the team decided *Half-Life* was not good enough to ship, went back to the drawing board and essentially started over. A second game, codenamed *Prospero*, was permanently shelved. When *Half-Life* finally came out in 1998, Valve says it won more than 50 game-of-the-year awards. The company had about 30 employees at the time.

That restart is the real origin of Valve's culture. A tiny studio, with one game and no guarantee of another, chose quality over its schedule. The handbook says Valve has never taken outside financing, and that after some legal wrangling with its first publisher following *Half-Life*, it now owns all of its own intellectual property. Self-funding and owning your work sound like boring business details. In practice they meant nobody outside could force a release date or a sequel.

items.label: Valve employees when Half-Life shipped in 1998
Game-of-the-year awards Valve says Half-Life won
Employees listed in the 2012 handbook timeline

blocks.source: Valve Handbook for New Employees, 2012; Valve About page

blocks.text: Hiring the people already making your game better

Look at Valve's catalog and you notice something strange: many of its biggest hits were not invented there. The handbook timeline records the company acquiring TeamFortress Software in 1998, whose creators came in to build *Team Fortress Classic*. *Counter-Strike* started as a fan-made modification of *Half-Life*. *Day of Defeat* was a popular mod that got full Valve support. And in the mid-2000s, Valve hired six students from the DigiPen Institute of Technology after seeing their student game, *Narbacular Drop*. That team's idea became *Portal*.

The handbook says Valve established a pattern of supporting the best mods and occasionally acquiring them. Think about what that does. Instead of guessing who might be talented, you watch people who are already building things your players love, for free, on your own tools. The audience has done the screening for you. Those creators have proven skill and taste, and they already understand your game better than most job applicants ever could.

The handbook's hiring advice explains why this matters so much to Valve. When interviewing someone, it tells employees to ask not just whether the candidate is talented and collaborative, but whether they could literally run the company, because in a flat organization they effectively will. Modders who had already built and shipped something on their own, with no one telling them what to do, had answered that question before they ever walked in the door.

For a small studio, especially on a platform like Roblox, this is the cheapest recruiting strategy in existence. The people who make fan art, build in your game's style, find bugs or run your Discord are your farm team. You do not need to acquire anyone. You just need to notice them.
Steam: plumbing that became the business

Valve announced Steam at the Game Developers Conference in 2002 and released it in 2003. The company's About page describes it as a digital distribution channel created before app stores existed. The handbook is more specific: Steam's tools and services were originally built to serve Valve's own games, *Half-Life* and *Counter-Strike*. Valve had a problem, which was getting updates, patches and anti-cheat protection to millions of players, so it built the pipes itself.

*Half-Life 2*, released in 2004, became the first game available both on Steam and in retail stores. Valve Anti-Cheat launched around the same time. In 2005, the first third-party games arrived on Steam, and PC developers suddenly had an alternative to fighting for shelf space at retail. By the time of the handbook, *Team Fortress 2* alone had shipped more than 280 updates, all pushed through Steam, including, eventually, its first hat.

blocks.text: This is one of the most repeated patterns in business: the tool you build for yourself becomes more valuable than the product it was built for. Steam turned Valve from a studio that needed hits into a platform that earns money whenever anyone's game sells. When this was written, Valve's About page showed more than 33 million Steam users online at once. Getting on Steam today costs a developer a $100 fee per game, which Valve pays back once the game earns $1,000 in adjusted gross revenue. The tollbooth sits on a road Valve paved for its own trucks.

Notice the order of events. Steam was not launched as a store hoping to attract games. It launched with a reason to exist that had nothing to do with other developers: Valve's own players needed it to get updates. Valve also added the Steam Community, with features for friends to find and play with each other. By the end of the 2000s, the handbook says, Steam had passed 25 million users and 1,000 games. A platform needs a first reason for people to show up, and Valve's was its own hit games. Most platforms that start with nothing but a promise die waiting for users.
Pay attention to the annoying problems you solve for yourself. A tool, template or system that makes your own work easier might be useful to thousands of people with the same problem.
Welcome to Flatland

The handbook's description of daily life is genuinely radical. Other companies let people spend a slice of their time on self-directed projects; at Valve, the handbook says, that share is 100 percent. Desks have wheels so people can roll to whatever project they think matters most. Teams form as *cabals* around work people believe in. When a lead emerges, the job is described as a clearinghouse of information, not a boss.

Two other lines stand out. First, nobody has ever been fired at Valve for making a mistake, because you cannot ask people to take risks and then punish them for failing. Second, long stretches of overtime are treated as a sign of failed planning or communication, not dedication. The company says it works hardest at hiring good people and wants them to stay, which means not grinding them down.

The money side is just as unusual. The handbook claims Valve's profit per employee is higher than Google's, Amazon's or Microsoft's, and says the company's goal is to pay each person what their work is actually worth: Valve loses if it underpays you, and you lose if you are paid more than you create. That is a company's own description of itself, written in 2012, and it cannot be checked from outside because Valve is private. But it shows the logic of the whole system. If you hire very few people and give each of them enormous freedom, every hire has to be exceptional, which is why the handbook calls hiring the single most important thing employees do.

It also explains Valve's preference for what it calls *T-shaped* people: broad skills across many areas, plus deep expertise in one. In a company without fixed job descriptions, the person who can only do one narrow thing gets stuck when the project changes. The person who can code a bit, design a bit and talk to players, while being excellent at one of those, can roll their desk anywhere.

blocks.title: Two ways to organize people

left.head: Hierarchy (what most of us know)
items: Managers assign work
Clear chain of command and accountability
Predictable, repeatable, easy to coordinate at scale
Risk: smart people wait for orders

right.head: Valve's "Flatland"
items: People choose their own projects
Teams form around work they believe in
Fast, creative, owner-like behavior
Risk: hidden power, weak mentoring, poor long-range planning

blocks.text: The fine print

Here is where the story gets more interesting than the legend. Valve is not actually structureless, and its own handbook says so. A section titled *Structure happens* admits that teams form temporary internal structures. Compensation is set by *stack ranking*, where peers rank each other's value to the company. Someone collects those rankings, and someone decides what they mean. That is a hierarchy; it is just not drawn on a chart.

Writer and activist Jo Freeman described this exact problem in an essay first given as a talk in 1970 and published in 1972, *The Tyranny of Structurelessness*. Her argument was that groups without formal structure do not stay equal. Informal elites form, made up of friends and early members, and because their power is unofficial, nobody can challenge it or hold it accountable. Formal structure, whatever its faults, at least makes power visible.

Valve's handbook is honest about some costs. In a section on what Valve is not good at, it lists helping new people find their way, mentoring, sharing information internally, hiring in completely new disciplines and making predictions longer than a few months out. It also notes that it loses talented people who prefer a traditional structure. That last item on predictions might explain why some Valve projects have taken famously long to appear, or never appeared at all.

So the honest lesson is not that bosses are bad. It is that Valve paid for creative freedom with specific, known weaknesses, and could afford to because Steam threw off enough money to absorb them. A company with no cash cow and a launch deadline might not survive the same design.
What a two-person studio can steal
A small team is flat by default. When there are two of you, nobody needs a manager. But Valve's story still has three useful ideas for that size.

blocks.title: Valve habits that scale down
items: Be willing to restart a project that is not good enough, early, before the sunk cost gets huge
Watch your community for people already making things for your game; they are your best future collaborators
Notice the tools you build for yourself; one of them might matter more than the game
Treat endless crunch as a planning problem, not proof of commitment
Write down your weaknesses as a team, the way Valve's handbook did, so they stop being invisible

blocks.text: One more habit from the handbook is worth copying exactly. In its section on mistakes, it tells employees to treat every belief as something to test: before you act, ask what you would expect to see if you are right, and what you would expect to see if you are wrong. Then go collect the data. For a game, that might mean predicting how many playtesters will finish the first level before you watch them try. When your prediction misses, you have learned something about your model of players, not just about one level.

There is also a lesson for anyone who lives inside a hierarchy every day. Valve's handbook frames military-style structure as the opposite of creativity, but that is too simple. Hierarchy is excellent at what it is built for: predictable, repeatable, high-stakes work where a mistake can kill people. A reactor plant should not be run by whoever rolled their desk over that morning. Creative work has different failure modes. The skill worth learning is recognizing which kind of work you are doing, and switching your style to fit, instead of assuming one way of organizing people is right for everything.

takeaways: Valve threw out its first version of Half-Life and started over; quality before schedule became its identity.
Many Valve hits came from modders and students it hired after seeing their work; your community is your talent pipeline.
Steam began as plumbing for Valve's own games and became the real business.
Flat organizations still have hierarchy; it is just informal, which can make power harder to see and challenge.
Match your structure to the work: hierarchy for high-stakes repeatable tasks, freedom for creative exploration.
