title: Cause of Death: Ran Out of Money
dek: Ask founders why their company died and the top answer is cash. That is like a coroner writing 'heart stopped.' The data on business failure gets far more useful once you separate the symptom from the disease.

blocks.text: Every coroner knows that a heart stopping is not a cause of death. It is what death looks like at the end. The useful question is always what came before: the blocked artery, the infection, the fall. Business failure has the same problem. When the research firm CB Insights read through 111 startup post-mortems written by founders and investors, the most common reason given for failure was running out of cash or failing to raise more. Of course it was. That is what failure looks like at the end.

The interesting part of failure is upstream. And the first thing to clear away is a number almost everyone has heard, that nine out of ten startups fail. It is repeated so often it sounds like a law of nature. The official data says something different, and more interesting.
The real survival curve

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks every private-sector business establishment, from law firms to food trucks, through its Business Employment Dynamics program. In January 2024 it published the fate of every establishment that opened in March 2013. A year later, about 80 percent were still operating. After five years, about half. After ten years, just over a third.

blocks.title: Share of U.S. establishments born in 2013 still operating
blocks.note: Covers all private-sector establishments, not only tech startups. Closing is not always failing.
blocks.source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, TED, January 2024

blocks.text: Two things stand out. First, the curve is steepest at the start. About one in five businesses is gone within a year, and the losses slow down every year after that. In the first year, about one in five closed. Between years nine and ten, fewer than one in twelve of the remaining survivors did. Getting through the first couple of years is the hardest part by far.

Second, these numbers include businesses that closed for reasons that are not failures at all. Owners retire, sell, move or simply decide they want a different life. Venture-backed tech startups are a different population with different math, aiming for huge outcomes and accepting that most will not get there. So the honest summary is not that 90 percent of businesses fail. It is that about half of new establishments in the U.S. are still around after five years, and the danger is concentrated early.
Survival risk is front-loaded. Whatever you are building, the first year or two is where most projects die, which is exactly when motivation is easiest to lose and evidence is hardest to read.
What founders say killed them

The CB Insights analysis, published in 2021, is the most widely cited look at why startups say they failed. Founders could name several reasons, so the percentages add up to well over 100. Running out of cash led the list at 38 percent, followed closely by no market need at 35 percent. Then came being outcompeted, a flawed business model, and regulatory trouble.

blocks.title: Reasons cited in 111 startup post-mortems
blocks.note: Multiple reasons per startup, so totals exceed 100%. Self-reported by founders and investors.
blocks.source: CB Insights, 2021, via SmartCompany

blocks.text: Treat this list with care. These are post-mortems people chose to write and publish, mostly from tech startups. Founders are also not neutral judges of their own failure; blaming the market or a competitor is easier than blaming your own decisions. And 111 stories is a small sample. The value of the list is not its precision. It is the pattern it reveals once you read it as a chain instead of a menu.

There is a deeper bias hiding in all failure research, and it runs in both directions. During the Second World War, the statistician Abraham Wald was asked where to add armor to bombers, based on where returning planes had bullet holes. His insight was that the holes on returning planes showed where a plane could be hit and survive. The armor belonged where the returning planes had no holes, because planes hit there never came back.

Startup stories have the same shape. The success stories everyone hears, the teenager whose game exploded or the channel that blew up after one video, are the planes that came back. Thousands of projects that did the same things and vanished left no story behind. And the failure stories that do get written skew toward founders articulate and secure enough to publish one. Neither set is a fair sample. The safest lessons are the ones that show up in both: build something specific people want, keep the team aligned, and do not run out of the resource your project actually runs on.
Reading the list as a chain

Running out of cash is rarely an independent event. Money runs out because revenue never arrived, and revenue never arrived because not enough people wanted the product at a price that worked. Read that way, no market need, a flawed business model, bad pricing and running out of cash are often the same story told at different stages: the first is the disease, the last is the death certificate.

blocks.title: How most failures actually unfold
items: A team builds something based on an untested belief about what people want.
Real users show up in smaller numbers than hoped, or do not come back.
The team adds features, spends on marketing, or lowers prices to compensate.
Costs keep running while revenue stays flat.
Cash or motivation runs out, and that gets recorded as the cause.

blocks.text: This is why the second item on the list, no market need, deserves more attention than the first. It is the one founders can actually do something about early, cheaply, before much money is at stake. The lean startup method, covered in its own article, is essentially a toolkit for catching this disease before it reaches the bloodstream.

For a side project, the chain has a twist. A game built by two people with day jobs has almost no burn rate, so it cannot literally run out of cash. It runs out of something else: hours, energy, belief. Burnout sits at the bottom of the CB Insights list at 5 percent, but for part-time builders it is the equivalent of the top line. When a side project has no players, the founders quietly stop opening the editor, and the project dies without anyone writing a post-mortem. (The articles on building on the side and on finishing one project take this problem head-on.)
Six ways good ideas die

Tom Eisenmann, a Harvard Business School professor, spent years studying failed ventures for his 2021 book Why Startups Fail. He was especially interested in startups that looked promising, with smart founders and decent ideas, and still collapsed. He sorted the deaths into patterns, which are more useful than the CB Insights list because they describe mistakes rather than outcomes.

items: **Bad bedfellows:** a good idea sunk by the wrong partners, team, or investors.
**False starts:** launching fast without first researching what customers need, then cycling through uninformed guesses.
**False promises:** early adopters love the product, the team scales, and mainstream customers turn out not to care.
**Speed traps:** growing faster than the business can support, until the cracks break it.
**Help wanted:** a fast-scaling company runs short of the money or people it needs at a critical moment.
**Cascading miracles:** a vision so big that too many things all have to go right at once.

blocks.text: Two of these matter most for a small builder. False promises are a trap for game makers in particular: the first players of a new game are often friends, fellow developers, or enthusiasts who will forgive anything. Their enthusiasm can be real and still say little about whether ordinary players will stick around. The fix is to find out early how strangers behave.

Bad bedfellows is the other. Eisenmann found that a good idea is not enough if the people around it are mismatched, and CB Insights' list shows team problems and disharmony appearing again and again. For two brothers building a game, the risk is not that one of you is a bad person. It is unclear roles, unspoken expectations about effort, and no agreed way to make decisions. (The article on partner roles covers this in detail.)
Who actually succeeds

If failure has patterns, so does success, and one of the best-documented findings cuts against the stereotype of the hoodie-wearing twenty-two-year-old. Pierre Azoulay and colleagues combined U.S. Census Bureau data on businesses, workers and owners to study millions of startups across the whole country, not just the famous ones. In a 2020 paper in American Economic Review: Insights, they found that the most successful founders tend to be middle-aged.

items.label: Average founder age of the 1-in-1,000 fastest-growing new U.S. firms

blocks.source: Azoulay, Jones, Kim & Miranda, AER: Insights, 2020

blocks.text: Their strongest predictor of success was not youth or genius but prior experience in the same industry. Founders who had worked in a field knew its customers, its suppliers and its hidden problems. They had, in effect, done years of free market research before starting.

It is worth being precise about what this does and does not say. It is an average, and plenty of young founders build great companies. It also does not mean age itself causes success. The likelier story is that age is a stand-in for what accumulates with it: industry knowledge, savings, contacts, judgment about people, and a track record that makes others willing to take a chance on you. Those can be built at any age, but they cannot be skipped.

For someone who is twenty and wants to own a business eventually, this is a more encouraging finding than it sounds. It means that the years spent learning a trade, a system, or an industry are not a detour from entrepreneurship. They are often the raw material for it. A nuclear-trained electrician understands power systems, maintenance, technical training and rigid procedure from the inside. Someone with ten years in gaming and content knows that world's players better than most outsiders ever will. Experience is the moat that founders often do not realize they are digging.
A pre-mortem for your own project

The psychologist Gary Klein proposed a simple exercise he called the pre-mortem. Before a project starts, the team imagines that it is a year in the future and the project has failed. Each person writes down why. Because the failure is treated as having already happened, people stop defending the plan and start explaining its death, and they surface risks they would not have raised in a normal planning meeting.

Applied to a small game or channel, the exercise takes fifteen minutes. Imagine it is next year and the project is dead. Did players never come back after their first session? Did the two of you stop agreeing on what to build? Did the project grow too big to finish in the time you actually have? Did the person doing most of the work burn out? Each answer points to a check you can run this month rather than discovering it in a year.

blocks.title: A fifteen-minute pre-mortem
items: Imagine it is a year from now and the project has quietly died.
Each partner writes, alone, the three most likely reasons it died.
Compare lists and circle the reasons that appear on both.
For each circled reason, name the earliest sign you would see.
Agree on one cheap check for each sign, and put a date on it.

blocks.text: The pre-mortem works best when it is honest about the one resource a side project lives on. For a funded startup that resource is cash, and the founders watch the bank balance every week. For a part-time project, it is the hours the builders are actually willing to put in. Watching that number, and noticing early when it starts to slide, is the side-project version of watching the runway.

The data on business failure is less frightening than the folklore and more useful. Most new businesses do not vanish in year one; half of them make it five years. The ones that die usually die of something upstream of money, most often building something too few people wanted, or of problems between the people building it. Both can be spotted early by anyone willing to look. Cash running out is just the last thing that happens.

takeaways: About half of new U.S. establishments survive five years; the 'nine in ten fail' line is folklore, but risk is front-loaded.
Running out of cash is usually the final symptom; no market need is the disease that most often causes it.
For side projects, the equivalent of cash is time and motivation; projects without users die quietly when builders stop showing up.
Prior industry experience is one of the best predictors of founder success; the fastest-growing firms have founders averaging 45.
Run a pre-mortem: imagine the project failed, list why, then check for the early signs now.

title: The Algorithm Doesn't Watch Your Video. It Watches the Viewer.
dek: In 2012 YouTube made a change that cost it a fifth of its views overnight, and kept it. What the company has actually said about its recommendation system since then is less mysterious, and more useful, than the myths creators trade.

blocks.text: In 2012, engineers at YouTube flipped a switch and watched views fall by about 20 percent almost immediately. For most companies that would be a crisis and a rollback by lunch. YouTube left the change in place. The company later described this moment itself, in a 2021 post by Cristos Goodrow, its vice president of engineering, as the point where it stopped treating a click as proof that a viewer was happy.

That small piece of history is a better guide to the algorithm than most of the theories passed around creator forums. It shows what the system was built to want, and what it was willing to give up to get it. A new channel that understands that one trade has a clearer picture than a channel that has memorized a hundred tips.

This article sticks to what YouTube has said on the record: its engineering blog, its public How YouTube Works pages, and interviews its growth team has given on Creator Insider, the company's own channel for creators. Those are the claims of an interested party, and they should be read that way. But they are the closest thing to a primary source anyone outside the company has.
From popularity to clicks to something harder

YouTube's account of its own history runs in clear steps. When recommendations began in 2008, the system mostly ranked videos by popularity and dumped the winners into a trending list. Everyone saw roughly the same thing. That works when a site is small and fails when it holds billions of videos aimed at very different people.

Next came clicks. By 2011, according to Goodrow's post, the team had concluded that clicks were a poor signal, because people often clicked on videos that turned out not to be what they expected. A misleading thumbnail could win the click and lose the viewer. So in 2012 the system began counting watch time, and that is when views dropped by a fifth: fewer people were tricked into starting videos they did not want.

Watch time had its own flaw. A person can sit through something and feel worse for it, or leave a video playing while doing something else. So YouTube added surveys. Some viewers are asked to rate a video from one to five stars, and only time spent on videos rated four or five counts toward what the company calls valued watchtime. Because almost nobody answers surveys, a machine learning model predicts how everyone else would have answered.

blocks.title: What YouTube says it has optimized for
items: Recommendations begin; videos ranked largely by popularity
Team concludes clicks are an unreliable signal of what viewers want
Watch time added as a signal; views drop about 20% at once
Later
Viewer surveys feed 'valued watchtime'; a model predicts answers for everyone else
Borderline content demoted in recommendations

blocks.text: Notice the direction of travel. Each step moved away from something easy to count and toward something closer to the viewer's actual experience. That does not make the system benevolent. It makes it a machine that keeps trying to measure satisfaction, because a satisfied viewer comes back tomorrow. (The general version of this, and its downsides, is covered in the article on recommendation algorithms.)
Pull, not push

The most common mental picture among creators is of YouTube as a distributor. You upload, the algorithm decides whether to push your video out, and if it likes you it pushes harder. Todd Beaupré, who leads YouTube's growth and discovery team, has said repeatedly that this is backwards.

In his description, recommendations are built at the moment a person opens the app. The system looks at that one viewer, their history and what similar viewers enjoyed, and pulls from the whole library the videos most likely to satisfy them right now. Your video is not being pushed. It is a candidate, competing in millions of tiny private auctions, one per viewer per session. Notifications are the main exception, for people who asked for them.

That reframe dissolves several popular fears. Beaupré has said the discovery system mostly judges individual videos rather than channel averages, so one weak upload does not doom the next one. He has denied that there is a penalty box for channels that take breaks, saying the system tries not to lean on historical data that does not predict how a new video will do. And because recommendations are not limited to recent uploads, an old video can find a second life when interest in its topic returns.

blocks.title: Creator folklore vs. YouTube's stated position

left.head: What creators often believe
items: YouTube pushes videos out to audiences
A bad video hurts the whole channel
Taking a break gets you punished
A video that flops in 48 hours is dead
Subscribers will see and watch everything

right.head: What YouTube staff have said
items: Each viewer's feed is pulled together when they open the app
Discovery judges mostly video by video
No penalty box; old data is down-weighted if it is not predictive
Old videos can be recommended again when interest returns
Most subscribers skip most uploads, and that is normal

blocks.text: Be fair to the skeptics, though. These reassurances come with no published data, and creators in the comments under these interviews regularly report experiences that do not match them. The honest position is that YouTube's description is probably true on average and may not feel true for any one channel in any one month.
What it is actually predicting

Goodrow's post says the system learns from more than 80 billion signals. The ones the company names are ordinary: clicks, watch time, survey answers, shares, likes and dislikes, plus the history a viewer has chosen to keep. The important detail is the one people skip. YouTube says there is no fixed formula. How much each signal matters changes from viewer to viewer, and Beaupré has added that the weights shift by time and device as well.

items.label: Signals YouTube says its recommendation system learns from
Immediate drop in views when watch time was added in 2012
Typical click rate from the subscriber row, per YouTube's growth lead

blocks.source: Goodrow, YouTube Official Blog, 2021; Beaupré on Creator Insider, Sept 2026

blocks.text: A 2016 paper by three Google engineers gives a rough picture of the plumbing behind those claims. The system works in two stages. A first network narrows a library of millions of videos down to a few hundred candidates that might suit a given viewer. A second network then scores and ranks those candidates in detail. The paper is a decade old and the models have changed many times since, but the shape is a good mental model: first a coarse question about whether a video belongs in this person's world at all, then a fine question about whether it is the best choice right now.

That shape explains why topic clarity matters so much for a small channel. A video that does not obviously belong to any recognizable interest has a hard time even making the first cut. A video that clearly belongs to one, say aim training for players returning to tactical shooters, at least gets into the pool where the finer judgment happens.

This is why asking which metric the algorithm rewards is the wrong question. Click-through rate matters only as one clue about whether a particular viewer wanted a particular video. A high click rate followed by people bailing in the first minute is a strong clue that the promise was false. A modest click rate with long, satisfied viewing is a clue that the video is right for a narrower group, and the system will go looking for more people like them. (The articles on thumbnails and on retention graphs dig into those two clues.)

There is a useful way to compress all of this. The algorithm does not watch your video. It cannot judge your editing or your jokes. It watches viewers, and it tries to predict which of them will be glad they spent their time on you. Everything a creator can do to grow on YouTube reduces to two moves: be clear about who the video is for, and then make those people glad they clicked.
Your subscribers are not your audience

In a Creator Insider interview in September 2026, Beaupré offered a number that surprises most new creators. Across uploads, he said, the click rate from the subscriber row on the home page is often around 10 percent or less. Even on a channel's best videos, the large majority of subscribed viewers who see the video do not choose to watch it. He called that normal: people who like a channel do not want every single thing it makes.

This matters because creators tend to treat subscribers as a mailing list. They are not. A subscription is one weak signal among many that a viewer might like your next video. The system still asks the question fresh for each upload and each person: of everyone who subscribed, who is likely to want this one? A video can underperform with subscribers and still do well with strangers, because, according to Beaupré, the system learns about those two groups separately.

For a brand new channel there is even less to go on. With no viewing history attached to the channel, Beaupré has said, early distribution leans on matching the topic of the video to viewers who like that topic. If no interested audience shows up, impressions stop. That is not punishment. It is the system running out of reasons to believe anyone wants the video.

A small channel's real problem is rarely being suppressed. It is being ambiguous. If the title, thumbnail and first thirty seconds do not make clear who the video is for, the system has nobody to test it on.
The part that is not about engagement

It would be easy to read all this as a pure engagement machine. YouTube's own history says otherwise. Goodrow's post lists a series of interventions that override what viewers would have clicked: classifiers that kept racy or violent videos out of recommendations from 2011, the demotion of sensational tabloid content in 2015, and in 2019 the demotion of what the company calls borderline content, videos that come close to breaking its rules without quite doing so.

YouTube reported that the 2019 change cut watch time of borderline content that came from recommendations to non-subscribers in the United States by 70 percent. The post adds that responsibility signals can outrank engagement signals. In other words, there is an editorial layer sitting on top of the prediction layer, and it reflects decisions made by people about what the platform wants to be associated with.

For a gaming channel this is mostly background, but not entirely. Shock titles, fake drama and rage bait sit in exactly the zone where a click can be cheap and a recommendation can be withheld. The pattern from 2012 repeats: the system is built to stop rewarding things that win attention without earning satisfaction, and it keeps getting better at spotting them.
Using this without being used by it

The deepest lesson in YouTube's account is that the company has been fighting Goodhart's law for over a decade. Every time a number became the target, creators learned to game it, and the number stopped meaning what it used to. Clicks, then watch time, then surveys. A creator who chases whatever metric is fashionable this year is running the same race the engineers are trying to make unwinnable.

The alternative is almost boring. Pick viewers you understand, because you are one of them. Make a specific promise in the packaging. Keep that promise fast, and give people a reason to feel the time was well spent. For a channel about rebuilding aim after years away from games, the viewer is easy to picture: someone who also drifted away and wonders whether they can come back. Every upload can be checked against that one person.

blocks.title: A pre-upload check based on what YouTube says it measures
items: Name the viewer: who, specifically, should want this video?
Read the title and thumbnail as that viewer. Is the promise clear in two seconds?
Check that the first 30 seconds start delivering on that promise.
Ask whether that viewer would rate it four or five stars, not just finish it.
After upload, judge it over weeks, not hours; old videos can still be found.

blocks.text: None of this guarantees growth, and YouTube's statements are not neutral science. They are a company describing its product in the most flattering honest terms it can manage. But they line up with the one thing the company proved it believed back in 2012, when it gave up a fifth of its views. The system wants viewers who are glad they came. Build for those people, and you are working with the machine instead of guessing at it.

takeaways: YouTube moved from popularity to clicks to watch time to surveys; each step tried to measure satisfaction more honestly.
Recommendations are pulled for each viewer when they open the app; your video is a candidate, not a package being pushed.
There is no fixed formula. Signal weights vary by viewer, time and device, so chasing one metric misses the point.
Most subscribers skip most uploads. Treat each video as a fresh pitch to a specific viewer.
Clarity about who a video is for is the most useful thing a small channel can control.

title: Designing for the Player You Forgot
dek: About one in six young American adults has a disability, and the most common kind isn't the one you'd guess. Accessible design is not an easy mode. It is the curb cut that ends up helping everyone.

blocks.text: In May 2018, Microsoft announced a controller that looked nothing like a controller. It was a flat white slab with two huge round buttons on top and a row of ports along the back. Those ports were the point. Players could plug in foot pedals, chin switches, joysticks mounted on wheelchair arms or big buttons that could be pressed with an elbow, and map each one to any input a game expected.

The Xbox Adaptive Controller was built with partners that included the AbleGamers Charity, the Cerebral Palsy Foundation, Craig Hospital, the UK charity SpecialEffect and Warfighter Engaged, a group that adapts gaming gear for wounded service members. It cost $99.99, far less than the custom rigs it replaced. And it carried a message the industry was only beginning to absorb: a lot of people who want to play are not being stopped by skill. They are being stopped by design decisions nobody thought about.

For anyone who builds games, that is not just a moral point. It is a practical one. Every barrier you leave in place quietly shrinks your audience, and most players who hit one never complain. They just close the game and go play something else, and you never learn why they left. Accessibility is one of the few design areas where small, cheap changes can open a game to people who were being turned away at the door.
Who is actually being left out

Ask people to picture a disabled gamer and most picture a wheelchair. The data says that picture is badly incomplete, especially for young adults. In a large 2016 CDC survey of US adults, about one in six people aged 18 to 44 reported some form of disability. The most common type in that age group, by a wide margin, was cognitive: serious difficulty concentrating, remembering or making decisions.

blocks.title: Disability among US adults aged 18–44
blocks.note: Self-reported; people can have more than one type.
blocks.source: Okoro et al., MMWR, 2018 (BRFSS 2016 data)

blocks.text: Then there are the conditions that do not even show up as disabilities in surveys like that. The National Eye Institute estimates that about 1 in 12 men have some form of color vision deficiency, most often trouble telling reds from greens. In a lobby of ten men, odds are decent that at least one cannot reliably tell your red enemy outline from your green teammate outline. Hearing is another quiet one: people who spend years around loud machinery, from factory floors to engine rooms, often lose some high-frequency hearing, which is exactly the range where footsteps and reload clicks live.

items.label: US adults aged 18–44 reporting a disability (16.6%)
Men with a color vision deficiency
Accessibility settings in The Last of Us Part II

blocks.source: Okoro et al., MMWR 2018; National Eye Institute; Sony/Naughty Dog

blocks.text: Disability is a mismatch, not a person

Microsoft's inclusive design team, whose thinking shaped the adaptive controller, makes a reframe worth borrowing. Disability, in their framing, is a mismatch between a person and the thing they are trying to use. That makes it something designers create, not just something players have.

They illustrate it with what they call the persona spectrum. A design that works for someone with one arm also works for someone with a broken wrist in a cast, and for a new parent holding a baby in one arm. The first limitation is permanent, the second temporary, the third situational. Solve for the permanent case and you quietly solve for a far larger group of people who would never call themselves disabled.

blocks.title: The persona spectrum, game edition

left.head: Permanent
items: One arm
Deaf
Color vision deficiency
ADHD or a brain injury

right.head: Temporary or situational
items: Wrist in a cast; eating with one hand
Playing on mute in a quiet berthing space
Glare on a phone screen outdoors
Exhausted after a long watch

blocks.text: Urban planners call this the **curb-cut effect**. In 1972, after years of pressure from disability activists, the city of Berkeley, California, installed its first official curb cut, a ramp from sidewalk to street, at an intersection on Telegraph Avenue. Curb cuts were meant for wheelchair users. They turned out to help everyone pushing a stroller, pulling a suitcase, riding a bike or rolling a delivery cart. Policy writer Angela Glover Blackwell later used the story to argue that designing for those most excluded often ends up benefiting everyone.

Games have their own curb cuts. Subtitles began as a feature for deaf and hard-of-hearing players. Today huge numbers of hearing players switch them on because they play late at night, in noisy rooms, on phones with the sound off or in a second language.

Remappable controls were for players who could not reach certain buttons, and now nearly every competitive player customizes their bindings. Studios have started acting on this. Microsoft's guidelines point to Gears 5, which turns subtitles on by default the first time it launches and then shows players the accessibility menu right after the opening video, before they can get lost.

Here is the uncomfortable flip side. If disability is a mismatch, then a game can disable people who are not disabled anywhere else in their lives. A rhythm section with no visual cue disables anyone playing on mute.

A 9-point font disables anyone on a small phone. A puzzle that depends on telling two shades of green apart disables a meaningful slice of the men who try it. The designer, often without noticing, decides who gets to play.
What great accessibility looks like

The Last of Us Part II, released in 2020, became the benchmark. Naughty Dog shipped it with more than 60 accessibility settings, including presets that switch on recommended options for vision, hearing or motor needs in one go. Blind and low-vision players got text-to-speech for menus and on-screen text, audio cues for traversal and combat, a high-contrast display that paints allies, enemies and items in solid colors, and an option to skip puzzles. Motor options let players change holds to taps and reduce rapid button presses. There were even settings for motion sickness: camera shake, motion blur and field of view.

Smaller games found smarter, cheaper wins. Celeste, a notoriously hard platformer from 2018, added an Assist Mode that lets players slow the game down, extend their stamina or become invincible, framed with a respectful note about the game being designed as a challenge. Valorant offers color-blind modes that recolor enemy highlights. Fortnite added an option to visualize sound effects on screen, so a player who cannot hear footsteps can still see which direction they came from. None of these change the game for players who leave them off.

blocks.title: Myths and reality

left.head: Myth
items: Accessibility means an easy mode
It only helps a tiny group
It's expensive and comes at the end
Players with disabilities don't play hard games

right.head: Reality
items: Most options change input, information or comfort, not difficulty
Situational limits make almost every player a beneficiary sometimes
The cheapest fixes are design choices made early
Many want the full challenge, just a way in

blocks.text: The invisible majority: thinking and focus

Go back to that CDC chart. For people in their twenties and thirties, cognitive difficulty was more common than mobility, vision and hearing difficulty combined. That covers a wide range: ADHD, learning disabilities, brain injuries, the after-effects of illness, and the simple reality that some days your memory and focus are not what they usually are. It is also the area games think about least, because it is invisible on a screenshot.

Cognitive accessibility mostly looks like plain good design. Tell players clearly what they are trying to do and let them check it again later, through a quest log, a marker or a one-line reminder. Let them pause, including in online games where a full pause is impossible, by giving them a safe spot to stand.

Keep menus and HUDs consistent so the same button always does the same thing. Avoid timers on reading and decision screens. Let tutorials be replayed. Every one of those helps a player with a brain injury, and every one also helps someone who just came back to your game after two months away and has forgotten everything.

One more danger hides here: flashing. For people with photosensitive epilepsy, rapid flashes can trigger seizures, and for many others they cause headaches and nausea. The web accessibility standard WCAG sets a simple bar: nothing should flash more than three times in any one-second period unless it stays below specific size and brightness thresholds. Explosions, lightning, damage flashes and strobing lights in a game are worth checking against that rule, and worth offering a way to tone down.
The difficulty argument

Accessibility gets most heated around difficulty. Some players and designers argue that for certain games, the struggle is the art: that beating a brutal boss means something precisely because the game refused to bend, and that an easy toggle cheapens it for everyone. It is a serious position, not just gatekeeping, and some of the most admired games of the last fifteen years were built on it.

The counterargument is that most accessibility features do not touch difficulty at all. Remapping a button, adding a subtitle, replacing a color cue with a shape or offering a toggle instead of a long button hold leaves the challenge exactly where it was. They remove barriers that have nothing to do with the skill being tested, the way a curb cut does not make a race shorter. Where options do touch difficulty, like Celeste's, they are optional, and the default experience stays exactly as the designer intended.

A useful test for any proposed feature is to ask what skill your game is actually testing. If it is reflexes and precision, then forcing someone to also read tiny red-on-green text is not part of the test. It is noise. Removing noise makes the real challenge cleaner, not weaker.

There is a middle path that many designers now take. Keep one intended experience as the default, protect its leaderboards and bragging rights, and offer separate options for players who need them, clearly labeled and never forced. A speedrun board can track assisted and unassisted runs separately. A tough boss can stay tough while its attack warnings get a visual cue as well as a sound. Players who want the full fight still get it, untouched, and players who were locked out now get to try.
Before calling a barrier part of the challenge, ask: is this the skill my game is about, or just an accident of how I built it? Accidents are worth fixing.
An accessibility pass for a small game

The industry has done the hard thinking already. The free Game Accessibility Guidelines sort recommendations into three tiers: basic ones that are easy to implement and apply to almost every game, intermediate ones that take some planning and advanced ones for profound impairments and niche mechanics. Microsoft's Xbox Accessibility Guidelines get specific. For subtitles, they recommend lines of no more than about 40 characters, no more than two lines on screen at once and either turning subtitles on by default or letting players set them before any opening cutscene starts.

blocks.title: A one-evening accessibility pass
items: Turn your game's color off: screenshot it in grayscale and check every important cue still reads
Add a shape or icon to anything color-coded, like team markers or safe versus deadly platforms
Make text bigger than feels necessary and test it on the smallest phone you can find
Give every sound that matters a visual twin: a flash, an arrow, a short caption
Replace long button holds and rapid tapping with toggles or single presses where you can
Ask one player who struggles with your game to play it while you watch silently

blocks.text: For a Roblox game, the stakes are high because the audience is enormous and plays on everything from gaming PCs to old phones and tablets. In a launcher obby, for example, deadly and safe surfaces should differ in pattern or shape, not only in red versus green. Launch timing cues should be visible as well as audible. Text should stay readable on a small phone screen. Each of those fixes takes minutes, and each one widens the group of people who can enjoy what you built.

Then let data point you at the barriers you missed. Roblox's analytics can show where players drop out of a game. If an unusual share quit at one obstacle, watch someone play it before assuming they simply lacked skill.

Maybe the timing cue was a sound they had muted, or the safe path was a color they could not see. A barrier and a challenge can look identical in a quit chart. Only watching a real player tells you which one you built.

The adaptive controller's real legacy was not a piece of hardware. It was a change in who designers picture when they picture a player. The player you forgot is not rare. Sometimes it is a kid with cerebral palsy, sometimes it is a veteran with an injured hand, and sometimes it is you, exhausted after a long watch, trying to play on mute.

takeaways: Among US adults 18–44, about 1 in 6 report a disability, and cognitive difficulty is the most common type (10.6%).
About 1 in 12 men have a color vision deficiency, so never signal anything with color alone.
Disability is often a mismatch the design creates; solving the permanent case helps temporary and situational cases too.
Most accessibility options change input, information or comfort, not difficulty.
A quick pass (grayscale check, shapes plus colors, bigger text, visual twins for sounds, fewer long holds) fixes most problems in small games.

title: What 682,000 Rounds of Gridshot Reveal About Aim
dek: A huge dataset from an aim trainer shows accuracy stalls within days while speed keeps climbing for months. What motor-learning science says about practicing aim, and what it can't tell you yet.

blocks.text: Between July 2020 and January 2021, thousands of people opened the aim trainer *Aim Lab* and played Gridshot, the 60-second mode where three targets sit on a grid and you click them as fast as you can. They weren't in a study. They were just trying to get better at Valorant, CS or Apex. But every run was logged, and a team of researchers later analyzed the records of 7,174 of those players.

That added up to 682,564 runs over up to 100 days of play per person, a sample far larger and longer than almost any lab study of motor learning. The paper, published in *Frontiers in Human Neuroscience* in 2021, found something every aim grinder should know. Accuracy barely improved. Speed kept improving for months.

items.label: Aim Lab players analyzed
60-second Gridshot runs logged
Share of each day's gains still there the next day

blocks.source: Listman et al., Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 2021

blocks.text: One important caveat before going further: the study was run and funded by Statespace, the company that makes Aim Lab, and it is observational. Nobody was randomly assigned to practice schedules. Treat the findings as strong clues, not commandments. They line up well with a century of motor-control research, which is a good sign.
Aim is a reach, and reaching has rules

Every flick you make is a version of one of the oldest experiments in psychology: move your hand quickly to a target. Back in 1899, researcher Robert Woodworth noticed that fast aimed movements come in two parts. There's a big, fast initial launch toward the target, then one or more small corrections as you home in. You can feel this in your own flicks: the big snap, then the tiny adjustment before you click.

In 1954, psychologist Paul Fitts put numbers to it. **Fitts' law** says the time it takes to hit a target grows with how far away it is and shrinks with how big it is, following a logarithmic curve. Double the distance or halve the target size and you add a roughly fixed chunk of time. This is why a head-sized target across the screen takes longer than a body-sized one near your crosshair, and why there is always a trade between speed and accuracy. Rush the launch and you land further off, needing bigger corrections or missing outright.

Do aim trainers really measure the same thing as a lab task? A 2023 study from the University of Leeds in *PNAS Nexus* checked. Participants shot targets either by moving a cursor across a still background, as in classic experiments, or by turning the camera as in a shooter. Their movements were nearly identical in both, which suggests the brain uses the same internal model to plan a flick whether the screen moves or the cursor does. In a second experiment modeled on aim trainers, the movements showed the classic signatures described in decades of reaching research.
A flick is two movements, not one: a fast launch and a small correction. Getting better mostly means making the launch land closer, so the correction shrinks or disappears.

Flicking and tracking lean on different versions of this machinery. A flick is mostly planned in advance: the launch is fired before visual feedback can steer it, and only the final correction uses what your eyes see. Tracking a strafing target is the opposite, a continuous loop of seeing, predicting and adjusting. That is why someone can be excellent at one and mediocre at the other, and why it makes sense to train both rather than assuming one covers the other.
Accuracy stalls, speed keeps climbing

Back to the Gridshot data. The researchers split performance into two numbers. **Hit rate** is the share of shots that hit. **Hits per second** combines speed and accuracy and is what they called motor acuity: the ability to be fast *and* accurate at once. Hit rate rose a little and then flattened within days. Hits per second kept rising across weeks of play, with no clear ceiling in the data, unlike most lab tasks where people plateau quickly.

The researchers built a model to show what this means for a typical player who plays ten Gridshot runs a day without skipping days. Their predicted hit rate inches from about 85.7 percent on day 1 to about 86.9 percent by day 40. Over the same period, hits per second climbs steadily.

blocks.title: Predicted Gridshot hits per second, typical player, 10 runs a day
blocks.source: Listman et al., Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 2021 (model predictions)

blocks.text: That is about a 22 percent gain in hits per second over forty days, while accuracy moved barely more than a point. In other words, practice did not mainly make people *more accurate*. It let them stay roughly as accurate while going much faster. In Fitts' terms, practice shifts the whole speed-accuracy trade-off, so you get more of both. That's the thing that wins duels: not hitting a slow, careful shot, but hitting it first.

A 2022 follow-up by the same company tested professional-level players on two Gridshot-style tasks, one with big targets that rewards speed and one with small targets that rewards precision. Pros' skill showed up in the fine detail of how their mouse moved, and their performance across the two target sizes was not well described by a simple Fitts' law fit. Elite aim, in other words, is more than raw speed; it's knowing how to adjust your movement to what the task demands.
From thinking to automatic

Motor-learning researchers often describe skill development in three rough stages, a model laid out by Paul Fitts and Michael Posner in 1967. In the first, *cognitive* stage, you think your way through the movement and make big, inconsistent errors. In the *associative* stage, the movement becomes smoother and errors shrink as you tune the details. In the *autonomous* stage, it runs on its own, freeing your attention for everything else happening in the game.

That last stage is the real goal for a shooter player. Nobody wins a clutch by consciously planning a flick. The aim has to happen by itself so your mind can track the enemy's likely position, your utility, the spike timer and your teammates. Aim practice is valuable less because it makes you a better clicker and more because it hands aiming off to the autopilot, so your attention is free for decisions.

There's a trap in the autonomous stage, though. Once a skill feels automatic, ordinary repetition stops improving it much. You can play for years at the same level because you are no longer pushing the edge of the skill. Gridshot's scoring hints at the alternative. Because points reward speed and penalize misses, every run nudges you to go a little faster than feels safe, and that pressure may be part of why hits per second kept rising for so long. The general rule from skill research holds: practice that feels comfortable is usually maintenance, not growth. Improvement lives just past the speed where you start to miss, with enough feedback to pull you back.
How much to practice, and when

The dataset also says something useful about dosage. Players kept a solid chunk of each day's improvement into the next session: about 65 percent from day 1 to day 2, settling to around 40 percent after the tenth day. The rest of each day's gain had to be rebuilt, which is normal for motor skills.

More practice in a day helped, but with sharply diminishing returns. Improvement in the next day's performance peaked at around an hour of Gridshot, and most of the benefit came well before that: depending on how you measure, roughly 90 percent of the gain arrived after somewhere between 33 and 49 runs, or about half an hour to fifty minutes of play. Grinding three hours did not buy three times the progress. Skipping a day between sessions had only a small negative effect in the model.

There was one more striking pattern: a warm-up effect. Every day, players' speed jumped over the first few runs before settling into steady improvement. The authors suspect this is the brain recalibrating to the mouse sensitivity, since desktop and in-game sensitivities usually differ. Their model suggested that with about three warm-up runs, peak next-day benefit came at around an hour of practice; without the warm-up, it took about 75 minutes.

blocks.title: A practice session built on the evidence
items: Warm up for 3 to 5 short runs before judging your performance.
Practice focused for about 20 to 45 minutes; quality drops long before three hours.
Mix flicking, tracking and small-target scenarios instead of grinding one mode.
Track speed and accuracy separately: expect accuracy to plateau and speed to keep rising.
Then play real matches so the skill gets used under game pressure.
Sleep. Skill consolidation continues after you stop practicing.

blocks.text: Variety, sensitivity and what the lab can't promise

Lab research on motor learning has a long-standing lesson that applies here: practicing a skill in varied forms tends to produce better long-term learning and transfer than repeating one fixed version, even though it looks worse during practice. Richard Schmidt's schema theory, published in 1975, argued that varied practice teaches the brain a general rule for producing a whole family of movements. The library's piece on interleaving covers why this kind of practice feels worse while working better. For aim, it suggests rotating through flick, tracking and micro-adjustment scenarios at different distances, rather than only playing Gridshot.

It also explains the near-universal advice to pick one sensitivity and keep it. Your brain is learning a precise mapping between how far your hand moves and how far the view turns. Change that mapping and some of what you learned must be relearned, which is the same recalibration the Gridshot warm-up effect seems to reveal. Many players match their sensitivity across games for exactly this reason.

Not every coaching tip holds up in shooters, though. In sports, telling athletes to focus on the target rather than on their own body movements usually helps performance. A 2023 study from the University of St Andrews tested this in Aim Lab with 37 players who had at least 200 hours of shooter experience, and found no difference between focusing on the target and focusing on their wrist and arm. It's one small study, but it's a reminder that results from other sports don't automatically carry over.

Sleep matters too, but carefully. A well-known 2002 Harvard study found a night of sleep boosted speed on a finger-tapping sequence by about 20 percent without any loss of accuracy, while the same time spent awake did not. Later analyses, including a 2015 meta-analysis in *Psychological Bulletin*, argued that much of that overnight gain could be explained by fatigue and other quirks of how the experiments were run. The safest reading is that sleep supports skill learning, but nobody should expect to wake up dramatically better. The library's piece on sleep and skill goes deeper.

Finally, the biggest gap: almost all of this research measures performance *inside* an aim trainer. Whether hours there turn into more round wins in Valorant or Apex has been studied far less. Real matches add crosshair placement, movement, game sense, audio cues and decision-making under pressure, none of which Gridshot trains. An aim trainer is a gym for the hands. It builds a capacity that the real game then has to use.
Aim trainers sharpen the raw movement. Matches teach you where to point it. A short daily trainer session plus deliberate real games beats endless hours of either alone.

For anyone stuck on a long deployment or away from a good setup, the dosage findings are encouraging. Skill retention across days was solid, short daily sessions captured most of the benefit, and gaps between sessions cost little in the model. Coming back to aim after months away mostly means paying the warm-up and recalibration cost again, then letting short, regular practice do its work. Expect the first week back to feel worse than your memory of your old self. That's the recalibration, not lost talent, and motor-learning research on what scientists call savings consistently finds that relearning a skill is faster than learning it the first time.

takeaways: In 682,564 Gridshot runs, accuracy plateaued within days while hits per second kept improving for months.
Practice mainly shifts the speed-accuracy trade-off: same accuracy, faster shots.
Most of a day's benefit came within roughly 30 to 50 minutes; more grinding gave diminishing returns.
Warm up before judging your aim, keep one sensitivity, and mix scenarios instead of grinding one mode.
Trainer skill is a capacity, not a rank. Real matches still teach crosshair placement and decision-making.

title: One More Turn: Compulsion Loops vs. Good Design
dek: Two games can keep you up until 3 a.m. One leaves you grateful and one leaves you drained. The difference is a design choice, and you can learn to spot it.

blocks.text: It is 2:47 a.m. and you have told yourself, three times now, that this is the last turn. In one version of this night you are deep in a strategy game, an idea for a new plan forming in your head, and you go to bed tired but happy. In another version you are tapping through a daily reward screen in a game you stopped enjoying weeks ago, because if you skip today the streak resets. Same hour, same glowing screen, same 'one more.' Completely different feeling the next morning.

Designers have a name for the machinery behind both nights: the loop. Every game repeats something. You act, the game responds, you get something, and that something makes you want to act again. The question that matters, for a player and especially for anyone building a game, is not *whether* a game loops. It is what the loop is feeding on: your curiosity and growing skill, or your fear of missing out.

This article is about telling those two apart, where the idea came from, what the research on players actually shows, and how to build a game people come back to because they want to rather than because they feel they have to.
A rat, a lever and a 2001 magazine article

In April 2001, a researcher named John Hopson published an article on Gamasutra called 'Behavioral Game Design.' His pitch was simple and a little unsettling. Every game, he argued, is already a behavioral experiment. It sets rules for when rewards arrive, and those rules shape what players do, whether the designer meant them to or not. Psychology had spent decades studying exactly this in labs. Game designers might as well learn the vocabulary.

The vocabulary came from B. F. Skinner's work on reinforcement schedules. Hopson retold the story, as it was passed down to him, that Skinner once ran low on food pellets and started rewarding his rats only every tenth lever press instead of every press. The rats did not quit. They changed *how* they pressed. Different reward rules produced very different patterns of behavior, and that discovery became a whole field.

Hopson walked through the main patterns. A fixed ratio rewards every Nth action, which tends to produce a pause before starting and then a sprint toward the payoff, and the pause grows as the ratio grows. A fixed interval rewards the first action after a set time, so players ease off after each reward and speed up as the next one comes due.

A variable ratio rewards after a number of actions that changes every time, so the player never knows if the next attempt is the one. Hopson noted that this last schedule produces the highest overall rate of activity of the ones he covered, steady and without the pauses. It is also the schedule a slot machine runs on.

blocks.title: Reward schedules, translated into games

left.head: Predictable rewards
items: Fixed ratio: a level-up every 1,000 XP
Fixed interval: a chest that refills every 4 hours
Typical behavior: pause, then sprint toward the payoff
Natural stopping points built in

right.head: Unpredictable rewards
items: Variable ratio: a rare drop with a 1-in-50 chance
Variable interval: a boss that spawns at random times
Typical behavior: steady, persistent effort
No obvious moment to stop

blocks.text: Hopson was not writing a manifesto for manipulation. Much of his article is practical advice about pacing, like avoiding long dry stretches that make players give up. But the frame he popularized, the player as a subject responding to contingencies, gave designers a powerful toolkit. Like most powerful toolkits, it can be used to build something good or something corrosive.
Why 'almost' keeps you pulling the lever

Unpredictable rewards hold attention partly because the brain cares a great deal about surprise. There is a second trick that matters just as much for game design: the near miss. In a 2009 study in the journal *Neuron*, Luke Clark and colleagues had people play a simplified slot machine while in a brain scanner. Near misses, where the reels stopped one position from a win, felt *less* pleasant than clean losses. Yet they increased people's desire to keep playing.

Two details make this study especially useful for designers. First, near misses recruited some of the same brain reward circuitry that responded to actual wins, even though the player got nothing. Second, the effect only appeared when the player had personal control over arranging the gamble. When the machine chose for them, near misses lost much of their pull. Feeling like your skill or choice *almost* worked is what makes 'almost' so sticky.
Here is the uncomfortable part. Near misses in a skill game are honest feedback. If you clip the edge of a jump by a pixel, the game is telling you something true, and you really are close.

Near misses in a random system are a lie dressed up as feedback. A spinning wheel that slows down dramatically next to the jackpot is not telling you that you are getting better. It is borrowing the feeling of progress without the substance.

A useful test: when the player almost wins, is the game telling the truth? In a skill challenge, 'almost' means they are improving. In a random roll, 'almost' means nothing, and dressing it up as close is a manipulation.
Wanting to play versus having to play

The core loop of a good game and a compulsion loop can look identical on a diagram. Act, get feedback, get a reward, want to act again. The difference is what the reward is for. In a core loop, the reward is mostly the activity itself: the jump feels good, the puzzle clicks, the fight teaches you something. In a compulsion loop, the activity is a toll you pay to reach the reward, and the reward is mostly a reason to keep paying tolls.

blocks.title: The compulsion loop, stripped down
items: Anticipation: a timer, a chest, a streak
Action: a short, repeatable task
Uncertain reward: sometimes great, usually small
New anticipation set up before you can stop

blocks.text: Psychologists have a framework that maps neatly onto this split. Andrew Przybylski and colleagues, writing in 2009, drew on the idea of harmonious versus obsessive passion. Harmonious passion is when an activity fits freely into your life and you play because you want to. Obsessive passion is when it feels like something you are compelled to do. Their study of gamers found that people whose basic psychological needs (feeling competent, free and connected) were poorly met in daily life were more likely to have obsessive passion for games, to play more hours, to feel tension after playing and to enjoy it less.

The flip side was just as telling. Players whose needs were well met did not necessarily play fewer hours, but they reported more harmonious passion, more enjoyment and more energy after playing. And heavy play was linked to lower well-being only for players who described an obsessive relationship with the game. Hours alone were not the villain. The *kind* of hold the game had on someone was.

Later studies with better data pointed in the same direction. In 2021, Niklas Johannes, Matti Vuorre and Przybylski partnered with Electronic Arts and Nintendo to match players' surveys with their actual logged play time in *Plants vs. Zombies: Battle for Neighborville* and *Animal Crossing: New Horizons*. Play time had a small positive relationship with well-being. Feeling autonomy and connection during play predicted feeling better, while playing out of pressure (extrinsic motivation) predicted feeling worse.

In 2022, the same group scaled up. They tracked six weeks of real play data from 38,935 players across seven games from seven publishers. The headline: time spent playing had essentially no detectable effect on well-being.

The model suggested a typical player would need to play about ten more hours *per day* than usual before noticing a change in how they felt. But motivation mattered again. Enjoyable, self-chosen play was linked to small improvements in well-being, and pressured play to small declines, though the authors noted these effects were modest and somewhat uncertain.

items.label: Players whose real play time was tracked across seven games
Extra daily play the model estimated it would take to notice any well-being change

blocks.source: Vuorre et al., Royal Society Open Science, 2022

blocks.text: Put together, the research reframes the whole debate. 'Is this game too addictive?' is usually the wrong question if you are measuring it in hours. The better question is whether the game pulls people in through what they enjoy or pushes them along with pressure. That is a design decision, and it shows up in specific mechanics.
The rat that pressed to avoid a shock

One of the most revealing parts of Hopson's 2001 article is a short section on avoidance. In the lab example he describes, a rat gets a mild shock every so often, but pressing a lever postpones the next shock for 30 seconds. The rat quickly learns to press at a slow, steady rate, not to gain anything, only to keep something bad from happening. His game example was *Ultima Online*, where houses decayed unless their owners visited regularly. He also pointed out why designers like this pattern: it is cheap, because the game never has to hand out anything new.

Look at modern game design through that lens and a lot of features change shape. A daily login streak that resets to zero if you miss one day is an avoidance schedule. Crops that wither if you do not come back in time are an avoidance schedule. A limited-time event that disappears forever is an avoidance schedule.
None of them reward you for playing. They punish you for *not* playing. That is the treadmill feeling of the second 2:47 a.m. in the opening: you are not chasing joy, you are dodging a loss.

Hopson also wrote about extinction: what happens when a reward stops. Players react with frustration, and how long they keep going depends on the schedule they were trained on. Under ratio schedules, he wrote, people keep working hard for a long time before gradually trailing off. That helps explain why games built around chance-based rewards can keep people grinding long after the fun has drained out. The habit outlives the enjoyment.

blocks.title: Same feature, two designs

left.head: Pull (want to play)
items: Daily challenge that is a fresh puzzle
Streak that pauses or forgives a missed day
Rare drop that rewards a skill milestone
Session ends at a natural, satisfying break

right.head: Push (have to play)
items: Daily login reward for showing up
Streak that resets to zero after one miss
Rare drop that rewards repeated paid rolls
Session ends on a cliffhanger timer

blocks.text: Designing a game people are glad they played

If you are building a Roblox game, every one of these tools is available to you, and the platform's metrics will quietly tempt you toward the push side. Retention and session length go up when people feel they must return. But a game that only holds people through pressure is fragile. The moment a better treadmill appears, they leave, and they do not miss you. The goal is retention that comes from the core activity being worth repeating.

Take an obby or a launcher-style game. The core loop is already strong: try a jump, fail, adjust, succeed. Every failure is honest feedback, and every success is earned. That loop is the asset. Most of the design work is protecting it from being buried under timers and pop-ups.

items: **Make rewards mean something.** A new pole skin for clearing a hard section tells the player they got better. A random skin for logging in tells them nothing.
**Keep near misses honest.** Show players how close they came on a real attempt, like a height marker or ghost of their best run. Never fake 'almost' on a random roll.
**Forgive absence.** If you add streaks, let them pause or bank missed days. People on irregular schedules, from students to sailors standing watches, will thank you by coming back.
**Build in stopping points.** Checkpoints and stage clears are natural moments to quit happy. A player who leaves on a high is more likely to return than one who leaves annoyed.
**Test the reward-removal question.** Imagine stripping out every currency, timer and chest. If the remaining loop is still fun for ten minutes, you have a game. If not, the extras are carrying it.

blocks.text: None of this means rewards are bad. Unlocks, collections and surprises add texture to good games all the time. The issue is which job they are doing. Used well, rewards are signposts that point at the fun and celebrate mastery. Used badly, they replace the fun with a feeling of obligation.
The cleanest design test is the morning after. If a player looks back on a long session and thinks 'that was great,' the loop is pulling. If they think 'why did I do that,' it is pushing.

There is a personal version of this lesson too. The same reward schedules that power games power phones, feeds and shopping apps. Knowing the names helps. When you catch yourself opening something just to keep a streak alive, or because 'almost' felt close, you are watching a contingency do its job. Seeing the lever does not make you immune, but it does give you a choice about whether to keep pressing it.

takeaways: Every game loops; the question is whether the loop runs on enjoyment and mastery or on pressure and fear of loss.
Unpredictable rewards and near misses are powerful because they borrow the feeling of progress, even when nothing real has changed.
Large studies with real play data find hours played barely matter for well-being; playing out of pressure is the warning sign.
Streaks that reset, withering crops and vanishing events are avoidance schedules: they punish absence instead of rewarding play.
For your own game: make rewards signal skill, keep near misses honest, forgive missed days and let sessions end on a high.
