title: The Level That Teaches Without Saying a Word
dek: Super Mario Bros. never told you to jump on a Goomba. How great games teach through level design, why good difficulty is a sawtooth not a ramp, and where players actually quit.

blocks.text: Press start on *Super Mario Bros.* and look at the screen. Mario stands near the left edge with open space stretching to the right. There's no arrow, no text, no tutorial. You just know which way to go. A few steps later, a brown mushroom-shaped creature walks toward you. It's the first enemy in the game, and it's the gentlest one Nintendo could design.

In a 2015 video interview with Eurogamer, Shigeru Miyamoto and his long-time collaborator Takashi Tezuka walked through that first level, World 1-1, and explained how much of it was arranged to teach. The Goomba was chosen as the first enemy for a reason. The first power-up mushroom pops out of a block and slides along, bouncing off a pipe so that it tends to come back toward you even if you tried to dodge it. And before one tricky, dangerous jump, the level gives you a nearly identical but safe version to practice on first.

That level is more than forty years old and it still gets taught in game design courses, because it does what most tutorials fail to do. It teaches through play. You learn by doing, in a space built so that the lesson is almost impossible to miss and failure is cheap.
Why tutorials so often fail

Most players have sat through the other kind of teaching: a wall of text boxes in the first five minutes explaining twelve controls, three currencies and a crafting system before you have done anything. Most of it evaporates. That is not because players are lazy. Memory research has long shown that people retain far more of what they actively do and retrieve than of what they passively read, and a list of instructions with no context gives the brain nothing to hook onto.

There's a second problem. A text tutorial teaches everything at once, at the moment the player cares least. Good level design teaches each idea at the exact moment it becomes useful, which is when the brain is most ready to keep it. The jump is taught when there is something to jump over. The new tool is handed over right before the obstacle it was made for.

That is why the strongest designers treat every popup as a small admission of failure. Sometimes text is unavoidable, especially for menus and complex systems like a card game's keywords. But the goal is always to make the space itself do the explaining, so the player feels like they figured it out rather than being told.
Every level is a lesson plan

The best-documented version of this approach comes from Koichi Hayashida, who directed *Super Mario Galaxy 2* and *Super Mario 3D Land*. In a 2012 interview with Gamasutra, he described building stages around a four-part structure he compared to *kishōtenketsu*, the shape of a classic four-panel Japanese comic strip. The article noted that Miyamoto, who drew comics as a kid, had brought the idea into Nintendo's design culture.

blocks.title: Hayashida's four-step stage structure
items: Introduce: show one new mechanic in a safe spot so players can learn how it works.
Develop: put that mechanic in a slightly more demanding situation.
Twist: change something unexpected so players must rethink what they learned.
Conclude: let players show off their mastery before the stage ends.

blocks.text: Look closely and you'll see why this works so well. Each stage is built around one main idea instead of five. The idea arrives in a low-stakes form, so the player's first encounter is curiosity rather than death. It then gets harder in a controlled way. The twist is the bit that makes it memorable: the moving platforms suddenly reverse direction, or the thing you've been dodging becomes the thing you ride. By the end, the player has learned a new skill without reading a word.

Then the next stage introduces a fresh idea, and the cycle starts again. Across a whole game, that adds up to hundreds of small lessons, each one taught, tested and retired before it can get stale. That is the same pattern-learning engine described in the library's piece on what makes games fun, built into the very floor plan.
A useful rule from this school of design: one new idea per space. Teach it safely, test it seriously, twist it once, then move on before it gets old.
Difficulty is a sawtooth, not a ramp

When people draw a difficulty curve they usually sketch a smooth line climbing from easy to hard. Good games almost never look like that. They look more like a sawtooth. Tension builds through a challenge, peaks, and then drops to a calm stretch before rising again, a little higher than last time. Without the drops, players burn out. Without the rises, they get bored.

Valve built that idea straight into *Left 4 Dead* (2008), a co-op zombie shooter. Its AI Director, designed by Michael Booth, kept a running estimate of each survivor's stress, raising it when they took damage, got knocked down or had zombies die close by, and letting it fade over time. Based on the most stressed player, the Director switched between phases.

blocks.title: Left 4 Dead's AI Director pacing loop
items: Build up: full threat population until intensity peaks
Sustain peak: keep the pressure on for 3 to 5 seconds
Peak fade: pull back to a minimal threat until stress drops
Relax: about 30 to 45 seconds of calm, then build again

blocks.text: Booth's slides summed up the philosophy in a single line: the algorithm adjusts *pacing*, not difficulty. The zombies didn't get weaker when you struggled. The game just gave you room to breathe before the next wave, the way a good action movie alternates chase scenes with quiet moments. Your Valorant or Siege matches have the same shape built in: the tension of a round, then the short buy phase between rounds.
Where players actually quit

Designers obsess over difficulty for a simple reason: it decides who stays. You can see this in public data. Steam tracks what share of a game's owners have unlocked each achievement, and *Celeste*, the famously hard 2018 platformer, gives an achievement for clearing each chapter. Here is the drop-off, as a share of everyone who owns the game on Steam.

blocks.title: Share of Celeste owners on Steam who cleared each chapter
blocks.note: Chapter-completion achievements; owners include people who barely played. Snapshot November 2026.
blocks.source: Steam global achievement stats, Celeste (app 504230), retrieved Nov 2026

blocks.text: Two things jump out. First, the biggest losses come early. Between finishing Chapter 1 and finishing Chapter 3, the game loses about 20 points of its owners. Between Chapter 5 and the summit at the end of Chapter 7, it loses only about 4. Once players are invested and skilled enough to reach the middle of the game, nearly all of them finish the story. Second, the optional Farewell chapter, added later and aimed at experts, is cleared by fewer than one in ten owners.

Some of the early drop is not about difficulty at all. Plenty of people buy games in a sale and play for twenty minutes. But the same shape shows up elsewhere. In *Hollow Knight*, about 71 percent of Steam owners have beaten the first boss, the False Knight, while the most common ending achievement is held by only about a quarter of them, with steady losses all along the way. The opening hour is where your difficulty curve does most of its killing, which is why it deserves most of your design attention.

There's a subtler reason a flat difficulty curve fails, too. The player is not standing still. Every minute they play, their skill grows, so a level of challenge that felt tense in the first hour feels trivial by the fifth. A designer is not tuning difficulty against a fixed person; they are chasing a moving target. That is why the sawtooth has to drift upward over the course of a game, and why the late game can demand things that would have been unthinkable at the start.

How fast you get back into the action after failing matters as much as how hard the challenge is. Celeste respawns you almost instantly at the start of the screen you died on, so a hundred deaths cost minutes rather than an evening. Compare that to a game that sends you back ten minutes after every mistake. The challenge might be identical, but one feels like practice and the other like punishment.
Forgiveness, options and the assist question

Celeste offers another lesson. It is hard on purpose, but it also includes an Assist Mode that lets players slow the game down, get extra dashes or even turn on invincibility. The game makes clear this is not how it is meant to be played, but it puts the choice in the player's hands. Its hidden forgiveness tricks, like letting you jump a fraction of a second after leaving a ledge, do quieter work: they make the hard parts feel fair rather than easier.

Other games bake help into the system itself. Mario Kart hands better items to racers in the back of the pack, keeping races close. Some Nintendo platformers offer to show you the solution after you've died repeatedly on a level. Each approach has a cost. Players who notice a game secretly going easy on them often feel patronized, and competitive players hate anything that props up the loser. The best-received help tends to be either invisible, like Celeste's coyote time, or clearly optional, like its Assist Mode.

blocks.title: Two ways to handle a wall of difficulty

left.head: Lower the wall
items: Hidden difficulty adjustment
Rubber-banding items or AI
Optional assist settings
Risk: players feel patronized if they notice

right.head: Teach them to climb it
items: A safe practice version before the hard version
Short retry loops and close checkpoints
Clear feedback on why you failed
Calm stretches between peaks so players recover

blocks.text: Building a curve for your own game

For an obby or a platformer-style Roblox game, all of this turns into a few concrete habits. Introduce every new obstacle type in a spot where falling costs almost nothing, ideally right after a checkpoint. Use it once more in a harder setting, then give it a twist. Space checkpoints so that a failure costs seconds, not minutes, especially early on. After every hard section, give players a short easy stretch with something nice to look at or collect.

Then watch real people play, and keep your mouth shut. Valve's developer commentary for games like *Portal* describes how heavily the team leaned on watching playtesters, changing levels whenever players got stuck or missed the lesson. The urge to explain is strong, but every time you have to say what to do, the level failed to teach it. Note where they hesitate, where they die repeatedly and where they put the controller down.

Finally, measure it. Roblox lets you log simple custom events, such as reaching each checkpoint or stage, and the resulting funnel will look a lot like the Celeste chart above. Find the steepest drop in your first few minutes and fix that before you build anything new. One badly placed spike early on can quietly lose you more players than a whole new world will ever win back.

Many Roblox obbies sell a skip-stage button, and it doubles as a free difficulty sensor. If skip purchases or deaths pile up on one particular stage, that stage is a spike, whatever you intended. Sometimes a spike is the point, a boss moment the player will brag about clearing. But it should be a choice you made on purpose, placed after the player has had time to get invested, not an accident sitting in stage four where it quietly ends most sessions.

A simple rule of thumb from everything above: early on, make failure cheap and lessons obvious; in the middle, raise the stakes in waves; near the end, trust the skills you have spent the whole game teaching.

The deepest lesson from World 1-1 is humility. Miyamoto's team did not assume players would understand. They assumed players would do the most natural thing, and then designed the space so that the natural thing was also the right thing. A great difficulty curve feels like your own skill growing. It's really someone else's careful planning, hidden so well that you never notice it at all.

takeaways: Teach through play: introduce each new mechanic in a safe spot before testing it for real.
Hayashida's structure: introduce, develop, twist, conclude. One main idea per stage.
Good difficulty is a sawtooth with peaks and calm stretches, not a smooth ramp. Left 4 Dead adjusted pacing, not difficulty.
Players quit most in the opening stretch. Celeste lost about 20 points of owners between chapters 1 and 3.
Make help invisible or clearly optional, and find your steepest early drop-off with data before building more content.

title: Every Game Is a Central Bank
dek: Gold, gems, coins and Robux follow the same laws as real money. Get the faucets and drains wrong and your game inflates until nothing players earn means anything.

blocks.text: Around 2001, an economist named Edward Castronova did something his colleagues found ridiculous. He studied *EverQuest*, a fantasy online game, the way you'd study a developing country. He surveyed players, tracked prices on eBay, where people sold in-game gold and items for real dollars, and worked out what an hour of play was actually worth.

His numbers were startling. The average player in the game world of Norrath produced about $3.42 of real-world value per hour. Its currency, platinum pieces, traded at about one cent each, more than the Japanese yen or the Italian lira at the time. Measured per person, Norrath's economic output landed somewhere between Russia's and Bulgaria's. A fantasy world running on servers in San Diego had a real economy.

That paper launched a whole field, and it holds a lesson every game developer eventually learns the hard way. The moment your game has a currency, you are running a central bank. You decide how much money gets printed, what it can buy and how it leaves the system. Do that badly and you get the same disease real countries get: inflation, inequality and a currency nobody trusts.
Faucets and drains

Designers describe every game economy with two words. **Faucets** are anything that creates currency out of nothing: enemy drops, quest rewards, daily login bonuses, idle income, selling items to a shop. **Sinks** are anything that destroys it: buying from the game's shop, repair bills, upgrade costs, consumables, taxes on trades, fees to respawn.

blocks.title: The basic economy loop
items: Faucet: the game creates currency (drops, rewards, income)
Wallet: players hold and trade it
Sink: the game destroys it (upgrades, fees, consumables)
Progress: what was bought makes earning faster

blocks.text: The balance between them decides everything. If faucets pour in more than sinks drain out, the total money supply grows. In a single-player game that just makes things easier. In any game where players trade, it's inflation in the textbook sense: more coins chasing the same goods. Prices in player markets climb, veterans sit on mountains of gold, and new players arrive to find that their first hour of earnings can't buy anything worth having.

MMO players have a name for a cousin of this problem: **mudflation**. Each expansion adds stronger gear, so last year's legendary sword becomes this year's junk, and everything earned before loses value. Inflation of gold and inflation of power do the same damage. They quietly tell players that the effort they already put in has been devalued.

There's a catch on the other side. Players hate sinks that feel like punishment. Repair bills, death penalties and taxes are efficient drains, but they feel like the game reaching into your pocket. Sinks that feel like *buying something* work far better: a new skin, a faster mount, a bigger backpack. The money disappears just the same, but the player walks away feeling richer instead of robbed. Good economy design is mostly the art of disguising drains as rewards.
Inflation is not just a number problem. It erases the meaning of past effort. If a player's hard-won stash buys nothing a month later, the game has told them their time didn't matter.
When the market ate the game

The most famous economic mistake in modern games is *Diablo III*. When it launched in 2012, Blizzard included two auction houses where players could trade loot, one using in-game gold and one using real money, with Blizzard taking a cut.

On paper it was clever: players were going to trade on shady third-party sites anyway, so why not make it safe and official? In practice it broke the game's heart. *Diablo* is about killing monsters and hoping for a great item. With an auction house, the best gear for your character was almost always for sale, so the smartest way to improve was to farm gold and go shopping. Item drops felt pointless, because someone else had already found a better version and listed it.

The real-money side added another layer. Once a sword had a dollar price, every hour of play had one too, and for a lot of players the game started to feel like a job with bad pay. Some players spent heavily to skip the grind; others felt that anyone with a strong character had probably just bought it. Either way, the thing that made loot exciting, the surprise of finding it yourself, was gone.

Blizzard announced in September 2013 that both auction houses would close, and they shut down on March 18, 2014. Production director John Hight said they ultimately undermined the core loop of the game, which he summed up as killing monsters to get cool loot. Alongside the closure, Blizzard reworked how loot dropped so that playing, not shopping, became the way to get stronger. The game was widely seen as much better afterward.

The lesson is bigger than auction houses. An economy should *serve* your core loop. Whenever spending currency becomes a faster path to the fun than playing, the economy is competing with your game, and it will win.
The game that hired an economist

Some games lean into a real economy instead of fighting it. *EVE Online*, a space MMO where nearly every ship and module is built by players from mined resources, is the extreme case. In June 2007 its developer CCP appointed Eyjólfur Guðmundsson, a university dean with a PhD in economics, as the game's lead economist. His job was to publish regular reports on the state of the economy and track inflation, growth and prices, much like a statistics office for a country.

What makes *EVE* work is its brutal sink. When a ship is destroyed, it's gone. Every battle wipes out materials that players spent hours mining, hauling and building, which creates constant demand for new ships, which keeps miners, traders and manufacturers in business. Loss is not a bug in that economy. It's the drain that keeps the whole system from flooding.

blocks.title: Two kinds of game economy

left.head: Designer-controlled
items: Prices set by the game's shop
Players can't trade, or trade only a little
Inflation mainly makes the game too easy
Easy to balance, fewer emergent stories

right.head: Player-driven
items: Prices set by supply and demand
Trading, crafting and markets between players
Inflation hurts new players and wrecks value
Needs strong sinks: taxes, decay, destruction

blocks.text: Most games sit somewhere between. *World of Warcraft* added a token in 2015 that players can buy with real money and sell to other players for gold, partly to undercut illegal gold sellers. Path of Exile famously uses consumable crafting orbs as its money, so the currency itself gets destroyed whenever someone uses it. Each is an attempt to answer the same question: where does the money go when it leaves?
Roblox: two economies stacked on top of each other

A Roblox game actually runs two economies at once. The first is Robux, the platform's currency, bought with real money. The second is whatever you invent inside your experience: coins, gems, power, wins. Roblox manages the first; you're the central bank for the second.

The Robux economy is now enormous. Creators who earn Robux from game passes, developer products and other sales can cash them out through the Developer Exchange program, called DevEx. On September 5, 2025, Roblox raised the cash-out rate from $0.0035 to $0.0038 per earned Robux. The total paid out has grown fast.

It helps to follow one Robux on its trip. A player buys it with real money, then spends it on your game pass. Roblox keeps a share of that sale and credits the rest to you in Robux. You can spend those Robux on ads or other creators' items, or cash them out through DevEx. At each step some value leaves the system, which is exactly why the platform's currency holds its value: Roblox is running the faucets and sinks at the top level, the same way you'll run them inside your game.

blocks.title: Roblox developer exchange fees paid to creators
blocks.note: Amounts earned by creators in the Developer Exchange Program, from Roblox's annual reports.
blocks.source: Roblox Corporation Form 10-K filings for 2022, 2024 and 2025

items.label: Average daily active users on Roblox in 2025
Average daily unique paying users in 2025
DevEx cash-out rate per earned Robux since Sept 2025

blocks.source: Roblox Corporation Form 10-K for fiscal 2025

blocks.text: Look at the middle number. Only about 1.4% of daily players paid anything on an average day. That means your in-game currency, the one everyone earns for free, is the economy that most of your players actually experience. If it's broken, the roughly 98% who don't spend Robux on a given day will feel it first, and they're the crowd that makes your game look alive to the few who do pay.
Designing currency sinks for your own game

Simulator and +1 style games on Roblox are basically economies with a game attached. Every second, something ticks up: strength, height, speed, coins. That's a faucet running nonstop. Without strong sinks, players hit the point where they can afford everything, and the game ends for them even if there's content left.

The most important sink in the genre is the **rebirth**, sometimes called prestige. A player gives up their currency and upgrades, resets to the start, and in return gets a permanent multiplier. It's a brilliant drain because it destroys the entire money supply of a player's run while making them *feel* richer. Every rebirth also sends them back through your early content, which is cheap to make and fast to replay.

Don't overcorrect, though. An economy with too many drains is just as broken as one with too few. If every upgrade costs more than a session's earnings and every boost is a rip-off, players feel permanently poor and quit. The goal isn't zero inflation; it's controlled growth, where players feel steadily richer while the next thing they want always stays slightly out of reach. Tuning that gap is most of the job.

items: **Rebirths and prestige:** wipe currency and upgrades for a permanent multiplier.
**Escalating upgrade costs:** make each level cost more, so earning speed and spending stay in a race.
**Consumables:** temporary boosts, launch pads or shields that are used up, not kept.
**Cosmetics:** trails, skins and effects that cost a lot but don't add power, so whales of the free currency have something to chase.
**Trading taxes:** if players can trade, destroy a percentage of every transaction.
**Limited-time shops:** rotating items that pull currency out at predictable times.

blocks.text: Then measure it. Roblox's analytics tools let developers log economy events, tagging each currency change as a source or a sink, and see the totals in the Creator Dashboard. The single most useful chart for your game's health is total currency created per day versus total destroyed per day. If the first line pulls far ahead of the second for weeks, prices and progression are about to break, and you'll see it in the data before players start complaining.

blocks.title: A starter plan for an in-game economy
items: Write down every faucet and every sink in your game, with rough amounts per minute of play.
Pick what the currency is *for*: one clear thing players want next, then the thing after that.
Make upgrade costs grow faster than income, and add a rebirth when the curve gets too steep.
Keep Robux purchases to convenience, boosts and cosmetics, not the core verb of the game.
Log sources and sinks, compare them weekly and adjust prices in small steps.

blocks.text: Money is a measure of time

Here's the reframe that ties it together. In a game, currency is really a measurement of player time. Ten thousand coins means 'you played this many minutes and made these choices.' When a designer prints too much money, they aren't just changing a number. They're changing what an hour of a player's life was worth.

Castronova's $3.42 an hour was the same idea seen from outside: players had turned their time into something other people would pay for. The best game economies honor that. They make earning feel like progress, spending feel like a real decision, and saving feel worthwhile. Get the faucets and drains right, and the currency fades into the background, which is exactly where it belongs. Get them wrong, and you'll spend your updates chasing inflation instead of making new content.

It's worth noticing how closely this mirrors real money too. A paycheck is a faucet; rent, food and car payments are sinks; savings are what's left when the drains run slower than the tap. The same discipline that keeps a game economy healthy, knowing exactly where the money comes from and where it goes, is the one that keeps a personal budget from quietly inflating away.

takeaways: Every currency needs faucets that create it and sinks that destroy it; when faucets win for long, you get inflation.
If buying is faster than playing, the economy is competing with your game. Diablo III closed its auction houses for that reason.
Destruction and loss can be healthy sinks, as EVE Online's exploding ships show.
Roblox paid creators about $1.5 billion through DevEx in 2025, but only about 1.8 million of 127 million daily users paid on an average day.
For a +1 or simulator game: rebirths, rising costs, consumables, cosmetics and logging sources vs sinks keep the economy healthy.

title: You Were Never Looking at the Same Moment
dek: The history of the online shooter, from Doom to Valorant, is really a thirty-year war on lag. Riot's own tests show how a hundredth of a second can flip a gunfight from 90% wins to 90% losses.

blocks.text: Before Valorant launched, Riot Games ran an experiment that sounds almost too precise to matter. They sat pairs of their best, evenly matched players down for days of blind peeking duels: one player held an angle, the other peeked around a corner at a moment of their choosing. Between rounds, the developers secretly nudged the network conditions by a few milliseconds.

The results, published by Riot's engineers in 2020, were startling. Skilled players could tell when the timing shifted by about 10 milliseconds, even without being told anything had changed. And a 10 ms swing in the peeker's favor was enough to flip a duel from a 90% win rate for a player holding an angle with an Operator to a 90% win rate for the player peeking with a rifle. A hundredth of a second decided the fight. Across all their tests, the gap between winning and losing a gunfight at that level often came down to 20 to 50 ms, and a 20 ms shift felt huge to the players even when they could not say why.

That is the hidden story of the first-person shooter. We usually tell its history through weapons, maps and graphics, from Doom's demons to Valorant's agents. But underneath, every generation of online shooter has been fighting the same enemy: the speed of light and the messiness of the internet. Every player sees a slightly different version of the past, and netcode is the art of deciding whose version counts.
Doom: everyone waits for everyone

Doom arrived in December 1993 and made multiplayer shooting a craze on office and university networks. Its netcode was elegant and brutally simple. The game world advanced in fixed steps called tics, 35 of them per second, and up to four players could join a game. In each tic, every computer needed every player's input before it could move the world forward.

This approach, called **lockstep**, has a big advantage: each machine runs the exact same simulation from the exact same inputs, so they never disagree and very little data needs to be sent. It also has a fatal weakness. The game can only run as fast as its slowest connection. On a local network where messages take a millisecond or two, that does not matter. Over a dial-up modem, every player feels every other player's lag, all the time.
It is worth remembering that even a game with no network at all has lag. In his 1996 notes, Carmack walked through the arithmetic. A game drawing 15 frames a second spends about 66 ms on each frame.

Your input arrives at a random point in the frame, so it waits about 33 ms on average before it is even read, then another frame passes before you see the result. That adds up to nearly 100 ms between your hand and your eyes, sitting at your own desk. Run the game at 25 frames a second and it drops to about 60 ms. Frame rate is latency.

items.label: Tics per second in Doom's simulation
Maximum players in a Doom game
Year Doom launched

blocks.source: id Software, DOOM source code (doomdef.h), released 1997

blocks.text: Quake: the client starts guessing

Quake, released in 1996, switched to a client-server model. A single server ran the authoritative world, and each player's computer, the client, sent inputs and drew whatever the server reported back. It played beautifully on a local network. On the internet it felt like wading through mud, because every step you took had to travel to the server and back before you saw yourself move.

In August 1996 John Carmack, Quake's lead programmer, wrote a public note admitting he had built the network code on the wrong basic assumptions for internet play. He had designed for connections under 200 milliseconds. But he estimated that 99% of players connected through modems and overcrowded internet providers, which meant round trips of 300 ms or more at a minimum.

His fix, in an experimental version called QuakeWorld, was **client-side prediction**. Your own computer stopped waiting for permission. It applied your movement instantly, using the same physics as the server, and quietly corrected itself if the server later disagreed. Carmack reported that even over a link of more than 200 ms, your own movement felt like a single-player game.

The latency did not disappear. It moved. Your rockets still came out of where the server thought you were, not where your screen showed you, and other players appeared where they had been a moment earlier, so you had to lead your shots by your own ping. Carmack also learned the limits of guessing: he concluded that simulating 300 ms of the world on the client was out of the question for a twitch shooter, because the guesses about other players would be wrong too often.

He fought for bytes as hard as for milliseconds. On a modem link, he noted, every couple of bytes saved per update translated into roughly a millisecond of latency saved, and he reported trimming an average of 17 bytes from each server-to-client message in a single day. He also added bandwidth estimation, so the game would send less rather than letting a clogged connection pile up seconds of delay. The tools have changed since then. The mindset has not.
Lag never goes away. Netcode only decides who pays for it: the shooter, the target, or the smoothness of the game. Every design choice since 1996 has been a different answer to that question.
Valve rewinds time

The next leap came from Valve, whose Half-Life engine also ran Counter-Strike, the mod that became one of the most played competitive games ever made. In a 2001 paper on latency compensation, Valve engineer Yahn Bernier described the trick most shooters still use. The server keeps a short history of where every player was, moment by moment. When your shot arrives, the server works out what you were seeing when you clicked, rewinds the other players to those positions, checks the hit, and then returns everything to the present.

For the shooter, this is magic: if your crosshair was on the target on your screen, the shot counts, with no need to lead by your ping. Riot's engineers describe the same rewind in Valorant and explain why it matters. Without it, players would have to aim ahead of moving targets by an amount that changes with their own network latency.

But someone pays. If you sprint behind a wall and die a split second later, you may have been shot in the server's rewound past, a moment when the shooter could still see you. That is why every game caps how far back the server is willing to rewind. Riot notes that without a limit, a player on a 500 ms connection could kill you half a second after you had reached cover.

Why favor the shooter? Because aiming is the skill a shooter is built to test. A player who lands a clean shot on their screen and sees it ignored feels robbed of the core of the game, and it happens on every shot. Dying just behind cover is frustrating too, but it is rarer and more ambiguous. Most modern shooters have made the same bet: protect the moment of aiming, and keep the rewind window short enough that the victims' complaints stay occasional.

blocks.title: What happens in a peek
items: The peeker presses a key, and their own screen moves them around the corner instantly (prediction)
The movement travels over the internet to the server
The server waits briefly in a buffer, processes the move on its next tick and sends it out
It travels to the holder's computer and waits in another small buffer
The holder's screen finally draws the peeker, often 100+ ms after the peeker first saw them

blocks.text: Valorant's war on milliseconds

That last step is the source of **peeker's advantage**, the most argued-about effect in tactical shooters. Because the peeker moves first on their own screen, they get to see the holder before the holder's screen shows them. Riot's engineers boiled it down to a relationship in plain terms: the time a holder has to react before dying equals the peeker's reaction time, minus the holder's round-trip ping, minus the buffering delays on the server and on both clients.

Plugging in typical numbers, Riot estimated that peekers got roughly 141 ms more time to react than holders, at a time when human reaction times often sit around 300 ms. So they attacked every term. They built Riot Direct, a private internet backbone, and placed servers around the world with the goal of 35 ms ping for 70% of players. They ran servers at 128 ticks per second, kept buffers as small as possible and optimized the game client to run at high frame rates.

blocks.title: Simulation updates per second
blocks.note: Quake's 20 is the default server frame rate Carmack described; it could be raised.
blocks.source: Carmack .plan, Aug 1996; id Software DOOM source; Riot Games, 2020

blocks.text: Riot calculated that 128-tick servers, 35 ms ping and a 60 frames-per-second client together cut about 40 ms, or 28%, off the baseline advantage. A player running at 144 frames per second brought it down to around 71 ms, a 49% reduction from where they started.

blocks.title: Peeker's advantage, Riot's estimates
blocks.note: Riot setup = 128-tick servers and 35 ms ping. Middle bar is Riot's 141 ms baseline minus its stated ~40 ms saving.
blocks.source: deWet & Straily, Peeking into VALORANT's Netcode, Riot Games, 2020

blocks.text: The same article spells out a subtler problem: two computers running the same physics can still drift apart. Running two 5 ms physics updates back to back gives a slightly different answer than one 10 ms update, because of how forces are added up step by step. A client simulating at 30 updates a second would slowly diverge from a server at 128 and need constant corrections, which show up on screen as rubber-banding. Riot's answer was to run movement on fixed time steps, so every machine does the same math in the same increments no matter its frame rate.

Even then, Riot admitted that zero is unreachable. So it used game design to tilt fights back toward the holder. Attackers usually have to come through a single entry point while defenders can choose among several angles. A character's shoulder appears around a corner before their eyes do, which buys the holder a few milliseconds.
Guns are inaccurate while moving, so a peeker has to stop before shooting reliably. And getting hit briefly slows you down. Technology shrank the advantage. Design did the rest.

blocks.title: The shooter's war on lag
items: Doom: lockstep, 35 tics a second, four players
Quake moves to client-server; QuakeWorld adds client-side prediction
Counter-Strike begins as a Half-Life mod
Valve publishes its server-rewind lag compensation method
Valorant launches with 128-tick servers and a private network backbone
Counter-Strike 2 adds timestamps for actions between ticks

blocks.text: What this changes about how you play and build

Once you see netcode, a few old arguments resolve. "I shot first" is often true on your screen and irrelevant on the server, because the server is judging a slightly different moment than either of you saw. Getting killed behind cover is not always a bug; it may be the rewind doing its job for someone with a worse connection. And your hardware matters more than it looks. By Riot's own math, a high-refresh monitor and a high frame rate shave real milliseconds off every duel you take as a holder.

It also explains the shape of modern competitive habits. Players who hold an angle and wait, instead of wiggling in and out of it, are not just being patient; they are refusing to hand the enemy the peeker's edge for free. Players who jiggle-peek for information are deliberately exploiting the same delay. At the top level, people are playing the netcode as much as the map.

For anyone building a multiplayer game, including a Roblox game, the same principles apply at a smaller scale. Riot designed Valorant around a server that never trusts a client's view of the world, because clients can be modified by cheaters. Roblox's own security guidance makes the same point: let the client predict and display, but have the server check anything that matters, such as damage, currency or a record-setting launch height. Keep your own character's movement responsive locally, and accept that everyone else on the screen is always slightly in the past.

The first-person shooter's history looks like a march of better graphics and bigger maps. Underneath, it is thirty years of engineers arguing with physics over a few dozen milliseconds, and of designers learning to make that argument feel fair. The next time a duel goes the wrong way, it is worth remembering that you and your opponent were never really looking at the same moment.

takeaways: Every online player sees a slightly different past. Netcode decides whose version of events counts.
Doom's lockstep model ran at 35 tics a second for up to four players but could only go as fast as the slowest link.
QuakeWorld's client-side prediction made your own movement feel instant; Valve's server rewind made what you see what you hit.
Riot estimated a ~141 ms baseline peeker's advantage and cut it to ~71 ms at 144 FPS with 128-tick servers and low ping.
For your own games: predict on the client for feel, but let the server decide anything that matters.

title: The Game Is Secretly Cheating for You
dek: Why some games feel incredible in your hands and others feel like steering a shopping cart, and the invisible tricks designers use to close the gap.

blocks.text: Run toward the edge of a cliff in *Celeste*, the brutally hard 2018 platformer, and press jump a split second too late. By the strict logic of physics you should already be falling. You jump anyway. You probably never noticed, and you were never supposed to.

In March 2020, Celeste's co-creator Maddy Thorson posted a list of the quiet tricks hidden in the game's movement. One was that very jump, a trick designers call **coyote time**, after the cartoon coyote who keeps running in midair until he looks down. Another was **jump buffering**: press jump a moment *before* you land and the game remembers, firing the jump on the first frame you touch ground. Bonk your head on the corner of a ledge and the game nudges you sideways so you slide past. Dash into a corner and it pops you up onto the platform instead of stopping you dead.

Thorson's point was that a game this hard only feels fair because it keeps tilting close calls in your favor. Players believe they are being precise. Often, the code is being generous. That gap, between what really happened and what the player feels happened, is what designers mean by game feel.
What game feel actually is

Designer Steve Swink wrote the book on this, literally. In *Game Feel* (2008) he described it as the experience of controlling something in real time inside a simulated space, with polish that makes the interactions vivid. All three parts matter. Real-time control means your input and the response form a tight loop. Simulated space means the thing you control bumps into walls, lands on floors and reacts to forces. Polish is everything layered on top so your senses believe it.

The first ingredient, responsiveness, is the least glamorous and the most important. If there is a noticeable lag between pressing a button and seeing the result, nothing else can save the feel. The control stops feeling like your hand and starts feeling like a request you have submitted. Competitive players know this in their bones, and research backs them up.

In a 2021 study, researchers at Worcester Polytechnic Institute and Intel had 43 experienced *Counter-Strike: Global Offensive* players play with different amounts of delay added between their mouse and the screen, from a total of about 25 to 125 milliseconds. Accuracy and score fell steadily as delay rose.

items.label: Experienced CS:GO players tested with added local delay
Accuracy lost per extra 100 ms of local latency
Score points lost per extra 100 ms

blocks.source: Liu, Claypool et al., EHPHCI '21 (ACM), 2021

blocks.text: Six percentage points may not sound dramatic, but these players' accuracy averaged under 18 percent, so a swing that size is a big chunk of their skill. The same paper found the relationship was remarkably close to a straight line: less delay meant better aim at every step they tested.

Feel also lives in numbers most players never see. Take the humble jump. In many well-loved platformers, gravity is stronger on the way down than on the way up, so a jump rises with a floaty arc and drops quickly and decisively. Letting go of the button early cuts the jump short, so a tap gives a hop and a hold gives a full leap. Characters speed up and slow down along curves instead of starting and stopping instantly. Each of these is a tuning choice, and small changes produce surprisingly different personalities: heavy, slippery, snappy, floaty.

Swink's book makes the point by comparing classic games that share almost nothing except a well-tuned feel. A spaceship that drifts on momentum and a plumber who skids when he turns are both satisfying, because their behavior is consistent and readable. Players adapt to almost any physics as long as it stays the same. What they hate is physics that seems to change its mind.
Juice: making every action feel loud

Responsiveness makes a game controllable. **Juice** makes it feel alive. The term was popularized in a 2012 talk called *Juice It or Lose It*, where indie developers Martin Jonasson and Petri Purho took a plain Breakout clone and, without changing a single rule, piled on effects: blocks that wobbled when hit, a ball that squashed on impact, particles, sound for everything, a screen that shook. The game went from forgettable to something people wanted to keep playing, and the rules never changed.

A year later, Jan Willem Nijman of the studio Vlambeer gave a talk called *The Art of Screenshake*, where he did the same to a bare-bones shooter, adding one effect at a time until it felt powerful. Developers have been passing both talks around ever since. The common toolkit looks something like this:

items: **Hit stop:** freeze the action for a few frames when a big hit lands, so the impact registers.
**Screen shake and camera kick:** move the camera in response to recoil, explosions and heavy landings.
**Squash and stretch:** deform characters and objects when they jump, land or get hit, borrowed straight from classic animation.
**Particles and debris:** dust on landing, sparks on impact, shells ejecting from a gun.
**Layered sound:** a crunchy hit sound with a deep thump underneath beats a single clean effect.
**Anticipation and follow-through:** a short wind-up before an action and a settle afterward, so motion has weight.

blocks.text: Every one of those tricks is a form of feedback. They tell your brain, instantly and through several senses at once, that your action mattered. That's why juice is not just decoration. A hit with no reaction feels like it might not have counted. A hit with a freeze-frame, a flash, a crunch and a little shake feels like it obviously did.

Shooters lean on the same idea, tuned for information. Hit markers, a distinct headshot sound and a kill confirmation tell you instantly what your shot did, so you can decide whether to keep firing or reposition without checking a single number. Apex Legends goes a step further and colors its damage numbers by the armor tier of the enemy you are hitting, so even your feedback is telling you how much fight they have left. Good juice in a competitive game is really a fast, wordless information channel.
Too much juice is a real failure

Can you overdo it? Yes, and researchers have started to measure it. Academic work on juice is young: a 2019 paper at the CHI PLAY conference, titled simply *Juicy Game Design*, was one of the first attempts to test how these embellishments change player experience under controlled conditions. In a 2020 study published in *Entertainment Computing*, game researcher Dominic Kao built four versions of the same action role-playing game that differed only in how much visual and audio feedback they had: none, medium, high and extreme. Players in the medium and high versions came out ahead of both the no-juice and the extreme-juice versions on every measure he tracked.

That shape, a rise and then a fall, makes sense once you think of juice as feedback. With none, players can't tell what is happening. With a reasonable amount, every action reads clearly and feels satisfying. With extreme amounts, the effects become noise: the screen shakes so much you lose track of enemies, particles hide the information you need, and constant explosions stop meaning anything. In a competitive shooter, too much shake would actually make you worse at the game.
Juice should make information louder, never bury it. If an effect hides something the player needs to see, cut it or tone it down.
The invisible half: forgiveness

Back to Celeste's hidden tricks. They are the other half of game feel, and they solve a problem players never consciously notice. Human timing is sloppy. You think you pressed jump at the edge, but you were a few frames late. You think you landed and then pressed jump, but you pressed it slightly early. A game that enforces perfect timing feels unresponsive even when it is technically correct, because it ignores what you *meant* to do.

I jumped the moment I landed
I barely cleared that ledge
My dash just made it onto the platform

right.head: What actually happened
items: You were already off the ledge; coyote time let you jump
You pressed early; the game buffered the input
Your head clipped the corner; the game nudged you past
You were short; corner correction popped you up

blocks.text: Celeste's list also included smaller touches. Holding jump at the top of an arc halves gravity for a moment, giving you a little extra hang time to adjust. Wall jumps work from a couple of pixels away from the wall, not only when you are touching it. Jumping off a moving platform adds its momentum, and the game keeps that bonus for a few frames after the platform stops, in case your timing was a hair late.

None of these tricks makes the game easier in the way players complain about. Celeste is still famously hard. What they do is make sure that when you fail, it is because of a real mistake rather than a frame you could not feel. That is what earns the player's trust, and a player who trusts the controls will attempt something hard fifty times without blaming the game.

Competitive shooters work on the same principle with different tools. Many use a bit of lag compensation so that a shot that looked like a hit on your screen counts as a hit, even though the target had technically moved a few milliseconds earlier on the server. Exactly how generous to be is a balancing act, since it can make the player being shot feel cheated. The goal is always the same: honor what the player intended.
A game feel pass for your own project

Game feel is usually something you add in focused passes once the core is working, rather than something you design on paper. For a Roblox game, the biggest single rule is to give feedback on the player's own device immediately, and let the server confirm afterward. If a player presses launch on a pole vault or swings a weapon and waits for a round trip to the server before seeing anything, the game will feel mushy no matter how good the art is.

blocks.title: A practical juice pass, in order
items: Fix responsiveness first: make sure every input shows a visible reaction on the same frame, on the player's own device.
Add forgiveness: coyote time on ledges, input buffering on landings and a little corner correction.
Give each big action an anticipation, an impact and a settle.
Layer feedback for the most important moments: sound, particles, a brief camera kick, maybe a tiny hit stop.
Playtest, then cut any effect that hides information or gets annoying after the hundredth time.

blocks.text: Start with the action players do most often, because they will feel its quality thousands of times. For a launcher game that is the launch and the landing: a short squash before takeoff, a whoosh and a slight field-of-view widening as speed builds, a thud and a puff of dust on landing. For a card game it is drawing and playing a card: a snap, a slide, a satisfying flip, enemies that flinch when hit.

Two cheap tests help. First, the gray-box test: strip out the art and play with plain blocks. If the movement is still fun to mess around with for a few minutes, with no goal at all, the foundation is solid. Second, the side-by-side test: pick a game whose controls you love, play it for five minutes, then immediately play yours. The differences jump out in a way they never do when you only play your own build, because your hands have quietly adapted to its flaws.

It also helps to keep every feel value in one place, like a single settings module for gravity, jump power, coyote time and shake strength, so you can tweak them quickly during a playtest instead of hunting through scripts. Feel is tuned by iteration, and fast iteration is the whole game.

Then, the hardest skill of all: restraint. Record a clip of your game and watch it with fresh eyes. If you can't tell what's happening, there is too much. If nothing seems to react to the player, there is too little. Somewhere between those two is the version that just feels *right*, and players will never be able to tell you why.

takeaways: Game feel starts with responsiveness: if input lags, no amount of polish can save it.
Juice is feedback, not decoration. Effects should make the result of an action instantly obvious.
More juice is not always better: in a controlled study, medium and high juice beat both none and extreme.
Hidden forgiveness like coyote time and input buffering makes hard games feel fair by honoring what players meant.
In online games, react on the player's own device right away and let the server confirm afterward.

title: Forty-Eight Hours to Make a Game
dek: Thousands of people now build complete games in a weekend. The constraints that sound crazy are exactly why it works, and why a jam might teach you more than a year on one big project.

blocks.text: In 2017, a Finnish developer named Arvi Teikari sat down at the Nordic Game Jam with a theme, a deadline and not much else. The game he made in that sprint was a strange little puzzle prototype in which the rules of each level were written as word blocks on the floor, and you could push the words around to change the rules. Want to walk through walls?

Break the sentence that says WALL IS STOP. It won the jam. Two years later, in March 2019, the finished version, *Baba Is You*, launched on Steam and became one of the most celebrated puzzle games of its generation.

Stories like that are why game jams have exploded. A jam is an event where people build a game from scratch in a fixed, short window, usually 48 to 72 hours, often around a theme announced at the start. No pitch meetings, no feature creep, no endless polishing.

Just a clock, an idea and a hard stop. It sounds like a recipe for junk. In practice it is one of the best training grounds in game development, and a surprisingly good way to find out whether an idea is any good.
How a jam works
The format varies, but the core is consistent. The theme is revealed at a set time, so no one can start early. Participants brainstorm, pick an idea and build until the deadline.

Then they submit, and other participants play and rate each other's games. The rating period matters as much as the building. Instead of shouting a game into the void, jammers get feedback from hundreds of people who just went through the same ordeal.

Ludum Dare, one of the oldest online jams, has two tracks. The Compo is the hardcore version: 48 hours, solo, and you must create all of the game's content yourself. The Jam is more relaxed: 72 hours, teams allowed. Global Game Jam takes a different approach, gathering people at physical sites around the world for the same weekend. A 2019 study of the event reported that the 2017 edition had 36,401 registered participants at 701 sites in 95 countries, who together built 7,263 games in two days.

items.label: Registered participants at Global Game Jam 2017
Countries with jam sites that year
Games made over the weekend

blocks.source: Borg et al., IEEE Transactions on Games (arXiv 2019), citing Global Game Jam data

blocks.text: Themes are deliberately short and open. Ludum Dare picks its themes through rounds of community voting, and past winners give a feel for the style: 'A Small World,' 'Running out of space,' 'Limited Space,' 'Collector.' A good theme is broad enough that a thousand people can interpret it a thousand ways, and specific enough to knock everyone out of their usual habits. Part of the fun of the rating period is seeing how many different games grew from the same two or three words.

Online jams have grown even faster. The GMTK Game Jam, run by the Game Maker's Toolkit YouTube channel, started in 2017 with a theme taken from one of its videos, 'Downwell's Dual Purpose Design.' It drew 722 entries. By 2025 it was pulling in more than 9,500, and the 2026 edition passed 10,000. The 2024 theme, 'Built to Scale,' produced 7,511 games in a single long weekend.

blocks.title: GMTK Game Jam entries per year
blocks.note: Entry counts as shown on each year's itch.io jam page.
blocks.source: itch.io jam pages, GMTK Game Jam 2017-2025

blocks.text: Not every jam grew. Ludum Dare's own stats show a different arc. Its April 2020 event, which landed during the first pandemic lockdowns with the theme 'Keep it alive,' was a huge spike.
Since then submissions have fallen well below their earlier levels, even as newer jams hosted on itch.io and tied to big creator communities have boomed. The jam scene did not shrink. It moved.

blocks.title: Games submitted to Ludum Dare (Compo + Jam + other)
blocks.note: Total games per event from Ludum Dare's public stats API.
blocks.source: Ludum Dare API (api.ldjam.com) event stats

blocks.text: Why tiny deadlines work
The obvious objection is that nothing good can be made in two days. That misunderstands what a jam is for. You are not making a finished product.
You are making the smallest playable version of one idea, and then finding out whether it is fun. Most big projects can go a year without answering that question. A jam answers it by Sunday night.

The constraints each solve a specific problem. The theme kills the blank page and pushes everyone toward ideas they would not have chosen on their own. The deadline kills perfectionism, because there is no time to rewrite the movement code a fourth time. The tiny scope forces you to find the core of your idea, the one mechanic that makes it interesting, and cut everything else. And the public rating forces you to ship, which is the step that most hobby projects never reach.

Interpreting the theme is itself a design skill. Take 'Keep it alive.' The obvious reading is a pet or a plant you have to tend. Less obvious readings might be a fire you keep lit while exploring a cave, a conversation you must not let die, or a song that stops if the player stops moving. Experienced jammers often throw out their first three ideas, because everyone else will have those ideas too. The fourth or fifth is where the surprising games come from.

Scope is where most first-time jammers stumble. The classic mistake is planning a game with ten enemy types, three levels and a story, then running out of time with none of it working. A better plan is one mechanic, one screen and one goal, with a written list of 'nice to have' features you only touch if the core is finished early. In practice, that list almost never gets touched, and that is fine. A small game that works beats a big game that doesn't.

blocks.title: Big project vs. jam project

left.head: The year-long project
items: Starts with a huge feature list
Core fun is assumed, not tested
Easy to keep polishing forever
Feedback arrives late, if ever

right.head: The 48-hour jam
items: Starts with one theme and one mechanic
Core fun is tested in the first day
Hard deadline forces you to ship
Hundreds of players rate it within days

blocks.text: Researchers have looked at how jam teams actually work. In a survey of 198 Global Game Jam participants, Markus Borg and colleagues found that iterative group brainstorming was by far the most common way to settle on an idea, used by 76 percent of respondents. The development practices people reported most often were continuous integration (merging everyone's work constantly), building a minimum viable product, scope management, version control and quick stand-up meetings. Teams were small, typically four to six people, and decisions were usually made by discussion rather than by a single boss. Only about 5 percent described a strong leader making most of the calls.
The authors noticed something else: the habits of a good jam team closely resemble the advice given to software startups.

Build the smallest thing that works. Test it with real users fast. Cut scope ruthlessly. Talk constantly. A jam is basically a startup compressed into a weekend, which is part of why so many developers describe it as the most educational 48 hours of their year.
The goal of a jam is not a finished game. It is an answer to one question: is this idea fun? Getting that answer in two days instead of two years is the whole point.
Prototypes that grew up

*Baba Is You* is the cleanest example of a jam game that became something bigger, but it is not alone. *Superhot*, the shooter in which time moves only when you move, began as a 2013 prototype built for a week-long shooter jam before becoming a commercial hit. *Celeste*, the acclaimed platformer about climbing a mountain, grew out of *Celeste Classic*, a tiny game its creators made for the PICO-8 fantasy console.

Notice what these have in common. Each had one strong, unusual mechanic that could be understood in seconds: rules you can push, time that only moves with you, a dash that resets when you land. Jams naturally select for ideas like that, because there is no time to build anything else. The polish, the content and the story came later, on top of a core that had already proven itself in front of real players.

It is worth being honest about the odds. The vast majority of jam games are never developed further, and that is not a failure. They did their job: they taught their makers something, tested an idea and ended cleanly. A folder of finished jam games is also a better portfolio than a single unfinished epic, because it proves you can ship. The rare jam game that grows into a full release is a bonus on top of all that.

There is a lesson here for anyone who has started and scrapped several ambitious projects. Big games often die not because the team is lazy, but because the core loop was never tested before the content piled up on top of it. By the time anyone realizes the central idea isn't working, months of work are tangled around it. A jam flips that order. You test the core first, cheaply, and only invest in the ideas that survive.
The dark side of the all-nighter

Jams have a mythology of energy drinks and no sleep, and it is worth pushing back on. The Borg study ends with a direct warning about crunch, the long overtime stretches that plague the game industry. The authors pointed out that jammers voluntarily enter a 48-hour crunch because they enjoy the urgency, which is fine as a rare event. The danger is when that feeling becomes normal. They argued that jam organizers are well placed to teach the next generation of developers that crunch should be the exception, not the way games get made.

Sleep deprivation also makes you worse at exactly what a jam demands: creative problem-solving, clean code and good judgment about what to cut. Experienced jammers often treat sleep as part of the plan, not an obstacle to it. A weekend jam should be an intense sprint you recover from in a day, not a template for how to make games all the time. If a project only moves forward when you are wrecking yourself, the project needs a smaller scope, not a bigger sacrifice.
Running your own jam

You don't need an official event to get the benefits. A personal jam works almost as well, and it fits around an irregular schedule: a long weekend on leave, a few days in port, or a stretch of evenings at home. Two people can do it together, each building their own prototype on the same theme and then swapping. Here is a simple structure that works in Roblox Studio or any engine.

blocks.title: A 48-hour personal jam
items: Pick a random theme (draw a word, or reuse an old jam theme) and set a hard deadline
Spend the first hour on paper: one-sentence pitch, one core mechanic, no extras
Gray-box it: get the mechanic playable with plain blocks by the end of the first evening
Cut half your remaining ideas at the halfway point, no exceptions
Spend the last quarter on feel and clarity: feedback, sounds, a clear goal
Publish it, even privately, and get at least five people to play it
Write down what was fun and what wasn't before starting anything new

blocks.text: Roblox is well suited to this. Studio's templates let you skip setup and start on the mechanic in minutes, Team Create lets two people build in the same place at once, and you can publish an experience privately and invite a handful of friends to test it without anyone else seeing it. For a two-person team, a useful rule is that each person owns one area, for example one handles the mechanic while the other handles the level, so you are not both editing the same script at 2 a.m.

The last step is the one people skip, and it is the one that turns a weekend into a skill. Over several jams, those notes become a personal record of which kinds of ideas work for you and which don't. They are also a pipeline. If one of your jam prototypes keeps pulling people back for 'one more try,' you have found something worth building into a full game, with evidence instead of hope behind the decision.

The biggest change a jam makes is psychological. After a few of them, finishing stops feeling rare. You know you can take an idea from nothing to playable in two days, so a bad idea costs you a weekend instead of a year. That makes it much easier to try bold things, drop the ones that don't work, and commit fully to the one that does.

takeaways: A jam's real product is an answer: is this one mechanic fun? You get it in days instead of months.
GMTK Game Jam grew from 722 entries in 2017 to over 9,500 in 2025; the jam scene has shifted toward creator-hosted itch.io events.
Successful jam teams look like tiny startups: brainstorm, build a minimum viable product, cut scope, talk constantly.
Baba Is You started as a Nordic Game Jam winner; jam hits share one strong mechanic understandable in seconds.
Run personal jams on leave or in port, protect your sleep and always write down what you learned.

title: The Tall Pointy Thing: How Levels Guide You Without Signs
dek: You think you chose where to go. A designer put a castle, a light, a color or a triangle exactly where it would make you choose it.

blocks.text: Walk through the gates of Disneyland and you're on Main Street, a long avenue of shops. Nobody tells you where to go. There's no arrow on the ground, no sign saying 'the fun is this way.' But almost everyone walks the same direction, toward the far end of the street, because standing at the end of it is a castle.

Walt Disney had a word for that castle. He called it a **wienie**, after the hot dog an animal trainer holds up to get a dog to move where they want. A wienie is a tall, visible, interesting thing that pulls people toward it without a word of instruction. Disneyland is full of them, and so is nearly every good video game level you've ever played.

Level design is often described as building spaces. A better description is persuasion. The player has a controller and free will. Your job is to make the place you want them to go feel like the place they want to go, using nothing but what they can see and hear. When it works, players never notice. They just feel smart.
Landmarks: the tall pointy thing

Game designer Stephen Clarke-Willson, who once worked at Disneyland and wrote an essay applying its layout to games, boiled the idea down to a phrase. His shorthand for a quick wienie: a tall pointy thing. A landmark you can see from far away does three jobs at once. It gives the player a goal, it gives them a way to orient themselves, and it promises that something worth seeing waits there.

You've seen this everywhere. In *Ocarina of Time*, Death Mountain looms over Hyrule with a ring of smoke at its peak, practically daring you to climb it. In *Journey*, a glowing mountain sits on the horizon from the very first scene, and the whole game is the walk toward it. In *Breath of the Wild*, Nintendo's team made the most important structures the tallest, so that importance and height became the same thing in the player's mind.

The opposite tool matters too. Clarke-Willson calls it the **anti-wienie**: a deliberately dull feature that tells people there's nothing to see. At Disneyland, backstage doors are small and plain, the opposite of a castle. In games, a dark, unremarkable side passage quietly tells you it's a dead end. Good levels are a map of things that pull and things that push away, and the player follows the gradient without thinking about it.
The first test of any level: stand where the player starts and look around. What's the most interesting thing you can see? If it isn't where you want them to go, they'll go somewhere else.
Light, color and the yellow paint war

Up close, landmarks are too big to help. You need smaller signals, and the two strongest are light and color. People drift toward brightness. A lit doorway in a dark hall, a beam of sun through a gap in a cave or a glowing object on a ledge will draw players far more reliably than any text prompt. Horror games use the reverse, making the way forward dark so that moving ahead feels like a choice made against instinct.

Sound is the signal people forget. Clarke-Willson points out that Disneyland's log flume announces itself with the crash of boats hitting water long before you can see it. Games do the same with a distant waterfall, music leaking from a doorway, or enemies talking around a corner. Sound works through walls and behind the player's back, which makes it perfect for pulling attention toward something the camera isn't pointed at yet.

Color works by building a language. *Mirror's Edge* (2008) painted the city mostly white and highlighted pipes, ramps and doors you could use in red. Its 2016 sequel kept the rule, summed up by its developers as 'follow the red,' and let players choose how much guidance to see, from off to a full red trail. Many games since, from *Uncharted* onward, mark climbable ledges with paint, wear or bright edges. Many modern games mark climbable surfaces and breakable crates with bright yellow.

That last habit blew up online in March 2023, when the *Resident Evil 4* remake's demo arrived with yellow-marked crates in its opening village. Plenty of players complained that the marks were too obvious and insulted their intelligence. Developers pushed back. Graphics programmer Ben Golus explained how hard it is to make interactive objects stand out in detailed modern scenes, where everything is lit and textured realistically. The original *Resident Evil 4* from 2005 made breakable objects stand out partly because they were rendered differently from the scenery; the remake swapped that for a contrasting color.

The debate never really ended, and that's because both sides are right about something. Obvious markers do break immersion for experienced players. But designers who watch real playtests routinely describe players walking right past the one ladder they need. The best answers tend to be consistent and optional: one clear color language used everywhere, taught early, and settings that let veterans turn the hints down.

blocks.title: Two ways to say 'go here'

left.head: Telling the player
items: Arrows, waypoints and text prompts
Fast and unmissable
Pulls attention to the screen edge, not the world
Players stop looking at the level itself

right.head: Showing the player
items: Landmarks, light, color and shape
Players feel they found the way themselves
Can fail if the signal is too subtle
Needs playtesting to tune

blocks.text: Triangles and gravity

The most detailed explanation of how a modern open world guides players came from Nintendo itself. At the CEDEC developer conference in 2017, *Breath of the Wild* director Hidemaro Fujibayashi and lead artist Makoto Yonezu explained the thinking behind its landscape, and one idea spread fast: the triangle.

Hyrule is full of triangular shapes, from hills and mountains to rock formations. A triangle on the horizon offers a choice. You can climb over it or walk around it, and either path leads somewhere interesting. A triangle also hides what's behind it. As you crest a hill, the far side is revealed all at once, which turns simple walking into a series of small surprises. Big triangles hide big things; small ones hide small things.

The team also talked about **gravity**. The game's towers were the big pulls, but the first layout, with towers spread over the map, felt too obvious in testing. So the team used heat maps of where testers actually walked and where they got bored or stuck, then repositioned towers and filled the space between them with smaller points of interest, each pulling players a little deeper. The result feels like freedom, but it's freedom inside a carefully tuned field of attractions.

blocks.title: The open-world pull loop
items: See something interesting on the horizon
Head toward it
A hill or ridge hides, then reveals, the next thing
Arrive, get a reward, spot the next landmark

blocks.text: This connects to something everybody who has played *Breath of the Wild* describes: you set out for one thing and end up somewhere else entirely, three hours later. That isn't an accident. It's the gravity of many small pulls overriding a single big one. The designers didn't take away your choice. They just made sure every choice led somewhere.
Most players never see what you hide

Guidance has a flip side. If good design pulls players along the main path, anything off that path is, by definition, easy to miss. Steam's public achievement data makes this visible. Here's *Portal 2*, one of the most carefully designed games ever made, comparing story achievements every player earns by progressing with achievements for finding hidden things.

blocks.title: Portal 2: share of Steam owners with each achievement
blocks.note: Percent of all Steam owners, including people who never played far. The first two come from simply progressing.
blocks.source: Steam global achievement statistics for Portal 2 (app 620), retrieved Nov 2026

blocks.text: Only about a third of owners finished the single-player story. The hidden portrait was found by roughly a third as many people as finished, and the signal tucked into one of the secret dens by about one in six as many. Those secrets were designed to be quiet, for the curious few. That's fine. Secrets are a reward for players who poke at the edges, and the thrill of finding one depends on most people missing it.

The original *Portal* shows the same pattern. About 52% of Steam owners have the achievement for completing it, but only 4.4% have the one for tracking down all of its hidden radios. A game can be famous for its flawless guidance and still have almost everyone walk straight past the things it doesn't point at.

The danger is mixing the two up. If something *required* to progress is guided as quietly as a secret, a large share of players will get stuck, and many won't come back. The rule many designers follow: the critical path should be impossible to miss, and the secrets should be impossible to find by accident. Most frustration in levels comes from breaking the first half of that rule.
Shapes that steer: lines, funnels and loops

Beyond landmarks and color, the shape of a space does a lot of quiet work. **Leading lines**, like a road, a cable, a row of lamps or a crack in a wall, pull the eye in a direction, and the feet follow the eye. A narrowing corridor speeds people up; a wide room with a view slows them down and invites them to look around. Designers use those rhythms to pace a level, alternating tight action with open spaces to breathe.

Collectibles double as guidance, too. Mario games have long laid out coins in arcs that trace the exact jump you should make, and in lines that lead toward a hidden pipe. Players think they're grabbing coins. They're actually being taught a path. For any game about launching or vaulting, a trail of pickups through the air is one of the clearest, least preachy ways to show where a great jump goes.

Some of the most satisfying guidance happens after the fact. *Dark Souls* is famous for long, winding areas that end at a door you can open from one side, revealing a shortcut back to a place you passed an hour ago. The level guides you outward, then folds back on itself, so the world clicks together in your head like a map you built yourself. Players remember those moments for years.

Then there's the problem of edges. Every level has a boundary, and invisible walls feel cheap. Disneyland hides its edges with trees, berms and distant scenery that suggest the world keeps going. Games do the same with cliffs, water, dense forest and mountains that look climbable but aren't marked as such. A boundary that looks natural keeps players inside the illusion.
A wayfinding pass for your own map

For a Roblox obby or adventure map built around a launching mechanic, all of this is directly usable. A launcher gives players speed and height, which means they'll see far and move fast. That raises the stakes on landmarks, because a player who's flying needs something on the horizon to aim at, and lowers the value of small signs, because nobody reads text in mid-air.

blocks.title: A wayfinding pass for any level
items: Place one big landmark visible from spawn that marks the next goal.
Pick a color language, such as one color for launch points and another for safe landings, and never break it.
Use light and leading lines to point toward the critical path.
Hide secrets behind ridges, under ledges and off the obvious line, where only the curious will look.
Watch a friend play with zero instructions and note every place they hesitate.
Log player positions and deaths to build a simple heat map, then fix the cold and crowded spots.

blocks.text: If players can vault from anywhere, the level's job shifts from telling them *where* to jump to making good jumps look inviting. A platform that's slightly brighter, a ring floating in the air, a tall structure in the distance with a visible landing zone: each one says 'try this' without saying anything. The freedom stays, but the best options rise to the top.

The deepest idea in all of this is about respect. Walt Disney didn't put up signs saying 'castle this way' because the castle was the sign. The best levels trust players to read the world, and then quietly make sure the world is easy to read. When a player finishes your map and says it felt natural, that's not a sign you did nothing. It's a sign you did your job so well they never saw you do it.

takeaways: A wienie is a tall, visible landmark that pulls players toward a goal without instructions. Start every level by checking what's most visible from spawn.
Light and color are the strongest small-scale signals; build one consistent color language and keep it.
Breath of the Wild used triangles to hide and reveal, and heat maps from playtests to place its 'gravity' points.
Most players miss hidden content. Make the critical path impossible to miss and secrets impossible to find by accident.
Test with someone who gets zero instructions, and log where players go to find your cold spots.
