title: The Slot Machine With a Sword Inside
dek: Loot boxes and gacha pulls made billions. Then regulators and researchers started asking whether they were gambling. Here is what they found, and what it means if you build a game.

blocks.text: In November 2017, Electronic Arts was days away from launching *Star Wars Battlefront II*, one of the biggest releases of the year. Then players got a look at how progression worked. Much of it ran through loot boxes: randomized crates you could earn slowly or buy with real money, which could contain items that made your character stronger.
The backlash was enormous. EA pulled the paid loot boxes shortly before launch. But the argument it had started did not go away.

A few months later, in April 2018, the Belgian Gaming Commission published a report that landed like a grenade. It examined four big games and concluded that the paid loot boxes in three of them, *Overwatch*, *FIFA 18* and *Counter-Strike: Global Offensive*, met every element of gambling under Belgian law. Companies that kept offering them, the report warned, risked prison sentences of up to five years and fines of up to 800,000 euros for a first offense, with penalties that could double if minors were involved.

Since then, researchers have collected years of data and regulators around the world have tried very different approaches. The story is messier than either 'loot boxes are evil' or 'it's just a game.' And if you are building a game on Roblox, the rules already reach you.
What makes something gambling

The Belgian report laid out a simple test. Gambling needs four things: a game, a wager (you put up something of value), chance (the outcome is random), and a win or loss. Paid loot boxes, the commission argued, check every box. You pay money, you can't control what comes out, and you either get the item you wanted or you don't. The report also noted that the industry's own age rating system, PEGI, did not systematically check whether games let players spend real money on chance.

Some of the commission's sharpest concerns were about kids. It worried that children who grow up experiencing wins and losses tied to money inside games learn to treat gambling as normal. It noted that anyone with an account could make payments without age checks, so a 13-year-old could buy loot boxes in a game rated for 16 and up. And it flagged the possibility that companies could tune random outcomes based on player behavior data, which would undercut the idea that the odds are even fixed.

Not every country agreed. In the Netherlands, the gambling regulator pursued EA over packs in its FIFA games, but the country's highest administrative court ultimately sided with EA, finding the packs did not fall under Dutch gambling law. Much of the legal fight hinges on one question: do the prizes have real-world monetary value? Belgian law does not require that. Most countries' laws do, which is why loot boxes escape gambling rules in most places.

blocks.title: Loot boxes on trial
items: Star Wars Battlefront II backlash; EA removes paid loot boxes before launch
Belgian Gaming Commission says paid loot boxes in three major games are illegal gambling
Zendle and Cairns survey of 7,422 gamers links loot box spending to problem gambling
Follow-up studies replicate the link and find it stronger in 16- to 18-year-olds
FTC reaches $520 million in settlements with Epic Games over Fortnite
Study finds most top-grossing iPhone games in Belgium still sell random paid items
South Korea begins requiring loot box odds disclosure by law
Brazil bans paid loot boxes in games accessible to minors

blocks.text: What the research found

The study that shaped the debate came from David Zendle and Paul Cairns, published in *PLOS ONE* in 2018. They surveyed 7,422 gamers about how much they spent on loot boxes and screened them for problem gambling. The more people spent on loot boxes, the more severe their problem gambling tended to be. Crucially, spending on *other* in-game items with real money showed only a tiny link. Something about the random, gambling-like structure of loot boxes seemed to be doing the work.

Critics pointed out that people who volunteer for a loot box study might not be typical. So in 2019, Zendle and Cairns ran it again with 1,172 gamers who didn't know what the study was about. The link came back at almost exactly the same strength. A separate 2019 study by Zendle, Rachel Meyer and Harriet Over surveyed 1,155 people aged 16 to 18 and found the relationship was stronger in these older adolescents than in adults.

blocks.title: How much of problem-gambling variation tracks spending
blocks.note: Effect sizes (eta squared) converted to percent. Higher means spending and problem gambling move together more strongly.
blocks.source: Zendle & Cairns, PLOS ONE, 2018 and 2019; Zendle, Meyer & Over, Royal Society Open Science, 2019

blocks.text: How big is that? An effect of about 5 percent of variance is meaningful but far from the whole story: most of the differences in people's gambling problems come from other things. The adolescent figure of 12 percent is the kind of number the authors described as moderate to large. These are correlations, not proof of cause.

The researchers were careful to name both possibilities. Loot boxes might act as a gateway that pushes some players toward gambling problems. Or people who already have gambling problems might be drawn to spend heavily on loot boxes. Either way, the authors argued, there was good reason to regulate.

It is worth being clear about the limits. Nearly all of this evidence comes from surveys that capture people at one moment and rely on them to report their own spending. That design can show that two things go together, but not which came first. Following the same players over years would answer the gateway question far better, and that kind of data is mostly locked inside game companies. Still, the basic link has now shown up across many samples and research groups, which is why it is taken seriously even by researchers who disagree about what to do.
Who actually pays

That second possibility points to a question about where the money comes from. Most players spend little or nothing on loot boxes. The revenue is driven by a small group of heavy spenders that the industry calls whales. In 2021, James Close and colleagues pooled open survey data from 7,767 loot box buyers to look at who those whales are.

items.label: Spenders (over $100 a month) who accounted for about half of loot box revenue
Correlation between loot box spending and problem gambling
Correlation between loot box spending and earnings (not significant)

blocks.source: Close et al., Addictive Behaviors, 2021

blocks.text: The middle and right numbers are the important ones. If whales were simply wealthy players treating themselves, spending would rise with income. It didn't.

Spending tracked problem gambling instead. In this self-reported data, the biggest spenders looked less like rich enthusiasts and more like people struggling to control their spending. Close and colleagues concluded that developers, knowingly or not, were profiting disproportionately from moderate- and high-risk gamblers rather than from high earners, a pattern that mirrors how gambling revenue works.
If half the revenue from a feature comes from the 5 percent of players least able to control their spending, that is not a side effect. That is the business model.
What regulators actually did

Regulation has taken three broad forms, and none has worked perfectly. The first is the outright ban, Belgium's approach. In 2023, legal researcher Leon Xiao checked the 100 highest-grossing iPhone games in Belgium years after the ban.

He found that 82 percent still made money through randomized paid features, including about 80 percent of the games rated suitable for ages 12 and up. The ban had changed the behavior of some big, well-known companies, but it was not being enforced across the market. Xiao warned that an unenforced ban carries its own costs, including giving consumers, parents and policymakers a false sense of security.

The second approach is mandatory odds disclosure: you can sell random items, but you must tell players the exact chances. China adopted this as law first. Researchers comparing compliance found that legally required disclosure in China was followed far more consistently than voluntary industry self-regulation in the UK.

South Korea began requiring disclosure by law in 2024. The third approach is age-based restriction. In 2025, Brazil's Digital Child and Adolescent Act banned paid loot boxes in games accessible to minors, framing it as child protection rather than gambling law.

In the United States, the most dramatic action came from a different angle. In December 2022, Epic Games agreed to pay $520 million in settlements with the Federal Trade Commission over *Fortnite*. That included a $275 million penalty for violating children's privacy law by collecting data from kids under 13 without notifying parents, and $245 million in refunds over what the FTC called dark patterns: confusing button layouts and billing practices that led players to make purchases they didn't intend. The case was not about loot boxes as such. It was about the whole purchase flow, and it showed regulators were willing to treat manipulative store design as a serious violation.
Gacha, pity and the rules on Roblox

Gacha games, named after Japanese capsule toy machines, take the loot box idea further. Characters or gear come from paid pulls with published rarity rates, and many games add a 'pity' system that guarantees a rare result after a certain number of failed pulls. Pity sounds generous, and it does cap the worst case. But it also gives players a target number to chase, and it turns 'I'll try a few pulls' into 'I'm only twenty away from guaranteed.'

Roblox's own rules treat all of this as paid random items. Its creator policy covers prize wheels, egg hatches, chests, random upgrades, combinations of items for a better roll, and probability modifiers such as luck boosts and pity systems, whenever they are bought with Robux or with in-game currency bought with Robux. If you offer them, you must show every possible outcome and its numerical odds as percentages that add up to 100, before purchase. If there are too many outcomes to display, a list behind a clearly labeled 'Info' or 'Details' button is acceptable, but a bare (i) icon is not. If a player buys a lucky potion, the game must show the updated odds while it is active.

Roblox also lets developers check, player by player, whether paid random items are restricted for that user. For restricted players, creators must either offer a free, earnable path to the item, show a fixed and disclosed sequence of outcomes, sell the item directly, or remove or block the random purchase. The policy's own example is quietly revealing: if a loot box costs 10 Robux and has a 5 percent chance of a rare sword, the direct price for restricted users should be 200 Robux. That is the sword's real expected cost, and it is the number a random box hides.

blocks.title: Roblox's options for players who can't buy paid random items
items: Offer a free, earnable path, like eggs granted at gameplay milestones
Use a fixed sequence of outcomes disclosed before purchase
Sell the specific item directly, priced around its expected value
Remove or hide the random purchase, or block it with a message
Move the player away from areas built around paid random items

blocks.text: Building a game you'd defend

Random rewards are not the problem in themselves. Loot drops from enemies, surprise unlocks and free chests can make a game exciting, and Roblox's policy explicitly does not require odds disclosure for random rewards that cost nothing. The trouble starts when randomness meets payment, especially in front of a young audience that cannot easily judge odds or set limits. Roblox's audience is young. That raises the bar for anyone building there.

items: **Sell things, not chances.** A pole skin for 99 Robux is honest. A 5 percent shot at it for 10 Robux is the same price on average, with a gambler's experience attached.
**Keep randomness free.** Use random drops for earned rewards, where surprise adds fun and nobody loses money.
**If you sell random items, over-disclose.** Show the odds on the purchase screen, not behind a menu. Show the expected cost of the rare item.
**Don't design for whales.** If your revenue model only works because a few players spend without limit, rethink it before launch.
**Use the parent test.** Imagine a parent watching their 11-year-old go through your store. If you'd feel the need to explain anything, change it.

blocks.text: The loot box era is a lesson in how a design choice that looks small, putting a price on a random roll, can grow into a legal and ethical fight across dozens of countries. For a small developer, the takeaway is freeing. You don't need slot machine mechanics to make money. Selling good things directly, at fair prices, to players who feel respected is a business you never have to defend.

takeaways: Belgium's 2018 report found paid loot boxes in Overwatch, FIFA 18 and CS:GO met every legal element of gambling.
Large surveys repeatedly link loot box spending to problem gambling, more strongly than other in-game spending and more strongly in teens.
The top 5 percent of spenders produce about half of loot box revenue, and their spending tracks problem gambling, not income.
Bans without enforcement, odds disclosure and age limits have all been tried; Roblox already requires full odds disclosure for paid random items.
For your own game: sell items directly, keep randomness free and show the true expected cost of anything random.

title: Who Picks Your Opponents?
dek: Matchmaking looks like a lobby timer, but underneath it is a prediction machine, and a 2017 paper asked whether it should aim for fair games or for keeping you playing.

blocks.text: You lose five ranked games in a row and the thought arrives, as it does for everyone: this is rigged. The game is feeding you bad teammates on purpose. Most players say it half as a joke.

But in 2017, a team of researchers working with Electronic Arts published a paper that took the idea seriously from the other side. What if a matchmaker *did* choose your opponents based on your recent streak? Not to punish you, but to keep you from quitting?

Their answer was that it could, that it would work, and that the 'fair match' every player assumes they are getting is not always what keeps players around. That paper sits at the end of a long story that starts with chess, runs through Xbox Live, and lands in every Roblox server you join. Understanding it changes how you see your own losing streaks, and how you would build matchmaking for a game of your own.
A rating is a prediction

The modern idea of a skill rating comes from Arpad Elo, a physics professor and chess master whose system was adopted by chess federations in the 1960s and 1970s. The key insight is that a rating is not a trophy. It is a forecast.

The gap between two players' ratings predicts how often each should win. If you beat someone the system expected you to beat, your rating barely moves. If you beat someone far above you, it jumps, because the system just learned it was wrong about you.

Elo's formula turns rating differences into expected scores. A 100-point edge means you are expected to score about 64 percent against that opponent. At 400 points, it is about 91 percent, roughly ten to one. The curve flattens quickly, which is why huge rating gaps produce games that are almost foregone conclusions.

blocks.title: Expected score for the higher-rated player (Elo)
blocks.note: Values calculated from the Elo expected-score formula, 1 / (1 + 10^(-gap/400)).
blocks.source: Calculated from Elo's expected-score formula

blocks.text: That framing explains why a good matchmaker feels invisible. If it pairs you with someone at the same rating, the prediction is a coin flip. Coin flips are exciting. You can win, you can lose, and your decisions decide which. A rating system's real job is to manufacture coin flips.
This also explains the rigged feeling. If the matchmaker is doing its job perfectly and every game is a true coin flip, losing streaks are not a sign of sabotage. They are guaranteed.

A quick calculation shows that a player who wins exactly half their games has about an 81 percent chance of hitting at least one streak of five straight losses somewhere in 100 games. Your brain notices the streak and goes looking for a villain. Usually the villain is probability.
Elo had a blind spot, though. It treats every rating as equally certain. A brand-new player and a veteran with ten thousand games both sit at a single number.

In 1999, the statistician Mark Glickman published a model that also tracked how *uncertain* the system was about each player's skill, an idea he built into his Glicko system. A new player's rating should move a lot after each game, because the system knows very little. A veteran's should barely budge.
Xbox Live and the problem of teams

Microsoft Research took that idea to online games with TrueSkill, which has rated players in Xbox Live titles from *Halo 3* to *Forza Motorsport 7*. Each player gets two numbers: an average skill estimate and an uncertainty around it. Microsoft's description is plain about the matching rule: the best opponent for you is someone you would be likely to *draw* with.

TrueSkill also exposes a problem that every team game faces. When your team wins, how much of that was you? In a free-for-all, every match tells the system a lot about you individually. In a big team match, your contribution is blended with seven teammates, so each result carries far less information about your personal skill. Microsoft published rough figures for how many games the system needs before it can pin down a player's skill, and the difference is striking.

blocks.title: Games needed for TrueSkill to identify a player's skill
blocks.note: Microsoft notes the real number can be up to three times higher depending on factors like performance variation and draw rates.
blocks.source: Microsoft Research, TrueSkill Ranking System project page

blocks.text: Ninety-one games is a long time to be mismatched. That is why so many team games feel rough in your first weeks and why a smurf, an experienced player on a fresh account, can wreck lobbies for a while before the system catches up. The fix Microsoft eventually shipped was to stop looking only at who won.

TrueSkill 2, described in a 2018 paper by Tom Minka, Ryan Cleven and Yordan Zaykov, added the information online shooters already record: kills and deaths, whether a player was in a party with friends, how experienced they were, whether they tended to quit mid-match, and their skill in other modes. Tested on *Halo 5* matches, the original TrueSkill predicted match outcomes with 52 percent accuracy, barely better than a coin. TrueSkill 2 reached 68 percent. Microsoft says the newer system launched with *Gears of War 4* and was later used in *Halo 5*, *Gears 5*, *Halo Infinite* and *Forza Motorsport*.

items.label: Classic TrueSkill's accuracy predicting Halo 5 match outcomes
TrueSkill 2's accuracy on the same task, using kills, parties, quits and experience

blocks.source: Minka, Cleven & Zaykov, TrueSkill 2 (Microsoft Research), 2018

blocks.text: Two of those added signals carry design lessons on their own. Parties matter because friends in voice chat coordinate better than strangers, so the paper models a squad as performing above its members' individual ratings. Quitting matters because a player who rage-quits shouldn't be rated as if they had simply lost, but punishing the whole team for it is unfair too. Fairness turns out to be a lot of small, careful choices about what counts.
Fair or sticky? The engagement question

Which brings us back to the 2017 paper. Zhengxing Chen and colleagues at Electronic Arts and Northeastern University called their framework EOMM, for Engagement Optimized Matchmaking. Their starting observation came from a real EA player-versus-player game. They grouped players by their last three results (win, loss or draw) and measured what share stopped playing for at least seven days after a match. The numbers varied more than you might expect.

blocks.title: Share of players who stopped playing for 7+ days, by last three results
blocks.note: The 'safest' streaks in the data, such as draw-loss-win or draw-draw-draw, sat at 2.6 to 2.7 percent. Three losses were roughly twice as risky.
blocks.source: Chen et al., EOMM, WWW 2017 (EA game data)

blocks.text: Look closely at that chart. Three straight losses was the most dangerous state, which makes sense. But three straight wins was also riskier than a mixed record.

A player on a hot streak was *more* likely to drift away than one whose results bounced around. Perfectly fair matches don't guarantee either outcome. They just make each game a coin flip and let streaks happen when they happen.

EOMM's idea was to treat matchmaking as an optimization problem: predict each player's risk of quitting after each possible pairing, then choose the pairings that keep the most people playing. The authors proved that pure equal-skill matchmaking is a special case of their framework that only comes out on top under a narrow assumption. Under some conditions, they showed, equal-skill matching could even be the *worst* option for engagement.

In their simulation, built on 36.9 million matches from 1.68 million players, EOMM retained on average 0.7 percent more players per round of matchmaking than skill-based pairing. That sounds tiny, but the authors pointed out that it compounds: over 20 rounds of play in eight hours, that edge would work out to about 15 percent more players still around. Two important caveats. This was a simulation, not a report of a live system, and the paper does not say EA shipped it. And the authors themselves noted the same machinery could optimize for other goals, including spending.
Every matchmaker is optimizing for something. 'Fair' is one choice. 'Keeps you playing' is another. 'Keeps you spending' is a third. Players rarely get told which one they are in.

This is where matchmaking meets ethics. Choosing a softer opponent after you lose three in a row could be kindness, the digital version of a coach putting you in against someone you can beat. It could also be a slot machine trick, timing a win to keep you on the hook. The math is identical. The difference is the goal, and whether players would feel cheated if they knew.
Fairness is more than skill

Skill is only one ingredient. Ask players what makes a match feel unfair and they will mention lag, queue times, stacked parties against solo players, smurfs and leavers long before they mention rating math. Every matchmaker trades these against each other.
Tighten the skill window and queues get longer. Loosen it to get people in faster and the matches get lopsided. Small player pools feel this trade-off hardest, which matters for any new game.

A newer game feels this most sharply. When only a few hundred people are online, there may simply be no one near your skill in the queue at that moment. The matchmaker then has three bad options: make you wait, give you a lopsided match, or pad the lobby with bots.

A common compromise is to start strict and widen the acceptable skill gap the longer someone waits. None of these is wrong in itself. What matters is that the designer chooses the trade-off deliberately instead of discovering it from angry reviews.

Roblox handles a version of this for every experience. Its documentation describes the flow: when a player tries to join, the system filters out servers that are full, private, reserved or about to shut down, then scores the rest using a weighted sum of signals and sends the player to the highest-scoring server. Built-in signals include things like location, latency, age group and language. Developers can adjust the weights or add custom attributes, such as a skill level stored in their own data, and preview the effect on mock servers before going live.

blocks.title: How Roblox picks a server for a joining player
items: A player requests to join your place
Servers that are full, private, reserved or shutting down are filtered out
Each remaining server gets a score from weighted signals like latency, language and custom skill attributes
The player is sent to the highest-scoring server

blocks.text: That gives even a small creator real control. If latency matters most in your game, you can weight it heavily so movement feels crisp. If you want new players grouped together, you can store a progress level as a custom attribute and favor servers with similar players. The design question comes first: what does a 'good' server mean for the experience you are trying to create?
Matchmaking lessons for your own game

Even a game that isn't head-to-head, like an obby or a launcher game, has matchmaking problems. Who is in the server shapes the experience. A brand-new player dropped into a lobby of maxed-out veterans may feel lost or outclassed. A veteran stuck with newcomers may get bored. Races, leaderboards and any player-versus-player mode raise the stakes further.

items: **Decide what you are optimizing.** Write one sentence: 'A good server is one where...' Then make your signals serve that sentence.
**Protect the first sessions.** New players are the most likely to leave. Group them with others at a similar stage where you can, so their first impression is a fair contest.
**Use more than wins.** If you rate skill, borrow TrueSkill 2's lesson and look at richer signals like clear times, heights reached or checkpoints, not just who finished first.
**Treat parties differently.** Friends playing together usually perform better than their individual stats suggest. Don't let a coordinated group farm solo players.
**Be honest about adjustments.** If you soften matches after a losing streak, consider saying so. A visible 'warm-up' or 'comeback' queue respects players more than a hidden thumb on the scale.

blocks.text: The deepest lesson from the EOMM paper is not about algorithms. It is that 'fair' was never the default. Every matchmaker reflects a choice about what its designers care about. When you build your own, you get to make that choice on purpose, and you will know what your players are actually getting when the countdown ends and the match begins.

takeaways: A skill rating is a forecast; good matchmaking turns each game into something close to a coin flip.
Team games learn your skill slowly: Microsoft estimates about 91 games for 8v8 versus 3 for a 16-player free-for-all.
Adding signals like kills, parties and quits lifted Halo 5 prediction accuracy from 52 to 68 percent.
An EA study found losing streaks and even winning streaks raised quit risk, and matchmaking tuned for engagement could beat 'fair' matching at keeping players.
Decide what your matchmaker optimizes, protect new players and be open about any adjustments.

title: The Unfinished Game That Ate the World
dek: Minecraft started as one programmer's side project with placeholder graphics. It became the best-selling video game in history by breaking almost every rule of how games were supposed to be made.

blocks.text: In May 2009, a Swedish programmer named Markus Persson posted a rough little project on an indie developer forum. It had no goal, no enemies worth mentioning, no story and no ending. You were a blocky figure in a world of blocky terrain, and you could remove blocks or place them. That was the whole thing.

Persson, who went by Notch online, had a day job at a game company and built this in his spare time. He'd been inspired by *Infiniminer*, a small mining game that had been abandoned by its creator, and he wanted to see what would happen if you added a bit more to it. The answer, sixteen years later, is the best-selling video game ever made, a franchise that has crossed a trillion views on YouTube, and a movie that pulled in more than $900 million worldwide.

The usual way to tell this story is as a lightning strike: lucky guy, right place, right time. That version is comforting, because it means there's nothing to learn. The more interesting version is that *Minecraft* won because of choices that looked like weaknesses at the time, and most of those choices are available to any small team today, including one building on Roblox.
Selling a game before it was done

The first strange decision was charging money for something obviously unfinished. Persson started selling *Minecraft* during its alpha phase, at a lower price than he planned to charge later, with a promise that anyone who bought early would get every future update for free. The price went up as the game matured. Early buyers got a discount for taking a risk; later buyers paid more for a better game.

Today this is called early access, and it's normal. In 2009 it was odd. Big studios polished games in secret for years and revealed them in a burst of marketing. Persson did the opposite. He posted constantly on his blog and on Twitter about what he was adding, asked players what they wanted, and shipped updates every few weeks. Players weren't just customers. They were watching the game get built, and many felt like they'd helped build it.

That openness had a practical side too. A solo developer can't afford a test team. Thousands of players poking at every update found bugs, invented uses for features and reported what felt boring, for free, while also paying the bills. The players became the QA department, the design committee and the marketing team at the same time.

Early access is not magic, and plenty of games have died in it, abandoned half-built after the money came in. What made it work for *Minecraft* was visible momentum. Updates kept arriving, each one added something players could feel the same day, and the developer was obviously still excited. Buyers weren't paying for a promise. They were paying to ride along with something that was clearly moving.

blocks.title: From side project to biggest game ever

blocks.text: Ugly on purpose

The second choice was the look. In an era chasing realistic graphics, *Minecraft* used chunky cubes and tiny pixel textures that were 16 by 16 pixels each. Critics called it ugly. It was also the reason one person could build an entire world.

Think about what blocks buy you as a developer. Every object in the world is made of the same unit, so the game can generate endless terrain from rules instead of hand-made art. Players can understand exactly how the world is built just by looking at it, which means they can build too. And a simple style ages slowly. A cutting-edge 2011 game looks dated now; *Minecraft* in 2011 looks basically like *Minecraft* today.

There's a lesson here for anyone building on Roblox with a blocky, stud-style art direction. A consistent, simple style isn't a compromise if it's chosen on purpose. It lets a two-person team make lots of content quickly, keeps the game readable on a cheap phone, and gives players a visual language they can build with. The failure mode is not 'too simple.' It's inconsistent, where some assets look hand-painted and others look like defaults.

Constraints that look like weaknesses can be your engine. Minecraft's blocks made procedural worlds possible, made building intuitive and made the game cheap to expand. Ask what your game's limitation makes easy.
A game you had to look up

The third choice was almost no explanation. Early *Minecraft* didn't tell you how to make a crafting table, that zombies come at night, or that you should never dig straight down. You died on your first night, confused, and then went looking for answers. The answers were on wikis, forums and above all YouTube.

This turned a weakness into a distribution machine. Every confused player became a viewer of tutorials, and every skilled player had a reason to make one. *Minecraft* videos were perfect for the platform: endlessly varied, easy to follow, safe for kids, and different every time because every world was unique. Let's Plays, building showcases, survival series and redstone computers turned the game into one of the biggest subjects on YouTube. By 2021, Xbox said Minecraft had become the first entertainment franchise to pass a trillion views there.

The day-night cycle shows how much design was hiding inside that silence. Nobody tells you to build a shelter. But the sun starts setting, the light drops, strange noises start, and suddenly you have an urgent goal you set for yourself. The game created a mission without a single line of instruction. That first frantic night of digging into a hillside is one of the most widely shared experiences in gaming, and it came from a single system, not a scripted tutorial.

Nobody at Mojang paid for that marketing. The game's design produced it. Secrets to find, stories that differ every time, and creations worth showing off are all things that make people want to record and share. That's a direct, testable question for any game: what in yours is worth filming?
Letting players build the game

The fourth choice was letting go. *Minecraft* players ran their own servers with their own rules, built minigames inside the game, and wrote mods that added everything from new machines to whole new worlds. Mojang tolerated much of this and later embraced it, with official server software, a marketplace for creators' content and features like command blocks that let players script their own adventures.

Redstone is the clearest example. It started as a simple wiring system for doors and traps. Players used it to build working logic gates, then calculators, then entire simple computers inside the game. Mojang didn't design those. It designed a system with simple rules that could be combined, and players did the rest. Good systems produce content their creators never imagined.

Multiplayer servers took the same idea further. Communities built entire games inside *Minecraft*: survival games, capture-the-flag variants, parkour maps, and team modes like Bed Wars and SkyWars, run on big minigame servers such as Hypixel. Many of those formats later spread to other platforms, including Roblox. Players weren't just playing *Minecraft*. They were using it as a game engine, years before Mojang officially treated it as one.

If this sounds like Roblox, it should. Roblox launched in 2006, before *Minecraft*, built on the idea that players make the games. *Minecraft* proved how huge the appetite was for a world you could reshape, and much of the generation that grew up on it went on to build in Roblox, Fortnite Creative and other platforms. The line between player and developer that *Minecraft* blurred is the line many young developers now cross on Roblox.
Success, then the cost of it

By the time version 1.0 launched at MineCon in Las Vegas in November 2011, the game already had millions of paying players. Persson soon handed lead development to Jens Bergensten, known as Jeb, who became the long-running face of its development. Mojang grew from a handful of friends into a real company, and the money kept coming.

The move to phones mattered just as much. *Minecraft: Pocket Edition* arrived in August 2011, first on a Sony Ericsson phone and then on iOS. It started stripped-down, but it put the game in the hands of kids who didn't own a gaming PC, on a device they already carried. Much of the generation that now plays Roblox met sandbox building on a phone or tablet first.

In September 2014, Microsoft bought Mojang for $2.5 billion. Persson and the other two founders left. In a blog post at the time he wrote, in effect, that the sale was about his sanity rather than money: he hadn't wanted to be the face of a giant franchise or to carry the expectations of millions of fans. His later public behavior and comments led Microsoft to remove most references to him from the game in 2019, an awkward footnote for a creator whose project outgrew him.

Many fans expected Microsoft to ruin it. Instead, the company mostly protected what worked. It kept Mojang semi-independent, shipped *Minecraft* to nearly every device, unified most versions so friends on phones, consoles and PCs could play together, and launched an Education Edition used in schools. Sales kept climbing long after most games fade.

blocks.title: Minecraft copies sold (millions)
blocks.source: Xbox Wire, 2020 and 2024; Minecraft.net, Oct 2023; Mojang via Guinness World Records, Apr 2025

blocks.text: That curve is the unusual part. Most games sell the majority of their copies in the first year. *Minecraft* sold its second hundred million copies between 2016 and 2020, its third by October 2023, and reached 350 million by April 2025, more than fifteen years after release. In 2016 it was selling about 53,000 copies a day. Its only rival for the all-time title is *Tetris*, whose total counts dozens of different versions from different publishers.
What actually transfers to a small team

It's tempting to treat *Minecraft* as unrepeatable, and in scale it probably is. Timing mattered: YouTube was taking off, indie games were finding an audience, and the market for open sandbox games was nearly empty. But luck only multiplies what's there. The choices underneath are things any builder can steal.

Be honest about survivorship bias, too. For every *Minecraft* there were hundreds of rough, early-access sandbox games that also shipped early, also updated in public and also had blocky art, and went nowhere. The playbook below raises your odds; it doesn't guarantee anything. What it does guarantee is that you'll learn fast what players actually respond to, which is the only information that really matters early on.

blocks.title: The Minecraft playbook, scaled down
items: Ship a playable core early, even if it looks rough, and let real players in.
Update often and in public, so players feel the game growing with them.
Pick a simple, consistent style that lets a tiny team make lots of content.
Build systems with simple rules that combine, instead of one-off scripted content.
Leave room for discovery so players have something to look up, share and film.
Keep improving the game for years instead of moving on after launch.

blocks.text: For a Roblox game with a launching or movement mechanic at its center, the lesson maps cleanly. Make that core verb feel great before adding anything else, because in *Minecraft* breaking and placing blocks was satisfying from day one. Then ask what players can combine it with. A launcher that interacts with terrain, momentum and other players' creations can produce moments you never scripted. Those moments are what people clip and share.

The deeper reframe is about what 'finished' means. *Minecraft* was never finished. It shipped as a toy, grew into a game, then into a platform, and it's still being updated. Persson didn't plan the best-selling game in history. He planned to see what would happen if he added a bit more to a mining game, then kept listening to the people playing it. The plan wasn't the genius. The listening was.

takeaways: Minecraft is the first game to sell over 300 million copies, and reached 350 million by April 2025, years after launch.
It sold early and cheap while unfinished, updated in public and treated players as collaborators.
Its blocky style was a strategy: cheap to produce, easy to understand, easy to build with, slow to age.
Its lack of hand-holding turned players into tutorial makers, which made YouTube its free marketing engine.
For your own game: nail one great core verb, add combinable systems, and keep updating for years.

title: The Story Is What You Do
dek: Most players never see a game's ending. The best game stories are built for that fact, told through rooms, verbs and failure instead of cutscenes.

blocks.text: In most games, dying is a failure state. The screen fades, you reload, and the story waits politely until you get it right. In *Hades*, dying is how the story moves forward. Every time you are killed trying to escape the underworld, you wash up back at home, and the characters there have something to say about it.
Your father has a cutting remark ready. Other residents of the house react to how far you got, or to someone you met along the way. The failure you just suffered becomes the next scene.

That one design choice solves a problem that has frustrated game writers for decades. Games are about repetition, choice and failure. Stories are about sequence, consequence and arc. Put a traditional story inside a game and the two often fight. Put the story *into* the repetition, as *Hades* did, and they reinforce each other.

The numbers show why this matters. On Steam, 46.7 percent of *Hades* players have escaped the underworld at least once. Only 23.3 percent have the achievement for completing the main quest of the story. If the story lived only at the end, more than three-quarters of players would never get it. Because it lives in every run, nearly everyone gets a story, just different amounts of it.

blocks.title: Hades: how far Steam players get
blocks.note: Steam global achievement percentages, retrieved November 2026.
blocks.source: Steam global achievement stats, Hades (app 1145360)

blocks.text: Why games and stories fight

Around the turn of the millennium, game scholars argued fiercely about whether games were a kind of storytelling at all. One camp treated games as a new form of narrative. The other insisted games were fundamentally systems of rules and play, and that bolting stories onto them was a category mistake. The debate cooled, but the tension it described is real for anyone who builds games.

A film director controls what you see and when. A game designer hands the camera, and often the plot, to someone who might skip the dialogue, run the wrong way, or spend three hours fishing. In 2007, designer Clint Hocking gave a name to the worst version of the clash: *ludonarrative dissonance*, when what a game's story tells you and what its mechanics make you do pull in opposite directions. The classic example is a hero who is gentle and principled in cutscenes but casually kills hundreds of people in gameplay. Players feel the mismatch even if they can't name it.

Branching stories, the obvious fix, carry their own trap. Every meaningful choice splits the story, and every split means content that most players will never see. Double the branches a few times and the writing budget explodes.

So many games quietly fold their branches back together, letting you pick a different line of dialogue that leads to the same outcome. Players are good at sensing when a choice is cosmetic, and when they notice, the sense of agency collapses. Real choice is expensive, and fake choice is fragile.

The way out is not to choose between story and play. It is to stop thinking of the story as something delivered *between* the play, and start treating space, mechanics and failure as storytelling tools in their own right.
Four ways a space tells a story

In a 2004 essay called 'Game Design as Narrative Architecture,' media scholar Henry Jenkins suggested looking at game designers less as storytellers and more as builders of story spaces, closer to theme park designers than novelists. He described four ways a space can create a narrative experience.

blocks.title: Jenkins' four kinds of spatial storytelling
items: Evoke: build on a world or genre players already know, like a pirate cove or haunted house, so they arrive with the story half-loaded
Enact: stage events that happen as the player moves through the space, like an ambush or a bridge collapsing
Embed: hide story information in the environment, waiting to be pieced together by a curious player
Emerge: give players tools and systems that let them create their own stories

blocks.text: Jenkins drew heavily on Don Carson, a former senior show designer at Walt Disney Imagineering who worked on attractions such as Splash Mountain. In a 2000 Gamasutra article on 'environmental storytelling,' Carson argued that in a theme park the physical space does much of the work of conveying the story. Every texture, sound and turn in the path should reinforce the theme, and anything that contradicts it breaks the spell. He also warned designers not to flood players with too many choices at once. Done right, the space is carefully orchestrated, but the visitor feels free.

This is the technique behind every abandoned room in a game that tells you what happened there without a word. A barricaded door, a half-eaten meal, a child's drawing on the wall. The player assembles the story themselves, and because they did the work, it sticks. Embedded narrative also respects players' time. Those who want lore can dig; those who don't can keep moving.
Environmental storytelling works because the player becomes a detective. A story you deduce from a ruined room feels like yours in a way a cutscene never does.
Verbs are the plot

The deeper move is making the mechanics themselves carry meaning. What the player *does* over and over is what the game is really about, whatever the script says. If the core verb is shooting, the game is about violence no matter how thoughtful the dialogue. If the core verb is listening and choosing what to say, the game is about relationships.

*Firewatch* is built almost entirely on that second verb. You play a fire lookout in the Wyoming wilderness whose only human contact is a supervisor on a handheld radio. The relationship that develops between them is the story, and it unfolds through what you choose to tell her, what you hold back, and when you stay silent. *What Remains of Edith Finch* goes further, giving each family member's story its own way of playing, so the controls themselves express who that person was. *Hades*, as we saw, turns the roguelike loop of dying and retrying into a family drama about a son trying to leave home.

There is even evidence that wrapping a story around an activity changes how people engage with it. In a small randomized study published in *Scientific Reports* in 2018, Jungyun Hwang and Amy S. Lu had young adults play an active, exercise-based video game with or without an added narrative. Adding the story led to higher step counts and more time in moderate-to-vigorous activity than the same game without it. It is one modest study, but it fits what designers see: a reason to act makes the same action feel different.

blocks.title: Telling versus playing

left.head: Story told at the player
items: Cutscene explains the villain's motive
Dialogue says the hero is merciful
Lore dumped in a text box
Death is a reload; the story pauses

right.head: Story told through play
items: Player discovers the motive in the villain's quarters
Mechanics reward sparing enemies
Lore hidden in props, notes and level layout
Death triggers new dialogue; the story continues

blocks.text: Most players never see your ending

Here is the uncomfortable fact behind all of this: a large share of players do not finish games, even short, highly praised story games. Steam's global achievement data makes it visible. In *Firewatch*, the hidden story achievements tied to the game's days show a steady drain from the first day to the last.

blocks.title: Firewatch: Steam players reaching each story day
blocks.note: Based on the game's hidden day-by-day story achievements; the game skips through the summer, so the days are not evenly spaced.
blocks.source: Steam global achievement stats, Firewatch (app 383870)

blocks.text: *Firewatch* is a game you can finish in an evening or two, and still only about 55 percent of Steam players reach its final day. *What Remains of Edith Finch*, another short story game, shows a similar pattern: 58.5 percent of players have the achievement for seeing a name in the ending credits. The biggest drop in *Firewatch* comes right at the start, between the first and second days. Players decide very early whether a story has its hooks in them.

Some caution is due when reading these numbers. Steam calculates achievement percentages across a broad pool of players, which almost certainly includes people who grabbed the game in a sale, played twenty minutes and moved on, so the true completion rate among committed players is higher. The exact drop-off also varies from game to game. Not finishing is not the same as disliking a game.

Life interrupts. A busy week, a new release, a move or a deployment can end a playthrough that was going perfectly well. But for a designer, the reason doesn't change the result: whatever you put at the end, many people will never get to it.

For a designer, that changes priorities. If roughly half your players will leave before the end, the ending cannot be where all the meaning lives. The first ten minutes need to carry real story weight. Each section should feel complete on its own, with a small payoff, so that a player who leaves halfway still had a satisfying experience. *Hades* does this brilliantly: every run, even a failed one, ends with a conversation.
Stories players tell each other

Jenkins' fourth category, emergent narrative, matters most for multiplayer games and especially for platforms like Roblox. These are stories nobody wrote. The time your friend made an impossible jump on the last try.

The server where everyone teamed up against one player who kept knocking people off. The run you lost by a pixel. Players retell these moments to each other for years, and they are often more memorable than anything in a script.

Sandbox games are built almost entirely on this kind of story. A survival world has no plot, yet players come away with sagas: the first night hiding from monsters in a dirt hut, the base a friend accidentally burned down, the long expedition that ended one block from home. The game supplied rules, risk and materials. The players supplied the narrative, and because it happened to them, they remember it better than any scripted twist.
You cannot write emergent stories, but you can design for them. They come from systems with clear stakes, visible skill, other people watching, and room for surprise. A leaderboard creates rivalries.

A shared space where players can see each other attempt the same challenge creates drama. A rare, hard-to-reach spot creates legends. The designer's job is to build a stage where good stories are likely to happen.
A story toolkit for a small Roblox game

You don't need a writing team or cinematic budget to put story into a game. Most of these techniques cost almost nothing, and they fit games like obbies and launcher games that seem to have no story at all. A pole vault game, for instance, already has a strong verb: launching yourself higher than you should be able to go. The story can grow from that.

items: **Write a one-line premise.** Why is the player climbing? Escaping a flood, chasing a stolen trophy, reaching a lighthouse at the top of the world. One sentence gives every asset a theme to reinforce.
**Let the world explain itself.** Use Carson's rule: every prop and sound should support the premise. Broken poles and scorch marks near a hard jump tell a story about everyone who failed there.
**Make failure talk.** A short, varied line from an NPC when a player falls for the tenth time, or reaches a new height, turns frustration into character. It is *Hades*' trick on a tiny scale.
**Front-load the story.** Assume half your players leave early. Put the premise and the first payoff in the opening minutes, not at the summit.
**Hide lore for the curious.** Notes, signs and secret rooms reward explorers without slowing down speedrunners.
**Build stages for player stories.** Shared spaces, visible attempts and leaderboards create the moments people screenshot and retell.

blocks.text: The best game stories are not the ones with the most words. They are the ones where what you do and what it means line up, so that every jump, death and discovery feels like part of something. When that happens, the story stops being a reward at the end of the game and becomes the reason to keep playing it.

takeaways: Game stories work best when they live inside the mechanics and repetition, not only in cutscenes between them.
Jenkins' four tools: evoke a familiar world, enact events in space, embed clues in the environment and enable emergent stories.
Only about 55 percent of Steam players reach Firewatch's final day, and 23 percent finish Hades' main story, so don't save all the meaning for the end.
Make failure part of the story: reactive lines and changing worlds turn deaths into scenes.
For small games, a one-line premise plus consistent environmental detail does more than pages of dialogue.

title: The Enemy That Is Built to Lose
dek: Game AI is not trying to beat you. It is trying to look smart, stay fair and lose convincingly. How NPCs actually decide what to do, from Pac-Man's ghosts to the director that reads your stress in Left 4 Dead.

blocks.text: Deep in the source notes for Left 4 Dead, Valve admitted to a small, deliberate cheat. If one of the computer-controlled survivors ever drifted far out of position, the game would teleport it back next to the team. There was one condition: no human player could be looking at it when it happened.

That single rule tells you most of what you need to know about game AI. It is not trying to be smart. It is trying to *look* smart, stay out of your way when it should and give you a fight worth having. A chess engine is built to beat you. A game enemy is built to lose to you convincingly, and that turns out to be a harder engineering problem than it sounds.
A magic trick, not a mind

When people hear "AI" today they picture large language models or programs that crush world champions at Go. Game AI is a different craft with a different goal. Its job is to produce behavior that players read as intentional, then hand that behavior a weakness they can learn to exploit. An enemy that never misses is not impressive. It is just unfair, and players quit unfair games.

Pac-Man is the classic example. Its four ghosts do not all hunt you the same way. Each one picks its target tile by a different rule, so one chases you directly while others try to cut you off or wander, and all of them periodically break off the chase and retreat toward their own corner of the maze. Those breaks are not a bug in their hunting. They are breathing room, timed so the player can recover and plan.

The ghosts are not intelligent in any meaningful sense. They run a handful of simple rules a few times a second. But because the rules differ, the ghosts appear to have personalities and to cooperate, and players spent decades arguing about their "strategy". That gap between simple rules and rich-seeming behavior is the entire game.

blocks.title: Two kinds of AI

left.head: AI built to win
items: Goal: maximize the chance of victory
Perfect information if it can get it
Never hesitates, never misses on purpose
Success = beating the human

right.head: AI built to be played against
items: Goal: a fight that feels fair and fun
Simulated senses: sight lines, hearing, memory
Reaction delays and readable tells built in
Success = the human enjoys winning

blocks.text: The state machine: the workhorse

Most game characters, from Roblox zombies to stealth-game guards, start life as a **finite state machine**. The character is always in exactly one state, such as Patrol, Investigate, Attack or Flee. Each state has its own behavior and a list of conditions that switch it to another state.
Hear a noise while patrolling, switch to Investigate. Spot the player, switch to Attack. Health drops low, switch to Flee.

blocks.title: A guard's brain as a state machine
items: Patrol: walk a fixed loop of waypoints and watch the cone in front of you
Investigate: a sound or a glimpse moves you toward where the stimulus came from
Attack: a confirmed sighting sends you after the target
Search: you lost the target, so check its last known position for a while
Return: nothing found, so give up and walk back to Patrol

blocks.text: State machines are easy to build and easy to debug, which is why they never go away. Their weakness shows up as characters get richer. Every new state needs transitions to and from many of the others, and the logic for when to switch ends up scattered across all of them. Add cover, grenades, ladders, squads and wounded allies, and the diagram turns into spaghetti that nobody on the team dares to touch.

Game programmers hit that wall in the early 2000s. The answer that spread through the industry was the **behavior tree**, popularized by the Halo 2 team at Bungie. Instead of a web of states pointing at each other, behaviors are arranged as a tree that the character checks from the top down, in priority order: am I about to die, then can I attack, then should I take cover, then patrol. A 2020 survey of the field notes that behavior trees were invented for games precisely because state machines scaled poorly, and that roboticists have since adopted them for real machines. Code written to make space aliens duck behind crates now helps physical robots decide what to do next.
Finding the way

Deciding what to do is half the problem. The other half is getting there. Almost every game that moves characters around obstacles leans on an algorithm published in 1968 by Peter Hart, Nils Nilsson and Bertram Raphael at the Stanford Research Institute, who were working on a mobile robot. They called it **A-star**, usually written as the letter A followed by an asterisk.

A-star explores possible routes by scoring each spot on two numbers: how far you have already traveled to reach it and an estimate of how far is left to the goal. It always expands the most promising spot next. As long as the estimate never overestimates the real remaining distance, A-star is guaranteed to find a shortest path, and it usually does so while exploring only a fraction of the map. Straight-line distance makes a perfect estimate, because no path can be shorter than a straight line.

If you have ever plotted the fastest way through a crowded ship, you have run a rough version of it in your head: you weigh how far you have come against how far you think is left, and you do not bother exploring the passageways that lead the wrong direction. Modern games run A-star not on a grid of squares but on a **navigation mesh**, a set of polygons covering every surface a character can walk on. Roblox Studio builds one automatically, and its pathfinding service will even mark the spots where a character has to jump. But the shortest path is not always the best-looking one. Valve's Left 4 Dead team found that A-star paths through a navigation mesh came out jagged, and that following them exactly made characters look robotic.

Their fix was to stop obeying the path literally. Characters steer toward a point some distance ahead on the path and use local obstacle avoidance for everything in between: props, corners and each other. The result stayed close to the optimal route but moved like a crowd of real bodies. The lesson repeats across game AI. Perfect is often less convincing than slightly sloppy.
Plans instead of scripts

In 2005 a shooter called F.E.A.R. got famous for enemy soldiers who seemed to think. They flanked, laid down suppressing fire, knocked over tables for cover and retreated when a fight went badly. The AI programmer behind them, Jeff Orkin, described the system in a paper that same year. Its core idea was to replace hand-written state transitions with a **real-time planner**.

Each soldier had a set of goals, such as killing the enemy, staying out of danger or investigating a disturbance, and a library of actions, each with conditions that had to be true before it could run and effects it produced afterward. Only one goal was active at a time. When the situation changed enough, the soldier searched for a sequence of actions that would satisfy its most relevant goal, much as A-star searches for a path through space.

items.label: Enemies F.E.A.R. typically threw at the player at once
How often one cover-finding sensor polled the world
Time budget for a soldier's whole plan search

blocks.source: Orkin, AIIDE 2005

blocks.text: Nobody wrote a script that said "flank when the player hides". Flanking fell out of the planner combining small, reusable actions. A soldier in a squad could even ignore an order: if a grenade landed nearby, the goal of staying alive outranked laying down cover fire for a friend, so he ran.

The hard part was speed. The planner had to finish inside a single frame while sharing the processor with physics, animation and rendering. Orkin's answer was to spread expensive work, like tracing lines of sight or scoring cover positions, across many frames through "sensors" that dropped their findings into a working memory. One sensor that hunted for places to hide or fire from polled the world three times per second. The planner then only had to read cached facts, not calculate them.

There is a quieter trick that designers lean on, too. Players only credit intelligence they can see. A flank that happens off-screen looks like an enemy teleporting behind you. So squads in many shooters bark their intentions out loud, and the same behavior suddenly reads as tactics instead of cheating.
The director behind the curtain

Left 4 Dead, released in 2008, pushed the idea of game AI up a level. Instead of only asking how one zombie should act, Valve built an "AI Director" that decided what the whole experience should feel like from moment to moment. Michael Booth, who led the work, explained it in a 2009 talk.

The director first solves replayability. If enemies and supplies are always placed in the same spots, players memorize them, settle on one optimal strategy and turn a cooperative game into a race. So the director populates each run on the fly using what Valve called structured unpredictability: not pure randomness, but rules with designer-chosen ranges. On Normal difficulty, a horde of 20 to 30 infected is spawned at a random interval between 90 and 180 seconds, and about three quarters of hordes come from behind, because the slower threats are usually met up ahead.

items.label: Random gap between zombie hordes on Normal
Infected in a typical horde
Length of a forced "relax" period after a peak

blocks.source: Booth, The AI Systems of Left 4 Dead, Valve 2009

blocks.text: The second job is pacing. The director keeps a running estimate of each survivor's "emotional intensity". It rises when a player takes damage, gets knocked down or is dragged off a ledge, and even when an infected dies close by. It decays over time, but not while enemies are still on the player. When the most stressed player crosses a threshold, the director stops sending new threats, lets the current fight end naturally and then holds off for 30 to 45 seconds before building pressure again.

blocks.title: Left 4 Dead's pacing loop
items: Build up: spawn the full mix of threats
Sustain peak: keep full pressure for 3–5 more seconds
Peak fade: stop new threats, let the fight finish
Relax: 30–45 seconds of near-quiet, then start again

blocks.text: Booth was blunt about how crude the intensity estimate was, and yet the pacing worked. One line in his slides is worth remembering: the algorithm changes pacing, not difficulty. The hordes do not get weaker when you struggle.

They just stop coming for a moment. The game breathes, and that rhythm of tension and relief is what players remember. It is the same rhythm Pac-Man's retreating ghosts were giving players back in 1980.

The same talk describes how much care went into making AI teammates feel trustworthy. Bots had simulated senses and reaction times, so they did not know things a human could not. And some outcomes were simply ruled out: bots never dealt friendly-fire damage and never threw Molotovs. Those are cheats too, but cheats that protect the player's trust.

Those bots earned their keep in more ways than one. Because a computer could always fill an empty slot, Valve could tune every level on the assumption of a full four-person team, and players could drop out mid-game without wrecking it for everyone else. The team also ran automated stress tests in which four bots played through the game with the clock sped up, hunting for spots where the AI got stuck. The AI was a design tool and a testing tool, not just an opponent.
Good game AI is judged by one question: does the player feel smart, challenged and treated fairly? If an NPC needs to cheat to deliver that, it cheats. It just never gets caught.
Using this in your own game
You do not need a planner or a director to make a Roblox game feel alive. You need a few of the same ideas at a smaller scale.

items: Start with a small state machine: three or four states with clear triggers. Draw it on paper before you script it.
Make intentions readable. A wind-up animation, a sound cue or a line of text before an attack turns a cheap hit into a fair one.
Build in imperfection: a short reaction delay, a first shot that misses, a chaser that slows slightly when it gets close.
Use the engine's navigation mesh and pathfinding service instead of hand-placing routes, then smooth the movement so it does not look robotic.
Think like a director. In an obby or a launcher game, alternate hard sections with easy ones and quiet stretches with busy ones. Pace, don't just escalate.

blocks.text: Notice that none of that is about making the computer clever. It is about making the player's experience well shaped. The enemies in your favorite games are actors reading from a script they help write on the fly, and the best ones know their real role: to lose, eventually, in a way that makes the person holding the controller feel like they earned it.

takeaways: Game AI aims to create fun, readable behavior, not to win. Hidden cheats are fine as long as they protect the player's experience.
Finite state machines run most NPCs; behavior trees came out of games when state machines grew unmanageable, and robotics later adopted them.
A-star (1968) finds shortest paths, but characters that follow optimal paths exactly look robotic; steering slightly loosely looks more alive.
F.E.A.R.'s soldiers planned their own actions toward goals, so tactics like flanking emerged instead of being scripted.
Left 4 Dead's AI Director changed pacing, not difficulty: build tension, let it peak, then force a break.
