title: Ten Thousand Bowls of Oatmeal
dek: Computers can generate endless worlds from a single number. Making those worlds feel different is the hard part, and the history of procedural generation is the story of designers learning to rig the dice.

blocks.text: Around 1980, two students at the University of California, Santa Cruz, Michael Toy and Glenn Wichman, were bored of adventure games that were identical every time you played them. The designers had invented every puzzle, so the designers could never be surprised. Their fix was radical for the time: let the program build the dungeon itself. Every game would be a new map, a new layout of monsters and loot, and even the people who wrote the code would not know what was around the next corner.

The game was Rogue. It spread to universities everywhere when it shipped with the Berkeley version of Unix, and its idea now runs through an enormous share of modern games, from Minecraft's terrain to every roguelike deckbuilder you have ever said "one more run" to. Wichman later wrote that the computer generating the adventure was the game's biggest contribution. He was right, and the decades since have taught designers something he could not have known yet: getting a computer to make content is easy. Getting it to make content anyone cares about is the real work.
Why let the computer design

Procedural generation means content created by rules and randomness at runtime instead of placed by hand. Designers reach for it for three different reasons, and it helps to know which one you are after, because each leads to different choices.

items: **Surprise and replay.** Rogue's reason. If the map changes every run, players have to read the situation instead of memorizing it, and the game stays fresh for hundreds of hours.
**Scale.** A small team cannot hand-build a planet, let alone a galaxy. Rules can.
**Memory.** Early computers could not store large worlds, but they could store the recipe for one and cook it on demand.

blocks.text: The reasons also come with costs that hand-built games never pay. A generated level cannot be playtested in advance the way a fixed one can, because there are too many of them. Bugs become statistical: a broken layout might appear once in five hundred runs, which means a streamer will find it on day one. And generated content has no intent behind it, so the designer has to find other ways to put meaning into the world. Every technique below is, in part, an answer to those costs.
That third reason produced one of the most impressive tricks in game history. It came from two young programmers and a home computer with almost no memory.
A galaxy folded into three numbers

In 1984, David Braben and Ian Bell released Elite on the BBC Micro, a home computer with 32 kilobytes of memory, less than a single small photo takes up today. Elite let you fly between thousands of star systems, each with a name, a government, an economy, a tech level, a position on the chart and a species living there. Storing all of that as data was impossible. So they did not store it.

Instead, every system in the game is described by three 16-bit numbers called seeds. Different bits of those numbers are read off as the system's economy type, its government, its coordinates, the letters of its name and so on. To get the next system, the game runs a short routine that "twists" the seeds along a sequence in which each number is the sum of the three before it. Start from one set of seeds, twist, read, twist, read, and out comes a whole galaxy.

items.label: 16-bit seed numbers that every system is built from
Star systems generated in each galaxy
Unique systems across Elite's 8 galaxies

blocks.source: Mark Moxon, Elite on the 6502 (fully documented source), bbcelite.com

blocks.text: The key idea is that a generator is a **function**: the same seed always produces the same output. That is why the galaxy was identical for every player in 1984, and it is why Minecraft players today can share a seed and walk through exactly the same mountains. A world can be both random and perfectly reproducible, because the randomness is a fixed sequence that only looks random.
Mark Moxon, who documented Elite's code line by line, notes that the authors could have generated far more galaxies and chose not to. More was free. Better was not.

Seeds also changed how players talk to each other. Minecraft communities trade seeds for worlds with a village next to the spawn point or a rare biome, and speedrunners split categories into set-seed and random-seed runs, because a known seed turns exploration into a route you can practice. Randomness that can be replayed becomes a shared object, something you can compare, argue about and master.
Noise that looks like nature

Pure randomness looks terrible. Fill a terrain map with independent random heights and you get static: every point unrelated to its neighbors, like a broken TV. Real landscapes are smooth at small scales and varied at large ones. The breakthrough that fixed this came from film, not games.

Ken Perlin had worked on the computer graphics for Disney's Tron and was frustrated by how clean and machine-like computer images looked. In a 1985 paper called "An Image Synthesizer" he described a way to make controlled, natural-looking randomness, now known as **Perlin noise**. Instead of choosing a random value for every pixel, you place random gradients only at the corners of a coarse grid and smoothly blend between them. The result rises and falls gently, like hills.

blocks.title: How noise becomes a landscape
items: Lay a coarse grid over the world and give each grid corner a random direction
For any point, blend smoothly between the influences of its nearest corners to get one height
That gives rolling hills, but they all look about the same size
Add a second layer at double the frequency and half the strength for smaller bumps
Keep stacking layers (octaves) until you have mountains, ridges and pebbles at once
Feed the final value into rules: below a level is water, above another is snow

blocks.text: In 1997 the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences gave Perlin a Technical Achievement Award for the technique, because it let artists fake marble, fire, clouds and water without modeling them. Games picked it up for terrain, and the family of noise functions it started still sits under countless worlds. Roblox ships it as a built-in function, math.noise, which returns the same value for the same coordinates every time. Its documentation points out one quirk worth knowing: at whole-number coordinates it returns exactly zero, so you sample between grid points.
Designing the dice

The biggest lesson of the last two decades is that the best generators are not very random at all. They are designers' hands, broken into pieces and reassembled by rules that guarantee the result works.

Spelunky, released by Derek Yu as a free game in 2008, is the standard example. Each level is a small grid of rooms. The generator first carves a guaranteed path from the entrance to the exit through that grid, then fills each room with a handmade template chosen to fit that path, and only then randomizes smaller chunks inside the templates. Players get a fresh cave every time, but never one that is impossible to finish, and never one that feels like it was assembled by a machine with no idea what a fun room is.

A newer approach flips the process around. In 2016 a developer named Maxim Gumin released an algorithm he called **wave function collapse**. You give it a small example, a handmade picture or tile layout, and it learns which little patterns are allowed to sit next to each other.

It then starts with an output in which every cell could be anything, picks the cell with the fewest remaining options, settles it and propagates the consequences to its neighbors, over and over until everything is decided. Games including Bad North, Caves of Qud and the town-building toy Townscaper use versions of it. Occasionally it paints itself into a corner where no pattern fits, and has to restart, but Gumin reports that this happens surprisingly rarely.

Townscaper shows where this can go. There is no goal and no failure; you click on water and a little building appears, and the algorithm decides how its walls, roofs, stairs and arches should connect to whatever is next to it. The player supplies intent and the generator supplies craft. Researchers call this mixed-initiative design, and it hints at a future in which generators act less like dice and more like a skilled assistant who fills in the details of your rough sketch.

blocks.title: Milestones in procedural generation
items: Rogue builds a new dungeon every game
Elite generates 8 galaxies from a few seed numbers
Ken Perlin publishes the noise technique
Perlin noise wins a technical Academy Award
Spelunky stitches handmade room templates along a guaranteed path
Wave function collapse learns layouts from an example

blocks.text: Ten thousand bowls of oatmeal

Here is the trap. The game designer and researcher Kate Compton named it in a 2016 essay on building generators. You can easily generate 10,000 bowls of oatmeal, she wrote, with every oat in a different position, and mathematically each bowl is unique. But a person looking at them just sees oatmeal.

Her distinction is between **mathematical uniqueness** and **perceptual uniqueness**. A 64-bit seed can produce roughly 18 quintillion different outputs; Compton used exactly that number to tease generators of planets. If those planets differ only in the arrangement of the same few ingredients, players figure out the ingredients within an hour, and the infinite universe collapses into a short menu. No Man's Sky ran into a version of this at its 2016 launch, when many players felt its vast universe repeated itself, and the studio spent years of free updates adding systems that give planets reasons to be different.

blocks.title: Variety that counts

left.head: Mathematical variety
items: Positions, colors and sizes shuffled
Huge numbers of possible outputs
Players learn the pattern fast
Looks impressive in a trailer

right.head: Perceptual variety
items: Changes that alter what you do or decide
Handmade pieces combined in new ways
Rare, memorable outliers on purpose
Feels different on the tenth play

blocks.text: The deeper point is about attention. Humans are pattern detectors, and we stop noticing anything we have learned to predict. A generator that only shuffles surface details is training players to ignore it. One that occasionally produces a structure they have never seen, or a combination that forces a new plan, keeps their attention alive, because their pattern detector keeps failing to close the loop.

The fixes all point the same way. Vary things that change decisions, not just looks: a cave with no light source plays differently from one with three. Mix handmade set pieces into generated filler so there are moments that feel authored. Put deliberate rare events in the table, so players occasionally see something they will tell friends about. And curate: throw away outputs that fail a quality check instead of shipping whatever the dice produce.

Procedural generation does not remove the designer. It moves the designer one level up: instead of building the level, you build the rules that build levels, and then you judge thousands of their outputs.
Generating for a small game

For a two-person Roblox team, procedural generation is tempting because it promises endless content without endless building. It can deliver, as long as the scope stays honest. A launcher obby, for instance, could generate bonus courses from a library of hand-built obstacle chunks, each tagged with a difficulty and the launch height it needs. The generator lays chunks along a path, checks that each gap is clearable with the player's current power and swaps in a different chunk when it is not. A shared daily seed would give every player the same course that day, which turns a random map into something people can compare times on.

The tools are already in the engine. Alongside math.noise, Roblox provides a Random object that you can create from a seed, so the same number always produces the same sequence of rolls. Use one seeded generator per course rather than the global random function, store the seed with any bug report and you can rebuild the exact course a player saw. That one habit saves hours of trying to reproduce a broken layout from a vague description in a Discord message.

items: Build pieces by hand, assemble them by rule. Never ask the generator to invent fun from nothing.
Guarantee solvability first, then add variety on top.
Use seeds so a bug report or a great run can be reproduced exactly.
Generate a few hundred outputs and look at them in bulk. Patterns of failure jump out fast.
Ask what decision each random element changes. If the answer is none, it is oatmeal.

blocks.text: Rogue's creators wanted to be surprised by their own game. That is still the best reason to let a computer design. But the surprise only lands if a human taught the machine what is worth being surprised by.

takeaways: A generator is a function: the same seed rebuilds the same world, which is how Elite fit 2,048 star systems into three numbers.
Perlin noise made randomness smooth and natural. Layered octaves of it still shape terrain, and Roblox ships it as math.noise.
The best generators assemble handmade pieces along a guaranteed-solvable structure, like Spelunky's room grid.
Mathematical uniqueness is cheap; perceptual uniqueness is what players notice. Vary what changes decisions, not just what changes looks.
Procedural design moves the designer up a level: you write rules, then judge their outputs in bulk.

title: The Species That Only Grow on Roblox
dek: Obbies, tycoons and simulators barely exist anywhere else, yet they rule one of the biggest game platforms on Earth. They are not accidents. They evolved to fit Roblox's bricks, players, screens and economy.

blocks.text: Roblox's public game data contains a number that would make most of the game industry do a double take. A game called Grow a Garden, whose page was created in March 2025, had logged more than 36 billion visits by early November 2026. In about a year and a half it passed Tower of Hell, one of the platform's most famous obbies, which had needed more than eight years to reach 29 billion.

Grow a Garden is, at its core, a game about planting seeds, waiting for them to grow and selling what comes up. Roblox files it under Simulation, subgenre Tycoon. Nothing like it would top a Steam chart or headline a console showcase. On Roblox it became one of the biggest games of all time.

That is not a fluke. It is evolution. Biologists have long noticed that islands grow strange species, shaped by local conditions that the mainland does not have. Roblox is an island, and its best-known genres, the obby, the tycoon and the simulator, are native species. If you are building a game there, understanding why they evolved is more useful than copying any one of them.
The conditions on the island

Every genre is an answer to a set of conditions: what is easy to build, who is playing, on what device, for how long and how the game makes money. Roblox's conditions are unusual, and they all push in the same direction.

items: **The tools are bricks.** Since its 2006 launch, Roblox has handed creators a physics engine and simple building blocks called parts. Things made of blocks, platforms and conveyors are easy; cinematic stories and complex animation are hard.
**The players are young and social.** Friends join each other's servers, so a game is often a place to hang out as much as a challenge to beat.
**The screens are small.** Many players are on phones and tablets, so controls have to be simple and sessions short.
**The games are free.** Money comes from optional purchases with Robux, so a game needs things worth buying without walling off the fun.
**Discovery runs on charts.** Games that keep players coming back climb the charts, and the charts send them more players.

blocks.text: Roblox has gone as far as writing its native forms into its official genre system. Its creator documentation lists 17 top-level genres, and among the subgenres sit Classic Obby, Tower Obby, Tycoon and Incremental Simulator, categories you will not find in most storefronts' menus. The platform's own taxonomy is a field guide to what grew there.
The obby: the first thing anyone builds

Roblox defines the obby, short for obstacle course, as a game where players navigate surfaces and obstacles to progress, mostly by jumping, climbing and changing direction. It is the platform's oldest native form for a simple reason: it is the easiest game you can make out of parts. One of Roblox's own beginner scripting tutorials teaches you to make a floor of lava that kills on contact, and then suggests using it as an extra challenge in an obby.

That simplicity is a strength, not a weakness. An obby needs no enemies, no story and no inventory. Failure costs seconds, because a checkpoint puts you right back. Friends can see each other succeed and fail, which turns a solo challenge into a social one. And because almost every Roblox creator builds an obby first, the platform is full of players who already know the language: red means danger, checkpoints mean safety, stages climb upward.

Tower of Hell, created in 2018, shows how far the form can go with one twist. Instead of a fixed course, it stacks randomly chosen sections into a tower, with no checkpoints and a timer that resets the whole thing. Roblox lists it as a Tower Obby, and its visit count passed 29 billion. Same parts, same lava, one clever rule.
The tycoon: progress you can walk through

Roblox's official description of a tycoon is a game simulating the management of a business or base, usually built around collecting money from "droppers" that you use to upgrade the base. If you have played one, you know the rhythm: a machine drops blocks onto a conveyor, the blocks become cash, the cash buys a better machine, a wall, a second floor.

The tycoon fits the island almost perfectly. Its pieces are made of exactly the things Roblox is good at: parts, conveyors and simple physics. Its progress is physical, so you do not just see a number grow; you see a building rise. And your base is a trophy your friends can walk through. Theme Park Tycoon 2's page dates to 2012 and Lumber Tycoon 2's to 2009, and both remain playable with well over a billion visits each, proof that the form has staying power.

Grow a Garden is a tycoon in the same family, with a farm where the factory used to be. Plants grow while you are away, so a five-minute check-in still moves you forward. That idle progress fits a young audience on phones with short sessions, and it gives players a reason to come back tomorrow, which is exactly what the charts reward.
The simulator: the number that goes up

The word simulator on Roblox rarely means simulating anything real. Roblox's own definition of the Incremental Simulator subgenre is a game where progress comes from simple repeated actions that increase a counter, with new abilities, areas and characters unlocking as the counter grows. Its ancestors are idle and clicker games such as Cookie Clicker, a 2013 browser game about making a number go up.

blocks.title: The classic simulator loop
items: Click or swing to collect
Fill your backpack, then sell
Buy a better tool or a bigger bag
Unlock a new zone with richer loot
Rebirth: reset progress for a permanent multiplier

blocks.text: Bee Swarm Simulator, Mining Simulator, Muscle Legends and the Pet Simulator series all run on versions of that loop. The rebirth step is the clever part. You throw away your progress in exchange for a permanent boost, which makes the early game fast and fresh again while the long-term number keeps climbing. It is the same idea as prestige in many mobile games, and it lets a game with a handful of zones stretch across months.

The simulator also suits free-to-play money without forcing a paywall. A game pass that doubles what you collect, a pet that boosts your speed, an extra backpack slot: each one speeds up a loop the player already enjoys. That is why these games tend to have long, layered stores. The same features can tip into compulsion design, a risk covered in more depth elsewhere in this library. The healthy versions are the ones where the loop is fun even without buying anything.

blocks.title: Lifetime visits, native-genre hits
blocks.note: Visits count sessions, not unique players. Snapshot of 5 Nov 2026.
blocks.source: Roblox games API (games.roblox.com), accessed Nov 2026

blocks.text: Step back and the three native genres turn out to reward three different things. The obby rewards skill: nothing you buy makes your jumps cleaner, and a good player can clear a stage a new player cannot. The simulator rewards time: anyone who keeps clicking long enough gets stronger, regardless of talent.

The tycoon rewards a mix of time and planning, since what you buy first shapes how fast the rest arrives. That split matters to a young audience. Some players want to prove they are good. Others want to feel themselves getting stronger without the risk of being bad at something.

blocks.title: What each native genre rewards

left.head: Skill-driven
items: Obby: precise jumps, route knowledge
Progress resets if you fall
Buying rarely helps
Bragging rights come from ability

right.head: Time-driven
items: Simulator and tycoon: steady accumulation
Progress is kept and compounds
Purchases speed up the loop
Bragging rights come from stats and size

blocks.text: Roblox's own retention guidance for creators speaks in exactly these terms. It tells developers to identify the core loop, the actions players repeat to make progress in a session, and gives a tycoon as an example: managing a business, balancing resources and competing with others. It then tells them to watch how long players take to reach each progression level, because progress that is too fast leaves nothing to explore and progress that is too slow makes people quit. Native genres are, in a sense, pre-tested answers to that tuning problem.
What the numbers do and don't say

Visit counts are the only lifetime numbers Roblox shows publicly, and they need care. A visit is a session, not a person, so a player who comes back daily for a year counts hundreds of times. That actually tells you something: the games at the top of this chart are the ones people return to, not just the ones they try. Creation dates need care too. They mark when a game's page was created, which can be well before its real launch or rise.

The data also shows the limits of the native genres. The very biggest Roblox games are not obbies or tycoons. Brookhaven, a town roleplay game, had over 89 billion visits, and Blox Fruits, an action role-playing game, over 65 billion. The native genres are where many players learn the platform and where many creators learn to build. The biggest hits usually take those lessons somewhere new.

The crowding is the other thing the data hints at. Because native genres are easy to build, they are also easy to copy, and every hit spawns a wave of near-identical clones. Roblox seems aware of the problem.

Its discovery documentation describes a hand-curated Standout Games section that favors games with novel mechanics, distinctive visual styles or genres that are underrepresented on the platform. On a platform full of obbies, being a slightly better obby is a weak position. Being a different kind of game, built from native parts, is a stronger one.

items.label: Top-level genres in Roblox's official taxonomy
Visits for Brookhaven, the top roleplay game
Minimum wait between genre changes on Roblox

blocks.source: Roblox Creator Hub, Genres; Roblox games API, Nov 2026

blocks.text: Where a launcher obby fits

Some of the most interesting recent Roblox games are hybrids, and the "+1" format is one of them. A number goes up on its own, every second or with every action, which is pure incremental simulator. Then you spend that number to clear obstacles, which is pure obby. A pole-vault launcher sits right on this border: the vault height grows like a simulator stat, and the course tests what you do with it.

That border is exactly why hybrids are hard to balance. If the number grows so fast that skill stops mattering, the obby half becomes decoration and the game is really a simulator with scenery. If the course ignores the number, the counter is just a clock. The sweet spot is a game where time opens new possibilities and skill decides how well you use them: a bigger vault unlocks a higher route, but only a clean run takes it. That way the player who wants to feel stronger and the player who wants to prove they are good can both find what they came for in the same server.

Roblox asks every game to pick one genre and an optional subgenre, and it shows that label on the game's page and uses it to place games in genre-specific charts. You can only change it once every three months, and Roblox may correct a label it thinks is wrong. Its advice is to choose by the primary purpose and core gameplay loop. That forces a useful design question for any hybrid: which half is the real loop, and which half is the reward?

blocks.title: Using the native genres without cloning them
items: Name your core loop in one sentence, then decide which native genre it belongs to
Keep the genre's proven strengths: fast retries for obbies, visible progress for tycoons, a satisfying counter for simulators
Add one twist that changes decisions, like Tower of Hell's random sections
Make sure the free loop is fun before designing anything to sell
Pick the genre label that matches the core loop, and live with it for at least three months

blocks.text: The deeper lesson of the island is that genres are not arbitrary fashions. They are solutions to a particular environment. Obbies, tycoons and simulators took over Roblox because they fit its bricks, its young social players, its small screens and its free-to-play economy better than anything imported from consoles. The builders who win there are rarely the ones who invent a form from scratch. They are the ones who understand why the native forms work, and then breed something new from them.

takeaways: Genres are solutions to an environment. Roblox's bricks, young social players, phones and free-to-play model produced its own forms.
Roblox's official taxonomy includes Classic Obby, Tower Obby, Tycoon and Incremental Simulator, defined by their core loops.
Visits count sessions, not people, so top visit counts reveal what players return to.
The very biggest Roblox games (roleplay, RPGs) usually build on native lessons rather than staying inside one native genre.
For a hybrid like a +1 launcher obby, decide which loop is core; Roblox lets you change your genre only once every three months.

title: Why You Always Click Embark Again
dek: Slay the Spire sold about 800 copies in its first three days. How a tiny studio built the most influential deckbuilder of its era, and what its design teaches anyone making a roguelike.

blocks.text: In November 2017, a small Seattle studio called Mega Crit put an odd little card game on Steam Early Access. It mixed a deckbuilder with a roguelike, two genres most players had never seen combined. Over the first three days it sold roughly 800 copies. Co-founder Casey Yano later said most of the keys they had mailed to YouTubers and press had simply vanished into the void.

Then a Chinese streamer picked it up. By April 2018, about three months into Early Access, the game had sold around 700,000 copies. By March 2019, two months after the full release, *Slay the Spire* had passed 1.5 million, with China accounting for roughly 30 percent of sales. Seven years later its sequel, *Slay the Spire 2*, launched in Early Access on March 5, 2026, and Mega Crit announced it had sold 3 million copies in its first week.

items.label: Copies of Slay the Spire sold in its first three days (2017)
Copies sold by March 2019
Slay the Spire 2 copies sold in its first week (2026)

blocks.source: Game Developer, 2019; PC Gamer, 2026

blocks.text: Those players had attempted around 25 million runs in that first week, by the studio's count, and Mega Crit said the tally was missing at least a few million. That works out to roughly eight runs for every copy sold, in seven days. That number is the real story. A run of Slay the Spire usually ends in death. Players lose, over and over, and click the button to start again. Understanding why that loss feels like an invitation instead of a punishment is the whole art of roguelike design.
What a roguelike actually is

The genre is named after *Rogue*, a 1980 dungeon crawler made by university students in which every dungeon was generated fresh and death was permanent. In 2008, developers at an international roguelike conference in Berlin tried to pin the genre down in a list now called the Berlin Interpretation. Its core ideas: levels generated randomly, death that wipes your run, turn-based decisions, and enough interlocking systems that the same problem can be solved many different ways.

Modern games bend those rules so often that a softer label, roguelite, is common. Those games keep some permanent progress between runs, like unlocks or upgrades. Slay the Spire sits close to the strict end. It unlocks a few cards and characters early on, but once those are open, the only thing you really carry into the next run is what is in your head.

That's the key to the whole genre. In most games, progress lives in your save file. In a roguelike, progress lives in *you*. Each death leaves you a slightly better player, and the next run is your chance to prove it. That is Raph Koster's idea that fun is learning (covered in the library's piece on what makes games fun) in its purest form.
Random, but never unfair

Randomness is dangerous. Done badly, it makes a player feel that luck decided the outcome, and nobody wants to practice at a slot machine. Slay the Spire's cleverest move is *where* it puts the randomness. The game is random about what you are *offered*: which cards appear after a fight, which relics you find, which path the map draws. It is almost never random about what *happens* once you act. A card that deals 6 damage deals 6 damage.

On top of that, the game shows you its enemies' intentions. Every monster displays an icon telling you whether it plans to attack, and for how much, or to defend or cast a buff next turn. That one feature turns a fight from a guessing game into a puzzle. When you lose, you can usually point to the exact turn where you made the wrong call. Losses that feel like your fault are losses you want to avenge.

blocks.title: Two places to put randomness

left.head: Random outcomes
items: Your attack might miss for no visible reason
Players blame luck after losing
Skill is hard to see, so practice feels pointless
Wins feel unearned too

right.head: Random options (Slay the Spire)
items: Random card offers, relics and map paths
Actions do exactly what the card says
Enemy intents are shown in advance
Losses are traceable, so you learn and retry

blocks.text: The map works the same way. At the start of each act you see the whole branching path to the boss, with icons for normal fights, elite fights, shops, campfires and unknown events. Do you take the route with two elites for better relics, risking your health? Or the safe route with an extra rest stop? The randomness built the map, but the decision is entirely yours.
Your deck is your character

In a role-playing game you level up a hero. In Slay the Spire the deck *is* the hero, and its growth is a chain of small, sharp decisions. After most fights you get to pick one of three cards, or skip. That skip button might be the most important design choice in the game. A bloated deck draws its best cards less often, so taking a mediocre card can actually make you weaker. Good players learn to say no.

Because every card choice depends on what you already hold, the same card can be brilliant in one run and useless in the next. That's what makes the game feel endless with a fixed set of content. The designers did not have to create millions of situations. They created a few hundred pieces that combine in ways even they could not fully predict.

The four characters of the original game push this further. The Ironclad, the Silent, the Defect and the Watcher each have their own pool of cards and their own way of thinking. The Silent wins by stacking poison and slipping damage past blocks; the Defect juggles orbs that trigger every turn. Switching characters is close to learning a new game with the same rules, which multiplies the content without multiplying the systems.
Why losing doesn't feel like losing

Most games treat death as a failure state you want to avoid. Roguelikes make it the main rhythm of play, and that only works if three things are true. First, a run has to be short enough that starting over isn't a disaster. A Slay the Spire run takes a good chunk of an evening, not a week. Second, the early part of a run has to be quick and low-stakes, so replaying it feels like a warm-up rather than a chore. Third, each run has to feel different enough that you want to see what this one will become.

There's also a psychological trick in how runs end. Because you choose every card and every path, a lost run feels like *your* story. You remember the boss that almost died, the relic that nearly made a combo work, the elite you should have skipped. That sense of a near miss, combined with full ownership of the decisions, is exactly what makes the next click on Embark feel urgent rather than tired.

Compare that to a game where you lose an hour of progress to a random crit you could not see coming. The time cost might be the same, but the feeling is opposite. One loss teaches; the other just takes. Players will forgive almost any amount of failure if they believe it was fair and that they understood it.
Balancing with data, not opinions

Here's the part most players never see. From the prototype stage, Mega Crit had the game report players' decisions to a metrics server. Co-founders Anthony Giovannetti and Casey Yano described the system in a 2018 Game Developer feature, and Giovannetti went into more depth in a 2019 Game Developers Conference talk titled *Slay the Spire: Metrics Driven Design and Balance*.

They tracked how often each card was picked when offered and what it was picked over, how often it showed up in winning decks, and how much damage players carrying it took from specific enemies. A card almost nobody picked was, in their view, effectively not in the game. A card that showed up in too many winning decks was probably overpowered. Their dashboard reportedly grew from three graphs to at least ninety.

Two examples show the method. A card called Dual Wield had a low pick rate, so they buffed it to copy any card in hand. The data then showed it was too strong and let players build infinite combos, so they limited it to copying certain card types. A late boss, the Awakened One, gains strength whenever you play Power cards, and the numbers showed it was crushing decks built around Powers. They cut that strength gain and raised its base damage instead, and later data showed more players getting past it.

The developers were clear that data was not the whole job. Numbers could not tell them how a change felt, so they still leaned on playtesters and a Discord community, and they found that one well-reasoned feedback post was worth more than a pile of complaints demanding a nerf. Weekly Early Access patches let them test, measure and adjust in short cycles.
Players are excellent at telling you something feels wrong. They are much worse at telling you why. Data shows you what is happening; players tell you what it feels like. You need both.
The ladder that never ends

Once you beat the game, Slay the Spire hands you Ascension mode: 20 stacked levels, each adding one more nasty modifier, like tougher elites or less healing. It's a difficulty curve the player climbs by choice, one rung at a time. Steam's public achievement data shows how steep that ladder is. The percentages below are shares of all Steam owners of the game, including people who barely played, so they understate how far active players get. But the shape is the point.

blocks.title: Share of Slay the Spire owners who unlocked each milestone
blocks.note: The Guardian, Ruby, Ruby+, Ascend 10 and Ascend 20 achievements; snapshot November 2026.
blocks.source: Steam global achievement stats, Slay the Spire (app 646570), retrieved Nov 2026

blocks.text: Notice that the hidden fourth act, where you fight the Heart, and the top Ascension levels are reached by a small fraction of owners. That is fine. Those layers aren't for everyone. They exist so that the players who fall in love with the game always have a next mountain,.
What this means for your own deckbuilder

Slay the Spire 2 adds one more lesson. Mega Crit had spent more than two years building it in Unity when Unity announced a fee per game install in 2023. The studio said it would leave unless the policy was reversed. Unity backed down, but Mega Crit switched to the open-source Godot engine anyway. For a small team, owning your tools and not betting everything on one platform's goodwill is part of design too.

If you are designing your own roguelike deckbuilder, with twists like corruption mechanics or cards slotted into each other, the Slay the Spire playbook gives you a checklist that matters more than any single card idea.

blocks.title: A Slay the Spire-style design checklist
items: Log every choice from day one: what was offered, what was picked, what was skipped, and how far that run got.
Put randomness in the offers, not the results. Make actions predictable once taken.
Show enemy intent. A visible threat turns a gamble into a puzzle.
Always allow a skip. Saying no should be a real strategy.
Treat a card nobody picks as missing content, and a card in every winning deck as a bug.
Add a voluntary difficulty ladder once the base game is beatable.

blocks.text: Mechanics like corruption fit this philosophy well, as long as the player can see the price before paying it. Slay the Spire is full of bargains like that: relics that give energy but blind you to enemy intents, events that offer power in exchange for a curse in your deck. A trade the player chooses with open eyes is a decision. A penalty that surprises them is just bad luck, and bad luck is the one thing a roguelike can't afford to feel like.

On Roblox you can do the logging part with simple event tracking: write a small record each time a player takes or skips a card, and when a run ends. Even a few hundred runs from friends will show you cards that are never picked and bosses that end most runs. Fix those first, then ask testers how the changes *feel*.

The deepest lesson is about death itself. A roguelike works when the player walks away from a loss thinking, I know exactly what I'd do differently. Build for that sentence, and your players will keep clicking the button to start another run, just like millions of people did with Slay the Spire.

takeaways: In a roguelike, progress lives in the player's head, not the save file. Every death should teach something.
Randomize what players are offered, not what their actions do. Show enemy intent so losses feel earned.
The skip button matters: in a deckbuilder, saying no to a card is often the strongest play.
Mega Crit balanced with pick rates and win rates from day one, then used player feedback for feel.
Add an optional difficulty ladder like Ascension so dedicated players always have a next goal.

title: Racing Against Perfection
dek: People have spent more than twenty years shaving a 1985 Mario game down by hundredths of a second. What speedrunners figure out about practice, mastery and limits applies far beyond games.

blocks.text: On October 31, 2026, a runner called Niftski finished *Super Mario Bros.* in 4 minutes and 54.299 seconds. The game came out in 1985. Its levels have been mapped pixel by pixel, every known trick catalogued, every route argued over. And yet his run beat his own previous record by about three hundredths of a second, roughly two frames of animation on an NES.

To most people, that sounds absurd. Why would anyone grind thousands of attempts at a game they finished as a kid, chasing a margin smaller than a blink? But speedrunning isn't really about Mario. It's one of the cleanest experiments in human skill ever run in public: a fixed task, an exact timer, thousands of competitors and decades of recorded data. Watch it long enough and you learn how mastery actually works, and what happens when people push toward a hard limit.

The hobby is older than most people think. It grew out of 1990s PC shooters like *Doom* and *Quake*, whose built-in demo recordings let players share proof of a fast run as a tiny file anyone could replay. Fan sites and forums collected those runs and argued over rules. Then live streaming in the 2010s turned a niche of forum regulars into something hundreds of thousands of people watch live.
The curve of diminishing returns

Speedrun.com, the community's main leaderboard site, keeps verified runs going back to the early 2000s. Plot the world record for *Super Mario Bros.* any% (finish by any means, warps allowed) and the shape tells a story.

It's also a crowded field. As of November 2026, the *Super Mario Bros.* any% category alone held 6,938 verified runs on speedrun.com, each one a video someone recorded, submitted and had checked by a moderator. Only a tiny handful ever held the record. For almost everyone else, the real opponent is their own personal best, which turns out to be motivation enough for years of attempts.

blocks.title: Super Mario Bros. any% world record
blocks.note: Best verified time on the leaderboard at each point. Early runs were timed less precisely.
blocks.source: speedrun.com Super Mario Bros. any% leaderboard, verified runs, retrieved Nov 2026

blocks.text: In the first five years, the record fell by about 25 seconds as players discovered better routes and tricks. Since 2011, it has dropped by less than five seconds total. The last three years of progress add up to about a third of a second. That's the classic shape of skill near a ceiling: big early gains from better strategy, then a long grind where each improvement costs more effort than the last.

Part of why *Super Mario Bros.* is so tight is a quirk of its code called the **framerule**. The game only checks whether to load the next level every 21 frames, about a third of a second. Finish a level a little faster and you may still wait for the same framerule, gaining nothing. So top runners don't just play fast. They have to play fast enough to catch an earlier framerule, which means cutting time in chunks, not smoothly. Many record attempts die not from mistakes but from barely missing one.

There's also a known floor. **Tool-assisted speedruns**, or TAS, are made with emulators that let a creator play frame by frame, rewind and redo inputs until they're perfect. They aren't competing with humans; they show what the game allows. Top human runs of *Super Mario Bros.* now use essentially the same route and the same frame-precise tricks the tool-assisted runs rely on. Runners are mostly no longer chasing new tricks. They're chasing a version of themselves that makes almost no mistakes for five straight minutes.
How runners actually get that good

From the outside a world record looks like reflexes. From the inside it's mostly memory and structure. Human reaction to a visual cue takes a good fraction of a second, many frames longer than a frame-perfect input allows. Top runners don't react to most tricks. They know them in advance and time them from rhythm, sound cues and landmarks, the way a musician doesn't react to each note but plays a piece they've memorized.

The training methods look a lot like what learning science recommends. Runners split a game into **segments** and practice the hardest pieces in isolation, often using save states to retry one trick hundreds of times in a row. Then they stitch the pieces back together with full runs, because consistency under pressure is its own skill. Timer software shows a split at the end of each segment, comparing it to their personal best, so they get exact feedback after every attempt instead of a vague sense of 'that felt good.'

blocks.title: How a runner learns a game
items: Watch top runs and learn the current route, including every skip and trick.
Break the route into segments and drill the hardest ones in isolation.
Track timing on each segment to see exactly where time is lost.
Run full attempts to build consistency and handle nerves.
Reset bad runs early; keep going only when a record is possible.
Revisit the route as the community finds new tricks.

blocks.text: That last part matters more than it looks. Speedrunning is a giant collaborative research project. Somebody discovers a glitch that skips a section; someone else figures out how to make it consistent; a third person finds a safer setup. Routes evolve the way scientific fields do, through many small contributions. Even a record holder is standing on top of hundreds of people's discoveries.

Then there's the mental side. A runner can execute a trick perfectly a hundred times in practice and miss it on the attempt that matters, because their hands are shaking from being on record pace with two minutes left. Many describe the last stretch of a good run as the hardest part of the whole game, not because the tricks are harder but because now there's something to lose. Learning to stay loose when it counts is as much a part of the training as the tricks themselves.

The speedrunner method works for anything you're learning: isolate the hardest piece, drill it with fast feedback, then put it back in context. Most people do the opposite and only ever practice the full thing.
Breaking games on purpose

Watch a run of *The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time* or *Super Mario 64* and you'll see characters clipping through walls, jumping backward at impossible speeds, or skipping most of the game. Speedrunners treat games as physics systems to be exploited, not stories to be followed. Categories help keep things fair: any% allows nearly everything, glitchless bans major exploits, and 100% requires collecting everything.

The most extreme technique is **RNG manipulation**. Many games generate 'random' events, like item drops or enemy movement, from formulas that depend on the player's inputs or timing. If you understand the formula, you can make the dice land the way you want by doing precise things at precise moments. Some runners walk in odd patterns or pause at exact frames because doing so makes a rare drop guaranteed. It looks like superstition. It's actually applied reverse-engineering.

For game developers there's a lesson here. Players will find every crack in your systems, and some of those cracks become the most loved part of the game. Movement tricks that let skilled players go faster, like bunny hopping in old shooters, often outlive the content around them. Some developers now design for runners directly, with built-in timers and leaderboards. For an obby or a movement-based Roblox game, a launch mechanic that rewards clever angles and momentum isn't just fun for new players. It's a skill ceiling that can keep your best players busy for years.

Concretely, that can mean an on-screen timer that starts when a player leaves the spawn, a leaderboard for each stage as well as the whole run, and replays or ghosts of the fastest attempts. Those features cost little to build and give your most dedicated players a reason to come back long after they've seen everything. They also generate content: a clip of someone shaving a second off a stage is exactly what other players want to watch and try to beat.
Trust, proof and the Dream scandal

Any competition built on self-recorded videos has a cheating problem. Speedrunning's answer is volunteer moderators who check footage, timing and sometimes game files. The most famous test came in 2020, when Dream, one of the biggest Minecraft creators on YouTube, submitted a fast run of Minecraft 1.16.

Minecraft speedruns depend on luck with two items: ender pearls traded from piglins and blaze rods dropped by blazes. Moderators pulled data from six of Dream's livestreams and found his luck was wildly off. In December 2020 they published a 29-page report concluding his game had been modified to boost drop rates, and removed the run.

The logic is the same as catching a loaded coin. At the game's 5% rate, 262 piglin trades should yield about 13 pearls, give or take a few. Getting 42 is not a lucky streak; it's roughly eight standard deviations above what you'd expect. Blaze rods told the same story at the same time. One lucky stat can happen to anyone. Two, both pointing the same direction, across six separate streams, is a pattern that needs an explanation other than luck.

items.label: Dream's ender pearl trade rate vs the game's expected rate (42 of 262 trades)
Blaze rod drop rate vs expected (211 rods from 305 kills)
Moderators' estimate of the odds his trades were legitimate

blocks.source: Minecraft speedrun moderators' report, Dec 2020, as reported by PC Gamer

blocks.text: Dream disputed it at first and paid for a counter-analysis. In mid-2021 he wrote that he had in fact been using a mod with boosted drop rates, one he'd built for his YouTube videos and believed was turned off, and said he hadn't meant to cheat. Whatever you make of his explanation, the episode showed something remarkable: a hobby community, with no lawyers or referees, used statistics to catch a huge creator and stood by the result.
Speedrunning as a spectator sport

The most visible face of the hobby is Games Done Quick, a charity marathon that streams speedruns around the clock for a week. The first Classic Games Done Quick in 2010 raised about $10,500. The winter event, Awesome Games Done Quick, now raises millions every January for the Prevent Cancer Foundation, and the summer event raises money for Doctors Without Borders.

blocks.title: Awesome Games Done Quick: money raised
blocks.note: Across all its tracked events since 2010, GDQ's tracker shows more than $62 million raised.
blocks.source: Games Done Quick donation tracker, retrieved Nov 2026

blocks.text: Part of the appeal is commentary. Runners talk through what they're doing while they do it, explaining why they're jumping at a wall or walking backward, and couch commentators fill in the history. You don't need to know the game to enjoy watching someone who knows it absolutely, explaining their craft while performing it under pressure. That combination of expertise, explanation and live risk is a format any content creator can learn from.
What the hundredths are really about

Go back to that 4:54.299. Nobody needs a faster *Super Mario Bros.* run. The value is in what the chase reveals. People will put in thousands of focused hours when the goal is crystal clear, the feedback is instant, the progress is visible, and there's a community that understands exactly how hard the last hundredth was. Those are the same conditions that make any skill grow, from watchstanding to weightlifting to coding.

The diminishing-returns curve has a lesson too. In almost anything you learn, the early gains come from strategy: a better route, a better method, a better plan. Later gains come from consistency, doing the same right thing more reliably. Most people stall in the middle because they keep looking for a new trick when what they actually need is fewer mistakes.

Speedrunners also prove that a 'solved' problem rarely is. The *Super Mario Bros.* record was called nearly perfect years ago, and it has fallen again and again since. The limit was real, but people kept underestimating how close they could get to it. That's worth remembering the next time something feels maxed out.

takeaways: The Super Mario Bros. record fell about 25 seconds in its first five years and under five seconds since 2011: classic diminishing returns.
Top runners rely on memorized timing and rhythm, not raw reaction speed.
Train like a runner: drill the hardest segment in isolation with exact feedback, then rebuild the full run.
Early progress comes from better strategy; late progress comes from fewer mistakes.
Games Done Quick events have raised more than $62 million for charity, and moderators used statistics to catch even the biggest creators.

title: What Video Games Actually Do to Your Brain
dek: Twenty years of research, two loud camps and a lot of small studies. The real answer is less exciting than either side wants, and more useful.

blocks.text: In the early 2000s, a student in Daphne Bavelier's vision lab at the University of Rochester kept wrecking the experiment. Shawn Green was helping build tests of visual attention, and his own results were so far above normal that the tests looked broken. They weren't. Green was a heavy action-game player, and when the lab started testing other gamers, the pattern held.

That accident became a 2003 paper in *Nature*, one of the most cited studies in the field. It also kicked off two decades of headlines that swing between 'games make you smarter' and 'games are rotting your brain.' Both headlines are mostly wrong, and the way they're wrong is worth understanding, because it teaches you how to read any science story about screens, sleep, supplements or anything else you care about.
The case for: action games train attention

The 2003 study had two parts. First, Green and Bavelier compared habitual action-game players with non-players and found the gamers better on several measures of visual attention, such as tracking more items at once and picking targets out of clutter. Then they ran a small training experiment. Non-gamers played about an hour a day for two weeks: nine played *Medal of Honor*, eight played *Tetris*. Only the shooter group improved noticeably on the attention tests.

Notice the sample size: seventeen people. That's normal for an early lab study, but it means the result was a promising lead, not a law of nature. The honest question is what happened when other labs piled on for the next twenty years.

The best summary comes from meta-analyses, which pool many studies to estimate an average effect. Bavelier's group published two. The 2018 version, in *Psychological Bulletin*, covered studies from 2000 to 2015. A 2023 update in *Technology, Mind, and Behavior* added newer work. Both separate two kinds of evidence: **cross-sectional** studies that compare gamers to non-gamers, and **intervention** studies that assign non-gamers to play an action game or a different game and test them before and after.

blocks.title: Action games and cognition: average effect sizes
blocks.note: 0.2 is usually called small, 0.5 medium. Training studies are the ones that can show cause.
blocks.source: Bediou et al., Psychological Bulletin, 2018; Bediou et al., Technology, Mind, and Behavior, 2023

blocks.text: The gap between those bars is the most important thing in this article. Gamers outperform non-gamers by about half a standard deviation or more. But when you take non-gamers and make them play, the gain shrinks to roughly a third of a standard deviation. Part of the gamer advantage is probably selection: people who are already quick and visually sharp are more likely to enjoy and stick with shooters. Training does seem to cause some improvement, mainly in top-down attention and spatial skills, but less than the gamer-versus-non-gamer comparison suggests.

The 2018 paper was also unusually frank about bias. It estimated that the published effects were about 30% larger than the full literature would show, because studies that find nothing tend to stay in desk drawers. The 2023 update found publication bias again in the cross-sectional studies, though not in the training studies.

There is brain-imaging evidence too, though it is thin. In a 2014 study in *Molecular Psychiatry*, Simone Kühn's team had adults play *Super Mario 64* for at least 30 minutes a day for two months. Compared with controls, players showed more gray matter in the right hippocampus, part of the prefrontal cortex and the cerebellum, regions tied to navigation, planning and movement. It's a neat result from a small group, and nobody should read it as proof that Mario grows your brain in any lasting, general way.
The case against: the far-transfer problem

Now the other camp. Also in 2018, also in *Psychological Bulletin*, Giovanni Sala, Kaan Tatlidil and Fernand Gobet published a larger and more skeptical set of meta-analyses. They looked at three things: whether game skill correlates with cognitive ability, whether players differ from non-players, and whether game training improves cognition. Across hundreds of effect sizes they found small or null effects, and concluded there was no good evidence that playing games causes better general thinking.

How can two teams look at the same field and disagree? Mostly by asking different questions. Bavelier's group focuses narrowly on fast action games and specific skills like attention. Sala and Gobet ask the bigger question that brain-training companies sell: does practice in one thing make you smarter at unrelated things? That's called **far transfer**, and the evidence for it is poor across the board. Chess, music lessons and working-memory apps all tend to fail the same test. You get better at what you practice and at things very close to it.

Bavelier's side has a plausible answer for why action games might be special. A good shooter forces you to keep switching between a narrow focus (the enemy in your crosshair) and a wide one (the flank, the minimap, the sound of footsteps), under time pressure, with outcomes you can't predict. Puzzle games and slower genres rarely demand that mix. If any game trains attention as a general skill, it would be this kind. The skeptics reply that a good story is not the same as a large, reliable effect, and that's a fair hit too.

blocks.title: Two camps, one literature

left.head: Bavelier and colleagues
items: Focus on action games specifically
Measure attention, perception, spatial skill
Find small-to-medium gains, including in training studies
Admit publication bias inflates published effects

right.head: Sala, Tatlidil and Gobet
items: Pool many genres and cognitive tests
Ask about general cognitive ability
Find small or null effects overall
Argue far transfer basically doesn't happen

blocks.text: The fair reading: fast, chaotic games probably sharpen some visual and attention skills by a modest amount, and those gains may matter in tasks that look a lot like games, like scanning busy displays. They don't raise your IQ, make you a better student, or replace studying. If you want to get better at qualifying on a new watchstation, flash cards and walking the plant beat *Apex* every time.
The violence fight that fizzled

For a generation, the loudest question about games was whether violent ones make kids aggressive. In 2010, a meta-analysis led by Craig Anderson concluded that violent games were a causal risk factor for aggressive behavior, thoughts and feelings, and for reduced empathy. That paper shaped policy debates and courtroom arguments for years.

Then the field changed how it did science. Researchers began pre-registering their predictions and analyses before seeing the data, which makes it much harder to find effects by fiddling. Re-analyses also found that many lab measures of 'aggression,' such as how much hot sauce someone gives a stranger, were used inconsistently from study to study. Christopher Ferguson's 2015 meta-analysis of 101 studies on children and teens found almost nothing, and later work on long-term studies agreed.

blocks.title: Violent games and youth aggression: correlations found
blocks.note: An r of 0.06 means game exposure accounts for less than half a percent of the variation in aggression.
blocks.source: Ferguson, Perspectives on Psychological Science, 2015; Drummond, Sauer & Ferguson, Royal Society Open Science, 2020

blocks.text: The 2020 analysis by Aaron Drummond, James Sauer and Ferguson pooled 28 long-term samples covering about 21,000 young people. The overall link was tiny, it got *smaller* over longer follow-ups rather than building up, and the best-designed studies were statistically indistinguishable from zero. A pre-registered 2019 study of 1,004 British 14- and 15-year-olds by Andrew Przybylski and Netta Weinstein, using parents' reports of aggression, also found no link and no tipping point at high play levels.

Some researchers still argue for small real effects, and 'tiny' is not quite 'zero.' But the scary version of the claim, that shooters turn ordinary kids violent, has not survived better methods. That arc, from confident alarm to near-null once studies got stricter, is a pattern worth remembering. It has happened in other corners of psychology too.
Hours don't predict how you feel. Reasons do.

The newest research skips self-reported playtime, which people estimate badly, and uses real data from game companies. In a 2022 study, Matti Vuorre, Przybylski and colleagues linked six weeks of actual play logs from 38,935 players, supplied by seven publishers, with repeated well-being surveys. They found little to no evidence that time spent playing changed how people felt, in either direction.

What did matter was *why* people played. Players who felt they played because they wanted to tended to be doing better than those who felt pushed to play, by guilt, pressure or obligation. A 2025 follow-up with 703 adult Nintendo Switch players, covering more than 140,000 hours of play, found the same: hours didn't predict well-being, but how well gaming fit into the rest of someone's life did.

Big studies of kids point the same way with a twist. Using data from the US ABCD study, Bader Chaarani's team found in 2022 that 9- and 10-year-olds who gamed 21 or more hours a week did slightly better on fMRI tasks of impulse control and working memory than kids who never played. It's an association, not proof of cause, and a later preprint from the same team linked very heavy play (3 or more hours a day) with more attention problems. Same game, different dose, different life around it.
Gaming disorder is real, rare and still argued over

In 2019 the World Health Assembly adopted the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases, which took effect in January 2022 and includes **gaming disorder**. The WHO's definition has three parts: impaired control over gaming, gaming taking priority over other interests and daily activities, and continuing despite clear negative consequences. The pattern has to cause significant problems in work, school, family or social life, and normally be visible for at least 12 months. Playing a lot, on its own, is not the definition.

items.label: Pooled global prevalence of gaming disorder across 53 studies
Estimate using only the best-sampled studies
Share of the variation between studies explained by which questionnaire was used

blocks.source: Stevens et al., Australian and New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry, 2021

blocks.text: That last number is the tell. How common gaming disorder appears depends heavily on which survey researchers use and where they set the cutoff. Przybylski's group, using the American Psychiatric Association's draft criteria in four pre-registered surveys of nearly 19,000 people, estimated that only 0.3% to 1% of the population might qualify. In 2017, a group of more than two dozen scholars published an open letter urging the WHO not to add the diagnosis yet, warning of moral panic and false positives. Supporters answered that people with real problems needed a recognized path to treatment. Both points can be true.

One of the most practical findings comes from a 2026 study of 1,149 male gamers aged 18 to 35 who played at least 12 hours a week. The researchers split playtime into two buckets. **Green Box** hours were played in genuine free time. **Red Box** hours were played instead of doing something you were responsible for. Red Box hours identified gaming disorder far better than total weekly hours did.

blocks.title: The question that matters more than 'how many hours?'

left.head: Green Box hours
items: Played in real free time
Chores, sleep, study and people already handled
Chosen because you want to
Mostly harmless, often good

right.head: Red Box hours
items: Played instead of something you owed
Sleep, quals, workouts or calls pushed back
Played to escape, not to enjoy
The stronger warning sign

blocks.text: A useful self-check after a long session: were those Green Box hours or Red Box hours? If your sleep, quals or relationships keep losing to the game, that's worth taking seriously and talking to a corpsman or counselor about, whatever the total hours.
How to read the next headline

Put the whole literature together and a fairly calm picture appears. Fast action games probably give modest, specific boosts to attention and spatial skills. They don't make you generally smarter. Violent content doesn't meaningfully drive real-world aggression. Average playtime has little effect on mood, while the reasons you play and what the play displaces matter a lot. A small minority of players develop a genuine problem, and researchers still argue about how best to define and count it.

The bigger lesson is about evidence. Notice how many striking early findings came from small samples, how meta-analyses kept shrinking them, and how pre-registration and real telemetry pushed estimates toward zero. When you see a headline that games, social media or anything else 'rewires your brain,' ask three questions: was it a comparison or a real experiment, how many people were in it, and has anyone replicated it with the analysis locked in first?

For someone building games, there's a design lesson too. The healthiest play, according to this research, is play people choose freely and that fits around their lives. Games that lean on guilt, streak anxiety or fear of missing out may raise daily logins while pushing players into exactly the motivation pattern linked with feeling worse. The best long-term retention probably comes from being a game people are glad they played, not one they feel they owe.

takeaways: Action games give modest, specific attention and spatial gains: about g = 0.3 in training studies, smaller than the gamer vs non-gamer gap suggests.
There's little evidence games make you generally smarter. Far transfer is weak for nearly all kinds of brain training.
Better-designed studies find violent games have almost no link to youth aggression (r near 0.01 to 0.06).
Hours played barely predict well-being; why you play and what it replaces matter more. Watch your Red Box hours.
Gaming disorder (WHO ICD-11) means impaired control and real harm, usually for 12 months, not just playing a lot.
