title: Fun Is a Pattern You Haven't Finished Learning
dek: Why tic-tac-toe dies by age eight, why Halo's most famous design rule gets quoted backwards, and how to find the loop a game lives or dies on.

blocks.text: Think back to the first time you played tic-tac-toe. For a few weeks it was a real game. You lost, you won, you set traps for your cousin. Then one day you noticed that if both players are paying attention, nobody ever wins. Every game ends in a draw. And just like that, it stopped being fun. Nothing about the game changed. *You* changed.

That small childhood moment holds the best working definition of fun that game designers have. In his 2004 book *A Theory of Fun for Game Design*, Raph Koster, lead designer of *Ultima Online*, argued that fun is what learning feels like from the inside. Your brain is a pattern-eating machine. While it is chewing on a pattern it hasn't cracked yet, it rewards you. Once the pattern is solved, the reward stops and you feel bored. Tic-tac-toe didn't get worse. You finished it.
If that's true, then a game is not a pile of content. It is a supply of patterns, served at a speed your brain can digest. Everything else in this article follows from that one idea.
Boredom and frustration are the same failure

Koster's framing explains both ways games die. If the patterns are too simple, you solve them fast and the game goes stale. That's tic-tac-toe, and it's also the tenth hour of a mobile game where you tap the same button for slightly bigger numbers. If the patterns are too complex or too random to read, your brain never gets a foothold. That feels like noise, and noise feels like frustration. Either way the learning stops, and so does the fun.

This is why grinding feels hollow even when the rewards keep coming. Numbers going up is not a pattern to learn. A new enemy that punishes your favorite strategy *is* one. The first makes you feel busy. The second makes you feel smart, and feeling smart is the thing you actually came for.

It also explains why skilled play stays fun for years in games like Valorant or Rainbow Six Siege. The core rules are simple, but the other players are a pattern generator that never runs dry. Every opponent brings new habits to read and exploit. A competitive shooter keeps feeding you fresh patterns for free, which is a big part of why the genre has such staying power.
Koster's test for any game: what is the player learning right now? If you can't answer, they are either bored or lost.
Thirty seconds of fun, misquoted

The most repeated line in shooter design comes from Bungie and the original *Halo*. Designer Jaime Griesemer is credited with the idea that Halo was built around about thirty seconds of fun repeated over and over. For years people have used it to argue that you only need one great short loop and you can stamp it out across a whole game.

Griesemer has said that reading is backwards. In a 2011 interview he explained that the point was the opposite: no thirty-second stretch of Halo ever repeats exactly, because the missions keep changing the weapons, vehicles, enemies and terrain around you. He described the combat as a three-second loop inside a thirty-second loop inside a three-minute loop, with the outer layers constantly shifting. The idea grew out of a 2002 talk he gave with Bungie programmer Chris Butcher, where the enemy AI made decisions on a scale of seconds and mission scripting worked on a scale of minutes.

blocks.title: Halo's nested loops, as Griesemer described them
items: About 3 seconds: see an enemy, aim, shoot, take cover. The verb itself must feel good.
About 30 seconds: one encounter. Read the enemy mix, pick a weapon, flank or hold.
About 3 minutes: one stretch of the mission. New terrain, new vehicles, new enemy types.
Whole mission and campaign: the context keeps changing, so the 30-second fight never plays the same way twice.

blocks.text: Put Koster and Griesemer together and you get a powerful rule. The tiny loop must feel good on its own, but the fun lasts because the bigger loops keep handing that tiny loop new problems. The verb stays the same. The pattern it is applied to keeps changing. That's how a game teaches you for twenty hours using the same two buttons.

blocks.title: Two ways to repeat a loop

left.head: Repetition (grind)
items: Same action, same situation, bigger numbers
Learning stops early; rewards have to carry everything
Players feel busy, then bored
Content has to be added constantly to keep people

right.head: Variation (the Halo idea)
items: Same action, new situation each time
Each change forces a small new decision
Players feel clever and in control
A few systems combine into many situations

blocks.text: What players actually need from you

Psychology has a complementary answer to the question of why games pull us in. Self-determination theory, developed by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, says people are driven by three basic needs: **competence** (feeling effective), **autonomy** (feeling that your choices are your own) and **relatedness** (feeling connected to other people). In 2006, Ryan, Scott Rigby and Andrew Przybylski published a set of studies in *Motivation and Emotion* applying this to video games. Across their studies, players who felt more competent and more autonomous while playing reported enjoying the game more and wanting to keep playing.

That maps neatly onto design choices. Competence comes from clear feedback and fair challenge, so you can feel yourself getting better. Autonomy comes from meaningful choices: which route, which loadout, which card. Relatedness comes from squads, guilds, trading and even just seeing other players in the world. A game that delivers all three doesn't need to bribe you with daily login rewards to bring you back.

The theory also predicts a quieter failure. When a game leans too hard on outside rewards, like streak bonuses, timed events and loot for logging in, it can start to feel like a job. The rewards are not evil, but they cannot stand in for the three needs. If the moment-to-moment play does not make you feel capable, free and connected, rewards only delay the day you uninstall.

Relatedness deserves special attention for anyone building a multiplayer game. Playing beside a friend who is trying as hard as you are changes the experience completely, and many players will put up with a mediocre game for years because it is where their group meets. That is a huge advantage, but it cuts both ways: if your game makes it awkward to play together, you lose the strongest glue there is.

The difficulty-versus-skill balance that keeps you absorbed is its own deep topic, covered in the library's piece on flow. The short version: competence only feels good when the challenge is close to the edge of what you can do. Too far below and there is nothing to learn. Too far above and it is just noise again.
Not everyone is chasing the same fun

One more wrinkle: there is no single kind of fun. In a 2004 paper that is still assigned in game design courses, Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc and Robert Zubek laid out the MDA framework: designers build **mechanics** (the rules), which produce **dynamics** (what happens when people play), which create **aesthetics** (what the player feels). They listed eight kinds of feeling a game might aim for, including challenge, discovery, fellowship, fantasy, narrative and expression.

MDA also points out a trap. Designers start from the mechanics and work outward, but players experience the game from the other end: they feel the aesthetics first and only later, if ever, notice the rules. So when a playtester says your game is boring, they are reporting a feeling. Your job is to trace that feeling backward through the dynamics to the rule that caused it.

Large-scale survey data backs up how differently people play. The analytics firm Quantic Foundry has had hundreds of thousands of gamers take its Gamer Motivation Profile, which measures twelve motivations such as competition, strategy, completion, discovery and story. When it looked at how those motivations change with age, competition fell faster than any other.

items.label: Gamers in Quantic Foundry's age analysis of competition
Competition's rank among 12 motivations for decline with age
Correlation of age with competition appeal (male gamers)

blocks.source: Quantic Foundry, The Appeal of Competition, 2016

blocks.text: The same data showed the decline was steepest between the early teens and the mid-thirties, and that age explained more than twice as much of the difference in competition appeal as gender did. In plain terms, the ranked grinder you were at fifteen is not the player you will be at thirty, and a game built for one of those people may bore the other. The data comes from a self-selected online survey, so treat it as a strong pattern rather than a census, but the lesson for a designer is sharp: decide whose fun you are building.
The same idea in games you already know

Once you see the pattern, you find it everywhere. *Minecraft*'s three-second verb is breaking and placing a block. On its own that is barely a game. What keeps it alive is how the world keeps changing the question: night falls and you suddenly need shelter, a cave opens and you need light, a new material appears and your old tools look weak, the Nether rewrites the rules of where it is safe to stand. The verb never changes. The problem it solves changes every few minutes.

*Fortnite* bolted two verbs together, shooting and building, and the storm circle forces a new context every couple of minutes. Each closing ring changes the terrain you are fighting on, the players left near you and how much material you can afford to spend. Apex does something similar with legends: the gunplay is shared, but each character's kit changes what a good thirty seconds looks like for the squad.

Now notice what happens when a game runs out of context changes. Most players have had the experience of a survival or building game that is gripping for a week and then quietly dies once the base is finished and every threat is handled. Nothing broke. The game simply stopped asking new questions, and the brain, true to Koster's theory, got bored and left.
Finding the loop your game lives on
If you are building a game, all of this boils down to a few practical questions you can test today, long before you have art, menus or a store.

items: **Name the 3-second verb.** Jump, shoot, place, swing, launch. Build it in a gray box with no art. If it is not satisfying to do fifty times in a row, nothing on top will save it.
**Design the 30-second problem.** What situation forces the player to use that verb in a slightly new way? An obstacle, an enemy, a timer, another player.
**Plan how the context changes.** List at least five ways the outer loop can twist the inner one: new hazards, new tools, new goals, new terrain.
**Watch for the moment learning stops.** In playtests, the instant a player's face goes blank is the instant the pattern ran out. That is where your next new idea needs to land.
**Pick your player.** A competition-hungry fifteen-year-old and a story-loving adult want different things. Choose, then design for them on purpose.

blocks.text: Many Roblox hits are good examples of the first two steps done well. The verb is dead simple, the very first minute is satisfying, and the game keeps handing that verb a slightly harder or stranger problem. Where many of them fall short is the third step. When the context stops changing, players drift, no matter how many cosmetic rewards are layered on top.

There's a useful self-check hiding in Koster's theory, too. When you design, you are also a player of your own game, and you will get bored of it long before anyone else does because you know every pattern. That boredom is not proof the game is bad. Your fresh testers are the only reliable judge of whether the patterns still have something to teach.
A good game is a teacher that never runs out of lessons and never lectures. The verb is the pencil. The changing situations are the lessons.

So the next time a game grabs you for a whole weekend, try asking what it's teaching you, and how it keeps changing the question right before you master the answer. Once you see that, you'll start noticing the exact moment every game you play stops being fun. Usually it's the moment it ran out of new questions.

takeaways: Fun is the feeling of learning a pattern. Boredom means the pattern is solved; frustration means it can't be read.
Halo's '30 seconds of fun' meant a great short loop placed in constantly changing contexts, not one loop repeated forever.
Players need competence, autonomy and relatedness. Fair feedback, real choices and other people beat bribes like login rewards.
Different players want different fun, and the appeal of competition drops more with age than any other motivation measured.
Prototype the 3-second verb with no art first. If it isn't satisfying fifty times in a row, fix that before anything else.

title: The Day That Wasn't Supposed to Happen
dek: The events that shape markets, careers and history are the ones our models call impossible. Black swans, fat tails, and how to live in a world you can't forecast.

blocks.text: Picture a turkey on a farm. Every morning a friendly human shows up with food. After a hundred days the turkey has a theory: humans are generous and the world is safe. After a thousand days the theory is rock solid, backed by a thousand data points and zero exceptions. The turkey's confidence peaks on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving.

The writer and former options trader Nassim Nicholas Taleb uses this bird (borrowed from Bertrand Russell, who told a similar story about a chicken) to open his 2007 book *The Black Swan*. The point is not that turkeys are dumb. The turkey did everything a good statistician is taught to do. It gathered data, found a stable pattern and extrapolated. The problem was that the single most important event in its life was, by construction, absent from its data.

Notice that the event was a catastrophe only from the turkey's point of view. For the farmer it was the plan all along. A Black Swan is relative to what you know, which means the most useful question is not "what is going to happen?" but "what is missing from my picture?"

That is the uncomfortable idea at the center of this article. In some parts of life, the past is a decent guide to the future. In others, the past is worse than useless, because it hands you confidence right before the thing that matters most.
Where the name comes from

For centuries, Europeans used the phrase *black swan* to mean something that could not exist. The Roman poet Juvenal used it as a figure of speech for an impossibly rare thing. Every swan anyone had ever seen was white, so "all swans are white" looked like as safe a fact as you could get. Then in 1697 the Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh sailed into a river in what is now Western Australia and found black swans paddling around. Thousands of years of confirming observations were overturned by one sighting.

Taleb's definition of a Black Swan event has three parts. It is an outlier, outside the range of what past experience suggested. It carries an extreme impact. And afterward, people cook up explanations that make it look predictable all along. That third part is sneaky. The story we tell after the fact ("the warning signs were everywhere") makes us think we would spot the next one, which is exactly why we won't.

There is a second trap, which Taleb calls silent evidence. He retells an old story from Cicero: an atheist named Diagoras is shown paintings of sailors who prayed during a storm and survived, offered as proof that prayer works. Diagoras asks where the paintings are of the sailors who prayed and drowned. The dead don't commission portraits. Every successful founder, streamer and trader you hear about is a painted survivor, and the graveyard of people who did the same things and failed is invisible. That makes risky paths look safer, and success look more like a recipe, than it really is.
Two kinds of randomness

Taleb's most useful idea is a split between two kinds of worlds, which he calls Mediocristan and Extremistan. Imagine putting 1,000 random people in a stadium and measuring their height. Now add the tallest person who has ever lived. The average barely moves. No single person can dominate the total, because human height has hard physical limits.

Now measure the same 1,000 people's net worth and add the richest person on Earth. Suddenly one person holds almost all of the stadium's wealth, and the average becomes meaningless. That is Extremistan: a world where one observation can outweigh all the others combined. Book sales, YouTube views, startup returns, war casualties, pandemics, earthquakes and stock market crashes all live there.

blocks.title: Mediocristan vs Extremistan

left.head: Mediocristan
items: Height, weight, calories eaten, hourly pay
No single case moves the total much
The bell curve works well
The past is a decent guide
Averages tell you something real

right.head: Extremistan
items: Wealth, views, book sales, crashes, quakes
One case can outweigh all others combined
Bell curve badly underestimates extremes
The biggest event may not be in your data yet
Averages can be dominated by one outlier

blocks.text: The technical term for Extremistan is a *fat-tailed* distribution. On a bell curve, the odds of an extreme value shrink so fast that anything far from the average is effectively impossible. In a fat-tailed world, the odds shrink much more slowly, so huge events are rare but not absurdly rare. If you use a bell curve to model a fat-tailed world, you will feel safe most of the time and be wrong exactly when it counts.
What real data look like

You can test this yourself. The Nasdaq Composite stock index has daily closing prices going back to February 1971. Over the 14,052 trading days through October 2026, the typical daily move (one standard deviation) was about 1.3 percent. If daily returns followed a bell curve, a move of four standard deviations, about 5 percent, should show up roughly once in the whole 55-year record. A move of five standard deviations should show up about once every 7,000 years.

blocks.title: Nasdaq days with moves bigger than...
blocks.note: A bell curve would expect about 38, 0.9, 0.008 and effectively zero days for 3, 4, 5 and 6+ std devs.
blocks.source: Calculated: daily log returns from FRED series NASDAQCOM, Feb 1971 to Oct 2026

blocks.text: Instead there were 95 days beyond four standard deviations and 43 beyond five. Two days went past ten: the 12.3 percent crash on March 16, 2020, as COVID shut the world down, and a 14.2 percent jump on January 3, 2001, when the Federal Reserve made a surprise rate cut. Under a bell curve, a single ten-sigma day should not happen in a span vastly longer than the age of the universe. The Nasdaq had two in 55 years.

Professionals have been burned by this exact mistake. In August 2007, as the financial crisis began, Goldman Sachs' finance chief David Viniar told the *Financial Times* that the firm was seeing "25-standard deviation moves, several days in a row." In a 2009 speech, Andrew Haldane of the Bank of England worked out that under a normal distribution, even a 7.26-sigma daily loss should happen about once in the age of the universe. A 25-sigma day was beyond silly. His conclusion was blunt: the simpler explanation is that the model was wrong.

Stock markets are not a special case. The U.S. Geological Survey catalog lists 44,393 earthquakes of magnitude 5 or larger worldwide from 2000 through 2024. Because each step up in magnitude means about 32 times more energy, the two biggest (Sumatra in 2004 and Japan in 2011) released more energy than all 44,366 quakes below magnitude 8 combined. A seismologist who studied only the first decade of the record would have been working from a sample that was missing the event that would dwarf it.

items.label: Earthquakes of magnitude 5+ worldwide, 2000 to 2024
Quakes (Sumatra 2004, Japan 2011) that released about 39% of their total energy

blocks.source: USGS earthquake catalog; energy share calculated using energy proportional to 10^(1.5 x magnitude)

blocks.text: A handful of days decide everything

Fat tails don't only bring disasters. They also mean that most of the gains arrive in a few bursts. If you had put $100 into the Nasdaq in 1971 and held it, ignoring dividends, it would have grown to about $25,400 by late 2026. Now run the same history but delete the 10 best days, which make up less than a tenth of one percent of all trading days. You end with about $9,800. Delete the best 50 days and you end with about $900.

blocks.title: $100 in the Nasdaq, 1971 to 2026
blocks.note: Price only, no dividends. Out of 14,052 trading days.
blocks.source: Calculated from FRED series NASDAQCOM

blocks.text: Before you take the wrong lesson from that chart: the best days tend to cluster right next to the worst days, in the middle of panics. Someone who tried to dodge the crashes would very likely have missed the rebounds too. The real lesson is about concentration. In Extremistan, outcomes are decided by a small number of moments you cannot see coming, so a strategy that requires you to predict them is a strategy that fails.

The same shape shows up in creative work. On most YouTube channels, a few videos bring in the bulk of all views. Most games on a platform like Roblox get almost no players while a tiny number get nearly all of them. A salary is Mediocristan: one day of work is worth about the same as the next. A channel, a game or a business is Extremistan: hundreds of days may produce almost nothing, and one upload or update can change everything.

This changes how you should read your own results. In Mediocristan, a bad month means you did something wrong. In Extremistan, ten flat uploads in a row are what the distribution predicts even if you are doing everything right, because the payoff is concentrated in a few hits you haven't landed yet. The danger is quitting on the turkey's logic in reverse: concluding from a long run of nothing that nothing is coming. Sometimes that is the correct conclusion. The trick is to judge whether your process is improving, not whether the tail has shown up yet.
The case against Taleb

Taleb's ideas are powerful, but they deserve pushback, and serious people have pushed. The first objection is that "black swan" has become a label people slap on anything that hurt them. Banks that loaded up on risk called 2008 a black swan, when plenty of people had warned about it. If every bad surprise counts, the concept explains everything and therefore nothing. Taleb himself argued that COVID was not a black swan at all but a *white swan*, a risk that epidemiologists had warned about for years.

The second objection is that prediction is not hopeless. Weather forecasts are dramatically better than they were a few decades ago. The psychologist Philip Tetlock found that some people, whom he called superforecasters, consistently beat others at predicting world events over horizons of months to a year. Fat tails do not make the future unknowable, they make certain kinds of forecasts unreliable, especially precise forecasts about the size and timing of extremes.

The third objection is that fat tails can be measured. Seismologists have known for decades that earthquake counts follow a regular pattern across magnitudes. Insurers price hurricane and earthquake risk using models built on exactly those patterns. Taleb's own term for this middle ground is a *gray swan*: an extreme event you can anticipate in general, even if not its date. The honest version of his argument is narrower than the slogan. It says: in fat-tailed domains, don't trust any model that implies the worst case is impossible.
How to live in Extremistan

If you can't predict black swans, you can still arrange your life so they hurt less and help more. Engineers already think this way. A reactor plant is not designed around the most likely day; it is designed with margins, redundant systems and procedures for casualties nobody expects to see. The design question is not "what will happen?" but "what happens to us if the unlikely thing does?"

blocks.title: Rules for a fat-tailed world
items: Ask what you'd lose in the worst case, not the likely case, and refuse bets that can wipe you out.
Keep slack: savings, spare time, backup skills. Slack is what lets you survive a bad tail.
Make many small bets with capped downside and open-ended upside, like videos, prototypes or applications.
Distrust smooth track records in risky areas. A thousand good days can be the turkey's thousand days.
Judge decisions by their process, since outcomes in Extremistan are mostly luck in the short run.

blocks.text: Taleb goes one step further with an idea he calls antifragility. Some things merely survive shocks; others get stronger from them. Muscles grow from the stress of lifting. A crew that drills casualties until the responses are automatic handles the real one better. A creator who puts out lots of small experiments learns something from every flop. The goal is not to predict the storm but to become the kind of system that the storm improves.

Taleb's preferred structure is what he calls a barbell: keep most of your resources extremely safe, and put a small slice into things with unlimited upside. A steady paycheck and no debt on one end; a game, a channel or a side business on the other. The safe end means a bad swan can't ruin you. The risky end means a good swan has somewhere to land.
The turkey's mistake was not ignorance. It was confidence built from data that couldn't contain the event that mattered. Ask of any track record: what would it look like right before it broke?

Some questions to sit with. What in your life is Mediocristan, where effort turns into results at a steady rate, and what is Extremistan, where nearly all the payoff comes from a few rare hits? Which of your plans quietly assume that the worst case won't happen? And if your next big break comes from one unpredictable moment, what are you doing now to make sure you are in the room when it arrives?

takeaways: In Mediocristan (height, pay) no single case matters much; in Extremistan (wealth, views, crashes) one event can outweigh all others.
Real markets are wildly fat-tailed: the Nasdaq had 43 days beyond five standard deviations where a bell curve expects almost none.
In fat-tailed domains, a long smooth track record is not proof of safety.
Don't try to predict black swans; avoid bets that can ruin you and keep exposure to rare big wins.
Black swan is often misused: many disasters were foreseeable gray or white swans that people chose to ignore.

title: Don't Tear Down the Fence Yet
dek: Chesterton's fence says you shouldn't remove something until you know why it's there. A forgotten step in cooking corn shows what happens when nobody asks.

blocks.text: For thousands of years, people in Mexico and Central America cooked their corn in a strange way. Before grinding it, they soaked and simmered the kernels in water mixed with lime or wood ash, an alkaline bath that loosened the hulls. It was extra work, and if you'd asked why, most cooks would have said that's just how it's done. The process is called nixtamalization, and it's why tortillas taste like tortillas.

When corn crossed the Atlantic and later spread through the American South, it traveled without that step. Corn was cheap and filled bellies. The lime bath looked like a quaint local habit, so nobody bothered with it. What nobody knew was that the alkali does something chemical: it makes the niacin in corn usable by the human body. Strip out the ritual and a diet built mostly on corn becomes a slow-motion deficiency.

The disease that followed was pellagra, remembered for its grim list of symptoms: rashes, diarrhea, dementia and eventually death. It was first reported in the United States in 1902 and soon reached epidemic levels among the rural poor of the South. Between 1900 and 1940, historians estimate, at least 100,000 people in the southern states died of it.

items.label: Pellagra deaths in the southern US, 1900–1940
Year pellagra was first reported in the United States

blocks.source: Marks, J Hist Med Allied Sci, 2003; Rajakumar, Southern Medical Journal, 2000

blocks.text: It would be too neat to blame all of that on one skipped step. Pellagra in the South was rooted in poverty and a monotonous diet of cornmeal, molasses and fatback, as the public-health doctor Joseph Goldberger showed. But the old processing was one of the things that had made heavy corn diets safe where corn came from. Generations of cooks had been carrying a piece of nutritional science that nobody could explain, and the people who dropped it had no idea what they were throwing away.
The fence in the road

In 1929 the English writer G. K. Chesterton put this problem in the form of a parable. Imagine a fence or a gate standing across a road, he wrote. A certain kind of reformer walks up to it, sees no use for it, and proposes to clear it away. The wiser reformer answers that if you can't see what it's for, you certainly may not remove it. Go and find out why it's there. Come back when you can explain its purpose, and then we can talk about taking it down.
Go away and think.
blocks.by: G. K. Chesterton, The Thing, 1929

blocks.text: That's **Chesterton's fence**: don't remove something until you understand why it was put there. Notice what the principle does *not* say. It doesn't say old things are sacred or that fences should stay forever. It says the burden of understanding falls on the person who wants to change things. Fences don't grow on their own. Somebody spent time and money building this one, and they probably had a reason, even if the reason turns out to be bad or out of date.

The idea has traveled far beyond Chesterton's essay. According to Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, a young John F. Kennedy jotted a version of it in a notebook in 1945. Engineers, doctors, managers and programmers all reinvent it, usually right after someone tears down a fence and finds out the hard way what it was holding back.

blocks.title: Corn, lime and a forgotten reason
items: Ancient
Mesoamerican cooks soak corn in lime or ash before grinding it
Pellagra described in Europe, where corn arrived without the lime step
Pellagra first reported in the US; epidemics follow across the South
Joseph Goldberger concludes within months that the cause is diet
At least 100,000 deaths from pellagra in the southern states
Researchers in Science link traditional maize processing to nutrition

blocks.text: Why old habits can be smarter than the people who follow them

The corn story points at something deep. Traditions often work even when nobody can say why. The anthropologist Joseph Henrich argues in *The Secret of Our Success* that much of human survival has rested on this kind of knowledge: practices refined across generations by trial, error and copying the people who were doing well, long before anyone understood the mechanism.

His favorite example is cassava, also called manioc, a starchy root that's a staple for hundreds of millions of people. Bitter varieties contain compounds that release cyanide. Traditional preparation in places where it's eaten involves long, tedious steps such as grating, soaking and fermenting. Cut those steps short and you don't drop dead at dinner. Instead, the damage builds quietly. Medical researchers have linked outbreaks of konzo, a permanent paralysis of the legs seen in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, to diets that rely on cassava that wasn't processed enough.

That delay is the key. When a shortcut kills you instantly, people learn fast. When it takes years, nobody can connect cause and effect within a single lifetime. A rule that protects against slow harm will always look pointless to the person following it, because the disaster it prevents never shows up. The fence is invisible precisely because it works.

Of course, tradition also preserves nonsense. Bloodletting was standard medicine in Europe for well over a thousand years and almost certainly killed far more patients than it helped. Cultural evolution is good at keeping practices that pay off visibly and reliably, and much worse at weeding out practices whose harm is hidden or blamed on something else. So the existence of a tradition is a clue, not a verdict. It tells you there may be a reason. It doesn't tell you the reason is good.

blocks.title: Two kinds of fence

left.head: Load-bearing fence
items: Prevents a harm you never see because it works
Reason is slow, rare or long-forgotten
Removing it looks harmless for a while
Example: lime-soaked corn, cassava processing

right.head: Vestigial fence
items: Built for a problem that no longer exists
Reason can be found and is clearly outdated
Removing it frees up time or money
Example: a step kept for equipment you replaced

blocks.text: Fences in code

If you write software, you meet Chesterton's fence weekly. You open an old script, find a strange check or a weird delay, and think: this is garbage, delete it. Sometimes you're right. Often that ugly line is a bug fix for some edge case that took somebody a whole weekend to track down.

In 2000 the programmer Joel Spolsky wrote a famous essay about Netscape, which had decided to throw away its web browser code and rewrite it from scratch. Nearly three years passed between major releases while the company's market share fell apart. Spolsky's argument was that old code looks messy because it's full of hard-won knowledge. Each odd-looking patch is a fence somebody built after getting burned. When you rewrite from zero, you throw all of that knowledge away and get to rediscover every bug yourself.

Building a game makes this vivid. Say a script spawns a player half a second late, and the delay looks like sloppiness. You delete it. Everything seems fine until players on slow connections start falling through the map before the world finishes loading. Somebody had already learned that lesson once. They just didn't write it down, so you paid for it again.

The practical fix is cheap. Before deleting something you don't understand, check its history: who added it, when, and with what note. And when you build a fence yourself, leave a sign on it. A one-line comment explaining *why* is the difference between a fence the next person respects and one they bulldoze. The same goes for any procedure. People who work in dangerous jobs often say their rules were written in blood. The trouble is that the blood isn't printed on the page, so a rule with its reason stripped off looks like pointless bureaucracy.
When the fence should come down

Chesterton's fence can be abused, and it's worth being honest about how. The first problem is that it can become an all-purpose excuse for never changing anything. Psychologists have documented a strong status quo bias: people prefer the current option largely because it's current. A principle that says 'understand before you change' can quietly turn into 'never change', especially in the mouths of people who benefit from the way things are.

The second problem is that sometimes the reason is known, and it's bad. Plenty of laws, rules and customs were built to exclude people or protect someone's turf. Understanding the original purpose of a fence is sometimes exactly what tells you to tear it down. Chesterton only asked for understanding. He didn't promise the answer would be flattering.

The third problem is that a lot of fences really are useless, and medicine offers a sobering measure of how many. In 2013 a team led by the physician Vinay Prasad went through ten years of studies in a top medical journal and pulled out every one that tested an already-established practice, something doctors were routinely doing. There were 363 of them. In 146 cases, the standard practice turned out to be no better than a lesser alternative or doing less. Only slightly fewer studies reaffirmed the existing practice.

blocks.title: When established medical practices were put to the test
blocks.note: Share of 363 studies (2001–2010) testing a standard of care; the rest were unclear
blocks.source: Prasad et al., Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 2013

blocks.text: Read that carefully. It doesn't mean four in ten medical practices are worthless; these were the practices someone thought worth testing, which skews toward doubtful ones. But it does mean that 'we've always done it this way' is weak evidence on its own. Many fences in medicine were built on reasoning that sounded right and was never checked. Chesterton's principle works best paired with a willingness to test. Understanding a fence's purpose tells you what it was *meant* to do. Only evidence tells you whether it does it.

The fourth problem is cost. Investigating every fence takes time, and some histories are simply lost. If you can't find out why something exists, you have to decide anyway. The smart move then is to estimate the downside. Removing an unexplained step from a game's menu flow is cheap to undo. Removing an unexplained step from a reactor procedure or a food safety rule is not. The less reversible and the more dangerous the system, the more respect an unexplained fence deserves.

This connects to a cousin idea, the Lindy effect: things that have survived a long time tend to keep surviving, because time has already tested them. Old fences have been stress-tested by decades of people wanting them gone. That doesn't make them right. It does make them worth a second look before you grab the bolt cutters.
How to treat a fence

blocks.title: Before you tear it down
items: Ask what problem this was built to solve, and who built it.
Look for the record: history, notes, incident reports, the oldest person who'd know.
If you find the reason, ask whether that problem still exists.
If you can't find it, judge the downside: how bad, how slow, how reversible?
Remove it in a way you can undo, and watch what happens.
Whatever you keep or build, write down why for the next person.

blocks.text: Step five matters more than it looks. A reversible test turns an argument into an experiment. Instead of debating whether a step is needed, you drop it in one small corner, for a limited time, with someone watching for the specific harm it was supposed to prevent. If nothing happens, you've learned something. If something does, you've learned it cheaply.

These steps scale from tiny to huge. They work on your own life, too. The habit your parents drilled into you that seemed pointless, the training rule you hated, the checklist item that never seems to matter: each one may be guarding against something you've just never seen happen. Or it may be junk. The point is to know which before you decide.

There's a neat symmetry with second-order thinking, which asks what will happen *after* you act. Chesterton's fence asks the same question backward in time: what was happening *before* someone acted, that made them put this here? Both are ways of seeing a system as something that responds, remembers and pushes back, rather than a blank board you can rearrange however you like.

The deepest lesson of the fence is humility about what you can't see. The world you walked into was built by people who solved problems you've never had to face, often because they solved them. The cook simmering corn in lime water didn't know the word niacin. She didn't need to. She needed to keep doing it, and the people who stopped needed to ask her why.

Chesterton's fence isn't a rule against change. It's a rule about the order of operations: understand first, then change. If you can't explain why something exists, you don't yet know what removing it will cost.

takeaways: Before removing a rule, step or habit, find out what problem it was built to solve.
Protections against slow or rare harms always look pointless, because the harm never shows up.
Knowing the reason can also tell you a fence should go; understanding isn't the same as keeping.
The less reversible and more dangerous the system, the more respect an unexplained fence deserves.
When you build a fence, write down why, so the next person doesn't have to guess.

title: The Math of Doing Good
dek: Effective altruism promised to calculate the most good you can do. Then its most famous donor went to prison. What the movement got right, what it got wrong, and what's worth keeping.

blocks.text: In the summer of 2022, the most famous effective altruist on the planet was a thirty-year-old in shorts and a wrinkled T-shirt who ran one of the world's biggest crypto exchanges. Sam Bankman-Fried said, in effect, that he was getting rich in order to give it away, and he had become a hero to a movement built on doing as much good as possible. His foundation had pledged huge sums to pandemic prevention, AI safety and other causes the movement cared about.

By November, his exchange, FTX, had collapsed. According to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, customer money had been secretly funneled to his trading firm, Alameda Research, and used for venture investments, lavish real estate and large political donations. A jury convicted him of fraud and money laundering in 2023, and in March 2024 he was sentenced to 25 years in prison.

For many people, that was the end of the story: effective altruism was a scam with a philosophy degree. But the idea at the movement's center is older than FTX, harder to dismiss, and still quietly moving hundreds of millions of dollars. To judge it fairly, you have to separate three things: the core idea, the movement that grew around it, and the man who became its most famous face.
The core idea

Effective altruism, or EA, starts from a claim most people agree with and then refuses to stop thinking about it. The philosopher Will MacAskill, one of its founders, defines it roughly as using evidence and careful reasoning to work out how to benefit others as much as possible, and then acting on what you find. The first half sounds like common sense. The second half is where it gets uncomfortable.

The intellectual seed was Peter Singer's 1972 essay *Famine, Affluence, and Morality*, with its drowning child in a shallow pond (covered in this library's article on utilitarianism). EA added something Singer's argument didn't have: measurement. If you're going to give money away, the obvious next question is which gift does the most good. And when people started checking, they found that the answer varied enormously.

In 2007 two young hedge-fund analysts, Holden Karnofsky and Elie Hassenfeld, founded GiveWell to evaluate charities the way analysts evaluate companies. Two years later the Oxford philosophers Toby Ord and Will MacAskill launched Giving What We Can, which asks members to pledge 10 percent of their income to the most effective charities they can find. The name 'effective altruism' was adopted around 2011.

GiveWell's estimates give a sense of the scale. Its top programs are cheap per unit: about $6 for an insecticide-treated bed net, about $7 to protect a child from malaria through a high-risk season with preventive medicine, about $2 for a year of vitamin A supplements. But not every net or pill saves a life, so the real cost per life saved is far higher. GiveWell estimates its recent top grants have cost a few thousand dollars per life.

blocks.title: GiveWell's estimated cost to save one life
blocks.note: Average estimated cost-effectiveness of GiveWell-directed funding, 2022–2024. Model estimates, not guarantees.
blocks.source: GiveWell, Top Charities page, accessed 2026

blocks.text: Those numbers are models, and GiveWell says plainly that they're uncertain and likely to rise over time. But compared with the typical charity, which never tries to estimate its impact at all, they represent a different way of thinking. The radical claim of EA isn't that you should give. It's that *where* you give may matter far more than *how much*.

items.label: People who have taken Giving What We Can's 10% pledge

blocks.source: Giving What We Can website, accessed November 2026

blocks.text: From bed nets to the far future

The same logic that led to malaria nets led to some much stranger places. If you care about all suffering equally, the reasoning goes, why stop at humans? Many EAs turned to animal welfare, especially the tens of billions of animals raised on factory farms each year. And if you care about all people equally regardless of *when* they live, then future generations, who could vastly outnumber everyone alive today, matter enormously.

That second step became **longtermism**, laid out in MacAskill's 2022 book *What We Owe the Future*. Its practical conclusion is that one of the best things you can do is reduce the risk of catastrophes that could end or permanently cripple civilization: engineered pandemics, nuclear war, and, increasingly, advanced artificial intelligence. A small reduction in the chance of extinction, multiplied by trillions of potential future lives, can outweigh almost anything else on paper.

The movement also popularized **earning to give**: instead of working directly for a charity, take a high-paying job and donate a large share. A good engineer at a bank, the argument went, might fund more good than the same person working at a nonprofit. Bankman-Fried was the most extreme example of where that idea could lead.

blocks.title: How a movement rose and stumbled
items: Peter Singer publishes the drowning-child argument
GiveWell founded to rank charities by evidence
Giving What We Can launches the 10% pledge
The name 'effective altruism' is adopted
MacAskill's longtermist book; FTX collapses in November
Bankman-Fried convicted of fraud and money laundering
Sentenced to 25 years in prison

blocks.text: What FTX exposed

When FTX fell, the damage spread well past Bankman-Fried. His foundation's grants evaporated, and researchers who had received FTX money found themselves under pressure to return it. Critics asked how a movement obsessed with careful reasoning had failed to notice that its biggest donor was running a fraud. Defenders replied, fairly, that sophisticated venture investors and regulators had missed it too.

The harder question was whether something in EA's thinking had made the fraud more likely. Bankman-Fried had talked publicly about being comfortable with enormous risks, the kind most people would never take, because expected-value math said the upside was worth it. If you believe your money will save thousands of lives, it becomes dangerously easy to tell yourself that bending a rule is a rounding error next to the good you'll do.

Leading EA thinkers had long warned against exactly that reasoning, and after the collapse they condemned the fraud and repeated the warnings loudly. But skeptics noted a pattern. A movement that treats ethics as an optimization problem, gives outsized influence to a few very rich donors and attracts young people who want to be heroes has some specific failure modes. The FTX scandal was not the only example people pointed to. In November 2023, board members at OpenAI with ties to the EA world briefly ousted the company's chief executive, a move that blew up within days and left many observers wondering who exactly the movement's influence answered to.
The serious critiques
Strip away the scandal and there are still real arguments against EA, made by serious people.

**It counts what's easy to count.** The philosopher Leif Wenar, writing in *Wired* in 2024, argued that charity evaluators tally the benefits of aid in precise decimals but rarely put numbers on the harms. Aid can strengthen corrupt local officials, pull health workers away from government clinics or attract violence. Malaria nets can be used for fishing. Wenar doesn't say aid never works. He says that an approach claiming to calculate the most good has to calculate the bad too.

GiveWell pushes back. It has called the evidence on fishing with nets limited and argued the concern largely doesn't apply to the nets its charities distribute, and its chief executive told *Wired* the group puts tens of thousands of hours of research into its recommendations each year. It also keeps a public page listing its own mistakes, which is more than most charities do. The disagreement is less about whether harms exist than about how hard an evaluator has to look for them.

**It treats symptoms, not causes.** The philosopher Amia Srinivasan argued in 2015 that EA mostly asks what an individual can do with spare money inside the world as it is, rather than asking why the world produces so much poverty in the first place. Political change, she suggested, is hard to measure, so a measurement-obsessed movement tends to skip it.

**It can be hijacked by tiny probabilities.** Longtermism multiplies small chances by astronomical numbers of future people. That kind of math can justify almost anything, and it uncomfortably resembles Pascal's famous wager about heaven and hell. Critics worry it lets a small group of people decide that speculative far-future risks matter more than children dying of malaria today.

**It asks too much, or the wrong thing.** If you take Singer's logic seriously, it's hard to justify spending money on anything beyond necessities. Most people find that impossible to live by, and some philosophers argue it ignores the legitimate pull of family, friends and personal projects.
The best replies
EA's defenders have answers to each of these, and some of them are strong.

On measurement, they argue that imperfect numbers beat no numbers. The realistic alternative to GiveWell isn't a perfect evaluator who tracks every side effect. It's the ordinary way people give: to whoever asked, whatever made them feel something, or a charity whose overhead looked low. On systemic change, they point out that political campaigns are even harder to evaluate, that their side effects can be bigger, and that many EA-funded groups do in fact work on policy.

On FTX, the strongest reply is also the simplest. An argument doesn't become false because a fraudster believed it. The drowning-child problem is exactly as hard as it was before 2022. A bed net that keeps a child alive works the same way regardless of who paid for it. The scandal is a real indictment of the movement's judgment about people and power, but it doesn't settle the philosophical question.

blocks.title: The argument in one view

left.head: The case for EA
items: Charities differ wildly in how much good they do
Measuring impact beats giving on feelings
A few thousand dollars can plausibly save a life
Future generations and animals count too

right.head: The case against
items: What's hard to measure gets ignored, including harms
Individual giving can dodge political causes
Tiny odds times huge stakes can justify anything
Big donors and hero complexes invite abuse

blocks.text: What to keep

The fairest verdict is probably that EA got one big thing right and several things dangerously wrong. The big thing is the question it forces you to ask: compared to what? Most giving, volunteering and even career choice runs on vibes, habit and whoever asked first. Asking whether your effort actually does good, and how much, is not cold. It's a form of taking the people you're trying to help seriously.
In practice, that question breaks into a few smaller ones you can ask about any cause, from a hometown food bank to a global health charity:

items: What exactly changes for someone because of this money or time?
How do they know? Is there evidence beyond stories and photos?
What would have happened without it?
What could go wrong, and is anyone checking?

blocks.text: None of these require a spreadsheet. They just require caring about the result more than the feeling of having helped.

The dangerous things are overconfidence in the numbers and a willingness to let a calculation override ordinary ethics. A spreadsheet can't see the side effects it wasn't built to track, and a person convinced they're saving the world is exactly the person who most needs someone to say no to them.

You don't need to join a movement to use its best idea. You can apply it to a donation, a volunteer weekend, or how you spend the next five years of your career. And you can borrow the lesson of its worst moment, too: any reasoning that ends with 'so it's fine to lie, cheat or hurt people this one time' has a bug in it somewhere, no matter how good the math looks.

Effective altruism's lasting contribution is a question, not an answer: if you're going to spend time or money trying to help, how do you know it's working? Ask it. Just don't let any answer talk you out of being honest.

takeaways: Charities can differ enormously in how much good a dollar does, so asking 'compared to what?' matters.
Cost-per-life figures are models with real uncertainty, not price tags.
Math that multiplies tiny odds by huge stakes can be made to justify almost anything.
Measuring benefits without measuring harms gives a lopsided picture.
Any plan that requires lying or cheating 'for the greater good' has a flaw, however good the numbers look.

title: Would You Plug In?
dek: In 1974 a Harvard philosopher offered readers a machine that could give them any life they wanted. Most refused. The reasons why say a lot about what a phone feed is really selling.

blocks.text: Here's the offer. Scientists have built a machine that can give you any experience you want, indistinguishable from the real thing. You can feel what it's like to win a world championship, build a company, fall in love, write a great novel, become the best player on the server. You float in a tank with electrodes on your brain, and while you're inside you won't know you're in a tank. It will all feel completely real.

You can program your next two years from a huge library of possible lives, then step out briefly to pick the next stretch. No pain unless you want some for contrast. No boredom. No setbacks unless they make the story better. Whatever you would most want to experience, you get to experience. Do you plug in for the rest of your life?

The philosopher Robert Nozick posed this question in 1974, in a few pages of his book *Anarchy, State, and Utopia*. He expected readers to say no, and most do. But the reasons people give, and the cracks that later research found in those reasons, make it one of the most useful thought experiments ever written. Especially now, when billions of people carry a small, crude version of the machine in their pockets.
Why the answer matters

Nozick was aiming at a specific target: *hedonism*, the idea that the only thing that's ultimately good for you is pleasant experience and the only thing bad is unpleasant experience. It's an old and serious view. Epicurus held a version of it, and so did Jeremy Bentham, the founder of utilitarianism. It sounds almost obviously right at first. What else could matter to you, except how your life feels from the inside?

The machine is a test. If hedonism is true, the machine is a no-brainer. It gives you more pleasure and less pain than real life ever could, so plugging in should be the best choice anyone ever makes. If you hesitate, even a little, then something other than experience matters to you. Your hesitation is the data.
Professional philosophers mostly hesitated. In the 2020 PhilPapers Survey, about 1,640 philosophers, mostly faculty in English-speaking departments, answered the question directly.

blocks.title: Would you enter the experience machine?
blocks.note: Philosophers who accept or lean toward each answer.
blocks.source: Bourget & Chalmers, 2020 PhilPapers Survey (Philosophers' Imprint, 2023)

blocks.text: More than three quarters said no. That's a remarkable level of agreement in a field that argues about everything. When people think about it, something in them resists trading their actual life for a perfect simulation of a better one.
What we want besides feeling good

Nozick offered three reasons for the resistance, and each is worth testing against your own gut. First, *we want to do things*, not just have the experience of doing them. The feeling of beating a hard boss is great, but you want to have actually beaten it, with your own hands and your own reaction time. A feeling of achievement without the achievement seems hollow once you know about it.

Second, *we want to be a certain kind of person*. Someone floating in a tank for decades isn't brave, or kind, or funny, or disciplined, Nozick argued. He's an indeterminate blob. You can't develop character when nothing you do has real consequences. The person you become through real effort is part of what you want, not just the feelings that come with it.

Third, *we want contact with reality*. The machine limits you to a world someone programmed. However rich it is, it can never be deeper than its designers' imagination. Real life, frustrating as it is, contains real people with their own minds, and a universe that can still surprise everybody.

Nozick then pushed further with two more devices. A *transformation machine* would turn you into whatever kind of person you wanted to be: braver, smarter, more disciplined, instantly. A *result machine* would produce, in the real world, whatever effects you would have produced through your own effort. Most people find these less creepy than the experience machine, but still not quite right. Something about earning it, about the change coming through you, seems to matter too.

blocks.title: Nozick's three tests, applied to any hour of your day
items: Doing: did I actually do something, or just watch or feel something?
Becoming: did this hour make me a little more the person I want to be?
Reality: did it connect me to real people, real skills or real consequences?

blocks.text: There's a fourth reason that many people add, and later philosophers have stressed: relationships. Would you rather have a friend who truly likes you, or one who secretly can't stand you but fakes it so perfectly you'll never know? Your experience would be identical either way. Almost everyone still wants the real friend. That single intuition is hard for hedonism to explain.
The case for plugging in

Before you feel too good about refusing, give the other side its best shot. The strongest argument for plugging in is that you are, in a sense, already plugged in. Everything you have ever known about reality has reached you as electrical signals in your brain. Your sense of a real world out there is itself a model your brain builds. The machine just swaps one source of signals for another, a better one.

Then there's an uncomfortable experiment. In 2010 the philosopher Felipe De Brigard ran the scenario in reverse. He told participants, a few dozen college students, to imagine they were already living in an experience machine, and had just been offered the chance to unplug and return to their real life. Would they?

Suddenly reality lost much of its pull. When told nothing about what their real life was like, the group split roughly evenly. When told their real life was in a maximum-security prison, most chose to stay plugged in. Even when told that their real life was as a wealthy artist in Monaco, about half still preferred to stay where they were.

De Brigard's conclusion was pointed. Maybe people aren't really choosing reality over illusion when they reject Nozick's machine. Maybe they're just doing what humans do with most big choices, sticking with the life they already have, a well-known tendency called *status quo bias*. If so, the classic answer to the thought experiment is less a deep insight into human values and more a symptom of fear of change.

That's a real challenge, though not a knockout. The study was small, and other researchers have argued that what people are protecting isn't the status quo itself but the specific relationships and people in their current life, real or not. Still, it should make you a bit more humble about why you said no.
It also connects to a stranger possibility. If, as some philosophers argue, we can't rule out that our whole universe is a computer simulation, are we already in the machine? Not quite.

Nozick's tank is a private, scripted fantasy built to please one person. A simulated universe full of other real minds, with its own physics and its own surprises, would still let you do things, become someone and meet people who push back. What makes the machine troubling isn't the hardware. It's that everything inside it exists only for you.

blocks.title: Plug in or stay out? The strongest case for each

left.head: Plug in
items: Experience is all you ever directly have
Your brain already turns the world into signals
Refusing may just be status quo bias
If real life is bad enough, staying out looks cruel

right.head: Stay out
items: You want to do things, not just feel them
Character is built only by real consequences
Real people have minds; programmed ones may not
A faked friendship is worse even if it feels the same

blocks.text: The machine in your pocket

Nobody has built Nozick's tank. But we've built something that runs on the same principle at much lower resolution. A social feed delivers the experience of social connection without most of the connection. It offers the feeling of learning from short explainers, the feeling of progress from watching other people grind, and the feeling of being in on the joke, all without doing anything. The library's article on dopamine and scrolling covers *how* the feed hooks you. Nozick helps with *what* it is selling.

In one way the feed is even more refined than Nozick's tank. His machine played back a life you chose in advance. The feed chooses for you, minute by minute, using recommendation systems trained to keep you watching. It isn't designed to give you the best possible experience. It's designed to give you the next experience you're least likely to swipe away from, which is not the same thing at all.
The difference is that nobody chooses the feed the way they'd choose the machine. You don't sign a contract to spend your life floating. You just pick up the phone for a minute, many times a day.

The feed doesn't offer a better life than your real one. It offers a slightly easier next minute than your real one, over and over. If someone offered you a deal for two hours a day of watching other people do the things you want to do, in exchange for not doing them yourself, you'd probably refuse. That's roughly what heavy scrolling adds up to.
Games are more interesting. A good competitive game with real teammates actually passes several of Nozick's tests. Your aim really improves. Your decisions have real consequences.

The people you play with have real minds, and the ones who play to get better push you to get better too. That's real doing and real becoming, even if the arena is digital. But some games are built mostly to deliver the *feeling* of progress, numbers going up and rewards dropping on a timer, with little skill involved. Those drift toward the machine.

Notice what this means: the line isn't between screens and real life. It's between activities that change something real, in you or in the world, and activities that only change how the next few minutes feel. Editing a video for your channel is screen time. So is a voice call home. Neither is the machine.

Underway, the machine gets unplugged for you. There's no feed to fall into. Pay attention to what you actually miss after a few weeks, and what you don't. The difference is a rough map of what you value versus what you were just used to.
Living with the question

You don't have to settle the philosophy to use it. The thought experiment's real gift is a simple question you can ask about any stretch of time: if I found out tomorrow that the last month had been a simulation, what would I lose? The hours spent on things that only felt good would cost nothing. The hours spent getting stronger, learning a system, building something, or actually talking to someone you care about would be the ones you'd grieve.

That question works better as a nudge than as a rulebook. You don't need to quit games or delete apps to take it seriously. The simplest version is a swap: the next time you reach for the feed out of habit, pick one small thing that would survive the simulation test instead. Ten minutes on a skill, a message to someone real, one task on the thing you're building. Then go back to the feed if you still want it. Often you won't.

Nozick himself wasn't against pleasure. Feeling good matters, and a life of grim, joyless effort isn't the alternative he was recommending. His point was that pleasure works best as a side effect of a life that's actually going somewhere, not as a substitute for one. The feeling of winning is great because you won.

Thought experiment: you're offered the machine, but with one change. It will only run for a year, and afterward you'll remember everything you experienced inside. Would you go in now? What about if you'd have no memory of it? Notice which version bothers you more, and why.

Most people say the second version is worse, and that's telling. If all that mattered were how life feels, a year of bliss you can't remember would still be a year of bliss. The fact that it feels like a loss suggests what we're really after is a life that is ours: done by us, remembered by us, and shared with people who are really there.

takeaways: Nozick's machine tests hedonism: if pleasure were all that mattered, plugging in would be obvious. About 77 percent of philosophers said no.
His three reasons: we want to actually do things, become a certain kind of person, and stay in contact with reality.
Reverse versions suggest part of our 'no' may be status quo bias, so hold your answer with some humility.
A feed is a low-resolution experience machine: the feeling of connection, learning and progress without the thing itself.
Quick test for any hour: if it turned out to be simulated, would you lose anything?
