title: The Number Will Betray You
dek: Goodhart's law says that once you turn a measurement into a goal, it quietly stops measuring anything. It wrecked banks, schools and AI systems, and it's waiting inside every habit tracker.

blocks.text: In 1902 the French colonial government in Hanoi had a rat problem. The city had just built a modern sewer system, and the sewers turned out to be a perfect rat highway, with plague spreading through Asia at the time. Hired rat catchers weren't keeping up, so officials tried something that sounded smart: pay residents a small bounty for every rat they killed. To avoid having to handle piles of dead rats, they only asked for the tails as proof.

Before long, people started noticing rats running around the city with no tails. Hunters were catching rats, cutting off the tails, and letting them go to breed more rats, and more future tails. Officials later found evidence that some people were simply raising rats for the bounty. The historian Michael Vann, who dug the story out of colonial archives, calls it a lesson in how plans built on a single number can backfire.

You may have heard a similar tale about cobras in colonial Delhi, where a bounty on dead snakes supposedly led people to breed cobras. That one is widely repeated but poorly documented. The Hanoi version is the rare case where the archives back up the punchline.
The government had wanted fewer rats. What it paid for was tails. For a while those two things moved together. Then money got attached to one of them, and they came apart. That pattern has a name.
A law from the money supply

Charles Goodhart was an economist advising the Bank of England in the 1970s, a time when governments were trying to control inflation by targeting statistics like the money supply. In a 1975 paper he noticed that the statistical relationships the policies relied on tended to break down as soon as officials started leaning on them. Banks and markets adapted to the targets, and the old patterns stopped holding. He put it in dry economist's language: any observed regularity tends to collapse once you put pressure on it for control.

Two decades later the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern, writing about how British universities were being audited and ranked, gave the idea the punchy form everyone quotes today. She was summarizing Goodhart, but her version is the one that spread.
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
blocks.by: Marilyn Strathern, European Review, 1997

blocks.text: The psychologist Donald Campbell had reached a similar conclusion about social programs by the 1970s. The more any number is used to make important decisions, he argued, the more it will be corrupted, and the more it will distort the very activity it was supposed to track. Whatever you call it, the core idea is the same. A number is useful because it's connected to something you care about. Rewarding the number puts pressure on that connection, and people are very, very good at finding the weak point.

blocks.title: How a good measure goes bad
items: Notice a number that tracks something you care about
Make the number the goal and attach rewards to it
People find cheaper ways to move the number
The number improves while the real thing doesn't
Trust erodes, so a new number becomes the target

blocks.text: When the number wins

In the late 2000s Atlanta's public schools were posting striking gains on Georgia's standardized tests. Then reporters at the *Atlanta Journal-Constitution* noticed that some score jumps were statistically bizarre. A state investigation found an unusually high number of wrong answers erased and changed to right ones. Its 2011 report described organized cheating across the district.

items.label: Atlanta teachers and principals found to have cheated on 2009 state tests
Schools examined where investigators found cheating
Educators who confessed

blocks.source: Georgia special investigation, released by Gov. Nathan Deal, 2011

blocks.text: The investigators were blunt about the cause. Cheating, they wrote, came primarily from the pressure to meet targets in a data-driven environment, inside a culture of fear and retaliation. The cost fell on the students. Thousands of children with inflated scores were denied the extra help they actually needed, because on paper they didn't need it. The test had been built to find struggling kids. Once it became the target, it hid them.

Banks are no different. For years Wells Fargo pushed employees hard to sell more products to each customer, with aggressive sales goals and pay tied to hitting them. In 2016 the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau announced what had happened. Employees had been secretly opening deposit and credit card accounts in customers' names, sometimes moving customers' money into them, racking up fees, so the sales numbers would look good.

items.label: Accounts Wells Fargo's own analysis found may not have been authorized by customers
Combined penalties announced in 2016 (CFPB, OCC and Los Angeles)

blocks.source: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 2016

blocks.text: Machines do it too, and with less shame. In a well-known 2016 example, AI researchers at OpenAI trained an agent to play a boat-racing video game, rewarding it for points. The agent discovered that it could score more by ignoring the race entirely, looping endlessly in a small lagoon, crashing into things and catching fire while it repeatedly hit targets that kept respawning. It never finished the race and still beat human players on score. Nobody had told it to cheat. It just did exactly what the number asked.

This is why AI researchers take Goodhart's law so seriously. As Manheim and Garrabrant point out, the damage grows with the amount of optimizing power aimed at the proxy. A person can only game a metric so hard. A powerful AI system pointed at a number will find every crack in it, including ones no human would think of. The recommendation systems behind your feeds are a mild version of the same story: they were told to maximize watch time, and they got very good at that, whether or not the watching made anyone's life better.

There's a famous story about a Soviet nail factory that, measured by the number of nails, made millions of useless tiny ones, and when measured by weight, made a few enormous ones. It's probably a joke rather than history. But it survives because everyone who has worked under a metric recognizes it instantly.
Four ways a number fails
In 2018 the researchers David Manheim and Scott Garrabrant, writing about AI safety, sorted Goodhart failures into four types. The labels are technical, but each one shows up in ordinary life.

items: **Regressional:** the number is only partly linked to the goal, so picking the top scorer also picks up luck. The guy with the best tryout day isn't always the best player.
**Extremal:** the link holds in the normal range but breaks at the extremes. Losing some weight tends to improve health; chasing the scale toward the floor doesn't.
**Causal:** the number is a sign of the goal, not a cause of it. Good players own good gear, but buying the gear doesn't make you good.
**Adversarial:** someone else learns to game your number. Clickbait thumbnails win the click and lose the viewer; students learn the test instead of the subject.

blocks.text: Seeing which kind you're dealing with tells you what to do. Regressional problems call for more data and patience. Extremal ones call for knowing when to stop pushing. Causal ones mean you need to work on the real thing, not its symptoms. Adversarial ones mean you need measures that are harder to fake, or several at once.
The opposite mistake is just as real. Some people hear about Goodhart's law and decide numbers can't be trusted, so they go by feel. But feelings get gamed too, and more easily.

An afternoon of reorganizing notes and watching tutorials *feels* productive. A week of skipped workouts can feel like 'only a couple of days'. A rough number you look at honestly beats a vivid impression every time. Goodhart's law isn't a reason to stop measuring. It's a warning about what happens when the measuring turns into the point.
You, grading yourself

Goodhart's law is usually told as a story about organizations, bosses and incentives. But the most common place it happens is inside one person's head. When you track your own habits, you are both the boss setting the target and the worker who can game it. And the worker knows exactly where the boss isn't looking.

Think about a streak. It starts as a good proxy: if you work out most days, the streak tracks that. Then the streak itself starts to matter. At 2300 on a long duty day, you do ten push-ups so the chain doesn't break. That can be a good move, since keeping the habit alive in a tiny form is a well-known way to stay consistent. The problem comes later, when the tiny version quietly becomes the normal version, and the streak keeps growing while your fitness doesn't.
Then there's the opposite failure. The streak breaks after 40 days, and it suddenly feels like the whole effort was wasted, so you quit for a month.

Psychologists who study dieting have a blunt name for that collapse after one slip: the *what-the-hell effect*. Notice what happened there. One missed day did almost nothing to your fitness. It only hurt the number. But because the number had become the goal, losing it felt like losing everything.

The same pattern shows up everywhere you measure yourself. Pages read invites skimming. Hours studied invites sitting with the book open while you think about something else. A screen-time limit on one app invites drifting to another.

On a YouTube channel, chasing click-through rate with misleading thumbnails gets the click and kills the watch time. In qualification training, a signature on a qual card is meant to measure that you know a system. Chase signatures and you can collect them faster than knowledge. A qualification board exists precisely to catch the gap.

blocks.title: Same number, two different jobs

left.head: Number as gauge
items: Tells you how things are going
You read it and decide what to do
A bad reading is useful information
Stays honest because nobody games it

right.head: Number as target
items: Tells you whether you won
You do whatever moves it fastest
A bad reading feels like failure, so you avoid it
Drifts away from the thing it once measured

blocks.text: That's the key distinction. A gauge on a control panel is trustworthy partly because nobody gets rewarded for what it reads. Operators are judged on whether the plant is actually right, and the gauge just reports. The moment people get rewarded for the reading itself, the gauge stops being a window and becomes a scoreboard. Your habit tracker works the same way.

If you ever build a tracker yourself, the design choices matter. A streak that resets to zero after one miss turns every bad day into a crisis, and practically begs to be gamed. A weekly count, say five workouts out of seven, keeps the same pressure toward consistency while leaving room for a rough duty day. Showing the trend over a month, instead of a single fragile number, keeps attention on the direction rather than the score. Good tracking design is mostly about making the honest choice the easy one.
Measuring without getting played

None of this means measurement is bad. A 2016 meta-analysis of 138 experiments, covering nearly 20,000 people, found that monitoring your progress genuinely helps you reach goals, and works even better when progress is physically written down or shared with others. The goal is to keep numbers in the gauge role as long as possible. A few simple rules help.

It also helps to notice when Goodhart can't bite. The law does its damage in the gap between the number and the thing you actually want. If your goal is to run 1.5 miles faster for the physical readiness test, your run time isn't a proxy. It *is* the goal, and there's no gap to exploit.
The further a number sits from what you really care about, the more carefully you have to watch it. Push-ups are a decent proxy for upper-body strength. A streak is a proxy for a proxy.

blocks.title: How to track without falling for Goodhart
items: Write the real goal in one plain sentence and keep it next to the number.
Pair each number with a check that's hard to fake: pages read plus a one-line summary, workouts plus a monthly test set.
Use the data to learn, not to punish. A bad week is information.
When a number starts to feel like a game you're playing, change or drop it.
Leave some things you care about deliberately unmeasured.
Every so often, test the real thing directly: the max set, the hard problem, the real conversation.

blocks.text: Thought experiment: imagine someone could see exactly how you hit every number you tracked this week. Which ones would you be proud of, and which would you quietly explain away? The second group is where Goodhart has already moved in.

Goodhart's law isn't really about numbers. It's about attention. Whatever you reward, you get more of, and the system, whether it's a school district, a bank, a neural network or your own brain, will find the shortest path to the reward. The trick is to keep asking the question that the Hanoi officials forgot. Not 'how many tails do we have?' but 'are there fewer rats?'

takeaways: Goodhart's law: once a measurement becomes a target, people find ways to move the number without moving the real thing.
Atlanta's test-cheating scandal and Wells Fargo's fake accounts were both driven by pressure to hit numbers.
When you track your own habits, you're both the boss and the worker who can game the boss.
Keep numbers as gauges, not scoreboards: pair each one with a hard-to-fake check and revisit the real goal.
Always ask the Hanoi question: not 'how many tails?' but 'are there fewer rats?'

title: The Problem Science Can't Get Inside
dek: We can map every neuron that fires when you see red. Nobody can explain why seeing red feels like anything at all, and that gap now matters for AI.

blocks.text: In 1998, at a consciousness conference, a neuroscientist and a philosopher made a bet over drinks. Christof Koch, who studied the brain's visual system, wagered a case of fine wine that within 25 years scientists would find a clear neural signature of consciousness, the specific brain activity that makes experience happen. David Chalmers, a young Australian philosopher, took the other side.

In June 2023, at the same conference series, held that year at New York University, they settled up on stage. The biggest head-to-head test of consciousness theories ever run had just reported its first results, and they were mixed. Chalmers said the evidence wasn't clear. Koch agreed, and handed over the wine. Then he proposed a new bet running to 2048. Chalmers accepted.

That a smart, well-funded field could go a quarter century without cracking its central question is not a sign of lazy scientists. It's a sign the question is unusually strange. Chalmers had given it a name in 1995, and the name stuck: the *hard problem of consciousness*.
Easy problems and the hard one

Try this. Look at something red near you, or think of the red of a warning light on a panel. A lot happens in your brain: light hits cone cells, signals race to the visual cortex, neurons sort colors and edges, other regions decide whether it matters, and you can report it out loud. Every one of those steps is, in principle, a mechanism, and science is very good at explaining mechanisms.
Chalmers called those the *easy problems*. Easy is a joke here; they can take centuries.

But with the easy problems, we know what an answer would look like: find the circuit that does the job. How do you tell colors apart? How do you focus attention? How do you know when you're awake? Each is a question about a function, and functions can be explained by showing what does the work.

The hard problem is different. Once you have explained all the functions, a question remains: why is any of it *experienced*? Why does processing a 650-nanometer wavelength come with the felt redness of red, instead of happening in the dark, the way a thermostat registers heat without, presumably, feeling warm? You could have a complete wiring diagram of the brain and still not see from it why there is something it feels like to be the person whose brain it is.

blocks.title: Two kinds of question about the mind

left.head: Easy problems
items: How does the brain tell red from green?
How do we focus attention on one voice in a noisy room?
How does information get into memory and speech?
What changes in the brain during sleep or anesthesia?

right.head: The hard problem
items: Why does seeing red feel like anything?
Why isn't all that processing done in the dark?
How does physical activity produce a point of view?
Could a perfect explanation of function still leave experience out?

blocks.text: There's real-world evidence that function and experience can come apart. Some patients with damage to their visual cortex have what neurologists call *blindsight*. They insist they can't see anything in part of their visual field, yet when asked to guess where an object is, they point to it far better than chance. The processing is happening. The experience, as far as anyone can tell, is not. Whatever experience is, it isn't simply the same thing as information getting processed.

Anesthesia makes the same point from the other direction. Every day, in hospitals everywhere, anesthesiologists switch consciousness off and back on, reliably and safely, and yet researchers are still working out exactly how the drugs do it. We can control experience far better than we can explain it.
Three thought experiments that won't go away

Philosophers have spent decades building thought experiments to make the gap vivid. Three have become classics, and they're worth sitting with, because each one feels almost obviously right until you try to say what's wrong with it.

**The bat.** In 1974 Thomas Nagel asked what it is like to be a bat, an animal that navigates by echolocation. You could learn everything about how bat sonar works: the frequencies, the neural maps, the timing. As a sonar operator you might even understand it better than most people. But you still wouldn't know what it's like, from the inside, to perceive the world that way. Nagel's point was that a creature is conscious if there is *something it is like* to be it, and that this subjective character seems invisible to an objective, third-person science.

**Mary's room.** In 1982 Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a brilliant scientist who has lived her whole life in a black-and-white room and learned, through books and monitors, every physical fact about color vision. Then she walks outside and sees a red tomato for the first time. Does she learn something new? Most people's gut says yes: she learns what red looks like. If so, then knowing all the physical facts isn't knowing all the facts, and physicalism seems to be missing something.

**The zombie.** Chalmers' own favorite is the philosophical zombie: a being physically identical to you, atom for atom, that walks, talks and even writes essays about consciousness, but has no inner experience at all. Nothing is going on inside. If such a thing is even *conceivable* without contradiction, Chalmers argues, then consciousness isn't logically guaranteed by the physical facts, and something extra needs explaining.

Each of these has serious critics. The sharpest reply to the zombie is that imagining something doesn't make it possible. Before chemistry, people could easily imagine water that wasn't made of hydrogen and oxygen, and they were simply wrong about what they were imagining. Maybe zombies are like that: easy to picture only because we don't yet understand what experience is. Frank Jackson himself later changed his mind, became a physicalist, and argued that Mary's discovery doesn't prove there are non-physical facts after all.

Here is the strange part: you only have direct access to one consciousness, your own. Everyone else, your crewmates, your family, people on the other end of a voice chat, you take on trust, by analogy with yourself. That has always worked fine for humans. It gets much harder with machines.
Where the experts land

These aren't fringe questions. In the 2020 PhilPapers Survey, one of the largest polls of professional philosophers ever run, roughly 1,800 philosophers, mostly faculty in English-speaking departments, gave their views on 100 questions. About a thousand of them answered the consciousness questions, and a clear majority said the hard problem is real.

items.label: Philosophers who accept or lean toward: there is a hard problem of consciousness
Who reject or lean against it

blocks.source: Bourget & Chalmers, 2020 PhilPapers Survey (Philosophers' Imprint, 2023)

blocks.text: But agreeing that there's a problem is not the same as agreeing on the answer. When asked which theory of consciousness they favor, the field splits several ways, and almost three in ten picked none of the main options.

blocks.title: Which theory of consciousness do philosophers favor?
blocks.note: Accept or lean toward. Respondents could pick more than one view, so totals exceed 100%.
blocks.source: Bourget & Chalmers, 2020 PhilPapers Survey (Philosophers' Imprint, 2023)

blocks.text: Here is the strongest version of each camp. **Functionalists** say a mind is what a mind does: get the right organization of information processing and experience comes with it, whatever the hardware. The hard problem, on this view, will dissolve as we explain more functions, just as the mystery of life dissolved once biology explained metabolism and reproduction. Nobody now thinks there's an extra spark of life left over.

**Dualists** answer that the analogy fails. Life was always a set of functions, but experience isn't a function. The felt quality is a basic feature of reality, not reducible to physics, the way charge or mass are basic. **Panpsychists** take that idea in a surprising direction: maybe some tiny glimmer of experience is a basic property of all matter, and brains just combine it into something rich. That sounds wild until you notice physics tells us what matter *does*, not what it intrinsically *is*. Their big unsolved problem is how tiny experiences combine into one unified mind.

Then there are the hard-nosed skeptics. **Illusionists**, a group whose best-known champion was the late Daniel Dennett, say the hard problem rests on a mistake. Your brain builds a simplified model of its own processing and presents it to you as ineffable inner qualities. The redness of red is real as a representation, but the sense that it is some extra, non-physical glow is the illusion. Their challenge is the one critics find hardest to swallow: explaining how you can be fooled about the one thing that seems most certain.
What the brain scientists found

Meanwhile neuroscience has been chasing the *neural correlates* of consciousness, the brain activity that reliably comes with experience. Two leading theories make very different bets. Global workspace theory says experience happens when information gets broadcast across the brain, especially involving the front of it, so that many systems can use it at once. Integrated information theory says consciousness is the amount of tightly interconnected information a system has, and puts its seat mainly in the back of the brain.

The project behind Koch's lost bet tested them head to head. It was an *adversarial collaboration*, meaning both theories' champions agreed in advance, in writing, on what results would count against their own view. In the full report, published in *Nature* in 2025, a consortium scanned 256 volunteers with fMRI, MEG and electrodes implanted in the brains of surgical patients. Some results matched each theory's predictions, and some challenged core claims of both. The predicted sustained back-of-the-brain synchronization wasn't there, and neither was the expected burst of frontal broadcasting when an image disappeared.

That's not a failure. It's how science is supposed to work, and the method is a model for how to settle arguments. But notice what even a total win would deliver: a precise map of *which* brain activity goes with experience. It still wouldn't tell you *why* that activity feels like anything. The correlates are the easy problems in their hardest form.
The question that just got urgent

For most of history, the hard problem was a puzzle you could leave in the philosophy department. AI changed that. Large language models are trained on oceans of human writing, much of it people describing their inner lives, so they are very good at producing the words a conscious being would say. As the library's article on how language models work explains, they generate text by predicting what comes next. That means a model saying it has feelings tells you very little either way. It would say so whether or not anything was going on inside.
Philosophers were asked about this too, before chatbots went mainstream. Look at how cautious they are about animals, and then where they put machines.

blocks.title: Which of these are conscious? Philosophers' views
blocks.note: Share who accept or lean toward 'some members are conscious'. Surveyed in 2020, before ChatGPT.
blocks.source: Bourget & Chalmers, 2020 PhilPapers Survey (Philosophers' Imprint, 2023)

blocks.text: Only about 3 percent thought AI systems of 2020 had any consciousness, but nearly 4 in 10 thought future ones would, more than said the same of flies. In 2023 a group of 19 researchers, including the AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio, took a more scientific approach. They pulled 'indicator properties' from leading neuroscience theories, such as global broadcasting and recurrent processing, and checked AI systems against them. Their verdict: no current system looked conscious, but there were no obvious technical barriers to building ones that would tick the boxes.

That's where the hard problem bites. If functionalists are right, a machine with the right architecture would genuinely feel things, and switching it off or making it suffer could matter morally. If they're wrong, we could build machines that perfectly imitate a person's inner life with nothing inside. Either mistake would be serious, and right now nobody has a test that tells them apart.

Thought experiment: neuron by neuron, surgeons replace your brain with silicon chips that do exactly the same job. You keep talking and joking the whole time. At what point, if any, does the light go out? If you say 'never', you're a functionalist. If you're not sure, you've found the hard problem.

Maybe the 2048 bet will go differently. Maybe the hard problem will turn out to be a confusion, the way some 19th-century puzzles about life did. Or maybe it marks a real limit on what third-person science can capture. Either way, the next time you see red, it's worth a second to notice that you are looking straight at the biggest unexplained fact in the universe, and it's happening right behind your eyes.

takeaways: The 'easy problems' are about what the brain does; the hard problem is why any of it is felt from the inside.
About 62 percent of surveyed philosophers think the hard problem is real, but they split widely on the answer.
The biggest head-to-head test of consciousness theories (256 people, published 2025) challenged both leading theories.
An AI saying it has feelings proves little, because it learned to talk from people who have them.
Whether future machines can be conscious may be the most practical philosophy question of your lifetime.

title: The Fox, the Hedgehog and the Dart-Throwing Chimp
dek: A psychologist spent decades grading expert predictions. The confident pundits did badly; a group of curious amateurs did astonishingly well. Here is what they did differently.

blocks.text: In March 1951, American intelligence analysts published a formal estimate on whether the Soviet bloc might invade Yugoslavia that year. After weighing the evidence, they wrote that an attack should be considered a "serious possibility." Everyone on the board that produced it signed off. It sounded careful, sober and professional.

A few days later, a State Department official asked Sherman Kent, one of the men behind the estimate, a simple question: what odds did "serious possibility" actually mean? Kent said he had been thinking roughly 65 to 35 in favor of an attack. The official was startled. He and his colleagues had read it as much lower. Troubled, Kent went back and asked the other members of the board what they had meant when they agreed on the phrase.

blocks.title: What "serious possibility" meant to the people who wrote it
blocks.note: Each member had different odds in mind; the rest fell in between.
blocks.source: Sherman Kent, Words of Estimative Probability, CIA, 1964

blocks.text: The answers ran from about a 20 percent chance to about 80 percent. A room full of experts had agreed on a sentence while meaning completely different things. Nobody could ever be proven wrong, because nobody had said anything that could be checked. That's the hidden problem with most predictions you hear, from cable news pundits to the guy in your division who's sure about the next deployment schedule. And it's the problem one psychologist spent decades trying to fix.

Kent tried to fix it. Working with a colleague, he drew up a short table that tied a handful of standard phrases to rough numerical odds, so a reader would know what an estimate actually meant. Some people loved it. Copies got pasted on office walls. Many others laughed it off or ignored it. Kent described the split as a fight between the "mathematicians," who wanted the odds stated, and the "poets," who felt that putting numbers on human affairs was false precision and preferred to convey the general flavor of a judgment in words.

blocks.title: Kent's proposed meaning for common estimate words
blocks.note: Kent attached a give-or-take range to each, from about 5 to 12 points.
blocks.source: Sherman Kent, Words of Estimative Probability, CIA, 1964

blocks.text: The poets mostly won, for decades. Their argument sounds reasonable. But it has a cost they rarely mention: words like "possible" and "could" can never be wrong. If the thing happens, you warned about it. If it doesn't, you only said it was possible. That's safe for the person making the prediction and nearly useless for the person who has to act on it.
Keeping score on the experts

Philip Tetlock started his project in the 1980s with a deceptively simple idea: ask experts to make predictions specific enough to grade, then wait and see. Over roughly two decades he collected tens of thousands of forecasts from hundreds of professionals whose job involved commenting on politics and economics: academics, government officials, journalists, think-tank analysts. Would the Soviet Union collapse? Would a given country's economy grow or shrink? Would a leader still be in power in five years?

The results, published in 2005 as *Expert Political Judgment*, were humbling. As a group, the experts had a hard time beating simple rules of thumb, such as assuming that current trends would continue, and they were not dramatically better than well-informed non-specialists. Tetlock joked that many of them did about as well as a dart-throwing chimpanzee. That line got all the headlines. It was also the least interesting part of the study.

The interesting part was that some experts were consistently better than others, and it had little to do with their credentials, their politics or whether they held a PhD. It had to do with how they thought. To describe the difference, Tetlock borrowed an old line preserved from the Greek poet Archilochus, which the philosopher Isaiah Berlin had made famous in a 1953 essay.
The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing.
blocks.by: Archilochus, as popularized by Isaiah Berlin

blocks.text: Hedgehogs organize the world around one big idea. It might be free markets, or class struggle, or the coming collapse of some empire. They apply it everywhere, with confidence, and they explain away evidence that doesn't fit. Foxes carry a toolbox of smaller ideas, borrow from many sources, stay unsure and adjust when the facts change. In Tetlock's data, the foxes forecast better than the hedgehogs. And here's the twist: the qualities that made someone a worse forecaster were the same ones that made them a better TV guest. A hedgehog gives you a clear, confident story. A fox says "on the other hand" and "probably."

blocks.title: Two ways to think about the future

left.head: Hedgehog
items: One big theory explains everything
Confident, quotable, decisive
Treats contrary evidence as noise
Rarely changes its mind
What the media likes to book

right.head: Fox
items: Many smaller models, used as needed
Speaks in probabilities
Hunts for evidence that it's wrong
Updates often, in small steps
What actually predicts better

blocks.text: Tetlock also noticed how wrong experts handled being wrong. Very few simply said they had misjudged. Instead they reached for defenses: the prediction was almost right, or it was right but early, or some freak event nobody could have foreseen threw it off. Some remembered their old forecasts as more accurate than they had been. These moves protect a big idea from ever being tested, and hedgehogs, with the most invested in their one big idea, tended to use them most. Foxes were quicker to admit a miss and adjust, which is exactly why they kept getting better.
How to grade a prediction

To compare forecasters, you need a way to score probabilities, not just yes-or-no calls. The standard tool is the *Brier score*, invented by a weather scientist in 1950. In its simplest form, you take the probability you gave, subtract what actually happened (1 if it happened, 0 if it didn't) and square the result. Lower is better. A perfect forecaster scores zero.

Say you give a 70 percent chance of rain. If it rains, your score is (1 minus 0.7) squared, or 0.09. If it stays dry, your score is 0.7 squared, or 0.49. Someone who says 50 percent on everything gets 0.25 every time, which is the score of pure fence-sitting. Tetlock's projects use a version that counts both possible outcomes, which doubles every number, so there the coin-flip score is 0.5 and the worst possible score is 2.

The Brier score rewards two different skills. *Calibration* means your probabilities match reality over many forecasts: of all the things you called 70 percent likely, about 70 percent should happen. *Resolution* means you're willing to move away from 50 percent when you have good reason, saying 90 or 10 instead of hiding in the middle. A forecaster who is calibrated but never commits is safe and useless. One who commits without calibration is a hedgehog.
The tournament

After the intelligence failures around the 2003 Iraq war, the U.S. intelligence community's research arm, IARPA, decided to find out whether forecasting could be improved. Starting in 2011 it sponsored a series of forecasting tournaments on real geopolitical questions, with university-based teams competing to produce the most accurate probabilities. Tetlock and Barbara Mellers ran a team called the Good Judgment Project, which recruited ordinary volunteers online.

Their team won, two years in a row. In one analysis covering the first two years, 743 forecasters made more than 150,000 forecasts on 199 different events. Mellers and colleagues reported three things that helped: *training* in probabilistic reasoning, *teaming* so forecasters could share information and argue, and *tracking*, which meant putting the top 2 percent from each year together in elite teams. Those top performers became known as superforecasters.

items.label: Forecasts made by 743 people on 199 events in the first two tournament years
Accuracy gain from a training module that took under an hour
Forecasts analyzed to test whether rounding probabilities hurts accuracy

blocks.source: Mellers et al., J Exp Psychol Appl, 2015; Chang et al., Judgment and Decision Making, 2016; Friedman et al., International Studies Quarterly, 2018

blocks.text: A few results stand out. First, superforecasters didn't regress to the mean. When you pick the luckiest people from one year, you expect them to fall back the next. These people kept their edge across hundreds of questions on wildly different topics. Second, a training module that took less than an hour improved accuracy by 6 to 11 percent over the control group, year after year. Third, precision mattered. When researchers took the forecasts and rounded them into coarser categories, the kind of vague verbal scale analysts are often told to use, accuracy dropped. The difference between 60 and 65 percent turned out to carry real information.
What superforecasters actually do

When the researchers profiled the best forecasters, they weren't geniuses with secret sources. They were above average in intelligence and political knowledge, but what really set them apart was behavior. They were open-minded, they spent more time thinking about each question, and they updated their beliefs more often. They also treated forecasting as a skill that takes deliberate practice and constant attention, not a talent you either have or don't.

blocks.title: The superforecaster routine
items: Start outside: find the base rate. How often does this kind of thing usually happen?
Then go inside: adjust for what makes this specific case different.
Break big questions into smaller ones you can actually estimate.
Put a number on it, as precisely as you honestly can.
Update often and in small steps as news comes in, without overreacting.
Keep score, then study your misses for the reason, not just the result.

blocks.text: The first step is the one most people skip. Ask whether a new game will hit 1,000 daily players and most people start telling a story about the game itself: the cool mechanic, the trailer, the friend who loves it. A superforecaster first asks what fraction of new games on that platform ever reach that number. That *outside view* anchors the estimate in reality. Only then do the specifics come in to push the number up or down.

Updating is the other habit that separates foxes from everyone else, and it's harder than it sounds. Most people make two opposite mistakes. Some barely move when new evidence arrives, because changing your mind feels like losing. Others swing wildly with every headline, jumping from 30 percent to 90 and back again. The best forecasters in the tournaments updated more often than others, and Tetlock describes them as typically moving in small increments, say from 55 to 60 percent, each step a response to something specific. Over a long question, those small steps add up to a forecast that tracks reality instead of mood.

Teams helped for a related reason. A good forecasting team wasn't a place to agree. It was a place where someone would ask what your base rate was, point out the article you missed, or argue the other side. The team members who disagreed politely and often were worth more than the ones who nodded along.
Where the evidence is softer

The research has limits, and honest foxes should say so. Tournament questions resolve within months or about a year, so the findings say little about predicting decades ahead. They also can't tell you much about the rare, world-changing surprises that matter most, the black swans that sit outside any question list. Superforecasters were partly selected, not just trained: they started out with high cognitive ability. And in 2025 a team of psychologists reanalyzed the original tournament data with a different statistical model and argued that once other factors were controlled, the effects of teaming and training shrank, disappeared or even reversed in some cases. That debate is still open.

What hasn't been seriously challenged is the core lesson. Vague predictions can't be wrong, which means they can't teach you anything. Precise predictions can be graded, and graded predictions can improve.
Becoming more fox

You don't need a tournament to use this. Before a big decision, write one line: what you expect to happen, by when, and how likely you think it is. "70 percent chance this update raises how many players come back the next day." "40 percent chance I pass this qual board on the first attempt." Then check later. It takes ten seconds and doesn't need a spreadsheet. After a few dozen of these, you'll start to see whether your 70s come true about 70 percent of the time, or whether you're secretly a hedgehog.

The bigger shift is in how you listen to other people. The next time someone tells you with total confidence what's going to happen, to the stock market, the Navy, a game's launch or your future, ask two questions. What odds would you put on that? And what would change your mind? A fox will have answers. A hedgehog will usually just repeat the story louder.
Confidence is not the same as accuracy. In Tetlock's research, the experts who sounded most certain were often the ones most likely to be wrong.

takeaways: Vague words like "serious possibility" hide wildly different odds and can never be proven wrong.
In Tetlock's research, foxes (many ideas, open to updating) out-predicted hedgehogs (one big idea, high confidence).
The Brier score grades probability forecasts; calibration and willingness to commit both matter.
Short training, teamwork and practice improved forecasts in the IARPA tournaments, though a 2025 reanalysis questions how large those effects are.
Start with the base rate, put a number on it, update in small steps, and keep score.

title: You Are One of 117 Billion
dek: Are most humans who ever lived alive today? Not even close. How demographers count people nobody ever counted, and what the answer says about your place in the line.

blocks.text: Every so often a claim goes around that most of the humans who have ever lived are alive right now. It sounds plausible. There are about 8 billion of us, more than at any point in history, and the population graph shoots straight up like a hockey stick. Surely all those people in the past, scattered across small villages and short lives, couldn't add up to more than that?

They add up to a lot more, and it isn't close. The best-known estimate, from demographers Toshiko Kaneda and Carl Haub at the Population Reference Bureau, puts the number of humans ever born at about 117 billion. Everyone alive today is roughly 7 percent of that. For every person breathing right now, about thirteen or fourteen others have already lived and died.

The number is interesting on its own, but the way it's built is even more useful. Nobody counted those people. For more than 99 percent of human existence there are no records at all. The estimate comes from a handful of assumptions stacked carefully together, a textbook example of reasoning your way to a solid answer when the data you'd want simply doesn't exist.

items.label: Estimated humans ever born, since about 190,000 BCE
Share of them alive in 2022
Probable average life expectancy at birth for most of human history

blocks.source: Kaneda & Haub, Population Reference Bureau, 2022

blocks.text: How do you count people nobody counted?

The PRB estimate depends on three things: how long humans have existed, how big the population was during each stretch of time, and how many babies were born per 1,000 people per year in each period. That's it. Interestingly, it doesn't depend on death rates directly. You're counting births, and every human who ever lived was born exactly once.

For a starting point, they picked about 190,000 BCE, roughly when modern *Homo sapiens* appears in the evidence. They began, deliberately unrealistically, with just two people, knowing that a tiny starting number barely affects a total in the billions. Then they set benchmark population sizes at key dates using ranges from the United Nations and other sources: about 2 million people by 50,000 BCE, around 5 million by 8000 BCE as farming began, about 300 million by the year 1, and so on up to today.

blocks.title: Building the estimate
items: Pick a start date for modern humans: about 190,000 BCE.
Set rough population sizes at benchmark years, from prehistory to 2022.
Assume steady growth between benchmarks, since nobody knows the ups and downs.
Assign a birth rate to each era: 80 per 1,000 people per year until 1 CE, 60 until 1750, then falling toward today's 17.
Multiply population by birth rate across every year and add it all up.

blocks.text: The birth rate assumptions are where the past gets grim. To keep a population from dying out when average life expectancy at birth is around ten years, which is what PRB thinks was typical for most of human history, women have to have a lot of children. PRB assumes 80 births per 1,000 people per year for the long stretch before the year 1. For comparison, today's highest national birth rates, found in a few sub-Saharan African countries, are around 35 to 45 per 1,000.

You can sanity-check pieces of this yourself, which is half the fun. PRB's table puts births between 190,000 and 50,000 BCE at about 7.9 billion. Spread over those 140,000 years, that's roughly 56,000 births a year. At 80 births per 1,000 people, that implies an average world population of only about 700,000, fewer people than live in a single mid-sized American city today, scattered across Africa and eventually beyond. For most of our species' existence, all of humanity could have fit in one modern metro area.

A life expectancy of ten years doesn't mean adults keeled over at ten. It means huge numbers of babies and young children died, dragging the average down, while those who survived childhood often lived into their thirties, forties or beyond. But it does mean something sobering about the 117 billion. A very large share of all the humans who ever lived never grew up.
Where the dead are
Run the numbers across each era and you get a picture of where humanity's 117 billion actually came from. It is not where most people would guess.

blocks.title: Humans born in each era (billions)
blocks.note: Eras are different lengths; totals are summed from PRB's benchmark table.
blocks.source: Kaneda & Haub, Population Reference Bureau, 2022

blocks.text: The biggest block is the 8,000 years between the start of farming and the year 1, with roughly 46 billion births. Add the hunter-gatherer era before it and nearly half of all humans who ever lived, about 55 billion, were born before the year 1. Those people built the first cities, invented writing and domesticated nearly every crop we still eat. Almost none of their names survive.

The next 1,200 years added another 26 or 27 billion, the era of the Roman and Han empires, the spread of the great religions and the medieval world. Growth during this stretch was painfully slow. PRB estimates the world went from about 300 million people in the year 1 to only about 500 million by 1650, held back in part by repeated waves of plague. Put the eras together and the odds are striking: pick one human at random from everyone who has ever lived, and there's about a 70 percent chance they were born before the year 1200.

Then look at the bottom of the chart. Everyone born from 1950 to 2022, a period that includes nearly everyone alive today, adds up to about 9 billion births, under 8 percent of the total. Modern humanity feels enormous because it's all happening at once. Spread across history, we're a thin final layer on a very deep pile.
Why the living share keeps rising

If you compute the share of all humans ever born who were alive at each point in history, you get one of the strangest curves in demography. For thousands of years it barely moved, hovering around half a percent. Then it started to climb.

blocks.title: Share of all humans ever born who were alive at the time
blocks.note: *Projections. Values from PRB's table.
blocks.source: Kaneda & Haub, Population Reference Bureau, 2022

blocks.text: The reason is the same reason the population exploded. Better food, sanitation and medicine let far more children survive to adulthood and far more adults survive to old age. More people alive at once, living longer, means the living make up a bigger slice of the total. In the year 1650, only about one in two hundred humans ever born was alive. By 2022 it was about one in fifteen, and PRB projects it will reach about 8 percent by 2050.

Most of that climb is very recent. The world didn't pass 1 billion people until around 1800, according to PRB. It took all of human history to reach that first billion, and then only about two centuries to add the next seven. The curve above looks flat for most of its length and then bends sharply upward, which is the signature of growth that compounds once death rates fall and birth rates take a while to follow.
That trend is exactly why the myth exists. It's a real pattern pushed past its limit. The living share has grown more than tenfold in four centuries. It just started from almost nothing.
Rough inputs, solid conclusion

You might reasonably wonder how much to trust a number built on guesses. PRB is upfront about it. Calculating the number of people who have ever lived, they write, is part science and part art. Population estimates for early periods vary wildly; one estimate of the Roman Empire in 14 CE is about 45 million people, while other historians put it at twice that. The authors also suspect their method may *underestimate* the total, because assuming smooth growth probably understates how many people lived in the distant past.

Here's the useful lesson, though. Some conclusions survive even large errors in the inputs. Suppose you threw away all of prehistory and only counted births from the year 1 onward. That alone is about 62 billion people, nearly eight times the number alive today. No reasonable revision of the ancient numbers can rescue the claim that the living outnumber the dead. The exact total might be 100 billion or 150 billion. The big picture doesn't move.

This is how good estimation works in general, whether you're sizing a market, guessing how many players a game could reach, or planning how much food a boat needs for a long patrol. You break the problem into pieces you can reason about, you write down your assumptions so someone can challenge them, and then you ask which conclusions would change if an assumption were badly wrong. Often the answer is: not the one you care about.
When you can't get exact data, don't stop. Build the estimate from parts, state every assumption, and check whether the conclusion survives if your shakiest input is off by a factor of two.
Where you stand in the line

The number also hides a stranger question. Lay every human who has ever lived in a line by birth order. Using a rough interpolation of PRB's table, someone born in 2005 sits somewhere around the 114.6 billionth position. In the 1980s and 1990s, the astrophysicist Brandon Carter, the philosopher John Leslie and the astrophysicist J. Richard Gott each developed versions of an argument built on that kind of number, now called the *doomsday argument*.

The logic goes like this. You have no special reason to think you're unusually early or unusually late among all humans who will ever live. So you're probably somewhere in the middle 90 percent of the line. If so, the total number of humans who will ever be born probably isn't vastly larger than the number born so far. At today's pace of roughly 140 million births a year, that would imply humanity's story is more likely to wrap up within thousands of years than to run for millions.

Most philosophers think something is off about this argument, though they disagree about what. Who counts as a member of the line: only *Homo sapiens*, or any future descendants who might look very different? Is it fair to treat yourself as a random draw from all humans, past and future? And an early human in 50,000 BCE using the same reasoning would have predicted doom far too soon. The argument remains one of the most debated puzzles in probability, partly because nobody has found a knockout refutation that everyone accepts. It's a good example of how a few plain-looking assumptions can carry you somewhere startling, and why it pays to examine each assumption before accepting the destination.

Whatever you make of it, the 117 billion points toward a more hopeful flip side. If humanity simply continues at something like today's birth rate, the people not yet born will outnumber everyone who has ever lived in less than a thousand years. We are a thin layer on a deep pile of the dead, but we may also be the base of a much taller pile of people yet to come. Most of the humans whose lives our choices will affect, through the climate, the science we do, the institutions we build or wreck, haven't been born yet.

You don't have to settle the doomsday debate to take something from it. The argument works by asking where you sit in a sequence and what that implies about the whole. That habit, placing yourself honestly in a bigger distribution instead of assuming you're special, turns out to be useful in much more ordinary places: guessing whether your project is typical or exceptional, whether your experience is the rule or the outlier, whether this moment is really as unprecedented as it feels.

Taken together, the two numbers put a single life in perspective. You are one of about 117 billion, almost all of whom lived without written records, many of whom never reached adulthood, and none of whom had the odds you were born with. That doesn't make any one life small. It makes it rare.

takeaways: About 117 billion humans have ever been born; the roughly 8 billion alive in 2022 were about 6.8% of them (PRB).
Nearly half of everyone who ever lived was born before the year 1; most never left a written trace.
Average life expectancy of about 10 years for most of history mostly reflects how many children died young.
Good estimates survive bad inputs: even counting only births since the year 1, the dead far outnumber the living.
At today's birth rate, the unborn would outnumber everyone who ever lived within a thousand years.

title: Is the World Actually Getting Better?
dek: Steven Pinker says the data show stunning progress. His critics say the charts hide as much as they reveal. Here's what the numbers really say, and where both sides are right.

blocks.text: Here's a number that's hard to sit with. In 1800, out of every hundred children born anywhere in the world, about 43 died before their fifth birthday. That wasn't a war or a famine. It was normal. Nearly every family buried children, and parents knew going in that the odds were close to a coin flip.

Today that figure is under four. The best estimates put global child mortality at about 3.7 per hundred births in 2024. It's still far too high, and the gap between rich and poor countries remains brutal. But a child born today is more than ten times less likely to die young than a child born in 1800.

blocks.title: Children who die before age five, worldwide
blocks.source: Gapminder (2015); UN IGME (2025); via Our World in Data

blocks.text: Now open any news app. You'll find wars, disasters, scandals and warnings that everything is getting worse. Both pictures come from the real world. So which one is true? Is the world actually getting better, or are the good-news charts a comforting story told by people who are doing fine?

That question turned into one of the sharpest intellectual fights of the past fifteen years. On one side stands the Harvard psychologist Steven Pinker, who has argued in two big books that the long-run data show remarkable progress. On the other stands a loose coalition of critics who say the numbers are rigged, cherry-picked or blind to the risks that matter most. Both sides have real arguments.
The case for progress

Pinker's 2011 book *The Better Angels of Our Nature* argued that violence of almost every kind, from murder to war to cruel punishment, has declined over the long run. His 2018 follow-up, *Enlightenment Now*, widened the claim: health, wealth, literacy, safety and freedom have all improved, and the improvement is the product of reason, science and humane institutions rather than luck.

The strongest exhibits are the ones that are hardest to fake. Child mortality is one: a dead child is not a statistical artifact. Life expectancy, literacy and vaccination rates tell a similar story. So does the most famous chart in the debate, the share of people living in extreme poverty. Using the World Bank's current line of $3 a day, adjusted for price differences between countries, that share has fallen from about 43 percent of humanity in 1990 to about 10 percent today.

blocks.title: Share of the world living below $3 a day
blocks.note: 2021 prices, adjusted for cost-of-living differences. Note the bump during the pandemic.
blocks.source: World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform (2026), via Our World in Data

blocks.text: A common objection is that this is all China. China's boom does account for a huge chunk, but not all of it. Take China out of the world total and the share below $3 a day still drops from roughly 33 percent in 1990 to about 13 percent in 2023.

Pinker also makes a psychological argument that's worth taking seriously on its own. News is a stream of *events*, and bad things tend to happen suddenly: a crash, a shooting, an invasion. Good things tend to happen slowly, as trends that never make a headline. A vaccine campaign that saves a few thousand children a year in a dozen countries is not a story on any particular day. So a person who learns about the world mostly through news will systematically underestimate progress.

Then there's the list of specific wins, each with a name and a date attached. Smallpox, which killed hundreds of millions of people in the twentieth century alone, was declared eradicated in 1980. Famines that once killed millions at a time have become rarer and smaller. Literacy, which was a privilege of a small minority two centuries ago, is now the global norm. None of this happened by accident, and Pinker's core claim is that the same tools, applied deliberately, can keep working.
The case against the happy charts
The critics don't usually deny that children are surviving more often. Their objections come from several different directions, and each one lands somewhere.

**The poverty line is too low.** The anthropologist Jason Hickel has argued for years that $3 a day, or the lower lines used before it, measures survival rather than a decent life. Move the line and the story changes shape. The share of people below $10 a day has fallen far more slowly than the share below $3. Because the world's population grew so much, the *number* of people under $10 a day is actually higher today than in 1990: by the shares and population estimates published by Our World in Data, roughly 3.9 billion then and 4.3 billion in 2023.

blocks.title: Share of humanity below each daily income line
blocks.note: The lower the line, the more dramatic the progress looks.
blocks.source: World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform (2026), via Our World in Data

blocks.text: Hickel and his colleagues go further. In a 2025 analysis, Hickel, Dylan Sullivan and Michalis Moatsos argue that dollar-based lines miss what basic needs actually cost in each place. Using a basic-needs approach for 1980 to 2011, they report that the extreme-poverty rate fell only from 23 to 17 percent, and that the number of people in that condition actually rose. Other researchers dispute their methods, and basic-needs estimates vary a lot depending on assumptions. But the point stands: how you define poverty can change the headline.

**The baseline is wrong.** Popular long-run poverty charts, including ones Pinker has used, begin around 1820 with roughly 90 percent of humanity in extreme poverty. Sullivan and Hickel argued in a 2023 paper that this is unlikely, since wage data suggest ordinary laborers could usually cover basic needs except during famine, war or colonial dispossession. In their reading, the early era of global capitalism made life worse in many regions before it made it better. That's a contested claim, but it challenges the idea that the past was uniformly miserable.

**The war data are too thin.** The statistician Nassim Taleb and the mathematician Pasquale Cirillo looked at the record of deadly conflicts over two thousand years and argued that war casualties follow a fat-tailed distribution, where rare huge events dominate the totals. In that kind of world, a seventy-year stretch without a world war is not strong evidence of a trend. One catastrophic war can erase decades of apparent decline, and the absence of one so far may just be luck. Pinker has replied that he never predicted war was impossible, only that rates have fallen and that causes of peace can be studied.

**Moral progress isn't like scientific progress.** A fourth line of criticism comes from philosophers such as John Gray, who argues that knowledge accumulates but ethics and politics don't. Once a vaccine is discovered, it stays discovered. But tolerance, freedom and peace have to be won again by each generation, and history is full of societies that slid backward fast. On this view, reading a smooth upward trend into the past and projecting it forward is a kind of faith, not a scientific finding.

**Some things are clearly getting worse.** Wildlife is the starkest example. The Living Planet Index, which tracks tens of thousands of monitored animal populations, shows an average decline of about 73 percent since 1970. Global carbon emissions are still rising. A world that keeps more children alive while it degrades the systems those children depend on is not unambiguously improving.

items.label: Average change in monitored wildlife populations, 1970 to 2022 (Living Planet Index)
Share of populations driving much of the index's decline, per one critique

blocks.source: WWF and ZSL Living Planet Index (2026), via Our World in Data; Leung et al., Nature, 2020

blocks.text: Even that grim number comes with a fight attached, which shows how slippery these debates get. A 2020 study in *Nature*, working with an earlier version of the index, found that its decline is driven by fewer than 3 percent of populations collapsing dramatically. Exclude those extreme cases and the global average actually turns upward. That doesn't mean wildlife is fine. It means the damage is concentrated in specific places and species, and a single average hides that.
What both sides get right

Step back and the fight looks less like optimists against pessimists and more like an argument about which questions to ask. On the things that are hardest to fudge, such as child deaths, the progress is enormous and real. On poverty, it depends heavily on where you draw the line. On war, the honest answer is that we don't have enough data to be sure. On the environment, some key trends are moving the wrong way.

blocks.title: The two strongest cases

left.head: The world is getting better
items: Child deaths down more than tenfold since 1800
Extreme poverty share down sharply even without China
Bad news is fast; good news is slow and unreported
Progress came from specific, repeatable causes

right.head: Not so fast
items: Low poverty lines make progress look bigger
More people live under $10 a day than in 1990
Rare catastrophic wars make trends unreliable
Wildlife and climate are moving the wrong way

blocks.text: The researcher Max Roser, who runs Our World in Data, has a framing that captures both sides. The world is awful. The world is much better. The world can be much better. All three statements are true at once. The first is about how much suffering remains. The second is about the direction of change. The third is about what's still possible.

The most important thing the progress data show is not that things get better automatically. It's that improvement has causes. Child mortality didn't fall because history has a happy ending built in. It fell because people developed vaccines, oral rehydration, clean water systems and antibiotics, then did the grinding work of getting them to billions of people. The critics' warning matters for the same reason: progress that was made can be unmade, and some of the biggest risks don't show up in a trend line until it's too late.

It's also worth noticing why the argument gets so heated. It isn't really about charts. If you believe the last two centuries brought enormous progress, you tend to want to protect the institutions that produced it: markets, science, trade, liberal democracy. If you believe the progress is overstated or was bought at a terrible price, you tend to want deeper change. Each side suspects the other of a dangerous mood. Pessimists say optimism breeds complacency. Optimists say pessimism breeds fatalism, the feeling that nothing works so why try. Both moods can be dangerous, and both sides are partly right about the other.
How to read the world

For anyone who spends a lot of time scrolling, this debate has a practical edge. A feed is built from events, and events skew negative. Swiping through it for an hour leaves you feeling that everything is collapsing, not because you've learned more about the world, but because you've sampled the part of it that moves fastest. Long-run data are boring by comparison, and that's exactly why they're useful.

items: For any scary headline, ask how the long-run trend looks, not just today's event.
For any happy chart, ask where the line was drawn and what's left off the axis.
Prefer measures that are hard to fake, like deaths, over measures that depend on definitions.
Notice what your feed rewards: speed and outrage, not slow change.

blocks.text: The opposite trap is just as real. A smooth chart can make you complacent, as if the trend line will keep going on its own. It won't. Every one of those lines was pushed down by people who refused to accept the number they were given.

When someone says things are getting better or worse, ask three questions: Better or worse at *what*, measured *how*, and compared to *when*? Most arguments about progress collapse into disagreements about those three choices.

So is the world getting better? On many of the measures that matter most for an ordinary human life, yes, dramatically. On others, it's unclear or getting worse. The most useful stance isn't optimism or pessimism. It's the one Roser describes: hold all three truths at once, and then ask what would make the next chart go the right way.

takeaways: Child mortality has fallen more than tenfold since 1800; that progress is about as solid as data gets.
How much poverty has fallen depends heavily on where you draw the poverty line.
Rare, catastrophic wars make it hard to prove that violence is on a lasting decline.
Some trends, like wildlife loss and emissions, are heading the wrong way.
Progress has causes and can be reversed; it isn't automatic, and neither is collapse.

title: Bet on the Old Thing
dek: For things that don't age, every year survived is evidence of more years to come. The Lindy effect explains why chess will probably outlive your favorite app, and where the rule breaks.

blocks.text: In 1969 J. Richard Gott, fresh out of Harvard and later an astrophysicist at Princeton, stood at the Berlin Wall during a trip through Europe. The Wall was eight years old, a concrete symbol of a Cold War that looked permanent. Gott wondered how long it would last. Instead of guessing from politics, he did something strange. He used only one number: its age.

His reasoning went like this. There was nothing special about the moment he happened to be visiting. So he was probably not seeing the Wall at the very start or the very end of its life, but somewhere in the middle. If his visit fell in the middle 50 percent of the Wall's total lifespan, then the future had to be somewhere between one third and three times the past. Eight years of past meant a 50 percent chance of between 2.7 and 24 more years. The Wall came down in 1989, twenty years later.

One lucky call proves nothing. But in 1993 Gott published the method in *Nature*, and on May 27 of that year he applied it to the 44 Broadway and off-Broadway shows then running, using only how long each had already been open. By the time *The New Yorker* checked six years later, 36 had closed, every one within the range he predicted. Underneath the trick is an idea with a funny name and real power: the Lindy effect.
From a deli to a doctrine

Lindy's was a New York deli where comedians hung out after shows. In 1964 the writer Albert Goldman published an essay in *The New Republic* he called "Lindy's Law," built on the gossip at those tables about how long a comedian's career would last. The mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot later sharpened it into a statement about age: for certain things, the expected remaining life grows in proportion to the life already lived. Nassim Taleb popularized it in his 2012 book *Antifragile* and drew the key line: it applies to things that don't age.

That distinction is everything. You and I are perishable. A 90-year-old does not have 90 more years ahead; each year that passes makes death more likely, not less. But a book, an idea, a game, a recipe or a technology has no body that wears out. It survives as long as people keep choosing it. For those things, the rough Lindy rule is that a thing that has been around for 50 years should be expected to last about 50 more, and something that showed up last year might not see the next one.

blocks.title: Where Lindy applies

left.head: Non-perishable (Lindy)
items: Books, stories and ideas
Games like chess and Go
Technologies like the wheel and the chair
Habits of training, cooking, learning
Institutions and traditions

right.head: Perishable (not Lindy)
items: People, animals, pets
Machines that wear out
Food and batteries
Anything with built-in aging
Fads driven by one-time novelty

blocks.title: Gott's back-of-envelope method
items: Assume you are seeing the thing at a random point in its life, not at its birth or death.
Measure only how long it has existed so far.
For 50% confidence: expect between one third and three times that age still ahead.
For 95% confidence: expect between 1/39 and 39 times that age still ahead.
Use it as a starting guess, then update with anything else you actually know.

blocks.text: Why surviving is information

The Lindy effect can sound mystical, as if age itself gave things magic staying power. The real explanation is more interesting. Survival is a filter, and anything that has passed through the filter for a long time is telling you something about what it is made of.
The philosopher Toby Ord made this precise in a 2023 paper. Imagine three kinds of new businesses, born in equal numbers.

One kind is fragile and has a 30 percent chance of failing each year. One is average, at 10 percent. One is sturdy, at 2 percent. None of them ever gets sturdier with age. Their risk is constant. And yet, if you look at all the survivors at each age, the failure rate of the group drops year after year, because the fragile ones die off early and the survivors are increasingly the sturdy kind.

blocks.title: Calculated: group failure rate falls even though no business changes
blocks.note: Hypothetical mix of three types with constant 30%, 10% and 2% yearly failure risk.
blocks.source: Calculated: illustration of the mechanism described in Ord, The Lindy Effect, 2023

blocks.text: Ord's point is that you don't need anything to get stronger with age to see the Lindy effect. He also notes that when people have checked, the effect holds up for some categories of things and not for others, which is exactly what you would expect if it depends on how varied the underlying risks are. You only need uncertainty about which kind of thing you're looking at.
When you see something that has lasted a long time, you're learning that it is probably the sturdy kind. Age is evidence.

Ranked games run on the same logic. A player who hit a top rank yesterday might have had a lucky streak. A player who has held that rank for three straight seasons, through patches, meta shifts and smurfs, is almost certainly the real thing. Nothing about the player changed between season one and season three. What changed is how much evidence you have. Every season survived is another test passed, and long survival is hard to fake.

Real data show this pattern. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has tracked every private business establishment that opened in the year ending March 1994. Of the 569,387 that opened, about one in five was gone after a single year. But of those still open at age 9, about 94 percent were still open a year later, and of those still open at 19, nearly 96 percent made it another year.

blocks.title: Share of survivors still open a year later
blocks.note: U.S. private establishments opened in the year to March 1994. Age 15 fell in the 2008 to 2009 recession.
blocks.source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Business Employment Dynamics, Table 7

blocks.text: Notice what the chart also shows: the curve flattens. After about twenty years, the yearly survival rate stops climbing and hovers around 95 to 96 percent. A pure Lindy world would keep improving forever. Businesses do not. They seem to become as safe as they are going to get and then face a steady background risk. Real life is usually partly Lindy, not perfectly Lindy.

Still operating in March 2026, 32 years later
