title: The Bet You Can't Refuse
dek: A 17th-century mathematician argued you should bet on God because the payoff is infinite. The argument fails in fascinating ways, and its ghost still haunts how we think about asteroids, AI and long shots.

blocks.text: When Blaise Pascal died in 1662, at thirty-nine, he left behind a pile of notes. Some were pinned together in bundles; some were scraps covered on both sides in handwriting running in every direction, full of crossings-out and second thoughts. Pascal had been a prodigy. As a teenager he built one of the first mechanical calculators, and in a famous exchange of letters with Pierre de Fermat he helped invent the mathematics of probability. He had also, in his last years, become intensely religious.

His friends published the notes in 1670 as the *Pensées*, or 'Thoughts'. Buried in one of the messiest fragments was an argument that has never stopped causing trouble. It didn't try to prove that God exists. Pascal thought reason couldn't settle that. Instead, he asked a gambler's question: given that you don't know, what's the smart bet?

That argument, **Pascal's wager**, is usually taught as a piece of religious philosophy. But it's really the first serious attempt to reason about a decision where the odds are unknown and the stakes are infinite. Philosophers still argue about it. And the same shape of argument now shows up in debates about asteroids, pandemics, artificial intelligence and how to plan a life.
The bet

Pascal set it up like a game. Either God exists or he doesn't. You can live as a believer or not. That gives four possible outcomes. If God exists and you believe, you gain eternal happiness, an infinite reward. If God exists and you don't, you lose it. If God doesn't exist, you either gave up some worldly pleasures for nothing or you didn't. Those last outcomes are finite either way.

blocks.title: Pascal's decision table

left.head: If God exists
items: Wager for God: infinite reward
Wager against God: infinite reward lost

right.head: If God does not exist
items: Wager for God: a finite loss (some pleasures given up)
Wager against God: a finite gain (those pleasures kept)

blocks.text: Now do the math the way Pascal had just helped invent it. The value of a bet is each payoff multiplied by its probability, added up. Any chance at all of an infinite reward, even one in a trillion, gives an infinite expected value. Nothing finite can compete. So as long as you don't think God's existence is *impossible*, Pascal concluded, you should bet on it. And you can't refuse to play, because not choosing is itself a choice.
You must wager. It is not optional.
blocks.by: Blaise Pascal, Pensées (W. F. Trotter translation)

blocks.text: The philosopher Ian Hacking later called the wager the first well-understood contribution to decision theory, the science of choosing under uncertainty. That's the part worth taking seriously even if you have no interest in religion. Pascal saw that when you can't know the truth, you can still reason about what to *do*, by weighing what's at stake on each side.

blocks.title: The wager in four moves
items: Reason cannot prove or disprove God, so you face real uncertainty.
You must act one way or the other; there's no neutral option.
Belief risks a finite loss for a chance at infinite gain.
Any nonzero chance of infinite gain beats every finite payoff, so bet on God.

blocks.text: Why it doesn't quite work

Almost as soon as the argument appeared, people started finding cracks. The most famous is the **many gods objection**. Pascal's table has only two columns, but there are countless possible gods, many of them jealous of each other. The French philosopher Denis Diderot pointed out in 1746 that an imam could run exactly the same argument for Islam. If any religion with an infinite reward gets the same treatment, the wager doesn't tell you which one to bet on. It just tells you that infinities make your math explode.

A second problem: can you even choose to believe something? Try believing, right now, that your shoes are made of cheese. Pascal anticipated this. His advice was to act as believers do, attend services and follow the rituals, and belief would follow from habit. That's psychologically shrewd. But it raises a moral question that William James and others pressed: would a just God reward someone who believed as a calculated bet? The wager may undermine itself by turning faith into a hedge.

Pascal even seemed to sense the cost. He admitted that following the rituals would dull the skeptic's sharp edges; his French phrase literally means it will 'make you a beast'. Later critics turned that into an ethical objection. The mathematician W. K. Clifford argued in 1877 that believing things on insufficient evidence isn't just a private matter, because it trains a habit of credulity that harms everyone around you. On that view, talking yourself into a belief because it pays is a kind of self-corruption, whatever the payoff.

A third crack is subtler and comes straight from the mathematics. The philosophers Antony Duff and Alan Hájek noticed that the wager, taken literally, proves too much. Suppose you flip a coin and only become a believer if it lands heads. That strategy still gives you some chance of infinite reward, so its expected value is also infinite, exactly as good as believing outright. So is a strategy of waiting to see if you win the lottery first. Once infinity enters the table, every strategy with any chance at all of reaching it looks equally good, which means the math has stopped guiding you.

blocks.title: The strongest objections

left.head: The objection
items: Many gods
Belief isn't a choice
Mercenary faith
Mixed strategies

right.head: What it shows
items: Infinite stakes can be claimed for any option
You can only act, then hope belief follows
A bet may not earn the reward it aims at
Infinity makes all chancy strategies equal

blocks.text: Getting mugged by small probabilities
You might think that's just a problem with infinity. Swap in very large but finite numbers and everything should behave. It doesn't.

In 2009 the Oxford philosopher Nick Bostrom published a short dialogue called *Pascal's Mugging*. A stranger approaches Pascal on the street. He has no weapon, but he asks for Pascal's wallet anyway, promising to return tomorrow with a reward many times its value. Pascal says the chance of that is tiny. The mugger simply raises the promised reward until even a tiny probability times the reward beats the money in the wallet. If you reason purely by expected value, you have to pay. Every time.

Something has clearly gone wrong. The mugger's promise is worth nothing, but the math says to hand over the cash. The lesson is that **expected value breaks down at the extremes**: when probabilities are tiny, hard to estimate, and attached to enormous payoffs, anyone willing to name a big enough number can hijack your decision.

Why does a tool that works so well most of the time fail so badly here? Expected value earns its reputation in situations you repeat. A casino doesn't care whether one spin of the roulette wheel goes its way, because over millions of spins the averages win out. The same is true for an insurance company or a poker player with a big enough bankroll. But a one-time bet with a tiny chance of an enormous payoff never gets the chance to average out. You either hit the long shot or, far more likely, you don't. The average is a number that describes no outcome you will ever actually experience.

Mathematicians had already met a cousin of this problem. In 1713 Nicolaus Bernoulli described a game in which a fair coin is flipped until it comes up heads, with the prize doubling on every flip. The expected value of the game is infinite. Yet nobody would pay more than a modest sum to play it. His cousin Daniel Bernoulli's answer in 1738, that each extra dollar matters less to you than the one before, became the foundation of how economists think about risk.
When the long shot is real

None of this means you should ignore small risks with huge consequences. Some of them are real, and the cost of ignoring them is enormous. The trick is telling a genuine long-shot danger from a mugging.

Asteroids are the clean case. The chance of a large impact in any given year is small, but it's not made up. Astronomers can track objects, measure orbits and count craters to estimate it. That's why spending money on planetary defense isn't a Pascalian gamble. In September 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately slammed into a small asteroid moon called Dimorphos to test whether an impact could shift its path. It worked, changing the little moon's orbit by about half an hour. That's the opposite of a mugging: a real but rare danger, a measurable probability, and a cheap, testable way to hedge against it.

items.label: Change in Dimorphos's orbital period after NASA's DART impact
Date of the first deliberate test of moving an asteroid

blocks.source: Lazzarin et al., Nature Communications, 2025

blocks.text: Other risks are murkier. Engineered pandemics, nuclear war and runaway artificial intelligence are all cases where the stakes could be civilizational but the probabilities are much harder to pin down. This is where modern debates sound a lot like Pascal. Some argue that even a small chance of catastrophe justifies serious investment now. Critics answer that numbers pulled from intuition and multiplied by billions of future lives can justify almost anything, which is the mugger's trick in a lab coat.

This isn't an abstract worry. Parts of the effective altruism movement embraced exactly this style of reasoning, arguing that because trillions of future lives could be at stake, even tiny reductions in extinction risk outweigh nearly everything else. Supporters say that's simply taking the future seriously. Critics, including some inside the movement, call it 'fanaticism', the willingness to let minuscule probabilities attached to astronomical numbers override everything you can actually see. The philosophers have not settled who is right. What they agree on is that Pascal's problem never went away; it just changed costumes.

Human intuition doesn't help much, either. Psychologists have found that people handle tiny probabilities badly in both directions. We overweight vivid long shots, which is why lottery tickets sell and why plane crashes feel more dangerous than car trips. And we often ignore dull ones entirely until they happen. Neither instinct is a reliable guide. That's one reason to slow down and check the numbers, and where they came from, whenever an argument leans on 'just a small chance'.

The reasonable middle ground looks something like insurance. You don't buy home insurance because you expect a fire. You buy it because a fire would be ruinous and the premium is bearable. Nuclear engineers design for accidents they never expect to see for the same reason. The question isn't only how likely the disaster is. It's how bad, how irreversible, and how cheap it is to guard against.
A field guide to extreme bets

blocks.title: Testing a high-stakes, low-odds argument
items: Ask where the probability came from: measured data, or a guess?
Ask whether the downside is recoverable or permanent.
Price the hedge: what does protection cost compared with the loss?
Run the many-gods test: does the same logic support opposite choices?
Run the mugger test: who benefits if you accept the argument?

blocks.text: Notice what's missing from the list: certainty. You'll rarely have it. The goal isn't to eliminate guessing but to know which parts of your reasoning are guesses, and to make sure the decision doesn't collapse if one of them is wrong.

The many-gods test is especially useful. If an argument would justify a wildly different action just by changing the story, it's not really telling you anything. And the mugger test catches a lot of real-world manipulation. Scams, crypto pitches and doomsday sales routines all work by promising huge outcomes at tiny but unknowable odds, then daring you to say no.

Pascal's deepest point survives all the objections, though. You are already in the game. Every big decision in life, whether it's enlisting, choosing a career, starting a business or betting years on a creative long shot, is a wager made without enough information. Refusing to decide is just another bet. What the wager's critics add is a way to bet well: take the long shot when the downside is survivable, protect yourself against the losses you can't recover from, and be very suspicious of anyone whose math only works when the numbers get infinitely large.

When someone says 'even a tiny chance of X justifies Y', ask two things. Where did the tiny chance come from? And would the same reasoning justify the opposite choice? If the answers are 'nowhere' and 'yes', you're being mugged.

takeaways: Pascal's wager is the first serious attempt to reason about choices under deep uncertainty.
Infinite or astronomically large payoffs break expected-value math; anyone can name a bigger number.
Separate measurable long shots, like asteroids, from guesses dressed up as probabilities.
Guard hardest against losses that are permanent, even if they're unlikely.
Not deciding is also a bet, so bet deliberately and keep a safety net.

title: And Then What?
dek: Most bad decisions aren't dumb. They get the first consequence right and never see the second. How to think one move further than everyone else.

blocks.text: In November 1989, Mexico City tried something that sounded airtight. The city sits in a high basin ringed by mountains that trap exhaust, and smog had hit record levels. So the government banned every car from the road one weekday a week, based on the last digit of its license plate. Plates ending in 5 or 6 stayed parked on Mondays, and so on down the week.

The rule covered about 2.3 million vehicles, and enforcement was serious: get caught and your car was impounded for two days. The arithmetic looked unbeatable. Take a fifth of the cars off the road each weekday and you take a big bite out of the pollution. Officials were right about that first step. They just never thought hard enough about the second one.

Families who needed to drive every day did the obvious thing. They bought another car with a different final digit, and the extra car was often cheap, old and dirty. When the economist Lucas Davis went through years of air-monitoring data, he found no evidence the program had improved air quality, and later work suggested pollution may have risen a year or two after the rules began. A policy meant to take cars off the road had helped put more of them on it.

The city didn't learn the lesson cleanly, either. In 2008 it extended the ban to Saturdays. Forecasts made beforehand predicted a drop of 15 percent or more in Saturday vehicle emissions. When Davis checked again, across eight major pollutants, the expansion had almost no detectable effect. He also found no sign that people had shifted onto the subway or buses. The forecast was a first-order prediction. The drivers made a second-order response.

That gap, between what a decision does first and what it does once people react, is what **second-order thinking** is about. It's the habit of asking one more question than everyone else in the room. Not just *what happens if we do this?* but *and then what?*

items.label: Vehicles covered by Mexico City's 1989 driving ban
That the ban improved air quality; drivers bought extra cars instead

blocks.source: Davis, Scientific Reports, 2017 (summarizing Davis, Journal of Political Economy, 2008)

blocks.text: The seen and the unseen

The investor Howard Marks draws a line between first-level and second-level thinking. First-level thinking says: this is a great company, so buy the stock. Second-level thinking says: everyone already knows it's a great company, the price already reflects that, so the real question is whether it will do *better than people expect*. The first is a reaction to a fact. The second is a model of how everyone else will react to the same fact.

The idea is much older than Wall Street. In 1850 the French economist Frédéric Bastiat wrote an essay called *That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen*. His example was a shopkeeper whose son breaks a window. The neighbors console him that at least the glass-maker gets some business. Bastiat's point was that the money spent on glass is money the shopkeeper no longer spends on shoes or a book. The glazier's gain is visible. The shoemaker's loss is invisible, so nobody counts it.

Ecologists have a blunter version, usually credited to Garrett Hardin: you can never do merely one thing. In 1935, Australian authorities released cane toads in Queensland to control insects eating the sugarcane. The toads turned out to be poor pest control. They were very good, however, at spreading. They are poisonous to the native predators that try to eat them, and the descendants of roughly a hundred imported animals now cover more than a million square kilometers.

items.label: Cane toads brought to Australia in 1935 for insect control
Area the toads now cover, harming native wildlife

blocks.source: Russo et al., Frontiers in Microbiology, 2021

blocks.title: Two ways to evaluate a decision

left.head: First-order thinking
items: What does this do right now?
Who benefits that I can see?
Assumes everyone else stays put
Judged by the first week's results
Fast, obvious, usually shared by everyone

right.head: Second-order thinking
items: What happens after people react?
Who pays that I can't see yet?
Assumes everyone else adapts
Judged at ten months and ten years
Slower, less obvious, where the edge is

blocks.text: The board moves back

A physics problem and a people problem differ in one crucial way. Atoms don't change their behavior because you wrote a rule about them. People do. Any decision that touches other humans is less like pushing a block across a table and more like moving a piece on a board where the other side gets a turn.

Rent control is the classic case, and a 2019 study gives it unusually clean numbers. In 1994, San Francisco extended rent control to small apartment buildings built before 1980, but not to similar buildings built after. That quirk of timing let the economists Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade and Franklin Qian compare tenants and landlords on either side of the line, almost like a natural experiment.

items.label: Drop in tenant mobility under rent control: renters stayed put, as intended
Cut in rental housing supply as landlords converted or redeveloped buildings

blocks.source: Diamond, McQuade & Qian, American Economic Review, 2019

blocks.text: The first-order effect was real and good. Covered tenants were less likely to be pushed out of the city. But landlords got a move too. Many sold units to owner-occupants or redeveloped their buildings, shrinking the supply of rentals in those buildings by 15 percent. Fewer rentals means higher rents for everyone not already protected. The authors conclude the law likely helped push up market rents over the long run, working against the very goal it was written for.

Sometimes the reaction is psychological instead of financial. The economists Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini studied day-care centers in Israel where parents kept showing up late. The centers introduced a fine for late pickups. Late arrivals went *up*, significantly, and stayed up even after the fine was dropped. Before the fine, being late meant imposing on a teacher, which felt bad. The fine turned it into a service with a price tag. Guilt went away and parents simply paid for extra babysitting.

Notice who adapted fastest in each case. Not the planners, but the people with the most at stake and the best local knowledge: drivers who needed to get to work, landlords who knew exactly what their buildings were worth, parents who just wanted an extra twenty minutes. A rule is written once, by people far away. The responses are written by thousands of people up close, every day, with strong motives to find the gap.

Notice what these stories share. The planners weren't stupid, and they predicted the first effect correctly. What they missed was that the people inside the system had goals of their own and would quietly reorganize around the new rule.
Why your brain stops at step one

If second-order effects are everywhere, why does almost everyone miss them? Partly because of how they show up. First-order effects are immediate, visible and easy to take credit for. Second-order effects are delayed, spread thin and usually land on someone else. The politician who caps rents gets the headline that week. The housing shortage arrives years later with nobody's name on it.

There's also an effort problem. Predicting the first effect takes one model: how the thing works. Predicting the second takes a model of every other player's model. That's expensive, and a tired brain grabs the cheap answer whenever it can.

And the second move is genuinely hard to call, because it can cut either way. In 1975 the economist Sam Peltzman argued that car safety rules might lead drivers to take more risks, eating up part of the benefit. That idea, now called risk compensation, holds up in some settings and is badly overstated in others. Seat belts still save lives. The lesson isn't that safety measures backfire. It's that behavior shifts, and you have to ask by how much.

Efficiency has its own twist. In 1865 the English economist William Stanley Jevons noticed that better steam engines had not cut Britain's coal use. They made coal-powered work cheaper, so people did more of it, and total consumption climbed. Make something cheaper to use, and you may get more of it used rather than less.
Think like a player, not a planner

If you've lived through a balance patch in a competitive game, you already understand this better than a lot of policymakers. The developer nerfs the dominant weapon. First-order effect: fewer people use it. Second-order effect: the next-best option becomes the new problem, and whatever used to counter it quietly falls out of the meta. Good designers patch with that second wave in mind.

The same thing happens when you build a game. Double a currency's drop rate to make new players happy, and within weeks the economy inflates and the old rewards feel worthless. Add a daily login bonus to boost retention, and you may train players to log in, collect and leave. Every system you add is an invitation for players to find the cheapest path through it, and they will find it faster than you did.

It works the same way inside an organization. A procedure step added after one incident makes that exact mistake harder. What it does next depends on the cost. Stack enough steps and people start skimming all of them, including the ones that matter. Rules written without asking how tired, busy people will actually respond tend to produce exactly that.
A toolkit for the next move

blocks.title: Running the second move
items: State the obvious first effect in one sentence.
Ask 'and then what?' at least twice more, writing each answer down.
List everyone affected and what each of them wants; every one of them gets a move.
Find the substitute: where will the money, effort or behavior go instead?
Check three horizons: ten days, ten months, ten years.
Run a premortem: imagine it failed a year from now and write the likeliest story why.

blocks.text: Time horizons matter because first- and second-order effects often point in opposite directions. Many good things feel bad first: training, saving, grinding through study for a qualification. Many bad things feel good first: one more hour of scrolling, the impulse buy, the shortcut on a checklist. A lot of what people call discipline is just second-order thinking pointed at yourself.

The substitute question is the one that catches the most mistakes. Behavior rarely vanishes when you block it; it moves. Ban driving on Mondays and people drive a different car. Make one route through a game harder and players crowd onto the next one. Delete an app from your phone and the same urge shows up in the browser. Before you celebrate stopping something, ask where it went.

The premortem, popularized by the psychologist Gary Klein, works because it flips the question. Asking a team what could go wrong invites defensiveness. Telling them the plan already failed and asking why gives everyone permission to say what they were already half-thinking.
The trap on the other side

Second-order thinking has an evil twin. Once you know actions have unintended consequences, you can argue against anything. The economist Albert Hirschman noticed this in his 1991 book *The Rhetoric of Reaction*. Opponents of change, he found, reach for the same three arguments over and over: it will backfire, it won't do anything, or it will wreck something we already have.

Sometimes those arguments are right, as Mexico City shows. Often they aren't. Plenty of changes, from vaccination campaigns to clean-water rules, did roughly what they promised. 'There might be unintended consequences' is not an argument. It's a prompt. The real work is naming the specific consequence, estimating how big it is, and comparing it with the cost of doing nothing, which has second-order effects of its own.

How far ahead should you look? Not forever. Each extra step is less certain than the one before, and by the fourth or fifth you're mostly guessing. In practice, the second move is where most of the value lives, with a quick glance at the third. Chess players don't calculate every line to checkmate. They calculate the forcing moves deeply, and trust judgment for the rest.

So the goal isn't to become the person who says 'it's more complicated' in every meeting. It's to be the one who has already played the next two moves and can say which consequences are big enough to matter and which are just noise.
Carry one question everywhere: *and then what?* Ask it until the answers stop changing. The first answer tells you what you're doing. The second and third tell you what you're actually causing.

takeaways: People adapt to every rule, so predict their move, not just yours.
First-order effects are fast and visible; second-order effects are slow and land on someone else.
Ask 'and then what?' at least three times, and check ten days, ten months and ten years out.
Many good choices feel bad at first, and many bad ones feel good at first.
'It might backfire' only counts once you can say how, and how much.

title: Are You Someone's Simulation?
dek: In 2003 an Oxford philosopher argued that one of three strange things has to be true, and the third is that you are almost certainly living inside a computer.

blocks.text: Minecraft players have built working computers out of redstone. Not mods, not plugins: actual processors made from in-game blocks, with memory and logic gates, slow and enormous, running simple programs inside a world that is itself a program running on a real machine. A computer inside a game inside a computer. Nobody inside that redstone CPU knows it's nested two layers deep, because there is nobody inside it. Yet.

Now push the idea forward a few centuries. Suppose game engines keep improving the way they have since Pong, and someday someone can simulate not just blocks and physics but brains, neuron by neuron, well enough that the simulated people think and feel. Then ask the uncomfortable question. If that day comes, and someone runs a lot of those worlds, how would anyone inside one of them know?

In 2003 the philosopher Nick Bostrom, then at Oxford, turned that late-night dorm question into a tight argument, published in *The Philosophical Quarterly*. It doesn't claim we live in a simulation. It claims something sneakier: that if you accept a few reasonable-sounding premises, you're forced to pick one of three surprising conclusions. And the third one is that you are almost certainly a simulated person.
Three doors, pick one

Bostrom calls the worlds in question *ancestor simulations*: detailed simulations of an earlier era of a civilization's history, run by its far-future descendants, which he calls posthumans. Then he says at least one of these must be true. First, almost every civilization at our stage goes extinct before it gets the technology to run such simulations. Second, almost no civilization that does get the technology has any interest in running many of them. Third, we are almost certainly living in one.

The logic is a counting argument. If even a small fraction of advanced civilizations run lots of ancestor simulations, then simulated minds will vastly outnumber original, biological ones. One real history, thousands or millions of copies. If you have no special evidence about which kind of mind you are, the honest bet is that you're one of the many, not the one. Bostrom calls this the *bland indifference principle*: if most observers with experiences like yours are simulated, your credence that you are simulated should match that fraction.

blocks.title: The simulation argument in five moves
items: Minds can, in principle, run on computers, not just on biological brains.
A technologically mature civilization would have enormous computing power to spare.
So it could run huge numbers of detailed simulations of its own past, cheaply.
If any meaningful fraction of civilizations did this, simulated minds would massively outnumber real ones.
Therefore: either almost no one gets there, almost no one bothers, or you are probably simulated.

blocks.text: The key word is *either*. Bostrom isn't selling door three. In the paper he says that, given how ignorant we are, it seems sensible to spread your belief roughly evenly across all three.

Each door is unsettling in its own way. Door one says humanity probably doesn't make it. Door two says every advanced civilization, without exception, loses interest in something we would find irresistible. Door three says the world around you is software.
Is that even possible?

The argument only works if the computing is affordable, so Bostrom ran rough numbers. He used two estimates of the processing it takes to match a human brain, one based on how much computation it takes to copy what the retina does, the other on synapse counts and firing rates. Then he multiplied out a full human history: about 100 billion people, living about 50 years each. He also cited estimates of what a computer the mass of a planet could do using nanotechnology designs already sketched on paper.

items.label: Operations per second Bostrom estimated a human brain performs
Operations to simulate the mental history of all humans who ever lived
Operations per second cited for one planet-sized computer

blocks.source: Bostrom, The Philosophical Quarterly, 2003

blocks.text: Put those together and the conclusion is startling. By his figures, one planet-mass computer could run the entire mental history of humanity using less than a millionth of its processing power for a single second. A civilization that could build many such machines wouldn't need to make sacrifices to run simulations. It could run them the way you leave a game server up overnight.

Notice the trick that keeps the cost down. The simulation doesn't need to model every atom in the universe. It only needs to model what its inhabitants actually look at, in the detail they look at it, the same way a game engine doesn't render the room behind you. Distant stars can be cheap points of light until someone builds a telescope. If a scientist zooms in on something, the system fills in detail on demand. As anyone who has written game code knows, that's just good optimization.

People sometimes point to quantum mechanics as a clue here, since particles seem not to have definite properties until they are measured. It sounds like rendering on demand. Physicists mostly treat that as a loose analogy, not evidence. Quantum theory makes the same predictions whether or not anyone is running it on a server, so the resemblance tells you more about how game-like our intuitions are than about what the universe is.
The strongest pushback

A lot of smart people find the argument clever but not convincing, and their objections are worth taking seriously. The deepest one goes straight at premise one. Bostrom assumes that a simulated brain would actually be conscious, that experience comes from the right kind of information processing, whatever it runs on. That is exactly the question nobody has answered. If consciousness needs biology, or something else computers lack, then simulated people would be empty puppets, and you, who definitely experience things, couldn't be one of them.

A second objection attacks the counting. In 2020 the Columbia astronomer David Kipping ran a Bayesian analysis of the argument. His point was that we don't know whether such simulations are even technically possible, and that uncertainty has to be counted alongside the huge number of possible simulated worlds. Once he did that, the probability that we are simulated came out below 50 percent, approaching 50 only in the limit of infinitely many simulations. The quantum-computing researchers Alexandre Bibeau-Delisle and Gilles Brassard reached a similar verdict the same year, arguing the odds are unlikely to be as high as earlier claims suggested, especially if simulations have to run simulations of their own.

A third objection is that the whole thing smuggles in assumptions about what posthumans would want. We have no idea what a mind a million years ahead of us values. Maybe running billions of suffering ancestors for fun would be considered monstrous. Maybe it's illegal. Maybe it's just boring, like asking an adult to keep playing with a toy they outgrew. Door two might be the boring, correct answer.

Then there's the falsifiability problem. A good scientific claim makes predictions that could prove it wrong. In 2012 three physicists, Silas Beane, Zohreh Davoudi and Martin Savage, tried to do exactly that. They imagined a simulation built on a cubic grid, like the lattices physicists already use to simulate the strong nuclear force, and asked what tell-tale signs that would leave. Their answer: the very highest-energy cosmic rays might show a subtle preference for certain directions, lining up with the grid. It's a long shot, but it turned a philosophy question into something a detector could, in principle, test.

blocks.title: Should you take it seriously?

left.head: Reasons to
items: The math of the counting step is simple and hard to dodge
Simulation power has grown relentlessly since the 1970s
A simulation only has to render what its inhabitants observe
It rests on premises many scientists already accept

right.head: Reasons to doubt
items: Nobody knows if simulated brains would be conscious
Bayesian analyses put the odds below 50 percent
We can't guess what posthumans would want
Hard to test, and so far no physics anomaly points to it

blocks.text: The twist: you can move the odds

Here is the part of the argument that gets under your skin. Suppose humanity, or some company, actually builds a convincing ancestor simulation full of conscious people. That would knock out doors one and two in one move: we'd have proof that civilizations can reach the tech and that at least one wants to use it. Kipping makes the same point. If we ever start producing such simulations ourselves, the odds that we are sims jump sharply.

Bostrom's paper ends on a related twist. Unless we are already living in a simulation, he notes, our descendants will almost certainly never run one. The two facts are chained together. Which means the people most excited about building the ultimate simulation are also, in a strange way, the people working hardest to prove they're probably inside one.

It gets stranger. Bostrom points out that computers can be stacked, the way a virtual machine runs inside your desktop. If our simulators can be simulated too, reality could have many levels, each one running on the one below. But every level costs the level beneath it, and a simulated civilization that grows powerful enough to start running its own simulations would get expensive fast. Bostrom notes, almost in passing, that this gives our hypothetical operators a reason to shut a simulation down right around the time its people are about to become posthuman.

If you build games, this has an odd ring to it. Every NPC you script lives in a world with rules you chose, physics you tuned, and corners you never bothered to render. Right now they're simple state machines with no inner life. But the direction of travel is clear. Characters in games are getting smarter every year, and some already chat back using language models. At what point would you owe them anything?

Flip the question around and it becomes a mirror. If we are someone's simulation, we would hope our creators cared whether we suffered, didn't delete us on a whim, and didn't run a few billion copies of history's worst years for entertainment. Whatever rules you would want them to follow are a decent first draft of the rules we should follow if we ever create minds of our own. The simulation argument, oddly, ends up being an ethics question about the future of game design.

blocks.title: The long history of doubting reality
items: c. 300s BCE
Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly, then wonders if he's a butterfly dreaming he is a man
c. 375 BCE
Plato's cave: prisoners mistake shadows on a wall for the whole of reality
Descartes imagines an evil demon feeding him a false world
Hilary Putnam's brain in a vat on a scientist's lab bench
The Matrix brings the idea to the mainstream
Bostrom's simulation argument appears in The Philosophical Quarterly
Beane, Davoudi and Savage propose a physics test
David Chalmers argues in Reality+ that virtual worlds can be genuinely real

blocks.text: Would it even matter?

Say door three is right. Does anything change? The philosopher David Chalmers, who has spent decades on consciousness, argues in his 2022 book *Reality+* that the answer is less than you'd think. His view is that a simulated world isn't fake.

It's made of digital processes instead of whatever the base level is made of, but the tables still hold your weight, the people are still people, and the causes and effects are all still there. Physics already says your desk is mostly empty space and quantum fields. Finding out those fields are running on someone else's hardware adds one more layer underneath, not a lie on top.

On that view, your effort in the gym still built muscle, the reactor plant you learned still behaves exactly as the books said, and the people you love are still conscious beings who love you back. What would change is cosmic context. There'd be a creator, though possibly a bored grad student rather than a god, and the universe might have an off switch. The economist Robin Hanson once half-jokingly suggested that if we're simulated, we should try to be interesting so nobody shuts the simulation down.

There's also a deeper lesson hiding here, and it doesn't depend on the answer. The argument shows how a few modest-looking assumptions, chained together, can force you somewhere wild. That's a skill worth having. Whenever a conclusion feels crazy, look for the premise doing the heavy lifting. In Bostrom's case it's the idea that a mind is just information processing, which is the very question the hard problem of consciousness says we can't yet settle.

Thought experiment to sit with: you're offered proof, today, that this world is a simulation. List three things you would do differently tomorrow. If the list is short, the question matters less than it feels. If it's long, ask why those things depend on what the universe is made of.

Most people who try that exercise find their list is short. They'd still want to see their family, finish what they started, and get better at what they care about. That might be the most useful answer the simulation argument gives: whatever the substrate, the life is still the one you're living, and it still counts.

takeaways: Bostrom's argument is a trilemma: civilizations die out, don't bother, or we're probably simulated. He spread his own belief roughly evenly across all three.
Its weakest link is the assumption that a simulated brain would be conscious, which nobody has proven.
Bayesian reanalyses put the odds of being simulated below 50 percent, not near certainty.
If we ever build conscious simulations ourselves, the odds that we are simulated jump.
Even if it's true, a simulated world can still be real in the ways that matter: effort, skills and people still count.

title: The Tragedy That Wasn't Inevitable
dek: For decades experts said shared resources were doomed unless governments or owners took over. Elinor Ostrom went and looked, and won a Nobel for showing ordinary people often do better.

blocks.text: For nearly five hundred years, the cod off Newfoundland seemed endless. European fishing fleets crossed the Atlantic for them before there were permanent colonies to come home to. Whole towns grew up around a single fish. Then, in the late 1980s, the catches started coming up short, and the fish that were caught were smaller and younger than they used to be. In July 1992 the Canadian government closed the northern cod fishery outright.

The moratorium put about 30,000 people in Newfoundland out of work. The closure was supposed to be temporary. Decades later, the northern cod still haven't returned to anything like their old numbers, and the fishing towns that survived switched largely to shellfish.

Nobody wanted that outcome. Not the fishermen, not the processing plants, not the government. Yet everyone kept fishing until the fish were gone. That pattern has a name, and for a long time it came with a grim conclusion: people sharing a resource will destroy it unless someone forces them to stop. Then a political scientist at Indiana University went out and checked, and won a Nobel prize for finding that the grim conclusion was only half true.
Hardin's pasture

In December 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay in *Science* called "The Tragedy of the Commons." He borrowed an image from an 1833 pamphlet by the English economist William Forster Lloyd: a pasture open to every herder in a village. Each herder asks a simple question. Should I add one more cow?

The math always says yes. The herder who adds the cow gets all the benefit of that extra animal: its milk, its meat, its sale price. The cost, a little more overgrazing, is split across everyone who uses the pasture. So adding the cow is rational for each herder individually, even though every herder doing it destroys the pasture they all depend on. Hardin's summary became one of the most quoted lines in environmental writing.
Freedom in a commons brings ruin to all.
blocks.by: Garrett Hardin, Science, 1968

blocks.title: The tragedy loop
items: A shared resource is open to everyone
Each user gains the full benefit of taking a bit more
The cost of overuse is spread across all users
Everyone takes more, and the resource shrinks
Scarcity makes grabbing your share now feel even more urgent

blocks.text: The logic is the same one behind the prisoner's dilemma. And Hardin's prescription followed from it. Since people won't restrain themselves, restraint must come from outside. Either a government steps in to regulate the resource, or the commons gets carved into private property so each owner bears the full cost of his own overuse. For decades, those were treated as the only two options, and policy around the world followed suit.
The woman who went and looked

Elinor Ostrom didn't argue with Hardin's logic. She argued with his evidence, because he didn't really have any. Ostrom was a political scientist at Indiana University whose first major study looked at how groundwater basins in Southern California were managed. Over the following decades, she and her colleagues collected detailed case studies of shared fisheries, pastures, forests, lakes and irrigation systems from all over the world.

What she found was that the tragedy was common but not inevitable. Many communities had managed shared resources well for generations, without either a central government in charge or private ownership. In Törbel, a village in the Swiss Alps, farmers have shared high mountain pastures under their own rules for centuries, including a limit tying how many cows you can send up to the summer meadows to how many you can feed through the winter. In Valencia, Spain, irrigators settle water disputes at a farmers' court that has met outside the city's cathedral every Thursday for generations.

Just as interesting were her stories of outside "fixes" that made things worse. The Nobel committee highlighted irrigation in Nepal. Farmers there had long maintained small, crude dams of stone, mud and timber. Upstream and downstream farmers needed each other, because the dams kept washing out and rebuilding them took everyone's labor. When government agencies and foreign donors replaced some of them with modern concrete dams, the dams no longer needed constant repair, so the farmers at the head of the canal no longer needed the farmers at the tail. They took more water, cooperation broke down, and crop yields were often higher around the primitive dams than around the modern ones.

Another example came from satellite images of grasslands across Mongolia, China and Russia. In Mongolia, nomadic herders kept moving their animals seasonally under traditional group arrangements. Across the borders, governments had imposed collective farms, and later China privatized much of its grassland into household plots. Both approaches settled herders in one place, and the land degraded far more than in Mongolia. Neither the state nor the market beat the old commons.

blocks.title: Two views of the commons

left.head: Hardin, 1968
items: Users are trapped by individual incentives
Shared resources trend toward ruin
Fix: government control or private property
Rules must come from outside

right.head: Ostrom, 1990
items: Users can create and enforce their own rules
Many commons have lasted for centuries
Fix depends on local conditions; no panacea
Rules made by the users tend to be obeyed

blocks.text: Eight features of commons that last

In her 1990 book *Governing the Commons*, Ostrom compared long-lived successes with failures and pulled out a set of design principles that the durable systems tended to share. They read less like economic theory and more like the rules of a well-run crew.

items: **Clear boundaries.** Everyone knows who has the right to use the resource and where its edges are.
**Rules that fit the place.** Limits on taking match local conditions, and what you put in is tied to what you get out.
**Users help make the rules.** Most people affected by the rules can take part in changing them.
**Monitoring by people accountable to the users.** Someone watches, and usually it's the users themselves.
**Graduated sanctions.** A first offense gets a mild penalty; repeat offenders face steeper ones.
**Cheap, fast conflict resolution.** Disputes get settled locally before they fester.
**Outside authorities respect the group's right to organize.** Higher governments don't override the local rules.
**Nested layers.** Larger systems are organized as smaller units within bigger ones, each handling what it can.

blocks.text: A 2010 review in *Ecology and Society* by Michael Cox, Gwen Arnold and Sergio Villamayor Tomás tested the principles against 91 later studies covering 77 cases. Every principle had at least twice as many supporting cases as contradicting ones, and the authors concluded the principles were well supported. They also found the most serious criticism was that the list is incomplete. Group size, the type of national government around a community, and especially how connected a village is to outside markets all mattered too. Communities close to markets were more likely to overexploit their resource, because the outside world changed what people needed from it.

items.label: Newfoundlanders put out of work by the 1992 northern cod moratorium
Studies reviewed in a 2010 test of Ostrom's design principles
Year Ostrom shared the Nobel memorial prize in economics

blocks.source: Ambio, 2026 (cod); Cox, Arnold & Villamayor Tomás, Ecology and Society, 2010; Nobel Prize press release, 2009

blocks.text: Why talking changes the game

Ostrom also took the commons into the lab. In experiments she ran with colleagues, groups of volunteers drew money from a shared pool where overuse shrank everyone's earnings. When players couldn't communicate, they overharvested, just as Hardin predicted. When they were allowed to talk to each other, cooperation improved a great deal. When they could also agree on their own rules and pay a small cost to fine people who broke them, they did even better. The title of one of those papers says it all: *Covenants With and Without a Sword: Self-Governance Is Possible*.

One of the findings the Nobel committee highlighted was that many people will pay out of their own pocket to punish free riders, even when they gain little from it personally. That sounds irrational, but it's the glue of every working commons. A shared resource survives when enough people are willing to spend a little effort calling out the person who takes too much.

Why would talking matter so much, when promises cost nothing to break? Part of the answer is that real commons aren't one-shot games. The herders in Törbel will see each other around the village, at community meetings and at every harvest for the rest of their lives. Breaking your word once buys you a little extra grass and costs you your reputation for good. In the language of game theory, repeated interactions with people who remember turn a prisoner's dilemma into something much closer to a coordination problem, where everyone just needs a clear, shared signal of what fair looks like.

That also explains why the principle about graduated sanctions matters so much. A first offender in a working commons usually gets a warning or a small fine, not banishment. Most people who break a rule do it once, under pressure, and a harsh first penalty can turn a decent neighbor into a permanent enemy of the system. Escalating penalties leave room to come back, while still making repeat cheating expensive.

Hardin himself eventually conceded part of the point. Writing in *Science* in 1998, he said his original essay should have described the tragedy of the *unmanaged* commons. A pasture with no rules really is doomed. A pasture where the herders know each other, talk, watch and punish is a completely different situation.
When local rules aren't enough

Ostrom was careful never to claim that communities always beat governments or markets. The Nobel committee pointed to an example on the other side: in the 1930s, oil fields in Texas and Oklahoma were wasted on a massive scale because the pools under many properties weren't consolidated under clear ownership. Sometimes privatization or regulation really is the answer. Ostrom's lesson was that there's no panacea, and that rules worked out over long periods by the people closest to a resource are often subtler than outsiders realize.

Her principles work best on resources with clear edges, users who know each other and expect to keep dealing with each other, and problems they can see. The northern cod failed every one of those tests. It was a vast offshore stock fished by large fleets from many places, and it collapsed under formal government management, not under a lawless free-for-all. The hardest commons of all, like the atmosphere or the high seas, are global, with billions of users who will never meet. That's why so much of the current thinking builds on Ostrom's idea of *polycentric* governance: many overlapping layers, local and national and international, each handling what it can rather than waiting for one perfect global deal.

blocks.title: The commons debate
items: William Forster Lloyd describes overgrazing on shared pasture
Hardin's "The Tragedy of the Commons" appears in Science
Ostrom publishes Governing the Commons
Canada closes the northern cod fishery
Hardin writes that he meant the unmanaged commons
Ostrom becomes the first woman to win the economics Nobel
A review of 91 studies finds her principles well supported

blocks.text: The commons you live in

Once you know the pattern, you see commons everywhere, especially in cramped places full of people. On a ship, the fresh water everyone draws from, the shared lounge, the gym equipment, the coffee pot that nobody refills and the laundry schedule are all small commons. The ones that work tend to have exactly Ostrom's features: everyone knows the rules, someone notices when they're broken, the first violation gets a joke or a reminder rather than a write-up, and people who use the resource have a say in how it's run.

Online spaces work the same way. A game community's Discord, a shared group project, even the codebase two people build a game in is a commons. A messy shortcut that saves you ten minutes costs your partner an hour later, which is Hardin's cow in software form. The fix is not to assume your partner is selfish. It's to agree on boundaries, a few clear rules, and a cheap way to flag problems early.

It also helps to notice which resources are quietly turning into commons without anyone saying so. Shared bandwidth when everyone is trying to download at once, a group chat that one person floods, a playtesting community that a single loud player dominates: all of them have the same structure as Hardin's pasture, and all of them respond to the same kind of fixes.

That's the deeper shift Ostrom offered. Hardin's story says shared things fail because people are selfish. Ostrom's evidence says shared things fail when there are no rules people helped make, no one watching, and no way to settle arguments. Human nature is the same in both stories. What differs is the structure people build around it.

If something shared keeps getting wrecked, don't just blame the people. Ask which of Ostrom's features is missing: clear boundaries, rules users helped make, monitoring, mild-then-escalating penalties, or a quick way to settle disputes.

takeaways: Hardin's tragedy is real: when each user gets the full benefit of taking more but shares the cost, an unmanaged commons tends toward ruin.
Ostrom showed many communities have governed shared resources for centuries without top-down control or privatization.
Durable commons share features: clear boundaries, rules users help make, monitoring, graduated penalties and quick conflict resolution.
Outside fixes can backfire when they remove the reasons people needed to cooperate, as with Nepal's concrete dams.
There's no panacea: big, global commons like the oceans and atmosphere need layered rules at many scales.

title: Design the World Before You Know Who You'll Be
dek: A World War II infantryman turned philosopher invented the most famous fairness test ever devised. When real people take it, they don't pick what he predicted.

blocks.text: Two brothers, one pizza, and a fight about who gets the bigger slice. Every parent eventually discovers the fix: one kid cuts, the other picks first. Suddenly the kid holding the knife becomes the most careful geometer in the house. He isn't being generous. He just knows that any slice he makes too small could end up on his own plate.

Now scale that trick up as far as it will go. Imagine you get to design the rules for an entire society: who gets what, who decides, what happens to the people who lose out. The catch is that you have no idea who you will be once the rules take effect. You might be born rich or poor, healthy or chronically sick, gifted or ordinary, into the majority or into a group everyone else looks down on. You won't even know which century you'll land in.

This is the *veil of ignorance*, the most famous thought experiment in modern political philosophy. Its inventor thought it settled the question of what a fair society looks like. Fifty years of argument, plus some surprising lab experiments, suggest it's more interesting than that. It doesn't hand you one answer. It shows you which of your opinions only survive because you already know which slice you're getting.
The infantryman's thought experiment

John Rawls was a Harvard philosopher, but before that he was an infantryman in World War II. He went into the war seriously considering the priesthood. He came out of it having lost his faith, in part, as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy puts it, from seeing how arbitrary death in combat was. Who lived and who died had nothing to do with who deserved what. That idea, that so much of what happens to us is morally arbitrary, runs straight through his work.

In 1971 Rawls published *A Theory of Justice*. Its central device was what he called the *original position*: a hypothetical meeting where people choose the basic rules of their society from behind a veil that hides every fact about themselves that could bias them. Your wealth, your talents, your race and sex, your social class, your health, even your personal idea of what makes life worth living all disappear. What you keep is general knowledge: how economies work, how people behave, what humans need.

One detail people often skip: Rawls also hid which generation you belong to. You might be born in this century or three centuries from now. That turns the veil into a question about the future. How much of today's wealth, forests, fish or public debt would you hand down if you might be the one inheriting the results? Rawls's answer was a *just savings principle*: each generation owes the next a fair share of what it was given, not everything and not nothing.

The point isn't that anyone ever stood behind such a veil. Rawls was clear that it's a thinking tool, a way to check whether a principle is fair or just convenient for the person proposing it. A billionaire who favors low taxes and a struggling student who favors free tuition might both be sincere. Behind the veil, neither can argue from where they happen to be standing.
The veil of ignorance is a bias filter. If you would only support a rule because of who you already are, the rule fails the test.
What Rawls thought you'd choose

Rawls argued that rational people behind the veil would agree on two principles. First, everyone gets the same basic liberties: speech, conscience, voting, a fair trial, equal protection under the law. Second, social and economic inequalities are allowed only if two conditions hold. Positions must be open to everyone under fair equality of opportunity, and the inequalities must work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society. That last condition is the famous *difference principle*.

Notice what the difference principle does not say. It doesn't demand equal outcomes. If paying surgeons more means there are more surgeons, and the poorest people get better healthcare as a result, the inequality passes. What fails is inequality that makes the people at the bottom worse off than they would be under some other arrangement.

Why would people choose that? Rawls's argument leaned on a decision rule from game theory called *maximin*: pick the option whose worst outcome is the best of all the worst outcomes. Normally maximin is far too cautious. You wouldn't use it to choose a lunch order. Rawls said the original position is a special case where it becomes the rational play.

blocks.title: Rawls's case for playing it safe behind the veil
items: You have no basis for guessing the odds of ending up in any particular position, so expected-value math has nothing to work with.
The choice is permanent. You can't renegotiate the rules of your whole life after you see where you landed.
Some alternatives have outcomes you could hardly accept, like slavery, starvation or persecution.
A guaranteed decent minimum is worth more to you than a shot at extra gains above it.
So you secure the floor first: protect the worst-off position, then let the rest of the system compete.

blocks.text: The gambler's reply

The sharpest pushback came from the economist John Harsanyi, who later shared the 1994 Nobel memorial prize in economics with John Nash and Reinhard Selten for work on game theory. Harsanyi had used a similar imagined veil in the 1950s and reached the opposite conclusion. If you truly don't know who you'll be, he argued, the reasonable assumption is an equal chance of being anyone. Then the rational choice is the society with the highest *average* well-being. That's utilitarianism, the exact view Rawls was trying to replace.

Harsanyi thought maximin was absurd outside the classroom. His best-known jab went roughly like this: a strict maximin chooser offered a far better job in another city would refuse to take the flight, because the worst outcome of flying is dying in a crash. Real people accept small chances of disaster for large chances of gain all the time. Why would they suddenly become ultra-cautious when designing a society?

Rawls answered that the original position is not an ordinary bet. The stakes are a whole life, the choice can never be revisited, and the rules must be ones you can actually live with once the veil lifts. He called this the *strains of commitment*. A society that sacrifices some people for a higher average asks those people to accept a deal they would find unbearable. A floor protects everyone from having to make that sacrifice.

blocks.title: Same veil, two answers

left.head: Rawls: secure the floor
items: Odds of each position are unknown
Choice is permanent and total
Protect the worst-off position first
Inequality allowed only if it helps the bottom
Result: equal liberties plus the difference principle

right.head: Harsanyi: maximize the average
items: Assume an equal chance of being anyone
Treat it like any rational bet
Count everyone's gains and losses equally
Some losers are acceptable if the total rises
Result: average utilitarianism

blocks.text: What happens when real people stand behind it

A thought experiment is supposed to reveal what reasonable people would choose. So researchers started asking real people. In the late 1980s the political scientists Norman Frohlich and Joe Oppenheimer ran experiments in which small groups had to agree on a rule for distributing income, without knowing which income class they would be assigned to afterward. Real money was at stake.

The groups rarely chose Rawls's difference principle. They also didn't choose pure average maximization. Most landed on a hybrid: make the average as high as possible, but guarantee a floor that no one can fall below. In other words, ordinary people split the difference between the two philosophers. They wanted a safety net and a growing pie.

That result makes a lot of sense once you think about insurance. Most people don't want to gamble their whole life on landing in the top half. They also don't want to cripple the economy to make everyone equal. A floor works like a policy you buy before you know whether disaster will hit: you accept a slightly smaller expected payout in exchange for never ending up with nothing. Many real welfare states look more like this hybrid than like either philosopher's pure theory.

A much larger set of experiments, published in 2019 in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* by Karen Huang, Joshua Greene and Max Bazerman, aimed the veil at specific moral dilemmas instead of whole societies. Across seven experiments with 6,261 participants, people first did a veil exercise. In one hospital case, for example, they imagined they had a 1-in-10 chance of being a single patient on oxygen and a 9-in-10 chance of being one of nine earthquake victims who needed that oxygen for surgery. Then they answered the standard version of the dilemma.

blocks.title: Share choosing the greater-good option, with and without the veil exercise first
blocks.note: Footbridge = push one person to save five. Car swerve = should self-driving cars sacrifice their passenger to save nine pedestrians. Charity = a real donation to a more vs less effective charity.
blocks.source: Huang, Greene & Bazerman, PNAS, 2019

blocks.text: The veil pushed people toward the choice that saved more lives in every case. The biggest jump came with self-driving cars. Asked whether cars should be programmed to swerve and sacrifice their own passenger to save nine pedestrians, 58 percent of control participants agreed. After imagining they had a 1-in-10 chance of being the passenger, 83 percent did. The effect also held for a real donation: more people gave to the more effective charity.

There's an irony here. Rawls built the veil to argue against utilitarian thinking. Yet when you give people even odds of being anyone affected, the veil nudges them toward exactly the greater-good math Harsanyi defended. The authors point out that this is the key difference: Rawls's version deliberately hides the odds, while theirs states them. Which version of the veil you use quietly decides which philosopher wins.
The veil in small places

You don't need to redesign a nation to use this tool. It works on any set of rules where the person writing them will also live under them. A watch rotation is a good test case. If you didn't know which section you'd end up in, which schedule would you actually sign off on? The answer is usually different from the one you'd defend once you know you've drawn the worst slot.

Game design is another. If you're building a game's economy, imagine you don't know whether you'll be a day-one player with every early reward, a free player who joins in month six, or someone who spends heavily. Rules that feel fine from the developer's chair can look brutal from the new player's. The veil turns that into a concrete question: would I still want to play this if I were dropped into the worst realistic position?

It also works on partnerships. The best time to agree on how ownership, credit and money get split in a project is before anyone knows who will end up doing the most work or getting the lucky break. Once those facts are known, everyone's sense of fairness bends toward their own slice. Agree on the rule while the veil is still down.

The same move works in an argument. When you catch yourself insisting that some rule is obviously fair, swap roles in your head. If you're the senior guy defending a perk, picture yourself as the newest person aboard who never gets it. If you're the new guy complaining, picture yourself as the senior one who waited years for it. Sometimes your position survives the swap. When it doesn't, you've learned that you were defending your slice, not a principle.

The tool has limits, and critics have spent decades pointing them out. Robert Nozick argued that justice is about how holdings came about, not what pattern they form, so no veil can tell you to redistribute what people fairly earned. Communitarian critics said a person stripped of every attachment is too thin to choose anything meaningful. And as the 2019 experiments showed, small changes in how the veil is framed can tilt the answer. The veil doesn't remove the need for judgment. It just makes it harder to hide your self-interest inside that judgment.

That may be the veil's real legacy. Rawls hoped it would prove one theory of justice. What it does even better is catch a habit everyone has: mistaking the view from your own seat for the view from nowhere. The kid with the pizza knife didn't become fair because he became a better person. He became fair because the rules stopped letting him know which slice was his. Good institutions, good games and good partnerships often work the same way.
Try it on your next argument about fairness: state the rule you want, then ask whether you'd still choose it if you were assigned the role of the person it hurts most.

takeaways: The veil of ignorance is a bias filter: choose the rules as if you didn't know which position you'd end up in.
Rawls argued people would protect the worst-off position first; Harsanyi argued they'd maximize the average. Both used the same veil.
In real experiments, groups usually chose a hybrid: grow the average, but guarantee a floor.
Telling people they have equal odds of being anyone pushes them toward the greater-good option (Huang et al., 2019).
Use it on small rule sets too: watch rotations, game economies, and splits with a partner, ideally before anyone knows who benefits.
