title: The Side Project That Ate the Day Job
dek: Minecraft started as a programmer's after-hours experiment. The research on side ventures says keeping the day job is not a lack of nerve. The hard part is making a few hours a week add up.

blocks.text: In May 2009, a Swedish programmer posted a short clip of a blocky cave game he had been tinkering with. He called it Cave Game. He had a real job at a photo software company, and the game was something he worked on around it. People started paying for early access. He kept the job. Only in 2010, once the money from those early sales was beating his salary, did he quit to work on it full time. The programmer was Markus Persson, and the game became Minecraft.

The usual story about building something is a story of leaping: quit the job, burn the boats, go all in. Persson's story is the quieter one. He did not leap. He built on the side until the side project proved it could carry him, and then he stepped across. That quieter path turns out to be the one the evidence favors, and it is the only path open to someone whose day job is a submarine.

Notice one more thing about the Minecraft story. Persson did not build in secret and reveal a finished game. He posted footage within days of starting and shared builds on an indie developer forum, and early players followed along as it grew. Building on the side and building in public fit together well: when you can only work a few hours a week, letting people watch the progress turns small steps into something that also attracts an audience.
Keeping the day job is a strategy, not a weakness

In 2014, management researchers Joseph Raffiee and Jie Feng asked a simple question: do people who start businesses while still employed do better or worse than people who quit first? They used a long-running U.S. government survey that has followed about 12,700 Americans since 1979, and looked at business starts from 1994 to 2008.

The people who kept their jobs while starting, whom the researchers called hybrid entrepreneurs, had a 33 percent lower rate of exiting their new business than those who jumped straight from a paycheck into full-time self-employment. Keeping the job did not signal weak commitment. It bought time to learn whether the idea worked before betting everything on it.

items.label: Lower rate of exiting the business for founders who kept their day job at first
People followed in the U.S. survey the study drew on
Years of business starts analyzed

blocks.source: Raffiee & Feng, Academy of Management Journal, 2014

blocks.text: A fair caveat: this is an observational study. People who choose the hybrid route may simply be more careful or less risk-hungry, and that could explain part of the gap. But the logic holds either way. A paycheck lets you make decisions based on what the project needs instead of what next month's rent needs. That freedom is worth more than the extra hours a full-time founder gets.

For a sailor, this reframes the situation. Ships, watches and duty days do eat time. But a steady paycheck, no debt and a career path with a civilian safety net are exactly the conditions under which experiments are cheap. The constraint is hours, not survival. That is a much better problem to have.
Your schedule is more optimistic than you are

The first enemy of a side project is not laziness. It is bad estimating. In a classic 1994 study, psychologist Roger Buehler and colleagues asked senior psychology students to predict when they would finish their honors theses. They also asked for a best-case guess and a worst-case guess, the date if everything went as badly as it could.

blocks.title: Thesis completion: estimates vs reality
blocks.note: On average, the students took longer than even their worst-case guess. Only about 30% finished by their predicted date.
blocks.source: Buehler, Griffin & Ross, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1994

blocks.text: Look at the last two bars. The average student took longer than their own *worst-case* scenario. This is the planning fallacy, and it gets worse, not better, for part-time work. A full-time builder who loses a day loses a fifth of a week. A part-time builder who loses a weekend to duty or a long underway loses everything that week had.

The fix the research points to is to stop estimating from the inside, picturing the steps going smoothly, and start estimating from the outside: how long did similar things *actually* take before? If the last few game ideas each died after a couple of months, that is your base rate. Plan the next one assuming the same pull, and build the plan to survive it. A practical rule: whatever your estimate, cut the scope until the estimate is half of the time you really have.
If a plan only works when nothing goes wrong, it is not a plan. It is a best-case guess, and the data says reality usually lands past the worst case.

Cutting scope is where most side projects are actually won or lost. For a launcher obby, that might mean one world instead of three, a handful of upgrades instead of a full tree, and no trading system until people are clearly coming back. Every feature that does not make the first version fun is a feature that makes it later. Later is the most dangerous word for a part-time builder, because every extra month is another month for life to interrupt.
The real tax is restarting

Programmer and investor Paul Graham wrote an influential essay about two kinds of schedules. Managers live in one-hour blocks, and an extra meeting costs them one hour. Makers need long stretches, often half a day, because building requires loading a whole problem into your head before you can do anything useful. A single interruption can wreck a maker's afternoon.

Side builders live in the worst version of this. Their sessions are short and scattered, so a large share of each session goes to remembering where they left off: which script was broken, what the next level needed, what the partner changed. If it takes 30 minutes to get your head back into the project and you only have 60, half your time is gone before you start.

That means the most valuable habit for a side project is not working longer. It is making restarts cheap. Ernest Hemingway famously advised stopping a writing session while you still know what comes next, so the next day starts with momentum instead of a blank page. Builders can do the same thing on purpose.

blocks.title: The parking routine: last five minutes of every session
items: Stop in the middle of something easy, not at the end of something hard.
Write one line: what you were doing and what is broken right now.
Write the very next action, small enough to start in two minutes.
Note anything you need from your partner, so it can happen while you are away.
Save, commit or back up, so the next session starts from a known state.

blocks.text: This feels too small to matter. It is not. The first ten minutes of a session decide whether it becomes productive or turns into scrolling. A clear next action is the difference between "open Studio and fix the jump pad" and "open Studio and figure out what I was doing."
Why small wins keep you going

The second enemy is motivation fade. Harvard researcher Teresa Amabile and Steven Kramer collected about 12,000 daily diary entries from 238 professionals across seven companies, each tracked for the length of a project. They wanted to know what separated people's best workdays from their worst.

The answer was almost embarrassingly simple. On the best days, the single most prominent event was making progress on meaningful work, even small progress. On the worst days, it was setbacks. They called this the progress principle. Feeling that you moved forward fuels the motivation to keep moving.

For a side project, this is a design requirement. If every session ends with "still not done" on a giant task, motivation drains. If tasks are cut small enough that most sessions end with something visibly working, a new obstacle, a fixed bug, a rough level, the project feeds itself. That is the same reason the parking routine ends with a tiny next step: it guarantees the next session starts with a quick win.

blocks.title: Two ways to build on the side

left.head: Waiting for big sessions
items: "I'll work on it when I have a free weekend"
Tasks sized like "build the level system"
Each restart takes half an hour
Long gaps kill momentum and the project fades

right.head: Small reps, cheap restarts
items: Short sessions on a fixed rhythm
Tasks sized to finish in one sitting
A parked next step makes restarts take minutes
Visible progress most sessions keeps motivation up

blocks.text: There is a related trap worth naming: confusing activity with progress. Watching tutorials, tweaking settings, rearranging a task list and redesigning the logo all feel productive, and all of them give you a little of the progress feeling without moving the project. A useful test at the end of a session is whether a player would notice what you did. If the answer keeps being no, the sessions are being spent on comfort work.

The same principle explains why fixed rhythms beat bursts of inspiration. Two or three sessions a week, at roughly the same times, mean the project never goes cold long enough for the restart cost to balloon. A burst of twelve hours one weekend followed by three weeks of nothing feels heroic but often produces less, because each return starts from zero.
Async: building with someone who is awake when you are not

Building with a partner while one of you disappears for weeks without reliable internet sounds like a dealbreaker. It is actually a known problem with a known shape. Remote teams across time zones solve it with asynchronous work: decisions and progress live in writing, so nobody has to be online at the same time.

The trick is splitting work by what needs a connection. Live operations, like publishing updates, answering players and posting clips, belong to whoever is on shore. Deep work that can be done offline belongs to whoever is underway: game design documents, level layouts sketched on paper, upgrade tables and pricing math, video scripts, lists of bugs and ideas to test. A deployment is not dead time for a project if the offline work is planned before it starts.

items: Before going underway: agree on one goal for the period and who owns which pieces.
Underway: work only on things that need no internet, and keep a running log of decisions and questions.
On return: hand over the log in one sitting, then merge, test and ship together.
Always: one shared written list of what is being built now, next and later, so nothing lives only in one person's head.

blocks.text: This also keeps the partnership healthy. Most friction between co-builders comes from surprise: one person changes something big while the other is away. Writing things down and agreeing on owners before a long absence prevents most of that.

Be realistic about energy, too. After a long watch or a duty day, deep design work may be out of reach, and forcing it usually produces work you redo later. Keep two kinds of tasks on the list: thinking tasks for when you are fresh, like designing a new mechanic, and low-energy tasks for when you are tired, like naming upgrades, cleaning up a bug list or sorting clips. Matching the task to the energy you actually have means a tired evening still moves the project a little, instead of becoming a reason to skip it entirely.
A few hours, every week, for a long time

Put the evidence together and a clear strategy appears. Keep the stable job; it makes experiments cheap. Distrust your schedule, and cut scope until the plan has room for duty days and surprises. Make every restart cheap with a parked next step. Size tasks so most sessions end with a small win. Split work with your partner by what needs a connection, and write everything down.

None of this needs a tracking spreadsheet or an elaborate system. It needs a rhythm: a few fixed sessions a week, each one starting with a written next step and ending with one. Minecraft did not need its creator to quit his job to get started. It needed him to keep coming back to it. The question to ask about a side project is not "How much time do I have?" It is "How little does it take for me to pick this back up?" Get that number close to zero, and a few hours a week compound into something real.

takeaways: Founders who kept their day jobs at first exited their businesses about a third less often; a paycheck makes experiments cheap.
People routinely blow past even their worst-case estimates, so cut scope until the plan fits half your real time.
The hidden cost of side projects is restarting; end every session with a written next step.
Small visible progress is the strongest daily motivator, so size tasks to finish in one sitting.
With a partner, split work by what needs internet: offline design underway, live operations on shore.

title: The 70-Hour Week That Did a 56-Hour Week's Work
dek: A century-old study of munitions workers, decades of game postmortems and the psychology of passion all say the same thing: past a point, more hours buy you almost nothing, and the cost comes due later.

blocks.text: In October 2018, just before *Red Dead Redemption 2* came out, the Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser gave an interview to *New York* magazine's Vulture about what it took to finish the game. The numbers were staggering: around 300,000 animations and 500,000 lines of dialogue. Then came the line that set off a long argument across the industry. Several times that year, he said, the team had been working 100-hour weeks.
We were working 100-hour weeks.
blocks.by: Dan Houser, Rockstar Games, to Vulture, 2018

blocks.text: Most people who heard that line reacted to it as a moral question: is it fair to ask people to work like that? There is an older and more practical question underneath. Does working like that even get more done? About a century ago, the British government ran what amounts to an experiment on that question, and an economist dug the data back up in 2014. The answer should change how anyone building something big in their spare time thinks about effort.
Hours are not output

During the First World War, Britain needed shells, and its munitions factories pushed workers, most of them women, through very long weeks, sometimes with no day off at all. A government body called the Health of Munition Workers Committee was set up to study the effects, and it recorded the weekly hours and output of groups of workers in detail. Its investigators concluded that longer hours often produced no more shells.

In 2014 the Stanford economist John Pencavel reanalyzed those records with modern statistics. Below about 49 hours a week, output rose in step with hours. Above that, each extra hour added less and less. Output peaked at around 63 hours, after which more hours actually reduced it. And output at 70 hours a week was barely different from output at 56.

items.label: Weekly hours after which each extra hour added less output
Point where total weekly output peaked, then began to fall
Output at 70 hours a week differed little from output at 56

blocks.source: John Pencavel, The Productivity of Working Hours, Economic Journal, 2014

blocks.text: Pencavel also tested the committee's complaint about Sunday work. Holding weekly hours constant, taking away the weekly day of rest cut output by about ten percent. Put the two effects together and a 48-hour, six-day week came out slightly ahead of a 70-hour week worked across all seven days. That is 22 extra hours every week for nothing, and Pencavel notes that his findings line up with modern research tying long hours to more accidents and injuries.

There are fair limits on how far to stretch this. These were factory workers doing physical, repetitive jobs a hundred years ago. Creative and technical work is different, and the evidence for it is thinner. But there is little reason to think that thinking, debugging and designing hold up better under exhaustion than turning shell casings. If anything, work that depends on judgment is the first thing fatigue erodes, because tired people do not notice their own mistakes.

Part of the reason long hours survive anyway is that they feel productive. Hours are easy to see and count; output is slow, lumpy and hard to measure. A night spent at the desk until 3 a.m. feels like progress even when half of it went into fixing bugs you introduced at 1 a.m. The munitions committee's investigators had a big advantage over the rest of us: they could count the shells.
The question is never how many hours you can put in. It is how many hours still produce good work, and what the extra ones cost you next month.
Crunch is a planning failure wearing a work ethic

Game development has its own name for long stretches of forced overtime: crunch. In 2017, Henrik Edholm and colleagues interviewed developers at four studios and reviewed 78 published postmortems on the subject. As summarized in a later review, 45 percent of those postmortems mentioned crunch. Small studios were the most prone to it, ahead of both the tiniest teams and medium-sized ones.

blocks.title: Postmortems mentioning crunch, by studio size
blocks.note: Published postmortems, not a random sample of studios.
blocks.source: Edholm et al., ICSE-SEIP 2017, as summarized by Politowski et al., 2021

blocks.text: The interesting part is not that crunch happens, but where it comes from. When Cristiano Politowski and colleagues coded 927 problems from 200 game postmortems, crunch itself was a small category. The bigger ones sat upstream: teams with too few people for the work, plans that underestimated how long things would take, and scope that kept growing. Crunch is usually what those problems look like at the end of a project. Someone promised too much, to themselves or to someone else, and the hours are the bill.

The single most common root cause in that dataset was insufficient workforce, logged 49 times: too few people for the work, or one person carrying too many jobs. Underestimation came up 34 times. A two-person team with part-time hours starts life with both problems built in. That is not a reason to quit. It is a reason to plan as if both are true from day one, because they are.

There is also a difference between studio crunch and side-project crunch that cuts the wrong way. A studio's crunch, however brutal, usually ends when the game ships. A hobby project often has no ship date at all, so self-imposed overtime has no natural end. Without a deadline to stop at, a burst of late nights can quietly become the normal way of working.

blocks.title: How a side project burns out
items: Plan more than the hours allow
Fall behind and feel guilty
Make it up with late nights
Get tired and make mistakes
Lose time fixing mistakes

blocks.text: That reframe matters for a side project, because there is no studio boss imposing the crunch. You impose it on yourself. The pole you wanted finished this week, the map your partner is waiting on, the update you told players was coming. Every one of those is a small promise, and every broken promise feels like it has to be paid back with hours you don't have.
Two kinds of passion

The usual advice is to work on something you love, so it won't feel like work. The research on passion says that is only half true. The psychologist Robert Vallerand distinguishes two kinds. **Harmonious passion** is when you love an activity and choose freely when to engage in it; it fits alongside the rest of your life. **Obsessive passion** is when the activity has become something you feel you *must* do, often because your self-worth or identity is riding on it. Both kinds involve caring a lot. They feel very different from the inside.

In a 2010 study, Vallerand and colleagues followed 258 nurses in Quebec over six months. Harmonious passion predicted more satisfaction with the work and less conflict with the rest of life. Obsessive passion predicted more conflict, because people couldn't let go of the work when they were supposed to be doing something else. And that conflict, in turn, predicted rising burnout. The damage didn't come from caring. It came from not being able to stop.

blocks.title: Same love, different relationship

left.head: Harmonious passion
items: You choose when to work on it
Skipping a day feels fine
A bad session is just a bad session
Other parts of life stay intact

right.head: Obsessive passion
items: You feel you have to work on it
Skipping a day brings guilt
A bad session feels like a verdict on you
Sleep, friends and duty get squeezed

blocks.text: Anyone building a game they really believe in should be honest about which column they are living in. Wanting the game to succeed is fine. Feeling that you are worth less on days it doesn't move is the warning sign.

One practical protection follows from the definition. Obsessive passion grows when one activity becomes the main source of your sense of worth. Keeping other anchors in your life, such as training, friends, reading or your job itself, means a bad week on the game is just a bad week on the game. People whose whole identity rides on one project have no shock absorbers when it stalls.
Recovery is part of the work

If long hours buy little, rest has to be doing something. Work psychologists study this under the name recovery, and one of its most consistent ingredients is psychological detachment: mentally switching off from work during time off, not just physically leaving. A 2017 meta-analysis by Johannes Wendsche and Andrea Lohmann-Haislah pooled 86 publications covering more than 38,000 employees. People who detached more reported less exhaustion, better sleep, more well-being and better task performance.

The same analysis has an honest twist. Detachment was slightly *negatively* linked with creativity. Some ideas arrive precisely because your mind keeps chewing on a problem in the shower. The goal is not to never think about the game. It is to be able to stop when you need to, which is exactly the skill obsessive passion destroys. Detachment is also a skill you can practice. A fixed ritual that marks the end of a session, like closing the laptop, writing the next-step note and doing something physical, teaches your brain that the work has stopped. That matters most when the place you work and the place you rest are the same few rooms.

Long breaks help less than people hope. A 2009 meta-analysis of vacation studies led by Jessica de Bloom found that holidays did improve health and well-being, but the effect was small and faded quickly once people went back to work. You cannot bank a week off to pay for months of overload. What protects you is the daily and weekly rhythm.

The psychologist Sabine Sonnentag calls the cruel part of this the recovery paradox. When work stress is highest, people need recovery most, and that is exactly when they are least likely to get it. They are too wound up to detach, too tired to exercise and too behind to take an evening off. For someone whose day job already runs on rotating duty and short sleep, filling every off-duty hour with a second job is the paradox in its purest form.
Pacing a long build
So what does a sustainable pace look like for a part-time project that will take months? A few rules follow straight from the evidence.

blocks.title: Rules for a project you want to finish
items: Set a weekly hour budget you could keep even in a bad week, and plan work to fit it, not the other way around.
Keep one full day a week with no project work at all. The munitions data says rest days pay for themselves.
End each session at a clean stopping point, with a one-line note on what to do next, so starting again is easy.
When you fall behind, cut scope before you add hours.
Treat deployments and duty weeks as planned pauses: leave handoff notes and let the project wait without guilt.
Watch for the signs of obsessive passion, and take them as seriously as a bug report.

blocks.text: That last-but-one rule deserves emphasis for anyone who disappears underwater for weeks at a time. A long absence is not a failure to manage. It is a fixed part of the schedule, and a plan that ignores it is a plan to crunch on the way back. The healthy version is boring: write down where things stand, agree with your partner what will and won't move while you're gone, and come back to a short list instead of a pile of guilt.

Pace is also a team agreement, not just a personal one. Two partners who quietly expect different speeds will each feel let down: one thinks the other is slacking, the other feels pushed. Say the numbers out loud. How many hours a week can each of you actually give, in a normal week and in a bad one? A plan built on the honest numbers will be slower on paper and faster in reality, because it won't collapse.

On bad days, lower the bar instead of skipping the plan entirely or forcing a full session. Fifteen minutes to fix one small thing, or simply reading your notes, keeps the thread alive without draining you. And some days the right amount is zero. The project will still be there tomorrow, and so, if you pace it, will you.

If exhaustion, cynicism or a sense that nothing you do matters starts hanging around for weeks, not days, take it seriously. Those are the three classic dimensions of burnout, and they are worth raising with a corpsman, a chaplain or someone you trust, not just pushing through. A hobby that is supposed to be your way out should not become one more thing grinding you down.

The game you finish at a steady 10 hours a week will beat the game you abandon after three months of 40. Pencavel's munitions workers made the point with artillery shells a hundred years ago: past a certain line, the extra hours were never really working. They were just being spent.

takeaways: Past roughly 50 hours a week, extra hours add little output; in WWI munitions data, 70 hours produced about what 56 did.
Crunch usually starts upstream, in over-promising and under-estimating; cut scope before adding hours.
Harmonious passion protects you; obsessive passion, the inability to stop, predicts burnout.
Daily detachment beats occasional long breaks, whose benefits fade fast.
Plan deployments and duty weeks into the schedule as pauses, not as debts to repay.

title: Your First Fifty Players Are a Design Tool
dek: Most of a Roblox audience can't even see your Discord link. Building a community for a small game starts somewhere else: with a handful of watched playtests, a quiet majority you design for, and rules that protect a very young crowd.

blocks.text: Here is a fact that should change how you plan your game's community. On Roblox, the Discord link you put on your game page is invisible to most of the people who will play it. Roblox only shows social media links to users who have verified their age as 16 or older, through a face scan or a government ID. Everyone under 16, and every adult who never bothered to verify, sees nothing. You are not allowed to post the link inside the game either. Roblox's rules permit links only on the game's main page, and writing a Discord invite into your game's text breaks them.

So the standard indie advice, "start a Discord on day one," only half applies. A Discord can still be valuable. But it will hold a small, older, unusually committed slice of your players, not your playerbase. If you want to build a community around a Roblox game, you need to know where the rest of it lives, what a small group of testers can and cannot tell you, and how to treat the people who show up first.
Where a Roblox community actually lives

Look at where the biggest games keep their crowds. Every Roblox game can be owned by a group, which Roblox now also calls a community, and players can join it in a couple of taps from the game page. Those groups get enormous. The group behind *Steal a Brainrot* had about 39.5 million members in November 2026. The one behind *DOORS* had more than 24 million.

blocks.title: Members of the Roblox group behind each game
blocks.note: Member counts of each game's owning group, rounded to one decimal.
blocks.source: Roblox public groups and games APIs, retrieved Nov 5, 2026

blocks.text: Those numbers dwarf any Discord server, and that is the point. A group membership is the community tool every player can see and use. It also powers practical things. Roblox's own beta-testing guide suggests running a closed test by inviting trusted players into the group and giving them a role that unlocks the unreleased game.

Roblox has added more built-in channels on top. **Experience notifications** let a game send personalized alerts, such as a friend beating your record, to players aged 13 and up who opt in, once the game has at least 100 visits. **Events** let you schedule an update or a weekend challenge that players can RSVP to, and an event with at least 1,000 RSVPs can appear in a trending events chart. **Invite prompts** let players pull their friends straight into a server. None of these depends on anyone leaving Roblox.

blocks.title: Two homes for a community

left.head: Roblox group and in-game tools
items: Visible to every player
A couple of taps from the game page
Notifications, events and invites built in
Little room for long conversation

right.head: Discord server
items: Link visible only to verified 16+ users on Roblox
A separate platform with its own age rules
Great for bug reports, feedback and devlogs
Needs active moderation, every day

blocks.text: Use the Roblox group as the front door for everyone and Discord as the back room for your most committed, older players. Don't build your whole plan around a channel most of your audience can't see.
Five testers find most of the problems

The most valuable thing a small community gives you is not hype. It is information you cannot get any other way: what happens when someone who isn't you plays your game. And you need fewer people for that than you might think.

In 2000, the usability researcher Jakob Nielsen published an argument that became famous in software design. Drawing on earlier work with Thomas Landauer, he estimated that a single test user reveals, on average, about 31 percent of the usability problems in a design. Each additional user finds fewer new ones, because they keep tripping over the same issues. By his formula, five users find around 85 percent. His conclusion: stop running big, expensive tests, and run many small ones instead. By the same curve, finding nearly every problem takes about 15 users. Nielsen's advice was to split those 15 into three rounds of five, fixing what each round finds before the next, because a redesign always creates new problems of its own.

blocks.title: Share of problems found as testers are added
blocks.source: Computed from Nielsen's formula with his average of 31% per tester; Nielsen, 2000

blocks.text: The curve is a model, not a law, and it has been challenged. In 2003, Laura Faulkner tested 60 users and then drew random groups of five from them. Some groups of five found 99 percent of the problems. Others found only 55 percent. With groups of ten, the worst group still found 80 percent; with twenty, 95 percent. The honest lesson is that five testers usually find the big problems but can miss a lot by bad luck, and that testing different kinds of players matters as much as testing more of them.

Both findings point the same way for a tiny team. Test early, test small and test again after every change. A batch of five strangers this weekend beats fifty next month, because the first batch will hand you the obvious problems, and you will fix them before the next batch finds new ones.
How to run a playtest that tells you something

Most first playtests are wasted, because the developer asks players what they think. Players are polite, and they are terrible at explaining their own behavior. What they *do* is the data. Where do they get stuck? Where do they stop reading? When do they leave? A player who says "it's fun" and quits after four minutes has told you two things, and only one of them is true.

blocks.title: A one-hour playtest for a two-person team
items: Pick one question for this test, such as whether new players understand the vault in under a minute.
Find testers who have never seen the game. Friends of friends beat your own friends.
Watch them play, on a call with screen share or in the server, and say nothing. Write down every stall, every wrong turn and every moment of delight.
Ask only at the end, with open questions: what was confusing, what did you want to do that you couldn't.
Fix the biggest problem first, then test the fix with new players.

blocks.text: For a launcher game, the most revealing things to watch are timings. How long until a new player does their first vault? Do they understand that holding longer launches farther, or do they tap and give up? How many attempts does the first real gap take? Where does the camera fight them? Note the moment each tester first smiles or laughs, too. That moment is your hook, and the job of the first minute is to get every player there faster.

Roblox also gives you options for testing at larger scale. Its documentation describes four: a **closed beta** run through group roles; **open paid access**, where players pay a one-time Robux fee, which shrinks the crowd but makes it more motivated; a **limited-time test** over a weekend, enough to see first-day retention and session length; and an **open beta**, with the game public but excluded from recommendations. Roblox's guide recommends the closed beta as the safest starting point for teams who are unsure, and that fits a two-person studio well.
The quiet ninety percent

Once you have a community space, expect it to be quiet, and don't take that personally. In 2006, Nielsen described what he called participation inequality: in most online communities, about 90 percent of users only read, 9 percent contribute occasionally, and 1 percent produce nearly everything. The exact ratios vary from place to place, but the shape shows up almost everywhere people gather online.

items.label: Of community members who only lurk
Who contribute now and then
Who account for almost all the activity

blocks.source: Jakob Nielsen, Participation Inequality, Nielsen Norman Group, 2006

blocks.text: That 1 percent is precious. They report bugs, answer newcomers and defend the game when it is down. But they are not your average player. The loudest voices in a Discord are usually older, more experienced and more invested than the kid who plays for ten minutes on a phone and never says a word. If you redesign the game around the 1 percent's wishes, you can build something they love and the other 99 percent quietly abandon.

So treat what the vocal few say as leads, not votes. Check their complaints against what the analytics show the whole playerbase doing. If they say the third stage is too hard and the numbers show a cliff of players leaving there, you have a real problem. If they say it's too easy and nobody is leaving, you have a request from experts.

The lurkers deserve design attention of their own, because they are most of your community. They will never post, but they read. A pinned changelog, a short weekly update and visible signs that the game is alive, like a new stage, a fixed bug or a weekend event, all tell them the place is worth returning to. A dead-looking server with one moderator arguing with one regular tells them the opposite. You are not writing for the people who reply. You are writing for the ones who scroll past and decide whether to come back.
How communities die from the inside

There is a cautionary tale from the biggest volunteer community on the internet. In 2013, Aaron Halfaker and colleagues published an analysis of why the number of active Wikipedia editors had been falling for years. Their answer was uncomfortable. The quality-control rules and automated tools built to protect the encyclopedia were rejecting so many well-meaning newcomers that fewer of them stuck around. The defenses designed to manage growth ended up choking it.

Small game communities do the same thing in miniature. A new player asks an obvious question and gets mocked. A first bug report gets ignored. A suggestion gets a curt "no" from a moderator. Each one feels minor. Together they tell newcomers that this place belongs to the regulars. The fix is boring and effective: welcome new people by name, thank every bug report, and explain decisions instead of just announcing them.

The flip side is that early players can become something more than an audience. People who see a suggestion of theirs show up in an update, or a bug they reported fixed with a thank-you in the patch notes, start to feel the game is partly theirs. Make that visible. Credit testers by name in a changelog or on a sign in the lobby, let regulars vote between two finished options, and show work in progress. That is also, not by coincidence, exactly the material a devlog channel runs on: the playtest footage, the fixes and the community's reactions are the story.

For someone who can disappear for weeks at a time, there is one more design constraint. A community cannot depend on you being online. Pick one or two trusted, older regulars, ideally people from your early playtests, and give them real moderator responsibility before you leave. Schedule posts in advance. Make the devlog, a short video or a pinned update, the heartbeat that keeps people around while you are gone.
Protect the kids first

Any Roblox game community will include children, and that puts real duties on the adults running it. Both Roblox and Discord have their own age rules, and Roblox applies its rules to every notification and link a game sends. Beyond the rules, a few habits are simply non-negotiable for an adult developer.

items: Keep conversations with players in public channels. Do not hold private one-on-one chats with minors.
Never ask players for personal information, photos or contact details outside the platform.
Turn on the strongest moderation and content filters your Discord server offers, and enforce your rules every time.
Do not use notifications or announcements to pressure players into spending. Roblox explicitly bans fake urgency and bait-and-switch messages.
If a player tells you something that suggests they are in danger, use the platform's reporting tools right away.

blocks.text: This is not paranoia. It is what makes parents comfortable letting their kids play your game, and what keeps you on the right side of platforms that can remove a game overnight.

Put all of it together and the first community you build is less like a fan club and more like an instrument panel. A few watched playtests tell you what is broken. A quiet majority tells you, through their behavior, what is working. A loud minority tells you where to look next. Built carefully, those first fifty players become the people who make the next five thousand feel welcome.

takeaways: On Roblox, social links are shown only to age-verified users 16 and older; make the Roblox group your main community and Discord the back room.
About five fresh testers usually reveal most of the big problems, but results vary, so test small and often with different kinds of players.
Watch what testers do; don't rely on what they say.
Most community members never post; treat the vocal 1% as leads, not votes.
Welcome newcomers, appoint moderators before you deploy, and never chat privately with minors.

title: Work That Keeps Working
dek: Most jobs pay you once for each hour. A few kinds of work pay you again and again for years. Knowing the difference changes how you should spend your scarce free time.

blocks.text: Stardew Valley came out on February 26, 2016. Its creator, Eric Barone, had built a farming game that sold about a million copies in its first two months, a huge result for an indie game. A normal story would end there: launch spike, slow fade, on to the next thing.

That is not what happened. Sales kept coming, year after year. Ten million by 2020. Twenty million by 2022. Thirty million by its eighth birthday in February 2024. In March 2024, when a big free update landed, the game set its all-time record for players online at once on Steam: 236,614, eight years after launch. By the end of that year it had passed 41 million copies, and in early 2026 its developer announced it had passed 50 million.

blocks.title: Stardew Valley lifetime copies sold
blocks.note: Milestones announced by the developer. Outlets report some dates a few months apart.
blocks.source: Game World Observer, 2024; Game Developer, 2024; VGChartz, 2026

blocks.text: Here is the part worth sitting with. Selling the fifty-millionth copy took no more work from Barone than selling the first. The work went into the thing once, and the thing kept selling. Updates, ports and new platforms mattered too, but each one built on an asset that already existed. That is the difference between work that pays once and work that keeps working, and it may be the most important idea for anyone trying to build something in their spare time.
Two ways to get paid

Most people earn money by trading time. A shift, a watch, an hourly job: you put in an hour, you get paid for that hour, and when you stop, the money stops. There is nothing wrong with this. It is reliable, it pays the bills, and a steady paycheck is the foundation that makes risky projects possible. But it has a hard ceiling. There are only so many hours, and you can only sell each one once.

The other way is to build assets: things that, once made, keep producing value without you being there for each unit. A game. A video. A piece of software. A skill. An audience that trusts you. Investor and writer Naval Ravikant popularized a useful way to see this. He describes kinds of leverage, including other people's labor, money and something newer: code and media. Hiring people or raising money requires someone else's permission. Writing code or publishing a video does not. And a copy of either costs almost nothing to make, so a game or video can serve one person or a million with the same original effort.

blocks.title: Time for money vs assets

left.head: Trading time
items: Paid once for each hour
Stops when you stop
Predictable and safe
Income capped by hours
Value mostly ends when the shift does

right.head: Building assets
items: Built once, pays repeatedly
Can keep working while you sleep or deploy
Uncertain; many earn little or nothing
Upside not tied to hours
Value can grow as it builds on itself

blocks.text: Notice the honest line on the right: many assets earn little or nothing. That is the trade. Time-for-money is a sure, capped return. Assets are uncertain bets with no cap. The smart move for someone with a stable job is not to choose one. It is to let the job fund your life and point your free hours at things that might keep paying.

There is a version of this that fits a submarine schedule especially well. Hours on watch only pay while you are standing them. A published game or video keeps working during the months you are underway and out of contact. Players can find the game, viewers can find the videos, and the audience can keep growing while you have no internet at all. Few kinds of work are compatible with disappearing for weeks at a time. Assets are one of them.
Old work keeps getting found

The clearest evidence that content compounds comes from companies that measure it closely. HubSpot, a marketing software company with a huge blog, analyzed where its traffic came from and found something its own writers had not expected. In the month it analyzed, the large majority of blog views and nearly all of the leads came from posts published in *earlier* months, not from that month's new posts.

items.label: HubSpot's monthly blog views that came from older posts
Monthly leads that came from older posts

blocks.source: Pamela Vaughan, HubSpot Marketing Blog

blocks.text: Every post they had ever written was still working, quietly pulling in readers through search and links. New posts got a burst of attention. Old ones were the base that kept the whole thing running. The same logic applies to video, especially videos people search for: a clear guide, a tutorial, a deep dive on a game mechanic. A reaction to this week's news fades in days. A great explanation of how a game's movement works can keep finding viewers for years.

For a gaming channel, this suggests a simple balance. Timely videos can bring bursts of attention, which matters early. But some share of your uploads should be evergreen: things someone will still want to find next year. Every evergreen video is a small asset that keeps showing up in search and recommendations long after you stopped thinking about it.
Audiences compound, and so does luck

Audiences grow on themselves in a way that hours never do. People who like your work share it; new people arrive; your next project starts in front of more people than your last one did. This is the flywheel every creator is trying to spin.

blocks.title: The creator flywheel
items: Make something worth sharing
A few people find it and stay
They share it or follow you
The next project starts with a bigger audience
Bigger reach brings more feedback and better work

blocks.text: A classic experiment shows how powerful that loop is, and how unpredictable. In 2006, sociologists Matthew Salganik, Peter Dodds and Duncan Watts built an online music market where 14,341 participants could listen to and download songs by unknown bands. Some participants saw how many times each song had already been downloaded. Others did not. When people could see what others chose, success became much more unequal and much harder to predict. Early leads snowballed.

The researchers also found something reassuring. Quality still mattered, within limits: the best songs rarely did poorly, and the worst rarely did well. But anything in between could happen, depending on early luck. Two lessons follow. First, early momentum compounds, so getting a project in front of people quickly matters. Second, any single release is partly a lottery, which means the builder who makes more good attempts gets more draws. Compounding rewards people who stay in the game long enough for one of the draws to hit.
You cannot control which project takes off. You can control how many good shots you take, and whether each one leaves something behind that the next one can build on.

Reputation works the same way. Each finished project, each honest devlog and each update you deliver on time adds to a record people can see. The first game from an unknown builder has to earn every player from scratch. The fifth game from a builder with a small, loyal following starts with people already willing to try it. That trust is invisible on any balance sheet, but it may be the most valuable thing a small creator owns.
Skills and code are assets too

Not every asset earns money directly. Some of the most valuable ones compound inside you. The first time you write a saving system for a Roblox game, it takes days. The second time, an afternoon. The third time, you paste in the module you already wrote. Each project you finish makes the next one cheaper, faster and better, as long as you carry the pieces forward.

This is a useful way to look at scrapped projects. A game idea that got abandoned is not automatically wasted. The question is whether anything durable came out of it: a working movement system, a shop interface, a data-saving script, art, or a lesson about what players actually do. If you can lift those pieces into the next game, the old project was an investment. If they are lost in a forgotten file, it was only an expense.

A small, practical habit makes the difference: keep a personal library. Every time you build something that works, from a launcher physics script to a clean menu or a thumbnail template, save it somewhere you will find it, with a one-line note on what it does. Over a few years, that library turns into a toolkit nobody else has, built from your own experience. It is also one of the few assets that survives every platform change, since it lives with you.

The same is true of skills that have nothing to do with code. Learning to edit a video, explain an idea clearly, or read a retention graph pays off in every future project, game or business. Those are assets with no expiration date.
The catch: compounding is slow, then sudden

If compounding is so powerful, why doesn't everyone do it? Because the early part of a compounding curve looks like failure. The first video gets twelve views. The first game gets forty players. The first library has three scripts. Measured against an hourly wage, the early returns on asset-building are terrible, and most people quit right there.

Simple math shows why. Anything that grows by a steady percentage each period does most of its growing at the end, not the start. A quantity that doubles every year looks tiny for the first several years and then becomes huge in the last few. Real creative careers are not that smooth, but the pattern holds: the payoff from years of building tends to show up late and all at once.

Run the numbers on something that doubles every year, starting from one. After five years it is at 32. After ten it is at 1,024. Half of everything it ever reached arrived in the final year alone. Someone who checked in at year three would have seen a value of 8 and concluded it was going nowhere. That is what quitting early looks like from the inside: a reasonable judgment based on the part of the curve that always looks flat.

There is a second catch, and it is the one people selling "passive income" leave out. Most assets need maintenance. Stardew Valley's sales kept growing alongside new platforms and big free updates, not by being left alone. Roblox games live or die by updates and events. A YouTube back catalog keeps working only while the channel stays alive and relevant. The honest phrase is not passive income. It is work that keeps paying, with upkeep. That is still a far better deal than work that stops paying the moment you stop.
Pointing scarce hours at assets

For someone with very little free time, this idea is a filter. Time underway, on duty or exhausted after watch is limited. The question for each free hour is not just "is this productive?" It is "will this still be working for me a year from now?"

blocks.title: Turning free hours into assets
items: Let the day job be the engine: it pays the bills so your projects do not have to yet.
Finish and publish things; an unfinished game or unposted video earns nothing and teaches less.
Save every reusable piece of code, art and template in a personal library you can find again.
Mix in evergreen videos people will still search for next year, not only reactions to the news.
Give fans a way to follow you so each project starts with a bigger audience than the last.
Keep going for years; judge the curve on a long time frame, not on the first month.

blocks.text: Look at scrolling through that same filter. An hour of short videos produces nothing that exists tomorrow. An hour writing one reusable script, cutting one evergreen clip or sketching one level produces something that will still exist next year, and might still be paying then. Neither hour feels very different in the moment. Over five years, they lead to completely different places.

This is not an argument for grinding every free minute. Rest, friends and family matter, and a burned-out builder makes nothing. It is an argument for being deliberate about the hours you do give to projects, so that they add up to something that lasts.

Barone's fifty-millionth sale did not come from working harder in 2026. It came from work that was done years earlier and kept on working. That is the shift worth making: stop thinking only about how much an hour pays today, and start asking how long it will keep paying.

takeaways: Time-for-money is safe but capped; assets like games, videos, code and skills can keep paying long after the work is done.
At HubSpot, older posts brought in 76% of monthly blog views; good evergreen content keeps getting found.
Social influence makes success snowball and partly a lottery, so take more good shots and stay in the game.
A scrapped project is an investment only if you carry reusable pieces forward; keep a personal code and asset library.
Most assets need upkeep, and compounding pays late; judge your projects over years, not weeks.

title: The Inventor's Share Is About 2 Percent
dek: Pioneers usually lose, pure clones usually vanish, and the biggest hits tend to be familiar ideas with one strange new part. How to copy like a professional.

blocks.text: In 2004, the Yale economist William Nordhaus tried to answer a question that sounds simple: when someone invents something valuable, how much of the value do they actually keep? He worked through decades of data on the US economy and arrived at a number that should be taped above every inventor's desk. Innovators, he estimated, capture about 2.2 percent of the total value their innovations create. Even his most generous estimate was only 3.3 percent.

blocks.title: Share of an innovation's value kept by the innovator
blocks.note: US nonfarm business sector, 1948 to 2001. The rest goes mainly to everyone else through cheaper, better products.
blocks.source: William D. Nordhaus, NBER Working Paper 10433, 2004

blocks.text: The rest flows outward, mostly to consumers, as competitors pile in, copy the idea, improve it and drive prices down. Nordhaus's explanation was that innovators manage to hold on to only a small slice at the start, around 7 percent by his estimate, and that even this slice erodes by roughly a fifth every year as rivals catch up. From society's point of view, that is wonderful. From the inventor's point of view, it is a warning: the market does not reward you for being first. It rewards you for what you can keep.

This matters for anyone making games, because the most common creative anxiety in game development is the fear of not being original. Is our game just a copy? Is the genre too crowded? Should we invent something completely new? The research on pioneers and imitators says those are mostly the wrong questions. The right one is more specific: what are you copying, what are you changing, and can you hold on to whatever you build?
The first-mover myth

Business books love the idea of first-mover advantage: get there first, grab the market, and latecomers can never catch you. In 1993, the marketing researchers Peter Golder and Gerard Tellis checked that story against history. Earlier studies had mostly relied on databases of companies that were still alive, which quietly left out pioneers that had died. Golder and Tellis used historical records instead and rebuilt the story of about 500 brands across 50 product categories.

items.label: Of market pioneers failed, in Golder and Tellis's historical study of about 500 brands
How long after the pioneer the eventual early market leaders entered, on average

blocks.source: Golder & Tellis, Journal of Marketing Research, 1993

blocks.text: Their results upended the legend. Almost half of the pioneers failed, and the survivors' average market share was much lower than earlier studies had claimed. The companies that ended up leading their categories for the long run had typically arrived an average of 13 years after the pioneer. Being first was not the advantage. Being good at the moment the market was ready was.

Why would latecomers do so well? Marvin Lieberman and David Montgomery laid out the logic in a classic 1988 paper. Being first can help, they argued, but only through specific channels. And being early carries specific costs that followers get to skip.

blocks.title: Being first: what helps and what hurts

left.head: First-mover advantages
items: A head start on learning and technology
Grabbing scarce resources before others can
Customers who would find it costly to switch

right.head: First-mover disadvantages
items: Followers copy your work for far less effort
You pay to discover what the market wants; they watch
Technology or tastes shift under you
Success makes you slow to change

blocks.text: Read the right-hand column as a developer and it is painfully familiar. The pioneer spends months discovering what players actually enjoy, through failed experiments and confusing early versions. The follower plays the finished result for an afternoon and knows. The pioneer has to convince players that a new kind of game is fun. The follower inherits players who already know what they want and are looking for more of it.
Why copiers win: complementary assets

In 1986, the economist David Teece wrote one of the most cited papers in business strategy, built around a puzzle: why do innovators so often fail to profit from their own breakthroughs? His examples were brutal. The British company EMI built the first commercial CT scanner, an invention so important that its engineer, Godfrey Hounsfield, shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in medicine. Yet EMI soon lost the market to established medical-equipment makers and left the business. RC Cola, a small drinks company, was first with cola in a can and first with a diet cola. Coca-Cola and Pepsi followed and took those markets.

Teece's answer had two parts. First, how easy is the idea to copy? He called this the appropriability regime. Where patents are weak and the idea is obvious once you see it, copying is fast. Second, who owns the **complementary assets**, the other things you need to turn an idea into a business, like distribution, manufacturing, service networks and brand? If the idea is easy to copy, the winner is usually whoever already owns those assets, not whoever had the idea.

Games sit about as far toward easy copying as any industry gets. Mechanics are visible the moment someone plays, and in most places the law protects specific art, code, music and names, not game ideas or rules. So on Roblox, Teece's question becomes: what are the complementary assets? The big ones are an existing audience, an established group, a team that can ship updates every week, enough players for full servers, and the skill to make a game feel polished. A big studio that spots your mechanic on a Monday can have a version out quickly and push it to millions of existing players. That is why the copiers who win on Roblox are almost never random newcomers. They are teams who already own the assets.

If your idea is easy to copy and you own no complementary assets, your idea is not your advantage. Your speed, your audience and your craft are the only things that stay yours, so build those on purpose.
But pure clones mostly vanish

None of this means copying is a safe strategy for a small team. It means copying is a safe strategy for teams that already have what small teams lack. When a new Roblox format takes off, a wave of near-identical copies follows. Most of them arrive after the trend's peak, with less polish, no players and nothing a player can't already get in the original. A player who loves a game has no reason to switch to a slightly worse copy of it. Timing makes this worse for part-time builders. A team with a few hours a week, and whole weeks when nobody can work at all, will finish a trend clone after the trend is over. Chasing waves is a strategy for studios that can ship in days. For everyone else, it is a way to arrive late to someone else's party.
So pure invention loses to followers, and pure imitation loses to incumbents. What wins? Research from two very different fields points to the same answer.

In 2013, Brian Uzzi and colleagues at Northwestern University analyzed 17.9 million scientific papers across every field to find what predicts a big hit. The papers most likely to become highly cited were not the most novel ones. They were papers grounded in exceptionally conventional combinations of earlier work, with a small intrusion of unusual combinations on top. Papers with that mix were twice as likely to be big hits. Teams, they also found, were 37.7 percent more likely than solo authors to add those novel combinations to familiar territory.

items.label: Scientific papers analyzed for what predicts a hit
Hit rate of work that is mostly conventional with a dose of the unusual
How much more likely teams were than solo authors to add novel combinations

blocks.source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer & Jones, Science, 2013

blocks.text: Product designers found the same pattern in aesthetics. The industrial designer Raymond Loewy famously called it MAYA: Most Advanced Yet Acceptable. In 2003, Paul Hekkert and colleagues at Delft University of Technology tested the idea across three studies of consumer products. Typicality and novelty each predicted what people found attractive, but they worked against each other: the most preferred designs were novel only as far as they still looked like what they were. People like new things that are recognizably the thing.

A player browsing Roblox is in exactly that position. They have seconds to understand what your game is from a thumbnail and a title. If it's completely unfamiliar, they don't know why they would want it. If it's completely familiar, they already have one. The sweet spot is a game they instantly recognize with one thing they have never seen.
How the big ones did it

The most famous copy in recent game history is *Fortnite*'s battle royale mode. In 2017, *PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds* turned the last-player-standing format into a phenomenon. Later that same year, Epic Games added a free battle royale mode to *Fortnite*, a game it already had. On the surface it was the same skeleton: a hundred players, a shrinking zone, scavenged weapons. But Epic changed the parts that shaped who could play and why: free instead of paid, bright cartoon art instead of gritty realism, and *Fortnite*'s existing building mechanic layered on top. And it already owned complementary assets: an engine, a live game and a large studio. Copy the skeleton, change a few bones, bring your own assets. That is Teece and Uzzi in one product.

The +1 genre on Roblox works the same way at a smaller scale. Its skeleton is proven: a number that grows every second, a world that rewards bigger numbers, rebirths that reset you stronger. Players already understand it. A game that keeps that skeleton and makes the growth power a pole vault launch, so players are flinging themselves across a world instead of watching a counter, is not a clone. It is the conventional core plus one unusual combination that the research says hits more often.

There is a second kind of copying hiding in that example, and small teams often get it backwards. Every genre has table stakes: features players expect so strongly that leaving them out reads as a broken game rather than a bold choice. In a +1 game those include visible numbers going up, a rebirth system, a reason to come back tomorrow and a leaderboard. Copy those without guilt. Players will not praise you for including them, but they will leave if you don't. Save your originality for the one place where it changes how the game feels in your hands.

Uzzi's team finding is worth noticing here too. Two people with different strengths are more likely than one to stumble onto an unusual combination, because each brings habits and references the other lacks. One person who builds maps and another who builds launch physics are already mixing two kinds of knowledge. The trick is to protect that mix instead of letting both people drift toward whatever the top games are doing this week.
Copy like a professional
Turn that into rules for a small team and it looks like this.

blocks.title: Copy the skeleton, change one bone
items: Pick a proven loop players already understand, and study why it works by playing the top games until you can explain their first five minutes.
Choose one change that is genuinely yours, and make it the center of the game, not a side feature.
Make that change visible in the thumbnail, the title and the first thirty seconds of play.
Test whether the twist is actually fun. If players ignore it and enjoy the copied parts, you have a clone.
Never copy art, models, code, music or names. Ideas and loops are fair game; someone else's work is not.

blocks.text: There is a hard line in that last step, and it is worth being blunt. Studying another game's loop is how every designer learns. Lifting its assets, its name or its look is theft, it breaks Roblox's rules on intellectual property, and it gets games taken down. The professional way to copy is to understand a thing so well that you could rebuild it from scratch, then rebuild something different.

And keep Nordhaus's 2 percent in mind. If your twist works, others will copy it, probably within weeks, and probably some of them will be bigger than you. You can't stop that. What you can do is make sure each game leaves you with something they can't copy: players who know your name, a channel that documents the work, a faster way of shipping and a better feel for what makes your twist fun. The idea was never going to be the thing you kept. The team that had it is.
Originality is not a virtue in itself. The question is whether your one new thing is the reason someone would choose your game over the familiar one they already have.

takeaways: Innovators keep only about 2% of the value their ideas create; plan around what you can hold on to, not what you can invent.
Almost half of market pioneers fail; long-run leaders typically arrived years later and executed better.
When ideas are easy to copy, owners of complementary assets win: audience, update speed, polish.
Hits are mostly familiar with one unusual twist; aim for a game players recognize instantly and have never seen.
Copy loops and ideas, never assets, names or art.

title: The Idea Nobody Wanted to Test
dek: A throwaway tweak to Bing's ads turned out to be worth more than $100 million a year, and it sat ignored for months. Data beats opinions, but only if you know how small numbers lie.

blocks.text: In 2012, someone at Microsoft working on Bing had an idea for a small change to the way the search engine displayed its ad headlines. It was unglamorous, the kind of tweak nobody gets promoted for. The managers who ranked ideas thought it was low priority, and it sat in the backlog for more than six months.

Eventually an engineer decided it was cheap enough to just try, and ran an A/B test: some users saw the old layout, some saw the new one, picked at random. Within hours, the test set off an alarm that fires when results look too good to be true. They were not too good to be true. The change raised revenue by 12 percent without hurting the user experience measures Bing tracked. Ronny Kohavi and Stefan Thomke, writing in Harvard Business Review, estimated it was worth more than $100 million a year in the United States alone.

The lesson is not "test everything and get rich." It is that even experienced people at one of the biggest software companies in the world could not tell which of their ideas were good. If they could not, neither can a two-person Roblox team or a new YouTube channel. The good news is that both platforms now hand small creators testing tools that used to need a data team. The bad news is that small numbers lie in very specific ways, and most creators fall for them.
Your opinions need a referee

Kohavi and Thomke reported that at Google and Bing, only about 10 to 20 percent of experiments produced positive results. Across Microsoft overall, about a third of tested ideas helped, a third did nothing and a third made things worse. These were ideas that smart people had already judged worth building.

items.label: Share of experiments at Google and Bing with positive results
Revenue lift from Bing's ignored headline idea
Estimated yearly U.S. value of that one change

blocks.source: Kohavi & Thomke, Harvard Business Review, 2017

blocks.text: Think about what that means for a game update. If you and your partner argue about whether a new upgrade shop will keep players around longer, the honest prior is that it probably will not move the number much, and might hurt it. That is not pessimism. It is the base rate. The point of data is not to prove you were right. It is to find out cheaply when you were wrong, before you spend a month building on a bad assumption.
Kohavi also pushes a rule he calls Twyman's law, which every new creator should tape to their monitor:
Any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong.
blocks.by: Twyman's law, as cited by Kohavi & Thomke, HBR

blocks.text: When a number jumps, the first suspect is a bug, a tracking glitch or a fluke, not your genius. At Bing, a surprising result from a tiny color change was rerun with 32 million users before anyone believed it. You will never have 32 million users in a test. That is exactly why you need to be more skeptical, not less.
The small-sample trap

Statistician Howard Wainer called it the most dangerous equation, a formula worked out by the mathematician Abraham de Moivre in the 1700s. Its message fits in one sentence: averages from small groups swing much more wildly than averages from big groups. That sounds obvious. Ignoring it has cost a lot of money.

In the late 1990s, people noticed that the smallest schools were overrepresented among the best-performing schools. The idea that small schools were better caught on, and the Gates Foundation alone had given about $1.7 billion in education grants by 2001, with smaller schools a major focus. Wainer and a colleague looked at Pennsylvania data. Small schools were indeed overrepresented at the top. They were also overrepresented at the bottom.

blocks.title: Smallest 3% of Pennsylvania schools: where they landed
blocks.note: Small schools showed up at both extremes, which is what extra random variation predicts. Being small did not make them better.
blocks.source: Wainer, The Most Dangerous Equation, American Scientist, 2007

blocks.text: Small schools were not better or worse. They were *noisier*. With few students, a handful of strong or weak kids moves the average a lot. The same pattern shows up in maps of U.S. counties: both the highest and lowest kidney cancer rates cluster in tiny rural counties, because one death in a county of a few hundred people swings the rate enormously.

Now apply this to your own dashboard. If 40 people played your game yesterday and 12 came back today, your day-1 retention reads 30 percent. If tomorrow 9 of 40 return, it reads 22 percent. Nothing changed except chance. Creators with small audiences see these swings constantly and invent stories for them: the new map ruined it, the thumbnail fixed it, the weekend killed it. Most of those stories are noise.

The fix is not to ignore small numbers. It is to read them correctly. Look at trends over several weeks instead of single days. Compare a full week to a full week. Be most suspicious of the most dramatic numbers, since those are the ones most likely to come from luck. And when you do see a big change, ask the dull questions first: did traffic come from a different source, like a TikTok clip or a friend's server? Did a bug stop the game from recording sessions? Did a holiday shift who was playing?
How many players does a test really need?

A standard sample-size calculation, the kind experimentation teams use, makes the problem concrete. Suppose your day-1 retention is 20 percent and you want a test that will reliably catch an improvement, at the usual 95 percent confidence and 80 percent power. To detect a lift to 22 percent, you need roughly 6,500 new players in *each* version. To detect a lift to 25 percent, roughly 1,100 per version. To detect a jump to 40 percent, fewer than 100.

The takeaway is blunt: small creators can only detect big effects. With a few hundred players a week, testing whether a slightly different button color helps is a waste of time; you will never get enough data to know. What you *can* test are big swings: a completely different first minute, a new core mechanic, a thumbnail with a different idea rather than a different shade. Save fine-tuning for when the traffic exists to measure it.
If a change is too small to show up in your numbers, it is too small to argue about. Test bold differences, and let small details be a matter of taste.
Let the platform run the test
Here is where small creators today have an advantage over the industry a decade ago: the two platforms that matter most to a Roblox developer with a gaming channel both run proper tests for you.

Roblox's thumbnail personalization lets you activate two to five thumbnails. Roblox shows each one to random sets of players, then gives more impressions to whichever performs best for each group of players while keeping some traffic on the others. The metric it uses is qualified play-through rate, meaning plays by people who actually stick around, divided by Home impressions. That choice matters: it rewards thumbnails that bring in players who stay, not just players who click. In Roblox's testing, games saw an average increase of 8.5 percent in qualified play-through rate, and some saw 50 percent.

YouTube's Test & Compare lets you test up to three titles, thumbnails or combinations on a long-form video, shown to viewers at the same time. YouTube picks the winner by **watch time share**, not click-through rate, and explains why: a title and thumbnail should help viewers understand what the video is, so they don't click into something they don't want. A test can end as a winner, as "performed same," or as inconclusive. That last option is the honest one: sometimes the data cannot tell, and pretending otherwise is how you fool yourself.

blocks.title: Built-in testing on the two platforms

left.head: Roblox thumbnail personalization
items: 2 to 5 thumbnails active at once
Shown to random sets of players
Judged on qualified play-through rate
Keeps adapting by player group over time

right.head: YouTube Test & Compare
items: Up to 3 titles and/or thumbnails
All versions shown at the same time
Judged on watch time share, not clicks
Can return winner, same, or inconclusive

blocks.text: Notice that neither platform judges on clicks alone. Both had the scale to learn what every clickbait creator learns eventually: a promise that the content does not keep wins the click and loses the viewer. When you design your own experiments, copy that choice. Pick a metric that reflects whether people got what they came for.
Choose the number that matters

Every analytics page offers a dozen numbers, and the dangerous ones are the ones that only go up. Total visits, total subscribers and total views feel great because they never shrink, and that is exactly why they teach you almost nothing. Eric Ries, author of *The Lean Startup*, calls these vanity metrics: numbers that make you feel good without telling you whether the thing is working or what to do next.

Useful numbers are rates and ratios that can get worse. For a Roblox game, that means things like the share of new players who come back the next day, how long a typical player stays, and how many bounce in the first minute. For a YouTube channel, it means the share of a video people actually watch and how many viewers return for the next one. If a number cannot drop when you make a bad change, it cannot tell you that the change was bad.

items: Vanity: total visits. Useful: share of new players returning on day 1.
Vanity: total subscribers. Useful: share of viewers who come back for more videos.
Vanity: likes on a devlog post. Useful: how many people from that post actually played for more than a few minutes.

blocks.text: Pick one main number for each project and stick with it for a while. Switching the metric every time the old one looks bad is one of the most common ways creators fool themselves.
A testing habit for a tiny team

Platform tools handle thumbnails and titles. For the game itself, you will usually be comparing before and after an update, which is weaker evidence because everything else changes too: weekends, holidays, a trend on TikTok, a big game launching the same week. A few habits make it much harder to fool yourself.

blocks.title: The small-creator experiment loop
items: Write the prediction first: what will change, which number should move, and by roughly how much.
Pick one main metric before you look, such as day-1 retention or average playtime, not whatever looks best afterward.
Change one big thing at a time, so you know what caused any difference.
Wait for enough players: at least a full week, so weekdays and weekends both count.
Compare against the same weekdays before the change, and treat a surprising jump as a bug until proven otherwise.
Decide and write down what you learned, then move to the next test.

blocks.text: Writing the prediction first is the step most people skip, and it is the most valuable. Without it, any result can be explained after the fact. With it, you build a record of how often your instincts are right, and that record is humbling in a useful way.
What numbers can't tell you

One last caution. Data tells you *what* is happening, rarely *why*. A dashboard can show that most new players leave in the first 90 seconds. It cannot show you the moment a confused player spins the camera, fails to find the launch pad and quits. For that, nothing beats watching five real people play while you stay silent. At small scale, those five sessions are worth more than any chart, because they generate the hypotheses worth testing.

Running one well is simple. Find someone who has never seen the game, ideally someone in your target audience, and let them play without any explanation. Do not help, do not defend the design, and do not ask leading questions. Note every place they hesitate, misread something or try an action the game does not support. Afterward, ask what they thought the goal was. If three out of five people get stuck in the same spot, you do not need a statistics test to know what to fix next.

Data also cannot tell you what to build in the first place. It can only judge between options you came up with. That is where taste, curiosity and play still matter. The best way to think about it: ideas are cheap and your gut is a useful source of them, but your gut is a terrible judge of them. Let your instincts propose. Let players vote. And when the vote comes back surprising, check the ballot box for bugs before you celebrate.

takeaways: Even top companies find that most tested ideas do nothing or hurt; assume your update probably won't move the number until shown otherwise.
Small samples swing wildly: with a few dozen players, daily changes in retention are mostly noise.
Small audiences can only detect big effects, so test bold changes, not tiny tweaks.
Use Roblox thumbnail personalization and YouTube Test & Compare; both judge on whether people stay, not just whether they click.
Write your prediction and metric down before looking, and treat surprising results as bugs until proven otherwise.
