title: Judge the Decision, Not the Dice
dek: The same choice gets rated as smart or foolish depending only on how it turned out, even by people who know better. A decision journal is the cheapest way to learn the right lessons from your own choices.

blocks.text: A man with chronic pain is offered an operation. If it works, his pain goes away and he can expect to live five years longer. But 8% of people who have this operation die from the operation itself. He decides to go ahead.

Now the question: was that a good decision? In a 2023 replication of a classic experiment, almost 700 people were asked to rate it on a scale from +3, clearly correct, to -3, inexcusable. Every one of them read exactly the same facts, with one difference. Half were told the operation succeeded. Half were told it failed.

The people who heard it succeeded rated the decision an average of 1.78. The people who heard it failed rated the identical decision 0.68. Nothing about the choice had changed: same odds, same information, same reasoning. Only the dice had landed differently, and the dice rewrote the verdict.

blocks.title: Rating of the same decision, by outcome
blocks.note: Identical scenario; only the outcome differed. 692 online participants.
blocks.source: Aiyer et al., International Review of Social Psychology, 2023

blocks.text: Psychologists Jonathan Baron and John Hershey first documented this in 1988 and called it *outcome bias*. The replication found something even more telling. Participants who said outright that outcomes should not count when judging a decision still showed the bias. Knowing about the trap was not enough to avoid it.

If you build things, you make a steady stream of decisions under uncertainty: which game to make, what to cut, when to release, how to price, whether to keep going. Outcome bias means you will learn the wrong lessons from many of them unless you have some record of what you were actually thinking at the time. That record has a name. It is a decision journal.
Good decisions, bad luck

The former professional poker player Annie Duke calls this mistake *resulting*: judging a decision by how it turned out. In poker, it is easy to see why that is a mistake. You can play a hand perfectly, put your money in as a big favorite and still lose when the last card comes. You can also play terribly and get bailed out by luck. Over one hand, the result tells you almost nothing about your skill. Over thousands, it tells you a lot.

Most of life works the same way, only with far fewer hands. A game that flops after launch might have been a bad idea. Or it might have been a fine idea released the same week the platform changed how it recommends games, or the same week a giant hit sucked up every player in the genre. A game that takes off might reflect great design, or a single streamer who happened to stumble onto it. If you judge only by results, you will repeat lucky mistakes and abandon unlucky good ideas.

blocks.title: Separating the decision from the dice

left.head: What you controlled
items: What information you gathered
Which options you compared
How you estimated the odds
Whether you were rested or rushed
Whether you set a way to check the result

right.head: What you did not
items: What other games launched that week
Platform algorithm changes
Whether a big creator noticed you
Random bugs in tools you depend on
Your partner's sudden schedule change

blocks.text: None of this means outcomes are meaningless. If the same kind of decision keeps going wrong, that is evidence. The point is that a single outcome is a noisy signal, and you need some way to look at the process separately from the result.

This matters most for small builders, because small builders live on small numbers. A game with thirty players on a given day can swing wildly from one week to the next for reasons that have nothing to do with anything you changed. If you treat every dip as proof that the last decision was wrong, you will spend your life reversing good choices and chasing noise. A record of what you expected, and why, is what lets you tell the difference between a real signal and a bad roll.
Your memory is not a neutral witness

The obvious objection is that you can simply remember what you were thinking. Unfortunately, you cannot, at least not reliably. In 1975 Baruch Fischhoff showed that once people learn how something turned out, they overestimate how predictable it was, and they misremember what they themselves had expected. He called it *hindsight bias*, often summed up as the I-knew-it-all-along effect.

Put outcome bias and hindsight bias together and you get a nasty combination. After a failure, you remember being more doubtful than you were, and you judge the choice as worse than it was. After a success, you remember being more confident than you were, and you credit your judgment for what may have been luck. Either way, the lesson you file away is distorted, and the distortion feels exactly like clear memory.

This is also why postmortems written months later are less reliable than they feel. By then, everyone already knows the ending, and the story bends toward it. A note written on the day of the decision is the one witness that cannot be influenced by what came next.

A decision journal fixes this the only way it can be fixed: by writing down your reasoning *before* the outcome is known, so that later you are comparing the result against what you really thought, not against a version your brain quietly edited.
What the forecasting tournaments learned

The most serious test of whether people can get better at judging uncertain events came from a series of forecasting tournaments sponsored by the U.S. intelligence community in the early 2010s. Large numbers of volunteers made probability forecasts on real questions, such as whether a given country would hold an election by a certain date or whether a treaty would be signed. Then the questions resolved, and every forecast was scored.

A team led by Barbara Mellers and Philip Tetlock at the University of Pennsylvania won. In a 2014 paper, they credited three psychological factors: training in probabilistic reasoning, working in teams that shared information and debated, and tracking, which meant putting the top 2% of forecasters from the first year into elite teams together. These *superforecasters*, as they came to be called, stayed accurate across hundreds of questions, beating the usual expectation that top performers drift back toward average.

The research has its critics. A 2025 reanalysis by Hauenstein and colleagues argued that once some overlooked factors were controlled for, the measured benefits of training and teaming shrank, disappeared or even reversed in some models. So be careful with any claim that a short course turns ordinary people into prophets. But one ingredient is common to every version of this story: forecasters were scored, relentlessly, against what actually happened. Nobody improves at a skill they never measure.

How scoring works: the Brier score, proposed by meteorologist Glenn Brier in 1950, squares the gap between your probability and what happened (1 if it did, 0 if it did not). Say 70% and it happens: (0.7 - 1) squared is 0.09. Say 90% and it does not: 0.81. Lower is better, and overconfidence is punished hard.

Scoring also exposes something subtler than right and wrong: *calibration*. A well-calibrated forecaster is one whose 70% predictions come true about 70% of the time, and whose 90% predictions come true about 90% of the time. Most untrained people are overconfident. Things they call near-certain fail more often than they expect, and things they call long shots happen more often than they expect. You cannot see your own calibration from one prediction. You can see it from fifty, which is another reason to write them down.

You do not need a spreadsheet to borrow the idea. The key move is attaching a number to your expectations. Not just *I think this update will help*, but *I think there is a 60% chance this update raises how many players come back the next day*. A number can be wrong in a way that a vague hunch never can, and that is exactly what makes it useful.
The five-line entry

A decision journal does not need to be elaborate. Most decisions do not deserve an entry at all. Save it for choices that cost real time or money, or that would be hard to undo: picking which game to build, cutting a major system, changing a price, committing to a release date, signing up for something long-term.

blocks.title: A decision journal entry
items: Decision and date: one sentence on what you chose.
Options: what else you seriously considered, even briefly.
Prediction: what you expect to happen, with a probability and a date to check.
Reasons: the two or three facts or beliefs that tipped it.
State: how you felt when deciding, such as tired, rushed, excited or annoyed.

blocks.text: The last line is the one people skip, and it is often the most revealing. After twenty or thirty entries, patterns start to show up. Maybe your worst calls cluster late at night after duty. Maybe every abandoned project was chosen while you were excited about a video you had just watched. You will not see patterns like that from memory, because memory does not store the boring context. Paper does.

Here is what a real entry might look like for a game decision. *Decision: cut the pet system from version one and spend the next three weeks on how the launch feels. Options: keep pets and delay release; ship pets in a stripped-down form. Prediction: 70% chance that playtesters describe the launch as fun without being prompted by the end of the month. Reasons: two testers said the jump felt floaty; pets add nothing to the core action. State: rested, Sunday morning, talked it through with my partner first.* That took about a minute to write. In a month it will be worth far more than a minute.

Notice that the prediction is specific enough to be wrong. *The game will be better* cannot fail. *Testers will call the launch fun without prompting by the 30th* can. The more checkable the prediction, the more the entry can teach you.
A small notebook works fine underway, where there may be no reliable way to sync anything. What matters is that the entry exists before the result does.
Reviewing without fooling yourself

Writing entries is half the habit. The other half is going back. Put the review date in the entry and actually open the notebook when it arrives. Then ask questions in a fixed order, so the outcome does not get to answer first.

items: Before looking at the result: given only what I knew then, was the process sound?
Now the result: did it land inside or outside what I predicted?
If it went wrong, was it the reasoning, the information, or plain luck?
If it went right, would I make the same choice again for the same reasons?
What one thing would I do differently next time a decision like this comes up?

blocks.text: Be fair to your past self in both directions. If a decision was reasonable but unlucky, say so and keep the reasoning. If it worked out but the reasoning was sloppy, say that too, even though it is less fun. The second case is the dangerous one, because unearned success teaches habits that will eventually cost you.

For a two-person team, a shared version is even more valuable. When you and your partner disagree about a decision, write down both predictions with probabilities. When the result comes in, nobody has to argue about who said what, and over time you both learn whose instincts are better calibrated on which kinds of questions. That turns disagreement from a contest of confidence into a source of data.

A builder who has started and dropped several projects already has the raw material for a remarkable record. Each one was a decision, made with certain hopes, at a certain moment, for certain reasons. Writing down why the next one is chosen, before anyone knows how it turns out, is how a string of dropped projects becomes a lesson instead of a pattern.

takeaways: Outcome bias makes the same decision look good or bad depending on luck; knowing about it does not switch it off.
Hindsight quietly rewrites what you expected, so record your reasoning before the result is known.
Attach a probability to your predictions; a number can be checked, a hunch cannot.
Write a five-line entry for big decisions: choice, options, prediction, reasons, state of mind.
Review on a set date and judge the process before you look at the result.

title: Nobody Is Coming to Find Your Game
dek: Among Us sat mostly unnoticed for two years before streamers found it. The game barely changed. What changed was distribution, and that lesson decides more indie projects than talent does.

blocks.text: In 2018, a three-person studio called Innersloth released a small social deduction game for five dollars. It was finished, it worked, and people who played it with friends liked it. For most of the next two years, almost nobody noticed. By August 2019 it had crossed a million downloads, which sounds big until you remember how many free mobile games pass that number and are never heard from again.

Then, in 2020, a handful of Twitch streamers started playing it. First a couple of mid-sized ones in May, then a big one in mid-July, who pulled his friends in. By the end of August the game had gone from a couple hundred average Twitch viewers to more than 100,000. In September it was the most-streamed game on Twitch, and Google Play downloads went from 10 million to over 100 million in less than three weeks. The game was **Among Us**. The code that went viral was basically the code that had been sitting there unnoticed since 2018.

That is the uncomfortable fact at the center of this article. A good product is necessary. It is nowhere near sufficient. Between "good" and "successful" sits a step most builders treat as an afterthought: getting the thing in front of the people who would love it. That step is called distribution, and for small builders it is usually the hardest part of the whole job.

blocks.title: Among Us: the same game, two different years
items: Released by a three-person team for $5. Modest sales.
Aug 2019
Passes one million downloads. Still a niche game.
May 2020
Streamers AdmiralBulldog and singsing start playing for hours at a time.
Sodapoppin tries it on stream and pulls other big streamers in.
Late Aug 2020
Average Twitch viewership jumps past 100,000.
Sep 2020
Most-streamed game on Twitch; Google Play passes 100 million downloads.

items.label: Developers on the team
Peak simultaneous Steam players during the 2020 surge
Google Play downloads by September 21, 2020

blocks.source: PC Gamer, How Among Us became so wildly popular, 2020

blocks.text: The flood you are swimming in

Here is why distribution matters more every year. In 2024, SteamDB counted 18,945 games released on Steam, the biggest one-year jump it had ever tracked. In 2025 the count passed 19,000 again, and nearly half of those games ended the year with ten or fewer user reviews. On a platform where a review is a rough proxy for sales, that means thousands of games were bought by almost nobody.
Another way to see it: Valve flags games that pass a popularity threshold, which unlocks extra community features. In 2024 only 3,964 games crossed it. That is roughly one in five releases.

blocks.title: Steam games in 2024
blocks.note: About one in five 2024 releases reached Valve's popularity threshold for community features.
blocks.source: PC Gamer, citing SteamDB, December 2024

blocks.text: Be honest about what those numbers include. A big chunk of the invisible games are low-effort asset flips and shovelware; one 2025 publisher released 138 games, and analyst Chris Zukowski doubted any of them had more than a single review. So the data does not prove that great games die in obscurity all the time. What it proves is that the default outcome of shipping is silence, and the store will not rescue you. You are one of about fifty new games every day.

Notice what this means for effort, too. Two games of identical quality can end up with wildly different results depending on whether anyone ever plays them in front of an audience. The store pages for most of those silent releases look much like the successful ones: screenshots, a trailer, a price. What separates them is almost never visible on the page.

Roblox is even more crowded, since making and publishing a game there costs nothing. YouTube is the same story at a bigger scale: hundreds of hours of video uploaded every minute. Whatever you build, it lands in a flood.
Why builders underrate distribution

Peter Thiel makes a sharp point about this in *Zero to One*. Engineers and makers, he argues, tend to believe that if the product is good enough, selling it takes care of itself. They see marketing as fluff, something people do when the product is weak. He argues the opposite: poor distribution, not a bad product, is behind a huge share of failures, and a business with great distribution can win even with a merely decent product.

You can see why makers fall for the myth. Building is visible progress: a new mechanic works, a new map loads, the commit history grows. Distribution feels like begging. It also gives feedback you might not want, because posting a clip that gets nine views is a more painful signal than a bug. So builders keep polishing, telling themselves they will promote it "once it is ready." Ready never comes, and when it does, nobody is waiting.

blocks.title: Two ways to think about a launch

left.head: Product-only thinking
items: Build until it is good, then tell people
Marketing is something you add at the end
Success means the game is fun
Waiting for the algorithm to notice

right.head: Distribution thinking
items: Decide who it is for and where they hang out first
Shareable moments are designed into the game
Success means the right players find it and stay
Giving the algorithm a reason to test you

blocks.text: On Roblox, the product is the distribution

Here is the twist that makes Roblox different from Steam. Roblox has published how its Home recommendations work, and the most important signals are almost all about what players do after they click. Roblox tests a game on small groups of new players, then shows it to more people if those groups engage and spend. Roblox calls this explore and expand.

The top-priority signals are telling. Roblox looks at how many people who see your game in recommendations actually play it, how many bounce in under a minute or within three minutes, how many come back on day 1 and across the first week and month, and how long they play, capped at 60 minutes per player per day. These are calculated per player, not as totals, so a small game with very engaged players is not punished for being small.

Two details matter a lot for a tiny team. First, players you buy with Sponsored ads do not count toward the recommendation ranking; Roblox only ranks you on players who arrived through recommendations. Ads can still bring traffic that helps you get considered, but you cannot buy your way into the algorithm. Second, a game without a custom thumbnail gets no impressions from Home recommendations at all. That one is free to fix, and people still miss it.

blocks.title: How a Roblox game earns reach (simplified from Roblox's docs)
items: Players arrive from anywhere: friends, search, social media, ads or a small recommendation test.
Roblox measures what recommended players do: play-through rate, quick bounces, return days and playtime.
If those per-player signals look strong, Roblox shows the game to a bigger group of similar players.
If the bigger group also sticks, the cycle repeats and impressions grow.
If signals weaken, through boredom, a bad update or a better competitor, impressions shrink.

blocks.text: So on Roblox, "distribution versus product" is a false choice. The first 60 seconds of your game *are* your marketing. A pole vault obby that confuses players for the first minute is not just a design problem; it is a distribution problem, because every quick bounce tells the algorithm to stop showing it.
The cold start: someone has to light the match

If recommendations reward good engagement, why do builders need outside distribution at all? Because the algorithm needs players to measure. Roblox's docs say signals from friends, search, social media sharing and other sources can speed up a game's consideration for organic recommendations. Translation: a spark from outside helps the machine notice you.

YouTube runs on a similar engine. Back in 2018, YouTube's product chief Neal Mohan said that about 70 percent of watch time on the site came from its recommendations, not from people searching. The system is enormous, but it still has to learn who your video is for, and it learns from the first viewers who show up.

Look at where the sparks came from in recent breakout hits. Among Us was lit by streamers. **Dress to Impress**, a Roblox fashion game started by a developer who was 14 when she began it, spread in 2024 as a TikTok meme: people posted ridiculous outfits and copied an emote called Pose 28 in real life, and high school students turned it into a trend. Big streamers followed. By September 2024 it routinely had the most concurrent players of any Roblox game. Neither spark was a paid campaign. Both were moments that people *wanted* to share.

There is a trap on the other side, too. A spark only helps if the game holds the people it brings. If a TikTok clip sends a thousand curious players into a game that confuses them for a minute, most of them bounce, and on Roblox those bounces are exactly the signals that shrink your impressions. Hype pointed at a weak first session can do more harm than silence. So the order matters: get the first five minutes right with a small group of real players, then go looking for the spark.

The blunt version: "the algorithm will find it" is not a distribution plan. The algorithm finds games that already have some players behaving well. Your job at the start is to supply the first few hundred, from friends, a small community, a creator who likes the genre, or your own videos, and to make sure they stick.
Distribution for a tiny team is not buying ads. It is building moments worth clipping, then putting them where your future players already spend time.
Designing a game that markets itself

The practical lesson is to think about distribution while you design, not after. Ask one question about every feature: would anyone record this? Among Us produced a story every round: accusations, betrayals, a friend lying badly. Dress to Impress produced a funny image every round. That is not an accident of marketing. It is a property of the game.

A pole vault launcher obby has a natural advantage here, if it is built for it. Huge launches, near misses, absurd fails and a visible number that climbs are exactly what short-form video rewards. A few design choices push that further:

items: Make the funniest failure visible from a distance, so a clip makes sense without explanation.
Give players a shareable number, like height or distance, that invites a challenge to beat it.
Make playing with friends better than playing alone, since co-play is one of Roblox's tracked signals.
Keep the first minute dead simple so the clicks a viral clip sends you don't bounce right away.

blocks.text: Then there is the asset most solo builders never connect: a YouTube channel. A gaming channel and a Roblox game made by the same person are not two projects competing for limited hours. The channel can be a distribution channel for the game, through devlogs, challenge videos, and clips of the best fails. Each video gives the game a spark, and each game update gives the channel a story.
Distribution on a deployment schedule

Limited time makes this harder, not irrelevant. You cannot post daily from a submarine. But distribution does not have to mean constant posting. The highest-leverage parts can be done in bursts: a sharp thumbnail and icon, a first minute that hooks, a few clips cut and scheduled before going underway, a Discord where early players and the other builder can keep things moving while you are gone. A partner on shore can handle posting and community while the person underway handles design and building work that can be done offline.

It also helps to treat distribution like any other skill: something you practice in small reps, not one big launch. Post one clip and watch what happens. Try a different first frame next time. Notice which moments other players react to in a playtest, because those are your future clips. A builder who has posted fifty small things knows far more about what spreads than one who saved everything for a single release day. And that knowledge carries over to every project after this one, which makes it one of the few skills that keeps paying even if this particular game does not.

The deepest point is a mindset shift. Most builders ask, "How do I make this good?" The ones who make it also ask, "How will the first thousand players hear about this, and why would they tell a friend?" If you cannot answer the second question, the first one does not matter yet. The Among Us team did not change much between 2018 and 2020. What changed was who was looking. Build for the moment people start looking, and give them something worth showing.

takeaways: The default outcome of shipping is silence: about one in five 2024 Steam releases passed Valve's popularity bar.
On Roblox, retention and the first 60 seconds are your distribution, because recommendation ranking is built on what recommended players do.
Paid ads do not count toward Roblox's recommendation ranking; you cannot buy your way into the algorithm.
Breakout hits are usually sparked by shareable moments on streams or TikTok, so design clip-worthy moments in from day one.
A YouTube channel and a game from the same builder can feed each other instead of competing for time.

title: Five Half-Built Games Are Worth Zero
dek: Starting a project is the most fun you will ever have with it. That is exactly why serial starters end up with nothing, and why the fix is a rule, not more willpower.

blocks.text: Open almost any young developer's old hard drive and you will find a cemetery. A folder called *rpg_test*. Another called *new_idea_FINAL_v2*. A map with a lighthouse and no enemies, a dragon that flies beautifully but has nothing to fight, a slick menu screen for a game that never got a second level. Every one of those folders was born on a great night, the kind where a new idea felt so obviously better that the current project suddenly looked tired.
Here is the uncomfortable math. A player cannot play 80% of a game. A viewer cannot watch 80% of a video that was never uploaded. A customer cannot buy from 80% of a store.

To the outside world, five projects that are each four-fifths done are worth exactly the same as zero projects. The hours were real and the skills you picked up were real, but the *value* only shows up at the finish line, and it shows up all at once.

That is why focus is not a productivity tip for a small builder. When you have a few hours a week, a partner with his own job, and long stretches where you cannot touch the project at all, focus is the entire strategy. Everything else in this library, from retention to moats, assumes you have something finished enough for real people to use.
The finish line is where the value lives
Programmers have an old joke, usually credited to Tom Cargill at Bell Labs: the first 90% of a project takes the first 90% of the time, and the last 10% takes the other 90%.

It is funny because it is true, and it is true because of *what* lives in that last stretch. It is the tutorial that gets a confused stranger to the fun. The bug that only shows up with twelve players in a server. The thumbnail, the title, the game icon, the settings menu, the save system that does not wipe progress. Nobody dreams about these parts. They are also exactly the parts that decide whether a stranger stays or leaves in the first minute.

This creates a nasty asymmetry in how a project feels. Starting pays you immediately: every hour produces something visible and new, and every problem is still hypothetical. Finishing pays you almost nothing until release day: the hours go into invisible fixes, the problems are now real, and the design choices you made months ago are locked in. Your brain is not broken for preferring the first one. It is responding sensibly to the rewards in front of it. The trouble is that the rewards in front of you are not the rewards that matter.

blocks.title: Why starting always feels better than finishing

left.head: Starting a project
items: Everything is still possible
Fast, visible progress every session
Problems are hypothetical
Feels like momentum
Earns nothing from players

right.head: Finishing a project
items: Choices are locked in
Slow, invisible fixes
Every problem is real and yours
Feels like grinding
The only part players ever see

blocks.text: The price tag you never see
Economists call the real cost of any choice its *opportunity cost*: whatever else you would have done with the same time or money. Everyone learns the definition. Almost nobody uses it in the moment.

In 2009, Shane Frederick and colleagues showed how easily people skip it with a tiny experiment. Students were asked whether they would buy a video of a favorite actor for $14.99. Half chose between buying it and simply not buying it. The other half got the same choice, except the second option was worded as keeping the $14.99 for other purchases.

Nothing about the deal changed. The money was always going to be available for other things. But spelling that out moved behavior by about 20 percentage points. People were not weighing the alternative until someone put it in front of them.

blocks.title: Students who chose to buy a $14.99 video
blocks.note: Same video, same price. Only the wording of the alternative changed (75 students per group).
blocks.source: Frederick et al., Journal of Consumer Research, 2009 (Study 1a data via OpenIntro)

blocks.text: New project ideas exploit the same blind spot. When an exciting idea shows up, you compare it to the current project's *problems*, not to the current project's *finish*. The new idea has no bugs yet, so it wins.

But the honest price of the new idea is not zero. For a two-person team working in scraps of free time, its price is something like: the current game does not ship this year. Said out loud, that trade is often a bad one. It just never gets said out loud.

A practical habit follows directly from the study. Whenever one of you pitches a new direction, the other asks a single question: *instead of what?* If the answer is that the current game will wait three more months, you are at least now making the real decision instead of the fake one.
What Apple learned by cutting 70% of everything

When Steve Jobs returned to Apple in 1997, the company was making a sprawling list of products: many overlapping Macintosh models, printers, the Newton handheld, and software lines that confused even employees. Jobs cut more than 70% of Apple's hardware and software products. He replaced the lineup with a simple grid of four: a consumer desktop, a consumer laptop, a pro desktop and a pro laptop. If a product did not fit one of those four boxes, it was gone.

items.label: Share of Apple's hardware and software products cut after Jobs returned
Apple's loss in fiscal 1997
Apple's profit in fiscal 1998

blocks.source: Macworld, Steve Jobs's seven key decisions; CNN Money, Oct 1998

blocks.text: Be careful with the lesson. Cutting products did not magically create a profit. What it did was free up engineers, money and attention so the company could make a few things well, including the iMac, instead of many things badly.
The cuts also had a human cost: thousands of layoffs. Focus is not free. It means saying no to things that are genuinely good, and sometimes to people you like.

A tiny team faces the same trade on a smaller scale. Two people cannot run a Roblox game, a second game prototype, a YouTube channel and a store at the same time and do any of them well. Each one needs its own learning curve, its own audience and its own maintenance. Picking one does not mean the others are bad ideas. It means they are *later* ideas.

There is one useful exception: projects that feed each other instead of competing. A gaming channel that documents building the game, or a devlog that turns each update into a short video, is not really a second project. It is distribution for the first one, made from work you are already doing.

The test is simple. If a side project uses the same hours to push the main project forward, it can stay. If it needs its own separate hours, its own audience and its own ideas, it goes in the parking lot until the main project ships.
Open loops are not free

Unfinished things also cost you when you are not working on them. Psychologists have long noticed that unfulfilled goals tend to keep popping back into the mind, an idea associated with Bluma Zeigarnik's work in the 1920s. In 2011, E. J. Masicampo and Roy Baumeister ran experiments showing that an unfinished goal could interfere with an unrelated task, and that simply making a specific plan for the goal reduced that interference. You did not have to finish it. You had to decide what would happen to it.

Abandoned projects are the worst kind of open loop because they are never officially dead. The scrapped game sits in the back of your head as *maybe we'll go back to it*, quietly competing with the current one. Switching between projects has its own price too. The American Psychological Association's summary of task-switching research notes that each switch costs time, and that the cost grows when tasks are complex or unfamiliar.

One researcher, David Meyer, has estimated that switching can eat up to 40% of productive time. That is an estimate, not a law of physics, but anyone who has reopened a project after a month away and spent the first hour just remembering how it works knows the feeling.
Quitting is not the enemy

None of this means you should never quit. The evidence actually points the other way. Economist Steven Levitt ran a large online experiment in which people stuck on a big decision, such as quitting a job, flipped a coin. Those whom the coin pushed toward making a change were more likely to make it, and they reported being happier six months later.

His interpretation: people may be too cautious about big changes. Former poker professional Annie Duke makes a similar argument in her book *Quit*: most of us quit too late, because walking away feels like admitting failure.

So how do you square that with focus? The answer is that serial starters do not quit too much. They quit for the wrong reason, at the wrong time. They quit when the work gets boring, which happens around the middle of every project that has ever existed. They do not quit because they learned something, such as players trying the game and not coming back even after several rounds of fixes.
The test before you abandon anything: am I quitting because of something I *learned*, or because of something I *felt*? Evidence is a good reason to stop. Boredom at the 60% mark is just the middle.

Duke's best tool is the *kill criterion*: a signal, chosen in advance, that tells you to stop. You write it down at the start, while you are calm and not yet emotionally invested. A useful one has two parts, a date and a measurable condition. For a game, that might be a specific number of weeks after launch and a minimum share of new players who come back the next day.

Pick your own numbers before you launch, because benchmarks vary a lot by genre and traffic source. The point is that the decision gets made by the plan you wrote when you were thinking clearly, not by the mood you are in at midnight after a frustrating bug.
A focus system for two people with almost no time

Limited time is not just a constraint here. It is a reason the rules have to be stricter. Someone working full time on a game can afford a week of wandering. Someone who gets a few free evenings between watches, then disappears underway for weeks, cannot. Every restart resets the clock on learning, testing and building an audience, and you have fewer clocks to spare than most people.

blocks.title: One active project, on purpose
items: Pick one active project. Every other idea goes in a written parking lot, not a new Studio file.
Define done as something strangers can touch: published, playable, with a first five minutes that works.
Set a ship date that fits your real hours, then cut features until the scope fits the date.
Write kill criteria now: a date plus a player-behavior number you choose before launch.
When a shiny idea shows up, park it and ask together: instead of what?
Finish or kill on purpose, then write a short close-out note so the loop actually closes.

blocks.text: The parking lot matters more than it sounds. Ideas are not the problem; partners who are excited about ideas are a good sign. Writing them down tells your brain they are safe and will not be lost, which is the Masicampo and Baumeister effect working for you. A good idea that waits six months is still a good idea. Many will look worse in six months, which is also useful information.

For a two-person team, the system also needs one agreement: neither of you can start a new project alone without the other's explicit yes. Most abandoned games die not in a big argument but in a slow drift, where one person starts tinkering with something new and the other quietly follows. Make the switch a decision, not an accident.

Long stretches away from the keyboard can even work in your favor. Time when you cannot build is good time for the parts that do not need a computer: sketching levels on paper, writing the parking lot, deciding what to cut, and listing the next three tasks so the first session back starts in motion instead of in confusion. Arriving with a plan turns a short window into real progress.
The person who finishes

There is a deeper reason to finish things, and it has little to do with any single game. Every finished project teaches you the parts that no unfinished project can: what launch day actually looks like, how strangers break your game in ways you never imagined, what the data says when real players vote with their time. The sixth time you start something, you mostly learn how to start. The first time you finish, you learn everything else.
That is the reframe worth keeping. Finishing is not just a result. It is a skill, built by repetition like any other, and like any skill it compounds.

The builder who has shipped three small, imperfect games will usually make a better fourth game than the builder who has started twenty brilliant ones. Pick the project. Write the kill criteria. Then get it into strangers' hands.

takeaways: An unfinished project is worth zero to players; its value arrives only when it ships.
Every new idea has a hidden price: the current project not getting finished. Ask: instead of what?
Quit on evidence, not on boredom. Write kill criteria with a date and a number before you start.
Keep one active project and a written parking lot for everything else.
Close loops on purpose: finish or formally kill a project, then write it down.

title: Relieve the Watch: Handing Off a Project Before You Disappear
dek: Hospitals cut preventable harm by 30% by fixing one short conversation. Software projects stall when the one person who understands them leaves. Both lessons apply to a game built by two people when one of them is about to go underway.

blocks.text: Every watchstander knows the ritual. You do not just walk up, sit down and start. You show up early, walk the space, read the logs, look at the indications and listen while the person you are relieving walks you through what is going on: what is running, what is out of service, what is weird, what to keep an eye on. You ask questions until you actually understand. Only then does the formal exchange happen, and only then does the watch change hands.

The Navy did not invent this because it loves ceremony. It exists because the moment of handoff is one of the most dangerous moments in any operation. Information that lived in one head has to move to another, and anything that does not make the trip is simply gone.

Side projects have handoffs too. They are just invisible, because nobody stands up and says *I relieve you*. When one partner on a two-person game goes underway for weeks or months, the project changes hands whether anyone plans it or not. The question is whether it happens like a proper turnover or like someone walking off watch without a word.
Why handoffs leak

The problem is not that people are careless. It is that the person handing off knows too much. After weeks inside a project, you stop noticing the things you know. You know the launch script breaks if a certain value goes negative. You know the map loader needs to run before the UI. You know which test place is the real one. None of it feels worth mentioning, because to you it is obvious.

Psychologists call this the *curse of knowledge*: once you know something, it is very hard to imagine not knowing it, so you badly misjudge what someone else needs to be told. The fix is not to try harder to remember everything. It is to use a structure that drags the hidden knowledge out, and a receiver who is expected to ask questions until the picture is complete.
One conversation, fewer mistakes

Medicine learned this lesson the hard way. Hospital residents hand off patients at every shift change, and for years the handoff was an improvised chat in a hallway. Miscommunication during these handoffs was recognized as a leading cause of serious medical errors. So a group of hospitals that train pediatric residents tried something simple: they standardized the handoff around a mnemonic called I-PASS, trained residents to use it and checked that they did.

The results, published by Amy Starmer and colleagues in the *New England Journal of Medicine* in 2014, covered 10,740 patient admissions at nine hospitals. After the program started, the medical error rate fell by 23%, and preventable adverse events, the errors that actually hurt patients, fell by 30%. The rate of harms that nobody could have prevented stayed flat, which is what you would expect if the change came from better communication rather than sicker or healthier patients.

blocks.title: Before and after a structured handoff program
blocks.note: Nine hospitals, 10,740 admissions. Error rates fell 23%; preventable adverse events fell 30%.
blocks.source: Starmer et al., NEJM, 2014

blocks.text: Here is the detail that matters most for a busy builder. The spoken handoff did not get longer. It averaged 2.4 minutes per patient before the program and 2.5 minutes after. The improvement came from structure, not from extra time. The same few minutes were simply spent on the right things in the right order.

items: I: Illness severity. How serious is this right now?
P: Patient summary. What is going on and what has been done.
A: Action list. What needs to happen next, and who does it.
S: Situation awareness and contingency planning. What might change, and what to do if it does.
S: Synthesis by receiver. The person taking over repeats it back in their own words.

blocks.text: That last step will sound familiar to anyone who has heard a repeat-back on a sound-powered phone. It is the cheapest error check ever invented. If the receiver cannot explain the situation back, the handoff is not done.
The truck factor

Software developers have a darker way of describing the same risk. A project's *truck factor* is the number of people who would have to be hit by a truck, or simply quit, before nobody left understands enough of the code to keep it going. It is a blunt measure of how concentrated knowledge is.

In 2016, Guilherme Avelino and colleagues estimated truck factors for 133 popular open-source projects on GitHub, including widely used tools such as the d3 charting library and the Elasticsearch search engine. A third of them had a truck factor of 1. Another 31% had a truck factor of 2. Linux, with a truck factor the team estimated at 57, was a rare exception.

blocks.title: Truck factor of 133 popular GitHub projects
blocks.note: Share of projects that one or two departures would leave without anyone who knows most of the code.
blocks.source: Avelino et al., ICPC, 2016

blocks.text: A follow-up study by the same group looked at 1,932 popular GitHub projects and found that 16% had been abandoned by the core developers who held most of the knowledge. Of those, 41% survived because new people stepped in and took over. When the researchers surveyed those rescuers, two obstacles stood out: lack of time, and the difficulty of getting permission to change the project at all.

A two-person game has a truck factor of two at best. In practice it is usually one, because each partner owns different parts and only half understands the other's work. If one of you writes all the launch code and the other runs the maps and the Studio sync, then for any given system, there is exactly one person who knows how it works. When that person is underway, the truck factor for that system is effectively zero for the duration.

You can raise that number without turning each partner into an expert on everything. Before a long absence, spend one session where the person who owns a system walks the other through it while he makes a small change himself, with the owner watching and not touching the keyboard. Pick something real but low-risk, like adjusting launch power or adding a checkpoint. The goal is not mastery. It is making sure that at least two people have successfully changed every important part of the game at least once.

The same goes for the boring infrastructure. Who can publish an update? Who can change prices? Who controls the group that owns the game? If the honest answer to any of those is one person, that is a single point of failure, and it will fail at the least convenient moment.

The survival study's lesson is practical: rescuers who knew the code still got stuck on access. Before a long absence, make sure your partner has every permission, account role and key he needs to keep the game running without you.
Distance is a tax

Even when nobody leaves, working apart slows teams down. James Herbsleb and Audris Mockus studied change records at a large software organization whose engineers were spread across several sites. Work items that crossed sites took about two and a half times as long to finish as similar items handled by people in one place.

The most interesting part was why. Distributed items tended to involve more people, and the number of people involved was strongly linked to how long the work took. Every extra person meant more waiting, more messages, more chances for something to sit in an inbox. The researchers confirmed the main result at a second organization with a different product.

Time zones add their own version of this tax. If your partner is a day behind you, or asleep when you are awake, every question costs a full round trip. A two-minute answer can take twenty hours to arrive. Remote teams that work well around this tend to write more, not less: decisions, reasons and open questions all go into a shared place, so most questions are answered before anyone has to ask.

For a partner who will be out of contact for weeks, the implication is clear. Do not split tasks so that both of you have to touch them. Draw ownership lines so that each piece of work can be finished by one person from start to end. The fewer handoffs inside a task, the less the distance costs you.
Write the turnover sheet

The practical tool here is a turnover sheet: a one-page document you write before going underway and walk through with your partner, ideally on a call where he can ask questions. It borrows its shape from I-PASS, adapted for a game.

blocks.title: A turnover sheet for a two-person game
items: Status: what works, what is broken, and what is half-built. Be honest about the broken parts.
Summary: the current goal for this stretch in one or two sentences, so every decision can be checked against it.
Action list: each task with one owner and a clear finish line. Mark which ones he can do alone.
Contingencies: if a bug wipes data, if a trend shows up, if a big update breaks something, what should he do, and what can he decide without you?
Access check: confirm he has every role, password vault entry and permission he needs.
Read-back: he explains the plan back in his own words. If he cannot, keep talking.

blocks.text: The contingency section deserves the most thought. You cannot predict what will happen while you are gone, but you can give your partner authority in advance. Something like this works well: anything that can easily be undone, like a price change, a map tweak or a new thumbnail, is his call. Anything that cannot easily be undone, like changing how revenue is split, deleting a system or publishing under a new name, waits for you. Clear decision rights turn a partner into a captain instead of a caretaker.

Add a short how-to for the code itself, the kind of file programmers call a README. Where does each system live? How do you run the game locally? What breaks if you touch it carelessly? Which tasks are safe for a beginner? Writing it will feel slow. It is also the single best test of whether your work is understandable by anyone other than you, which is the whole point of a turnover.

If you will have occasional email or messages while away, agree on a format before you go rather than improvising. A short weekly status with the same three headings every time, what changed, what is blocked, what is next, is far easier to read on a slow connection than a long thread, and it keeps both people looking at the same list.

Keep a shared decision log as well, one line per decision with the date and the reason. It costs seconds to write and saves hours of confusion when the person coming back wants to know why something changed.
Coming back aboard

The turnover runs in both directions. When you come back after weeks without internet, the temptation is to dive straight in, pull the latest code and start building whatever you planned in your notebook. Resist it for one session. Ask your partner for his turnover first: what changed, what broke, what he decided and why. Read the decision log. Play the current build start to finish as if you were a new player.

Then sync the work you did offline. Underway time is often good for design work that needs no connection: level sketches, upgrade tables, scripts for videos, lists of bugs to test. That work only becomes valuable when it is merged with what happened while you were away, and the first conversation decides whether it slots in cleanly or collides with a dozen changes you did not know about.

Watch turnover works because it treats knowledge as something that has to be deliberately handed over, not something that leaks across on its own. A project you care about deserves the same respect. Ten minutes of structure before you leave is what lets the game still be alive, and still be yours, when you come back.

takeaways: Handoffs are where information gets lost; structure matters more than time spent.
A two-person project usually has a truck factor of one for each system, so plan for absence.
Split work so one person can finish each piece alone; every extra hand on a task slows it.
Before leaving, write a one-page turnover: status, goal, actions, contingencies, access, read-back.
Give your partner clear decision rights: reversible calls are his, irreversible ones wait.

title: Anyone Can Copy Your Game. Now What?
dek: Hit games get cloned within weeks. Hamilton Helmer's 7 Powers explains what actually protects a business, and which of the seven a two-person team can realistically build.

blocks.text: In February 2014, a small team released a sliding-number puzzle game called *Threes* on the iPhone. They had spent 14 months on it. The first prototype came together in a single night, and most of the rest went into testing variations until the game felt exactly right. Critics loved it. Apple later named it the best iPhone game of the year.

Within weeks, the copies arrived. One iPhone game openly advertised itself as a free alternative to *Threes*. Then a browser game called *2048*, built on that copy, exploded across the internet and spawned dozens of its own imitations.

A British newspaper called it a clone of a clone. For a huge number of players, *2048* became the version they knew. The original team, clearly frustrated, published a 45,000-word post walking through how *Threes* was designed and why it thought the copies fell short.

If that sounds like ancient history, look at Roblox in 2025. *Steal a Brainrot* launched in May and at its peak had as many as 24 million people playing at once. By early 2026, Bloomberg reported that hundreds of competing titles had appeared on Roblox, with more arriving daily, plus clones on app stores, Fortnite and Meta's platform. The developers had filed at least four lawsuits against alleged knockoffs. There is an irony buried in the story, too: the game's creator has said *Steal a Brainrot* was inspired by an earlier game, *Steal a Character*, whose rights he acquired and then improved on. On Roblox, the line between copying and building on something is blurry, and everyone is standing on someone else's idea.

items.label: Peak simultaneous players of Steal a Brainrot
Competing brainrot titles that appeared on Roblox
Estimated in-game spending since launch (third-party estimate)

blocks.source: Bloomberg, March 2026 (spending estimate from Romonitor data)

blocks.text: This is the question every small builder eventually runs into. If anyone can copy what you made, what is the point of making something good? The answer comes from one of the clearest books ever written on business strategy, and it starts with an uncomfortable idea: being good is not a strategy.
Good is not a moat

Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant and investor, wrote *7 Powers* to answer one question: what lets a business keep earning more than its competitors over time? His answer is a concept he calls *Power*, which needs two ingredients at once. The first is a **benefit**, something that makes you better off, like lower costs or the ability to charge more. The second is a **barrier**, something that stops competitors from copying the benefit even when they can see it working.

Most small builders have plenty of benefit and no barrier. A fun game is a benefit. But the mechanics of a game are generally easy to copy, and in many cases the law does not stop people from copying ideas and mechanics, only specific art, text and code. The *Steal a Brainrot* lawsuits, for example, were about the game's visuals, layout, menus and overall look, not about owning the idea of stealing characters. Epic Games summed up the line neatly when it removed some clones from Fortnite: making games in popular genres is allowed, but direct copying is not. (This is general background, not legal advice.)
So the real question is not whether someone *can* copy your game. They can. The question is what you will have that a copier cannot get by copying.

Roblox makes this sharper than almost anywhere else. Every developer uses the same engine, the same free tools and the same storefront, and publishing costs next to nothing. That is exactly why it is such a good place to start: the barrier to entry is close to zero. It is also why it is such a hard place to defend a position. Whatever lets you get in easily lets everyone else in easily too, including the person who will copy your best idea a week after it starts working.
The seven powers in plain English
Helmer argues that every durable advantage in business falls into one of seven types. Here they are, translated from boardroom language into something closer to a game studio's reality.

items: **Scale economies:** costs per unit fall as you grow, so a giant can always undercut a newcomer. Think of a studio that can spread one engine across ten games.
**Network economies:** the product gets better as more people use it, like a game where your friends already are, or a trading economy that only works with a big player base.
**Counter-positioning:** a newcomer uses a model the leader cannot copy without hurting its own business.
**Switching costs:** leaving would cost customers something they value, such as progress, collections or a group of friends.
**Branding:** people trust or prefer you because of your history, and will choose you over an identical product.
**Cornered resource:** you control something valuable that others cannot get, like a unique team, a key piece of IP or an audience.
**Process power:** your way of working is so refined that rivals cannot copy it even when they study it.

blocks.text: Helmer's examples range from Vanguard's low-cost index funds to Pixar's creative team and Toyota's production system. The striking thing about the list is what is missing. Working hard is not on it. Having a great idea is not on it. Being first is not on it either, unless being first lets you build one of the seven.
Power comes in stages

The most useful part of Helmer's framework for small builders is what he calls the *power progression*. Different powers become available at different stages of a business, and trying to build the wrong one at the wrong time wastes effort.

blocks.title: Which powers are available when
items: Origination
Before you have traction: counter-positioning and cornered resource
Takeoff
During rapid growth: scale economies, network economies, switching costs
Stability
Once growth slows: branding and process power

blocks.text: This is good news and bad news. The bad news: a two-person team with a new game has, realistically, none of the takeoff or stability powers yet. You do not have scale. You do not have a network.

Nobody has spent months building progress they would lose by leaving. Your brand is a name people have not heard. Pretending otherwise leads to bad decisions, like spending weeks on a trading system for a game with forty players. The good news is that the two powers available at the start are exactly the ones a tiny team can build, because they do not depend on size at all.
Counter-positioning: do what the leaders won't

Helmer's favorite example is Vanguard. When it launched cheap index funds, the big fund companies could easily have offered the same product. They did not, for years, because doing so would have pulled money out of their own expensive actively managed funds.

The barrier was not that the idea was secret. It was that copying it would hurt the incumbents more than it helped them. Netflix's move from mailing DVDs to streaming put Blockbuster, with its stores and late fees, in a similar bind.

On Roblox, the incumbents are the large studios running many games at once, often optimized around trends, heavy monetization and rapid releases. A small team can look for a position those studios would find costly to copy. That might be a game built around skill and mastery rather than paying to skip ahead, a game for a niche that is too small to interest a big studio, or a community where the developers are visibly present and reply to players.

None of these are guaranteed to work. The test is always the same: if a bigger rival copied this, would it damage something they currently depend on? If yes, you may have a real counter-position. If they could copy it for free, you just have a feature.

Here is what that might look like for a launcher-style obby. Suppose the big games in the genre make most of their money by selling power: buy a pass, launch twice as far, skip the grind. A small team could build its game around movement skill instead, where the best players are the ones who mastered the jump, with cosmetics as the main thing for sale.

A big studio could copy that design, but only by giving up the power-selling that pays its bills. Whether players actually want it is a separate question that only shipping can answer. But if they do, you have a position that a richer rival may be reluctant to take from you.
Cornered resource: what only you have

A cornered resource is something valuable that rivals cannot simply acquire. For Pixar, Helmer argues, it was a rare group of creative leaders who kept producing hits. For a small builder, the honest answer is usually smaller, but it is still real.

The strongest cornered resource most solo creators can build is an **audience they own**. A copycat can clone your game in a weekend. They cannot clone the few thousand people who follow your devlog, watch your channel, and show up on launch day because they like *you*.

A distinctive art style, a recurring character, or a personal story that nobody else has also count. A builder who designs games around launchers and movement, documents it on video, and has an unusual background is harder to copy than any single mechanic. These barriers are weaker than Pixar's, but they grow with every project instead of resetting to zero.

The same logic is the entire strategy of a creator channel. There are thousands of gaming channels, and every format can be copied. What cannot be copied is a specific person's voice, humor and story. The more a channel is built around *who* is talking rather than *what* is being shown, the closer it gets to a cornered resource.
The game can be copied. The studio cannot. Every project should leave you with something a copier will not get by copying: an audience, a brand, a faster process, or players who know your name.
The powers you grow into

Once a game has traction, the takeoff powers open up, and they can be designed in from the start even if they only pay off later. Roblox's own discovery system lists intentional co-play days per user among its important signals, which hints at why social design matters: players who play *with friends* have a reason to come back that a clone cannot easily steal. Trading economies, guilds, leaderboards and long progression all create mild switching costs. A player with hundreds of hours in your game is unlikely to restart from zero in a copy.

Process power is the rarest of all, but it is worth noticing where small studios get close to it. The studio behind *Grow a Garden* is known on Roblox for shipping weekly updates, a habit that turned a simple game into a record breaker. Any single update can be copied. A team's ability to produce good updates every week, reliably, for months, is much harder to replicate. Brand comes last: *Steal a Brainrot* survived hundreds of imitators at least partly because players knew which one was the original, although that is an interpretation, not something anyone has measured.
A moat plan for a two-person team

blocks.title: Building power when you have none yet
items: Accept that your first game has no moat. Speed and focus are your edge for now.
Choose a counter-position: something bigger studios would find costly to copy.
Start building an owned audience early: a devlog channel, a Discord, a mailing list.
Design social play and long progression into the game so leaving has a real cost.
Keep one studio name, style and voice across projects so each launch starts warmer.
Protect what the law can protect: your own art, names and code, not the mechanic.

blocks.text: Notice that most of these steps survive the death of any individual game. That is the real point of thinking in powers. If your strategy depends on nobody copying your next game, you have no strategy, because someone will. If your strategy is to come out of each game with a bigger audience, a more recognizable name and a faster way of working, then even a game that gets cloned or flops moves you forward.

Most builders ask: how do I stop people copying my game? It is the wrong question, because the honest answer is usually that you cannot. Helmer's framework swaps in a better one: what am I building that gets stronger the longer I do this, and that a copier cannot take with them?

*Threes* lost the clone war to *2048*. But its creators kept making games, and the reputation they earned from building something original went with them. The copycats got a moment. The originals got a career. For a small builder, that is what a moat really looks like: not a wall around one game, but an advantage that keeps compounding across all of them.

takeaways: Real advantage needs a benefit and a barrier. A fun game is a benefit with no barrier.
Early on, only two powers are realistic: counter-positioning and cornered resource.
The strongest cornered resource for a small creator is an audience they own.
Design social play and long progression early; they become switching costs later.
Ask what each project leaves you with that a copier cannot take.

title: Most Doors Swing Both Ways
dek: Amazon's founder sorted decisions into reversible and irreversible. Research on fast-deciding teams, why half of organizational decisions fail, and a strange catch about keeping your options open shows how to use that idea well.

blocks.text: In October 1984, a computer company called Gavilan filed for bankruptcy. It had an early lead in a promising market and $31 million from venture capitalists. It did not die because the idea was bad or the money ran out too early. According to the Stanford researcher Kathleen Eisenhardt, it died of delays and indecision. While the team deliberated, its leading-edge technology turned into a me-too product, and competitors filled the market it had found first. One executive summed it up in four words: we missed the window.

Eisenhardt opened her 1989 study of decision speed with that story because it captures something builders rarely think about. People worry constantly about making the wrong decision. They worry much less about the cost of making the right decision too slowly, or of never quite making it at all.

Two decades later, a businessman who had built one of the fastest-moving companies on Earth offered a simple tool for this problem. It is worth understanding properly, including the part most people leave out.
Two kinds of doors

In his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders, Jeff Bezos divided decisions into two types. Some are consequential and irreversible, or nearly so. He called those one-way doors, or Type 1 decisions. Once you walk through, you cannot get back to where you were, so they deserve to be made slowly and carefully, with plenty of consultation.

But most decisions, he argued, are not like that. They are changeable and reversible: two-way doors. If you make a weak Type 2 decision, you do not have to live with it for long. You open the door again and walk back through. Those decisions should be made quickly, by individuals or small groups with good judgment.

His warning was about what happens when the two get mixed up. As organizations grow, he wrote, they tend to use the slow, heavyweight process meant for one-way doors on almost everything. The result is slowness, risk aversion that has not been thought through, too little experimenting and, eventually, less invention. A two-person team is nowhere near Amazon's size, but the same disease shows up in miniature as endless discussion about things that could simply be tried.

blocks.title: Doors in a two-person game project

left.head: Two-way doors: decide fast
items: A game pass price
A thumbnail, icon or game title tweak
Launch power, gravity, course layout
Which small feature to test next
The order of tasks on the Now list

right.head: One-way doors: slow down
items: How revenue and ownership are split
Which account or group owns the game
Signing a contract or paying a large sum
Deleting work with no backup
Anything involving players' data or safety

blocks.text: Watch out for one-way doors that do not look like doors. A promise to players, such as a permanent item that will never be sold again, is hard to take back without losing their trust. So is a public name once a community has formed around it, or a rule your partner relied on while you were away. If a choice creates expectations in other people's heads, it is usually less reversible than it looks.

The opposite mistake is just as common. Builders often treat technical choices as permanent when they are not. Which color the UI uses, how a menu is laid out, even which framework handles a particular system can usually be changed later at modest cost. Spending a week agonizing over them is the slow, heavy process applied to a door that swings freely.
Speed comes from the right kind of thinking

The tempting conclusion is that fast deciders simply think less. Eisenhardt's research says the opposite. She studied eight companies in the microcomputer industry of the 1980s, a business where products and competitors changed so quickly that she called it a high-velocity environment. Some teams made big strategic decisions quickly. Others dragged on.

The fast teams used *more* information, not less, but it was a different kind: real-time information about what was happening right now, rather than forecasts and long reports. They developed *more* alternatives, not fewer, and weighed them side by side instead of studying one option at a time. They used a two-tier advice process, leaning on a few experienced advisers. And they had ways to resolve conflict instead of waiting for everyone to agree. Crucially, the fast decisions were linked to better company performance.

That is a useful correction for anyone who hears move fast and decides it means skip the thinking. Speed comes from cutting the waiting, not the thinking. Looking at live data, comparing two or three options at once and having a clear way to break ties all make decisions faster *and* better.
Why half of decisions fail

If speed alone were the answer, careless managers would be the best decision makers. Paul Nutt of Ohio State University spent years studying how decisions actually go inside organizations, and his findings show how slow and careless can fail in the same way.

In a 1999 summary of 358 decisions made in medium and large organizations in the United States and Canada, Nutt reported that about half of them failed. The failures traced back to a few habits. Managers imposed a solution they already liked, cut the search for alternatives short and then used their power to push the plan through. Those failure-prone tactics were used in two out of every three decisions he studied.

items.label: organizational decisions studied by Paul Nutt
of those decisions failed
decisions used tactics prone to failure

blocks.source: Nutt, Academy of Management Executive, 1999

blocks.text: The decisions that worked looked different. The people involved made the need for action clear at the start, set objectives, searched broadly for options before settling and brought key people into the process. Put Nutt next to Eisenhardt and a pattern emerges. The single most common way to decide badly is to consider only one option, a yes-or-no question about an idea you have already fallen for. The cure is the same whether you are fast or slow: put at least two real alternatives on the table before choosing.

Nutt's earlier work points the same way. In a study of 168 decision cases, he found that the most common tactic was to impose a fully formed solution, and that this tactic seldom succeeded. Approaches that searched for and combined ideas from several sources worked far better, but were rarely used. People reach for the answer they walked in with because it feels decisive. Very often it is just the first idea, wearing a confident face.
A quick upgrade for any decision: before asking should we do this, ask what else could we do with the same time. One extra option is often enough to expose a bad idea.
Decide with less than you want

In his 2016 letter, Bezos added a rule of thumb. Most decisions, he suggested, should be made with about 70% of the information you wish you had. Waiting for 90% usually means you are being slow. And in either case, you need to be good at quickly noticing and correcting bad decisions. If you can correct course fast, being wrong costs less than you think. Being slow, he wrote, is expensive for sure.

items.label: of the information you wish you had is usually enough to decide, by Bezos's rule of thumb

blocks.source: Bezos, Amazon letter to shareholders, 2016

blocks.text: The 70% figure is not a measured fact. It is one experienced executive's heuristic, and it only makes sense for two-way doors. Its value is in naming a feeling every builder knows: the urge to research a little more, watch one more video and ask one more person before committing to something that could simply be tested in an afternoon. For a reversible choice, a quick test usually beats more research, because the test produces the information you were waiting for.
The catch: open doors can make you less happy
Here is the part that usually gets left out. Reversibility has a hidden cost, and Harvard psychologist Daniel Gilbert and his colleague Jane Ebert found it in a photography class.

In their 2002 study, photography students had to choose which of their own prints to keep. Some were told their choice was final. Others were told they could still change their minds. The students predicted that the option to change their minds would not affect how much they liked the photo they kept. They were wrong. The students whose choice was final liked their prints more than the ones who could still switch. Even so, when asked in advance, most participants wanted the freedom to change their minds.

The explanation is that once a decision is truly made, the mind gets to work making peace with it. It focuses on the good parts and stops comparing. While the door stays open, that settling process stalls, and you keep weighing what you have against what you might have had. These were small studies, so treat the result as suggestive rather than settled. But anyone who has switched game ideas several times in a month will recognize the feeling.

This changes how to use the door model. Some choices are technically reversible but behave like one-way doors because of what reversing them costs. Which game to build is the classic example. You can always switch, so it feels like a two-way door. But every switch throws away weeks of work, resets everything you learned about the current game and leaves you just as restless about the new one. The useful question is not *can this be undone?* but *what does undoing it cost?*

For decisions like that, the smart move is to close the door on purpose. Pick the game, then commit to it for a fixed period, say three months, with a clear test at the end. Until that date, the question of whether to switch is not open. You may find you like the game more once you stop shopping for a better one.

There is a practical side for a builder who disappears for weeks. An open question is not neutral. If the two of you leave a decision hanging when one of you goes underway, the other is stuck: either he waits, and the project stalls, or he decides alone and risks friction later. Closing the big questions before you leave, and agreeing which kinds of doors he can open alone, keeps the project moving while you are out of reach.
Disagree and commit

The last tool matters most for a partnership. In the same 2016 letter, Bezos described a phrase he used to save time: *disagree and commit*. When someone has strong conviction about a direction and the team has not reached agreement, the person who disagrees can say so plainly and then commit fully anyway, rather than dragging out the argument or quietly undermining the plan. He was explicit that this applies to the boss as well, and described approving a project he had doubts about with a note saying he disagreed, committed, and hoped it would be a huge success.

Between two partners, especially brothers or close friends, this can prevent a lot of slow damage. Long disagreements over two-way doors are almost never worth it. One person can make the call, the other can state his concern for the record and both can agree to check the result on a set date. If the doubter was right, the door swings back. Nothing is lost except a little time, and much less of it than the argument would have taken.

blocks.title: Sorting a decision in under a minute
items: Ask what undoing it would really cost in time, money and trust.
Cheap to undo: the owner of that area decides today and sets a date to check the result.
Expensive to undo: list at least two alternatives and talk it through together.
Still split: one person decides, the other says disagree and commit, and both write down what result would change their minds.
Close the door on purpose when switching would cost more than staying, like which game to build.

blocks.text: Gavilan did not need perfect decisions. It needed to tell which doors swung both ways, walk through those quickly and spend its real care on the few that did not. That is the whole skill. Most of your choices this year will be two-way doors. Treat them that way, and save your hesitation for the handful that are not.

takeaways: Most decisions are two-way doors: decide them fast, check the result and reverse if needed.
Fast decision makers use more live information and compare more options, not fewer.
The most common way to decide badly is to consider only one option; always put two on the table.
Judge a door by what undoing it costs, not by whether undoing it is possible.
With a partner, disagree and commit on reversible calls instead of arguing them to death.
