title: Have the Hard Conversation Before You Need It
dek: Partnerships rarely die from bad ideas. They die from the conversations two people skipped at the start, and the research says friends and family skip them most.

blocks.text: In 2010, two brothers from Regina, Saskatchewan, started making a video game on the side. Chad and Jared Moldenhauer both had full-time jobs, so the game began as a weekend project with a team of three. It had an absurdly ambitious art style: every frame hand-drawn to look like a 1930s cartoon. They called it *Cuphead*.

When they finally showed it publicly in 2014 and then let people play it in 2015, the reaction was huge, and so was the criticism: the game was only boss fights, and players wanted more. The brothers faced the kind of decision that ends partnerships. Expanding the game meant years more work. Doing it properly meant quitting their jobs and remortgaging their homes. They made the call together, took the risk, and *Cuphead* came out in 2017 and went on to sell millions of copies.

blocks.title: Two brothers, one very risky game
items: Chad and Jared Moldenhauer start Cuphead as a side project while working full time
The game is unveiled publicly for the first time
Players can try it; the boss-only design is criticized
The brothers expand the scope, quit their jobs and remortgage their homes
Cuphead releases and goes on to sell millions of copies

blocks.text: Stories like this get told as stories about talent and passion. But look at what the studio said about how it worked. New ideas had to be approved by everyone on the team, and the debates over them could get heated. They had a rule for deciding, and they used it on the biggest bet of their lives. That is the less glamorous half of every successful partnership, and it is the half most partners skip.
What 10,000 founders reveal

Noam Wasserman, then a professor at Harvard Business School, spent about a decade studying nearly 4,000 startups and 10,000 founders for his book *The Founder's Dilemmas*. His central finding is that the decisions that sink new ventures are often made in the first days, when everyone is excited and nobody wants to spoil the mood.

The clearest example is how founders split ownership. Wasserman found that most teams settle it almost immediately, and that a third simply split everything equally. A related study he co-wrote with Thomas Hellmann, covering 1,476 founders in 511 ventures, found that equal splits were linked to lower valuations when the companies later raised money, especially in teams that agreed on the split in under a day. The founders who brought more to the table, such as the original idea, previous experience or their own money, gave up an estimated 10% of the company by accepting an equal split, according to the researchers' model.

items.label: Founding teams that settled equity in their first month
Teams that split ownership exactly equally
Estimated share of the company a stronger founder forgoes by accepting an equal split

blocks.source: Wasserman, The Founder's Dilemmas (HBS Working Knowledge, 2012); Hellmann & Wasserman, NBER, 2011

blocks.text: The lesson is not that equal splits are wrong. For two people contributing similar work, equal may be exactly right. The lesson is that a split decided in a rush, to avoid an awkward conversation, tends to stop matching reality later. And when ownership stops matching who is doing the work, resentment grows quietly until it does not stay quiet.

Why do so many teams rush? Hellmann and Wasserman's explanation is simple: negotiating is uncomfortable and costly, so many founders accept an equal split rather than pay the price of an honest conversation about who is bringing what. In other words, the 50-50 split is often not a decision at all. It is a way of avoiding one.

Wasserman has also been widely quoted as saying that about 65% of high-potential startups fail because of conflict among co-founders. Treat that number with care: it gets repeated far more often than it gets explained, so think of it as a strong signal rather than a precise measurement. But the direction matches everything else in his research. People problems kill more ventures than product problems.
Why family makes it harder, not easier

Here is the counterintuitive part. Wasserman found that teams made of friends and family were among the most fragile, not the most stable. The reason is not that relatives are worse partners. It is that they are more likely to avoid tough conversations to protect the relationship.
Strangers who start a company together have to write things down because they do not trust each other yet. Brothers assume they will figure it out.

blocks.title: Partnering with family: the trade

left.head: What you get for free
items: Trust from day one
Fast, honest communication
Shared history and humor
Someone who will not just vanish

right.head: What you risk
items: Skipping the awkward money talk
Unclear roles because 'we'll figure it out'
Old family dynamics showing up in decisions
A failed project hurting the relationship

blocks.text: Old dynamics matter more than people admit. An older sibling may expect to have the final word without either of you noticing. A younger one may defer on things they actually know better, then resent it later. None of this is anyone's fault, which is exactly why it is worth naming out loud. The goal is to make sure the partnership runs on the roles you chose, not the ones you inherited.

The stakes are also different. If two strangers fall out over a failed game, they lose a project. If two brothers fall out, they risk every holiday for the next decade. That is a reason to be *more* formal with family, not less.
Rich or king: know what each of you wants

Wasserman's most famous idea is that founders face a choice between being *rich* and being *king*. Rich means maximizing the value of what you build, which often means bringing in partners, money or a bigger studio and giving up some control. King means keeping control of the decisions, even if the thing you build stays smaller. His research suggests you usually cannot fully have both, and the founders who get hurt are the ones who never decided which they wanted.

This is not a theoretical question on Roblox. *Grow a Garden* began as one teenager's project; when it was still small, he sold a share to an established studio, which brought in weekly updates and a team. By the studio's account, the original creator kept a stake and still contributes and suggests updates.

That was a rich choice, and it worked spectacularly. Another creator in the same position might have refused, preferring to keep full control. Neither is wrong. What would be wrong is two partners discovering they want opposite things on the day a studio sends an offer.
How to disagree without damage

Even with clear roles, you will disagree, and that is healthy. Two people who never argue about a game are usually not thinking hard enough about it. The goal is not fewer disagreements. It is disagreements that end in a decision instead of a grudge.

A few habits make a big difference. Before arguing against your partner's idea, explain it back in your own words until they agree you understood it. That one step removes a surprising number of fights, because many arguments turn out to be two people defending different versions of the same idea. Argue about the game, never about who is smarter or who works harder.

Give a design debate a time limit, then decide using your agreed rule. And once a decision is made, both of you commit to it fully, even the person who lost the argument. Amazon built a leadership principle around this idea: disagree openly, then commit. A half-hearted version of a plan, built by a partner who is quietly hoping it fails, is the worst of both worlds.

Finally, go back and check. When an update ships, look at what players actually did and talk honestly about who called it right. Over time, you learn which of you has better instincts in which areas, and the roles can shift to match. The data becomes the neutral third partner that neither of you has to argue with.
Split roles, not just revenue

Most partners talk about money and never talk about decisions. But day to day, decisions cause far more friction than money. Who decides whether the launcher upgrade costs 50 coins or 80? Who decides whether to start a second game? What happens when you both feel strongly and disagree?

A simple structure works well for two-person teams. Give each person clear ownership of specific areas, such as one owning scripting and systems while the other owns building, art and the store page. In your own area, you make the final call after hearing the other person out. A short list of big decisions, like starting a new project, selling a share, spending real money or changing the revenue split, requires both of you to say yes. And when you are stuck on a design argument, you agree in advance to settle it the way good studios do: build the cheapest version of both ideas and let players decide.

blocks.title: A one-page partnership agreement
items: Roles: who owns which areas, and who makes the final call in each.
Big decisions: the short list that needs both partners to agree.
Tie-breaks: test both options with players, or alternate who decides.
Money: who owns the group, how revenue is split, and when you will revisit it.
Goals: rich or king, and what offer you would actually accept.
Exit: what happens to the game and the money if one person stops working on it.

blocks.text: Writing it down is the point. A one-page document you both agree to on a calm day is worth more than a hundred conversations remembered differently by each of you during a fight.

Clear ownership pays off in a less obvious way, too: it lets work continue when one partner disappears for a while. When one of you is away for weeks with no connection, a team where every decision needs both people simply stops. A team where each person owns an area keeps moving.

Leave a short written handoff before going dark: what you finished, what is next, and which decisions the other person can make without you. Keep a simple decision log, a running list of what you agreed and why, so nobody has to rely on memory when you reconnect. These habits feel like overhead for a two-person team. In practice, they are what make a part-time partnership work at all.
A written agreement is not a sign of distrust. It is shared memory. Six months from now, both of you will remember the original deal slightly differently, and the paper will not.
The money mechanics on Roblox

On Roblox, the practical version of ownership is usually a *group*. A game owned by a group can automatically split its earnings with recurring percentage payouts to members, set per game or across the whole group. That makes revenue sharing easy. It also means whoever owns the group, or holds the permission to manage payouts, controls the money and can change the split. Roblox's documentation is blunt about what happens if things go wrong: it says it cannot help arbitrate or resolve disagreements inside a group.

The per-game setting is more useful than it looks. Because splits can be set game by game, partners do not need one split for everything forever. A game you built together can be split one way, and a smaller project that one person builds mostly alone can be split another. That flexibility only helps if you use it deliberately, so add a line to your agreement about how new projects inside the group will be divided before anyone starts building them. The worst time to negotiate the split on a game is after it starts earning.

So decide, in writing, who owns the group and what the split is. Startups solve a version of this problem with *vesting*, where founders earn their ownership over time, often over four years with nothing earned until the first year is complete. The point is that if one founder leaves early, they do not walk away with a large share of something the other person keeps building.

A two-person game team does not need legal paperwork to borrow the idea. You can simply agree that the split will be reviewed every few months against who is actually doing the work, and that someone who stops contributing stops earning new shares. Once real money is involved, talk to a lawyer. If either of you serves in the military, also check your command's rules on outside business activity before income starts flowing.
The cheapest fight you will ever have

Every partnership has hard conversations. The only choice is when. Have them early, when the game earns nothing and nobody is hurt, and they cost an awkward evening. Have them late, when there is real money, years of work and two different memories of what was promised, and they can cost the project and the relationship.

That is the reframe worth keeping. A written agreement between brothers is not a sign that you do not trust each other. It is the thing that lets you *keep* trusting each other when the stakes go up. The Moldenhauers bet their homes on a game and stayed partners. Their talent made *Cuphead* good. Their way of deciding together is what let them survive making it.

takeaways: Decide equity, roles and decision rules on purpose, not in a rush to avoid awkwardness.
Family partnerships need more structure, not less, because the relationship is at stake.
Know whether each of you wants to be rich or king before an offer arrives.
Give each partner clear areas to own; reserve a short list of big decisions for both.
On Roblox, the group owner controls payouts, so put ownership and splits in writing.

title: You Are Building on Rented Land
dek: Roblox and YouTube give a small builder reach no one could buy. They also set the rules, the payout rate and who is allowed in, and they can change all three overnight.

blocks.text: In September 2023, thousands of game developers woke up to news that their engine maker wanted a new cut. Unity, the engine behind a huge share of indie and mobile games, announced a Runtime Fee: a charge tied to how many times a game was installed, set to begin in January. Developers were furious, partly because of the money and partly because of the principle. They had picked Unity years earlier under one set of terms. Now the terms were changing under games they had already built.

Unity backed down in stages. Within weeks it narrowed the fee so it would not apply to existing games and would only hit paid tiers. On September 12, 2024, a year after the uproar, a new CEO cancelled it for game developers entirely and went back to subscription pricing, with price rises for the paid plans. But for a year, every studio built on Unity learned something uncomfortable: the ground under their business belonged to someone else.

That is platform risk. If you build a Roblox game and a YouTube channel, you are building on two of the most generous platforms that have ever existed for small creators. You are also building on land you do not own. Neither fact cancels the other.
The landlord always writes the lease

Platforms make a trade with builders. They bring the audience, the payments, the hosting and the discovery. In return, they set the rules and keep the right to change them. When interests line up, it is a fantastic deal. When they diverge, the platform wins, because it owns the lease.

Zynga, the company behind FarmVille, is the classic case. Around 2011, roughly 90 percent or more of its revenue was generated on Facebook, and Zynga alone accounted for $445 million, about 12 percent of Facebook's revenue that year. Even so, Facebook began requiring Zynga to pay its 30 percent fee on purchases through Facebook's own currency, which squeezed Zynga's profits and pushed it to try to diversify. The biggest tenant in the building still paid the rent the landlord set.

Size does not protect you either. In August 2020, Epic Games added its own payment option to Fortnite on iPhone to get around Apple's cut, and Apple pulled Fortnite from the App Store. It took a long legal fight and court orders against Apple's fees before Fortnite returned to the U.S. App Store on May 20, 2025, nearly five years later. One of the richest game companies in the world could not simply negotiate its way back.

blocks.title: When the platform changed the deal
items: Jan 2018
YouTube raises the bar for ad money to 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 watch hours.
Aug 2020
Apple removes Fortnite from the App Store over payments.
Sep 2023
Unity announces a per-install Runtime Fee.
Aug 2024
Turkey blocks access to Roblox.
Sep 2024
Unity cancels the Runtime Fee for games.
May 2025
Fortnite returns to the U.S. App Store.
Sep 2025
Roblox raises its standard DevEx cash-out rate.

blocks.text: What changing the rules looks like on YouTube

YouTube's version arrived on January 16, 2018. Until then, a channel could earn ad money after 10,000 lifetime views. Overnight, the requirement became 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 hours of watch time in the past year, and existing channels below that line were reviewed and dropped from the program. YouTube said the change would affect a significant number of channels.

Why would a platform squeeze the people who fill it with content? Usually because someone more important to its business needs something. In 2018, the change came as YouTube worked to win back advertisers who had been burned by ads appearing next to objectionable videos. Raising the bar gave YouTube more control over which channels could carry ads. Small creators were not the target; they were simply in the way. That is the normal shape of platform risk: decisions made for the platform's biggest customers, felt hardest by its smallest suppliers.

items.label: Affected channels that had earned under $100 in the past year
Affected channels that had earned under $2.50 in the past month

blocks.source: YouTube, via 9to5Google, January 2018

blocks.text: Those numbers cut both ways. They show YouTube was right that most affected channels were earning almost nothing, so the money lost was small. They also show who absorbs rule changes: the smallest creators, who have the least voice and the fewest alternatives. If you are just starting, you are in that group. The rules will be written with someone else in mind, and you will adapt to them.

Rules are not the only lever. YouTube's own product chief said in 2018 that about 70 percent of watch time came from recommendations. Any change in how that system weighs videos can move a small channel's views far more than anything the creator does that week. No contract guarantees you a share of it.

Discovery itself can shift. Roblox's own documentation lists changes to its algorithm as one of the reasons a game's Home impressions can rise or fall, alongside the developer's own updates and seasonal traffic. A game can lose a chunk of its players in a week without its creators changing a single line of code. If you ever see that happen, it is worth checking for announcements before assuming the game suddenly got worse.
The fine print on Roblox

Roblox controls every part of the money pipeline for its developers. Players buy Robux from Roblox. Developers earn Robux. Developers who qualify can convert earned Robux to real dollars through the Developer Exchange, known as DevEx, at a rate Roblox sets. Roblox's own documentation says the exchange rate is subject to change, that Roblox decides at its discretion what counts as earned Robux, and that it can reject requests.

The rate has moved, and in this case in developers' favor. Before September 5, 2025, the standard rate was $0.0035 per earned Robux. It is now $0.0038, and a higher rate of $0.0054 applies to some purchases made by U.S. players who are verified as 18 or older. Robux earned before the change still cash out at the old rate.

blocks.title: What 30,000 earned Robux pays out through DevEx
blocks.note: 30,000 is the minimum to cash out. The 18+ rate applies only to certain purchases by age-verified U.S. adults; that bar is calculated from Roblox's published $0.0054 rate.
blocks.source: Roblox Creator Hub, Developer Exchange documentation, 2025

blocks.text: The lesson is not that Roblox is stingy. It is that every number in that chart is a policy, and policies move. The newest one rewards games that attract verified adults, which tells you where Roblox wants developers to point their work. A platform's incentives quietly steer what gets built on it.

Rule changes are also openings for anyone paying attention. When a platform shifts its incentives, builders who adapt early tend to find less competition for the new thing being rewarded. A developer who reads Roblox's announcements and asks what the platform is trying to encourage will usually spot those shifts months before someone who only notices when their numbers change. Reading the landlord's plans is not paranoia. It is market research.

Eligibility is also a rule set. To cash out, you need to be at least 13, hold at least 30,000 earned Robux, have a verified email and tax forms on file, and stay in full compliance with Roblox's Terms of Use and Community Standards. Breaking the rules can mean suspension from DevEx. For a game made by two people, that means the account and group that own the game are business assets, and a careless mistake by either person is a risk to both.

Then there is access itself. Turkey blocked Roblox in August 2024 over child safety concerns. Several countries followed in 2025 and early 2026, including Qatar, Iraq and Egypt, while others such as Kuwait and Russia blocked it and later restored access with conditions like disabled chat. If a big share of your players lives in one country, a government decision you never saw coming can erase them in a day.
Rented versus owned

None of this means you should avoid platforms. At your stage, that would be a bad idea. Building your own game launcher or video site would be slower, more expensive and almost certainly reach nobody. Roblox and YouTube are the right places to start. The goal is not to leave rented land. It is to know which of your assets are rented and to build some that are owned.

blocks.title: What you build on a platform vs what goes with you

left.head: Rented (the platform can change it)
items: Your place in recommendations
The payout rate and eligibility rules
Your subscriber count and channel
Access in each country
The Robux balance before it is cashed out

right.head: Owned (goes with you anywhere)
items: Your skills: scripting, design, editing
Design docs, source files and art you made
Your reputation and name as a builder
Direct ways to reach fans, like an email list
Cash already paid out and saved

blocks.text: Look at the right column. Almost everything on it is either knowledge or a direct relationship. Those survive a policy change. A builder who has shipped three Roblox games has skills that transfer to any engine. A creator who has learned to edit and tell stories can move to another video platform. A team with a few hundred players who chose to hear from them directly can announce the next game no matter what an algorithm decides.

Be careful about what counts as owned. A Discord server is extremely useful, but it is also another platform with its own rules. An email list is about as close to owned as a small creator gets, because the addresses travel with you. The honest version is that nothing online is fully owned. The point is not to have zero dependence. It is to not have *one* dependence.
Concentration is the number to watch

The simplest way to measure platform risk is one question: if this platform disappeared or changed its rules tomorrow, what share of my income and audience would go with it? For Zynga, the honest answer was about 90 percent. That is what made Facebook's decisions so painful. The risk was not that Facebook existed; it was that almost everything ran through it.

For a beginner, the answer will be close to 100 percent, and that is fine. A first game on Roblox and a first channel on YouTube should be fully committed to their platforms, because splitting attention across five platforms before anything works is a much bigger risk than any policy change. Concentration becomes dangerous as the stakes grow: when the income starts paying real bills, when a team depends on it, when it becomes the business you plan to leave the Navy for. That is the point to start deliberately building the owned column, not before.
Early on, concentration is focus. Later, the same concentration is fragility. The skill is noticing when one has turned into the other.
A platform-risk checklist for a two-person studio

blocks.title: Protecting what you build
items: Read the rules that pay you: Roblox's Terms of Use, Community Standards and DevEx terms, and YouTube's monetization policies.
Stay clearly inside the lines; avoid gray-area tactics like misleading titles or copied assets that could put the account at risk.
Keep backups of place files, scripts and art outside the platform, so a lost account is not a lost game.
Put ownership in writing: which group owns the game, who controls it and how payouts are split.
Give fans a way to follow you that you control, and invite them to it from inside the game and videos.
Watch where your players come from and avoid depending on a single country, source or feature.

blocks.text: Money also deserves a rule. Robux sitting in a balance is a promise from Roblox, not dollars in a bank. Rates and eligibility can change, so once a game earns past the cash-out minimum, it is reasonable to turn platform money into real money on a regular schedule. Taxes apply to DevEx income; if it gets meaningful, check with a tax professional or the base legal or finance office.

One more habit costs nothing: keep a short record of the rules you are relying on and check it when you come back from time away. Coming home from a long underway to find that a policy changed weeks ago is a real risk when you cannot check announcements regularly. A partner on shore who reads platform news and passes along anything important is worth a lot here.
The portable asset is you

The deepest protection from platform risk is not a contract or a backup drive. It is the builder. Unity developers who knew their craft could switch engines if they had to. Small YouTubers who lost ad revenue in 2018 still had the skills and viewers they needed to cross the new bar and earn it back.

So use the platforms fully, follow their rules carefully and enjoy the reach they give you. Just never confuse renting with owning. Every game you finish, every video you edit, every player who chooses to follow you directly is something no landlord can take back. Build those on purpose, and a rule change becomes a setback instead of an ending.

takeaways: Platforms give reach in exchange for control: they set the rules, payout rates and access, and can change them.
Even giants like Zynga and Epic could not escape platform decisions, and the smallest creators absorb rule changes first.
Roblox's DevEx rate, eligibility and country access are all policies; read them, follow them and expect them to move.
Skills, source files, reputation and direct contact with fans are the assets that survive any policy change.
Back up your work, put game ownership in writing, and turn platform balances into real money regularly.

title: The Autopsy You Owe Every Dead Game
dek: Teams that review their failures, and their successes, get measurably better. Most builders skip it for projects they abandon, which is exactly where the cheapest lessons are buried.

blocks.text: In a study published in 2005, the Israeli researchers Shmuel Ellis and Inbar Davidi followed Israeli soldiers through a series of land-navigation exercises. Every day the soldiers set out with maps and checkpoints, and every evening their units held an after-event review. The researchers changed one thing. Some groups reviewed only what had gone wrong that day. Others reviewed both their failures and their successes.

The soldiers who studied both improved significantly more over the following exercises. The researchers also measured what was going on in the soldiers' heads. At the start, their mental models of failures were far richer than their models of successes: they had thought hard about what went wrong and barely at all about why things went right. With full reviews, that gap gradually closed. Studying success turned out to be a skill the soldiers had been neglecting.

Most people building games do neither. When a project dies, especially one that never shipped, the natural move is to shrug, close the folder and start something new. That feels like resilience. It is often just a way of throwing away the most expensive data you will ever collect, and then paying for it again on the next game.
Why nobody does the autopsy

There are emotional reasons to skip it. Looking closely at something that failed is unpleasant, and between partners or family members it can feel like an invitation to blame. But there is also a cognitive trap that makes even honest reviews misleading, and it was named half a century ago.

In 1975, the psychologist Baruch Fischhoff gave people accounts of historical events and told some of them how the events turned out. People who knew the outcome judged it to have been much more predictable than people who didn't. Worse, they could not undo it: even when asked to answer as if they did not know the outcome, they couldn't. Fischhoff called this creeping determinism. It is now known as hindsight bias, the feeling that you knew it all along.

Hindsight bias poisons postmortems of abandoned projects in a specific way. Once a game is dead, it is very easy to say, "That idea was never going to work." That sentence feels like a lesson, but it isn't one. It erases the actual decisions you made, with the information you had at the time, and replaces them with a story in which the ending was obvious. If the ending was obvious, there is nothing to learn. And so the next idea dies at the same stage for the same reason.

A second force pushes in the same direction: the pull of the next idea. Starting something new is the most exciting moment in any project. Every new concept looks clean and full of promise, because none of its problems have shown up yet, while the old one is covered in every bug and compromise you have already met. Comparing a real project to an imagined one is not a fair fight. A postmortem forces a fairer comparison by making you write down what actually happened to the last idea that looked this good.
"It was a bad idea" is not a postmortem. The useful question is what you believed when you started, what evidence would have changed your mind, and when that evidence actually arrived.
Debriefs work, and the numbers are big

The US Army has used after-action reviews for decades, and medicine and aviation have adopted structured debriefs too. In 2013, Scott Tannenbaum and Christopher Cerasoli pulled the research together in a meta-analysis of 46 samples covering 2,136 people, comparing teams and individuals who debriefed with those who didn't.

items.label: Average performance improvement from debriefs versus no debrief
Research samples pooled in the meta-analysis
People in those samples

blocks.source: Tannenbaum & Cerasoli, Human Factors, 2013

blocks.text: Debriefs improved effectiveness by roughly 20 to 25 percent on average, an effect size that is large by the standards of workplace interventions. It held for teams and individuals, in simulations and in real settings, and in medical and non-medical work. The researchers found that debriefs worked best when they were structured and when the discussion was aligned with what the participants were actually trying to improve. A vague "so how did that go?" is not the same thing.

Ellis and Davidi's result adds a twist that most people get backwards. Teams tend to treat success as needing no explanation: it worked, move on. But a success you can't explain is a success you can't repeat. If the launching mechanic felt great in a prototype, the review should ask why. Was it the camera shake, the sound, the arc, the speed of the reset? Knowing which parts did the work is what lets you keep them when everything around them changes.

That should sound familiar to anyone trained in a nuclear plant. A critique after an incident, with its timeline, root causes and corrective actions, is the same tool wearing a uniform. The habit of asking what happened, why, and what changes now is already drilled into the people who run reactors. It works just as well on a game that never launched.
What 355 game postmortems say

Game developers have a long tradition of public postmortems, usually split into "what went right" and "what went wrong." Two research teams have mined them. In 2016, Michael Washburn and colleagues, including researchers from Microsoft Research, analyzed 155 postmortems published on the trade site Gamasutra.

blocks.title: What developers said went right and wrong
blocks.note: 155 postmortems; each could list several categories.
blocks.source: Washburn et al., ICSE, 2016

blocks.text: Notice that game design and development process appear on both sides of the ledger. When design went right, developers kept mentioning two things: a hook that grabbed players and a clear vision. When it went wrong, the cause was often overly ambitious designs that couldn't be built in time, or concepts that confused players. When the process went right, teams had planned before building, made prototypes and iterated. The same few levers decided success and failure; teams just pulled them in opposite directions.

In 2021, Cristiano Politowski and colleagues went further, coding 200 postmortems from 1997 to 2019 into 927 individual problems. The most common problem types were technical and game design, each about one problem in eight, followed by team problems, tools and planning.

blocks.title: Problems found in 200 game postmortems
blocks.note: Top 8 of 20 problem types, out of 927 problems in total.
blocks.source: Politowski et al., Game Industry Problems, 2021

blocks.text: Their most striking conclusion was about root causes. When they traced problems back, most of the main causes were related to people, not technology: too few people for the work, a poor team environment, underestimation, an unclear design vision, misaligned teams. The code was rarely the real reason a game struggled. The decisions around it were.

There is a caveat built into all of this, and it matters for anyone with a folder of abandoned projects. Published postmortems come overwhelmingly from games that shipped. Studios rarely write public autopsies of the projects they killed in pre-production. So the research is a picture of what goes wrong in games that survived long enough to launch. The lessons from games that never got that far mostly go unrecorded, which is exactly why you have to record your own.
Make it blameless

Google's site reliability engineers, who keep some of the largest computer systems on Earth running, write a postmortem after serious incidents, and they insist it be blameless. In their own guide, a blameless postmortem focuses on identifying the contributing causes without indicting any person or team for bad behavior. The reasoning is practical. If people expect to be blamed, they hide information, and a postmortem built on hidden information is useless.

blocks.title: Two ways to review a dead project

left.head: Blame review
items: Who dropped the ball?
Ends with a culprit
People get defensive and leave things out
Same mistake returns with a new owner

right.head: Blameless review
items: What conditions made this likely?
Ends with changes to how you work
People share what really happened
The system gets harder to fail

blocks.text: For two people building together, especially family, this is the difference between a review that makes the next game better and one that makes the next conversation worse. "You never finished the inventory system" is blame. "We started the inventory before we knew the core loop was fun, so it was hard to stay motivated" is a cause you can fix.
A postmortem for a game that never shipped

A scrapped game needs slightly different questions from a shipped one, because there are no sales or reviews to analyze. What there is, is a record of decisions. And when you have scrapped several concepts in a row, the most valuable data is the pattern across them, not any single one.

Imagine a team that starts four game ideas in about five weeks and drops each one. It is tempting to treat that as four separate bad ideas. A better reading lines them up side by side. Did each die at the same stage, say, right after the fun first prototype and right before the grinding systems work? Did each die when a newer, shinier idea appeared? Did any of them get in front of real players before being cut? If the answers rhyme, the problem was never the ideas. It was the process, and the next idea will die the same way unless the process changes.

It is also worth counting what a dead game leaves behind, because the answer is rarely zero. A movement system, a data-saving module, a shop interface, an art pipeline, a working setup for two people sharing code: all of that can be carried into the next project if it was built to be reused. So can skill. A team that scrapped four concepts but learned to script, sync and test together along the way has not wasted those weeks. It has paid tuition. The postmortem is where you decide which parts of that tuition you are keeping.

blocks.title: A 30-minute autopsy for an abandoned game
items: Write a short timeline: when you started, key decisions, and the day you decided to stop.
Write down what you believed at the start: why this game, who it was for, what would make it fun.
Name the actual reason you stopped. Was it evidence from players, a technical wall, or a loss of interest?
List what went right, not just what went wrong: systems, skills or assets worth carrying forward.
Compare with your previous scrapped projects and look for the stage where they keep dying.
Write one or two concrete changes for the next project, and decide now what evidence would justify killing it.

blocks.text: Here is what a filled-in version might look like for an imaginary scrapped game, kept deliberately short.

items: **Timeline:** started a monster-collecting game; first prototype in a week; dropped after three weeks when a new concept came up.
**What we believed:** players would love catching rare creatures; we assumed the economy would be easy to build.
**Why we stopped:** no player ever tested it. We stopped because the economy work felt slow and the next idea felt exciting.
**What went right:** the catching mechanic was fun in our own tests; the shared code setup worked well.
**Pattern:** third project in a row dropped at the economy-and-progression stage, before any outside player saw it.
**Change for next time:** put a rough version in front of five outside players within two weeks, and do not start a new concept until that test has happened.

blocks.text: That last step is the bridge between a postmortem and the next game. Before you start, write down the conditions under which you would stop: for example, if ten fresh testers can't understand the core mechanic in a minute, or if the first public test shows most players leaving in the first stage. Kill criteria set in advance protect you from both mistakes, quitting a good game because a new idea feels exciting, and clinging to a bad one because you have sunk months into it.

Keep the write-ups short and keep them all in one place. Six honest paragraphs per dead project are worth more than a perfect template you never fill in. Read them before you pitch the next idea. Over time they turn into something no tutorial can give you: a record of how *you* tend to fail, which is the only kind of knowledge that stops you failing that way again.

Ellis and Davidi's soldiers got better because every evening they asked what had gone wrong and what had gone right, and why. A scrapped game deserves the same evening. It cost you weeks. Thirty minutes to find out what it was trying to teach you is the cheapest part of the whole project.

takeaways: Review successes as well as failures; soldiers who did both improved more than those who studied only failures.
Structured debriefs improve performance by roughly 20 to 25% on average.
Beware hindsight bias: "it was always a bad idea" erases the real lessons.
Most root causes in game postmortems are about people and decisions, not technology.
For scrapped games, look for the stage where projects keep dying, and set kill criteria before starting the next.

title: On Any Given Day, 98 of 100 Players Pay Nothing
dek: What Roblox's biggest games actually charge, why their stores look nothing like a beginner's, and how to price a game when almost nobody pays.

blocks.text: Open the store in *Steal a Brainrot* and something looks wrong. This is one of the most visited games Roblox has ever had, with more than 74 billion visits on its counter in November 2026, and it sells exactly three game passes: an admin pass, a VIP pass and a double-money pass. A first-time developer would expect a hit game to have a wall of passes. It doesn't.

Look one layer down, at the repeatable purchases Roblox calls developer products, and the picture flips. The same game lists 126 of them for sale, from a 19-Robux skip timer on an egg up to an 11,992-Robux bundle of eight lucky blocks. At roughly a cent per Robux, that ladder runs from about 20 cents to about $120. *Grow a Garden* goes further still: no passes on sale at all, and more than 1,400 developer products listed in Roblox's system.

That shape is not one studio's quirk. It is the rational answer to a single number buried in Roblox's annual report. Understanding that number is the most useful thing you can do before you put a price tag on anything.
The number that shapes everything

In its filing for 2025, Roblox reported 127 million average daily active users. Of those, only about 1.8 million were daily paying users, roughly 1.4 percent. Put the other way, on a typical day about 98 of every 100 people on the platform spend nothing at all.

items.label: Average daily active users on Roblox, 2025
Average daily paying users, about 1.4% of them
Average daily spend per paying user, versus $0.15 per user overall

blocks.source: Roblox Corporation, Form 10-K for fiscal year 2025

blocks.text: The same filing gives the other half of the picture. Average daily bookings per active user were 15 cents. Per paying user, they were $10.36, nearly seventy times as much. Spending on Roblox is not spread thinly across everyone. It is concentrated in a small group, and it is lopsided even inside that group.

This changes the question you are answering. You are not setting "the price" for "your players." You are designing for two populations at once: a huge crowd who will never pay, and a small minority who will, some of them a lot. The crowd is not freeloading. They are part of what the payers are buying: full servers, people to race, someone to show off a rare skin to. Roblox's own filing says that keeping and growing its users, including the ones who never spend, is important to its success. The same logic holds inside a single game.

Pricing on Roblox is not about finding one right number. It is about building a range of prices so a player with 25 Robux to spend and a player with 2,500 both find something worth buying, while the player with zero still has a great time.
Ladders, not prices

Economists call this price discrimination: charging different people different amounts for related things. You can't usually ask each customer how rich they are, so the version that works is self-selection. Offer a menu and let buyers sort themselves. Airlines do it with seat classes. Software companies do it with basic, pro and enterprise plans.

In 1998 the economists Carl Shapiro and Hal Varian gave the digital version a name in the *Harvard Business Review*: versioning. Because an extra copy of a digital product costs almost nothing to make, a seller can offer as many versions as buyers can tell apart, each aimed at a different willingness to pay. A Roblox store is a versioning machine, and the developer product is its main tool.

Look at how *Steal a Brainrot* sells in-game cash. There are five packs. After a cheap entry point, each rung roughly doubles the one below it, so a player choosing between them is picking a spending level, not haggling over a few Robux. The 59-Robux pack is for a kid with a little left on a gift card. The top rung is for the rare player for whom money is not the constraint.

blocks.title: One game's price ladder: cash packs
blocks.note: Steal a Brainrot's five cash packs as listed for sale. At about $0.01 per Robux, the range is roughly 60 cents to $25.
blocks.source: Roblox public developer-product listings, retrieved Nov 5, 2026

blocks.text: The same pattern repeats across its store: speed boosts at 39, 99 and 229 Robux, wheel spins at 99 for one and 499 for ten, lucky blocks from 175 up to nearly 12,000. Every rung exists for a different wallet. When paying players are scarce and spending is concentrated among them, the top rungs can carry far more revenue than their tiny number of buyers suggests.
Durable versus consumable

Roblox gives you two main things to sell. A **pass** is bought once and kept forever: VIP access, a permanent boost, a special item. A **developer product** can be bought again and again: a currency pack, a spin, a skip. Designers describe the same split as durable versus consumable items, and sort both by purpose: enhancement (it makes you stronger, faster or luckier) versus expression (it makes you look different).

blocks.title: Two ways to sell

left.head: Passes
items: Bought once, owned forever
Clear value, easy to explain
Spending ceiling: you cannot buy VIP twice
Fits small, simple games

right.head: Developer products
items: Bought as often as the player wants
No ceiling on what one player can spend
Needs an economy and systems to spend into
Where randomized items usually live

blocks.text: The money logic is simple. A pass has a ceiling: once a player owns everything, they are done paying. A consumable has none. That is why the most successful games tilt so hard toward developer products. In a survey of 14 well-known Roblox games, the number of passes on sale ranged from zero to 22, while several listed hundreds of products.

blocks.title: Developer products listed for sale
blocks.note: Products marked for sale at a real price. Old seasonal items may still be listed, so not all are offered in-game at once.
blocks.source: Roblox public developer-product API, retrieved Nov 5, 2026

blocks.text: But consumables are also where Roblox monetization gets ugly. A lot of them are randomized: spins, eggs, lucky blocks. Roblox requires that any paid random item show every possible outcome and its actual percentage odds before purchase, including when the player pays with an in-game currency bought with Robux. For some players in some countries, Roblox flags paid random items as restricted, and the game must offer another path, such as a free way to earn them or a direct purchase priced from the expected value.

There is a reason regulators care. In a 2018 survey of 7,422 gamers, the psychologists David Zendle and Paul Cairns found that the more people spent on loot boxes, the more severe their problem gambling tended to be, and that link was much stronger than for ordinary in-game purchases. The study cannot say which causes which. But Roblox's audience is young, and a business that depends on children buying spins is a choice with real costs. Make it with your eyes open, or don't make it.
What a pass actually costs, and what you keep

For passes specifically, the market has a clear middle. Across the same 14 games, there were 92 passes on sale with a median price of 395 Robux. Most hits cluster between roughly 300 and 500. The two obby-style games in the sample sit well below that: *Tower of Hell* at a median of 195 and *Natural Disaster Survival* at 80.

blocks.title: Median game pass price
blocks.note: Passes on sale on one account; regional pricing can show some players lower prices.
blocks.source: Roblox public game-pass API, retrieved Nov 5, 2026

blocks.text: Now translate a price into what reaches you. Roblox's filing says creators selling their own items in their own games keep 70 percent of the Robux spent. Since September 5, 2025, the standard Developer Exchange rate has been $0.0038 per earned Robux. A 299-Robux pass therefore earns you about 209 Robux, worth roughly 80 cents. DevEx won't pay out until you hold 30,000 earned Robux, about $114, which takes around 144 sales of that pass. The higher $0.0054 rate, live since June 8, 2026, applies only to qualifying purchases by age-verified US players aged 18 and up. For a game full of kids, that is a sliver of revenue, not a raise.

Two Roblox systems then reshape whatever price you pick. **Regional pricing**, now part of what Roblox calls Managed Pricing, is on by default for passes and automatically lowers prices in poorer economies, never below 30 percent or above 100 percent of your price. **Price optimization** runs automatic tests that show different prices to different groups of players and recommends winners. The catch: Roblox says a test generally needs about 60,000 transactions over the previous 30 days. A new game from a two-person team will not get near that. You will set your first prices by hand.

There is one more way to charge: paid access, a one-time entry fee of 25 to 1,000 Robux. Roblox's own documentation warns that it limits how many people join, and in a world where almost nobody pays, a gate at the front door shrinks the crowd that makes the game fun. Its best use is narrow. Roblox notes that some developers switch it on briefly to run a closed beta for their most motivated players, then open the game for free.

And not every Robux you earn comes from a store. Roblox's Creator Rewards program, which replaced Premium engagement payouts on July 24, 2025, pays creators 5 Robux a day when their game is one of the first three an active spender plays for at least ten minutes that day. An active spender is someone who has bought at least $9.99 of Robux or Premium in the previous 60 days. In other words, a player can be worth something to you without ever opening your shop, simply by choosing your game first.
Practical tip: never hard-code a price into your shop UI. Read it at runtime through MarketplaceService, or regional and tested prices will charge players one number while your button shows another.
Pricing a launcher obby

Put this together for a game where players vault, launch and climb for bigger numbers. The first decision is not a price. It is what kind of game you are. If the fun is skill, meaning a great vaulter beats a rich one, then selling raw power undercuts the thing that makes the game good, and expression should carry the store. If the fun is growth, meaning numbers go up and the joy is watching them climb, then multipliers are the genre's norm and players expect them. Most +1 games are the second kind. Know which one yours is before you open the Creator Hub.

items: **A cheap first purchase.** The classic is a starter pack, an offer a new player sees in the first few minutes. Keep it small, generous and clearly a deal.
**Expression at every level.** Pole skins, trails and landing effects at a few price points, so the best vaulters can show off and everyone else can look like they might be.
**A VIP or multiplier pass near the market middle.** Obby comparables sit low, so starting around 150 to 300 Robux and testing upward is safer than starting high.
**Consumables with a reason to exist.** Short boosts or a stage skip for players stuck on a hard section, priced low enough that buying one feels like a convenience, not a ransom.
**A high rung or two.** A big bundle for the rare player who wants everything. Few will buy it. That is fine; it is not for most players.

blocks.text: Then watch what happens, because the comparables are only a starting anchor. A pass nobody buys is telling you something about value, not just price. A product many players open but few buy is telling you the price is wrong. And a game where the free players leave is telling you that you priced for the wrong population entirely.

The deepest lesson in Roblox's numbers is that the store is built on top of the free player, not the other way around. The 98 who pay nothing are the reason the two who pay want to be there. Design the free game first, make it worth being in, and only then build the ladder that lets people pay to enjoy it more.

takeaways: About 1.4% of Roblox's daily users pay on a given day; price for two audiences, the payers and the crowd that makes the game worth paying for.
Build a price ladder, not a price: cheap entry, middle rungs, and a rare high rung.
Hit games sell few passes and many repeatable products, because passes have a spending ceiling.
A 299-Robux pass earns you about 80 cents at the standard DevEx rate; do the math before dreaming.
Paid random items must show their odds, and they carry real ethical weight with a young audience.

title: The Urgent Thing Is Usually the Wrong Thing
dek: People pick tasks with fake deadlines over ones that pay more, and busy doctors pick easy cases over the ones that make them better. A small team's to-do list has the same trap built in.

blocks.text: In a 2014 paper, psychologist David Rosenbaum and colleagues at Penn State set up what should have been the most boring experiment imaginable. Two buckets sat along a hallway, one near the start and one closer to the finish. Participants were told to pick up whichever bucket seemed easier and carry it to the end.

The sensible choice is the bucket nearer the finish, because you carry it a shorter distance. Most people grabbed the nearer one at the start and lugged it the whole way. Across nine experiments, the pattern kept showing up. Participants' own explanations pointed to wanting to get part of the job out of the way as soon as possible. Rosenbaum named the habit *pre-crastination*: rushing to finish a small piece of a task, even when it costs extra effort.

That hallway is a decent model of a to-do list. Some items sit right in front of you and can be grabbed immediately. Others are farther off and matter more. A surprising amount of research now suggests that people, including highly trained professionals, consistently grab the wrong bucket. For a two-person team with a few hours a week, that habit is the difference between a game that improves and a game that merely stays busy.
The pull of a fake deadline

In 2018, Meng Zhu, Yang Yang and Christopher Hsee published a paper in the *Journal of Consumer Research* with an unsettling title: *The Mere Urgency Effect*. Across five experiments, they gave people a choice between tasks. One paid more. The other paid less but carried a sense of urgency, such as an expiration window that made it seem like it had to be done now.

People kept choosing the urgent, lower-paying task, even when the researchers removed the usual good reasons for doing so. The urgent task was not easier, not more certain and not a stepping stone to the important one. It just felt like it was expiring. The authors point out that this breaks one of the most basic rules of rational choice: never pick an option that is worse in every way that counts. People behaved as if urgency had a value of its own.

This is the old urgent-versus-important distinction, usually drawn as a four-box grid and credited to Dwight Eisenhower. The grid has been on office walls for decades. What the research adds is a warning that knowing the grid is not enough. Even when people can plainly see which option pays more, the ticking clock still often wins. The bias does not live in what you know. It lives in the moment you choose.

Most of what makes a side project feel urgent is exactly this kind of spurious urgency. A message from a friend who found a typo. A notification that another game updated. A sudden worry that a certain feature needs to be in before some imagined launch date. None of those is necessarily important. All of them pull.

Rosenbaum's own explanation for the bucket result points to the same root. Unfinished tasks take up room in working memory. Grabbing the near bucket clears one item off the mental list immediately, and that relief feels good even when it costs more effort overall. Urgent and easy tasks both offer that relief. Important tasks usually do not, at least not soon, which is why they lose the contest so often.
A useful test for any task that feels urgent: what actually happens if this waits 48 hours? If the honest answer is nothing, the urgency is a feeling, not a fact.
The easy-task trap

Urgency is not the only distortion. The other one is ease. In a study published in *Management Science* in 2020, Diwas KC, Bradley Staats, Maryam Kouchaki and Francesca Gino looked at six years of data from a hospital emergency department. When the department got busy, doctors increasingly picked easier patients from the queue. They called it *task completion preference*.

On the surface, it seemed to work. More patients were being seen per shift. But once the researchers adjusted for how complex each case was, the picture flipped: choosing easy cases was linked to *worse* overall throughput. It was also linked to slower learning, because the doctors were dodging exactly the hard cases that would have made them faster later. In follow-up lab experiments, the same behavior appeared, driven by fatigue and by the pleasant feeling of crossing something off.

A second team, Ibanez and colleagues, studied 2.4 million diagnoses by radiologists, who are supposed to read scans in a set order but often reshuffle their queue. The doctors tended to jump to the tasks they expected to finish fastest and to batch similar ones. Because cases were assigned randomly, the researchers could measure the effect cleanly: these deviations hurt productivity, and picking the shortest tasks first was especially costly.

items.label: of emergency department data showing busy doctors drift toward easy cases
radiology diagnoses showing shortest-task-first hurts productivity
experiments showing people pick urgent tasks over better-paying ones

blocks.source: KC et al., Management Science, 2020; Ibanez et al., Management Science, 2018; Zhu, Yang & Hsee, JCR, 2018

blocks.text: Translate that to a game project. After a long day, the easy tasks are irresistible: rename some buttons, tweak a color, reorganize the folder structure, make a new icon. Each one gives a little hit of progress. Meanwhile the hard problem, say, making the launch feel powerful or fixing the bug that resets player data, sits untouched for another week. The list gets shorter. The game does not get better.

The researchers did not conclude that the doctors were lazy. They were overloaded and tired, and the easy case offered a quick sense of progress. That is the uncomfortable part: the trap catches conscientious people precisely when they are working hardest. The fix is not to try harder in the moment. It is to arrange the work so the hard thing gets the fresh hours, and the easy things fill the tired ones.
Value is lumpy

The reason this matters so much is that value is rarely spread evenly across a list. In a classic study of a large commercial software system, Norman Fenton and Niclas Ohlsson found that a small number of modules contained most of the faults discovered in testing, and a very small number contained most of the failures users actually hit in the field. Problems clump. So does impact.

Games work the same way. A handful of things decide whether a new player stays: the first minute, how the core action feels, whether anything crashes or erases progress, whether the player understands what to do next. Fifty smaller improvements elsewhere can add up to less than one fix in that short list. Prioritizing is mostly the skill of finding the few items that carry the weight, and then protecting time for them from everything that merely feels pressing.
Scoring instead of guessing

One reason people fall for urgency and ease is that the alternative, comparing tasks on value, is mentally expensive. A scoring system does the comparison on paper. One of the best known was described in 2018 by Sean McBride, a product manager at the software company Intercom, who called it RICE.

blocks.title: RICE, adapted for a two-person game team
items: Reach: how many players will this touch in the next month? Every player, or only the few who reach world three?
Impact: how much will it change each of those players' experience? Intercom's scale runs 3 (massive), 2, 1, 0.5, down to 0.25 (minimal).
Confidence: how sure are you of those guesses? 100% means you have data, 80% means a decent hunch, 50% means you are mostly hoping.
Effort: how many evenings or hours will it take, counting both of you?
Score: multiply reach, impact and confidence, then divide by effort. Sort the list by score and argue about the top five, not the bottom fifty.

blocks.text: Here is how it plays out with made-up but realistic numbers. Say 100 players try the game next month. Fixing a camera that hides the landing touches all 100 of them, has an impact of 2, deserves 80% confidence because testers complained about it, and takes about two evenings. That scores 100 times 2 times 0.8, divided by 2, which is 80. A brand-new world touches only the 10 players who get far enough to see it, might have an impact of 3, gets 50% confidence because nobody has asked for it yet, and takes ten evenings. That scores 1.5. The exciting option loses by a factor of more than fifty, and seeing it written down makes the argument almost unnecessary.

The numbers are guesses, and McBride was upfront about that. Their value is in the conversation they force. The confidence factor is especially useful for a team that loves new ideas, because it punishes exciting projects that nobody has evidence for. The reach factor punishes features only the builders would use. And dividing by effort makes the cost of a big system impossible to ignore.

Do not let the score become the goal, though. Anyone can game a spreadsheet, including the person who filled it in. If a score surprises you, that is a prompt to talk, not an order. The point is to make the reasoning visible so two people can disagree about something specific instead of about a vague feeling.
A list two people can actually use

Big companies have whole teams for prioritization. Two people sharing a game need something that fits on one screen and survives long stretches when one of them is gone. The simplest version is a list with three sections.

blocks.title: Feels urgent versus actually important

left.head: Feels urgent
items: A friend's small bug report from today
Matching a feature another game just added
Polishing a menu almost nobody opens
Reorganizing files and folders
Replying to every comment right away

right.head: Actually important
items: Anything that loses player progress
How the core action feels in the first minute
Whether new players know what to do next
Crashes and broken purchases
The next thing players keep asking for
Now: no more than three items, each with one owner and a clear finish line. Nothing else gets worked on until one of these is done or deliberately dropped.
Next: the few items that move up when a Now slot opens. Ranked, so there is no debate when it happens.
Later: everything else, including the exciting new ideas. Writing them down here is how you keep them without letting them hijack the week.
Rule for new items: they go into Later by default. Moving one into Now means moving something else out, out loud, with your partner.

blocks.text: Some things really do deserve to jump the line, so agree in advance on what they are. A short interrupt rule keeps genuine emergencies from being confused with ordinary pressure: anything that loses player data, crashes the game, breaks a purchase or creates a safety problem for players gets handled right away. Everything else, no matter how loud, goes onto the list and waits its turn.

The cap of three matters more than it looks. Limits force trade-offs into the open. With an unlimited list, every request can be accepted and nothing has to be refused, which is how teams end up working on twenty things at once and finishing none. With three slots, saying yes to one thing means saying no to another, and that is exactly the conversation prioritizing is supposed to produce.

It also matches how people actually work after a long day. When you sit down tired, you do not want to choose. A short, already-ranked Now list removes the choice and with it the temptation to grab the nearest bucket.

A ranked list has one more benefit for a team where one person can vanish for weeks at a time. The ranking is the decision. When your partner finishes a Now item while you are out of contact, he does not have to wait for you to agree on what comes next. He takes the top of Next, and you both know it was the plan you made together. A ranked list is a way of being present in the project when you cannot actually be there.
Choose the far bucket

None of these studies says urgent or easy tasks are worthless. Some urgent things really are urgent, and quick wins can keep morale alive. The problem is the default. Left alone, people drift toward whatever is closest and whatever is ticking, and they feel productive the whole way.

The fix is not more discipline in the moment. It is deciding ahead of time, when you are fresh and with your partner, which buckets are worth carrying. Then, when the evening comes and the nearby bucket looks tempting, the decision has already been made.

takeaways: Urgency feels valuable even when it is not; ask what really happens if a task waits 48 hours.
Picking easy tasks first feels productive but can lower real output and slow your learning.
Value is lumpy: a few items decide whether players stay, so find them and protect time for them.
Score ideas on reach, impact, confidence and effort to turn vague feelings into a specific argument.
Cap the Now list at three items; adding one means removing one.
