title: Why Good Practice Feels Like Losing
dek: Mixing up your practice makes you look worse while you train and better when it counts. The research on desirable difficulties explains why.

blocks.text: In a study published in 1994, a junior college baseball team agreed to an experiment. Thirty players were split into three groups. Ten got no extra practice. Ten got two extra batting sessions a week for six weeks, seeing 15 fastballs, then 15 curveballs, then 15 changeups, in neat blocks. The last ten got the same 45 pitches per session, but in random order, so they never knew what was coming next.

Anyone who has played sports can guess how the sessions felt. The blocked group got into a groove: by the tenth fastball in a row, you are timing it well. The random group kept getting fooled. Yet when everyone was tested at the end on randomly mixed pitches, like a real game, the random group had improved by about 57 percent from their starting level and the blocked group by about 25 percent. The group that looked worse at practice got better at baseball.

That pattern, where the practice that feels worse produces the learning that lasts, has a name. The UCLA psychologists Robert and Elizabeth Bjork call it a *desirable difficulty*. Once you see it, you notice it everywhere, including in the way most people study for exams, train in games and learn to code.
Performance is not learning

The core idea is a distinction that sounds pedantic and turns out to be huge. Performance is what you can do right now, during practice. Learning is the lasting change that shows up later, in a different setting, after time has passed. You can watch performance. You can only infer learning, and the two often move in opposite directions.

Blocked practice is a performance-booster. When you do ten problems of the same type in a row, the method stays loaded in your head from one problem to the next, so you get them right and feel fluent. But that fluency is borrowed from the previous problem, not stored in long-term memory. Take away the crutch, by mixing types or adding a delay, and performance drops in practice. The Bjorks argue that this drop is often what drives durable learning, because it forces you to reconstruct the knowledge each time instead of coasting on what is already in your head.

In the Bjorks' framework, this is the gap between how accessible a memory is right now and how deeply it is stored. Easy practice inflates the first. Effortful practice, where you have to work to retrieve or reconstruct something, builds the second. Your feeling of mastery mostly reads the first, which is why it so often misleads you.

Their list of desirable difficulties is short: space your study sessions out instead of massing them, test yourself instead of rereading, interleave different topics instead of blocking them, and vary the conditions of practice. Spacing and testing each get their own article in this library. This one is about the less famous member of the family, interleaving, and about the crucial word in the phrase, *desirable*.
The math experiment

In 2007, Doug Rohrer and Kelli Taylor at the University of South Florida taught college students to find the volume of four unusual solids, such as a wedge and a spheroid. Everyone did the same practice problems in two sessions. Blockers did all the wedge problems together, then all the spheroids, and so on. Mixers did the same problems shuffled. A week later, everyone took a test.

blocks.title: Blocked vs mixed math practice
blocks.note: Test given one week after the final practice session. Small study: 18 students completed it.
blocks.source: Rohrer & Taylor, Instructional Science, 2007

blocks.text: Practice scores made blocking look like the clear winner. Test scores told the opposite story, by a factor of three. The sample was small, just 18 students who finished all sessions, so treat the exact numbers with caution. But the reason for the reversal is the important part, and it generalizes.

When problems come in blocks, you never have to decide which method to use. The worksheet decides for you: it says Section 4.2 at the top. On a real test, or a real job, nobody tells you what kind of problem you are facing. Identifying the problem type is half the skill, and blocked practice skips it entirely. Mixed practice forces you to ask, every single time, what kind of problem this is and how you know.

There is a second, quieter benefit. Mixing problem types automatically spaces out each type, because between two wedge problems you do three others. Each time you return to a type, you have to pull the method back out of memory rather than reading it off the previous problem. So interleaving smuggles in both spacing and retrieval practice, which may be part of why its effects can be so large.
Blocked practice teaches you how to solve a problem once you know what it is. Interleaved practice teaches you to recognize what it is. Real life mostly tests the second.
From a lab to 787 students

Small lab studies are easy to dismiss, so Rohrer and his colleagues went big. In a randomized trial published in 2020, 54 seventh-grade math classes across five Florida schools used either mostly interleaved homework or the usual blocked kind for about four months. Both groups did the same problems, only in a different order. About a month after a review session, the students took an unannounced test.

items.label: Test scores, interleaved vs blocked homework, one month later
Effect size, which is large for a classroom study

blocks.source: Rohrer, Dedrick, Hartwig & Cheung, Journal of Educational Psychology, 2020

blocks.text: For an educational intervention that costs nothing but reshuffling homework, that is an unusually large effect. It is also one trial, in one subject and one age group, so the precise size should not be taken as a law of nature. But it shows the lab finding survives contact with real classrooms, real teachers and real teenagers.
The illusion that protects bad habits

If interleaving works so well, why does almost nobody do it on their own? Because it fools the people doing it. In a 2008 study, Nate Kornell and Robert Bjork had students learn the styles of 12 painters of landscapes and skies, from Georges Seurat to lesser-known artists, either seeing each artist's paintings in a block or mixed with the others. Later the students tried to identify the artists of new paintings they had never seen. Those who studied mixed paintings were right about 61 percent of the time on the first test block; those who studied in blocks managed about 35 percent.

Then the students were asked which method had worked better for them. Seventy-eight percent said blocking had been as good as or better than mixing, even though 78 percent had actually done better with mixing. They had just experienced the result and still believed the opposite. Blocked study felt like learning. Mixed study felt like confusion.

A second experiment in the same paper repeated the trick, with the same result. Of the students who expressed a preference, 64 out of 72 believed blocking had worked better. The bias was not a fluke of one group. It seems to be how people read their own learning.

This is the real obstacle. Your in-the-moment sense of progress is a performance meter, and desirable difficulties are designed to push that meter down. If you choose methods by how they feel, you will choose the wrong ones almost every time. That makes these techniques less a study tip and more a matter of trust: trusting evidence over your own feeling of fluency.

The same illusion traps teachers, coaches and training programs, not just learners. An instructor mostly sees performance during training: how smoothly the class works through problems, how many get the practice set right, how confident everyone looks at the end of the day. Every one of those signals rewards blocked, predictable, easy practice. Over time, curricula drift toward whatever makes training look good, which is not always what makes people good. Motor-learning researchers have studied this for decades under the name contextual interference, and the baseball study is one of its best-known demonstrations.
When difficulty is just difficulty

The word *desirable* is doing real work. The Bjorks are explicit that a difficulty helps only if you can respond to it successfully. If you lack the background knowledge to make sense of the challenge, it is not desirable, it is just hard. Shuffling problem types before you understand any of them produces confusion, not learning. Learn each method first, then mix.

The evidence also says interleaving is not universal. A 2019 meta-analysis by Brunmair and Richter pooled 238 effect sizes from 59 studies. Overall, interleaving beat blocking by a moderate margin, an effect size of 0.42. But it varied enormously.

Paintings and other visual categories showed the biggest benefit, 0.67. Math showed a smaller benefit, 0.34. Results for expository texts were mixed, and for learning lists of words, blocking actually did better.

The pattern underneath was intuitive. Interleaving helped most when the categories were easy to confuse with each other, when the hard part was telling similar things apart. That is the situation where blocking hides the most and mixing reveals the most. When categories are already obviously different, there is little to gain.

It is also worth admitting how small some of the famous studies are. The baseball study had ten players per group, and the math study had 18 students. The large classroom trial and the meta-analysis are what make the overall picture credible, not any single striking chart.
Building difficulty into your practice

Technical training is full of easily confused categories, which is exactly where interleaving pays off. Electrical faults that present with similar indications. Thermodynamics problems that look alike but need different equations.

Casualty procedures with overlapping symptoms. Bugs that throw similar errors for different reasons. In each case, the real skill is discrimination: noticing the one detail that tells you which situation you are in.

blocks.title: How to interleave without drowning
items: Learn each new method or system on its own first, until you can do a basic example.
Then build mixed practice sets: shuffle problem types so no two in a row need the same approach.
Before solving each one, say out loud which type it is and what tipped you off.
Mix in older material, not just this week's, so earlier topics stay in rotation.
Expect your practice scores to drop. Judge the method by delayed tests, not by how practice feels.

blocks.text: For a board or a big exam, that means quizzing across systems rather than finishing one system completely before touching the next. For math and physics, it means pulling problems from different chapters into one set rather than doing the end-of-section exercises in order. For coding, it means building small projects that need several concepts at once instead of drilling one concept per tutorial. For game skills, it is the same lesson as the batting cage: training against one predictable bot pattern feels great and transfers poorly to opponents who do not cooperate.

Interleaving also changes how you should read your own results. If you switch to mixed practice sets and your scores drop from 90 percent to 60, that does not mean the method failed. It means the old 90 was partly an illusion created by the format. The fair comparison is how you do on a mixed, delayed test, the kind you will face on a board or in a real casualty, and on that measure the 60 is the more honest number and the one that climbs.

Varying conditions counts too. Practicing a procedure only at one panel, in one order, with one instructor watching, builds a skill tied to that setting. Changing the setup, the order of questions, or the person quizzing you makes your knowledge less dependent on any single set of cues.

blocks.title: Same problems, different order

left.head: Blocked
items: Ten of one type, then ten of the next
Method stays loaded between problems
High practice scores, smooth feeling
Weak at telling problem types apart

right.head: Interleaved
items: Types shuffled, no two alike in a row
Must choose the method every time
Lower practice scores, feels messy
Builds recognition of what you are facing

blocks.text: If you doubt all this, test it on yourself. Next time you have two similar topics to learn, practice one in blocks and the other mixed with older material, and quiz yourself on both a week later without warning. Personal experiments are not science, but they are a good way to stop trusting the feeling and start trusting the result.

The hardest thing about desirable difficulties is not using them. It is tolerating how they feel. Every one of them makes you look worse in the short term, to yourself and to anyone watching. The payoff arrives later, quietly, when the pitch you were not expecting comes in, and you hit it anyway.

takeaways: How well you perform during practice is a poor guide to how much you are learning.
Mixing problem types forces you to identify the problem, which is half of real-world skill.
Learn each method first, then interleave; difficulty without background knowledge is just confusion.
Interleaving helps most when categories are easy to confuse, and can hurt for simple word lists.
Judge study methods by delayed tests, not by how smooth practice feels.

title: The Dread Before the Equation
dek: Math anxiety is not the same as being bad at math. It is a second job your brain takes on at the worst possible moment, and it can be unlearned.

blocks.text: In 2012, two University of Chicago researchers put adults into a brain scanner and showed them a series of cues. One kind of cue meant a word puzzle was coming. Another meant a math problem was coming. Then, after a short pause, the problem appeared and the person solved it. The researchers were not interested in the solving. They were interested in the pause.

In people with high math anxiety, the few seconds of waiting for a math problem lit up the dorsal posterior insula on both sides of the brain, a region involved in detecting bodily threat and in the experience of pain. The more anxious the person, the stronger the response. Here is the strange part: the effect showed up while they were *anticipating* math, not while they were doing it. Math itself did not hurt. Expecting math did.

That finding, from Ian Lyons and Sian Beilock, captures what makes math anxiety so slippery. It is not mainly a gap in skill. It is a reaction that kicks in before you have even read the problem, and that reaction then shapes how well you can think once you do. Understanding the mechanics of it turns out to be the first step toward taking it apart.
More common than people admit

Math anxiety is not a rare condition. The OECD's PISA assessments, which survey 15- and 16-year-olds across dozens of countries, asked students in 2012 how math made them feel. Across the 34 OECD member countries, a majority said they often worry that math classes will be difficult for them. About a third said they get very tense when they have to do math homework, and a similar share said they get very nervous doing math problems.

items.label: Often worry math class will be difficult
Get very tense doing math homework
Get very nervous doing math problems

blocks.source: PISA 2012, as reported by Luttenberger, Wimmer & Paechter, 2018

blocks.text: Does the anxiety actually cost anything? A 2021 meta-analysis pooled 747 effect sizes from research published between 1992 and 2018. It found a consistent negative correlation between math anxiety and math achievement of about r = -0.28. That relationship showed up from childhood through adulthood and across nearly every kind of test the researchers looked at.

Read that number carefully, because it says two things at once. A correlation of -0.28 is real and reliable; anxious people do tend to score lower. But it is also modest. It means there are plenty of people who are good at math and anxious about it, and plenty who are weak at it and perfectly calm. Anxiety and ability are related, but they are not the same thing. You can be the person who passed every reactor theory exam and still feel your stomach drop when someone says 'run the numbers on the spot.'

The PISA data also show that the link between anxiety and scores appears in every participating country, though its strength varies, and that in most countries teenage girls report more math anxiety than boys. Researchers who study this generally do not read the gap as a difference in ability. It tracks beliefs and expectations about who is supposed to be good at math, which, as later sections show, can be picked up surprisingly early from the adults around a child.
Worry is a second task

The leading explanation for how anxiety hurts performance comes from Mark Ashcraft, who spent years studying it. Anything beyond memorized facts, such as carrying digits, holding an intermediate result, or keeping track of which step you are on, runs through working memory, the small mental workspace where you juggle information in the moment. That workspace is tiny. Most people can actively hold only a handful of items at once.

Ashcraft's argument is that math anxiety acts like a dual task. Part of your working memory is busy solving the problem. Another part is busy running a stream of commentary: I'm going to get this wrong, everyone is waiting, I've always been bad at this. That worry is not just unpleasant background noise. It takes up workspace. The more complex the problem, the more workspace it needs, and the more the worry crowds it out.

This explains a pattern that confuses anxious people about themselves. They often handle simple, memorized math fine. It is the multi-step problems, the ones that need every slot of working memory, where they fall apart. They conclude they are 'not math people.' A better reading is that they are trying to do math with part of their brain tied up on another job.

Picture a qual board. Someone asks you to work out, in your head, how long a tank takes to fill at a given flow rate. The arithmetic is not hard on paper. But now you are holding the numbers, the unit conversion and the next step, while also tracking the faces across the table and a voice in your head asking whether you look stupid. Every one of those things competes for the same few slots. Lose one slot and the intermediate result falls out, you start over, and the delay makes the worry louder. Nothing about your actual knowledge changed between the paper version and the spoken one. The load on your workspace did.
The anxious mind is not less capable at math. It is doing math with fewer free hands, because some of them are busy holding the worry.
Chicken or egg?

There is an obvious objection. Maybe people are anxious about math because they are bad at it, not bad at it because they are anxious. A 2016 review from Cambridge researchers took the question seriously and found evidence for both directions. Long-term studies of children suggest that early struggles can come first and create the anxiety. Experiments that raise or lower anxiety directly show that anxiety, in turn, lowers performance.

The most likely answer is that it runs both ways, in a loop. A bad experience creates worry. Worry eats working memory and leads to another bad experience. Worry also drives avoidance, and avoidance is where the real damage is done, because skipped practice means skills fall further behind, which justifies more worry. Ashcraft's work notes that highly anxious people avoid elective math courses, math-heavy majors and math-heavy careers altogether.

blocks.title: The math anxiety loop
items: A hard or embarrassing math moment
Worry the next time math comes up
Worry crowds working memory, so performance drops
Avoidance: less practice, less exposure
Skills fall behind, confirming the fear

blocks.text: The useful thing about a loop is that you can cut it anywhere. You do not have to fix the anxiety before you practice, or fix the skill before you feel calm. Breaking any single link weakens the whole cycle. That is a genuinely hopeful structure. The same feedback that drives the slide downward also drives recovery: a few small successes reduce worry, reduced worry frees working memory, freed working memory produces more successes, and practice stops feeling like a threat.
It is learned, which means it can be unlearned

Some of the most striking research shows math anxiety being passed from adults to children. A 2010 study of first- and second-grade classrooms found that at the start of the year, female teachers' math anxiety had no relation to their students' math scores. By the end of the year, the more anxious the teacher, the more likely girls in her class were to believe that boys are good at math and girls are good at reading, and the girls who believed that scored lower.

A 2015 study found a similar effect at home. When parents were anxious about math, their children learned less math over the school year and ended the year more anxious, but only when those parents frequently helped with math homework. Anxious parents who helped less often did not pass the effect along. And parents' math anxiety did not predict their children's reading scores at all.

These findings are uncomfortable, but they carry good news. If math anxiety were simply a fixed trait, it would not spread through a classroom in a single school year. It behaves more like a learned reaction, absorbed from the people around you. Learned reactions can be retrained.
What actually helps

The first tool is almost absurdly simple. In a 2011 study published in *Science*, Gerardo Ramirez and Sian Beilock had students spend about ten minutes before a high-stakes test writing freely about their worries regarding it. In lab experiments and in a real high school biology class, this expressive writing improved exam scores, and the boost was biggest for the students who were habitually most anxious about tests. A 2014 follow-up applied the same idea specifically to math anxiety. Without writing, highly math-anxious students did much worse on math problems than calm students. After writing, that gap shrank significantly.

Why would writing help? The working memory explanation predicts it. Putting worries on paper seems to get them out of the mental workspace, freeing up room for the actual problem. Notably, in the 2014 study, anxious students who used more words about cause and insight in their writing did better, which suggests the benefit comes from processing the worry, not just venting it.

The second tool is reframing the physical feeling. A separate line of research, covered elsewhere in this library, found that telling students their racing heart could actually help performance improved their scores on the math section of a real graduate admissions exam. The pounding heart is the same. What changes is whether you read it as a threat or as fuel.

The third tool is the slowest and the most durable: exposure plus skill. A 2015 Stanford study gave 46 third-graders eight weeks of intensive one-on-one math tutoring. The highly anxious children came out significantly less anxious, and brain scans showed calmer responses in the amygdala, a key region for fear. The children whose amygdala reactivity dropped most showed the biggest drops in anxiety. The researchers compared it to exposure therapy: repeated, supported contact with the feared thing, paired with growing competence.

blocks.title: A ten-minute routine before a test, board or calc
items: Write for about ten minutes about exactly what you're worried will happen and why
Notice the physical arousal and name it as energy your body is supplying, not a warning
Start with one problem you know you can do, to get a quick early win
Write intermediate steps down instead of holding them in your head
If you blank, move on and come back; the answer often returns once the worry fades

blocks.text: Turning the loop around

Put the research together and the strategy is clear: interrupt the loop at the cheapest link. Writing intermediate steps on paper instead of holding them in your head offloads working memory directly, which is why the calculations you do on paper go better than the ones someone asks you to do out loud. Doing a little math often, at low stakes, steadily erodes the avoidance that keeps the cycle going.

That second point matters for anything you want to build. Game development eventually brings in vectors, angles and a bit of physics. Quals bring in calculations you will be asked to do under someone's gaze. The temptation is to dodge the math-heavy parts until you feel ready. The research suggests you will feel ready only after you start: short, frequent, private practice with problems slightly above your comfort level is exactly the exposure that shrinks the reaction.

A concrete version: when a game mechanic needs math you don't know yet, such as making a projectile fly toward the player or a camera orbit smoothly, resist the urge to paste in a formula and move on. Draw it. Sketch the two positions, the arrow between them, the angle. Work one example by hand with simple numbers. Ten minutes like that is low-stakes exposure, it builds the actual skill, and it turns a vague dread of 'the math part' into a specific, finished thing you understand.

The pain-network study ends with an idea worth keeping. The dread lived in the waiting, not in the work. For most anxious people, the math itself is far more manageable than the anticipation of it. The fastest way to shrink the anticipation is to make math ordinary: something you do a little of most days, write down instead of carry in your head, and stop treating as a verdict on who you are.

takeaways: Math anxiety and math ability are linked only modestly (r = -0.28); strong performers can be very anxious.
Worry uses up working memory, so anxiety hits multi-step problems hardest. Write intermediate steps on paper.
Ten minutes of writing about your worries before a high-stakes test has improved scores, especially for anxious students.
Avoidance keeps the loop alive. Short, frequent, low-stakes practice is exposure that shrinks the fear.
The dread peaks before the problem, not during it. Starting is usually the hardest part.

title: The Memory Palace: Why Your Brain Remembers Places Better Than Lists
dek: An ancient trick for memorizing speeches turns out to run on the brain's navigation system, and 20 hours of practice rewired ordinary brains to look more like those of memory champions.

blocks.text: A poet named Simonides of Ceos is reciting at a banquet when someone calls him outside. While he is gone, the roof of the hall comes down and kills everyone at the table. The bodies are crushed beyond recognition, and the families cannot tell whom to bury. Simonides walks back through the hall in his mind, seat by seat, and names every guest by where they sat.

Whether it happened that way is anyone's guess. Cicero told the story about four centuries later as the origin of an idea: if you want to remember things in order, put them in places. Roman orators used it to give speeches lasting hours without notes. Medieval scholars and preachers adapted it. Today people who compete in memory sports use it to memorize the order of a shuffled deck of cards in under a minute.

The method has a dull academic name, the *method of loci* (loci is Latin for places), and a better popular one: the memory palace. The surprising part is not that it works. It is *why* it works, and what brain scans of trained memorizers reveal about how ordinary their brains are.
How the trick works

The oldest surviving how-to guide is a Latin textbook on public speaking called the *Rhetorica ad Herennium*, written around the 80s BC by an unknown author. It splits artificial memory into two parts: *backgrounds* and *images*. The backgrounds are places you already know cold, like rooms in a house or spots along a street. The images are vivid pictures that stand for the things you want to remember, placed one per spot.

blocks.title: Building a memory palace
items: Pick a route you know so well you could walk it in the dark, such as your house, your commute, or the path from your rack to your workspace.
Fix a set of stations along it, always in the same order: the door, the sink, the locker, the ladder.
Turn each item you need to remember into a concrete, ridiculous image. Abstract words get a stand-in object.
Place one image at each station and make it interact with the spot: melting into it, smashing it, shouting from it.
To recall, walk the route in your head and look at what is sitting at each station.

blocks.text: Say you need to remember five things to pick up from the ship's store: batteries, socks, a notebook, sunscreen and gum. Station one is your rack, where a battery the size of a torpedo is leaking acid onto your pillow. Station two is the sink, overflowing with wet socks that are singing. Station three is your locker, which has been stuffed so full of notebooks that it bursts open when you touch it. It feels silly. That is the point. Silly is memorable, and you will be able to walk the route backward too.

The ancient guide is surprisingly practical. It says to mark every fifth station with something distinctive, a golden hand at the fifth, a friend named Decimus at the tenth, so you never lose count. It advises choosing quiet, uncrowded places, because passing crowds blur the images. It even suggests spacing stations about thirty feet apart in your mind, the way your eye works best at a moderate distance.

Most of all, it insists the images must be strange. The author notes that we forget sunrises because they happen every day but remember eclipses because they are rare. In the old translation, "ordinary things easily slip from the memory." A plain image of a hammer fades. A hammer made of raw meat, bleeding on your rack, does not.
Memory champions are not born different

If you watched someone recite a thousand random digits, you would assume they were born with a freak brain. In 2003, neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire and colleagues at University College London tested that assumption on people known for top performances at the World Memory Championships. They gave them cognitive tests and scanned their brains.

The memorizers were not exceptionally intelligent, and their brains showed no structural differences from those of ordinary people. What set them apart was strategy. While memorizing, they leaned on brain regions used for spatial memory and navigation, including the hippocampus. They were, in effect, walking through places.

In 2017, a team led by Martin Dresler at Radboud University in the Netherlands took the question further. They recruited 23 memory athletes ranked in the world's top 50 and compared them with controls matched for age, sex, handedness and IQ. Both groups saw a list of 72 words and were asked to recall them 20 minutes later.

blocks.title: Words recalled out of 72, after 20 minutes
blocks.note: 17 of the 23 athletes did this task; most athletes hit the ceiling of all 72 words.
blocks.source: Dresler et al., Neuron, 2017

blocks.text: The gap is striking, but notice what the controls were: people of the same age and IQ, not a random sample of the struggling. Matching on IQ is what makes the result interesting. Whatever the athletes had, it was not raw intelligence.
Most of the athletes simply hit the ceiling. The interesting question was whether an ordinary person could get there.
Six weeks to rewire

Dresler's team then took 51 young men with no mnemonic experience and split them into three groups. One trained in the method of loci for 30 minutes a day over 40 days, at home on a web platform. One trained on a working memory game (an n-back task) for the same time. One did nothing. Everyone memorized 72 words before and after.

The loci group improved far more than either control group. In their training sessions, their best score at memorizing random words in five minutes rose steadily, from about 17 words on day one to about 42 by the end. When they came back four months later, without having been required to keep practicing, the advantage was still there.

items.label: Words memorized in 5 minutes, first day vs. end of 6 weeks of loci training
Total training: 20 hours, at home
How long the memory advantage was still measurable afterward

blocks.source: Dresler et al., Neuron, 2017

blocks.text: The brain scans told the more interesting story. After training, the way different brain networks talked to each other, especially visual areas, the medial temporal lobe (which includes the hippocampus) and the default mode network, had shifted toward the pattern seen in the champions. The more a person's brain had moved toward that pattern, the better their memory four months later. A follow-up analysis by Isabella Wagner, Dresler and colleagues in 2021 found that trained brains actually worked *less* hard during memorizing, showing lower activity in several regions, which they read as a sign of efficiency.

Twenty hours of practice is a small investment for a skill that changed the way the brain's networks were organized. It is also a good reminder that "I have a bad memory" usually means "I have never been taught a memory strategy."
Why places work so well

Your brain has been mapping places for as long as there have been brains. Knowing where the food, water and danger are has always mattered for survival, and the hippocampus is deeply involved in both navigation and forming new memories. A list of unrelated words is the opposite of what memory evolved for. A walk through a familiar house is exactly what it evolved for.

The memory palace borrows that machinery in three ways. First, it gives you a ready-made order: you never wonder what comes after the sink, because the route tells you. Second, it gives you retrieval cues. Each station is a hook you can check, so instead of fishing in the dark you look in a specific spot. Third, turning a word into a weird scene forces you to process it deeply, building connections to things you already know, which is one of the most reliable ways to make anything stick (see the article on how memory works).

This also explains why the images have to be bizarre and active. A boring picture gives the brain nothing to grab, while something gross, funny or violent grabs attention for a moment longer and gets tied more firmly to its spot. It also explains why abstract material is harder. "Resistance" is not a picture, so you have to invent one, maybe a crowd of people shoving through a narrow doorway. Building that stand-in image is itself a little act of understanding.

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis by Jan Ondřej at Masaryk University pulled together the research on adults. Compared with simple rehearsal, the method of loci produced a large improvement in recalling items in order (an effect size of about 0.88, which is big by the standards of psychology). Brain imaging studies consistently showed activity in navigation regions. But the review also rated the quality of the evidence as low to very low, because many studies were small or had a high risk of bias. The technique clearly works; exactly how much it helps in real life is less certain.
What it can't do

Here is the trap. A memory palace is a filing system, not an understanding system. You can memorize every component on a system drawing in order and still have no idea what happens when one of them fails.

A 2021 study at a Chinese university trained young adults for several weeks either in the method of loci or on a dual n-back working memory task. Both groups got much better at the task they practiced and on a digit-span test. Only the n-back group improved on a different kind of visual memory task. The loci training made people better at memorizing, not smarter in general.

A major 2013 review of study techniques led by John Dunlosky also gave low marks to two close cousins of the memory palace: the keyword mnemonic (linking a new word to a sound-alike image) and imagery for learning from text. Not because they fail, but because their benefits were narrow, short-lived in some studies, and limited to certain kinds of material.

blocks.title: Where a memory palace earns its keep

left.head: Good fit
items: Lists that must be recalled in order
Steps in a sequence you already understand
Names, numbers and arbitrary facts with no logic to them
Key points of a talk or brief
The order of components along a flow path

right.head: Poor fit
items: Understanding why a system behaves the way it does
Problem solving and troubleshooting
Physical skills and reflexes
Anything that changes often
Replacing a written procedure you're required to follow

blocks.text: There is also evidence that the classic Greek and Roman version is not the only way to tie memory to place. In a 2021 study at Monash University in Australia, first-year medical students learned word lists after training in either a memory palace or an Australian Aboriginal technique that links information to a story told across a landscape. Both improved recall compared with no training. The Aboriginal narrative method did slightly better at getting entire lists perfectly right. Humans have invented this trick more than once, which says something about how our memory is built.
Building one for real study

Medical educators have tried the technique on dense, list-heavy material. In a 2014 study in Pakistan, students who built memory palaces for the topic of insulin and diabetes scored better on assessments than classmates who used self-directed study instead. It was one small study at a single school, so treat it as promising rather than proven. But it fits the pattern: the method shines when there is a lot of arbitrary detail to hold.

Life on a boat offers an unusual advantage here. You walk the same passageways every day, and you know them in more detail than most people know their own homes. That is a ready-made set of palaces. The route from berthing to the mess deck could hold one list, and the path through your division's spaces could hold another, so long as each route is used for one subject so the images don't collide.

A memory palace helps you hold information so you can study and recall it. It is never a substitute for the procedure, the reference or the qualified watchstander. Use it to learn faster, not to skip the book.

The palace also pairs perfectly with the other two tools that matter most for memory. Walking it from memory is retrieval practice, because you are pulling information out instead of rereading it. Walking it again a few days later, then a week later, is spaced repetition. A palace you build once and never revisit will crumble like any other memory. A palace you walk every few days can last for years.

And start small. Build a ten-station route, memorize a shopping list or the order of the planets, and test yourself tomorrow. Most people are startled by how well it works on the first try. That surprise is the point: memory turns out to be less a talent you have and more a tool you can learn to use.

takeaways: Memory champions are not born with special brains; they use a learnable strategy that taps spatial memory.
In one study, 30 minutes a day for six weeks more than doubled how many words beginners could memorize, and the benefit lasted months.
A memory palace stores information; it does not create understanding or make you smarter in general.
Use one familiar route per subject, make the images absurd, and mark every fifth station.
Walk the palace from memory on a spaced schedule, or it will fade like anything else.

title: When a Reward Turns Play Into Work
dek: Paying people to do what they already love can make them love it less. But rewards are not the villain either. The research is about when, how, and for what.

blocks.text: In the early 1970s, researchers at Stanford watched a nursery school classroom through a one-way mirror. They were looking for children who, given free time, chose to draw with a new set of felt-tipped markers. Then they took those kids, the ones who already liked drawing, and split them into three groups. One group was told in advance that if they drew pictures, they would get a certificate with a gold seal and a ribbon. A second group got the same certificate as a surprise afterward. A third got nothing.

One to two weeks later, the markers went back out during free play, with no rewards on offer. The children who had drawn *in order to* earn the certificate now spent noticeably less of their free time drawing than the other two groups. The surprise-reward kids were fine. Only the expected reward changed things. Something that had been play had, in the children's minds, become a job, and when the pay stopped, so did the work.

Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett called it the *overjustification* effect: give someone an outside reason for doing something they already enjoy, and they may start to explain their own behavior by the outside reason. The study became one of the most famous in psychology, and it launched a fight that ran for decades. The fight matters, because almost everything in modern life, from paychecks to game achievements to habit apps, runs on rewards.
Two engines, not one

Psychologists distinguish two broad kinds of motivation. *Intrinsic* motivation is doing something because the activity itself is satisfying: you play a game because playing it is fun, you tinker with code because figuring it out feels good. *Extrinsic* motivation is doing something for a separate outcome: money, a grade, a qualification, avoiding trouble.

Edward Deci and Richard Ryan built the most influential theory of this, called self-determination theory. Its core claim is that people have three basic psychological needs, and that intrinsic motivation thrives when those needs are met. *Autonomy*: feeling that you chose this. *Competence*: feeling that you are getting better and can handle it. *Relatedness*: feeling connected to other people in it. Rewards affect motivation, in this view, mostly through what they do to those three needs.

A reward that feels like control, as in 'do this and you get that,' chips at autonomy. A reward that carries information, as in 'you did this well,' feeds competence. That distinction turns out to explain most of what happened in the decades of experiments that followed.

The theory adds one more nuance that matters a lot in real life. Extrinsic motivation is not one thing. At one end is pure pressure: you do it because you will get in trouble if you don't. Further along is doing something for an outside reason you have genuinely adopted as your own, such as studying a system thoroughly because you want to be the kind of operator people trust in a casualty. That second kind still points at an outcome, but it feels chosen, and it behaves much more like intrinsic motivation. Moving a task from 'they make me' to 'I want this for my own reasons' is one of the most practical motivation upgrades available.
What 128 experiments found

In 1999, Deci, Richard Koestner and Ryan pooled 128 experiments on rewards and intrinsic motivation. The usual measure was the one from the marker study: after the reward phase ends, how much free time do people spend on the activity when nobody is paying them?

blocks.title: Effect on later free-choice motivation
blocks.note: Negative values mean people chose the activity less after the reward ended.
blocks.source: Deci, Koestner & Ryan, Psychological Bulletin, 1999

blocks.text: Tangible rewards that people expected, whether for simply doing the task, finishing it, or hitting a performance target, all reduced later free-choice motivation. The effects were small to moderate, not catastrophic. Tangible rewards also tended to be more damaging for children than for college students. And one kind of reward pushed in the opposite direction: positive feedback, simply being told you did well, increased both time spent on the activity and self-reported interest.

Not everyone accepted this picture. A rival 1994 meta-analysis by Judy Cameron and David Pierce concluded that rewards overall do not decrease intrinsic motivation, and that the only negative effect was a minimal one when people expected tangible rewards just for doing a task. The two camps argued over which studies to include and how to group them. But look at what they agreed on: verbal praise helps, and expected tangible rewards for simply showing up are the riskiest kind. The disagreement was about how big and how general the harm is, not whether the pattern exists.
The research does not say rewards are bad. It says rewards that feel like control can crowd out enjoyment, while rewards that tell you you're getting better tend to feed it.
Quality versus quantity

If rewards can undermine motivation, why does every workplace on Earth use them? A 2014 meta-analysis by Christopher Cerasoli and colleagues helps resolve the puzzle. It covered 40 years of research, 183 samples and more than 200,000 people in school, work and sports, and asked a more practical question: what actually predicts how well people perform?

Intrinsic motivation predicted performance moderately to strongly, whether or not incentives were also present. But the two engines specialized. Intrinsic motivation was the better predictor of the *quality* of performance. Incentives were the better predictor of *quantity*. And when incentives were tied very directly to performance, intrinsic motivation mattered less, a crowding-out effect. When incentives were only loosely connected, intrinsic motivation mattered more.

blocks.title: What each engine is good at

left.head: Extrinsic incentives
items: Drive quantity: more reps, more units, more hours
Work well for simple, clear, measurable tasks
Can crowd out interest when tightly tied to output
Stop working when the reward stops

right.head: Intrinsic motivation
items: Drives quality: care, creativity, depth
Matters most for complex, open-ended work
Survives when nobody is watching or paying
Grows with autonomy, progress and connection

blocks.text: Economists found a related twist. In a well-known study of Israeli day care centers, Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini introduced a small fine for parents who picked up their kids late. Late pickups went up, not down, and stayed up even after the fine was removed. The fine had turned a moral obligation (don't make the teacher wait) into a price (it costs a few shekels). Once people thought of lateness as something you could pay for, many happily paid. The researchers' title said it plainly: a fine is a price.
What it looks like in the brain

In 2010, a team led by Kou Murayama tried to watch the undermining effect inside the brain. Participants played a simple stopwatch game: stop a running watch at exactly five seconds. One group was paid for each success; the other was not. Then came a free-choice period in which nobody was being paid, and the researchers counted how often each person chose to play anyway.

The paid group played less on their own time, the classic undermining effect. In the brain scanner, that drop in motivation came with a drop in activity in the anterior striatum and in prefrontal areas, regions involved in valuing outcomes. It was as if the brain's valuation system had re-priced the task: once it had been worth money, doing it for nothing looked like a worse deal.
That is a useful way to think about any reward you attach to an activity. You are not just adding a bonus. You may be changing the price tag your brain puts on the activity itself.
Why games feel different

Games are packed with rewards: experience points, loot, badges, daily login bonuses. By the overjustification logic, they should kill the fun of playing. Usually they don't, and self-determination theory explains why. A 2006 study by Ryan, Scott Rigby and Andrew Przybylski found that how much players enjoyed a game and wanted to keep playing tracked closely with how much the game satisfied autonomy, competence and relatedness. Good game rewards are mostly *information*: they tell you that you got better, that you can now handle the next challenge.

A 2009 study by the same group added an important warning. Players whose basic needs were well met in daily life tended to have a 'harmonious' passion for games: they played because they wanted to and came away energized. Players whose needs were poorly met were more likely to have an 'obsessive' passion: they felt they *had* to play, played more, and came away tense and enjoying it less. The same hobby can be play or compulsion depending on what it is filling in for.

For anyone building a game, this is a design guide. Rewards that mark mastery, open new choices and are shared with friends tend to strengthen the reasons people play. Rewards that exist mainly to pull people back on a schedule, regardless of whether they feel competent or free, push the experience toward the obsessive side. That may raise short-term numbers, but it is the opposite of building something people love.
The timing trick

One more finding changes how to use all of this. Kaitlin Woolley and Ayelet Fishbach studied people pursuing long-term goals like exercising and studying. People said they pursued these goals mainly for delayed rewards, like health or good grades. But what actually predicted whether they kept at it was the presence of *immediate* rewards, such as whether the activity itself was enjoyable. Delayed rewards motivated setting the goal; immediate rewards predicted sticking with it.

In a follow-up, they found that making a reward more immediate, even a small bonus paid right away rather than later, increased intrinsic motivation for the task. Their explanation is that an immediate reward fuses with the activity in your mind, so the activity itself starts to feel rewarding. A delayed reward stays separate, so the activity stays a means to an end.

Applied to learning, this suggests a trick. Don't just promise yourself the payoff at the end of a six-month project. Build small rewards into the session itself: a mechanic that works by the end of the hour, a playtest clip you can send to a friend that night, a hard quals topic you can now explain out loud. Those moments fuse the reward to the work. A vague future payoff mostly gets you to start; rewards you feel during the session are what keep you coming back.
Using this on yourself

Much of military life is run on extrinsic motivation, and that is not a failure. Qualifications, evaluations and pay drive quantity and get necessary, sometimes boring work done, which is exactly what the research says incentives do well. The problem comes when you try to run the things you *want* to be great at, such as a game, a channel, a skill, on the same engine.

items: Use extrinsic rewards for chores and volume: logging study hours, finishing a quals card, clearing a backlog. Make them immediate rather than distant.
For work where quality matters, protect autonomy. Choose what to build next, even within limits, rather than only taking assignments from a list.
Make progress visible. A changelog, a before-and-after clip, or a note of what you can do now that you couldn't last month is the kind of feedback that strengthens motivation.
Build with someone. Relatedness is one of the three needs; a partner who cares about the same project is a motivation source, not just extra hands.
Be careful about attaching money or metrics too tightly to something you love. If views or revenue become the only reason, the activity can get re-priced into a job.

blocks.text: The kids with the markers did not stop liking drawing because rewards are evil. They stopped because the reward told them a story about why they drew. Every reward you set up for yourself tells a similar story. The goal is to pick rewards that say 'you are getting better at something you chose' rather than 'you are doing this because someone is paying you.'

takeaways: Expected tangible rewards for simply doing an activity can lower your later desire to do it; positive feedback tends to raise it.
Incentives best predict quantity of work; intrinsic motivation best predicts quality.
Immediate rewards predict sticking with long-term goals better than delayed ones; make the payoff show up during the work.
Autonomy, competence and connection fuel motivation. Build projects you chose, track visible progress, and work with people who care.
A fine or a price can turn an obligation into a transaction. Watch what story a reward tells about why you do something.

title: Should You Study With Music On?
dek: Lyrics cost you a little, instrumentals mostly cost nothing, and the boost people feel from a study playlist is mood, not memory.

blocks.text: There's a famous animated loop on YouTube: a girl in headphones writing at a desk by a window, a cat on the sill, rain outside, and an endless stream of mellow instrumental hip-hop. Millions of people have studied to channels like it. The genre even has a name, lo-fi beats to study to. The unspoken promise is that the right soundtrack makes studying easier.

In 2023, psychologists Alessandra Souza and Lauren Leal Barbosa put that promise to a direct test. College students did four kinds of tasks, memorizing words, memorizing visual patterns, reading comprehension and arithmetic, in three conditions: silence, lo-fi instrumental music, and popular songs with lyrics in the students' own language. Each student did a task under all three conditions, so every person was compared with themselves rather than with someone else.

blocks.title: Words recalled correctly, by background sound
blocks.note: Verbal memory task. Lyrics hurt verbal memory, visual memory and reading by about d = 0.3; instrumental music had no credible effect.
blocks.source: Souza & Leal Barbosa, Journal of Cognition, 2023

blocks.text: The results were tidy. Music with lyrics hurt verbal memory, visual memory and reading comprehension, by a small but real amount. Its apparent harm to arithmetic was weaker and not credible. Lo-fi instrumental music did not reliably help or hurt anything. The students noticed the lyrics costing them. But some believed the instrumental music was *helping*, even though their scores said it wasn't doing much either way.

The students' own habits were all over the map. Asked how often they study with music, about 14 percent said always, 20 percent often, 23 percent sometimes, 25 percent rarely and 18 percent never. There is no single "normal" way people study, which is part of why the question keeps coming up.

Their sense of what was happening was partly right. After the verbal memory task, students rated how much each kind of music had affected them on a scale where zero meant no effect. They rated the lyrics clearly negative, at nearly minus 3, and the instrumental music at almost exactly zero. They also predicted lower memory scores while the lyrics were playing. Awareness, in other words, isn't the whole problem. Plenty of people know the lyrics cost them something and play them anyway, because the music makes the session more pleasant.

That combination, a real cost from lyrics, roughly nothing from instrumentals, and a feeling of benefit that doesn't show up in scores, is close to what decades of research suggest. The interesting part is why.
Your ears have no eyelids

You can close your eyes to stop seeing. You can't close your ears. Your brain keeps processing sound whether you want it to or not, and certain kinds of sound collide with the mental machinery you use for words.

Psychologists call this the *irrelevant sound effect*. In the classic version, people see a sequence of digits or words and must recall them in order, while something plays in the background that they're told to ignore. In 1989, Salamé and Alan Baddeley tested background music this way. Vocal music disrupted memory more than instrumental music. When they compared instrumental music with speech and with noise that rose and fell in volume, the steady-ish noise was no worse than silence, instrumental music did some harm, and speech did the most. Earlier work had shown that speech disrupts this kind of memory even in a language the listener doesn't understand.

Why would speech you aren't listening to interfere with words you're reading? One leading explanation focuses on change. Work by Dylan Jones and his colleague Macken in 1993 found that even a sequence of tones changing in pitch could produce the same kind of disruption as speech. The idea is that your brain automatically tracks the order of distinct sounds as they change, and that automatic order-tracking competes with your effort to hold words or steps in order. Lyrics are the worst offenders because they are full of distinct, changing units that your brain is especially tuned to: syllables.

The same study also hinted at a role for practice. In a second experiment with more highly trained participants, vocal music still caused significantly more disruption than instrumental music, while instrumental music was no longer reliably worse than silence. Instrumental music sits in a gray zone: some cost for some people on some tasks, often too small to measure.

It also explains why lo-fi study music is built the way it is. The best-known streams are slow, repetitive and mostly wordless, with few sudden changes. Whether by design or by trial and error, that is close to the kind of background sound the research says is easiest to ignore. A playlist that keeps switching songs, genres and volume is a different story.

This explains a useful detail: lyrics in a language you don't speak are not a free pass. Your brain still chops them into speech sounds. And it explains why the cost shows up most on tasks that involve holding things in sequence, like remembering a list, following a chain of reasoning or reading a dense paragraph.
The feeling of benefit is real, but it's about mood

If music can hurt, why does it so often feel like it helps? Part of the answer comes from the strange history of the "Mozart effect," the 1990s claim that listening to Mozart made people temporarily better at spatial reasoning (see the article on brain myths for how that claim fared).

In 2001, William Forde Thompson, Glenn Schellenberg and Gabriela Husain tested an explanation. Some people listened to an upbeat Mozart sonata before a spatial test. Others listened to a slow, sad adagio by Albinoni. Others sat in silence. Only the Mozart group did better than silence. But Mozart also left people more aroused and in a better mood, and when the researchers statistically accounted for arousal and mood, the Mozart effect disappeared. It wasn't Mozart. It was feeling energized and good.

That's the real, useful benefit of music: it changes how you feel. It can wake you up, make a boring session tolerable and get you to sit down in the first place. If studying in silence means you don't study at all, music that gets you to the desk is a net win. The mistake is assuming the good feeling during the session means you're learning more.
What the big reviews say
Single experiments only test a few kinds of music and tasks, so researchers have tried to pool them. The results are honestly mixed, and the reasons are informative.

A 2011 meta-analysis by Kämpfe, Sedlmeier and Renkewitz looked broadly at the effect of background music on adults. Averaged across everything, the effect was essentially zero. But the authors argued that this null result came from averaging out opposite effects. Background music tended to disturb reading and had small harmful effects on memory, while it improved emotional reactions and sports performance.

A 2023 meta-analysis focused on learning, by de la Mora Velasco and colleagues, pooled 47 studies and found a small positive average effect of background music. The benefit was larger when music was played *before* the learning assessment rather than during it, and classical music looked better than other genres. That fits the mood explanation: music as a warm-up helps, music competing with the work helps less.

Why would two careful reviews disagree? Because "background music" covers almost everything: a quiet piano piece or a loud rap track, music during learning or a song before the test, a word list or a physics lesson, measured minutes later or days later. Average enough different situations together and the specific effects cancel out. The useful question is never "is music good for studying?" It is "is this music good for this task, for me?"

Other studies add a twist: it depends on you and on the task. In 2019, Gonzalez and Aiello found that music generally hurt performance on complex tasks, but complex music actually helped on simple ones, and people who crave outside stimulation, those quickest to get bored, were affected differently. A 2011 study by Johansson and colleagues found that students' reading comprehension dropped with music they didn't normally study to, yet their eye movements didn't change. They weren't slowing down or rereading to compensate, because they didn't realize they were missing anything.

blocks.title: Matching sound to the task

left.head: Keep it quiet or steady
items: Reading dense technical text
Memorizing lists, sequences or procedures
Working through multistep problems
Writing anything that needs careful wording

right.head: Music is fine or helpful
items: Warming up before a study session
Repetitive or simple tasks like cleaning and organizing
Exercise and PT
Long boring tasks where the risk is quitting, not errors

blocks.text: Noise, engine rooms and white noise
Not everyone gets to choose silence. Working spaces on a ship hum, roar and clank, and berthing is rarely quiet. Here the research on noise is more relevant than the research on music.

A 2011 meta-analysis by James Szalma and Peter Hancock pooled 797 effects from 242 studies of noise and human performance. The effects varied a lot, but the biggest factors were whether noise was continuous or intermittent, what type of noise it was, and what type of task people were doing. Steady, predictable sound is generally easier to tune out than sound that starts, stops and changes, which matches the changing-state idea. Loud, persistent noise also has a separate and permanent cost to your hearing, which is why hearing protection rules exist in high-noise spaces (see the article on sound and hearing).

What about deliberately adding white or pink noise to cover distractions? A 2024 meta-analysis led by Joel Nigg looked at this for attention tasks. For young people with ADHD or high ADHD symptoms, white and pink noise produced a small benefit. For people without ADHD, it produced a small *harm*.

items.label: Effect of white/pink noise on attention tasks in youth with ADHD or high symptoms (small benefit)
Effect in comparison groups without ADHD (small harm)

blocks.source: Nigg et al., Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 2024

blocks.text: None of this is a way to diagnose yourself. If focusing has always been a real struggle for you, in every setting and not just on hard material, that's worth raising with a corpsman or doctor rather than trying to solve with a sound app.

The takeaway isn't that noise machines are bad. It's that the same sound can help one brain and hurt another, so the only way to know what works for you is to test it rather than trust the feeling. If you're studying in a noisy berthing area, foam earplugs that cut the changing sounds of conversation may do more for your focus than any playlist.

The same logic applies to the soundscape you can control. A steady fan or ventilation hum is easy to ignore. A nearby conversation, a show playing on someone's phone or a running commentary from the next rack is the kind of sound that pulls at your attention, because it is speech and it keeps changing. If you can only fix one thing, fix that.
Run the experiment on yourself

Because the effects are small and personal, the most useful thing you can do is test them on your own work. Pick a type of material you study often. On some days study it in silence or with earplugs, on others with your usual music, and quiz yourself at the end of each session without looking. A week or two of honest scores will tell you more than any study.

Until then, a sensible default comes straight from the research. Lyrics and dense material don't mix. Steady instrumental music is mostly harmless and can make you more willing to start. Music before a session is a better mood tool than music during one. And when the work is truly hard, a little silence, or the closest thing a ship can offer, is still the cheapest performance boost available.

takeaways: Music with lyrics reliably hurts reading and memorizing by a small amount, even in a language you don't speak.
Instrumental music mostly neither helps nor hurts; the benefit people feel is mood and motivation.
Play music before a session to get going, and keep dense reading and memorizing quiet or steady.
Changing sounds (speech, intermittent noise) distract more than steady ones; earplugs can beat playlists in noisy spaces.
Effects are small and personal, so test your own study conditions with quick self-quizzes.

title: Pen, Keyboard, or Your Own Voice
dek: A famous 2014 study said handwritten notes beat laptops. The replications tell a messier story, and point to what actually matters: whether your brain is transcribing or thinking.

blocks.text: In 2014 two psychologists, Pam Mueller of Princeton and Daniel Oppenheimer of UCLA, published a paper with one of the best titles in the history of the field: *The Pen Is Mightier Than the Keyboard*. Students watched short TED talks while taking notes either on a laptop or by hand, then answered questions about what they had seen. Across three studies, the laptop users wrote more and copied the speaker word for word much more often. And on questions that required understanding rather than recall, they did worse.

The explanation was elegant. Typing is fast enough to transcribe a lecture almost verbatim, so laptop users did exactly that, letting words flow from ear to fingers without passing through much thought. Handwriting is too slow for that. If you write by hand, you are forced to choose, summarize and rephrase, and that processing is what makes ideas stick. Even telling laptop users not to transcribe did not stop them.

It is easy to see why the result was so believable. Anyone who has sat behind a row of laptops in a lecture has seen screens full of messages, shopping tabs and games. Handwriting feels old-fashioned and virtuous; typing feels lazy. A finding that confirmed what teachers already suspected, with a clever mechanism attached, was always going to travel fast.

The paper became a sensation. It was covered by news outlets around the world, cited more than a thousand times by 2021, and used to justify laptop bans in lecture halls. It was also, as it turned out, one of those findings that looked sturdier in its first telling than it did after other scientists tried it again.
What happened when others tried it

In 2019 Kayla Morehead, John Dunlosky and Katherine Rawson ran a direct replication, adding groups who took notes on an e-writer tablet and a group who took no notes at all. Some trends leaned toward longhand, but test performance did not consistently differ between the groups. When students got to study their notes before the test, the differences shrank further. Pooling the direct replications, they found small effects favoring longhand that were not statistically reliable, and concluded that declaring one method superior was premature.

That pattern is common in psychology. The first studies on a new effect are often small, and the ones that happen to find large, clean results are the ones that get noticed. Later, larger studies that follow the same procedure tend to find smaller effects, or none. It does not mean the original researchers did anything wrong. It means a single striking paper, however elegant, is a starting point, not a settled fact.

Two years later, Heather Urry and a team that included 87 of her students at Tufts published another direct replication of the original first study, with 142 participants. They reproduced the part about behavior almost exactly: laptop users wrote more words and copied more verbatim. But they did not reproduce the part about learning. Laptop and longhand students scored about the same on factual and conceptual questions. A small meta-analysis of eight similar studies, including the original ones, pointed the same way.

items.label: Students in the Urry et al. direct replication
Similar studies pooled in their mini meta-analysis
Longhand advantage on the quiz, factual or conceptual

blocks.source: Urry et al., Psychological Science, 2021

blocks.text: Then, in 2024, Abraham Flanigan, Kenneth Kiewra and colleagues published a broader meta-analysis of 24 studies comparing typed and handwritten lecture notes, looking at both taking notes and reviewing them afterward. Typing produced far more notes. But handwriting was linked to modestly higher achievement.

items.label: Achievement advantage for handwritten notes (small)
Advantage for typing in the amount of notes taken (large)

blocks.source: Flanigan et al., Educational Psychology Review, 2024

blocks.text: So which is it? Probably this: there is no large, reliable longhand advantage for understanding a single lecture right after you hear it, which was the original headline. There may be a small advantage for handwriting in real courses, where other things come into play, like the distraction of a laptop with messages and games one click away, and how useful each type of notes is when studying later. The effect is real enough to consider and far too small to be the thing that decides how well you learn.
The idea underneath was right

Here is the interesting part. The replications mostly undercut the *device* claim, not the *mechanism* claim. In both the original study and the Tufts replication, students who wrote more words tended to do better, and students whose notes copied the speaker word for word tended to do worse, though that second pattern was weaker in the replication. What seems to matter is not the tool in your hand, but whether the information got processed on the way through.

Think about what verbatim note-taking actually is. Your ears receive a sentence, your fingers reproduce it, and at no point does your brain have to decide what it means or how it connects to anything. It feels productive because the page fills up. But you have built a transcript, not an understanding. Writing by hand happens to make transcription harder, which nudges you toward summarizing. A disciplined typist who paraphrases can get the same benefit, and a careless writer who scribbles fragments without thinking will not.

blocks.title: The same lecture, two kinds of notes

left.head: Transcribing
items: Captures the speaker's exact words
Feels productive, page fills fast
Brain mostly bypassed
Hard to use later: long and unsorted

right.head: Processing
items: Captures ideas in your own words
Feels slower, gaps are obvious
Forces you to decide what matters
Shorter, organized, easy to quiz from

blocks.text: This is the real lesson, and it applies far beyond lectures. Any study activity that lets information pass through you without transformation, rereading, highlighting, copying a tutorial's code line by line, gives you the feeling of learning without much of the substance. Activities that force you to generate something, a summary, a diagram from memory, an explanation, are the ones that build durable understanding.

One practical upgrade, whatever you write with: leave a margin, and after the lecture or reading, turn your notes into questions. Next to a paragraph about a system's interlocks, write the question it answers, such as what stops this pump from starting with the discharge valve shut. Later, cover the notes and answer the questions. That converts a passive record into a self-test, which is where most of the value of good notes comes from.
The illusion of knowing how things work

That brings us to the second half of this story: explaining. In 2002 Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil at Yale asked people to rate how well they understood how everyday devices work, things like a zipper or a flush toilet. Most people rated themselves fairly high. Then they were asked to write out a detailed, step-by-step explanation of how the thing actually works. Faced with the blank page, they realized they could not, and their ratings of their own understanding dropped.

Rozenblit and Keil called it the *illusion of explanatory depth*. It is strongest for exactly the kind of knowledge you need in technical work: how mechanisms work, how parts cause each other to change. It is weaker for simple facts or procedures. Seeing a diagram many times, or watching someone else operate a system, creates a sense of familiarity that the brain happily mislabels as understanding. Only trying to explain it reveals the gaps.

The illusion is sneaky because it does not feel like an illusion. When you have looked at a schematic a dozen times, it really is familiar, and familiarity produces a warm sense of knowing. Nothing in that feeling tells you whether you could rebuild the logic from scratch. The only reliable way to find out is to try, ideally before someone with a clipboard asks you to. A gap you find on your own on a quiet evening costs nothing; the same gap found at the board costs a lot more.
If you cannot explain a system out loud, step by step, without notes, you do not know it yet. You recognize it. The difference shows up at the qual board, not before.
The Feynman technique, and why it works

Online, this insight usually goes by the name *the Feynman technique*, after the physicist Richard Feynman, famous for explaining hard ideas in plain language. Feynman did not package a numbered method under that name; the label was attached later by writers and study coaches inspired by his style. But the core is sound: pick a concept, explain it in simple terms as if teaching a beginner, notice where you get stuck or fall back on jargon, go back to the source to fill the gap, and repeat until the explanation is simple and complete.

The jargon check matters more than it sounds in a technical job. Acronyms and system names are efficient for people who already understand them, but they are also a perfect hiding place. It is possible to recite a sentence full of correct terms without being able to say what physically happens in the plant. Forcing yourself to explain in plain words, as you might to a family member who has never seen a submarine, exposes whether the terms are attached to anything.

Research on learning by teaching helps explain why it works. In a 2014 study, John Nestojko, Elizabeth Bjork and colleagues told some students they would have to teach a passage to someone else, while others were told to expect a test. Nobody actually taught; everyone took the test. The students expecting to teach recalled more, and organized what they recalled better, especially the main points.

A 2018 study by Aloysius Koh, Sze Chi Lee and Stephen Lim went further and pinned down the active ingredient. After studying a text, students either taught the material on camera without notes, taught it by reading from a prepared script, did unrelated arithmetic, or simply wrote down everything they could recall. A week later, the students who had taught from memory did better than those who had taught from a script, and about the same as the students who had just practiced recalling. Teaching helped because it forced retrieval. Teaching from notes, which skips retrieval, did not.

blocks.title: The explain-it method, done properly
items: Pick one concept or system, small enough to explain in a few minutes.
Close the book, put away the notes, and explain it out loud or on paper as if to a new crew member.
Mark every spot where you stall, wave your hands or hide behind a term you cannot define.
Go back to the source for those spots only.
Explain it again from scratch, then once more a few days later.

blocks.text: Putting it to work

For submarine qualifications, this means the standard advice to talk through systems is better advice than it sounds, as long as you do it without the print in front of you. Draw the system from memory, then explain each component and what happens if it fails. Compare against the real drawing afterward, and fix only what you missed. Explaining to a shipmate who is also qualifying works even better, because their questions find gaps you did not know you had.

For programming, the same idea has a well-known version: rubber duck debugging, where you explain your code line by line to an inanimate object until the bug becomes obvious. When you are learning Luau or any other language, add one more step after a tutorial: close it and rebuild the feature from memory, then write a few sentences in your own words about why each part is there. If you cannot, you copied the code; you did not learn it.

The same goes for game design. If you are building a game with a partner, writing a one-paragraph explanation of a mechanic, how a player earns progress, what makes them come back tomorrow, is a fast way to discover that you both have different versions of it in your heads. Explaining is not only a study tool. It is a way of checking whether an idea is as clear as it feels.

As for pen versus keyboard, use whatever lets you think. A paper notebook works well underway, where it is quiet and never runs out of battery, and it avoids the distractions that sit one click away on a laptop. If you type, resist the urge to capture everything; aim for fewer, shorter notes in your own words. Either way, the notes are not the learning. The learning happens when you put them away and try to explain what they said.

takeaways: The famous longhand advantage largely failed direct replication; a 2024 meta-analysis found only a small edge for handwriting.
What matters is processing, not the device: paraphrase instead of transcribing.
Feeling that you understand something is not evidence; try explaining it step by step without notes.
Teaching helps learning mainly because it forces retrieval. Explaining from notes skips the useful part.
For quals and code: draw or rebuild from memory, explain each part, then check and fix only the gaps.
