title: Practice Where It Counts
dek: Skills learned in calm, comfortable practice often fall apart under pressure. The fix is not more practice. It is practice that feels more like the real thing.

blocks.text: In a Dutch experiment published in 2009, expert dart players threw darts at a board under two conditions. In one, they stood low on a climbing wall, close to the floor. In the other, they hung high up the same wall, safely roped in but with the drop very much in view. The height made them anxious: their heart rates rose and the throws took more effort. These were experienced players, the kind of people you would expect to be steady.

Then the researchers trained them. Half practiced low on the wall, where it felt safe; half practiced high up, where it did not. At the final test, with the anxiety switched back on, only the players who had trained high kept their accuracy. They were just as anxious, their hearts pounded just as hard and they reported working harder, but their throws held up. A companion experiment found the same thing with expert basketball players who practiced free throws for five weeks with or without induced pressure: only the pressure-trained group stopped getting worse when the stakes went up.

The lesson from Raôul Oudejans and his colleagues is easy to state and widely ignored. What you practice is not just the skill. It is the skill *in the conditions you practiced it in*. If those conditions are calm, private and comfortable, you have trained a calm, private, comfortable version of the skill. The real test, whether it is a qualification board, a casualty drill, a ranked match or a live demo of your game, rarely looks like that.
Memory is picky about how it was stored

The deeper principle has a clunky name: *transfer-appropriate processing*. It comes from a classic 1977 study by Donald Morris, John Bransford and Jeffery Franks. Students studied words while answering questions about them. Some questions were about meaning, such as whether the word fit in a sentence. Others were about sound, such as whether the word rhymed with another word.

On a standard memory test, processing meaning won, as everyone expected. But when the test was about sound, asking people to pick words that rhymed with the ones they had studied, the students who had processed sound did better. Neither kind of studying was simply 'deeper' or 'better.' What mattered was the match between how the knowledge was practiced and how it was later demanded.

This explains a lot of frustrating experiences. You can know a system perfectly well when reading the manual and still freeze when someone asks you to trace a flow path from memory, out loud, while standing up. You did not forget the material. You practiced recognizing it on the page, and the board demanded producing it under scrutiny. Those are different skills, and only one of them got trained. Related research on context, covered in this library's article on how memory works, shows that even the physical setting where you learn can act as a retrieval cue.

Comfortable practice has a second problem: it lies to you about how ready you are. When you study in the same quiet spot, with the same notes, in the same order, everything feels familiar, and familiarity feels like mastery. You walk into the real test confident, and the confidence evaporates the moment the conditions change. Realistic practice feels worse while you are doing it, because it exposes the gaps. That bad feeling is information you want to get in your rack at 2300, not in front of the board.

blocks.title: Comfortable practice versus realistic practice

left.head: Comfortable practice
items: Reading over notes in your rack
Solving problems with the answer key open
Running the drill when you already know it's coming
Testing your game alone on your own PC

right.head: Realistic practice
items: Explaining it out loud, standing, to someone who asks follow-ups
Working problems timed, closed-book, then checking
Responding to a surprise scenario someone else picked
Watching a stranger play it while you stay silent

blocks.text: Strong memories survive stress

Stress is the most common difference between practice and the real thing, and it has a well-documented effect: it makes recalling memories harder. That is why people blank on things they know cold. But a 2016 study in *Science* by Amy Smith, Victoria Floerke and Ayanna Thomas found an important exception.

Participants learned material either by restudying it or by retrieval practice, meaning repeatedly testing themselves. A day later, half of each group went through a stressful procedure designed to spike their stress response before being tested. The restudy group showed the usual stress-related drop in memory. The retrieval-practice group did not; their recall held up under stress. The authors concluded that whether stress damages recall may depend on how strong the memory is to begin with.

Why would that be? A weak memory is like a faint trail through the woods: easy to follow on a calm day, easy to lose when you are rushed and panicked. Stress shifts the brain toward fast, well-worn responses and away from slow, effortful searching. A memory that has been retrieved many times is a well-worn path, so it stays reachable. A memory that has only been reread is a faint trail that needs exactly the kind of calm, deliberate searching that stress takes away.

Classroom data point the same way. In a 2014 survey of 1,408 middle and high school students whose classes used regular low-stakes quizzing, 72 percent said retrieval practice made them less nervous for unit tests and exams. That is self-report, not a controlled experiment, but it fits the lab results. Testing yourself repeatedly is not just a good study method, as this library's retrieval practice article explains; it is also rehearsal for the feeling of being tested.
The best insurance against blanking under pressure is not calming down. It is having pulled the answer out of your head so many times, in testing conditions, that stress can't knock it loose.
Pressure is something you can train

The darts study was one of a growing set of experiments in which people practice under deliberately added pressure. The pressure varies: audiences, video cameras, being evaluated, competition, money on the line, or something physically intimidating. In one study with police officers, the officers practiced shooting against an opponent who shot back with colored soap cartridges. At the start, anxiety hurt everyone's accuracy. After training with anxiety, the experimental group's accuracy no longer dropped under pressure, while the control group's still did. Four months later, the advantage remained.

In 2021, researchers pooled the studies that tested this kind of pressure training against regular training, 14 studies with 394 participants from sport and law enforcement. Performance under pressure improved by a medium-sized amount, and the effect was fairly consistent across studies. It worked for novices and experienced performers, on both predictable skills like free throws and unpredictable ones. Their practical conclusion: create pressurized training environments rather than relying on more hours of ordinary practice.

items.label: Average boost to performance under pressure from pressure training, across 14 studies

blocks.source: Low et al., Sport, Exercise, and Performance Psychology, 2021

blocks.text: The evidence base is still modest: 394 people is not a lot, and the authors called for more studies of real competitions rather than lab-built pressure. But the military has run on a version of this idea for a long time under the name *stress inoculation*, and a 1996 meta-analysis of stress inoculation training found it reduced anxiety and improved performance under stress. The principle is borrowed from vaccines: a controlled, survivable dose of the threat builds resistance to the real thing.

The pressure itself does not have to be dramatic. In these studies it has come from things like a video camera, an evaluator with a clipboard, a competition with a ranking, a small cost for failure or a tight time limit. Most of those are free. Pair up with someone studying the same quals and grill each other with a timer running. Record yourself explaining a system and watch it back. Put a small, real consequence on missed questions, like push-ups. None of this feels like the real thing exactly, but each one adds a piece of the pressure your brain needs to get used to.

There is one more counterintuitive finding about pressure. Sian Beilock and Thomas Carr studied golfers putting under pressure and found that what helped was not dual-task practice with distractions. It was practicing while being watched and filmed, so that the self-conscious attention pressure brings was no longer new. Skilled performers often choke because pressure makes them start monitoring movements they normally run on autopilot. Practicing with an audience gets you used to that spotlight before it matters.
Realism isn't about graphics

If realistic practice works, does that mean you need expensive, high-fidelity simulators? Medicine tested this directly. In 2012, Geoffrey Norman and colleagues reviewed 24 studies that compared training on high-fidelity simulators, which can cost close to six figures, with cheap low-fidelity versions. Both beat no training. But nearly all the studies found no significant advantage for the expensive version, with average differences of only 1 to 2 percent.

What does matter is training to a real standard and transferring to the real task. In a small but influential 2002 study, eight surgical residents trained on a simple virtual reality simulator until they hit expert-level benchmarks, while eight others had no simulator training. When all 16 then performed real gallbladder surgeries, scored by reviewers who did not know who was who, the simulator-trained residents dissected 29 percent faster and the untrained residents were nine times more likely to stall and fail to make progress.

items.label: Faster surgical dissection by residents trained to criterion on a VR simulator
More likely to stall for residents without simulator training

blocks.source: Seymour et al., Annals of Surgery, 2002

blocks.text: The realism that counts is psychological and cognitive: the same decisions, the same demand to produce answers rather than recognize them, the same time pressure, the same feeling of being watched. A buddy with a list of questions in a passageway can recreate most of what makes a board hard. A whiteboard and a timer can recreate most of what makes a casualty hard to think through. You do not need the real plant to practice thinking like you're in it.
Building a ladder of realism

Realistic practice is uncomfortable, and that is the point, but you do not have to start at full intensity. The basketball players trained under pressure over five weeks, and the police officers trained with anxiety across several sessions. The research suggests a gradual climb: master the basics in calm conditions, then steadily add the features of the real test until practice feels harder than the real thing.

One caution. The goal is a controlled, survivable dose of pressure, not maximum misery. Pressure training in the meta-analysis helped beginners as well as experts, but in those studies the pressure was added on top of skills people were already practicing, not used as a substitute for learning them. If every practice session leaves you overwhelmed, you are no longer training the skill; you are training the panic. Raise the realism a step at a time, and step back down when your performance collapses instead of just wobbling.

blocks.title: Raising the realism, one rung at a time
items: Learn it calmly: understand the material or mechanic with notes and examples available
Close the book: recall it from memory on paper and check your gaps
Say it out loud: explain it standing up, as if to a board, without notes
Add a stranger: have someone who isn't your friend ask follow-ups and interrupt
Add stakes and surprise: time limits, scenarios you didn't pick, a small penalty for misses
Debrief: write down where you blanked and drill exactly that next time

blocks.text: The same ladder works outside the Navy. For coding, it means building small features from a blank file with a time limit instead of following tutorials where the answer is always one click away. For a game you're making, it means watching real players without explaining anything, because the real launch won't come with you standing behind every player. For competitive games, it means spending some of your practice in actual ranked or scrimmage conditions, not only in an aim trainer, because the trainer never makes you nervous.

There is a reason the Navy runs drills that feel uncomfortably real, at inconvenient hours, with people watching and grading. Those drills are not a test of whether you have studied. They *are* the studying, in the only form that reliably carries over to the day it counts. The dart players on the wall learned the same thing: you do not rise to the occasion so much as fall back on the conditions you trained in. Choose those conditions on purpose.

takeaways: Skills are stored with the conditions you practiced them in. Practice in conditions that resemble the real test.
Retrieval practice makes memories sturdy enough to survive stress; restudied material is more likely to vanish when you're nervous.
Training under mild, controlled pressure, such as being watched, timed or graded, improves performance under real pressure.
Expensive realism isn't required. A buddy asking board questions in a passageway captures most of what matters.
Climb a ladder: calm practice, closed-book recall, out-loud explanation, a stranger asking questions, then surprise and stakes.

title: You Read the Whole Chapter. Did You Understand It?
dek: The feeling of understanding a technical manual is a poor guide to whether you do. Here is what decades of reading research say actually works.

blocks.text: In 1982, psychologists Arthur Glenberg, Alex Wilkinson and William Epstein gave college students short passages of expository text and told them exactly what to look for: some of these passages contain a contradiction, so find it. Then the researchers planted contradictions, two sentences that could not both be true, and asked readers to rate how well they understood each passage.

Many readers sailed right past the contradictions and still rated their comprehension as high. They had been warned, they were looking for a problem, and they missed it while feeling confident. The researchers called this the *illusion of knowing*: the belief that you have understood something when your understanding has actually failed.

A follow-up study in 1984 found the illusion got worse in exactly the situations that dense technical writing produces. Readers missed more contradictions when spotting them required an inference, when the clashing sentences sat in different paragraphs, and when the second sentence paraphrased the idea instead of repeating the same words. In other words, the harder a text makes you work to connect ideas, the more likely you are to feel fine while missing the point.

Anyone who has studied a thick technical manual knows the sensation: you reach the end of the chapter, every sentence made sense as you read it, and an hour later you couldn't draw the system or explain why it works. Reading and understanding are different activities. The good news is that the research on what turns one into the other is fairly clear.
Why rereading feels like learning

The most popular study method is also one of the weakest. In 2009, Jeffrey Karpicke, Andrew Butler and Henry Roediger surveyed 177 college students about how they study. Most said they repeatedly read their notes or textbook. Relatively few tested themselves. The researchers argued that students were falling for *illusions of competence*: rereading makes the text feel familiar, and familiarity feels like knowledge.

A 2013 review led by John Dunlosky at Kent State University rated ten common study techniques for how well their benefits generalize across students, materials and tests. Rereading, highlighting and summarization were all rated *low utility*. Not useless, but inconsistent: they help some people some of the time, and they routinely lose to better methods.

Familiarity is the problem. The second time through a page, it reads smoothly because you have seen it before. Your brain reads that smoothness, which psychologists call fluency, as a sign of mastery. But recognizing something when it's in front of you is a much easier job than producing it from scratch when it isn't, which is what any board, exam or casualty will actually ask of you.

blocks.title: Feels productive vs. actually works

left.head: Feels productive
items: Rereading the chapter until it reads smoothly
Highlighting most of the page
Copying the text into neater notes
Reading straight through without stopping

right.head: Actually works better
items: Asking yourself questions before you read
Stopping each paragraph to explain why it's true
Working the text and diagram together
Closing the book and reconstructing it from memory

blocks.text: There is a deeper reason rereading underdelivers on technical material. Understanding a system is about relationships: this valve affects that pressure, which changes this reading. Those relationships often aren't written in any single sentence. You have to build them, and passive reading doesn't build them. It just lets you meet the same sentences again.
The truth about highlighting

Highlighting deserves a closer look, because the full story is more interesting than "it doesn't work." In 2022, Héctor Ponce, Richard Mayer and Ester Méndez pooled 36 published studies from 1938 to 2019 that tested highlighting under controlled conditions. They separated two situations: students highlighting the text themselves, and students reading a text where an instructor had already highlighted the important parts.

blocks.title: Effect of highlighting on learning (effect size)
blocks.note: Roughly, 0.2 is a small effect and 0.5 a medium one. Self-highlighting's comprehension effect was not reliable.
blocks.source: Ponce, Mayer & Méndez, Educational Psychology Review, 2022

blocks.text: Highlighting your own text helped people remember the highlighted facts but did not reliably improve understanding. Text highlighted by an expert improved both. The difference makes sense once you see what highlighting really is: a decision about what matters. When an expert makes that decision, it guides your attention. When a beginner makes it, they often can't tell the key idea from a detail yet, so they either mark everything or mark the wrong things.

The age difference in the study fits this explanation. Self-highlighting helped college students more than younger students, who may have had a harder time judging what was important. Expertise in the subject is what makes a highlight useful, which is a bit of a catch-22 for a beginner.

Technical manuals already come with expert highlighting built in. The warnings, cautions, notes, bold terms and boxed summaries are an author's judgment about what you must not miss. Read those with extra care before you reach for your own highlighter. And when you do mark the text, make it earn its place: mark only after you have read the whole paragraph, and only what you could explain to someone else.
Explain it to yourself, one line at a time

The single best-studied habit of strong readers is something called *self-explanation*. In the late 1980s, cognitive scientist Michelene Chi and her colleagues watched students study worked examples in physics while thinking aloud. The students who went on to solve problems well were not the ones who read the most. They were the ones who kept stopping to explain each step to themselves: why this formula, where this number came from, how it connects to the last line.

Was that just a sign of being a good student, or could it be taught? In a 1994 study, Chi's team had 14 eighth graders read a textbook passage on the human circulatory system and simply asked them to explain each sentence to themselves after reading it. A comparison group of 10 students read the same text twice instead. The prompted group learned more. Among them, the students who generated the most explanations all ended up with a correct mental model of how blood circulates, while many of the others did not. The study was small, but the idea has held up.

items.label: Average benefit of prompting people to self-explain while studying (a medium effect)
Research reports pooled in the meta-analysis

blocks.source: Bisra, Liu, Nesbit, Salimi & Winne, Educational Psychology Review, 2018

blocks.text: Here is what it looks like in practice. Suppose a manual says a motor's starting current can be several times its running current. A passive reader nods and moves on. A self-explaining reader stops: why would that be? Because a motor that isn't turning yet isn't generating the back voltage that will later push against the supply, so much less stands in the way of the current. Then what follows? The breaker has to tolerate that surge without tripping, and the supply voltage may sag for a moment. Two sentences of the manual have just been tied to three things you already knew. That web of connections is what you'll pull on later.

Notice that the explanation might be partly wrong. That's fine. Researchers in Chi's tradition have argued that even an imperfect explanation helps, because it gives you a specific idea that the next paragraph can confirm or correct, and noticing the mismatch is itself a moment of learning. A reader who never commits to an explanation has nothing to correct.

A 2018 meta-analysis led by Kiran Bisra at Simon Fraser University pooled 69 effects from 64 research reports and found that prompting learners to self-explain produced a medium-sized benefit across many subjects, levels and task types. Dunlosky's review rated it *moderate utility*, held back mainly because it hadn't been tested enough in real classrooms.

Self-explanation is not the same as summarizing. A summary restates what the text says. A self-explanation asks *why* it's true and *how* it fits: why does this pump need a minimum flow? What would happen downstream if this breaker opened? Which earlier paragraph does this depend on? It is closely related to explaining a topic to an imaginary student (see the article on note-taking and the Feynman technique), but it happens while you read, sentence by sentence, instead of afterward.

A practical sign of where to slow down comes from the 1984 contradiction study. Readers were most likely to miss problems when connecting two ideas required an inference, when the ideas were paragraphs apart, or when the wording changed. Technical writing does all three constantly. When a sentence refers back to something earlier, or a new term seems to describe an old idea, that is your cue to stop and check that the pieces really fit.
Ask before you read

A strange but well-supported trick is to quiz yourself on material *before* you have studied it. In a 2023 review, Steven Pan and Shana Carpenter summarized the research on *prequestions* and *pretests*. Answering questions you are almost guaranteed to get wrong can improve learning, as long as you then study the material and find the correct answers. The effect has been shown with texts, videos and lectures, though how much it helps varies with the procedure and with what the final test measures.

Part of the reason seems to be that a question changes how you read. Instead of letting the text wash over you, you're hunting for something specific, and when you find it, it lands on a prepared spot. For a technical chapter, that can be as simple as reading the review questions at the end first, or writing down three questions from the headings: What does this system do? What are its main parts? What happens when it fails?
Read the drawing and the words together

Technical material is rarely just text. It comes with schematics, one-line diagrams, piping drawings and cutaways, and the way you combine them matters. In 1993, Mary Hegarty and Marcel Just tracked readers' eyes as they studied descriptions of pulley systems with text and a diagram. Readers moved back and forth, connecting a sentence to the matching part of the drawing a component or a group of connected components at a time. Understanding was built in the integration, not in either source alone.

That integration costs mental effort, which is why layout matters. Cognitive load researchers, starting with Paul Chandler and John Sweller in 1991, showed that when learners must hunt between a diagram on one page and its explanation on another, part of their limited working memory gets spent on the hunting. Putting labels and explanations right on the diagram freed that capacity for learning. A 2026 meta-analysis of 28 studies with 4,720 learners found a moderate-to-large benefit from placing related words and pictures close together, with novices benefiting most.

You can't redesign the manual, but you can redesign how you use it. Put the drawing beside the text rather than flipping pages. Trace the flow path with a finger or pencil as you read about it. Write notes on a copy of the diagram itself rather than in a separate list. Then close everything and redraw the system from memory, which turns reading into retrieval practice (see the article on retrieval practice).
A reading protocol for dense material

blocks.title: Reading a technical chapter
items: Survey first: skim headings, figures, warnings and the end-of-chapter questions. Two minutes.
Write two or three questions you expect the chapter to answer, and guess the answers.
Read one section at a time. At the end of each paragraph, explain to yourself why it's true and how it connects.
Work the diagram alongside the text, tracing paths and labeling the drawing directly.
Close the book. Redraw the system or write the key points from memory, then check what you missed.
Come back to it in a few days and do the memory check again before rereading anything.

blocks.text: This is slower than reading straight through, and it will feel slower. That's not a flaw. The goal of reading a technical manual is not to reach the last page; it's to be able to answer questions the manual never asked, at a time when the manual isn't open in front of you.

The illusion of knowing never goes away entirely. Even experienced readers feel that smooth sense of understanding when they've only recognized the words. The fix is to stop trusting the feeling and start testing it: explain, predict, redraw. If you can do those things with the book closed, you understood it. If you can't, you just read it.

takeaways: Readers often miss contradictions while rating their own comprehension as high; trust tests, not feelings.
Rereading and self-highlighting mostly build familiarity; expert highlighting (warnings, notes, bold terms) helps more.
Stop after each paragraph and explain to yourself why it's true and what it connects to.
Write questions before you read, and work diagrams and text side by side.
Finish every chapter by redrawing or explaining it with the book closed.

title: The Test Is the Lesson
dek: Rereading feels like studying. Pulling information out of your own head, even badly, is what actually makes it stick.

blocks.text: In an experiment at Washington University in St. Louis, a group of undergraduates sat down with a short science passage, a few hundred words about the sun or about sea otters. Some read it four times. Others read it once and then spent the remaining sessions trying to write down everything they could remember, with no feedback and no peeking. The first group saw the text about 14 times in total. The second group saw it about three and a half times.

Five minutes later, the readers won easily. One week later, the result had flipped: the students who had mostly tested themselves remembered half again as much as the students who had mostly reread. The experiment, published in 2006 by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, became one of the most cited demonstrations of what psychologists call the testing effect, or retrieval practice. Its message runs against almost every study habit people have: a test is not just a way to measure learning. Taking one is learning.
The scoreboard that flipped
The design was simple. In the second experiment, 180 students were split into three study schedules made of five-minute periods. One group studied the passage in all four periods (SSSS).
One studied three times and took one recall test (SSST). One studied once and took three recall tests (STTT). Then each student took a final test, either five minutes later or a week later.

blocks.title: Share of the passage recalled one week later
blocks.note: At five minutes the order was reversed: 83%, 78% and 71%.
blocks.source: Roediger & Karpicke, Psychological Science, 2006

blocks.text: Look at the forgetting rates rather than the raw scores. Over the week, the reread-only group lost about 52 percent of what they had shown at the five-minute mark. The mostly-testing group lost about 14 percent. Rereading builds something that looks impressive right away and drains fast. Retrieval builds something that looks weaker at first and holds.

The first experiment in the same paper showed the same crossover with 120 students. Restudying was slightly ahead at five minutes, 81 percent to 75 percent. Two days later, testing led 68 to 54. After a week it led 56 to 42. If you only ever check your learning right after studying, you will reliably pick the wrong method.
Your confidence is lying to you

Here is the most uncomfortable detail. After the learning phase, the students rated how well they expected to remember the passage in a week on a scale of one to seven. The repeat-readers were the most confident, averaging 4.8. The repeat-testers were the least confident, at 4.0. The group that would do best felt worst about its chances, and the group that would do worst felt best.

The reason is fluency. When you reread something, it flows. The words are familiar, the diagram looks right, and your brain mistakes that ease for knowing. But recognizing an answer when it is in front of you is a different skill from producing it when it is not, and a qual board, a casualty and a coding interview all demand the second. Testing feels harder because it exposes the gaps, which is exactly why it is useful.

blocks.title: Two ways to spend the same hour

left.head: Rereading and highlighting
items: Feels smooth and productive
Builds recognition: I have seen this
Hides what you cannot produce
Strong at five minutes, fades fast

right.head: Retrieval practice
items: Feels slow and frustrating
Builds recall: I can produce this
Shows you exactly what is missing
Weaker at five minutes, lasts weeks

blocks.text: A 2008 study by Karpicke and Roediger in *Science* made the point with Swahili vocabulary. Students who kept being tested on words even after they had got them right recalled about 80 percent a week later. Students whose words were dropped from testing once they had recalled them, whether or not they kept restudying, managed only 33 to 36 percent. Once a word could be recalled, extra studying added little; extra retrieval added a lot. The students' own predictions of how they would do bore little relation to any of this.
Better than the fancy methods, too

Retrieval does not only beat passive rereading. In a 2011 study, also in *Science*, Karpicke and Janell Blunt compared it with concept mapping, a popular active technique where students draw diagrams connecting the main ideas. Eighty Purdue students read a passage about sea otters, then either stopped, reread it repeatedly, built a concept map, or practiced recalling it. A week later they took a test with both factual and inference questions.

blocks.title: Test score one week after studying a science text
blocks.source: Karpicke & Blunt, Science, 2011 (as summarized by the What Works Clearinghouse)

blocks.text: Retrieval won on the inference questions as well as the facts, which matters, because a common objection is that testing only builds parrot memory. A fair caveat, flagged by the US Department of Education's What Works Clearinghouse when it reviewed the study: the retrieval and concept-mapping groups spent more total time studying than the two reading groups, so the comparison with rereading is not perfectly clean. The head-to-head with concept mapping, at equal time, is the stronger result.

One more detail from that work is worth sitting with. Right after the learning session, students who practiced retrieval and students who mapped concepts could recall about the same amount. The difference only showed up a week later. Students also tended to overestimate how well they knew the material whenever it was sitting in front of them, which is precisely the condition rereading and concept mapping create. Methods that keep the source in view keep the illusion running.
How big is the effect, really?

Single studies can mislead, so the better question is what happens across many. In 2014, Christopher Rowland pooled 159 effect sizes from 61 studies comparing testing with restudying. The average advantage was an effect size of 0.50, which is moderate: large enough to move a typical student well up the class, not large enough to be magic. A 2013 review led by John Dunlosky rated ten common study techniques and gave its top rating, high utility, to only two: practice testing and spacing your study out. Rereading and highlighting were rated low.

items.label: Average effect size of testing over restudy when tests gave feedback
Average effect size without feedback

blocks.source: Rowland, Psychological Bulletin, 2014

blocks.text: The meta-analysis also found which details matter. Tests with feedback roughly doubled the benefit compared with tests without it. Recall tests, where you produce the answer, generally beat recognition tests like multiple choice. And the advantage was bigger when the final test came a day or more later rather than the same day, which is exactly when it matters.

There are real limits. Most of this research uses word lists, facts and short passages. In 2015, Tamara van Gog and John Sweller argued that the testing effect shrinks and may even disappear for highly complex material, where many elements must be understood together; other researchers dispute how far that goes, and the debate is not settled. And testing only works if you can retrieve something. Quizzing yourself on a chapter you never understood just produces blank pages; learn it first, then test.
Why pulling beats pushing

A useful mental model: memory is less like a hard drive and more like a trail through a forest. Reading the trail map does little to the trail. Walking it, especially when it is overgrown and you have to push through, wears it deeper. Every successful retrieval changes the memory itself, strengthening the routes you used and often linking the item to new cues. The effort is not a side effect; it is the work.

Testing also has an indirect benefit that is easy to overlook. It tells you, precisely, what you do not know. A reread chapter gives you a vague warm feeling about the whole thing. A blank page where the third interlock should be gives you a target. That is why good testing is followed by checking: retrieve, compare, fix the misses, and come back later to retrieve again.

Robert and Elizabeth Bjork at UCLA offer a sharper version of this idea. Every memory, they argue, has two separate strengths. Storage strength is how deeply it is embedded and connected to other knowledge. Retrieval strength is how easy it is to pull up right now.

Rereading pumps up retrieval strength, which is why the material feels known, but does little for storage. Retrieving something when retrieval strength has dropped, when it takes effort to dig out, is what builds storage strength. The feeling of strain is the sensation of the deeper number going up.

That model also explains why cramming and rereading are so seductive. Your sense of how well you know something reads the retrieval-strength gauge, because that is the only one you can feel. The storage-strength gauge, the one that decides what you will know in a month, is invisible. You have to infer it from evidence, and the best evidence is a test taken after a delay.
If a study method lets you feel good without ever being wrong, it is probably not doing much. Productive studying includes a steady stream of small, private failures.
Turning it into a method
For technical material, retrieval practice can look like many things besides flashcards. The common thread is that the answer comes out of your head before you look at the source.

blocks.title: A retrieval session for technical material
items: Read or watch the material once, carefully, until it makes sense.
Close everything. Write or draw all you can: the system, the steps, the equations.
Check against the source and mark every miss and error in a different color.
Rework the misses from memory, not by copying them.
Come back in a few days and do the blank-page test again before reviewing.

blocks.text: For systems, sketch the line diagram from memory and label every valve and interlock you can, then compare. For procedures, recite the immediate actions in order before you open the book. For math and physics, do practice problems cold instead of rereading worked examples, and only look at the solution after a real attempt. For coding, close the tutorial and rebuild the feature from a blank file; the errors you hit are the lesson. For game design, explain a mechanic to a friend without your notes.

Format matters less than effort, but a few rules hold up. Producing an answer beats picking one, so prefer blank-page questions over multiple choice when you can. Always check your answer afterward, since feedback was the biggest single booster in the meta-analysis.

And once you can retrieve something, do not retire it. The Swahili study showed that dropping items from testing as soon as you get them right throws away most of the benefit. Instead, push them further out and test them again later, which is where retrieval practice and spacing become the same habit.

Nuclear training already contains a version of this, whether or not anyone calls it that. Boards, walkthroughs and oral checkouts force you to produce knowledge on demand, out loud, under mild pressure. That is retrieval practice with feedback built in. The trap is the preparation for them: hours of rereading notes and highlighting the manual, which feels like getting ready and is mostly not. Swap half of that time for self-quizzing and the board itself becomes less of a shock, because you have already been doing the thing it measures.

The same goes for anything you are learning on your own time. A tutorial you follow line by line is rereading with extra steps. You get the warm feeling of progress, and a week later you cannot start the project without it open.

The fix costs nothing: after each lesson, shut it, open a blank file, and try to build the thing again. You will get stuck within minutes. Getting unstuck, with the tutorial as a last resort instead of a first, is the moment the knowledge actually moves into your head.

Study partners help if you use them right. Quizzing each other before a board is retrieval practice with built-in feedback. Listening to someone else explain the system is mostly rereading with a voice.

The hardest part is psychological. Retrieval practice will make you feel less prepared than rereading, right up until the moment it counts. The students in 2006 who did best were the ones who felt worst about it. Learning to trust that feeling of strain, instead of chasing the comfort of familiarity, may be the single most valuable study skill there is.

takeaways: Closing the book and recalling beats rereading for anything you need to remember beyond tomorrow.
Your confidence after rereading is a poor predictor; the method that feels worse often works better.
Check your answers. Feedback roughly doubled the benefit of testing in the 2014 meta-analysis.
Produce answers (draw, write, recite, code) rather than just recognizing them.
Understand material first, then test it; quizzing yourself on what you never learned only yields blanks.

title: Forgetting Is Part of the Plan
dek: A 140-year-old self-experiment and a 1,354-person study agree: when you review matters almost as much as whether you review.

blocks.text: Picture two sailors with the same qual card and the same five weeks before the board. The first coasts for a month, then spends the last three nights grinding the material for hours. The second does short sessions spread across all five weeks and comes back to each system only after he has half-forgotten it. On board day they may score about the same. Ask them the same questions six months later, mid-deployment, when a drill actually needs that knowledge, and the difference between them is enormous.

The second sailor is using one of the oldest and most replicated findings in psychology: the spacing effect. It has been known since the 1880s, confirmed in hundreds of experiments, and almost everyone still studies as if it did not exist. Why that happens is the interesting part, because it reveals how poorly the feeling of *I know this* predicts what you will actually remember.
The man who memorized nonsense

In the early 1880s the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus ran what may be the most tedious experiment in the history of science, with himself as the only subject. He memorized lists of meaningless syllables, chosen precisely because they gave his mind nothing to hook onto. In his main series each list had 13 syllables. He drilled a list until he could recite it without error, waited a set amount of time, and then measured how long it took him to learn it again.

That last step was the clever part. Instead of asking how much he could still recall, he measured *savings*: the share of the original learning time he no longer needed. If a list took 1,000 seconds to learn and 600 seconds to relearn, the savings was 40 percent. The method could detect memories too faint to produce a single recalled syllable, because even a faint trace makes relearning faster.

blocks.title: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve
blocks.note: Savings = how much less time relearning took than the original learning.
blocks.source: Ebbinghaus, Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology (1885; English trans. 1913)

blocks.text: The shape is the famous forgetting curve. Most of the loss happens fast: within an hour, more than half of the benefit of his original effort was gone. Then the curve flattens.

A month later he still kept about a fifth of the savings, and that remnant was fading only slowly. In 2015, Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros at the University of Amsterdam redid the experiment with a single subject, Dros himself, over roughly 70 hours. The new curve closely resembled the original, with one odd bump: memory looked slightly better at the 24-hour mark than the trend predicted, which the authors tentatively linked to sleep.

Notice what the curve actually says, because it gets misquoted constantly. It does not say you lose everything. It says that material studied once and never touched again leaks away fast and then settles into a thin, durable residue.

It also says something hopeful: even after you feel you have forgotten, relearning is cheaper than learning. The trace is still in there. The real question is how to make it thicker each time you come back to it.
Half the work, same result

Ebbinghaus also noticed that repetitions spread across several days did more for him than the same number crammed into one sitting. That observation became the spacing effect, and it has been tested exhaustively since. A 2006 review by Nicholas Cepeda, Harold Pashler and colleagues pooled 839 assessments from 317 experiments in 184 articles. Spaced practice beat massed practice for verbal recall, and the best gap between sessions grew as the time you need to remember grew.

One of the most striking demonstrations came from four psychologists who all shared the surname Bahrick. Over nine years they learned and relearned 300 foreign-language word pairs, then tested themselves up to five years after training ended. Thirteen sessions spaced 56 days apart produced retention similar to 26 sessions spaced 14 days apart. Wider spacing bought the same memory for half the sessions. With only four subjects it is a vivid case study rather than proof, which is why the big controlled experiments matter.

Spacing is not just for vocabulary. In a 2007 study, Doug Rohrer and Kelli Taylor taught college students a type of math problem and gave them the same practice problems either in one block or split across two sessions a week apart. During practice the two groups performed almost identically. On a test a week later, the spacers scored 74 percent and the massers 49 percent. The extra practice the massers did in a single sitting added almost nothing; a third group that did less massed practice scored about the same as them.
The ridgeline: how long to wait

The most useful of those experiments was published in 2008 by Cepeda, Ed Vul, Doug Rohrer, John Wixted and Pashler. They recruited 1,354 people online and had them learn 32 obscure but true trivia facts, the kind of thing you would never already know. Each person reviewed the facts once after a gap ranging from zero to 105 days, then took a final test after a retention interval of 7, 35, 70 or 350 days. Every person got exactly the same amount of study; only the timing changed.

Two results stood out. First, the payoff from spacing was large. For people tested a year later, reviewing at the best gap improved recall by 77 percent compared with reviewing immediately, and at the 70-day test the improvement was 111 percent. Second, the best gap was not a fixed number. It depended on how long you needed to remember, and as a fraction of that time it shrank.

blocks.title: Best review gap as a share of how long you need to remember
blocks.note: Estimated optimal gap for recall: about 3, 8, 12 and 27 days respectively.
blocks.source: Cepeda et al., Psychological Science, 2008

blocks.text: Translate that into your calendar. If the board is a week out, review a few days after you first learn something. If it is five weeks out, wait about a week. If you want to still know it a year from now, as in when you are standing a watch and the indication in front of you is not in the book, the ideal second look comes three or four weeks later. The authors called the pattern a temporal ridgeline: a ridge of best gaps that climbs as the target date moves further away.

There is a forgiving detail buried in the data. Retention climbed steeply as the gap grew toward the optimum and then declined only gradually past it. In the authors' words, the cost of a too-long gap was much smaller than the cost of using too short a gap. If you are unsure, err late. Reviewing the same evening feels productive and is the least useful choice of all.

items.label: Better recall after a year when the review came at the best gap instead of right away
People in the 2008 spacing study

blocks.source: Cepeda et al., Psychological Science, 2008

blocks.text: Why spacing works, and why it feels wrong

Researchers still argue about the mechanism. One leading idea is that a review helps most when the memory has partly faded, so retrieving it takes real effort, and that effort strengthens it more than an easy repeat would. Another says that studying at different times attaches the memory to more varied contexts and cues, giving you more routes back to it later. A third says that a second pass right after the first gets lazy processing because the material still feels fresh. These ideas are not mutually exclusive, and the honest answer is that the effect is far better established than its explanation.

Whatever the cause, spacing has a public relations problem. Cramming produces a feeling of mastery that is real, just short-lived. Spaced review feels worse in the moment because each time you return, you have forgotten some of it and have to struggle. That struggle is the point, but your brain reads it as failure. The psychologists Robert and Elizabeth Bjork have a name for this, desirable difficulties, and it is a big enough idea to deserve its own article.
The moment you feel a little rusty on something is not a sign that you studied it wrong. It is usually the best time to review it.

Schools make this worse by rewarding the short game. Unit tests reward cramming, and then the material is never examined again. Nuclear training is unusual because it keeps coming back: the facts from power school show up on boards, in quals, in drills and in real casualties years later. That is exactly the situation where the ridgeline says spacing pays off most.

The best part is that spacing is close to free. In the 2008 study, every group got identical study time; the only variable was the calendar. In the Bahrick study, wider gaps actually cut the number of sessions in half.

You do not need more hours to benefit. You need to take the hours you were going to spend anyway and stop stacking them on the same night. For someone whose free time comes in scattered chunks between watches, that is good news: scattered is exactly the right shape.
Building a spacing habit for technical material

Flashcard software built on spaced repetition, such as Anki, automates the ridgeline. Each time you answer a card correctly, its next appearance is pushed further out, so cards you know well show up rarely and shaky ones keep coming back. It runs offline on a phone, which matters on a submarine. It is ideal for crisp facts: setpoints, alarm meanings, component names, formulas, the steps of a procedure in order.

It has limits worth respecting. The big studies used word pairs and trivia, and spacing evidence is thinnest for deep conceptual understanding. A card that asks you to recite a number teaches you the number, not why the system behaves the way it does. For systems knowledge, space bigger units: redraw a system from memory every couple of weeks, rework a problem set you did a month ago, or explain a casualty response out loud without notes. The same logic applies when learning to code: rebuild a small feature from scratch a week after the tutorial instead of rereading it.

Card design decides whether the app helps or just feels busy. Keep each card to one fact, phrase it as a question you must answer before flipping, and actually say or write the answer rather than nodding at it. Make cards from material you already understand; a card can preserve knowledge, but it is a poor way to acquire it. And prune ruthlessly. A deck of a few hundred cards you review daily beats a deck of five thousand you abandon in week three.

You may hear arguments about whether gaps should expand (one day, then three, then ten) or stay equal. Expanding schedules are what most software uses and they are convenient, but the research comparing them to equal spacing is mixed, and some studies found equal gaps held up as well or better over the long run. The big, reliable effect is spacing versus cramming. The fine-tuning matters much less than simply coming back.

blocks.title: A spaced plan for one qual system
items: Day 0: learn it properly, then close the book and write down what you remember.
Day 1 or 2: redraw the system and list its interlocks from memory, then check.
About one week: answer practice board questions cold, no peeking first.
About three to four weeks: explain the whole system out loud, including casualties.
After that: put the facts you keep missing into flashcards and let the app space them.

blocks.text: Two practical rules make this survivable on a busy watch rotation. Keep sessions short, because spacing works with many short visits rather than a few heroic ones. And when you miss days, do not try to catch up all at once; just restart the queue. A slightly late review costs little, as the 2008 data showed.

The deeper lesson is about trusting the right signal. Your sense of fluency in the moment is a measure of how recently you saw something, not how well you will know it later. Ebbinghaus showed that forgetting is fast and that it never quite reaches zero.
Spacing turns that leftover trace into the foundation of the next session. Forgetting, used well, is not the opposite of learning. It is part of the mechanism.

takeaways: Forgetting is steep at first, then flattens; what is left makes relearning cheaper.
Space reviews at roughly 10 to 20 percent of how long you need to remember something.
When unsure, review later rather than sooner; too short a gap costs far more than too long.
Use spaced flashcards for facts, and spaced redraws or re-explanations for whole systems.
Feeling rusty at a review is a feature, not a sign you studied wrong.

title: The Speed Limit on Reading
dek: Speed reading courses and apps promise to triple your pace with no loss in understanding. Your eyes, and fifty years of research, say otherwise. Here is what actually makes readers faster.

blocks.text: In 1959, a Utah schoolteacher named Evelyn Wood launched a course called Reading Dynamics. The pitch was irresistible: with the right training, ordinary people could read thousands of words a minute and remember all of it. The course spread nationwide, and the idea never went away. Today it lives on in apps that flash words one at a time in the center of your screen, promising you can finish a novel on your lunch break.

If that were true, it would be the most valuable skill a person could learn. More books, faster study, quals knocked out in half the time. So in 2016, five reading scientists, led by the late Keith Rayner, one of the most prolific researchers of eye movements in reading, wrote a long review for the journal *Psychological Science in the Public Interest*. They asked a simple question: what does the science of reading say about speed reading?

Their answer was blunt. There is a trade-off between speed and accuracy. It is unlikely that readers can double or triple their speed, from around 250 words per minute to 500 or 750, while understanding the text as well as they would at a normal pace. Push past that, and you are no longer reading in the sense most people mean. You are skimming. To see why, you have to look at what your eyes are actually doing right now.

Part of the confusion comes from how speed reading gets measured. If the comprehension check only asks about the general gist, almost any reading method looks fine, because you can often guess the gist from a few key words and some background knowledge. The differences show up on questions about specific details, arguments and implications, which are exactly the things you need when you are studying for something real. When researchers in the 1980s compared graduates of a speed-reading course with ordinary readers who were simply told to skim, the two groups behaved much alike: decent on the big picture, weaker on the details.
What your eyes are really doing

Reading feels smooth, like your eyes glide along the line. They don't. Your eyes move in quick jumps called *saccades*, and between jumps they stop on a word for a brief *fixation*. Fixations in reading last on average about a quarter of a second, roughly 250 milliseconds. During that pause, you pull in information about the word you're looking at, plus a little about the next one. During the jumps themselves, you take in almost nothing useful.

The reason for all this stopping and starting is the structure of the eye. Only a tiny central region of the retina, the fovea, sees fine detail. A few letters away from where you're looking, your vision is too blurry to identify words reliably. That is why one of the classic speed-reading promises, taking in a whole line or a whole page at a glance, runs into a hard physical limit. You can't read what your eye can't resolve.

blocks.title: One beat of reading
items: Your eyes land on a word and hold still for a fixation, about a quarter second on average
Your brain identifies the word and starts fitting it into the sentence
You get a blurry preview of the next word in your peripheral vision
Your eyes jump forward several letters in a saccade, taking in almost nothing mid-jump
Sometimes your eyes jump back to an earlier word to check or repair your understanding

blocks.text: Crucially, the time each fixation lasts is not fixed. It stretches for rare words and words you didn't see coming, and shrinks for common, predictable ones. In other words, the eyes are not the bottleneck. They wait on the brain. The limiting step in reading is how fast you can recognize words and build meaning from them, and that is a language skill, not a visual one.
How fast people actually read

Ask people how fast an average adult reads and you will often hear 300 words a minute or more. In 2019, Belgian psychologist Marc Brysbaert gathered 190 studies with more than 18,000 participants to pin down the real figure for English. The averages came in lower than the numbers usually quoted.

blocks.title: Average adult reading rate in English
blocks.note: Most adults fall between 175 and 300 words/min for silent non-fiction.
blocks.source: Brysbaert, Journal of Memory and Language, 2019

blocks.text: Non-fiction is slower than fiction largely because it uses longer words. Most adults fall somewhere between 175 and 300 words a minute for silent non-fiction reading. Brysbaert also noted something telling: silent reading rates sit in line with the upper limit of how fast people can comfortably understand speech. That suggests reading speed is set by the same language-processing machinery we use for listening, not by some visual skill that training could unlock separately.

For a sense of scale: at about 238 words a minute, a 2,000-word article like this one takes around eight or nine minutes. A speed-reading claim of 1,000 words a minute would put it at two minutes. Ask yourself whether you could explain this article's main arguments to someone after two minutes with it, and you have the problem in a nutshell.
Taking away the eye movements

Modern speed-reading apps tried an engineering solution. If eye movements waste time, eliminate them. The method, called rapid serial visual presentation, flashes words one after another in the same spot, so your eyes never have to move. You set the speed, and the words keep coming.

The flaw is that eye movements are not just wasted motion. A meaningful share of the saccades in normal reading actually go *backward*, quick glances back at an earlier word. These are called regressions, and they look like inefficiency. In 2014, Elizabeth Schotter, Randy Tran and Keith Rayner tested what happens when you take them away. Using an eye tracker, they masked each word on the screen the instant a reader's eyes moved past it, so there was nothing to go back to.

Comprehension dropped. And it didn't drop only for tricky, ambiguous sentences where you would expect rereading to help; it dropped for ordinary ones too. Those small backward glances turn out to be part of how understanding gets checked and repaired as you go. An app that removes them is not removing waste. It is removing a quality-control step.

A 2017 study tested the apps directly. Participants read easier and harder passages either normally on a static page or in a flashing-word format at 700 or 1,000 words a minute. Reading a normal static page produced better comprehension than either app speed. Comprehension was driven mainly by speed, not by people's working memory capacity, so being sharp didn't rescue you. Reading at a thousand words a minute mostly meant understanding less.

There is also a trap in how these apps feel. Words arrive at a steady clip, nothing ever stalls, and the experience is smooth and oddly satisfying. That smoothness is easy to mistake for understanding. It is the same illusion that makes rereading notes feel productive: the input is flowing, so it seems like learning must be happening. The only honest check is to close the app afterward and try to explain what you just read.
Speed reading doesn't break the speed-accuracy trade-off. It just picks a different point on it, trading understanding for pace, and usually doesn't tell you that's what you're doing.
The inner voice is not a bad habit

Another common speed-reading target is *subvocalization*, the quiet inner voice that 'says' the words as you read. Courses often treat it as a crutch slowing you down to talking speed. The research tells a different story. Converting written words into a sound-based code appears to be a normal part of skilled silent reading, and Rayner's review concluded that the inner voice is part of how skilled readers understand text, so trying to suppress it costs comprehension rather than buying speed.

Psychologists have studied this for more than a century, and a 2014 review in *Psychological Bulletin* by Mallorie Leinenger laid out the debate in detail: whether the inner voice helps identify words, helps hold a sentence in memory while you work out its meaning, or both. Researchers still argue about exactly when and how it kicks in. What the field does not support is the idea that skilled readers can simply switch it off and read at the speed of sight with no cost.
Where you read matters too

There is one more factor that affects reading more than any speed technique: the screen. A 2019 meta-analysis by Virginia Clinton pooled 33 studies with nearly 2,800 participants that randomly assigned people to read on paper or on screens. Screen readers understood less. Interestingly, the drop came without any time savings, and screen readers were also worse at judging how well they had understood what they read.

items.label: Effect of reading on screens vs paper on comprehension (g)
Same effect for informational, non-fiction text
Same effect for stories: no real difference

blocks.source: Clinton, Journal of Research in Reading, 2019

blocks.text: The gap showed up mainly for informational, expository text, not for stories. That pattern is a useful clue for anyone who does most of their reading on a phone. A novel on your phone is fine. A dense technical article on your phone deserves a slower pace, a deliberate pause at the end of each section, and a quick self-test of what you actually took away, because the screen makes it easier to feel like you understood more than you did.

Researchers are still sorting out why screens have this effect. Possible reasons include scrolling, which makes it harder to remember where on the page something was, a habit of reading screens quickly and shallowly because that is how we read most online content, and the overconfidence the calibration results point to. Whatever the mix, the practical upshot is the same: on a screen, build in the checks that paper seems to provide for free.
How to actually read faster

None of this means reading speed is fixed. Rayner and his co-authors were clear about what does work: become a more skilled language user. Readers with bigger vocabularies and more background knowledge recognize words faster and predict what comes next more accurately, so their fixations get shorter and their regressions rarer. The way to get there is unglamorous: read a lot, especially in the areas you care about. Speed is a side effect of fluency, not a trick layered on top of it.

If your reading of technical manuals sped up over a training pipeline like nuke school, this is why. You did not learn an eye trick. You learned the vocabulary, so words like 'enthalpy' or 'reactivity' stopped being speed bumps, and you built mental models so each new sentence slotted into something you already knew. The same will happen with programming documentation or game design writing: the first month is slow, and then it isn't.

The other legitimate tool is skimming, used on purpose. Rayner's review notes that if thorough understanding is not your goal, skimming gets you through text faster with moderate comprehension. Good readers do this constantly. They decide before they start whether a text needs to be learned, understood or just triaged, and they read accordingly.

items: Decide your goal first: learn it, understand it, or just find out whether it matters.
To triage, skim headings, first sentences of paragraphs, charts and the conclusion. Then decide whether to read properly.
For anything you need to know cold, read at normal speed, let your eyes go back when they want to, and stop after each section to recall the main points without looking.
Build vocabulary in the field you're studying. Every unfamiliar term you master permanently speeds up every future page.
Read dense material on paper when you can; on a phone, slow down and check your understanding more often.

blocks.text: Evelyn Wood's promise was that reading could be made effortless. The science says reading is the effort: the effort of turning marks into meaning, one fixation at a time. You can't skip that step. But you can make it faster by knowing more, the slow, compounding way, and you can stop wasting full-speed reading on text that only ever deserved a skim.

takeaways: Typical adult silent reading is around 240 to 260 words per minute; claims of doubling or tripling that with full comprehension are not supported.
Your eyes stop on words about a quarter second at a time, and the brain, not the eyes, sets the pace.
Backward glances and the inner voice help comprehension; apps that remove them trade understanding for speed.
The real way to read faster is fluency: more vocabulary and background knowledge in the field you're reading.
Skim deliberately to triage, read properly to learn, and slow down for dense text on a phone screen.

title: Water or Crowds? How the Picture in Your Head Decides How You Fix Things
dek: Research on electricians, naval technicians and doctors shows that troubleshooting runs on mental models and search strategy, and that most failures come from stopping too soon, not knowing too little.

blocks.text: Picture electricity. Most people see one of two things. Some see water flowing through pipes: the battery is a pump, wires are pipes, a resistor is a narrow section, voltage is pressure. Others see a crowd of people moving through corridors: the battery is something urging them forward, a resistor is a narrow gate they have to squeeze through.

In the early 1980s, cognitive scientists Dedre Gentner and Donald Gentner gave people circuit puzzles and then asked which picture they had used to solve them: what happens to the current with two batteries in series, or in parallel? Two resistors in series, or in parallel? The answers depended on the picture. People who thought in water did better on the battery problems. People who thought in crowds did better on the resistor problems, especially resistors in parallel.

Neither picture is electricity. Both are analogies, and each one makes some answers easy and others almost invisible. That is the core lesson of research on how people understand and fix complex systems: you never reason about the machine directly. You reason about the model of it in your head. When the model is good, troubleshooting feels like intuition. When it's off, you can be smart, careful and completely wrong.
Every technician runs a simulation

Psychologists call these internal pictures *mental models*: simplified working versions of a system that you can run forward in your head. If I open this valve, what happens to that pressure? If this breaker trips, what loses power? You don't calculate the answer from first principles every time. You run the model and see what it predicts.

The idea is older than modern psychology. In 1943 the Scottish psychologist Kenneth Craik argued that the mind carries a small-scale model of the outside world and uses it to try out actions before taking them. A good model lets you rehearse the future. It also means that every prediction you make is only as good as the model that made it, and the model is invisible to you most of the time. You notice it only when reality disagrees.

The Gentners' study shows why the choice of model matters. Take two identical resistors in parallel. In the water picture, people often reason that two narrow sections means twice the obstruction, so less flow. In the crowd picture, two gates side by side obviously let more people through. The correct answer is more current, and the crowd model hands it to you. For batteries, the water picture, especially reservoirs stacked one above another, makes the series-versus-parallel difference easy to see.

In a second experiment, the researchers taught small groups of high school and early college students one of three models: water with a pump, water with a reservoir, or a crowd of mice pushed along by a loudspeaker. Then they asked how two parallel resistors would change the current.

blocks.title: Avoided the "less current" error on parallel resistors
blocks.note: Share of answers saying current would be equal or greater (the correct answer is greater). Tiny groups of 7, 5 and 6 students.
blocks.source: Gentner & Gentner, in Mental Models (Gentner & Stevens, eds.), 1983

blocks.text: The samples were tiny, so the exact percentages shouldn't be taken too seriously. The pattern is the point: the analogy someone carries shapes which mistakes they make. A technician with only one way of picturing a system will be strong on the problems that picture handles well and blind to the rest. Experts usually carry several models and switch between them, which is why they can explain the same system three different ways depending on the question.
What a navy taught the researchers

If troubleshooting depends on models, you might think the fix is simply to teach more theory. The research says that isn't enough. In a 1985 review of troubleshooting studies, Nancy Morris and William Rouse concluded that how much training improved troubleshooting depended on how explicit it was about *actions*: what to check, and in what order. Teaching how a system works, without teaching how to use that knowledge to search for a fault, often didn't transfer.

A Dutch team led by Alma Schaafstal ran into exactly that problem with naval weapons engineers. Their observations traced the technicians' difficulties partly to insufficient training, to technical documentation written from a designer's point of view rather than a maintainer's, and to a gap between the theory they had learned and the practice of finding faults.

So they built a new training method they called *structured troubleshooting*. It combined two things: a general step-by-step strategy for finding faults that works on any system, and a way of breaking each specific system into functional blocks at several levels of detail, from the whole system down to individual circuits. The results, published in 2000, were striking. Technicians trained this way solved twice as many malfunctions, in less time, than those trained the traditional way, and the course itself took less time to teach.

items.label: Malfunctions solved by technicians trained in structured troubleshooting vs. traditional training
To find faults, and to teach the course

blocks.source: Schaafstal, Schraagen & van Berlo, Human Factors, 2000

blocks.text: The documentation point is worth pausing on. A manual written by designers explains how a system is supposed to work, part by part. A troubleshooter needs something different: how it fails, what each failure looks like from the outside, and where to put the meter to tell the possibilities apart. When the book doesn't provide that view, you have to build it yourself, and most people never do it deliberately.

The lesson is that knowledge and search strategy are separate skills. You need a model of how the system works, organized by what each part *does*, and you need a disciplined method for hunting through it.
Two ways to hunt a fault

The Danish engineer Jens Rasmussen spent years studying how technicians and plant operators diagnose problems, starting with think-aloud recordings of electronics technicians in the early 1970s. He described two broad ways to search. In *symptomatic* search, you match the pattern of symptoms against faults you've seen before: this alarm plus that reading usually means a failed sensor. It's fast and powerful when you have experience, and useless when the fault is new.

Symptomatic search has a hidden cost. The more often a familiar pattern turns out to be right, the faster you jump to it, and the harder it becomes to notice when this time is different. It's the same shortcut that makes an experienced watchstander quick, and the same one that can send them confidently down the wrong path.

In *topographic* search, you follow the system's structure, checking points along the path and asking a simple question at each: is the signal, flow or voltage normal here? If it's good at point A and bad at point B, the fault is somewhere between them. This is slower, but it works even on faults you've never seen, because it relies on the layout of the system rather than your memory of past failures.

In practice, good troubleshooters blend the two. They use symptoms to make a smart first guess about where to look, then switch to methodical checks along the system's structure the moment the guess doesn't pan out, instead of guessing again and again.

The most efficient version of topographic search is called *half-splitting*. Instead of checking components one by one from the start, you test in the middle of the suspect section. Whichever half is bad becomes your new search area, and you split again. With 16 suspect components in a line, checking them one at a time could take up to 15 tests. Splitting in half each time isolates the fault in 4, because 16 halves to 8, 4, 2 and finally 1.

blocks.title: A structured troubleshooting loop
items: Define the problem precisely: what is wrong, what is still right, and when it started.
Use the system's functional blocks to list every section that could produce these symptoms.
Choose the next check: the one that rules out the most possibilities, adjusted for what's cheap, safe and likely.
Make the check and update the list. Cross out what's proven good.
Repeat until the fault is isolated, then confirm the repair actually fixed the original symptom.

blocks.text: Real systems are messier than a line of 16 boxes. Some checks are quick and some require tearing things apart, and some components fail far more often than others. Good troubleshooters weigh that. But the principle holds: every check should cut the search space, and you should be able to say which possibilities it eliminates before you make it.

Search strategy never overrides safety. Troubleshooting on real equipment happens inside your procedures, tag-outs and supervision. The thinking in this article is about where to look, not about skipping steps to look faster.
The trap: falling in love with the first answer

The most dangerous moment in troubleshooting is the moment you think you've found it. Medicine has studied this carefully, because a doctor diagnosing a patient is doing the same job as a technician diagnosing a fault: reasoning from symptoms to a hidden cause.

In 2005, Mark Graber and colleagues analyzed 100 cases of diagnostic error involving internists. In most cases, several things went wrong at once. Problems in the system around the doctor, such as procedures, teamwork and communication, contributed to 65 percent of the errors. Problems in the doctor's thinking contributed to 74 percent.

blocks.title: What contributed to 100 diagnostic errors
blocks.note: Most cases involved both, so the bars add to more than 100.
blocks.source: Graber, Franklin & Gordon, Archives of Internal Medicine, 2005

blocks.text: The most common single cause was *premature closure*: settling on an answer and no longer considering reasonable alternatives. And the finding that should stick with anyone who fixes things for a living: faulty or inadequate knowledge was uncommon. The doctors mostly knew enough. They stopped searching too soon, or misjudged which findings mattered.

Nuclear power learned the same lesson the hard way. Investigations after serious accidents have repeatedly found operators who acted reasonably on the picture in their heads while that picture had drifted away from what the plant was actually doing (see the article on Three Mile Island). Rasmussen's work on diagnosis was shaped by exactly that concern. A wrong model held with confidence is worse than an uncertain one, because it tells you to stop looking.

A few habits push back against fixation. Before you commit, name at least one other cause that could explain the same symptoms. Ask what you would expect to see if your theory were wrong, then go look for it. Pay special attention to the reading that doesn't fit, rather than explaining it away. And when you fix something, confirm that the original symptom is actually gone, not just that you replaced a part.
Building better models

Good mental models aren't something you have or lack. They're built, and they're built by prediction. Every time you predict what a system will do and then see what it actually does, your model gets corrected. Before you watch a start-up, a shift in lineup or a test, say to yourself what the meters should do. When they surprise you, that's the most valuable moment of the day, because it shows you exactly where your picture is wrong.

Carry more than one picture. Water and crowds are both useful for electricity; the same goes for any complex system. Learn it as a flow path, as a set of functions, and as a physical layout, because different faults are easiest to see from different angles. And organize what you learn by function: what is this part for, what feeds it, and what depends on it. That's the structure the Dutch training used, and it's what lets you split a problem in half instead of wandering through it.

Keep a fault log, even a short one in a notebook: the symptom, what you suspected first, what it actually was, and what check would have found it fastest. Over time it becomes a personal library for symptomatic search, built from your own mistakes. It also shows you your habits. If your first guess is wrong in the same direction again and again, that's your mental model telling you where it's biased.
The best troubleshooters aren't the ones who never guess wrong. They're the ones who hold every guess loosely, check it efficiently, and let the system tell them when their picture needs to change.

takeaways: You troubleshoot your mental model of a system, not the system itself; different analogies make different answers obvious.
Knowing how a system works and knowing how to search it are separate skills; train both.
Half-splitting finds a fault among 16 components in 4 checks instead of up to 15.
Premature closure, stopping at the first plausible answer, causes more errors than lack of knowledge.
Predict before you observe; every surprise shows you where your model is wrong.
