title: Why the Cook Knows Where the Valves Are
dek: Submarine qualification forces everyone aboard to learn the whole boat. The history of the dolphins, and the learning science hiding inside the qual card, explain why that works.

blocks.text: On most ships, a culinary specialist's job is food. On a submarine, the same sailor is expected to know where the damage control gear is stowed in every compartment, how to help plug and patch a leak, how to fight a fire and how to rig a space for a casualty. That is not a nice extra. According to the Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC), qualifying in submarines is a requirement of service, precisely so that everyone aboard can take immediate action when an emergency happens.

Most organizations do the opposite. They divide work into specialties, let each person go deep in one narrow lane, and trust that someone else knows the rest. The submarine force made a different bet nearly a century ago, and it built a ritual, a badge and a whole learning system around it. Looking closely at that system says a lot about how people actually learn hard things, on a boat or anywhere else.
A badge designed by a future fleet admiral

The insignia came first. In the summer of 1923, NHHC records, Captain Ernest J. King, then commanding Submarine Division Three, proposed that the Navy create a warfare device for qualified submariners and even sketched a design himself: a shield on a submarine with dolphins forward and aft of the conning tower. The Bureau of Navigation also looked at a shark-and-shield idea before hiring a Philadelphia jewelry design firm. The final design was approved on 24 March 1924. King would later lead the entire Navy as Chief of Naval Operations in World War II.

The approved device shows the bow of a surfaced O-class submarine with two dolphins resting their heads on the bow planes. Those dolphins, NHHC points out, are actually dolphinfish, better known as mahi-mahi, not the marine mammal. It is one of the oldest warfare devices in the Navy.

items.label: Year the submarine insignia was approved (24 March)
Typical time to complete submarine qualification, officer or enlisted
First enlisted woman earns silver dolphins

blocks.source: NHHC, Submarine Warfare Insignia (Dolphins), 2023

blocks.text: The way the badge was worn tells its own story about rank. From 1924 to 1947, qualified enlisted men wore an embroidered cloth version on the right sleeve, halfway between wrist and elbow, while officers wore a gold-plated metal pin on the left breast. In 1947 enlisted sailors moved the insignia to the left breast, the same position as officers. In 1950, when officers were allowed embroidered gold insignia, enlisted sailors got a silver-plated metal pin. Gold for officers and silver for enlisted remains the rule, but the badge sits in the same place on both, because it certifies the same thing.

World War II added a second pin that sat alongside the dolphins in photos of the era. NHHC describes the submarine combat patrol insignia, awarded to men who served on a submarine during a patrol in which it sank an enemy ship or did something comparable. A gold star was added for each successful patrol, and a silver star stood for five. The dolphins said you knew the boat. The patrol pin said what the boat had done with you aboard.

blocks.title: How the dolphins evolved
items: Capt. Ernest King proposes a submariner's insignia and sketches a design

blocks.text: How qualification actually works

NHHC's description of the process will be familiar to anyone who has carried a qual card. Officers and enlisted follow similar paths, and it typically takes about a year. The card lists the boat's systems, compartments and equipment. You collect a signature for each item only after you have been trained and have shown a qualified person that you understand it. When the card is full, you face an oral board. And if you transfer to a different class of submarine, you requalify on the new boat.

blocks.title: The qualification loop
items: Study a system, compartment or piece of equipment
Walk it down in person and trace how it actually works
Explain it to a qualified sailor and answer their questions
Earn the signature only when your explanation holds up
Repeat across the whole boat over many months
Pass an oral board that pulls from everything at once
Teach the next unqualified sailor what you learned

blocks.text: The requalification rule is worth pausing on. A sailor who already wears dolphins and moves to a different class of submarine does not get to assume that what he knows carries over. Valves are in different places, systems are laid out differently, and the habits that were right on the last boat can be wrong on this one. The force treats knowledge as tied to a specific machine, and makes you prove it again. That is humbling, and it is also exactly how expertise works in most fields: skills transfer, but details do not, and the details are what save you in an emergency.

On paper this looks like bureaucracy: a card, a lot of signatures, a board. In practice it is one of the best-designed learning systems most people will ever go through, and it happens to line up with several of the most solid findings in learning research.
The science hiding in the qual card

Start with the signatures. You do not get one for reading about a system. You get one for explaining it, out loud, to someone who will push back. That is retrieval practice: pulling knowledge out of your own head instead of putting it in again. In a classic 2006 study, the psychologists Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had students either reread prose passages or take recall tests on them. On a test five minutes later, rereading came out ahead. On tests two days and a week later, the students who had practiced recalling the material remembered substantially more.

The most important detail in that study is easy to miss. Rereading made students *more confident* that they would remember, even though they actually remembered less. Familiarity feels like knowledge. Anyone who has read a system manual three times and then frozen when asked to trace the flow path has felt this. A qual board exists, in part, to break that illusion before a real casualty does.

Retrieval also builds understanding, not just memory for facts. In a 2011 study in *Science*, Karpicke and Janell Blunt compared retrieval practice with building concept maps, a popular study method where students draw diagrams linking ideas. Retrieval practice produced more learning, including on questions that required making inferences, and even when the final test asked students to draw a concept map. Explaining how a system works without notes is harder than drawing a diagram with the book open. That difficulty is the point.

If studying feels smooth and easy, be suspicious. The struggle of pulling an answer out of your own memory, in front of someone who can catch your mistakes, is what makes knowledge stick and what shows you where the gaps are.

Then there is the teaching. Qualified sailors are expected to help qualify the people behind them, and research suggests that helps the teacher too. In a 2014 study, John Nestojko and colleagues told some participants they would study a passage in order to teach it to another student, while others expected a test. Nobody actually taught anyone; everyone took the test. The group expecting to teach recalled more and organized it better, especially the main points. Simply expecting to explain something changed how they learned it.

The oral board adds one more ingredient: pressure. Answering questions in front of senior people, with no notes and no time to look things up, is uncomfortable by design. It is much closer to the conditions in which the knowledge will actually be needed than a quiet written quiz would be. Practicing under conditions that resemble the real thing is a long-standing principle in training, from flight simulators to fire drills, and the board applies it to memory. The goal is not to make people sweat for its own sake. It is to make sure the first time someone has to recall a system under stress is not during a real casualty.

Finally, the timeline. A qual card is worked over months, a system at a time, with earlier material resurfacing in later walkthroughs and again at the board. That spreads practice out across time, which memory research has long shown works better than cramming. These studies were done with students and text passages, not submariners and piping diagrams, so the fit is an analogy rather than proof. But the overlap is striking: the submarine force arrived at a method by necessity that labs later confirmed by experiment.
Why a sealed hull needs generalists

The deeper idea behind qualification is about who you can count on. On the surface, a ship in trouble can sometimes get help from other ships, aircraft or shore. A submerged submarine is far more alone. The people on board are the whole response team, and an emergency will not wait for the right specialist to arrive from the other end of the boat. So the force spreads the critical knowledge across everyone.

blocks.title: Two ways to organize knowledge

left.head: Specialist-only organization
items: Each person knows one area deeply
Fast and efficient when things are normal
Fragile if a key person is missing
Problems wait for the right expert

right.head: Qualified-crew organization
items: Everyone knows the whole system at a working level
Slower and costlier to train
Resilient when someone is hurt or busy
Whoever is closest can act first

blocks.text: Software engineers have a darkly funny name for the risk the submarine force is avoiding. They call it the bus factor: how many people on a team would have to be hit by a bus before the project could not continue. If the answer is one, the project is fragile no matter how talented that one person is. Qualification is a deliberate decision to push the bus factor for critical knowledge as high as possible, even though it costs every new sailor a year of extra study.

The same logic applies to anything built by a small team. If only one partner understands how a game's code, economy or save system works, the project is one deployment or one burnout away from stalling. A simple version of a qual card, a short list of the systems that matter and a rule that each one has to be explained to the other person before it counts as understood, costs an afternoon and can save a project.
Who gets to wear them

Because the dolphins certify knowledge rather than job title, their history also tracks who the Navy has allowed to serve under the sea. Separate versions were created for medical officers in 1943, engineering officers in 1950 and supply officers in 1964. Sailors who loved the diesel era even made unofficial badges marked "DBF," for "diesel boats forever."

The Navy lifted its ban on women serving on submarines in 2010. In June 2012, Lieutenant Britta Christianson, a supply officer on USS *Ohio*'s Gold crew, became the first woman supply corps officer to qualify. That December, three women unrestricted line officers, Lieutenants (junior grade) Marquette Leveque, Amber Cowan and Jennifer Noonan, earned their dolphins. In 2016 Chief Culinary Specialist Dominique Saavedra, who qualified aboard *Ohio*, became the first enlisted woman to wear silver dolphins. Fittingly, the first enlisted woman to qualify was a cook, the job this article started with.

The badge has hardly changed in a century, and that is part of its weight. A sailor pinning on dolphins today joins the same line as the World War II crews who wore them on their sleeves. What connects them is not a rating or a rank. It is the fact that each of them, at some point, stood in front of a board and proved they knew the whole boat.

That method is portable. Whatever you want to learn next, whether it is a programming language, a game engine or how a small business handles its money, the qual card offers a template: break the subject into systems, explain each one aloud to someone who can catch your mistakes, spread the work over weeks instead of a weekend, and finish by teaching it to someone else. It is slower and more uncomfortable than watching another tutorial. It also works far better.

takeaways: Qualification is required so that anyone aboard can act immediately in an emergency, not just the specialist.
The dolphins were proposed by Capt. Ernest King in 1923, approved in 1924, and show dolphinfish (mahi-mahi), not mammals.
Qual signatures and oral boards are retrieval practice, which beats rereading for long-term memory even though rereading feels better.
Expecting to teach improves how you learn; helping qualify others strengthens your own knowledge.
Raise your project's "bus factor": make sure more than one person can explain every critical system.

title: The Day an Aircraft Carrier Powered a City
dek: From one dynamo on a wooden frigate to warships that run everything off a single electric bus, the Navy's 140-year love-hate relationship with electricity, and why it keeps coming back.

blocks.text: In December 1929, the city of Tacoma, Washington, was running out of electricity. A drought had dropped the lake behind its main hydroelectric dam so low that the water fell below the intakes. The city asked the federal government for help, and the help that arrived was an aircraft carrier.

USS *Lexington* steamed in from the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard in Bremerton. Crews ran heavy cables from the ship into the city grid. From December 17 to January 16, 1930, the carrier's generators fed Tacoma, delivering a total of 4,520,960 kilowatt-hours until rain and melting snow refilled the reservoir. A warship had become the power plant for a city.

That could only happen because *Lexington* was an unusual ship. Her propellers were not turned by steam turbines through gears, like most warships of her day. They were turned by electric motors, fed by giant turbine-driven generators. She was, in effect, a floating power station that happened to have a flight deck. The story of how she got that way, and why the Navy kept abandoning and then rediscovering the idea, is the story of the electrician's trade at sea.

December 17, 1929 to January 16, 1930
Average output that works out to, around the clock

blocks.source: Wikipedia, USS Lexington (CV-2); average calculated from the total and dates

blocks.text: One dynamo on a wooden ship

The Navy's electrical history starts modestly, in the summer of 1883, aboard USS *Trenton*, a wooden-hulled steam frigate. Workers installed a dynamo, an engine to spin it and a set of electric lamps. *Trenton* became the first US Navy ship lit by electricity. The experiment worked well enough that electric lighting went into the first ships of the new steel Navy that was being built in the 1880s.

That same year, 1883, the Navy created a rating called Electrician. It did not last: it was disestablished in 1884. In 1898, as ships filled up with more and more electrical equipment, it came back for good. In 1921 the rating took the name it still has, Electrician's Mate. Every EM and EMN today is the descendant of a job that the Navy started, cancelled and then decided it could not live without.

*Trenton* herself met a dramatic end. In March 1889 she was anchored in the harbor at Apia, Samoa, one of thirteen ships there, when a cyclone struck. *Trenton* was wrecked, along with several other warships. Electric lights could not help her against wind and sea. But the idea she carried had already spread through the fleet.

blocks.text: The speed problem

To see why anyone would want electric propulsion, you need to know one awkward fact about steam turbines. They are most efficient spinning very fast, thousands of revolutions per minute. Ship propellers work best turning slowly, around a hundred. Something has to connect a fast machine to a slow one.

The usual answer is a reduction gear: a big, heavy, precisely machined set of gears that trades speed for torque. The alternative, championed by a General Electric engineer named William Le Roy Emmet, was to skip the gears entirely. Let the turbine spin a generator as fast as it likes. Send the electricity through cables to a motor on the propeller shaft, and let the motor turn at whatever speed the propeller wants.

There is a catch, and it explains everything that follows. Each conversion, from spinning shaft to electricity and back to spinning shaft, loses a little energy, and generators, cables and motors take up weight and space. Electric drive only wins when the flexibility it buys is worth more than those losses.

The Navy tried Emmet's idea on a coal-carrying ship, the collier *Jupiter*, commissioned in April 1913. A single Curtis turbine drove an alternator at 2,000 rpm and 2,200 volts. That electricity fed two motors, each connected directly to a propeller shaft, turning at about 110 rpm and pushing the ship at 14 knots. The electric machinery weighed 156 tons, against 280 tons for the conventional engines in her sister ship *Cyclops*, a saving of more than 40 percent. *Cyclops* was the collier that would later vanish without a trace in the First World War.

blocks.title: Propulsion machinery weight, sister colliers
blocks.source: Wikipedia, USS Langley (CV-1), citing the ships' design data

blocks.text: *Jupiter* had an interesting career. In 1914 she became the first vessel to pass through the Panama Canal from the Pacific to the Atlantic. In 1920 she was converted into the Navy's first aircraft carrier and renamed *Langley*. So the first US carrier was also the first US turbo-electric ship.
Battleships, carriers and a reversal

Encouraged, the Navy put turbo-electric drive into its newest battleship. USS *New Mexico*, commissioned in May 1918, was the first battleship with turbo-electric transmission, rated at 27,500 shaft horsepower. Then came the carriers *Lexington* and *Saratoga*, converted from unfinished battlecruisers in the 1920s, *Lexington* had four turbo-generators rated at 35,200 kilowatts each, feeding eight 22,500-horsepower propulsion motors. On trials in 1928 *Lexington* produced almost 203,000 shaft horsepower and made more than 34 knots.

Those numbers put the Tacoma episode in perspective. Four generators of 35,200 kilowatts add up to about 140 megawatts of capacity. Tacoma's month of emergency power averaged roughly 6 megawatts. The carrier kept a city running on less than a twentieth of what she could generate, because machinery built to push a 33-knot warship through the sea dwarfed what Tacoma needed from her. She also carried six smaller 750-kilowatt generators just for the ship's own lighting and equipment.

It is worth pausing on what that meant for the crew. A turbo-electric ship turned the electricians from the people who looked after the lights into the people who made the ship move. The switchboard was no longer an accessory to the engine room. It *was* the engine room.

And yet the idea retreated. During a modernization between 1931 and 1933, *New Mexico*'s turbo-electric plant was ripped out and replaced with conventional geared turbines. Most later American warships used geared turbines instead. A turbo-electric plant tends to be heavier than a simple geared one, and for a ship whose main job is to go fast, that was hard to justify. For decades, turbo-electric warships were a curiosity of the 1920s.

blocks.title: Rated propulsion power of electric-drive Navy ships
blocks.note: Zumwalt's figure is total generator output, shared between propulsion and everything else on board.
blocks.source: Wikipedia: USS Tullibee (SSN-597), USS New Mexico (BB-40), Zumwalt-class destroyer, USS Lexington (CV-2)

blocks.text: The quiet idea under the sea

Electric drive came back for a reason that had nothing to do with weight: noise. Reduction gears hum. Gear teeth meshing thousands of times a second make sound that travels a long way through water, and for a submarine, sound is life or death.

In 1956 the Chief of Naval Operations, Admiral Arleigh Burke, asked the National Academy of Sciences to study future submarine needs. The study, called Project Nobska, stressed deep-diving, very quiet boats with long-range sonar. One result was USS *Tullibee*, commissioned in November 1960: a small nuclear attack submarine whose reactor steam drove a turbo-generator, with an electric motor turning the shaft. Her rated power was a modest 2,500 horsepower. Over her career she dove and surfaced about 730 times and steamed roughly 325,000 nautical miles.

The Navy then tried the idea at full size. USS *Glenard P. Lipscomb*, commissioned in December 1974, was built to test whether turbo-electric drive could make a full-sized attack boat quieter and safer; one argument was that reversing an electric motor gives instant reverse thrust. The Tullibee plant had to be scaled up about six times, which made her a 6,400-ton, 365-foot boat, bigger than comparable submarines with conventional drive, and by later accounts she was underpowered and maintenance-hungry. She was decommissioned in 1990 after less than 16 years, one of the shortest careers of any US nuclear submarine.

Electric drive kept losing for the same reason: the electrical hardware of each era was too heavy or too fragile at the power levels warships needed. Each time the hardware improved, the idea came back.
Everything on one bus

A big part of what changed in the last few decades is power electronics: compact, efficient devices that can convert and control huge amounts of electrical power. That made a different design philosophy possible, usually called integrated electric propulsion. Instead of one set of machinery for moving the ship and another for making electricity, you generate all of it as electricity and send it wherever it is needed.

The Zumwalt-class destroyers are the clearest example. Their two main gas turbines, each about 35 megawatts, drive generators rather than shafts. The resulting electricity, up to about 78 megawatts in total, feeds electric motors on the propeller shafts and every other system aboard, from the ship's computing network to its automated fire-fighting and pipe-rupture isolation systems, which were part of a design meant to need a smaller crew. At one point the Navy considered putting a railgun on one of the class, because a ship that can shift tens of megawatts from propulsion to a weapon can do things a geared ship cannot.

The Columbia-class ballistic missile submarines, now being built by Electric Boat in Groton to replace the Ohio class, will also use electric drive, according to public Navy and Congressional Research Service descriptions. The reactor will still make steam and the steam will still spin turbines, but the turbines will turn generators, and an electric motor will turn the propulsor instead of reduction gears. The stated reasons are lower life-cycle cost and a smaller acoustic signature. Tullibee's idea, sixty years on, is going into the most important submarines the Navy will build this century.

blocks.title: Two ways to connect a turbine to a propeller

left.head: Geared drive
items: Turbine and propeller linked mechanically through reduction gears
Proven, efficient, well understood
Gear noise is a constant concern for submarines
Separate generators needed for ship's electrical load

right.head: Electric drive
items: Turbine spins a generator; a motor turns the shaft
Each machine runs at its own best speed
No main reduction gears to hum
One electrical plant can feed propulsion, sensors and weapons

blocks.text: The trade that kept growing

Step back and the arc is striking. In 1883 the Navy's entire electrical plant on its first lit ship was a single dynamo and some lamps, and the job of looking after it was so new the Navy could not decide whether it needed a rating for it. A century and a half later, the question for the newest warships is not whether the electricians run part of the plant, but whether there is any part of the plant they do not run.

The training reflects that. The modern nuclear electrician's path runs through roughly six months of EMN "A" school in Goose Creek, South Carolina, six months of nuclear power school and six months at a prototype, an operating training reactor in Goose Creek or Ballston Spa, New York, before a sailor reports to a boat or carrier. That is a year and a half of schooling for a rating that, in 1884, the Navy briefly decided it did not need at all.

There is a broader lesson in the way electric drive kept failing and returning. Good ideas are often not wrong, just early. Emmet's logic, let each machine run at its best speed and connect them with wires, was sound in 1913. What it lacked was hardware light, efficient and reliable enough to beat the alternative at scale. Every generation of engineers who tried it again was not repeating a mistake. They were checking whether the world had caught up.

That is worth keeping in mind for any idea you have shelved, whether it is a game mechanic that did not work on your first engine, a business that did not make sense with the tools you had, or a skill you dropped because it felt out of reach. The useful question is not just whether it failed. It is what, specifically, made it fail, and whether that thing has changed.
When an old idea failed, write down why. If the reason was the technology or the timing rather than the logic, put a date on when to check again.

takeaways: USS Trenton got the Navy's first electric lights in 1883; the Electrician rating dates to 1883 and 1898, and became Electrician's Mate in 1921.
Turbo-electric drive solves a speed mismatch: turbines like thousands of rpm, propellers about a hundred.
The carrier Lexington's generators powered Tacoma for a month in 1929-30, about 4.5 million kWh.
Electric drive was dropped from battleships and tried and shelved on submarines, then revived for Zumwalt and Columbia as power electronics improved.
Ideas that fail for reasons of hardware or timing are worth revisiting when those reasons change.

title: The Schoolteacher Who Built the Submarine Force
dek: John Holland's designs were called unworkable, stolen by his own backers and finally bought for $150,000. Then the company with his name on the patents moved on without him.

blocks.text: In the winter of 1873, a recently arrived Irish immigrant slipped on an icy street in Boston and broke his leg. He was a former teacher with weak health, no money and no engineering degree. Stuck in a hospital bed with nothing to do, he pulled out an idea he had been sketching for years and started refining it: a boat that could run under the sea.

Twenty-seven years later the United States Navy bought that idea for $150,000. The date it did so, April 11, 1900, is still marked as the birthday of the US Submarine Force. Every boat in the fleet today, including the one you may be reading this on, sits at the end of an unbroken line that starts with John Philip Holland's sixth attempt.

Holland's story is usually told as an inventor's triumph. It is more interesting than that. It is about how long it takes for a correct idea to be accepted, how many times it has to fail in public first, and what happens to the person who had the idea once it starts making money.
A math teacher with a strange hobby

Holland was born in 1841 in a coastguard cottage in Liscannor, County Clare, on the west coast of Ireland. He grew up in an Irish-speaking area and learned English properly only at school. He joined the Irish Christian Brothers, a teaching order, and spent years teaching in schools around Ireland, including a stint as a mathematics teacher. Ill health forced him out of the order in 1873, and that same year he emigrated to the United States.

After the broken leg and a brief job at an engineering firm, he went back to teaching, this time at a Catholic school in Paterson, New Jersey. In 1875 he sent his submarine design to the US Navy. The Navy turned it down as unworkable. For most people that would have been the end of a hobby. For Holland it was the start of a 25-year loop: design, build, fail, learn, repeat.

Funding came from an unusual place. The Fenian Brotherhood, Irish-American revolutionaries who wanted a weapon to use against the British Navy, paid for his work, enough that he could quit teaching. In 1878 he demonstrated a small prototype, Holland I. In 1881 he launched a larger boat that a New York newspaper nicknamed the *Fenian Ram*.

blocks.title: Six boats to get one right

Holland I, a small prototype, is demonstrated
Fenian Ram launched, funded by Irish revolutionaries

Holland Torpedo Boat Company founded
Holland VI launched on May 17

blocks.text: The boat that wanted to float

The *Fenian Ram* already contained Holland's central insight. Most would-be submarine builders of the era tried to sink their boats by flooding tanks until the boat lost its buoyancy and went down, a bit like a stone. Holland did something different. His boat kept a slight positive buoyancy, meaning it always wanted to float, and used angled horizontal fins near the stern to drive itself under while moving forward, the way a fish or a torpedo does.

That choice matters more than it sounds. A boat that dives by losing buoyancy is balanced on a knife edge: take on a bit too much water and it keeps going down. A boat that dives by driving itself under has a built-in safety. If the engine stops, it drifts back up. The *Ram* also carried a compressed-air gun firing a dynamite projectile through a bow tube with an inner and outer door, the same basic logic as a modern torpedo tube: load from inside, shut the inner door, open the outer, fire, reverse the sequence.

Then the project collapsed for a reason that had nothing to do with engineering. The Fenians quarrelled among themselves and with Holland about money, and in November 1883 a group of them simply took the *Ram* and a smaller test boat. The smaller boat sank by accident in the East River. The Fenians towed the *Ram* to New Haven, Connecticut, and discovered that nobody but Holland knew how to operate it. He refused to help. The boat ended up sitting in a shed for decades. It survives today in the Paterson Museum.

The Fenians owned the hardware but not the knowledge. A machine nobody can run is just a very expensive object. The same thing is true of a reactor plant, a codebase or a game project whose only expert leaves.
Holland VI: getting the combination right

Through the 1880s and 1890s Holland kept building. One boat was financed by an Army officer, Edmund Zalinski; another, his fifth design, named *Plunger*, was launched in 1897 and tried out but never accepted by the Navy. In 1896 he formed the Holland Torpedo Boat Company, and on May 17, 1897, he launched his sixth design, built at Lewis Nixon's Crescent Shipyard in Elizabeth, New Jersey.

Holland VI was small even by the standards of the day: about 54 feet long and 10 feet across, displacing around 64 tons, with a crew of seven according to the Navy's official ship history. What made her important was the combination of parts. She was the first submarine able to run submerged for a meaningful distance, and the first to pair a gasoline engine for running on the surface with an electric motor and battery for running underwater.

That pairing is the whole trick of the pre-nuclear submarine. An internal combustion engine needs air, so it can only run on the surface. An electric motor does not, but it needs stored energy. Holland's answer was to use the gasoline engine both to drive the boat on the surface and to recharge a 66-cell battery, then switch to the electric motor to dive. The same basic split, diesel on the surface, battery below, would define submarines for the next half century, until the reactor on *Nautilus* removed the need to come up for air at all.

blocks.text: The specs look tiny now. Published figures vary between sources, but the boat made roughly 6 knots on the surface and about 5 submerged, with a submerged range of around 30 nautical miles and a maximum diving depth of about 75 feet. Her armament was a single reloadable 18-inch torpedo tube with three torpedoes, plus a dynamite gun in the bow. She was less a warship than a proof that the concept could work.
Proof, then purchase, then a fleet

The Navy did not buy Holland VI on faith. She went through trials before she was accepted, and only after that, on April 11, 1900, did the government pay $150,000 for her. She was commissioned as *Holland* on October 12, 1900, at Newport, Rhode Island. Strictly speaking she was never called SS-1 while in service; that hull-number system was introduced in 1920, and historians apply it to her after the fact.

Her real job turned out to be teaching. She spent most of her career at Annapolis, training midshipmen and the officers and enlisted men who would crew the boats that came next. Her success led directly to orders for more Holland-type boats, the Plunger class, which became the Navy's first real submarine fleet. The Royal Navy's first submarine was a Holland design too, and the first five submarines of the Imperial Japanese Navy were modified versions of it.

blocks.title: How deep the early boats could go
blocks.note: Rated diving depths for Holland and the Plunger class; G-1's figure is a test-depth record.
blocks.source: Wikipedia: USS Holland (SS-1), USS Plunger (SS-2), Simon Lake

blocks.text: Holland was not the only American trying. Simon Lake, a New Jersey engineer, built the *Argonaut* in the late 1890s and in 1901 the *Protector*, which used four diving planes to stay level while changing depth rather than tilting nose-down. The Navy accepted neither. Lake, without Holland's financial backing, sold *Protector* to Russia in 1904 and spent years designing boats for European navies before founding his own company in 1912. Its first boat for the US Navy, G-1, set a depth record of 256 feet that November. Lake's level-diving idea, and his diver lock-out chamber, were good ideas that simply arrived without the money behind them.
When the money men arrive

Here is the part of the story that rarely makes the plaque. The firm that sold Holland VI to the Navy was not really Holland's anymore. Building boats that the Navy might or might not buy is expensive, so in 1899 the business was reorganized as the Electric Boat Company, with the financier Isaac Rice as president and Elihu Frost as vice president and chief financial officer. Holland had the patents and the know-how. They had the capital and the control.

Accounts of what came next differ in detail, and some writers have argued that Holland's partners, such as the shipyard team at Crescent, deserve more credit than the lone-genius version allows. What is clear is that the company soon mattered more than the man. Electric Boat licensed Holland designs to Britain, Japan and Russia, grew into the defense giant General Dynamics, and is still building submarines in Groton, Connecticut, today. Holland's name stayed on more than twenty patents, among them, late in life, one for a flying machine. His name is not on the company.

blocks.title: Two ways to own an idea

left.head: What Holland had
items: The core design insight
Decades of hands-on failures
Patents on the hardware
Knowledge nobody else had

right.head: What decided who controlled it
items: Money to build boats before anyone ordered them
A company structure with someone else in charge
Patience to wait for Navy contracts
Willingness to sell the design abroad

blocks.text: The ship herself had a quieter fate than her name deserved. She was decommissioned in 1905, struck from the Navy list in 1910 and sold in 1913 to a Philadelphia scrap dealer for $100, who had to post a $5,000 bond promising she would be broken up rather than used. Instead her stripped hull drifted through a series of owners and exhibitions, including a science fair in the Bronx in 1917, before she was finally scrapped in 1932. The first submarine of the US Navy did not survive to become a museum piece.
Six weeks too early

John Holland died in Newark, New Jersey, on August 12, 1914, aged 73. By one count he had spent 56 of those years working on submersibles. Europe had gone to war less than two weeks earlier, and many naval officers still regarded submarines as a curiosity.

On September 22, about six weeks after his death, the small German submarine U-9 found three British armored cruisers patrolling the southern North Sea. In less than an hour, reloading her tubes while submerged, she sank all three. 1,459 British sailors died. Admiralty officials who had dismissed submarines as toys stopped saying so. The man who had spent four decades arguing for the weapon did not live to see the argument settled.

That gap between being right and being recognized is the thread worth pulling. Holland was right in 1875, when the Navy called his design unworkable. He was right in 1881, when his backers stole a boat they could not run. He was right in 1897, and the Navy still took three years to buy. What finally made the case was not his reasoning but a working machine that people could watch dive, surface and fire.

Ideas rarely win on the strength of the argument. They win when someone can see the thing working. If you are building something, a game, a channel, a business, a version people can actually use will persuade more people than any pitch.

There is a second lesson, and it is less comfortable. The skills that make someone a great builder are not the skills that keep them in control of what they build. Holland could solve problems of buoyancy and propulsion that defeated better-funded rivals. He could not stop the company with his designs from being run by people whose priorities were capital and contracts. If you ever start something with partners or investors, it is worth deciding early, in writing, who owns what and who decides what. Holland's story suggests that the person with the idea should not assume the idea protects them.

Every April 11, submarine crews mark the birthday of their force. It is worth remembering that the date is not the day a submarine was invented, or first dove, or first fired a shot. It is the day a government finally agreed to pay for one, 25 years after a schoolteacher in a hospital bed decided to try anyway.

takeaways: Holland's design was rejected in 1875 and bought in 1900; persistence through public failure was most of the job.
His key idea was a boat that stayed slightly buoyant and drove itself under, so it floated up if power failed.
Gasoline on the surface, battery below: Holland VI set the pattern for submarines until nuclear power.
Owning the hardware is not the same as owning the knowledge, and owning the idea is not the same as controlling the company.
A working prototype persuades people in a way that arguments rarely do.

title: Eight Men at Their Stations
dek: The first submarine to sink a warship never came home. When she was raised 136 years later, her crew was still sitting in place, and the fight over what killed them turned into a lesson in how to solve a mystery.

blocks.text: When archaeologists finally cleared the silt out of the submarine *H. L. Hunley* in the early 2000s, they found something that did not fit any of the stories people had been telling for a century. The skeletons of all eight crewmen were at their stations along the hand crank that drove the propeller. Nobody was piled at the hatches. Nobody seemed to have tried to get out. The forward hatch was closed, and the aft one was still locked.

Whatever killed them had done it fast, or quietly, or both. Figuring out which turned into a scientific argument that is still running. It is worth following, because the way investigators narrowed down the answer is the same way you troubleshoot anything, from a tripped breaker to a bug in your code.
The fish boat

*Hunley* was built in Mobile, Alabama, in 1863 by private backers for the Confederacy, and named for one of them, Horace Hunley. She was about 40 feet long and very narrow, with a hull only around four feet across, so cramped that the crew sat in a row and turned a crank by hand to drive the propeller. The commander stood forward, looking out through a small conning tower. The two hatches were about 16 by 21 inches, barely big enough to squeeze a body through.

She was shipped by rail to Charleston, South Carolina, in August 1863, to attack the Union ships blockading the harbor. She then proceeded to kill her own crews. On August 29, during preparations for a test dive, her commander apparently stepped on the lever controlling the diving planes while a hatch was still open. She went under and five men drowned. On October 15, during a practice attack, she failed to surface and all eight men aboard died, among them Horace Hunley himself. Both times she was raised and put back into service.

blocks.title: Men lost in each sinking of the Hunley
blocks.note: Twenty-one men in all. The Union ship Housatonic also lost five men in the 1864 attack.
blocks.source: Wikipedia, H. L. Hunley (submarine), citing Confederate and Union records

blocks.text: Think about what it took to volunteer for the third crew. Every man knew the boat had killed thirteen people in two months. They went anyway, under Lieutenant George Dixon. Dixon carried a bent $20 gold coin. At the Battle of Shiloh in 1862 a bullet had struck it in his pocket, probably saving his leg and possibly his life, and a forensic examination later found a healed wound on his hip bone. When the coin was found beside his remains in 2002, the inscription he had engraved on it was still legible: "My life Preserver."
One night, one attack

The weapon was a spar torpedo: a copper cylinder holding about 135 pounds of black powder, mounted on the end of a long pole sticking out from the bow. The idea was to push the charge against an enemy hull and set it off. It was less a torpedo in the modern sense than a bomb on a stick.

Even the delivery method was a product of the earlier disasters. The original plan had been to dive under a target while towing a floating charge, which risked the line fouling or the charge drifting back onto the submarine. After Horace Hunley's death, the Confederate commander in Charleston, General P. G. T. Beauregard, ordered that the boat should no longer attack while fully submerged. A spar angled down from the bow let her place the charge below an enemy's waterline while running at or near the surface, the same method used by the small Confederate torpedo boats called Davids.

On the night of February 17, 1864, *Hunley* attacked USS *Housatonic*, a 1,240-ton wooden steam sloop on blockade duty about five miles off Charleston. The charge went off against the Union ship's hull at about 8:45 p.m. *Housatonic* sank in about three minutes, taking five of her crew with her. It was the first time a submarine had ever sunk an enemy warship.

*Hunley* did not come back. Soldiers ashore reported seeing the agreed signal, and a lookout on the sinking *Housatonic* said he saw a blue light on the water afterward. Then nothing. The boat stayed lost for more than 130 years. She was located in 1995, though who found her first became its own long dispute: an underwater archaeologist said he had found her in 1970, the novelist Clive Cussler's team announced a find in 1995, and the two sides ended up suing each other. She was raised on August 8, 2000. Since then she has been under conservation in North Charleston.

blocks.title: From the attack to the evidence

Wreck located off Charleston

blocks.text: Eliminating suspects

For a long time the leading stories were dramatic ones. Maybe small-arms fire from *Housatonic*'s crew had damaged the submarine enough to let in water: the lucky-shot theory. Maybe the crew had run out of air while waiting on the bottom for the tide to turn. Maybe a Union warship rushing to help *Housatonic* had run her down. Each story explained some facts. The question was whether it explained all of them.

The ramming theory died quickly: when the boat was raised, there was no damage of the kind a collision would have caused. The other clues piled up from the conservation work. The crew were at their stations with no skeletal injuries. In 2008 researchers reported that the bilge pump had not been set to remove water from the crew compartment. In 2018 they reported that the keel blocks, iron ballast weights that the crew could release from inside to make the boat shoot to the surface in an emergency, had never been released. Whatever happened, the crew did not fight it.

Rachel Lance, then a biomedical engineer specializing in blast injury at Duke University, took a different approach: test each theory against physics. With colleagues, she published a series of papers that treated the *Hunley* like a forensic case.

blocks.title: How the Duke team tested the theories
items: Suffocation: calculate how fast eight working men would use up oxygen and build up carbon dioxide in the boat's air volume.
Lucky shot: fire Civil War-type bullets at cast iron, check historical tests, and model how the tide would have carried a damaged boat.
Blast: set off scaled black-powder charges underwater near a model hull and measure the pressure wave inside.
Compare each result with what was actually found: crew seated, hatches shut, pump not set, ballast still attached.

blocks.text: The suffocation study, published in 2016, found that the crew would have had at least ten minutes between feeling uncomfortable from carbon dioxide and being in danger of passing out from lack of oxygen. That is plenty of time to notice something is wrong and try to surface, release ballast or open a hatch. The *Hunley* had no way to scrub carbon dioxide or make oxygen; her crew lived on the air sealed in with them, which is exactly why the calculation was possible. On a modern submarine, keeping that same air breathable for months is a full-time engineering job. Men slowly suffocating do not usually sit quietly at their cranks. The lucky-shot study found that bullets of the era were unlikely to have breached the iron in the way the theory needed, and that the tides did not fit a slow leak carrying the boat to where she was found.

That left the blast. Conservators had already reported in 2013 that the torpedo had been fixed directly to the end of the spar, not released and set off from a distance. That meant the charge exploded less than five meters, about 16 feet, from the submarine's bow. In their 2017 paper the Duke team ran scaled underwater explosions and measured how a blast wave passes through a thin hull. Their argument was that the pressure wave would flex the iron, sending a strong secondary wave through the air inside the crew compartment. Air-filled organs like the lungs are especially vulnerable to that kind of wave.

items.label: Black powder in Hunley's torpedo
Distance between the charge and the submarine
Each crewman's calculated chance of surviving the blast wave inside the hull

blocks.source: Lance et al., PLOS ONE, 2017

blocks.text: If they were right, the crew died, or were fatally injured, within moments of the explosion, from their own weapon, without the hull being breached at all. The submarine then drifted with the current and slowly filled with water. That would explain the seated skeletons, the shut hatches, the unset pump and the unreleased ballast in one stroke.
Not case closed

It would be neat to end there, and many news stories in 2017 did. But the blast theory is not universally accepted. Archaeologists with the Naval History and Heritage Command, which has been involved in the *Hunley* project since the recovery, have disputed the Duke team's conclusions. The kind of injury the Duke team proposed mainly damages soft tissue like the lungs, which did not survive 136 years underwater, so it cannot be confirmed directly from skeletons. Scale models and calculations, however careful, involve assumptions about the real boat that can be argued over.

That is not a weakness of the investigation. It is what honest investigation looks like. The ramming theory was falsified by the hull. The suffocation and lucky-shot theories were made much less likely by calculation and experiment. The blast theory fits the evidence best so far but rests partly on modeling rather than direct proof. A good investigator holds it as the leading explanation, not the final word, and says so.

blocks.title: Strong evidence versus a good story

left.head: Good story
items: Explains the most dramatic fact
Easy to picture
Hard to test
Survives by being repeated

right.head: Strong explanation
items: Explains every fact, including the boring ones
Makes predictions you can check
Rules out its rivals by test, not by vote
Says how sure it is

blocks.text: What the Hunley teaches a submariner

There is a hard engineering lesson in this boat. Her designers solved the problem they were focused on, getting a charge against an enemy hull, and badly underestimated the one right next to it: what the charge would do to them. A weapon whose safe distance is longer than its delivery pole is not a weapon, it is a gamble. The fix came fast. Self-propelled torpedoes, which carried the charge away from the boat under their own power, were already being developed in the 1860s, and by the time the US Navy bought its first real submarine in 1900, USS *Holland*, she carried Whitehead torpedoes fired from a tube. Putting distance between the boat and the bang became the first rule of submarine weapons. Modern submarine design and safety culture, from shock testing to the SUBSAFE program born after *Thresher*, exist because the sea has repeatedly punished that kind of narrow focus.

There is also a lesson about troubleshooting that applies far beyond submarines. The *Hunley* investigators did not argue about which story felt right. They listed every observation, especially the boring ones like a pump setting and a ballast block, and asked which explanation accounted for all of them. They tested each idea in a way that could have proved it wrong. When you are hunting a fault in an electrical system, chasing a bug in a script or trying to work out why your sleep is wrecked, the same moves work: write down all the symptoms, list every plausible cause, test the cheapest ones first, and do not fall in love with the most exciting answer.

In April 2004, the eight men of *Hunley*'s last crew were buried in Charleston. A Smithsonian physical anthropologist, Douglas Owsley, had studied their remains; chemical signatures in their teeth showed that four were born in America and four in Europe. Tens of thousands of people came. Whatever you think of the cause they served, they climbed into a boat that had already killed two crews, did what they set out to do, and stayed at their posts. The science says it was probably over for them before they knew it. The argument about exactly how will go on, which is the right outcome for a question the evidence has not fully settled.
When something fails, list every observation before you pick a theory, especially the boring ones. The explanation you want is the one that fits all of them, not the one that makes the best story.

takeaways: Hunley killed 21 of her own men in three sinkings and was the first submarine to sink a warship, USS Housatonic, in 1864.
Her final crew was found at their stations, hatches shut, pump not set and ballast still attached: they did not try to escape.
Tests made suffocation and a lucky bullet unlikely; the leading theory is that the blast wave from their own torpedo, under 5 m away, killed them.
Navy archaeologists dispute that conclusion; the honest answer is a leading explanation, not proof.
Good troubleshooting explains every observation, tests ideas in ways that could prove them wrong, and resists the most exciting story.

title: Nine Days Over the Kursk
dek: A submarine sank in water shallower than its own length, at least 23 men survived the blasts, and nobody reached them. The reasons were set long before that day.

blocks.text: At 11:29 in the morning on August 12, 2000, seismometers in Norway picked up a small jolt from the Barents Sea. Two minutes and fourteen seconds later they picked up a second one, and this one was not small. Stations thousands of kilometers away recorded it. Seismologists who studied the traces later estimated that the second event was roughly 18 times the size of the first, the kind of energy you get when several torpedo warheads go off at once.

The source was the *Kursk*, one of the largest attack submarines ever built: 155 meters long, nine watertight compartments, two reactors, 118 men aboard. She came to rest on the seabed at 108 meters, which is shallower than the length of the boat itself. For a submarine designed to operate far deeper, that is practically a parking lot.

And yet over the next nine days, nobody got in. The story of the *Kursk* is usually told as a tragedy of bad luck and worse politics. It is both. But underneath it is a harder lesson that applies to any crew on any boat: the outcome of a casualty is mostly decided years before the casualty happens.

items.label: Gap between the first and second explosions
Depth where the Kursk came to rest
Men who survived the blasts and gathered aft

blocks.source: Science News, 2001; Kursk submarine disaster (Wikipedia summary of official findings)

blocks.text: Two blasts, two minutes apart

The *Kursk* was taking part in the first major Russian naval exercise in more than a decade. She was near periscope depth, preparing to fire a practice torpedo. That torpedo used **high-test peroxide** (HTP), a concentrated hydrogen peroxide that decomposes violently into steam and oxygen when it meets the wrong material. It is an attractive fuel because it lets a torpedo run fast and far without carrying air. It is an unforgiving one for exactly the same reason.

Russia's official investigation concluded in 2002 that HTP leaked from the practice torpedo in the forward torpedo tube, apparently through a faulty weld, and set off the first explosion. The torpedo's manufacturer disputed that finding. Either way, the first blast started a fire in the torpedo room. A bit over two minutes later, with the boat already headed for the bottom, the fire reached the warheads of the combat torpedoes stowed nearby. That second detonation tore open the bow and killed almost everyone in the forward compartments within seconds.

HTP was not a mystery hazard. Britain had experimented with it in the 1950s and dropped it after an HTP torpedo exploded aboard HMS *Sidon* in 1955. Russia kept using it for decades. After the *Kursk*, it pulled this torpedo type from service. A known hazard, tolerated because it had not killed anyone lately, is one of the oldest patterns in accident history. Engineers have a name for it: the normalization of deviance.

blocks.title: What was said versus what the evidence showed

left.head: Early official explanations
items: A collision with a foreign submarine
A leftover World War II mine
The crew died within minutes
Weather and conditions blocked rescue

right.head: What investigators later found
items: A leaking HTP practice torpedo started the chain
A second, far larger blast came from the boat's own warheads
At least 23 men were alive for hours afterward
Russian rescue vehicles repeatedly failed to seal on the hatch

blocks.text: The ninth compartment

The reactors and heavy machinery in the middle of the boat soaked up much of the blast. Behind them, men from the sixth, seventh and eighth compartments moved aft to the ninth, where the escape hatch was. A young officer, Lieutenant Captain Dmitry Kolesnikov, wrote a note in the early afternoon, well over an hour after the explosions. It said 23 people were gathered in the ninth compartment and that none of them could reach the surface. A later, barely legible entry, timed around 3:15 p.m., included the line that he was writing blind. The power was gone.

The note was found in his uniform pocket when divers recovered his body that October. Until then, Russian officials had said the crew died almost instantly. The note made that impossible to keep saying. It also raised the question that has haunted the case ever since: if men were alive, could they have been saved?

The note also hinted at how close escape might have seemed. According to the parts that were released, two or three men had planned to try leaving through the after hatch, and the attempt failed. Escaping from a hundred meters is survivable with the right equipment, training and a working trunk. It is not survivable with a hatch you cannot open. After that, Kolesnikov wrote, the men prepared themselves for what was coming.

Russia's prosecutor general gave the official answer in 2002: all of the sailors were dead within about eight hours. Investigators believed the survivors tried to change a chemical oxygen cartridge, the kind that releases oxygen from potassium superoxide. It fell into oily seawater, which made it react violently, and the resulting flash fire burned through the air that was left.

The note proved the official story wrong once. That is why many families never fully trusted the second official story, the one saying nothing could have saved the men. When an organization is caught shading the truth, it loses the benefit of the doubt on everything that follows.
Nine days on the surface

Russia declared an emergency late on August 12, after the *Kursk* missed her scheduled check-in. The navy had rescue submersibles of the Priz and Bester types, small crewed vehicles designed to dock over a submarine's escape hatch, form a watertight seal and ferry men up. Over the next four days they tried again and again. One collided with the hull and had to surface. Others could not get a seal on the hatch, which had been damaged and sat on a tilted, battered hull.

It helps to know why a seal is so hard. A rescue vehicle has to settle a rubber-rimmed skirt squarely onto a flat ring around the escape hatch. Then it pumps the water out of the space inside the skirt, so the weight of the ocean presses the vehicle down onto the hull and holds it there. Only then can anyone open a hatch. If the ring is bent, the hull is tilted, or the current keeps nudging the vehicle sideways, water leaks back in and the grip never forms. Precision that is routine in a calm drill becomes nearly impossible on a wreck.

Meanwhile, Britain, Norway, France, Germany, Italy, Israel and the United States offered help. For days the answer was no. There were real reasons for reluctance, including a sunken boat full of secrets, and less admirable ones, including pride. On August 17, five days after the sinking, the Kremlin accepted British and Norwegian assistance. Norwegian divers worked down to the after escape hatch and opened it on August 21. The escape trunk was full of water. The navy announced that day that there were no survivors.

blocks.title: Days after the sinking
blocks.note: Day 0 is August 12, 2000.
blocks.source: Kursk submarine disaster, Wikipedia (compiled from Russian and Norwegian accounts)

blocks.text: The public watched all of this live. President Putin stayed on vacation at a Black Sea resort during the first days, and the footage of it played badly. When he finally met the families ten days after the sinking, the meeting was raw and angry, and footage of a grieving relative being sedated at a news conference went around the world. For many Russians, the *Kursk* became shorthand for a state that lied first and grieved later.
Would faster have mattered?

Here is the uncomfortable part. If the official eight-hour estimate is right, then no rescue on any realistic timeline would have arrived in time. The emergency was not even declared until the evening. Even a perfectly maintained Russian rescue force, with the boat found instantly, would have struggled to be docked on the hatch within eight hours of the blast.

In the first days, Russian officials said rescuers had heard knocking from inside the hull, which some reports described as SOS signals. Officials later attributed the sounds to machinery or other noise. After the note was found, those early reports took on a terrible new weight, and the official timeline never fully put them to rest. The eight-hour finding was politically convenient, and it may also be true. Both things can hold at once. But notice what the question does. *Would faster have mattered* treats the nine days as the place where the outcome was decided. It was not. By the morning of August 12, most of the outcome was already locked in by choices made long before.

The emergency rescue buoy, which would have floated to the surface and marked the wreck, had reportedly been disabled before the exercise. The rescue vehicles were aging, in a navy that had been starved of money through the 1990s. The torpedo fuel was a known risk. The system for asking allies for help did not really exist, because nobody had planned for needing it. None of that could be fixed in a week.

blocks.title: How the outcome was set before the accident
items: A volatile fuel stays in service because it has not hurt anyone recently
Maintenance and drills slip as budgets shrink, and nobody notices the loss of skill
Safety gear like the rescue buoy is disabled for convenience or secrecy
No agreement exists for fast international help, so asking takes days of politics
When the casualty comes, everyone improvises, and improvisation is slow

blocks.text: This is the real lesson of the *Kursk*, and it is one any watchstander will recognize. A casualty drill can feel like theater on the hundredth run. The point of the hundredth run is that on the real day nobody is improvising. The crew in the ninth compartment did what they could with what they had. What they had was decided by people far away, years earlier.
What changed afterward

In 2001, a Dutch team led by the heavy-lift company Mammoet, working with Smit International, raised the wreck in one of the most ambitious salvage jobs ever attempted. They cut away the shattered bow, then lifted the rest of the hull from the seabed using 26 hoisting cables and towed it to a dry dock. The bodies of 115 of the 118 men were recovered. The bow section was later destroyed on the bottom.

The salvage was put at roughly 65 million dollars. That is worth sitting with for a moment. Within about five months of getting the contract, a commercial team designed custom equipment, rigged a giant barge and lifted a wrecked nuclear submarine from the Barents Sea. The engineering capability to reach the *Kursk* existed in the world in 2000. What did not exist was a way to get it there in hours instead of days.

The bigger change was international. After the *Kursk*, navies set up the International Submarine Escape and Rescue Liaison Office, known as ISMERLO, to coordinate rescue assets across countries before anyone needs them: who has what vehicle, which ships can carry it, how fast it can fly, which hatches it fits. More than 40 countries operate submarines today, and almost none can handle every rescue alone. The *Kursk* made it obvious that the time to sort out cooperation is not the day a boat goes down.

Russia, for its part, withdrew the HTP torpedo type and eventually acknowledged that the disaster began inside its own boat. The final report in 2002 called it an accident for which no one was responsible. No one was charged. A separate report by the families' lawyers blamed failures to follow safety procedures. Those two documents describe the same event and draw opposite conclusions about what it means.

A useful question for any system you are part of: if the worst happened tomorrow, which parts of the response would be practiced, and which would be improvised? The improvised parts are where the time goes.
The ninth compartment, again

It is worth ending where the survivors were. Twenty-three men in a cold, darkening steel room more than a hundred meters down, with an escape hatch they could not use and a sea that would not let them go. They organized. They wrote down who was there. They tried to keep the air going. They did not panic so badly that they left no record. Their discipline is the reason we know anything at all.

Their story also explains why modern submarine rescue is built around partnerships, standard hatches, pre-planned logistics and drills that look boring until the day they are not. The engineering matters. The honesty matters too. The *Kursk* showed that a navy can lose a crew twice: once to an explosion, and again to the slow erosion of trust that comes from being caught not telling the truth.

takeaways: The Kursk was sunk by its own torpedo fuel and warheads, not by a collision.
At least 23 men survived the blasts for hours; official findings said all died within about eight hours.
Rescue failed because of choices made years earlier: aging gear, lost proficiency, a disabled buoy, no plan for foreign help.
After the Kursk, navies created ISMERLO to coordinate international submarine rescue in advance.
Drills exist so that nobody improvises on the real day; improvisation is where the time goes.

title: The Atmosphere Is Something You Manufacture
dek: On a sealed hull, every breath is a product that someone made from seawater and electricity, and every exhale is waste that has to be hauled away.

blocks.text: Here is a number worth sitting with. According to NASA life-support engineers, an average person breathes in about 0.84 kilograms of oxygen a day and breathes out about 1 kilogram of carbon dioxide. That is a bag of sugar's worth of gas in, and a little more than that out, every single day, for every person aboard.

On land, nobody has to think about it. The planet handles the bookkeeping: plants and plankton pull carbon dioxide out and put oxygen back, and the atmosphere is so huge that one person's output disappears into it. Seal a hundred-plus people inside a steel hull for weeks and that safety net vanishes. The air becomes a closed system, and a closed system with people in it only stays breathable if a machine keeps it that way.

This article walks through how that machine works, using public sources: how water gets split into oxygen, how carbon dioxide gets pulled back out, what the limits are, and how fresh water is made from the sea. The details of any particular class of boat are left out. The chemistry is the interesting part anyway.

items.label: Oxygen used per person per day (average)
Carbon dioxide exhaled per person per day (average)
Moisture given off per person per day, from breath and sweat (average)

blocks.source: Perry et al., NASA life-support technology paper (c. 2012)

blocks.text: When the air ran out on a schedule

For the first half of the twentieth century, submarines did not make air at all. They carried it. A boat submerged with whatever atmosphere was inside the hull when the hatch shut, plus some stored oxygen and chemical absorbent for carbon dioxide. The diesel engines that charged the batteries also needed air, so the boat had to come up regularly anyway. A long submerged day meant the air got steadily worse: stuffy, warm, hard to think in, and finally hard to breathe.

In that world, the length of a dive was set partly by chemistry. The battery set how far you could go, and the air set how long you could stay. Snorkels, which let diesel boats draw air through a mast while just below the surface, eased the problem without solving it.

Nuclear power changed the equation completely. A reactor needs no oxygen, so the propulsion plant no longer competed with the crew for air. And because the reactor produces enormous amounts of energy, the boat could afford to spend electricity making oxygen and heat regenerating scrubbers. For the first time, the limiting factor on staying down stopped being the atmosphere. It became food, maintenance and people. The machines described below are what made that shift real.
Splitting water to make breath

The core trick is one most people learned in high school chemistry with a battery, two wires and a glass of water. Run direct current through water and it splits: hydrogen bubbles off one electrode and oxygen off the other. Two water molecules become two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule.

The National Research Council, in a 2004 report written for the Navy on submarine air contaminants, describes it plainly: oxygen generators add oxygen through electrolysis, and the hydrogen produced is discharged to the sea. That second part matters as much as the first. Hydrogen is light, flammable and easy to ignite, so a system that makes it in quantity also has to get rid of it safely and continuously.

The water itself is the raw material. By mass, oxygen makes up about 89 percent of a water molecule, so producing one person's daily 0.84 kilograms of oxygen consumes a little under a kilogram of water. That water has to be extremely pure; dissolved salts and impurities would wreck the electrodes and create unwanted byproducts. So the oxygen system depends on the fresh-water system, which depends on the power plant. On a nuclear boat, breathable air is ultimately a product of the reactor.

Electrolysis is also energy-hungry, and there is no way around that. Hydrogen and oxygen release a lot of energy when they recombine into water; that is why hydrogen burns so fiercely. Splitting water means paying that energy back, plus losses. This is the basic reason that making oxygen on demand only became practical once a boat carried a power source large enough to spare the electricity.

blocks.title: From seawater to a breath
items: Seawater is taken aboard and distilled into fresh water.
That water is purified further so it is clean enough for electrolysis.
Electricity splits the water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Hydrogen is sent overboard, safely away from people and ignition sources.
Oxygen is fed into the ship's ventilation and spread through the boat.
Sensors and watchstanders track oxygen levels and adjust production to match the crew's use.

blocks.text: Pulling carbon dioxide back out

Making oxygen is only half the problem. Carbon dioxide is the bigger threat, because it builds up quickly in an enclosed space and causes headaches, sluggishness and, at high enough levels, real danger long before oxygen runs short.

According to the same NRC report, US submarines remove carbon dioxide with scrubbers that use a chemical called monoethanolamine, usually shortened to MEA. MEA belongs to a family called amines, and its useful property is that it grabs carbon dioxide when it is cool and lets go of it when heated. That makes the process regenerable: the same chemical can be used over and over rather than thrown away.

blocks.title: The amine scrubber loop
items: Ship's air passes through cool MEA solution
MEA chemically binds the CO2
The loaded solution is heated
CO2 is released and sent overboard
The cleaned solution is cooled and reused

blocks.text: There is a lovely symmetry here. The same basic amine chemistry is used at industrial scale to strip carbon dioxide from natural gas and power plant exhaust, and it is one of the leading candidates for carbon capture on land. A submarine is, in a sense, a small floating carbon capture plant that has been running for decades, because it had no choice.

A third machine handles the minor gases. The NRC report describes a carbon monoxide and hydrogen burner that catalytically oxidizes carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide and hydrogen into water, which the other systems can then deal with. At the time of that report, the report noted, the main source of carbon monoxide aboard was cigarette smoking, and hydrogen came largely from charging the battery. Smoking has since been banned aboard US submarines, which made life easier for the burner and for everyone's lungs.
How clean is clean enough?

No submarine atmosphere matches the air on a beach, and none needs to. The question engineers and doctors argue about is how much carbon dioxide people can breathe for weeks or months without harm. The NRC's 2004 review, written at the Navy's request, gives a rare public look at the numbers behind that debate.

blocks.title: Carbon dioxide levels, from the NRC's 2004 review
blocks.note: Submarine averages come from measurements cited in the report. The 90-day limit is the Navy's continuous exposure level at the time; the NRC subcommittee recommended 8,000 ppm.
blocks.source: National Research Council, Submarine Contaminants Vol. 1, 2004

blocks.text: Two things jump out. First, typical submarine air ran roughly ten times the outdoor level, with averages around 3,500 to 4,100 parts per million and wide ranges around them. Second, the Navy's own 90-day limit at the time was 5,000 ppm, and the expert subcommittee concluded that, based on the evidence it reviewed, a 90-day level of 8,000 ppm would be acceptable. The Navy had proposed 7,000.

Those numbers can feel alarming next to studies of offices, where a few thousand ppm is considered stuffy. Whether moderate carbon dioxide actually dulls thinking is a genuinely open scientific question, and Navy researchers have tested it directly on submariners. That debate gets its own treatment in this library's article on crew health. The short version is that one well-known office study found decision-making declines at levels as low as 1,000 ppm, while a later Navy lab study of submariners found no measurable effect even at 15,000 ppm for a short exposure.

Underneath all of this sits monitoring. A manufactured atmosphere can only be managed if it is measured, so oxygen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, hydrogen and other trace gases are sampled continuously and checked against limits. The NRC exercise itself existed because the Navy wanted every one of those limits grounded in the best available evidence rather than habit. The report's job was to weigh animal studies, human chamber experiments and workplace data, and turn them into numbers a watchstander can act on.

The useful mindset is not that the air is bad or good. It is that the air is a managed variable, measured and logged like any other plant parameter, with limits set by people who argued about the evidence.
The backups: chemistry in a can

Electrolysis and amine scrubbing need power, water and working machinery. If any of those fail, a crew needs a way to keep breathing that does not depend on the plant. The answer, on submarines and spacecraft alike, is stored chemistry.

blocks.title: Running systems vs. emergency chemistry

left.head: Regenerable systems
items: Oxygen made by splitting water with electricity
CO2 removed by amine that is heated and reused
Can run for as long as power and water hold out
Need machinery, maintenance and trained operators

right.head: Expendable backups
items: Oxygen candles: a chlorate compound that releases oxygen as it burns
Lithium hydroxide canisters that soak up CO2 chemically
Work with no power at all
Used up once spent, so supply is limited

blocks.text: Lithium hydroxide is the same chemical that made one of the most famous improvisations in engineering history. During Apollo 13 in 1970, the crew retreated into the lunar module, whose carbon dioxide canisters could not keep up. The command module's canisters were the wrong shape. Engineers on the ground worked out how to adapt one to the other with materials that happened to be on board, and the crew built it from instructions read over the radio.

The lesson from that story applies anywhere air is manufactured. The scary failure is rarely running out of oxygen. It is carbon dioxide creeping up because the removal system stopped keeping pace, often quietly and gradually enough that the people breathing it do not notice right away.
Turning the ocean into drinking water

Fresh water is the other thing a boat cannot carry enough of. People drink it, cook with it, wash with it, and, as described above, the oxygen system eats it. The solution is to make it from the endless supply of seawater outside the hull.

The classic method is distillation. Boil seawater, and the water evaporates while the salt stays behind; condense the vapor and you have fresh water. The engineering refinement is to boil it under a partial vacuum. Lower pressure means a lower boiling point, so the water can be boiled with modest waste heat instead of a dedicated flame. The leftover brine, now saltier than seawater, goes back over the side. Some vessels also use reverse osmosis, which pushes seawater through a membrane that lets water through but blocks most of the salt.

Making water costs energy and machinery time, so it is never infinitely available. That is the real reason behind the famously short shipboard shower: water on, get wet, water off, soap up, rinse. It is not a tradition for its own sake. It is the visible tip of a supply chain that starts with seawater and ends, through a long chain of equipment, at your showerhead and the air vents.
A planet in miniature

Step back and the whole arrangement is a scale model of a planet. Oxygen comes from splitting water, which is what plants do with sunlight in photosynthesis. Carbon dioxide gets captured and removed, which is what oceans, forests and rocks do slowly on Earth. Water is purified by evaporation and condensation, which is the water cycle. The submarine just does it with electricity and steel instead of sunlight and time.

The difference is ownership. Inside the hull, the atmosphere has an owner. Someone measures it, logs it, compares it to a limit, and takes action when it drifts. Outside, the same carbon dioxide reading that would be logged and discussed aboard ship is spread across a whole planet where nobody stands that watch. Outdoor air has climbed steadily since the 1950s, and by the time the NRC report was written it had reached 372 ppm.

That is a thought worth carrying off the boat. Closed systems teach you to see the hidden machinery behind things that seem free. Clean air, fresh water and a stable climate are never actually free. They are always being produced by something, whether that is an electrolysis cell in a machinery space or a few trillion phytoplankton. The only question is whether anyone is watching the gauges.

Next time you take a breath underway, it is worth remembering the chain: reactor heat, distilled seawater, purified water, an electrical current, and a bubble of oxygen that did not exist an hour before.

takeaways: Each person uses about 0.84 kg of oxygen and exhales about 1 kg of CO2 a day, so a sealed crew needs constant manufacturing of air.
Oxygen comes from electrolysis of purified water; the hydrogen byproduct goes overboard.
CO2 is captured by an amine (MEA) that grabs it when cool and releases it when heated, so it can be reused.
Expendable backups like oxygen candles and lithium hydroxide work without power but run out.
Fresh water is distilled from seawater under vacuum, which is why water, and showers, are always budgeted.
