title: The Interview Is a Test You Can Study For
dek: Years of experience barely predict how well someone will do a job. A well-run interview predicts it better than almost anything else, and the best interviews are built to be predictable. What hiring science says, and how to prepare like it is a qualification board.

blocks.text: Here is a number that should change how you think about your resume. In a 2022 reanalysis of decades of hiring research, the link between how many years of experience someone has and how well they actually perform in a job came out at a correlation of 0.07. On a scale where zero means no relationship and one means perfect prediction, that is close to nothing. The line most people list first, and that many job postings demand, tells a hiring manager very little about how you will actually do.

At the top of the same list sat something you have far more control over: the structured interview. Not the vague, chatty kind where a manager asks about your hobbies and goes with their gut, but the kind built around a fixed set of job-related questions and a scoring guide. It came out as the single best predictor of job performance in the analysis.

That is good news for anyone moving from the military to civilian work. Experience in years is hard to translate and easy to discount. Performance in an interview is a skill, and like any skill, it can be trained.
What actually predicts performance

The analysis, led by industrial psychologist Paul Sackett, revisited the classic summaries of hiring research and argued that earlier statistical corrections had inflated many of the numbers. After fixing that, almost every method's predictive power dropped by 0.10 to 0.20 points. The rankings mostly held, but the overall picture got humbler: no hiring method predicts performance especially well. Some are just much better than others.

blocks.title: How well hiring methods predict job performance
blocks.note: Higher means a stronger link to later job performance. Values are corrected estimates.
blocks.source: Sackett, Zhang, Berry & Lievens, Journal of Applied Psychology, 2022

blocks.text: Look at what rises to the top. Structured interviews, job knowledge tests and work samples all measure something close to the actual work: what you know, what you have done, and how you would handle real situations. The methods that do best are the ones that look most like the job. Raw time served does not, because two people with the same years can have learned wildly different amounts.

Notice too what the chart cannot show. These are averages across thousands of hires and many kinds of work. A 0.42 is modest. Plenty of strong interviewers turn out to be average employees and the reverse. But if an employer is going to use one tool to choose between you and other candidates, the interview is likely to be it, and the better employers will use the structured kind.

Also notice what is missing from the top of the list: the gut feeling. Unstructured interviews, where the conversation goes wherever it goes and the manager decides afterward, consistently do worse than structured ones. They feel more insightful to the person running them, because a free-flowing chat gives you a strong sense of someone. But that sense is more open to the pull of charm, similarity and snap impressions, which predict performance less well than people tend to believe.

The second-place finisher on that chart is worth a thought too. Many technical employers use knowledge tests or technical interviews alongside the behavioral ones. If you are aiming at a technical field, reviewing the fundamentals you learned in training is not wasted effort. Being able to explain a system clearly to someone who did not learn it your way is a skill all by itself, and it shows up in both kinds of question.
What structure means for you

Structured interviews have a few features in common. Every candidate gets the same core questions. The questions come from an analysis of what the job actually demands. And answers are scored against a guide, often with examples of what a weak, average and strong answer sound like. Research has long found that this beats the unstructured chat, both for predicting performance and for reducing bias from impressions formed before the interview and *similar to me* effects.

Most structured questions come in two flavors. Behavioral questions ask about your past: *Tell me about a time you had to deal with a conflict on your team.* Situational questions ask about a hypothetical: *What would you do if you noticed a coworker skipping a safety step?* Both are testing the same thing, whether you have the judgment and habits the job needs, and both reward specific, concrete answers over general claims.

Here is the useful part. A structured interview is predictable by design. Employers in the same field ask about the same handful of things: teamwork, conflict, mistakes, working under pressure, leading or influencing others, learning something hard, following procedures when nobody is watching. If you walk in with a prepared story for each of those, you are not gaming the system. You are giving the interviewer exactly the evidence the scoring guide asks for.

blocks.title: The STAR answer
items: Situation: one or two sentences of context. Where, when, what was going on.
Task: what you specifically were responsible for.
Action: what you did, step by step. Say I, not we, for your part.
Result: what happened, with a number or concrete outcome if you have one.
Lesson: one line on what you would keep or change. Optional, but strong.

blocks.text: The most common failure in behavioral answers is drifting into *we*. Teams do get things done together, and military culture rightly trains you to credit the team. But the interviewer is scoring you. Name the team's success, then be precise about your piece: *I was the one who caught the discrepancy, and I wrote up the fix.* That is not bragging. It is answering the question.
The first few minutes count

Interviews usually open with a few minutes of small talk: how was the drive, tell me a little about yourself. It is tempting to treat that as warm-up before the real questions. The research says otherwise.

Murray Barrick, Brian Swider and Greg Stewart studied students interviewing for internships and tracked what happened afterward. Candidates who made better impressions during the opening rapport-building phase got higher interview ratings at the end and received more actual internship offers. The key detail is what those early impressions were made of. The judgments that carried over to separate interviewers were about competence, not just liking or similarity. In the opening minutes, interviewers were already picking up on how clearly people thought and spoke.

items.label: Correlation between opening-minutes impressions and final interview ratings
Correlation between opening-minutes impressions and actual job offers

blocks.source: Barrick, Swider & Stewart, Journal of Applied Psychology, 2010

blocks.text: So the small talk is part of the test. A firm, short answer to *how was your trip in* followed by a question back shows the same things the hard questions will: that you are calm, that you listen, and that you can say something clearly and stop. Prepare a sixty-second version of *tell me about yourself* that ends with why you want this particular job, and practice it until it sounds natural rather than memorized.

The same goes for the end of the interview. When they ask if you have any questions, *no, I think you covered everything* is a missed chance. Ask about the work itself: what a normal week looks like, what the best person in this role does differently, what the biggest challenge for the team is right now. Good questions show you are already thinking about doing the job, and they give you real information about whether you want it.
The translation problem

A 2025 study asked civilian hiring professionals who regularly interview veterans what they see, then surveyed 93 veterans about the same things. The strengths were consistent: veterans came across as professional and confident, with strong soft skills. The weaknesses were consistent too. Veterans often failed to translate the technical skills they had built in the military into terms the interviewer understood. They leaned on military jargon. And they were often nervous.

The jargon problem is easy to underrate from the inside. After a few years, acronyms stop feeling like acronyms. They feel like normal words. But a civilian interviewer who hears a string of them does not think *impressive*; they think *I have no idea what this person did*. And they will not interrupt to ask, because nobody wants to look clueless in their own interview. They will just score you lower.

blocks.title: Say what you did, not what it was called

left.head: Lost in translation
items: I stood EO watches and qualified early.
I was LPO for my division.
I did PMS and troubleshooting on the plant.
We had an ORSE and I was on the drill team.

right.head: Lands with a civilian
items: I operated and monitored the electrical system for a nuclear power plant on rotating shifts.
I supervised and trained a team of junior technicians.
I ran scheduled maintenance and diagnosed faults on high-voltage equipment.
I helped prepare our team for a demanding external safety inspection, and we passed.

blocks.text: A good exercise: write out what you actually do in a week, then go line by line and replace every term your parents would not understand. If an outsider could not picture it, rewrite it. The goal is not to dumb anything down. It is to let the real substance through, because the substance is often impressive. Running and maintaining equipment in a nuclear plant under tight procedures is exactly what many civilian employers are looking for, but only if they can tell that is what you did.

Nervousness, the third weakness, responds well to the same medicine as public speaking fear: repetition under realistic conditions. Most of the jitters come from novelty. The fifth time you tell a story out loud to someone playing an interviewer, it stops feeling like a performance and starts feeling like a conversation about something you know well, because it is.
The over-talker's interview

Nerves do different things to different people. Some freeze. Others talk, and talk, and keep going because stopping feels like admitting they are done. In a structured interview, long answers are costly. The interviewer is listening for specific points on a scoring guide. Bury those points in five minutes of context and they may not get credit.

A rough rule of thumb used by many interview coaches is to aim for about one to two minutes per behavioral answer, then stop. That is not a research finding, just a practical target, but it fits how scoring works. Hit the STAR points cleanly and end with the result. If the interviewer wants more, they will ask, and a follow-up question is a good sign: it means they are interested.

There is a hidden strength in this for people who like to talk. Juliana Schroeder and Nicholas Epley found that when employers and professional recruiters heard a candidate's pitch spoken aloud rather than read the same words on paper, they rated the person as more competent and intelligent and were more interested in hiring them. Your voice, with its pauses and emphasis, shows a mind at work. The skill is to give it room by saying less and saying it well. Pausing to think before a hard question does not look weak. It looks like thinking.
How to prepare

Treat the interview like a qualification board. You would never walk into a board having only read the material. You would talk it through, out loud, until it came easily. Interviews reward the same thing.

items: Build a story bank: six to eight real situations that cover teamwork, conflict, a mistake, pressure, leadership, learning something hard and doing the right thing unobserved.
Write each one in STAR form, then say it out loud and time it.
Translate every story into civilian language. Have someone outside the military listen and flag every term they do not get.
Record yourself answering three common questions. Watch for answers that wander, filler words and the word we.
Prepare two or three real questions for them about the work, the team and what success looks like in the first year.
Do at least one full mock interview with someone who will be honest with you.

blocks.text: Transition programs can help with all of this, including resume translation and practice interviews, and some programs allow service members to spend time working with a civilian employer before separation. Rules and eligibility change, so check the current details with your command's transition office well before you need them.

The deeper point of the research is encouraging. Hiring is noisy, and nobody can predict performance perfectly. But the best tool employers have is built around a predictable set of questions about real situations, scored on clear, specific answers. That is a format you can practice for, the same way you practiced for everything else that once seemed impossible.

takeaways: Structured interviews are the best single predictor of job performance hiring research has found. Years of experience barely predict anything.
Structured interviews are predictable by design. Prepare a story for teamwork, conflict, mistakes, pressure and leadership.
Answer in STAR form, say I for your part, and stop after the result.
The opening small talk is scored too. Have a clear sixty-second answer to tell me about yourself.
Translate every acronym. If an outsider can't picture what you did, rewrite it.

title: The Word That Gets You to the Front of the Line
dek: Cialdini's principles of persuasion are some of the most famous ideas in psychology. Some of the evidence is rock solid, some is smaller than the legend, and all of it works best when there is something real behind it.

blocks.text: In the 1970s, a researcher at a university library in New York waited until someone was about to use the photocopier, then stepped up and asked to cut in. The request was small, five pages. The experiment, run by Ellen Langer and colleagues and published in 1978, tested one thing: how the request was worded.

With no reason given, 'Excuse me, I have five pages. May I use the Xerox machine?', 60 percent of people let the researcher go ahead. Add a real reason, 'because I'm in a rush,' and it jumped to 94 percent. The interesting condition was the third one. The researcher said 'because I have to make copies.' Which is not a reason. Everyone at a copier has to make copies. Compliance: 93 percent.

blocks.title: Letting a stranger cut in line at the copier (5 pages)
blocks.note: The empty reason worked almost as well as the real one, but only for a small favor.
blocks.source: Langer, Blank & Chanowitz, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1978

blocks.text: The word *because* seemed to do the work by itself. People heard the shape of a reason and said yes without processing the content. But there is a twist that usually gets left out of the retelling. When the favor was bigger, twenty pages instead of five, the empty reason stopped working. It did no better than giving no reason at all. Only the real reason helped. When the stakes rose, people actually listened.

That twist is the key to understanding persuasion psychology as a whole. The famous tricks are shortcuts our brains use when a decision feels cheap. They are real, they can be powerful, and they are fragile. Once someone starts paying attention, substance takes over again.
Six shortcuts, then a seventh

Robert Cialdini, a social psychologist at Arizona State, spent years studying how people get others to say yes, partly by going undercover in sales trainings, fundraising operations and marketing outfits. In 1984 he published *Influence*, which organized what he found into six principles. In 2016, in the book *Pre-Suasion*, he added a seventh. Each one names a rule of thumb that is usually sensible, which is exactly why it can be exploited.

items: **Reciprocity:** we feel obliged to return favors, even small unrequested ones.
**Commitment and consistency:** once we take a stand, we like to act in line with it.
**Social proof:** when unsure, we copy what people like us are doing.
**Authority:** we defer to people who seem to know what they're talking about.
**Liking:** we say yes more easily to people we like, who are similar to us or who compliment us.
**Scarcity:** things seem more valuable when they're rare or about to disappear.
**Unity (added 2016):** we are swayed by people we see as part of our group, a shared 'we.'

blocks.text: If you play games, you have seen every one of these. The free daily login reward (reciprocity). The streak you don't want to break (consistency). '2.3 million players own this skin' (social proof). The limited-time shop item that leaves at midnight (scarcity). The clan tag (unity). Game designers did not invent these. They borrowed from the same playbook used by car dealers, charities and recruiters.
The best evidence, and the shakier stuff
Some of the classic studies hold up well. Some have shrunk on contact with replication. It's worth knowing which is which, because the size of an effect tells you how much to rely on it.

Start with commitment. In a 1966 study by Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser, researchers asked California homeowners to put a large, ugly 'Drive Carefully' sign in their front yard. Among people who got that request cold, only 17 percent agreed. But a group who had been asked two weeks earlier to put a tiny 'Be a Safe Driver' sign in their window, a request almost everyone accepted, said yes to the big sign 76 percent of the time.

blocks.title: Agreeing to a big, ugly yard sign
blocks.note: The classic foot-in-the-door result. Later reviews found the average effect much smaller.
blocks.source: Freedman & Fraser, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1966

blocks.text: That is the foot-in-the-door technique, and the original result is huge. The later picture is more modest. Reviews of the many follow-up studies since the 1980s found that the effect exists on average but is much smaller and less consistent than that first study suggested, and in some settings it barely appears. The underlying idea, that a small yes shifts how people see themselves, is plausible. Treat it as a nudge, not a lever.

Social proof has a similar story. In a widely cited 2008 study, Noah Goldstein, Cialdini and Vladas Griskevicius tested signs in hotel bathrooms asking guests to reuse towels. The standard environmental message got 35.1 percent of guests to reuse. A message saying most fellow guests reused their towels got 44.1 percent. It became a textbook example and a favorite of consultants.

Then other researchers tried it. Several later experiments found little or no effect. In 2016 Benjamin Scheibehenne and colleagues pooled seven towel experiments in a Bayesian meta-analysis. The effect survived, but smaller: in a reanalysis of that pooled data, reuse ran about 50 percent with the plain message and 56 percent with the social norm message.

blocks.title: Hotel towel reuse: original study vs pooled evidence
blocks.note: Pooled values are approximate estimates from a reanalysis of seven experiments.
blocks.source: Goldstein, Cialdini & Griskevicius, J. Consumer Research, 2008; Scheibehenne et al., Psychological Science, 2016, as reanalyzed by van der Linden & Chryst, 2017

blocks.text: So social norms do something, about six points' worth here. That is useful at the scale of a hotel chain or a government tax letter. It is not mind control. The same pattern shows up across a lot of persuasion research: the first flashy study finds a big effect in one place, and the long run settles on something real but smaller.

Reciprocity is one of the sturdier principles, and it shows up in odd places. In a 2002 restaurant study, David Strohmetz and colleagues found that servers who left a piece of candy with the check got bigger tips than servers who didn't, and that both the size of the gift and the way it was offered changed the result. The authors argued that reciprocity explained the pattern better than a simple good-mood boost. Notice what that implies: the candy worked because it read as a gesture, not as a tactic.

A rule of thumb from the replication era: if a persuasion trick claims a giant effect from a tiny change, expect the real-world version to be smaller. Shortcuts work best on decisions people don't care much about.
Scarcity, liking and the messenger

Scarcity has one of the most charming classic demonstrations. In a 1975 study, Stephen Worchel and colleagues offered people a chocolate chip cookie from a jar and asked them to rate it. When the jar held only two cookies, people rated the identical cookie as more desirable than when the jar held ten. The effect was strongest when the jar went from ten down to two in front of them, as if other people had just grabbed the rest. Same cookie. Different story about how rare it was.

That is the engine behind every limited drop and every 'only 3 left in stock' banner. It also explains why things you might lose feel more valuable than things you might gain. A battle pass that expires motivates you more than one that sits there forever, even though the rewards are the same.

Liking and authority are about the messenger rather than the message. People say yes more readily to someone who seems similar to them, who is friendly, who has helped them before. They also defer to people with real or apparent expertise, which is why a confident tone and the right title can carry an argument further than the argument deserves. Stanley Milgram's obedience studies in the 1960s are the darkest illustration of authority, and they have their own long list of critiques about how the experiments were run and reported. The everyday lesson is milder: the same request lands differently depending on who says it and whether they have earned credibility on the topic.

For a junior person, that cuts both ways. You may not have rank, but you can have credibility on specific things: you're the one who actually knows that system, ran that procedure last week, or did the reading. Speaking from that ground, briefly and specifically, is a legitimate form of authority. Pretending to know more than you do is the counterfeit version, and in a technical job it gets caught fast.
Why the shortcuts exist at all

It's easy to read this as a list of human bugs. Cialdini's own framing is kinder and more useful. Each principle is a heuristic that usually leads to good decisions. Copying what others do is a fast way to learn in an unfamiliar place. Deferring to experts is how you avoid relearning everything yourself; it's why you trust the procedure written by people who've thought harder about the reactor than you have. Returning favors is the glue of every functioning group, including a crew.

blocks.title: How a persuasion shortcut gets exploited
items: A rule of thumb works most of the time
People stop checking it on small decisions
Someone fakes the signal (fake scarcity, fake reviews, fake authority)
The fake triggers the yes without the substance
People get burned and grow suspicious of the real thing too

blocks.text: The problem comes when someone fakes the signal. A countdown timer that resets every time you reload the page is counterfeit scarcity. Paid reviews are counterfeit social proof. A guy in a lab coat selling supplements is counterfeit authority. The shortcut fires, but there's nothing behind it. And because these tactics are now everywhere, people have gotten better at smelling them, which is one reason the textbook effects keep shrinking.
Using it without being that guy

Cialdini draws a sharp line between using the principles honestly and manufacturing them. The honest version is simple: if a real reason, a real expert opinion, real popularity or a real deadline exists, make it visible. Don't make people dig for it. The dishonest version invents those things. The first is just good communication. The second works once and costs you trust you won't get back.

blocks.title: Honest persuasion for a normal request
items: Lead with the real reason. The copier study shows a reason helps, and for anything that matters, it has to be a good one.
Point to genuine social proof if it exists: 'the other watch sections already switched to this.'
Borrow real authority: cite the procedure, the tech manual or the person who actually knows.
Ask for a small, reasonable first step rather than everything at once.
Find the shared 'we': same division, same goal, same problem.
Give before you ask: help people when you don't need anything, and you build credit for when you do.

blocks.text: For someone working on speaking professionally, the most practical lesson is the one from the copier. When you ask for something, a schedule swap, a favor, an exception, give the reason in one clean sentence. Then stop. People who over-talk tend to stack reason on reason, apology on apology, and that can backfire: it signals that you don't think your first reason was good enough. One real reason, stated plainly, is usually stronger than five nervous ones.

There's a defensive lesson too. When you feel an urge to decide right now, because it's leaving the store, because everyone's doing it, because the person seemed so likable, that urgency is a good moment to ask a single question: would I want this if the shortcut weren't there? If the item weren't limited, if nobody else had it, if a stranger were offering it? If the answer is still yes, go ahead. If not, you just caught a shortcut doing the deciding for you.

Persuading up the chain of command is where this gets real. A chief or division officer has heard every flavor of pitch and is busy. What tends to work is boring: the request in one line, the real reason, what you've already checked, and what it costs them to say yes. That structure leans on the honest versions of several principles at once. The reason is real, the homework is a signal of competence, and making it easy to agree respects their time. Nothing about it is a trick, which is exactly why it holds up the second and third time you ask for something.

The deeper reframe is that persuasion is not mainly about tricks at all. The strongest form of every principle is the real thing. Real reciprocity is being someone who helps. Real authority is knowing your stuff. Real liking is being decent to be around. Real unity is actually being on the same team. The principles describe why people say yes. The shortcut versions are just attempts to get the yes without doing the work.

takeaways: Persuasion shortcuts work best on low-stakes decisions; when it matters, people check the substance.
Many famous effects are real but smaller than their original studies: hotel towel norms shrank from about 9 points to about 6.
When you ask for something, give one clear real reason and stop talking.
Make genuine reasons, expertise and deadlines visible; never fake them.
If you feel rushed to say yes, ask whether you'd still want it without the scarcity, crowd or charm.

title: The First Minute Is the Worst Minute
dek: Public speaking fear is close to universal, mostly invisible to the audience, and it peaks almost as soon as you start. That is exactly why it can be beaten quickly.

blocks.text: When stress researchers need a reliable way to make healthy people anxious in a lab, they have a favorite tool. It is not a needle, a loud noise or a cold-water bath. It is a speech. In the Trier Social Stress Test, developed in Germany in the early 1990s and used in a huge number of studies since, a volunteer is given a few minutes to prepare a talk, then has to deliver it to a panel of stone-faced judges who take notes and offer no encouragement. It reliably spikes heart rate and stress hormones.

Think about what that means. Out of everything scientists could use to stress a person safely, they chose standing up and talking. Not because talking is dangerous, but because being judged by a group is one of the most dependable alarm buttons the human brain has. If your hands go cold before a brief at quarters, nothing is wrong with you. You are running standard equipment.
Not worse than death, just more common

You have probably heard that people fear public speaking more than death. The claim traces back to a 1973 survey that asked Americans to check off their fears from a list. Public speaking came out on top, checked by about 40 percent of respondents. Comedians ran with it, and it became a cliché that at a funeral, most people would rather be in the casket than at the podium.

In 2012, Karen Kangas Dwyer and Marlina Davidson at the University of Nebraska Omaha tested the cliché properly. They surveyed 815 college students who had not yet taken a speech class, using the same list of 14 fears. When students simply checked which things they feared, public speaking was again the most common, chosen by about 60 percent. But when they were asked to rank their fears, death came first. So the cliché is half right. Public speaking is the fear the most people share. It is not the one they rank as worst.

blocks.title: Share who checked public speaking as a fear
blocks.note: In the 2012 study, death still ranked first when students ordered their fears from worst to least.
blocks.source: Dwyer & Davidson, Communication Research Reports, 2012 (via KIOS/UNO)

blocks.text: It is also worth separating ordinary nerves from a clinical problem. The large National Comorbidity Survey Replication estimated that about 12 percent of Americans meet criteria for social anxiety disorder at some point in their lives, a condition where fear of judgment seriously disrupts daily life. That is real and treatable, and if fear of speaking is wrecking your career or keeping you from basic tasks, a doctor, corpsman or chaplain can point you to help. But the much larger group, the majority who just get sweaty palms before a brief, are dealing with a normal reaction that responds well to practice.
The shape of the fear

Here is a useful fact that most nervous speakers do not know: the fear has a predictable curve. In a 2006 study, Ralph Behnke, Chris Sawyer and Paul Witt at Texas Christian University tracked 96 students giving a five-minute speech. They measured anxiety symptoms like a lump in the throat and knots in the stomach at four moments: the minute before speaking, the first minute of the speech, the last minute, and the minute right after.

For the more relaxed students, anxiety peaked just before they started and fell from the first word onward. For the high-anxiety students, it peaked in the first minute of actually speaking, then declined as the speech went on, dropping substantially by the end. In other words, even for the most nervous people, the worst part was front-loaded. If you can get through the first sixty seconds, the curve starts working for you.

blocks.title: Where speech anxiety peaks
items: Minute before
Peak for low-anxiety speakers. Waiting is the worst part.
First minute
Peak for high-anxiety speakers. Highest symptom load of the talk.
Last minute
Anxiety has fallen for both groups, a lot for the nervous ones.
Minute after
A small bounce back as people replay how it went.

blocks.text: That shape suggests a very specific tactic. You do not need to rehearse the whole talk to the point of memorizing it. That often backfires, because a memorized script shatters the moment you lose a word. You need to over-prepare the first minute. Know your opening sentences cold, so that when your anxiety is at its peak, your mouth is running on rails while the rest of your body catches up.
They cannot see what you feel

A second reason the fear is worse than it needs to be is that speakers badly overestimate how visible their nerves are. Kenneth Savitsky and Thomas Gilovich at Cornell studied this in 2003. In their first experiment, speakers rated how nervous they had looked, and observers rated the same thing. Speakers consistently judged themselves as more visibly anxious than the audience saw them.

In the second experiment, they split speakers into three groups before a short, unprepared talk. One group got no special instructions. One got reassurance that nerves are normal. The third was told about the illusion of transparency: the well-documented tendency to think your inner state is far more obvious to others than it is. That third group gave better speeches, and not just in their own eyes. Observers, who did not know which group anyone was in, rated their speeches higher too.

blocks.title: The same speech, two views

left.head: What the speaker feels
items: Heart pounding, voice shaky
A two-second pause feels endless
Every um sounds like a disaster
Sure the whole room can tell

right.head: What the audience sees
items: Someone a little serious
A normal pause to think
Ordinary speech, barely noticed
A person giving a talk, mostly fine

blocks.text: The interesting part is how cheap that fix was. The informed group did not get coaching or practice. They got one fact about perception, and it changed their performance. Part of what wrecks a nervous speech is the spiral: I think they can see I am nervous, which makes me more nervous, which makes me try to hide it, which takes attention away from what I am saying. Knowing the audience mostly cannot see it breaks the first link.
Call it excitement, with an asterisk

If you cannot calm down, what should you do? A widely cited 2014 study by Alison Wood Brooks at Harvard Business School suggested an odd answer: do not try. In one experiment, 140 people were told they would give a persuasive speech on camera, judged by a committee. Right before speaking, half said out loud I am excited and half said I am calm. Independent raters judged the excited group's speeches as more persuasive, more competent and more relaxed, and their speeches ran longer.

Her other experiments pointed the same way. When people sang karaoke scored by the game's own rating system, those who first said I am excited averaged around 80 percent accuracy, compared with 69 percent for those who said they were calm, angry or sad, and 53 percent for those told to say they were anxious. On a hard math test, people told to get excited scored about 8 percent higher than those told to stay calm.

blocks.title: Karaoke accuracy by what people said first
blocks.source: Brooks, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2014 (APA summary)

blocks.text: The theory is elegant. Anxiety and excitement are both high-arousal states: racing heart, sharp focus, energy. Going from anxious to calm requires dumping all that arousal, which is hard to do on command. Going from anxious to excited only requires relabeling it, from a threat to an opportunity. Same body, different story.

Now the asterisk. In 2025, Michelle Poynter and Marcia Smith Pasqualini published a direct replication of the speech experiment. Saying I am excited again made people report feeling more excited. But this time, independent raters saw no difference in how good the speeches were, and an indirect measure of anxiety showed no change either. So the honest summary is this: reappraisal probably changes how the moment feels, and that is worth something. Whether it reliably makes the speech itself better is not settled. Use it, but do not expect it to replace practice.
How to get better fast

The good news hiding in all of this is that public speaking anxiety is not a fixed trait you are stuck with. It behaves like most fears: it shrinks with repeated exposure that ends without disaster. Each time you speak and nothing terrible happens, your brain gets one more data point against the alarm. The first five briefs are the hardest. By the twentieth, the curve from the TCU study has flattened.

Structure helps too, and the military has already solved part of it. Army correspondence rules have long told writers to put the bottom line up front, usually shortened to BLUF: lead with the conclusion or the recommendation, then support it. That is not just a writing rule. It is the single best structure for a brief to a senior, because it answers the question they actually care about while their attention is highest, and it gives a nervous speaker a short, fixed opening to over-prepare.

blocks.title: Prepping a five-minute brief
items: Write your bottom line in one sentence: what you want them to know or decide.
Pick at most three supporting facts, each a short sentence.
Script and rehearse only the first minute until it is automatic.
Record a full run on your phone once and watch it. It will look calmer than it felt.
Run it out loud two more times, standing, with no notes for the opening.
Right before, breathe out slowly and tell yourself you are excited, not calm.

blocks.text: A few small habits make a big difference in the room. Slow down, because nerves speed you up and a slightly too slow pace sounds confident to listeners. Talk to one face at a time for a sentence or two, rather than the whole room at once. Allow pauses. A one-second silence while you find your next point feels long to you and looks thoughtful to them. And when you finish, stop. A strong last sentence followed by I can take questions beats a trailing so yeah, I think that's about it.

Underway, opportunities to practice are everywhere and mostly low stakes: walking through a system at a qual board, giving a turnover, leading a training session for the division, explaining a drill debrief. Each is a rep. Treat them that way. Volunteer for the short ones on purpose, the way you would choose a drill in a game you are trying to get better at, not a match you are trying to win.
Over-prepare the first sixty seconds and the bottom line. Anxiety peaks right at the start and falls after, so the opening is where preparation pays most.
When the questions start

For a lot of people, the speech is not the scary part. The questions are. You can rehearse a talk, but you cannot rehearse what a department head will ask, and the fear is that one question will expose that you do not know your stuff. In a briefing up the chain of command, that fear tends to produce two bad habits: talking around a question you cannot answer, and over-answering one you can.

The first habit is the dangerous one. Anyone who has been through nuclear training has heard the standard: if you do not know, say so, then go find out. It sounds simple and it feels terrible in the moment. But a senior can work with I don't know, I'll find out and report back by end of watch. What they cannot work with is a confident guess that later turns out to be wrong, because now they have to wonder about everything else you said. An honest gap costs you a little. A bluff that gets caught costs you your credibility for a long time.

The second habit, over-answering, is the nervous speaker's version of filling silence. A yes-or-no question gets a three-minute history. The fix mirrors the bottom-line rule: answer in the first sentence, then stop and let them pull for more. Yes, it is on track for Thursday; the part came in this morning. If they want the backstory, they will ask. Short answers under pressure read as control, and control is most of what an audience means when they say a speaker seemed confident.

Here is the reframe to carry into the next brief. Your nerves are evidence that your brain takes the situation seriously, not evidence that you are bad at it. They are mostly invisible. They peak right at the start and then fade. And they get smaller every time you stand up and speak anyway. Fear of public speaking is common enough that scientists use it as the standard stress test. It is also one of the fears people most reliably get past, by doing the thing.

takeaways: Public speaking is the most commonly reported fear, but people still rank death as worse. Your nerves are standard equipment.
For anxious speakers, anxiety peaks in the first minute and then falls, so script and rehearse the opening most.
Speakers overestimate how visible their nerves are; just knowing this improved speeches in a Cornell experiment.
Relabeling nerves as excitement helps how you feel; its effect on performance did not replicate in a 2025 study.
Lead briefs with the bottom line, then three facts. Collect reps on purpose.

title: Small Talk Is Not Small
dek: Everyone claims to hate it, and almost everyone predicts it will go worse than it does. The research says the dread is the bug, not the conversation.

blocks.text: Picture a commuter train heading into downtown Chicago at rush hour. Nobody is talking. Headphones in, eyes on phones, everyone silently agreeing that the polite thing is to leave each other alone. In 2014, two University of Chicago psychologists, Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder, decided to break that agreement on purpose. They handed riders envelopes with instructions. Some were told to strike up a conversation with a stranger. Some were told to sit in solitude. Some were told to do whatever they normally did.

Before the experiment, a separate group of commuters was asked to predict how each option would feel. They picked solitude. Talking to a stranger, they guessed, would be the least pleasant ride of the three. Then the real riders got off the train and filled out their reports. The people who had talked had the *most* positive commute. They also got no less done. The researchers repeated versions of this on buses, in a waiting room and in the lab, nine experiments in all, and kept finding the same mismatch: people expect connection to feel worse than it does.

That gap between prediction and reality is the whole story of small talk. Most people do not avoid it because it is bad. They avoid it because they are bad at *forecasting* it. And if you are the kind of person who either dreads it or overcompensates by talking too much once it starts, both problems come from the same source.
What small talk is actually for

In 1923 the anthropologist Bronislaw Malinowski gave a name to talk that exists mainly to create a bond rather than to pass along information. He called it phatic communion. 'Cold today, huh' is not a weather report. Nobody leaves that exchange knowing more about the temperature. What both people learn is something more important: *this person is friendly, this person is safe, the channel is open.*

That makes small talk less like a conversation and more like a handshake protocol. Before two computers trade real data, they exchange short, almost content-free messages to confirm the connection works. Skip the handshake and the data never arrives. People who say they 'only like deep conversations' often miss that most deep conversations started as shallow ones. The weather comment is the SYN packet.

There is a practical payoff too. In 1973 the sociologist Mark Granovetter argued that acquaintances, the people you only make small talk with, are disproportionately useful because they move in different circles and hear about things your close friends don't. For decades that was mostly a correlation. Then in 2022 a team from MIT, Stanford, Harvard and LinkedIn published a test of it in *Science*, using experiments across more than 20 million LinkedIn users over five years, during which 2 billion new connections formed and 600,000 new jobs were recorded.

items.label: LinkedIn users in the experiments
New ties formed over 5 years
New jobs recorded

blocks.source: Rajkumar, Saint-Jacques, Bojinov, Brynjolfsson & Aral, Science, 2022

blocks.text: The finding: moderately weak ties, not your closest contacts, produced the most job mobility. The people you know well tend to know what you already know. The guy from the other division you talk to for two minutes at the gym knows about the job you've never heard of. Small talk is how weak ties get built and maintained. It is cheap, and it compounds.
Does small talk make you less happy?

You may have heard the opposite claim: that small talk is empty and the happiest people skip it. That idea traces to a 2010 study by Matthias Mehl, Simine Vazire and colleagues. They had 79 college students wear a small recorder for four days that captured 30-second snippets of sound every 12.5 minutes. Coders then sorted the conversations into small talk and substantive talk. The happiest participants had about one third as much small talk as the unhappiest, and about twice as many substantive conversations.

items.label: Small talk among the happiest vs the unhappiest (2010)
Substantive conversations among the happiest (2010)
People in the 2018 replication, which found no link for small talk

blocks.source: Mehl et al., Psychological Science, 2010; Milek et al., Psychological Science, 2018

blocks.text: It made headlines. But 79 students is a small sample, and in 2018 the same lab ran a much bigger check. Anne Milek and colleagues pooled 486 people from four different studies, including breast cancer survivors, recently divorced adults and people in a meditation program. Substantive conversation still went with higher life satisfaction. Time spent alone went with lower. But small talk showed no link to happiness at all, positive or negative.

That is the honest version: deep conversation seems good for you, and small talk does not seem to hurt. Both studies are correlational, so they can't say whether depth makes people happy or happy people seek depth. What they clearly do not support is the snobby take that small talk is a waste. If small talk is the on-ramp to substantive talk, the people who refuse the on-ramp are not getting to the highway faster.
Why it feels so much worse than it is
If small talk is useful and mostly pleasant, why does it trigger so much dread? The research points at a few specific forecasting errors, and naming them helps, because each one is fixable.

blocks.title: What you predict vs what tends to happen

left.head: The forecast
items: They want to be left alone
I'll get shut down
It will be awkward
Going deeper would be weird
I have to be interesting

right.head: What studies find
items: Others want to connect more than we assume
Rejections are rare
Both shallow and deep chats beat expectations
Strangers are more interested in depth than we think
Being friendly and curious does most of the work

blocks.text: First, we underestimate how much other people want to talk. In the train studies, that was the main driver: riders assumed strangers would be uninterested, so they never tried, so they never found out they were wrong. It is a self-sealing belief. Avoidance protects the prediction from ever being tested.

Second, we overestimate rejection. In a 2022 study, Gillian Sandstrom, Erica Boothby and Gus Cooney had people use a scavenger hunt app for a week. Each day they picked a mission, like finding someone wearing a hat, and then either talked to that person for a few minutes or just observed them. Across 1,336 conversations, 87 percent happened with the very first person approached. People's predicted rejection fell day by day as they practiced. Their actual rejection had been low all along.

items.label: Of 1,336 stranger conversations happened with the first person approached
Of talkers swapped contact info and followed up with someone

blocks.source: Sandstrom, Boothby & Cooney, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 2022

blocks.text: Third, we expect deeper topics to be awkward. Michael Kardas, Amit Kumar and Epley ran a series of experiments, published in 2021, in which strangers discussed either shallow topics or deeper ones like something they were grateful for. Both kinds of conversation went better than people predicted. The deep ones beat expectations the most, and when people tried both, most preferred the deep one, even though beforehand they'd said they would prefer shallow. People assumed the other person didn't want to go there. Usually they did.

Even the most minimal version counts. In a 2014 study, Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn had people buy coffee either as efficiently as possible or while smiling, making eye contact and having a short exchange with the barista. The social group reported more positive feelings and a stronger sense of belonging. A brief exchange with someone whose name you don't even know moved the needle.
How to do it without dreading it

Most small talk advice is a list of opening lines. That misses the point. The opener matters very little; almost anything friendly works. What separates smooth small talk from painful small talk is what happens in the next 60 seconds, and when it ends.

blocks.title: A simple small talk arc
items: Open with the shared situation: the line, the weather, the drill, the food. It is low-risk because you are both in it.
Ask one easy question that invites more than yes or no: 'How'd the inspection go?' beats 'Busy day?'
Listen for free information, the extra detail they volunteer, and ask about that instead of your next planned topic.
Offer a small piece of yourself so it isn't an interview, then hand the turn back.
If it's going well, nudge one level deeper: why, how it felt, what's next.
Exit while it's still good, with a warm line and a reason.

blocks.text: The free information step is the real skill. If you ask someone how their weekend was and they say 'good, finally got out to the lake,' the word *lake* is an invitation. People drop these hooks constantly. Grabbing one shows you were actually listening and lets them talk about something they chose, which is far more pleasant for them than whatever topic you rehearsed.

The give-and-take step matters most for anyone who tends to over-talk. Small talk is a game of short turns. A good rhythm is roughly: they say something, you react and add a little, you hand it back with a question or a pause. If you notice you have been talking for a full minute straight in a casual chat, that is the signal to land the plane and toss them the ball. Nervous talkers fill silence because silence feels like failure. In small talk, a brief pause is just the other person's turn arriving.

Two failure modes are worth knowing by name. The first is the interrogation: question, short answer, question, short answer, until it feels like an intake form. The fix is to react before you ask again. 'No way, I've never been there' or 'that sounds brutal' gives the other person something to respond to besides your next question. The second is the monologue, where one story becomes three and the other person's contributions shrink to 'yeah' and 'huh.' That one usually comes from nerves rather than ego, which is why it is fixable. Watch their answers. When they get shorter, you have been holding the ball too long.

And sometimes it just goes flat. The other person is tired, distracted or not in the mood, and your friendly opener gets a one-word reply. That is not a verdict on you. In the scavenger hunt study, fear of rejection shrank with each day of practice, and part of the reason is simple: every new attempt is a fresh draw. A flat exchange costs you about ten seconds. Say something pleasant, let it go and do not replay it in your rack that night. The other person has almost certainly forgotten it already.
Small talk is supposed to be small. A two-minute exchange that ends warmly does more for a relationship than a fifteen-minute one that drags. Leaving people wanting a little more is a feature.

The ending is where a lot of over-talkers lose ground. The fear is that wrapping up will seem rude, so the conversation keeps going past its natural finish. But a clean exit, 'Good catching up, I need to grab chow before it's gone,' is not a rejection. It is a signal that you respect their time, and it leaves the last impression on a high note.
Practicing in a small world

Life on a boat is an odd small talk environment. You can't avoid people, so you never get the stranger-on-a-train version, but you also see the same faces in passageways a dozen times a day, which creates its own pressure. Do you say something every time? Nod? The research suggests the stakes are much lower than they feel. A quick, friendly acknowledgment is all a weak tie needs to stay warm.

The best place to practice is where the shared context is already built in: the mess line, the gym, the wait before a brief, watch turnover once the actual turnover is done. These are low-stakes reps with a built-in exit. Treat them the way you'd treat drills in a game you want to get better at. Not every rep has to go well. The point is to collect evidence against the forecast in your head.

Small talk with seniors is its own skill. With a chief or an officer, keep it shorter, stay on shared ground like the ship, the schedule or the qual board, and let them set the depth. If they open up, follow. If they give short answers, a brief, friendly exchange still counts as a win. Professional small talk is not about being memorable. It's about being easy to be around.

The deepest reframe from this research is about who is actually uncomfortable. When you hesitate to say something to the person next to you, you assume you are the only one who wants the silence broken. The studies keep finding the opposite. The other person is often sitting there making the exact same wrong prediction about you. Somebody has to go first, and the data says it usually goes fine.

takeaways: People reliably predict talking to strangers will feel worse than it does; the dread is a forecasting error.
Small talk is a handshake: it builds weak ties, and weak ties carry outsized value, including for jobs.
The best evidence says deep talk goes with well-being and small talk is neutral, not harmful.
Grab the free information people offer, keep turns short, and hand the conversation back.
End while it is still good; a short warm exchange beats a long one that drags.

title: Why Your Brain Keeps the Story and Drops the Number
dek: In one classroom test, 63 percent remembered the stories and 5 percent remembered any statistic. But stories are not magic, and some of the most-quoted storytelling science is shakier than the stories told about it.

blocks.text: At Stanford, the business professor Chip Heath has run the same small exercise in his classes for years. Students get a sheet of government data about crime in the United States. Half are told to argue, in a one-minute speech, that nonviolent crime is a serious problem. The other half argue that it is not. They split into small groups, give their speeches, and vote on who was most persuasive.

Then Heath distracts them with a short video. When it ends, he asks them to write down everything they remember from the speeches they just heard. The results, which Chip and his brother Dan Heath describe in their book *Made to Stick*, are remarkably consistent.

blocks.title: What students remembered from one-minute speeches
blocks.note: Classroom demonstration, not a controlled experiment. Only about 1 in 10 speakers told a story at all.
blocks.source: Heath & Heath, Made to Stick, 2007

blocks.text: The typical speaker used about two and a half statistics. Only about one student in ten told a story. Yet when it came to recall, 63 percent of listeners remembered a story, and only 5 percent remembered any individual statistic.

This is worth taking seriously, but also worth taking carefully. It is a classroom demonstration run many times, not a controlled experiment with random assignment and a published dataset. It is a vivid illustration of a pattern that better-controlled research also finds. And it carries a delicious irony: a book about why stories stick made its case, in part, with a story.
One girl against millions

The most famous experiment on stories and numbers involves charity. In a study published in 2007, Deborah Small, George Loewenstein and Paul Slovic paid people five dollars for filling out an unrelated survey, then gave them a chance to donate some of it to Save the Children. What changed was the letter asking for the money.

One version described the statistics of a food crisis in Africa: millions of people facing hunger across several countries. Another described a single girl, Rokia, seven years old, from Mali, desperately poor, with a photo. A third gave people Rokia's story and the statistics together.

blocks.title: Average donation out of $5
blocks.source: Small, Loewenstein & Slovic, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 2007 (Study 3)

blocks.text: People gave more than twice as much to the single girl as to the statistics about millions. The most unsettling part is the third bar. Adding the big-picture numbers to Rokia's story did not boost giving. It cut it. The authors argued that facts pushed people into a calculating mode that dampened the feeling that drove generosity in the first place. One child moved people. One child plus a spreadsheet made them stop and think, and thinking made them stingier.

Slovic, one of the authors, has spent much of his career on a related idea he calls psychic numbing. Our feelings do not scale with numbers. One person in danger can grip us completely. A thousand people in the same danger does not feel a thousand times worse; it often feels like less, because the mind stops seeing individuals and starts seeing a blur. Numbers tell you how big a problem is. They are poor at making you feel it.

Now the caveat, which a fair article has to include. Psychology has spent the last fifteen years re-testing its famous findings, and this one has not come through untouched. A 2024 replication led by Maier and colleagues, published in *Collabra: Psychology*, reported no empirical support for the identifiable victim effect. That does not mean single stories never move people more than numbers. It means the effect is probably smaller and less reliable than its fame suggests, and that it depends heavily on the details.
What a story does inside two brains

Why would stories have any special grip on memory? Part of the answer is that the brain seems built to turn the world into narratives whether we ask it to or not. In a classic 1944 experiment, Fritz Heider and Marianne Simmel showed people a short animated film of two triangles and a circle moving around a box. Asked to describe it, nearly everyone told a story: the big triangle was a bully, the little ones were trying to escape, someone was trapped. The shapes had no faces and no intentions. The viewers supplied them anyway.

A more recent experiment shows what happens when a story passes from one person to another. In 2010, Greg Stephens, Lauren Silbert and Uri Hasson at Princeton used fMRI to record a speaker telling an unrehearsed personal story, then played the recording to listeners in the scanner. The listeners' brain activity tracked the speaker's, region by region, usually with a short delay. When communication failed, as when listeners heard a story told in a language they did not speak, that coupling disappeared.

The most interesting detail was that in some areas, the listeners' brains ran slightly ahead of the speaker's, as if predicting what came next. The more of that anticipation a listener showed, the better they understood the story afterward. A good story, in other words, is not just received. It is something the listener actively runs, alongside the teller, guessing at the next beat. That is a very different mental state from reading a list of numbers.

blocks.title: What the listener's brain is doing

left.head: Hearing a list of facts
items: Each item stands alone
Nothing to predict, so little to hold on to
Weighed and filed, often skeptically
Easy to forget by the next day

right.head: Hearing a story
items: Events hang on cause and effect
The listener predicts what happens next
Attention shifts into the scene and the people
Details come back attached to the plot

blocks.text: You may have heard a more dramatic explanation: that stories release oxytocin, a so-called trust hormone, which makes people more generous and connected. It was a popular idea for a while, with its own talks and articles. A 2015 critical review by Gideon Nave, Colin Camerer and Michael McCullough looked at the human evidence and found it weak. The headline result of oxytocin boosting trust had not replicated well, blood measures of oxytocin were unreliable, and large genetic studies found no consistent link. Stories clearly change people. The single-molecule version of why is not supported.
Transportation: how stories slip past your guard

The better-supported explanation has a strange name: transportation. In 2000, Melanie Green and Timothy Brock asked people to read a story, then measured how absorbed they had been, how much they lost track of the room and saw the scenes in their heads. The more transported readers were, the more their beliefs shifted toward the ones the story implied. They were also less likely to spot false notes, the small details that did not ring true.

That second finding is the key. When you are absorbed in a story, you are not busy arguing with it. A list of claims invites counterarguments; you weigh each one as it comes. A story sweeps you along, and by the time you would have objected, you are three scenes further on. A 2014 meta-analysis led by Tom van Laer pooled 132 effects from 76 papers with more than 21,000 participants and found that being transported by a narrative reliably shifts what people believe and intend to do.

items.label: Effects pooled in a meta-analysis of narrative transportation
Participants across 76 papers

blocks.source: van Laer, de Ruyter, Visconti & Wetzels, Journal of Consumer Research, 2014

blocks.text: This is a power that cuts both ways, and it is worth knowing for defense as much as offense. Advertising runs on it. So do scams, recruiting pitches, conspiracy videos and every game that makes you care about a character made of pixels. When a message comes to you as a gripping story, that is the moment to pause and ask what the claim would look like stripped down to a sentence, and whether you would still believe it.

There is a good illustration of this sitting in plain sight on the internet. You will often see the claim that stories are 22 times more memorable than facts, usually credited to the psychologist Jerome Bruner. It is a great line. People who have tried to trace it to an actual study have come up empty. It spreads because it is a neat story about stories, which is a little too perfect.
Building one that works

Most stories you will tell are not campfire epics. They are thirty-second examples inside a brief, a pitch or a conversation. The bones are simple, and they are the same ones found in almost every good narrative: a specific person, something they wanted, something in the way, and what changed.

blocks.title: A thirty-second story
items: Start with a person in a place: last underway, a new mess cook on midwatch.
Say what they wanted or needed.
Show the problem, with one concrete detail.
Describe the turn: what they did, or what happened.
Land the point in one sentence, then stop.

blocks.text: Concrete detail is what makes it work. The girl in the charity study had a name, an age and a country. Compare a sailor who did not know the procedure with a nub who opened the wrong valve at 0300 because the label had worn off. The second version is barely longer and it is far more memorable, because listeners can picture it, and pictures are what memory holds on to.

Numbers deserve the same treatment. A statistic sticks when you translate it into something a listener can see. Suppose a part fails a few percent of the time. Saying so to a division is abstract. Saying that, across enough boats, someone in the squadron will probably be the crew that deals with it is a scene, and it changes how people listen. The goal is not to replace the number. It is to give it a body.

The same structure shows up anywhere attention is scarce. The first seconds of a good gaming video do not open with the creator's name and a list of topics. They open with a moment: a clutch round, a fail, a question the video will answer. A good game tutorial does not hand you a manual. It drops you into a situation where you need the mechanic, and teaches it as part of what happens next. Both are applying the same rule the Stanford students stumbled into: people follow a character with a problem far more willingly than they follow a list of points. If you are building anything people have to choose to pay attention to, the opening is a story whether you plan it or not. Better to plan it.

In a chain of command, though, a story has a job and a place. Seniors still want the bottom line first. The trick is to lead with the conclusion, then use one short story as the evidence that makes it stick. We need to replace the valve labels in the lower level. Last week a qualified watchstander almost opened the wrong one at 0300 because the tag was unreadable. That sequence gives the officer the decision up front and the image that will make it memorable when he walks away.

Use stories as evidence, not decoration. Lead with the point, tell one specific story that proves it, and let a number follow if it adds scale. One vivid case plus one clear figure usually beats either alone.

Stories also work in less formal ways, and this is where a lot of people who like to talk go wrong. A story in conversation is a loan of attention, and it has to be paid back. The best social storytellers keep it short, end on the punchline or the point, and hand the floor back. A story that wanders through every detail you remember is not a story. It is a tour of your memory, and listeners can feel the difference.

The deepest lesson in this research is not a speaking trick. It is that humans do not really think in statistics. We think in people and scenes and consequences, and we translate numbers into those when we can. A good communicator does that translation for the listener, honestly, without inventing details and without letting the vivid case hide the big picture. Use the power of a story to carry a true idea further than a number could carry it alone. And when someone else's story has you completely absorbed, remember that is exactly when you have stopped checking.

takeaways: In a long-running classroom exercise, listeners remembered stories far better than statistics, even though few speakers told them.
A single identifiable person can move people more than numbers, though the classic charity effect replicated poorly in 2024.
Good listeners actively predict a story as it unfolds, and stories that absorb you lower your guard against weak claims.
The oxytocin trust-hormone explanation and the stories are 22 times more memorable stat are both shaky. Be skeptical of neat stories about stories.
In briefs, lead with the bottom line, then one short, concrete story as evidence. In conversation, keep stories short and hand the floor back.

title: Your Text Doesn't Sound Like You Think It Does
dek: When you type, you hear your own tone of voice. The reader gets only the words. The research on why messages get misread, why one period can change the meaning, and when to just call.

blocks.text: Someone asks if you are still coming tonight. You reply *yup.* Your friend reads it and wonders what they did wrong.

This is not oversensitivity. It is a measurable effect. Psychologists at Binghamton University showed people short text exchanges that ended in a one-word reply, either with a period or without one. Readers judged the replies with a period as less sincere. The same exchange written as a handwritten note did not show the effect. In texting, that little dot is not grammar anymore. It is a tone of voice, and the tone it carries is clipped, final and a bit cold.

Later work from the same lab found that people read *No. Just. Go.*, with a period after every word, as frustrated or even disgusted, the way you would hear someone saying it slowly through their teeth. Writers have quietly rebuilt the voice that text strips out, using punctuation, spacing and emoji. The trouble is that the rebuild is crude and everyone reads it a little differently. Every message you send is a performance whose audience cannot hear you.

Anyone who has played ranked games knows a version of this already. Typed chat starts fights that voice comms would have defused in a second. *nice* after a teammate whiffs can be sincere or brutal, and in text there is no way to tell. On voice, the same word comes with a laugh or a groan, and everyone knows exactly what you meant. The words are identical. The message is not.
The voice in your head does not ship

In 2005, Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and colleagues ran five experiments on a simple question: can people communicate tone over email as well as they think they can? Senders wrote messages meant to be sarcastic, serious, funny or sad, and predicted how often readers would get it. Over and over, they overestimated. Readers misjudged tone far more often than writers expected.

The researchers traced the overconfidence to egocentrism. When you write a sarcastic line, you hear it in your head with the sarcastic voice you intended, so it seems obvious. You cannot unhear that voice and imagine reading the words cold. The reader, of course, has nothing but the words. If the sarcasm is not in the words themselves, it does not arrive.

Monica Riordan and Lauren Trichtinger tested whether knowing someone well fixes this. Across three experiments, both writers and readers were highly confident they had read emails correctly, but their accuracy did not match their confidence. Writers were more confident that friends would understand them than strangers. Friends were not actually any more accurate. Closeness makes you *feel* understood without making you understood.

The people you text most are the ones you are most likely to assume will get your tone. They are not much better at it than anyone else. A short message to someone close still deserves a second look before you send it.

There is a quick way to catch yourself. Before sending anything with an edge, read it aloud in a flat, robotic voice, the way a stranger with no context would hear it. Sarcasm usually dies on the spot. So do jokes that depend on a raised eyebrow, and criticisms you thought you had softened. Whatever survives the robot test will probably survive the trip.

This matters most for the messages you write fastest. Long, careful messages tend to get a reread. It is the quick reply, typed in ten seconds between tasks, that goes out with a tone you never intended. The faster you write, the more of your own voice you are hearing and the less of the reader's.
Why the default reading runs negative

When tone is missing, readers do not land on neutral. Kristin Byron, reviewing research on email at work, argued that receivers often read messages as more negative, or at best flatter, than the sender intended. A quick *see me when you get a chance* from a supervisor reads like trouble. *Fine* reads like *not fine*. A short reply from someone who usually writes paragraphs reads like anger, when they may just have been busy.

Part of this is the brain filling a gap. In speech, warmth comes through a dozen channels at once: pitch, pace, a laugh, a softened face. Strip them out and the brain does not assume they were warm; it assumes they were absent. And absence of warmth, from someone you know, feels like coldness. That asymmetry is why polite, efficient writing can come across as curt. It is not enough to avoid being rude. You often have to put the warmth in on purpose.

At work, this is how a two-line email from a chief or a manager can ruin an afternoon. The writer dashed it off between three other tasks and thought nothing of it. The reader rereads it six times looking for the hidden meaning. Both are reacting to the medium, not to each other. Once you know that, you can stop reading tea leaves in short messages, and you can stop sending messages that force other people to read them.
What text cannot carry: timing

There is another channel text destroys that people rarely think about: timing. In live conversation, people take turns with remarkable speed. The gap between one person finishing and the other starting is usually a fraction of a second, and both people are tracking it constantly without knowing it. A pause that runs a little long tells you something is off before a word is said. A quick, overlapping laugh tells you the joke landed.

That speed carries meaning. Emma Templeton, Thalia Wheatley and colleagues at Dartmouth recorded pairs of friends and strangers talking, and found that faster responses predicted feeling more connected. The effect came mostly from your partner's speed in replying to you, and it operated at a scale under a quarter of a second, too fast to fake on purpose. Outside listeners picked up on it too, judging fast-response conversations as more connected.

items.label: Scale of the response-time differences that signaled two people had clicked

blocks.source: Templeton et al., PNAS, 2022

blocks.text: Text throws all of that away. A reply can come after four seconds or four hours, and the gap means nothing about how the person felt, but readers treat it as a signal anyway. If you have ever stared at *read* with no reply and invented a story about why, you have felt the brain trying to read timing that is not there. On a submarine, where messages may go out and come in batches with long gaps in between, this effect is huge. Silence is just the schedule, but at home it can read like distance.
Hearing someone changes your opinion of them

If text loses so much, why do people default to it? Because they expect voice to be awkward. Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley asked people to reconnect with an old friend either by phone or by email, and had others chat with strangers by video, voice or text. People expected the voice conversations to be more awkward. They were not. And they produced noticeably stronger feelings of connection. People chose text based on a fear that did not come true.

Voice also changes how smart you seem. Juliana Schroeder and Epley had employers, including professional recruiters, evaluate job candidates' pitches either by reading them or by hearing them. When evaluators heard the same words spoken, they rated the candidates as more competent, thoughtful and intelligent, and were more interested in hiring them. Adding video on top of audio did not change much. It was the voice itself, with its pauses and emphasis, that showed a thinking mind behind the words.

A call has one more advantage for anyone who tends to over-talk: it gives you feedback while you are still talking. You can hear the other person's energy rise or drop, catch a pause that means they want in, and wrap up when the call has done its job. In text, there is no such signal. You can type three paragraphs without ever learning that the reader lost interest after the first line.

The same research is worth remembering for anything high stakes. If you are applying for a job, a short phone call or a recorded intro can show a hiring manager something that a page of text cannot. People judge your mind partly by hearing it work.

blocks.title: Pick the channel for the job

left.head: Text works well for
items: Logistics, times, places, facts
Things the reader needs to look back at later
Quick check-ins and reminders
Sending something they can read when they're ready

right.head: Use your voice for
items: Disagreements and criticism
Apologies and bad news
Anything sarcastic or jokey that could misfire
Reconnecting with someone you've drifted from

blocks.text: The lesson is not that text is bad. It is that text is a narrow pipe. It is excellent for facts and terrible for feelings. Most misfires happen when people push emotional content through the narrow pipe because it feels safer, then wonder why it arrived damaged.

Notice where the gains came from. In the hiring study, adding video on top of audio did not change the evaluations, and in the connection study, every option that included a voice, whether phone, video or voice chat, beat text. You do not need a perfect video call to get most of the benefit. A plain phone call, or even a voice memo, carries the pauses, emphasis and warmth that text loses.
Writing messages that survive the trip

Sometimes text is all you have. Underway, email may be the only line home for weeks, and at work a lot of real decisions happen in writing. A few habits, borrowed from what the research says goes wrong, make messages much more likely to land the way you meant.

blocks.title: Before you hit send
items: Reread it in the voice of someone who's annoyed with you. Anything that sounds bad that way, fix.
Say the intent out loud: no rush on this, or just checking in, nothing's wrong.
Add the warmth on purpose. A thanks, a name, an exclamation point where it fits.
Drop the sarcasm unless the person knows your humor well and the stakes are zero.
If it has emotional weight, use the message to set up a call, not to have the conversation.

blocks.text: Length is its own trap. People who talk a lot in person often write a lot too, and a wall of text has the same effect as a monologue: the reader skims, misses the one thing that mattered and replies to something else. Put the point or the question in the first line. If a message needs five paragraphs, that is often a sign it should be a conversation.

Long-gap messaging, like email home from a deployment, needs its own adjustments. Messages may arrive in a bunch, out of order, or days after you wrote them, and the reader cannot ask a quick follow-up. Answer the questions they asked you, by name, so they know their last message landed. Mention when you wrote it if timing matters. Include one concrete detail about your day, not just *all good here*, because specifics are what make a message feel like it came from a person rather than a status report. And if something is bothering you, say so plainly instead of hinting, because hints are the first thing to get lost in a narrow pipe.

Emoji and exclamation points deserve less scorn than they get. Researchers who study texting describe them as a kind of emotional labor: readers notice that you took the trouble to add warmth, and that effort itself sends a signal. In casual messages, a well-placed one is not unprofessional; it is the closest thing text has to a smile. In formal writing to a boss or a hiring manager, words do that work better: *thanks for the quick turnaround* beats a thumbs-up.

Finally, read incoming messages with the same charity you want for your own. When a text seems cold, the most likely explanation is the medium, not the person. Before you react, ask yourself how it would sound if your most easygoing friend had sent it. If the answer is fine, assume that is what they meant. If you are not sure, the cheapest fix in the world is a short call or a simple question: *all good?*

The deeper shift is this. Clear communication is not about what you meant. It is about what arrived. Once you start judging your messages from the receiving end, you will catch most misfires before they leave your hands.

takeaways: You hear your own tone when you write. Readers get only the words, and they misread tone more often than you'd guess.
Knowing someone well makes you feel understood in text without making you more understood.
With tone missing, messages get read as colder than intended. Add the warmth on purpose.
Use text for facts and voice for feelings: disagreements, apologies, bad news and jokes that could misfire.
Lead with the point, say your intent and keep it short. If it needs five paragraphs, call.
